lessons.title: Scope, authority and exclusions for appliance cleaning
learningOutcomes: Describe the external and accessible components that this course covers for each appliance type
Identify the work that is excluded because it needs a licensed trade or is internal reprocessing
Explain why the written booking or work order sets the limit of your authority on site
Apply the stop, record and refer step when a request goes beyond the approved scope

instructionSections.heading: What this course covers
instructionSections.body: This course teaches you to clean specialty appliances and machines at the external level and at the level of accessible components. Specialty appliances include commercial dishwashers, commercial ovens and fryers, coffee machines, ice machines, commercial washing machines and dryers, and light-duty workshop machines. For each of these, the in-scope work is the outside of the machine, the surfaces around controls, removable trays and racks, drip trays and grounds bins, door seals and door glass, and any other part that the manufacturer's care instructions say can be cleaned by the user. The cleaning of a surface is the job. Taking a machine apart, reaching inside a housing or changing a part is a different job with different hazards, and it is not covered here. Read the scope every time you start a job, because the same model can be set up differently at different sites.

instructionSections.heading: What this course excludes, and why
instructionSections.body: Five kinds of work are excluded. The first is electrical repair and any work inside an electrical enclosure, which needs a licence under state or territory rules. The second is gas appliance servicing, including cleaning or touching burners, igniters, gas valves and flues, which needs a gasfitter or a person registered for that work under the rules of the state or territory. In Victoria, internal cleaning of a Type A unit is covered work for plumbers in the specialised class. The third is refrigerant handling and work on refrigeration circuits. Regulation 111 makes it an offence to do work on RAC equipment without the required licence, and the regulation reads that work broadly (check the current compilation on legislation.gov.au before relying on the wording). The fourth is internal reprocessing, such as opening panels to clean inside, descaling heating elements or boilers, or working on internal fryer oil systems or pumps. The fifth is resetting safety devices such as thermostats, interlocks and tripped switches. Some work near these items is covered elsewhere in the Skilled curriculum, such as domestic oven cleaning in the kitchen group and kitchen exhaust cleaning in commercial and office cleaning. This lesson does not cover those lessons. Each exclusion matters because a worker who opens a housing has taken on a risk the course has not prepared them for, and in some cases has done regulated work without the required licence.

instructionSections.heading: Authority comes from the booking, not from the person on site
instructionSections.body: You may clean an appliance only when the owner, operator or site manager has authorised the work. The authority is set by the booking or work order, which should name the equipment, the tasks included, the tasks excluded, and any special conditions. A manager who asks you to do something verbal on site has not changed the booking. You should record the request and get it confirmed in writing before you act on it. If the request is for something outside this course, you must refuse that part, complete any in-scope work that was booked, and report the refusal to your supervisor. Refusing excluded work is not a failure of service. It protects the customer, the worker and the business, and it keeps the record accurate. This applies even when the customer is insistent or the machine appears to be faulty and the customer expects you to fix it.

instructionSections.heading: Stop, record and refer
instructionSections.body: When a task is outside scope, or you are unsure whether it is, stop before you touch the item. Record what you saw, what was asked, who asked, and the time. Tell the customer in plain words what you can do under the booking and what needs a different provider. Refer the item to the business's escalation contact for the site or to the owner's nominated service provider. Do not start a partial task to see whether it will work. A partial task on an appliance can leave it unsafe, can void the warranty, and can cause a fault that you then have to explain. If you are unsure about a single component, treat the component as out of scope until the supervisor confirms otherwise.

lessons.title: Identifying the appliance and reading the manufacturer's care instructions
learningOutcomes: Identify an appliance's make, model and serial number from its data plate and label
Find and read the manufacturer's care and cleaning instructions for the model
Record the pre-clean condition of an appliance, including damage, leaks and fault codes
Decide whether a cleaning method is allowed for a specific appliance and finish

instructionSections.heading: Know what you are cleaning before you touch it
instructionSections.body: Two machines that look alike can have different care rules. A commercial dishwasher from one manufacturer may allow a rinse of the spray arms, while a model from another manufacturer may forbid water on the same part. Before you clean, locate the data plate. It is usually on the back, side or inside the door frame and carries the make, model and serial number. Copy these into the job record. If the plate is missing or unreadable, record that fact and the visible brand and model, and treat the appliance as having unknown care rules. Unknown rules mean you use the most conservative method you have been trained in, which is dry removal of debris and a light damp wipe with an approved product, and you stay away from any part that carries a warning label.

instructionSections.heading: Read the manufacturer's care instructions first
instructionSections.body: The manufacturer's care and cleaning instructions are the first reference for every method. They are often in the owner's manual, in the installation guide, or on the manufacturer's website. Your business should hold the link to the correct manual for each machine in the equipment record, and it should be checked before the job. When you read the instructions, look for four things: which parts may be cleaned by the user, which cleaning products are approved, which methods are forbidden, such as direct spray or steam on certain parts, and any warranty statements about cleaning or third-party work. Where the manual and the business procedure disagree, the more protective instruction governs, and you report the disagreement to the supervisor. Do not rely on a memory of how a model used to be cleaned, because manufacturers change their guidance between model years.

instructionSections.heading: Record the condition before you start
instructionSections.body: A pre-clean record protects you, the customer and the business. Walk around the appliance and note anything that is already wrong. Look for leaks or wet patches on the floor under the machine, cracked or missing panels, loose or hanging covers, scorch marks, a burnt smell, unusual sounds when it is idle, damaged door seals, and any fault code on the display. Photograph each point with the appliance and its data plate in the frame. Do not test the machine by running it. If the machine is running when you arrive, record that it is running and go to the isolation step in lesson “Making a machine safe before cleaning: isolation, stored energy and moving parts” before you do anything else. A fault that you find before the job is a fault you did not cause, and the record should say so clearly. If you find a fault that is outside the course, stop, record it and refer it, as in lesson “Scope, authority and exclusions for appliance cleaning”.

lessons.title: Making a machine safe before cleaning: isolation, stored energy and moving parts
learningOutcomes: Identify the energy sources and moving parts that can stay active on a machine after it is turned off
Apply the site's isolation procedure before cleaning near powered parts
Confirm that a machine is off and cannot restart during the clean
Explain when isolation needs a qualified person, and what to do when no safe isolation point is available

instructionSections.heading: Why switching off is not enough
instructionSections.body: Turning a machine off with its control switch does not always make it safe. Many machines keep energy in them after the switch is turned off. An electrical capacitor can hold a charge. A water or steam system can stay under pressure. A heated element, a fryer's oil, a dishwasher's rinse water and an oven's walls stay hot for some time. A motor, fan, drum, conveyor, slicer or pump can keep moving while it spins down, and a spring-loaded door or lid can close or swing. A control switch can also fail, be bypassed or be pressed by accident. For these reasons, isolation means removing the supply at a point the machine cannot override, and then confirming the machine is off by a method that does not involve touching live or moving parts. The Safe Work Australia model code on managing risks of plant includes appliances in its definition of plant (no page date shown). The page does not describe isolation or stored energy. The duty to manage those risks applies to the cleaning work, and an isolation step is one of the controls that reduces the risk.

instructionSections.heading: The isolation sequence
instructionSections.body: The first step is to switch the machine off using its normal control. The second is to isolate the supply at the isolator, switchboard or plug, as set out in the site's procedure. Where the site provides a lock and tag, apply your own lock and tag to the isolator so that nobody can re-energise the circuit while you work. Where there is no lock, use the site's alternative procedure, such as a notice and a person at the switchboard. The third step is to confirm the machine is off. Look at the display and the indicator lights, and listen for fans or pumps. Do not press start to test the machine. The fourth step is to allow stored energy to dissipate. Let hot surfaces cool and let any pressure or stored water settle, following the manufacturer's sequence. The fifth step is to keep the isolation in place until the cleaning is complete and all people have moved clear of the machine. Only the person who applied the isolation removes it, and only after checking that the machine is clear and that the handover is complete.

instructionSections.heading: When isolation is not safe or not possible
instructionSections.body: Some machines have no accessible isolator, the isolator is inside a locked switchboard, or the site procedure requires a qualified person to isolate. In those cases stop. Do not open a switchboard, do not remove a panel to reach a breaker, and do not bridge or defeat an interlock. Record the situation, tell the site contact, and refer the job. Never reset a tripped breaker or safety device to test whether the machine is working. Moving parts such as fans and drums need a second point of control: the power must be off, and the part must be stopped or held before your hands go near it. Guards and covers are not removed to make cleaning easier. If a guard is missing or damaged when you arrive, record it and refer it, because cleaning near an exposed moving part is a risk you should not take.

lessons.title: Electrical hazards on appliance jobs and the stop-and-refer rule
learningOutcomes: Identify the electrical hazards that appear when water, cleaning products and cords meet powered appliances
Carry out a pre-use visual check of leads, plugs and safety switches
Keep water and cleaning products away from controls, sockets, motors and terminals
Apply the stop-and-refer criteria for any electrical fault found during a clean

instructionSections.heading: Where the electrical hazard sits on an appliance job
instructionSections.body: Most electrical injuries on appliance jobs come from water reaching a live part, a damaged lead, or a missing protective device. A cleaning cloth that is too wet, a spray that drifts onto a control panel, a lead that has been run under a machine, or a socket that is warm to the touch can each create a shock or fire path. Commercial appliances often draw more current and have more connections than domestic ones, so the effect of a fault can be larger. Electrical hazards also sit on the equipment you bring: extension leads, pressure cleaners, vacuums and lights. Treat every powered item you bring to a job as part of the electrical risk, and check each one before use.

instructionSections.heading: Pre-use checks and protective devices
instructionSections.body: Before you use any powered item near an appliance, check the plug, the lead, the housing and the switch. Look for cracked insulation, exposed conductors, a damaged plug or socket, a cord that is pinched or crushed, a missing earth pin, and any sign of heat or scorching. Check that the item suits the environment, because a standard indoor item is not suitable for a wet floor or outdoor use. Where the site has a residual current device (RCD), also called a safety switch, confirm it is in place and test it using the site's procedure before you use water on the job. Tag and remove from service any item that fails the check, and tell the supervisor. AS 3760:2022 covers the testing and tagging of portable equipment (text not read here). WorkSafe ACT's view is that a licence-holding electrician, or a certified competent person, carries out those inspections. Do not assume that a worker may test and tag their own equipment unless the business compliance record confirms it.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping water and product away from live parts, and stopping when a fault appears
instructionSections.body: Use the least amount of water that does the job, apply it to a cloth rather than the machine, and wipe away from the control panel. Keep product and water away from sockets, switches, terminal blocks, motor housings, fan vents and any data plate that has an electrical connection. Never use a hose or pressure jet near an appliance's electrical parts. When a fault appears, stop. Signs that require you to stop and refer include a tripping safety switch, a burning smell, scorch marks, sparks, a warm plug or socket, a flickering display after cleaning, a cord that is damaged or heated, water visible inside a control panel or housing, and any exposed wire. Do not reset the safety switch to continue the job, do not open a housing, and do not repair a cord yourself. Make the machine safe if you can do so without touching the fault, by isolating the supply as in lesson “Making a machine safe before cleaning: isolation, stored energy and moving parts”, and then refer the fault.

lessons.title: Gas appliances: recognising gas components and stopping work safely
learningOutcomes: Identify the gas components on an appliance that are outside the scope of this course
Recognise the signs of a gas leak, incomplete combustion and ignition risk
Describe the stop, evacuate and report sequence for a suspected gas leak
Explain which gas work needs a licensed or registered gasfitter or plumber, and why this course does not grant it

instructionSections.heading: Which parts of a gas appliance are off limits
instructionSections.body: Many commercial ovens, fryers, combi ovens, some dishwashers and laundry machines use gas for heating. Gas components include the burner and burner tray, the pilot or igniter, the flame sensor, the gas valve, the regulator, the gas supply pipe and its flexible connector, the flue and the flue outlet. Under this course you do not clean, touch, adjust or remove any of these. You may clean the outside surfaces of a gas appliance, but you keep clear of the gas supply connector and the flue, and you do not wipe or spray near the burner openings or the igniter. Where the manufacturer's care instructions say that a gas component must be cleaned by a qualified person, the instruction governs and the task is excluded. Cleaning or servicing gas appliances is regulated work. In Victoria, internal cleaning of a Type A unit under AS 4575 counts as covered work, and only plumbers holding the specialised Type A servicing class may do it (no page date shown). A cleaner who opens the appliance is doing work they are not authorised to do.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising a gas leak and an unsafe flame
instructionSections.body: A gas leak may show as a distinct smell, often described as rotten eggs, a hissing sound near a connector or valve, a dead or dying plant near a pipe, or a bubbling in a wet area near a line. Incomplete combustion can show as a yellow or sooty flame, scorch marks around a burner, a soot deposit on a surface, or a headache or dizziness among people in the room. Any of these is a reason to stop. Do not light, relight or operate the appliance, do not operate electrical switches or tools in the area, and do not use a flame or spark to check for a leak. Increase ventilation only if you can do so without any risk of ignition. Keep people clear of the area and report the situation immediately to the site contact.

instructionSections.heading: The stop, evacuate and report sequence
instructionSections.body: If you suspect a gas leak, stop all work at once. Do not switch any device on or off, including lights and extraction fans. Move people out of the area and keep them clear of the appliance and the pipe. Make the area safe to leave by closing an accessible manual gas valve only if the site procedure tells you to do so and you can reach it without any risk. Call the emergency number for the gas supplier or the emergency services from outside the area, and tell the site contact. Do not re-enter until the emergency responder has said that the area is safe. Afterwards, record what you saw and smelled, the time, the people involved, and the actions taken. Do not attempt to fix a leak, tighten a fitting or replace a flexible connector, because those are gasfitting tasks.

lessons.title: Hot surfaces, hot oil and burn prevention on specialty appliances
learningOutcomes: Identify the hot surfaces, hot liquids and steam sources on common specialty appliances
Confirm an appliance is cool enough to clean before starting
Describe the response to a hot oil splash or a suspected oil fire
Apply safe handling for hot trays, racks, filters and doors

instructionSections.heading: Where the heat is on an appliance
instructionSections.body: Heat can come from more than one place on a single appliance. A commercial fryer holds hot oil in its vat and may have hot heating elements or gas burners beneath the vat. An oven's door glass, racks, tray runners and cavity stay hot after use, and the door handle can conduct heat. A dishwasher's rinse water, wash arms and internal surfaces can be hot, and steam escapes when the door opens. Coffee machines and steam wands carry hot water and steam. Each of these sources has a different time to cool. Never assume a surface is cool because the display is off. Check it with the back of a hand, or with an approved surface thermometer if the site provides one, and wait until the surface is cool enough to touch safely before you start.

instructionSections.heading: Oil splashes and oil fires
instructionSections.body: Hot oil can splash when a basket is lifted, when water is introduced to hot oil, or when a fryer is moved while it still contains oil. Hot oil on skin causes serious burns. If oil splashes on you, cool the skin with cool running water, keep the area covered, and get first aid. The fire response is set by the site's fire procedure and by the appliance's own fire protection, such as a suppression system fitted over the fryer or hood. Do not disturb, disconnect or cover a fire suppression system or its nozzles during a clean. Your business must record the extinguisher type and the site fire procedure in the safety field before you clean any fryer. Do not use water on a burning fryer or a burning oil pan.

instructionSections.heading: Safe handling of hot parts and steam
instructionSections.body: Hot trays, racks, filters and doors need the right gloves and a safe handling method. Use heat-resistant gloves rated for the task, check the gloves for holes before you use them, and handle parts only when they are cool enough for the gloves to be safe. Do not lean over a hot appliance when you open a door, because steam can escape. Open the door slowly, stand to one side, and let the steam clear before you put your face or hands close. Use a damp cloth and let the surface cool. Keep flammable materials, such as paper, cloths and aerosol cans, well away from hot surfaces and never leave a damp cloth or towel on a hot element. Do not spray cold water onto a hot oven door glass.

lessons.title: Manual handling of heavy appliances and equipment
learningOutcomes: Assess the weight, shape and handling points of an appliance before moving it
Plan a move using the right equipment, team size and route
Identify the hidden hazards of moving an appliance, such as leads, hoses and drains
Decide when a move is outside the safe limit and must be referred

instructionSections.heading: Why moving an appliance is a risk of its own
instructionSections.body: Moving a machine to clean behind it is one of the most common causes of back and joint injury on appliance jobs. The weight of a commercial dishwasher, oven or ice machine can be far above what one person can lift safely, and the weight is often poorly placed, with the centre of gravity high or to one side. Appliances also have sharp corners, exposed fittings, hoses and leads that can catch, and their feet or castors may not roll on the floor where you need them to. Moving a machine can also disconnect a hose or lead, damage a drain, or cause a fitting to leak. The Safe Work Australia model code on hazardous manual tasks requires these risks to be assessed and managed, and it aims at removing or reducing them (no page date shown). The page does not list weight or posture factors. A machine that does not need to be moved should not be moved.

instructionSections.heading: Plan the move before you lift
instructionSections.body: Before you move any appliance, check its weight from the manufacturer's specification or the data plate, and compare it with the team size and equipment on site. If the appliance cannot be moved safely by the team available, do not attempt it. Check the route for steps, thresholds, ramps, wet or greasy floors, narrow doorways, and obstacles. Identify the handling points that the manufacturer allows, which are usually the base or designated lifting points, and avoid lifting by panels, doors, handles or control housings, because they can bend or break. Disconnect nothing without isolation under lesson “Making a machine safe before cleaning: isolation, stored energy and moving parts”. Check for leads, hoses and drain lines that will become stretched, and check whether the site has a trolley or a platform truck suited to the load. Agree the signal and the direction of travel with your team before you start, so that everyone moves together.

instructionSections.heading: Moving, positioning and returning the machine
instructionSections.body: Keep the load close to the body, bend the knees, keep the back straight and avoid twisting while lifting. Tilt a machine only when the manufacturer allows it, and only by the method the manufacturer sets out, because tilting can move oil, water, or internal parts. Slide a machine on a sheet or a board where the floor is hard and the machine's base allows it, rather than dragging it across the floor. Keep feet clear of the path and stop if the load shifts. Set the machine down on a level floor, and check that the castors lock and that the machine is stable before you leave it. When you return the machine to its position, check that all leads and hoses are free and not crushed, that the drain is clear, and that the machine sits level. Do not move a machine with an oven door open, a drawer out or a fryer holding oil.

lessons.title: Cleaning chemicals for appliances: selection, compatibility and safe use
learningOutcomes: Select an approved cleaning product for an appliance and surface using the manufacturer's care instructions and the business product list
Explain the hazards of mixing incompatible cleaning chemicals, including acid with chlorine
Read a safety data sheet and label to identify the PPE, first aid and storage requirements for a product
Store, dilute and dispose of cleaning products without creating a new hazard

instructionSections.heading: Matching the product to the appliance and the surface
instructionSections.body: Specialty appliances are built from several materials at once: stainless steel panels, painted or powder-coated surfaces, plastics, rubber door seals, glass, membrane control panels and sometimes aluminium. A product that is safe on one of these can damage another. Alkaline degreasers remove cooking fat and oil but can attack some painted surfaces and some finishes if left on too long. Acid descalers remove mineral scale from water-carrying parts, but are not suitable for every metal or seal, and the manufacturer's instructions govern where they may be used. Chloride-containing products can damage some stainless steel finishes, and some rubber seals are damaged by strong solvents. Choose the product from the business's approved list for the appliance type, and check the manufacturer's care instructions for any product that is forbidden for that model. If the product you need is not on the list, do not substitute a product you have at home or in your van. Ask the supervisor to approve it, with its SDS, before use.

instructionSections.heading: Mixing hazards and what must never be combined
instructionSections.body: Never mix cleaning chemicals, and never use one product to 'boost' another. The most important combination to avoid is an acid with a chlorine-based product or bleach. Ammonia-based products must not be mixed with chlorine either. Alkaline products and acids can react strongly when mixed, producing heat and splash. Rinse the surface and the equipment between products, using the method set by the business, and leave a surface dry before changing to a product of a different type. Store products separately by type, so that an acid and a chlorine product are never next to each other on a shelf or in the van. Keep product in its original labelled container, and never decant an acid or a caustic into an unlabelled bottle.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the SDS and the label before you use a product
instructionSections.body: Every hazardous product must come with a safety data sheet, which sets out its hazards, the first aid steps, the PPE required, the storage and handling advice, and the disposal method. Read the SDS for each product before you use it for the first time, and keep it accessible in the vehicle or on the device. The label is the short version, and it must match the SDS. Check the signal words, the hazard statements, the dilution rate, the contact time and the PPE on the label. Follow the dilution rate and contact time exactly. A stronger solution does not clean faster and can cause corrosion, residue or injury. The Safe Work Australia model code on managing risks of hazardous chemicals covers safety data sheets and labelling.

lessons.title: Exterior cleaning methods that keep water and product out of the machine
learningOutcomes: Select a low-moisture exterior method that suits the appliance's finish and controls
Keep water, steam and product away from vents, seals, connections, motors and labels
Clean stainless steel and painted surfaces without causing scratches, streaks or residue
Check the finished surface for residue, moisture and damage before handover

instructionSections.heading: Start dry, then use the least water that works
instructionSections.body: The method that protects an appliance is the one that removes the soil with the least water. Begin by removing loose debris with a dry cloth, a soft brush or a vacuum with a non-metal nozzle, and only then apply a damp cloth. Use a microfibre or other lint-free cloth dampened with the approved product, and wring it out until it is damp rather than wet. Work from the top of the appliance down, so that drips do not run over areas you have already cleaned. Keep the cloth moving and turn it often, so that the soil is lifted rather than smeared. Use a second clean damp cloth to remove product residue, and finish with a dry cloth. Avoid hosing, pressure washing and steam for exterior surfaces of most specialty appliances, because the water and heat can enter vents, seals, switches and electrical boxes, and they can drive grease into joints.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting the parts that water must not reach
instructionSections.body: Some parts of an appliance are sensitive to water even when they are on the outside. Control panels and membrane keypads can let water in at their edges, and water inside a control panel can cause a short. Vents and fan grilles draw water into motors. Door seals can be damaged by solvents or by heat from steam. Data plates and labels can lift or fade. Connections, sockets and electrical plugs must stay dry. Motor housings and bearings must not be wetted. Drip trays and drain outlets should be emptied and wiped, not flooded. Use the cloth only, keep spray off these parts, and wipe away from the control panel. Where the manufacturer's instructions name a part that must not be wetted, the instruction applies even if it is on the outside.

instructionSections.heading: Stainless steel, painted surfaces and glass
instructionSections.body: Stainless steel should be wiped along the grain using a clean damp cloth and a product suitable for stainless steel, then dried to prevent water marks. Do not use steel wool, abrasive pads or scouring powder, because they scratch the finish and make it easier for soil to stick. Painted and powder-coated surfaces should be cleaned with a mild product, because strong alkaline or solvent products can dull or lift the coating. Glass, including oven door glass, should be cleaned with a product approved for glass and a clean cloth, and never with a wet cloth on a very hot surface. Plastic parts should be cleaned with a mild product, and rubber seals with a product that the manufacturer or the SDS confirms is compatible. Test any product on a small hidden area first if the finish is unfamiliar, and record the test.

lessons.title: Refrigeration, ice and coffee machines: the cleaning boundary
learningOutcomes: Identify the refrigerant circuit and water-carrying parts that are outside the cleaning scope
Clean the accessible drip tray, grounds bin, bin lid, door seal and exterior of an ice or coffee machine
Explain why refrigerant handling and refrigeration circuit work need a refrigerant handling licence
Record and refer a water, drain or refrigeration fault without attempting a repair

instructionSections.heading: What sits inside the refrigeration boundary
instructionSections.body: Ice machines, coffee machines with refrigerated milk units, and refrigerated display cabinets contain a refrigerant circuit made of a compressor, a condenser, an expansion device and an evaporator. The circuit is sealed, and it is the part of the machine that carries refrigerant gas. Water-carrying parts include the water inlet valve, the inlet filter, the water distribution system, the evaporator plate or bin on an ice machine, the boiler or heating element of a coffee machine, and the internal water lines. These parts are outside this course. In practice, the cleaning boundary is the outside of the cabinet, the door and door seal, the accessible drip tray and grounds bin, the bin lid and its outside surface, and the exterior of the condenser grille where it is accessible without tools. Until the business compliance record confirms the position, treat the coil as outside the scope, record it, and refer it.

instructionSections.heading: Why refrigerant work is a licensed task
instructionSections.body: Regulation 111 makes it an offence to carry out work on RAC equipment without a licence (2018 compilation; check the current version). That work includes any act with refrigerant, or with a component that carries a risk of refrigerant escaping, and the regulation reaches decommissioning where refrigerant is in the equipment. A cleaner who opens a refrigeration housing, disturbs a pipe, or touches the compressor, the condenser coil or a service valve is doing work that may need the licence, and this course does not grant it. Refrigerant can cause frostbite on contact, and some refrigerants are flammable, so a leak is a hazard in its own right, not just a loss of cooling.

instructionSections.heading: Water, drain and bin areas: clean, check, refer
instructionSections.body: The drip tray, grounds bin and ice bin are the most cleaned parts of these machines, and they hold water and food residue, so they need regular wiping. Empty the drip tray and bin into the approved waste container, rinse with clean water, and dry before refitting. Check the drain outlet for blockage without inserting tools into the internal drain line. If water is leaking, if the drain is blocked, if the water inlet appears to be leaking, or if the machine makes a new sound, stop cleaning around that part and record it. Do not reset the machine, do not remove the water inlet filter, and do not open the cabinet. Ice machines and coffee machines can have hot or very cold surfaces, and some have a water supply under pressure, so isolate the machine as set out in lesson “Making a machine safe before cleaning: isolation, stored energy and moving parts” before you clean near its water connections.

lessons.title: Customer communication, warranty, access and privacy on appliance jobs
learningOutcomes: Confirm the customer's authority, access and the state of the appliance before the job starts
Explain the limits of the cleaning service without promising repair, safety or warranty outcomes
Handle warranty and damage questions by recording facts and referring them to the right person
Take and store job photographs in a way that respects the customer's privacy and confidential information

instructionSections.heading: Confirm authority, access and the appliance's state before you start
instructionSections.body: The first conversation on the job sets the terms. Confirm the name of the person who has authority to approve the work, the site contact for the day, the access arrangements, the parking, the times when the kitchen or workshop is available, and whether the appliance is in service. Ask whether the machine has been used recently, whether it still holds oil or hot water, and whether any fault has been reported. If the machine is in use, ask the owner to shut it down under the site procedure, and make sure the owner understands that you will not operate it. Confirm that the cleaning is the job that was booked, and tell the contact about any part of the scope that you cannot clean under this course. Record each confirmation with the time and the person's name, because these facts protect the customer, the worker and the business if a question comes up later.

instructionSections.heading: Explain the limits without promising a result
instructionSections.body: Customers often expect a cleaner to make an appliance look new, work better, or be free of faults. Explain what the job can and cannot do. You can say that the exterior and accessible parts will be cleaned to the agreed standard, and that internal parts, electrical parts, gas parts and refrigeration parts are not part of the service. You should not say that a machine is safe, will work properly, or will pass an inspection, because you cannot know that from cleaning alone. You should not say that cleaning will restore a finish that has worn away, or that a stain will come out without testing. If the customer asks for a repair or an adjustment, tell them who can do it and that the business will refer the job. Keep the tone plain and honest, and avoid technical jargon that suggests you have more authority than you do.

instructionSections.heading: Warranty, damage claims and photographs
instructionSections.body: Warranty terms are set by the manufacturer and are often conditional on how the appliance is cleaned, serviced and used. Consumer guarantees are separate: they apply automatically and a warranty cannot remove them. If a customer asks whether the clean will affect the warranty, do not answer from memory. Say that the manufacturer's warranty sits on top of the consumer guarantees, and record the question. If you find a fault or damage before you clean, photograph it with the appliance in view and record it, so that it is not blamed on the clean. If damage occurs during the job, stop, make the item safe, photograph it, and report it to the supervisor the same day. Do not admit liability on site, and do not promise compensation. Photographs of the appliance are normally taken to show the condition before and after the clean. Take only the photographs that the job needs. Do not photograph people, screens showing customer information, paperwork, staff rosters, security codes or private areas. Store job photographs in the business system only, and remove them from personal devices in line with the business's privacy procedure. Whether the Privacy Act binds the business depends on turnover and activity: businesses with turnover at or under $3 million are generally outside it unless an exception applies.

lessons.title: Quality check, evidence and handover for specialty appliance cleaning
learningOutcomes: Inspect a cleaned appliance against the agreed standard and the safety checks
Restore the appliance to its pre-job arrangement, including guards, covers, trays and labels
Record photographs, product use, exclusions and referrals accurately
Write a handover statement that is accurate, within scope and free of safety or warranty promises

instructionSections.heading: What the finished check must confirm
instructionSections.body: A finished appliance clean is checked by eye and by hand before it is handed over. The eye check confirms that the surfaces are clean and dry, that there are no streaks, residue, scratches or moisture at seams, that the labels and data plate are readable, and that the door seal sits correctly and has no visible tear. The hand check confirms that the control panel is dry at its edges, that trays and bins are seated and not loose, and that covers and guards are fitted correctly. Check that no water has entered a vent, socket, switch or motor housing, and that no tool or cloth has been left in or near the machine. Check that every part you were asked to clean is done, and that every part you excluded is recorded as excluded. The finish check is about the agreed standard. It does not test whether the appliance works, and it does not confirm that the appliance is safe to use.

instructionSections.heading: Restore the machine and leave it as the site expects
instructionSections.body: Put back everything you removed, including trays, racks, drip trays, bin liners and guards, and return them to their correct positions. Confirm that the isolation applied under “Making a machine safe before cleaning: isolation, stored energy and moving parts” is removed only by the person who applied it, and that the removal is recorded. Do not switch the machine on to test it unless the site procedure and the manufacturer's instructions allow it, and the site contact has agreed, because switching on is not part of the cleaning service. Tell the site contact in plain words what state the machine is in, and what they should check before they use it. If the machine must remain off, say so and record it. Leave the work area clean and dry, and remove all waste, cloths and product containers from the area. A tidy site is part of the job and protects the next user.

instructionSections.heading: Evidence and handover statement
instructionSections.body: Every job needs an evidence record that someone else could read and understand without you. Record each appliance by make, model, serial number and location. Record the before and after photographs with the data plate in shot where the business requires it. Record the products used, from the approved list, with the dilution and the surface. Record the parts excluded and the reason, such as gas components, refrigerant circuits, internal water parts, or internal electrical parts. Record every defect, leak, fault code or damage found, and the referral made and to whom. The handover statement should say what was cleaned, to what standard, what was excluded and why, what was referred, and what the site must arrange next. It must not say that the machine is safe, that it works, or that it complies with any regulation. If the record shows a fault, the handover says so plainly. The defect reporting route and the evidence needed are set by the business's quality record.

lessons.title: Water sampling and records for freshwater and marine tanks
learningOutcomes: Keep freshwater and marine records on separate sheets, and state which parameters each system needs from the owner's plan
Choose a sampling point and dedicated equipment that give a reading describing the tank, not the equipment or the water at the return or the heater
Check that a salinity or specific gravity instrument is calibrated, and apply its temperature correction before a result is recorded
Record and correct a result without overwriting it, and identify a result that is not valid

instructionSections.heading: Keep freshwater and marine records apart
instructionSections.body: Freshwater and marine tanks are different systems, with different chemistry, different equipment and different animals. A freshwater tank is usually tested for temperature, ammonia, nitrite, nitrate and pH, and for hardness where the owner's plan asks for it. A marine tank is usually tested for temperature, salinity or specific gravity, pH, ammonia, nitrite and nitrate, and for alkalinity, calcium, magnesium and phosphate where the plan lists them. Use a separate record sheet, or a separate record in the system, for each type of tank. Never write a marine reading on a freshwater sheet, or the reverse. Mixing the two produces records that look normal and mean nothing. The routine of testing and what each reading means are covered in the water testing lesson (“Water testing, trends and records”). This lesson concentrates on where the sample is taken, the instruments, and the records.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the sampling point and the equipment
instructionSections.body: Sample the open water at the point the owner's plan names, and keep that point the same on each visit. Avoid the heater, the filter outlet, the return, an air stone, the area under a feeding spot and the surface film, unless the plan asks for one of them, because each can give a reading that does not describe the whole tank. Use a container, syringe or pipette dedicated to one tank. Do not use the same sampling equipment for two tanks without cleaning it between them, and never move water from one tank into another as a top-up without checking the plan. Water, plants and animals moved between tanks can carry disease.

instructionSections.heading: Salinity, specific gravity and instrument checks
instructionSections.body: For marine tanks, salinity or specific gravity is measured with a refractometer, a hydrometer or a meter. Before each session, check the instrument against the calibration solution that the manufacturer specifies, and record the date. Some instruments give a reading that depends on temperature, so apply the temperature correction given in the instructions and record the temperature at the time of the test. An instrument that is out of calibration, or a calibration solution that is out of date, gives a result that is not valid. Do not record a salinity reading that you have estimated from the look of the water or from the last visit.

instructionSections.heading: Records, corrections and out-of-range results
instructionSections.body: Write each result with its value, its unit, the time, the temperature, the location, the method, the reagent or instrument batch, the tester and any observation about the animals or the water. A test that was not completed is recorded as not completed, with the reason. Do not back-fill a result, and do not average a freshwater reading with a marine reading. Never overwrite an original entry. To correct an error, draw a single line through it, write the correct value beside it, then initial and date the correction and give the reason. In an electronic system, use the amendment function that keeps the original. If a result is outside the range the owner's plan sets, follow the plan's action, tell the responsible person, and leave the measured record as it was taken.

instructionSections.heading: Sampling more than one tank in a round
instructionSections.body: A technician who visits several tanks in one round uses a fixed order, cleans the sampling equipment between sites, and records each tank on its own sheet before moving on. Where the round includes both freshwater and marine tanks, sample the freshwater tanks first and clean the equipment between sites. This is a practical method for limiting the chance of carrying material from a marine system into a freshwater one. It is not a legal rule in this draft. The order matters less than keeping each record in its own place.

lessons.title: Water chemistry and pH interpretation for freshwater and marine tanks
learningOutcomes: Explain how pH, ammonia, nitrite and nitrate are linked in an established tank, and why a tank that is not yet established shows a different pattern
Describe the chemistry that matters for marine tanks, including salinity, alkalinity and calcium, separately from freshwater tanks
Use conditioners, salt mixes and any medicine only as the label and the owner's plan direct, and refuse any product or dose that the plan does not cover
Refer any result, product request or animal health concern that the plan does not cover, rather than experimenting with treatment

instructionSections.heading: Two systems, two sets of chemistry
instructionSections.body: A freshwater tank and a marine tank share the same basic cycle of waste, bacteria and water change, but the rest of the chemistry differs. A freshwater tank is read for temperature, ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH and, where the plan asks, hardness. A marine tank adds salinity or specific gravity, alkalinity, calcium and magnesium, and often phosphate, which affect the stability of the pH and the health of corals, invertebrates and fish. A target that is right for one type of tank is not right for the other, and the two sets of targets must not be mixed. Set them from the owner's plan or a qualified aquatic specialist, not from numbers remembered from another system.

instructionSections.heading: The nitrogen cycle and reading the results together
instructionSections.body: Fish waste and uneaten food release ammonia. Bacteria in the filter and on the tank surfaces convert ammonia to nitrite, and another group of bacteria converts nitrite to nitrate. Nitrate is removed by water change and by plants, and in some systems by other processes. A tank that is new, recently cleaned or has lost its filter bacteria can show ammonia or nitrite while the cycle is re-established. A rising nitrate with falling ammonia and nitrite usually means the cycle is working. Read the whole set of results, and the trend since the last visit, before deciding anything. The relationship between pH, alkalinity and calcium in a marine tank is a technique point with no source checked in this draft, so follow the owner's plan for marine chemistry targets.

instructionSections.heading: Conditioners, salt mixes and medicines
instructionSections.body: Water conditioners, salt mixes and medicines are products with their own labels, and each must be used as its label and the owner's plan direct. Measure salt mixes accurately, mix them in water at the right temperature, and check the salinity after mixing and before use. Use a conditioner that removes chlorine and chloramine from tap water only at the dose on its label. Do not mix two products in one container, and do not add a product that is not in the owner's plan. Medicines for fish and other animals are a health matter. Pool chemicals and other non-aquarium products are never used in an aquarium. Keep all products apart in storage and on the vehicle, as their safety data sheets direct.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer
instructionSections.body: When readings do not respond to the plan, do not add a larger dose to force a result. Recheck the sample and the reagent, compare with the trend, and follow the plan. If the plan does not cover the situation, stop chemical adjustment and refer it to the responsible person. Animals that gasp at the surface, lie still, show sores, change colour, behave unusually, or die without explanation need a qualified person, and the record should describe what you saw and the readings you took. Do not treat an animal outside the plan. A sudden change in salinity or temperature is a reason to stop and check the equipment and the top-up water before any other step.

lessons.title: Filtration and circulation diagnostics for freshwater and marine tanks
learningOutcomes: Describe the circulation path of a freshwater filter and of a marine sump system, including the skimmer where one is fitted
Diagnose low flow and poor filtration by observation of the intake, the impeller, the media and any gauge the system has
Isolate a tank pump, filter or skimmer safely before opening any part of it
Price, record and refer diagnostic work under the business's approved method and the scope in this lesson

instructionSections.heading: Circulation in freshwater and marine systems
instructionSections.body: A freshwater tank usually uses a canister, a hang-on-back or an internal filter. Water is drawn in, passed through mechanical and biological media, and returned to the tank. A marine system often adds a sump, a return pump and a protein skimmer. In the skimmer, water passes through a column of bubbles that removes dissolved waste before the water returns. The skimmer is a marine-specific piece of equipment, and a freshwater tank does not need one. Diagnose the circulation in the order the water travels: intake, pump or impeller, media or skimmer, return. Record the layout you find before you change anything, because each system is installed differently.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the signs of a fault
instructionSections.body: Weak flow at the outlet, a noisy pump, a pump that loses its prime, air in the intake, a filter that gurgles, and a skimmer that produces less foam than before are common signs. A blocked intake, a clogged media basket, a worn impeller, an air leak on the suction side and a partly closed valve can all give similar symptoms. Clean or replace media only as the owner's plan and the manufacturer direct, because biological media holds the bacteria the tank depends on. Record the flow you observe, the state of the intake and media, and the skimmer cup level before you clean, and record them again after the work.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating before you inspect
instructionSections.body: Switch off the pump, the heater and any other equipment in the circuit at the isolator or the safety switch before you open a filter, a skimmer or a sump lid, or touch an impeller. Confirm that the pump is off before you put your hands in the water. Disconnect or isolate the equipment as its manufacturer directs, and do not open a pressurised filter. Record the position of each valve before you move it, so that it can be restored. Keep cords out of the water, do not use a damaged cord, and keep the area dry. Do not reach into a running skimmer or pump.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning media in tank water, and the scope boundary
instructionSections.body: Rinse biological media in water removed from the tank, not in tap water, so that the bacteria are kept. Clearing an intake, cleaning a skimmer as the manufacturer directs, and rinsing media are generally within the scope of aquarium maintenance work. Replacing a pump, changing its wiring, altering a fixed electrical connection and changing plumbing are not general maintenance, and they are referred. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work is licensed whatever its cost (last updated 23 June 2026). The NSW page says plumbing, draining and gasfitting work is licensed whatever its cost (last updated 31 July 2026), and in Queensland a QBCC licence is needed for plumbing or drainage work of any value (last reviewed 16 April 2026). Refer such work to the person the rules name.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing and documenting diagnostic work
instructionSections.body: Diagnostic time is priced under the business's approved method, not absorbed as free time. Record the symptoms, the flow and readings, the checks you made, the action taken, the parts or work referred, and the time spent. A record that says the system is working is valid only if the readings and the checks support it. Where a fault is outside scope, write a referral note that describes the symptoms and readings, so that the licensed person can start from the facts.

lessons.title: Electrical, mechanical and confined-space boundaries for aquariums
learningOutcomes: Identify the electrical, mechanical and confined-space hazards around a tank heater, light, controller, pump, sump or cabinet void
Isolate, secure and prove off the power to aquarium equipment before any inspection that needs it
Recognise when a cabinet, sump or void may be a confined space, and refuse entry without authority and a procedure
State where aquarium maintenance scope ends and licensed work begins, without implying that this lesson grants any licence

instructionSections.heading: Water and electricity around a tank
instructionSections.body: Heaters, lights, pumps, controllers and their cords sit in or close to water, and a fault can deliver a shock through the water, through a damaged enclosure or through a wet connection. A residual current device, or safety switch, reduces the risk. The Queensland Electrical Safety Office page recommends using electrical equipment through a safety switch (no date shown). It does not make live work safe and does not give anyone permission to work on the equipment. Treat any aquarium equipment as live until it has been isolated and proven dead by a competent person. Check each heater and cord for cracks, discolouration and damage before use. Take a damaged heater out of service, isolate it, and refer its repair. Keep cords and extension leads out of the water, and never use a damaged lead.

instructionSections.heading: Where electrical work becomes licensed work
instructionSections.body: In New South Wales, electrical wiring work is licensed whatever its cost, and the page defines wiring work to include repairing (last updated 23 June 2026). WorkSafe Queensland's page on testing and tagging electrical equipment names AS/NZS 3760 for in-service inspection and testing in industries such as manufacturing, service, office, amusement and rural work (no date shown). The page gives no edition year and does not mention home aquarium equipment, so do not treat it as a rule for this trade without checking. A maintenance worker may isolate equipment, inspect its outside, check a cord for damage and report a fault. Repair, rewiring, a new connection or the opening of a fixed enclosure is for a licensed person. Completing this lesson does not give the authority to do electrical work.

instructionSections.heading: Mechanical hazards and large glass tanks
instructionSections.body: Pumps, impellers and skimmers can start again when power returns, and a switch that looks off can still leave the circuit live. Before you reach into a pump, sump or skimmer, isolate the power, check that the isolator is off, and secure it so that it cannot be switched on while you work, as the site procedure directs. Do not reach into a running pump to clear a blockage. A full glass tank is heavy and can fail if it is lifted, moved or knocked. Do not lift, tilt or move a full tank alone, and do not move a tank without the method the owner's plan or the manufacturer gives.

instructionSections.heading: Confined spaces in cabinets, sumps and voids
instructionSections.body: A sump, a cabinet void, an under-tank space or an enclosed stand can be a confined space. A confined space has limited openings for entry and exit, is not designed for people to work in continuously, and can hold a hazard such as low oxygen, gas, engulfment, or a hazard from the water or the equipment. Assess the space before any entry. Entry needs a documented procedure, an assessment of the atmosphere and hazards, a standby person and, where the rules require it, a permit. The model Code of Practice from Safe Work Australia says it guides work in a confined space, and that you should check with your regulator whether it has legal effect in your jurisdiction (no publication date shown). Do not crawl into a cabinet or sump alone, and do not enter a space with standing water to inspect it.

instructionSections.heading: The scope boundary
instructionSections.body: Aquarium maintenance scope covers cleaning, inspection, reading equipment from the outside, isolating power as the procedure allows, cleaning intakes and baskets, and reporting faults. Replacing or rewiring a heater, light or pump, opening electrical enclosures, entering a confined space, altering a controller, and changing plumbing are outside that scope, unless the client, the work order and the worker's licence and competence all cover them. When a task is outside scope, make the equipment safe as far as the procedure allows, stop, and refer the task in writing with the symptoms and readings.

lessons.title: Water conservation and environmental release for aquariums
learningOutcomes: Separate evaporation from a leak in a tank by running a bucket test and recording the result
Carry out routine partial water changes on the owner's plan schedule, and make extra changes only where the test results or the plan call for them
Refuse to release tank water, sand, rock, plants or animals to stormwater, a waterway or bushland without an approved route and any permit the state requires
Record the volume moved, the route, the approval and the person who approved it

instructionSections.heading: Why tank water loss and water changes cost money
instructionSections.body: Every litre lost from a tank has to be replaced, and each top-up or water change changes the temperature, the salinity and the chemistry that the animals live in. Evaporation from an open tank on a warm, dry day is normal. A steady loss on a cool, still night can point to a leak, a worn seal, a misaligned overflow or a splash from the filter outlet. Water changes that the plan does not call for cost money, add stress for the animals, and can disturb the bacteria that keep the tank stable. Cost reduction starts with finding the cause of the loss, rather than topping up at every visit without knowing why.

instructionSections.heading: The bucket test
instructionSections.body: A bucket test separates evaporation from a leak. Fill a bucket with tank water, stand it in the tank so that its water level is close to the tank level, and mark the level inside and outside the bucket at the start. Leave it for the same period and compare the two marks. If the tank has dropped more than the water in the bucket, the loss is more likely a leak or an overflow problem, and it should be reported. The method is a practical technique and not a certified test. Record the weather, the times and the result.

instructionSections.heading: Routine water changes, extra changes and new water
instructionSections.body: Routine partial water changes are a normal part of aquarium care, and they follow the schedule in the owner's plan. Extra changes are made only where the test results, the plan or a qualified specialist calls for one, and the reason is recorded each time. Match the temperature and, for a marine tank, the salinity of the new water to the tank before it goes in. Tap water must have chlorine and chloramine removed before it is added to a tank, because both harm fish and the bacteria in the filter. Use a conditioner at the dose on its label, and check the label for the dechlorination method. Add new water slowly and away from the animals. Do not add water from an unknown source, such as a dam, a bore, a natural waterway or the sea, without first checking the state rules with the regulator.

instructionSections.heading: Releasing tank water, sand, rock, plants and animals
instructionSections.body: Tank water, sand, rock, plants and animals should not be released into stormwater, a kerb drain, a gutter, bushland or a waterway until a route is confirmed. Confirming the route with the client, the council and the water authority is practice in this draft, not a rule read from an official page. For animals, the rules are stricter. In New South Wales, the Department of Primary Industries says that listed prohibited and notifiable species may not be kept, purchased, sold or transported, and that releasing fish into public waters needs a fish stocking permit (no date shown). In Queensland, listed prohibited species must not be held or brought in, and a person who has or suspects one should inform Biosecurity Queensland without delay (last updated 28 May 2026). Do not release, donate or sell an animal under this lesson, and do not move plants or live rock between tanks or sites without checking the rules. Do not assume that any discharge route is allowed.

instructionSections.heading: Recording tank water movements
instructionSections.body: Record the volume drained, changed or topped up where you know it, the route, the approval or permit relied on, the time, the reason and the person who approved the move. Where the route is unknown, stop and refer rather than moving the water. A record that shows an approved route protects the business and the client. A record that shows the water went somewhere unknown protects neither.

lessons.title: Freshwater, brackish, marine and planted systems
learningOutcomes: Describe the main aquarium system types (freshwater, brackish, marine, reef, fish-only and planted) and what each one needs from its water and equipment
Explain why freshwater and marine systems must not share equipment without a cleaning and transfer plan
Prepare tap water and marine salt mixes as the product label and the owner's plan direct, and confirm marine salinity with a calibrated instrument before use
Keep aquarium products and pool chemicals apart, and refuse any product that is not approved for the system

instructionSections.heading: Six common system types
instructionSections.body: Aquarium systems are grouped by the water they hold and by the animals and plants they keep. A freshwater system holds water with no added salt. Cold-water freshwater systems run near room temperature, and tropical freshwater systems need a heater. A brackish system sits between the two, with a low level of salt that suits some estuarine and river-mouth fish but not a full marine community. A marine system holds seawater-level salinity made from a salt mix. Within marine keeping, a fish-only system holds fish, perhaps with a few algae-eating or detritus-eating animals, and uses decorative rock, dried coral or artificial items instead of living coral. A reef system is built around living coral and needs more control of its chemistry, lighting and water flow. A planted system can be freshwater, brackish or marine, and it adds plants that depend on light and nutrients. Identify the system type from the owner's plan and from the equipment labels before you start work, because the same product or tool can be correct for one type and wrong for another.

instructionSections.heading: Why systems stay separate
instructionSections.body: Freshwater and marine animals are adapted to different salt levels and water chemistry, and a brackish system is a third set of conditions. Nets, siphons, buckets, scrapers, sponges, heaters, test kits and sampling containers can carry organisms, parasites or product residues from one system into another, even when they look clean. Keep each item dedicated to one system, label it, and store it dry. If equipment must move between systems, clean and dry it as the owner's plan directs, and record the move. Do not share a net between a freshwater tank and a marine tank in the same visit.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing water
instructionSections.body: Its chlorine or chloramine content, hardness, pH and metal content all differ between suppliers and sometimes within a supply area. Check with the local water utility about what is in the supply before you assume that a conditioner or a water source is right, and test the tap water if the owner's plan asks for it. Use a conditioner that removes chlorine and chloramine, at the dose on its label. For a marine system, dissolve the salt mix in the water and at the temperature that the product instructions give, mix until it is fully dissolved, and allow it to stabilise before use. Check the salinity or specific gravity with a calibrated instrument before the water goes into the tank (see the sampling lesson). Do not estimate salinity by looking at the water or by feel, and do not use amounts copied from another product's label.

instructionSections.heading: Temperature and placement
instructionSections.body: Temperature affects how quickly animals use oxygen, how quickly the bacteria in the filter work, and how stressed livestock become when conditions change. Use the livestock plan or a qualified aquatic specialist to set the target. Keep the thermometer away from the heater so that it reads the tank, not the heater. Record the temperature at each visit, and investigate a sudden change before you adjust the heater. Keep the tank out of direct sunlight, which encourages algae and can overheat the water, and away from draughts and doorways.

instructionSections.heading: Products and pool chemicals
instructionSections.body: Pool chemicals, including chlorine, pool pH products and algaecides, are never used in an aquarium. Aquarium products are used only where the product label and the owner's instruction allow, and only in the system type named on the label. Some planted systems use liquid nutrients or added carbon dioxide. Those products and gases are used at the rates on their labels and within the owner's plan, and this course does not set those rates. Store aquarium products apart from pool chemicals, as the separation principle for incompatible chemicals on the Safe Work Australia storage page directs (no date shown). Keep them away from food and out of reach of children and pets as good practice, because that page addresses container labelling and says nothing on food storage. Read the safety data sheet for each product, because the storage and handling rules are recorded there, and a business has to keep hazardous chemicals stored safely and share hazard information with its workers (page text refers to the model WHS laws created in 2011; no revision date shown).

lessons.title: Water testing, trends and records
learningOutcomes: Test tank water for temperature, pH, ammonia, nitrite and nitrate with an in-date kit or meter, in the same order and from the same sampling point each visit
Explain in general terms what each core reading means, and read the results together and against the previous visit
Record each result with its time, temperature, method, equipment and observations so that trends can be seen
Respond to an out-of-range result by retesting, checking the equipment and recent changes, and following the owner's plan one change at a time
Identify when a result or a pattern must be referred to the owner or a qualified person

instructionSections.heading: Why testing is the core skill
instructionSections.body: Testing is the main way to see what the water is doing, because livestock often show stress only after conditions have moved for some time. A single reading shows one moment. A short run of readings taken with the same method shows a trend, and a trend is what lets you act before the animals show a problem. A consistent record also lets the next visit compare like with like. Test the source water as well as the tank, including the tap water used for top-ups and water changes, because a poor source water can cause a tank problem.

instructionSections.heading: What the core readings mean
instructionSections.body: Temperature: a stable temperature matters more than hitting one exact number, because a sudden change stresses animals. Record it at every visit. pH: pH measures how acidic or alkaline the water is. A pH that swings or drifts is a warning sign in its own right. pH also changes how much of the ammonia in the water is in the more toxic form, so a high pH makes the same ammonia reading more dangerous. Ammonia: ammonia comes from fish waste, uneaten food and decaying matter. It is toxic to fish. In an established tank it should not be detectable, and any reading in a new, recently disturbed or overfed tank is a reason to act under the owner's plan. Nitrite: nitrite is an intermediate step, formed when bacteria convert ammonia, and it is also toxic. In an established tank a nitrite reading points to a problem with the bacteria, the load or the water change. Nitrate: nitrate is the end product of the usual conversion. It is much less harmful than ammonia or nitrite, but it builds up between water changes and is reduced by partial water changes and by plants. Its target is set by the owner's plan. Other parameters, including dissolved oxygen, hardness and the marine parameters, are tested only where the plan asks for them.

instructionSections.heading: A consistent test routine
instructionSections.body: Use a test kit or meter with reagents in date and, for a meter, a current calibration. Test in the same order each visit, from the same sampling point and at about the same time of day, so that differences come from the tank and not from the method. Follow each kit's instructions for shaking, timing and colour reading, and read the colour in good light against the card that comes with the kit. If a test cannot be completed, record it as not completed and give the reason. Store test kits and reagents as their safety data sheets direct (page text refers to the model WHS laws created in 2011; no revision date shown), and keep incompatible chemicals at a distance from one another (no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Reading the results together
instructionSections.body: Read the whole set before you decide anything, and compare it with the previous visit. High ammonia with low nitrate usually points to a cycle that has not been established or has been disrupted. Ammonia falling while nitrite and nitrate rise can show that the bacteria are doing their job. A rising nitrate with stable ammonia and nitrite is common, and the question is whether it stays within the plan's target. A single high reading that falls back on retest is a different problem from a reading that keeps rising, and the trend tells you which one you have.

instructionSections.heading: Responding to an out-of-range result
instructionSections.body: Retest the sample with an in-date reagent. If the first result looks wrong, take a fresh sample. Check the equipment that could change the reading, including the filter, the heater, the top-up water, any recent water change, feeding changes and any livestock added. Then follow the owner's plan. Change one variable at a time, allow time for the effect to show, and retest. Do not add a large amount of any product to force a result, and do not change the water rapidly. If the plan does not cover the result, or the livestock show stress, stop adjusting and refer the matter to the owner and to a qualified specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Electronic monitors support manual testing
instructionSections.body: Continuous electronic monitoring, such as a logged probe with alerts, can show trends between visits. A student project described a system that logged pH and temperature and sent alerts to a phone. The general point is that a monitor supplements manual tests and does not replace them. Sensors drift over time and need calibration, a failed sensor can give a false reading, and a connection or power failure can stop the alerts. Record the sensor's calibration date, and compare the sensor reading with a manual test at each visit.

instructionSections.heading: Records that are useful
instructionSections.body: A useful record shows the date and time, the sampling point, the temperature, each result with its unit, the test method and the reagent expiry date, any water change and its volume, any equipment change, any feeding change and any livestock observation. Corrections follow the same rule as any other record: the original stays readable, and the correction is initialled and dated with the reason. A run of consistent records is the best evidence for the owner, and for any specialist asked to help.

lessons.title: Livestock stress, quarantine and animal welfare boundaries
learningOutcomes: Recognise common signs of stress and illness in aquarium livestock, and record them with the time and the conditions
Explain why new stock is quarantined, and how the owner's quarantine plan is applied
Separate the contractor's role from the role of the owner and of any animal health professional
Refuse to medicate, move or release animals without written authority

instructionSections.heading: Signs of stress
instructionSections.body: Stress in fish and invertebrates shows as hiding, clamped fins, gasping at the surface, pale or dark colouring, erratic swimming, rubbing on surfaces, loss of appetite, sitting on the bottom or hovering near the top. Some of these signs are normal for a short time in an animal that has just been introduced. A pattern that continues or gets worse needs attention. Stress often follows a change in water conditions, temperature, handling, transport or crowding. Record the signs, the number of animals affected, the time and the conditions, rather than assuming the behaviour is normal. The sources also describe signs of disease, including white spots, red streaks, open sores, cloudy eyes, white growths on fins and damaged fins. Record and refer these. Do not diagnose them yourself.

instructionSections.heading: Quarantine
instructionSections.body: New or returned livestock is commonly held in a separate quarantine system before it joins the main tank, so that disease or parasites can be seen before they spread. A quarantine system is a separate tank or container with its own equipment, which must not be shared with the main system without cleaning. The set-up, the length of quarantine and any treatment are set by the owner's plan and by the species guidance the owner uses. A contractor does not start, stop or change a quarantine without the owner's instruction, and does not move stock between systems without a plan (see the system types lesson).

instructionSections.heading: Your role and the owner's role
instructionSections.body: A contractor or technician observes, records, feeds where the plan authorises it, cleans, and reports. Diagnosis, treatment, medication, euthanasia and any decision to move or release animals belong to the owner and, where needed, to a qualified animal health professional. Do not treat an animal with a medication or chemical without authority, and do not use a pool product as a treatment. Report what you observed and when, and refer the decision in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Movement and release
instructionSections.body: Moving live fish between waterways is regulated. The Western Australian page says authority is needed to move fish within the state, and the detail varies by fish type (page metadata dated 2 October 2024, no date in the body). The New South Wales Department of Primary Industries says that listed prohibited and notifiable species may not be kept, purchased, sold or transported, and that releasing fish into public waters needs a fish stocking permit under the Fisheries Management Act (no date shown). In Queensland, listed prohibited species must not be held or brought in, and a person who has or suspects one should inform Biosecurity Queensland without delay (last updated 28 May 2026). Releasing an aquarium animal into a natural waterway can introduce disease and non-native species, and it is never a contractor decision.

instructionSections.heading: Welfare and handling
instructionSections.body: Minimise handling. Use the owner's nets and containers, handle animals in ways that avoid injury, and keep them in water as far as possible. Where an animal has died, record it, and handle the remains as the owner directs. Record deaths and suspected disease in writing, and refer them. Do not put remains down a drain or into a waterway.

lessons.title: Heaters, filters, lights and electrical safety
learningOutcomes: Identify the electrical hazards in aquarium heaters, pumps, filters, lights and controllers, and explain how water raises the risk
Isolate and check each item before any inspection or cleaning in the water area
Recognise a damaged heater, cord, plug or outlet, and take it out of service
Refer any wiring, repair, fixed lighting or controller work to a licensed person, without implying that this lesson grants any licence

instructionSections.heading: Water and mains power
instructionSections.body: Aquarium heaters, pumps, lights, controllers and filters work in water or beside it, and they are powered from mains outlets. Water on a connection, a damaged cord or an unsuitable outlet can cause an electric shock or a fire. Common causes described in the sources include a heater running out of water, a cracked heater, a cord hanging into the water, and several devices on one double adaptor. Treat every aquarium electrical item as live until it has been unplugged or isolated, and check it before you use it.

instructionSections.heading: Heaters and thermostats
instructionSections.body: A heater must be fully submerged, or used only as the manufacturer directs, because a heater that runs out of water can overheat and crack. Check the heater for cracks, discolouration, loose parts and a damaged cord before it is used, and take a damaged heater out of service. Set the heater within the range the livestock plan gives (see the system types lesson). Keep a separate thermometer where it can be read easily, away from the heater, and compare the two readings at each visit. Do not repair a heater by taping or wrapping a damaged part. Replace it with a suitable unit, as the owner's plan and the product instructions direct.

instructionSections.heading: Filters, pumps and air
instructionSections.body: Filters and pumps need a clear intake and a working impeller. Check both for blockage before you reconnect the power, and never run a pump dry.
