A power filter that is opened or refilled must be full of water before it is plugged in. Check the flow at the outlet against the filter's rating on its label. Air pumps, air lines and air stones supply oxygen and circulation. Check the air line for kinks and leaks, and clean air stones as the manufacturer directs. A battery air pump is a useful backup in a power failure, and that choice belongs to the owner.

instructionSections.heading: Lights and timers
instructionSections.body: The light period is set by the owner's plan. Leaving the light on for long periods encourages algae, and a timer is commonly used to keep the period steady. The sources do not agree on the exact hours, so use the plan. Unplug a light before you remove it from the tank or clean it. Metal halide lamps run very hot, and a lamp must cool before it is handled, or be handled with gloves as the manufacturer directs. Bulbs are replaced at the manufacturer's interval.

instructionSections.heading: Cords, outlets and layout
instructionSections.body: Keep cords out of the water and away from splash zones. Make a drip loop, so that water runs down the cord and drips away rather than into the outlet. Do not use damaged cords, and do not use double adaptors that overload the outlet. Use one suitable power point, or a power board whose rating is checked against the load, and keep the outlet dry and above splash level where practical. Do not plug equipment into an outlet that is wet or looks damaged.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating before work
instructionSections.body: Unplug or isolate equipment before you remove it from the water, clean a filter, change media or check a connection. Check that the device is off before you put a hand in the tank. Wet hands, metal tools and water on the floor increase the risk, so dry your hands and keep the area dry. A safety switch, or residual current device, reduces the risk on the circuit, but it does not make live work safe and does not make the work allowed.

instructionSections.heading: Repairs and licensed work
instructionSections.body: Repairing or rewiring a mains connection, a controller or a fixed lighting installation is electrical work. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work, repairs included, needs a licence or certificate whatever its cost, except for electrical equipment operating at not more than 50 volts AC or 120 volts ripple-free DC (last updated 23 June 2026). A maintenance worker's role is to isolate, inspect the outside of the equipment, report the fault and refer it. Completing this lesson does not give electrical authority.

lessons.title: Cycling a new tank and client handover
learningOutcomes: Explain the nitrogen cycle and why a new tank must be cycled before it carries a full livestock load
Check a new tank site for a level, supported floor, power and water access before any water is added
Run and record a cycle using the owner's plan and the test results, rather than a calendar
Prepare a written handover pack, and price the set-up and cycle work under the approved method

instructionSections.heading: What a cycle is
instructionSections.body: A new filter has few of the bacteria that break down ammonia. One group of bacteria converts ammonia from food and waste to nitrite, and another group converts nitrite to nitrate. Until both groups are established, ammonia and nitrite can build up to toxic levels. A cycle is complete when the test results show it, not when a date passes.

instructionSections.heading: Check the site before any water goes in
instructionSections.body: Choose a flat, hard, level site that can carry the filled weight of the tank, the stand and the equipment. A slanted or uneven base can put stress on the glass. Keep the tank out of direct sunlight, away from draughts, doors, windows and high-traffic areas. Confirm there is a suitable power point with a safety switch, that cords can be kept out of the water, and that the water supply is within reach. A filled tank is heavy, so plan the lift and use enough people. Check the tank for leaks at the seams and the base while it is empty and dry, and again during the first fill, and record what you find. This course covers setting up a tank, not building one. Building or modifying a glass tank is outside this course.

instructionSections.heading: Clean, fill and condition
instructionSections.body: Wash the substrate in a bucket until the rinse water is clear enough for the plan, because new substrate often clouds the water. Rinse decorations and new filter media in clean water before they go in, and do not use detergents. Fill the tank slowly, using water at about room temperature, and condition it with a product that removes chlorine and chloramine at the dose on its label. Start the heater and the filter as the plan directs, with the heater set in the range for the livestock (see the system types lesson). A cloudiness that persists or worsens is reported.

instructionSections.heading: Running the cycle
instructionSections.body: There are two broad approaches: a cycle with fish, which needs close monitoring and a plan for feeding and water changes, and a cycle without fish, which uses an ammonia source to feed the bacteria. The owner and the plan choose the method. Any product used to start the bacteria, and any ammonia source, is used strictly at the label dose and as the plan directs. This course does not set amounts or name products. Test ammonia, nitrite, nitrate and pH at the interval the plan sets, and record every result. Keep the light on a timer, so that algae does not take hold while the tank is young. Overfeeding is a common cause of a spike, so feed the amount the plan sets and remove uneaten food.

instructionSections.heading: Adding livestock in stages
instructionSections.body: Do not add livestock until the cycle is complete and the plan agrees. Add livestock in small groups over the period the owner's plan sets, rather than all at once, because a large sudden load can push the bacteria past what they can handle. New livestock must be held in quarantine as the owner's plan directs (see the livestock lesson). Acclimatise each animal by floating its sealed bag in the tank for the period the plan sets, then net the animal out. Do not pour the transport water into the tank. Record each addition with its date, the number of animals and the test results before it.

instructionSections.heading: The client handover pack
instructionSections.body: A handover pack lets the owner keep the tank safe after you leave. It should include the tank size and the system type; the equipment list, with each item labelled and each isolation point marked; the maintenance plan (see the routine visit lesson); the test log and the cycle record; the water source and the conditioning method used; the livestock list supplied by the owner; the emergency steps for a power failure, a heater fault or a leak; a list of things that must never be added, such as pool chemicals; and referral contacts for electrical, plumbing and animal health matters. State the limits of your service in writing, and get the owner's sign-off.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing the set-up and cycle work
instructionSections.body: Set-up and cycle management is skilled work, and its value comes from the checks, the records and the handover. Price it as a defined scope under the business's approved method. Price the set-up, the test visits during the cycle and the handover pack as separate items, so the client can see what each one covers. Do not absorb test visits as free work. Charge for materials under the materials cost policy. Do not sell animals unless the business is authorised to do so.

lessons.title: Routine maintenance visit and checklists
learningOutcomes: Run a routine visit in a fixed order that covers the livestock, equipment, testing, water change, cleaning, filters and records
Use a checklist that sets out daily, weekly, monthly and longer tasks, and separates the owner's tasks from the contractor's
Carry out a staged partial water change that keeps the animals safe and keeps the bacteria in the filter
Reduce repeat work by sequencing tasks and recording only the exceptions

instructionSections.heading: A fixed order saves time
instructionSections.body: A routine visit goes faster and misses less when it follows the same order every time. A good order is: check safety and the work order, observe the livestock and the equipment, test the water, make the planned water change, clean the glass and décor, care for the filter, check the equipment and the lights, and then complete the records. Testing comes before the water change, because the results may change what the change should be. Observing the livestock before the work starts gives a baseline to compare with afterwards.

instructionSections.heading: Daily, weekly, monthly and longer tasks
instructionSections.body: Most daily tasks belong to the owner: feeding to the plan, a glance at the equipment and the livestock, and a check of the water level. The contractor's visit covers the tasks that need skill or access. Weekly tasks usually include the planned partial water change, glass and décor cleaning, a check of any top-off reservoir, and the planned tests. Monthly tasks include rinsing filter media in tank water, checking the lighting timer, and checking the expiry dates on test kits. Longer tasks include cleaning pumps and powerheads, calibrating probes, replacing bulbs at the manufacturer's interval, and checking heaters for age and condition. The intervals in the sources differ from one another and are examples only.

instructionSections.heading: The staged partial water change
instructionSections.body: A partial change removes waste from the bottom and replaces part of the water in small volumes. The method in the sources is to change part of the water, not all of it. Loosen the debris, siphon it from the gravel and the bottom, and refill slowly with treated water. Prepare the new water before you start, conditioned as the label directs and close to the tank's temperature. For a marine tank, match the salinity as well. Do not return siphoned water to the tank. When the siphon is finished, close the line so that the water in the hose does not run back into the tank. Keep the animals safe while you work. Where the plan allows, move them to a container of tank water with an air supply, and do not hold them out of water for long. Before you open a filter, check it for trapped fish, and never run a filter that has been opened and left dry.

instructionSections.heading: Glass, lights and décor
instructionSections.body: Clean the glass with a scraper or pad made for aquarium use, moving slowly so that the animals are not disturbed. Use only aquarium-approved supplies or clean water. Household cleaners are never used on glass, décor or equipment. Keep buckets for tank water only, because a bucket contaminated with cleaning residue can harm the animals. Before you remove a light from the tank or clean it, unplug it. Keep the light period to the plan, and set a timer if the owner forgets to switch the light off. Remove algae from décor and plastic plants by rinsing them in clean water, and replace any item that cannot be cleaned without damage. For live plants, remove dead leaves and keep the planting as the plan says.

instructionSections.heading: Filter care
instructionSections.body: Rinse biological media in tank water that was removed during the change, never in tap water, so that the bacteria survive. Clean mechanical media, such as sponge or floss, in the same way. If you replace floss, replace only part of it, and leave some of the original in the filter, because the old material keeps the bacteria the tank needs. Replace chemical media, such as activated carbon, only as the plan directs. Doing too much at once can strip the bacteria, so change one part at a time, and check the flow before you leave.

instructionSections.heading: The equipment check
instructionSections.body: Check the heater setting against the separate thermometer, the pump's flow and noise, the air line and air stone, the top-off device if one is fitted, the lighting timer, and every cord and outlet. Look for leaks at the tank seals and at the equipment joints. Any damaged item is taken out of service and referred (see the electrical safety lesson).

instructionSections.heading: Records and checklists
instructionSections.body: Use one checklist for each visit, with the same headings every time, and record only the exceptions in detail. A completed checklist shows that each task was done, or deliberately skipped with a reason. Record the time on site, each test result, the volume of any water change, the equipment checked, anything changed, and any observation about the animals. Save the record to the client's file on the day of the visit.

instructionSections.heading: What is outside a routine visit
instructionSections.body: A routine visit does not include adding medicines, treating animals, buying or moving animals, releasing water or animals, electrical or plumbing repair, or structural work. Record anything the owner asks for that is outside the visit, and refer it.

lessons.title: Saltwater and reef-specific water basics
learningOutcomes: Distinguish marine fish-only, marine community and reef systems, and state what each one needs from its water and equipment
Explain why evaporation is topped up with fresh water rather than salt water, and how that choice affects salinity
Describe what the main reef chemistry parameters measure, and explain why they are changed one at a time under a plan
Refuse any dosing or product addition that the owner's plan does not cover, and refer it to a qualified person

instructionSections.heading: Marine system types
instructionSections.body: Marine systems differ in what they hold. A fish-only system holds marine fish, perhaps with algae-eating or detritus-eating animals, and uses decorative rock, dried coral or artificial items, with no living coral. A marine community system can hold a wider range of invertebrates, depending on the plan. A reef system is built around living coral, and it needs closer attention to its chemistry, lighting and water flow. Reef systems are the most demanding of the three. One aquarium types reference in the sources notes that a marine system needs a sizeable tank for its livestock, a steady schedule of checks, and regular testing for minerals and chemical balances. Confirm the system type from the owner's plan before you test or change anything, because the targets and the products differ by type.

instructionSections.heading: Why evaporation is topped up with fresh water
instructionSections.body: Water leaves an open tank by evaporation, and the salt stays behind. A top-up with fresh water therefore keeps the salinity steady, while a top-up with salt water raises it. This is why a top-off device, or a manual top-up, uses fresh water, and why a top-up with the wrong water is a common cause of a salinity swing. Check the top-off reservoir regularly so that its pump does not run dry. Evaporation changes with the season, so the check interval should be adjusted to the time of year, as the owner's plan directs.

instructionSections.heading: Salinity and the instrument
instructionSections.body: Measure salinity or specific gravity with a calibrated refractometer, hydrometer or meter, and apply any temperature correction the instrument needs (see the sampling lesson). Measure after the salt mix has fully dissolved and stabilised, and again before any water is added to the tank. Do not record a salinity you have estimated.

instructionSections.heading: The reef chemistry set
instructionSections.body: Reef water is tested for more than the nitrogen compounds. Alkalinity measures how well the water resists a change in pH. Calcium and magnesium are used by animals with hard skeletons, and they are linked to alkalinity. Phosphate is a nutrient that feeds algae when it is high. Nitrate is tested as in other systems. These parameters are linked, so a change to one changes the others. A reef checklist in the sources gives a testing frequency for the reef set. Change one parameter at a time under the plan, and retest before the next step. Do not chase a number by adding products. Dosing is done only with a product approved for the system, at the label dose, under the owner's plan. Where the plan is not clear, refer it.

instructionSections.heading: Water source for marine work
instructionSections.body: Marine salt mixes are made with water of known quality. Reef keepers commonly use water from a treatment process that removes most dissolved material, such as reverse osmosis, sometimes followed by deionisation. The sources suggest monitoring that output with a TDS meter and changing the cartridges as the manufacturer and the use indicate. Treat that equipment as a water-treatment item, with its own records, storage and maintenance. Do not collect seawater or live rock from the sea, because that is not covered by this course.

instructionSections.heading: Marine-specific equipment
instructionSections.body: A protein skimmer removes dissolved waste by producing foam in a collection cup. Empty and clean the cup at the interval set by the manufacturer and the load on the tank. Low foam output, a full cup, or foam of an unusual colour is a sign to check the pump, the air intake and the cup, and to record what you find. Specialised equipment, such as calcium reactors, chillers and ozone generators, is maintained by the specialist or the manufacturer. This lesson does not cover adjusting it.

instructionSections.heading: Pests, disease and treatments are referred
instructionSections.body: Pests, coral disease and the treatment of marine animals are outside this lesson. If a coral or a fish shows damage, unusual colour or pests, record what you see, photograph it only if the owner agrees and the business policy allows, and refer it. Do not add a treatment or a coral additive that the owner's plan does not cover.

lessons.title: Service offers for aquarium maintenance
learningOutcomes: Define a service offer for aquarium maintenance with a written scope, a tier, a price basis and the exclusions
Identify recurring and add-on offers that stay within the business's scope and authority
Describe referral arrangements, and check their disclosure and fee rules before they are used
Explain honestly what the service does and does not promise to the client

instructionSections.heading: What the offer is
instructionSections.body: A service offer is a written statement of what you will do, how often, for what price, and what the client needs to do in return. For aquarium maintenance, the core is a routine visit: testing, a planned partial water change, glass and filter care within scope, equipment checks and records. Other offers build on that core: set-up and cycle management, a trend report from the test records, an equipment check, and referrals to licensed trades. Describe every offer in the same terms, so that the client can compare them. Under the Australian Consumer Law, a service must be performed competently, suit the purpose stated, and be delivered within a reasonable time unless a timeframe was agreed (published and modified 7 October 2026 (page metadata)). Businesses owe customers honest information about services, and should keep hidden fees out of contracts (dated 27 May 2025).

instructionSections.heading: Three tiers that match the hobby
instructionSections.body: Clients differ in their experience and in how much work they want to do themselves. A basic tier covers the visit, the planned tests and the planned water change. A standard tier adds an equipment check, the records and a short monthly trend note. A full-care tier adds cycle or set-up support for a new tank and a handover pack. Use the tiers to match the client's need, not to push the most expensive one. A small study of aquarium shops in India, published in 2012 and therefore historical and not Australian, found that customers' questions centred on fish care, tank cleaning and water quality. The study's figures are not used here. It is a prompt for what to explain, and it is not evidence about the Australian market.

instructionSections.heading: Recurring and add-on offers
instructionSections.body: A recurring plan at a set interval gives the client predictable care and gives the business predictable work. Add-ons can include a test report, a filter media refresh (with materials charged under the materials cost policy), a timer or light check, and a quarantine set-up under the owner's plan. Do not sell animals, medicines or chemical treatments as add-ons. Absence care, where someone checks a tank while the owner is away, is a separate service with its own staffing, access, emergency and insurance rules.

instructionSections.heading: Referral partners
instructionSections.body: Some work is outside the business's authority and needs a licensed electrician, a licensed plumber or an animal health professional. Refer that work in writing, with the symptoms and the readings. Before you accept any payment or commission for a referral, check the rules that apply to referral fees, to advertising and to inducements in the state where you work. Disclose any arrangement to the client before they agree to the referral.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing for value
instructionSections.body: Price each offer on the work it includes: time on site, testing, records, travel, materials and the risk the work carries. Show the scope as line items, so the client can see what is included. Use the approved pricing method and quoting approval for each offer, and state the minimum charge. A receipt is needed once a transaction passes $75, and also whenever the customer asks for one (published and modified 7 October 2026 (page metadata)). Value comes from the reliability of the checks and the records, and that is what the owner is paying for.

instructionSections.heading: What you must not promise
instructionSections.body: Do not promise that the fish will live, that the water will sit at a particular value, or that a visit will fix a problem. Do not diagnose disease, and do not recommend treatments outside the owner's plan. Explain the limits of the service in writing, and keep client details private as the business policy requires.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping clients and growing the work
instructionSections.body: Clients stay with a service that is explained and recorded. A trend report, a clear handover, a reliable visit time and a plain explanation of any change are the reasons people keep a service. Ask for referrals only in ways the marketing rules allow (see the referral incentives lesson, “Referral incentives that respect consumer and spam rules”). Never send unsolicited messages to people who have not agreed to receive them.

lessons.title: Mobile beauty scope and skin-treatment boundaries
learningOutcomes: Explain why cosmetic injectables are outside the scope of this course and must not be offered under it
Decide whether a proposed service is inside the approved service list and inside the regulatory position for the location
Identify the chemical hazards that WorkSafe Victoria names for beauty products, and the step each one requires

instructionSections.heading: What is excluded from this course
instructionSections.body: Cosmetic injectables, including botulinum toxin and dermal fillers, are excluded from the mobile beauty course. This is a team decision recorded in the course plan. This lesson does not teach injectable treatments, does not describe how they are given, and no lesson in this course gives authority to offer them. Whether a business offering injectables needs a licence, is restricted, or is classed as a higher-risk service depends on the state and the council, and that is outside what this course covers. Gold Coast City Council places procedures that put foreign material beneath the skin in its higher-risk category, which needs a licence, and its page gives cosmetic injectables as an example (no date shown). Any future consideration of injectables is a separate scope decision with its own licence check.

instructionSections.heading: Skin penetration and where the lines fall
instructionSections.body: Beauty work sits under different rules in each state and territory. In Victoria, the Department of Health lists beauty therapy and cosmetic applications among services that must register under the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008 (page updated 22 May 2026). The same page exempts mobile beauty therapists from registration, but the exemption stops short of the principal place of business, and exempts mobile cosmetic application services only where the service does not involve skin penetration or tattooing. Classification is also council-specific. Macedon Ranges Shire Council places facials or body treatments, manicures or pedicures, artificial nails, electrolysis and waxing in its high-risk group, which needs periodic renewal, and places eyelash and eyebrow tinting, spray tans and temporary make-up in its low-risk group (no updated date shown). Other councils may classify differently. In Queensland, beauty therapy does not need a licence, but higher-risk services do, including cosmetic tattooing, semi-permanent make-up, implanting substances under the skin, body piercing, with the exception of closed ear and nose piercing, and scarring (no date shown). In the ACT, mobile practitioners doing skin penetration work fall under the infection control licence. In the Northern Territory, a business that receives payment for beauty therapy must register; the register's beauty list runs from facial and body work through nail services to semi-permanent make-up and cosmetic tattooing (no date shown). Before you add any service to the menu, check which list it falls under in your state, and do not assume that a service is outside the rules because it looks minor.

instructionSections.heading: Chemical hazards that set the boundary
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria's page on hazards in hairdressing and beauty (reviewed 12/09/2025) names nail acrylics and dip powders, where airborne particles and vapours can arise; eyelash glue, which can include a cyanoacrylate that may sensitise the skin and irritate the eyes; and chemical peels, which may contain TCA, phenol or glycolic acid that can irritate skin and damage eyes. The business must hold a safety data sheet for each product. WorkSafe's safety data sheet page (reviewed 30/07/2022) requires an up-to-date SDS for every product, kept accessible. Its safety basics page (reviewed 30/07/2022) says employers need a register listing every hazardous substance on site. Whether a chemical peel is offered at all is a business scope decision. The approved list of services is held in {{business:services.service_description}}. Do not offer a mobile peel until the business has reviewed it with the regulator.

lessons.title: Hygiene, single-use tools and product sanitation
learningOutcomes: Choose single-use or reusable tools for each treatment and explain the choice
Clean and disinfect reusable tools using the product label contact time
Prevent cross-contamination of products during a treatment, including the rule against returning used product to a container

instructionSections.heading: Single-use first, then clean and disinfect
instructionSections.body: Infection in beauty work spreads through skin, blood, body fluids and shared products. The first control is to use single-use items wherever a product allows. Disposable applicators, spatulas, wax sticks, cotton items and gloves are discarded after each client. Reusable tools must be cleaned, then disinfected. Cleaning removes visible soil and product. Disinfection kills the organisms that remain, and it works only after the surface is clean and for the contact time stated on the product label. The Victorian Department of Health's page on hair, beauty, tattooing and skin penetration industries (updated 26 October 2026) names the 2019 infection prevention and control guidelines for these industries. The business's approved method is recorded in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instructionSections.heading: Product sanitation during a treatment
instructionSections.body: Products become contaminated during use. A spatula dipped into a jar and then returned to it can carry skin cells and organisms into the whole product. The rule is to decant the amount needed for each client into a clean dish, never return used product to the main container, and discard the dish or clean it after the service. Pumps and lids are kept closed when not in use. Products that are labelled for single use are not reused. Record each product's name, batch and date where the business procedure requires it, and keep products in the approved storage in {{business:materials.storage_procedure}}. WorkSafe Victoria's page on this industry names nail acrylics and dip powders, eyelash glue and chemical peels as sources of hazard. WorkSafe's safety data sheet page requires an up-to-date SDS to be held for every product (reviewed 30/07/2022), so the product's safety data sheet must be checked before use.

instructionSections.heading: Cross-contamination in a mobile setting
instructionSections.body: A mobile therapist works in rooms that are not clinics, often without a dedicated sink. Cross-contamination risk rises when a single kit is carried from client to client. Keep a clean and used area apart within the kit, carry used tools in a sealed container, and clean the work surface before and after each client. Wash hands with soap and water, or use an approved hand sanitiser where the business procedure allows it, before and after each client and after touching a used item. Waste from wax, cotton and gloves goes in a sealed bag for disposal. Western Australia's hairdressing guideline (last reviewed February 2024) requires mobile operators to have easily accessible hand-washing with warm water, soap and disposable towels, and to send wastewater into the sewer, not stormwater drains.

lessons.title: Client consent, patch testing and contraindications
learningOutcomes: Complete a written client intake that records allergies, previous reactions, medical conditions and current treatments
Identify the contraindications in the business's approved list that require the service to be postponed or refused
Explain what the therapist can and cannot decide about a client's medical condition

instructionSections.heading: Consent starts before the first product touches the skin
instructionSections.body: Consent is the client's agreement to a service after being told what it involves, what it does, what the risks are, and what the alternatives are. In a mobile setting the therapist is often in a home the client has chosen, and the client may feel pressure to agree. The therapist must explain the service in plain words, answer questions, and give the client time to decide. The consent is recorded on the intake form before the service starts, and it can be withdrawn at any time. The business's consent form and intake questions are held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}. Where the client is under a guardian or has a substitute decision-maker, the business procedure must say how consent is recorded. The business must check the consent form and wording for each location.

instructionSections.heading: Contraindications and the duty to refer
instructionSections.body: A contraindication is a condition or circumstance where a treatment should not go ahead, or should be changed or postponed. Common examples in beauty work include an open wound, a skin infection, a recent reaction to a product, and a skin condition the therapist cannot assess. The WA hairdressing guideline (last reviewed February 2024) does not require formal health screening of staff or clients. For a client with an open wound, an infection or a skin condition, it advises that the hairdresser recommend a visit to a general practitioner, and it allows the service to go ahead only where the operator believes it can be appropriately provided around the condition and infection-prevention processes are in place. That is a WA position for hairdressing, used here as practical good practice for beauty work. The therapist must not diagnose a condition. The safe action for any unclear condition is to postpone the service and refer the client.

instructionSections.heading: Patch tests and what the record must show
instructionSections.body: A patch test checks a client's reaction to a product before a full treatment. The product's instructions set the method, and where the instructions say a test is needed, the test is required. Record the product name, the site on the skin, the time applied, the time read, the result and the client's response. If there is a reaction, stop, do not apply the product, advise the client to seek medical advice, and record the decision. A client who has had the same product before should still be tested if the instructions say so, because a reaction can develop with repeated exposure.

lessons.title: Service menus, add-ons and packages
learningOutcomes: Build a service menu from the approved list, and keep every item inside the scope of the approved service
Design an add-on or package that adds volume without adding unreviewed risk or shortening required steps
Explain how the menu, the add-ons and the packages are recorded for the client and the business

instructionSections.heading: The menu is the scope, in print
instructionSections.body: A service menu tells the client what the business does. It is therefore a statement of scope. Every item on the menu must be on the approved service list, and every item must have been checked against the state and council rules in “Mobile beauty scope and skin-treatment boundaries”. A menu item that is not on the approved list, or that is in a category the business has not reviewed, is a scope error even if the therapist has the skill. The approved list is held in {{business:services.service_description}}. The menu should describe each service in plain words, state the time it takes, and state any product the client should know about. It must not describe a result that the treatment cannot deliver, and it must never include an injectable treatment, which is excluded from this course.

instructionSections.heading: Add-ons that add value without adding risk
instructionSections.body: An add-on is a small extra service sold with a main treatment, such as a hand treatment with a nail service. Add-ons are useful because they raise the revenue from each visit without adding travel. The risk is that an add-on may need its own patch test, its own processing time or its own consent. A tinting add-on, for example, needs the product's patch test and the processing time from its label, as “Client consent, patch testing and contraindications” explains. An add-on should be checked for the same steps as the main service, and it should be recorded on the job record so that the materials cost is included in the price. The rule is that an add-on may not shorten a required step, and may not be offered as a replacement for the consent or the intake.

instructionSections.heading: Packages and the record they create
instructionSections.body: A package is a set of visits sold together at a set price. Packages are useful for clients who return regularly, but they create a record that the business must keep. The package should state the services included, the number of visits, the period it covers, and what happens if the client does not use all the visits. The package record must link each visit to the services delivered, and each visit must have its own intake and consent record, because a client's health can change between visits. The package terms are set in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}.

lessons.title: Mobile setup, power and wet-area safety
learningOutcomes: Check the power supply and the electrical equipment before use, and remove equipment that is unsafe
Plan a wet-area set-up that keeps electrical equipment away from water and wastewater away from stormwater
Apply the general WHS duty that a self-employed therapist owes to others, and record the set-up check

instructionSections.heading: The general duty that applies to a mobile therapist
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria states that a self-employed person's work must not expose others to risk, within what is reasonably practicable, and that an employer's work must not endanger customers or members of the public (reviewed 03/04/2025). Both duties are confirmed for Victoria. In a mobile setting, the therapist's work is done in someone else's home, so the set-up must be checked for the power, water and fire risks that the therapist brings. The safe approach is to apply the duty in the client's home as though it applies, and to record the set-up check. The business's set-up checklist is recorded as {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instructionSections.heading: Power, leads and equipment checks
instructionSections.body: A mobile therapist depends on a power outlet the client provides. Before plugging in, check that the outlet is in working order, that the cable is not damaged, and that the load of the equipment does not exceed what the cable and outlet can take. Do not run leads across walkways where people can trip. Do not use a damaged appliance, and remove it from use until it has been repaired or tested. Where the business supplies a residual current device or a portable tester, use it. Keep the power cord away from water. Equipment that has been wet should not be switched on until it has been checked by a competent person.

instructionSections.heading: Wet-area planning and wastewater
instructionSections.body: Beauty work often involves water, for hand washing, cleaning tools and rinsing. Water and electrical equipment must be kept apart. Set the electrical equipment on a dry surface away from the sink and the wet area, and never put a plugged-in appliance into water. Wastewater must be planned. The WA hairdressing guideline (last reviewed February 2024) says that holding tanks for wastewater from mobile work must be emptied into the sewer rather than into stormwater; that rule is confirmed for WA hairdressing. Use a sealed container for wastewater where the sewer connection is not known, and do not tip it into a stormwater drain. Record where the wastewater went.

lessons.title: Bond-clean scope, inclusions and exclusions
learningOutcomes: Read the accepted work order and separate cleaning from restoration and specialist work.
Document pre-existing damage, inaccessible areas and fragile materials before work.
Decline to promise bond return or extra work that has not been priced and approved.

instructionSections.heading: The work order decides the scope
instructionSections.body: A bond or end-of-lease clean is defined by the customer's accepted work order and the applicable tenancy arrangements. It is not a promise that the bond will be returned. Identify the rooms, fixtures, surfaces, access conditions and the specific deliverables before you start. Where the work order and the customer's expectation differ, record the difference and get approval before you proceed.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning is not restoration
instructionSections.body: Normal soil removal differs from repairing damage, removing permanent stains, remediating mould, controlling pests or working at height. Record these as exclusions, and refer them to a qualified service where they are needed. A cracked tile is recorded as damage, not as a cleaning failure.

instructionSections.heading: Checkpoints and changes
instructionSections.body: Before work, document pre-existing damage, inaccessible areas, fragile materials, power and water constraints, and unusually heavy soil. In Victoria, the start-of-tenancy condition report, together with any photos taken then, is the comparison point at the end of the tenancy, and a rental provider cannot claim for ordinary wear (Consumer Affairs Victoria, releasing or claiming the bond, last updated 14 Oct 2026). When a client asks for an extra oven, balcony or carpet extraction, check training, tools, hazards and pricing authority before agreeing. Do not promise extra work on behalf of the business without approval. Conditions vary by state, territory and country. The local law and the manufacturer's instructions govern, and this lesson does not substitute for them.

lessons.title: Room-by-room deep-clean execution and sequencing
learningOutcomes: Prepare the site and a clean equipment staging area before starting.
Sequence the work high-to-low and dry-remove dust before wet processes.
Check each zone against its acceptance criteria before moving on.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing the site
instructionSections.body:
Before the first cloth is wet, confirm the basics of the property. Check access to the building and to each room, the position of the power, water and gas controls, and the ventilation that is available. Walk the property with the agreed scope and note any hazards: loose floor coverings, wet or slippery areas, damaged electrical fittings, fragile glass, pest activity, and any product or chemical left by the occupant. Record the surface condition as you find it, room by room, so that a later question about a mark or a chip can be answered from the record. The record is the baseline for the whole job.

Photograph pre-existing issues only with the permission of the occupant or the owner, and only within the privacy rules that apply to your business. The federal Privacy Act generally does not apply to a business with an annual turnover of $3 million or less, but it does apply to some small businesses regardless of turnover, including health service providers and businesses that trade in personal information. Check your own position before you rely on the exemption (OAIC, small business page; last modified 5 September 2024). Keep photographs focused on the surfaces and fixtures, and avoid personal papers and belongings.

Set up a clean equipment staging area near the entry, outside the path of the work. Place the cloths, buckets, products and the vacuum there, with the SDS for each product in a folder on site. Keep products on a tray or trolley rather than on the floor, and keep the staging area separate from the dirty water and used cloths. A staging area that sits in the middle of a room gets knocked over, and a spill from a product on the floor can cause a slip or a contaminated surface.

instructionSections.heading: Sequence: high to low, and dust before water
instructionSections.body:
Work high to low, and from less soiled to more soiled where practicable. Start with the high points: light fittings and covers, ceiling fan blades and the tops of wall units, then the upper walls and door frames, then the windows and sills, then the lower walls, the fixtures and the cupboard fronts, and finally the floors. Floors are cleaned last where it is safe to do so, because the dust and drips from above fall onto them. A team that cleans floors first and then removes overhead dust creates rework, and the sequence must change.

Dry-remove loose dust before any wet process, so that the dust does not turn into a film or mud. Use a dry cloth, a dusting tool or an approved vacuum with a suitable filter. Where the dust may contain crystalline silica, which can come from concrete, grout, stone or tile, the national guide on silica states that dry sweeping, compressed air and general-purpose vacuums must not be used to clean dusty surfaces. It recommends wet methods, low-pressure water, wet sweeping or a vacuum of the class the guide describes. It also warns that handheld spray bottles and sponges are not adequate for suppressing silica dust, so a dusty surface that contains silica needs the controls in the guide, not a quick wipe. Check the SDS or the supplier's data before you decide that a dust does not contain silica.

Protect completed areas from recontamination. Close a finished room, or mark it with a clear sign and a boundary, so that the team does not walk back through it with dirty shoes or equipment. Work from the far end of a room towards the exit, so that you do not step on finished areas.

instructionSections.heading: Kitchens, bathrooms and fixtures
instructionSections.body: In bathrooms, clean from the top down: fan covers and vents, the shower head and the screens, the walls and tiles, the basin, the bath, the toilet, and then the floor. Use dedicated sanitary cloths and tools for the bathroom only, and keep them out of the kitchen and the living areas. Apply product to the cloth, rather than spraying it into fittings, and follow the product's dwell and rinse instructions. Protect finishes that a product can dull or mark, and test a product on an inconspicuous area first. In kitchens, clean from the top down as well, and clean the surfaces that food touches with a product that the label says is suitable for that purpose. Clean inside cupboards and drawers that are empty, and keep residue out of the stored items. Do not disassemble an appliance to clean behind or inside it. Clean the accessible parts, note what you could not reach, and report it. Moving furniture, appliances and heavy fittings is a manual task. Identify the items that need moving before the clean starts, and remove the hazard where you can, for example by agreeing that the occupant empties a cupboard before you arrive. Where the item must move, reduce the risk with a mechanical aid, a change to the layout, a second person where the item needs it, and training. Safe Work Australia states that the business must identify and manage the risk of manual tasks, and that elimination comes first, followed by ways to minimise the risk that remains (Safe Work Australia, lifting, pushing and pulling manual tasks; no date shown). Stay within the agreed scope, and check every zone against its acceptance criteria before you move on.

instructionSections.heading: Zone sign-off before moving on
instructionSections.body: Each zone is checked against its acceptance criteria before the team moves to the next one. The criteria are written before the work starts, and they name the surfaces, the fixtures and the standard expected for each. Check the zone under a good light, from the doorway and from close up, because a room can look clean from one position and still have missed cleaning behind a fixture or in a corner. Mark the zone as signed off only when every criterion is met, or record the item that is not met and why. Where a mark or a stain remains after the approved method, record it as unresolved, with a photograph where permitted, and note that it was not removed by the method used. Do not describe an unresolved mark as cleaned.

lessons.title: Bond-clean verification, defects and photographic handover
learningOutcomes: Inspect against the signed checklist, not subjective impressions.
Classify findings as missed cleaning, pre-existing wear, permanent damage, inaccessible or out of scope.
Hand over with approved evidence, exceptions and follow-up, without guaranteeing a bond outcome.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect against the agreed list
instructionSections.body:
Inspect with the signed checklist in your hand, not with a general impression of the room. The checklist was agreed and signed before the work started, and it names each surface, fixture and standard that the clean covers. Walk the property in the same order as the checklist, so that nothing is skipped and the record can be checked line by line later. Use a good light, held low across walls and cupboard fronts where marks show best, and check from the doorway and from close up.

Check the accessible surfaces, the corners, the top of the door frames, the inside of cupboards that were agreed to be cleaned, the rear of the toilet and the basin, the gaps around the cooktop, and the floor edges and skirting. A room that looks clean from the doorway can still have missed cleaning in those places. Confirm that products have been rinsed or removed as the label requires, because residue can look like a stain or a film. If a line on the checklist cannot be checked, mark it as inaccessible rather than passing it.

instructionSections.heading: Classify findings fairly
instructionSections.body:
Separate each finding into one of five groups. Missed cleaning is an area that the agreed clean covered and did not clean properly, and it is corrected. Pre-existing wear is a mark or condition that was present before the clean, and the pre-work record shows it. Permanent damage is a defect that cleaning will not remove, such as a crack, a chip or a burn, and it is recorded and referred for assessment. Inaccessible means the area could not be reached safely or without damage, and the reason is recorded. Out of scope means the item was not part of the agreed clean, and it is recorded as such.

Do not alter the evidence to fit a classification. Do not imply that a stain is removable until it has been assessed, and do not describe a permanent defect as cleaning. An inspector who flags a cracked tile may be looking at damage that was present before the clean, and the pre-work record shows it. Compare the finding with the photographs and notes from the start of the job. Where the record does not show the condition, say so, and do not claim that it was present or absent.

instructionSections.heading: Standards, reports and what the checklist is
instructionSections.body: The standard a renter must meet is set by the tenancy law of the state or territory, and it varies. In Victoria, the Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance says that a renter must leave the property reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear. For rental agreements signed from 29 March 2021, the page says a rental provider cannot require professional cleaning unless the property needs to be returned to its starting state, or is in a state that requires professional cleaning. It does not require renters to use a particular cleaner (Consumer Affairs Victoria, moving out of a rental property; last updated 14 October 2026). In Queensland, the Residential Tenancies Authority page says a tenant must leave the property in the same condition as at the start, apart from fair wear and tear, and that a landlord or property manager cannot require a better condition, require a particular cleaning or pest service or provider, or require a set fee for it (RTA Queensland, carpet cleaning and pest control page; no date shown). In Victoria, the rental provider or agent completes the exit condition report, within 10 days after the rental agreement ends. The renter must be present or have a reasonable opportunity to attend. The exit section is part of the original condition report, and bond-claim evidence such as invoices, receipts, quotes or photographs must be given to the renter at least 3 business days before a claim is made (Consumer Affairs Victoria, condition reports; last updated 14 October 2026). Your checklist is a separate record of the clean. It is not the condition report, and it must not be presented as one.

instructionSections.heading: Evidence, bond release and the handover
instructionSections.body:
Take authorised photographs that show the area and its context, with the timestamp on. Avoid people, private documents, mail and personal possessions in the frame. Obtain the occupant's and the owner's consent before photographing their property, and keep the originals and their timestamps under the business's retention and access rules. Store them securely and share them only with the people entitled to them.

Bond release in Victoria is decided by the parties named on the bond, or by an order. The Consumer Affairs Victoria page says the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority repays a bond when everyone listed agrees, or when the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal, or Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria for a binding order, has made an order. A renter who starts a claim gives the other parties 14 days to contest it, and the bond may be repaid as the claim directs if nobody contests it (Consumer Affairs Victoria, releasing or claiming the bond; last updated 14 October 2026). Your handover does not decide that outcome, so do not guarantee acceptance by a property manager, the return of a security deposit, or the release of a bond.

Correct any missed cleaning, reinspect the corrected area against the checklist, and record that you did so. Record what could not be resolved within scope. Then give the customer the completed checklist, the exceptions and classifications, the approved photographs and the follow-up contact. Describe the clean and the evidence only. The local law and the manufacturer's instructions govern, and this lesson does not substitute for them.

lessons.title: Pricing and quoting for detailing packages
learningOutcomes: Build the variable cost of one detailing package from labour, consumables, travel, water and power.
State the pricing basis on every quote, and show whether a price is quoted with or without GST.
Calculate break-even jobs per month and compare the figure with the jobs the business can realistically book.

instructionSections.heading: Build the cost before the price
instructionSections.body: A price is only as good as the cost it covers. Start with the cost of one job of each package. Labour is the time on site, plus the time to travel to and from the client, plus set-up and pack-down, multiplied by the hourly cost you need to earn. Consumables are the chemicals, pads, towels and small items used on that job. Travel is the distance driven for the job multiplied by your running cost per kilometre, which you should take from your own vehicle records rather than from a generic figure. Water and power are the amounts used on site, and they matter most for mobile work where the client supplies them. Fixed costs are the costs that do not change with one job: insurance, phone, storage, software, licence and registration costs, bookkeeping fees, and depreciation on equipment. Keep the two groups separate. Variable costs go into the price of each job. Fixed costs are spread across the number of jobs you expect to book in a month. A package that looks profitable when fixed costs are ignored may not cover the business's running costs at all.

instructionSections.heading: Choose a pricing basis and state it
instructionSections.body: A pricing basis is the reason a price is what it is. Common bases are cost-plus, where a margin is added to the variable cost; time-based, where a rate per hour is applied; package pricing, where the price reflects the result the package delivers; and market-referenced pricing, where you compare with prices you have verified yourself. The mobile car wash business plan uploaded for this course describes a market-price approach and a decision to avoid price wars, and that approach is a model for thinking about the choice, not a source of figures. Whichever basis you use, write it on the quote, for example that the price reflects the package scope, travel within a stated radius and the consumables used. Do not state a competitor's price as a market fact unless you have a dated record of it. Decide how travel is charged: as a call-out fee, as part of the package, or with a minimum charge that covers the time lost on a short job. State whether the price includes GST. A GST-exclusive price and a GST-inclusive price can differ by the GST amount, and a quote that does not say which one it is will be misunderstood. The ATO page on GST registration gives $75,000 in GST turnover as the point at which registration is required.

instructionSections.heading: Break-even and the written quote
instructionSections.body: Break-even tells you how many jobs you must book in a month before the business covers its fixed costs. Divide the monthly fixed costs by the contribution per job, which is the price excluding GST minus the variable cost of that job. Then compare the answer with the jobs you can realistically do in a week, allowing for travel, weather and rest. If the break-even figure is higher than your capacity, the price, the costs or the mix of packages has to change. A written quote should include the package and its scope, the included items, the excluded items, the conditions the client must meet for water, power and access, the price and whether GST is included, the validity period, any deposit, and the payment terms. Keep the quote short enough for the client to read, and long enough that a later dispute can be settled from the document. Review each price after three months, using the actual costs recorded on the job cards.

lessons.title: Running a mobile detailing round
learningOutcomes: Plan a round of mobile jobs with an order, time windows, travel buffers and access checks for each stop.
Confirm water and power at each site, and choose a wash-water method that keeps run-off out of stormwater drains.
Load, run and close a round in a fixed order, and record start, finish and any delay.

instructionSections.heading: Plan the round before the first job
instructionSections.body: A mobile round is planned from the booking list, not from memory. Group the bookings by suburb, then set the order so that the most time-critical job comes first and the shortest travel is between stops. For each job, set a time window, and add a buffer for parking, set-up, pack-down and the drive to the next stop. A round that looks possible on a map can fail when a client's gate is locked or a driveway is blocked, so confirm access for each stop before you leave. Write down the gate code, the parking, the location of the tap and the power point, and any pets. The mobile car wash business plan uploaded for this course describes a mobile operation with set operating hours and a stated service radius. Use that structure as a model: write the hours and the area in the round sheet, and do not accept jobs that take you outside the area without a decision recorded. A round sheet should show, for each stop, the order, the window, the address, the access notes, the water and power arrangement, the vehicle, the package and the estimated time on site.

instructionSections.heading: Water, wash water and power on site
instructionSections.body: Water and power are often the constraints on a mobile round. Before you travel, confirm that the client has a tap and a hose within reach, and that the flow is adequate for the work. Carry enough water for the stops that do not have a tap, and measure how much water a typical job uses in your own practice before you plan a tank size. Wash water must not run into a stormwater drain. Capture the run-off with a containment method, and take it away for disposal at an approved point, or discharge it where the local rules allow. Do not let it run onto neighbouring property. For power, read the rated power on the nameplate of each tool before you connect it. Plug tools into an outlet with residual current device protection, and check the lead for damage before use. Do not overload a generator by running more tools than its rating allows. Place a generator outdoors, away from doors and windows, so that its exhaust cannot enter a building. Never run a petrol generator inside a garage or enclosed space.

instructionSections.heading: Vehicle, kit and handover
instructionSections.body: Load the vehicle in a fixed order, so that the same item is always in the same place. Store chemicals upright, labelled, in a secure compartment, and keep the safety data sheet for each product in the vehicle. Lift heavy tanks and generators with a plan, and use a trolley where one is available. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling chemicals, and closed footwear on wet or sloping driveways. On arrival, stop and reassess if the site has a hazard you did not expect, such as a slippery surface, live traffic, exposed wiring or an unstable load. When the work is done, walk the client through the finish, note any limit, and complete the handover note. Pack down the kit, check that no item has been left on the client's property, and clear the run-off area. At the end of the round, log the start and finish times, the travel time, the water and power used and any delay, and restock the vehicle for the next round.

lessons.title: Service boundaries and consent
learningOutcomes: Verify consent, scope and the vehicle condition before any work starts.
Separate routine washing from correction and restoration in a two-tier work order.
Stop and obtain authorisation before changing the scope of the work.

instructionSections.heading: Agreeing the scope
instructionSections.body: Begin with the agreed work order, the vehicle condition record, the product instructions and the site risk assessment. Before work, verify the consent, the scope, the surroundings, access, weather, the surface condition, and whether the activity is permitted at this site. A booking that says basic wash does not include paint correction or stain removal, and the difference is written into the work order.

instructionSections.heading: Routine work and specialist work
instructionSections.body: Prepare a two-tier work order. The first tier lists the authorised wash tasks, with the price and estimated duration. The second tier lists the specialist work, such as paint correction or stain removal, that needs its own agreement, its own price and its own assessment. Record the protected personal possessions and any unresolved damage before the vehicle is touched. Show the specialist tier as its own price line, because the Australian Consumer Law stops a business making false claims about price or about what a service will achieve (ACCC, false or misleading claims, metadata 28 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: When the scope changes
instructionSections.body: If a customer expects work that was not agreed, such as paint correction at no extra cost, do not absorb it into a routine wash. Record what is known, what is uncertain, the immediate safe action, and who has authority to approve the next step. Do not continue on assumptions. Services must be performed competently and must suit a purpose the customer has told you about (ACCC, consumer rights and guarantees, metadata 17 July 2026). The customer decides the extra work only after it has been priced and agreed. Conditions vary by state, territory and country. The local law and the manufacturer's instructions govern, and this lesson does not substitute for them.

instructionSections.heading: Stop rules
instructionSections.body: Stop when equipment is defective, when a substance is unidentified, when wastewater cannot be lawfully controlled, when exposed vehicle electronics could be damaged, when the public cannot be protected, or when the task exceeds your demonstrated competence. Isolate the hazard and seek a competent supervisor or specialist.

lessons.title: Vehicle condition and evidence
learningOutcomes: Carry out a systematic walk-around and log fragile and defective components before wetting the vehicle.
Agree an exception plan with the owner for any component that could be damaged.
Avoid claiming that a pre-existing defect was caused or repaired by detailing.

instructionSections.heading: Why the record comes first
instructionSections.body: Before any water touches the vehicle, its condition needs to be recorded as it is found. The reason is practical. The Auto-Detailing guide notes that most swirls, scratches and water spots are added to paint during washing and drying, so a careless wash can add marks to a finish that already had some. Without a before record, a customer who reports a mark after collection and a detailer who knows the wash was careful have only memory to rely on. A written and photographed record turns that argument into evidence. It also shows where the risk sits before products, tools and water pressure are chosen. This lesson covers how to walk the vehicle, how to log what you find, how to agree a plan for parts that could be damaged, and how to write down what was there without blaming the work for it.

instructionSections.heading: Walk-around and condition map
instructionSections.body: Walk the vehicle in a fixed order so nothing is skipped. A practical sequence is paintwork, glass and mirrors, trim and seals, lights, wheels and tyres, the engine bay if it is in scope, and then the interior. Work around the car in one direction and note each defect as you pass it. Look at each panel under a directional light, a torch held low across the surface, because flat light hides fine marks. The Spanish-language manual advises avoiding washing in direct sun and using a light close to the surface to show how badly the surface is damaged. A dark vehicle can hide swirls that appear only under a directional light, so check each panel from more than one angle. Number each defect on a simple condition map and photograph each numbered item, with the owner's permission. Where the clear coat is peeling, flaking or hazy in a patch that does not respond to light cleaning, record it as a suspected clear-coat failure. The show-car sample notes that this kind of breakdown cannot be fixed by abrading the surface, so the record should say that the finish may need specialist assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Fragile parts and the exception plan
instructionSections.body: Some components are more likely to be damaged by water, pressure or product than others. Log fragile seals, any repaired panel that is not sealed, loose trim, open ports and vents, modified accessories, exposed aftermarket air filters and interior electronics. A cracked light lens may admit water, so the water risk is recorded even if the lens looks sealed. The Auto-Detailing guide advises covering exposed electrical connections and protecting air intakes with a plastic bag where water could reach them, and avoiding a direct stream on visible electrical parts. Agree an exception plan with the owner before work starts. The plan names the component at risk, what will be done to protect it (covering, masking or leaving that area alone), who agreed, and what happens if the part moves or leaks. Where a component is unstable, add a stop-work note and do not use force on it. The plan belongs in the job file next to the condition map, not in a conversation alone.

instructionSections.heading: Recording what the work did not cause
instructionSections.body: Keep two entries in the record: what was there before work, and what the work changed. Never write that detailing caused, repaired or removed a defect unless the record shows it. A pre-existing scratch is recorded as found, with its location and photograph. A step you take, such as removing a bonded residue, is recorded separately, with the product, the area and the result. Avoid wording that suggests the vehicle is now restored or defect-free, because it is not. The record also protects the business where an owner's expectations are too high. If the customer expected a scratch to disappear, the written agreement shows the scope and the limits. Keep the record factual and short, and date it at the point it is made.

lessons.title: Product selection and SDS
learningOutcomes: Quarantine any unidentified chemical and refuse to use it.
Match each product to the surface and task using the label and the SDS.
Reject an unlabelled product and never reuse food containers.

instructionSections.heading: What the label and the SDS each tell you
instructionSections.body: A product label and its safety data sheet (SDS) answer different questions, and both are needed. The label is the supplier's instruction for use: the surfaces the product is intended for, the dilution, the dwell time, the ventilation and the general precautions. The SDS is the longer technical document. Safe Work Australia guidance says an SDS covers the chemical's hazards and safe handling, including storage and disposal, along with physical and chemical properties and emergency measures. In practice, look in the SDS for the hazard identification section, the first-aid section, the handling and storage section, and the exposure controls and personal protection section. Those tell you which gloves and eye protection to use, what to do after a splash, and how to keep the product stable. A label alone does not show the full hazard picture, and an SDS does not set the strength of a dilution. Read both before first use, and check the review date on the SDS, because the sheet shows when it was last reviewed.

instructionSections.heading: Matching product to surface and task
instructionSections.body: Match each product to the surface and the task. The guides in the source set repeat one rule: check that the product is safe for the surface before using it. Wheel cleaners are the clearest example. The Auto-Detailing guide advises a pH-neutral wheel cleaner for most wheels, because acidic cleaners can oxidise or tarnish polished and sensitive finishes and suit only factory wheels with a thick clear coat. Interior products follow the same logic. The guide says products designed only for cleaning or only for protection usually work better than combined products, so a serious interior clean uses a cleaner and then a separate protectant. Glass cleaners should not contain ammonia on tinted windows, and protectants should not go onto moving belts or fans. A degreaser can remove sealant or wax, so a degreaser used before a wash strips protection that must then be reapplied. To compare two labelled products, ask the same questions of each: which surfaces are listed, what the label says about dilution and dwell, what the SDS says about PPE and ventilation, and whether the product conflicts with anything already on the vehicle. Where the label and a general practice disagree, the label governs.

instructionSections.heading: Quarantine, the register and storage
instructionSections.body: An unidentified product is not used on any vehicle. Keep it out of use, away from cabin and detailing products, label it as quarantined, and report it to the person who keeps the register. Do not test it, identify it by smell, or pour it into another container to see what it does. Safe Work Australia guidance says a workplace that uses hazardous chemicals must keep a register of them, kept up to date, with the current SDS for each listed chemical, and easily reached by workers and emergency services. Keep products in their original labelled containers. Do not decant into drink bottles or food containers. Decanting into a food or drink container is a common cause of accidental swallowing, and this is working practice rather than a stated legal rule. Separate incompatible products, keep the storage area away from food, and record each product with its label, its SDS location and the surfaces it is approved for. Remove any product that is no longer on the register.

lessons.title: Skin and eye exposure
learningOutcomes: Identify the repeated wet-work and splash exposures in a detailing shift.
Select chemical-resistant gloves using the SDS and use them correctly.
Plan task rotation and drying breaks to reduce wet-work exposure, and refer persistent symptoms.

instructionSections.heading: Wet work and what it does to skin
instructionSections.body: Detailing involves repeated wet work. Safe Work Australia defines wet work in three ways: having body parts in liquids, or wearing waterproof gloves or other waterproof PPE, for more than two hours a shift; handling wet items for more than two hours; or washing hands more than 20 times a shift. A two-bucket wash, a decontamination session and drying can meet several of these tests in a single day. The most common work-related contact dermatitis is irritant contact dermatitis, which develops from repeated or long exposure that damages the skin's protective barrier. Detergent, degreaser and solvent can all do this, and so can wet hands kept inside gloves. Early signs include dry, red, painful or itchy skin, cracking, peeling, and a stinging or burning feeling. The hands are affected most often, but the condition can spread to the arms and face and can take months to heal. Allergic contact dermatitis is different. It is an allergic reaction, can appear up to 72 hours after exposure, and is likely to last once it develops. A worker who reports a rash or ongoing skin change should not be told to keep working through it.

instructionSections.heading: Splashes to the eyes and face
instructionSections.body: Eye exposure happens when spraying and rinsing, when product or water bounces back from a surface, or when a hose is moved. Degreasers are often misted onto the lower body first and worked up the vehicle, which can throw droplets towards face height. Splashes also happen when a worker bends to clean a wheel arch, or wrings a cloth over a bucket. Eye protection is needed whenever a splash is possible, and it has to fit and be worn for the whole task. PPE is the last line of defence. The Safe Work Australia guidance on PPE says it is one of the least effective controls and should be considered only after higher-level measures, such as removing or substituting the hazard. In a detailing business, the higher-level measures are choosing a less hazardous product, diluting to the label, spraying low and away from the face, and using a bucket and wringing method that limits splashes. PPE is worn in addition to those controls, not instead of them. The business must provide the PPE the worker needs, train workers to use, clean and store it, and make sure it fits and protects the wearer.

instructionSections.heading: Gloves: choosing and using them
instructionSections.body: Choose gloves from the SDS. Section 8 of an SDS covers exposure controls and personal protection, and it names the glove material suited to the product. A thin disposable glove is useful for some light tasks, but it is not a substitute for a chemical-resistant glove when handling a concentrate. Replace gloves that are torn, swollen or contaminated on the inside. Put on clean, dry hands, and remove gloves by peeling them inside out so the outside does not touch bare skin. Wash and dry hands after removal. Gloves trap sweat, which makes wet work worse, so change gloves at breaks and do not reuse disposable ones. Where a worker is sensitive to latex, choose a glove material that does not contain latex. Where a worker has an existing skin condition, discuss the glove choice and the task rotation with the worker and their medical adviser before the shift.

instructionSections.heading: Task rotation, drying breaks and escalation
instructionSections.body: Plan the shift so wet work is spread out. Pair the wash with dry tasks such as interior vacuuming, checklists and applying products that do not need wet hands, and schedule drying breaks between wet tasks. Write the plan on the shift sheet, including the break times. If a worker reports persistent skin symptoms, stop the task that causes them, take the worker off wet tasks, and refer them for medical or occupational advice. Record the symptom report, the task that came before it, the action taken and the advice received, with the worker's agreement to the record. Review the plan if the symptoms return. Use the business's own rule for when to seek advice, and do not wait for symptoms to become severe.

lessons.title: Pre-wash and equipment control
learningOutcomes: Remove loose grit with non-contact methods before any contact with the paint.
Inspect hoses, couplings and spray pattern, and keep pressure away from sensitive parts.
De-energise equipment before servicing it.

instructionSections.heading: Grit before contact
instructionSections.body: Loose grit can scratch paint when a cloth or brush moves over it. Remove the loose grit first, using a non-contact pre-wash and the product's own instructions, before the paint is touched. A heavily soiled car with loose stone chips needs this step before anything else.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment and spray
instructionSections.body: Inspect hoses and couplings before use, and check that the spray pattern and pressure suit the surface. Do not direct pressure into seals, sensors, electrical connectors, damaged paint or occupants. Keep the spray away from camera housings and fragile trim, and use a low-risk test area or a gentler method where a fragile component is close to the work. Hoses and fittings should be rated for at least the equipment's maximum operating pressure. A jet of water at high pressure can puncture the skin, and a loose hose can whip and strike someone (WorkSafe Victoria, high-pressure water jetting alert, reviewed 11 May 2023). Depressurise and secure the equipment when a component is being replaced or repaired, and isolate it with locking and tagging before maintenance (Safe Work Australia guide, December 2013).

instructionSections.heading: Stop and check
instructionSections.body: Stop if the equipment is defective, if a seal is damaged, or if the spray is reaching a sensor or connector. Check the pre-use condition each shift, and record any defect and the equipment taken out of service. Operators should be retrained, and the retraining recorded, at intervals no longer than two years (WorkSafe Victoria, reviewed 11 May 2023). Operators should limit themselves to minor adjustments and swapping listed parts; anything more belongs with the manufacturer or a suitably qualified person (Safe Work Australia guide, December 2013).

lessons.title: Paint and clear-coat care
learningOutcomes: Carry out a clean-media wash sequence before any correction.
Inspect the finish under suitable lighting and identify the defect.
Refer uncertain defects and decline aggressive correction that is not agreed.

instructionSections.heading: Clean before you correct
instructionSections.body: Correction removes material from the surface, so the surface must be clean first. Grit left on the paint is pushed around by the pad and can leave new marks. The Auto-Detailing guide puts washing ahead of every other step and notes that most swirls come from the wash and dry. Use a two-bucket method: one bucket of shampoo solution and one of clean rinse water with a bucket insert that traps grit at the bottom, and rinse the wash mitt after each panel. Use separate wash media for wheels and tyres, and wash lightly soiled areas before heavily soiled ones. Degrease tar, sap and bird droppings before the shampoo wash, following the degreaser label for dilution and dwell, and rinse the degreaser fully so none remains on the paint. Dry by sheeting the water off and blotting with a clean microfibre towel rather than dragging it across the paint. Only then decontaminate with clay or a decontamination pad (“Clay bar and decontamination”), and check the surface by touch. A paint that still feels rough after the wash is not ready for correction.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect the finish under suitable light
instructionSections.body: The inspection decides what correction is needed, so do it properly. Wash in shade, but inspect with a light that shows the surface. A directional torch held low across the panel reveals swirls and water spots that flat light hides. The Spanish-language manual makes the same point, advising a light close to the surface, and the show-car sample describes a baggie test, where a clean plastic bag over the hand makes rough spots easier to feel. Name each defect by type: a fine swirl pattern, a hazed or oxidised surface, water spotting, etching, or a scratch that catches the light. Note the depth where you can.
