The Auto-Detailing guide says a finishing polish typically will not remove anything deeper than a very light swirl, so a deeper mark needs a different plan. Check each panel separately, because a single car can have different paint on different panels. The show-car sample describes a car that was clear-coated everywhere except the trunk lid, which had single-stage paint, so each panel needs its own check; “Polishing and paint correction: the difference” gives the pad test.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding whether to correct
instructionSections.body: After inspection, decide whether correction is appropriate and at what level. Correction means removing a thin layer of clear coat to level the surface. The clear layer on a modern car is thin. The show-car sample gives roughly 50 micrometres (2 mils in its own measurement), though the figure varies between manufacturers. Every cut removes part of a finite layer, so deep work carries real risk. A deep scratch may pass through the clear coat into the colour coat, and aggressive correction can remove too much of what is left. A colleague may propose a compound to chase a deep scratch. Do not start on that suggestion alone. Identify the defect and its depth as well as you can, and refer uncertain defects to a competent specialist or to the owner, with the risk stated. Clear-coat failure, where the clear coat peels or hazes and will not level, cannot be polished out. The show-car sample describes repainting as the only remedy. A detailer records the failure and declines to promise its removal.

instructionSections.heading: Record, agree and decline
instructionSections.body: Record each defect with its location, your assessment of its type and depth, and a photograph taken under the same light each time. Agree the correction and its limits with the customer in writing before work starts. State the risk that a deep defect may not be removable without damage, and that the result cannot be guaranteed. Decline aggressive correction that has not been agreed, and record the decline. Claims about the result must be accurate and must not leave out material facts. The ACCC guidance says intent does not matter when a claim misleads, and that leaving out an important detail can itself mislead. A promise that a scratch will be removed, made before any test, is a claim the business may not be able to support.

lessons.title: Wheels, tyres and trim
learningOutcomes: Identify the finish of a wheel or trim piece before choosing a product.
Choose a conservative treatment, and refuse an acidic product for an unknown finish with a damaged coating.
Produce a product-compatibility test record before a wider treatment.

instructionSections.heading: Identify the finish before you choose a product
instructionSections.body: Wheels and trim come in several finishes, and each responds differently to chemicals. The Auto-Detailing guide separates factory alloy wheels, which often carry a clear coat, from aftermarket or upgraded wheels with a high polish or bare metal, which are more sensitive. Painted alloy, powder-coated wheels, polished lips, and plastic, rubber and vinyl trim each need their own care. Check each wheel in good light and ask the owner where the wheels came from. A wheel with an intact clear coat can be treated much like paint. A polished or bare-metal wheel, or one of unknown origin, should be treated as sensitive until a test shows otherwise. Trim may be unpainted plastic, rubber or vinyl, and a product suited to one may leave a greasy or uneven finish on another. Where the finish is unknown, choose the gentlest approved product, and move up only after a test shows no damage.

instructionSections.heading: Gentle products and techniques
instructionSections.body: For most wheels, use a pH-neutral wheel cleaner, or a car shampoo with a dedicated wash media, on wheels that are cool to the touch and in shade. The Auto-Detailing guide says a pH-neutral cleaner can be used on any wheel finish, and that dwell time can be extended in shade for stubborn build-up, following the label. Use soft brushes or natural fibres. A stiff nylon brush can put swirls into a wheel face. Brake dust on a clear-coated wheel may be removed with a clay product, but the Car-Detailing-Guide warns that clay can add marring to a highly polished wheel. Bare-metal lips can be polished with a metal polish after a test. For tyres, water-based dressing soaks into the rubber, while silicone-based dressing sits on the surface, can sling onto the paint, and can dry and brown the rubber over time. Apply tyre dressing in thin, even coats, and keep it off the paint. For trim, clean first and degrease where old polish or wax has built up. Then apply a protectant with UV protection, wiped on with an applicator, and keep it off the paint.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing an unsuitable product
instructionSections.body: An acidic wheel cleaner may be proposed for an alloy of unknown finish with a damaged protective coat. The Auto-Detailing guide says acidic cleaners are highly effective but should be used only on factory wheels with a thick clear coat, because they oxidise or tarnish polished and sensitive finishes. A damaged coat leaves metal exposed, and exposed metal is where a product can do the most harm. Refuse the acidic product, choose the gentler approved option, and record the decision and the reason. If the owner insists on the acidic product, decline the treatment in writing rather than accept a risk the business has not assessed. An unidentified product from the bench is not used because it is described as strong. Keep the reasoning on the record.

instructionSections.heading: Test before a wider treatment
instructionSections.body: A product-compatibility test is a small trial on an inconspicuous part of the wheel or trim before the wider treatment. Choose an area that is not seen in normal use, such as the inside of the barrel or a spot behind a spoke. Apply the product as its label directs. Record the product, the area, the wait time and the result: no change, a change in colour, a haze, a stain or a loss of gloss. Check the test area after it has dried, not while it is wet, because a product can look fine and then mark. Widen the treatment only when the test shows no damage and the customer has agreed to the work. The Auto-Detailing guide's practice is to test a polish or cleaner on a small area before the entire wheel, and the written record makes that test auditable. Keep the test record with the job file.

lessons.title: Cabin air and vapour exposure
learningOutcomes: Identify the vapour risk of solvent-rich products in a closed vehicle cabin.
Plan ventilation, exclusion and a safe re-entry decision for an interior treatment.
Refuse a solvent treatment in a closed, hot cabin without controls.

instructionSections.heading: Closed cabins concentrate vapour
instructionSections.body: A closed vehicle cabin, especially in hot weather, can concentrate the vapour from a solvent-rich stain remover. The vapour can irritate the eyes and airways, and can make people feel unwell. Before any interior treatment, check the product's SDS for vapour and ventilation requirements. Air concentrations at work must stay below the workplace exposure standard for each airborne contaminant, and the employer must monitor the air where needed to show that (Safe Work Australia, exposure standards, no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Planning the treatment
instructionSections.body: Plan the interior treatment with ventilation, exclusion of people and pets, a chemical inventory and exposure controls. Set a safe re-entry time as the SDS and the plan direct, and do not re-enter a sealed cabin that still smells of solvent. An employee who plans to use a solvent in a closed cabin on a hot day is proposing an uncontrolled treatment, and it is refused until the controls are planned.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and record
instructionSections.body: Stop if the cabin cannot be ventilated, if someone becomes unwell, or if the product is not on the register. Record the proposal, the controls in place, the re-entry time and who approved it. A hazardous chemicals register kept at the workplace must list the current SDS for each chemical on it (Safe Work Australia, hazardous chemicals register, no date shown). The new workplace exposure limit list is due to take effect on 1 December 2026, so confirm which list applies on the day of the job (Safe Work Australia, exposure standards, no date shown).

lessons.title: Interior materials and electronics
learningOutcomes: Identify interior materials and match the cleaning method to each.
Keep liquid away from electronic controls, screens and airbag areas.
Stop and record a warning light, a fault or exposed wiring.

instructionSections.heading: Identify the material before you choose a product
instructionSections.body: Most vehicle interiors combine several materials, and each one reacts differently to a cleaner or a dressing. Fabric seats and carpet hold dirt in the fibres. Leather, vinyl and rubber can dry, crack or go tacky when the wrong product sits on them. Plastic trim can mark under a harsh solvent. Many surfaces described as leather are coated or synthetic, sometimes sold as leatherette, so check each surface by look and touch and by the owner's information rather than assuming. Where the surface is unclear, choose the mildest product the label allows and test it first. Record the material you decided on before the product goes on. The order of an interior clean and the protection step are covered in “Interior cleaning and treatment” (interior cleaning and treatment). This lesson covers the material, electronics and fault checks that come first, so read it alongside that lesson rather than in place of it.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a product and testing it
instructionSections.body: The label and the safety data sheet decide what a product may be used on. The guides this lesson is drawn from show dressings that can be diluted to give anything from a natural finish to a high gloss, and very glossy results on leather or trim are seldom what an owner wants. For this lesson, a natural, non-greasy finish is the default on leather and trim, unless the owner's written instruction and the product label both allow something else. Dilute only as the label directs, and label every spray bottle with the product, the dilution and the date. Test on a hidden area first, such as under the edge of a seat or inside a door pocket, and let the test area dry fully before you judge it. A test that dries tacky, cloudy or discoloured means the product is wrong for that surface, so stop and choose another. Do not use heat to speed up a product. The Auto-Detailing guide describes using a hair dryer or heated seats to make leather more receptive to a product. Heat inside a closed cabin needs its own risk assessment, so this lesson does not adopt that method.

instructionSections.heading: Screens, controls and sensors
instructionSections.body: Screens, instrument displays, switches, dash buttons, steering wheel controls and seat sensors are electronic, so keep liquid off them. Do not spray any product onto these components. Put the product onto an applicator or cloth first, wipe the surface with that, and use a dry microfibre cloth alone for dust. The Spanish-language manual warns against spraying dressing directly onto plastic because it can leave marks, and the same reasoning applies to a display. Screen coatings vary, and the manufacturer's care guidance governs where it is available. Where no guidance can be found, use a dry or lightly dampened cloth and stop if the surface does not respond. Keep the cloths used on screens separate from those used on leather and trim, so residue from a trim product is not carried onto a display. This separation is working practice, not a regulatory requirement.

instructionSections.heading: Airbags, wiring and warning lights
instructionSections.body: Airbag covers, the steering column area, side airbag modules and any exposed wiring are outside detailing work. Do not remove, pry or press on a cover, do not clean inside a gap around a module, and do not disturb a loose wire. If you find a loose cover or an exposed wire, stop work on that part, photograph it, record its location, and tell the customer in writing that a qualified repairer should inspect it. If a warning light or fault message is showing when the vehicle arrives, or appears during the work, record it as found. Do not reset it, clear it or try to diagnose it. Electrical and airbag diagnosis and repair are not part of detailing, and completing this lesson does not qualify anyone to carry out that work.

instructionSections.heading: Cabin conditions and handover
instructionSections.body: Plan the handover around dryness. Keep carpets and seats as dry as you can, because damp material holds moisture against the floor and cushioning for longer than the owner expects. Check seats, mats and the floor for damp patches before handover. Record anything still wet, and tell the owner how to dry it. Protectants go on only to dry surfaces, as “Interior cleaning and treatment” describes. Ventilate the cabin when the label or safety data sheet calls for it. Read “Cabin air and vapour exposure” (cabin air and vapour exposure) before any solvent-containing product is used in a closed cabin, because vapour in a hot, closed vehicle is a separate risk with its own controls. A written record of what you found, with the time and location, protects the owner and the business if a later question arises about a surface or a component.

lessons.title: Quality assurance and handover
learningOutcomes: Complete an end-to-end checklist in adequate light and record remaining limitations.
Check that glass, mirrors and controls are safe and unobstructed, and that no slippery residue remains on pedals or controls.
Explain rectification, seek approval for extra work, and keep traceable evidence.

instructionSections.heading: The final check
instructionSections.body: Carry out the end-to-end checklist in adequate lighting, comparing the finish with the condition photographs taken at the start. Check that the glass and mirrors are clean and unobstructed, and that the vehicle controls work freely. Make sure that no slippery residue is left on the pedals or controls, because residue there is a driving hazard. Record any limitation that remains, such as a defect that was present before the work.

instructionSections.heading: Explaining the result
instructionSections.body: Explain the result to the customer in plain terms: what was done, what was not done, what remains as found, and what was rectified. Where further work would help, seek approval for it and price it before doing it. If no completion date was agreed, the work must still be delivered in a timely way, judged by the nature of the job and the availability of parts (ACCC, consumer rights and guarantees, metadata 17 July 2026). Never describe a pre-existing defect as caused or repaired by the detailing, because a false or misleading statement about the result of a service is prohibited (ACCC, false or misleading claims, metadata 28 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Handover evidence
instructionSections.body: Keep the traceable evidence: the start and end photographs, the checklist, the customer's sign-off and the record of any disputed defect. A disputed defect is handled with an escalation record, not with a verbal argument at the kerb.

lessons.title: Interior cleaning and treatment
learningOutcomes: Sequence an interior clean from loose debris to protection, in the order the guides describe.
Select a cleaner and a protectant for fabric, leather, vinyl and plastic from each product's label and SDS.
Keep liquids off screens, controls and electrical parts, and leave the interior dry at handover.

instructionSections.heading: Order of work
instructionSections.body: Interior work follows a fixed order, because each step makes the next one easier. Start by removing the mats carefully so debris does not fall onto the carpet, and shake them outside the vehicle. Clear loose items, then vacuum and brush from the top of the cabin downward, so dust falls onto areas you have yet to clean. The Spanish-language manual describes this top-to-bottom sweep for the same reason. Use a firm bristle brush to loosen debris embedded in carpet, working from the outside of each area towards a central pile, and then vacuum the pile. Small brushes and detail tools reach the gaps around door panels and air vents. Spot treat stains only after the loose soil is out, because a cleaner applied over grit smears the grit into the fibres. An extraction machine can deepen the clean on fabric. The Spanish manual calls it expensive and optional, and this lesson treats it the same way.

instructionSections.heading: Matching the product to the material
instructionSections.body: Each material needs its own approach. Fabric and carpet take a cleaner suited to the fibre, applied to a brush or applicator, worked in, left for the dwell time on the label, and lifted with a clean towel or the vacuum. The Auto-Detailing guide's dwell example of one to two minutes is an example only, so the label governs. Leather is cleaned and conditioned, and the guide's example applies a conditioner first and a separate cleaner second, with both removed afterwards. Whatever the sequence, the finish should be neither greasy nor glossy, and the guide advises against products that add shine. Do not use heat as a shortcut. The guide describes a hair dryer or heated seats to open the leather, and that method is not adopted here, because heat inside a closed cabin needs its own risk assessment. Vinyl, plastic and rubber take a cleaner followed by a protectant. The Spanish manual warns against spraying dressing directly onto plastic, because it can leave marks, so apply it to an applicator, wipe it on, and buff off the excess with a clean dry towel.

instructionSections.heading: Protection and finishing
instructionSections.body: Protect fabric only when it is completely dry, because a protectant sealed onto damp fabric traps moisture. The guides describe a light mist from the product's label, which leaves the fabric feeling natural while adding resistance to moisture and stains. Treat trim with a protectant that gives UV protection and a non-greasy finish, and wipe off any excess so nothing pools on surfaces a driver touches. Keep microfibre in groups, wash it only with other microfibre, and avoid fabric softener, because softener coats the fibres and reduces absorbency and cleaning power. Interior glass needs little cleaner and several towels to avoid streaks. The Auto-Detailing guide notes that the top edge of the glass and the window seal are often missed, so roll the window down a little to reach them.

instructionSections.heading: Electronics, moisture and handover
instructionSections.body: Screens, instrument clusters, switches and airbag covers are not places for liquid. Spray product onto an applicator or towel rather than onto the surface, and wipe screens with a dry microfibre towel. Do not disturb airbag covers or exposed wiring. If you find loose trim or an exposed wire, record it, stop work on that item, and refer it to a qualified repairer. Keep carpets as dry as possible, because a wet carpet can hold moisture against the floor for longer than the owner expects. Check the seats and carpets for damp patches before handover, and record anything still wet. Some interior products release vapour in a closed cabin, so ventilation and the cabin risk described in “Cabin air and vapour exposure” apply.

lessons.title: Clay bar and decontamination
learningOutcomes: Test a washed panel by touch and identify embedded contamination before deciding to decontaminate.
Decontaminate in small, lubricated sections, and reshape or replace the clay as it loads.
Choose a fine-grade clay for most vehicles and explain why a medium grade needs polishing afterwards.

instructionSections.heading: What decontamination removes
instructionSections.body: Washing removes loose dirt but not everything. Embedded contamination includes tree sap, tar, brake dust, bird droppings and insects, and industrial fallout, which is embedded iron particles that leave a surface feeling rough after a wash. Some contamination lodges in the pores of the clear coat and cannot be seen, so touch is needed to find it. Decontamination does not remove swirls or scratches. A clay bar has no effect on those marks, so clay is preparation for polishing rather than a substitute for it. Iron removers react with iron deposits and can reduce the need for clay on some vehicles. Use an iron remover only as its label directs, and rinse it off fully before drying.

instructionSections.heading: Touch test and choosing the method
instructionSections.body: After a wash and dry, glide clean fingertips lightly over the paint in shade. A surface that does not feel smooth like polished glass has contamination. A clean plastic bag over the hand also makes rough spots easier to feel. Map the rough areas on the condition record, then choose the method. Iron remover suits iron deposits. Tar and sap often need the clay itself. Decontamination pads and towels, which have a urethane face, can be washed and reused and often replace clay for light contamination. A clay bar must be discarded once it has picked up heavy contamination or has been dropped on a dirty floor. Chemical decontaminants must not be used on a finish with a protective coating unless the coating's label allows it.

instructionSections.heading: Lubrication and technique
instructionSections.body: Clay works only on a lubricated surface. Without lubricant the clay sticks and drags, and marring follows. Use the clay maker's recommended lubricant, a quick detailer with cleaning power and little protection, or a diluted wash solution, following the label. Work in small sections, about 45 centimetres square, so the lubricant does not dry. Use straight, overlapping passes, horizontally or vertically, with light pressure, and let the clay absorb the contamination. The clay is finished when it glides without grabbing and makes no grinding sound. Wipe off the excess lubricant with a clean microfibre towel, using a fresh face for each section. Reshape the clay to expose clean material after each section, and break off a new piece if no fresh surface remains. A dropped piece is discarded. Avoid claying in direct sun, because the lubricant evaporates quickly.

instructionSections.heading: Grade, rewash and check
instructionSections.body: Use a fine-grade clay for most vehicles. A medium grade is more aggressive and usually leaves marring that needs polishing to remove. Fine grade cleans and leaves the surface ready. After the clay, rewash to remove loosened contamination and any clay residue, and dry by sheeting and blotting. Check the surface by touch again. A panel that still feels rough is decontaminated only as far as you have achieved, so record what remains and do not describe it as clean. The next step is polishing (“Polishing and paint correction: the difference”) or protection (“Paint protection choices: wax, sealant and coating”). Keep the clay and decontamination record with the condition map from “Vehicle condition and evidence”.

lessons.title: Polishing and paint correction: the difference
learningOutcomes: Explain what polishing removes, and why correction removes more material than a finishing polish.
Identify the paint system with a test, and record the result before choosing products.
Choose the least aggressive product and pad combination that works, and step up only after a recorded test.
Inspect each panel under a directional light and measure its paint thickness with a calibrated gauge, recording the readings before any correction.
Refer or decline a panel when a referral trigger applies, such as thin or uneven clear coat, a prior repair, a deep defect or clear-coat failure, and record that decision.
Run the compounding, polishing and finishing sequence panel by panel, with heat and residue checks, and state the PPE and SDS controls that apply before work starts.

instructionSections.heading: What correction is, and what it is not
instructionSections.body: Polishing levels the clear coat. Correction is the wider term: it covers any abrasive step that removes a measured amount of paint to reduce a defect, and it takes away more material than a finishing polish does. The difference matters because clear coat is a finite layer. Each cut removes some of it, and that loss cannot be reversed. Waxes, sealants and glazes can hide some defects for a while, but they leave the surface itself unchanged. A correction job is therefore a decision about how much material to remove, from which panel, for which defect, and within limits agreed in advance. That is why this lesson puts inspection, measurement and referral ahead of any machine work. Basis: the principle that polishing levels the surface and removes thin material is drawn from the Auto-Detailing guide and the show-car sample, reworded. The decision process and the limits are working practice.

instructionSections.heading: Paint defects and how they differ
instructionSections.body: Each defect looks different, has a different cause and has a different limit. Swirls are fine, curved marks that show mainly in direct light. The Auto-Detailing guide describes them as very thin, shallow scratches that scatter light instead of letting it pass through the clear coat, which dulls the finish. Light scratches run in straighter lines or in random directions, and they cut deeper than swirls, so they catch a fingernail more readily. Oxidation is a dull, chalky or hazy change in the surface. The show-car sample notes that single-stage paint oxidises more readily than clear-coated paint, so it is most often met on older vehicles. Water spotting is a mineral deposit left when water dries. If it sits too long it can etch the surface, and the Auto-Detailing guide sorts water spots into three types by how deep they have gone. Etching is damage to the clear coat from a deposit or contaminant that has sat on the paint, and it can remain after the deposit has gone. Basis: the list of imperfections and the water-spot types are from the Auto-Detailing guide. The single-stage oxidation point is from the show-car sample. The fingernail check is working practice: it is a rough guide to depth, not a measurement.

instructionSections.heading: Inspection under lighting
instructionSections.body: Inspect before any product or machine touches the paint. Wash and decontaminate first, as “Clay bar and decontamination” describes, because contamination hides defects and can scratch under a pad. Use a directional light held at a low angle, and check each panel from several angles, since a defect can vanish from one direction and show clearly from another. Walk the vehicle in a fixed order and mark each defect on a diagram or photograph it with a reference point, so the record can be matched to the panel later. Compare each panel with its neighbours. A panel that looks different from the rest is often the first sign of a prior repair. Repeat the inspection under the same type of light after each stage of correction, so that results can be compared. Basis: working practice. The directional-light method is also used in the guides, reworded.

instructionSections.heading: Measuring paint thickness
instructionSections.body: A paint thickness gauge reads total film build, which is the combined thickness of primer, colour and clear coat if present. It does not read the clear coat alone, so a single reading cannot tell you how much clear is left to cut. Calibrate the gauge before use on a reference shim of known thickness, following the instrument's own instructions. The show-car sample describes recalibrating its gauge on a shim before trusting any reading. Gauges also differ in accuracy. The sample compares a more accurate class of gauge with a common less accurate one, and notes that the difference matters most on coatings that are already thin. Take several readings on each panel, spread across the panel and kept away from edges, trim, badges and stickers. Record each reading, the average and any outlier, along with the gauge model, the calibration method and the date. Units matter: one mil is 25.4 micrometres, so the sample's figure of about 2 mil is about 50.8 micrometres. The sample also says the figure varies by manufacturer, so compare a vehicle with its own panels, not with a figure from a table. Example figures only, not standards: a door reading 110 micrometres when the other panels read about 90 micrometres is a difference to record and refer, not a number to correct down to. Basis: the mil-to-micrometre conversion is arithmetic. The calibration, accuracy and total-film points are from the show-car sample, reworded. The reading procedure and recording are working practice.

instructionSections.heading: Identifying the paint system and why test spots come first
instructionSections.body: Most cars built since the 1980s have a basecoat with a clear coat over it. Single-stage paint has its colour through one layer and no separate clear. The show-car sample describes single-stage paint as softer and more prone to oxidising, which changes how it polishes. A pad test can help tell them apart. Polish a small area with a light-coloured pad, then check the pad. If colour transfers onto it, the pigment runs through the layer, which suggests single-stage paint. A clean pad suggests a clear coat. Tinted clear coats can mislead, so test each panel instead of assuming the whole vehicle matches. A test spot is a small, representative area, usually low-visibility, where you try the process before any wider work. The show-car sample calls this dialling in. Start with the least aggressive combination. If it does not work quickly enough, step up one variable at a time, either the product or the pad, and test again. A test that fails is information, so it tells you to stop and reassess rather than push harder. Record the area, the product, the pad, the machine setting range from the label or tool manual, the passes and the result. Photograph the result under the same light used for inspection. Basis: the test-spot and dialling-in concept is from the show-car sample, reworded. The pad-test interpretation and the tinted-clear caution are working practice. Speeds, passes and dwell times come from the product label and the tool manual, not from this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: When to refer rather than correct
instructionSections.body: Some panels should not be corrected in-house. Refer, or decline and record, when any of these triggers applies, and tell the owner in writing. Thin clear coat, or clear coat that reads thin in places, leaves little margin, so a cut can go through to colour. A reading well above the rest of the vehicle suggests filler, a respray or another prior repair, and that repair is outside detailing. A defect that catches a fingernail, or a scratch that reaches the colour, needs a qualified repairer to assess options. Clear-coat failure, where the clear peels, lifts or cracks, cannot be levelled, and abrasive work only exposes more damage. The show-car sample describes this failure as a breakdown the layer cannot recover from, with repainting as the remedy. Edges, panel seams, plastic trim and paint around sensors or badges are also high-risk areas. Basis: the clear-coat failure point is from the show-car sample. The triggers themselves, and the thresholds the business sets for them, are working practice. No number in this lesson is a universal limit.

instructionSections.heading: Sequence: compounding, polishing and finishing
instructionSections.body: Correction runs from the most aggressive step to the least, and each step leaves the surface ready for the next. Compounding is the cutting step. It removes the deepest defects and usually leaves marring that a finer step must refine. Polishing refines the surface and removes lighter marring. Finishing removes micro-marring, haze and very light swirls, and brings out gloss. The Auto-Detailing guide notes that finishing polishes generally cannot remove imperfections deeper than a very light swirl. Do not skip steps to save time, and do not use a compound where a finishing polish already gives the agreed result. Between steps, wipe the surface clean and inspect it, so that you can see what the last step achieved. Move to the next step only after a recorded test, as the procedure below sets out. Basis: the three-level description is from the Auto-Detailing guide, reworded. The step order as a working rule, and the decision to move between steps, are working practice. The number of steps is a business decision, recorded in the approved SOP.

instructionSections.heading: Pads and products in general terms
instructionSections.body: Pads and products are chosen as a pair, and the pair should match the defect. A firmer pad used with a cutting product removes more material. A softer, finer pad used with a finishing product refines the surface. Foam pads differ in density, thickness and diameter, and each changes how much cut and how much heat the pad produces. Some pads use grooves, a centre hole or a beveled edge to help reduce heat, and the Car-Detailing-Guide describes such designs. Wool and microfibre pads are used for cutting and for some polishing steps, and they behave differently from foam. Clean or replace pads as the job requires, because a loaded pad cuts unevenly and can scratch. Each product label states the surfaces it is for, how to apply it and how to remove it. Follow the label, and do not mix products unless the label allows it. The Spanish-language manual reports that some protectants should be applied by hand only, which the label governs. Basis: the aggressiveness principle and the heat-reducing pad designs are from the Auto-Detailing guide and the Car-Detailing-Guide, reworded. Product choice is decided by the test spot, not by a table in this lesson. Brand names and product-specific settings are not used here.

instructionSections.heading: Machine choice, speed and heat
instructionSections.body: Dual-action and random orbital machines oscillate, which makes them safer for learners and less likely to burn paint than a rotary machine. A rotary machine spins the pad on one axis, removes material faster and needs more practice. The Auto-Detailing guide treats rotary buffers as a tool for experienced detailers only. The detailing handbook excerpt warns that high-speed buffing can burn through clear coat when a pad is held in one place. Speed should come from the machine's manual and the product label, not from memory or from this lesson. A common working rule is to start with a lower speed to spread product and then increase only as the test requires. Reduce speed and pad firmness as the process moves toward finishing. The Spanish-language manual makes the same point: firmer pads at higher speed early in the process, and softer pads at lower speed later. Control heat by keeping the machine moving, using light pressure, avoiding edges and high spots, and stopping to check the surface by hand. If the panel feels hot, or the product is drying out, stop, let the panel cool and re-wet the area as the product label directs. Stop at once for smoke, a burning smell or a sudden change in gloss that you cannot account for. Basis: the rotary-versus-orbital comparison and the handbook warning are from the Auto-Detailing guide and the detailing handbook excerpt, reworded. The speed-sequence rule is from the Spanish-language manual, reworded. The touch check and stop rules are working practice.

instructionSections.heading: Working panel by panel, residue and final inspection
instructionSections.body: Work in small sections, one panel at a time, so that you can control coverage and inspect each area before moving on. Before you start, tape off trim, badges, panel gaps and edges with full strips of tape, and cover glass and fragile parts. Apply product in controlled amounts, and spread it before the machine runs. Work each section to the test result, then move on. Polish residue is the main reason a result looks worse than it is. When the polish breaks down it can look like a clear or milky haze, and that haze can hide both the defect and the result. When you see it, stop the machine, wipe the area with a clean microfibre and inspect under the directional light. Refold towels to a clean face often, and keep each product's towels separate. Basis: the section-by-section approach is from the Auto-Detailing guide, reworded. The breakdown-haze observation is from the Auto-Detailing guide. The tape, towel and final-inspection steps are working practice. Record a final inspection of each panel under the same light, compared with the reference panel, before protection is applied.

instructionSections.heading: Protection after correction, and removing residue
instructionSections.body: Once the surface is level and clean, protection locks in the result. Remove residue first with a clean microfibre. If the product label or the surface calls for a wipe-down before protection, use a product whose SDS and label cover that use, and apply the controls the SDS lists. Choose a protectant listed for the surface, such as a sealant or a wax, and apply it as the label directs. Some protectants are hand-applied only, and the label decides the method. Wipe off the excess so nothing pools on trim or edges. Do not promise durability. Tell the owner that protection needs regular maintenance and that deep defects remain. Coatings and ceramic products are not taught in this lesson. Any claim about how long a coating lasts or what it does needs evidence the business can support, and the ACCC point below applies to it. Basis: the protection steps are working practice, with the hand-applied note taken from the Spanish-language manual, reworded.

instructionSections.heading: Safety: PPE, vibration, electrical equipment and machines
instructionSections.body: Start with the controls that remove or reduce the hazard, and treat PPE as the last line. The WorkSafe Victoria hierarchy of control places personal protective equipment at the bottom. It describes PPE as a last resort or a temporary measure while a better control is put in place, so it does not replace guarding, layout or safe procedures. Eye protection: wear it for all polishing and cleaning tasks, because splatter and pad debris can reach the eye. Gloves and any other PPE: follow the SDS of each product. Respiratory protection: a polisher used on a clear-coated panel is not expected to create airborne dust. If an SDS names a respiratory hazard, or a task produces dust or mist, such as sanding, wet abrasive work or heavy product fallout, use respiratory protection at the level the SDS and a risk assessment require. Sanding and wet abrasive work are not taught in this lesson. Hand-arm vibration: Safe Work Australia lists exposure to vibration among the risk factors for musculoskeletal disorders, and it publishes a guide to managing hand-arm vibration. In practice, lighter machines, shorter sessions and breaks reduce exposure, and Safe Work Australia's guidance on manual tasks recommends rotating workers between repetitive tasks. Electrical safety: check cords and plugs before use, keep cords clear of the work area and pads, and keep electrical equipment away from water. Machine guarding: check the backing plate, the pad fitting and any guard or shroud the manufacturer fitted, and never run a machine with a part missing. Product SDS: read the SDS for each product before use and note its flammable, irritant and respiratory warnings. Safe Work Australia states that almost every hazardous chemical needs an SDS, and that copies must be kept in the workplace.

instructionSections.heading: Claims, documentation and the record
instructionSections.body: A claim about the result must match what you showed. The ACCC states that a business's intention does not matter, and that leaving out important information can make a claim misleading. A statement that all swirls have been removed, when the test covered one door, is a problem even if you did not mean to mislead. Describe the likely result and its limits, and record them. Keep a record for each job: the paint-system note, the thickness readings with gauge model and calibration, the test spot record, each referral or decline with photographs, the products and pads with their label or SDS references, the passes, the final inspection, the protection applied and the owner's acknowledgement. Keep the record with the job file, so that the next detailer can see what was done and why. Basis: the ACCC principles are sourced from the ACCC page. The documentation list is working practice.

lessons.title: Paint protection choices: wax, sealant and coating
learningOutcomes: Compare natural wax, synthetic sealant and coating on durability, application method and maintenance.
Prepare the paint before protection, including removing residues that would stop the protection bonding.
Apply protection thinly, observe the label's cure and levelling times, and state only the durability the maker supports.

instructionSections.heading: Protection is a layer, not a repair
instructionSections.body: Protection sits on top of the paint and does not repair it. The show-car sample says clear coat still needs washing, clay, polishing and protection on a regular schedule to keep its appearance, and that a clear layer is not an invisible force field. Protection products do three jobs: they add gloss and depth, they make dirt release more easily, and they shield the surface from sun and weather. Each type does those jobs differently and for a different time. Choose the product from the owner's use of the car (garage or outdoor parking, daily driving or shows), the paint's condition, the time available for application, and the owner's budget. A protective layer over damaged paint seals the damage in, so the condition record from “Vehicle condition and evidence” and the polishing decision in “Polishing and paint correction: the difference” come first.

instructionSections.heading: Natural wax
instructionSections.body: Carnauba wax is the classic natural product. The Auto-Detailing guide describes it as giving a deep, wet look and good water beading, but as lasting three to eight weeks, depending on use and conditions. The Spanish-language manual says natural waxes are applied by hand, because machine heat can soften the wax before it is spread thinly. Apply a very thin layer, allow it to dry for the label's time, and remove the residue with a clean microfibre towel. The guide's example is 10 to 20 minutes before buffing, but the label governs. Work in shade. Two or three thin coats can add depth, but each coat needs its own cure time, and a wax does not level swirls. A wax suits the owner who wants a short-term, deep finish, such as before a show.

instructionSections.heading: Synthetic sealant
instructionSections.body: Synthetic sealants are polymer products. The Auto-Detailing guide describes them as lasting about three to six months, longer than carnauba, and as applied by hand or with a dual-action or random orbital polisher fitted with a soft foam pad. Spread the product as thinly and as far as possible, and remove the excess after the label's time. The guide suggests at least one hour before a second coat, and a longer wait is safer. The Spanish-language manual warns that a sealant left too long before removal becomes much harder to take off, so timing matters. A sealant can be topped with a wax for extra gloss. The guide suggests reapplying a sealant about once a season, or sooner when water stops beading and begins to pool.

instructionSections.heading: Coatings
instructionSections.body: Coatings are semi-permanent layers, usually applied panel by panel because they dry quickly. The Auto-Detailing guide describes a timer-led process: apply a few drops to an applicator, work the coating in thinly, and level it with a clean towel within the window the label allows. A coating that dries too far before it is levelled leaves haze that may need polishing out. The Car-Detailing-Guide says most manufacturers want 24 hours before water exposure and no detergent washing for four to seven days, with full cure in one to four weeks. The Spanish manual gives 12 to 24 hours depending on humidity. The label governs. A second layer usually has to go on within a stated window, often 30 to 60 minutes, or it will not bond. The guide gives a life of one to three years or more, but that is the manufacturer's claim and must be presented as one. Do not clay a coated surface; the guide says clay can diminish the coating, and suggests iron and tar removers instead. Heat lamps to speed the cure are not adopted in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing and what you may promise
instructionSections.body: Match the type to the owner's use. A car parked outdoors under trees gains more from a longer-lasting layer, while a short show finish suits a wax. Explain that durability depends on washing, parking, weather and the state of the paint at application. The durability of any product is the maker's figure, and the business must be able to support what it tells the owner. The ACCC guidance says claims must be accurate and backed by evidence the business can produce, and that intent does not matter when a claim misleads. Do not promise lifetime protection, a never-polish result, or a fixed number of months unless the maker's documentation supports it and the owner has the same information.

lessons.title: Exterior and interior handover checklists
learningOutcomes: Complete an exterior checklist covering painted surfaces, the engine compartment, wheels and tyres, critical details and glass.
Complete an interior checklist covering hard surfaces, leather and fabric, glass and mirrors.
Record items that are not finished, and why, rather than ticking them.

instructionSections.heading: Why the checklist is the evidence
instructionSections.body: A checklist turns a finished job into a record that someone else can check. The detailing checklist in the source set is organised into exterior and interior sections, with a box for each item and a comment line at the end of each section. Use it as the basis for the handover, alongside the condition map from the intake record. Its purpose is not to show that everything was perfect, but to show what was done, what was not done, and why. A tick against an item that was not completed is worse than a blank, because it is a false record. Complete the checklist at handover, in good light, with the vehicle in the state the owner will see it.

instructionSections.heading: Exterior items
instructionSections.body: The exterior section covers the painted surface: contaminants removed, metallic fallout and acid-rain spotting removed, marks treated to the level agreed, residues removed, and a final finish evenly applied. The engine compartment section records whether contaminants were removed from the engine, the compartment and the inner bonnet, and whether the engine was dressed. Wheels, tyres and wheel wells are checked as cleaned and, where agreed, dressed. Critical details include the grille, air dam and bumpers; the door, boot and fuel-cap jambs; rubber and vinyl trim; and the exterior glass and mirrors. Check each item against the work order that was agreed, not against what the detailer would like to achieve. Where the agreed scope excludes an item, mark it as not in scope rather than complete.

instructionSections.heading: Interior items
instructionSections.body: The interior section has two parts: hard vinyl, rubber and glass surfaces, and leather and fabric surfaces. Hard surfaces include the dashboard, console and instrument panel, which are dressed; the steering wheel, foot pedals and vinyl seats, which are not dressed; the glove box and storage areas; door-frame weather-stripping; interior glass and mirrors; the rear window deck; and the ashtrays. Leather and fabric surfaces are cleaned while damp, not saturated, and the same areas are checked. The checklist separates dressed from not dressed, and the difference matters. The steering wheel and pedals are left undressed, because a dressing on them creates a slip risk for the driver. Check the pedals and wheel by touch before handover.

instructionSections.heading: Exceptions, comments and sign-off
instructionSections.body: Use the comment line for each exception, with its reason. For example: a loose trim piece not touched, under the exception plan; a cracked lens masked and not treated; a stain that did not come out and is recorded with the owner's agreement. Record the owner's sign-off on the completed checklist, and record the permission for any photographs. Take handover photographs in shade and under a directional light, so the record shows the true state. A precise handover record also helps when a customer returns with a question, because the file shows the condition at handover rather than a recollection of it.

lessons.title: Detailing, restoration and the scope of a service
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between detailing and restoration, using the source definitions.
Classify a booking as basic, full, commercial or show detailing, and describe what each includes.
Refer restoration, body repair and other specialist work to an appropriate provider instead of promising it as detailing.

instructionSections.heading: What detailing is
instructionSections.body: Detailing is a total cleaning of a vehicle, inside and out, top to bottom, with each surface treated to suit its material. The Detailing Hand Book describes it as more than a good wash and wax. The small things decide the result: wax buildup around trim, dirt in the seams, and grime in the wheel wells are the details that separate a detailed car from a washed one. The handbook stresses that choosing the correct chemical, wax or sealer for each surface is one of the most important things a detailer learns, because the correct treatment protects the surface as well as improving its appearance. Detailing works with the vehicle's existing finish. It cleans, corrects within agreed limits, and protects.

instructionSections.heading: Detailing versus restoration
instructionSections.body: Restoration returns a car to its original condition. The handbook describes it as tearing the car apart, examining each part, reworking or replacing it, and reassembling it with great care. That is time-consuming and costly, and most cars do not need it. Detailing does not dismantle the vehicle. The handbook makes a practical point: even a restored show car is detailed before a show, because detailing makes a car look its best. The source overview describes detailing as restoring a car to its original condition, which conflicts with the handbook. This lesson uses the handbook's distinction, because it matches the scope of the course. Replacing a part, re-spraying, or fixing a cracked lens or dashboard is outside detailing, and should be referred. This course also treats spray painting, live electrical work, airbag work and hazardous remediation as outside its scope.

instructionSections.heading: Service types
instructionSections.body: Booking types differ in scope. A basic detail covers exterior washing, waxing and interior cleaning, and suits regular maintenance. A full detail adds polishing, waxing and conditioning of the interior, and takes several hours. A mobile detail is the same kind of service delivered at the customer's home or office, which adds water, power and site questions (see “Manual handling, wet floors and site hygiene” and “Service boundaries and consent”). A commercial or used-car preparation is a minor detail that makes a car presentable for sale, done quickly. The handbook warns that quick services sometimes use a clear lacquer to make engine bays and trims look new, which can trap dirt under the cover. A fast finish is a different service with a different promise, and it must be described as such. A show detail is the most complete and the most time-consuming. The handbook notes that, except to the sharpest eye, there is little visual difference between complete and show detailing on an ordinary vehicle.

instructionSections.heading: Dents, chips and other repairs
instructionSections.body: The Detailing Hand Book lists minor dent removal and paint-chip touch-up among the services of a complete detailing shop. In this course the approach is different. A dent that needs reshaping, a chip that needs touch-up paint, or a scratch that needs filler is a repair with its own materials, skills and promises. Treat repair as a separate service with its own scope and quote, and do not describe it as part of the detail unless the business has the skill and the authority to carry it out. Where a repair is to be referred, say so in the work order and record the referral.

lessons.title: Preventive maintenance and client aftercare
learningOutcomes: Set a maintenance interval for each protected surface using the product label and the source guidance.
Explain to the owner the signs that protection is wearing, such as poor water beading or dullness.
Give written aftercare advice that does not promise results the product cannot give.

instructionSections.heading: Why maintenance matters
instructionSections.body: A detail that is not maintained starts to slip. The Detailing Hand Book describes preventive maintenance as the stage after the first complete detail, when periodic cleaning and the right treatments keep the appearance. It also gives the practical reasons. Dirt works like sandpaper as people get in and out, and it wears fabric and carpet. Acid rain and bird droppings can damage the finish. Dirt that sits in the wheel wells or under the car holds moisture against the metal, and rust can follow. Maintenance also keeps protection working, because protection is a layer that wears away with washing, weather and sun.

instructionSections.heading: Intervals for each surface
instructionSections.body: The source guides give typical intervals, and the product label always overrides them. Wash every one to two weeks. Clean wheels at each wash, and give them a thorough clean and a protective layer every two to three months. Clay about twice a year, or before polishing in heavy-contamination areas. Polish one to two times a year, as needed, during a full detail. Reapply sealant about once a season, or sooner when water stops beading. Reapply carnauba wax every three to eight weeks, depending on use and conditions. Clean trim with a light degreaser every one to three months, and re-dress it every one to two months. Clean and protect the engine bay every three to six months. Coatings last one to three years or more, according to the manufacturer. Give the interior a thorough clean once or twice a year. Record these intervals for each vehicle, tie each one to the product it applies to, and explain them in the owner's language.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the signs
instructionSections.body: Protection is wearing when water no longer beads and sheets off the paint, when water pools and looks flat, when the surface looks duller after a wash, or when dirt sticks more easily. Teach the owner a simple check: after a wash, see how the water behaves on the bonnet. The Auto-Detailing guide uses this test. Dull wheels and dressing that slings onto the paint are signs that the wheels or tyres need their own treatment. Explain these signs in the aftercare note, so the owner knows when to book rather than waiting for the appearance to fail.

instructionSections.heading: Aftercare advice the owner can keep
instructionSections.body: Write aftercare advice the owner can keep. Include the wash frequency, how to dry (blotting with a clean, dry towel rather than dragging it), where to park if possible, and the signs of wear. Advise against degreasers on protected surfaces unless the protection is to be removed, because the Auto-Detailing guide notes that most degreasers remove sealant or wax. Where the product names a maintenance product, use that product rather than a general cleaner that may strip the layer. Advise the owner to wash microfibre towels without fabric softener. Do not promise a result the product cannot give. A statement that a coating lasts for life is not supportable; a statement that the maker's figure applies under stated conditions is. Keep a copy of the advice in the job file, and make the next maintenance date part of the record, not a sales pressure point.

lessons.title: Manual handling, wet floors and site hygiene
learningOutcomes: Identify the manual handling risks in a detailing job and set up the work to reduce them.
Control slip risks on wet driveways, floors and paved areas, using footwear and clean-up.
Keep the work area clear of hoses, cords and spills, and report spills promptly.

instructionSections.heading: Manual handling in detailing
instructionSections.body: Detailing involves repeated, sustained and awkward movement. Safe Work Australia describes hazardous manual tasks as those with repetitive movement, high or sudden force, sustained or awkward postures, or vibration, and names musculoskeletal disorders such as strains, back injuries and nerve compression as the risk. In detailing, the common tasks are lifting buckets and pressure equipment, carrying kits between vehicles, bending to clean wheels and lower panels, and holding a machine over a bonnet for long periods. The duty is to assess and manage these risks, and to consult workers as far as is reasonably possible. The best control is to design the task out. Use a trolley for kits, fill buckets to a sensible level, arrange the vehicle and the work so the operator is not bent or reaching for long periods, and rotate buffing with other tasks. Where a task cannot be designed out, use mechanical aids, job rotation and training in the method.

instructionSections.heading: Slips on wet ground
instructionSections.body: Wet driveways, forecourts, garage floors and the paved ground under a car are common slip surfaces. Safe Work Australia lists polished, wet or greasy floors among the causes of slips, and notes that wet or slippery surfaces are hazards that can cause falls. A detailing site adds soap, wax and polish residue, which makes a wet surface more slippery than water alone. Control the risk at the source: keep the wash area clear, plan a clear route for hoses, sweep loose grit and water where it is safe, and dry the floor when work is finished. Clean up any spill as it happens, not at the end of the job. Set up the wash area on the most level ground available. Where a slope cannot be avoided, plan the water so it runs away from the work area and the route to the vehicle.

instructionSections.heading: Footwear and housekeeping
instructionSections.body: Use slip-resistant footwear suited to the work, and check that it is in good condition. Safe Work Australia guidance says tread should be deep enough to penetrate surface water in wet conditions, and that urethane and rubber soles are more slip resistant than vinyl and leather. Keep cords and hoses off walkways, because a hose across a path is a trip hazard. Store products and equipment on a tray or shelf, not on the floor, and set up a dry, clean place for breaks. Working in wet boots for a whole shift reduces grip, so dry the feet and change socks at a break; this is working practice. Keep absorbent material or a spill kit on site, and treat any product spill as both a chemical hazard and a slip hazard.

instructionSections.heading: Mobile and home-site hazards
instructionSections.body: On a customer's driveway, the surface, the gradient, traffic, and the presence of children or pets are site hazards. Carry out a quick site check on arrival and record the hazards in the job file, with a clear route for equipment and a safe area for the owner and others to stay away from the work. Do not let customers or children walk through wet work areas. Use a trolley or a second person for heavy items, rather than carrying a full bucket up a step or kerb. Lift from a close position with a straight back, and ask for help when a load is awkward; this is working practice.

lessons.title: Chemical storage, disposal and pressure equipment
learningOutcomes: Store and dispose of detailing chemicals and rinse water following the SDS, the label and the waste rules that apply where the work is done.
Inspect and use pressure equipment so that high pressure does not damage weakened paint or injure a worker.
Explain how high-pressure jets and whipping hoses cause injury, and which personal protective equipment the risk requires.

instructionSections.heading: Storing chemicals
instructionSections.body: The SDS storage and handling section sets the conditions for each product, and the register must list each hazardous chemical with its current SDS (Safe Work Australia). Store products in their original labelled containers, out of reach of children, and away from food and drink. Keep incompatible products apart, so that strong acids and strong alkalis are never stored together, and keep flammable products away from ignition sources; the SDS gives the flash point. Keep a stock list, and remove any container whose label is damaged or unreadable. Store chemicals in a dry, ventilated, secured area where the site allows. Keep the spill kit where it can be reached quickly. Temperature limits come from each label and SDS.

instructionSections.heading: Disposing of chemicals and rinse water
instructionSections.body: The SDS covers disposal, and a label may give its own instruction. Never pour concentrates or unused product into a drain, a stormwater pit or a garden. Victorian EPA guidance, the main reference for this course, says stormwater drains should carry only rainwater, and that washing a car on a driveway can send soap, grime and oils into waterways. Commercial car washes that capture and treat wash water are presented as the more responsible option. Where wash water cannot be captured, use a containment or sewer route approved for the site, and check the local water authority's trade waste rules. Dispose of empty containers as the label and the local waste service direct, and rinse them only where the label allows.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure equipment and weakened paint
instructionSections.body: Pressure equipment is useful for rinsing, but it can damage paint that is already weak. The force of a pressure washer can remove paint that is already thin or damaged. Avoid a direct high-pressure stream on visible electrical parts and on air intakes. Check the paint condition on the intake record before choosing the pressure. Keep the nozzle at a distance and an angle that does not focus the stream on one spot. Stand back from weak paint and use a wider spray or hand washing. Do not use pressure near the edges of loose or cracked trim, badges and seals. Where the paint is weak, the method is chosen for the paint, and the choice is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: High-pressure hazards and PPE
instructionSections.body: High-pressure water jetting can pierce skin and inject contaminated material into the body. Flying debris can strike the eyes. A whipping hose, an uncontrolled nozzle or a separated coupling can strike a worker. The Victorian WorkSafe safety alert on high-pressure water jetting names these risks, and it lists eye protection and a face shield near jetting, with body armour and hearing protection where the hazards cannot be controlled. It names AS/NZS 4233.1 as the standard for high-pressure water jetting. Before use, check hoses for cuts, bulges and kinks, check that couplings are secure, and check that the trigger gun or lance and its safety parts are in order. Never point a stream at a person or at yourself, and never test a stream on skin. Keep bystanders out of the spray zone. Electrical equipment such as pressure washers, vacuums, polishers and lights needs checks too: check cords and plugs, keep cords off wet ground and away from the spray, and use each tool only as its label directs. AS/NZS 3760 is commonly referenced for in-service testing of portable electrical equipment.

lessons.title: Headlight restoration: inspection, referral and protection
learningOutcomes: Explain why polycarbonate lenses haze and yellow, and separate a surface problem from a crack, internal fogging or a housing fault.
Inspect a headlamp and choose between surface restoration and referral, applying the referral rule in this lesson.
Mask and protect surrounding paint, trim and seals, and handle dust and wet slurry in line with the product label and SDS.
Describe to the customer what restoration can and cannot achieve, and record consent and before and after evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Why lenses haze and yellow
instructionSections.body: Most modern headlamp lenses are made from polycarbonate, a plastic chosen for toughness and light weight. The Spanish-language manual in the source set names sun exposure as the main factor in the dulling, and this lesson starts from the same point. Sunlight wears the outer face of the lens over time, and the surface loses its clarity, so light scatters instead of passing cleanly through. The cloudy, yellowish look most owners recognise is a surface condition. Restoration works on that outer layer only. It does not reverse damage that goes deeper. A crack, moisture trapped behind the lens, or a failed seal belongs to a different category, because a surface process cannot close a gap in the plastic or dry out the inside of a housing. Check the lamp or lens manufacturer's material information before you state it to a customer as fact. This lesson does not claim that restoration returns light output to factory standard. That needs a measurement and is outside this service.

instructionSections.heading: Inspecting the lamp and choosing restore or refer
instructionSections.body: Inspect every lamp before you quote. Look at it in daylight and, where it is safe to do so, at night with the lamp working, as the owner directs. Note the type of haze and where it sits on the lens. Even surface haze that feels smooth to the touch is the condition restoration is designed for. Also note any crack or chip, pitting, a peeling coat, condensation or water inside the lens, a cracked or distorted housing, broken or loose mounting points, a discoloured or melted housing, and any sign of an electrical fault such as a dim, flickering or failed lamp. Photograph each finding before any work starts. Choose restoration only when the lens is intact and sealed, the damage is on the outer face, and no trigger in the referral rule applies. Skipping this inspection creates a scope problem as well as a workmanship problem, as “Service boundaries and consent” explains.

instructionSections.heading: Masking and protecting paint and trim
instructionSections.body: Masking protects the paint, the grille, badges, bumper edges and any rubber seal around the lamp. Use a low-tack masking tape with a clean, firm edge, so it does not lift when the surface is wet. Some restoration work carries liquid and slurry across the lamp and its surroundings, so cover any area the liquid could reach that tape does not protect. Check every tape line before you start, and again after the first wet stage, because tape can loosen when it is wet. Keep tape off the lens seal where you can, since adhesive residue there makes the final seal harder to inspect. The English guides in the source set describe masking headlights and trim as routine. The tape type and how long it stays on come from the tape maker's and the product's labels, not from this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Wet sanding and polishing in general terms
instructionSections.body: The aim is to remove the thin, damaged outer layer of plastic, then bring the surface back to a clear, smooth finish. Work on a wet surface with light, even pressure, and keep it wet throughout. Dry sanding generates heat and dust and can mark the lens. Begin with the abrasive that the restoration product or its label names for the first stage, then move through the finer stages the label lists. The specific abrasives, their order, the speed and the water-to-product mix are product-specific. This lesson does not state them, and the sequence in the Spanish manual is not adopted here. After each stage, rinse the lens and inspect it under good light for an even haze and for deeper scratches. If an area stays dull or a scratch remains, return to the previous stage rather than pressing harder. Stop and reassess if the plastic becomes warm, if the surface turns cloudy or changes texture, or if you think the lens is getting thin. Then polish with a labelled polish to bring out clarity and smoothness, and inspect again before any protection is applied.

instructionSections.heading: UV-protective clear coat and when it is needed
instructionSections.body: Once the surface is clean and clear, the lens is bare plastic and has lost any protection it had. The Spanish manual lists a protective varnish or seal as an option for longer-lasting results, and the English guides stress UV protection whenever a plastic surface is treated. Apply a UV-protective clear coat when the restoration removed the outer layer that carried protection, or when the lens has no protection left, and when the product label names polycarbonate lenses as a suitable surface. Apply it only to a clean, dry, polished lens, within the temperature and humidity range the label gives, and in the number of coats the label specifies. A protective coat is not a repair. It does not fill a crack or stop moisture getting inside the housing. Do not promise how long the protection lasts. Durability depends on the product, the surface, the conditions and how the car is used, so state only what the label supports.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning and drying afterwards
instructionSections.body: When the last stage is complete, rinse the lens and the surrounding area with clean water, so polish and slurry do not dry on the paint or the seal. Dry the lens with clean, dry microfibre, and do not rub it into the seal. Look closely at the lens edge and the seal for water or fog inside the housing. Water inside the lens is a referral trigger, not something to dry and hand back. Remove the masking slowly, pulling back on itself at a low angle, and check the paint edges for residue. Then inspect the lamp again in the same light as the first inspection, so the before and after photographs can be compared fairly. If you can switch the lamp on safely, check that it works and looks as it did before. Do not open the housing to check the wiring. That is electrical work and sits outside this service.

instructionSections.heading: Dust and wet-slurry handling
instructionSections.body: Sanding produces dust, and the way you handle it matters for the worker and for the surroundings. Wet methods keep dust down, so keep the surface and the abrasive wet throughout. Dry sweeping, blowing with compressed air and dry buffing spread dust into the air and onto nearby surfaces, so avoid them. Slurry from sanding and polishing contains the abrasive, the product and fragments of the lens. Do not let it run into a stormwater drain. Collect it, let the solids settle or absorb the liquid, and dispose of it as the product's SDS waste section directs and as local council or water authority rules require. Clean the work area with a wet method after each job. Wash cloths and applicators used for restoration separately from other cleaning items, and keep food and drink out of the area while dust or slurry is present.

instructionSections.heading: PPE and respiratory protection for dust
instructionSections.body: Read the SDS for each product before the job, and focus on the sections for personal protection and handling, because that is where the practical instructions sit. Eye protection and gloves are usually needed for polish, slurry and abrasive products, but the SDS decides which types. For dust, the first control is to reduce it at the source, using wet methods and ventilation that moves air away from the worker. Respiratory protective equipment is the last line of control. Basic dust masks and surgical masks do not protect against small particles, so they are not a substitute for a respirator. Where a respirator is needed after other controls, use a tight-fitting type that seals to the face. Each worker needs their own fit test before first use, at least once a year, and after a significant change in facial features such as major weight change. Each person also does a fit check every time they put the respirator on. Facial hair that breaks the seal can stop a respirator sealing. Particulate filters are classed P1, P2 or P3, with P3 giving the highest protection, and the class is chosen from the hazard assessment and the SDS. Respirators used at work should comply with AS/NZS 1716.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical and lamp safety
instructionSections.body: Headlamps are electrical components, even when the work is on the lens. Restoration sits on the outside of the lens and does not include wiring, connectors, control units, ballasts or diagnosis of any fault. Only licensed or registered electricians should carry out electrical work, and this lesson does not grant any licence or authority to do it. Check leads and power tools for damage before each use, and remove any damaged lead from service. Keep leads off the floor where they can be damaged or reached by water, and use leads rated for damp conditions where the work is near water. Halogen lamps can stay hot after use, so let them cool before you touch the housing. Treat a lamp that flickers, is dim or will not light as an electrical fault. Record it and refer it. Do not attempt to make it work.

instructionSections.heading: Chemical hazards from the SDS
instructionSections.body: Each product in a restoration kit, and each cleaner or protective coat you use, has an SDS. Read its sections on hazard identification, first aid, handling and storage, exposure controls and personal protection, and disposal before the job starts. Check for skin and eye hazards, inhalation hazards, flammability and any incompatibility with other products you use. Under the WHS duties for hazardous chemicals, a business must identify and assess the risks, control them, store the chemicals safely and communicate hazard information to workers. Safe Work Australia's SDS guidance says that workers who use, handle or store a chemical should be able to reach its SDS, and that the business must make it easy to access. That page covers access, not practical handling, so the handling and PPE details come from the SDS itself. Keep products in their original labelled containers, and keep the SDS where the team can reach it, either in the vehicle or in a file at the site.

instructionSections.heading: What restoration can and cannot promise
instructionSections.body: Restoration improves the clarity of the outer surface of an intact lens. It does not repair cracks, seal a housing, remove moisture from inside a lamp, fix an electrical fault, or guarantee that the lamp will pass any inspection. Outcomes depend on the lens age and material, the damage, any earlier treatment, the product used, and how the car is kept and driven. Consumer law applies to what you say. Under the ACCC's guidance, claims about a product's benefits and performance must be provable, and leaving out relevant details can mislead a customer even without any intent to mislead. Do not say that a restored lamp will stay clear for a set time, or that it is protected for life, unless you hold evidence that supports the statement. Set out in the quote what is included, what is excluded, the condition of each lamp, and any referral items. Ask the owner to confirm the agreed scope in writing before work begins.

instructionSections.heading: Documentation and consent
instructionSections.body: Documentation protects the owner, the business and you. Before work, photograph each lamp from the front and from one side, in the same light, and record its condition, including any damage that was already there. Record the owner's consent to restoration, the agreed scope and the limits you explained. After the work, take matching photographs in matching light. Record the products used by name, the label reference, the SDS reference, the stages used in general terms, the protective coat applied and its label conditions, the drying check, and any referral. Keep photographs to the job, and keep them only as long as your business's privacy and records practice allows.

instructionSections.heading: Referral rule
instructionSections.body: Refer, rather than restore, when any of the following is present: a crack in the lens; moisture or fog inside the lens that does not clear after the lamp has dried; a cracked, broken or distorted housing; a broken or loose mounting point or seal; a melted, scorched or discoloured housing; or an electrical fault such as a dim, flickering or failed lamp. A referral means stopping work on that lamp, recording the finding with photographs, telling the owner in writing what you found and what restoration cannot fix, and passing the repair to a qualified repairer. Where the referral affects other work on the vehicle, agree the next step with the owner before you continue. A referral is part of a responsible service, not a failure of it. This lesson does not grant authority to repair a lamp, a housing or any wiring.

lessons.title: Fibre and construction identification
learningOutcomes: Identify common carpet and upholstery fibres by look, feel and the care label.
Recognise the construction, such as loop pile, cut pile or woven backing, and its effect on cleaning.
Treat an unidentified fibre as sensitive until it is tested.

instructionSections.heading: Why the fibre comes first
instructionSections.body: The fibre decides how an item responds to water, heat, brushing and product, so it has to be identified before anything else is chosen. The broad groups matter most. Protein fibres, such as wool, are usually treated with more care than cellulose fibres, such as cotton and linen, and synthetic fibres, such as nylon, polyester and polypropylene. General practice is that protein fibres are more easily damaged by heat and strongly alkaline products, and that some synthetics tolerate water better but can be marked by some solvents. These are general cleaning points. The colour of an item tells you very little about its fibre.

instructionSections.heading: Looking at and feeling the fibre
instructionSections.body: Work in good light and use a magnifier. Look at the sheen, the depth of the colour, the twist of the yarn, and whether the fibres are short and crimped or long and straight. Feel the surface and the pile. Natural fibres often feel different from synthetics, but that is a tendency, not an identification, and two fibres can feel alike. Where a loose fibre can be taken from an inconspicuous spot without damage, look at it closely. Do not use an open flame or a burn test on any item, on site or in the workshop, because the fire risk to the item, the premises and the operator is not acceptable and the test is not part of this course. Where the look and feel do not give a clear answer, record the fibre as unidentified.

instructionSections.heading: Construction: pile, backing and seams
