instructionSections.body: Construction changes the method as much as the fibre does. A loop pile holds soil in the loops, and it can distort or fuzz when it is scrubbed hard. A cut pile shows brush marks and can crush under pressure, so the direction of the pile matters. A cut-and-loop pile combines both. A flatweave or woven construction has little pile to protect it, and water can move through into the backing and stay there. Look at the backing as well as the face. Check the seams and the edges. A seam that is already lifting, or a loose binding, is a condition to record before any water is used. Decide whether the item is a loose rug, a fixed carpet or a fabric upholstery, because the handling of a loose rug and a fixed carpet differs.

instructionSections.heading: The care label and the manufacturer's code
instructionSections.body: Where a care label exists, it gives the manufacturer's cleaning code. The code states what the manufacturer considers suitable, and it is the first source to follow. A code is not permission to use any product. A code that calls for a particular cleaning approach does not make every product on the market suitable for it. Read the label before the inspection, record it exactly as written, and compare it with the fibre and construction you have identified. Where the label and your identification disagree, treat the item as the more sensitive of the two until a test decides which one is right.

instructionSections.heading: The unidentified fibre and the conservative default
instructionSections.body: When the fibre cannot be identified with confidence, treat the item as sensitive. Choose the most conservative method available. In general practice that means the least water, the lowest heat and the mildest product that will do the job, and a test on an inconspicuous area before the main treatment. Record the item as unidentified, with the photographs and the reasons, so that the next person does not repeat the same guess. Never guess, and never choose the strongest method to save time or to satisfy the customer. A mild result that leaves some soil is acceptable if the limit is recorded and agreed; a damaged fibre is not.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the identification
instructionSections.body: Write down the fibre group, or the word unidentified, the construction, the backing, the label code exactly as written, and the reasons for the identification. Add a photograph taken with permission and record the method chosen and why. This record protects the business if the customer later asks why a method was used or refused. Keep the record with the job file rather than relying on memory, because the identification affects the inspection, the test and the scope agreed with the customer.

lessons.title: Inspection and scope
learningOutcomes: Inspect the carpet or upholstery for soil, stains, wear, colour change and damage before work.
Agree the scope, the limits and the known risks with the customer in writing.
Record items that the cleaning cannot be expected to remove.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect in good light, from several angles
instructionSections.body: Inspect the item in good light, and walk it or move around it so that you see it from more than one angle. A raking light, a torch held low across the surface, shows the pile direction, flattened traffic lanes and marks that a flat light hides. Look at the traffic lanes, the high-use areas near doors and stairs, the edges and the areas under furniture where the customer allows furniture to be moved. An inspection done only from the doorway misses most of the soil that the customer cares about. Note the soil, the stains, the wear, any colour change, fading, seam damage, loose edges and any pre-existing marks, and check for odour. Photograph the condition with the customer's permission, and include a reference object so that the size of a mark can be judged later.

instructionSections.heading: Separate soil, stains, wear and damage
instructionSections.body: Soil is the loose or embedded dirt that cleaning is expected to remove. Stains are marks that have a source, such as food, drink, oil, ink or dye, and each responds differently to the same method. Wear is the loss of pile height or colour where the item is walked on, sat on or rubbed, and cleaning cannot restore lost pile. Colour change includes fading and dye movement, and it can be permanent. Damage includes burns, tears, cuts, shrinkage, delamination of the backing and failed seams. Record each one separately. Any sign of wetness that has not dried, a musty smell or visible growth is not routine soil; it is a moisture or biological concern, and it is handled as set out below.

instructionSections.heading: Agree the scope and the limits in writing
instructionSections.body: Agree the scope in writing before work starts. The scope covers the areas to be cleaned, the method, the result the customer can reasonably expect and the limits. State plainly that some stains and wear may not come out, that colour change or fibre damage may be permanent, and that the result is assessed after the clean. Do not promise a result that the inspection does not support, and do not let the customer's hope stand in for the evidence. Where the customer wants more than the inspection supports, say so, record the difference, and offer a specialist assessment or a separate job. The signed scope is the document that protects both parties when the result is discussed later.

instructionSections.heading: Claims about results need a basis
instructionSections.body: Any statement about what the cleaning will achieve is a claim, and it needs a basis. The ACCC guidance expects a business that speaks about a future matter to have its grounds in place when it speaks, and to be able to show them later (ACCC, False or misleading claims, fetched 2026-11-03). The same guidance cautions against forecasts that lack firm support. In practice, a phrase such as removes everything, or guaranteed, is not used unless there is evidence for it. The page does not name those particular words, so the test is the basis, not the word. Keep a note of the basis for the result you describe, such as the inspection, the test and the product information.

instructionSections.heading: Record what cleaning cannot be expected to remove
instructionSections.body: Record items that cleaning cannot be expected to remove, such as old dye stains that have set into the fibre, pet damage, scorch or burn marks, bleach marks, and permanent colour loss. Record items that need a specialist, such as repairs, re-stretching of loose carpet, and fabric replacement. Refer any mould, moisture or biological contamination to a qualified service, and do not treat it as routine cleaning. Stop and do not disturb any suspected contamination until the referral has been made and recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Moving furniture and manual handling
instructionSections.body: Inspection often means moving furniture, rolling up rugs or lifting an upholstered item. Safe Work Australia's model Code of Practice on hazardous manual tasks says that manual tasks must be identified, that their risks must be assessed, and that the risks must be managed. In practice, plan the lift, ask for help with heavy or awkward items, use the equipment you have, and do not move anything that you cannot control.

lessons.title: Method selection
learningOutcomes: Compare dry, low-moisture and wet methods and choose the one that suits the fibre and the soil.
Explain the risks of each method, including shrinkage, colour change, residue and wicking.
Refuse a method that is not suitable for the fibre or the construction.

instructionSections.heading: The main methods
instructionSections.body: Cleaning methods for carpet and upholstery are usually grouped by how much water they put into the item. Dry methods use powders or compounds that are worked into the pile and then removed by vacuuming, and they add little or no water. Low-moisture methods use a small amount of water or solution, worked in with pads or rotary equipment, and they leave the item damp rather than wet. Wet methods, including hot-water extraction, inject a larger volume of solution and then pull it back out. Equipment makers and suppliers use their own names for these approaches, so the name of a method matters less than the water load, the dwell time, the residue left behind and the drying time. The general practice is that the method is chosen from the fibre, the construction, the soil and the test result, not from habit.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the method
instructionSections.body: Work through five questions before any method is chosen. What is the fibre group, and is it treated as sensitive? What is the construction, and in particular is the backing woven, latex-backed or otherwise slow to dry? What is the soil: dry grit, greasy soil, a protein stain or a dye stain? What did the test show on an inconspicuous area? How long can the item stay out of use, and what drying time is practical in the room or the premises? The answers point to a method. Where two methods are both possible, choose the one that puts less water into the item, and move up to the wetter method only if the lighter method has been tried and has not worked. Record the reasons for the choice.

instructionSections.heading: Risks of each method
instructionSections.body: Wet methods carry the most risk of shrinkage, colour bleed, wicking of soil and product to the backing, and a long drying time. They can also leave a residue that attracts soil if the rinse is poor, and a backing can delaminate if it is over-wetted. Low-moisture methods can leave residue behind if the product is not fully removed, and they can build up soil if the pads are not changed often enough. Dry methods can grind soil deeper into the pile if they are used without enough vacuuming, and they remove less soil from heavily soiled areas. Explain the risks to the customer in plain terms, and record the explanation and the customer's agreement.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment, settings and electrical checks
instructionSections.body: Set the machine as the equipment maker's manual directs, including the water temperature, the solution flow, the pressure and the tank levels. Do not set the water hotter than the method and the test allow, and do not exceed the setting the maker gives. Before each use, look over the hoses, the tank, the cord and the plug for damage. WorkSafe ACT's guidance on electrical equipment describes an external inspection of the cords and connections as one of the checks, with protective earth, insulation and polarity testing to AS/NZS 3760:2022, and says that a licensed electrician or a person certified as competent carries out the testing (fetched 2026-11-03). Keep a record of the last test date and the tag on each machine.

instructionSections.heading: Drying, residue and the job's pace
instructionSections.body: Plan the drying before the method starts. Confirm how long the item needs to dry in the conditions on site, and keep traffic off until it is dry. A method that leaves the item wet for many hours is a poor choice for a room that must be used that evening. Remove product residue as the label directs. Where the label does not give a rinse step, the general practice is to extract the residue with clean water as the method allows, and to check for tide marks after drying. Record the drying time and the residue check.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing an unsuitable method and offering an alternative
instructionSections.body: Refuse a method that is not suitable, such as hot water on a wool carpet, or extraction on a woven backing that cannot be dried in the time available. Do not accept the booking simply because the customer asked for the method. Offer a conservative alternative, such as a low-moisture method after a test, or a dry method for a sensitive item, and explain what that alternative can and cannot do. Record the refusal, the reason, the alternative offered and the customer's response. A refusal written down at the time protects both the business and the customer.

instructionSections.heading: Wastewater and the work site
instructionSections.body: Wet methods produce wastewater that contains soil and product. The research brief for this course treats discharge to stormwater as out of bounds. Record how the water was disposed of.

lessons.title: Chemical and spot testing
learningOutcomes: Carry out a chemical and spot test on an inconspicuous area before the main treatment.
Read a test result for colour change, fibre damage, residue and bleed.
Never mix products and never test an unidentified product.

instructionSections.heading: Why test, and where
instructionSections.body: A test shows how the fibre and the dye react to a product before the whole item is treated. It is the only practical way to learn whether a dye will move, whether a fibre will mark, or whether a residue will form, and it is done even on familiar fabrics, because the same fibre can be dyed differently by two makers. Choose an inconspicuous area, such as the back of a corner, a hidden edge, the underside of a cushion or an area under furniture where the customer allows it. Where the item has several colours or several fibre types, test each one, because a test on one colour says nothing about another. The number of test spots is set by the item; for example, one spot per colour zone is a reasonable working approach (example only). The test must use the same product, the same dilution and the same method that will be used on the main area. A test with a weaker product is not a valid test of a stronger one.

instructionSections.heading: Carrying out the test
instructionSections.body: Prepare the test area in the way the planned method would prepare the main area, and apply the product as the method would apply it. Leave the product for the dwell time stated on its label, and do not extend the time to get a stronger result. Blot the area with a white cloth if the method calls for it. Allow the test area to dry fully, because a damp area can look different from a dry one, and judge the result only then. Keep the test spot unaffected by other work during the drying period, so that the result is not confused by a second product or by traffic. Photograph the test spot, with permission, before and after drying.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the result
instructionSections.body: Read the result against an untouched area in the same light. Look for colour change, which can be a lightening, a darkening or a shift in shade. Press a white cloth onto the test area and look for bleed, which shows as colour transfer. Look for fibre damage, such as fuzzing, fraying, crushing or a dull, stripped look. Feel for stiffness, which shows the product has affected the fibre or the backing. Look for residue and tide marks, which show as a ring or a film where the product dried. A result that shows any of these means the product or method is not suitable for the main area. A slight change that the customer has accepted in writing can be recorded as a limit, but a bleed or a fibre damage result is a stop.

instructionSections.heading: What to do when the test fails
instructionSections.body: Stop. Do not use the product on the main area, and do not try a stronger version of the same product. Record the product, the dilution, the test area, the method, the time and the result, with a photograph taken with permission. Choose a different approved method, test it in the same way, and check the new result. If no method passes, refer the item for a specialist assessment, and tell the customer what the test showed and what the next step is. A failed test is not a failure of the business; a treatment carried out after a failed test is.

instructionSections.heading: Products, mixing and safety data
instructionSections.body: Use one approved product at a time. Never mix products, because two products can react with each other and the result is not predictable. Never test or use a product from an unlabelled container, because the hazards and the directions are not known. Each product on the job needs a current safety data sheet, and the supplier can provide one at no cost on first supply or on request. A safety data sheet has 16 headings, including hazards, first aid, handling and storage, exposure controls and disposal, and it should have been prepared within the last five years (Safe Work Australia, fetched 2026-11-03). Each hazardous chemical on the workplace register is matched to a current safety data sheet, and the register is kept where workers can reach it.

instructionSections.heading: Records and the customer conversation
instructionSections.body: Record each test as a separate entry: the product, the dilution, the area tested, the time the product was left, the drying time, the result and any photographs. Record what was explained to the customer and what the customer agreed. Where a test leaves a visible but acceptable change, the customer's written agreement is part of the record. A test record that shows the reasons for a decision protects the business if the result is questioned later.

lessons.title: Machine and moisture control
learningOutcomes: Set up and check an extraction machine before use, including hoses, tools and the water recovery.
Control moisture so that the item is not over-wetted.
Stop and act on electrical or moisture faults during the job.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the machine
instructionSections.body: Check the machine before use: the cord, the plug, the hoses, the tools, the seals and the recovery tank. Confirm that the water recovery works and that the tank is emptied as the procedure requires. Keep the cord clear of the work area, and keep the machine away from water on the floor. Do not use a machine with a damaged cord or a cracked hose. Portable equipment used in harsh conditions should be checked and tested on a regular basis by a qualified person, and commercial cleaning equipment should be tested at least every six months (Safe Work Australia, electrical risks fact sheet, no date shown). Equipment that has not been tested should stay out of use until it has been tested (same fact sheet).

instructionSections.heading: Controlling moisture
instructionSections.body: Use the least water that gives the result, and extract well after each pass. Over-wetting leaves water in the backing, which can cause shrinkage, colour bleed, odour and mould. Monitor the moisture, and do not leave the item wet overnight. Use air movement where the setting allows.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping on faults
instructionSections.body: Stop and make the item safe if the machine trips, sparks, smells of burning or leaks into the power connection. Disconnect the machine as the procedure directs, and report it. Do not repair the machine or the electrical parts yourself. Unsafe electrical equipment must be disconnected or isolated and kept out of service until it is made safe by repair, testing, replacement or permanent removal (Safe Work Australia, electrical risks fact sheet, no date shown). In Victoria, doing electrical work requires an Energy Safe Victoria licence (Energy Safe Victoria, reviewed 19 August 2024). This lesson does not grant any electrical licence.

lessons.title: Drying, inspection and handover
learningOutcomes: Dry the item fully using airflow and the approved method, and confirm dryness before release.
Inspect the cleaned item against the agreed scope and record any limits that remain.
Hand over without promising a result beyond the inspection.

instructionSections.heading: Drying properly before release
instructionSections.body: Drying is part of the cleaning, not an afterthought. Moisture moves into the lowest and thickest parts of an item, which means the backing, the edges, the seams and the underside of an upholstered cushion are the places that stay damp longest. The surface can feel dry while the layers below remain wet, and that hidden dampness is where odour and growth start. Use airflow across the item, such as fans or air movers placed according to the equipment maker's instructions, and keep traffic and furniture off the item until it is dry. Check the backing, the edges and the seams by touch and, where the business has an approved moisture check, by reading. Record the time the drying started, the checks made and the time the item was confirmed dry. Where an item stays wet well beyond the time the method and the conditions would normally allow, stop and find out why before release.

instructionSections.heading: Inspecting against the agreed scope
instructionSections.body: Inspect the cleaned item against the scope and limits signed before the work. Work from several angles and in good light, and compare the item with the pre-work photographs and the record. Record the stains that remain, any change in colour or texture, any residue or tide marks, any change in pile direction or pile height, and any damage. Separate what the cleaning achieved from what it did not achieve. A short, factual record is more useful than a general statement that the item looks good, because the record is what the customer and the business rely on if the result is questioned.

instructionSections.heading: Dampness, odour and suspected growth
instructionSections.body: Persistent dampness can lead to odour and to growth, which are outside routine cleaning. If the item smells musty after drying, if a damp area remains at the backing after the expected time, or if any growth is visible, do not release the item as complete. Keep the item out of use, record the location and the observations with photographs taken with permission, and refer it to a qualified service. Do not treat a damp item as dry because the customer wants it back.

instructionSections.heading: Stains that can return
instructionSections.body: Some soils and stains can wick back up as the item dries and is used, and a residue left behind can attract new soil. The customer should understand this before the handover, because a stain that looks removed can reappear after use. Explain the likely behaviour in plain terms, and record that it was explained. Do not describe any stain as permanently removed unless the inspection and the test support that statement, and even then, describe it as the result seen on the day.

instructionSections.heading: Handover with the record
instructionSections.body: Hand over with the written record: the scope that was done, the method used, the drying check, the remaining limits, any items referred, and the follow-up the business offers. Explain the result plainly, and show the customer the areas where the result is limited. Agree any further work separately, with its own scope and price. Give the customer any maintenance advice the product label or the maker gives. Any statement about the result needs a reasonable basis at the time it is made, and the business must be able to show that basis if asked (ACCC, False or misleading claims, fetched 2026-11-03). Obtain the customer's signature on the handover record.

instructionSections.heading: After the handover
instructionSections.body: Keep the handover record with the job file. If the customer reports a change after the handover, compare the report with the pre-work record, the inspection record and the drying record, and respond with the evidence. Do not change the record after the event; add a dated note instead, and keep both.

lessons.title: Upholstery fabric identification and colourfastness
learningOutcomes: Identify the common upholstery fabrics and their sensitivity to water and products.
Carry out a colourfastness check before a treatment.
Refuse a treatment where the fabric or colour is not suitable.

instructionSections.heading: Common upholstery fabrics
instructionSections.body: Upholstery covers are made from many materials, and each responds differently to water, heat, brushing and product. Cotton and linen are cellulose fibres; they can shrink and some of their dyes can run when they are wet. Wool is a protein fibre and is treated with more care. Synthetic blends and microfibre are common in modern furniture; microfibre is a fine fibre that can hold soil in its surface and can be marked by friction. Velvet, chenille and other pile fabrics have a direction, and a pile can crush or mark under hard brushing. Leather is a natural hide with a finish, and it is not treated like a textile. Vinyl and polyurethane coatings are a surface layer over a backing, and some solvents can damage that layer. The label, the feel and the pile are the first clues, and no single clue is conclusive.

instructionSections.heading: Identifying the fabric on the job
instructionSections.body: Read the manufacturer's care label first, where one is present, and record it exactly as written. Then look at the fabric in good light with a magnifier. Look at the weave or knit, the pile and its direction, the sheen and the surface finish. Feel the fabric, and check the back and any hidden seam allowance for the backing and the construction. Where the fabric cannot be identified with confidence, record it as unidentified and treat it as sensitive, with the most conservative method and a test before any main treatment. Do not guess the material from the colour or the price of the furniture.

instructionSections.heading: The colourfastness check
instructionSections.body: Test colourfastness on an inconspicuous area, such as the underside of a cushion, a hidden seam or the back of a panel. Use the planned product at the planned dilution. Apply a small amount to a white test cloth and press it gently onto the test area, rather than rubbing it. Check the cloth for colour transfer, and check the test area for any change in shade or any damage. Compare the cloth with a blank white cloth held in the same light, because a faint mark is easier to judge that way. Repeat the test on a second colour or a second fabric panel if the item has more than one. Allow the test area to dry fully before the result is judged, and record the time and the result.

instructionSections.heading: Reading a failed result
instructionSections.body: A colour transfer onto the white cloth means the product is not suitable for that fabric and colour, and the fabric is not treated with that product. Do not try a stronger version of the same product, and do not switch to a product that the test has not been run on. Look also for shrinkage, stiffness, pile crush and cracking or lifting of a coating. Any of these results is a reason to refuse the treatment or to choose a gentler approach. Record the test, the result and the decision, and tell the customer what was found and what the next option is.

instructionSections.heading: Pile fabrics and gentle handling
instructionSections.body: Pile fabrics need a gentle method. Work with the direction of the pile, using a soft brush rather than a stiff one, and avoid hard brushing in all directions, because it can flatten the pile, mark the surface or lift the nap. Test the method on an inconspicuous area before the main treatment, and check the result after drying in the same light. A pile that has been crushed may not recover, so record its condition before the work starts, and tell the customer if a change is likely.

instructionSections.heading: Leather and vinyl are not fabric
instructionSections.body: Leather and vinyl are not treated like fabric. Leather has a finish over a natural hide, and the finish can be damaged by products that work well on textiles. Vinyl and polyurethane have a coating over a backing, and the coating can be softened, marked or lifted by some solvents. Identify the material first, check the label, and test the approach on an inconspicuous area. Where the material is unclear, or the finish is already cracking or peeling, refer the item for a specialist assessment rather than treating it as fabric.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing treatments and offering alternatives
instructionSections.body: Refuse a treatment where the colour transfers, the fabric shrinks, the pile is damaged or the coating reacts in the test. Offer a conservative alternative that has been tested, or refer the item for a specialist assessment. Explain the limit to the customer, and do not promise that a stain will come out of a fabric that has failed the test. Record the test, the result, the decision, the alternative offered and the customer's response.

lessons.title: Upholstery stain treatment and soil assessment
learningOutcomes: Assess the soil and the stain type before treatment, and record its age and appearance.
Choose a stain treatment that is compatible with the fabric and the test result.
Explain what may not be removable, and avoid promising the removal of a stain.

instructionSections.heading: Assessing the stain
instructionSections.body: Start by naming the soil or stain as closely as you can: food, drink, body oil, ink, pet urine, dye transfer from clothing, or a mix. Ask the customer how and when it happened, and record the answer as the customer's account rather than as your own finding. Note the age in hours, days or months, and the appearance: whether the stain is wet, tacky, crusted or dry, whether it has a ring or halo, and how far it reaches. Older and dried stains usually need a different approach from a fresh one. A stain that has been wetted and dried several times may have moved deeper into the fibre or into the padding. Check the care label, if there is one, for the fibre content and any cleaning code. Do not apply heat until the stain has been assessed, because some stains set with heat, and heat can change some fabrics permanently. Photograph the stain before any work, with the customer's permission, in even light.

instructionSections.heading: Testing before you treat
instructionSections.body: Choose a hidden test area, such as the underside of a seat cushion or the back of a skirt panel, and test the planned product there first. Watch for colour change, fibre damage, dye bleeding onto the cloth, and any change in feel as the area dries. Give the test time to dry before you judge it, and record the result. If the test area changes, stop and reassess before you touch the stain. For example, if a test patch leaves a light ring after it dries, the product is not suitable for that fabric, and you need a different approach or a referral. A test does not prove the stain will respond, but it does show whether the fabric can take the product at all.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing and working the treatment
instructionSections.body: Choose a treatment that is compatible with the fabric and with the result of the test. Remove loose solids gently before any liquid goes on, so that they are not pushed deeper. Work from the outside of the stain inwards to stop it spreading, and blot with a clean white cloth rather than rubbing. Rubbing spreads the stain and roughens the fibre. Use the least product that works, and apply it as the label directs, including dilution, contact time and rinsing or extraction. Do not leave the fabric over-wet, because excess moisture can carry the stain outwards as it dries and can leave a tide mark or an odour. Stop if the fabric starts to change, if the dye begins to move, or if the stain does not respond after the label's contact time. Dry the area as the procedure directs, with air movement, and check it again once it is dry before you decide on the result.

instructionSections.heading: What may not come out
instructionSections.body: Explain that some stains may not come out fully. The usual cases are old dye, pet damage, stains that have been set by heat or by an earlier product, and tide lines left by drying. Pet urine can leave an odour and a discolouration in the padding under the fabric, and surface treatment may not reach it. Record the stain and its likely limit before you start, and give the customer the limit in writing. If an odour persists after treatment, refer it to a specialist rather than covering it with fragrance. A fragrance can hide the problem, and it can also create a claim you cannot support.

instructionSections.heading: Products, labels and safety data
instructionSections.body: Read the product label and its safety data sheet (SDS) before you use a product. The SDS describes the hazards, first aid and the PPE that the product needs, and you must be able to reach it easily while you work. Keep to the products your business has approved. Do not mix products unless the label allows it, because mixing can create a hazardous reaction. Wear the gloves and eye protection the SDS or label sets. PPE is the lowest level of control, so also keep the amount of product to the minimum, ventilate where the label requires it, and keep bystanders away from the work area.

instructionSections.heading: What you say about the result
instructionSections.body: Any claim about the result must be accurate, and you must have reasonable grounds for it when you make it. Do not promise that a stain will be removed, that the fabric will look as new, or that the treatment is guaranteed. Silence can also mislead, so if you know a limit applies, say so before the work starts. Under the consumer rules, intention does not matter: a statement that creates a false impression can breach the rules even if each word is accurate. Describe the expected result as uncertain, for example 'may improve', and record the limit you agreed.

lessons.title: Workstations, shared electronics and office fixtures
learningOutcomes: Confirm workstation boundaries from the contract, induction and desk-cleaning policy before touching a desk.
Clean shared electronics and touchpoints with site-approved methods that keep liquid away from powered equipment.
Stop, withhold and report when a desk holds confidential material or an access issue exists.

instructionSections.heading: Setting the boundary before the desk
instructionSections.body: Review the contract, the site induction and the desk-cleaning policy before the first desk. Identify the clear-desk rules, the occupied desks, the restricted offices and any surface that is excluded from the service. Confidential papers are not moved, drawers are not opened, and computer accounts are not accessed. If a desk holds a laptop left open, a spill and confidential documents, you do not touch the laptop or the papers. You report the spill and ask for the authorised instruction.

instructionSections.heading: Electronics and shared devices
instructionSections.body: Clean screens, keyboards, phones and shared touchpoints only with site-approved methods. Do not spray liquid directly onto powered electronics, do not disconnect cables without authorisation, and do not use wet tools near outlets. Report damaged cords and equipment. A shared device is cleaned only where the site lists it as authorised for cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Sequence and touchpoints
instructionSections.body: Work from lower contamination risk toward higher risk, and change cloths as the procedure requires. Clean door handles, switches, meeting tables and authorised shared devices with products suited to each material. Where a disinfection product is used, follow its label directions for contact time, and do not describe the surface as disinfected unless the label supports that claim. Claims about cleaning and disinfection must be accurate and provable, because consumer law looks at the impression a claim creates rather than the intent behind it (ACCC, page metadata dated 28 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Handover and exceptions
instructionSections.body: Check for streaks, residue, missed high-touch points, unsecured cords and disturbed items. Log any desk that could not be accessed, and any incident, through the approved reporting channel. The handover says what was done and what was not.

lessons.title: Office access, keys, alarms and confidentiality
learningOutcomes: Verify authority and identity before entering a site, and keep to the approved entry route.
Handle keys and access codes under the site register, and report losses immediately.
Respond to an alarm or access failure by withdrawing, reporting and recording it, without bypass.

instructionSections.heading: Entering with authority
instructionSections.body: Your right to be on a site comes from the roster, the site induction and the access the site has granted you. Before you enter, confirm that the roster names this site and this time, that you have completed the induction the site requires, and that you carry whatever identification the site asks for. Use the approved entry route every time, even when a door is already open. Holding a door for someone else, or following someone through a controlled door, defeats the access record, because the site can no longer tell who was inside. Your credentials are issued to you alone. Do not lend a card, a fob or a code, and do not use another person's access even when that person is beside you and offers help. If you are unsure whether your access covers an area, stop and ask the designated site representative before you go further. Restricted areas, plant rooms, server rooms and areas closed for a meeting or inspection are not open to you simply because a door happens to be unlocked.

instructionSections.heading: Keys, codes and information
instructionSections.body: Keys are a form of access, so handle them with the same care as a card. Sign each key out and back in on the site register or the electronic access record at the moment it changes hands, and keep it under your personal control while it is with you. Do not leave keys on a trolley, in a cleaning cart in a corridor or in a jacket you have left unattended. If a key is lost, report it at once to the designated site representative and to any contact the register names. Give the time it was signed out, the last place you knew it to be, and the key's label or number. Do not spend a long time searching in a way that delays the report. Access codes are secret. Do not photograph a keypad, write a code on a product bottle or a checklist, or send a code in a message, including to a colleague who is also on site. Visible information is confidential too. Documents on desks, screens, visitor sign-in sheets and conversations about people in the building are not yours to read, copy or discuss. If you see or hear something you should not have, report the accidental exposure through the site privacy procedure and do not repeat it.

instructionSections.heading: Alarms and access failures
instructionSections.body: An alarm exists to protect the site, and it is not an obstacle to work around. If the supplied code does not disarm an alarm, stop trying. Do not try guessed codes, codes remembered from another site, or another door, window or service entrance. Each of these actions can set off the alarm response, can damage a door, and can make a genuine intruder harder to detect. Withdraw to a safe place that the site has named, which may be outside the building, and contact the designated site representative. Record the access failure with the date, the time, the area, the fact that the supplied code did not work, who you contacted and what they told you. Do not write the code in the record. If an evacuation alarm sounds, follow the site emergency plan, go to the assembly point and do not return for equipment or keys. Do not try to repair a sensor, a lock, a door closer or any part of the security or electrical system. Those repairs belong to authorised people, and a repair attempt can leave the site less secure than before.

instructionSections.heading: Lock-up and the exception log
instructionSections.body: Lock-up is a check, and it is finished only when every item has been checked. Work through the lock-up checklist in order. Isolate the equipment you used, confirm that the authorised doors and windows are closed and secured, return all keys to the register, complete the alarm procedure the site has set, and record each item in the exception log. If you cannot check an item, for example a window you cannot see, a door that will not latch, or a zone you were not allowed to enter, record it as unresolved and escalate it to the site representative. Do not tick it to complete the list, and do not write a note that suggests the site is secure. An unresolved item means the lock-up is not signed off. The next person to use the site, and the site itself, need to know what is still open. A clear exception log protects you as well as the site, because it shows that you did not claim a check you did not make.

lessons.title: Occupied-office cleaning, shift handover and quality verification
learningOutcomes: Plan a commercial cleaning route from the service specification, with zones, windows and exclusions.
Set up safe operations in an occupied office, including cable routes and public access.
Hand over to the next shift with completed tasks, exceptions and unresolved issues recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the service specification
instructionSections.body: The service specification is the working document for the shift. Before you start, identify the frequencies (which tasks run daily, weekly or on a set cycle), the priority zones that must be finished before the office opens, the consumables the client supplies and those the business supplies, the cleaning windows when occupants are present or absent, the exclusion areas, and the quality criteria the client will use to judge the result. Confirm the site contact and the emergency arrangements for the shift. If the specification and the contract disagree, do not settle the difference yourself. Note it and refer it to the supervisor, following the variation process in the contract (see “Site contract and scope”). Build the route from the specification, not from memory of the last shift, because a route built from memory tends to miss the tasks that have changed.

instructionSections.heading: Safe operations in an occupied office
instructionSections.body: An occupied office has risks that an empty building does not. People walk through the work area, cables cross the floor, and staff are concentrating on their own tasks. Before you start, carry out a pre-start risk assessment for the shift. Name the zones you will enter, the equipment you will use, the walkways that will be affected and the people who may be present. Check electrical equipment before use: look at the cord, the plug and the casing, and check insulated parts for damage. The Code of Practice on managing electrical risks says that equipment should not be used where there is doubt about its insulation, and that insulated covers and mats should be visually inspected before and after each use. Remove any damaged item from use and report it. Plan cable routes so that they do not cross the public route, or cover them with approved covers where the site allows. Keep the public access route open, and place signs and barriers where a hazard remains. Wet floors are a slip hazard. The SafeWork NSW guidance notes that cleaning products and methods can leave floors slippery and that poor drainage lets liquid pool, so contain spills, keep the floor clean and maintained, and use wet-floor signs. Drying the floor as you go is working practice. Never leave hazardous equipment or a trolley unattended in a walkway, and coordinate with occupants so that confidential meetings and sensitive work are not disturbed.

instructionSections.heading: Working the route and verifying
instructionSections.body: Work the route in zones, and finish each zone before you move on. Segregate tools and cloths by zone, so that cloths used in washrooms do not reach desks or the kitchenette. A common order is to start at reception, move through meeting rooms and workstations, then the kitchenette and washrooms, and finish with waste areas, so that clean areas are not contaminated by later work. This is working practice, and the specification may set a different order. Verify as you go, not only at the end. Check high-touch surfaces such as door handles, rails and lift buttons, the floors, the waste areas, the consumables and the secured storage. Record missed rooms, spills that need a specialist response, and maintenance concerns such as a loose tile or a dripping tap. Use privacy-safe evidence. A photograph of a desk or a whiteboard may capture confidential material, so take photographs only where the site allows, and frame them around the defect. The quality check is the checklist, not your general impression of the room.

instructionSections.heading: Chemicals, SDS and the register
instructionSections.body: Every chemical used on site has a label and a safety data sheet. Before you use a product, check that it is on the site's hazardous chemicals register and that you can reach its SDS quickly. Use the product only as the label and the SDS direct. Choose gloves and eye protection to match the SDS and your shift risk assessment. Do not use a product that has no SDS on the register. Set it aside, refer it to the supervisor and record the hold. The Safe Work Australia guidance expects the register to be readily accessible to workers and to anyone who may be affected, so a register kept in a locked office that workers cannot reach does not meet that expectation.

instructionSections.heading: Shift handover
instructionSections.body: A shift handover is the point where responsibility moves to the next worker. Record what was completed and when, which access exceptions you met, which equipment is faulty or out of use, which stock is short, which incidents were reported, and where every key is. Write outstanding work in plain terms, so that the next worker can act without guessing. A damaged vacuum is isolated, removed from use, labelled and recorded in the handover, so that nobody reaches for it. A meeting room that is still in use is rescheduled to an authorised alternative time, and the rescheduling is recorded as outstanding work. Write the handover, and confirm in conversation any decision that was made at the end of the shift.

lessons.title: Site contract and scope
learningOutcomes: Identify the contract scope, exclusions, frequencies and the people who authorise changes.
Record variations in writing before the work changes.
Refuse to promise work that the contract does not include.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the contract
instructionSections.body: The contract sets the scope of the work. It names the areas, the tasks, the frequencies, the standards, the exclusions and the people who may authorise changes. Read it before you price the work or start it, and read the attached scope schedule as part of the contract, not as a separate note. Look hard at the exclusions. A missing or vague exclusion is the most common cause of disputes, because the site and the cleaner remember different things about what was agreed. Words such as as required, periodic, regular or as needed do not give a frequency, so ask the contract owner to replace them with a number of visits or a cycle before work starts. Check who signs for the client, who receives service reports and who can approve a change. A person who can request work is not always a person who can approve it. Where a standard is named, check how it will be measured, for example by a checklist or an inspection, so the standard can be shown to have been met.

instructionSections.heading: Variations
instructionSections.body: A variation is any change to the agreed scope. That includes an extra area, a different product, a different frequency, a new task, a change of time that affects the price, or a removal of work the business has agreed to do. Record each variation in writing. Describe the change, the reason it was asked for, the time and product it needs, the price, and the person the contract names as the approver. Get that approval before the extra work starts. A verbal request from a site staff member is a request, not a variation, even when the request is reasonable and the staff member has authority within the building. Note the request, tell the staff member that it needs to go to the contract owner, and send it through that route. Where a contract allows approval to be given after work has started, follow the wording of that contract, and record the approval when it is given. Keep the variation register in the same file as the contract so that the current scope can be read in one place.

instructionSections.heading: Promises and representations
instructionSections.body: Do not promise work, results or standards that the contract does not include. Saying the stain will never return, that a room will be dust-free for a week, or that the business will add a service next month are all statements about what the business will do or achieve. The ACCC's guidance says that claims about services must be accurate and based on reasonable grounds, and that a business must be able to back up what it says when it makes the claim. Predictions about the future also need reasonable grounds at the time they are made, and the business should allow for uncertainty. Misleading impressions count, even where they were not intended. When a request falls outside the contract, explain what the contract covers in plain terms, and refer the request to the contract owner. Keep the wording factual: say what is included, rather than guarantee what the result will be.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the records together
instructionSections.body: A contract is only useful if the current scope can be found quickly. Keep the signed contract, the scope schedule, every approved variation, the approval for each one, and the service reports in one file. When a variation is approved, update the scope schedule, the checklist and the staff briefing so that they match. Mark old versions as superseded rather than deleting them, so that the history can be shown if a dispute arises. The file is also the first place to look when a new team member asks what they should be doing on a site.

lessons.title: Waste and recycling
learningOutcomes: Separate general waste, recycling and regulated waste streams in the labelled containers.
Reduce waste where the contract and the site allow it, without mixing streams.
Refer any unclear or regulated waste to the site for disposal under its plan.

instructionSections.heading: Separating the streams
instructionSections.body: Waste on a client site usually falls into a few streams: general waste, recycling, food waste where the site has a food waste service, and any material the site has identified as regulated or special. Keep the streams apart from the point where the waste is created. Use the labelled containers and the collection routes the site sets, and do not place a bag in a bin because it is nearest. A mixed bin usually goes to general waste, and a single item in the wrong bin can spoil a whole load of recycling. Check the label on a container before you use it, not just its colour, because a colour may mean one thing at one site and something else at another. If a container has no label, treat its contents as unknown until the site has identified them. Keep the waste areas tidy, with lids closed and bins not overfilled, so that the streams stay identifiable and no leak reaches a drain.

instructionSections.heading: Reducing waste within the rules
instructionSections.body: Reducing waste is part of good service. The EPA's guidance on the general environmental duty describes the same approach in a different setting: avoid creating waste where possible, reuse what can be reused, recycle what can be recycled, and separate and store each type safely. In a cleaning job, that means ordering consumables to need rather than in excess, reusing cloths and mop heads where the method allows, and refilling only from approved, labelled bulk containers. Do not refill a spray bottle from an unlabelled drum, because nobody can then say what is in the bottle. Do not reuse single-use items in a way the site does not permit, for example a disposable glove or a sachet that the site has said to discard after one use. Where a reduction would change the cleaning method or product, the change belongs to the contract or site procedure, not to the cleaner.

instructionSections.heading: Unclear and regulated waste
instructionSections.body: When you cannot say what a material is, do not decide its stream yourself. Leave it in place, do not put it in a bin, and record its location and the time. Refer it to the site contact so that the site can identify it and dispose of it under its plan. Victoria's general environmental duty requires a business to reduce or eliminate the risk of harm from its waste, so far as reasonably practicable. The duty applies to businesses as well as households, and the EPA states that businesses that fail to meet it face significant penalties (EPA Victoria, updated 4 August 2026). EPA Victoria's industrial waste guidance also says that anyone who manages industrial waste must classify it and meet the duties for that classification, and that managing waste includes collecting, transporting, storing and disposing of it (EPA Victoria, updated 9 April 2026). The cleaner does not classify waste. The site does, under its plan and any authorisation it holds.

instructionSections.heading: Leaks and spills in the waste area
instructionSections.body: A leaking bag or container in a waste area is both a hazard and a pathway to a drain. Stop, keep other people away, and check the label and the SDS for any chemical involved before touching it. Use the absorbent material and the gloves the site supplies. Do not wash the leak into a floor drain or a stormwater drain. The EPA's stormwater guidance says that waste should be kept out of stormwater drains so far as reasonably practicable (EPA Victoria, updated 7 May 2025). Record the leak, the time, the area and the action taken, and refer the clean-up of anything beyond the routine to the site.

lessons.title: Multi-site service standards
learningOutcomes: Set a service standard that applies across sites while allowing for site-specific rules.
Keep the standard checkable through checklists, training and records at each site.
Escalate where one site's rules conflict with the common standard.

instructionSections.heading: One common standard, with site rules recorded separately
instructionSections.body: A multi-site service works best when every site runs on the same standard for method, approved products, checklists, training and records. Keep that common standard in one controlled document, with a version number and a date. Record each site's differences in a separate site schedule: access arrangements, opening hours, exclusions, product restrictions, the location of the SDS folder and the hazardous chemicals register, and the emergency contacts. Keeping the two records apart means that a change to the common standard is made once, and that a site difference is not mistaken for a company-wide rule. A site rule that conflicts with the common standard is not quietly accepted and not quietly ignored. It is escalated, as described below.

instructionSections.heading: Making the standard checkable
instructionSections.body: A standard that cannot be checked is only a hope. Turn each task into a checklist that names what is done, the method and the product, and the result that counts as complete. Record training for each cleaner against the checklist and the approved products. Keep a visit record for each site, showing who visited, when, what was checked and what was found. Run the same check at every site, so that results can be compared. If two inspectors would score the same room differently, the checklist is not clear enough, and it should be reworded before it is relied on. Do not rely on memory, and do not assume that sites with similar buildings have the same rules. A site that looks the same from the outside may have a different access arrangement, a different product restriction or a different waste route.

instructionSections.heading: Chemicals across sites
instructionSections.body: Each site has its own list of hazardous chemicals that are used, handled or stored there. The Safe Work Australia guidance describes a register that lists those chemicals, includes the current SDS for each one, is kept up to date, and is readily accessible to workers and anyone affected. For a multi-site service, the common product list should match each site's register. When a site introduces a product that is not on the common list, the product is not used until it has been approved and added to the register for that site. The SDS and the label then govern how the product is used.

instructionSections.heading: Escalating conflicts
instructionSections.body: A conflict arises when a site rule and the common standard point in different directions. It may be a product the standard does not approve, a method the site restricts, or a frequency that the site cannot accommodate. Do not decide the conflict in the field. Stop the change, record the request and the site rule, and escalate to the supervisor and the client. Record the decision in writing, including who made it and when. If the decision changes the standard, the change is made to the controlled document, communicated to every site it affects, and reflected in the checklists and training. Until that happens, the approved standard continues to apply at all sites.

lessons.title: Stakeholder coordination
learningOutcomes: Identify the stakeholders for a site and what each needs to know.
Use one agreed communication channel for schedules, changes and issues.
Record decisions and send confirmations to the right people.

instructionSections.heading: Who needs to know
instructionSections.body: A cleaning site has several stakeholders, and each needs different information. The building manager or client needs the schedule, the changes, the access arrangements and any incident. The site staff need the zones that will be worked, the times when areas are occupied, and any restriction on entry. Other contractors need to know the times they share with you, the areas they will use, and any isolation or delivery that affects the route. Occupants need to know when their area will be disturbed and how to raise a concern. Your supervisor needs every request that falls outside the agreement, every issue that is not resolved on site, and every change that affects the team. Emergency contacts for the site are held on the site schedule. For each site, list the stakeholders, the information each one needs, how often they need it, and the channel through which it reaches them. A one-page table is enough for most sites, and it should be checked when the site changes.

instructionSections.heading: One agreed channel
instructionSections.body: Use one agreed channel for schedules, changes and issues at each site. The channel might be a shared email thread, a messaging group, a logbook at reception or a ticketing system, but it must be agreed with the client and written into the site arrangement. Mixing channels is a common cause of lost information. A change sent by text to one person, an email to another and a remark in a corridor will not reach everyone who needs it. Keep each message brief, dated and factual: what changes, when it takes effect, who is affected, and why. A change that is given verbally is not a recorded change until it is confirmed in the channel. Ask the person who gave the change to confirm it in the channel, or send the confirmation yourself and ask them to reply.

instructionSections.heading: Confirmations and disputes
instructionSections.body: Send confirmations of schedule changes, access arrangements and reported issues to the people who need them, and keep a copy. A confirmation should state the change, the time it takes effect, the reason, the area affected, the person who approved it, and the people it has been sent to. When a stakeholder asks for something outside the agreement, refer it to the supervisor rather than agreeing it at the door. Describe an issue in facts: what you saw, where, when, and who was told. Do not speculate about cause or blame, and do not promise a fix. If a dispute arises over what was agreed, the channel record and the confirmations are the first reference, followed by the contract and any variation (see “Site contract and scope”).

instructionSections.heading: Handling a difficult conversation
instructionSections.body: Some stakeholders will be unhappy about a delay, a noise, or a change they did not expect. Listen to the concern, repeat it back in plain words so that the person knows it has been heard, and say what you will do next. Do not promise a change you cannot make. Record the concern in the channel, and pass it to the supervisor if it needs a decision. Keep your tone calm and factual. A short, accurate message in the channel protects the relationship better than a long conversation at the door that nobody else can see.

lessons.title: Contract improvement
learningOutcomes: Review service records to find the areas where the contract and the work do not match.
Propose a change to scope, frequency or method in writing, with the reasons.
Refrain from promising changes until the contract owner has approved them.

instructionSections.heading: Reviewing the record
instructionSections.body: Review the visit records, the checklists, the client feedback, the complaint log and, where kept, the time records, to see where the contract and the work do not match. A recurring complaint, a repeated missed item, or an area that always takes more time than the scope allows is a sign that the scope, the frequency or the method may need to change. Start with a defined period, such as the last few months of visits, and count what happened in it. Separate one-off events from patterns. A single bad visit is not evidence of a scope problem, but the same item missed across several visits is. Note the conditions that may explain the pattern, such as a season, a staffing change, a building works period or a new product, so that the proposal does not blame the team. Use the record, not impressions, and mark any gaps in the record so that they are not filled by guesswork.

instructionSections.heading: Building the evidence
instructionSections.body: For each proposed change, build a short evidence summary. It should state the source records and their dates, the count or frequency of the event, the time or product it consumes, and any conditions that affect it. Where time is measured, compare the planned time with the recorded time. For example, a bathroom planned at a set time that routinely takes longer may need its time reviewed, but the figures in your proposal must come from your own records. Do not use invented figures in a proposal. If an example figure is needed to explain a calculation, label it clearly as an example. Be careful to separate routine cleaning from work that is outside routine cleaning. Removing growth from a surface, repairing a leak, or replacing a damaged fitting is not part of routine cleaning and should be referred to the appropriate person.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the proposal
instructionSections.body: Write the proposal in plain, factual language. Include the current scope, the observed mismatch, the evidence summary, the proposed change to scope, frequency or method, the time and product implications, what the client would gain, and any limits or risks. Include an option to keep the current arrangement and monitor the result, where that is reasonable. The proposal is not a promise and does not change the contract. Send it to the contract owner for a decision. Do not include a new price unless the pricing rules for the contract allow you to propose one, and label any price as a proposal for approval.

instructionSections.heading: Approval and follow-up
instructionSections.body: The contract owner decides. Do not start the changed work, promise a new frequency, or quote a new price until the change has been approved in writing and recorded. A forward-looking promise about frequency or price is a claim about future performance, and the ACCC's guidance says that such claims need reasonable grounds when they are made (ACCC, page dated 28 June 2026). If the change is approved, update the contract schedule, the checklist and the staff briefing, and monitor the result for the period agreed in the approval. Report back on the monitoring. If the change is refused, record the decision and revisit only when new evidence is available.

instructionSections.heading: Where the proposal meets remediation
instructionSections.body: Some records describe a problem that cleaning cannot fix. Mould is a useful example. SafeWork NSW guidance says that investigating mould can be difficult and is in some cases best left to an experienced professional. It also says that where the source of growth is unclear and people may be at risk, sampling should be carried out by a competent person with suitable equipment and PPE, and that cleaning starts by fixing the moisture or ventilation problem, because mould returns otherwise (SafeWork NSW, modified 4 December 2025). A proposal that asks for more frequent cleaning of a mould-prone area without addressing the moisture source is not a fix. Refer the underlying problem, and propose only the cleaning scope that remains after the referral.

lessons.title: Site authorisation and sanitation task boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify the operator-approved sanitation procedure and the person who authorises work before any task starts.
Mark restricted spaces, unknown hazards and off-limits equipment on a site plan.
Stop the planned work when production release or task ownership is unclear, and record a hold rather than an unapproved workaround.

instructionSections.heading: The site owns the sanitation programme
instructionSections.body: On a food-processing site, the facility's food safety team owns the sanitation programme, not the visiting cleaner. Before any sanitation work, you need three things in writing: the operator-approved sanitation procedure, confirmation of the production shutdown, and the name of the food safety or production supervisor who authorises the work. Explain who can grant access, who reviews deviations, and who can authorise restart of production. If any of these is missing, the work does not start.

instructionSections.heading: Observe without disturbing production
instructionSections.body: Review the signed production release, and identify which manager owns access and sanitising clearance. On the site plan, mark every restricted space and every unknown hazard before you propose any activity. Treat machinery, ingredients and processing surfaces as off-limits until they are specifically authorised for the work. A cleaner who moves a product or touches a line to see what is there has already changed the situation.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping on unclear ownership
instructionSections.body: When the production line has not been released, or when it is not clear who owns the task, stop. Do not look for a workaround. Escalate to the responsible authorised person, protect the zone, and document the hold and the referral. Do not claim that the area is sanitised or released, because that decision belongs to the facility.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the hold
instructionSections.body: Record the date, the zone, the issue, the source of the authorisation, the action that was withheld, the person notified and the decision that is still pending. The record must never describe validated sanitation, allergen freedom or microbiological clearance, unless an authorised person has issued that result.

lessons.title: Water use, drainage and environmental control
learningOutcomes: Trace where wash water could reach drains, production areas and the environment.
Recognise aerosol, drainage overflow and slip hazards from wet cleaning and high-pressure devices.
Stop and escalate for unapproved water use, and record the hold.

instructionSections.heading: Where the water goes
instructionSections.body: Wash water on a food-processing site can reach floor drains, product areas, equipment and surfaces that contact food, wastewater systems, and, where a drain connects outside, stormwater. Trace each path before you use water. Start from the point where the water is applied and follow it to the floor, then to the nearest drain, then to the point where the drain goes. Check whether the drain has the capacity for the volume you will use, and check the drain map the site holds. A drain that backs up or overflows can carry contamination back into a production area, and water that runs toward ingredients, packaging or equipment is a contamination pathway in its own right. If you cannot trace the path, treat it as unknown and do not use water there until the site has confirmed it. Food safety law in Australia requires food premises and equipment to be kept clean and sanitary, and the FSANZ guidance on cleaning and sanitising under Standard 3.2.2 describes the sequence of rinsing, washing and sanitising. Water is part of that sequence, so its path matters as much as the cleaning method.

instructionSections.heading: Aerosols and high-pressure devices
instructionSections.body: High-pressure and spray devices create aerosols, which are fine droplets that can carry soil and micro-organisms into the air and onto surfaces that are not being cleaned. This is the main reason spray is restricted near open product. Use water-based methods only where the site instruction permits them, and keep spray away from exposed product, open containers, packaging and open equipment. Consider the aerosol path as well as the floor path: a jet that is safe at the floor can still carry droplets onto a nearby surface. Floors become slippery when wet. The SafeWork NSW guidance notes that cleaning products and methods can leave floors slippery, and that poor drainage lets liquid pool, so the controls are containment of spills, floor maintenance and drainage, and non-slip footwear in wet conditions. The use of barriers and drying as additional controls is site practice, not a requirement stated in that guidance.

instructionSections.heading: Environmental controls and discharge
instructionSections.body: Wash water, detergent residues and rinse water can reach waste systems and the environment. In Victoria, EPA guidance says that waste should be kept out of stormwater drains so far as reasonably practicable, and that the general duty applies to wastewater as well as to other waste (EPA Victoria, updated 7 May 2025). Discharging trade waste into a sewer also has its own approval rules. A Victorian water corporation states that businesses must have a trade waste consent or agreement before discharging trade waste to the sewer, and that discharging without one is an offence (Goulburn Valley Water, a Victorian water corporation). Before using a detergent or a cleaning product in a drain or near one, check the site's approval and the product's SDS, and do not assume that a product is acceptable to discharge.

instructionSections.heading: Food safety program status
instructionSections.body: A food safety program under Standard 3.2.1 applies to food businesses that the enforcing agency has placed in a priority classification, and the classification is decided under state or territory law. The FSANZ guide to Standard 3.2.1, a first edition from June 2007, explains this. The guide is explanatory and is not the standard, so the clauses of the standard itself govern. Because the guide is dated 2007, its statements about which jurisdictions require a program are historical. This lesson does not confer any food safety clearance or qualification, and it does not establish that a site is compliant.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping, holding and recording
instructionSections.body: Stop the task where there is aerosol risk, drainage overflow, or water use the site has not approved. Do not look for a workaround, and do not use more pressure to clear a drain. Escalate to the responsible authorised person, protect the area and any exposed product, and record the hold, the referral and the pending decision. Protecting exposed product means covering it or keeping people away from it, and any move of product is for the authorised person to decide. Do not record the area as clean, safe, sanitised or released. Those statements are decisions for the authorised person, based on checks you did not make.

lessons.title: Pest evidence, waste and by-product management
learningOutcomes: Recognise signs of pest activity and improperly contained waste.
Segregate food by-product streams so that waste does not contaminate ingredients or packaging.
Preserve evidence and refer unidentified pest contamination or regulated waste, without disturbing it.

instructionSections.heading: Why pests and waste belong in the same lesson
instructionSections.body: Pests and waste are linked. Rodents, insects and birds are drawn to food residue and to waste that is not sealed, and they can carry harmful micro-organisms into the areas where food is handled. The FSANZ pest guidance places the obligation with the operator. Under Standard 3.2.2, the operator is expected to take every reasonable step that keeps pests out of the premises and clears out any that get in, including from vehicles that carry food. It is not a duty that a cleaner can discharge by acting alone. Your job on a food site is to notice, protect and refer. You are not the pest-control provider, and you are not the person who decides how waste is classified or moved. Keep that boundary clear from the first shift.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising pest signs and loose waste
instructionSections.body: Pest evidence takes several forms. Look for droppings, gnawing on packaging, timber or cable sheathing, nesting material, shed skins, live or dead insects, trails in dust or grease, and an unusual smell that does not match the product. Insects may appear as small clusters near drains, under bins or in the seams of stored packaging. Waste that is not contained is also a warning sign. Watch for lids left open, bags that are split or torn, bins that are overfull, residue on the floor beneath a bin, and waste stored close to ingredients, packaging or a wash-down point. The FSANZ guidance recommends that a pest management plan names the areas to inspect, such as behind equipment and inside cupboards, and that traps and bait stations are placed away from food and food-contact surfaces, with a site map. Check these areas as part of your normal walk, but do not disturb a station or trap that is not yours to service. Report it instead.

instructionSections.heading: Segregating by-product streams
instructionSections.body: Food processing produces several streams of material: edible by-product that the site has approved for a defined use, inedible food waste, general waste, packaging, recyclables, and regulated or chemical waste. Each stream needs its own labelled container, its own route and its own holding point. The reason is simple. When streams are mixed, a single contaminated item can carry risk into ingredients, packaging or a clean zone. The contamination controls in the Safe Food Australia guide (p. 35) also keep chemicals for cleaning and pest control away from food processing areas, which means a waste route should not pass a chemical store or a pest-control station. Plan your route before you start. Use the approved path that keeps waste away from exposed product and wrapped packaging, and avoid carrying a full bin across a clean line. Storage of garbage is covered in Standard 3.2.3, which the guide locates under the garbage storage clause; the wording of that clause was not read for this draft, and it should be checked against the current standard.

instructionSections.heading: Preserving evidence and referring
instructionSections.body: Pest evidence is information for the people who investigate and control pests. If you sweep up droppings, empty an unidentified container or move a nest, you destroy the record of where the activity was and you may spread material. Preserve the scene where it is safe to do so. Close off the immediate area so that work and foot traffic do not move the evidence, and keep people from entering the zone without the responsible person's approval. Do not apply a pest-control product yourself. Record the location, the time, what you saw, how you know, who you told and what action you withheld. If the site's procedure allows photographs, take them without moving items. Then refer the matter to the authorised person and record the hold, the pending decision and the name of the person who will decide next. A hold is not a finding that the area is contaminated, and it is not a clearance. It means the question is open and the responsible person must answer it.

instructionSections.heading: Regulated waste and unknown containers
instructionSections.body: Some waste is regulated because of what it contains, how it reacts or how it can harm people or the environment. A cleaner does not classify waste, decide its route or choose a waste contractor. Those decisions sit with the site's waste procedure and the lawful waste contractor. Victoria's current EPA page on transporting hazardous waste places a general environmental duty on those who carry waste, asks that drivers be trained, and requires that some priority waste be logged in an online tracker and covered by a permission. That guidance is Victorian and is included here only as an example of the kind of control that applies. If a container is unlabelled or its contents are unknown, do not open it, add to it or move it. Stop, record and refer.

instructionSections.heading: Pest-control products and who may use them
instructionSections.body: Pest-control products are regulated. The FSANZ guidance expects a food business to pick products that suit food premises and to keep their labels in view, and it treats pest control as a managed program in which inspections and treatments are logged and any recommended fix is acted on without delay. Only the people authorised by the business and, where required, licensed under state or territory rules may apply a pesticide. A cleaner who finds evidence reports it. A cleaner does not treat it. Where the pests cannot be managed through the site's own program, the business is expected to call in professional help, and that call is made by the authorised person, not by the cleaner.

lessons.title: Pre-operational inspection and sanitation records
learningOutcomes: Distinguish a completed cleaning checklist from environmental monitoring, ATP swabs, microbiological sampling and official production release.
Compare observed conditions with the operator's sign-off checklist without certifying production readiness.
Record unverified tasks clearly, and refuse to sign off a premature restart.

instructionSections.heading: What a checklist can and cannot show
instructionSections.body: A completed cleaning checklist is a record that the listed cleaning steps were carried out and that someone says so. It is useful evidence of work done, and it is one part of the food safety program. It does not prove that micro-organisms are absent, and it does not prove that a line is ready to run. Those are different questions with different evidence. The Safe Food Australia guide to the standards describes cleanliness and the cleaning and sanitising of equipment as separate matters under Standard 3.2.2 (clauses 19 and 20, located from the guide's contents; the clause wording was not read for this draft).
