The guide also quotes the definition of 'clean' in Standard 3.1.1 as a physical test: the surface is clean to touch and free of visible extraneous matter. A surface can pass that physical test and still need verification by other means. Keep the cleaning record, the verification results, the monitoring results and the release decision in separate places in your head and in the record.

instructionSections.heading: Verification tools and what their results mean
instructionSections.body: Several tools are used to check cleaning, and each answers a narrower question than the checklist. The NSW Food Authority guide on environmental swabbing (undated, reference FI170/1303) describes swabs as a way to verify cleaning and sanitation, and notes that counts from swabs, contact plates and dipslides are semi-quantitative. Single results are of limited value; trends over time are more useful. ATP tests detect residue on a surface and give fast feedback, which suits a pre-start check, but the same guide says results are site-specific and are best read as a trend. Contact plates and dipslides are not conclusive for detecting specific pathogens such as Salmonella or Listeria. The guide also advises waiting for the sanitiser's contact time to pass before sampling, commonly five to fifteen minutes, which is a useful example of why timing must be recorded. Importantly, the guide presents sampling as verification and monitoring. It does not say that a test result replaces cleaning or that it is a production release. Your role is to carry out the steps you are assigned, record them, and make sure the right test is done at the right time by the person authorised to do it.

instructionSections.heading: Comparing observed conditions
instructionSections.body: Before a shift starts, compare what you can see with the operator's sign-off checklist. Look at each item and ask whether you have observed it yourself. Where you have seen a step done, record what you saw. Where you have not seen it, or cannot see the area, mark it as not verified. Do not tick a step that you have not observed, and do not carry a tick forward from a previous shift. Be specific about the zone, the time and the method. If a checklist line covers a large item, such as a whole conveyor, note which sections you checked and which you did not reach, for example the underside of a belt. A cleaner's sign-off covers the cleaning and observations that the cleaner made. It is not a release of the line, and it is not a certification that the line is free of hazards. If the checklist asks for a judgement you are not competent to make, record the observation and pass the judgement to the person who is.

instructionSections.heading: Production release and premature restart
instructionSections.body: Production release is a separate decision made by the authorised person under the site's food safety program. It depends on the completed cleaning record, the verification and monitoring results that the program requires, any maintenance that changed the equipment, and the owner's written decision. A line may be restarted only after that decision has been made. A premature restart is one where production resumes while some of those inputs are missing or unresolved. Treat any request to restart early as a stop-work trigger. Where a restart follows maintenance, the earlier sign-off no longer describes the equipment, which is why the plant-state checks in the related degreasing material matter here too. A supervisor's pressure, a customer's deadline or a visual impression that the line looks clean does not change the release process. None of these is a substitute for the test results or the authorised decision.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing a premature restart
instructionSections.body: If someone asks you to sign that a line is ready to restart while tests, monitoring or release decisions are still pending, refuse to sign. Explain plainly what is pending. You might say that the cleaning is recorded, that the results are not back, and that you cannot sign for release. Then record the request, the person who made it, the time, the tasks that are unverified and the person you escalated to. Escalate to the authorised supervisor or food safety owner, and keep the stop in place until they confirm in writing how the matter is resolved. Do not sign a version of the record that describes the line as ready. Do not agree to add a note that cancels the concern. A refusal is a normal and required part of the job, and recording it protects the site, the team and the customers.

instructionSections.heading: Writing a record that can be checked
instructionSections.body: A useful sanitation record shows what was done, where, when, by whom, and how it was checked. Write the date, time, zone, the item checked, the observed condition, the method of checking and your initials. Use plain words. Avoid describing the line as sterile, pathogen-free, allergen-free or clear, because you cannot establish those claims from a cleaning checklist. Mark unverified steps and state why. Corrections should be made by striking through the entry with a single line, initialling it and giving the reason and date, rather than rubbing out or rewriting. Keep the record with the other site records, and retain it for the period the site procedure requires. An auditor or the owner should be able to follow each line from the checklist to the observation to the person who recorded it.

lessons.title: Safe handover, audit and jurisdiction review
learningOutcomes: Prepare an evidence-based closeout package with unresolved items clearly labelled.
Identify the responsible site food-safety authority and the stop-work trigger for a handover.
Refuse a single universal sanitation certificate that spans several jurisdictions.

instructionSections.heading: The closeout package
instructionSections.body: A closeout package is the bundle of records that describes a cleaning job at the point it is handed over. It should show which zones were cleaned, using the site map and the zone names the site uses. It should list the exceptions: areas not reached, equipment not opened, steps not verified and anything removed from scope. It should name who signed each part, and who is responsible for each open item. It should also contain an evidence index that tells the reader where each supporting record is kept, for how long the site keeps it, and who can retrieve it. The package describes the cleaning that was done and the evidence that supports it. It does not describe the site as validated, allergen-free, microbiologically clear or ready for production. Those statements are outside a cleaner's authority, and an owner who reads them may rely on them.

instructionSections.heading: Who holds the food safety responsibility
instructionSections.body: The operator of the food business holds the food safety responsibility for the site, and the operator's food safety program sets out how that responsibility is carried out. The Safe Food Australia guide explains that a food safety program is a written set of controls kept at the premises, and that the standards in the Food Standards Code include evidence requirements for some prescribed activities (Standard 3.2.2A, with the evidence tool at section VII(iii) and the record-keeping attachment at Attachment 2, located from the guide's contents; the clause wording was not read for this draft). The enforcement agency is the state or territory food regulator for the premises. The practical point for a cleaner is simple. Identify the named food-safety owner for the site before you hand anything over, and do not accept a handover that has no named owner.

instructionSections.heading: Why one certificate cannot cover several countries
instructionSections.body: A multinational operator may ask for a single sanitation certificate that covers an Australian site and its export markets. A cleaner cannot issue that document, and cannot assert that a site complies with the law of any other country. Food safety obligations differ between jurisdictions, and the rules of New Zealand, the United States and the United Kingdom are not Australian law. Consumer law also applies to any statement a business makes about its own services. The ACCC's page on false or misleading claims (dated 28 June 2026) treats a claim as needing accuracy, reasonable grounds and evidence to back it. Whether the speaker meant to mislead is not the test, and leaving out a material detail can also produce a misleading impression. A universal certificate that cannot be substantiated for every jurisdiction is therefore a claim the business cannot safely make, and it should go to the food-safety owner for a decision.

instructionSections.heading: Audit readiness without altering records
instructionSections.body: An audit or inspection looks at what the records show, and at whether the records match the work. Your task is to keep the records as they were made. Do not backfill a checklist, do not tidy an entry that was made late, and do not replace a page. If an entry is wrong, correct it using the site's method: a single line through the error, initials, date and reason. If an entry was made after the event, record the date it was made, not the date of the job. If a record is missing, say so in the package and do not recreate it from memory and present it as the original. Present unresolved items honestly, because a clearly labelled gap is easier to manage than a discovered inconsistency. An auditor who finds a gap that was disclosed usually has a simpler conversation than one who finds a gap that was hidden.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer triggers
instructionSections.body: Stop and refer the handover where the food-safety owner has not signed it, where a cross-jurisdiction assertion is being made without an approved basis, or where records are missing or contradict one another. Also stop where unidentified pest contamination or regulated waste is present, as covered in the pest and waste lesson, and where a restart is requested before the release decision has been made, as covered in the pre-operational lesson. Record each stop with the time, the requester, the trigger and the decision that is pending. Do not resolve the stop yourself by changing the record or by asking a colleague to sign on the owner's behalf. The handover waits until the responsible person has decided each item in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Completing the handover
instructionSections.body: A handover is complete when the receiving person has received the closeout package, has read the exceptions and the open items, and has confirmed in writing that they understand who holds each open decision. Both the person who performed the cleaning and the person who received the handover should sign and date it. Keep a copy with the site records and give the receiver a copy if the site procedure requires one. A handover that is signed before the owner has reviewed the open items is incomplete, however complete the cleaning looks. Completing a handover does not give the cleaner any certificate, approval or authority, and it does not make the cleaner an auditor.

lessons.title: Authorisation, task limits and contractor interface
learningOutcomes: Confirm the written authorisation and the limits of the degreasing task before starting.
Identify the interface with other contractors and who controls it.
Stop and refer any task that goes beyond the authorised limit.

instructionSections.heading: What an authorisation is
instructionSections.body: An authorisation is the written permission that tells you what work you may do, where, with which product and method, under whose supervision, and for how long. It is the starting point for every degreasing task. A verbal instruction, a text message or a contractor's assumption is not an authorisation, however sensible it sounds. Before you touch a tool, a container or a surface, read the document in full. Check the named supervisor, the defined area on the site plan, the product and its SDS, the method, the hours, the isolations that the owner has put in place, and the list of exclusions. If any of these is missing or unclear, the task is not yet authorised. Record that and ask the supervisor to complete the document. This lesson does not grant an authorisation, and completing it does not make you the person who gives one.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the limits
instructionSections.body: Limits tell you where your authority stops. A typical degreasing authorisation covers the external surfaces of a named machine, or a defined bay, and excludes the interior of tanks, electrical enclosures, guarding that is not yours to remove, and any product not listed. Read the exclusions as carefully as the scope. Some limits are obvious, such as a request to degrease inside a tank. Others are easy to miss. For example, a task that begins as wiping a panel can become removing a guard to reach a gearbox, and that is a change of scope. Any change needs approval from the named supervisor, in writing, before the new work starts. Confined spaces are a particular case. Where a task involves entering a tank or vessel, the Safe Work Australia confined spaces code requires an entry permit that a competent person issues before entry, specifying the space, the workers, the work period and the controls. A degreasing authorisation does not replace that permit.

instructionSections.heading: The contractor interface
instructionSections.body: Industrial sites often have several contractors working in the same area at the same time, for example maintenance, electrical, production and cleaning. Each party has its own duties under the model WHS laws, and those duties can overlap. The Safe Work Australia guidance on managing WHS risks recognises that several parties can carry the same duty at once, and that a party sharing responsibility for a matter needs to talk with the others about it. It also warns against presuming that someone else has a matter covered, and asks each party to confirm who is doing what. In practice, identify each contractor on the job, the area each controls, and the person who releases each area. Agree the handover between contractors in writing, including the isolation status and any restriction. Do not start work in an area another contractor controls until that contractor has released it to you, and record the release. A release from one contractor does not cover an area they do not control.

instructionSections.heading: Duties you cannot hand off
instructionSections.body: A business that engages you still carries its own duties. The Safe Work Australia WHS duties page sets out the business's core obligations: remove risks where that can be done, and otherwise reduce them to the lowest level that is reasonably practicable, while involving workers in decisions that affect them. The guidance on shared duties also makes clear that a party's obligations stay with that party when work is passed on. This matters for you in two ways. First, you keep your own duty of reasonable care for yourself and others, so you cannot rely on a contractor's word that a hazard is gone. Second, a supervisor cannot give away the duty to check the work by saying that the other party will check it. Each person in the chain needs the information to act on their own duty.

instructionSections.heading: Isolation and whose isolation it is
instructionSections.body: Before cleaning or maintenance on plant, the plant should be isolated, or measures should be in place to prevent it operating by accident. The Safe Work Australia plant code of practice recommends isolating plant before cleaning starts, and where it cannot be isolated, using controlled procedures to prevent accidental operation. It also says that the isolation should cover all potentially hazardous energy, and that the process should include a verification step. Isolation is not something a cleaner can assume. If the isolation status is unknown, the machine is not authorised for your work. Ask the controlling contractor or the responsible supervisor for the isolation record, and confirm that the isolation covers your area.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer
instructionSections.body: Stop and refer when a task goes beyond the authorised scope, when a contractor asks you to start without a written release, when isolation status is unclear, when you are asked to enter a confined space without a permit, when a chemical is not identified on the SDS register, or when you feel pressure to proceed before the question is settled. Stop means stop work in that area and keep people out of it where that is safe. Refer means tell the named supervisor, give them the facts you have observed, and say what you have not been able to verify. Record the request, the limit or gap, the person you informed and the time. Do not decide the question yourself, and do not accept a contractor's assurance in place of the supervisor's written decision.

lessons.title: Plant hazards, guarding and exclusion zones
learningOutcomes: Distinguish ordinary walkways from guarded, moving, elevated, hot and restricted machinery zones.
Recognise that an unguarded machine is a stop, regardless of a request to hurry.
Record the concern and refer to the responsible supervisor and competent plant specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the machinery zones
instructionSections.body: On an industrial site, machinery creates zones: ordinary walkways, guarded areas, moving parts, elevated platforms, hot surfaces and restricted areas. A floor plan shows these zones, and the site decides who may enter each. Check the plan before you move, and do not assume that a zone is open because it looks quiet.

instructionSections.heading: Guarding is a stop
instructionSections.body: A guard is there to keep people away from moving or dangerous parts. If a guard is missing, damaged or bypassed, the machine is not safe to clean near. Under the national plant code, guards have to go back on before plant restarts after maintenance, and plant should not be run with its guarding removed (instrument dated 17 December 2015). A supervisor who says that the cleaning can proceed quickly despite an unguarded conveyor is asking you to work in a stop condition. Refuse, withdraw, and record the request. Any worker may stop unsafe work where they reasonably fear serious harm from an immediate or imminent hazard (Commonwealth WHS Act section 84, compilation dated 1 July 2024).

instructionSections.heading: What a cleaner records and refers
instructionSections.body: Record the equipment or location identifier, the observed concern, the source of the evidence, the people notified and the immediate restriction. Say what is unknown. Ask the responsible supervisor to assign the competent plant specialist. A cleaner does not sign off plant as safe. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

lessons.title: Energy isolation and verification boundaries
learningOutcomes: Explain why isolation of energy sources is done by an authorised person, not the cleaner.
Identify the energy sources that need isolation before cleaning plant.
Refuse to clean or enter plant until isolation has been verified by the authorised person.

instructionSections.heading: Energy sources
instructionSections.body: Plant can hold energy that is not obvious: electrical supply, stored pressure, hydraulic and pneumatic lines, gravity-held loads, stored heat and moving parts that coast after switch-off. Before cleaning plant, the authorised person must identify and isolate these sources, and verify that they are isolated.

instructionSections.heading: Verification
instructionSections.body: Isolation is verified, not assumed. Switching off a control is not isolation. The national plant code treats a lock as the effective isolation device, not a tag alone, and its lock-out procedure includes a trial restart (instrument dated 17 December 2015). The authorised person checks that the energy is removed, and that the machine cannot be restarted while the work is done. Only after verification does the cleaner work, and then only within the agreed area.

instructionSections.heading: The cleaner's boundary
instructionSections.body: A cleaner does not isolate or verify plant on their own authority. The national plant code expects each worker doing cleaning to hold their own lock at an isolation point, under a documented isolation procedure, so a cleaner applies a lock only where the person in control of the plant has set up that procedure and authorised it. Otherwise, refuse to clean or enter plant that has not been verified isolated, and refer the request to the authorised person. Record the request, the status and the time. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

lessons.title: Solvent, vapour and ignition risks
learningOutcomes: Recognise vapour build-up, hot work, ventilation restrictions and fire risk near solvents.
Refer product selection for solvents to a competent specialist.
Stop solvent use where the authority, machine state or chemical controls cannot be established.

instructionSections.heading: Solvents and ignition
instructionSections.body: Many solvents give off vapour that can ignite when it meets a heat source, a spark or an electrical fault. Vapour is heavier than air in some cases and can collect in pits and low areas. Ventilation may be restricted in a plant room. Before any solvent is used, identify the ignition sources, the ventilation and any hot work nearby.

instructionSections.heading: A proposal near heat or electricity
instructionSections.body: A contractor suggests solvent cleaning near hot equipment and an electrical panel. That is a stop condition. Solvent vapour near these sources is a fire risk, and the cleaner cannot establish that the controls are in place. Withhold the task, record the proposal, and refer to the competent specialist and the site.

instructionSections.heading: Product and record
instructionSections.body: Product selection for solvents is referred to a competent chemical specialist, not chosen by the cleaner from the shelf. Check the label and the SDS, and record the product name and the controls that the specialist confirms. Safety details for every chemical, hazardous or not, need to reach all people on site, and they sit on the label and the SDS. The register has to cover hazardous chemicals that are used, handled or kept on site, each entry needs an up-to-date SDS attached, and the register must be easy for workers to reach (Safe Work Australia, no date shown). Check your state or territory regulator for extra rules. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

lessons.title: PPE, hygiene and exposure escalation
learningOutcomes: Recognise exposure symptoms and follow the site's emergency and escalation route.
Refuse to use an unidentified agent or an unknown glove type.
Record the exposure concern and refer it through the site response route.

instructionSections.heading: How degreasing chemicals reach the body
instructionSections.body: Industrial degreasers include solvents, alkaline cleaners, emulsifiers and water-based products, and each carries its own hazards. Exposure can happen through the skin, through the eyes, by breathing vapour or mist, and, less often, by swallowing material that has been carried on the hands. Splashes during pouring or spraying, soaked rags, and open containers in a warm or poorly ventilated area all increase the chance of contact. The safety data sheet for each product is the main source of information. It describes the health effects, the hazardous ingredients, safe handling and storage, emergency procedures and first aid, and the PPE that the supplier recommends. The Safe Work Australia code on managing hazardous chemicals says that the current SDS should be readily accessible to the workers who use the chemical, and near the work area. If you cannot find the SDS for a product in front of you, you do not have the information you need to start work with it.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising exposure
instructionSections.body: Symptoms depend on the product and the route of exposure. Skin contact can cause dryness, cracking, redness, burning or a rash. Eye contact can cause stinging, watering, blurred vision or more serious damage. Breathing vapour can cause headache, dizziness, nausea, a sore throat or cough, or a feeling of being unwell. Some effects appear later, which is why a person who feels fine after a splash should still report it. Do not decide for yourself that a symptom is trivial, and do not wait to see whether it passes. Know the site's emergency route, the first-aid contact and the location of the eyewash and first-aid kit before you begin any task. Follow the first-aid section of the SDS for the product you were using, and follow the site's emergency policy.

instructionSections.heading: PPE chosen from the SDS, not from habit
instructionSections.body: PPE is the last line of protection, not the first. The Safe Work Australia code ranks controls so that elimination, substitution, isolation and engineering controls come before administrative controls, and PPE comes last, to be relied on mainly where higher controls are not yet in place or are not enough. In practice, that means ventilation, enclosure and a safer product should be considered before a glove is chosen. Where PPE is needed, it must suit the product. The code says gloves should be chosen for the best resistance to the chemical in use, because some gloves resist some solvents and fail with others. It also notes that the SDS and the product label may specify PPE, for example a particular glove material for hydrocarbon or chlorinated solvents. Choose the glove the SDS or the site procedure names, check it for damage before use, and replace it when it is torn, swollen or contaminated. Eye protection and face protection are chosen the same way, from the SDS and the task. If you are offered an unknown glove for an unidentified agent, refuse it, ask for the SDS and the approved PPE, and record the request.

instructionSections.heading: Hygiene that protects you and others
instructionSections.body: Hygiene reduces the chance of carrying residue away from the work area. Remove contaminated PPE before you leave the work area and store it where the site requires. Do not wear degreasing gloves or overalls into a break room, a canteen or a vehicle. Wash your hands and face before eating, drinking or smoking, and do not eat or drink in the degreasing area. Launder contaminated work clothing separately, as the site procedure states, and do not take it home with other laundry. Keep disposable PPE in a closed bin, not on the floor. If you handle rags or absorbents that have been used with a product, treat them as contaminated until the SDS and the site procedure say otherwise. These habits are simple, but they are the ones most often missed, and they matter most at the end of a long shift.

instructionSections.heading: Escalating a possible exposure
instructionSections.body: If you or a colleague may have been exposed, stop the task at once and move away from the source, using the route the procedure sets out. Follow the emergency route and the first-aid section of the SDS. Tell the named supervisor immediately, and make sure the person affected is seen by the first-aid contact. Record the time, the product if it is known, the route of exposure if it is known, the symptoms, the first aid given, and the people informed. Keep the product container or its label, if it can be done safely, so that the product can be identified. Do not return to the area to finish the task until the supervisor has confirmed that the area is safe and the controls have been checked. The site's incident procedure governs what happens next, and the report is made whether or not the symptoms seem minor.

instructionSections.heading: Register, records and health monitoring
instructionSections.body: A site that uses hazardous chemicals must keep a register of them, and each chemical on the register must have a current SDS. The Safe Work Australia code says the register should be kept at the workplace, be readily accessible to workers and others who may be affected, and be kept up to date, with an SDS that is no more than five years old. Health monitoring is a separate duty, which applies to some exposures and not others. A site's occupational health advice, or the advice of the person who holds the monitoring duty, decides whether monitoring is needed.

lessons.title: Waste oil, absorbents and environmental controls
learningOutcomes: Distinguish approved waste containers and authorised handlers from unverified oils and absorbents.
Stop where a waste container has no label or approved collection path.
Record the concern and refer waste decisions to the competent person.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as waste in a degreasing job
instructionSections.body: Degreasing produces several kinds of waste. There is spent degreaser, rinse water that has picked up oil or solvent, rags and wipes soaked with product, absorbents laid down under spills, waste oil drained from machines, sludge from tanks, and empty containers that still hold residue. Each of these can carry hazards of its own, such as flammability, toxicity or environmental harm, and the risk depends on what it has been mixed with. The classification and disposal route are decided by the competent person and the lawful waste contractor, not by the cleaner. Your job is to recognise that a material is waste, keep it in the right container, label it accurately as the site requires, and refer any question about what it is or where it goes. The Safe Work Australia code on hazardous chemicals says that containers holding waste, and decanted containers, must be correctly labelled, and that chemicals of unknown content must be disposed of under the local waste requirements. That is a point of law for the site to confirm, not something a cleaner decides on the spot.

instructionSections.heading: Containers, labels and storage
instructionSections.body: A waste container should have a lid that closes, be made of a material that suits the content, and carry a label that says what is inside and what hazard it presents, in the form the site requires. Keep containers closed when they are not being filled. Store them where they cannot be knocked over, where spills can be contained, and away from ignition sources, heat and drains. Keep incompatible materials apart, so that a container of oxidising material is not stored with a flammable one, and do not place chemicals where they could contaminate food or personal items. The Safe Work Australia code also advises keeping chemicals clear of incompatible materials, including when stacking them. Historical Victorian guidance from 2009 described bulk tanks or 200 litre drums in an enclosed, bunded area, preferably under cover, or on spill containment pallets.

instructionSections.heading: Waste oil and oily absorbents
instructionSections.body: Waste oil and oily absorbents need special care. Used engine oil, gear oil and similar fluids are waste that must not be poured down a drain, put onto soil or burnt in an unlicensed fire. The 2009 Victorian guidance for motor and degreasing workshops said that oily rags, sand and sawdust contaminated with oil or solvent should be stored in a separate bin until a suitable disposal route is found, and that used oil filters should be recycled rather than sent to landfill. Current EPA Victoria guidance on transporting hazardous waste (updated 14 May 2025) does not name waste oil, so it does not settle the question either. The practical rule for a cleaner is firm. Keep oily rags out of ordinary bins, keep waste oil in its approved container, and refer the choice of route to the competent person.

instructionSections.heading: Environmental controls and spills
instructionSections.body: In Victoria, the EPA's general environmental duty (updated 4 August 2026) asks businesses to deal with the risk of harm from their waste or pollution, removing what can be removed and reducing the rest, to the extent that is reasonably practicable. That applies to waste oil and absorbents as much as to any other waste. In practice, keep waste sealed and within the approved area, keep spills off the ground and out of drains and stormwater, and use the approved absorbent to contain a spill. Do not hose an oil spill toward a drain, and do not use a drain as a way out of a spill. Stop the source where it is safe to do so, keep people clear, and report the spill immediately to the supervisor. Record what was spilled, roughly how much, where it went, and what was done.

instructionSections.heading: Stop, record and refer
instructionSections.body: Stop where a container has no label, where the content is not known, where the collection path is not approved, or where a container is in poor condition or leaking. Do not add material to the container, do not move it, and do not decide where it goes. Keep people away from the container where that is safe. Record the location, the label status, the lid condition, the visible condition, the source of what you know, the people informed and the restriction you put in place. State what is unknown, rather than guessing. Refer the matter to the supervisor, who should assign the competent person and the lawful waste contractor. Do not sign off a disposal route yourself, and do not accept a verbal assurance from another contractor that the material is fine to remove.

instructionSections.heading: Transport and handover of waste
instructionSections.body: Waste leaves a site with a carrier, and the carrier must be authorised for the waste type. Current EPA Victoria guidance on transporting hazardous waste (updated 14 May 2025) sets out the same general duty for carriers, asks that drivers complete waste-handling training, and notes that certain priority waste has to be tracked online in the EPA's Waste Tracker and covered by a permission. The site receiving the waste must also be authorised to take it. A cleaner should not load, carry or transport waste unless the site and the carrier have confirmed in writing that the cleaner is authorised to do so and the training and permissions are in place. This lesson does not grant any transport or disposal authority.

lessons.title: Work coordination, change control and simultaneous operations
learningOutcomes: Recognise an unexpected restart, another contractor entering or a shifted boundary as a stop-and-reauthorise event.
Explain why a cleaning sign-off does not survive a later change to the machine.
Record the change and refer the restart to the authorised person.

instructionSections.heading: What a sign-off describes
instructionSections.body: A cleaning sign-off describes the machine as it was when the cleaning was checked. It records a state: the plant was isolated or otherwise made safe, the boundaries were agreed, the people and areas were known, and the cleaning was observed. The sign-off is a record of that moment, and it is only as good as the conditions behind it. Once those conditions change, the sign-off no longer describes the situation in front of you. Many degreasing incidents, and many near misses, begin with someone acting on an earlier record as if it were current. Treat every sign-off as dated and conditional. When the state of the machine, the boundary or the people working around it changes, the question of whether it is safe to proceed has to be asked again by the people who have the authority to answer it.

instructionSections.heading: Events that call for a stop and reauthorisation
instructionSections.body: Some events always trigger a stop. An unexpected restart of the plant, even a brief one, is a trigger, because the energy state has changed without the knowledge of the people nearby. Another contractor entering the area, or starting work on the same machine, is a trigger, because their work may depend on a different isolation or may affect yours. A shifted boundary is a trigger, because the area you cleared may no longer be the area you were authorised to work in. Other triggers include a guard removed or refitted, a change in the product or method, the isolation being added or removed, an alarm or fault that was not present at sign-off, and the end of a shift where handover is incomplete. When a trigger happens, stop work in the affected area, keep people clear where that is safe, and do not resume until the authorised person has confirmed the state of the machine and the authority to proceed.

instructionSections.heading: Isolation, guarding and restart
instructionSections.body: The Safe Work Australia plant code of practice recommends that plant is isolated before cleaning or maintenance begins, and where it cannot be isolated, that controlled procedures prevent accidental operation. It also says that isolation should cover every potentially hazardous energy source, including electricity, stored energy and gravity, and that a verification step is needed to confirm the isolation worked. The code describes lock-out as the most effective method, with each worker using their own lock, tag and key, and it does not treat a tag alone as an isolation device. Verification is done by trying to start the plant from a safe position, so that you confirm the isolation before you rely on it. Where guarding is removed for cleaning or maintenance, the code says the energy source should be eliminated first, and the plant should not restart until the guarding has been put back. A cleaner should not do any of these steps. A cleaner should confirm that they have been done, by the person who controls the plant, before work starts.

instructionSections.heading: Maintenance changes after sign-off
instructionSections.body: Consider a case where maintenance personnel change the machine's configuration after the cleaning sign-off. They may have adjusted a valve, swapped a part, changed a setpoint or taken a guard off to reach a component. The cleaner cannot know from outside the machine whether it is now safe to be near it, and should not assume that the change was minor. Work stops until the machine state and the authority to proceed are confirmed by the competent site personnel. The sign-off is not reinstated by a conversation with the maintenance team. It is replaced by a new check, recorded at the time it was done, against the new machine state. The same principle applies to the confined space code, which says that an entry permit should be re-validated if the person in direct control changes, if the work is interrupted or if new hazards appear. The sign-off and the permit are both tied to the conditions they were issued under.

instructionSections.heading: Simultaneous operations and shared responsibility
instructionSections.body: When several parties work on the same plant or in the same area, each has its own duty, and those duties overlap. The Safe Work Australia guidance on managing risks says that parties who share responsibility should consult, co-operate and co-ordinate, and that a party should not assume another is handling a matter. In practice, agree at the start of the shift which party controls which area and which isolation, and how changes will be communicated. Confirm each change with the party that made it. A verbal assurance from a contractor that a machine is fine is not confirmation from the person who controls it. Where there is a dispute about who holds a control, stop and refer it to the site supervisor who holds the overall control of the area.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the change and handing over
instructionSections.body: Record each change at the time it is noticed. Note the time, the area, the machine or boundary involved, what changed, what you observed, the source of your information, the people you told, and the restriction you applied. Say what you do not know. Do not describe the machine as safe, clear or ready. Compare what you can see against the planned and authorised housekeeping only, not against what you hope is still true. Handover is restricted until the responsible owner has confirmed the outstanding restricted work, the state of the machine, and who may decide on restart and on any chemical matter. If the handover is to a new shift, the outgoing person should note the open items clearly, and the incoming person should not start on the basis of the old sign-off.

lessons.title: Release, handover and no-certification claims
learningOutcomes: Describe what a cleaner's handover covers, and what it does not.
Refuse a request to certify plant or chemical safety.
Record exclusions and restricted work in a handover that the owner can verify.

instructionSections.heading: What a cleaner's handover covers
instructionSections.body: A cleaner's handover is a factual account of the housekeeping and inspection work that was carried out, with the areas, the methods and the products named. It lists what was cleaned, what was looked at, what was seen, and how it was checked. It lists the exclusions, which are the parts of the job that were not done, could not be reached or were removed from scope. It lists the restricted work that remains open, and it names the person who holds each open decision. Above all, it says what the handover is not. It does not describe the plant as safe to operate, the chemicals as cleared for disposal or reuse, or the area as released for production or restart. Those are decisions for the owner and the competent person, and they are made on evidence that the cleaner's handover does not provide.

instructionSections.heading: Why a cleaning completion is not a certificate
instructionSections.body: A completed clean is a record of work, not a statement about the safety of the plant. A cleaner who has wiped a machine has not tested its isolation, verified its controls, assessed its chemicals or checked its guarding. The handover should make that distinction plain. Where a document is presented to a customer or the owner as a statement about the safety, condition or compliance of a plant or product, it is a representation the business is making. The ACCC's page on false or misleading claims (dated 28 June 2026) treats such statements as needing accuracy, reasonable grounds and evidence behind them, and it does not treat the speaker's intention as the test. A cleaner should not sign a document that says the plant is safe or the chemicals are cleared when the cleaner has no evidence of those things.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing a certificate and referring it
instructionSections.body: If someone asks you to sign a certificate that a plant or chemical is safe, or that a degreasing area may restart, refuse. Keep the refusal calm and factual. You might explain that your handover covers the cleaning and inspection you performed, that it does not cover the isolation, the controls or the chemical assessment, and that the decision belongs to the competent person. Refer the request in writing to the person who holds that decision, and name the document you were asked to sign. Record the request, the requester, the time, the document, your response and the referral. Do not offer a softer version of the certificate, such as one that says the work was 'done to a safe standard', because that phrasing still describes safety and is not supported by your evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Exclusions and restricted work
instructionSections.body: List exclusions and restricted work plainly so that the next person knows what remains open. Every area not cleaned should be named, with the reason it was not done. Every item not inspected should be listed, along with what stopped the inspection, such as access, an active isolation or a missing permit. Restricted work should be described in terms of what cannot be done until someone else decides, and who that person is. A handover that hides an exclusion is a false record, even if each line in it is accurate, because the reader will assume the work is complete. If the owner asks you to remove an exclusion from the handover to make it look finished, refuse and record the request. The exclusion stays in the record until the owner, in writing, confirms it has been resolved.

instructionSections.heading: A handover the owner can check
instructionSections.body: A handover the owner can check has an evidence index that points to where each supporting record is kept, a date and time on each entry, the names of the people who did each part, and the signature of both the person who performed the work and the person who received the handover. Corrections are made with a single line through the error, initials, a date and a reason, so that the original is still readable. Records are not replaced, backfilled or rewritten after the event. If a record is missing, state that in the handover and explain what has been done to find it. Photographs are taken only where the site procedure and the owner permit them, and they should show the condition without moving anything. The owner should be able to read the handover and decide, on the evidence, what is still to be done.

instructionSections.heading: Restart and release belong to someone else
instructionSections.body: Release for restart and clearance for chemical use are decisions made by the owner and the competent person, after they have checked the plant, the isolation, the guarding, the controls and the chemical assessment. The Safe Work Australia guidance on managing WHS risks makes clear that a duty holder keeps its obligations when it passes work on, and warns against presuming that another party has a matter covered. For a cleaner, this means the handover supports the owner's decision and does not replace it. Once the handover is signed, the restart decision still needs its own record, made by the person who holds it. The cleaner should not be asked to make that decision, and should refuse to be drawn into making it in the course of a handover conversation.

lessons.title: Authority, scope and specialist eligibility
learningOutcomes: Identify the authority, scope and specialist eligibility for kitchen exhaust work.
Separate the accessible surface tasks a cleaner may do from specialist work.
Refuse and refer any task that needs specialist eligibility the cleaner does not hold.

instructionSections.heading: Why authority comes before the cloth
instructionSections.body: A commercial kitchen exhaust system is one connected arrangement. It starts with the grease-capturing canopy or hood, runs through filters and plenums, continues into ductwork, reaches one or more fans, and often ends above the roof. Fire-suppression components may sit within or alongside that arrangement, depending on the site. Because the parts are connected, a task that looks small, such as wiping the underside of a hood, can change the condition of another part of the system. Before you pick up a tool, you need two answers in writing: who has authorised the task, and which parts of the system the authorisation covers. This lesson teaches you to find those answers, to classify the task, and to decide whether you may do it, need to refer it, or must decline it. It does not teach you to do any specialist task. It teaches you where your own work stops.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the authority and the scope
instructionSections.body: The authority normally comes from the person who controls the premises or the exhaust system, such as the site operator, the facilities manager or the owner of the building. A tenant's chef, a shift supervisor or a contractor's site lead may give day-to-day instructions, but each of them should be able to show where their authority comes from. The scope is the written description of what the job includes. A good scope names the parts of the system in scope, the parts excluded, the access that is allowed, the method that may be used and the products that may be used. If a scope says only 'clean the hood', you should not assume that filters, ducts, fans or roof components are included. In this course, the working categories are accessible surface, ductwork, fans, fire suppression and roof or high access. These categories are teaching labels, not legal categories. The written scope and the site's own procedures decide which category a task falls into, and where the scope is unclear you ask before you act.

instructionSections.heading: Eligibility, not experience
instructionSections.body: Eligibility is the set of qualifications, licences, competency records, insurances and approvals that a person must hold before they may perform a particular task. It is separate from experience. A cleaner who has cleaned many hoods has not, by that fact alone, become eligible for internal duct work, fan work or fire-suppression work. Where a task falls in a specialist layer, the question to answer is which eligibility the site, the regulator or the contract requires, and whether the person doing the task holds it. That answer is recorded by the site or the contractor, and the cleaner checks it rather than assuming it. Completing this lesson does not give you any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and it does not make you a specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Classifying a task before you start
instructionSections.body: Each task you are asked to do should be given a short classification before work begins. Write down the task in plain words, the part of the system it touches, the layer it falls in, and whether the written scope includes that part. Then decide one of three outcomes. The first outcome is to proceed, which is allowed only when the task is in the accessible surface layer, is inside the written scope, uses the approved method and products, and does not require removing a panel, opening a duct, isolating equipment or working above the roof. The second outcome is to hold, which means you stop, make the area safe as the site requires, and ask the authority for a written decision. The third outcome is to refer or decline, which applies when the task is a specialist layer you are not eligible to perform. A verbal request does not change the outcome. Any change must be in writing, and the eligibility check must be recorded before the task starts.

instructionSections.heading: Referral and the record
instructionSections.body: A referral is a handover, not a dismissal. When you decline a task, state what was asked, which layer it belongs to, why it is outside your scope or eligibility, and who you have told. The authorised contractor or the site's competent person then takes the task forward. Record the date, time, the person who asked, the person informed, and any instruction given. Do not promise that a specialist will 'fix' the system, and do not suggest what the specialist will find. If a client asks you to do the duct while you are on site for the hood, decline the duct, keep the hood work within its scope if that is what was agreed, and send the duct request to the authorised contractor through the agreed route. Keep the referral record with the job file so that the scope is clear to the next person who comes to the site.

lessons.title: Fire triangle and grease accumulation
learningOutcomes: Explain how cooking heat, ignition sources, exhaust airflow and grease deposits contribute to fire risk.
Recognise that a clean-looking canopy is not evidence of a clean, safe duct.
Escalate visible or reported grease accumulation for an approved fire-risk assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Why grease is a fire risk
instructionSections.body: A fire needs fuel, heat and an oxygen source, and in a kitchen exhaust system the grease deposit is the fuel. Cooking produces heat, the exhaust carries grease vapour into the hood and duct, and the vapour condenses on the cooler surfaces. Over time a layer of grease builds up in the filters, the hood and the duct. Visible grease is a warning. Food premises rules also expect grease buildup to be controlled rather than left to collect (FSANZ, page updated 30 September 2025). Grease in sections you cannot see is a risk you cannot judge from the kitchen floor.

instructionSections.heading: Appearance is not evidence
instructionSections.body: A canopy can look clean while a maintenance record lists inaccessible, grease-laden duct sections. Do not treat the visible part as proof of the whole system. Separate what you can see, what a record says, and what remains unknown, and label each. Where the records and the appearance disagree, the disagreement is itself a reason to stop and escalate.

instructionSections.heading: Escalation
instructionSections.body: Escalate immediately for visible or reported grease accumulation where there is no approved fire-risk assessment. Record what you observed, where, and when, and inform the site operator. Do not clean the inaccessible sections yourself, and do not invent a maintenance interval or a safe grease level. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

lessons.title: System anatomy and access boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify hoods, filters, ducts, fans and concealed or inaccessible sections of an exhaust system.
Separate what is observed from what is reported and what is unknown.
Refuse to sign off a system beyond the scope of the work order, and refer the question to the owner.

instructionSections.heading: The parts of the system
instructionSections.body: A commercial kitchen exhaust system usually includes a hood over the cooking line, grease filters within the hood, a duct that carries air away, a fan, and an outlet. Parts of the duct may run through walls, ceilings and roofs, so they are concealed or inaccessible from the kitchen floor. Knowing where the accessible parts end and the concealed parts begin is the first boundary in any exhaust task.

instructionSections.heading: Observation and assumption
instructionSections.body: Consider a work order that covers a hood, while a contractor proposes to sign off the whole connected system. Work through what you observe, what you are only told, and what remains unknown, and label each separately. A clean hood does not show that the duct is clean or that the fan is safe. A missing or conflicting authority is grounds to withhold action, so the sign-off is refused and the question is referred.

instructionSections.heading: Access and referral
instructionSections.body: Use the duct and access diagram to decide whether an ordinary cleaner may carry out the permitted surface task, or must stop and refer. Describe the components as you see them, without climbing, entering ductwork or operating any component. Escalate at once where ducting is inaccessible, where system ownership is unclear, or where access would need an alteration to the building or the system.

instructionSections.heading: Recording without certifying
instructionSections.body: Complete a dated record with the site zone, the authorising party, the observations, the excluded access, the evidence gaps, the referral owner and the response requested. Do not backfill permissions, and do not issue a compliance certificate. Whether the system is safe is decided by the owner and the competent person, not the cleaner.

lessons.title: Standards, local codes and contract scope
learningOutcomes: Identify the standards and codes that a site instruction cites, and their source and edition.
Explain that a course reference is a lead for specialist review, not a binding site rule.
Read the contract scope and record the adopted local requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Why the citation matters
instructionSections.body: A site instruction often names a standard, a code or a local requirement. The name sounds authoritative, and it is tempting to act on it without checking what it says, which edition applies or whether the site has adopted it. That shortcut causes three kinds of error. You may follow a superseded edition. You may apply a national text where a state has changed it. You may treat a general reference as a rule for the specific site. This lesson does not teach the content of any standard. It teaches you to identify the document, to check its status, to record what the site relies on, and to refer any doubt to the person who can decide. The reader of this lesson is not expected to interpret an engineering standard. Interpretation belongs to the competent person named in the contract.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the source and its edition
instructionSections.body: Each citation needs five pieces of information on the record: the document type (for example a standard, a code, a regulation, a council requirement, a contract clause or a manufacturer's instruction), its number or title, its edition or amendment, its date of issue, and where you obtained it. Standards are revised over time, and a revised edition can replace an earlier one. The course's research notes list two related Australian standards for kitchen exhaust fire systems, AS 1851 on routine service of fire protection systems and AS/NZS 1668.1 on a related installation topic. A local council, a fire authority or a state adoption may apply a different text.

instructionSections.heading: Course references are leads
instructionSections.body: Course material, including this course, can point you to a standard, a topic or a question. It is not the site's rule. A course note may give example numbers, such as a grease depth or a cleaning interval, to show how a record might look. Those numbers are illustrations. They are not legal thresholds and must not be quoted as the threshold at a site. A legal inspection interval, a safe grease level or a fire-compliance result is set by the owner, the regulator or the competent person for the site, and recorded in the site documents. When a course reference is useful, record it as a lead, note what question it raises, and send that question to the competent person for review.

instructionSections.heading: Contract scope and the adopted local requirements
instructionSections.body: The contract defines what the cleaner has agreed to do. Read it alongside the site instruction. Look for the scope, the exclusions, the standard of finish, the method limits, the products allowed, the access arrangements and any clause that adopts a named standard or local requirement. Record the adopted local requirements as the site has stated them, with the document reference. Where the contract and the site instruction disagree, or where a citation conflicts with another citation, do not decide the conflict yourself. Refer it to the contract owner, record the conflict and the referral, and hold the affected task until the owner confirms the position in writing. A contract can allocate work and set standards between the parties. Until that question is answered, treat the legal duty as still applying, and send the question to the competent person, not to the cleaner.

instructionSections.heading: Duties are shared, so the record is shared
instructionSections.body: Under the model work health and safety framework, a person conducting a business or undertaking has a primary duty to manage risks so far as is reasonably practicable, and where more than one party has a duty for the same risk, each keeps its own responsibility and must consult and coordinate with the others. Safe Work Australia's model code on biological hazards restates this shared-duty approach in its section on duty holders. For this lesson, the practical point is that the cleaner's record is one part of the wider site record. Send the citation, the conflict and the adopted requirement to the other duty holders in writing, so that the site does not rely on a single person's memory.

lessons.title: Initial survey and access planning
learningOutcomes: Recognise that safe specialist work depends on documented access, hazards, fall prevention, isolation and site operations planning.
Identify the authorised contractor, the evidence owner and the escalation decision.
Hold a task where safe access, authorisation or specialist competence is missing.

instructionSections.heading: Access before the survey
instructionSections.body: A survey of an exhaust system depends on safe access. Some fans and sections sit on roofs, at height, or in spaces that are hot. A fan that looks reachable may only be reachable by crossing an unprotected roof edge. Before anyone goes up or in, confirm the access route, the fall protection, the heat conditions and the authority for the work. The national falls code says fall controls are needed whatever the height and singles out roofs with fragile material for particular attention; it also addresses guard rails at roof edges (instrument dated 17 December 2015). Routine housekeeping does not include specialist survey, removal or certification.

instructionSections.heading: Observed, reported and unknown
instructionSections.body: Work through what is observed, what is only reported and what remains unknown, and label each assumption separately. A missing or conflicting authority is a reason to withhold action. Do not read a surface appearance as proof of the condition of the whole system.

instructionSections.heading: Holding the task
instructionSections.body: Use the inspection hold sheet to decide whether an ordinary cleaner may carry out the expressly permitted administrative or surface task, or must stop and refer. Hold the task when safe access, authorisation or specialist competence is missing. Escalate at once for uncontrolled work at height, or unsafe access to fans, roof spaces or ducts. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

lessons.title: Plant shutdown and protected systems
learningOutcomes: Identify which parties hold authority over electrical, gas, ventilation and fire-suppression dependencies.
Separate what is observed from what is assumed when a shutdown is proposed.
Stop and refer any shutdown, bypass or re-energisation to the site-authorised competent person.

instructionSections.heading: Dependencies that cannot be assumed
instructionSections.body: Exhaust fans, gas supplies, electrical controls and fire-suppression systems depend on one another. Switching one off can leave another unprotected. Routine housekeeping is not inspection, removal or certification of an exhaust system. Before any task that touches the system, identify who holds the authority for each dependency, and get that authority in writing.

instructionSections.heading: A proposed bypass is a stop
instructionSections.body: Suppose a kitchen team offers to silence the suppression system temporarily to speed up cleaning. That is an unauthorised bypass, and it is a stop-work trigger. Note what you can observe, what you were told, and what remains unknown. Do not treat a clean-looking surface as evidence that the duct or the system is safe. A missing or conflicting authority is grounds to withhold action.

instructionSections.heading: Standards and local requirements
instructionSections.body: Site instructions cite standards and local requirements. Compare the site instruction with its source and its effective edition before relying on it. Treat course references as leads for specialist review, and not as binding site rules. Do not state a legal inspection interval, a safe grease level or a fire compliance result that you have not seen in a verified document.

instructionSections.heading: Boundary and handover
instructionSections.body: Refer shutdown and re-energisation to the site-authorised competent personnel. Electrical isolation, fire-suppression interference, live duct access, rooftop work, hot equipment and degreasing are outside a cleaner's scope. Record the site zone, the authorising party, the observations, the excluded access and the referral owner, and escalate at once for live electrical or mechanical plant, or any bypass of suppression or interlocks.

lessons.title: Specialist cleaning method boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify which cleaning methods sit within routine boundaries and which are specialist methods.
Explain why a specialist method is not used by a general cleaner.
Refuse to offer or agree to a specialist method without eligibility and written scope.

instructionSections.heading: Method is a boundary, not a preference
instructionSections.body: When people talk about cleaning an exhaust system, they often name a method: wipe, soak, scrape, brush, spray, foam, steam, pressure-wash or 'degrease'. Each method carries a different risk. A wipe on an accessible hood surface is a different task from a brush run through a duct, and a foam applied in an enclosed canopy void is different again. The method you choose decides what you touch, what you disturb, what you wet, what you spread, and what chemical you expose yourself and others to. For that reason, the method is a boundary, and you must check it before you choose a tool. This lesson separates the methods that sit within a routine boundary from those that are specialist methods. It also explains how to refuse a specialist method politely and in writing, without offering it as a favour.

instructionSections.heading: Routine boundary and specialist methods
instructionSections.body: A routine method is one that the written scope and the site procedure both allow for an accessible surface, with a product named in the site's approved list and a safety data sheet on file. In practice, that can include wiping an accessible hood surface with an approved detergent, and cleaning removable filters in the place the site designates. Those examples are teaching examples. The site decides what is routine, and it must be written down. A specialist method is one that reaches into concealed or connected parts of the system, changes the system's condition, requires isolation, opening of access panels, use of equipment that is not approved for the site, or chemistry outside the approved list. Internal duct cleaning by brush, air or mechanical means is specialist. So are fan internals, fire-suppression components, and any roof or high-access work. Chemical methods for concealed or heavily fouled surfaces are specialist unless the site has approved them and the person applying them is eligible. When a method is not clearly routine, treat it as specialist until the site says otherwise.

instructionSections.heading: Detergent, degreaser and sanitiser are different tasks
instructionSections.body: Chemistry is part of the method. Detergents remove dirt and grease from a surface but do not, on their own, kill micro-organisms. Sanitisers destroy micro-organisms, but some sanitisers must be rinsed off and others are food-safe only when used as directed. Degreasers are formulated to dissolve heavy oily residue and are often more aggressive. Western Australia's health guidance for food premises describes this difference between detergents and sanitisers, and gives example heat-and-chemical steps for food-contact utensils and surfaces; those steps are a food-premises practice, not an exhaust-cleaning method, and the Food Standards Code clauses that the guidance cites were not read for this lesson. For exhaust work, the question is simpler: which product is approved for this surface, what does its safety data sheet say about handling, dilution, ventilation and disposal, and is the product within the scope you were given? If the answer to any of those is unclear, the method is not routine.

instructionSections.heading: Why a general cleaner does not take on specialist methods
instructionSections.body: A general cleaner may be competent at routine surface work and still be outside the eligibility, equipment and authority needed for a specialist method. Specialist methods can spread contamination into areas that were not cleaned, disturb grease that was previously stable, damage components that protect against fire, or create a hazard for the next person who opens the system. The specialist also needs to see the condition of the system before work starts, and that often means access the cleaner does not have. This is why the question is not 'can I do it?' but 'am I eligible and authorised to do it, in writing, for this part of the system?' When the answer is no, the method is declined and referred. Declining is not a failure of service. It protects the customer, the site and the cleaner, and it keeps the record accurate.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing and referring a specialist method
instructionSections.body: When a client or supervisor asks for a specialist method, state the method you have been asked to use, say which boundary it crosses, and say what you are able to do within your scope. Do not offer a 'quick version' of the specialist method, and do not agree to try it. Give the request to the person who can approve a change of scope, and record it. If the request comes from a sales conversation, the cleaner should not quote a specialist price or promise a result. Keep the message short and factual. A written method change, if approved, should name the method, the layer, the products, the people who will do the work, the eligibility held, the access arrangements and the exclusions. Until that document exists, the specialist method is not authorised.

lessons.title: Grease waste, runoff and environmental controls
learningOutcomes: Recognise grease residues and greasy washwater as fire and contamination hazards.
Identify approved waste handling and wastewater protections.
Stop an unapproved discharge, and route waste decisions to the site operator and a lawful waste contractor.

instructionSections.heading: Where the grease goes
instructionSections.body: Kitchen exhaust cleaning removes a material that has been building up for a long time. It is oily, it contains food residue, and it is often mixed with detergent and hot water when it is loosened. Every step of the job creates a waste stream: the grease scraped from a canopy, the saturated filter wash, the rinse water that runs down a drain, the rags and absorbent material, and the containers that hold the residue until it is collected. Each stream has its own risk. Grease that is left in a bin near a heat source is a fire risk. Washwater that enters a stormwater grate reaches the environment without treatment. Greasy washwater that enters a sewer without the right pre-treatment can block pipes and breach trade waste conditions. The job is therefore not finished when the surface is clean. It is finished when every waste stream has been handled, stored and recorded in a way the site operator has approved.

instructionSections.heading: Fire and contamination hazards of greasy waste
instructionSections.body: NSW Fire and Rescue's restaurant guidance identifies the ignition of fatty residue in hoods and ducting as a risk, and the same logic applies to waste that has been removed from the system but is still oily. Keep greasy waste in closed, labelled containers, away from cooking equipment, heat sources and electrical outlets, and out of direct sun. Do not store rags soaked in grease in a pile. Do not leave a bucket of greasy washwater standing near an open flame or a fryer exhaust. The fire hazard is the reason for the storage rule, and the contamination hazard is the reason for the discharge rule. Both are the site operator's responsibility to control, and the cleaner's responsibility to report when they see a breach.

instructionSections.heading: Trade waste and approved pre-treatment
instructionSections.body: Greasy washwater from a food premises may be a regulated trade waste, depending on the premises and the utility. Trade waste rules are set by the water authority or the council that serves the premises, and the rules differ between utilities. Sydney Water's published guidance for food businesses states that a grease trap or arrestor should be sized to the maximum hourly flow, installed by a licensed plumber, fitted with the lid or cover the manufacturer specifies, and kept with overhead clearance at least equal to its deepest part so that it can be cleaned and inspected safely. The same guidance says that unlisted pre-treatment products may have to be removed. That guidance does not say who must maintain the unit, and it gives no cleaning or pump-out frequency. For this lesson, the principle is that a pre-treatment device is a protection that must not be bypassed, blocked or opened by a cleaner without the site's authority. Where a trade waste approval or a pre-treatment requirement applies at a site, it is recorded in the site file.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping an unapproved discharge
instructionSections.body: A cleaner who sees greasy water heading for a stormwater grate, a floor drain that is not connected to pre-treatment, or a neighbour's yard should stop the discharge at its source if it is safe to do so. Use absorbent material, sealed containers and drip trays to contain the flow. Do not pour water, detergent or degreaser down any drain to clear the path. Do not add more product to 'dilute' the water. Tell the supervisor and the site operator at once. Record the time, the location, what was seen, what was done to contain it, and who was told. The decision about the discharge route, the treatment and any notification to the utility or the regulator belongs to the site operator and, where applicable, the regulator. It does not belong to the cleaner, and it is not decided by the cheapest contractor on the day.

instructionSections.heading: Lawful waste handling and the record
instructionSections.body: Greasy waste leaves the site through a waste contractor who is authorised to collect and transport it. Confirm the contractor's details before the waste is loaded, and keep a record of the collection with the date, the quantity or number of containers, the contractor's name, the destination and the person who signed for it. State requirements for waste transport and for tracking regulated wastes differ between jurisdictions, and this lesson does not confirm them. Where a state requirement applies, the site operator must confirm it before the first collection. The cleaner's part is to keep the containers sealed, labelled and separated by stream, to hand over only to the approved contractor, and to keep the record that proves it.

lessons.title: Inspection, photos and access limitations
learningOutcomes: Distinguish documented observation, photographic evidence and access limitations.
Identify before-and-after evidence and any section that has not been seen.
Refuse to describe incomplete access as full-system verification.

instructionSections.heading: Three kinds of record
instructionSections.body: An inspection record contains three different kinds of statement, and they must not be mixed. The first is an observation: something you saw, touched within your scope, or measured with an appropriate tool, recorded as you saw it at a time and place. The second is photographic evidence: an image that supports an observation and shows where it was taken from. The third is an access limitation: a part of the system you could not see, reach or check, and the reason. Most bad records fail because one kind is written as another. A photograph of a clean hood face is treated as proof that the duct behind it is clean. A missing access panel is written as 'nothing unusual'. A report says the system was inspected when only the accessible surfaces were seen. This lesson teaches you to keep the three kinds separate, so that the owner and the competent person can see exactly what is known and what is not.

instructionSections.heading: Writing an observation
instructionSections.body: Write observations in plain, specific language. State the location using a fixed reference, such as the hood canopy, the left filter bank or the duct take-off above the cooking line, and use the same reference names on every visit. Say what you saw, not what you think it means. 'Grease film visible on the lower edge of the left canopy panel, approximately across the panel width' is an observation. 'Hood is a fire hazard' is a conclusion that needs a competent person's assessment, and it is not for the inspection record. Include the date, the time, your name, the scope reference, and the lighting condition if it affects what you could see. If you could not see a surface clearly because the light was poor, write that down as a limit.

instructionSections.heading: Photographs that support, not replace
instructionSections.body: A photograph supports the observation it is attached to. Take it from a stated position, label it with the date, the location reference and the observation number, and keep the original file unaltered. Include a reference object or the panel edge where that helps the reader judge the scale. A photograph shows only what the lens captured, in the light available, from where it was taken. It does not prove that unseen surfaces are clean or dirty, and it does not prove the absence of a defect. Where the site uses photographs, check the site's rules on what may be photographed. Photographs can show staff, customers, screens and documents, and their storage is a site decision. Store images in the approved location only.

instructionSections.heading: Access limitations and sections not seen
instructionSections.body: An access limitation is a statement that a part of the system was not seen or checked, with the reason. Common limitations include a duct run behind a fixed ceiling, a fan housing that could not be opened, a roof component that was not reached, a canopy void that was closed, or a surface blocked by equipment that the site did not move. Record each limitation as a separate entry. Name the section, say what was not seen, state why, and say who was told. Mark the section as not inspected. Do not write 'no defects found' for a section you did not see. If the owner gives permission for a later access, record the permission and the date, and leave the section open until it is inspected. An access limitation is not a finding that the section is clean, safe or compliant. It is a statement of what the record does not cover.

instructionSections.heading: Before and after evidence
instructionSections.body: Before-and-after evidence is a pair of records taken from the same position under comparable light. The 'before' record is taken before any work starts and shows the condition as found. The 'after' record is taken when the work within scope is complete and shows the condition as left. Use the same reference names, the same angle and the same light where you can. Where a surface was not cleaned because it was out of scope, the after record should say so next to the photograph. A set of before-and-after pairs shows the change within the work you did. It does not show that the whole system is clean, and it does not show that any part is fire-safe. If a before photograph was not taken, say so and record the reason.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing to call partial access full verification
instructionSections.body: Owners and managers sometimes ask for a single sentence that says the system is clean, fully inspected or fully cleaned.
