Where the record covers only some sections, that sentence is not accurate, and it must not be written. Offer an accurate alternative: the sections inspected, the sections not inspected, the observations made, and the limitations that apply. If the owner insists on a wording that covers the unseen sections, refer the request to the competent person and record the referral. Do not sign a statement that describes access you did not have.

lessons.title: Defects, fire-risk escalation and scheduling
learningOutcomes: Recognise defects such as damaged access panels, persistent seepage and non-operating extraction.
Escalate serious grease accumulation and known fire or system integrity hazards to competent people.
Record recurrence without inventing a maintenance interval or a safety approval.

instructionSections.heading: Seeing a defect without fixing it
instructionSections.body: A cleaner working on an exhaust system will see things that are wrong. A panel may be missing its fixings. Grease may be seeping from a joint. The extraction fan may not run when the cooking line is on. A fire-suppression component may be covered, loose or disconnected. Each of these is a defect, and each must be recorded. The cleaner's first duty is not to repair it. Most defects in this system sit in a specialist layer, and the cleaner's scope and eligibility do not cover repair. The cleaner's job is to notice, to make the area safe in the way the site requires, to record what was seen, and to escalate to the people who can decide. This lesson covers how to recognise the defect, how to escalate it and how to record it. It does not cover how to repair it.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising the signs
instructionSections.body: The signs that matter fall into a few groups. Access and integrity signs include an access panel that is missing, cracked, held shut with tape, or no longer seals. Leak signs include grease or oily water seeping from a joint, seam or fixing, or a stain that grows between visits. Operating signs include a fan that does not run, makes an unusual noise, or vibrates strongly when it is on, and a canopy that appears to draw poorly, as reported by the kitchen staff. Fire-suppression signs include a component that is covered, damaged, disconnected or obstructed. Heat signs include discolouration or a smell of burning on or near the system. Describe what you see in plain language, with its location and time, and do not guess the cause. The observed sign is the record. The cause is decided by a competent person.

instructionSections.heading: Escalating serious grease accumulation and integrity hazards
instructionSections.body: Escalate at once, and do not wait for the end of the shift, where you see a known fire or integrity hazard. That includes heavy grease accumulation that you can see in an accessible area and that the site has not planned to clean, a missing or unsealed access panel where grease is visible nearby, a suppression component that is obstructed or damaged, a fan that has stopped with grease visible on or around it, and any heat sign. Stop the work in the affected area as the site requires, keep people away from the area, and tell the supervisor and the site operator. Where the site's escalation contact or the competent person is named in the site file, call them. The cleaner does not switch equipment off, reset it, open it or cover it unless the site procedure specifically allows that action for that person. NSW Fire and Rescue's restaurant guidance identifies fatty residue in hoods and ducting as an ignition risk, which is the reason for escalating grease accumulation without delay.

instructionSections.heading: Recurrence and scheduling
instructionSections.body: A defect that comes back is a recurrence. Keep a recurrence log that records each occurrence: the date, the time, the location reference, the observed sign, the action taken, the person told and the response. A log like this lets the owner and the competent person see a pattern that a single visit would not show. The log does not set a maintenance interval, a cleaning frequency or a safety approval. Those decisions belong to the owner and the competent person, who must consider the system, the use, the site's risk assessment and the requirements that apply. In the log, you may write that a recurrence has occurred at a location three times in the period recorded, and recommend that the owner review the schedule. You may not write that the system is safe at a given interval, or that the next clean is due on a particular date unless the owner has set it.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the escalation record
instructionSections.body: A good escalation note states what was seen, where, when, who was told, what was done to make the area safe, and what has been left for the competent person. It contains no speculation about the cause and no words such as 'fixed', 'cleared', 'safe' or 'compliant' unless a competent person has written them. Attach the photograph taken under the site's rules and reference it in the note. Keep the note with the job file and send a copy to the owner in the way the site has set. If the response is delayed, follow up in writing and record the follow-up.

lessons.title: Handover, records and honest compliance claims
learningOutcomes: Write a handover that states the work done, the access limits and the exclusions.
Refuse to describe the system as compliant or fire-safe.
Keep records that the owner and the competent person can check.

instructionSections.heading: What a handover is for
instructionSections.body: A handover is the document that carries the job from the people who did the work to the people who will rely on it. The owner needs it to decide what happens next. The competent person needs it to decide whether a further assessment is needed. The next cleaner needs it to know what is already done and what is not. A good handover is short, specific and limited to what was actually seen and done. A poor handover is long on reassurance and short on facts, and it tends to create the impression that the system has been checked more thoroughly than it has. This lesson teaches you to write a handover that a reader can rely on, because it says exactly what it covers and what it does not.

instructionSections.heading: The parts of a handover
instructionSections.body: A handover normally contains the site and location, the date and time, the names of the people who did the work and the people who received the handover, and the scope reference. It then lists the work done, grouped by layer and by location reference, so that the reader can see which accessible surfaces were cleaned and which were not. It states the access limits: sections not seen, panels not opened, areas blocked, and parts outside scope. It lists the exclusions in plain words, such as internal duct, fan internals, fire-suppression components and roof work, where those were not part of the job. It records the observed defects and the escalations, with the times and the people told. It refers to the photographs and their labels, and it identifies the records that go with it. It is signed and dated by the person who prepared it. Each part should be short and precise.

instructionSections.heading: The language you must not use
instructionSections.body: Certain words make a claim that the cleaner has no authority to make. Do not write that a system is compliant, certified, fire-safe, passed, approved or inspected in full. Do not write that the fire-suppression system is working, that the duct is clear, or that the fan is safe to run, unless a competent person has said so in writing and the statement is attributed to them. Do not write that the job is complete if any section in the scope was not done. Use exact statements instead: the surfaces cleaned within the written scope, the sections not inspected, the observations made and the limitations that apply. Where the owner wants a sentence for an insurer, a landlord or an authority, the cleaner must not write it. Refer the request to the owner and the competent person, and record that the referral was made.

instructionSections.heading: Records that the owner and the competent person can check
instructionSections.body: A record is useful only if another person can check it. Each entry should carry a date, a time, a location reference, the person who made it, and the scope reference. Photographs should be labelled and linked to the entry they support. Escalations and referrals should show who was told and when. Keep the original files and any later amendments, marked with the date and the person making the change, rather than overwriting an earlier entry. Store the records in the approved location for the site.

instructionSections.heading: Shared duties and the handover
instructionSections.body: Under the model work health and safety framework, where more than one party has a duty for the same risk, each party keeps its duty and must consult and coordinate with the others. Safe Work Australia's current model code on biological hazards restates this shared-duty approach. The handover is the cleaner's way of meeting that duty in practice. It gives the owner, the competent person and any other duty holder the information they need in a form they can act on. Where the handover shows a gap, send the gap to the people who must close it, and record that you did so.

lessons.title: Site authority and laboratory access
learningOutcomes: Confirm that a named laboratory contact has released the documented room, zone and time window.
Recognise that a cleaning ticket does not override a restricted-entry sign.
Deny entry while an experiment is active, and defer the task with a record.

instructionSections.heading: A laboratory is not an ordinary room
instructionSections.body: A laboratory holds people, equipment, chemicals, samples and experiments that may be in progress. Some rooms are shared between groups, some hold material that must not be disturbed, and some have controls on who may enter and when. A cleaner who treats a laboratory as an office with more glassware will eventually disturb something that cannot be restored: a running incubator, a cold chain, a sealed sample, a bench that has been left in a particular state for a reason. This lesson concerns the first step, which is not cleaning at all. It is establishing whether you may enter, which parts you may enter, and when. Everything in later lessons depends on getting this step right. Laboratory decontamination, the handling of biological waste and biosafety-level work are specialist programmes. They are not general housekeeping, and nothing in this lesson teaches them.

instructionSections.heading: Who gives the release
instructionSections.body: A cleaning booking is a request. It shows that someone asked for a room to be cleaned on a date. It does not show who controls the room, whether it is occupied, or whether an experiment is in progress. The person who can release the room is normally the named laboratory contact, such as the laboratory manager, the chief investigator or the facilities contact the site has named, and the release should be in writing. The release should state the room, the zone within the room, the time window, the tasks allowed and the tasks excluded, and any conditions such as escort or protective equipment. If the site uses a separate facilities or safety officer, that officer may also need to confirm the release. Where the release is verbal, record who gave it and when, and ask for written confirmation before you enter. If the contact is not available, the room is not released.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the signs and the status
instructionSections.body: Before you enter, read the door. Look for restricted-entry signs, biological or chemical hazard signs, notices that name a responsible person, and any status indicator the site uses, such as a light, a board or a sign that shows an experiment is running. Where the sign is unclear, or the indicator is not set, treat the room as not released. A cleaning ticket never overrides a restricted-entry sign, and it does not cancel a notice placed by the person who controls the room. If a sign has been removed or looks old, do not assume it no longer applies. Ask the named contact, and record the answer. Do not enter to check whether an experiment is running, because your entry may be the disturbance the sign was placed to prevent.

instructionSections.heading: When an experiment is active
instructionSections.body: An active experiment means the room is in use, even if nobody is standing at a bench. Equipment may be running, samples may be incubating, and a bench may be set up for a process that must not be interrupted. The correct response is to deny entry for the period the experiment is active, to tell the named contact that the task has been deferred, and to record the deferral with the time, the reason, the person told and the new window requested. Do not clean around the experiment, do not move equipment, and do not wipe a surface you think is 'safe'. If the laboratory contact says that the experiment will run for a long time, agree a new window in writing, and keep the original booking on hold rather than cancelling it without a record.

instructionSections.heading: Your scope and the handover
instructionSections.body: Once you have a written release, the release defines your scope. A release for general floor cleaning in a corridor does not cover benches, fume enclosures, freezers or cabinets. A release for a shared office inside the laboratory does not cover the bench area. Where the scope is unclear, ask before you start. At the end of the visit, record what you did, which zones you did not enter, and what you left as found. Do not write that the laboratory is clean, decontaminated or safe. Those words belong to the laboratory's own procedures and to the competent people who make such statements. Your handover states the release, the scope and the areas you did not enter.

lessons.title: Risk assessment and hazard signage
learningOutcomes: Treat new hazard signage as a changed-condition trigger, not as something to interpret into permission.
Record the sign's location without approaching the hazard.
Route away and ask laboratory staff to revise the cleaning boundary.

instructionSections.heading: What a risk assessment is for a cleaner
instructionSections.body: A risk assessment is the record of what could hurt someone in a particular task, who could be hurt, and which controls reduce that risk. For a cleaner, the relevant assessment is the one written for the cleaning task in that laboratory, together with the site's hazard information. You do not write the laboratory's risk assessment, and you do not extend it on your own. Your job is to know the boundary it sets, to notice when the conditions have moved outside it, and to stop when they have. The service specification you were given is a snapshot taken on the day it was written. A laboratory changes its occupancy, its signage, its equipment and its procedures, and each change can alter what is safe to clean. Treat the assessment as a current document that must match the room you are standing in, not as a permission slip that stays valid until someone tells you otherwise.

instructionSections.heading: New signs are a changed condition
instructionSections.body: A new warning sign in a laboratory corridor is a change in the condition of the workplace. A service specification written before the sign was posted does not account for it. Treat the sign as a trigger to stop and reconfirm the boundary. The sign may mark a biological hazard, a chemical store, a radiation or laser area, a room that is being decommissioned, or a space that is awaiting an inspection. You will not know which from the sign alone, and you should not try to work it out by reading the sign closely. Do not decide for yourself what the sign means, and do not read it as permission to go in. The absence of a sign is not permission either, so a corridor that was open last week is only open this week if the site confirms it. The stop is not a judgement about the sign. It is a recognition that the job as written no longer describes the room.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping a distance while you record
instructionSections.body: Record the location of the sign from a safe distance, and note the time. Stand where you can see the sign and the entry point without moving closer to read small print or to look through a door panel. Note the corridor, the room number or the nearest landmark, the position of the sign on the door or wall, and what the sign shows in general terms, such as a symbol, a colour and any wording you can read from where you stand. Do not open doors, lift lids, look under benches or photograph inside a room. If a photograph is needed to make the location clear, take it only of the outside of the door and only if the site allows photographs in that area. Check the laboratory hazard map with the site management if it is available, and note any difference between the map and what you can see. Record what you observed, not what you assume the sign means.

instructionSections.heading: Routing away and asking for a revised boundary
instructionSections.body: Route away from the area by the way you came in, and keep other people away from it where you safely can. Do not stand in the corridor to wait for an answer if it puts you in the path of a hazard. Once you are clear, contact the laboratory staff or the site management and ask them to revise the cleaning boundary in writing. The written request should say what you saw, where, when, which part of the job is affected and what you need: an updated scope, a decision about the affected area, and any instructions for the rest of the job. A verbal answer in the corridor is not enough. The revised boundary must name the areas that are open, the areas that are closed, the people who decided and the time the decision was made. Until that written boundary arrives, the affected area stays out of the job and the rest of the job waits for the same confirmation.

instructionSections.heading: Returning to work after a stop
instructionSections.body: Resume only when the site authority has supplied an updated scope and you have been trained and equipped for the work it describes. If the new scope allows some areas but not others, clean only the areas named as open, and leave the rest untouched. The handover at the end of the job covers housekeeping only. It does not imply sterilisation, decontamination or clearance of any kind. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission states that claims about a business's services must be accurate and based on reasonable grounds, that a business must be able to prove the claims it makes, and that the rule covers statements made by staff as well as advertising. A handover that says a corridor is sterile, or that a sign no longer applies, would be a claim you cannot prove as a cleaner. Record what was tidied and what was not touched, and leave any other conclusion to the people who can test and decide it. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Worked boundary: one corridor, three signs
instructionSections.body: Consider a laboratory corridor with three doors. The service specification covers the general floor and two rooms that are open for housekeeping. A new sign now appears on the third door, and the floor plate outside the first room has a new yellow marking that does not appear on the plan. Under this lesson, the general floor and the two open rooms are still in scope only if the site confirms they are unchanged, because the new sign and the marking are changes that were not in the specification. The third room is closed to you. The yellow marking is treated as a changed condition, so you stop at the marking and do not step over it. You record the door position, the time and the marking from where you stand, route back the way you came, and ask the laboratory staff for a written revision. Until the revision arrives, you do not clean the corridor, including the parts you could reach from the middle. The point of the example is that a booking covers a plan, and a plan does not cover a changed room.

lessons.title: Biological agents and exposure boundaries
learningOutcomes: Explain why biological agents are outside a cleaner's authority.
Recognise the signs that biological material may be present, and keep clear.
Stop, record and refer any exposure concern or unidentified material.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as a biological agent in a laboratory
instructionSections.body: In a laboratory, a biological agent is any living or once-living material that could cause disease or harm if people were exposed to it. The group includes bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, and some toxins produced by living things. A sample tube, a culture plate, a waste container, a centrifuge, a freezer, or a spill on a bench may each contain material of this kind, and nothing about the outside of the item tells you what is inside. For a cleaner, the practical point is simple. You cannot tell by looking whether a material is safe, and the people who can tell are the laboratory staff who know the agent, the containment and the procedure for it. This is why the work of identifying, sampling, containing and decontaminating biological material belongs to trained laboratory personnel working under the laboratory's own documented methods. A cleaner's role is to recognise that the material may be there, keep clear, and pass the matter on.

instructionSections.heading: Why this sits outside routine cleaning
instructionSections.body: Routine housekeeping assumes that the surfaces and items in the room are ordinary. A laboratory cannot make that assumption. Wiping a bench that has a biological spill on it spreads the material, and so does lifting a lid, moving a rack or sweeping a floor where containers have been dropped. The Commonwealth security sensitive biological agents scheme covers entities and facilities that handle suspected or known security sensitive biological agents in Australia, and it sets registration duties for those who handle these agents on an ongoing basis. The list of agents is set by the Minister for Health and Aged Care and is not published on the scheme page, so a cleaner cannot tell from the scheme alone whether a particular material is listed. Nothing in this lesson gives a cleaner any role under the scheme, and a cleaner working to this lesson does not handle these agents. Whatever the laboratory's own registration and procedures are, the cleaner's job is to stay out of that work.

instructionSections.heading: Signs that material may be present, and keeping clear
instructionSections.body: Signs that biological material may be present include biohazard signage, sealed containers with a biological label, restricted-entry signs, equipment marked not to be opened, cold storage with a warning label, and an unfamiliar spill or leak on a bench or floor. Some signs are only words, and some are only a colour or symbol. Treat any sign that you do not fully understand as a reason to keep clear, and do not decide that it is out of date. Keep clear of the marked area, the area under it, and any path that would take you past it. Do not touch the material, do not pick up a container that has been dropped, and do not try to identify the content by smell, colour, or appearance. Record the location, the sign or condition, and the time, from a safe distance. If you need to note what you can see, describe it in plain words, such as a dropped tube with a label, rather than guessing what is in it.

instructionSections.heading: Possible exposure: stop, leave and report
instructionSections.body: If you may have been exposed, stop what you are doing, leave the area by the route you came in, and follow the site's emergency and exposure route. Exposure can happen through a cut or puncture, through a splash to the eyes, nose or mouth, through skin that has been in contact with the material, or through breathing an aerosol or an unfamiliar odour. Do not wait to see whether symptoms develop, and do not carry on with the job. Use the site's first aid and washing facilities as the exposure route describes, and do not attempt treatment beyond that. Report the concern to the laboratory supervisor or site contact at once, and tell them what happened, where, when, and whether you touched anything. Record the time, the location, the people informed and the first aid given, and ask for medical advice through the route the site has set. Medical follow-up is a matter for the treating clinician, and this lesson does not give any clinical instructions.

instructionSections.heading: Unidentified material and the refer-on rule
instructionSections.body: Sometimes you will find material that nobody has labelled, such as a container of unknown liquid, a plate with growth on it, or a box of small tubes left on a trolley. The rule is the same as for a labelled leak. You do not identify it, open it, move it to a cleaner place, or put it in a general bin. You record it and refer it. The record names what is visible, where it is, the time, and who you informed, and it asks the laboratory staff to make the decision about collection, containment or any further step. The refer-on rule also applies when a person asks you to help with something outside the cleaning task, such as moving samples to a fridge or taking a container to the sink. The answer is that the task is outside your authority, and the request goes back to the laboratory staff in writing. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Worked boundary: a sealed container and a second, quieter risk
instructionSections.body: Imagine a corridor with a sealed container labelled as biological. The container has been left on a bench and there is a small wet mark beneath it. The cleaner's task is to tidy the bench. The correct boundary is that the bench is excluded from the cleaning until the laboratory staff have dealt with the container and the mark, and the cleaner keeps clear of both. There is a second, quieter risk in the same corridor, which is a small glass fragment on the floor near the wet mark. The fragment is not a biological item in itself, but it may have been part of a container that held one. Do not pick the fragment up, and do not wipe the mark, because wiping spreads whatever is there. Record the fragment, the mark, the container and their locations from a distance, and tell the laboratory staff. The lesson for the cleaner is that a small or ordinary-looking item in the same spot as a biological sign is treated as part of the sign, not as a separate, cleanable job.

lessons.title: Approved surfaces and equipment boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify the approved surface inventory and treat ambiguous surfaces as excluded.
Explain why specialist equipment, such as biological safety cabinets, stays under its equipment manager.
Refuse and reassign a request to clean inside specialist equipment, and log it as out of scope.

instructionSections.heading: What the approved surface inventory is
instructionSections.body: The approved surface inventory is the laboratory's written list of the surfaces that may be cleaned as housekeeping, the method and products that apply to each, and the no-touch margins around equipment that must not be cleaned by the cleaning team. It is usually a set of plans or a table tied to room numbers, and it is maintained by the laboratory or its equipment manager. Your authority to clean a surface comes from this list and nothing else. A surface that looks like an approved surface, is next to one, or was cleaned last month is not automatically on the list. Before you start, compare the room you are in with the inventory, check the room number and the date of the inventory, and identify each surface you plan to touch. If the inventory has been changed since your last visit, ask the equipment manager for the current version before you begin.

instructionSections.heading: Ambiguity is an exclusion
instructionSections.body: Where a surface is not clearly on the inventory, treat it as excluded until the equipment manager clarifies it. Ambiguity is not permission. Common ambiguous cases include the top of a piece of equipment, a shelf above a bench, a panel that may be part of an enclosure, a splash guard, the frame around a door to a controlled room, and a tray that sits on or under equipment. Each of these may be part of a containment or airflow system even when it looks like an ordinary surface. Do not clean it, do not move it, and do not decide that the nearby approved surface covers it. Note the surface on your record, describe where it is, and ask the equipment manager to classify it in writing. The written answer then goes on the inventory or the job file, so that the next cleaner does not have to guess.

instructionSections.heading: Specialist equipment stays with its equipment manager
instructionSections.body: Biological safety cabinets, centrifuges and fume hoods are specialist equipment. They are operated, checked and maintained by people who are trained for them, and their interiors and airflow can be disturbed by unapproved cleaning. A biological safety cabinet uses controlled airflow through its front opening to protect the people and work inside it, and wiping the inside without the approved method can change that airflow or contaminate the work surface. Some interiors are cleaned only by trained laboratory personnel under a documented method, and that method may include steps that a housekeeping cleaner is not trained to carry out. A cleaner does not clean the inside of this equipment unless the equipment manager has put that task in writing, with the method and the person authorised to do it. The outside of the equipment may be in scope, but only where the inventory lists it, and the no-touch margin around the opening is excluded unless the inventory says otherwise.

instructionSections.heading: A request to clean inside equipment
instructionSections.body: Suppose a cleaner is asked to wipe the inside of a biological safety cabinet. The request may come from a senior person, a researcher, or a colleague who is trying to save time, and the source does not change the answer. The request is out of scope for the cleaner. Decline it politely and clearly, reassign it to trained laboratory personnel, and log the request as out of scope with the time, the person who asked, the reason and the name of the person it was reassigned to. Do not treat the request as a quick favour, and do not wipe the outside and report that the inside was done. If the person insists, ask them to put the request in writing from the equipment manager or the laboratory supervisor. A cleaner who cannot get that instruction in writing does not carry out the task. The log protects the cleaner, the laboratory and the equipment, because it shows what was asked and what was done.

instructionSections.heading: Products, SDS and the chemical register
instructionSections.body: Use only the cleaning products approved for the surfaces you are working on, and check the label and the safety data sheet before you use any product. The Safe Work Australia guidance says the hazardous chemicals register must cover the hazardous chemicals used, handled or stored at the workplace, that each entry needs a current safety data sheet attached, and that the register must be readily accessible to workers. A product that is not on the approved list, or that has no current safety data sheet available, is not used. Ask for the product's entry on the register before you start, and do not mix products to make a stronger solution. The products you use must match the surfaces in the inventory, because a product approved for a bench may not be approved for an instrument surface.

instructionSections.heading: Recording and returning
instructionSections.body: Make a minimal record of the zone, the surfaces classified as approved, the surfaces classified as excluded, the excluded task, the responsible contact, the time, the follow-up and the return criteria. Resume only when the site authority has given an updated scope, and only in the areas that scope names. The handover covers housekeeping only, with no sterilisation or decontamination claim. A record that says a cabinet was cleaned, or that a room is sterile, is a claim that the cleaner cannot prove, and it must not be written. State what was tidied, what was not touched, and what remains with the equipment manager. This lesson does not authorise cleaning inside biological safety cabinets, centrifuges or fume hoods, and it does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority.

lessons.title: Sharps, glass and biological waste
learningOutcomes: Recognise sharps, broken glass and biological waste, and keep clear of them.
Explain why a cleaner does not pick up sharps or biological waste.
Record and refer these items through the laboratory's waste procedure.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as a sharp, a broken glass hazard and a biological waste item
instructionSections.body: A sharp is any item that can cut or puncture the skin: a needle, a scalpel blade, a pipette tip with an edge, a broken slide or cover slip, a sharp instrument part, or a piece of glass with a fine edge. Broken glass from a laboratory is a sharp in its own right, and it is also a possible carrier for whatever it held. Biological waste is material that came from a process involving living or once-living material, such as used cultures, contaminated plastic, tissue, body fluids in containers, and other items the laboratory has set aside for specific disposal. Some of these items look ordinary once they are dry or inside a bag. You cannot tell by looking whether a piece of glass or a plastic tube has held a biological agent, and the laboratory staff are the people who know what each container held and how it must be disposed of. For a cleaner, the job is to recognise these items as a category, keep clear, and refer them on.

instructionSections.heading: Sharps and broken glass: keep clear, do not pick up
instructionSections.body: Needles, scalpels, broken glass and sharp instrument parts can cut and transmit infection. Do not pick them up with your hands, and do not sweep them into a general bin, even if they are small or look clean. A broom and dustpan used for ordinary floor debris can push a fine fragment into a gap or into the edge of a container, and it can cut the person holding it. Keep the area clear of people, mark the location of the items where you can do so safely, such as by standing a sign or cone at a safe distance, and tell the laboratory staff at once. If a sharp has been stuck in your skin, or if you have been cut by glass, stop, leave the area by the entry route and follow the site's exposure route, as described in the earlier lesson on biological agents. The cut is reported and recorded whether or not you think the glass held anything. The laboratory staff decide how the sharp is collected, and under what procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Biological waste containers: report, do not handle
instructionSections.body: Biological waste is collected and disposed of by trained laboratory staff, in the containers and routes the laboratory sets. A cleaner does not handle, move, lift, top up, tie off, or empty biological waste containers, and does not carry them to a waste store. Where a bin is full or leaking, report it, keep people out of the area, and ask the laboratory staff to arrange collection. Check the label on the container rather than relying on its colour, because colours and labelling systems differ between sites. If the label is missing or cannot be read from a safe distance, treat the container as unidentified, leave it where it is, and refer it. The EPA Victoria guidance states that clinical waste comes from settings that include laboratories, can cause disease or injury, and must be treated before final disposal, and it places the responsibility on the waste generator to ensure that waste goes only to facilities approved for that type of waste. These duties sit with the laboratory and its contractors, and not with a cleaner.

instructionSections.heading: Recording and referral
instructionSections.body: Record the item, its location, the time and the person informed, from a safe distance. Describe the item in plain words, such as a broken glass tube near a general waste bin, or a full biological container with a lid that is not closed. Do not describe the contents as harmless, and do not guess what the item held. Refer the item to the laboratory staff in writing or by the site's form, and ask for collection under their procedure. Keep the area closed to other people until the staff have dealt with the item and given a written updated scope. The record is the cleaner's evidence that the item was seen, kept clear and passed on, and it protects the cleaner if a later question is asked about the item. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Worked boundary: a general bin, a sharps container and a full biological bin
instructionSections.body: In a laboratory corridor, three items may be found together. A general waste bin sits beside a sharps container with a lid that has been left open, and a full biological waste container is on the floor beside a door with its lid not sealed. The cleaner's task is to empty the general bin. Under this lesson, the general bin is emptied only if it contains ordinary waste and nothing that could be a sharp, and the cleaner checks the top of the bin from a safe distance before lifting it. The open sharps container is not touched, closed or emptied by the cleaner, because the laboratory decides how it is closed and removed. The full biological container is not moved, emptied or tied. The cleaner records the three items with their positions and the time, keeps people clear of the corridor section, and refers all three to the laboratory staff. The general bin is not emptied until the staff confirm that it is ordinary waste and that the sharps container has been dealt with.

lessons.title: Ventilation, cabinets and specialist zones
learningOutcomes: Explain why airflow equipment and controlled enclosures are not disturbed by routine cleaning.
Confirm exclusions with the equipment owner before housekeeping nearby.
Decline a request to move a cabinet or clean inside a live fume hood, and redirect it to the owner.

instructionSections.heading: Why airflow and enclosures are treated as equipment
instructionSections.body: Ventilation equipment, cabinets and fume hoods control airflow and contain materials. An exhaust grille, a supply vent, a fume hood or a biological safety cabinet does its job by moving air in a particular direction at a particular speed, and by keeping a barrier between the people in the room and whatever is being worked on inside. A cleaner who wipes a grille, moves a cabinet, blocks a vent with a trolley, or leans into an open hood can change that airflow without knowing it. The effect can expose people nearby, disturb the work inside the enclosure, or affect the readings that the owner uses to decide whether the equipment is working. The equipment is therefore treated as a fixed boundary, not as ordinary furniture. Routine housekeeping in these zones is limited to what the owner has approved in writing, and anything the owner has not approved is excluded by default.

instructionSections.heading: Confirm the exclusion diagram before you approach
instructionSections.body: Confirm the current equipment exclusion diagram with the engineering or laboratory equipment manager before any housekeeping near the equipment. The diagram should show the fume hoods, cabinets, vents and grilles, the no-touch margins, the services that run to the equipment, and any points where a cleaner must not stand or place a trolley. Compare the diagram with the room, and check the date and the version. Find the approved local procedure for the zone, and distinguish what is permitted from what is only assumed. An assumption is not a permission. Permission given by a colleague in a hurry is not permission either, unless it is confirmed by the owner in writing. If the diagram and the room do not match, the room is treated as changed, and you stop until the owner confirms the scope.

instructionSections.heading: Changed condition and uncertain hazards
instructionSections.body: When a staff member proposes moving a cabinet and cleaning near a live fume hood, note the difference between the original job and the changed condition. The original job was housekeeping on the approved surfaces. The changed condition involves moving equipment, which may disconnect or strain services such as power, gas, water or exhaust ducting, and may place the cleaner close to an open hood. Any uncertain hazard stops the task, and an uncertain hazard includes a hood whose sash position is unclear, a cabinet with a warning label, an alarm or indicator that is showing, or any service that is not on the diagram. Decline the request to move the cabinet or clean inside a live fume hood, and redirect it to the equipment owner, who decides on a revised scope. Do not adjust the sash, switch a control, or try to make the equipment safe for cleaning. Those decisions belong to the equipment owner and to people trained for them.

instructionSections.heading: Recording and returning
instructionSections.body: Make a minimal record of the zone, the observable condition, the excluded task, the responsible contact, the time and the follow-up. Describe what you saw in plain words, such as a cabinet with a lifted panel or an open hood with items on the work surface, without assuming why. Resume only after the site authority gives an updated scope and the cleaner is trained and equipped for it. The handover covers housekeeping only, and it never implies sterilisation or contamination clearance. A handover that says the zone is safe, certified or sterile is a claim the cleaner cannot prove. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission states that claims must be accurate and based on reasonable grounds, that a business must be able to prove its claims, and that statements by staff are covered by the same rule. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Worked boundary: a cabinet, a hood and a request to help
instructionSections.body: A laboratory has a mobile cabinet beside a fume hood. The hood is in use, and a research assistant asks the cleaner to shift the cabinet a short distance so the floor under it can be mopped, and then to wipe the front of the hood while the sash is open. The request has three parts, and each is handled separately. The mopping is in scope only if the diagram shows the floor between the cabinet and the hood as open, and the cleaner can confirm that with the owner. Moving the cabinet is excluded, because it may disturb services and the airflow around the hood, and the decision belongs to the owner. Wiping the front of an open hood is excluded because it is a live enclosure, and the sash and the work surface inside are not in the cleaner's scope. The cleaner declines the move and the hood work, redirects both to the owner, records the request and the changed condition, and asks for a written decision on the floor. If the owner confirms only the floor, the cleaner mops only that floor, with the cabinet left where it is.

lessons.title: Verification, audit and restricted handover
learningOutcomes: Explain that a visibly clean surface is not evidence of decontamination, sterility or biological clearance.
Use housekeeping-only inspection criteria and a signed handover with explicit exclusions.
Reject a request to certify laboratory biological safety and refer verification to the laboratory owner.

instructionSections.heading: Looks clean is not clean enough
instructionSections.body: A visibly clean surface is not evidence that it has been decontaminated, sterilised or cleared of biological material. Mopping makes a floor look clean, and wiping makes a bench look clean. Neither action shows that a biological hazard is gone, because the hazard may be invisible, may sit below the surface, may be in a crack or drain, or may have been moved rather than removed. A clean appearance is the result of housekeeping, which is a tidy-up with a defined scope. Verification of decontamination, sterility or biological clearance is a different activity. It is carried out by the laboratory owner and by qualified testers, using their own method, sampling plan and acceptance criteria. A cleaner's role is to finish the housekeeping in scope, record what was done, and hand over the zone with its limits stated clearly. The cleaner does not take the verification step, and does not describe the result of it.

instructionSections.heading: Housekeeping-only inspection criteria
instructionSections.body: Use inspection criteria that match the housekeeping scope and nothing more. A housekeeping inspection asks whether the approved surfaces listed on the inventory were tidied, whether general waste was removed from the approved bins in line with the site procedure, whether floors were left free of ordinary debris, whether consumables were restocked where the site requires it, and whether any excluded or unclear surface was left untouched and recorded. It does not ask whether the area is sterile, whether a surface has been decontaminated, or whether any biological material is absent. Those questions belong to the verification step. Write the criteria on the inspection sheet in plain words, and tick only what was seen. A tick against a criterion that the inspection does not test is a false record, so do not tick a criterion simply because the room looks tidy.

instructionSections.heading: The signed handover and its exclusions
instructionSections.body: Sign a handover that lists the exclusions and the unresolved work. The handover states what was tidied, what was inspected against the housekeeping criteria, and what was not touched and why. It lists the excluded equipment, the ambiguous surfaces that are awaiting classification, any items referred to the laboratory staff, and the return criteria for any deferred area. A handover that is signed without exclusions invites the reader to assume that everything in the room was in scope and that the room is therefore safe, and this is the most common way in which housekeeping turns into an unsupported claim. Do not write that the laboratory is sterile, decontaminated, certified safe, or cleared. Where a reader asks for a conclusion of that kind, state the limits of the housekeeping, and refer them to the laboratory owner for the verification question.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing a clearance request
instructionSections.body: Consider a supervisor who asks you to certify laboratory biological safety after mopping. Refuse politely and clearly. Document the cleaning completed, state that the cleaning was housekeeping only, and refer the verification to the laboratory owner, who holds the method and the testers. Explain to the supervisor that a certificate based on mopping would state something the cleaning cannot show. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission states that claims about a business's services must be accurate and based on reasonable grounds, that a business must be able to prove the claims it makes, and that statements made by staff are covered by the rule. A certificate of biological safety that the cleaning cannot support would be a claim of that kind. Make a minimal deferral record with the supervisor's request, the responsible contact and the return criteria. If the supervisor persists, ask for the request in writing from the laboratory owner, and do not sign any clearance document in the meantime. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Worked boundary: three handover statements
instructionSections.body: After a housekeeping visit to a laboratory bench room, a cleaner has three possible statements to choose from for the handover. The first says that the approved benches, floor and general bin were tidied, that the excluded fume hood and the cabinet were not touched, and that the ambiguous panel is awaiting classification. This is a housekeeping statement with explicit exclusions, and it is the correct one. The second says that the room was cleaned and is now sterile. It is a clearance claim that the cleaning cannot support, and it must not be written. The third says that the room is clean and that the owner can rely on it for research work. This goes beyond housekeeping, because the reliance is a claim about the room's suitability, and it is not a claim the cleaner can make. The correct handover is the first, and any request for the second or third is referred to the laboratory owner in writing.

lessons.title: Work authorisation and warehouse operating boundaries
learningOutcomes: Confirm the written work authorisation and the named supervisor before entering a warehouse work zone.
Identify the operating boundaries: traffic routes, dock areas, racking, plant and restricted zones.
Stop and refer when the authorisation does not match what is observed on site.

instructionSections.heading: Authority before entry
instructionSections.body: An operating warehouse is a busy workplace with vehicles, plant and stored goods moving around, and the work of the people on site depends on the routes and zones being used as planned. A cleaner who enters a zone without the site's authority can block a route, stand in a path of moving plant, or disturb stock that someone else is counting or loading. Before you enter a work zone, confirm four things: the written work authorisation, the named supervisor, the agreed zone and the time window. A cleaning booking is not an authorisation to enter a zone that the site has closed or reassigned. The booking records what someone asked for, and the authorisation records what the site has agreed to. If the two differ, the authorisation governs. Keep a copy of the authorisation with you while you work, or have the supervisor's contact available, so that you can show it on request.

instructionSections.heading: Site induction and the traffic plan
instructionSections.body: A site induction is the point at which the site explains its own rules to people who are new to it, and it is where the traffic plan is explained. The Safe Work Australia guidance on warehouse traffic management says that the plan should document how traffic risks are managed, and that it may include designated vehicle travel paths, the entry and exit points, crossing points, pedestrian routes, how often plant and people interact, the traffic controls for each expected interaction, and the responsibilities of the people who manage traffic. The guidance also says that workers and contractors must know and understand the traffic rules and procedures, and that site induction should cover the plan. Ask for the induction and the plan before the first entry, and do not rely on a plan you were given when the booking was made. If you have not been inducted, you are not authorised to enter a zone where plant moves, and the induction is the first step, not the cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Operating boundaries on the site plan
instructionSections.body: Identify the boundaries on the site plan before you start: traffic routes, pedestrian walkways, dock areas, racking, plant and restricted zones. Mark anything that is not in scope. Traffic routes are the paths that vehicles use, including the aisles where forklifts run and the lanes at a dock. Walkways are the paths that people are meant to use, and they should be separate from routes, where the site can make them so. Dock areas include the edges, the leveller plates, the trailers and the door openings, all of which can move without warning. Racking is storage structure, and it is not part of the cleaning scope unless the site says so. Plant includes any machine that moves or lifts, and restricted zones include areas closed for maintenance, for hazardous storage, for testing or for another contractor. Do not enter a restricted zone to check whether it is clear, and do not cross a traffic route without the site's control. A zone that looks empty may be waiting for a vehicle, a load or a repair.

instructionSections.heading: When the site has changed
instructionSections.body: If the zone looks different from the plan, or the operations have moved, stop and check with the supervisor before you go on. A delivery may have arrived early, a pallet may be standing in an aisle, a barrier may have been moved, or a bay may have been reassigned for the day. Record the difference, the time and who you told. The authorisation follows the site's current plan, not the plan you were given at booking, so a change on the ground means the old plan no longer applies until the supervisor says it does. Do not decide that a change is minor, and do not work around it because the rest of the zone is open. The supervisor decides whether the zone is still in scope, and that decision is written down before you resume. A change that is reported and recorded is a normal part of the job, and a change that is not reported is the point at which an incident begins.

instructionSections.heading: Licences, plant and what this lesson does not authorise
instructionSections.body: Operating a forklift is one of the activities that Safe Work Australia's guidance on high-risk work licences lists as needing a licence. That guidance states that workers must have a licence before undertaking high-risk work, and it lists forklift trucks among the work covered. This lesson does not teach you to operate plant, and it does not grant a licence, a plant authority or a site authority. Do not move a pallet, climb onto a dock edge, use a plant attachment, or drive any vehicle to get a cleaning tool into place. Ask the site for a plant operator to move anything that is in the way, and wait.

lessons.title: Forklift traffic routes and pedestrian segregation
learningOutcomes: Identify forklift traffic routes and pedestrian walkways on the site plan.
Keep clear of forklift routes, and use segregated walkways only.
Stop and withdraw when a forklift route crosses the cleaning area.

instructionSections.heading: Why routes and walkways are separated
instructionSections.body: Forklifts move on set routes, and pedestrians should use walkways that are kept apart from those routes. The reason is that a forklift driver has a limited view, a load can block the view ahead, and a forklift turning at speed covers more space than the driver can always see. A cleaner who works close to a route is exposed to a strike, to being crushed against racking or a wall, or to being hit by a load that has been lifted or lowered. The Safe Work Australia guidance on warehouse traffic management states that the best approach is to keep pedestrians and forklifts apart, and that where that is not possible, the layout should be changed to reduce the time people spend in forklift areas. The same guidance says that access to forklift areas should be limited to operators and supervisors. Mark both the routes and the walkways on the site plan before you start, so that you know which area is which before you are in it.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping clear of blind spots and turning areas
instructionSections.body: Keep clear of forklift routes and of blind spots. A blind spot is any place a driver cannot see from the cab, such as the area behind a stacked load, the corner of an aisle where racking meets a cross-aisle, the space beside a forklift when it turns, and the gap at a dock door as a trailer is backed in. The guidance uses the term blind spots, and it recommends safety railings or bollards to stop pedestrians stepping into traffic from those points, and mirrors, cameras, sensors or alarms so that drivers can see around vehicles. Do not step into a route to reach a corner, and do not work in a route while a forklift is moving. A forklift that has stopped is not safe to work next to, because it can start again without warning. Where a route crosses the cleaning area, withdraw to a safe location that is not in a blind spot, and ask the site controller for a revised pedestrian route before you go back.

instructionSections.heading: Segregation, barriers and the stop-work right
instructionSections.body: Use barriers, signs and the site's segregation where they are provided. The guidance suggests high-impact barriers, containment fences and enforced exclusion zones where people and plant must be close, and it notes that a load should not block a driver's view. Report a missing barrier, a blocked walkway or a near miss at once, and record the location and time. Do not move a barrier to shorten a route, and do not climb over one. Under the Commonwealth Work Health and Safety Act, a worker may cease, or refuse to carry out, work where they have a reasonable concern that doing the work would expose them to a serious risk to their health or safety from an immediate or imminent exposure to a hazard. That right may be relevant to a cleaner who sees a forklift route cross the area without warning. Other state and territory laws may apply to the site, so check the law that applies where the site is located. Record the stop on the job file, with the reason and the site's response.

instructionSections.heading: Forklifts, licences and what this lesson does not authorise
instructionSections.body: Operating a forklift is a licensed activity. The SafeWork NSW guidance states that a worker needs a high risk work licence with the relevant class to operate a forklift in NSW, and it describes the forklift truck class (LF) as covering a forklift with a mast and an elevating load carriage with fork arms or another attachment, and the order picking class (LO) for order-picking trucks. The SafeWork SA class list shows the forklift truck class LF and the order picking forklift class LO. The SafeWork NSW page does not say whether a licence is needed to direct or supervise a forklift, and this lesson does not decide that question. This lesson does not teach or authorise you to operate, move or direct a forklift, and completing it does not grant any licence or plant authority.

instructionSections.heading: Worked boundary: a route, a corner and a stacked load
instructionSections.body: A cleaning corridor runs parallel to a forklift route for part of its length, and at one end it meets a cross-aisle where a stacked load of cartons blocks the view. A barrier is in place along the route side, but it has a gap where a cart has been pushed through. The cleaner's task is to clean the floor of the corridor. Under this lesson, the part of the corridor beside the route is kept clear, and the cleaner works only on the far side of the barrier. The corner at the cross-aisle is a blind spot, so the cleaner does not clean it, and does not stand near it while a forklift is in the area. The gap in the barrier is reported at once, and the cleaner does not move the cart, which belongs to the site. The cleaner records the gap, the stacked load, the time, and the person told, and asks the site controller for a revised pedestrian route for the corridor. If a forklift route moves across the corridor while the cleaner is in it, the cleaner withdraws to a safe location, and does not return until the site confirms the route is clear of the area.

lessons.title: Pallet racking and stored-load instability
learningOutcomes: Recognise signs of racking damage and unstable stored loads.
Keep clear of racking and loads that look unstable, and do not touch them.
Report the condition at once and stop work in the area.

instructionSections.heading: What you are looking at
instructionSections.body: A pallet racking system is a frame that holds stock in bays. The main parts are the upright frames that carry the load down to the floor, the horizontal beams that the pallets sit on, the diagonal and horizontal braces that stop the frame racking sideways, the connectors that join beams to uprights, the safety clips that stop beams lifting out of their connectors, and the floor fixings that anchor the frame. Each part is designed to carry a rated load. When one part is damaged, the rated load of the whole bay can fall, and the stored goods above a walkway can come down on whoever is below. A cleaner rarely knows the rated load of a bay, so the working rule is simple: if a bay looks wrong, treat it as unsafe until the site's competent person says otherwise.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising damage
instructionSections.body: Damage can be seen from the floor if you know what to look for. State regulator guidance on racking lists several common signs. Beam connectors that have bent into a V shape can point to overloading. Impact marks on beams from a pallet or forklift, and cracked welds, are another sign. Missing connectors and missing safety clips leave a beam free to lift out. A beam resting on only one end connector has popped out of its upright. Uprights that are twisted, split, cracked or badly spliced need attention, and so do bent braces. A frame that is out of plumb, meaning it leans away from the vertical, can result from impact, overloading or settlement in the floor. Damaged or missing floor fixings and a capacity sign that can no longer be read are further signs. On the load side, look for goods that overhang the pallet, pallets that are unstable or unlevel, goods that are not secured, loads that touch uprights or beams, and bays carrying more than their rated load. A load that leans over a walkway, or a pallet that sags in the middle, is an immediate concern rather than a tidy-up task.

instructionSections.heading: Keep clear, do not test, and use your right to stop
instructionSections.body: Do not climb, push, lean on or touch the racking or the stock to find out whether it is safe. Testing is the wrong method because a load that moves under a push can fall, and a frame that flexes may already be past its limit. Move out of the zone below and beside the damaged area, and keep other people out. Under the Commonwealth Work Health and Safety Act 2011, a worker who has a reasonable concern about an immediate or imminent serious risk to their health or safety may cease or refuse unsafe work (Work Health and Safety Act 2011, section 84, compilation dated 1 July 2024). State versions of the law may differ, so check the one that applies on your site. The right to stop is a right to stop your own work and to withdraw from the area. It is not a right to repair the rack, move stock, or decide that the area is safe.

instructionSections.heading: Close, report and record
instructionSections.body: Once you have moved clear, close the area with barriers or signs, following the site's method, and tell your supervisor straight away. State guidance says employees must report racking damage immediately so that a competent person can assess it. Where the site uses a tagging system for damaged bays, follow the site procedure, but do not classify the damage yourself. Your report should name the aisle, bay and level, describe what you saw, say when you saw it, and state who you told and what they said. If the site allows photographs, take them from outside the danger zone without touching the rack. Keep the restriction in place until the site confirms in writing that the area can be used again.

instructionSections.heading: Who decides and what happens next
instructionSections.body: Formal racking inspections are carried out by a competent person at intervals of no more than 12 months, and a competent person should inspect racking that shows signs of overloading. State guidance says that very serious damage should lead to the affected bays being unloaded before reuse, and that changes to a rack should be made only by the supplier, their representative or a suitably competent person. Employers and workers should not modify uprights, bracing or beams, for example by welding on extra cleats, and replacement parts should come from the equipment manufacturer. A cleaner does not re-stack stock, move a damaged beam, decide that a rack is safe because it has stood for years, or approve a bay for loading. Those decisions belong to the site and its authorised people.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning near racking in practice
instructionSections.body: Before you start an aisle, look up and along the bays for the signs listed above. Keep cleaning tools, mop buckets and vacuum hoses clear of the bases of uprights, because repeated knocks weaken frames. Do not use ladders, steps or shelving to reach a high surface near racking unless the site has authorised that task. Keep out of the zone where forklifts are working, and follow the site's traffic management plan. Where a walkway has a damaged bay above it, do not clean underneath until the site has dealt with the bay. Plan the work so the cleaning route can be moved if a bay is closed.

instructionSections.heading: The limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Completing this lesson does not make you a racking inspector, a rigger or a specialist, and it does not give any licence, certificate or authority to inspect, repair, re-stack or approve racking. Those tasks are done by authorised or competent people under the site's procedure. This lesson teaches you to recognise a warning sign, keep clear, stop, and report.

lessons.title: Loading docks, trailers and vehicle movement
learningOutcomes: Identify reversing vehicles, open dock edges and trailer movement as separate access risks.
Mark vehicle approach zones and dock-edge restrictions on a site plan.
Stop and refer any cleaning beside an active dock without approved segregation.

instructionSections.heading: Three different access risks
instructionSections.body: Reversing delivery vehicles, open dock edges and trailer movement are separate hazards, and each needs its own control. A reversing vehicle can strike a person who is out of sight. An open dock edge can produce a fall. A trailer can move when it is not secured. Treat each as a distinct risk on the site plan and do not assume that one control covers the others.

instructionSections.heading: The decision gate
instructionSections.body: Before work starts, review the work order, the named supervisor, the risk controls and the site movement plan. Compare what you see with the authorised plan. If the plan and the observed conditions diverge, suspend the affected task and document the difference. A wet-cleaning job scheduled beside reversing vehicles and an open dock edge is a stop-work condition until documented authority and specialist controls are in place.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and referral
instructionSections.body: A cleaner may identify and report hazards, but may not stand in for a traffic controller, a plant isolation officer, an engineer or a hazardous-material specialist. Do not cross or clean an active loading dock without approved segregation. Leave the affected area restricted until the authority is documented.

instructionSections.heading: Recording
instructionSections.body: Record the time, the location, the work-order identifier, what was observed as distinct from what was inferred, the supporting record, the person notified and any response. Keep the referral traceable, so that the site can see why the area remained restricted.

lessons.title: Dust, airborne contaminants and exposure uncertainty
learningOutcomes: Identify uncertain particulate sources and airborne visibility changes in a warehouse.
Explain why unidentified dust is never dry-swept, and why authorised supervision is needed.
Stop and refer a powder spill of unknown origin, leaving the area restricted.

instructionSections.heading: Where warehouse dust comes from
instructionSections.body: A warehouse can produce dust from many sources at once. Stored goods can shed fine material, and packaging, cardboard, pallets and dunnage (the timber or packing used to protect loads) generate fibres and fine particles. Bulk materials such as grains, minerals, plastics, fertilisers or powders can leave residues on floors, ledges and the tops of racking. Chemicals can leak, be spilled or be stored in damaged containers, and their residues can look like ordinary dust. The same ordinary-looking powder can be harmless in one place and a serious hazard in another, because its risk depends on what it is, how much there is, how it is spread into the air, and what is stored nearby. A cleaner cannot tell these apart by looking, and that is the core reason this lesson exists.

instructionSections.heading: Signs that a source is uncertain
instructionSections.body: Treat a particulate source as uncertain when you cannot say what it is from its label, its packaging or the site's records. Other warning signs include a visible haze in the air that was not there earlier, a change in the colour or texture of a residue, a sharp or unusual smell, a powder on surfaces with no matching stock nearby, a leaking or damaged container, and any report from a colleague of breathing or eye irritation. A report of irritation is a signal to stop the task and get the source checked, even if nobody feels unwell at the time. Do not disturb an unidentified residue in order to find out what it is. Disturbing it can put it into the air, and the act of checking then becomes the exposure.

instructionSections.heading: Why unknown dust is never dry-swept
instructionSections.body: Dry sweeping lifts fine material into the air, where it can be breathed in or settle onto other surfaces, equipment and food. The same action can also make dust cloud in a way that becomes a fire or explosion risk. State regulator guidance says that combustible dust can create a hazardous area when it is present in a suitable quantity and form, and that the person managing the workplace must manage hazardous atmospheres, including ignition sources. Do not use dry sweeping, compressed air or a leaf blower on unidentified dust. Wet methods and vacuums are not automatically safe either, because some materials react with water and standard vacuums are not designed for fine or hazardous dust. Any cleaning method for an unknown residue is chosen by the site authority and the specialist, and not by the cleaner.

instructionSections.heading: Stop conditions and the chemicals register
instructionSections.body: A powder spill of unknown origin near bulk chemical storage is a stop condition. Keep people out of the area, do not switch electrical equipment on or off in or beside the spill, and keep ignition sources away. Then check whether the site has a hazardous chemicals register. The register must list the hazardous chemicals used, handled or stored at the workplace, each entry must have a current safety data sheet (SDS), and the register must be easy for workers to reach. Model duties also require the supplier to provide the SDS with the chemical, and require the business to identify, assess and control risks and to store chemicals safely. If the site cannot match the powder to an entry, that is a finding to record, not a reason to guess. Never assume a powder is harmless because it looks like something on the register.

instructionSections.heading: Recording, referral and restriction
instructionSections.body: Your job is to make the condition safe to leave, record it accurately, and refer it. Write down the time, the exact location, the work-order number, and what you observed. Keep what you saw separate from what you think it might be, and label your guesses as guesses. Record the supporting evidence, such as a photograph taken from a safe distance if the site allows it, and the names of the people you told. Specialist identification and any sampling are arranged by the site and carried out by a qualified person. A cleaner does not take samples, does not identify the material, and does not decide that an area is clear. The restriction stays in place until a documented authority releases it, and a quick wipe by the cleaner does not end the restriction.

instructionSections.heading: Respiratory protection and symptoms
instructionSections.body: Respiratory protection is used only as the site's dust assessment requires, and only by workers who have been fitted and trained for it. A worker should not enter a restricted area because they are wearing a mask. Where the site requires a respirator, a fit check is done each time it is worn, and the choice of respirator is made by the site, not by the cleaner. If you or a colleague develop breathing trouble, skin or eye irritation, or any other symptom, stop, move to fresh air where it is safe to do so, and follow the site's first aid and emergency procedure. Report the symptoms to the supervisor and record them.

instructionSections.heading: The limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and it does not authorise sampling, identification, clearance or entry into a restricted area. Completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist in hazardous materials, dust control or atmosphere testing.

lessons.title: Powered conveyors and machinery interfaces
learningOutcomes: Identify moving parts, guards and interfaces on powered conveyors and machinery.
Keep clear of moving parts and do not clean them while they are running.
Refer isolation and cleaning of machinery to the authorised person.

instructionSections.heading: Moving parts, pinch points and transfer points
instructionSections.body: A powered conveyor moves product on a belt, a chain or a set of rollers, and it is driven by a motor, gearbox and drive pulley. Around the drive, the return and the tensioners there are pinch points, where a belt, chain or roller can draw in a hand, a sleeve, a glove or a cloth. Transfer points, where product moves from one conveyor to another or into a machine, are often the places where material builds up and where people reach in. Powered machinery such as wrapping machines, compactors and labellers has similar hazards: rotating or reciprocating parts, moving tables and rollers, and drives hidden under covers. Before you go near any machine, identify its moving parts, its guards, its interlocks and its emergency stops from the site plan or from the machine itself. A conveyor that is running is not a surface to clean, and a conveyor that is stopped is not necessarily safe until the authorised person confirms that its energy sources are controlled.

instructionSections.heading: Guards and interlocks
instructionSections.body: A guard is a physical barrier or device that stops a person from reaching a dangerous part, or that controls access to a dangerous area. Guards can be fixed, can be a physical barrier linked to an interlock that stops the machine when the barrier opens, or can be a presence-sensing device. Under the national plant code, guarding must prevent contact with moving parts or control access to dangerous areas, and must not be easy to bypass or disable. An interlocked physical barrier is one of the recognised types of guarding. A guard that has been removed must be put back before the plant returns to normal operation, and the plant should not be able to restart while the guarding is missing. For a cleaner, this means three things: do not remove a guard, do not prop open an interlock gate, and report any guard that is missing, damaged or bypassed. A guard that looks as if it could be moved by hand is still a guard, and moving it is not your job.

instructionSections.heading: Isolation comes before any cleaning inside the machine
instructionSections.body: Cleaning near or inside machinery needs the machine to be isolated, and the isolation is carried out by an authorised person under the site's documented procedure. The national plant code says plant should be isolated before maintenance or cleaning starts, and that the shutdown must not create a new hazard elsewhere (section 3.7). It treats lock-out as the most effective form of isolation (section 4.5). The steps it describes are: shut the plant down, identify every energy source and isolation point, isolate and lock out, tag, and then test that the plant will not start. A tag on its own is not an isolation device. Each worker who is working on the plant should have their own lock, tag and key at each isolation point, so that no one can restart the machine while another person is inside it. As a cleaner, you do not isolate machinery, you do not hold the key for someone else's lock, and you do not decide that the machine is safe to enter. If the cleaning cannot be done while the machine runs, that is a referral to the authorised person, not a reason to reach in.

instructionSections.heading: Spills on a belt and jams
instructionSections.body: A spill on a running belt is a common reason for an unsafe reach. Do not wipe, scrape or catch falling product on a moving belt, and do not clear a jam by hand while the belt runs. Keep people away from the spill and from the point where material is falling. Warn the supervisor and ask for the conveyor to be stopped and isolated by the authorised person. Once it is isolated, the authorised person decides how the spill is removed, and the cleaning method is chosen against the product and the chemicals that the site uses. Where a degreaser is used on a machine, the cleaner checks the safety data sheet for the product before use, follows the ventilation and personal protection it specifies, and does not mix it with other cleaners.

instructionSections.heading: Reporting, records and handover
instructionSections.body: Report a missing guard, a damaged interlock, a gate that opens without stopping the machine, a damaged emergency stop, a jammed belt, or a spill on a belt to the supervisor at once. Keep people away from the machine until the supervisor confirms in writing or by the site's method that it is safe. Do not restart a machine to test a fault. Record the machine's name or number, its location, the condition you saw, and the time, and say who was told. A referral for cleaning that needs isolation should name the task, the person who asked for it, the authorised person who will isolate, and the result. The record protects both the worker and the site if a machine is later found to have a guard missing.

instructionSections.heading: The limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority to isolate, operate, guard, repair or clean machinery. Completing it does not make a cleaner a competent person for plant. Competent person, isolation and maintenance decisions are made by the site and its authorised people.

lessons.title: Deck and fence scope, permits and boundary survey
