learningOutcomes: Identify when a deck or fence needs a building permit, a planning approval or a licensed contractor, by state.
Confirm property boundaries and the owner's authority before a deck or fence is set out.
Refer permit, planning and boundary questions and record the referral.

instructionSections.heading: Three separate questions
instructionSections.body: Deck and fence jobs raise three questions that are easy to mix up. The first is whether a building permit or planning approval applies. The second is whether the work is licensed work, so that the person doing it must hold a particular licence. The third is where the property boundary sits, and whether the owner has the right to build on that line. The answers come from different sources. A deck can be exempt from planning and still need a licensed contractor, and a fence can need no permit while being in dispute at the boundary. Answer each question separately, write down the source for each answer, and keep the answers apart in the job file. A single 'yes, it's fine' is not a usable record.

instructionSections.heading: Victoria: permits for decks and fences
instructionSections.body: The Victorian Building Authority practice note on building permits sets out the rules for decks, verandahs and fences. An attached deck needs a building permit irrespective of its size, and a detached deck that forms part of the amenity of a building also needs one. The size of the deck does not create an exemption for attached work, so a small deck still needs the permit position confirmed. For fences, the note exempts a fence that is not more than 2 metres high, but fences near a street are capped. Within 3 metres of a street, the limit is 1.5 metres for non-masonry fences and 1.2 metres for masonry or concrete fences. Within 9 metres of a street intersection, the limit is 1 metre above the footpath. Fences that form part of a pool barrier, and fences around children's outdoor play spaces, are outside the exemption. The cover of the note is dated April 2022, but its version history refers to a 2021 publication, so the current version must be checked before the note is relied on.

instructionSections.heading: New South Wales: exempt decks and fences
instructionSections.body: In New South Wales, exempt development rules set the limits within which a deck or fence needs no development approval. The planning page for decks and patios sets the top of an exempt deck at no more than 3 metres above existing ground at its highest point, and the floor no more than 1 metre above existing ground. The setback from the lot boundary is 5 metres in the listed rural and R5 zones and 900 millimetres in other zones. The structure must also not extend beyond the building line of a road frontage. For fences in the listed residential zones, a side or rear boundary fence must not exceed 1.8 metres, or 1.2 metres if it is built of masonry, and a fence along a primary or secondary road frontage must not exceed 1.2 metres. These are the exempt limits. A fence or deck above them, or outside a listed zone, needs the planning route that applies to the property. Check the zone for the property before relying on these numbers.

instructionSections.heading: Queensland and other states
instructionSections.body: Brisbane City Council states that building approval is needed for a fence more than 2 metres above the natural ground surface, measured across screens, fences and retaining walls combined. The page shows only a copyright year, so it is not dated. This rule applies to Brisbane only. Do not apply the Victorian or New South Wales limits to another state. Ask the local council or the building certifier, record the answer, and keep the source name and the date the answer was given.

instructionSections.heading: Boundary and the owner's authority
instructionSections.body: Before a deck or fence is set out, two things must be confirmed. The first is the owner's authority. The owner, or a person the owner has authorised in writing, must confirm the property address and the work to be done. The second is the boundary. Use the owner's title or survey documents to locate the boundary, and do not set out a line on the owner's word alone or from the position of an existing fence. Where a neighbour disputes the line, or where the documents are unclear, stop setting out and refer the question to a licensed surveyor or the owner's legal adviser. The record should show what was relied on for the boundary, not only that the boundary was marked.

instructionSections.heading: Licences are a separate question
instructionSections.body: A planning exemption does not change the licence position. In New South Wales, a contractor licence is needed for fencing work valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials, including GST, and the page applies this to fences regardless of materials. The deck licence question in New South Wales is covered in “Footings, post setting and levels”. In Queensland, the QBCC fence guide says a licence is not required for a fence on non-agricultural land valued under $3,300, and the QBCC licence page sets the same $3,300 figure for building work. These licence positions are explained further in “Footings, post setting and levels”. This lesson does not decide whether a particular contractor needs a licence. It asks that the question is asked, answered and recorded before work is quoted or started.

lessons.title: Timber selection, treatment and fixings
learningOutcomes: Select timber and treatment suited to the exposure, the use and the manufacturer data.
Select fixings that suit the timber, the treatment and the load.
Identify the risk of mixing incompatible metals and treatments.

instructionSections.heading: Match the timber to the exposure
instructionSections.body: A timber deck or fence is chosen for the conditions it will meet, not for its appearance. Before a board, post or rail is selected, record where it will sit and what it will meet. Ground contact, rain, standing water, sun and the timber's position relative to the ground are all part of that record. Treated timber is labelled with a treatment class, and the class tells you the conditions it is intended for. The Queensland government guidance describes H1 to H3 as classes for timber kept off the ground, with H3 for timber exposed to weather or periodic wetting. It describes H4 as the class for timber in contact with the ground or continually damp, and H5 for timber in contact with the ground or fresh water. The same guidance says each class suits the conditions described for the lower classes as well. The practical rule is simple: a post in the ground needs a ground-contact class, and a rail above the ground needs a class for above-ground exposure. Use the class on the supplier's label and data sheet for the product you are actually buying, not the class you expect.

instructionSections.heading: Read the supplier data and keep the reference
instructionSections.body: Each product has its own supplier data. The data names the treatment class, the intended use and sometimes the species and grade. Read it before purchase, and record the product name, the grade, the treatment class and the date of the data sheet on the job record. If the supplier data does not name the class, or names a class that does not match the use, do not use the product for that use. Do not assume that because a timber is treated it is suitable for every use. A treated product in the wrong class can look sound for years and then fail at its base, so the record matters as much as the choice. Where the supplier does not give treatment instructions for cut ends or drilled holes, record that the instruction was not available and refer it, rather than inventing a method.

instructionSections.heading: Cut ends, holes and field treatment
instructionSections.body: Cutting and drilling exposes untreated timber. The Australian standard for timber preservation (AS 1604) is the usual reference for this work, but its text was not read in this pass, so its requirements are not stated here. Use the supplier's written instruction for field treatment where one is given, and record the product used and the area treated. Do not use an unlabelled or decanted preservative. Dust from cutting treated timber is also a hazard. Use dust control and the dust protection named in the product label or safety data sheet, and, as a working practice rather than a verified rule, avoid sweeping the dust up dry in an enclosed space.

instructionSections.heading: Fixings and compatibility
instructionSections.body: A fixing has to suit the timber, the treatment and the load. Some treatments corrode standard steel fixings, and some metals react when they are in contact with each other. Use fixings whose rating or coating is stated, in the supplier or manufacturer data, as suitable for the treatment and the exposure. Do not assume that a galvanised, stainless or coated fixing is suitable for every treatment. Pre-drill near the ends of boards to reduce splitting. Where a connection carries load into the structure, such as a post to a bearer or a handrail to a post, the fixing must be rated for the load and fixed into the structure. A surface screw through a deck board does not make a structural connection, and it should not be relied on for one. Corrosion and incompatibility often show up years after the work, which is why the fixing record matters.

instructionSections.heading: Handling and chemical safety
instructionSections.body: Preservatives, stains and other products used on timber are hazardous chemicals, and the safety data sheet for each product is the starting point for their use. Keep a current copy where workers can reach it, and make sure the people using the product can see it. Store products apart from any chemical they are incompatible with, and keep containers suited to the product, as the Safe Work Australia storage guidance describes. Do not decant products into unlabelled containers.

lessons.title: Footings, post setting and levels
learningOutcomes: Describe the footing and post-setting checks that must be done before a deck or fence is loaded.
Set posts and levels to the approved design, and record the check.
Identify when footing and structural work is licensed or needs a permit, and refer it.

instructionSections.heading: Footings carry the structure
instructionSections.body: A footing transfers the load of a deck or fence into the ground. Its size, depth, and the concrete or fixing method come from the approved design, the ground conditions and the load. They are not chosen on site from habit or convenience. Before any excavation, confirm that the design is approved for the job, that the permit position has been checked under “Deck and fence scope, permits and boundary survey”, and that the footing details on site match the approved drawing. Where the ground is different from the design assumes, such as rock, soft fill or a slope, stop and refer the change. Do not change the depth or the size on site to suit the conditions. Concrete footings and timber or metal posts are the parts of a deck or fence that most often fail when they are set wrongly, and they are also the parts that are hardest to correct once the work is finished.

instructionSections.heading: Services and excavation
instructionSections.body: Check for underground services before digging. The Before You Dig Australia guidance says that anyone working near underground assets must understand their duty of care, and that plans show that infrastructure is present but not its exact position. The guidance describes lodging a plan request at least one day before the work begins, and checking that every asset owner has responded before work starts. Look for surface clues such as meters, marker posts, inspection points and warning signs. Use a skilled locator where one is available. Where a cable or pipe is found, the guidance describes exposing it by hand where that is safe and appropriate. Stop and refer if services are found where the design did not show them.

instructionSections.heading: Set posts and check levels
instructionSections.body: Set each post plumb and at the design height, and check the level across the structure before the concrete cures. Brace each post so it cannot move while the concrete sets, and check the brace again after the first pour. A post that looks plumb at ground level can be well out of line at the top of a long deck or fence, so take readings at the height the design names, not only at the base. Record the readings for each post, and photograph the set posts before backfilling. Where a reading falls outside the tolerance in the design, do not force the post into line. Reset the post, or refer the change. Forcing a post after the concrete has begun to set can crack the footing and loosen the post.

instructionSections.heading: Concrete cure and loading
instructionSections.body: Do not load a post, a rail or a deck frame until the concrete has cured for the period the supplier and the design state. The cure period depends on the mix, the weather and the placement, so use the supplier's stated period for the product, and record the time the concrete was placed and the time it may be loaded. Keep the record of the cure time with the footing record, and do not load a post early to meet a programme date.

instructionSections.heading: Licence positions by state
instructionSections.body: The licence question for footing and structural work depends on the state and on the exact wording of the licence page. In New South Wales, the carpentry page names timber decks and timber and metal fencing, but only under concreting for footings or structural support. A contractor licence is needed for building or trade work valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials, including GST. The fencing page applies the same $5,000 threshold to fencing work regardless of materials. In Queensland, the QBCC licence page sets a $3,300 threshold for building work, and does not name fences or decks. The QBCC fence guide says a fence on non-agricultural land valued under $3,300 does not need a licence, and it does not say whether labour and GST count. In Victoria, the Consumer Affairs Victoria page says domestic building work with a contract over $10,000 needs registration, and it does not mention decks. Confirm the position for the state and the job before pricing.

lessons.title: Balustrade and height-compliance boundaries (refer to building surveyor)
learningOutcomes: Recognise the balustrade and height issues that are referred to a building surveyor or competent person.
Describe why a balustrade cannot be certified by the worker.
Record the referral and the height and gap measurements without making a compliance claim.

instructionSections.heading: Why balustrades are referred
instructionSections.body: A balustrade protects people from falling from height. For Class 1 housing, the NCC 2022 Housing Provisions call for a barrier wherever a person could fall 1 metre or more, and set the minimum barrier height at 1 metre above a deck or balcony floor, or 865 mm on stairs and ramps (no date shown). A worker can measure and record a balustrade, but the worker cannot certify that it complies. Refer balustrade height and gap questions to a building surveyor or other competent person, and do not state that a balustrade complies.

instructionSections.heading: Record the measurements and the referral
instructionSections.body: Record the measured height from the finished surface, the gaps through the balustrade, and the fixing method, with photographs and the date. Record which person the matter was referred to and what was asked. A Queensland government guideline dated March 2017 gives a barrier of at least 1 metre and a maximum gap of 125 mm for decks or balconies more than 1 metre above ground. It is older guidance, so check the current NCC rule before relying on it. Do not rebuild a balustrade to a target height without the referral outcome. A balustrade that is measured and referred is more useful to the owner than one that is changed without a record.

lessons.title: Dog walking scope, keys and home access
learningOutcomes: Check whether a dog walking activity needs a council permit at the place and for the number of dogs planned
Hold, record and return client keys and access details under a written procedure
State which state registration points were found.

instructionSections.heading: Dog walking is council-dependent
instructionSections.body: Dog walking is not a licensed activity in the sources this course relies on, but it is regulated by councils where it takes place on public land. In Victoria, Agriculture Victoria's list of domestic animal business types (no date shown) names boarding establishments, breeding businesses, dog training establishments, pet shops and shelters or pounds, and it does not name dog walking. No state registration for walkers was found. Councils regulate dog walking on their own land. Port Phillip's dog walker page (no date shown) requires a permit once a walker has four or more dogs at one time. Yarra's commercial dog walker page (no date shown) requires a permit for a paid dog-exercise business operating on council-owned land or in public spaces, and caps the number of animals at one time at four. Ryde's open space dog minding form (July 2026) allows a single commercial minder under a permit, for up to four dogs, in named off-leash areas. The ACT Government's registered pet businesses page (no date shown) lists pet shops, operators that board animals, and prescribed businesses as pet businesses, and it does not mention dog walking.

instructionSections.heading: Keys, home access and the record you must keep
instructionSections.body: Dog walkers often hold a key or a code to a client's home. The key is the client's property and the access is the client's trust. Record the key in a register with the client's name, the date received, the person who holds it, and the date returned. Store keys in a locked place, and never copy a key without the client's written agreement. Never leave a key with a third party, and never enter a home outside the booked time. Record the access instructions, including any alarm, gate and pet door, in {{business:customers.access_instructions}}. If the client's home is unsafe, or the access fails, do not enter, and contact {{business:safety.escalation_contact}}. Security and privacy of client information are covered under the shared privacy lesson “Privacy, security and customer property”, and the business must apply it to keys and addresses.

instructionSections.heading: Insurance, WorkCover and the council conditions that follow
instructionSections.body: Council conditions often include insurance. Yarra's page (no date shown) sets a public liability minimum of $20 million, and requires the policy to list the council among the interested parties, with an end date stated. The page does not name a currency. Ryde's form (July 2026) requires APRA-approved public liability of $10 million, with evidence supplied at application. Port Phillip's dog walker page (no date shown) does not mention insurance. For businesses with staff, WorkSafe Victoria's WorkCover page (reviewed 19/05/2026) says registration is generally expected once a business takes on any employees, and a sole trader who employs nobody else does not need to register. A company that pays its owner as an employee is also required to register. A contractor that operates through a company and relies on one client may be treated as a deemed worker of that client, unless it is an owner-driver, and that can remove its own registration duty. Check every permit's insurance condition before taking a booking on council land, and record the check in {{business:compliance.policy_reference}}.

lessons.title: Dog handling, leash and group walking
learningOutcomes: Handle a dog on a lead with control, and keep each dog under effective control in public
Set group limits for each walker and each place, using the council and business limits
Recognise the signs of stress or aggression in a dog and separate it from the group before harm occurs

instructionSections.heading: Control on the lead and under effective control
instructionSections.body: A dog on a lead must be under the walker's control at all times. Port Phillip's dog walker page (no date shown) asks for dogs to be under effective control, asks handlers to carry a chain, cord or leash for each dog, and requires each dog to wear a collar or harness with the council's identification marker. Those are council-specific requirements that apply in Port Phillip. The principle of control is good practice everywhere. Use a lead of a length and type that lets you hold the dog without being pulled off balance. Do not wrap the lead around your hand or wrist. Keep the dog beside you or behind you where possible, and check the road, the footpath and the verge before crossing. Section 6.1 of the Victorian boarding code (revision 1, updated October 2004, printed April 2025) allows dogs to be walked on roads only when several conditions are met. Those include keeping every dog leashed the whole time, having an adult supervisor who is at least 17, no more than two dogs per person, and the owner's written approval. The business should adopt them as good practice and confirm the position.

instructionSections.heading: Group limits and the council rules
instructionSections.body: A walker with a group of dogs is taking on a risk that grows with each dog. Port Phillip's dog walker page (no date shown) requires a permit when a walker handles four or more dogs at one time, and sets a limit of eight dogs per person and twelve dogs in total across all handlers. Yarra's page (no date shown) caps the number of animals one person may exercise at one time at four. Ryde's form (July 2026) allows up to four dogs under a commercial minder permit. These are council-specific figures and apply in those councils only. The business limit must be set at or below the lowest limit that applies to the walk, and it must be recorded in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}. Where the walk crosses a council boundary, the lower limit of the two councils applies to the walk as a whole.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the dog and separating before harm
instructionSections.body: A dog that is stressed may pant, yawn, lip-lick, turn its head away, lower its tail, stiffen, freeze or hide. A dog showing aggression may growl, bare its teeth, raise its hackles, stare or lunge. Watch for these signs before a conflict starts. Move the dog away from the trigger, such as another dog, a child, a bicycle or a loud noise, and do not force the dog past it. In a group, keep dogs that do not get along apart and walk them separately. Never grab a fight between dogs by the collar or the body, because you can be bitten. Record each incident, including the dogs involved, the time and the action taken. The bite prevention and emergency steps are in “Bite prevention and emergency response”, and the business's group-walk procedure is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

lessons.title: Bite prevention and emergency response
learningOutcomes: Apply the bite prevention steps that reduce the chance of a bite during a walk or a home visit
Respond to a bite or dog attack, looking after the people and dogs involved and calling for help
Record and report a bite or attack, including the council reporting step where a permit applies

instructionSections.heading: Preventing a bite starts before the walk
instructionSections.body: Most bites happen when a handler does not notice the warning signs, or when a dog is put in a situation it cannot manage. Before each walk, read the dog's notes, its temperament record and any warnings from the client. Ask the client about the dog's history with other dogs, children and strangers, and about any medication, pain or illness that could make the dog defensive. Do not walk a dog that is injured or unwell without the client's written agreement and veterinary advice. On the walk, keep a safe distance from other dogs and people, and step aside rather than letting a dog be approached. Never leave a dog unattended on a lead, and never tie a dog to a fixture while you go elsewhere. The business's bite prevention procedure is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instructionSections.heading: Responding to a bite or an attack
instructionSections.body: If a dog bites or attacks, the first priority is to stop the attack without putting yourself at greater risk. Do not put your hands between the dogs. Use a barrier, such as a bag, a jacket or a lead loop, or call for help and move people away. Once the dogs are separated, check the person bitten, control the dog that bit, and call emergency services if the injury is serious. Keep pressure on any bleeding wound, and seek medical attention for any bite that breaks the skin. Keep the injured dog calm, and get it to a vet for any wound. Exchange details with the other owner and record names, addresses and the dog's registration where known. Do not admit blame in writing. The escalation contact in {{business:safety.escalation_contact}} must be called, and the emergency contact in {{business:safety.emergency_contact}} must be used for serious injuries.

instructionSections.heading: Reporting, records and council duties
instructionSections.body: Port Phillip's dog walker permit sets a 48-hour window for the council to be told about dog rushes and dog attacks, and requires records to be kept. Those records cover the dates and times each dog is in the walker's care, the owner's details and the council tag number. That is a council-specific condition for Port Phillip. Yarra's page (no date shown) sets no reporting or record-keeping duty, but it requires the permit to be carried and shown to an authorised officer on request. Ryde's form (July 2026) contains no incident-reporting requirement, although the council may end a permit where a minder fails to follow directions. The business should report every bite and attack to its own escalation contact the same day, and record the time, the place, the dogs involved, the injuries, the people called and the action taken. Keep the record for the period the council requires. Where the council does not require a report, the business should still keep the record and review it.

lessons.title: Pet taxi: vehicle restraint and transport
learningOutcomes: Restrain each animal in the vehicle with a method that prevents injury to the animal and to the driver
Plan a pet transport journey that keeps the animal safe from heat, cold, water loss and distress
State which transport rules are confirmed, and which licence or permit questions for a pet taxi remain open.

instructionSections.heading: Restraint in the vehicle: the NT page and the NSW code
instructionSections.body: A pet taxi carries animals in a vehicle, and the way they are held in the vehicle is the most important safety control. The Northern Territory Government's animal welfare page (no date shown) lists, among its recent changes, a rule on securing dogs while they ride in cars or on trailers, and it states that the changes took effect on 3 November 2025. Restraint is good practice everywhere. Use a secured crate, a harness connected to a seat belt anchor designed for it, or a partition that keeps each animal in its own space. Never let an animal ride loose in the cabin or the boot, and never let it stand on the driver's seat or in a position where it could distract the driver or be thrown forward. Keep the restraint in good order, and check the anchor points before each journey. The business's vehicle and restraint procedure is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the vehicle is recorded as {{business:equipment.primary_tool}}.

instructionSections.heading: What the transport codes cover, and what they do not
instructionSections.body: The New South Wales Animal Welfare Code of Practice No 1 covers companion animals, including dogs and cats, from collection and holding, including overnight stays, through transit to delivery. The code names no licence or registration. Its vehicle rules (section 7.1) call for protection from injury, non-slip floors, ventilation and control of extreme temperatures, with cats and small dogs kept in fixed cages or carriers and larger dogs separated by compartments or partitions. Section 7.2 rules out keeping animals in a stationary vehicle in sun or heat unless the vehicle has both shade and airflow. The code does not address driver welfare. The ACT's land transport instrument DI2018-90 (notified 17 May 2018) is limited to livestock: clause 3(2) covers the people responsible for livestock being transported, and it sets no rule for companion animals. The Queensland compulsory codes list (last updated 1 July 2026) names nine codes, none of them for companion animal transport.

instructionSections.heading: Journey planning: heat, water, time and records
instructionSections.body: A journey is a period when the animal cannot leave the vehicle, so the journey must be planned as a welfare step. Plan the shortest route with the fewest stops. Do not leave an animal in a parked car, even for a short time, because the temperature inside can rise quickly, and the NSW code restricts parked vehicles in sun or heat. Carry water and a bowl, offer water at each stop, and keep the cabin ventilated. Check the animal at each stop for distress, breathing and toilet needs. Record each journey, with the pickup and drop-off addresses, the time, the animals carried, the restraint used, the stops and any incident. Where a journey is long or the weather is hot or cold, the business should plan a break and a cooling or warming step, and record it. The NSW code sets heat and cold provisions.

lessons.title: Pet first aid and emergency vet referral
learningOutcomes: Recognise the signs of an animal emergency that need a veterinarian without delay
Carry out a basic first response that keeps the animal calm, safe and warm, and gets it to care
State the limit of the walker's role: first response and referral, not diagnosis or treatment

instructionSections.heading: The walker's role in an animal emergency
instructionSections.body: A dog walker or pet taxi operator is not a veterinarian. The role in an emergency is to recognise that the animal needs a vet, to give a first response that keeps it safe, and to get it to a vet or an emergency service. The walker must not diagnose the cause of the animal's condition, must not give human medication to the animal, and must not decide that the animal does not need a vet. Pet first aid training is a useful skill, but it is not a veterinary qualification and it does not give any authority to treat an animal. The walker's written authority from the owner, and the owner's vet details, are the basis of any decision to take an animal to care. The business's emergency procedure is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the owner's emergency details are held on the client file.

instructionSections.heading: Signs that need a vet without delay
instructionSections.body: Signs that need a vet without delay include difficulty breathing, collapse, seizure, uncontrolled bleeding, a suspected broken limb, a wound that is deep or gaping, signs of heat stress such as collapse, heavy panting or drooling, a suspected poisoning, a swollen or distended abdomen, and any sudden change in behaviour that is severe. The list is practical guidance and is not a confirmed legal list. Where the animal shows any of these signs, the walker must stop the walk or the journey, call the vet or the emergency service, and follow the vet's instructions. If the walker cannot reach a vet, the walker should take the animal to the nearest emergency vet and keep the owner informed at every step. Do not wait to see whether the animal improves.

instructionSections.heading: First response: calm, safe, warm, and to care
instructionSections.body: The first response is to keep the animal calm, safe and warm, and to avoid making the injury worse. Approach a hurt animal slowly, speak quietly, and use a muzzle or a towel where the animal may bite, but only if it can be done safely. Control bleeding with firm pressure using a clean dressing, and do not remove an embedded object. Keep a heat-stressed animal in shade, offer small amounts of water if it is conscious, and move it to a cooler place. Do not force water into an animal that is not conscious. Keep the animal still if a limb or spine may be injured, and move it on a flat board or towel. Record the time, what was seen, what was done and who was called. The walker should not delay transport to a vet while performing the first response. The shared emergency lesson “Emergency procedures and evacuation” and the incident steps in “Incident response and reporting” apply to the walker's own safety.

lessons.title: Route planning, bookings and walk records
learningOutcomes: Plan a daily route that stays inside each permitted place and within each group limit
Build a booking schedule that allows for pickups, walks, travel and records
Keep walk records that a council, client or insurer can rely on

instructionSections.heading: Routes inside the permits
instructionSections.body: A route is a list of places, and each place has its own rules. Before planning a route, identify each council park, reserve or footpath area on it, and check the permit for each place that requires one. Port Phillip's dog walker page (no date shown) requires a permit once a walker has four or more dogs, with limits of eight per walker and twelve in total. Yarra's page (no date shown) requires a permit for a paid dog-exercise business on council land, and caps the animals at one time at four. Ryde's form (July 2026) covers specific off-leash areas, with one commercial minder and up to four dogs. Where a route includes a place with no permit, or a place where the permit does not apply, the route must avoid it or the business must confirm the position. Plan the route so that the group size never exceeds the lowest limit for any place on the route, and record the plan.

instructionSections.heading: Booking so the day works
instructionSections.body: A dog walking day has a time for each pickup, each walk, each drop-off and each journey between them. Build the booking from those steps, and leave a margin for delays such as a dog that needs a longer walk, a traffic delay or a client who is late. Record each booking with the client's name, the dog or dogs, the pickup and drop-off times, the access instructions and the cancellation rule. Where the business uses a group walk, record the group size and the permit for each place. The scheduling method is held in {{business:jobs.scheduling_method}}, and the time tracking method in {{business:jobs.time_tracking}}. Do not book a walk that cannot be completed inside the permit's hours. The Port Phillip page read for this review does not state walking hours, so any time limit must be confirmed with the council before the booking.

instructionSections.heading: Walk records that stand up to scrutiny
instructionSections.body: A walk record shows what happened. It should include the date, the walker, the dogs walked, the places visited, the time the walk started and ended, the group size, any incident, any stop, the condition of each dog on return, and the handover to the client. Port Phillip's dog walker page (no date shown) expects a log of when each dog is in the walker's charge, the owner's name and how to reach them, and the council tag number. It also requires the permit to be available on the job, in paper or electronic form, and produced when a council officer or a member of the community asks. Record the permit reference for each walk. Photos of the dog can help a client see that the walk happened, but they must be taken and stored under the client's privacy consent, and the business must follow {{business:jobs.photo_requirements}}. Keep the records for as long as the business procedure or the council requires, and make them available to the client on request. Where a record has been changed, record the change, the date and who made it.

lessons.title: Flat-pack assembly from manufacturer instructions and parts control
learningOutcomes: Check a flat-pack delivery against the parts list before assembly starts.
Assemble furniture in the manufacturer's sequence without substituting parts.
Record missing, damaged or unsuitable parts and refuse assembly where a part is unsafe.

instructionSections.heading: Check the delivery before you start
instructionSections.body: Before assembly, open the delivery and count the parts against the parts list and the packing list. Check each panel and fitting for damage, such as split board edges, bent metal, stripped threads and missing hardware. Keep the packaging until the job is accepted, and photograph any missing or damaged part with consent. Do not assemble from a partial set or substitute a part from another product, even one that looks the same. A substituted part can change the load rating or the fit.

instructionSections.heading: Assemble in the manufacturer's sequence
instructionSections.body: Follow the manufacturer's assembly sequence and use the fixings specified for each joint. Keep the instructions at hand and check each step before moving on, because many fixings are hidden by later steps. Tighten fixings to the point of a firm joint without stripping the board. Do not use a fixing that is not specified, and do not force a panel that does not align, because the misalignment usually means a step has been missed or a part is wrong. Stop and check the instructions rather than forcing the joint.

lessons.title: Fixture anchoring and load limits in walls
learningOutcomes: Identify the load each fixture carries and the substrate that must carry it.
Choose anchors and fixings rated for the load and the wall type, using the manufacturer's data.
Refuse or refer a fixture whose load cannot be carried safely by the wall.

instructionSections.heading: Work out the load before choosing an anchor
instructionSections.body: A wall-mounted fixture carries its own weight plus whatever is put on it, and the force on each fixing point is greater than the weight alone when the load sits at the end of a shelf or when someone pulls on the item. Work out the load from the item's specification, the contents it will hold and the way it will be used. Record the weight of the empty item, the weight of the expected contents, and the force at each fixing point, including the force from use. Use the worst-case load, not the average, because a shelf is often loaded unevenly and pulled from one end. Choose an anchor rated for that load. Manufacturers state a load rating for each anchor in each wall material, and that rating is the limit. A rating for a different wall material does not apply to the wall in front of you.

instructionSections.heading: Identify the substrate before drilling
instructionSections.body: Identify what the wall is made of before any fixing is chosen. Plasterboard is light and needs a fixing that spreads the load across the board, or a fixing into a stud or a noggin behind it. Masonry such as brick, concrete or block needs a masonry fixing of the right size and depth, and a drill and bit that suit the material. A hollow or cavity wall needs a fixing rated for a hollow substrate. Timber framing is a common target, but its position must be confirmed, not assumed. Use a stud finder and check the result by a second method where possible.

instructionSections.heading: Match the anchor to the wall and check for services
instructionSections.body: Once the substrate is known, choose a fixing that the manufacturer rates for that substrate and the calculated load. Where the load is heavy, fix into studs or solid substrate, with fixings that take the load into the structure. Do not rely on a plastic plug in plasterboard for a heavy load unless the manufacturer rates that plug for the load and the board. Before drilling, check for concealed cables and pipes, and stop if one is found or suspected. Concealed wiring is electrical work, and concealed pipes are plumbing or gas work, and both are licensed work in the states covered below. Refer the fixing to the licensed person, and do not drill into the service yourself to find out what it is. If the position of the fixing cannot be confirmed as clear of services, choose a different position or a different method, or refer the work.

instructionSections.heading: Install, test and record
instructionSections.body: Install the fixings to the manufacturer's directions, including the drill size, the depth and the torque or tightening method. After installation, test the fixing with a controlled load before the item is used. Do not use a fixing that moves, pulls out, cracks the surface or shows any sign of failure under the test. Record the item, the load, the substrate, the fixing used with its rating, the position of each fixing, the test result and the date. Where the wall cannot be confirmed as able to carry the load, do not hang the item on it. Refer the fixture or choose a different method, and record the referral and the reason.

instructionSections.heading: Dust, drilling and personal protection
instructionSections.body: Drilling into masonry or fibre-cement produces dust, and drilling into plasterboard produces fine material. Eye protection is needed whenever drilling. Hearing protection is needed where the noise cannot be eliminated. Dust controls and any respiratory protection depend on the site risk assessment. Do not assume that a dust mask is enough for masonry drilling without checking the risk assessment and the manufacturer's data for the mask.

lessons.title: Wall-mounted fixture and electrical boundaries (referral)
learningOutcomes: Identify the wall-mounted fixtures whose electrical connection is referred to a licensed electrical worker.
Describe the safe response when an electrical connection is needed or a cable is found.
Record the referral without making any electrical connection.

instructionSections.heading: Mounting is not the same as connecting
instructionSections.body: A wall-mounted item such as a television bracket, a wall light, a heated towel rail or a mirror with lighting may need an electrical connection. Mounting the item to the wall may be within your scope if the mounting is only structural and the item has no fixed electrical supply. Connecting it to a fixed circuit, running a new cable, or altering a switch is electrical work and is referred to a licensed electrical worker. Check the item's requirements before mounting, and stop if it needs a fixed supply that is not present.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer when a cable is found
instructionSections.body: If a cable is found while locating a fixing point, stop drilling in that area and do not move, cut or join it. Record the location and refer the connection to a licensed electrical worker. If the item needs a fixed electrical supply that is not at the wall, refer the supply to the licensed electrical worker and do not run a cable yourself. Complete the structural mounting only where the wall has been confirmed clear and the approver agrees.

lessons.title: Scope, intake and the boundary with carpet and upholstery
learningOutcomes: Describe the scope of furniture restoration and separate it from in-place carpet and upholstery cleaning.
Ask the intake questions that decide whether a piece is in scope.
Record a scope decision, with its reason, before any work or quote is issued.

instructionSections.heading: What furniture restoration covers
instructionSections.body: In this course, restoration means working on a furniture piece in a workshop or at the business's premises. It includes stripping and refinishing timber, repairing joints and veneer, and renewing the fabric, foam and backing of an upholstered piece. It does not mean cleaning fabric in place in a client's home or office. That work is taught in the carpet and upholstery cleaning course, including the fibre identification lesson “Fibre and construction identification” (Fibre and construction identification). The two courses are kept apart so that a cleaner does not take on a restoration job without the checks taught here.

instructionSections.heading: Intake questions
instructionSections.body: Ask what the piece is, where it came from, and its age if known. Ask what finish or fabric the client believes it has, whether it has been stripped, repaired or re-covered before, and whether it has been kept in a damp, smoky, flooded or contaminated place. Ask whether children or pets use it, and what result the client wants. Record the answers. They decide whether the job is in scope and which checks come first. If the piece has been affected by mould, fire, smoke, flood or biohazard contamination, stop intake and refer the job to the High-risk cleaning module. Do not start restoration on it.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding in, conditional or out
instructionSections.body: A job is in scope, conditional, or refused. A conditional job goes ahead only after a named check is passed, such as the screening in “Screen for lead and asbestos: test, stop and refer”. A refused job is one the business cannot do safely or lawfully with the people, equipment or licences it holds. Refuse work that needs a licence the business does not hold, and say so in writing. Record every decision and its reason before work starts or a quote is sent, using the business's approved procedure {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

lessons.title: Identify timber, finish and fabric before any work
learningOutcomes: Identify the timber construction, the finish layers and their condition, and the fabric and backing of an upholstered piece.
Recognise age and origin clues that call for screening before work.
Record unknowns and the screening step they trigger.

instructionSections.heading: Why identification comes first
instructionSections.body: Each finish, fabric and backing reacts differently to heat, solvent, water and abrasion. Identification decides the method, the tests and the hazards that apply. An unidentified surface is treated as the most hazardous likely case until it has been tested or reviewed. Identification is not a guess at the piece's value or its history. It is a record of what is there and what is not yet known.

instructionSections.heading: Timber and finish
instructionSections.body: Look at the grain, colour, wear pattern and edges. Check whether the piece is solid timber or veneer over a core, and whether joints move. Veneer edges and worn corners often show the difference. Identify the finish by the approved test set: sheen, the point where the finish has worn through, feel, and a small test in a hidden area where the approved procedure allows it. Shellac, lacquer, varnish, oil and paint behave differently under the same method. Old paint may contain lead, so the finish is not identified as safe because it looks sound. Follow the approved procedure {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instructionSections.heading: Fabric and backing
instructionSections.body: Read the fibre from a label where one exists, and otherwise from look and feel. Look at the backing, foam, webbing and adhesive. Old backings can be bitumen-backed hessian, board or fibrous layers, and their adhesives can be unknown. Treat any material that cannot be identified as needing screening under “Screen for lead and asbestos: test, stop and refer” before cutting, stripping or removing it. Do not pull a backing off to see what it is.

instructionSections.heading: Age and origin as screening prompts
instructionSections.body: Age clues include construction methods, the number of paint layers, labels and where the piece came from. Age does not confirm lead or asbestos, and it does not rule them out. NSW's house guidance links lead-based paint to homes built before 1970 (page metadata modified 20 July 2026). That is a prompt to screen. It is not a finding about any particular piece. The same guidance names furniture only in its cleaning advice for renovation work, and it gives no furniture screening rule. Age is a reason to test or refer, not a reason to assume a result.

lessons.title: Screen for lead and asbestos: test, stop and refer
learningOutcomes: Explain why old finishes and backings are screened for lead and asbestos before they are disturbed.
Apply the stop-and-refer rule when a result is positive or unknown.
Record a screening decision that a reviewer can follow.

instructionSections.heading: Lead in old paint and finishes
instructionSections.body: NSW's house guidance links lead-based paint to homes built before 1970 and says the risk rises when old paint is disturbed (page metadata modified 20 July 2026). Lead can be a hazard without renovation too, but disturbing old paint raises the risk. That same house guidance allows intact paint to be left or painted over, and it mentions furniture only in its cleaning advice. Safe Work Australia's lead page treats sanding, grinding and welding as lead processes when they throw off lead-bearing dust or smoke, and it names abrasive blasting and water-jet treatment of lead-based paint. It does not mention heat stripping or furniture. This course therefore does not rely on that gap. Until a finish is screened or reviewed, do not sand, heat strip, dry scrape or use an open flame on it. Where a test is available through the approved method, use it and record the result. Where the result is positive or unknown, stop and refer to a person trained in lead work practices.

instructionSections.heading: Asbestos in old furniture
instructionSections.body: Asbestos can be found in some older backings, adhesives, insulation and fibrous or board-like layers. The rule in this course is simple. If you suspect asbestos, stop. Do not disturb the material further, keep people and pets away from it, record where it is, and refer it. Removal is licensed work, and the rules depend on the state or territory. Queensland requires a Class A licence even for small amounts of friable asbestos, and a Class B licence once non-friable asbestos exceeds ten square metres (no page date shown). South Australia places friable and non-friable removal under Class A with no area cap, and reserves Class B for non-friable material above ten square metres (no page date shown). Ten square metres or less of non-friable material needs no licence in Queensland, though safe work procedures still apply. The restorer does not make the call from memory. The business refers the material to the right licensed person or business.

instructionSections.heading: Records and the stop decision
instructionSections.body: A screening record states the item, the method used, the result, the decision, and who was told. A positive or unknown result stops the job. Work resumes only when the decision is written, the basis for it is recorded, and the client has been told about the delay or refusal. A quick look does not count as a screening result. Do not tell a client that an item is lead-free or asbestos-free without a result that supports it.

lessons.title: Strippers, solvents and finishing chemicals
learningOutcomes: Find the controls for a product in its SDS and label before first use.
Explain why stripping products must not be mixed unless the label or SDS allows it.
Store, use and dispose of solvent-soaked materials and residues safely.

instructionSections.heading: Read the SDS before the first use
instructionSections.body: A safety data sheet is the product's main safety record. Safe Work Australia's SDS guidance expects a workplace to hold an SDS for each chemical it uses, filed in its hazardous chemical register (no page date shown). It also asks that the SDS be easy to reach for people who use or store the chemical, emergency responders, and anyone who may be exposed. Read the sections on hazards, first aid, handling and storage, exposure controls and personal protection, and disposal before the first use. Keep the SDS where workers can reach it at the work area. The business's SDS list is recorded at {{business:materials.sds_links}}.

instructionSections.heading: Strippers and solvents differ
instructionSections.body: Strippers and solvents do not share one set of hazards. Some are solvent-based, which means vapour and flammable liquid hazards. Some are alkaline or caustic, which means skin and eye damage. Some are water-based, which still needs gloves and eye protection because the label may say so. Dilution, dwell time, ventilation and PPE come from the label and SDS for that product. Do not mix products unless the label or SDS allows it. A mixture can create a hazard that neither product has alone.

instructionSections.heading: Ventilation, ignition and waste
instructionSections.body: Work where vapour can move away from people and from ignition sources, including heat guns and any open flame. Keep containers closed when not in use. Store flammable products as the SDS and the business's storage procedure set out. Solvent-soaked rags carry a fire risk and a vapour risk. The approach taught here is to keep these rags in a closed metal container, away from heat, and to dispose of them as the SDS and local council rules set out. Collect spent residue and dispose of it in the same way. Do not pour it down a drain unless the SDS and local rules allow it.

lessons.title: Wood dust and sanding controls
learningOutcomes: Set up on-tool extraction and a dust collector to the minimum dust class in the guidance.
Clean sanding areas without compressed air.
Choose and fit a respirator as the last control, not the first.

instructionSections.heading: Why sanding dust matters
instructionSections.body: Sanding makes fine dust that can be breathed deep into the lungs. WorkSafe Victoria's wood dust guidance (reviewed 17 April 2026) includes sanding in its list of common wood-dust sources and asks that extraction sit as near as practicable to every dust source. The guidance covers wood dust generally, so this course applies it to furniture sanding as well. Timber floor sanding has its own controls, which are taught in the timber floor restoration course.

instructionSections.heading: Extraction first
instructionSections.body: For portable sanders, use on-tool extraction connected to a portable collector. WorkSafe Victoria recommends a minimum Dust Class M for that collector, and the same class for an industrial vacuum used in cleaning. A dust bag alone does not meet the at-source approach that page describes. Inspect the extraction system for leaks, because a leaking hose or joint lets dust out at the work area. Keep the extraction running while sanding.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning up without lifting the dust
instructionSections.body: Do not use compressed air to clean sanding areas, because it can put settled dust back into the air as a second exposure. Use a HEPA-filtered vacuum with the required dust class, or a wet cleaning method. Clean the area at the end of each session, and keep food and drinks out of the sanding area.

instructionSections.heading: Respirators are the backup
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria treats respiratory protection as the backup for when higher controls cannot keep exposure within the exposure standards, and it usually points to a reusable half-face model with P2 filtering. Respirators should meet the Australian Standard named on that page, AS/NZS 1716:2012. NSW's house guidance names AS/NZS 1716 for respirators and masks with P1 or P2 filters. NSW's guidance also describes simple paper masks as a poor fit that offers little protection from fine dust. The exposure figures WorkSafe Victoria lists are set out in the safety notes below.

lessons.title: Stripping timber furniture: choosing and controlling the method
learningOutcomes: Choose a stripping method after identification and screening, starting with the least aggressive method that does the job.
Apply chemical, abrasive and heat methods within their controls.
Record the method, the controls and the reason for the choice.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a method is a decision
instructionSections.body: Stripping methods fall into three groups: chemical (apply a product, allow it to dwell, then remove the softened finish), abrasive (sanding or scraping), and heat (a heat gun to lift the finish). Each group has its own hazards, and the choice is made only after identification in “Identify timber, finish and fabric before any work” and screening in “Screen for lead and asbestos: test, stop and refer”. The first choice is the least aggressive method that does the job on that piece. Sanding is the most dust-producing method. Heat carries a fire and a veneer risk. Chemical methods carry product hazards. The method is recorded with the reason for the choice.

instructionSections.heading: Chemical stripping
instructionSections.body: Follow the product's label and SDS for application, dwell time, removal and any neutralising step. Safe Work Australia's SDS guidance expects the SDS to be easy to reach for workers who use the product. Test the product on a hidden area first. Keep the product off skin and out of the eyes. Collect the softened residue and dispose of it as the SDS sets out. Do not scrape spent residue into a drain, and do not leave residue on the timber, because it can stop the next finish from bonding.

instructionSections.heading: Abrasive stripping
instructionSections.body: Sanding produces the most dust, so the extraction and respirator controls in “Wood dust and sanding controls” apply in full. If the finish has not been screened for lead, do not sand until the screening is done. Work with the grain, use the coarsest grit that does the job, and keep to the depth needed. Over-sanding removes veneer and changes the shape of mouldings and edges. Stop and reassess when the timber shows through in some places and not others.

instructionSections.heading: Heat stripping
instructionSections.body: NSW's house guidance on lead paint sets a heat gun to its lowest setting, asks users not to linger in one spot, and warns against open-flame torches, which release lead fumes (no page date shown). That guidance is written for houses, so this course applies the same caution to furniture until screening says otherwise. Apply the same caution to furniture until screening says otherwise. Keep an extinguisher and a water source nearby, and keep solvent rags away from the heat. Heat can lift veneer and soften heat-sensitive adhesive, so test a hidden area before using heat near veneer edges or joints.

lessons.title: Joint, veneer and surface repair
learningOutcomes: Assess a joint or veneer fault and record its condition before repair.
Stabilise a joint or veneer with adhesive, clamping or pressing, and allow the stated cure time.
Explain why a higher-skill repair is priced on assessment and stages, not on area alone.

instructionSections.heading: Assess before repair
instructionSections.body: Check whether a joint is loose, cracked or missing glue, and whether veneer is lifted, bubbled or chipped. Feel for movement by gently rocking the joint, and look for old glue lines and gaps. The aim of the repair is to stabilise the piece, not to hide the fault. Record the condition with photographs before any repair. A filled joint that still moves has not been repaired.

instructionSections.heading: Adhesive, clamping and cure
instructionSections.body: Choose an adhesive suited to the joint and the timber, and follow the product data sheet for mixing, open time and cure. Remove old glue and dust where the approved method requires it, because adhesive does not bond well to old residue. Clamp evenly, check that the frame is square, and wipe off squeeze-out before it sets. Allow the full cure time before putting load on the joint.

instructionSections.heading: Veneer lifts and bubbles
instructionSections.body: Lift veneer only as far as needed to get adhesive under it. Apply glue under controlled pressure, using a press, cauls or evenly spread clamps. Heavy weights can crush the veneer or crack the surface. Test heat on a hidden area first if the approved method calls for heat to soften old adhesive, and keep the heat away from edges. Check the surface flat before finishing.

instructionSections.heading: Filling and levelling
instructionSections.body: Use fillers that suit the finish method, and fill only what is needed. Fill the surface defect, not the structural gap. Colour matching is taught in “Staining, sealing and finish application”. Level the repair only after the filler has cured, so that the surface is not dug into.

lessons.title: Staining, sealing and finish application
learningOutcomes: Judge a colour match on a test piece before the visible surface is stained.
Apply seal and finish coats in thin, even layers, with sanding between coats controlled as taught in “Wood dust and sanding controls”.
Hand back a piece only after the stated cure time, and record the products and times used.

instructionSections.heading: Colour and stain
instructionSections.body: Judge the colour match on a test piece of the same timber, or on a hidden area, and check it in good daylight-equivalent light before stain goes on the visible surface. Stain takes up unevenly in some timbers and may need a seal coat first to even the absorption. Record the product and mix used for the match. Follow the product SDS and the approved procedure. Do not promise an exact match, because the same stain can look different on a different timber or a different light.

instructionSections.heading: Sealing and sanding between coats
instructionSections.body: Seal the timber where the approved method calls for it. Sand between coats only with the extraction and respirator controls in “Wood dust and sanding controls”, using a fine grade that does not cut through the stain or the seal. Wipe off dust before the next coat, using a method that does not lift the dust back into the air.

instructionSections.heading: Finish application and cure
instructionSections.body: Apply finish in thin, even coats, and do not overload the brush or cloth. Work with the grain, and keep the room ventilated, away from ignition sources. Oil-based products, shellac and lacquer each have their own SDS and their own recoat and cure times. Dry to touch is not the same as cured. Do not stack, wrap or hand back a piece until the stated cure time has passed.

instructionSections.heading: Rags and waste
instructionSections.body: Some finishing materials, including oily rags, carry a storage risk. Use the approved storage and disposal procedure, and do not leave used rags in a pile. Keep them as the approved procedure and the SDS set out.

lessons.title: Upholstery restoration: strip-back, foam and fabric renewal
learningOutcomes: Screen the old fabric, backing, adhesive and filling before cutting or stripping them back.
Inspect and repair the frame, springs and webbing before covering.
Document the foam and filling fitted, and the basis for any fire-related statement made to the client.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of the work
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers restoration of upholstered furniture in the workshop: removing old fabric and filling, checking the frame and springs, repairing or replacing webbing, and fitting new foam and fabric. Cleaning fabric in place on a client's premises is taught in the carpet and upholstery cleaning course, and in particular its fibre identification lesson “Fibre and construction identification”. Keep the two jobs separate in the quote and the records.

instructionSections.heading: Strip-back and screening
instructionSections.body: Before cutting off the old fabric, screen the backing, adhesive and filling as taught in “Screen for lead and asbestos: test, stop and refer”. Stop if you see fibrous or board-like material, bitumen-backed hessian with an unknown layer beneath, or an adhesive of unknown content. Do not cut, pull or disturb the material further. Record the location with photographs and refer it to the right licensed business. Queensland and South Australia both require a Class A licence for any amount of friable asbestos, and a Class B licence for more than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos (no page dates shown); other states and territories have their own thresholds. This course does not grant that licence. Keep old materials that are safe to keep, so that the next step can be checked against them.

instructionSections.heading: Frame, springs and webbing
instructionSections.body: Inspect the frame joints, using the method in “Joint, veneer and surface repair”, and check the springs and webbing for breaks, sag and corrosion. Record what is found. Repair the frame and webbing before covering. Covering a frame that has not been repaired hides a fault the client will pay to fix later.

instructionSections.heading: Foam, filling and fire-related claims
instructionSections.body: Ask the supplier for documentation on the foam and filling, and record what was fitted, including density and grade where the supplier gives them. Do not tell a client that the foam or fabric meets a fire standard unless the supplier documentation says so.

instructionSections.heading: Fabric renewal
instructionSections.body: Cut the fabric with the pattern direction and nap in mind, and check the cut against the old piece before trimming. Keep the fabric clean in the workshop. Remove pins, staples and fixings carefully, because a released spring or a cut staple can cause injury. Tension the cover evenly and check the seams before the final trim.

lessons.title: Quoting restoration work from a condition assessment
learningOutcomes: Separate the assessment, screening and restoration stages in a quote.
Write the scope, assumptions, exclusions and price-changing conditions on a quote.
Present hazard findings as stops or conditions, not as upsells.

instructionSections.heading: Price the assessment and the work
instructionSections.body: A restoration quote has three parts: the assessment, the restoration work, and the items that could change the price. Charge for assessment time, including screening, even if the client does not go ahead. Price the restoration by the stages the method requires, such as strip, repair, finish and cure. Price on the condition of the piece as found, not only on its size or number of pieces. The business's approved pricing method is {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}, and the minimum charge is {{business:pricing.minimum_charge}}.

instructionSections.heading: Scope, assumptions and exclusions
instructionSections.body: Write what is included, the assumptions the price depends on, and what is excluded. Typical exclusions are asbestos or lead removal, structural repair beyond the agreed scope, and colour matching to an item the business has not seen. Write what changes the price, such as a positive screening result, hidden damage found during strip-back, or a change of finish. A quote that depends on a screening result says so.

instructionSections.heading: Options and hazard findings
instructionSections.body: Offer a standard finish and a more durable finish where both are real options, and explain the difference. Do not present a higher price as the fix for a hazard. A positive or unknown screening result is a stop and a referral. It is not an upsell. Show it on the quote as a condition, and say what happens next.

instructionSections.heading: Approval before sending
instructionSections.body: Send the quote only after the business's quoting approval step is complete. The approval step is {{business:pricing.quoting_approval}}. Record the approval with the quote. A quote without a recorded approval is not sent.

lessons.title: Client expectations, value and authenticity claims
learningOutcomes: Set out what restoration will and will not change, and put the limits in writing.
Avoid claims of age, value, authenticity or lead-free and asbestos-free status that the evidence does not support.
Handle client photos and item details with the business's privacy approach.

instructionSections.heading: Set expectations early
instructionSections.body: Restoration shows the piece's history and its wear. It does not return the piece to new. Explain what will change, what will stay, and what cannot be guaranteed, such as an exact colour match, full removal of every mark, or a fixed cure outcome. Show a test piece or sample where you can, and put the main limits in writing before work starts.

instructionSections.heading: Age, value and authenticity
instructionSections.body: Do not describe a piece as an antique, original, heritage or valuable unless the client has documentation, or a qualified appraiser has confirmed it. Do not say that a repair will raise the piece's value. Describe what the work does to the piece. Where the client asks about age or value, suggest a qualified appraiser and record the conversation.

instructionSections.heading: Lead, asbestos and health statements
instructionSections.body: Do not tell a client that an item is lead-free or asbestos-free without a result that supports the statement. Do not describe a finish as safe for children or pets without the product's label and SDS. If screening found a positive or unknown result, tell the client plainly, record the advice given, and refer the material as “Screen for lead and asbestos: test, stop and refer” sets out. Share results as results. Share the regulator's or specialist's advice with them as well.

instructionSections.heading: Privacy and complaints
instructionSections.body: Store photographs and item details securely. Ask for the client's permission before sharing photographs of their home, belongings or the piece, including on social media. Whether the Privacy Act binds the business depends on turnover and activity: businesses with turnover at or under $3 million are generally outside it unless an exception applies. Use the approved wording in {{business:customers.communication_policy}}. If a client complains, record the complaint, acknowledge it, and escalate it as {{business:customers.complaint_escalation}} sets out.

lessons.title: Final inspection, handover and records
learningOutcomes: Inspect a finished piece against the agreed scope, quote and quality standard.
Check for residue, dust and uncured finish before handover.
Complete the handover and file the records the business's policy requires.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect against the scope
instructionSections.body: Compare the piece with the scope and the quote. Check the structure and joints, the finish and its colour, the fabric and its seams, the hardware, and the cleanliness of the piece. Use the business's inspection checklist, {{business:quality.inspection_checklist}}. Check the piece in good daylight-equivalent light, because most finish defects show only in good light.

instructionSections.heading: Check the finish and the cure
instructionSections.body: Look for runs, bubbles, dull patches, dust nibs and colour that does not match the agreed test piece. Check that the finish is cured to the time on the product data sheet. A touch test is used only where the approved method allows it, and never on a fresh finish. A defect found at this stage is recorded and reworked before handover.

instructionSections.heading: Check residue and cleanliness
instructionSections.body: Confirm that no stripper residue, sanding dust or solvent smell remains. Confirm that waste has been disposed of as the procedure sets out and that the work area has been cleaned with an approved method, such as a HEPA-filtered vacuum or a wet method. Do not clean with compressed air, because WorkSafe Victoria advises against it.

instructionSections.heading: Handover and records
instructionSections.body: Explain the care and cure time, and the limits agreed at quote. Give care instructions that suit the finish and the fabric, and record the client's sign-off. File the before and after photographs, the method and product records, the screening results, the supplier documents and the sign-off. Keep these records as the business's policy sets out, {{business:quality.evidence_requirements}}.

lessons.title: Scope, client approval and exclusions
learningOutcomes: Describe the scope of a garden clean-up using the client's written request, the site walk and the agreed boundaries.
Identify exclusions, including tree work above a set height or near power lines, and explain why they are excluded.
Handle a client request that goes beyond the agreed scope by pausing work and getting written approval.
Record the scope, access, exclusions and any variation so that the job can be verified at handover.

instructionSections.heading: What a garden scope is and why it matters
instructionSections.body: A garden clean-up looks simple until the crew reaches the back fence. A client may ask for the whole yard to be cleared, but the boundary might include a neighbour's tree, a garden bed the client has forgotten, an irrigation valve under the leaves or a protected plant. The scope is the written statement of what will be done, where, how far, with what waste removal and within what time. It turns a vague request into a job everyone can check. Without a clear scope, workers make decisions on the spot, clients expect results you did not agree to, and disputes about cost and damage follow. Your first job on any garden site is to compare what the client asked for with what the written scope says, and to ask for clarification before cutting anything you cannot confidently identify or are not authorised to touch. Use {{business:services.service_description}} as the reference for what the business normally offers, and record any difference from the standard service.

instructionSections.heading: Boundaries, access and protected items
instructionSections.body: Walk the boundary with the client before work starts. Identify the property line, any shared fences, easements, paths and areas that belong to a neighbour or to a public authority. Note the garden beds, lawns, planted areas and structures that are inside the scope and those that are outside it. Ask about protected or sensitive plantings, such as heritage-listed trees, specimen plants, native vegetation and any vegetation that the client or council has told you not to disturb. Where a planting is unidentified, treat it as protected until the client confirms otherwise. Record access arrangements, including gates, pets, working hours, water and power supply, and the places where material may be stored or staged. Photograph the agreed boundary and the disputed areas with the client's permission and label the exclusions on the photograph. If a neighbour's property is affected, do not work on it without the owner's written permission.

instructionSections.heading: Exclusions and licensed work
instructionSections.body: Exclusions are work you agree not to do. They are as important as the inclusions. Typical exclusions for a garden clean-up include: work on structures; irrigation and electrical repairs; removal of large stumps; pesticide or herbicide application unless the business holds the licence or authority that applies at that location; and tree work. In New South Wales, the EPA's 2018 fact sheet says that people who spray weeds commercially need a ground-applicator licence. Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business. Council tree rules decide whether a tree needs a permit, and they differ between councils: one NSW council exempts trees under five metres from its permit rule (no date shown), while Brisbane requires a permit ahead of working on protected vegetation that is not exempt (no date shown). This lesson does not grant any licence. If a client asks for a tree to be felled, lopped above a council threshold or cut back near a power line, record the request, state the exclusion in writing, and refer the client to a suitably licensed arborist. Do not begin any part of that work, including preparation, and do not promise that the business will do it later under the same job.

instructionSections.heading: Variations, approval and handover
instructionSections.body: Clients change their minds. A new request for extra cutting, a larger skip, or a different area is a variation. A variation is valid only after the client approves it in writing, for example by message or signed job update, and only once the price and time change is recorded. Stop the work that depends on the variation until approval is in place. Keep the variation with the original scope so that the final inspection can compare what was agreed with what was done. At handover, walk the site with the client and point out the completed areas, the exclusions and any remaining issues. Explain why any excluded item was not touched. A clear record of scope, approval and exclusions protects the client, the business and the crew.

lessons.title: Site walk-through and dynamic risk assessment
learningOutcomes: Walk a garden site and identify slopes, holes, trip hazards, irrigation components, overhead and buried services, fragile surfaces and public access routes.
Set safe work zones and choose methods that use higher-order controls before personal protective equipment.
Define the triggers that require the risk assessment to be reviewed, and apply the stop-work rule.
Produce a site hazard map that the supervisor can check.

instructionSections.heading: Why a walk-through comes before any tool
instructionSections.body: Most garden incidents happen because a hazard was not noticed before the work started. A hose hidden under leaves catches a foot, a paver lifts under a barrow, a sprinkler head is cut by a trimmer, or a child runs out from behind a hedge. A walk-through is a structured look at the site before any equipment is moved. Its purpose is to identify hazards, decide the methods, and set the conditions under which the job will stop. It is not a formality, and it should be repeated whenever the conditions change. Use the walk-through to decide what you can do safely, what needs a different method, and what must be referred. If the site has features that are outside your training or authority, stop, record them and inform the supervisor before you start.

instructionSections.heading: What to look for on a garden site
instructionSections.body: Walk the whole area slowly and make notes. Look for slopes and uneven ground where a mower or a loaded barrow can tip. Check for holes, pits, steps and changes of level that are hidden by long grass or leaves. Look at surfaces such as pavers, decking, glass, ponds and steps, and note any that are cracked, loose or slippery. Identify irrigation pipes, valves, controllers and sprinkler heads, and mark them so that they are not cut or driven over. Look up for overhead lines, branches that may be dead or hanging, and any structure that may be damaged by equipment. Look at the ground for buried services, such as electrical cables, gas lines, water pipes and drains, and for signs such as markers, meter boxes and inspection covers. Treat any service you cannot identify as live until a qualified person confirms otherwise. Note where the public, neighbours, children and pets can reach the work area, and where vehicles will be parked and turned.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing methods and setting work zones
instructionSections.body: Once you have the hazard list, plan the methods. Use the hierarchy of control. Elimination means removing the hazard before work begins, for example by moving a hose or a planter out of the path.
