Substitution means using a safer method, for example a hand saw in place of a powered tool near a service box. Separation means keeping people away from the hazard, for example by setting up a barrier, a clear route for barrows and a one-way path for material. Engineering controls include equipment guards, a residual current device on the supply and a stable platform for loads. Administrative controls include a sequence of tasks, a spotter for reversing vehicles and a start and finish briefing. Personal protective equipment is the last control, and it is not a substitute for a safe method. Mark the work zones on the hazard map and brief the team on where they can and cannot go.

instructionSections.heading: Dynamic risk assessment and stop-work triggers
instructionSections.body: A dynamic risk assessment is the process of reassessing risk while work is happening. Set the triggers in advance. Examples include: a new service is found; the ground becomes wet or slippery; a neighbour, child or pet enters the zone; a tool begins to vibrate or cut unevenly; the weather changes; or the material moved is not what was expected. When a trigger occurs, stop the affected work, make the area safe, and review the method. Do not carry on because the job is nearly done. Any worker may stop work when they consider it unsafe, and no worker should be penalised for doing so. Record the trigger, the decision and who was informed. A stop-work decision is a control, not a failure of the crew.

instructionSections.heading: Site hazard map, verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: Record the walk-through on a simple two-zone site map. The first zone is the work area, and the second is the buffer area around it where the public or other workers may be. Mark trip hazards, service locations, slopes, pedestrian routes, emergency access and stop-work triggers. Your supervisor should check the decisions you made rather than only the completed map. A competent worker can explain why a method was chosen, what a service means for the work, and which trigger would stop the job. Escalate to the supervisor for any suspected overhead or buried service, any tree that may need a licence to work on, any site that is unsafe to enter, and any hazard you cannot control. Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business. Council permit rules for trees vary; one NSW council's exemption for trees under five metres is an example only. Refer such work and do not begin it.

lessons.title: Hand tools, cutting tools and sharp waste
learningOutcomes: Inspect hand and cutting tools before use and remove defective tools from service.
Use cutting tools with control of hand position, cut direction and body position.
Separate and package thorns, glass, needles and other sharp waste without hand-sorting mixed heaps.
Store cutting tools safely during and after the job.

instructionSections.heading: Why hand tools cause garden injuries
instructionSections.body: Hand tools look simple, and that is why they cause so many cuts and puncture wounds in garden work. A blade that has been left unsharpened slips rather than cuts, so the worker pushes harder and loses control. A rake with a bent tine catches on a root and throws the user off balance. A loppers handle with a split grip pinches a finger. Sharp waste adds another layer. Broken glass, thorny stems, rusty wire and discarded needles can be hidden in leaves, mulch and soil. The safe approach is to inspect the tool before use, control the cut, and keep your hands away from anything you have not yet seen clearly.

instructionSections.heading: Inspecting and selecting tools
instructionSections.body: Before each shift, inspect the tools you will use. Check that blades are sharp and free of nicks, that the pivot or bolt is tight, and that the spring on secateurs opens fully. Check that saw teeth are intact and the blade is not bent, and that the handle is firm and free of cracks or splinters. Replace or remove from service any tool with a loose head, a cracked handle, a damaged guard or a blade that cannot be sharpened safely. Select the tool for the job. Use secateurs for stems within their rated diameter and loppers for thicker stems. Use a hand saw for material that a pruner cannot cut cleanly. Do not force a tool beyond its capacity. Do not use a hand tool as a lever on a pallet, a branch under load or a stone. Keep sheaths, scabbards and guards in place when tools are not in use.

instructionSections.heading: Cutting with control
instructionSections.body: Plan each cut before you make it. Identify where the cut will land and where the stem or branch will fall, and keep your feet and other people's feet out of that line. Use a stable stance, keep your free hand clear of the cutting line, and cut away from your body. When cutting a stem under tension, expect it to spring or split. Support heavy material before the final cut. Use two hands on loppers and keep the handle grip clean and dry. Do not reach over or through dense growth to cut. Move the stems you are cutting toward you, or move your position. If a stem is caught in a fence, a wire or a service, stop and assess before continuing. Clean and oil blades at the end of the job, and store tools with the blades protected and the handles dry.

instructionSections.heading: Sharp waste and safe packaging
instructionSections.body: Garden debris often contains sharp hazards. Thorny stems, broken glass and metal, rusted wire and needles all require care. Do not hand-sort a mixed heap. Use a rake, fork or shovel to move the pile, and look before you reach. If a needle or unknown sharp object is found, stop, keep others away, and do not pick it up by hand. Follow the site procedure for needles and report the find to the supervisor. Place broken glass and sharp metal in a rigid, labelled, puncture-resistant container, and keep thorny plant waste separate in a bag or bin that resists puncture. Do not overfill containers. Seal them and mark them so that the next person knows what they contain. Sharp waste that is not clean green waste goes to the stream that the business has confirmed for it, which is covered in the waste separation lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should observe the inspection, the cutting technique and the packaging. A competent worker can show that they inspected their secateurs, select the right tool for a given stem, explain where a falling branch will land and identify the packaging for sharp waste. Stop and report any tool that cracks, slips or behaves unexpectedly, any cut that causes a deep wound, any needle find, and any sharp waste that cannot be contained. Injuries must be treated under the business's first-aid procedure and recorded, even when they seem minor.

lessons.title: Plant hazards, allergens and hazardous contamination
learningOutcomes: Identify plants and plant materials that commonly cause skin, eye, respiratory or allergic reactions.
Recognise suspicious sap, thorns, needles, animal droppings and other contamination without touching or smelling them.
Apply the control steps for plant hazards, including the use of gloves, eye protection and barriers.
Isolate and refer unidentified or hazardous contamination to the authorised person and record the referral.

instructionSections.heading: Why plant hazards are easy to underestimate
instructionSections.body: Plants are part of the job, and their hazards are often treated as minor. Yet many garden plants and their parts irritate skin, cause blistering when the sap meets sunlight, damage the eyes or trigger allergic reactions. Pollen, spores, fine dust from dry leaves and mould in damp mulch can irritate the airways. Thorns and spines cause punctures that can become infected. A worker who knows which plants are common hazards, and who protects against them before the job starts, avoids many of the minor injuries that take a team off the job. This lesson does not replace a full medical or allergy assessment. Anyone with a known allergy or sensitivity should tell the supervisor before the job starts, and the business should record it in the safety plan.

instructionSections.heading: Plants, sap, thorns and allergens
instructionSections.body: Begin each job by looking at the plants in the work area. Look for plants with milky or coloured sap, plants with spines or thorns, plants with irritant hairs, and plants with berries or seed pods that may be toxic. Do not identify a plant by touch or smell. Some sap causes a burning rash after exposure to sunlight, and some berries are toxic if eaten. Wear gloves that resist sap and punctures, and eye protection when cutting. Keep tools clean so that sap does not build up on blades and handles. Wash exposed skin with water and soap after the job, and wash contaminated clothing separately. If a worker develops a rash, swelling, breathing difficulty or eye irritation, stop work, move away from the plant, and follow the first-aid and emergency procedure. Severe reactions require urgent medical help.

instructionSections.heading: Suspicious contamination and unknown material
instructionSections.body: Sometimes the hazard is not the plant but what is with it. Animal droppings, unknown liquids, needles, syringes, stained soil, dead animals, unusual residues and containers with no label can all appear in a garden. Do not touch, smell or move these items with bare hands. Stop work in the area, keep others back and place barriers or markers where the material is located. Take a photograph from a safe distance with the client's consent, and record the location. Do not attempt to clean, spray, bag or dispose of the material unless the business's procedure and the applicable licence or authority allow it for that exact material. Regulated biological or chemical contamination must be handled by authorised personnel only. Do not use a pesticide or cleaning product to treat the material, and do not improvise a disposal method. Inform the supervisor and the client, and follow the escalation route.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting people while work continues
instructionSections.body: When a hazard has been isolated, the rest of the work can often continue. Set a barrier around the hazard, move the team away from it and check that the barrier holds. Do not work on the rest of the garden in a way that moves the contamination, for example by using a blower across the hazard area. If the hazard is in a hedge or dense growth, cut the vegetation around it and leave the hazard in place for the authorised person. Do not allow children, pets or neighbours into the marked area. Record the hazard, the barrier, the time and the person informed. Stop the work if the barrier cannot be maintained or if the hazard spreads.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and referral
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the hazard decision rather than the paperwork. A competent worker can name the plant hazards on a job, describe the controls they chose, explain why they did not touch an unknown material and identify the authorised person to call. Escalate to the supervisor for any unknown material, any suspected biological or chemical contamination, any exposure, any reaction or injury, and any situation where the hazard cannot be contained. Do not certify that an area is clean or safe. Record only what has been observed and what has been done.

lessons.title: Work sequence, property protection and public safety
learningOutcomes: Sequence a garden clean-up from secure access and protected surfaces through to collection and transport.
Protect windows, paving, lawns, irrigation fittings and other property from damage during the work.
Set up barriers, exclusion zones and one-way material routes to keep the public and bystanders clear.
Stop work when barriers cannot be maintained and reset the zone before restarting.

instructionSections.heading: Planning the order of the work
instructionSections.body: A well-sequenced garden clean-up is safer, faster and less likely to damage the property. Start by confirming access: gates open, paths clear, vehicles able to park, and a safe place to stage tools and waste. Plan the order so that the team works from the cleanest and most secure area toward the messiest, and from the area furthest from the exit toward the gate, so that material is not carried back across finished ground. Clear obstructions such as furniture, pot plants and garden ornaments before cutting. Remove the heaviest or most dangerous items in a controlled way, rather than dragging them across lawns and paving. Plan the route for barrows and trailers before the first load moves. Write the sequence on the job sheet, and brief the team on it before starting.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting the property
instructionSections.body: Protect the client's property as carefully as you would protect your own. Cover or move windows, doors and glass that could be struck by a branch, a blower or a thrown clipping. Keep trimmer and mower discharge away from windows, vehicles, and any fragile item. Lay boards or protective matting where a barrow or trailer will cross lawn or soft ground. Do not drive or stand heavy equipment on paving, timber decking, pond edges or raised garden beds unless the surface is known to carry the load. Identify irrigation fittings, valves and sprinkler heads and mark them so that they are not cut or driven over. Report any damage immediately, record it with photographs taken with consent, and tell the client before leaving the site. Never attempt to repair damage to a service or fitting that belongs to a licence holder.

instructionSections.heading: Public safety and barriers
instructionSections.body: Garden work is often done close to footpaths, driveways, neighbours and children. Set up exclusion zones around the work area before cutting starts. Use barrier tape, cones or a temporary fence to keep people out, and check that the barrier is still in place at each stage. Where a footpath crosses the site, a spotter should stop pedestrians while material is moved and should watch for vehicles. Do not allow loads to cross public paths unless the route is controlled. Keep material off the footpath and kerb, and keep the stormwater drain clear. If a pedestrian enters the zone, stop the affected work until they have left the zone, and restart only when the barrier is restored. Many people do not realise how far a cutting tool or a flying clipping can travel, so set the zone wider than seems necessary.

instructionSections.heading: Material movement and stop conditions
instructionSections.body: Set a one-way material route, so that barrows and bags move from the cutting zone to the collection point without crossing back. Keep the collection point clear of traffic and away from the front entrance. Load barrows and trailers in a balanced way and do not overload them. Secure loose material on trailers before leaving. Stop work and reassess when a barrier cannot be maintained, when a person or animal enters the zone, when material begins to spill onto a footpath, or when a vehicle is manoeuvring nearby. Do not continue because the job is almost complete. Record each stop, the reason and the action taken, and inform the supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the layout and the decisions, not only the finished site. A competent worker can point to the work zone, the exclusion zone, the one-way material route, the protected surfaces and the stop conditions, and can explain how they would respond to a pedestrian entering the work zone. Escalate to the supervisor when property damage occurs, when a service or fitting is damaged or exposed, when a barrier cannot be kept in place, and when a member of the public is injured or distressed.

lessons.title: Final inspection, handover and incidents
learningOutcomes: Inspect completed garden work against the approved scope, photographs and the job sheet.
Correct safe defects before handover and record any defect that cannot be corrected on site.
Assemble a handover pack that includes the waste record, photographs and the client acknowledgement.
Record and escalate incidents and near misses without overstating what has been achieved.

instructionSections.heading: Why the final inspection matters
instructionSections.body: The final inspection is where a garden job is checked against what was agreed. Clients judge the result from the first look at the site, and disputes often arise from things the crew did not notice: a clipping left on the path, a cut that was not made to the agreed height, a branch lying on a neighbour's fence, or a waste bag still at the gate. The inspection is also where incidents that occurred during the job are recorded, while they are still fresh. Treat the final inspection as a formal step with its own record, not a quick walk. It protects the client, the crew and the business, and it gives the supervisor evidence that the job meets the standard.

instructionSections.heading: Checking against the scope and the evidence
instructionSections.body: Start with the approved scope, the exclusions and any written variations. Walk the site with the job sheet and compare each area with what was agreed. Check cut heights and the extent of clearing, and look at boundary edges and corners that are easy to miss. Look for remaining hazards, such as sharp debris in the lawn, exposed irrigation fittings, loose paving, pooled water and unsecured material. Compare the finished work with the before photographs taken with consent. Where the work has changed the site in a way the client did not expect, explain it, and record it. Do not sign off an area that is outside the scope or that still contains a hazard. Correct any safe defect straight away, such as a missed clipping, a loose stake or a stray bag, and then record that it was corrected.

instructionSections.heading: Waste, disposal and what cannot be certified
instructionSections.body: Check that all waste has left the site or is held in a documented and approved location. Compare the waste record with the receipts from disposal facilities. Do not certify that invasive species have been removed, that hazardous waste has been disposed of, or that a site is free of contamination unless the evidence supports the statement, and the authorised person has confirmed it. Phrase the handover in terms of what was done, what was verified and what remains open. A clear statement of limits protects the client and the business.

instructionSections.heading: Handover, client acknowledgement and incident records
instructionSections.body: Walk the completed area with the client, point out the work that was done, the exclusions and any remaining issues, and explain why excluded work was not carried out. Give the client a copy of the handover pack or a written summary, and record their acknowledgement with the date. Where a defect cannot be corrected on site, agree a plan and date with the client and record it. Record any incident or near miss during the job, including minor cuts, slips, property damage and stop-work events. Include the time, the people involved, the actions taken and the person informed. Do not describe an incident as a minor matter in the client's handover if it required first aid, damage or a stop event. Those details belong in the incident record, and the supervisor decides what is communicated and when.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and continuous improvement
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check a sample of completed jobs against the scope and the inspection record. A competent crew leader can explain each area that was signed off, name the exclusions and the open items, show the waste record and describe the incidents that occurred. Use the findings to improve the next job: a repeated defect may point to a poor method, an unclear scope or a missing control.

lessons.title: Hedge trimming and shaping
learningOutcomes: Distinguish a hedge, which is trimmed and shaped as a row of shrubs, from a tree, which is excluded when above a set height or near power lines.
Trim and shape a hedge to a level and line that suits the species, the site and the client's approved scope.
Identify when a hedge renovation needs more time, equipment or a different method, and price it accordingly.
Apply the stop conditions that apply to hedge work at height, near power lines and near services.

instructionSections.heading: Hedge or tree: where the line sits
instructionSections.body: Hedge trimming is one of the most common garden jobs and one of the easiest to take too far. A hedge is a planted row of shrubs or small trees that is kept at a managed height and width. A tree is a single plant, usually with a main trunk, that is allowed to grow to its natural height. The line between them is not always clear. A tall cypress that has been planted as a screen, a row of old trees that has been left to grow, or a hedge that has become a canopy can each be treated as a tree in the scope. Before cutting, agree in writing whether the planting is a hedge and what height and width the client expects. Whether a tree needs a council permit depends on the council. One NSW council exempts trees under five metres from its permit rule, but other conditions still apply (no date shown). Brisbane City Council requires a permit ahead of working on protected vegetation that is not exempt (no date shown). Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business. Where a planting may need council approval, or the work would bring tools or people near a line, record the exclusion, tell the client and refer the work to a licensed arborist.

instructionSections.heading: Planning the cut
instructionSections.body: Before cutting, look at the hedge as a whole. Note the species, the growth habit, the age and the condition. Check the base for dead wood, gaps and any sign of disease or pests. Check the ground for slopes, steps, services and any irrigation pipes that can be damaged. Decide the target height and width and mark them with a string line or stakes. Most hedges are shaped with a wider base than top so that light reaches the lower growth. Check the agreed scope for any part of the hedge that is excluded, such as the section above a fence or a plant the client wants left alone. Plan the access so that the operator can reach the full length without standing on unstable ground or on a structure. If the hedge needs a ladder or a platform to reach the top, check whether that work is inside the business's authorised access method. If it is not, the work is outside the scope and must be referred.

instructionSections.heading: Trimming and shaping technique
instructionSections.body: Trim in an even, controlled pattern. Work from the bottom up on the sides and from one end to the other along the top. Keep the blade moving in a steady sweep and avoid stabbing into dense growth, which can damage the blade and the hedge. Use the string line to check the height and the width at regular intervals, not just at the start and end. Cut back to a healthy lateral or a bud where possible rather than leaving stubs. Avoid cutting a hedge back into bare, leafless wood on one side unless the species can regrow from that point, because it may not recover. If a hedge needs renovation, plan the work over more than one season and tell the client. Clean up the trimmings as you go so that people do not trip over them and so the site stays safe. Check the cut edges and surfaces, and remove any leaves and clippings from the footpath and the drain.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment, safety and stop conditions
instructionSections.body: Powered hedge trimmers are electrical or battery tools with sharp reciprocating blades. Check the cord or battery, the blade guard, the handle grip and the blade condition before use, and keep the cord clear of the blade. Keep the blade away from people, pets and fences, and do not cut while anyone is in the cutting arc. Stop work when the blade contacts wire, metal, a stone or a service, when the hedge is above the height that the authorised access method allows, when the operator loses balance or footing, or when a line or service is near the cut. Do not reach over or through the hedge to cut the far side. Walk around, or move the ladder or platform if it is an authorised method. Hearing and eye protection are required for powered trimming, and gloves should resist cuts and sap.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing and quoting higher-value hedge work
instructionSections.body: Hedge work is a higher-value service when it is priced for what it involves, not for the time it takes to cut. Factors to price include the length and height of the hedge, the species and its growth rate, the condition of the base, the need for renovation rather than routine trimming, the access method, the waste to be removed, the risk controls needed, and any excluded areas that the client wants reviewed by another contractor. Quote a renovation separately from routine trimming so that the client understands the difference. Record the quote, the scope, the exclusions and any conditions, and get written approval before starting. Do not promise a result, such as the hedge growing back in a set period. Use the business's pricing method, shown in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}, and do not quote a price that is not approved for the business.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the line, the shape and the safety. A competent worker can show the target height and width with the string line, explain the difference between a hedge and an excluded tree, describe how they would handle a planting above the authorised height, and describe the stop conditions. Escalate any planting that is above the excluded height, any work that would bring people or tools near a power line, and any renovation that is larger than the approved scope.

lessons.title: Leaf clearance and debris removal
learningOutcomes: Choose a leaf-clearance method that suits the surface, the volume of debris and the site conditions.
Control the hazards of blowers, rakes and vacuums, including dust, noise, flying debris and slips.
Keep drains, gutters, paths and boundaries clear without spreading debris onto neighbouring property.
Recognise when debris is outside routine leaf clearance and must be referred, including roof and gutter work.

instructionSections.heading: What routine leaf clearance covers
instructionSections.body: Routine leaf clearance is the removal of fallen leaves, bark, small twigs and general garden debris from lawns, beds, paths, driveways and garden surfaces at ground level. It usually happens in the autumn, but many gardens need it through the year after windy weather or near deciduous trees. The job is straightforward, but the method matters. A crew that clears leaves quickly but spreads dust over the neighbour's car, blows debris into the stormwater drain or leaves a wet path slippery has not done the job well. The business's scope will say whether leaf clearance includes the gutters, the roof, the trees above the work area and the bin area. Unless the scope says so, do not clear gutters or roofs, and do not work at height. Those tasks need the access method and the training that apply to them, and are outside this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the method
instructionSections.body: Choose the method for the surface and the volume. Rakes are best for lawns and beds where the leaves are damp and heavy, and they reduce the spread of dust and fine debris. Blowers are quicker on paved areas and driveways, but they move dust, seeds and fine particles and can damage plants and carry debris onto neighbouring property. Vacuums and collection tools suit small areas and fine debris. Use the least dusty method that will finish the job within the scope. Work with the wind, not against it, so that leaves do not blow back onto cleared areas. Do not use a blower near open windows, vehicles, pets or people. Where dust is visible, stop and change the method, or wet the surface lightly if the business's procedure allows it. Use a leaf-collection method that keeps the debris contained, such as a tarp or a covered trailer.

instructionSections.heading: Hazards: noise, dust, slips and debris
instructionSections.body: Blowers and vacuums generate high noise and can expose workers to fine dust, spores and seeds. Wear hearing protection that suits the noise level and eye protection against flying debris. A mask may be needed where dust is significant, and the mask must suit the hazard. Wet leaves and moss make surfaces slippery, especially on paths, steps, decking and the edges of ponds. Clear slip hazards first, and use boots with good grip. Keep the path clear of loose debris as you go so that people and equipment do not slip on leaves. Watch for sharp hidden items under leaves, such as broken glass, nails, wire and thorny stems, and handle them with the methods in the sharp-waste lesson. Keep drains and stormwater pits clear, and do not put leaves or debris into them. Stop work when visibility is poor, when the surface is too wet to stand on safely, or when debris contains anything you cannot identify.

instructionSections.heading: Debris that is not routine leaf clearance
instructionSections.body: Some debris is outside routine leaf clearance and must be referred. Heavy accumulations of dead wood or large branches, clearing that involves roofs and gutters, debris that has become mouldy, debris contaminated by animal waste or unknown material, and debris that has been dumped on the property may all need a different method, a different team or a licence holder. Mould-affected or contaminated material is not part of routine clearance and must not be cleared by the crew without the business's authorisation and the relevant controls. Where a large branch is hanging over the work area, stop and refer. Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business. Whether a tree needs a council permit depends on the council; one NSW council exempts trees under five metres, as an example only.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the method, the containment and the finish. A competent worker can explain why they chose a method, show the containment for the debris, identify the slip risks, and describe what debris they would refer. Escalate any gutter or roof request, any unknown or contaminated material, any dust problem that cannot be controlled, and any debris that will enter a drain or neighbouring property.

lessons.title: Mulching: materials, depth and sourcing
learningOutcomes: Choose a mulch material that suits the planting, the site and the client's approved scope.
Measure the bed area and calculate the volume needed so that the order is accurate and wasteful over-ordering is avoided.
Spread mulch to the correct depth and keep it away from stems, crowns and trunks.
Check the source and contents of mulch to avoid contamination, weeds and treated timber.

instructionSections.heading: Why mulch saves time and money
instructionSections.body: Mulch reduces water loss from soil, suppresses weeds, moderates soil temperature and gives beds a finished look. For a garden maintenance business, mulching is a cost-saving service when it is done well, because it reduces the frequency of weeding and watering that the client pays for later. It can also become a cost problem when the wrong product is used, the bed is measured wrongly, or the material has to be carted away because it is contaminated. This lesson shows you how to plan the volume, choose the material, spread it correctly and avoid the sourcing mistakes that cost money and damage plants.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the material
instructionSections.body: Common mulch materials include wood chip, bark, pine straw or needles, sugarcane mulch, and compost. Each behaves differently. Coarse bark and wood chip break down slowly and suit shrub beds and paths. Fine mulches pack down more easily and can form a crust that repels water. Compost is a soil improver as well as a mulch, but it can carry weed seed and may need a different depth. Choose the material by its suitability for the planting and the site. Consider the slope, wind, fire-prone areas and whether the bed is near a path or a boundary where material can wash out. Ask the client whether they have preferences, but do not recommend a material that the business is not able to source in a way it can document.

instructionSections.heading: Measuring, calculating and ordering
instructionSections.body: Measure each bed in square metres. For a rectangle, multiply length by width. For an irregular bed, divide it into simple shapes, measure each, and add them together. Subtract the area of permanent structures such as paving, tree trunks and garden ornaments. Multiply the area by the planned depth to find the volume. Convert the volume into the units the supplier sells, and add a small allowance for settling and waste, not a large one. Order in bulk where the site and delivery make it economical, and check the delivery access and the drop-off point before ordering. A mulch order that is too large leaves material to be disposed of, which is an extra cost and a waste-handling task. A mulch order that is too small leaves a patchy finish and forces a second trip. Record the measurements, the volume and the order in the job sheet.

instructionSections.heading: Spreading to the right depth
instructionSections.body: Spread mulch evenly and to the depth set by the product guidance and the planting needs. Keep mulch away from the stems and crowns of plants and away from the base of trees, where it can cause rot and attract pests. Pull mulch back from the trunk so there is a clear ring around it. Rake the surface level and check that no mulch has fallen onto paths, lawns or drains. Water the bed if the client expects it, and tell the client how the material will settle over the following weeks. Do not bury plants or cover the crown of a shrub, because that can kill it.

instructionSections.heading: Source checks and contamination
instructionSections.body: Check where the mulch comes from before it arrives. Ask the supplier for the product description and its source, and keep the supplier's documentation with the job record. Watch for weeds and invasive plants in the material, including seeds, runners and fragments. Do not use mulch that has visible weed growth, mould or an unusual smell. Keep any contaminated load separate and do not spread it. Where the material contains an invasive plant, follow the biosecurity lesson and refer the decision. Do not claim that a mulch is free of weeds, chemicals or contamination unless the supplier's evidence supports the claim.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and records
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the measurement, the material and the finish. A competent worker can show how they calculated the area and volume, explain why they chose the material, point to the source documentation, identify a contaminated load and describe how a bed should look when the mulch is pulled back from the stems. Records should show what was ordered, what was delivered, what was spread and where any load was referred. Escalate any load with treated timber, weeds, mould or unknown material, and any request to mulch over plant crowns or into a restricted area.

lessons.title: Animal handling, restraint and calm handling
learningOutcomes: Handle and restrain an animal using methods that keep the animal calm and safe, and that never leave it unattended
Recognise signs of stress, fear or aggression, and stop the work before the animal is harmed

instructionSections.heading: Calm handling is the first skill
instructionSections.body: Grooming is a process the animal must tolerate, so the groomer's first job is to make the animal feel safe enough to take part. Approach slowly, speak quietly, and let the animal see and smell you before you touch it. Work in an order that suits the animal, leaving the parts it dislikes most until it is settled. Give breaks where the animal needs them. A groomer who rushes an animal into a restraint creates fear, and fear raises the risk of a bite or scratch for both the animal and the groomer. The business's handling method is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the procedure should describe the handling steps for each type of animal the business accepts.

instructionSections.heading: Restraint: the animal is never left alone
instructionSections.body: Use the restraint the least forceful way needed to keep the animal safe during the task. A grooming loop, a harness or a non-slip table surface can help. The rule is that an animal is never left tethered, fixed or unattended on a table or in a bath. Keep one hand on the animal when it is on a raised surface. Do not restrain the animal by the neck, by pulling a leg, or by holding its muzzle shut for long periods. A muzzle may be used only where it is safe, for the short time needed, and fitted by a person trained to fit it. Stop at once for signs of distress such as a stiff body, a tucked tail, a pulled-back head, growling, lip-licking, panting that does not settle, or a bid to escape. Let the animal rest, and resume only when it is calm.

instructionSections.heading: Welfare law and the standard to use
instructionSections.body: The sources read for this course did not confirm the welfare law that applies to pet grooming in Victoria. The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1986 (Vic) is listed as in force, with its current version effective 22 October 2025. Agriculture Victoria's domestic animal business list (no date shown) does not include mobile pet grooming, and that is a list position only. Until the welfare law is checked, the groomer must apply the good-practice standard in this lesson: no unattended restraint, no force, stop at distress, and record any injury or incident. The NT Government page lists a dog restraint requirement for vehicles among its recent changes.

lessons.title: Coat and skin checks; refer abnormal findings
learningOutcomes: Carry out a systematic coat and skin check on each animal at the start and end of a groom
Describe what was seen without naming a diagnosis, and identify the findings that need a vet referral
Record the findings and the owner notification with the date and time

instructionSections.heading: A systematic check, every time
instructionSections.body: A coat and skin check is part of the groom, not an extra. Check the animal at the start, before the bath or clip, and again at the end. Work in a set order, such as head, ears, eyes, mouth, neck, body, legs, paws, nails, tail and underside, so that no area is missed. Look at the coat for matting, dullness, bald patches, dry skin, flaking, lumps and parasites. Check the skin for redness, heat, sores, scabs, swelling, wounds and any odour. Check the ears for smell, discharge and redness. Record what you see in plain terms, using the business's approved check sheet, which is held in {{business:quality.inspection_checklist}}. Do not diagnose the cause of a finding. The purpose of the check is to see what is there and to refer it.

instructionSections.heading: What to refer, and what not to do
instructionSections.body: A groomer must not diagnose or treat a skin or ear condition, must not lance a lump, must not remove a tick or other parasite in a way that could injure the animal unless the owner has agreed, and must not give any medicine or product as a treatment. Refer the owner to a vet for any finding that is open, bleeding, swollen, hot, painful, has discharge, has a lump that is new or growing, or where the animal shows pain or sensitivity when touched. Refer the owner for any finding the groomer is unsure about. Describe the finding factually, such as 'a raised red area about two centimetres across on the left flank', and do not say what it is. The owner decides whether to see a vet, and the groomer should advise that a vet visit is recommended before the next groom.

instructionSections.heading: Record, notify and keep the evidence
instructionSections.body: Record each finding on the job record with a description, the location on the body, the size, the time, the photo where the owner has consented, and the owner notified. Tell the owner at the time of the groom, or at the end of the groom if the animal is stressed, and record the time the owner was told and the response. If the owner cannot be reached, record the attempts. Photos can help the owner and a vet see a finding, but they must be taken and stored only under the owner's written consent, and the business's photo rule applies. The business's evidence requirements are held in {{business:quality.evidence_requirements}}, and the defect reporting method is in {{business:quality.defect_reporting}}.

lessons.title: Pet-safe grooming products and dilution
learningOutcomes: Read the label and the safety data sheet for each product before first use, and file the sheet in the kit
Dilute products to the label ratio, and label every decanted or diluted product with its name, date and dilution
Apply the label and the safety data sheet to pet grooming products.

instructionSections.heading: The label and the safety data sheet come first
instructionSections.body: A pet product is a chemical product, even when it is sold as a gentle shampoo. Before first use, read the label and the safety data sheet for each product. The label gives the dilution, the contact time and the warnings. The safety data sheet gives the hazards, the first aid and the handling controls. WorkSafe Victoria's safety data sheets page (reviewed 30/07/2022) says a business that uses or stores hazardous substances needs an up-to-date sheet for each product, and must make it reachable by workers, contractors and emergency responders. Its hazardous substances page (reviewed 19/05/2026) asks employers to obtain MSDSs for hazardous chemicals and dangerous goods, and to make them available to staff. The GHS page (reviewed 22/11/2022) assigns the labelling of hazardous substances to manufacturers or importers, who must do it before a product reaches a workplace. Keep each safety data sheet in the kit, and record the date it was checked. The approved products are listed in {{business:materials.approved_products}}, and their sheets are linked in {{business:materials.sds_links}}.

instructionSections.heading: Dilution, decanting and labelling
instructionSections.body: Dilute to the label ratio, not to a feel. Measure the product with a measuring device, not by eye, and mix only the amount needed for the animal. Label every diluted or decanted container with its name, the date made, and the dilution. Never return unused diluted product to the main bottle, and discard or clean the container after the session. Do not mix products together unless the label allows it, because some combinations release gases or change the product's properties. Store products in the approved storage in {{business:materials.storage_procedure}}, away from food and out of reach of animals and children, and dispose of waste as the procedure in {{business:materials.waste_procedure}} says.

instructionSections.heading: Pet product rules
instructionSections.body: Flea products may be regulated as medicines or as agricultural chemicals, and that position was not researched. A groomer should not apply a flea or tick product unless the owner has asked for it in writing and the product is one the business has approved, and the groomer must follow the product's label. Where the owner brings a product, the groomer checks the label and the safety data sheet before use, and records the product name in the job record. Where the groomer is not sure a product is suitable for the animal, the groomer does not use it and asks the owner to check with a vet.

lessons.title: Dryer, clipper and equipment safety
learningOutcomes: Inspect dryers, clippers, blades and cables before each groom, and remove any unsafe item from use
Use dryers and clippers so that heat, noise and moving parts do not harm the animal or the groomer
Apply the confirmed Victorian WHS duty for self-employed people to the equipment and the client's home

instructionSections.heading: Inspect before every groom
instructionSections.body: Grooming equipment is used close to an animal's skin, eyes and feet, and close to the groomer's hands. Inspect each item before the first groom of the day. Check the dryer for a cracked housing, a loose nozzle, a fan that is noisy or stiff, and a damaged cord or plug. Check each clipper for a cracked body, a loose blade, a blade that is blunt, and a cord that is frayed or taped. Check the blade for heat after use, and for blunt or chipped teeth. Check the anchor point for any restraint in use. Remove any item that fails, label it, and record the removal on the equipment record. The business's inspection checklist is held in {{business:equipment.inspection_checklist}}, and the manufacturer's instructions are in {{business:equipment.manufacturer_manual_url}}.

instructionSections.heading: Heat, noise and moving parts
instructionSections.body: A dryer produces hot air and noise. Keep the nozzle moving and never hold it on one spot, because heat builds on the skin quickly. Start on the lowest heat and speed that dry the coat, and check the skin of the animal and your own hand for heat. Never leave a dryer running unattended, and never dry an animal in an enclosed space with no ventilation. Clippers have a moving blade and can heat up during long use. Let them cool between animals, and clean them as the manufacturer directs. Keep a grip on the animal when a blade is near the face, ears, feet or tail. Use hearing protection if the noise is high for long periods.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical safety at a client's home
instructionSections.body: A mobile groomer depends on a power outlet the client provides. Check the outlet, the cable and the load before plugging in, as “Mobile setup, power and wet-area safety” explains. Keep cords off the floor where the animal or the groomer could trip, and keep electrical equipment away from water. WorkSafe Victoria's responsibilities page (reviewed 03/04/2025) says a self-employed person must manage their work so that it does not put others' health and safety at risk, to the extent that is reasonably practicable. The same page extends the employer's duty to the people a business's work reaches, such as clients and the general public. Treat the home as one for set-up and safety, and record the set-up check. Where equipment is damaged or wet, switch it off and do not use it until it has been checked by a competent person.

lessons.title: Grooming bookings and recurring packages
learningOutcomes: Build a grooming booking that allows for the full groom, the checks, the clean-down and the travel
Set the terms of a recurring package, including the frequency, the price basis and the cancellation rule

instructionSections.heading: Booking the whole groom
instructionSections.body: A grooming booking has more steps than the clip. It includes the arrival check, the set-up, the consultation, the bath or the dry, the clip, the coat and skin check in “Coat and skin checks; refer abnormal findings”, the clean-down, the handover to the owner, and the travel between homes. A booking that allows only the clipping time puts the groomer under pressure to skip the checks. Build each booking from its steps, and record the time for each step. The business's scheduling method is held in {{business:jobs.scheduling_method}}, and the arrival steps are in {{business:jobs.arrival_procedure}}. Where an animal needs extra time, such as a large or nervous dog, the booking should say so before the appointment is confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Recurring packages and the terms they need
instructionSections.body: A recurring package sells a set of grooms at a regular interval, such as every four or six weeks. The package must state the frequency, the services included, the price basis and how it is paid, what happens if an appointment is missed, the cancellation rule, and how changes to the animal's needs are handled. The ACCC's guidance says the consumer guarantees apply to services, and that a business's own refund policy must sit alongside them, not replace them. Each groom under a package still needs its own check, consultation and record, and the package should not be used to shorten those steps. The package terms are recorded in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}, and the minimum charge in {{business:pricing.minimum_charge}}.

instructionSections.heading: Registration for mobile grooming
instructionSections.body: Mobile pet grooming is not among the Victorian domestic animal business types that Agriculture Victoria lists, and Stonnington's permit page does not name it either. Those are list positions only, and they are not exemptions. No Victorian council registration for mobile groomers was confirmed. The ACT's pet business licensing page does not mention grooming. The position in other states was not researched in this course. Before a mobile grooming service is offered in any place, the business must confirm the council and state position and record the source and the date. The absence of a confirmed rule is not permission to operate without one. Completing this lesson does not register the business or approve any grooming service.

lessons.title: Mobile salon setup, hygiene and tool sterilisation
learningOutcomes: Set up a mobile work station that has hand-washing, a treatment area, a sharps container and a wastewater plan
Clean, disinfect and store tools between clients using the method the cited guideline describes
Identify which registration or notification rule applies in your state or territory before the first visit

instructionSections.heading: Why set-up and hygiene come first
instructionSections.body: A mobile hairdresser has no salon fit-out to rely on. Every visit starts with an empty room, a borrowed sink or a van, and a client who expects the same standard as a salon. The set-up is therefore the first control you apply to every job. Hair services involve cutting, shaving with blades, and chemicals applied to the scalp and skin. A poorly set-up station can spread infection between clients and can leave chemical residue, sharps and wastewater in a client's home. This lesson teaches the set-up routine, the cleaning and disinfection routine, and the registration questions you must settle for your own state or territory. The content is drawn from research notes.

instructionSections.heading: Mobile facilities in the WA guideline (confirmed for Western Australia only)
instructionSections.body: The Western Australian Chief Health Officer guideline for the hairdressing industry, issued under the Public Health Act 2016 and last reviewed in February 2024, has a section for mobile operators (section 13.1). The guideline says mobile operators must have hand-washing facilities that are easily accessible, with warm water, soap and disposable towels, and that hands are cleaned both before and after every client. It requires equipment to be cleaned after each client, a container for sharps, and wastewater sent to the sewer instead of the stormwater system. It also says that an unsuitable treatment area, such as a kitchen, must not be used for hairdressing procedures. These are confirmed requirements for Western Australia. Your set-up checklist should record which source you used. Do not assume that a van, a bathroom or a kitchen sink meets the requirement until you have checked it against the source for your location.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning, disinfection and blood-contaminated tools
instructionSections.body: The title of this lesson uses the word sterilisation. The WA guideline does not use that word. Where equipment is contaminated with blood, the guideline suggests cleaning it first and then placing it in a 70 per cent alcohol solution or a disinfectant of hospital grade. The routine is: remove visible hair and debris, clean with detergent, rinse, then disinfect for the time the product label states. The guideline requires dye mixing bowls to be cleaned after each use, and food should not be prepared in the space where dyes are mixed, and drinks are to be kept away from hairdressing supplies. For blood or body-fluid spills, the guideline allows bleach as a disinfectant for hard-to-clean areas after a detergent clean, and it advises against using chemical disinfectants for everyday cleaning. Every product you make up should carry its name, the date it was made up, and its dilution; that is a business rule in this course. Keep blood-contaminated tools separate from clean tools until they have been cleaned and disinfected.

instructionSections.heading: Registration and notification: where this lesson stops
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not register you, and completing it does not give any authority to operate. The rules differ by state and council. In Victoria, the Department of Health lists hairdressing among services that must register under the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008 (page updated 22 May 2026). The same page lists mobile hairdressers as exempt from registration, but the exemption stops short of the principal place of business. In the Northern Territory, a business that receives payment for hairdressing must register, and the NT page gives a fee of $91 to register or renew for hairdressing (no date shown). In Queensland, hairdressing is not a higher-risk personal appearance service and needs no licence, but the business must still follow the infection control guidelines for personal appearance services (no date shown). In the ACT, hairdressing needs no infection control licence but must still follow the 2005 infection control Code of Practice for office practices and other community-based services (no date shown). In Western Australia, a home-based operator must contact the local government authority before operating (guideline section 13.2). Check your own state and council before your first client visit.

lessons.title: Client consultation, allergy patch test and consent
learningOutcomes: Run a written consultation that records a client's history of reactions, open wounds, infections and skin conditions
Decide when to stop, postpone or refer a service and explain the decision to the client
Describe what a patch test record must contain.

instructionSections.heading: The consultation is the first safety control
instructionSections.body: Before any colour, bleach or chemical service, the hairdresser must find out what the client's skin and scalp are like and whether the client has had a reaction before. A consultation is also where consent is given. In a mobile setting you may be the only trained person in the room, so the consultation must be complete before the chemicals are opened. The questions should be written down, asked the same way for every client, and kept with the job record. Clients should be told what the service involves, including the products used and the time the products will stay on the hair or scalp. Your business's approved procedure for the consultation is recorded as {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}. Follow that document and use this lesson to understand why each question matters.

instructionSections.heading: Health screening, open wounds and when to refer
instructionSections.body: The Western Australian hairdressing guideline does not require formal health screening of staff or clients. For a client with an open wound, an infection or a skin condition, the guideline advises that the hairdresser recommend a visit to a general practitioner. If the hairdresser is uncomfortable, the service may go ahead only if they believe they can appropriately provide it around the condition and have processes in place to prevent transmission to other clients. The guideline also says that head lice do not bar a person from a salon. These are WA positions, used here as good practice everywhere. Where a client has an open wound, an infection or an unexplained skin condition, the safe business action is to postpone and refer, and the record should say why. Do not proceed because the client says they feel fine.

instructionSections.heading: Allergy patch tests and their record
instructionSections.body: A patch test checks whether a client reacts to a product before a full service. Colour products contain substances such as PPD (paraphenylenediamine) and hydrogen peroxide. WorkSafe Victoria's hairdressing and beauty page (reviewed 12/09/2025) calls PPD and hydrogen peroxide toxic and notes that both are widespread in dye products, and notes that a typical peroxide product holds 7 to 12 per cent hydrogen peroxide, and that stronger mixes carry more hazard. It also names persulphate bleach, which can cause irritation. Follow the product manufacturer's instructions and your business procedure. Record the product, the date, the test site, the time, the result and the client's response. If the client reacts, do not apply the colour. Record the reaction, advise the client to seek medical advice, and do not offer the service again without a new assessment.

lessons.title: Colour and chemical safety: processing times and skin protection
learningOutcomes: Name the main hazards of hair colour, peroxide and powdered bleach, using the WorkSafe Victoria list
Apply processing times and mixing ratios from the product label, not from memory or habit
Describe the hazardous substances duties that apply to a self-employed or employing hairdresser in Victoria

instructionSections.heading: The hazards in hair colour and bleach
instructionSections.body: Hair colour and bleach are chemical products used close to the face, eyes and skin, often in an enclosed room. WorkSafe Victoria's hairdressing and beauty page (reviewed 12/09/2025) names several hazards. The page calls PPD and hydrogen peroxide toxic and notes that both turn up widely in dye products. A typical peroxide product holds 7 to 12 per cent hydrogen peroxide, and stronger mixes carry more hazard. Powdered bleach contains persulphate salts that can irritate the eyes and nose, and even a small quantity of bleach dust is enough to irritate. Aerosol colours are classed as hazardous, and the page rules out their use on eyelashes and eyebrows. Hair sprays are usually treated as non-hazardous, though they can irritate skin and eyes. The page does not label any control as mandatory or suggested, so check the safety data sheet for the control it specifies, and treat the page's advice as guidance that supports the duties below.

instructionSections.heading: Processing times and mixing: follow the label
instructionSections.body: Processing time is the period a product is left on the hair or scalp before it is rinsed. It is set by the manufacturer for each product and each mix. A stylist who works from habit may leave a product on for longer than the label allows, which increases exposure to the skin and scalp. The safe rule is to set the timer from the label, mix only the quantity needed for the client, and check the mixing ratio before the product is applied. Your business's approved procedure for mixing and timing is recorded as {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the products you use are listed in {{business:materials.approved_products}}. Where a product's label conflicts with a habit, follow the label. Where the label does not give a time for a service, stop and check with the manufacturer before the service continues.

instructionSections.heading: Duties, exposure limits and the change on 1 December 2026
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria's safety data sheet page (reviewed 30/07/2022) requires an up-to-date SDS to be held for every product, with access open to workers, contractors and emergency responders. Its safety basics page (reviewed 30/07/2022) says employers need a register listing every hazardous substance on site, and that workplace risks to health and safety need evaluating. A self-employed person carries a duty to keep others from harm arising from their work, limited to what is reasonably practicable. From 1 December 2026, Safe Work Australia states that the WEL schedule takes over from the WES schedule.

lessons.title: Barbering techniques and skin care
learningOutcomes: Describe the cutting and trimming techniques the business offers and the hygiene steps that come with each
Decide whether a skin-care service is inside the approved service list before offering it
Explain how a higher-rate service earns more per hour without adding unapproved risk

instructionSections.heading: What a higher-rate barbering service is
instructionSections.body: A barbering service that pays more per hour does so because it takes more skill and time, or because the client values it more, not because it cuts more corners. Examples include a beard shape with a hot towel finish, a full-head cut with a detailed fade, or a scalp and face treatment that uses an approved product. The extra revenue comes from the higher price, and the risk stays the same or grows. A barber who offers a premium service must still follow the consultation, hygiene and set-up steps in “Mobile salon setup, hygiene and tool sterilisation” and “Client consultation, allergy patch test and consent”. The service list the business uses is recorded as {{business:services.service_description}}. Any premium service that is not on that list is outside the approved scope and must not be offered until the business has reviewed it.

instructionSections.heading: Cutting and trimming techniques
instructionSections.body: Cutting uses clippers, guards and scissors to shape hair to a set length and style. Work from the consultation, so the length and the shape agreed with the client are the target. Check each side against the other, and step back to view the cut from the client's angle. Trimming refines the outline of the hair and the beard. Use a trimmer and check the neckline and the sideburns with the client seated upright. If the skin is broken during a cut or trim, stop, clean the area and record the incident as the steps below direct. These are working techniques, not regulatory requirements. The hygiene steps that go with them are set out in the next sections.

instructionSections.heading: What the business offers and the skin-penetration question
instructionSections.body: This business offers cutting, trimming, beard work and approved skin-care services. It does not offer blade shaving, and a client who asks for one should be offered a cut, trim or approved service instead. The ACT Government's page on skin penetration procedures treats skin penetration as a procedure that breaks the skin, and it excludes cutting from that definition. The page requires a licence for businesses that perform skin penetration procedures and covers mobile practitioners. NSW Health's page, current as at 10 August 2023, explains that hairdressing is not regulated under its skin penetration rules unless the work deliberately breaks the skin, and that other activities may be regulated by the local council under different legislation. Neither page is a licence, and neither settles the position in every state. If any work during a cut or trim breaks the skin, treat it as an incident and record it.

instructionSections.heading: Skin conditions, open wounds and referral
instructionSections.body: Before any tool or product touches the skin, check for a rash, an open wound, an infection, open sores, abrasions or a skin condition. The WA Health guideline says that a hairdresser who is uneasy about serving a client with one of these should steer the client toward a general practitioner and treatment before the next visit. The guideline also says the hairdresser may still go ahead where they judge the service can be given safely around the condition, with controls that stop spread to other clients. The business procedure decides which course applies, and the default for any work over broken or irritated skin should be to postpone and refer. Record the check, the decision and the reason.

instructionSections.heading: Mobile set-up and hygiene at the client's location
instructionSections.body: A mobile barber works away from a fixed salon, so the set-up must be checked at each location. The WA guideline expects basin access at each location, stocked with drinking-quality warm water, soap and paper towels, and hand hygiene before and after each client. The treatment space must be fit for purpose, and a space that is untidy or otherwise unfit is not used for treatments. Tools need cleaning between each client. A sharps container and disposable gloves are both needed on site. Keep clean and used equipment apart, and hold linen and waste in separate receptacles. A vehicle used for the service needs a sewer connection or a holding tank, and the tank's contents go to the sewer rather than stormwater. These are WA requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Skin care products and the limits of a claim
instructionSections.body: Skin-care add-ons can include a cleanser, a moisturiser or a beard oil. Each product must come from the approved product list, {{business:materials.approved_products}}, and must have a safety data sheet on file. Do not make medical claims about a product. A claim that a product treats acne, rashes or any other condition is outside what a barber is qualified to say in this course, and it may breach the business's own policy and consumer rules. Describe the product by its ingredients and its label instructions. Where a client has a skin condition, an open wound or an infection, follow the referral step above and do not proceed with the skin-care service.

lessons.title: Booking, travel routing and cancellation policy
learningOutcomes: Build a booking schedule that allows the full processing time and the travel time for each visit
Plan a daily route that keeps the team inside safe working hours and leaves time for hygiene steps
Apply the cancellation policy the business has approved, and record each change

instructionSections.heading: Booking around the real time a service takes
instructionSections.body: A mobile hairdresser loses money and breaks safety rules when the schedule is too tight. A colour service needs the full processing time from the label, the set-up time from “Mobile salon setup, hygiene and tool sterilisation”, the consultation time from “Client consultation, allergy patch test and consent”, and the clean-down time after the service. Build each booking as the sum of those steps, not as a fixed slot. If a booking is shortened to fit the day, the processing time is shortened too, and that breaks the label instruction as explained in “Colour and chemical safety: processing times and skin protection”. The booking form should record the services, the processing time, the access instructions for the home or venue, and any health question that needs a referral. The business's booking method is recorded as {{business:jobs.scheduling_method}}, and the access instructions for each client are held in {{business:customers.access_instructions}}.

instructionSections.heading: Routes, travel time and lone working
instructionSections.body: A mobile operator often works alone, drives between clients, and enters homes where they have not worked before. Route planning should leave a buffer between visits, so that the operator is not rushed in the next client's home. Use the lone-worker check-in method in “Lone-worker safety and check-ins” for each visit, and record the time the operator arrives and leaves. Record the travel time as part of the job. Do not plan a route that requires a colour service to be rinsed in the car. Where a client's address is unsafe or an entry is unclear, the operator should contact {{business:safety.escalation_contact}} before going in. Consider the time of day and the daylight where the route includes unfamiliar roads, and include the travel time in the quote.

instructionSections.heading: Cancellations and the limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Cancellation policies are a business decision. The business should write a policy that states the notice period, any fee, and what happens if the client does not attend. Do not describe a cancellation fee as legal or required until a source has been checked. Record each cancellation, the notice given, and the decision taken. A cancellation caused by the client's health or a wound is a referral matter under “Client consultation, allergy patch test and consent”, and the decision should be recorded as a referral, not as a no-show. The policy is recorded in {{business:customers.communication_policy}}.

lessons.title: Pricing mobile visits and add-on services
learningOutcomes: Build a quote from the visit, the travel, the materials and the approved add-ons
Apply the business pricing method and minimum charge without changing the approved service
Identify which insurance and registration costs affect the price.

instructionSections.heading: What a mobile price has to cover
instructionSections.body: A mobile hairdresser's price must cover more than the cut or the colour. It must cover the travel to the client, the time spent setting up and cleaning down, the products used, the disposable items, the insurance and registration costs that apply, and a fair return for the time. A quote that only covers the service time often leaves the business short. The business's pricing method is recorded as {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}, and any minimum charge applies as recorded in {{business:pricing.minimum_charge}}. Prices are set by the business and are not stated in this course. Any figure a learner sees in a sample quote is an example only, and it must be replaced with the business's approved figures.

instructionSections.heading: Add-ons inside the approved scope
instructionSections.body: An add-on is an extra service sold with the main visit. A colour client may add a scalp treatment, and a barber may add a beard shape. Add-ons must come from the approved service list, which is held in {{business:services.service_description}}. An add-on that is not on the list must be reviewed first, as “Barbering techniques and skin care” explains. Add-ons that use bleach or colour need the consultation in “Client consultation, allergy patch test and consent” and the processing time from the label. An add-on should never make the processing time shorter, and it should never be offered as a replacement for the consultation or the patch test. Record each add-on on the booking so that the materials cost is included in the quote.

instructionSections.heading: Insurance, registration and the cost of compliance
instructionSections.body: In Victoria, WorkCover registration is generally required where a business employs any workers. WorkSafe's registration guide (last updated 19 May 2026) says that a sole trader or individual partner who has no other workers on staff is not required to register, and that a contractor who depends on one business may be counted as that business's worker for registration purposes. Councils may set their own conditions. In the Northern Territory, a business that receives payment for hairdressing must register, and the NT page gives a fee of $91 to register or renew (no date shown), so that cost must be included in the price. Do not price a service on the assumption that a cost does not apply. Record every compliance cost the business pays, so that it can be built into the minimum charge.

lessons.title: Scope, consent and trade boundaries
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between having the skill to perform a task and having the authority to perform it.
Classify a requested task as within scope, outside scope, or referred to a licensed trade.
Record the agreed scope, the approver and any variation before work starts.

instructionSections.heading: Skill is not authority
instructionSections.body: A handyman job is usually small: hanging a fixture, patching a wall, adjusting a door, or replacing a worn part on something that is not part of a regulated system. The work is often ordinary and you may be able to do it well. Ability does not answer the first question, which is whether the person asking holds the authority to approve the work and whether the task is one a non-licensed worker may carry out at that property. Authority comes from the owner or from a property manager acting for the owner, and it is set out in the written work order. Which state or territory law applies depends on where the property sits, and the state positions checked for this course appear under trade boundaries below. Your own competence does not create either form of authority.

instructionSections.heading: Scope, consent and variations
instructionSections.body: Before you touch anything, read the work order and confirm three things in writing: what will be done, where it will be done, and who approved it. Identify the occupant as well as the owner. A tenant or other occupant may need to agree to access and may need to be present. If the request changes during the job, stop that part, record the new request, and obtain approval from the person who holds authority before you perform it. Verbal changes made on site are the most common source of disputes about who approved what. A short written message from the approver is enough, provided it names the change and the date.

instructionSections.heading: Trade boundaries and referral
instructionSections.body: Some work belongs to licensed trades, and the state position decides where the line sits, so check it for your state before you rely on it. Wiring jobs in New South Wales need a licence or certificate whatever their price, and the NSW electrical page sets no dollar threshold (electrical page, last updated 23 June 2026). Plumbing, draining and gasfitting licences in New South Wales cover those trades at any price, by category (plumbing page, last updated 31 July 2026). The NSW minor trade work threshold is more than $5,000 across labour and materials, GST included (minor trade work page, last updated 23 June 2026). In Queensland, plumbing, drainage and gasfitting need a QBCC licence at any dollar value (QBCC page, last reviewed 11 August 2021). Handyman work valued at $3,300 or less needs no QBCC licence when it is not electrical or plumbing and no occupational licence applies; that page is dated 2021 and does not say how labour, materials or GST are counted (QBCC page, last reviewed 11 August 2021). A lesson saying a task is ordinary handyman work does not confirm that the task is lawful for you in the state where you work. When a task touches a licensed trade, your job is to stop, record the boundary, and refer it to a person who holds the correct licence.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the decision
instructionSections.body: Each job needs a short record: the agreed scope, the approver, the date, any task refused or referred, and the reason. A refusal or referral that is recorded protects the client and the worker, because it shows the boundary was considered and not ignored. Keep the record with the work order. Do not rewrite it later to fit what was done.

instructionSections.heading: Everyday tasks and state requirements
instructionSections.body: The everyday tasks in this course are taught to every learner, so you can recognise them on a job, scope them properly and know when to stop. Hanging a fixture, patching a wall, adjusting a door and replacing a worn part are ordinary handyman tasks, but a state can restrict any of them once the work touches a regulated trade. Each task is taught here for recognition and where the state note confirms the work is allowed, and each one must be checked against the state note before you do it. In New South Wales, you must have an electrical licence or certificate before you can do any electrical wiring work, regardless of the cost of the work (electrical page, last updated 23 June 2026). In New South Wales, plumbing, draining and gasfitting licences cover those trades at any price, by category (plumbing page, last updated 31 July 2026). In Queensland, the QBCC handyman exemption does not cover electrical or plumbing work, a QBCC licence is needed for drainage, plumbing and gas fitting work at any value, and the QBCC page directs electrical questions to the Electrical Safety Office, so confirm the Queensland electrical rule with that office before you start (QBCC page, last reviewed 11 August 2021). In Victoria, Energy Safe Victoria states that installation and maintenance of PV systems are required to be carried out by licensed electrical workers (page reviewed 15 April 2025). The sources for this lesson do not state the Victorian rule for other fixtures, or any plumbing rule for Victoria. They also do not cover South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, the Northern Territory or the Australian Capital Territory, so treat a task that touches wiring, plumbing, drainage or gas in those states as a referral until the state regulator confirms the position.

lessons.title: Site survey and pre-start risk control
learningOutcomes: List the occupant, utility, finish, access and nearby-activity hazards that must be checked before an occupied-property task begins.
Set an exclusion zone and state the stop-work trigger for a task.
Record hazards, controls and the go, defer or refer decision before starting.

instructionSections.heading: Why the survey comes first
instructionSections.body: Most avoidable harm in occupied properties happens because a task starts before the site has been read. The survey is the step that finds what the work order does not say: a child asleep in the next room, a cable behind the plaster, a fragile tiled floor, an access code that expired, or a neighbour's scaffold above the work. Survey before the first tool is switched on, and repeat the survey whenever the task or the occupants change.

instructionSections.heading: What to check on the walk-through
instructionSections.body: Walk the route from the entry to the work area with the site contact. Identify occupants and their needs, including children, older people, people with limited mobility, and pets. Ask where concealed services run, because a cable, pipe or gas line is not visible in a wall and an assumption is not a check. Note fragile finishes such as glass, stone, old tiles and painted timber. Confirm access rules, including strata or building rules, lift bookings, key handling and parking. Note nearby activity such as other trades, traffic, machinery and weather. In older buildings, look for materials that may contain asbestos and do not disturb them. Refer any suspicion to the owner and to a competent specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Controls, exclusion zones and stop-work
instructionSections.body: Apply controls in this order: eliminate the hazard, substitute a safer method or material, separate people from the hazard with barriers and timing, and use personal protective equipment only for what remains. Safe Work Australia's model code of practice (dated December 2011) sets the same order of controls and asks that risk be removed where that is reasonably practicable. Set an exclusion zone around the work, and agree with the occupants how it will be kept. Decide in advance what would stop the task.
