The usual trigger is that the exclusion zone cannot be kept, or that a new hazard appears that the survey did not cover. If the trigger is met, stop, make the area safe, and inform the supervisor or client before anything resumes.

lessons.title: Hand tools, PPE and safe work area
learningOutcomes: Select a hand tool that suits the fastener, the substrate and the task.
Inspect hand tools and reject any that are defective.
Set up and keep a safe work area with protection matched to the task risks.

instructionSections.heading: Match the tool to the job
instructionSections.body: A hand tool is safe when it is the right tool for the fastener, the material and the force required. A screwdriver used as a chisel, or a spanner used as a hammer, may slip or break and cause injury. Before you start, identify the substrate (timber, plasterboard, masonry, metal), the fastener, and the force needed. Choose the tool that fits the fastener head exactly and that gives control. Use a pilot hole or a suitable bit rather than forcing a fixing.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect before use
instructionSections.body: Inspect each tool before it goes into use. Reject a hammer with a mushroomed striking face or a loose head. Reject a screwdriver with a rounded or cracked tip. Reject a wrench with splayed jaws. Reject a handle that is split, loose or greasy, and any cutting tool with a damaged edge that cannot be sharpened safely on site. A rejected tool is tagged out of service and removed from the work area. Do not compensate for a faulty tool with extra force, because that is when the tool fails.

instructionSections.heading: Work area and personal protection
instructionSections.body: Keep the work area clear of trip hazards, cords and loose material. Secure the workpiece so it cannot move while you apply force. Keep cutting edges and fingers away from the line of force. Choose eye and hand protection from the actual task risks identified in the survey, and check the protection is in good condition. Store tools in a way that stops them falling, and never leave tools on ladders, steps or window ledges where they can fall on people below.

lessons.title: Portable power tools and energy isolation
learningOutcomes: Identify guarding, cord, battery and attachment defects before a power tool is used.
Describe the main kickback, dust and noise hazards and the controls for each.
Isolate a portable power tool safely and refuse any tool that cannot be used safely.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect the tool before the first cut
instructionSections.body: Read the manufacturer instructions for the tool and any attachment. Inspect the cord, plug, housing, guards, switches, bits, blades and batteries. Look for cracked housings, damaged cords, missing guards, worn brushes, bent or blunt attachments, and battery damage such as swelling or leaking. A guard that has been removed or taped back is a defect and the tool must not be used with it bypassed. Test the tool's trigger and switch while it is unplugged or the battery is removed.

instructionSections.heading: Hazards: kickback, dust, noise and hidden services
instructionSections.body: Kickback happens when a blade or bit binds and the tool is thrown back toward the operator. Keep both hands on the tool, stand clear of the line of the blade, and do not force the cut. Power tools produce fine dust, including silica dust from masonry and wood dust from timber, and noise that can damage hearing. Use extraction where it is provided, and select respiratory and hearing protection from the task. Safe Work Australia's silica guidance (no date shown) names dry cutting of brick, concrete or stone as the higher-risk method and lists wet cutting and dust-collecting tools among the controls. Where respiratory protection is needed, the same guidance cites a half-face respirator with a P2 rating as a minimum. Before drilling or cutting, check for hidden services. A drill that has no side handle or a damaged cord is not safe to use on a surface that may hide cabling, and the surface must be checked by a competent process first.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating energy and refusing unsafe tools
instructionSections.body: Isolate the tool before any adjustment, blade or bit change, or cleaning. For corded tools, remove the plug from the supply. For battery tools, remove the battery. Do not rely on a switch alone. If a tool cannot be used safely, refuse it and tell the supervisor, and do not perform a repair that goes beyond the tool's manufacturer instructions or the worker's authority.

lessons.title: Ladders, elevated access and fall prevention
learningOutcomes: Choose a ground-level or safer access method before a ladder is considered.
Judge whether a ladder is suitable for a task, including ground, weather and overhead conditions.
Identify the licence and duty boundaries for elevated work and refer tasks outside training or equipment limits.

instructionSections.heading: Ground-level methods come first
instructionSections.body: Before you choose a ladder, ask whether the work can be done from the ground, by reaching with a tool, or from a properly designed platform that is set up for the task. Many fixtures, gutters and fascia repairs can be reached without climbing. A ladder is a last-resort access method for short, low-risk tasks, and it is not a substitute for a platform when the task needs both hands, heavy material or sustained work. A short job does not make an unstable ladder acceptable.

instructionSections.heading: Judge the ladder and the setup
instructionSections.body: Check the ground condition. Soft, sloped, wet or uneven ground can make a ladder unstable, and a ladder should not be placed on loose material or on a surface that moves. Check the ladder itself for cracked rails, bent steps, missing feet and loose joints. Check the weather, because wind and rain change the risk. Check overhead hazards, including power lines and cables, before you lift a ladder. Do not work on a ladder when you cannot maintain three points of contact, and do not lean out beyond the belt line. If the task needs the top step or a step beyond the manufacturer's limit, the ladder is not suitable.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and duty boundaries for elevated work
instructionSections.body: In Victoria, operating a boom-type elevating work platform needs the WP licence class, and WorkSafe lists scissor lifts as outside the high risk licence requirement (WorkSafe Victoria page, reviewed 30 June 2026). Victoria's WP class sets no boom length. In New South Wales, the WP licence applies at a boom length of at least 11 metres, measured by the longer of two distances (SafeWork NSW licence page). A shorter boom may not need that licence there. In New South Wales, construction work that carries a fall risk above 2 metres needs a SWMS (SafeWork NSW working-at-heights page, no visible date; page metadata shows 21 October 2026). In Queensland, the WP licence covers boom-type platforms of 11 metres or more, and platforms under 11 metres fall outside that definition, so a shorter boom may not need the licence there (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). These are statements of position for the licence classes and do not decide whether a specific handyman task is permitted. Refer any elevated task outside your training or equipment to a competent person.

lessons.title: Electrical boundaries and referral
learningOutcomes: Identify the electrical tasks that are treated as referral for a handyman, with the reason.
Describe the safe response to a suspected electrical fault found during other work.
State the licence positions recorded for electrical work in each state, without implying any authority to perform it.

instructionSections.heading: Where electrical work begins
instructionSections.body: Many handyman tasks look simple but touch fixed wiring: replacing a light fitting, adding a power point, moving a switch, mounting a wall fitting with a hard-wired feed, or fixing a socket that is loose. Treat any task that involves the fixed installation as a referral to a licensed electrical worker unless the state rules and your written authority clearly place it within your scope.

instructionSections.heading: The licence picture by state
instructionSections.body: In New South Wales, a licence or certificate is needed for wiring work whatever the price, and the NSW electrical page sets no dollar threshold (electrical page, last updated 23 June 2026). That page does not mention solar or battery systems. Energy Safe Victoria's renewable energy licence questions page (reviewed 4 June 2024) is UNVERIFIED for this lesson: the page was not fetched, so the claims that it covers inspection of battery and generation systems and does not name the class for installing or isolating PV are unconfirmed. These positions are a summary of what the sources say. They do not authorise any worker to carry out the work, and they must be checked with the regulator before a job is accepted.

instructionSections.heading: A suspected fault found on site
instructionSections.body: If you find a warm plug, scorched outlet, flickering light, burning smell, exposed conductor or a switchboard that is damaged, stop work near it. Do not open covers or touch exposed parts. Isolate the area from people where that is safe, and advise the occupant not to use the affected point. Record what you saw, where and when. Refer the fault to a licensed electrical worker and tell the approver in writing. Report the completed non-electrical work separately from the electrical referral, and do not mark the whole property safe.

instructionSections.heading: Everyday electrical tasks: state requirements
instructionSections.body: Replacing a light fitting, adding a power point, moving a switch, mounting a hard-wired wall fitting and fixing a loose socket are taught in this course for recognition, so you can spot them on a job and refer them correctly. Each one may be restricted by state law, so check the state note for the job location before you accept the task. In New South Wales, you must have an electrical licence or certificate before you can do any electrical wiring work, regardless of the cost of the work (electrical page, last updated 23 June 2026), so any of these tasks that involves wiring needs a person holding that licence or certificate. In Queensland, the QBCC handyman exemption does not cover electrical work, and the QBCC page directs electrical questions to the Electrical Safety Office, so confirm the Queensland electrical rule with that office before you start (QBCC page, last reviewed 11 August 2021). In Victoria, Energy Safe Victoria states that installation and maintenance of PV systems are required to be carried out by licensed electrical workers (page reviewed 15 April 2025). The sources for this lesson do not state the Victorian rule for light fittings or power points, so confirm it with Energy Safe Victoria first. The sources for this lesson do not cover South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, the Northern Territory or the Australian Capital Territory, so treat these tasks as referral work in those states until the state regulator confirms the position.

lessons.title: Water, plumbing and gas boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify the water, drainage and gas tasks that are referred to a licensed plumber or gasfitter.
Respond safely to a leak, a suspected gas smell or a blocked drain found during other work.
State the licence positions for plumbing, drainage and gasfitting in each state, without implying authority to perform the work.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as plumbing, drainage and gas work
instructionSections.body: Plumbing and drainage work includes installing, altering, repairing and removing water supply pipes, fixtures connected to them, and drainage lines. Gas work includes gas appliances, gas pipes and their connections. Some everyday tasks sit close to these boundaries: changing a tap washer, fitting a shower head, clearing a blocked drain, or fitting a flexible hose to a gas appliance. Do not assume that a small change is outside the licence. Check the state position first, and refer when it is unclear.

instructionSections.heading: The licence picture by state
instructionSections.body: In New South Wales, a licence or certificate is needed for plumbing, draining or gasfitting work at any price, by category (NSW plumbing page, last updated 31 July 2026). In Queensland, a QBCC licence is needed for plumbing, drainage and gasfitting at any dollar value (QBCC page, last reviewed 11 August 2021). In Victoria, gasfitting covers work on items, and the definition excludes cleaning, painting or preparing gas pipes unless the work connects, disconnects or alters them (BPC page, last updated 30 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Everyday water and gas tasks by state
instructionSections.body:
Four everyday tasks sit on these boundaries: changing a tap washer, fitting a shower head, clearing a blocked drain, and fitting a flexible hose to a gas appliance. They are taught here so that you can recognise them and apply the state rule. Each state note below is a requirement, not a permission. One line per task and state:
- Tap washer and shower head, NSW: the water plumbing category covers work connected with supplying or conveying water, including fittings, and the page does not name tap washers or shower heads. UNCONFIRMED: that this task must be done by a licensed worker in New South Wales.
- Tap washer and shower head, QLD: a QBCC licence is needed for plumbing at any value, and the handyman exemption for work at or under $3,300 does not cover plumbing work. UNCONFIRMED: that this task must be done by a licensed worker in Queensland.
- Tap washer and shower head, VIC: the cited gasfitting page does not cover water plumbing, so the Victorian position for this task is not confirmed in this lesson and it must be referred.
- Blocked drain, NSW: draining covers sanitary drainage connected to a sewer (UNCONFIRMED: this scope is not checked against the NSW page in this review), and a licence or certificate is needed at any cost, so this work must be done by a licensed worker in New South Wales.
- Blocked drain, QLD: a QBCC licence is needed for drainage at any value, so this work must be done by a licensed worker in Queensland.
- Blocked drain, VIC: the drainage position is not confirmed in the cited sources, so it must be referred.
- Flexible gas hose, NSW: gasfitting covers connecting or disconnecting gas appliances, so this work must be done by a licensed worker. UNCONFIRMED exclusion: connections where the point of connection is a gas outlet socket are not gasfitting work. Confirm this with the NSW regulator before relying on it.
- Flexible gas hose, QLD: a QBCC licence covers gas fitting at any value, so this work must be done by a licensed worker in Queensland; the skill is taught here for recognition.
- Flexible gas hose, VIC: gasfitting covers work on items, and the cited page does not mention flexible hoses, so this must be referred.
The sources in this lesson do not confirm a licence-free position for any of these four tasks in any state. The NSW gas outlet socket exclusion above is unconfirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Responding to leaks, gas smells and blocked drains
instructionSections.body: A visible leak should be stopped at the source only if you can do so without altering the plumbing, such as by asking the occupant to switch off a known isolation point. Otherwise, place a container, protect the floor and surfaces, and refer. If you smell gas, do not operate light switches or appliances, and do not light anything. Leave the area and keep others away from it. Leaving the area and calling from outside are general safety practice, not a legal requirement. Energy Safe Victoria's gas emergency guidance (reviewed 29 January 2023) supports avoiding electrical switches and devices, putting out flames, keeping people away, and contacting the gas distributor using the emergency number on the gas bill, with 000 for any other emergency. The Victorian page does not say where to call from, so calling once you are clear of the area is general safety practice. Which number applies by state: in Victoria, the distributor's number on the gas bill or 000 (Energy Safe Victoria page, reviewed 29 January 2023). In New South Wales, Jemena, which describes itself as the largest gas distributor in the state, lists 131 909 for gas faults and emergencies and says to call it any time of day, 7 days a week (Jemena gas pages, no date shown, copyright 2026); the page does not say which areas the number covers, so for a property on another network, contact that network's emergency line or call 000. In Queensland, the Queensland Government gas safety page (last updated 3 September 2026) says to call 000 if a gas smell persists after the gas supply is turned off, and to call 000 immediately for a fire, an explosion or an uncontrolled leak. No Queensland distributor emergency number is confirmed here: the APA page for Allgas customers in south-east Queensland lists only a connection line, so use the emergency number on the gas bill or call 000. A blocked drain found during other work is recorded and referred. Do not use drain-cleaning chemicals or tools on a drain beyond your authority.

lessons.title: Surface fastening and concealed services
learningOutcomes: Choose a fixing suited to the substrate, the load and the finish.
Locate studs, joists and concealed services before drilling or fixing.
Stop and refer when a concealed service is found or suspected.

instructionSections.heading: Match the fixing to the substrate and the load
instructionSections.body: A fixing that holds in one material can fail in another. Timber framing takes screws into the stud or noggin. Plasterboard needs a fixing that spreads the load across the board, or a fixing that locates a stud. Masonry needs a masonry anchor of the correct size for the material and the depth. Hollow walls and cavity walls need fixings rated for hollow substrates, and the rating should come from the fixing manufacturer. Estimate the load before you fix anything: a shelf with a load on it, a grab rail, or a wall-mounted fixture carries force that must reach solid structure. If you cannot confirm the substrate or the load path, do not proceed on assumption.

instructionSections.heading: Locate studs, joists and services before drilling
instructionSections.body: Use a stud finder, a detector, and a visual check of the wall, including skirting, switch and power point positions, and the line of pipes beneath sinks. Concealed electrical cables often run vertically above and beside switches and power points, and horizontally at set heights, but a cable can be run in any direction. Do not rely on the position of a single outlet as proof of where cables run. Mark the wall with the located positions and confirm before you drill. If a detector gives an unclear reading, stop and use a different location or refer.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer when a service is found
instructionSections.body: If you find or suspect a concealed electrical, gas or water service, stop drilling or fixing in that area. Do not move or cut the service. Record the location, the time and what was observed, and refer the work to a licensed trade. Continue with other fixings only where the wall has been confirmed clear and the approver agrees. Fixing into a service is a common cause of injury and of costly damage (UNCONFIRMED: no source is cited for this statement), and it is also work that falls under licensed trade boundaries, as set out for the states checked in this course (see “Electrical boundaries and referral” and “Water, plumbing and gas boundaries”).

instructionSections.heading: Everyday fixings and the state position
instructionSections.body: Everyday fixings such as towel rails, shelves and grab rails are taught here so that you can match the fixing to the substrate and the load, and locate services first. The cited pages do not set a state licence rule for the fixing itself. The licence rule applies when a concealed service is found or disturbed. In New South Wales, a licence or certificate is needed for wiring work regardless of the cost of the work, except for equipment operating at not more than 50 volts AC or 120 volts ripple-free DC, and a licence or certificate is needed for plumbing, draining or gasfitting work at any cost, so a concealed service found there must be referred to a licensed worker. In Queensland, a QBCC licence is needed for plumbing, drainage and gas fitting at any value (see Water, plumbing and gas boundaries), and the Queensland electrical position is not in this lesson's sources, so a suspected concealed cable must be referred. In Victoria, the gasfitting definition covers items (see Water, plumbing and gas boundaries), and the Victorian electrical and water positions are not confirmed in this lesson's sources, so a suspected concealed service must be referred.

lessons.title: Paint, patch and surface compatibility
learningOutcomes: Assess a surface for condition, contamination and compatibility before painting or patching.
Choose a patch material and primer that suit the substrate and the existing finish.
Identify when older surfaces need specialist assessment before disturbance.

instructionSections.heading: Read the surface before you touch it
instructionSections.body: Before patching or painting, look at the surface in good light. Note cracks, bulging, damp, staining, flaking paint, grease, mould, and any sign of previous repairs. Test the surface by pressing it with a fingertip and by scraping a small area to see whether the paint lifts. Decide whether the surface is sound, needs cleaning, or needs specialist assessment. Damp, active staining, and any surface that is crumbling or moving are not ready for paint until the cause is known. Painting over a moisture problem hides the evidence and makes the next repair harder.

instructionSections.heading: Patch and prime to suit the substrate
instructionSections.body: Use a patch material that suits the substrate and the depth of the repair. Filler suits shallow gaps in painted surfaces; deeper repairs may need a different material. Prime bare or patched areas before finishing, and select a primer that suits the substrate and the finish: a stain-blocking primer for staining, an alkali-resistant primer for new plaster or masonry where the product label requires it, and a bonding product where the surface is glossy or smooth. Check the product label and data sheet for the surface and the conditions. A patch that has not cured or dried will show through the finish.

instructionSections.heading: Older surfaces, dust and licence boundaries
instructionSections.body: In older buildings, paint and plaster may contain lead or asbestos. Do not sand, scrape, cut or demolish older paint or plaster until its composition is confirmed by a competent specialist. Asbestos removal above a state's allowance is licensed work. In Victoria, unlicensed removal of non-friable asbestos is limited to 10 square metres in total, and to one hour in any period of seven days which is cumulative across all employees (asbestos.vic.gov.au page, which shows an 'Updated' label and no date). In Queensland, non-friable jobs at or under 10 square metres need no licence (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). In New South Wales, a Class B licence applies once the area of non-friable material passes 10 square metres (SafeWork NSW page, published 12 November 2025, modified 12 March 2026). Do not apply one state's figure to another. Painting and plastering licence positions are set out in the safety and regulatory points below.

lessons.title: Doors, hinges and hardware upkeep
learningOutcomes: Diagnose common door faults: sticking, rubbing, sagging, loose hinges and worn closers.
Decide what minor upkeep is within scope, and what must be referred, including fire and security doors.
Price and record door upkeep so the higher-rate work is clearly scoped.

instructionSections.heading: Diagnose the door before adjusting it
instructionSections.body: Most sticking or rubbing doors have one of a few causes: a loose or sagging hinge, a screw pulled out of the frame, a door out of square, swelling from moisture, or a latch that does not line up with the strike plate. Check the gaps around the door, open and close it slowly, and watch where it binds. Check the hinges for play and the screws for tightness. A screw that spins in a worn hole needs a longer screw or a packed hole, not more force. A door that is out of square may need planing, which removes material and should be recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Minor upkeep and referral boundaries
instructionSections.body: Tightening loose screws, lubricating hinges, adjusting a latch strike, and replacing a worn door stop are minor upkeep. Adjusting or replacing a door closer, a fire-rated door or its hardware, or any security hardware that controls access, needs a check first. Security hardware, including locks and locking systems, may involve licensing rules. In Queensland, removing and reinstalling household locks needs a security equipment installer licence, except where the building is being constructed, repaired or renovated (Queensland Government page, last updated 21 October 2026). Installing basic security items while such works are underway is exempt on the same page. Refer any task that changes a lock, a fire door or a door closer. A fire door is part of a fire safety system, so do not alter its hardware by guesswork.

instructionSections.heading: Price the work and record the outcome
instructionSections.body: Upkeep of doors is often low in price per visit, and a worker can raise the rate by scoping the work properly. Write each task on the quote with its status: included, optional, or referred. Record the door's condition before and after, the parts used, and any defect that was not fixed. Do not quote a fire door or security hardware repair as minor upkeep. A quote that names the referral clearly is more credible and avoids disputes later.

lessons.title: Waste, housekeeping and client protection
learningOutcomes: Prevent trip hazards and protect the occupant's property during a repair.
Control dust so that it does not reach sleeping areas, food or people with breathing conditions.
Segregate controlled waste and stop work when a suspect material is found.

instructionSections.heading: Protect the occupant and the property
instructionSections.body: Lay protection before you start, not after. Cover floors, furniture and fittings in the route and in the work area, and keep the route to the work clear of tools, cords and offcuts. Keep a clean path for occupants to move through the property. Protect any food preparation area and any sleeping area from dust. A repair that leaves the property cleaner than before is credible; a repair that leaves dust and debris behind damages trust even when the repair itself is sound.

instructionSections.heading: Dust, waste and segregation
instructionSections.body: Separate waste as you go. Use containment and damp methods for dust, and do not dry sweep or use compressed air on dusty material. Keep products away from children and pets, and close containers once used. When material is suspected to contain asbestos, stop disturbing it, keep the area sealed, keep occupants away, and obtain a specialist assessment before any further work. Keep sharps, batteries, solvent and paint waste out of general refuse.

instructionSections.heading: Stop when a suspect material is found
instructionSections.body: A repair can expose fibrous fragments, unexpected fine dust, or material that smells or looks different. Stop the disturbing work, keep people clear, and do not sweep or vacuum the suspect material with ordinary equipment. Record what was seen, where, and the steps taken. Refer for a specialist assessment, and tell the approver. Asbestos removal above a state's allowance is licensed work. In New South Wales, a Class B licence applies once the area of non-friable material passes 10 square metres (SafeWork NSW page, published 12 November 2025, modified 12 March 2026). In Victoria, the unlicensed allowance is 10 square metres in total, and one hour in any period of seven days which is cumulative across all employees, for non-friable material only (asbestos.vic.gov.au page, which shows an 'Updated' label and no date). Work above either limit needs a licence. In Queensland, non-friable material at or under 10 square metres needs no licence (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). This lesson does not grant any removal authority.

lessons.title: Quality control, records and handover
learningOutcomes: Check completed work against the signed scope and the product instructions.
Record defects, exclusions and referrals separately from completed work.
Hand over a job without implying that the whole property is safe or compliant.

instructionSections.heading: Check the work against the scope
instructionSections.body: Compare what was done with the signed scope, line by line. Check that each item was completed, that each product was used as the manufacturer instructions say, and that the finish is sound. Check the surfaces around the work for marks, and clear the area before you leave. A task that was agreed but not done is an exclusion, and it must be recorded as such. Do not record something as completed because it looks finished from the doorway.

instructionSections.heading: Record defects, exclusions and referrals separately
instructionSections.body: Keep three lists: completed work, exclusions (agreed but not done, or refused), and referrals (issues found during the work that need another trade). A referral is not a failure of the job; it shows the worker saw a risk and passed it on. Keep the lists separate so the client can see what is done and what remains. Photograph the finished work and any defect only with consent, and keep the images only for the job record.

instructionSections.heading: Handover without overclaiming
instructionSections.body: When you hand over, state what was done, what was not, and what needs referral. Never say that the property is safe or compliant unless a competent person has confirmed that. Under the Australian Consumer Law, statements that mislead or are likely to mislead are unlawful, and intent is not needed for a breach (ACCC guide, dated March 2016). A completed cabinet fix does not clear an unrelated electrical hazard found on the same visit. Obtain the client's sign-off on the completed items and the exclusion list, and keep a copy of the signed record with the work order.

lessons.title: Asset inventory and maintenance records
learningOutcomes: Build an asset register that gives each item a unique identifier, a location and a condition record.
Keep service and repair history so that identical items are never confused.
Correct a record without overwriting the earlier entry.

instructionSections.heading: Why an asset register matters
instructionSections.body: A property manager partner is asked, again and again, what is in a property, where it is, and when it was last serviced or repaired. Without a register, the answer depends on memory and the worker who last visited. An asset register gives each fixed item and piece of equipment a unique identifier, a location, a description, its condition and its service history. It turns a series of visits into a record that the owner, the manager and the next worker can rely on.

instructionSections.heading: What to record for each asset
instructionSections.body: Record the unique asset identifier, the room or area, the item description, and the label details that identify the item, such as make, model and serial where visible. Record the condition on the day, the date of the record, the last service date where known, any manufacturer documentation held, and photographs taken with consent. Where two items look identical, the register must still hold two different records. Use the location and the label to tell them apart, and write down how each was identified.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the record honest
instructionSections.body: Never overwrite an older record. Add a new dated entry that shows the change, so the history stays visible. If you cannot identify an item, say so and record what you could see. An entry that says the pump was serviced needs evidence: the date, the worker, and the work done. An unverified entry is a risk, because the next person will rely on it.

lessons.title: Structured property inspections
learningOutcomes: Carry out a repeatable visual walk-through that records observations separately from diagnoses.
Triage findings by immediate risk, water damage and cosmetic condition.
Turn inspection findings into a proposed scope of work that the owner can approve.

instructionSections.heading: Observe, do not diagnose
instructionSections.body: A visual inspection records what can be seen, heard and smelled from a safe position. It does not establish the cause of a defect, and it cannot show that a concealed system is safe. Record the observation as seen: a stain on a ceiling, a tap that drips, a scorch mark on a switch plate. Keep the diagnosis for a competent person. Do not remove covers, drill, open ceilings or access heights during an inspection unless you are trained, authorised and equipped for that work.

instructionSections.heading: Walk the property in a fixed order
instructionSections.body: Use the same route and checklist each time so that inspections can be compared. Start with the points of greatest risk: electrical equipment, gas appliances, the roof and ceiling spaces that can be seen from below, and any sign of water. Move through the water and drainage points, then the doors, windows, locks and access points, and finish with cosmetic items. Triage findings in that order. A cosmetic chip is not a priority above a scorched switch or a leak that is active.

instructionSections.heading: Turn findings into a proposal
instructionSections.body: Each finding that needs work becomes a line in a proposed scope: the observation, the risk level, the proposed action, the owner of the action, and whether a specialist is needed. Price the work separately and do not start it until the owner or manager approves it in writing. Findings that need a licensed trade are referred, not proposed as handyman work. A clear inspection report with approved follow-up work is the revenue of this module.

lessons.title: Risk prioritisation and escalation
learningOutcomes: Rank defects by life safety, water ingress, security, service continuity and cosmetic impact.
Decide when to control access, stop work, or escalate to an authorised person.
Write an escalation that names the risk, the immediate protection and the owner of the next action.

instructionSections.heading: The priority order
instructionSections.body: Rank defects in this order: threats to life and to people's safety first, then water ingress and damage that spreads, then security of the property, then loss of essential services, and finally cosmetic defects. Within each band, consider how quickly the defect can get worse and who is affected. A defect can be urgent even when the cause is unknown. A ceiling panel that hangs over a corridor is urgent because of what could fall, whatever the reason it is loose.

instructionSections.heading: Control access before anything else
instructionSections.body: When a defect creates an immediate hazard, the first action is to control access. Keep people out of the affected area, mark it, and move occupants if necessary, in line with the site procedure. Do not attempt to fix the defect yourself if it needs a competent person, a licensed trade or specialist equipment. Summon the authorised person and record the time and the protection put in place.

instructionSections.heading: Write the escalation
instructionSections.body: An escalation states what was found, where, the risk, the protection put in place, the person who now owns the next action, and the date and time it was raised. Keep it factual. If the response is not received within the agreed period, escalate to the next person on the list and record that step. Do not promise a cause or a repair date that you have not established.

lessons.title: Moisture ingress and mould warning signs
learningOutcomes: Recognise the visible and indirect signs of moisture ingress and mould growth.
Identify the most common moisture sources to be investigated before any finish is changed.
Stop work and refer where growth is extensive, hidden, or disturbed, using safe handling rules.

instructionSections.heading: Signs that moisture is getting in
instructionSections.body: Moisture usually shows before mould does. Look for staining that spreads or returns, paint that bubbles or peels in patches, plaster that feels soft or crumbles, skirting that swells, and corners where condensation collects. A musty smell with no visible cause is also a sign. Mould can appear as dark, green, grey or white patches, often where moisture sits: around windows, in bathrooms and laundries, under sinks, in the corners of cold rooms and behind furniture placed against external walls. Record each sign as seen, with its location and time, and do not assume that a clean surface means a dry one.

instructionSections.heading: Finding the moisture source
instructionSections.body: Common sources include roof and gutter leaks, failed flashings, window and door seals, plumbing leaks and drips, drainage problems, rising damp at the base of walls, and poor ventilation that lets condensation build up. Work out where the water is coming from before any finish is covered or changed. Painting or sealing over a damp wall hides the evidence and lets the damage continue. Where the source is not clear, refer for a competent assessment and record the observation.

instructionSections.heading: Safe handling and the limit of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Do not disturb visible growth. Do not dry brush, dry sand, scrape or use a household vacuum on it, because that releases spores into the air. Do not use high-pressure water on mould, because it can drive growth into the structure. Keep occupants away from the area, especially children, older people and people with breathing conditions, and ventilate only if it is safe to do so. Observation and recording do not need special equipment beyond normal inspection kit. Remediation of mould is not part of this module. Where growth is extensive, hidden behind a finish, or in a ceiling or subfloor space, stop, keep people clear, and refer to a trained, competent worker under the controls in the High-risk cleaning module.

lessons.title: Structural, roof and facade warning signs
learningOutcomes: Recognise warning signs of structural movement, roof failure and facade deterioration from ground level.
Decide what can be recorded from safe ground-level positions and what must not be done.
Refer structural, roof and facade concerns to licensed or competent persons, and record the referral.

instructionSections.heading: Warning signs from ground level
instructionSections.body: Structural problems often show as change over time. Look for cracks that are wider than a hairline, cracks that have grown since an earlier record, doors and windows that have started to stick in a new way, floors that slope, and gaps opening at junctions between walls and ceilings. On the roof and facade, look for loose or missing tiles and sheeting, sagging gutters or roof lines, rusted or loose fixings, crumbling or spalling concrete and render, and balustrades or handrails that move. Record each sign from a safe position, with photographs taken from the ground where possible and with consent.

instructionSections.heading: What not to do
instructionSections.body: Do not climb onto a roof, a ladder or a platform to inspect a warning sign unless the access is authorised, safe and within the worker's training and equipment. Do not push, lean on, or test a balustrade, wall or structure to see how it moves. Do not remove finishes or cover cracks to see what is behind them. Keep people clear of the area below any loose item, and control access as set out in “Risk prioritisation and escalation”.

instructionSections.heading: Refer and record
instructionSections.body: Structural, roof and facade concerns are referred to a licensed building trade or to a competent specialist, as the site requires. Record the sign, its change over time if known, the protection in place, and the referral. Do not say the building is structurally sound or that the roof is watertight. A referral that says what was seen and what was not inspected is more useful to the owner than a reassuring statement that cannot be supported.

lessons.title: Minor repairs and materials suitability
learningOutcomes: Decide whether a minor repair fits the worker's skill, tools, manufacturer instructions and the property's permissions.
Recognise fire-rated and security items that must be referred rather than adjusted.
Select materials that suit the substrate, the load and the environment.

instructionSections.heading: Four checks before a minor repair
instructionSections.body: Before any minor repair, check four things. First, the permission: is the owner or manager approving this exact repair in writing? Second, the skill: does the worker have the training and experience for this task? Third, the manufacturer instructions: does the product or item have instructions, and do they allow this repair? Fourth, the item itself: is it a fire-rated, security or regulated item? If any check fails, the repair is referred. A minor repair is only minor if all four checks pass.

instructionSections.heading: Materials that suit the job
instructionSections.body: Choose materials for the substrate, the load and the environment. A fixing for a damp area should resist corrosion. A filler for a wet area should be suited to damp. Small fasteners can have safety-critical functions, such as holding a closer, a hinge or a grab rail. Replace a missing or damaged fastener with one of the same type and rating, and do not substitute a smaller or cheaper item. Keep the product record so that the next person knows what was used.

instructionSections.heading: When the item is rated or regulated
instructionSections.body: A security lock or access system controls who can enter. Both are referred to a competent person, and the state licence position for security and locking work is recorded in “Doors, hinges and hardware upkeep”. Do not adjust a rated item because it looks like a simple fix, and do not replace it with a non-rated part.

lessons.title: Tools, access equipment and manual tasks
learningOutcomes: Check tools and access equipment for defects, and tag out any that are unsafe.
Plan load handling and manual tasks so that improvisation is avoided.
Refuse to proceed when access or equipment is unsafe, and record the decision.

instructionSections.heading: Check the equipment before it is used
instructionSections.body: Check every tool and item of access equipment before the job, and at the start of each day. A drill with a frayed cable is not safe to use, and it must be tagged out. A ladder with a cracked rail or a missing foot is not safe to climb. Record defects, tag out what is unsafe, and remove it from the work area. Do not use a damaged item because it is needed for a small task.

instructionSections.heading: Plan access and manual handling
instructionSections.body: Choose the access method before the task, not after. A proposal to use a ladder on uneven ground should lead to a different method, not to a compromise. For manual handling, plan the route, the weight and the number of people needed. Use a trolley or a mechanical aid where the load is heavy or awkward. Share a heavy lift with another person when the load requires it, and set the load down rather than twisting while holding it. Ergonomic load management prevents strain injuries in tasks that look light but are repeated.

instructionSections.heading: Refuse unsafe conditions
instructionSections.body: The job does not proceed merely because the repair appears brief. If the equipment is unsafe, the access is unsafe, or the load cannot be moved safely, stop and record the decision. Tell the approver the reason and the alternative method needed. A refusal recorded with a reason protects the worker and gives the owner a clear next step.

lessons.title: Preventive maintenance scheduling
learningOutcomes: Set maintenance intervals from manufacturer guidance, criticality and site history.
Replace a calendar-only plan with condition-based checks where failures recur.
Schedule preventive work so that it is visible, approved and recorded against each asset.

instructionSections.heading: Start from the asset register and the manufacturer
instructionSections.body: A preventive plan is built from the asset register. For each item, use the manufacturer's recommended service intervals where they are available, and record where they come from. Where no manufacturer guidance is held, say so and set an interval based on the item's criticality and history, and review it. Rank items by consequence: an item whose failure would cause water damage, loss of heat or a safety hazard is scheduled earlier and more often than an item whose failure is an inconvenience.

instructionSections.heading: Use history, not only the calendar
instructionSections.body: A calendar-only plan may miss recurring failures. If a pump has failed repeatedly before its annual service, a fixed yearly date is not enough. Review fault dates, running hours or usage where known, and the criticality of the item, and propose condition-based inspections between services. Propose authorised servicing where the failure pattern points to a fault the planned service would not address. Record the reason for each change to an interval.

instructionSections.heading: Schedule, approve and record
instructionSections.body: Each scheduled item needs an owner, a due date, and an approval status. Preventive work is proposed to the owner or manager, and it is not started until it is approved. Record each visit against the asset, with what was checked, what was done, what was found, and what is due next. A schedule that is never updated after a visit is out of date from the first day.

lessons.title: Contractors, residents and site coordination
learningOutcomes: Confirm notice, permission and access before any contractor or worker enters an occupied property.
Coordinate sequencing and work instructions so that residents and contractors are not put at risk.
Protect the privacy and accessibility needs of residents during the work.

instructionSections.heading: Permission is separate from competence
instructionSections.body: A contractor's competence does not replace the property's access permission. Before anyone enters, confirm that the resident has been notified in the way the tenancy or building arrangements require, that the owner or manager has approved the entry, and that the contractor has been given the access details. Record the notice, the approval and the time of entry.

instructionSections.heading: Coordinate the work and protect the occupant
instructionSections.body: Issue a written work instruction that states the scope, the area, the time, the access route and the exclusion zone. Agree how the occupant will be kept clear of the work area. Where a resident has limited mobility, check the access route, the need for an accompanying person, and any evacuation constraints before work starts. Protect privacy: a contractor should not enter rooms or open personal items beyond the scope, and should keep any information about the resident confidential.

instructionSections.heading: Sequence and communicate
instructionSections.body: Sequence the trades so that one does not undo the work of another, and so that services are not disconnected without notice. Keep a single point of contact for the resident and the contractors. When something changes, tell everyone affected in writing. A change in the sequence that is not communicated is a common cause of damage and of disputes.

lessons.title: Closeout, quality evidence and follow-up
learningOutcomes: Record before and after evidence that shows what changed and what did not.
Mark the source of a problem as resolved only with evidence.
Schedule follow-up monitoring and propose the follow-up work for approval.

instructionSections.heading: Evidence before and after
instructionSections.body: Closeout starts with evidence. Take before and after photographs from the same position, with consent, so the change can be compared. Record the measurements, the materials used and the condition when the work ended. A clean appearance is not proof that the cause has been fixed. A patch can look finished while the moisture behind it is still active, and a closeout must say so where that is the case.

instructionSections.heading: Record what is unresolved
instructionSections.body: Record defects that were not fixed, the limits of the work, and the reason. Where the cause of a problem is not yet known, say so. Do not mark the source of a leak, a draught or a movement as resolved unless the evidence shows it. Keep the unresolved item open, with an owner and a follow-up date, so it is not lost when the job is closed.

instructionSections.heading: Follow-up and proposed work
instructionSections.body: Schedule follow-up checks where the risk requires them, such as a return visit after a repair near water. Propose any further work as a separate, approved scope, and do not start it because the closeout revealed it. Follow-up work is a source of revenue for this module, and it is priced and approved like any other work. Record the follow-up date and the person responsible.

lessons.title: Hard floor identification: timber, stone, tile, vinyl, concrete
learningOutcomes: Identify the common hard floor types by their appearance and feel.
Explain why each type needs a different method and product.
Treat an unknown floor as sensitive until it is identified.

instructionSections.heading: The main types and how to recognise them
instructionSections.body:
Five families cover most hard floors you will meet. Timber includes solid boards and engineered boards with a timber top layer. It may be sealed with a film finish, oiled, or left unfinished. Natural stone includes marble, limestone, travertine, slate and granite. Ceramic and porcelain tile are fired clay products, usually glazed, though some are unglazed. Resilient flooring such as vinyl and linoleum is a manufactured sheet or plank, often printed to look like timber or stone. Concrete may be plain, sealed, coloured or polished.

Appearance gives a first view, not a final answer. Timber shows grain and board joints, and it usually feels warm underfoot. Stone shows natural veining or mottled colour, and it feels cool and dense. Glazed tile has a uniform face with grout lines between units. Vinyl often has a repeating print, and it can feel slightly softer than tile. Concrete shows control joints, colour variation and, when dry, a fine powder if it is worked on. Printed vinyl and some manufactured stone look very like the real thing, so a visual check alone is not enough. Look at the joints, the sheen, the wear pattern and the edges, and then confirm with records or a simple test.

instructionSections.heading: Why the type decides the method
instructionSections.body:
The material decides which products are safe. Marble, limestone and travertine are calcium-based, and acid reacts with them. The reaction etches the surface and leaves dull marks that cleaning does not remove. This is why an acidic descaler is the wrong choice on a floor that might be stone, however strong the stain looks.

Timber takes up water along the grain, at board edges and through joints. Too much water can swell the boards, lift edges, leave dark stains and allow cupping. Sealed timber resists water better, but the seal still needs a limited moisture method. Finishes on any hard floor can be dissolved by solvents, dulled by alkaline or abrasive products, or stripped by products that are not made for that finish.

Vinyl and linoleum can be marked by some oil-based and solvent products, and by rubber-backed mats or furniture feet left in place. Ceramic and porcelain tile are generally durable, but the grout between them is porous, and abrasive pads can scratch glazed surfaces. Concrete is porous, so stains can soak in, and dry work on the surface can release fine dust. Where that dust may contain crystalline silica, the national guide on silica sets out wet methods and warns against dry sweeping and compressed air (see the safety notes in this lesson).

Before you choose a product, confirm the type and the finish, check the manufacturer's care guidance where it exists, and read the product label and the safety data sheet (SDS). Then test the product on an inconspicuous area and allow it to act for the time the label states before you judge the result.

instructionSections.heading: Simple identification checks
instructionSections.body: Start with a visual check under a light held low across the surface. Note the sheen, the pattern, the joints and any worn traffic lanes. Then use a water-drop test in an inconspicuous spot. Place a single drop of clean water on the surface and watch it for a short time. A drop that beads and stays on top suggests a sealed or glazed surface. A drop that darkens or soaks in suggests an unsealed or porous surface. Never use acid, a strong solvent or a harsh abrasive to test a floor. A test that damages the surface gives you a new problem and no answer. Record what you observed and what you could not confirm. A clear record of uncertainty is more useful to the next person than a confident guess.

instructionSections.heading: When the type is unknown
instructionSections.body:
If the floor cannot be identified, treat it as sensitive and use the most conservative approved method. In practice this means a pH-neutral or otherwise mild product that your business has approved for unknown surfaces, applied with a damp cloth or microfibre pad. Use no acid, no solvent, no steam and no abrasive pad. Keep the water to a minimum and dry the surface as you go.

Ask the client or supervisor for flooring information. Useful sources include the builder's or installer's records, the strata or property manager's maintenance file, and the manufacturer's care sheet if the flooring brand is known. Do not guess, and do not move to a stronger product until the type is confirmed. Record the floor as unidentified, state the method used, and note the information you requested and from whom.

lessons.title: Timber floor cleaning and finish limits
learningOutcomes: Identify whether a timber floor is sealed, oiled or unfinished before cleaning.
Use a method and product that suit the finish, with minimal moisture.
Stop and refer when the finish is worn, lifting or damaged.

instructionSections.heading: Finish first
instructionSections.body: The finish decides the method, so identify it before any product or water goes on the floor. A sealed timber floor has a film on the surface that resists water and most everyday soil. An oiled floor has oil or an oil-and-wax finish worked into the wood, so it is more sensitive to products that strip oil and to water that stays on the surface. An unfinished or raw timber floor has no protective layer, so it takes up water and product quickly. Even a sealed floor still needs a moisture-limited method, because water that stands at the edges and joints can get underneath the finish. Sources of information include the installer's or finisher's records, the strata or property manager's file and any maintenance history. Where those are not available, use a simple test in an inconspicuous spot. Apply a small amount of clean water and watch whether it beads, slowly darkens or soaks in. Beading suggests a sealed surface. Darkening or soaking suggests an oiled or raw surface. Treat the result as an indicator, and record the uncertainty if the answer is not clear.

instructionSections.heading: Method and product limits
instructionSections.body:
Use a damp-mop method with minimal moisture. A mop is damp when it is wrung until it is barely wet and does not drip when lifted. Work in small sections, along the grain where practical, and do not let the cloth or the mop sit in one place. Dry the section promptly with a clean microfibre cloth before you move on. Avoid steam, flooding and any method that pushes water into the seams or the edges. Keep the work area ventilated where a product has an odour, and follow the product label for dilution and contact time.

Use only products that the timber, the finish and your business have approved. Mild, pH-neutral cleaners made for timber are the usual starting point. Avoid ammonia-based cleaners, solvent-based products, abrasive pads and oil soaps on a sealed floor unless the product is approved for that finish, because these can cloud, soften or strip the finish. On an oiled floor, avoid products that are designed to strip finishes. Test the product on an inconspicuous area before wider use, and watch the area for a while after it dries.

Do not sand, screen, strip, recoat or re-oil a floor as part of routine cleaning. Those tasks change the finish and the surface of the wood. They are specialist finishing work, and a cleaner who carries them out outside a defined scope creates a dispute about what the work did.

instructionSections.heading: When to stop and refer
instructionSections.body:
Stop wet cleaning and refer the floor when you see any of the following: the finish is worn through to bare wood, boards are lifting at the edges or ends, boards are cupping or crowning, water is pooling on the surface, dark marks are spreading after a damp clean, or a stain does not respond to the approved method after a test. These signs can mean moisture has entered the timber, and more water will make them worse.

Record the condition with dated photographs taken in shade and under a light held low across the surface. Note the area, the signs you observed, the method you used and the moisture steps you took. Tell the client that the floor needs assessment by a qualified person, and that you cannot promise to restore the finish or remove the stain. Do not describe a floor as restored, sealed or repaired unless you carried out and recorded that work under a defined scope.

lessons.title: Stone, tile and grout cleaning and sealing boundaries
learningOutcomes: Choose a pH-appropriate method for stone, tile and grout.
Explain why sealing and stone restoration are outside routine cleaning.
Record the limits of cleaning where grout or stone is stained or etched.

instructionSections.heading: Stone, tile and grout: what each one is
instructionSections.body: Natural stone such as marble, limestone and travertine is calcium-based, and an acid will etch it. Granite and slate are often described as less reactive to acid than marble, but this lesson does not confirm that for any particular stone, and a product that is not made for stone can still dull a polished finish. Honed, polished and textured finishes behave differently. A polished surface shows dullness and scratches most easily, and an abrasive pad can remove the polish. Tile is usually more tolerant than stone. Glazed ceramic and porcelain tiles have a hard, fired surface, but the glaze can still be marked by some products, and an abrasive pad can scratch it. Unglazed quarry tile and some porcelain have a more open surface that takes up soil more readily. Grout is the porous material between tiles. Cement-based grout is absorbent and can take up soil, oils and coloured liquids. Epoxy grout is less absorbent and more resistant to staining, but it can still be damaged by the wrong product or a harsh abrasive. Check the product's compatibility with both the tile and the grout before you use it.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a method and a brush
instructionSections.body: Confirm the stone or tile type and the grout before you choose a product, and use the identification steps from “Hard floor identification: timber, stone, tile, vinyl, concrete” where the type is unclear. Where the stone is natural, use a stone-compatible product from the approved list and keep acidic products off it. Where the tile is glazed, use a product that is compatible with the glaze and the grout. Test the product on an inconspicuous area, and wait for the time the label gives before you judge the result. Use a brush that suits the grout and the surface. A soft or medium nylon brush is a common choice for grout lines, and a soft cloth or a non-scratching pad suits polished stone. Do not use a steel brush, steel wool or a harsh abrasive on stone or grout, because the scratch marks hold soil and will make the next clean harder. Work in small sections and rinse as the product label directs. Remove the rinse water as you go, so that residue does not dry on the surface or film over the grout. Do not mix products. Some combinations can release hazardous gases or cause a dangerous reaction. Use one product at a time, and rinse the area between products when the label requires it.

instructionSections.heading: Sealing, polishing and restoration are outside routine cleaning
instructionSections.body:
Sealing, polishing, honing, re-grouting and stone restoration all change the surface, the grout or the finish. They are specialist tasks and are outside routine cleaning. A cleaner records the condition of the grout and the stone, and refers any request to seal, polish or restore. Do not promise that a stain will come out, and do not describe a floor as sealed, polished or restored unless that work was carried out and recorded under a defined scope.

Deep grout staining and stone etching may not respond to routine cleaning. Record these as limits of the clean, with photographs taken in shade and under a light held low. Tell the client that the stain or etch may need a specialist assessment, and that the cleaning does not change the underlying condition. This keeps the record accurate and protects the business from a claim that a cleaning step caused or repaired a defect.

lessons.title: Water control and slip prevention on hard floors
learningOutcomes: Control water so that it does not pool, run into joins or create slip hazards.
Use signs, barriers and drying to keep people safe during and after wet cleaning.
Check that a floor is dry and safe before releasing it to traffic.

instructionSections.heading: Controlling water
instructionSections.body: Use only as much water as the method needs, and change the solution when it is dirty. Standing water on a hard floor is a slip hazard and can run into joins, edges and electrical outlets. Keep the mop damp rather than wet, and work in sections so that each section can dry before traffic returns.

instructionSections.heading: Signs, barriers and routes
instructionSections.body: Set out wet-floor signs and barriers before you start, and keep a safe route open for people where the site allows it. A sign alone does not stop a person from walking onto a wet floor, so use a barrier or supervision at busy points. Plan the route so that you do not have to walk over the wet floor you have just cleaned.

instructionSections.heading: Release
instructionSections.body: Release the floor to traffic only when it is dry and safe to walk on. Check the edges, corners and joins, which dry last. If the floor is still slippery, keep it closed and record the time and the reason.

lessons.title: Floor polishing and buffing
learningOutcomes: Explain what polishing and buffing change on a floor, and when they are outside routine cleaning.
Select a compatible polish and machine, and test the result on an inconspicuous area.
Control dust, slip and equipment hazards during buffing.

instructionSections.heading: What polishing changes
instructionSections.body: Polishing and buffing add or change a finish on the floor. They change the surface, so they are a different service from cleaning, and they must be priced and agreed as such. Check whether the floor is sealed, and whether the polish is compatible with the existing finish. A polish that is not compatible can cloud or lift.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment and test
instructionSections.body: Select a buffer and pad suited to the floor and the polish, and check the machine's cord and guard before use. Test the polish and the machine on an inconspicuous area, and let the test dry before judging it. Keep the cord clear of the path of the machine, and control dust from the buffing.

instructionSections.heading: Slip and the record
instructionSections.body: Polished floors are slippery until they cure, and that slip risk falls under the slip duty (page date: no date shown), so set signs and barriers and tell the client how long the floor should be kept clear. Record the product, the machine, the test result, the cure time and the client's agreement. Do not promise a finish that the floor cannot take.

lessons.title: Work authorisation and resident-centred scope
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between environmental cleaning by a cleaner and infection prevention and control decisions made by clinical and IPC staff.
Identify the written authority needed before work starts in a residential aged care or healthcare setting.
Describe how resident dignity, consent and privacy limit where and how a cleaner may work.
State the stop-and-refer triggers and the record that must follow a stop.

instructionSections.heading: Why this lesson comes first
instructionSections.body: A cleaner in a residential aged care facility, a clinic, a dental practice or an NDIS setting works in the place where people live, receive care and are most vulnerable to infection. Environmental cleaning is one of the controls that reduce the spread of infection, and the NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (document dated 2019) treat cleaning and spill management as part of preventing transmission from the environment to patients. But cleaning is not clinical care. Decisions about which precautions apply to a resident, which area is restricted, what product may be used near a clinical device, and whether a person has an infection belong to clinical staff and the infection prevention and control team. This lesson explains where the cleaner's authority ends.

instructionSections.heading: Written authority and the work order
instructionSections.body: Before you start, you need written authority for the task. A work order or site instruction should name the area, the surfaces or items, the approved product and method, the time window, and the person who gave the direction. A verbal request from a resident, a family member or a visitor is not authority to change the scope, and a request from a colleague does not replace the written list. If the facility's current infection prevention plan or outbreak instruction differs from the work order, follow the current instruction and tell your supervisor. Do not follow the work order where it would be unsafe under the current instruction.

instructionSections.heading: Resident-centred scope: dignity, consent and privacy
instructionSections.body: Residents are people in their own home or room, not only locations to be cleaned. A cleaner should knock, introduce themselves, ask before entering personal space, and explain what they will do. Do not move a resident, their belongings or their aids without permission, and do not read, move or photograph personal papers or medical charts. Privacy and dignity are part of the infection prevention approach, because a resident who feels that staff respect them is more likely to accept care. Where a resident refuses, asks you to stop, or appears distressed, stop that part of the task and tell the carer. Do not argue, and do not continue to force access.

instructionSections.heading: Where the cleaner's authority ends
instructionSections.body: Cleaning staff do not decide which precautions apply to a resident, do not set or lift isolation, do not give clinical advice, and do not decide that a room may be entered or left when the clinical team has set a restriction. They do not handle body fluids beyond the facility's spill procedure, and they do not handle clinical waste or sharps unless the facility has trained and authorised them to do so. They do not touch clinical devices, change their settings, or clean the interface of a device used on a resident unless the facility authorises that task in writing. When any of these comes up, stop and refer to the clinical team or the IPC contact, and record the referral.

instructionSections.heading: Licences, screening and the limit of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Completing this lesson does not give you a licence, a registration, a clearance or an authority to do regulated work. For NDIS settings, the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission states (page with no date shown) that a worker delivering NDIS supports and services may need an NDIS worker screening clearance, and that meeting worker screening obligations is a condition of provider registration. Residential aged care commenced under the Aged Care Act 2024 on 1 November 2025, and the strengthened Aged Care Quality Standards started on the same date (Department of Health news page, no date shown).

lessons.title: Transmission pathways in residential aged care
learningOutcomes: Describe contact, droplet and airborne transmission in plain terms, and state how they affect environmental cleaning.
Explain why the cleaner does not diagnose infection, identify a transmission route, or select a precaution.
Identify high-risk features of a residential aged care setting, such as shared spaces, high-touch surfaces and frail residents, that increase the importance of cleaning.
State the referral route when staff report new symptoms in a resident or a colleague.

instructionSections.heading: Why cleaners need to understand transmission
instructionSections.body: Infections move from person to person and from surfaces to people by a few main routes. A cleaner who understands these routes can do the environmental part of their job well: clean the places where contamination collects, avoid carrying it from one room to another, and stop when a risk is not in the plan. Understanding transmission does not mean diagnosing anyone, deciding which precautions a resident needs, or telling staff or families what a symptom means. Those decisions belong to the clinical team and the infection prevention and control team, and the facility's current instructions set what applies.

instructionSections.heading: Contact, droplet and airborne routes in plain terms
instructionSections.body: Contact transmission happens when an organism passes from a person or a surface to another person's hands or body, often through touch. Droplet transmission happens when larger droplets from a cough, sneeze or close conversation reach another person's eyes, nose or mouth, usually over a short distance. Airborne transmission happens when smaller particles stay suspended in the air and can be carried further in a room or through ventilation. In residential aged care the first route is the most common concern for cleaners, because touched surfaces, shared equipment and hand contact carry the organism between people. Which precautions apply for each route in a given case is decided by clinical staff, not by the cleaner.

instructionSections.heading: Why a care home is a higher-risk setting
instructionSections.body: Residents in residential aged care are often older and frail, may have reduced immunity or existing health conditions, and share bathrooms, dining rooms, lounges and corridors. Staff move between rooms many times a shift, and handrails, door handles, call bells and shared equipment are touched by many people. These features make environmental cleaning more important, and they also make it important that a cleaner does not carry a contamination from one resident's room into another. Plan the work from the most protected area to the most exposed, and never move from a room with a known risk to a clean room without the procedure for that situation.

instructionSections.heading: What to do when symptoms are reported
instructionSections.body: A resident or colleague may report new symptoms, or a carer may tell you that someone is unwell. Do not diagnose, do not name an infection, and do not tell anyone whether the symptoms are serious. Protect residents by following the current instructions, stop any task that would bring you into a risk you have not been trained for, and tell the nurse or the infection prevention contact immediately. If a notice is posted on the room, read it, follow it, and do not remove it. Record the report you made, the time and the person you told. The clinical team decides what happens next.

instructionSections.heading: Worked scenario: symptoms after the schedule was printed
instructionSections.body: A care unit reports new respiratory symptoms in several residents after the room cleaning schedule was printed. You are booked to clean three rooms on the unit. The first step is not to start work from the printed schedule as if nothing has changed. Ask the nurse in charge for the current instruction for the unit, and do not infer a cause from the symptoms. Follow the instruction you are given, and if the instruction changes the rooms, the sequence or the products, confirm it in writing before you start. Record the instruction you followed, who gave it, and the time.

lessons.title: Risk assessment and IPC instructions
learningOutcomes: Explain what the facility risk assessment and infection prevention and control (IPC) instructions are for, and who owns them.
Read an IPC instruction and identify the parts that apply to a cleaner's task.
Recognise a hazard or mismatch between the risk assessment, the instruction and the work order, and state the stop-and-refer step.
Record the instruction source, its effective time and any postponed task.

instructionSections.heading: What the risk assessment is for
instructionSections.body: A facility risk assessment identifies where infection could move and what controls reduce that risk. It considers the people in the setting, the activities carried out, the shared spaces, the equipment, and the products and waste handled. For a cleaner, the risk assessment explains why one room is cleaned before another, why some touch points are cleaned more often, and why certain items must stay separate. The assessment is owned by the facility, usually by its infection prevention and control lead, and it is reviewed when conditions change. The cleaner's job is to understand the parts that affect their work, and to follow them.

instructionSections.heading: What an IPC instruction is
instructionSections.body: An IPC instruction is a direction from the facility, a clinical team or the IPC lead that sets how a task must be done in a given area or situation. It may set the product, the sequence, the frequency, the protective equipment, the entry rules or the waste process. It may be a standing procedure, a unit notice on a door, or an outbreak direction. Where it is written, read it fully. Where it is verbal, ask for it to be confirmed in writing before you act on it, unless it is an immediate safety direction, which you follow and then confirm. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare treat environmental cleaning as part of a wider control framework, so an IPC instruction applies the guideline to the facility.

instructionSections.heading: Reading an instruction for your task
instructionSections.body: Read the instruction and sort it into three groups: what you must do, what you must not do, and what you must refer. The must-do items are your task steps, such as the cleaning sequence and the product to use. The must-not items include products not on the list, entry to restricted rooms, and handling of clinical equipment. The refer items include any clinical decision, any change to precautions, and any situation the instruction does not cover. If the instruction does not give a product, a contact condition or a method, do not invent one. Ask for it, and record that you asked.

instructionSections.heading: Spotting a hazard or a mismatch
instructionSections.body: A hazard or mismatch is any difference between the risk assessment, the IPC instruction, the work order and what you see on the ground. Examples include a room booked for routine cleaning that has a notice on the door, a product on the trolley that is not on the approved list, a high-touch surface missing from the schedule, or a resident whose situation has changed since the assessment was written. When you see one, stop the affected task, do not resolve it yourself by choosing whichever document is easier, and tell the nurse in charge or IPC contact. Postpone the affected task, record the hazard and the time, and do not diagnose the cause.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the instruction you followed
instructionSections.body: Your record should show which instruction you followed, who gave it, when it became effective, and any task you postponed and why. This matters because the facility may later need to show what was done and under which direction. Do not record a clinical reason you were not given.

lessons.title: Hand hygiene and personal protective equipment
learningOutcomes: Describe the hand hygiene points a cleaner passes through between rooms, using the facility's sequence.
Choose and use protective equipment for a room task in line with the facility assessment and product safety data sheet.
Prevent cross-contamination between resident rooms by controlling gloves, cloths and equipment.
Stop and report when protection is missing, damaged or contaminated, and record the event.

instructionSections.heading: Why hand hygiene is the first control
instructionSections.body: Hands are the most common way that organisms move from one surface or person to another. A cleaner touches door handles, handrails, call bells, equipment and clean stock many times in a shift, and each touch can carry an organism to the next place. The NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4 of November 2021, require that standard precautions are implemented in settings where supports are provided, and that workers are trained in hand hygiene and respiratory hygiene. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (document dated 2019) set the national framework. Hand hygiene is not a single action; it is a practice at the points where the risk changes.

instructionSections.heading: The transition points in a resident room
instructionSections.body: Perform hand hygiene at the points the facility specifies. In a typical resident room these include before entering the room, after removing gloves, after any contact with a resident's body fluid or their immediate surroundings, after touching a shared surface where the facility requires it, and before touching clean stock or leaving the room. A common failure is to clean a bedside table with gloves and then open a clean supply cupboard. The gloves must be removed, hand hygiene performed, and new gloves put on before the clean supply is touched. Follow the facility sequence, not habit.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing protection for the room task
