instructionSections.body: Select protective equipment from the facility's task assessment and the product safety data sheet, as set out in the medical equipment cleaning lesson on PPE and hand hygiene. Gloves are chosen for the task and the product, not for the room. A task that involves a spill, body fluid, or a sharp needs the protection the facility specifies for that task, and the cleaner does not decide to use less because the spill looks small. Check gloves and other protection before each use, and replace any that are torn, contaminated or the wrong type. Where the facility provides a gown, mask or eye protection for a room, follow the notice or instruction for that room.

instructionSections.heading: Preventing cross-contamination between rooms
instructionSections.body: Cross-contamination happens when something dirty touches something clean. Keep one room's cloths, gloves and waste out of the next room. Do not use the same cloth in more than one room unless the facility's procedure allows it, and do not carry used cloths in your pocket or on the trolley's clean shelf. Work from the area the facility's procedure directs as least contaminated to most contaminated, and keep used items in a closed container until they reach the holding area. A cloth used in a bathroom placed on a clean trolley shelf is a cross-contamination event to be stopped and reported.

instructionSections.heading: Exposure and stop-work
instructionSections.body: If your protection tears, you touch a body fluid with bare skin, or you are exposed through a splash or a sharp, stop the task, remove yourself from the immediate area, and follow the facility's exposure procedure. Report to the nurse in charge or supervisor the same shift. Do not continue a room because the protection was only slightly damaged. Stop work when the required protection is not available, and record the event and the decision. The facility, not the cleaner, decides any follow-up for an exposure.

lessons.title: Cleaning versus disinfection and product selection
learningOutcomes: Distinguish cleaning, which removes soil, from disinfection, which is an additional step where a facility or instruction requires it.
Explain why the NHMRC guidelines place detergent cleaning as the routine base, with disinfection used where indicated.
Select an approved product from a facility list, using its label, its approved use and its compatibility with the surface.
Stop and refer when a product is not approved, the label does not match the surface, or the required condition cannot be met.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning and disinfection are different steps
instructionSections.body: Cleaning removes soil, organic matter and visible contamination from a surface, usually with a detergent solution and a physical action. Disinfection reduces the number of living organisms on a surface to a level the facility has decided is appropriate, and it depends on a product, a dilution and a wet contact condition. A surface that looks clean can still carry organisms, and a surface that has been disinfected but not cleaned may still hold soil that blocks the product from working. For this reason, the approved sequence is usually to clean first and then disinfect where the facility or the instruction requires it. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (document dated 2019) recommend cleaning frequently touched surfaces with detergent solution at least daily and when visibly soiled, and recommend that shared clinical equipment is cleaned with detergent between patient uses and disinfected where indicated.

instructionSections.heading: Where disinfection is used
instructionSections.body: The guidelines (document dated 2019) state that sodium hypochlorite disinfection may be used as an adjunct to standard cleaning in healthcare facilities. They do not suggest routine use of hydrogen peroxide vapour or ultraviolet light, and note that either may be considered in high-risk settings or outbreaks after other options are exhausted. For a cleaner this means that disinfection is not applied to every surface every time as a habit. The facility decides where disinfection applies, how often, and with which product, and the cleaner follows that decision. Do not add disinfectant to a routine clean unless the facility's schedule or instruction calls for it.

instructionSections.heading: Selecting a product from the approved list
instructionSections.body: Choose a product from the facility's approved list for the surface and the purpose. Read the label for the approved use, the dilution, the wet contact condition, the surfaces it must not be used on, and the protection required. A familiar product is not automatically approved, and a product labelled for one use may not be approved for another. If the product you need is not on the list, do not use a similar one. Ask the supervisor or the IPC contact, and record the request. Where the label and the facility list disagree, stop and refer the conflict.

instructionSections.heading: Compatibility and the stop rule
instructionSections.body: Products can damage surfaces, displays and devices, and some products must not be mixed. Check that the product is compatible with the surface, that the surface can stay wet for the required condition, and that no products will be combined. Where a product would be applied to a clinical device interface, a keep-dry area or electrical equipment, stop and refer, because the device manufacturer's instruction and the clinical team govern that surface. Do not improvise a concentration, a contact time or a product.

instructionSections.heading: Worked case: the familiar disinfectant
instructionSections.body: A cleaner finds a familiar disinfectant on a shelf and plans to use it on the bathroom rails because it is strong. The facility's approved list names a different product for rails. The correct action is to use the approved product, or to ask the supervisor for it if it is missing, and not to substitute the familiar one. Record the shortfall, the product requested and the time. The familiar product may be suitable for another purpose under its own approval, but that approval is not a substitute for the facility list.

lessons.title: High-touch surfaces and risk-based frequencies
learningOutcomes: Identify the high-touch surfaces in a care or clinical area and explain why they are prioritised.
Apply a facility cleaning frequency schedule and explain how risk changes it.
Recognise when a schedule change is needed and state who authorises it.
Record the frequency applied, the surfaces cleaned and any change requested.

instructionSections.heading: What a high-touch surface is
instructionSections.body: A high-touch surface is one that many people touch with their hands, often in quick succession. Examples in a care or clinical setting include door handles, handrails, call bell buttons, light switches, bed rails and tables, taps and sink handles, toilet flush levers, commode lids, lift buttons, shared phones and keyboards, and trolley handles. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (document dated 2019) recommend cleaning frequently touched surfaces with detergent solution at least daily and when visibly soiled. The NDIS Practice Standards, Version 4 of November 2021, require routine environmental cleaning in settings other than participants' homes, with particular attention to frequently touched surfaces. The list of surfaces and the frequency for each are set by the facility's risk assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Risk-based frequency
instructionSections.body: Frequency is decided by risk, not by convenience. A handrail in a busy corridor used by many residents and visitors needs more frequent cleaning than a wall in a storeroom. A bathroom used by several residents in one day needs more attention than a single room used by one resident. The facility's schedule records these decisions, and it may set a higher frequency for a unit with known risks or after an event. Your job is to apply the frequency on the schedule, and to recognise when the actual use of an area has changed so that the schedule may no longer match the risk.

instructionSections.heading: Mapping the surfaces in your area
instructionSections.body: Before you start an area, walk it and list the high-touch surfaces it contains. Compare that list to the facility schedule. If a surface is missing from the schedule, or a surface on the schedule is no longer used, note the difference and tell your supervisor. Do not add or remove surfaces from the schedule yourself. In a resident room, check bed rails, call bells, bedside tables, the bathroom door, and any shared equipment that is part of the room's approved list, and leave clinical devices to the clinical team.

instructionSections.heading: When a change is needed
instructionSections.body: A schedule may need to change when an outbreak is declared, when a resident's needs change, when a new piece of equipment arrives, or when an inspection finds a gap. A change to frequency or to the list of surfaces must be authorised by the person responsible for the schedule, usually the IPC lead or the facility manager, and it must be confirmed in writing. Until the change is confirmed, follow the current schedule and report the concern. A change that is suggested by a resident or family member is passed on for review, and it is not applied directly.

instructionSections.heading: Worked scenario: the handrail that is touched all day
instructionSections.body: A resident repeatedly touches a handrail that several other residents also use, while the schedule lists only end-of-day cleaning for the handrail. You notice the handrail looks used several times in the morning. The appropriate response is to follow the schedule as written, tell the supervisor what you observed, and ask for the frequency to be reviewed. Record the observation, the time and the person told. Do not increase the frequency yourself, and do not clean the handrail in a way that is not approved.

lessons.title: Clean-to-dirty flow and equipment segregation
learningOutcomes: Plan a clean-to-dirty route through a care or clinical area that follows the facility's direction of travel.
Allocate and separate cloths, equipment and products between clean and used zones.
Recognise a cross-contamination event and state the containment and reporting step.
Record the route, the segregation used and any breach.

instructionSections.heading: Why the direction of travel matters
instructionSections.body: In a care or clinical setting, the most common way contamination spreads from one area to another is by the cleaner. A cloth used in a bathroom, a trolley wheel that rolls through a soiled corridor, or a glove that touched a bin and then a clean handle can carry an organism to the next place. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (document dated 2019) treat environmental controls, including cleaning and spill management, as part of preventing transmission from the environment to patients. A clean-to-dirty flow is one way the facility applies that control: work moves from the least contaminated areas toward the most contaminated, and used items move out without crossing back through clean areas.

instructionSections.heading: Planning the route through the area
instructionSections.body: Before starting, decide the route with your supervisor or the schedule. Identify the clean store, the least exposed rooms, the more exposed rooms, the holding area for used items, and the route between them. The facility may set a specific order, such as clean common areas first, then resident rooms in a set sequence, and then bathrooms and the holding area last. Follow it. If the route is blocked or the sequence cannot be followed, stop and tell the supervisor before you change it, rather than making a shortcut that crosses a contaminated area.

instructionSections.heading: Allocating cloths, equipment and products
instructionSections.body: Use separate cloths, equipment and product containers for clean and used zones, as the facility procedure directs. Many facilities use colour coding for cloths and buckets to show the zone. Keep each colour for its zone, and do not use a cloth from the bathroom in a resident room, or from one resident's room in another. Dedicated equipment is used in isolation areas or for specific residents where the facility requires it. Do not share equipment between areas unless the procedure allows it, and clean or replace it as directed.

instructionSections.heading: Containing a cross-contamination event
instructionSections.body: If a used item reaches a clean area, a clean item reaches a used area, or a glove touches clean stock after touching a soiled surface, treat it as a cross-contamination event. Stop, do not use the affected item or stock, set it aside in a clearly marked place, and tell the supervisor. Do not try to clean it and return it to stock. Record the item, where it was found, what it touched, the time and the person told. The supervisor decides the next step under the facility procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Worked scenario: the cloth on the clean shelf
instructionSections.body: You used a cloth in a bathroom and then, without thinking, placed it on the clean trolley shelf to free your hand. You notice it some minutes later. The correct response is to remove it from the clean shelf, put it in the used container or bag, set aside any clean items it has touched, and tell the supervisor. Record the event as a cross-contamination event with the time and the affected items. Do not reuse the cloth or the items that were on the shelf until the supervisor decides.

lessons.title: Bathrooms, shared areas and resident equipment boundaries
learningOutcomes: Describe the cleaning sequence for a shared bathroom, using the facility's approved method and frequency.
Identify the boundary between permitted environmental surfaces and resident equipment, including clinical devices and assistive equipment.
Respect resident privacy, dignity and personal belongings while cleaning shared and personal areas.
State the referral step for a request that crosses the equipment boundary.

instructionSections.heading: Why shared bathrooms need a structured method
instructionSections.body: A shared bathroom in residential aged care is touched by several people in a short time: handrails, taps, flush levers, toilet seats, grab rails, shower chairs and the door. It is also a place where body fluids and soil are more likely to be present, which increases the risk of spreading organisms. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare treat cleaning with detergent as the routine base, with disinfection where indicated. A structured method keeps the sequence consistent: clear the area, clean from the cleanest to the most soiled surface, use cloths for one zone, and finish with the high-touch points. Follow the facility method for the product, the contact condition and the frequency.

instructionSections.heading: The sequence in a shared bathroom
instructionSections.body: Enter the bathroom with clean equipment and the approved products. Check the notice on the door and the list of resident equipment that must not be moved or cleaned by you. Start with the fixtures and surfaces that are least soiled, and work toward the toilet and floor. Clean the high-touch points as a set, including rails, taps, flush levers and the door handle inside and out. Use separate cloths for the toilet and the washbasin where the facility requires. Keep the floor cleaning separate from the surfaces, and remove soiled water and cloths by the designated route. Leave the bathroom in the state the schedule and the product label require.

instructionSections.heading: The boundary with resident equipment
instructionSections.body: Resident equipment includes assistive devices such as walking frames, wheelchairs, hoists, shower chairs and commodes, and clinical devices such as monitors, pumps and call systems. Some of these are part of the room's cleaning list and may be cleaned by you using the approved product. Clinical devices, and any equipment that a clinician has set up for a resident, are not cleaned by you unless the facility has authorised the task in writing. Do not move a resident's equipment to reach a surface, and do not remove a clinical lead or cable to clean around it. Where the boundary is unclear, leave the item as found and refer to the nurse or carer.

instructionSections.heading: Privacy, dignity and personal belongings
instructionSections.body: Personal belongings, medication, papers and photographs in a resident's room or bathroom are not yours to move, read or handle. Ask the resident or carer before moving a personal item to clean under it, and return it to the same place. Knock, introduce yourself and close doors while you work, and keep residents' dignity in mind when a resident is in the bathroom. If a resident asks you to stop, or appears distressed, stop that part of the task, tell the carer, and record the event. Do not continue to force access or to finish a task at the cost of a resident's comfort.

instructionSections.heading: Worked scenario: the monitor in the shared bathroom
instructionSections.body: A resident asks you to wipe the screen of a clinical monitor that is mounted in a shared bathroom, saying that it has fingerprints and that their family will be upset. The monitor is a clinical device, and the boundary is not yours to cross unless the facility has authorised that task in writing. Explain politely that the nurse will attend to it, do not touch the device, tell the carer or nurse the same moment, and record the request, the referral and the time. Continue with the rest of the bathroom using the approved method.

lessons.title: Linen, waste and spill escalation
learningOutcomes: Distinguish ordinary linen and general waste from items that the facility treats as potentially infectious, and state the handling rule for each.
Recognise a body-fluid spill, a sharp or an uncertain waste item, and state that these are escalated to trained personnel under the facility procedure.
Describe the immediate containment steps for a spill a cleaner is authorised to attend, and the stop-and-escalate steps for one they are not.
Record the item, location, action and escalation for linen, waste and spill events.

instructionSections.heading: Linen and general waste: the ordinary rules
instructionSections.body: Ordinary linen and general waste are handled under the facility's linen and waste procedure. Bag and close linen at the point of collection, do not shake it, and keep it away from your face and clean stock. Place general waste in the correct bin, and do not overfill it. The facility decides which items go in which stream, and it may treat some linen as potentially infectious, for example after a known exposure. Follow the colour, label and stream the facility uses, and do not mix streams. If you are unsure which stream an item belongs in, do not guess. Set it aside and ask.

instructionSections.heading: Potentially infectious items and uncertain waste
instructionSections.body: Some items are treated by the facility as potentially infectious, and a cleaner may not be trained to decide that from appearance. These can include linen or dressings soaked with body fluid, items from an isolation area, and any waste whose origin you do not know. Do not open, sort, compact or reach into a bag or bin to identify its contents. Close it if it is safe to do so, label it as the facility directs, place it in the designated holding area, and tell the supervisor. The facility decides the stream, and the handling is done by staff trained for it.

instructionSections.heading: Body-fluid spills: what a cleaner may and may not do
instructionSections.body: The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare recommend that anyone cleaning a spill wears gloves and other personal protective equipment appropriate to the task. Where the facility has trained you and written your role into the spill procedure, you may contain and clean a small, identified, non-blood spill using the approved product. For blood or other body-fluid spills, larger spills, spills of unknown origin, spills that have reached carpet or soft furnishings, or spills near sharps, do not clean them unless the facility has trained and authorised you in writing. Restrict access, keep people away, and call the trained spill response person. Do not wipe a spill to reduce the visible mess before the trained person arrives.

instructionSections.heading: Sharps and clinical waste: escalate, do not handle
instructionSections.body: Sharps, such as needles, lancets and broken glass that may be contaminated, are not handled by a cleaner by hand. Do not pick them up, reach into a sharps container, push sharps into a bin, or attempt to recap a needle. If you find a sharp, stop, keep others away, and call the designated sharps response person under the facility procedure. If you are stuck or cut, follow the exposure procedure at once. Clinical waste is handled by staff trained and authorised for it, and the cleaner's role is to recognise it, keep it separate, and escalate.

instructionSections.heading: Worked case: the unidentified spill by the laundry trolley
instructionSections.body: You find a wet, unidentified mark near a laundry trolley in a corridor. It may be a spill of body fluid, or it may be water. Do not touch it or clean it. Put a warning sign or cone in place if the facility provides one, keep people away, and call the trained spill response person and your supervisor. Record the location, the time, the description and who you called. Only after the trained person has assessed the spill and given a written instruction should a cleaner clean it, and only using the procedure the instruction gives.

lessons.title: Outbreaks and transmission-based precautions
learningOutcomes: Explain that an outbreak declaration or an additional precaution changes the instruction that governs cleaning, and that the cleaner follows the current formal instruction.
Identify the changes an outbreak instruction may make to entry, protection, product choice and cleaning frequency, and state who authorises each.
Recognise a conflict between a planned clean and a newly announced outbreak instruction, and state the stop-and-refer step.
Record the instruction followed, its effective time and any task postponed.

instructionSections.heading: What changes in an outbreak
instructionSections.body: An outbreak is a cluster of infections that the facility or public health authority has identified as a risk to residents, workers or visitors. When an outbreak is declared, the facility's infection prevention and control team may add precautions to the normal routine. These can include restricting entry to some areas, requiring particular protection, changing the products used, increasing the frequency of cleaning on specified surfaces, and using dedicated equipment. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare set the national framework on which these facility decisions are based. The detail of what applies is set by the current formal instruction, not by a general memory of how outbreaks are managed.

instructionSections.heading: The governing instruction
instructionSections.body: The instruction that governs during an outbreak is the current formal instruction issued by the facility's clinical or IPC lead, usually in writing and posted in the area or sent to the supervisor. A verbal rumour, a message between colleagues, or a printed schedule that was prepared before the outbreak does not govern. If you hear that an outbreak has been declared and you have not received the formal instruction, ask your supervisor or the nurse in charge for it before starting the affected work. Confirm that the instruction is current and that it applies to the area you are about to clean.

instructionSections.heading: Entry, protection and dedicated equipment
instructionSections.body: Under an outbreak instruction, you may be asked to enter an area only after a particular step, to wear protection that is not part of routine work, or to use equipment that is dedicated to that area and not shared. Do not enter a restricted area without the instruction, do not substitute protection, and do not take equipment from the restricted area to a clean area. If the instruction requires you to wait outside until a clinical step is completed, wait, and record the time you waited and why.

instructionSections.heading: Products and frequency
instructionSections.body: Outbreak instructions may name a product, a dilution or a contact condition for a surface, and may require an increased frequency for specified high-touch surfaces. Use only the named product and the frequency in the instruction. If the named product is not available, do not substitute, and tell the supervisor so that the product is supplied. Do not increase the frequency beyond the instruction without written authority, and do not reduce it because the workload is high. Record each change in frequency or product as the instruction states it.

instructionSections.heading: Worked scenario: the planned clean and the outbreak briefing
instructionSections.body: A planned isolation-room clean overlaps with a newly announced outbreak briefing. The briefing may change the entry rules, the protection or the product for that room. The correct first step is not to enter the room until you have confirmed the current instruction with the clinical lead or IPC contact. If the instruction is not clear by the time you need to start, postpone the room, tell the supervisor, and record the time and the person you asked. Do not start the room on the assumption that nothing has changed.

lessons.title: Audit, handover and quality improvement
learningOutcomes: Complete a traceable task record that shows what was cleaned, how, when and by whom, without claiming clinical sterility or certification.
Describe a supervisor observation and a handover that lets the next person act without asking the cleaner.
Record a missed area or a variance honestly and arrange a safe correction under the approved procedure.
Identify a quality improvement point from audit findings and pass it to the responsible person.

instructionSections.heading: What an audit is for
instructionSections.body: An audit checks whether the work was done as the schedule and instruction require, and whether the controls are working. In residential aged care, clinics and NDIS settings an audit may be a supervisor walk-through, a checklist against the schedule, a review of the work records, or an external inspection. The NDIS Practice Standards, Version 4 of November 2021, require that the risk management system includes, where relevant, measures to prevent and control infections. The Aged Care Quality Standards Action 3.17 guidance resource (no date shown) refers to traceability of reprocessed items, which depends on accurate records. An audit only helps the facility if the record is honest. A record that says a task was complete when it was not defeats the purpose of the audit.

instructionSections.heading: A complete task record
instructionSections.body: A complete record shows the area or item, the date and time, the schedule or instruction followed, the product and method used, the frequency, the surfaces covered, any exception, the person who did the work and the handover. Write the record at the time of the task. Do not describe a result in terms that suggest clinical sterility, certification or a disinfection that was not achieved. A cleaner records what was done, not what the facility would like to be true. Where a field cannot be completed, leave a clear note rather than a guess.

instructionSections.heading: Variance, missed areas and honest correction
instructionSections.body: A variance is any difference between the schedule or instruction and what was done. A missed area is a surface or room on the schedule that was not cleaned. When you find a missed area, or an audit finds one, record it as found, not as already fixed. Arrange a correction under the approved procedure, such as cleaning the area now, and record the correction with the time. If the correction cannot be done safely or in time, tell the supervisor and record the postponement. Do not reopen a record to hide a gap, and do not add a completion time that was not observed.

instructionSections.heading: Handover that works
instructionSections.body: A handover tells the next person what is done, what is not done, what is blocked and who must be contacted. Keep it short and factual: the area, the status, any stop or referral, any product shortfall, any resident request, and the next step. Handover to the supervisor or the next shift in the way the facility requires. Do not assume that the next person knows about a restriction or a stop. If an area is restricted, the handover must say so, and the restriction notice must stay in place until the responsible person removes it.

instructionSections.heading: Quality improvement from audit findings
instructionSections.body: A repeated finding is a signal that the system needs attention, not only that one cleaner made a mistake. If the same surface is missed each week, the schedule, the route or the workload may need review. Pass the finding to your supervisor in writing, with the evidence and the pattern you observed, and suggest a change for the responsible person to consider. Do not change the schedule yourself. The improvement is made by the facility, and your role is to make the problem visible and accurately recorded.

lessons.title: Dental aerosols and operatory access control
learningOutcomes: Explain that environmental cleaning of a dental operatory is a facility-controlled task, and that access to the room alone does not confer authority.
Recognise post-procedure restrictions, aerosol or splash contamination, and barriers set by the dental clinical team.
Identify the stop-work triggers in an operatory, including patient presence, unknown contamination, sharps, restricted room status and contradictory instructions.
Record a room task without certifying that the room is clinically ready or pathogen-free, and without recording patient information.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and clinical boundaries
instructionSections.body: Environmental cleaning of a dental operatory is a task the facility delegates to cleaning staff under its own infection prevention and control procedure. It is not clinical care. Dental equipment, instruments, handpieces, suction and delivery systems, and any device the dental team uses on patients are clinician-owned or reprocessing matters, and they are outside your role unless the clinic policy authorises a specific task in writing. This lesson covers the environmental surfaces you may clean within your written scope. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course and are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the clinic procedure. Never infer authority from access to the room alone. Being allowed into the room does not mean you may clean everything in it.

instructionSections.heading: Aerosols, splashes and post-procedure restrictions
instructionSections.body: Dental procedures can produce aerosols and splashes that settle on surfaces around the chair, the light, the bench and the floor. The dental team decides the post-procedure restriction, which can include a period in which the room must not be entered, a barrier that must not be removed, or a waiting time before the room is opened for cleaning. The period is set by the clinic's procedure and the clinical team, and this lesson does not set a time. Do not enter a restricted operatory, do not remove a barrier the clinical team has placed, and do not start cleaning until the room has been released to you in the way the clinic specifies. Ask if you are unsure whether a room is released.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work triggers in the operatory
instructionSections.body: Pause work and notify the designated professional when a patient is present, when the contamination is unknown, when sharps or instruments are visible, when the room is restricted, or when two instructions contradict each other. Use the site risk plan to distinguish the environmental surfaces you are authorised to clean from clinician-owned equipment. If the chair, light, handpiece, delivery unit or suction is not on your written list, leave it as found. A contradictory instruction, such as a notice saying the room is clear and a clinician saying it is not, is a stop condition. Do not choose the instruction that lets you finish the room.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing the approved workflow
instructionSections.body: Before the first task in an operatory, confirm the room is released, check the hand hygiene station, read the product instructions for the approved surfaces, and select the protective equipment the task requires. Keep clean supplies and used cloths separate, and plan the route out of the room so that used items do not cross clean areas. Follow the clinic's actual contact time, dilution and compatibility instructions. Do not use a generic recipe from a website or from memory. If an instruction is missing for a surface, record it as missing and refer, rather than inventing one.

instructionSections.heading: Controlled cleaning and documentation
instructionSections.body: Within your authorised environmental scope, follow the clinic's risk-based cleaning sequence and frequency. Do not handle instruments, sharps, blood spills or medical devices unless you have been trained and expressly authorised under the clinic policy. Record the task you completed, the surfaces covered, any exclusion, any incident and the person you handed over to. Enter only the approved room identifier and non-patient information. Do not record patient names, appointment details or clinical notes in the cleaning record. Record an unresolved issue as unresolved. Never certify that a dental operatory is pathogen-free or ready for clinical use, because the cleaning record is not a clinical clearance.

lessons.title: Sharps, blood and clinical waste escalation
learningOutcomes: Recognise a sharp, a blood or body-fluid contamination and a clinical waste container, and explain why a cleaner does not handle them.
State the escalation steps for each, including keeping others away and calling the designated clinical contact.
Describe the exposure response if a cleaner is stuck, cut or splashed.
Record the item, location, time and person notified, without handling the item.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: recognition and escalation only
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches you to recognise sharps, blood and body-fluid contamination, and clinical waste, and to escalate them. It does not teach you to handle, collect, sort, compact, transport or dispose of them. Those tasks are performed by staff the clinic has trained and authorised for them, under the clinic's waste procedure and any state or territory requirement. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course, and are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the clinic procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising sharps
instructionSections.body: A sharp is any object that can puncture or cut the skin, such as a needle, a lancet, a scalpel blade, a broken glass ampoule or a dental instrument tip. A sharp that may be contaminated must be treated as a hazard even if it looks clean. Common places to find them include the floor beside a chair, in a drawer, between cushions, in a bin that has not been sorted, and in a corridor after a procedure. Do not reach into a bin, drawer or cushion without looking first. If you cannot see the whole of an area, do not reach into the gap. Ask for the area to be checked by the trained person.

instructionSections.heading: Blood and body-fluid contamination
instructionSections.body: Blood and body fluids are treated as potentially infectious. A visible spot of blood on a chair, a bench or the floor, or a dressing with a stain, is a contamination that you do not clean unless you have been trained and authorised for that specific task. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare recommend that anyone cleaning a spill wears gloves and other personal protective equipment appropriate to the task, and the clinic's procedure defines which spills a cleaner may attend. For anything beyond the clinic's authorised list, restrict access, keep people away, and call the designated clinical or spill contact. Do not wipe the spot to make it less visible.

instructionSections.heading: Clinical waste containers
instructionSections.body: Clinical waste containers, including sharps containers and bags for clinical waste, are labelled and placed by the clinic. Do not open, move, tip, compact or reposition a sharps container, and do not push items into it. If a container is full, damaged, overfilled or not closed, leave it as found, keep people away from it, and tell the designated clinical contact. Do not carry clinical waste from one area to another on your trolley. The NHMRC guidelines state that facilities must follow state and territory clinical waste laws.

instructionSections.heading: Exposure and the stop-and-report response
instructionSections.body: If you are stuck by a sharp, cut, or splashed by blood or another body fluid on broken skin or the eyes, nose or mouth, stop the task immediately. Remove yourself from the immediate area, and follow the clinic's exposure procedure at once. Do not squeeze the wound to make it bleed. Tell the designated clinical contact and your supervisor the same shift, and record the exposure with the time, the source where known, the first aid given and the person notified. The clinic decides any follow-up assessment, and the cleaner does not decide it alone.

lessons.title: NDIS participant homes and support-worker boundaries
learningOutcomes: Explain that a participant's home is the participant's own home, and that the participant's choices, privacy and consent govern the work.
Describe how the NDIS Practice Standards treat environmental cleaning in participants' homes compared with other settings.
Identify the boundaries of a cleaner's or support worker's role in a participant's home, including household items, personal care and clinical tasks.
State the stop-and-refer steps when a request or a hazard is outside the agreed scope.

instructionSections.heading: Whose home it is
instructionSections.body: When you work in an NDIS participant's home, you are a guest in someone's home. The participant decides how the home is used, who may enter, what may be moved, and what they want done. Your agreed task is the scope, and the participant's wishes within that scope come first. Respect the participant's privacy, their belongings and their routines. Knock or announce yourself, ask before entering rooms the participant is not in, and do not read papers, open drawers or look through personal items. The participant may have other people living in the home, and their privacy matters too.

instructionSections.heading: How the standards treat cleaning in homes
instructionSections.body: The NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4 of November 2021, Core Module, require that infection prevention and control standard precautions are implemented in every setting where supports are provided. The routine environmental cleaning indicator applies in settings other than participants' homes, and it expressly excludes participants' homes. This is not a reason for a worker to ignore hygiene in a home. Standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE use and safe handling of waste still apply to the worker's own conduct, and the participant's agreed support plan defines what cleaning, if any, is part of the service.

instructionSections.heading: Boundaries of the role in a home
instructionSections.body: Your role in a participant's home is the agreed support, and nothing more. Cleaning of the participant's own home is done only if it is part of the agreed service and the support plan. Do not perform clinical tasks, administer medication, change or manage equipment the participant uses for health reasons, or make decisions about care. Do not move or use the participant's assistive equipment beyond what the plan allows. Do not discard or sort the participant's belongings, medicines or waste unless the plan and the participant ask you to do so, and then only as directed. If a task is outside the plan, tell the participant and the provider, and do not do it.

instructionSections.heading: Hazards in a participant's home
instructionSections.body: Homes are not set up as clinical settings. A home may have soiled items, pets, unsafe steps, mould, chemicals stored in unsafe places, or needles or medical waste from the participant's own care. Stop and assess before you start if a hazard is present, and do not handle sharps, body fluid or unknown waste by hand. Report the hazard to the provider and, where a participant is at risk, to the appropriate contact. Where the home has a hazard that the provider's risk assessment does not cover, the work pauses until the provider decides how it is managed. Mould and other serious hazards in homes can be outside your role and need specialist assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Worked scenario: the participant asks for something else
instructionSections.body: A participant asks you, while you are there to clean the kitchen, to help them take their medication and to sort through a box of old papers. Neither task is in your agreed support plan. Medication administration and clinical tasks are outside your role, and sorting papers is outside the scope unless the plan includes it. Politely explain that you can only do the agreed tasks, record the request, and tell your supervisor and the provider the same day so the plan can be reviewed. Do not do the tasks, and do not refuse in a way that leaves the participant without a safe alternative. The provider should arrange it.

lessons.title: Licence classes and what this add-on does not grant
learningOutcomes: Identify the states in this add-on that list a boom-type elevating work platform class as a high-risk work licence.
State that this add-on grants no licence, certificate or authority.

instructionSections.heading: What a high-risk work licence is
instructionSections.body: Some plant and platform work is licensed as high-risk work. WorkSafe Victoria's high risk work licence page names a boom-type elevating work platform operation licence as a class (page reviewed 30 June 2026). SafeWork NSW also lists a boom-type elevating work platform (WP) class among its high-risk work licences (page last modified 15 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: What this add-on does not do
instructionSections.body: This add-on explains the licence rules. It does not grant a licence, certificate or authority for any regulated work, and finishing it does not qualify a learner to operate a boom-type platform. Check the rule for the state or territory where the work is done with that regulator before any work at height or on a platform.

instructionSections.heading: How to use this add-on
instructionSections.body: Take this add-on alongside the main courses. Each lesson marks the points that no official source confirms, so that they are checked before anyone relies on them.

lessons.title: Boom-type platforms: the 11 metre threshold by state
learningOutcomes: Apply the boom-length rule for each state that this lesson covers.
Explain why Queensland's platform definition excludes platforms under 11 metres.

instructionSections.heading: Where the 11 metre rule applies
instructionSections.body: Several states set the boom-type platform licence by boom length. SafeWork NSW's licence page states a WP licence where the boom is 11 metres or more. WorkSafe Tasmania states that a WP licence applies where the boom length is 11 metres or more, and that no licence is needed for a boom under 11 metres (page last updated 1 December 2023). WorkSafe WA's WP licence class page applies the same 11 metre boom length (published 11 August 2026, last updated 13 August 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Northern Territory and ACT
instructionSections.body: The Northern Territory's elevating work platform bulletin states the 11 metre threshold for the WP licence (no date shown). The ACT high risk work licence page lists a WP licence where the boom is 11 metres or more; the page shows a fee period and no publication date.

instructionSections.heading: Queensland's platform definition
instructionSections.body: Queensland's boom-type platform page says a WP licence is needed to operate a boom type elevating platform, and that platforms under 11 metres are not included in that definition (no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: What is not confirmed
instructionSections.body: How boom length is measured is not confirmed by an official source in this add-on. Confirm the measurement rule with the state regulator before relying on a length figure.

lessons.title: Victoria: the WP class and the boom-length question
learningOutcomes: Identify the Victorian WP class by its official name.
Distinguish a confirmed class from a boom-length rule that is not confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: What the Victorian class covers
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria's high risk work licence page names a boom-type elevating work platform operation licence as a high risk work licence class (page reviewed 30 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: The boom-length question
instructionSections.body: Whether the Victorian WP licence applies at any boom length is not confirmed by an official source. WorkSafe Victoria's page states the class without a boom length. A page that states no length does not confirm that there is no length threshold.

instructionSections.heading: What to do
instructionSections.body: Ask WorkSafe Victoria about the length rule before relying on it, and do not assume a short boom is outside the licence or inside it until the rule is confirmed.

lessons.title: Scissor lifts and operator competency
learningOutcomes: State where the WP licence does not apply to scissor lifts, as confirmed by an official page.
Explain why operator competency still applies to scissor lifts.

instructionSections.heading: Victoria
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria's high risk work licence page indicates that scissor lifts do not need the WP licence (page reviewed 30 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Northern Territory
instructionSections.body: The Northern Territory bulletin says a high risk work licence is not required for scissor lifts (no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Competency still applies
instructionSections.body: The same Northern Territory bulletin says the PCBU must ensure scissor lift operator competency so far as reasonably practicable (no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Limit of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not confirm the scissor lift rule for other states. Check the regulator for your state before using a scissor lift.

lessons.title: Scaffolding and work above 2 metres in New South Wales
learningOutcomes: Apply the NSW scaffold licence threshold of 4 metres.
Identify the SWMS trigger at 2 metres and the point that is not confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Scaffold licence
instructionSections.body: SafeWork NSW's work at heights page says a scaffold licence is needed to erect, alter or dismantle a scaffold where the fall or falling-object risk is more than 4 metres (no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Safe work method statement
instructionSections.body: The same page says a safe work method statement is needed where a person could fall more than 2 metres (no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: What is not confirmed
instructionSections.body: Whether the high-risk work licence rules apply to work over 2 metres is not confirmed by an official source. The page sets out the SWMS and fall-prevention duties at 2 metres, but it does not tie a high-risk licence rule to that height.

lessons.title: Falls from roofs and guardrails: what the sources confirm
learningOutcomes: Describe what the WorkSafe Victoria 2024 alert confirms and what it does not.
Explain why a guardrail must be checked against its supporting structure.
State the SA height-threshold announcement and its in-force status.

instructionSections.heading: A WorkSafe Victoria alert on a guardrail
instructionSections.body: A WorkSafe Victoria safety alert published 30 May 2024 describes a guardrail that came loose from a parapet wall. The alert does not state the cause of the failure.

instructionSections.heading: The supporting structure
instructionSections.body: The alert says a guardrail may fail where the supporting structure has not been verified.

instructionSections.heading: What is not confirmed
instructionSections.body: That the guardrail failed because its structure could not carry the load is not confirmed by an official source.

instructionSections.heading: The model falls code
instructionSections.body: Safe Work Australia's model code on managing the risk of falls says to check with the regulator whether it has legal effect in the jurisdiction (no date shown). That the model code has legal effect only where a jurisdiction adopts it is not confirmed by an official source.

instructionSections.heading: South Australia's height threshold
instructionSections.body: SafeWork SA announced on 5 June 2026 that the high-risk construction height threshold moves from 3 metres to 2 metres from 1 July 2026. The announcement is confirmed; the regulation text and in-force status are not confirmed by an official source.

lessons.title: Roof and platform work: the licence questions still open
learningOutcomes: List the boom-length rules that are confirmed and the ones that are not.
Identify the South Australian points that are not confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: What is confirmed
instructionSections.body: Lesson 2 sets out the 11 metre boom-length rules that official pages state for New South Wales, Tasmania, the Northern Territory, Western Australia and the ACT, and Queensland's exclusion of platforms under 11 metres.

instructionSections.heading: South Australia
instructionSections.body: SafeWork SA's high risk work licence page (last updated 10 January 2024) does not list a WP class and gives no boom length. Whether South Australia requires a WP licence is not confirmed by an official source.

instructionSections.heading: The South Australian pressure equipment class
instructionSections.body: The same South Australian page lists a 'pressure equipment operation' licence class. The class name is confirmed; whether it covers high-pressure water jetting is not confirmed by an official source, so do not treat it as covering jetting.

instructionSections.heading: Victoria
instructionSections.body: Victoria's WP class is confirmed; its boom-length rule is not confirmed by an official source (see lesson 3).

instructionSections.heading: Before any roof work from a platform
instructionSections.body: Check the licence rule for the state and the boom length with the regulator before work. This add-on does not give the answer for every state.

lessons.title: Professional scope and restricted-work triage
learningOutcomes: Separate routine cleaning from trauma-related work using the scope, authority and hazard information available.
Name the approver, source documents, boundaries and unresolved risks in a triage record.
Stop and refer when the authority, the hazard or the competence is not confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and restricted work
instructionSections.body: Routine cleaning and trauma remediation are different jobs. They carry different safety, legal, insurance and waste conditions, so a coordinator has to separate them before a quote is given or a worker is assigned. A client who describes a job as just a deep clean after a serious incident has not established what material is present, so the enquiry stays unverified until a competent assessment says otherwise. Before anything moves forward, confirm who gives access, who has released the site, the insurance position, the training held by the people who would attend and the waste rules that apply. Each open unknown is a reason to pause. The triage record names the approver, the source documents, the boundaries of the work, the unresolved risks and the person who receives the handover.

lessons.title: Pathogen and exposure risk fundamentals
learningOutcomes: List the exposure routes for a biological hazard and the uncertainty attached to each.
Explain why appearance cannot establish that an area is safe.
Stop a task that would produce aerosols or uncontrolled contact until an approved control exists.

instructionSections.heading: Pathogen and exposure risk
instructionSections.body: Biological hazards can be visible, such as a spill, or hidden in porous materials, gaps, equipment and waste. Workers cannot identify a pathogen by looking at it, so unknown fluids and sharps are treated as potentially infectious. Uncertainty is a reason to pause for a professional assessment. It is never evidence that an area is safe. The main exposure routes are contact with broken skin, splashes to the eyes, nose or mouth, puncture, and inhalation where aerosols or dust are produced. A photograph cannot show whether residue has reached underlay, timber joints or the space behind a wall, so appearance cannot support clearance. Build a hazard inventory that lists each route, the uncertainty attached to it, who assesses it and who owns the escalation.

lessons.title: Scene entry permissions and site isolation
learningOutcomes: Identify every party with an interest in a site before entry is considered.
Explain why one party's permission does not release a site for all others.
Set up an entry log and a controlled boundary for a fictional site.

instructionSections.heading: Entry permission and site isolation
instructionSections.body: Several parties can have an interest in a trauma-related site, including police, the property manager or landlord, the insurer, next of kin and the occupants. Permission from one of them does not release the site for all of them. Before entry is considered, confirm in writing who controls the site, who has released it, what the entry conditions are and who keeps the entry log. Plan for privacy protection, controlled entry, the welfare of nearby people, communications and separation of the public from any potentially contaminated area. A neighbour who offers access to a sealed property is not a source of authority. Missing from such an offer are the written authorisation of the responsible party, the release by the controlling authority, the insurer's position, a documented hazard assessment and an entry log.

lessons.title: Sharps and concealed hazards recognition
learningOutcomes: Describe the stop, isolate, record and report steps for a found sharp.
Explain why hand searches for sharps are refused.
Complete a reporting card for a fictional sharp without handling any object.

instructionSections.heading: Sharps and concealed hazards
instructionSections.body: Needles, broken glass and concealed debris are hazards in their own right. Do not search for sharps by hand, sort through debris to find them or move unidentified objects to speed the work. Sharps need trained people, approved equipment, a specified collection process and approved disposal. When a sharp is found, stop, keep people out of the area, do not touch it, record its location and report it to the authorised supervisor. If the location may be under police or coronial process, leave the object and the scene undisturbed unless that authority directs otherwise. The NHMRC guidelines advise that single-use sharps are disposed of at the point of use in an approved container, that the container is never filled past its maximum fill line, and that needles are never recapped, bent or broken.

lessons.title: Blood and bodily fluid exposure control
learningOutcomes: Confirm that an approved plan and a site assessment cover a body-fluid task before work starts.
Apply standard precautions and the planned PPE before a spill is touched.
Refuse product use outside its label or the approved procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Blood and body-fluid exposure control
instructionSections.body: Blood and body-fluid contamination requires an employer-approved exposure-control plan and a site-specific assessment by a competent person. Standard precautions apply to every such situation. The Victorian spill guidance describes applying standard precautions, wearing PPE for all cleaning, clearing up the spill before cleaning the area, avoiding aerosols and using leak-proof bags for waste. It also says sodium hypochlorite is generally unnecessary for spill management. That guidance is written for healthcare and public settings, so it does not settle the rules for trauma work. Controls depend on the setting, the material, the extent of contamination and local rules. Training material does not supply product strengths, contact times, spray methods or clearance claims, and a product's marketing does not authorise its use on biological contamination. If a worker may have been exposed, the activity stops and the exposure response begins.

lessons.title: PPE selection, fit and removal
learningOutcomes: Select PPE from a documented assessment and the approved plan rather than from availability.
Explain why a respirator is not used without a recorded fit check and training.
Describe the trained removal sequence and the reason it is taught and checked.

instructionSections.heading: PPE selection, fit and removal
instructionSections.body: Personal protective equipment does not replace removing the hazard, site controls or worker competence. It is selected from a documented risk assessment, must suit the task and must fit the worker. Workers do not choose their own equipment from a supply cupboard. Removal, sometimes called doffing, can cause self-contamination if done wrongly, so removal sequences are taught and checked by a qualified trainer in a controlled training setting. A worker given an unfamiliar respirator without a fit check must stop until suitability, fit, training and authorisation are confirmed. The Victorian spill guidance says PPE is worn for all cleaning and is then disposed of or cleaned. The NHMRC guidelines treat PPE as part of standard precautions. Both describe PPE as one control among several.

lessons.title: Cleaning and disinfection boundaries
learningOutcomes: Separate soil removal, disinfection and verification in a work record.
Refuse a disinfection or clearance claim that the work does not support.
Write a refusal note that states what was done and what was not verified.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning, disinfection and verification
instructionSections.body: Removing visible soil, disinfecting and sterilising are three separate outcomes, and a job can achieve one without the others. An authorised procedure identifies the surface or material, the cleaning steps needed first, any product and the efficacy its label supports, the manufacturer's instructions and the limits of the method. The Victorian spill guidance says to clear up visible material before cleaning the area, and that small spills can be wiped and cleaned with detergent and warm water, with a hospital-grade disinfectant optional. Visual inspection does not establish clearance. A request for a fully disinfected certificate after a wipe-down is not supported by the work done. Decline the unsupported claim, explain the difference between soil removal, disinfection and verification, and refer the verification question to the party with authority.

lessons.title: Porous surfaces and unsalvageable materials
learningOutcomes: Explain why porous materials can hold contamination that is not visible.
Hold a porous item out of use until a specialist decision is recorded.
Record property, risk and disposal decisions as three separate entries.

instructionSections.heading: Porous materials and disposal decisions
instructionSections.body: Soft furnishings, underlays, timber joints and similar porous materials can keep contamination that cannot be seen on the surface. Decisions to keep, remove or dispose of such material must be made by a competent, authorised person and must follow the property, insurance and waste controls that apply. A proposed treatment for a potentially contaminated item, such as a mattress, needs specialist review first, because a method that moves material or changes the contamination can make things worse. Keep three questions apart in the decision memo: the preservation of property, the risk evaluation and the authorisation for specialist disposal. Do not prescribe intrusive treatment of unknown contamination.

lessons.title: Regulated waste identification and handoff
learningOutcomes: Hold unclassified waste separately and mark its classification as pending.
Name the documents a licensed handoff needs.
Refuse transport by an unlicensed or undocumented carrier.

instructionSections.heading: Waste identification and handoff
instructionSections.body: Waste descriptions and classifications differ between jurisdictions and receiving facilities. Contaminated material is not assumed to belong in general waste, and holding a cleaning qualification does not permit anyone to transport it. The Victorian guidance describes three waste groups, general, clinical and pharmaceutical, and says clinical waste goes into yellow biohazard bags. It says clinical and pharmaceutical waste is collected by waste companies licensed by the EPA and taken to EPA-licensed facilities. Other states and territories have their own waste rules. A compliant handoff can require licensed operators, suitable containers, labelling, manifests and an approved treatment destination. A contractor who offers to take bagged material in a private vehicle without documents cannot provide that chain of custody.

lessons.title: Equipment segregation and transport
learningOutcomes: Label equipment used on a suspect task as dirty or quarantined.
Explain why a tool is not booked for another job until its release is documented.
Refuse improvised cleaning of powered or sensitive equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment segregation and transport
instructionSections.body: Reusable equipment and vehicles can carry contamination from one zone or site to another. Equipment choice, handling, decontamination, storage and vehicle segregation need approved protocols and competent oversight. Do not improvise cleaning methods for contaminated tools, especially powered or sensitive equipment, because an improvised method can damage the tool or leave contamination behind. Equipment used on a suspected contamination task is not booked for another job until its release is documented. Keep a clean and a dirty equipment register, store items separately and labelled, and treat any item without a documented history as quarantined.

lessons.title: Incident reporting and exposure escalation
learningOutcomes: Describe the first-response steps and the reporting route after a possible exposure.
Stop work after a possible exposure, even when the worker feels well.
Complete an anonymised exposure report with the required fields.

instructionSections.heading: Incident reporting and exposure escalation
instructionSections.body: Needlestick injuries, splashes, skin contact and suspected inhalation need prompt reporting and medical guidance under the employer's response procedure. A worker does not decide whether help is needed based on how they feel. The Victorian guidance on exposures says the first response is to remove contaminated clothing, wash the area with soap and water, flush mucous membranes with water, rinse eyes gently and report immediately. It says the person should be removed from duty for a risk assessment, and that medical evaluation, with post-exposure prophylaxis where appropriate, should follow. It says the date, time, type and circumstances of the exposure should be documented. Health services have written protocols, and outside them the guidance points to a general practitioner or the nearest emergency department.

lessons.title: Verification, records and release boundaries
learningOutcomes: Separate work done, checks made, exclusions and unverified outcomes in a handover.
Refuse a clearance or re-entry claim that the authorised party has not made.
Correct an unsupported claim in a fictional handover.

instructionSections.heading: Verification, records and release
instructionSections.body: Job completion evidence must state what was authorised, what was done, what was inspected, which exclusions remain and which sign-offs were given. Photographs and the appearance of a surface do not validate microbiological safety. Clearance or any claim of unrestricted re-entry can be made only by a party that is competent and authorised under the applicable scheme. A property manager may ask for an unconditional safety certificate while areas remain excluded. The correct response is a limited handover that states the authorised scope, the work done, the excluded areas, the unverified outcomes and who can make any clearance claim. A scene is not declared medically or legally safe without the authority to do so.

lessons.title: Scope and referral boundaries
learningOutcomes: Classify an intake request as general cleaning, specialist remediation, waste transport or possible evidence-controlled scene.
Record every authority that must still be confirmed before any step.
Hold work and issue a written hold notice when authority is missing.

instructionSections.heading: Scope, classification and referral
instructionSections.body: The intake coordinator's first task is to classify the request. It may be general cleaning, specialist remediation, waste transport or a possible scene where official authority applies, and the classification decides who must be involved next. A client request, an insurance work order or a set of keys does not establish authority to start. Record the requesting party, the party that controls the property, the location, what is uncertain about what happened there and every authority still to be confirmed. Separate what has been observed from what has been assumed. Where forensic cleaning after a work-related death is involved in Victoria, WorkSafe's guidance describes a provider scheme that requires registration, a recognised certification and insurance. That is a provider and funding scheme, not a general licence for trauma cleaning, and it does not confirm authority to enter a scene.

lessons.title: Scene release and evidence preservation
learningOutcomes: Distinguish official release, owner permission and employer authorisation.
Describe the steps for a potentially relevant object that is found during work.
Record the released boundaries exactly as the authority states them.

instructionSections.heading: Scene release and evidence preservation
instructionSections.body: Release of a scene by police or a coroner is a separate matter from the owner's permission and from the employer's health-and-safety authorisation. All three must be considered, and none of them replaces the others. Treat photographs, found property and any unexpected physical evidence as controlled. Do not move them, do not speculate about what they mean and do not alter the area around them. Record the authority that issued the release and the exact boundaries it covers. A general building access code does not reach a room that remains under investigation. Suspend work where the release is unclear, where a potentially relevant object has been found or where a boundary is unmarked, and notify the authorised lead. The specific procedures of each police and coronial authority are not set out in this lesson and must be confirmed with that authority.

lessons.title: Consent, dignity and privacy
learningOutcomes: Limit personal details in records and communications to what the task needs.
Name the designated contact who answers requests for information.
Refuse to share images or incident details outside the authorised process.

instructionSections.heading: Consent, dignity and privacy
instructionSections.body: Traumatic incidents involve real people, bereavement and highly sensitive information. Limit personal details to what the operational task needs, protect photographs and records, and use consent to define access and the scope of service. Workers do not photograph a scene or share images for social media, training examples or promotion. A respectful point of contact is named for the family, the occupants and the property party. When a neighbour asks a cleaner for photographs or incident details, the cleaner does not provide them. The request goes to the designated manager, who decides what, if anything, can be disclosed and to whom, under the rules that apply to the records.

lessons.title: Exposure pathways and occupational controls
learningOutcomes: Name the plausible exposure routes at a scene with unknown blood or body fluids.
Explain why appearance cannot be used to diagnose infection or confirm safety.
Stop any uncontrolled contact or aerosol-producing task until an approved control exists.

instructionSections.heading: Exposure pathways and occupational controls
instructionSections.body: Treat unknown blood, body fluids and contaminated surfaces as exposure hazards until they have been assessed under the employer's plan. The presence, scale and location of a hazard can be uncertain, including on materials and behind fixtures. Recognise the plausible routes: contact with broken skin, splashes to the eyes, nose or mouth, puncture, and inhalation where aerosols or dust are produced. The NHMRC guidelines describe standard precautions as the baseline for all people, including gloves and suitable protective equipment for spills, containment of the spill and removal of visible matter with disposable absorbent material. The Victorian spill guidance says to clear up the spilled material before cleaning the area. Verify worker training, exposure controls and the incident procedure for the specific environment before any task begins. Stop any uncontrolled contact, any aerosol-producing task and any work without an approved exposure-control plan.

lessons.title: Sharps and concealed hazards
learningOutcomes: Describe the no-touch boundary and withdrawal steps for a suspected sharp.
Refuse hand searches of bags, upholstery and blind spaces.
Name the sharps escalation chain for a fictional scene.

instructionSections.heading: Sharps and concealed hazards
instructionSections.body: Needles, scalpels, broken glass and concealed metal fragments can be present even where a room appears clear. A worker who sees a point of metal through a bag during a visual survey does not press, open or reach into the bag. Search and removal are carried out by trained people under the site procedure, never by hand exploration of upholstery, waste bags or blind spaces. Check the condition of any sharps container and whether disposal has been authorised before anything is moved. Isolate the item, mark the no-touch boundary, withdraw people nearby and refer the matter to authorised staff. The NHMRC guidelines advise that sharps are not passed hand to hand, are never recapped, bent or broken, and are disposed of immediately at the point of use in an approved container.

lessons.title: PPE assessment and doffing boundaries
learningOutcomes: Select PPE from a documented hazard assessment rather than from a standard kit.
Explain why a worker is not permitted to enter until PPE is approved and competence is verified.
Describe the boundary between clean and contaminated areas for removal.

instructionSections.heading: PPE assessment and doffing
instructionSections.body: PPE is selected from a documented hazard assessment for the specific task. It is not chosen from a one-size kit or from appearance. Check product compatibility, each worker's training, the fit requirements where a respirator is needed, the limits of each item and the boundary between clean and contaminated areas. Incorrect removal can transfer contamination onto the worker and beyond, so removal is taught and assessed by a supervisor using clean training equipment and no infectious substance. A new worker who offers ordinary gloves and a disposable mask for an unidentified incident scene is not equipped for the job. Entry waits until the responsible qualified person has approved the PPE and verified the worker's competence.

lessons.title: Containment and contamination zoning
learningOutcomes: Define clean, restricted, support and possibly contaminated zones for a fictional site.
Recognise that a zone drawing is a planning tool and not proof of clearance.
State the triggers that require reassessment of a boundary.

instructionSections.heading: Containment and zoning
instructionSections.body: Clean, restricted, support and possibly contaminated zones are defined only after a site assessment. Consider how people, waste and tools will move, and keep the approach practical for rooms, stairwells and shared areas. A zoning drawing is a planning tool. It does not prove environmental clearance. A shared hallway may have been used to move contaminated belongings, so its status is reassessed rather than assumed. Unexpected spread, including migration outside the approved boundary or uncontrolled public access, requires a new assessment and an escalation. Containment protects the people who are not doing the work, as well as the worker.

lessons.title: Surface and porous material decisions
learningOutcomes: Identify which materials need a specialist decision rather than a cleaning method.
Refuse a request to return a stained or unverified item to use.
Record a keep, quarantine or refer decision with its basis.

instructionSections.heading: Surface and porous material decisions
instructionSections.body: Hard non-porous surfaces, porous fabrics, absorbent building materials and electronic devices cannot be assumed to accept the same cleaning method. Material damage, incomplete penetration and manufacturer compatibility all matter. The authorised remediation specialist decides whether a material is kept, removed, isolated or investigated further. A visibly clean appearance is not proof of decontamination. A request to return a stained mattress or nearby electronic devices to use straight away is declined. Those items stay out of use until the required specialist evidence exists, and each decision is recorded with its basis.

lessons.title: Waste identification and chain of custody
learningOutcomes: Hold potentially infectious waste apart from evidential objects.
Name the custody and manifest records a waste handoff needs.
Refuse disposal in ordinary building waste or a private vehicle.

instructionSections.heading: Waste identification and custody records
instructionSections.body: Waste may fall into infectious, clinical, hazardous or general classes depending on the location and the source. The classification governs packaging, transport and disposal, and a cleaning certificate does not create permission to transport waste. The Victorian guidance describes three waste groups and says clinical waste goes into yellow biohazard bags. It says clinical and pharmaceutical waste is collected by waste companies licensed by the EPA named on the page. Record every change of custody, the authorised carrier and the supporting manifest. Potentially infectious waste is kept apart from evidential objects, and custody of evidence belongs to the authority that holds it. A contractor who suggests putting unidentified contaminated material into ordinary building rubbish is proposing something that must not happen.

lessons.title: Equipment controls and decontamination limits
learningOutcomes: Quarantine equipment whose exposure history is unknown.
Describe dedicated transport containment and separate storage.
Identify a decontamination claim that still needs validation.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment controls and limits
instructionSections.body: Equipment and reusable supplies can carry contaminants between work zones, vehicles and future clients. Choose reusable or disposable items only through an approved work procedure, and confirm the manufacturer's instructions before any cleaning process is used. Dedicated transport containment and separate storage prevent cross-use. A team that proposes using the same vacuum on a domestic job straight after an incident job has not met the control. The equipment is quarantined until its exposure history is known and specialist direction is given. Any claim that equipment is decontaminated needs validation before it is relied on.

lessons.title: Exposure incidents and worker wellbeing
learningOutcomes: Stop work and activate the exposure-incident protocol after a possible puncture or splash.
Describe the reporting content for a simulated incident.
Explain how confidential wellbeing support is offered without requiring graphic detail.

instructionSections.heading: Exposure incidents and worker wellbeing
instructionSections.body: Exposure incidents need immediate reporting, followed by the employer's medical evaluation and any public-health response the procedure requires. The Victorian exposure guidance says the first response is to remove contaminated clothing, wash the area with soap and water, flush mucous membranes and report immediately. It says the person is removed from duty for a risk assessment and that a medical evaluation should follow. Workers may also experience stress, grief or an acute reaction after a traumatic site. Offer confidential support and make clear that a worker can stop work. Never require a worker to recount graphic detail beyond what the operation needs.

lessons.title: Documentation, verification and handover
learningOutcomes: Write a scope-limited completion report with separate fields for evidence, exclusions, unresolved issues and referrals.
Withhold a forensic, biological-safety or habitability claim that the work does not support.
Name the party that holds the next review or clearance decision.

instructionSections.heading: Documentation, verification and handover
instructionSections.body: A handover separates the tasks performed, the independent checks made, the hazards still outstanding and the work expressly excluded. Photographs and disposal receipts are kept only with permission and under controlled retention. Do not claim forensic clearance, biological safety, zero pathogens or habitability unless a competent authority has verified that specific basis. A client who demands a certificate that a building is completely safe after limited specialist work is asking for something the work does not support. Withhold the unsupported claim, escalate the unresolved hazards and make no return-to-use recommendation until the authority has decided. Record the sign-off and the owner of the next review.

lessons.title: Scope, scene history and limits
