learningOutcomes: Distinguish suspected use, storage and manufacturing, and state why each calls for a different response.
Separate observed facts from reported history and mark unanswered questions.
Pause access when scope, history or a site assessment is missing.

instructionSections.heading: Scope, history and limits
instructionSections.body: Scope, scene history and limits is a decision and documentation competence. It is not permission to carry out hazardous remediation. The first task is to separate suspected drug use, storage and manufacturing, because each suggests a different risk pathway and a different response. The WA Department of Health guidance describes manufacturing sites as the highest-risk type. Do not judge the level of residue from its appearance. Establish the task boundary through an employer-approved procedure, verified site information and a qualified specialist before accepting any physical work. Record each claim with its date and source, separate what was observed from what was reported, and list each question still unanswered. Unknown conditions stay recorded as unknown. They are never treated as proof of safety.

lessons.title: Scene authority, permissions and release
learningOutcomes: Identify who controls access and what written permission exists before any step.
Explain why keys, verbal assurances and a general building code are not authority.
Record the authority chain and the referral decision in the job file.

instructionSections.heading: Authority, permissions and release
instructionSections.body: Before any progress, confirm who controls access, what written permission exists, whether police or another relevant authority has released the site where that applies, and whether an independent competent person has assessed the potential hazards. Authority is not established by a key, a verbal assurance or a general building code. Owner, manager, tenant and insurer permission do not replace an official release. Where the legal position is unclear, pause access. Rules can differ between jurisdictions, so the local rules are identified before the authority is treated as settled. The WA Department of Health guidance recommends checking home insurance first and reporting suspected manufacturing to WA Police, and this lesson does not extend those steps to any other jurisdiction.

lessons.title: Contamination routes and uncertainty
learningOutcomes: Name the routes by which drug-related contamination can reach people and surfaces.
Record a concern without guessing at concentrations.
Distinguish an observation from validated laboratory evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Contamination routes and uncertainty
instructionSections.body: Contamination can reach people and surfaces through contact, through inhalation of dust or airborne material, and through cross-transfer on shoes, tools, clothing, bags and vehicles. Identify each route for the premises in front of you and record the concern without guessing at concentrations, because a concentration cannot be judged from the look of a room or from a smell. Never substitute appearance, odour, a customer's assurance or an unverified reading for an authorised assessment. Uncertainty is itself a reason to pause and refer. The WA guidance on testing treats sample testing as a formal stage, separate from observation, so an observation is recorded as an observation.

lessons.title: Laboratory versus residue-only properties
learningOutcomes: Describe why a suspected laboratory calls for a different response from a residue-only property.
List the signs that suggest a possible laboratory and the steps that follow.
Record what was seen, where, when and who was notified, without touching any item.

instructionSections.heading: Laboratory versus residue-only properties
instructionSections.body: Residue associated with drug use and contamination from a manufacturing site create different risks, different investigations and different remedial needs. The WA Department of Health describes manufacturing sites as the highest-risk type. Recognition, not analysis, is the skill taught here. Signs that suggest a possible laboratory or manufacturing activity include unusual chemical containers, improvised equipment, strong unexplained chemical odours, heavy staining, and ventilation or sealing that does not fit a home. If any of these is seen, do not enter further and do not touch or move any item. Leave the area, keep others away, contact emergency services or the police and the authorised specialist, and record what was seen, where, when and who was told. Do not identify or handle the materials.

lessons.title: Independent sampling and chain of custody
learningOutcomes: Explain why sampling belongs to independent professionals.
Identify the representativeness limits of a single result.
Treat a result without a plan, laboratory and custody record as unverified.

instructionSections.heading: Independent sampling and custody
instructionSections.body: Sampling plans, laboratories, sample locations and documented chain of custody are the work of independent professionals. This lesson describes their purpose so that you can recognise when they are needed and question an unsupported result. It does not train any unqualified person to collect samples. The WA guidance describes a sequence of screening and detailed testing, then validation testing, with reports at each stage. A single result from one place may not represent a whole property, so a result from one room does not clear another. When a result is offered without a documented sampling plan, a named laboratory and a custody record, treat it as unverified and ask for competent interpretation before relying on it.

lessons.title: Worker exposure prevention and PPE decisions
learningOutcomes: Explain why PPE is chosen from a formal assessment and used by trained workers.
Stop the activity and follow the employer's procedure when exposure is suspected.
Refuse improvised protection and self-treatment beyond approved first-response steps.

instructionSections.heading: Worker exposure prevention and PPE
instructionSections.body: Respirators, protective clothing, ventilation and entry controls depend on a formal assessment and on operators who have been trained to use them. A worker who chooses equipment from whatever is available, such as ordinary gloves or a disposable mask, has not met the requirement. The NHMRC healthcare guidance treats PPE as part of standard precautions, and this lesson applies that principle by analogy. Where an exposure is suspected, stop the activity, restrict access to the affected area and follow the employer's incident and medical referral procedure. The Victorian exposure guidance sets out a first response of removing contaminated clothing, washing the area, flushing mucous membranes, reporting immediately and arranging medical evaluation. Do not improvise protection and do not self-treat beyond the approved first-response steps.

lessons.title: Containment and cross-contamination
learningOutcomes: Define supervised zones and handoff points on a fictional diagram.
Explain why a route through occupied or shared space is assessed before items move.
State the triggers that require the containment boundary to be reassessed.

instructionSections.heading: Containment and cross-contamination
instructionSections.body: Containment protects the people who are not doing the work as well as the worker. A crew that plans to carry items through an occupied corridor creates a route that can spread contamination, so the route is assessed before anything is moved. Define the supervised zones and the handoff points on a diagram, and keep clean and possibly contaminated areas apart. Do not move contents through shared spaces or into vehicles until the containment plan is approved. Stop if public access, migration outside the zone or uncontrolled movement is observed, and reassess the boundary.

lessons.title: Material classification and specialist decisions
learningOutcomes: Identify each material type that needs a specialist decision.
Refuse a universal salvage request for contaminated furniture or textiles.
Record any exception to the decision path with the approver's name.

instructionSections.heading: Material classification and specialist decisions
instructionSections.body: Materials differ in how contamination behaves within them. Hard surfaces, porous materials, upholstered furniture, carpet, textiles and electronic items each need a specialist decision on whether to keep, clean, remove, isolate or investigate further. A customer's demand for universal salvage of upholstered furniture cannot be accepted, because the work done cannot support it. Identify each point at which a specialist decision is needed, and document any exception to the normal decision path together with the person who approved it. The WA guidance describes validation testing after clean-up. A decision to keep or reuse a material needs evidence of that kind, not appearance alone.

lessons.title: Waste and environmental obligations
learningOutcomes: Identify debris and material that must not go into household bins.
Stop a removal that has no written handler arrangement.
Record the stop-work decision and the referral to a waste handler.

instructionSections.heading: Waste and environmental obligations
instructionSections.body: Debris from a former laboratory, contaminated materials and other drug-related waste are not ordinary household rubbish. A crew that plans to put unknown former-laboratory debris into residential bins has made an error that must be stopped. Waste is identified, packaged, transported and disposed of through handlers and destinations approved for that purpose, under the environmental and waste rules that apply where the work is done. Do not remove any waste until the handler has been engaged and has confirmed the arrangements in writing. Record the stop-work decision and the referral.

lessons.title: Country-specific rules and thresholds
learningOutcomes: Identify the jurisdiction and its current rules before any authority is treated as settled.
Explain why rules and thresholds are not carried from one place or property type to another.
Flag any unresolved rule and refer it.

instructionSections.heading: Jurisdiction, rules and thresholds
instructionSections.body: Rules about drug contamination, testing and remediation differ between countries and sometimes within them. Those rules must not be applied to Australia, to other countries or to property types they do not cover, and older standards must not be substituted for current rules. Some rules set a numerical threshold for a particular type of premises. The WA Department of Health guidance refers to health investigation levels for particular drugs, and says the aim is to reduce residue below levels that pose a risk and below the relevant health investigation level. This lesson gives no numerical value. The current value and its scope come from the authority that publishes it, for the jurisdiction and premises type concerned. Flag any unresolved rule and refer it.

lessons.title: Independent verification and clearance claims
learningOutcomes: Refuse a zero-contamination or clearance statement that the work cannot support.
Specify the independent competent verification that is needed.
Record the refusal and the limits of what has been confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Independent verification and clearance claims
instructionSections.body: A worker who is asked to sign a certificate of zero contamination must refuse, because no one can truthfully make that statement on the basis of a visit, a wipe, a photograph or a verbal account. The WA Department of Health guidance says a validation report, showing residues below levels that pose a health risk, is obtained before renting or selling, and that validation is done by a company separate from the clean-up company. Clearance is a decision for a competent, independent party acting under the applicable scheme, using documented sampling and laboratory evidence where the scheme requires it. Specify the verification that is needed, record the refusal of the unverified statement and state the limits of what has been confirmed. A customer's assurance does not change this.

lessons.title: Handover, health concerns and privacy
learningOutcomes: Write a factual, scope-limited handover that records verified facts, unresolved issues and referrals.
Refuse disclosure of personal or medical information about a past occupant.
Stop work and follow the health referral procedure when an exposure concern is raised.

instructionSections.heading: Handover, health concerns and privacy
instructionSections.body: A handover is factual, limited to the scope actually done and privacy-conscious. It records the verified facts, the unresolved issues, the referrals made and the scope limits. It does not disclose personal information about a past tenant or occupant, including medical history or drug use, to a customer who asks for it. Those details are sensitive, and disclosure is decided by the authority that holds the record and the privacy rules that apply. Refer any such request to the designated manager. If an event has raised a health or exposure concern, stop work, restrict access and follow the local emergency, employer incident and medical referral procedures. Do not promise that a property is free of contamination. The WA guidance says occupants should not enter or clean the property themselves, and that qualified environmental professionals should be used.

lessons.title: Authorisation and fire-scene release
learningOutcomes: Identify the authority that controls a fire-damaged property and the written release it has given, and refuse work that is not released.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to check who controls a fire-damaged property and whether that authority has released it for the work proposed. It does not grant authority to enter, release, re-occupy or disturb a fire-damaged property. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Authorisation and fire-scene release
instructionSections.body: Authority and access are assessed only after access, permitted tasks and responsibility are established. An owner may ask for immediate salvage while the fire investigation or structural survey has not released the premises. Ask who controls access, what has been formally released and which safety reviews are still open. Customer urgency is never a substitute for verification. Check the written authority that controls the property, the scope of permitted access and any restriction on disturbing contents. Where clearance is ambiguous, remain outside and request confirmation from the responsible authority. Before acting, record the site evidence, the decision owner, the uncertainties and any specialists needed. An unverified scene-release claim must stop work. In training, compare three mock release documents and decide which, if any, permits the proposed activity. Record why keys or a verbal permission on their own are insufficient. The handover from this stage should state the scope, the observations, the unresolved hazards, the consent or authority held, the responsible professional and the next review step.

lessons.title: Post-fire structural and utility hazards
learningOutcomes: Recognise structural and utility hazards after a fire and stop work until qualified parties resolve them.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to recognise structural and utility hazards after a fire, and how to stop work and refer them. It does not authorise entry, isolation, reconnection or repair of any structure or utility. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Post-fire structural and utility hazards
instructionSections.body: A room may look stable while a damaged electrical distribution board or a sagging ceiling is visible in photographs. Use non-intrusive visual observation only. Treat damaged wiring, gas lines, overhead loads, weakened stairs and unstable walls as stop-work hazards. Qualified utility and structural personnel decide on isolation and entry permissions, and no entry is made until competent parties have resolved these hazards. In training, mark unsafe entry routes on a mock floor plan and produce a referral request. Do not propose do-it-yourself electrical or structural work.

lessons.title: Ash, soot and combustion-residue exposure
learningOutcomes: Treat ash and combustion residue as uncertain material, keep it undisturbed and refer it for qualified assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to treat ash, soot and combustion residue as uncertain material and how to choose the escalation path. It does not approve any cleaning method, product or disturbance of residue. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Ash, soot and combustion-residue exposure
instructionSections.body: Ash and combustion residues are uncertain material. Assume that their composition is not known, keep the dust undisturbed, assess the respiratory and surface hazards, and identify the qualified cleaning methods approved for the site. Visible soil removal is not the same as exposure control, so a clean-looking surface is not evidence that the residue is gone. Do not dry-disturb unidentified residues. A proposal to sweep black powder from a burned office with a domestic vacuum must be refused, because it would disturb the material and spread fine particles. In training, use sample material photographs and a task-risk worksheet to select the escalation, the zoning and the equipment-review steps.

lessons.title: Asbestos and legacy hazardous materials
learningOutcomes: Recognise when a building may contain asbestos or legacy hazardous materials, stop work and refer for competent assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to recognise when fire-affected building materials may contain asbestos, stop work and refer for competent assessment. It does not allow anyone to disturb, remove or clean asbestos-suspect material. Completing it does not give an asbestos licence or any authority to remove asbestos.

instructionSections.heading: Asbestos and legacy hazardous materials
instructionSections.body: Before touching any material, determine the age of the building and check any prior records of hazardous materials. Fire-damaged asbestos-containing material may become friable, so ceiling sheeting and insulation of unknown composition must not be disturbed. Qualified investigation and, where the local rules require it, licensed removal may be needed. Requirements differ between states and territories. In training, prepare an asbestos-suspect stop-work notification based on a fictional site record, and identify the competent assessment that is missing.

lessons.title: Site zoning and occupant protection
learningOutcomes: Define exclusion zones and access routes with the site controller, and refuse unsupervised passage through restricted areas.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to set exclusion zones, plan clean and restricted routes, and protect occupants, including vulnerable occupants. It does not allow occupants or visitors into restricted areas, and it does not replace the release from the controlling authority. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Site zoning and occupant protection
instructionSections.body: Define the exclusion areas and make the access decisions with the site controller. Consider vulnerable occupants, adjacent occupied areas and the movement of contaminated materials. A neighbouring tenant may want to walk through a partly damaged corridor to collect medication. The answer is not unsupervised passage. Coordinate a safe alternative with the property manager or emergency services, so that the item is retrieved under supervision or by an authorised person. In training, draw a mock access map that shows the clean route, the restricted zones, the signage and the escalation path to the property manager or an emergency service. Do not allow access through a restricted or unassessed zone.

lessons.title: PPE and respiratory protection decisions
learningOutcomes: Explain why PPE and respiratory protection depend on hazard characterisation, fit, training and the employer's program.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how PPE and respiratory protection follow from the hazard assessment, and how to refuse inadequate controls. It does not select, fit or approve any respirator, and PPE does not make unsafe access acceptable. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: PPE and respiratory protection decisions
instructionSections.body: PPE and respiratory protection depend on the access, the permitted tasks and the hazard characterisation. Identify the contaminant uncertainty, the worker's medical fitness and training needs, the fit-testing requirements and the local respiratory program. PPE is not a substitute for safe access, hazard characterisation or source control. A worker who offers a disposable dust mask for an unknown ash exposure is proposing an inadequate control. Never infer that a respirator is suitable from its appearance. Where the hazard is beyond the program, flag the case for a competent hygiene adviser. In training, compare PPE requests against a simulated hazard register and flag each case that needs a competent adviser.

lessons.title: Content salvage and material suitability
learningOutcomes: Distinguish salvageable items from items that need specialist or client decisions, and refuse the immediate handling of damaged electronics.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to list, prioritise and record fire- and smoke-affected contents, and when to refer them. It does not allow cleaning, testing or operating electronics, appliances or heritage items. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Content salvage and material suitability
instructionSections.body: Catalogue the items, establish who owns them, set salvage priorities, and seek qualified guidance for heat-damaged electronics, fragile finishes and heritage objects. Secure the client's consent and record any repairability that is uncertain. A homeowner who asks that smoke-affected photographs and electronics be wiped immediately is asking for work that has not been assessed. Do not operate exposed electrical devices without authorisation. Keep a salvage register that distinguishes protected items, items needing restricted handling and items that need professional referral. In training, complete a mock salvage register using fictional items.

lessons.title: Controlled cleaning methods and limitations
learningOutcomes: Identify cleaning methods that are unsuitable for fire-affected finishes and recognise when a compatibility test or referral is needed.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to test whether a cleaning method suits a fire-affected finish, and when a method must not proceed. It does not give cleaning formulas and does not approve any destructive method. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Controlled cleaning methods and limitations
instructionSections.body: Before selecting any cleaning method, assess the stability of the substrate, the contamination and any manufacturer restrictions. High-value or fragile finishes need controlled testing by an authorised specialist. Document any damage that was there before the work. A technician who proposes abrasive scrubbing of painted historic timber to remove staining is proposing a destructive method, and it must not proceed without approval and evidence that it is suitable. In training, evaluate three fictional materials and record a compatibility-test or referral decision for each one.

lessons.title: Chemical and odour-treatment boundaries
learningOutcomes: Treat chemical and odour-treatment proposals as separate exposure decisions, and refuse unverified treatments in occupied spaces.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to review proposed chemical and odour treatments as separate exposure decisions, and when to refuse them. It does not select, dilute or approve any product, and it gives no method. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Chemical and odour-treatment boundaries
instructionSections.body: Treat each proposed chemical or air-treatment method as its own exposure decision. Review the safety data, the label permissions, the ventilation, the exclusion of occupants and the evidence that the method works. Some odour treatments create additional hazardous by-products, so a method that removes one odour may create another hazard. A vendor who recommends ozone treatment and solvent fogging while residents remain inside has proposed something that must be refused. No chemical mixing, fogging or ozone use in occupied spaces is permitted without verification and authority. In training, audit mock chemical treatment proposals for missing permissions, missing exposure controls and missing manufacturer instructions. No product, dilution or method is given in this lesson.

lessons.title: Waste segregation and environmental controls
learningOutcomes: Characterise waste before moving it, and refer suspect streams to specialist segregation and licensed handling.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to characterise fire-damaged waste before it is moved, and how to route suspect streams to specialist or licensed handling. It does not authorise anyone to transport, store or dispose of waste. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Waste segregation and environmental controls
instructionSections.body: Characterise waste before anyone moves it. Suspected asbestos, chemical containers, batteries and other hazardous residues may need specialist segregation and licensed handling. Record who will transport and who will receive each waste stream. Never classify unknown contaminated waste as general rubbish by default. A customer who asks cleaners to place charred debris and unknown insulation in normal bins is asking for something that must be refused. In training, complete a simulated waste-transfer log and identify the streams that need confirmation from the local authority or a specialist.

lessons.title: Records, damage mapping and insurer handoff
learningOutcomes: Build an impartial record of damage and handover that separates observed conditions from conclusions about cause or safety.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to build an impartial record of fire damage, the client's decisions and the chain of custody, and how to hand that record to an insurer without overstating it. It does not establish cause, contamination or safety. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Records, damage mapping and insurer handoff
instructionSections.body: Build an impartial inventory with dated photographs, condition descriptions, locations, the client's decisions and any authorised disposal notes. Distinguish observed conditions from conclusions about cause or contamination clearance. An insurer may ask for before-and-after photographs while the owner disputes the removal of some items. Record both positions and the chain of custody. Do not present photographs as proof of structural or environmental safety. In training, produce a fictional photo log and claims handover that records the unknowns and the chain-of-custody limits.

lessons.title: Verification and safe handover boundaries
learningOutcomes: Write a handover that reports only completed cleaning and unresolved limitations, and refuse a safe-to-occupy certificate.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to verify the scope actually completed and write a limited handover that does not certify the property as safe. It does not issue any clearance, safe-to-occupy or contamination-free statement. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and safe handover boundaries
instructionSections.body: Verification checks the scope that was actually completed, the defects still unresolved, the independent testing needed, any moisture or odour concerns and the professional clearance that is still required. Report only the cleaning work that was done and the limitations that remain. When all visible soot has gone and a customer asks for a certificate stating that the home is safe, the answer is no. Cleaning completion is not a safe-to-occupy certificate and is not a contamination-free certificate. In training, draft a fact-based completion statement and a referral list for the qualified clearance or re-occupancy decisions.

lessons.title: Site release, permissions and restoration scope
learningOutcomes: Identify the site authority, the permissions and the exclusions before any flood restoration scope is set, and separate a customer request, an insurer authorisation and a professional safety clearance.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to separate a customer request, an insurer authorisation and a professional safety clearance, and how to set a restoration scope from documented authority. It does not authorise entry, restoration, energisation or certification. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Site release, permissions and restoration scope
instructionSections.body: Site release, permissions and restoration scope need a documented decision based on the facts of the site, not on assumptions. Distinguish an observable condition from a qualified technical determination. A customer request, an insurer authorisation and a professional safety clearance are three separate documents, and none of them can be treated as the others. Start a scope sheet that names the party responsible for access, for utilities and for environmental hazards. Confirm the site authority and the approved procedure, identify who can make the technical decision, set the exclusions, and then collect only the information that can be gathered safely. Record each unresolved uncertainty. Stop work when permission, controls or competent supervision are missing. Produce an access decision that names the approver, the date, the zones, the limits on activity and the unresolved hazards. Never turn an observation into a technical certificate.

lessons.title: Floodwater origin and contamination screening
learningOutcomes: Explain why water appearance cannot prove biological safety, and record contamination as an uncertainty until it is classified by a competent person.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to screen floodwater and debris for contamination, and how to record the uncertainty until a competent person classifies it. It does not classify water from its look or smell, and it gives no treatment method. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Floodwater origin and contamination screening
instructionSections.body: Water appearance cannot prove that the water is biologically safe. Consider the possible sources of contamination before selecting a work scope: sewage entry, outdoor floodwater, chemical release, the time since the intrusion and the risk of cross-contamination. Produce a contamination uncertainty log. Do not assign a contamination category on the basis of odour or colour. Treat unknown contamination as a stop-work concern and refer its classification to competent personnel. Pass the observations, the uncertainties and the next authorised decision to the receiving supervisor.

lessons.title: Structural instability, slips and confined spaces
learningOutcomes: Recognise structural instability, slip and confined-space hazards that water can conceal, and refuse to treat a visual inspection as structural clearance.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how structural instability, slips and confined spaces after water exposure are recognised and excluded. It does not give structural clearance and does not authorise entry to an uncleared space. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Structural instability, slips and confined spaces
instructionSections.body: Water can conceal weakened ceilings, unstable stored loads, undermined flooring and blocked escape routes. Floors that look sound may be slippery, and spaces under floors or behind walls may be confined. Visual inspection is not structural clearance. Exclude any area that has not been cleared, record the exclusion zones and evacuation paths, and request a qualified structural assessment. Submit the engineering referral records with the scope sheet. Do not enter a confined space or an undermined area to look for the problem.

lessons.title: Electrical, gas and solar system hazards
learningOutcomes: Identify electrical, gas and solar and battery hazards after water exposure, and refuse to energise any affected system without licensed clearance.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how water-affected electrical, gas and solar systems are recognised, kept de-energised and referred to licensed professionals. It does not authorise isolation, reconnection, testing or repair of any system. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical, gas and solar system hazards
instructionSections.body: Water-exposed power outlets, damaged cables, gas appliances, and solar and battery systems can remain hazardous even when they appear to be switched off. A cleaner cannot certify that a system has been isolated. Create a utility verification checklist that names the authorised professional and the energisation that is prohibited. Do not energise any water-affected system until a licensed clearance has been issued. Do not attempt to isolate, reconnect or test electrical or gas equipment. Refer each hazard to the authorised professional and record the referral.

lessons.title: PPE, hygiene and biological exposure
learningOutcomes: Explain how biological exposure reaches workers, and apply hygiene, PPE and exposure-reporting controls from the site assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how biological exposure reaches workers after a flood, and how hygiene, PPE and exposure reporting follow from the site assessment. It does not approve any exposure work without controls. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: PPE, hygiene and biological exposure
instructionSections.body: Biological contamination can reach workers through broken skin, mucous membranes, inhalation or ingestion. Controls must follow the site hazard assessment, the training held by each worker and the washing facilities that are actually available. Record each exposure route, the hygiene limitations and the escalation route to a supervisor or to occupational-health advice. Suspend exposure work until suitable controls and hygiene facilities have been provided. Where an exposure occurs, follow the employer's incident and medical referral procedure, and keep the record confidential.

lessons.title: Moisture mapping and baseline records
learningOutcomes: Explain why moisture readings need a documented method and baseline, and why a single number cannot prove drying or safe occupancy.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how moisture readings are recorded with their method, instrument and baseline, so that a reading can be compared and interpreted. It does not set a moisture threshold, prove drying or clear a building for occupancy. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Moisture mapping and baseline records
instructionSections.body: Moisture readings depend on the instrument type, the material and the reference conditions, so a reading without its method cannot be compared with another. A single number cannot independently prove drying or safe occupancy. Record the material, the instrument, the locations and the baseline before work begins. Keep a measurement register that shows the instrument identifier, the method, the material, the location, the time and the limitations. Require calibrated and appropriate measurement, with expert interpretation of the results.

lessons.title: Water removal planning and equipment limitations
learningOutcomes: Select water-removal equipment by contamination, location, electrical supply and operator training, not by capacity alone.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to select and authorise water-removal equipment by contamination, location, supply and operator training. It does not authorise connecting equipment to a water-affected supply, or operating it without a verified supply. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Water removal planning and equipment limitations
instructionSections.body: Water-removal equipment must be suitable for the contamination and the location. Its use depends on a safe electrical supply and on trained operators. Capacity alone is not a selection criterion, because a machine that is large enough but unsuitable for the contamination or the power supply creates new hazards. Before any work, create an equipment suitability and authorisation matrix. Confirm that the utilities are safe, that the operators are trained and that the equipment suits the contamination before the work starts.

lessons.title: Porous contents, salvage and contamination
learningOutcomes: Recognise that porous contents may hold contamination that a wipe-down does not remove, and route salvage decisions to authorised assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how porous contents are quarantined, and how each salvage decision is linked to evidence, consent and an authorised assessor. It does not restore, clean or dispose of porous items on the basis of a wipe-down. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Porous contents, salvage and contamination
instructionSections.body: Porous furnishings, insulation and wallboard may keep contamination that cannot be seen on the surface, so a visual wipe-down is not sufficient evidence of restoration. Quarantine the items and defer any decision to restore or dispose of them to an authorised, competent assessment. Prepare a chain-of-decision record that links the identity of each item, the contamination concern, the owner's consent and the authority for its disposition. Keep the record so that any later decision can be traced back to the evidence.

lessons.title: Drying principles and monitoring logs
learningOutcomes: Explain why drying is a measured trend, and document monitoring without setting universal pass thresholds.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how drying is tracked as a measured trend, and how a monitoring chart and an escalation notice are kept. It does not set pass thresholds, and it does not state that drying is complete. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Drying principles and monitoring logs
instructionSections.body: Restoration progress is a measured trend, not simply a finish that looks dry. Covering a surface too early can trap moisture and hide damage. Prepare a monitoring chart and an escalation notice for any moisture that remains unresolved. Do not set universal pass thresholds in a training or operational document, because the appropriate values depend on the material, the method and the building, and must come from the competent professional. Document any ongoing moisture and prevent premature reinstatement of finishes.

lessons.title: Mould prevention and concealed damage
learningOutcomes: Recognise hidden microbial contamination and concealed damage, and refer rather than disturb suspect material to prove a point.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to recognise signs of possible hidden microbial contamination and concealed damage, and how to refer them. It does not identify organisms, test for microbes or certify a space as free of contamination. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Mould prevention and concealed damage
instructionSections.body: Musty odour, staining, repeated moisture events and concealed cavities can signal conditions that need specialist investigation. Do not disturb suspect materials in order to prove a hypothesis. File a hidden-damage referral that records the scope exclusions and the route for notifying the occupants. Pause the normal restoration work and escalate any suspected hidden microbial contamination to a competent professional. Occupant communication must be factual and must not state that the building is safe.

lessons.title: Wastewater, debris and lawful disposal
learningOutcomes: Separate flood debris into streams, identify hazardous streams and route them to lawful disposal.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how flood debris and wastewater are separated into streams, how hazardous streams are escalated, and how a draft waste manifest is kept. It does not authorise discharge of wastewater or disposal of waste. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Wastewater, debris and lawful disposal
instructionSections.body: Flood debris can combine ordinary material with sewage contamination, oils, chemical containers and regulated substances. Local collection and discharge permissions cannot be assumed. Separate the hazardous streams and escalate them, and follow only the locally authorised disposal routes. Complete a draft waste manifest that records the source, the storage controls, the authorised carrier and the regulatory checks that remain unanswered. Do not discharge wastewater or place debris in ordinary collection until the route has been confirmed in writing.

lessons.title: Verification, documentation and handover limits
learningOutcomes: Write a handover that separates cleaning completion, drying verification, hygienic release and occupancy clearance, and refuse to merge them.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and authority
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches how to keep four separate claims apart in a handover: cleaning completion, drying verification, hygienic release and occupancy clearance. It does not issue any of them. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Verification, documentation and handover limits
instructionSections.body: Cleaning completion, drying verification, hygienic release and building occupancy clearance are separate claims, and each has a different responsible professional. Create a defensible handover that records the work completed, the evidence, the outstanding defects, the referrals made and the customer's acknowledgement. Report actual observations and refer formal clearance to the qualified authority. Do not present the completion of cleaning as proof that the building is dry, hygienic or safe to occupy.

lessons.title: Scope, goals and client-defined success
learningOutcomes: Define the scope of work from the objective the resident has approved.
Distinguish a safety improvement from a full-property clearance and state which one is being done.
Record the permitted areas and the decisions that need fresh permission before any item is moved.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson is training content. It does not authorise entry to a home by force, clearance of belongings, handling of hazardous material, or welfare or clinical assessment. Completing it gives no licence, certificate or approval. Work is done only under an authorised support plan and a written agreement with the resident, within the limits set by the employer and the law that applies where the work takes place.

instructionSections.heading: Start from the resident's objective
instructionSections.body: Every job in this area starts with an objective the resident has approved. The objective may be narrow, such as keeping the route to the bathroom and the front door clear, or broader. A safety improvement reduces a specific named risk, such as a blocked exit or combustible material near a heater. A full-property clearance removes most of the contents. It is a different decision that needs its own consent, handling, waste and support arrangements. Workers drift from one to the other when a deadline or a property manager's demand replaces the resident's own words. Keep the two apart on paper. Fire Rescue Victoria recommends that risk reduction be a priority rather than large scale removal, which is a sound reason to keep the aim narrow and to agree it with the resident first.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the scope and what is unverified
instructionSections.body: Write a short scope record: the objective in the resident's words, the areas for work, the actions allowed, the items that need a fresh decision, and the people who may decide. Note what you have seen yourself, what others have told you, and what is still unverified. Any change needs supervisor clearance and a note of who asked for it. Permission is never inferred from a key, a deadline or a family member's view. Where the resident has not clearly agreed to a change, the work stays within the existing record, and the request is referred.

lessons.title: Consent, belongings and decision authority
learningOutcomes: Match each proposed action to a specific, current consent for a named area, action and item.
Use the four decision categories (retain, relocate, undecided and authorised disposal) in an item-decision log.
Pause and record a contested removal instead of acting on a third party's request.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers consent and the recording of decisions about belongings. It does not give legal advice on who may decide in a tenancy, guardianship or other arrangement, and it does not authorise the disposal of anyone's property. Those questions depend on the law that applies, and the coordinator confirms the position before any disposal.

instructionSections.heading: Consent is specific
instructionSections.body: Consent must be specific to the area, the action and the possession. Access to a home, a key, or a family member's wish is not blanket permission to dispose of its contents. The WA Department of Health guidance on help with hoarding advises getting the person's permission before touching or removing their things, and notes that a written agreement with the cleaning service can set out which items will be removed. Use that as the baseline: the agreement names the items, and anything not named stays where it is. Consent can also be withdrawn, and a withdrawal stops the action at once.

instructionSections.heading: The item-decision log
instructionSections.body: Keep an item-decision log with four categories: retain, relocate, undecided and authorised disposal. Each entry records the item or its location, the decision, who made it and the date. Let the resident revisit decisions. An undecided item is never treated as disposal-ready because it is in the way. If a relative asks the crew to discard sealed boxes while the resident is away, the relative does not hold that decision. Pause the handling, leave the boxes where they are, record the request, and seek a valid, documented decision from the resident or from the person the support plan names.

lessons.title: Respectful communication and coordinated support
learningOutcomes: Use neutral, person-centred language in a role-play about the work.
Agree communication roles, privacy rules and an escalation contact with the resident.
Stop and report a privacy breach, and record it through the incident procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers communication, privacy and coordination. It does not give welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments, and completing it does not qualify a worker to make them. Those decisions belong to the people responsible for them under the support plan.

instructionSections.heading: Language and dignity
instructionSections.body: Describe the situation in neutral, factual words. Clutter and environmental neglect are not personal failings. The Victorian Department of Families, Fairness and Housing describes hoarding as keeping many things that others think are useless or have little or no value, and notes that hoarding is different from collecting, where collectors are usually well organised and collect one type of thing. Avoid words that shame the person, and avoid photographs that expose the home to others. Speak to the resident about what they want to achieve, not about what others think should go.

instructionSections.heading: Coordinated support and privacy
instructionSections.body: Agree communication roles, break times, privacy rules and one escalation contact with the resident before the first session. Invite only the supporters the resident has authorised. The DFFH page refers to Make Safe guidance written for services such as councils, healthcare providers and housing providers, and that guidance should be used through the coordinator rather than applied alone. The CFA says hoarding is a complex issue which requires intervention and long-term support, so a cleaning crew should not be the only service involved. A worker who shares a before-photograph of the home in a group chat has breached the resident's privacy. Stop sharing, tell the coordinator, follow the incident procedure and keep the information confidential.

lessons.title: Fire loads, heating and electrical ignition
learningOutcomes: Identify combustible loads near heat sources and electrical points from a safe position.
Stop work and escalate fire-load findings without touching stacks or equipment.
Record the hazard with its location, date and referral.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers recognition and escalation only. It does not authorise work on heaters, electrical wiring, power boards or appliances, and it does not authorise moving stored items away from a heat source without an agreed plan.

instructionSections.heading: Why accumulated possessions raise the risk
instructionSections.body: The CFA says that clutter can easily catch fire and increase the intensity of a fire, and that hoarding makes fires more likely to start. Fire Rescue Victoria says hoarding increases the risk of having a fire, and that accumulated possessions create an abnormally high fuel load. Combustible storage near a heat source or an electrical point raises both the chance of ignition and the speed at which a fire spreads. The consequence is greater where escape routes are blocked, which is the subject of the next lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising ignition points from a safe position
instructionSections.body: Look for combustible material stacked near heaters, cooking areas, electrical boards, power boards and appliances, for cords running under piles, and for heat sources left among paper. Observe from the doorway or another safe vantage point. Do not touch or move anything, and do not test appliances. Record what you see, with the room and the date. Where a source looks active or the risk looks immediate, leave the area and follow the emergency procedure named in the plan. Fire-risk decisions belong to the competent fire service and to the specialists the plan names, so report the condition to the coordinator the same day and suspend work in the affected rooms until the risk has been assessed.

lessons.title: Safe egress and emergency access
learningOutcomes: Walk and map the planned evacuation route before any material is staged.
Recognise a blocked exit and stop the affected work.
Record a partly complete job honestly, with the outstanding exit referred.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers mapping and recognising blocked exits. Moving an obstruction is allowed only where the plan authorises that move and the resident agrees. This lesson does not authorise forced entry or structural work.

instructionSections.heading: Exits are part of the job
instructionSections.body: The CFA says that hallways, windows and doors can become blocked, and that getting in and out is harder as a result. Blocked routes stop residents from escaping and can stop rescuers reaching people. Before any material is staged, walk the planned route from the main entrance to each exit and to the agreed meeting point. Note trip hazards, narrow passages and any point where a stack or cart could block the way. Keep every route clear of work materials at all times.

instructionSections.heading: Re-checking and partial completion
instructionSections.body: Mark the routes on a simple plan agreed with the resident, and recheck them at the start and end of each session and after any change in staging. If a cart or stack blocks the only practical exit during work, stop. Move the obstruction only where the plan authorises that move, and recheck the routes before work continues. A cleared doorway does not finish the job while another exit remains blocked. Record the open exit, record the blocked one, and refer the outstanding hazard.

lessons.title: Structural instability and unstable piles
learningOutcomes: Identify at least three signs that a stack, shelf or floor may fail.
Withdraw, set a boundary and refer the zone without moving the load.
Record the signs, the time and the boundary set.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers recognition and withdrawal. Assessing or altering any stack, shelving or floor is a decision for a competent person. Completing this lesson does not qualify a worker to make that assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Signs of a possible collapse
instructionSections.body: Piles, overloaded shelving and damaged floors can give little warning before they fail. Watch for a stack that leans or bows, a cabinet pressing against boxes, shelving that sags or pulls from a wall, staining or softening on the floor beneath a load, and a floor that gives or moves underfoot. Any one of these is enough to withdraw. Do not test a stack by pushing it, and do not climb onto it to look. The signs listed here are recognition cues from this module. No structural standard was read for this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Withdraw, set the boundary and refer
instructionSections.body: Withdraw to a place where nobody is under a load and the exit is clear. Mark the boundary with barrier tape or signage, and keep residents and other workers outside it. Refer the zone for a competent structural or specialist assessment through the coordinator before any load is changed. Record the signs you saw, the time, the position of each load and the boundary you set. Work elsewhere may continue only if it is outside the boundary and the plan allows it.

lessons.title: Pests, contamination and hygiene triage
learningOutcomes: Record pest and contamination indicators as observations, not diagnoses.
Restrict access and avoid aerosol-producing actions in a described scene.
Route the case to the specialist named in the plan.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers recognition, access restriction and referral. It does not cover pest treatment, decontamination, or the disposal of contaminated goods, and completing it does not qualify a worker to undertake them.

instructionSections.heading: What to observe
instructionSections.body: Droppings, insects, mouldy goods and unknown liquids can signal contamination that ordinary cleaning does not manage. The WA Department of Health mould guidance advises against dry brushing, because dry brushing breaks the fungi up into small fragments. This module applies the same caution to mouldy goods found in a hoarded home: do not disturb the material to see more. Note the location, the extent and the odour from outside the affected area. Record what you see. Do not name a pest or a contaminant, because identification belongs to the specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Restrict access and refer
instructionSections.body: Restrict access to the affected area and keep residents and other workers out until guidance is in place. Avoid dry sweeping, vacuuming and any action that creates dust or aerosols. Do not open sealed containers or probe enclosed spaces. Record the indicators as observations, keep the record dated, and route the case to the specialist the plan names. Pest and contamination decisions belong to specialists.

lessons.title: Sharps, chemicals and unknown materials
learningOutcomes: Recognise sharps, unlabelled containers and unknown materials as stop-work items.
Isolate the area and escalate to suitably trained personnel without touching the items.
Record the hazard in a log that states what was not done.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers recognition, isolation and referral. It does not cover handling, sorting, testing, transporting or disposing of sharps, chemicals or unknown materials. Completing it does not qualify a worker to do any of these.

instructionSections.heading: Recognise the stop-work situation
instructionSections.body: Needles, syringes, lancets, unlabelled containers, leaking bottles and unidentified powders or liquids are stop-work items. Do not pick them up to see what they are, do not sort the material around them, and do not bag them. A loose needle among clothes beneath unknown bottles is a stop-work situation. Cease handling in the area, isolate it and escalate to suitably trained personnel. Keep people, including children and animals, away from the area as far as the plan allows. A photograph of the hazard is taken only where the plan authorises it.

instructionSections.heading: Record, refer and do not dispose
instructionSections.body: Prepare a hazard log entry without touching the suspect items. Record the type of item, its location, its condition and the time, and state what you did not do. Request specialist removal through the coordinator. Waste routing, health referral and any notification are decisions for competent personnel. Do not transfer the material into general waste. A skip contractor who declines a leaking, unidentified container has made a correct decision, and the crew should not treat that refusal as an obstacle to be worked around.

lessons.title: Safe handling and staged work zones
learningOutcomes: Set a work zone, its boundary and an order of work with the resident.
Separate items into four labelled categories and keep the traffic route clear.
Reconcile the daily inventory with the item-decision log.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers planning and handling limits in a staged job. It does not set numerical lifting limits, which come from the employer's plan and manual-handling controls, and it does not authorise the removal of possessions.

instructionSections.heading: Small, agreed zones
instructionSections.body: Controlled work in small, named zones reduces re-accumulation, manual-handling strain and the loss of items the resident values. Agree the zones with the resident, one room or one area at a time. Set a work and rest pattern, the lifting limits from the plan and a daily inventory review. A crew that rushes several rooms at once and mixes keepsakes with waste has breached the agreed plan.

instructionSections.heading: Four labelled categories and a clear route
instructionSections.body: Keep items the resident is keeping, items for relocation, undecided items and items for authorised disposal in four separate, labelled zones. Keep the traffic route clear and separate from the staging zones. Handle each item once and move it to its labelled zone. If a category is unclear, the item moves to the undecided zone, not the disposal zone. The daily review confirms that the zones still match the item-decision log, and it records any change and the reason for it.

lessons.title: Waste, reuse and property records
learningOutcomes: Sort items into the five waste and property streams before anything leaves the home.
Record the owner or decision maker, the permission to remove and the destination for each item.
Refuse to place an unknown or leaking container into general waste.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers separating streams and keeping records. It does not authorise the transport or disposal of hazardous waste, and it does not authorise the disposal of anyone's property. Local waste rules decide each destination.

instructionSections.heading: Five streams
instructionSections.body: Sort material into five streams before anything leaves the home: authorised ordinary waste, retained property, recyclable material, unknown material and regulated material. Waste rules differ by material and by jurisdiction, so the destination for each stream is the one set by the plan and confirmed by the coordinator under the local rules. Unknown material is not general waste until someone competent has identified it. A skip contractor who declines a leaking, unidentified container has made a correct decision, and the crew must not move that container into general waste to get round the refusal.

instructionSections.heading: Owners, permissions and mould-related material
instructionSections.body: Record the owner or decision maker for each item, the permission to remove it and the destination for each stream. Keep reusable property separate and labelled so that it is not lost or thrown away by mistake. The WA Department of Health mould guidance says that mould is not considered a hazardous waste and that bagged mouldy material can go in normal waste. That is WA guidance about mould itself. It does not settle the stream for goods that are also contaminated with other hazards, or whose contents are not known.

lessons.title: Privacy, tenant rights and multidisciplinary handoff
learningOutcomes: Refuse a request for information that has no authorised purpose, and record the refusal.
Write a handoff record that separates agreed, done, unresolved and referred items.
Send information only to authorised recipients through the agreed channel.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers the limits of information handling and referral. It does not give legal advice on tenancy, guardianship, privacy or safeguarding. Completing it does not qualify a worker to make welfare, clinical or safeguarding decisions.

instructionSections.heading: Only the minimum needed
instructionSections.body: Collect, keep and share only the information needed for the agreed work, and only where the resident or the lawful authority allows it. The rules on tenancy, safeguarding referral and information sharing differ by jurisdiction, and the coordinator confirms the legal basis for any disclosure. An agency that asks for photographs of every room and copies of personal documents is asking for far more than the work requires. Refuse requests that are not tied to an authorised purpose, and record the refusal and the reason.

instructionSections.heading: The handoff record
instructionSections.body: A handoff record states what was agreed, what was done, what is unresolved, who is responsible for each open issue, and what has been referred. Refer welfare, health and safeguarding concerns to the people responsible for them, not to the crew. Give the receiving service only the minimum needed. Mark anything that is unverified as unverified, and never present a person's health, drug use or circumstances as established fact unless a responsible person has confirmed it.

lessons.title: Verification, follow-up and recurrence prevention
learningOutcomes: Write a partial-outcome handover that claims no full remediation or cure.
List unresolved risks with a named responsible person.
Arrange and record follow-up with dates.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers honest recording of partial outcomes and follow-up. It does not certify that a home is safe, clean or free of hazards, and it does not record a clinical outcome. A handover is not a certificate of safety.

instructionSections.heading: A one-time clear-out is a partial outcome
instructionSections.body: The CFA says that one-off clean-ups do not deal with the underlying reasons for hoarding behaviour, and that hoarding is a complex issue requiring intervention and long-term support. A cleared room, a clear exit or a removed stack is a real outcome, and it is still only a partial one. Record what was achieved, what was not, and what remains unresolved. Do not describe the home as fully remediated, and do not describe the resident as cured.

instructionSections.heading: Follow-up and recurrence
instructionSections.body: Recurrence prevention belongs to the support plan and the people named in it. Describe the follow-up that has been arranged, with dates and responsible people. Record the factors the resident identified as risks, such as the items they keep returning to, and pass them to the support team. Fire Rescue Victoria recommends risk reduction as a priority rather than large scale removal, so the aim is a lower and ongoing fire risk, not one dramatic result. Health support is provided by the health and human services named in the plan, not by the cleaning crew.

lessons.title: Scope, competence and site authority
learningOutcomes: Identify who holds authority for the work and refuse work outside the contract or work order.
Separate observed, uncertain and unverified information in a written record.
Refer any scope mismatch before work continues.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson is training content. It does not authorise remediation, demolition, disturbance of building materials, handling of contaminated water or waste, or any statement that a space is safe or free of mould. Completing it gives no licence, certificate or approval. Restricted remediation is carried out only by a competent, appropriately qualified professional under an approved plan.

instructionSections.heading: Who decides before work starts
instructionSections.body: Before any practical work, confirm the contract boundary in writing, the responsible remediation manager, the access permission for the property, and the competence of each worker. Where the contract covers only routine cleaning, that is the limit of the task. The WA Department of Health guideline describes three duties that bear on mould: a general public health duty for anyone whose actions could foreseeably cause harm, a workplace duty, and a residential tenancies duty under which owners or agents must keep rental premises habitable and occupants help manage water, heating, ventilation and appliances. Which duty applies to a job depends on who controls the premises and the work. The coordinator confirms that position before work starts.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising a scope mismatch
instructionSections.body: A tenant who asks a cleaner to treat a damp bedroom after a long leak is asking for remediation, which the work order may not cover. The cleaner does not have authority to treat the room. Establish who may decide, what information is missing and which actions must stop. The absence of visible growth does not mean there is no hidden damage, so it cannot be used to widen the scope. A cleaning certificate also does not establish remediation competence for a particular job.

lessons.title: Moisture sources and building history
learningOutcomes: Complete a non-invasive moisture-history questionnaire for a fictional property.
Separate observed, reported and assumed information in a photograph log.
Refer the question of the moisture source to a qualified building investigation.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers history-taking and referral. It does not authorise opening walls, roofs, subfloors or cavities to find the source. A qualified building investigation does that work under an approved plan.

instructionSections.heading: Mould follows moisture
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says the source of moisture must be located so that the cause is addressed and recurrence is prevented. It lists common sources as water accumulation, condensation, poor ventilation, severe weather and occupant behaviour. It also says mould is likely if building foundations or porous components stay wet for more than 48 hours. The same guideline's flood appendix says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes, so the time since a water event matters. Find out when the water came in, not only where the stain is.

instructionSections.heading: Building history and the photograph log
instructionSections.body: Use a non-invasive moisture-history questionnaire. Ask when the stain first appeared, what happens during rain, showers, cooking and drying, whether the roof, gutters or plumbing have been repaired, and what the occupants have done about it. Keep a photograph log with the date and the location of each photograph, and note who reported each fact. Keep observation and assumption apart. A newly painted wall that smells musty after rain, while the carpet next to it feels dry, shows that the source may be somewhere other than where it seems. Refer the question of source to a qualified building investigation.

instructionSections.heading: Why the source must be corrected first
instructionSections.body: Cleaning or repainting a source that is still wet will not stop the growth. The guideline says surfaces should not be painted, sealed or covered until they are dry, and it treats repair of the source as a core part of remediation. Map the order of the work: source identified and repaired, moisture re-evaluated, drying complete, and only then cleaning and finishing.

lessons.title: Inspection, concealed damage and escalation
learningOutcomes: Classify a described contamination as simple or complex from recorded facts.
Identify warning signs of concealed damage and escalate without opening material.
Record the classification, the facts used and the escalation route.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Inspection here is visual and non-invasive. Do not open wall cavities, lift flooring or remove material to look for hidden growth without an approved plan and a competent person. Classification and the decision to use professional help belong to the competent supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Simple or complex
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline separates simple contamination from complex contamination. Simple contamination is new, isolated and visible, no greater than one square metre, and has causes that are easy to identify and correct. Complex contamination is larger than one square metre, or is found in multiple rooms or places. It also includes evidence of recurring and persistent mould or dampness, and situations such as HVAC involvement, suspected hidden mould, or other hazards such as asbestos. The guideline calls the one-square-metre size an arbitrary figure, and notes that larger areas may still be handled without professional help. It states that complex contamination typically requires professional help, so the classification decides the escalation route.

instructionSections.heading: Warning signs of concealed damage
instructionSections.body: Recurring staining, a musty odour, bulging or softening surfaces, and cold or wet patches on walls are warning signs of concealed damage. Record them and escalate. A request to demolish a sealed cupboard that has recurring staining is not a decision a cleaner can accept. Demolition needs a revised scope, a competent assessment and specialist investigation, and work stops until those are in place.

lessons.title: Occupant health and communication
learningOutcomes: Identify occupants the WA guideline names as susceptible and agree how they are kept away from the work.
Give a scope-based answer to a health or safety question without making a clearance.
Refer health questions to a clinician and record the referral.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers communication and referral. It does not give medical advice, and it does not give a clearance that a space is safe for any person. Health questions go to a clinician.

instructionSections.heading: Who is more sensitive
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline names people with existing respiratory, immunocompromising and allergic conditions as susceptible, and it also names infants, children and older people. It notes an association between mould exposure in pregnancy and poorer outcomes in offspring. Its flood appendix says susceptible people should avoid mould exposure. Plan the communication and the separation of these occupants before work starts, so that they are kept away from the work area.

instructionSections.heading: Keep three things apart
instructionSections.body: Keep observations, medical advice and clearance decisions apart. The guideline states there are no defined quantitative or qualitative exposure thresholds for mould or dampness, and that evidence suggests any mould or dampness may pose a risk. A worker therefore cannot describe a level as acceptable. When an occupant with respiratory symptoms asks whether the room is now safe, the worker does not answer with a clearance. Record the scope of the work, state what has and has not been verified, and refer the health question to a clinician. Explain the controls and closed areas in plain language, and make sure the answer is written down.

lessons.title: Hazard screening and contaminated water
learningOutcomes: Identify flood or sewage water and suspected asbestos or lead in a described scene, and stop work.
Isolate the area without disturbing material.
Record the hazards and the escalation in the risk register.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers screening and escalation. It does not authorise disturbing suspected asbestos or lead, handling contaminated water, or sewage clean-up, and it does not set out how to clean or dry a flood-affected home.

instructionSections.heading: Contaminated water changes the job
instructionSections.body: Water from floods, and sewage, must be treated as contaminated, and the job changes once it is present. The WA guideline has an appendix on managing mould risk after flooding. It says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes, and that homes should be cleaned and dried as soon as possible. It advises removing wet items, floor coverings and wet plasterboard, discarding soft materials with mould growth, and not using diesel equipment indoors. Those are remediation steps that depend on the flood assessment and the approved plan, so a screening worker stops, isolates and refers them rather than starting them.

instructionSections.heading: Suspected asbestos and lead
instructionSections.body: Older building materials may contain asbestos or lead, and disturbing them can release those hazards. A ceiling that collapses to reveal suspicious old insulation under sewage-affected plasterboard presents both hazards together. Stop work, isolate the area and escalate. Presumed asbestos is not disturbed by an ordinary cleaner, and any sampling or removal is carried out by a competent person and, where the law requires, a licensed one. The Victorian asbestos guidance says a limited amount of asbestos removal can be done without a licence, sets limits for non-friable material and contaminated dust, does not list friable material among those exemptions, and advises considering a licensed removalist where obligations may not be met. A cleaner does not rely on any allowance.

lessons.title: PPE, respiratory protection and worker readiness
learningOutcomes: Match a described exposure to the PPE set out in the approved plan, and identify an unsuitable choice.
Stop a worker who is not ready, and record the reason.
Complete a PPE readiness check for a fictional crew.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers selecting and checking PPE. It does not replace an exposure assessment, a respirator programme or the fit of a respirator, and it does not clear a worker to enter a contaminated area.

instructionSections.heading: What the guideline sets as minimum points
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says the respiratory tract, eyes and skin must be protected during remediation. Its PPE appendix says a P2 or N95 respirator face-mask should be worn to reduce exposure to airborne mould spores, and that powered air-purifying respirators should be used when remediating complex mould situations. These are minimum points for mould work in Western Australia. The approved plan sets the actual selection for each job, based on the exposure that has been assessed.

instructionSections.heading: Readiness before entry
instructionSections.body: Before anyone enters a contaminated area, confirm the respirator programme, the worker's training and the fit of the respirator. A worker who brings a loose disposable mask and says it is enough for major demolition has not met the requirement. Equipment does not replace exposure controls, and it cannot be relied on alone. Stop until a competent person has assessed the exposure, selected the equipment and confirmed that the worker is ready. Record each check, including the checks that failed.

lessons.title: Containment and cross-contamination prevention
learningOutcomes: Recognise when containment is required and stop work that lacks it.
