Plan a worker and waste route that avoids clean and occupied areas.
Record the zoning and any breach of it.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Containment is an approved, supervised measure. This lesson covers recognising the need for it and the planning it requires. It does not authorise a general cleaner to set up or alter containment.

instructionSections.heading: What the guideline sets for complex work
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says containment is a core principle of remediation, and that for complex contamination a site-specific remediation plan should be developed with professionals. The plan should cover containment, drying, surface and contents remediation, HVAC work, waste disposal, scheduling, PPE, environmental controls and post-remediation evaluation. The guideline says the affected area must be completely isolated or sealed with heavy grade plastic covers, kept under negative pressure, and that occupants should be evacuated. Those are the guideline's points for complex work, and the approved plan sets how each is done on the job.

instructionSections.heading: Cross-contamination in practice
instructionSections.body: Cleaning activity can carry airborne particles into an occupied corridor, so the route through the building must be planned before work starts. Keep clean materials away from the contaminated zone, and keep occupants who are not doing the work outside it. Containment decisions belong to the competent remediation manager. A general cleaner recognises the signs, stops and refers. An experienced remediation manager is needed where containment is complex or occupants are close to the work.

lessons.title: Porous, semi-porous and hard material decisions
learningOutcomes: Classify described items as hard, semi-porous or porous.
Refuse to keep a porous item on appearance alone.
Record each material decision and its referral.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers recognising material types and referring decisions about them. It does not decide that a porous item can be cleaned, and it does not authorise demolition or salvage.

instructionSections.heading: What the guideline says
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned should be removed or discarded in simple remediation, and that such items are often not economically salvageable as part of typical remediation. For hard surfaces it advises scrubbing with soapy water, and it says the physical action of scrubbing is the most important component. It also says that chemical products may be used in some cases, but will not fully remove mould, and that their use is a case-specific decision. Hard surfaces are therefore cleaned by the approved method, and porous items are judged against whether they can be adequately cleaned.

instructionSections.heading: Decisions in practice
instructionSections.body: Saturated drywall and timber beside washable metal fixtures need different decisions. Porous material that has held moisture and growth is judged for salvage by the competent supervisor. Mark each item as hard, semi-porous or porous, record its condition and any uncertainty, and refer the decision. Do not decide that an item is safe to keep because it looks clean. Looks clean is an observation, not a result of cleaning.

lessons.title: Cleaning methods and equipment limits
learningOutcomes: Identify an unsuitable cleaning method and state why it is unsuitable.
Check equipment for fit, seals and maintenance, and stop a defective item.
Record the method used and any deviation from the approved plan.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Cleaning methods for a contaminated area come from the approved remediation plan. This lesson identifies methods that are unsuitable and explains why. It gives no product, dilution, quantity or contact time.

instructionSections.heading: Methods the guideline rules out
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline advises scrubbing hard surfaces with soapy water, and says the physical action of scrubbing is the most important component. It says dry brushing should be avoided, because dry brushing breaks the fungi into small fragments. It also advises cleaning at least 30 to 50 centimetres beyond the visible mould, so cleaning that stops at the edge of the visible growth falls short of the guideline. Methods that spread dust or fragments into the air need the approval of the plan, and the plan names the equipment and the method to use.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment limits
instructionSections.body: Equipment that captures particles is only as good as its fit, its seals and its maintenance. Fit, maintain and use equipment under the manufacturer's instructions and the approved plan. A machine that is leaking, cracked or not sealed can increase exposure. Check the equipment before the job, record the check, and stop it if it leaks or is damaged. Defective equipment comes out of the job.

lessons.title: Waste segregation and environmental handover
learningOutcomes: Identify the waste stream of each load in a described scene.
Refuse an unauthorised waste route.
Record each load, its stream, its destination and its handover.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers segregating and recording mould-related waste. It does not authorise the transport or disposal of hazardous waste, and local waste rules govern each destination.

instructionSections.heading: What the guideline says about mouldy material
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says that mould is not considered a hazardous waste, and that bagged mouldy material can go in normal waste. It also says porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned should be removed or discarded. Those statements are WA guidance about mould itself. They do not settle the stream for material that is also contaminated with water from a flood or sewage, asbestos, lead, chemicals or other hazards. Those loads follow the stream set by the competent person.

instructionSections.heading: Plan before handling
instructionSections.body: Plan the containment of suspect waste before it is handled, and verify the local disposal, transport and contractor authorisations first. A contractor who proposes putting demolition debris into ordinary office waste bins is proposing something that must be refused. Keep the streams separate, record each bag or load, and hand over only by an authorised route.

lessons.title: Moisture correction, drying and recurrence prevention
learningOutcomes: Order the repair, re-evaluation, drying and finishing steps for a described job.
Refuse a finishing request made before drying is recorded.
Schedule follow-up monitoring for recurrence with a named person.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers the dependencies between the moisture fix, drying and any finishing or reoccupation decision. It does not decide that a home is ready for occupation, and it does not set a drying method.

instructionSections.heading: Dry before finishing
instructionSections.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says surfaces should not be painted, sealed or covered until they are dry. It lists complete drying of construction and building materials, furnishings and carpet as a core principle of remediation, and it says the source must be repaired. Painting over affected surfaces does not remedy dampness, and the mould can return. A landlord who wants new paint before the leak is fixed is asking for a result that will not last. Map the order: source repaired, moisture re-evaluated, drying complete, then cleaning and finishing, and only then the reoccupation decision.

instructionSections.heading: Prevention and monitoring
instructionSections.body: The guideline has a prevention section and a moisture-reduction appendix that set out ways to reduce the conditions that allow growth. Its flood appendix says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes, so drying should start as soon as it is safe under the plan. After the work, monitor for recurrence. The guideline lists no recurrence within two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success. It does not describe a formal clearance, and it recommends that the evaluation be done by a different entity from the one that did the work.

lessons.title: Verification, records and release boundaries
learningOutcomes: Write a closeout report that separates task completion, visual review and independent clearance.
Refuse a clearance or pathogen-free statement from the crew.
Name the unverified areas and the reviewer with authority.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers records and the limits of what can be claimed. It does not give a clearance, a pathogen-free result or a reoccupation decision. A closeout report is not a certificate.

instructionSections.heading: Three things kept apart
instructionSections.body: Keep task completion, visual review and independent clearance apart. Task completion means the agreed work was done. Visual review means someone looked and recorded what could be seen. Independent clearance is a judgement made by a different, competent reviewer under the requirements that apply to the job. A visual clean cannot establish a pathogen-free result, so a cleaner who writes one has claimed something the work does not support. The WA guideline recommends that the post-remediation evaluation be done by a different entity from the one that carried out the work. It states that there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment or for who carries it out.

instructionSections.heading: The closeout report
instructionSections.body: Prepare a factual closeout report. Record the observations, the methods used as the plan sets them, the changes made, the limitations, the areas not verified, and who has authority for post-remediation verification. Do not describe unverified areas as safe. Reoccupation is a separate decision that follows the applicable local and contractual requirements, so the report does not declare a home safe to occupy.

lessons.title: Irrigation system components and inspection
learningOutcomes: Name the main components of a residential or commercial garden irrigation system and state the function of each.
Carry out a visual and functional inspection of a system, zone by zone, and identify faults such as leaks, blocked emitters and coverage gaps.
Recognise the boundary between servicing permitted under this business and plumbing, backflow and electrical work that needs a licence holder.
Record inspection findings so that the client can see what was checked, what was fixed and what needs referral.

instructionSections.heading: The parts of an irrigation system
instructionSections.body: A garden irrigation system takes water from a supply point, controls it, distributes it through pipe and delivers it to plants through heads, drippers or emitters. The supply point is usually a tap or a connection that is part of the property's plumbing. Between the supply and the garden there is often a backflow prevention device, which stops water from returning to the supply. A filter and a pressure regulator protect the emitters. A controller, usually wall-mounted or in a shed, sends signals to electric valves, called solenoid valves, that open and close each zone. Each zone is a group of heads or drippers with similar water needs, fed by lateral pipe from a valve. Rain sensors and soil moisture sensors may be fitted to adjust the run times. Knowing these parts lets you work out where a fault is before you dig, and which parts you are allowed to service.

instructionSections.heading: Inspecting the system
instructionSections.body: Start with the paperwork: the system drawing, the controller settings and any previous service record. Walk the garden and look for wet spots, dry spots, sunken ground, broken heads and damaged emitters. Check the condition of the controller, its enclosure and the visible wiring for damage, corrosion or moisture, but do not open the mains supply section or work on wiring inside the controller. Run each zone in turn using the controller's manual test function. Watch for even coverage, heads that do not rise or rotate correctly, heads that spray onto paths, walls or windows, and drippers that are blocked or leaking. Note the operating pressure at a convenient point if the business has the approved gauge. Check the filter and clean it if the business's procedure allows. Record every zone, the run result and the faults found. Do not change valve settings or repair the mains connection without authority.

instructionSections.heading: Backflow devices and the licence boundary
instructionSections.body: Backflow prevention devices protect drinking water from contamination, and their installation, testing and repair are regulated. In some states, testing must be done by a person authorised for that work, and the test records must be lodged with the water authority. In New South Wales, the plumbing licence categories include urban irrigation water plumbing, which covers connecting an irrigation system to a water main (NSW Government page updated 31 July 2026). This lesson does not grant a plumbing, backflow or electrical licence. When you find a fault on the mains side of the system, a backflow device, a supply connection or the controller's wiring, stop, make the area safe, record the finding and refer the work to the licence holder under the business's referral procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Recording findings and handover
instructionSections.body: A good inspection record lets the client and the next technician see what was done. Record the date, the property, the zones tested, the run results, the faults found, the parts removed or replaced, the parts left in place, and any referral to a licence holder. Take photographs of faults with the client's consent, and show the location and the fault clearly. Explain the findings to the client in plain language before leaving the site, including any faults that cannot be fixed under the current scope. Ask the client to sign or confirm the report. A report that says what was checked is more valuable than one that says the system works, because it describes evidence and leaves no room for a promise that the system is leak-free.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the inspection method and the record. A competent technician can name the components on a drawing, run a zone test without damaging the valve or the head, identify a leak or coverage problem, and explain why a backflow or mains fault is referred. Escalate any suspected leak in the supply line, any exposed or damaged wiring, any backflow device that appears damaged or untested, and any system that is not safe to run.

lessons.title: Controller programming and water-efficient scheduling
learningOutcomes: Set zone run times and start times on a controller using the zone map, plant type, soil and sun exposure.
Adjust schedules for season, rainfall and sensor input so that water is not wasted.
Check that water restrictions and local rules are followed before a schedule is set.
Record each schedule change and explain it to the client in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Why scheduling saves water and money
instructionSections.body: Most irrigation waste comes from schedules that never change. A controller set in midsummer keeps running through a wet autumn, a zone that waters shade and sun equally wastes water on the shaded part, and a sprinkler that throws water onto a path wastes it entirely. Good scheduling matches the water each zone gets to what the plants and soil need. That saves water for the client and reduces the energy used by pumps, and it can reduce plant losses caused by overwatering. Scheduling is a cost reduction lesson because the client pays for water and for the consequences of a poor schedule, such as lawn disease, waterlogging or fungal problems in beds. Start with the zone map, not with a default programme.

instructionSections.heading: Setting zone run times
instructionSections.body: Each zone should be scheduled according to its plant type, soil, slope, sun exposure and the type of head. Sandy soils drain quickly and may need shorter, more frequent runs. Clay soils take water slowly and may run off on slopes, so they need short runs with rests between them. Lawns, shrubs and garden beds usually have different needs and should be on separate zones. Measure the precipitation rate of each zone if the business has a catch-can test method, because the same run time delivers different depths of water from different heads. Set the run time from the target depth and the precipitation rate, not from a guess. Record the settings for each zone, and label the controller so that the next technician can see the basis for the programme.

instructionSections.heading: Seasonal, rain and sensor adjustments
instructionSections.body: A schedule is a starting point, not a permanent setting. Adjust the programme for the season, since plants use less water in cool weather and more in hot, windy weather. Use a rain sensor or soil moisture sensor where it is fitted and working, so that the controller skips irrigation after rain. Check that the sensor is positioned correctly and not blocked. Review the schedule when the client reports a problem, after a major rain event, and at the start and end of each season. Where a water restriction applies to the property, the controller must follow it. Water restriction rules are set by the water authority and local council. Check the current rules before setting the schedule, and record the rule that was followed.

instructionSections.heading: Controller safety and the licence boundary
instructionSections.body: Programming a controller through its keypad or app is normal service work. Do not open the enclosure to change wiring, and do not bypass a rain sensor or a safety device to make a schedule work. If the controller is wet, damaged, or making unusual sounds, turn it off using its external control if that is safe and refer the fault. Keep the controller's manual or the manufacturer's instructions with the service record, and use the recommended settings for the model.

instructionSections.heading: Recording and explaining the schedule
instructionSections.body: Every schedule change needs a record that a later technician can follow. Write down the zone, the old setting, the new setting, the reason for the change, the date, the rule checked and the sensor status. Label the controller with the current season's basis, so that the next visit does not rely on memory. When you explain the schedule to the client, use plain language: say which zones run, when, for how long and why. Explain the trade-off where there is one, for example a shorter run that means the lawn may look slightly less green for a few days. Give the client a written copy and ask for confirmation. A client who understands the schedule is far more likely to keep it, and far less likely to override it with a manual run that wastes water.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the zone map, the run times and the record. A competent technician can explain how a run time was set, show the sensor setting, identify a schedule that wastes water and describe the change they would make. Escalate any schedule that conflicts with a water restriction, any controller fault, and any client request to water beyond the approved schedule or outside the restriction.

lessons.title: Leak detection and repair boundaries (backflow and plumbing)
learningOutcomes: Recognise the signs of a leak in an irrigation system, including wet ground, falling pressure and unexpected water use.
Locate and isolate a leak on the zone side of the system using the approved method, where it is safe to do so.
Distinguish leak repairs that fall within a non-licensed irrigation service from repairs on the supply side, backflow devices and plumbing, which need a licence holder.
Refer, record and communicate supply-side and plumbing faults without attempting licensed work.

instructionSections.heading: Finding leaks and understanding the signs
instructionSections.body: Leaks in irrigation systems show in a few predictable ways. The lawn or bed is wet or soft in one area even when the zone is not running. A zone takes longer than usual to pressurise, or the pressure at the other zones drops when one runs. The water bill rises without a change in use, or the water meter keeps moving when everything is off. A pipe that has been pulled by a mower or dug by a dog may leak at a joint or a fitting. Start with a visual walk of the system when the zones are off, then run each zone and watch the ground and the heads. Use the business's listening or meter test if it has one. Mark every wet area and every leak you find on the zone map before you dig. Do not assume a wet area is the leak; water travels along pipe trenches and can surface some distance away.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating the leak safely
instructionSections.body: Once a leak is located, isolate the affected part of the system if the isolation is on the zone side and the procedure allows it. Turn off the zone valve manually or at the controller, and confirm the water has stopped before you go further. Do not isolate the supply side, the backflow device or the main line unless your procedure specifically allows it for that work and you have the authority. Turn off the power to the controller only at its external isolation point and only if that is safe. Buried electrical cables, gas lines and other pipes may be close to the leak, and some are live or pressurised. Stop digging if you find an unexpected service, and do not continue until the owner or a qualified locator has confirmed its location and status.

instructionSections.heading: What is in scope and what needs a licence
instructionSections.body: Work on the supply side is different. Repairs to the supply connection, the water meter area, the backflow prevention device, the main line before the zone valves, or any plumbing connection are plumbing work. In New South Wales, the plumbing licence categories include urban irrigation water plumbing, which covers connecting an irrigation system to a water main (NSW Government page updated 31 July 2026), so supply-side connection work needs a licence there. This lesson does not grant a plumbing, backflow or electrical licence, and the crew must not repair supply-side or plumbing faults under it.

instructionSections.heading: Recording, referral and the client
instructionSections.body: Record every leak with its location, the cause if known, the photographs taken with consent, the time, the zone isolated, the action taken and the water pressure before and after if measured. For any supply-side or plumbing fault, write a referral to the licence holder that describes the location and the symptoms, and give the client a copy. Explain to the client what was found, what is in scope, what has been isolated, and what is needed next. Do not promise a repair date or a cost for licensed work that the business does not control. Keep the zone isolated until the repair is complete or the client has instructed otherwise, and record that instruction.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the leak location, the isolation and the referral. A competent technician can explain how they located the leak, show the isolation point, identify the boundary between in-scope and licensed work, and describe the referral. Escalate any leak on the supply side, any leak near a service, any water running that cannot be stopped at the zone valve, and any leak that is causing damage to a building or neighbouring property.

lessons.title: Irrigation service reports and maintenance contracts
learningOutcomes: Write a service report that records what was checked, what was done, what was referred and what the client needs to decide.
Design a maintenance agreement with defined visits, inclusions, exclusions and approval steps.
Price maintenance agreements and repair follow-up so that revenue reflects the work and the risk.
Describe water-saving outcomes only as far as the measurements support them.

instructionSections.heading: Why service reports create repeat work
instructionSections.body: A clear service report is the most useful sales tool an irrigation business has. It shows the client what was found, what was done and what needs attention, and it builds trust that the business is looking after the system. A client who receives a report with a list of zone faults, a referral for a supply-side leak and a suggested seasonal schedule is far more likely to book the next visit and to approve the referred work. A vague report that says the system was checked does the opposite. The report should be written for the client to read, not only for the technician, and it should separate what the business can do from what needs a licence holder.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the service report
instructionSections.body: Structure the report in the same order each time so that clients learn to read it. Start with the property, the date, the technician and the zones tested. Record the run results for each zone, the faults found with photographs taken with consent, and the actions taken on site. Then list the referrals, each with the reason and the licence class needed, and the items that need the client's decision, such as a head replacement that is in scope but has a cost. End with the schedule that is in place and the next recommended visit. Keep the language plain. Avoid promises such as the system will be leak-free or will save a set percentage of water, unless the measurements in the report support them. A report that is honest about limits is more credible than one that promises everything.

instructionSections.heading: Designing a maintenance agreement
instructionSections.body: A maintenance agreement sets out the visits, the inclusions and the exclusions, and the approval steps for extra work. A common structure is a seasonal check at the start of the warm and cool seasons, with a schedule review and a report. Inclusions may be the zone run test, the filter clean, the schedule adjustment and the service report. Exclusions should be listed clearly: supply-side and plumbing repairs, electrical work, backflow testing and any repair that needs a licence holder. The agreement should say how extra work is approved, typically by a written quote from the business or its licensed partner, and how a visit is rescheduled for weather or access problems. Do not describe the agreement as a licence, a certification or a guarantee of a leak-free system.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing and referral revenue
instructionSections.body: Price maintenance agreements from the work they contain. Build the price from the time for each visit, travel, the report time, a materials allowance for filters, washers and minor parts, and an allowance for the risk that a system in poor condition will need more attention. Set a separate price for extra in-scope work, such as a head replacement, and make sure the client sees the difference between the agreement and extra work. Referral work for licence holders is not revenue the business earns from its own labour. Where the business has an arrangement with a licence holder, record the arrangement in writing, state how the client will be billed for the licensed work, and make clear who carries out the work. Do not invent a commission or fee arrangement; check the state or territory rules first.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the report, the agreement and the pricing against the work done. A competent office or crew lead can show how each price was built, identify the exclusions, and explain how a referral is handed over to a licence holder. Escalate any report that describes licensed work as completed by the business, any agreement that includes supply-side or electrical work without a licensed partner, and any claim about water savings that the measurements do not support.

lessons.title: Landscape scope, design boundaries and approvals
learningOutcomes: Define the scope of a landscape job, separating design, supply, installation and maintenance.
Identify the approvals, permits and consents that a landscape project may need before work starts.
Recognise design elements that fall outside the business's scope, such as structures, retaining walls over the threshold, drainage connections and elements that need an engineer.
Record the scope, approvals and exclusions in a form the client signs and the crew can follow.

instructionSections.heading: What a landscape scope covers
instructionSections.body: Landscaping covers a wide range of work, from a simple garden refresh to a full backyard transformation with paving, planting, lighting, drainage and structures. The scope is the first and most important document, because it decides what is designed, what is supplied, what is installed and what is maintained afterwards. Separate these four parts in the quote. Design means preparing a layout, plant list and materials list. Supply means providing plants, stone, soil or hard materials. Installation means the physical work on site. Maintenance means the care after installation, usually for a set period. A client who understands the four parts is less likely to expect the business to do work it has not quoted, and the crew knows exactly what it is building. Confirm the scope in writing before any materials are ordered.

instructionSections.heading: Site information and design boundaries
instructionSections.body: Before designing, gather the site information. Measure the site and draw a plan with the boundary, the levels, the existing trees and plants, the existing structures, the services, the drainage paths, the access route and the orientation. Note the soil type and any visible drainage problems. Identify the features the client wants to keep. Design boundaries are the limits that the business will not cross without another party's input. A plant layout is generally within a landscape design. A new structure, a retaining wall above the threshold, an outdoor kitchen with gas, an electrical lighting circuit or a stormwater connection is not.

instructionSections.heading: Approvals, permits and consents
instructionSections.body: Many landscape projects need an approval before work begins, and a crew that starts without checking can face stop orders, forced removal of work and disputes with the client. Common approval points include building permits for new structures above the thresholds set by the local authority, consents for work that affects trees or native vegetation, approvals for works near public land, and strata or body corporate approval for common property. Two state positions were checked. In New South Wales, residential structural landscaping work valued over $5,000 in labour and materials, including GST, needs a contractor licence. The listed work includes retaining walls outside habitable buildings, whatever their material, and decks, pergolas and other non-habitable structures (page updated 23 June 2026). In Victoria, a retaining wall under 1 metre generally needs no building permit, unless it forms part of other building works or protects neighbouring land (practice note dated April 2022). Make the approval check part of the design stage, not a last-minute step. Record the authority, the application reference, the status and the person responsible for chasing it. Do not allow construction to start on an element until its approval is in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the scope and handling change
instructionSections.body: Write a scope document that lists the design items, the supply items, the installation items and the maintenance items, each with quantities and a clear description. List the exclusions, including the items that need approval or licensed work. Include the access arrangements, the working hours, the waste removal, the site protection and the payment milestones. Attach the plan and the plant or material list, and ask the client to sign or confirm them. Changes during the project are variations. A variation must be written, priced and approved before the extra work is done. Keep the variation with the original scope so that the handover can compare what was agreed with what was built.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the scope document against the site plan and the approvals list. A competent designer or crew leader can explain each part of the scope, identify the approvals that may be needed, name the exclusions and describe the variation process. Escalate any design element that appears to need an engineer, a building permit or a licence holder, any request to change a structure after approval, and any site where the services or the boundary are not clear.

lessons.title: Paving, edging and soft-landscape installation
learningOutcomes: Prepare a compacted base for paving with the right depth, falls and drainage for the surface and the load.
Lay pavers and install edge restraints so that the surface is level, stable and free from trip hazards.
Cut and handle pavers and stone with controls for silica dust, manual handling and noise.
Price paving and edging work by area, base depth, edge length, cutting, waste and access, rather than by a flat rate.

instructionSections.heading: Why the base decides the result
instructionSections.body: Most paving failures begin below the surface. A base that is too thin, poorly compacted or laid on soft ground will settle, rock and crack under foot and vehicle traffic. Good paving is a sequence of decisions: how deep the base must be for the expected load, how the surface will drain, how the edges will be held, and how the finished surface will feel underfoot. Paving is a higher-value service because it takes skill and materials, and because clients judge the result by its levels and finish. Spend the time on the base, check it before the bedding goes down, and record its depth and compaction.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing the base and drainage
instructionSections.body: Excavate to the depth for the planned base, allowing for the bedding layer and the paver thickness, and mark the finished levels with stakes or a string line. Remove soft and organic material, and check for services before any digging. Compact the subgrade in layers, using a plate compactor where it is suitable, and check the compaction at each stage. Build the base from a granular material in layers, compacting each layer, and check the depth as you go. Set falls so that water runs away from buildings and does not pool on the surface. The fall needed depends on the surface and the site, and the client's drainage path must be checked on the plan. A plate compactor is noisy and vibrates the body. The Safe Work Australia noise code (October 2018) sets the noise exposure standard at 85 dB(A) averaged over an 8-hour day, with a peak limit of 140 dB(C). It treats hearing protection as the last line of defence, after the noise source has been controlled, so use it and rotate workers where the procedure requires it.

instructionSections.heading: Laying pavers and edge restraints
instructionSections.body: Lay a thin bedding layer, screed it level to the stakes, and lay the pavers from a fixed starting line. Set each paver firmly, check its level with a straightedge, and keep the joints even. Fill the joints with the approved material, sweep it in, and compact the surface. Install edge restraints before the final pavers are placed, so that the edges do not move under load. Soft-landscape edging, such as timber or metal edging for garden beds, is set to a line and fixed firmly so that it does not heave or sink. Check that the finished surface has no trip hazard, such as a lip between two pavers, and that the falls are right. Re-check the levels after the first rain or wetting, and record any settlement.

instructionSections.heading: Cutting, handling and dust control
instructionSections.body: Pavers and stone are heavy, and cutting them creates both dust and noise. Plan the cutting before the work starts, so that most cuts are made in one controlled place rather than in the middle of the laying. For masonry and concrete, use wet cutting or local exhaust ventilation. Safe Work Australia's silica guidance (July 2024) treats wet processing and local exhaust ventilation as engineering controls, and gives the workplace exposure standard for respirable crystalline silica as 0.05 mg/m3, averaged over an 8-hour day. Wet cutting or exhaust does not by itself remove the need for a risk assessment, and where practicable the cutting should be done outdoors in a designated area away from other people. Where dry cutting is unavoidable, use an extraction system approved by the business and a respirator selected for the hazard. Keep bystanders and neighbours away from the cutting zone, and clean up slurry and waste with methods that do not raise dust. Lift pavers with a trolley or a clamp rather than carrying them by hand. Safe Work Australia's manual tasks guidance says a business must assess manual tasks and manage their risks as far as reasonably practicable (no date shown). Keep walkways clear of cut offcuts and slurry, which are slip and trip hazards.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing and quoting paving work
instructionSections.body: Paving is a higher-value service because it needs skill, materials and time to prepare the base. Price it from the components: the area, the base depth and material, the bedding and jointing material, the edge restraints, the cutting and waste, the access and the time for levels and checks. Quote soft-landscape edging separately from the paving, because its length and fixing method differ. Give the client a clear quote showing these components, and explain what is included in the base depth. Do not promise a surface that will never settle, because ground conditions and drainage affect the result. Record the quote and the client's approval before materials are ordered, and use the business's pricing method and approval steps.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the base, the levels, the cutting controls and the quote. A competent installer can show the base depth and compaction record, explain how falls were set, identify a trip hazard, describe the dust controls used and explain how the quote was built. Escalate any soft ground or unexpected service found during excavation, any level or fall that cannot be achieved on the approved plan, any cutting that cannot be controlled, and any request to change the surface or the drainage path after approval.

lessons.title: Retaining walls and structural boundaries (refer to engineer)
learningOutcomes: Identify the features of a site that signal a retaining wall or structural element, such as a level change, a load from a neighbour's ground or a surcharge from a driveway.
Explain why a wall that holds back soil can become a structural matter that needs an engineer, and why height alone is not the only test.
Apply the boundary between landscape work the business may carry out and structural work that must be referred.
Write a referral that describes the site, the drawing needs and the client's decision points without designing the structure.

instructionSections.heading: Why retaining walls are a structural matter
instructionSections.body: A retaining wall holds back soil that would otherwise move. It has to resist the pressure of the soil behind it, any water that builds up behind it, and any load placed on the ground above it, such as a driveway, a car, a fence or a neighbour's building. A wall can look modest and still fail. A poorly drained wall can fill with water and push over. A wall that is built on soft ground can settle and tilt. A wall that holds up a neighbour's ground can collapse onto their property. For these reasons, retaining walls are one of the clearest examples of a boundary between landscape design and structural work. The business may plan the planting and finishes, but the structural design and the decision about whether the wall is safe belong to a qualified engineer or other authorised person.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising a structural element on site
instructionSections.body: Look at the site before quoting anything. A level change of any size, a slope that the client wants to flatten, a new terrace, a raised bed with a heavy retaining edge, a wall that supports a path or a driveway, and a wall that is close to a building or a boundary all need a closer look. Check whether the ground behind a wall belongs to the client or a neighbour. Check for surcharge, which is any load placed near the top of the wall, such as a car, a shed, a fence or a stockpile of soil. Look for water: downpipes, paths, overland flow and the drainage behind any wall. Note any existing wall, its condition, its materials and any cracking, leaning or bulging. Record these facts on the site plan. Do not assume a wall is safe because it has stood for a long time.

instructionSections.heading: Where the boundary sits
instructionSections.body: The boundary depends on the jurisdiction and on the wall's height, location, load and purpose. In Victoria, the Victorian Building Authority practice note dated April 2022 says a retaining wall under 1 metre needs no building permit, unless it forms part of other building work or protects neighbouring land. In New South Wales, a retaining wall built from any material, sitting outside a habitable building, needs a contractor licence when the residential structural landscaping is valued over $5,000 in labour and materials, including GST (page updated 23 June 2026). In Brisbane, building approval is needed for a fence more than 2 metres above natural ground, and the council counts retaining walls within fence height (page undated). Even where no permit or licence is needed, a wall that holds a neighbour's ground, carries a surcharge, sits near a footing or changes drainage may need an engineer's design. Treat the boundary as a referral point, not a number to remember. This lesson does not grant a building, engineering or structural licence or approval.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the referral and communicating with the client
instructionSections.body: A referral should give the engineer or building surveyor what they need without designing the structure yourself. Describe the site location, the level change, the height as measured on site, the ground behind and below the wall, any surcharge, the drainage observations, the neighbour's position, the existing wall condition and the client's purpose for the wall. Attach the photographs taken with consent and the site plan. State clearly what the business proposes to do outside the structural element, such as planting or paving, and what it will not do. Tell the client in writing that the wall requires a referral, that the referral may cost money and take time, and that the business will not start the wall until the structural advice and any approval are in place. Record the referral, the date and the client's decision.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the referral and the scope. A competent designer can show where the structural boundary sits on the site plan, explain the features that triggered the referral, and describe what the business will and will not do. Escalate any wall that is cracked, leaning or bulging, any wall that holds a neighbour's ground, any wall near a building or a footing, and any client request to start construction before the referral is complete.

lessons.title: Planting, soil preparation and establishment care
learningOutcomes: Assess a site's soil, drainage and light conditions and decide the preparation needed before planting.
Select plants that suit the site and check them against local restrictions, including declared or restricted species.
Plant to the correct depth and spacing, and protect the root zone during handling and placement.
Plan and record an establishment care period, and price planting work for its labour, materials and aftercare.

instructionSections.heading: Why planting succeeds or fails below ground
instructionSections.body: The soil may be compacted builders' fill, waterlogged clay, sand that drains too quickly, or a mix of rubble and topsoil. The drainage may send water toward a building or hold it around the roots. The site may get more sun or shade than the plant can tolerate. Preparing the site and matching the plant to it is the largest single factor in how well a planting establishes. It is also the basis for higher-value planting work, because a client who sees healthy plants after the establishment period recommends the business. Start with the site, not the plant list.

instructionSections.heading: Soil assessment and preparation
instructionSections.body: Dig a test hole in several places and look at the soil profile. Note the colour, the texture, the depth of topsoil and any layers of rubble, clay or gravel. Fill the hole with water and see how fast it drains. Feel the soil: a sandy soil falls apart in the hand, while a clay soil forms a ribbon. Test the pH and nutrient levels only if the business has a test method and the result will change the plan. Prepare the soil to suit the plants: loosen compacted ground, remove rubble, and mix in organic material where the plant needs it. Do not add large amounts of material that will create a different soil in the hole from the soil around it, because the roots will not spread. Where drainage is poor, the plan may need a raised bed or a different plant list, and that decision is recorded with the client.

instructionSections.heading: Selecting plants and checking restrictions
instructionSections.body: Select plants for the site conditions: the light, the drainage, the wind, the space available at maturity and the maintenance the client is willing to accept. Use local plant lists and native plant references where they exist for the region. Check that the plants are not declared or restricted weeds in the state or territory, and do not supply or plant a species that the local rules restrict. Check the plant's mature size against the space, the distance from buildings, services and boundaries, and the expected root spread. Where a tree is planned near a building, service or boundary, record the check and refer any question about the root zone or the tree's future height to a qualified arborist. Record the plant list with the quantities, the sizes and the source of each plant.

instructionSections.heading: Planting technique and handling
instructionSections.body: Keep the root ball intact and the plant upright from the moment it leaves the container until it is in the ground. Water the container thoroughly before removing the plant, so that the root ball holds together. Dig a hole about two to three times the width of the root ball, but no deeper than the root ball, so the plant sits on firm ground rather than loose soil. Roughen the sides of the hole if the soil is smooth and compacted, so that roots can grow out. Set the plant so that the top of the root ball sits at the same level as the surrounding soil, and check the level from two sides. Backfill with the prepared soil, firming it gently with the hands rather than stamping, and water in to settle the soil around the roots. Use mechanical aids or a team lift for large containers, and keep the lift low and close to the body to protect the back. Do not pull a plant by its stem, and do not leave the roots exposed to wind or sun while the planting continues.

instructionSections.heading: Establishment care, pricing and records
instructionSections.body: New plantings need regular water and checks until the roots spread into the surrounding soil. Write the schedule in the planting record: the watering frequency, the check dates, the mulch top-up, the pruning of damaged growth and the date for the first review. Price planting work from the labour, the materials, the soil preparation, the plant supply, the mulch and the aftercare visits. Keep the plant supply price separate from the planting labour, and explain any replacement policy in writing, without promising that every plant will survive. Keep the planting record with the plant list, the date, the preparation carried out, the mulch used and the client's sign-off.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the soil record, the plant list and the planting depth. A competent planter can show the soil test result, explain how the planting level was set, identify a plant that is too large for the space or in the wrong position, and describe the establishment care the client needs to provide. Escalate any planting near a service or building that needs a qualified check, any plant that is restricted or unidentified, any plant that is root-bound or damaged on arrival, and any request to plant in a way that conflicts with the preparation or the drainage plan.

lessons.title: Turf species, mowing height and lawn health
learningOutcomes: Identify the common turf types on a site and state how their growth habit affects mowing.
Set a mowing height appropriate to the species, season and site conditions.
Recognise early signs of poor lawn health, including compaction, thatch build-up, water stress, pests and disease.
Describe safe mower operation on slopes, around obstacles and near people and pets.

instructionSections.heading: Turf is a living surface
instructionSections.body: A lawn is a planted surface that responds to every cut, every walk across it and every change in water and nutrition. The crew who mows it is the most frequent visitor, so the crew's habits shape the result. A lawn that is cut too short or with blunt blades becomes stressed, thins out and invites weeds. A lawn that is never cut becomes uneven and the client expects a rescue. Good lawn work starts with knowing what the turf is, what height it should be kept at and what it looks like when it is healthy. Identify the species before you mow, because two lawns of similar appearance may need very different heights and care.

instructionSections.heading: Identifying the common turf types
instructionSections.body: Lawns across Australia commonly contain warm-season grasses such as couch, kikuyu, buffalo and zoysia, and cool-season grasses such as perennial ryegrass and tall fescue. Warm-season grasses are usually active in warmer months and may go dormant in cold periods. Cool-season grasses are usually most active in cooler months. Many lawns are mixed, and weeds can be mistaken for turf. Look at the leaf width, colour, runner pattern, stolon and rhizome habit, and the seedhead if present. Check the client's notes for the species they have been told they have. If you cannot confirm the species, record the uncertainty and mow at a height that does not stress the turf. The species list in this draft is a working guide and is not verified against a named reference. Confirm it with a local turf guide or a qualified turf advisor before relying on it for a height recommendation.

instructionSections.heading: Setting the mowing height
instructionSections.body: The mowing height is the most important single setting on a lawn mower. Cutting too low removes too much leaf, weakens the roots and exposes the soil to heat. Adjust the height gradually when a lawn has been neglected, and do not drop it by a large amount in one pass. Set the height on a level surface and check it on each wheel. Note that high-traffic lawns and shaded lawns usually need a different height from open sunny lawns.

instructionSections.heading: Lawn health checks
instructionSections.body: Walk the lawn before mowing and look for signs of stress. Compaction shows as soil that is hard to push a screwdriver into, water that pools after rain and thin grass in paths. Thatch is a layer of dead and living stems and roots between the soil and the leaf, and it shows as a spongy surface and brown patches. Water stress shows as blue-grey leaves that do not spring back and dry patches that remain after watering. Pests such as lawn grubs and caterpillars cause patchy dieback that can be pulled up like a loose carpet. Disease shows as rings, spots or discoloured patches that are not explained by dogs, traffic or fuel spills. Record what you see, and do not diagnose a pest or disease without a clear identification. Refer the question to the client and to a qualified advisor, and do not apply a product under this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Mower safety on the lawn
instructionSections.body: Mowers can throw objects, cut feet and fingers, tip on slopes and cause injury when refuelled or restarted with the blade still turning. Walk the lawn before you mow and remove sticks, stones, pet waste, toys, hoses and cords. Keep children and pets indoors or well away from the mowing zone. On slopes, follow the manufacturer's guidance and the business's slope rule, and mow across the face rather than up and down where the machine is unstable. Do not mow on wet or very steep ground where the mower can slip. Clean the blade and the deck when you have finished. Refuel only when the engine is off and cool, and keep fuel away from the mower's hot parts. Switch off and disconnect or remove the battery before clearing a blockage or checking the blade. Use eye and hearing protection and footwear with grip.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the height, the finish and the safety set-up. A competent worker can name the species they have identified, explain how they set the height, point to the signs of stress they checked for and describe the safe operation of the mower on a slope. Escalate any lawn that shows widespread dieback, any suspected pest or disease, any lawn where the species is uncertain and the height cannot be confirmed, and any slope that the mower cannot safely work.

lessons.title: Edging, aeration and dethatching
learningOutcomes: Explain what edging, aeration and dethatching achieve and when each is the right service.
Set up and operate edging, aeration and dethatching equipment safely, with the hazards controlled.
Identify the lawn conditions that make these services unsuitable, such as drought stress, flooding or heavy traffic damage.
Quote and price the services for their labour, equipment and disposal content rather than for the area alone.

instructionSections.heading: What the three services do
instructionSections.body: Edging, aeration and dethatching are three distinct services that improve a lawn in different ways. Edging cuts a clean line between lawn and beds, paths, driveways and kerbs, which improves the look of the property and reduces the amount of hand trimming the client pays for later. Aeration creates holes or slits in the soil to relieve compaction and let air, water and nutrients reach the roots. Dethatching removes the layer of dead and living stems and roots that builds up above the soil. Each service has its own timing and its own risks. A lawn that needs aeration may not need dethatching, and vice versa. Diagnose the lawn before quoting any of them, using the health checks in the mowing lesson.

instructionSections.heading: When each service is the right answer
instructionSections.body: Edging is the right answer when the lawn edge has spread into beds, paths or kerbs, or when the line has become soft and uneven. It is usually done after mowing so that the edge is visible. Aeration is the right answer when the soil is compacted, water runs off or pools, the surface is hard, or the lawn is heavily used. Dethatching is the right answer when a spongy layer of thatch is visible, when water does not soak in, or when the lawn looks yellow and thin over a layer of dead material. Do not aerate or dethatch a lawn that is in drought stress, that has been flooded and not yet recovered, or that is dormant. Stress makes the lawn slower to recover and can cause more damage. Record the reason for the recommendation, and tell the client when the service is not appropriate and why.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment and method
instructionSections.body: Use equipment that suits the area and the lawn. Edgers can be powered or hand tools, and both need a guard, a sharp blade and firm footing. Keep the blade a safe distance from fences, pipes and irrigation fittings, and mark them before starting. Aerators remove small plugs of soil or push tines into the soil, and they can throw soil and debris. Set the depth and spacing for the lawn, and walk the lawn in straight, overlapping passes. Check for buried services and sprinkler heads before using tines deeper than the topsoil. Dethatchers use tines or blades to lift thatch to the surface, and they can throw debris. Set the depth so that the blades remove thatch without cutting into the soil and roots. Work in a logical pattern and stop when the lawn is recovering poorly. Collect and remove the material, which is part of the cost and must be planned for.

instructionSections.heading: Safety, services and waste
instructionSections.body: All three services involve moving machinery and flying debris. Wear eye protection, hearing protection, sturdy footwear and gloves suitable for handling soil and debris. Clear the area of people, pets and vehicles. Mark sprinkler heads, valves, cables and any service you can see or find using the business's method, and do not use deep tines or blades near a service. If a service is damaged or exposed, stop, make the area safe and refer the repair to the licence holder for that service. The removed material from dethatching and aeration is organic waste and may contain debris, weeds or seed. Follow the waste lesson and the biosecurity lesson when choosing a disposal route, and do not allow the material to go into a drain.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing and quoting
instructionSections.body: These services are higher-value because they require skill, equipment and disposal, but the value is in the work, not the area alone. Price for the labour and equipment time, the access and setup, the depth and intensity of the service, the waste to be removed, and any follow-up needed, such as topdressing or a second pass. Quote the service separately from routine mowing so that the client understands what they are buying. Explain that the lawn may need recovery time and may need more than one service. Record the quote, the scope, the exclusions and the client's approval in writing. Do not promise a result, and do not quote a price that is not approved for the business. Use the pricing method in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the diagnosis, the depth, the finish and the waste. A competent worker can explain why a service was chosen, show the depth setting, identify the services they marked and describe the aftercare they recommended. Escalate any lawn that is in stress, any damaged or exposed service, any suspected pest or disease, and any job where the scope or depth is larger than the approved quote.

lessons.title: Lawn weed and fertiliser product boundaries
learningOutcomes: Describe the boundary between lawn maintenance, which the crew may do under the business's scope, and product application, which may need a licence or authority.
Read a product label and safety data sheet and identify the conditions of use that apply.
Store, handle and record weed and fertiliser products safely, including spill and drift control.
Refer any weed-control or fertiliser task that is outside the business's authority.

instructionSections.heading: Why product rules matter on a lawn
instructionSections.body: Weed control and fertiliser are among the most common requests from lawn clients, and they are also the easiest to get wrong. A product that is safe on the label can still harm people, pets, waterways, neighbouring gardens and the lawn itself if it is mixed wrongly, applied in wind, sprayed near a boundary or applied at the wrong rate. In many jurisdictions, applying some pesticides or herbicides to other people's property for payment is regulated, and the rules may depend on the type of product, the method and the setting. This lesson teaches you to recognise the boundary, read the product information and stop where the task is outside the business's authority. It does not grant any licence, certificate or authority to apply a regulated product.

instructionSections.heading: Where the boundary sits
instructionSections.body: Maintenance tasks such as mowing, edging, raking and watering are normal lawn work and are described in other lessons. Product application is different. Applying a weed killer, a selective herbicide, a broadleaf treatment, a fertiliser or a soil amendment is a separate task with its own risks. New South Wales has the clearest official position checked so far. The NSW Environment Protection Authority's fact sheet, dated August 2018, says that people who spray weeds commercially have needed a ground-applicator licence since 1 July 2018, and it places routine garden and lawn maintenance, including bindii spraying, within an amenity horticulture exemption. Check the rules where the job is located before any product is applied, and record the rule that applies. If the business is not authorised for product application in that location, offer the client the mowing and maintenance work only, and refer the product work to a licence holder who is authorised for it.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the label and the safety data sheet
instructionSections.body: Read the product label before opening the container. Look for the active ingredient, the target weeds, the approved crops or settings, the rate of use, the mixing instructions, the protective equipment, the re-entry period, the pets and people restrictions, the buffer distance from waterways and the storage and disposal instructions. Read the safety data sheet for the hazards, first-aid measures, fire-fighting, spill response and storage requirements. If the label and the safety data sheet do not agree, stop and refer. Do not use a product for a purpose the label does not cover. Keep the label and the safety data sheet with the product, and make them accessible to the crew at the job site. Record the product name, batch, rate and the area treated on the job record.

instructionSections.heading: Handling, storage and drift control
instructionSections.body: Store products in their original labelled containers, in a locked, ventilated and dry store, away from food, animals, children, heat and incompatible products. Never decant products into drink containers. Mix only the amount needed, and mix in a well-ventilated area, following the label. Apply products only in calm conditions, and check the forecast for wind. Keep spray drift away from neighbours, waterways, gardens and vehicles, and maintain the label's buffer distances. Keep people and pets off the treated area for the period stated on the label. Clean equipment after use, and dispose of rinse water and empty containers only as the label and the approved waste process allow. For any spill, stop, contain the spill with absorbent material, keep people back and inform the supervisor. Do not wash spilt product into a drain.

instructionSections.heading: Fertiliser and nutrient run-off
instructionSections.body: Fertilisers are usually applied to lawns to supply nutrients, and they can be a pollutant when they reach waterways. Apply fertiliser at the rate and in the manner that the product label specifies, and avoid application before heavy rain or onto hard surfaces, paths and drains. Sweep any spilt fertiliser back onto the lawn or into a suitable container, and do not wash it into the stormwater system. Keep fertiliser stored separately from weed products and in a dry place. Record the product, the rate and the area. Fertiliser recommendations should follow the client's soil and lawn assessment, not a standard schedule alone.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the product decision, the label, the record and the handling. A competent worker can name the product, state its conditions of use, identify whether the job is inside or outside the business's authority in that location, show the storage and the spill kit, and explain how they would manage drift. Escalate any request for a product that is outside the business's authority, any label that is unclear, any spill, and any product that is found without a label or safety data sheet.

lessons.title: Lawn quoting, recurring schedules and seasonal calendar
learningOutcomes: Build a lawn quote that separates recurring mowing from seasonal services and one-off work.
Design a recurring schedule that matches the lawn's growth, the site's access and the client's expectations.
Use a seasonal calendar that sets out when each service is appropriate and when it should be deferred.
Explain the scope, exclusions and variation rules to the client in writing.

instructionSections.heading: How recurring lawn work creates volume
instructionSections.body: Recurring lawn work is the base of many lawn businesses because it creates predictable volume. A client who signs up for a fortnightly mow, or a weekly mow in peak season, gives the business regular income and a steady route. Volume grows when the business adds seasonal services such as edging, aeration, dethatching and topdressing, and when it sells them to the same client in the right season. The key is to design the offer so that each service fits the lawn's needs at that time of year. A calendar that sells the wrong service at the wrong time damages trust and leads to disputes. Build the offer from what the lawn needs, not from what is easiest to sell.

instructionSections.heading: Quoting the recurring service
instructionSections.body: Quote the recurring mowing separately from the seasonal services. The recurring quote should state the frequency, the mowing height, the edging included, the waste removal, the access, the site area and the exclusions. Price the recurring visit for the time, the equipment, the travel, the waste and the risk controls, not for the area alone. Adjust for difficult sites such as slopes, many obstacles, long travel or restricted access, and record the reason for the adjustment. Exclusions should be listed in writing, including product application unless the business is authorised for it at that location, tree work, irrigation repairs and any work at height. Use the business's pricing method, shown in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}, and get written approval through {{business:pricing.quoting_approval}} before the schedule starts.

instructionSections.heading: Building the seasonal calendar
instructionSections.body: A seasonal calendar sets out the services that suit each part of the year for the species and the region. Use the species identified on the job record, and use the local climate and the client's site conditions. In general, the calendar should show when mowing frequency rises and falls, when edging is done, when aeration or dethatching is appropriate, when fertiliser is considered, and when weed control is considered under the product rules. Mark the periods when services should be deferred, such as drought, flood recovery or dormancy. The calendar is a planning tool and is not a guarantee.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the schedule and the variation rules
instructionSections.body: Write the schedule with the dates or the frequency, the services included, the services that require separate approval, and the conditions under which a visit may be moved or cancelled. Include the weather rule: when rain or extreme heat makes a visit unsafe or damaging, the business may reschedule, and the client is told in advance where possible. Set out the variation rule in writing. A change to the schedule, the area or the service is a variation that needs approval before the work starts and a price change recorded. A recurring client who asks for an extra service mid-season should receive a written variation, not a verbal add-on. Review the schedule with the client at least once a season, and record the review.

instructionSections.heading: Client communication and records
instructionSections.body: Explain the offer in plain language at the first meeting, and check that the client understands what is included, what is seasonal, what is excluded and what needs approval. Use the same terms in the quote, the calendar and the schedule so that the client does not receive three different descriptions. Keep a record of every conversation that changes the scope, including the date, who was present and what was agreed. Store the calendar and schedule in the client file, and give the client a copy. A clear, consistent record protects the business if a dispute arises about what was promised, and it helps the crew arrive prepared for each visit.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the quote, the schedule and the calendar against the job record. A competent office or crew leader can show how the recurring quote was built, explain the exclusions, describe the seasonal calendar and identify what must be approved before work starts. Escalate any quote where the scope is unclear, any request for product application without confirmed authority, any schedule that conflicts with the lawn's condition, and any client who disputes a variation.

lessons.title: Locksmith licence scope and restricted work
learningOutcomes: Describe the locksmith licence position recorded for New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria, and what is still unresolved.
Identify lock work that is restricted or referred under the state position.
Refuse or refer locksmith work where the licence position is not established for the state.

instructionSections.heading: The position differs by state
instructionSections.body: Locksmith work is licensed differently in each state, so the state position must be checked before any lock work is accepted. In New South Wales, locksmiths must be licensed through the NSW Police Force Security Licensing and Enforcement Directorate (SLED). The SLED locksmith FAQ states that a Class 2C licence applies to locksmiths (page shows no date). In Queensland, the Queensland Government security equipment installer licence page (last updated 21 October 2026) says a locksmith generally needs a licence, and that retail key cutting is exempt. The Security Providers Act 1993 sets the offences for carrying on security work without a licence (version dated 9 December 2016 in the version reviewed, so check the current version). In Victoria, the Victoria Police private security page (last updated 26 October 2026) lists the security equipment installer licence and does not mention locksmiths or key cutting. Refer Victorian locksmith and key-cutting work to the Licensing and Regulation Division before accepting it.

instructionSections.heading: Restricted and referred work
instructionSections.body: Treat lock work as restricted until the state position is confirmed for the job. In Queensland, taking out and refitting household locks needs a licence, except where the job forms part of new construction, repairs or renovations to the building. Fitting basic security items, such as household locks, as part of building works is exempt, but that exemption does not cover later upkeep, replacement or removal of those items once the building work is over. Where the position is unclear, refer the work and record why. Do not accept lock work for a company or business until its licence status has been checked with the regulator. In Victoria, do not accept locksmith work until the Licensing and Regulation Division has given a written position.

lessons.title: Lock types, mechanisms and security-grade selection
learningOutcomes: Identify the main lock types and mechanisms and their typical use in residential doors.
Select a lock grade that matches the door, the frame and the risk, using the manufacturer data.
Identify when a lock must be referred because it is a fire door, an access system or a master-keyed installation.

instructionSections.heading: Lock types and what each one does
instructionSections.body:
A residential door usually has two kinds of lock working together. A latch is a spring-loaded bolt that holds the door closed when it is pulled shut, and it releases when the handle is pressed. It gives convenience, but it does little to resist force. A deadlock, which is also called a deadbolt, is a solid bolt that is thrown by a key or a turn-knob. It holds the door against pressure and is the part that resists a forced entry. Many doors combine a latch in the handle set with a separate deadlock, and the two should be considered together.

The mechanism is only one part of the lock. A cylinder is the keyed part that operates the bolt. Cylinders differ in their keying system, the number and type of pins or other components inside, and their resistance to picking and drilling. Lock bodies are fitted into the door in different ways. A mortice lock sits in a pocket cut into the edge of the door. A rim lock is surface-mounted. A cylinder-only lock is a cylinder that works with a separate bolt in the same door.

A lock mechanism, its cylinder, the strike plate and the door frame all share the load of a forced entry. A strong cylinder in a weak frame does not give a secure door, because the force travels into the frame, and the strike plate and its fixings are where the door gives way. Check the whole assembly, not one component alone.

instructionSections.heading: Measuring, specifying and selecting by grade
instructionSections.body: Select a lock grade that the manufacturer rates for the door, the frame and the risk. The grade ratings and the test standards are set out in the manufacturer's data. Record the model, the grade rating as stated, and the manufacturer data reference. Before you fit anything, measure the door and check the lock specification. Measure the door thickness. Measure the backset, which is the distance from the edge of the door to the centre of the lock spindle or bore. Many residential locks are listed for a particular backset, and for example a lock may be listed for a 60 mm or a 70 mm backset; the lock you have must match the measurement you take, and the example values are not a rule for any product. Check the cylinder length against the door thickness and the lock specification. A cylinder that is too long can protrude or foul the mechanism, and one that is too short may not engage properly. Check the frame and the strike plate. The strike plate and its fixings must reach solid timber or a fixing rated for the frame material. Screws into soft or split timber, or into a frame that is loose in the wall, do not give the grade the lock is rated for. Where a frame is weak, recommend remediation and quote it separately rather than fitting a high-grade cylinder that the frame cannot support. Where the door is a fire door, the lock and its hardware are part of the fire-resistance system. Refer the work as set out in “Door installation: frame, hinge and fire-door boundary”, and do not treat a fire door as an ordinary door for lock selection.

instructionSections.heading: Keys, master keying and access systems
instructionSections.body: Some lock jobs are more than a single lock. A master-keyed system uses several cylinders that open with a common key, and the key plan decides who can open which door. An access system uses cards, codes or electronic readers to control entry. Both need a documented key plan or access design, a record of who holds each key or credential, and an agreed process for lost keys and changes. Refer these installations rather than fitting them as standard hardware, unless the scope and the licence position for that work are confirmed for the job. Record the key numbers and the people issued with them, and check the licence position before any work begins.

lessons.title: Door installation: frame, hinge and fire-door boundary
learningOutcomes: Check a frame and opening for square, plumb and fixing before a door is hung.
Identify the boundary between standard door installation and fire-door work that must be referred.

instructionSections.heading: Frame and opening before the door
instructionSections.body:
A door can only work as well as the frame and opening it hangs in. Before the door is offered up, check that the opening is square, plumb and level. Measure the diagonals of the opening, because a difference between them shows that the opening is out of square. Check the head and the sides for plumb, and the sill or floor for level. Check that the clearances around the door will be even at the hinge side, the latch side and the head. A frame that is racked, twisted or loose causes a door to bind, fail to latch, rub at one corner and wear the hinges early.

Fix the frame to solid structure with fixings suited to the wall material. In timber framing, that means fixings into the studs or noggins; in masonry, it means fixings rated for the masonry and the load. Packing shims help set the frame square and plumb, but they do not hold a frame in place on their own. Pack behind each fixing point so the frame is supported where it is fixed, and then secure the fixings. Check the frame again after the fixings are tightened, because a frame can move as the screws are driven.

Before you hang the door, check its size against the opening, the hinge positions against the frame and the handing of the door. A door hung the wrong way round will not latch in the frame, and a door that is cut to fit an out-of-square opening will look wrong and fail early.

instructionSections.heading: Hanging, checking and handing over
instructionSections.body: Hang the door, then check its movement through the full range. Look for even gaps at the hinge side, the latch side and the head. Check that the door opens and closes without binding, that the latch engages the strike cleanly and that the door does not drop or rub at the hinges. Where the door has a closer or a self-closing device, check that it closes the door fully, without slamming and without leaving the door open. Check the lock and any hardware fitted at the same time, and confirm that the lock operates from both sides as the lock type allows. Record the door type, the frame material, the fixings used and the checks made. Hand over with the client's sign-off on the completed work, and state the exclusions in writing.

instructionSections.heading: The fire-door boundary
instructionSections.body: A fire-rated door, its frame, its seals, its hinges and its hardware form part of a fire-safety system.
