The rating is built into the whole assembly, so a door that is fitted in a fire-rated opening must carry the rating required for that opening. The Queensland Fire Department information sheet (version 09/2025) states that fire doors must be self-closing and latching, and that hardware such as closers, handles, locks and vision panels is part of the fire-resistance rating and must be tested and approved by a registered testing authority. The sheet also says that licensed carpenters or joiners can install and repair fire doors, but that only a person holding the Queensland passive fire protection licence for fire doors and fire shutters can certify, inspect or test them (Queensland Fire Department, fire doors information sheet; version 09/2025). This course takes a stricter position than the minimum that the Queensland sheet describes. Refer any fire-rated opening where the rating cannot be confirmed, and refer any work that would change a rated component, such as the hinges, seals or closer of an existing fire door, to a competent specialist. Do not hang a door in a fire-rated opening that does not carry the required rating. Record the door's rating marking where it is visible on the door or the frame, and if the rating cannot be confirmed, refer the job and record that it could not be confirmed.

lessons.title: Key control, records and client identity verification
learningOutcomes: Keep a key register that records each key, its holder and every issue and return.
Verify the client's identity and authority before any key is cut, issued or a lock is changed.
Store key records securely and limit access to them.

instructionSections.heading: Key control is a record, not a memory
instructionSections.body: Every key that is cut, issued, changed or returned must be recorded. A key register holds the key or lock identifier, the holder, the date of issue and return, and the authority under which it was issued. Without it, nobody can say who holds a key to a property, and a lost key becomes a security problem for the whole site. Keep the register current, and reconcile it at the end of each job.

instructionSections.heading: Verify identity and authority
instructionSections.body: Before a key is cut or a lock is changed, verify that the person asking holds the authority to ask. Check identification against the property record, and confirm that the owner or the authorised manager has approved the work in writing. A phone call that cannot be verified is not sufficient. Refuse the job where identity or authority cannot be verified.

lessons.title: Massage scope, contraindications and referral
learningOutcomes: Explain what this lesson does and does not grant, including the limits of any health or therapy authority
Apply a contraindication check from the approved list before any session, and postpone or refer where a contraindication is present
Describe the referral step, and the point at which a client must be advised to seek urgent medical care

instructionSections.heading: What this lesson grants, and what it does not
instructionSections.body: Completing this lesson does not register you, does not give a licence to massage, and does not give clinical, diagnostic or therapeutic authority. It teaches a safe method for deciding whether a session is suitable and when to refer. In Victoria, the Department of Health's list of services that must register under the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008 names beauty therapy, cosmetic applications, colonic irrigation, hairdressing, skin penetration and tattooing, and does not name massage (page updated 22 May 2026). In the ACT, the government's skin penetration page lists massage as one of the services that need no infection control licence but must still follow the 2005 infection control Code of Practice for office practices and other community-based services (no date shown). In Queensland, Gold Coast City Council lists massage therapy among services that do not require a licence (no date shown). Your state and council position must be checked and recorded before the first visit.

instructionSections.heading: Contraindications: a check, not a diagnosis
instructionSections.body: A contraindication is a reason a session should not go ahead as planned, or should be changed or postponed. The therapist's job is to identify the reason, not to decide the medical cause. Typical items on a massage contraindication list include recent surgery or injury, a bleeding or clotting condition, an infection or skin condition at the treatment site, a recent deep-vein or blood-clot concern, certain heart or circulation conditions, pregnancy, and medications that change how the body responds to pressure or heat. These examples come from general massage practice and are not a confirmed legal list. The business's approved contraindication list is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the therapist must use that list rather than a memory of it.

instructionSections.heading: Referral and when to stop
instructionSections.body: Where a client's answers show a contraindication, the therapist should postpone or change the session and recommend that the client speaks to a general practitioner or the relevant medical professional before any further session. The therapist must not tell the client what the condition is, must not advise on medication, and must not promise that a session will help a condition. During a session, stop at once if the client reports chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness, sudden severe pain, numbness, or any sign of a serious reaction. Keep the client safe, do not leave them alone if they are unwell, and advise them to seek urgent medical care. Contact the emergency contact recorded in {{business:safety.emergency_contact}} and the escalation contact in {{business:safety.escalation_contact}}, and record the incident. Do not resume the session.

lessons.title: Consent, draping and client privacy
learningOutcomes: Obtain and record consent for each part of a massage, including the right to stop at any time
Drape the client so that privacy and warmth are kept, and only the area being treated is exposed
Store and share client information in a way that protects the client's privacy

instructionSections.heading: Consent for the whole session and for each area
instructionSections.body: Consent for massage is an ongoing agreement, not a single signature at the start. The client agrees to the session as a whole, and may also agree or decline particular areas, pressure levels or techniques. Explain what the session involves, the areas to be treated, the oils or products used, and the client's right to stop at any time without giving a reason. Record the agreement on the intake form, and check again before any area that was not covered in the original agreement. Where a client is unable to give consent, for example because of a disability or a medical condition, the business procedure must say how consent is obtained and from whom. The approved consent process is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}. The business must check the consent wording and process for each location.

instructionSections.heading: Draping and privacy during the session
instructionSections.body: Draping means covering the client with towels or linen so that only the area being treated is exposed. Good draping protects the client's dignity and keeps them warm, and it also keeps the therapist's focus on the area. Explain the draping method before the session, and ask the client to say if they are uncomfortable. Keep the rest of the body covered at all times. Do not leave the room with a client partly undressed. Where other people are in the home, ask the client whether they want the door closed, a chaperone present, or another arrangement, and record the answer. Check the client's preference for a therapist of a particular gender or with a particular background, and record it where the business policy allows it. Where the client is a child, the consent and presence of a parent or guardian must follow the business procedure, and the children's-service rules in “In-home safety, lone-work and room setup” apply.

instructionSections.heading: Client information and privacy at home
instructionSections.body: A massage therapist holds information that can be personal and sensitive: health history, medication, and the address and access details of the client's home. This information must be kept secure, used only for the service, and not shared with anyone without the client's agreement, unless the law or a health emergency requires it. Store paper records in a locked case, and keep digital records on a password-protected device. Do not leave intake forms in a client's home or in a vehicle where others can read them. The business should follow the privacy approach in the shared privacy lesson “Privacy, security and customer property” and check the local rule before relying on it.

lessons.title: Linen, oil and hygiene management
learningOutcomes: Choose between single-use and reusable linen for each type of session, and explain the cost and hygiene effect of the choice
Store, dispense and handle massage oils and creams using the safety data sheet and the approved procedure
Identify two cost reductions that do not reduce hygiene or the required steps

instructionSections.heading: Linen: single-use, reusable and the cost of each
instructionSections.body: A massage session uses sheets, towels and bolster covers that touch the client's skin. Single-use linen costs more per session but removes the laundering step and reduces the risk of carrying contamination between clients. Reusable linen costs less per session, but the business must launder it to a standard and keep it separate from used linen until it is washed. The choice is a cost decision, but it must not reduce hygiene. The business should record the method it uses for each type of session. The approved laundering method, including the temperature and detergent recorded on the linen supplier's instructions, is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instructionSections.heading: Massage oils and creams: the safety data sheet governs
instructionSections.body: Massage oils, creams and lotions are products, and each one needs a safety data sheet. WorkSafe Victoria's safety data sheet page (reviewed 30/07/2022) requires an up-to-date SDS to be held for every product, with access open to workers, contractors and emergency responders. Its safety basics page (reviewed 30/07/2022) says employers need a register listing every hazardous substance on site, and that workplace risks to health and safety need evaluating. Whether a massage oil counts as a hazardous substance depends on its ingredients and the classification on its safety data sheet. The GHS labelling duty on WorkSafe's GHS page (reviewed 22/11/2022) falls on manufacturers and importing suppliers, so the business should check the label on each product it receives. Store products as the safety data sheet and the label direct. Decant only what is needed for each client into a clean dispenser, and never return used oil to the main bottle.

instructionSections.heading: Where cost reduction is safe
instructionSections.body: Cost reduction in a mobile massage business is worth doing where it does not change the steps that protect the client. Buying oil in larger containers is safe only if the storage and decanting method keeps the product clean and labelled. Choosing a reusable linen service can reduce the per-session cost if the service confirms its laundering standard in writing. Scheduling sessions to reduce travel reduces cost, provided the processing and set-up steps are still allowed. Cost reduction must never remove a contraindication check, a consent step, a clean-down step or a required product test. Where a cheaper product is considered, check its safety data sheet and its label before it is used, and record the review.

lessons.title: In-home safety, lone-work and room setup
learningOutcomes: Set up a treatment room that is stable, clear of trip hazards and safe for the therapist and the client
Apply a lone-worker check-in routine and an escalation step for threats or unsafe conditions
Explain the self-employed WHS duty as it applies in a client's home.

instructionSections.heading: The duty that applies in a client's home
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria states that a self-employed person's work must not expose others to risk, within what is reasonably practicable, and that employers must do the same for customers and the public (reviewed 03/04/2025). The safe approach is to treat the client's home as a workplace for the purpose of set-up and safety, and to record the set-up check each visit. The business's home-visit procedure is recorded in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the access instructions for each client are held in {{business:customers.access_instructions}}.

instructionSections.heading: Room setup for a stable and safe treatment
instructionSections.body: Choose a room that is quiet, warm, and has enough space to move around the table on all sides. Place the table on a firm, level floor, away from doors and windows where a draught or a person could disturb the treatment. Clear the path between the door and the table of cables, rugs and furniture. If you use a heater, keep it away from the table, the linen and the cables, and check that its cord is not under the client's weight. Keep your products within reach and on a surface that will not tip. Do not work in a room where the client has to stand on an uneven surface, and check the step at the entrance before the client walks in. Where the room has a water source, keep electrical equipment dry, as “Mobile setup, power and wet-area safety” explains for mobile beauty work.

instructionSections.heading: Lone work, check-ins and threats
instructionSections.body: A mobile therapist often works alone in a home they have not visited before. Use the lone-worker check-in method in “Lone-worker safety and check-ins” at arrival and departure, and record the times. Before entering, confirm the address and the access details against the booking. If the client's conduct, the household or the environment appears unsafe, the therapist should leave, and contact {{business:safety.escalation_contact}}, rather than stay to finish the session. The threats and unsafe-environment steps are set out in “Threats, unsafe environments and escalation”, and the decision to stop work is the therapist's to make. Children and pets in the home are a separate matter. The Victorian Working with Children Check list (updated 12 October 2026) names commercial gyms and play venues aimed at children, coaching for children, and sport, recreation and culture clubs that deal with children. It does not name massage.

lessons.title: Premium session pricing and memberships
learningOutcomes: Price a premium session from the time, the skill and the costs, and state what the session does not promise
Design a membership or prepaid plan that keeps each session's screening, consent and set-up steps
Identify the consumer-law and advertising points to check before the plan is sold.

instructionSections.heading: Why a premium session can earn more per hour
instructionSections.body: A premium massage session earns more per hour when it takes more skill, more time, or more specialised training, and when the business has the experience to deliver it safely. The price should cover the time for the intake and consent, the set-up and clean-down, the products, the linen, the travel and the cost of any compliance step. A session that is longer but has the same set-up time earns more per hour only if the extra time is real. A premium price must never remove the contraindication check in “Massage scope, contraindications and referral”. The approved list of premium sessions is held in {{business:services.service_description}}, and the pricing method is set out in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}.

instructionSections.heading: What a premium session must not claim
instructionSections.body: A premium session can be described by its length, its technique and its products. It must not be described as curing a condition, reducing a medical risk or treating an injury. Claims about health outcomes must not appear in an advertisement or a menu unless the business has a source for them. Advertising rules and consumer-law rules for health claims were not researched for this course. The safe practice is to describe the session as a relaxation or wellbeing service, state its length and what is included, and tell the client that the session does not replace medical treatment. The therapist must not promise that a session will help a condition.

instructionSections.heading: Memberships and prepaid plans
instructionSections.body: A membership gives a client a set number of sessions for a fixed period, often paid in advance. The plan must state the sessions included, the period it covers, what happens to unused sessions, how it can be cancelled, and how it is refunded. Each session under a membership needs its own intake, consent and contraindication check, because a client's health can change between sessions. Record each session against the membership so that the business can show what was delivered and when. The membership terms should be checked by the business before they are sold.

lessons.title: Scope, authority and prohibited tasks
learningOutcomes: Explain that this course covers external cleaning only, and name the tasks that are outside the course.
Identify the written authority needed before any medical equipment task starts.
Classify a requested task as permitted, needs authorisation, or prohibited, and state the action for each.
State when and how to stop work and escalate a request that goes beyond the authorised scope.
Recognise that completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to reprocess or disinfect medical devices.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. External cleaning means removing visible soil from the outside of equipment or environmental surfaces, using a product and method that the manufacturer and the facility have approved for that item. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure, and are carried out by staff who hold that authority. Nothing in this lesson describes how to reprocess, disinfect for re-use or sterilise a device, and nothing here should be read as a method for those tasks. If a task appears to involve any of them, treat it as outside your scope and stop.

instructionSections.heading: Why the boundary matters
instructionSections.body: The Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare, published by the National Health and Medical Research Council, distinguish cleaning from disinfection and set out how shared clinical equipment is handled between patient uses. The guidelines (document dated 2019) recommend cleaning with detergent and disinfecting where indicated, and they place the decision on the facility's infection prevention and control arrangements. The same device can need different processes depending on whether it contacts intact skin, mucous membranes or sterile tissue. A cleaner who treats a device that needs validated reprocessing as if it needed a wipe can damage the device, leave it unsafe for the next patient, and create a false record that the item is ready for clinical use. The boundary protects the patient, the worker and the facility.

instructionSections.heading: Where authority comes from
instructionSections.body: Authority to work on medical equipment comes from a written instruction that names the task, the equipment or equipment class, the approved product and method, the location, and the person who gave the direction. A verbal instruction from a nurse, doctor or site manager may be a real request, but it is not authority to change what the written procedure permits. The facility decides who may do which task. For a cleaner, that usually means a short list of authorised tasks, such as cleaning the exterior of named noncritical items with named products. If the list does not name the item, the product or the method, the task is not authorised until someone with authority adds it in writing. You may not authorise yourself, and you may not extend your authority because a task looks similar to one you are allowed to do. Record the source of your authority on the work record. Facility procedures are reflected in {{business:staff.authorised_tasks}}, and the facility contact for direction is {{business:staff.supervisor_contact}}.

instructionSections.heading: Permitted, authorised-only and prohibited tasks
instructionSections.body: Sort every requested task into one of three groups before you touch anything. Permitted tasks are on your written authorised list, for the named equipment, with the approved product and method. Authorised-only tasks need a specific written decision each time, such as an electrical check or an unusual surface, and you may not start them until that decision is recorded. Prohibited tasks are never yours to do under this course. These include reprocessing or disinfecting any reusable device for return to clinical use, sterilising any item, opening or disassembling equipment, cleaning inside a lumen or channel, reusing a single-use device, touching patient-connected equipment or changing its settings, testing or repairing electrical equipment, and returning any equipment to clinical service. When a task falls in the middle, choose the more restrictive group and ask.

instructionSections.heading: Licences, permissions and the limit of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Completing this lesson does not give you a licence, a certificate or any authority to do regulated work. Some reprocessing activity is regulated under the Therapeutic Goods Administration framework. The ACIPC position statement on single-use devices, version 4.0 of February 2024, states that reprocessing of single-use devices in a health service facility must not be undertaken unless the facility is licensed as a manufacturer, and that the TGA treats reprocessing or reuse of a single-use medical device as remanufacture. Check any state or territory requirements for your role with your employer and the relevant state health authority before work begins. Your facility's licence and permission requirements are recorded in {{business:compliance.licence_requirements}}, under {{business:compliance.jurisdiction}}.

lessons.title: Medical equipment classification and infection risk
learningOutcomes: Describe the difference between critical, semicritical and noncritical equipment categories by the tissue or skin contact they involve.
Explain why a classification decision belongs to the facility and cannot be made from appearance.
Identify the evidence needed before any medical equipment task starts, and the point at which work must stop.
Explain why a noncritical external surface and a reusable invasive device need different processes, without describing those processes.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It teaches you to recognise the categories that facilities use to decide which equipment a cleaner may touch and which equipment is outside your role. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure, and they are carried out by staff with that authority. This lesson does not describe how to process any device in the critical or semicritical categories.

instructionSections.heading: The three categories
instructionSections.body: The Spaulding classification, as used in the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) framework, is an international reference and not an Australian requirement, but it is a useful guide to why equipment is handled differently.

instructionSections.heading: Why appearance is not a classification
instructionSections.body: Two items can look almost identical and sit in different categories. A blood pressure cuff and a flexible endoscope may both be grey plastic objects beside a bed, but one contacts intact skin and the other passes into a body cavity. Appearance does not show the contact site, the reprocessing history, the manufacturer's labelling, or whether the item is single-use. Clean-looking equipment can still carry microorganisms. The lesson for a cleaner is simple: a classification comes from documented facility information, and where that information is missing, the item is treated as unknown and left for the responsible team.

instructionSections.heading: Professional decision process
instructionSections.body: Before you touch any item, decide three things from the written record: what the item is, what it touches, and whether your written authority covers an external clean of that item. If the item is in the critical or semicritical category, or its category cannot be confirmed, the task is outside your role. If the item is noncritical and on your authorised list, you may perform only the external clean the facility has approved. Keep environmental touchpoints separate from reusable instruments, and never move an unknown item to a cleaner's trolley to sort it later. The facility is responsible for classifying each device and for deciding who may clean which class. Your task is to confirm, not to reclassify.

instructionSections.heading: Worked case: a cuff beside an endoscope
instructionSections.body: You are cleaning the bedside area of a procedure room and find a blood pressure cuff sitting next to a flexible endoscope in its carry case. The cuff may be on your authorised list for external cleaning with an approved product. The endoscope is not. Do not clean either item until you have confirmed the authority for each one separately. Do not wipe the endoscope to tidy the room. Leave it where the team placed it, tell the nurse in charge, and ask for the endoscope to be collected by staff who hold the reprocessing authority. Record which items were present, what you did, and who you escalated to.

lessons.title: Manufacturer instructions and asset identification
learningOutcomes: Identify a medical device by its model and serial label, and match it to the correct written instructions.
Explain why the manufacturer's current external cleaning instructions govern the product choice, contact conditions and limits.
Recognise a missing, illegible or conflicting instruction and state the stop condition that follows.
Record asset identity and the instruction version used on the work record.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It explains how to identify the equipment and find the instructions that govern an approved external clean. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure, and this lesson does not teach any of them.

instructionSections.heading: Why identity comes first
instructionSections.body: A cleaning instruction belongs to a specific model, not to a family of devices that look alike. Two monitors from the same range can have different permitted surface products, different ingress protection ratings, and different rules about liquid near connectors. Before you open a product or wipe a surface, confirm the asset label: model number, serial number or asset tag, and the facility asset identifier if one is fitted. If the label is missing, worn or cannot be read, the item cannot be matched to its instructions. Treat it as unidentified and stop.

instructionSections.heading: Finding the instruction that governs
instructionSections.body: The governing instruction is the current manufacturer document for that model, together with any facility supplement that adds a restriction. Check three things: the document matches the model and serial range on the label, the revision date or version is current, and the cleaning section covers the external surface you are asked to clean. A facility supplement may only tighten the manufacturer's instruction, never loosen it. If the manufacturer says no liquid on a surface and the facility supplement lists a product for that surface, stop and refer the conflict. Do not choose the more convenient of two instructions. The facility location of the current instructions is recorded in {{business:equipment.manufacturer_manual_url}}.

instructionSections.heading: What the instruction tells you
instructionSections.body: A usable external cleaning instruction states the approved product or product class, the dilution or form of the product, the method of application, the wet contact condition if one applies, the surfaces and openings to keep dry, and the prohibited products or materials. Read every one of these before starting. Do not make up a concentration, substitute a stronger chemical, or apply a product to a surface that the instruction keeps dry. If an instruction requires a contact condition you cannot achieve on that surface, mark the task incomplete and escalate rather than adjusting the method.

instructionSections.heading: Worked case: two monitors that look alike
instructionSections.body: Two patient monitors sit side by side on a ward. Their casings look identical, but one label gives a different model number and its instruction permits only a specific detergent wipe, while the other permits a different product. The first step is to read both labels, not the casings. Clean each unit only with the product its own model allows, and record the asset identity against each clean. If either label is illegible, leave that unit alone and report it.

lessons.title: PPE, hand hygiene and exposure prevention
learningOutcomes: Describe the standard precautions that apply to every cleaning task in a healthcare setting, including hand hygiene at the correct points.
Select the personal protective equipment for a named task from the product safety data sheet and the facility assessment, and explain why it is task-specific.
Demonstrate the donning and doffing sequence in a supervised setting, and describe the exposure response for a splash or needlestick.
State when the cleaner must stop, withdraw and report instead of continuing.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It explains the protection a cleaner needs when cleaning the outside of medical equipment and healthcare environments. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure. Protection rules in this lesson do not authorise any reprocessing task.

instructionSections.heading: Standard precautions as the baseline
instructionSections.body: The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare treat hand hygiene and the use of personal protective equipment as core parts of routine infection prevention. The NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4 of November 2021, require that infection prevention and control standard precautions are implemented throughout all settings where supports are provided, and that each worker is trained, with refresher training, in standard precautions, hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette. A cleaner should treat every surface and item as potentially contaminated, perform hand hygiene at the transitions the facility specifies, and not wait for a visible soil before protecting themselves.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing personal protective equipment for the task
instructionSections.body: Protective equipment is task-specific. Gloves suitable for a dilute detergent may not resist a stronger product, and a gown that is right for a splash-prone task may be excessive for a dry dust wipe. Select the equipment from three sources: the product safety data sheet for the chemical you are using, the facility's risk assessment for the area, and the task itself. Where the task involves a splash risk, body fluids or a sharps hazard, the facility's specific requirements apply and may be stricter than general guidance. Check the equipment before use, and replace it when it is torn, contaminated or past its date. The facility supplies the approved equipment, and the NDIS Practice Standards require that personal protective equipment is available to each worker who needs it.

instructionSections.heading: Donning, doffing and hand hygiene
instructionSections.body: Put equipment on in an order that protects the clean parts of your body: hand hygiene first, then gown or apron, mask or eye protection if required, then gloves last so that they cover the cuffs. Remove equipment in the reverse order and in a way that keeps the outside of each item away from your skin and clothing. Perform hand hygiene immediately after removing gloves, and before touching clean stock, a trolley handle or your face. A common failure is touching a shared handle with contaminated gloves and then handling clean supplies. Stop, remove the gloves, perform hand hygiene, put on new gloves, and continue. Do not wash gloves to reuse them unless the facility procedure allows it.

instructionSections.heading: Exposure, stop and report
instructionSections.body: If you are splashed on broken skin or the mucous membranes of the eyes, nose or mouth, or you are stuck by a sharp, stop the task. Remove yourself from the immediate area, follow the facility's exposure procedure, and report the event to your supervisor the same shift. Do not handle sharps with your hands. The exposure response is set by the facility and may include immediate first aid, medical assessment and recording, and it is not a decision for the cleaner to make alone. Record the exposure, the time, the source if known, the first aid given and the person notified. Stop work whenever the protection you need is not available, damaged, or not the type the task requires.

lessons.title: Disinfectant compatibility and contact conditions
learningOutcomes: Read a product label and manufacturer instruction and identify the approved use, dilution, wet contact condition and material limits.
Explain why the wet contact condition is a requirement, and what happens when the surface dries before the time is reached.
Identify when two products or a product and a surface are incompatible, and stop before applying either.
Record product, lot, dilution and contact condition, and mark a task incomplete when the condition was not achieved.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. A disinfectant label can describe approved uses for surfaces, and a manufacturer instruction can describe approved uses for a device. This lesson teaches you to follow the label and the instruction for an approved external clean. It does not teach disinfection for reusable devices for return to clinical use, reprocessing or sterilisation. Those are outside this course and are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the label and the instruction
instructionSections.body: Before you open any product, read four things. The first is the approved use: some products are approved for environmental surfaces and not for medical devices, and a product approved for one does not carry over to the other. The second is the dilution or form, which must be exactly as stated. The third is the wet contact condition, which is the time the product must remain visibly wet on the surface. The fourth is the list of materials and surfaces the product must not be used on. If any of these is unclear, or the product is not on the facility's approved list, do not use it. Never make a stronger mix to save time, and never add one product to another.

instructionSections.heading: Wet contact condition is a requirement
instructionSections.body: The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare treat cleaning with detergent as the first step, and disinfection as an adjunct where indicated. A disinfectant only works as the label says if the surface remains wet for the stated time. If you wipe a surface and it dries before the wet contact condition is reached, the surface has not been treated as required, even if it looks clean. Apply enough product to keep the surface wet, avoid saturating electronics and openings, and time the condition from the moment the surface is wet. When the condition cannot be achieved, mark the task incomplete and escalate. Do not reapply in a way that breaks the instruction.

instructionSections.heading: Compatibility between products and surfaces
instructionSections.body: Compatibility has two parts: the product with the material, and the product with other products. Some plastics and display films discolour, craze or lose clarity after contact with certain alcohols, solvents or strong oxidisers. Electronics may need to stay dry even when a label permits a liquid. Never mix products, and never rinse one product into a container of another. Where a product label and a manufacturer instruction disagree on a surface, stop and refer the conflict. Keep a clear record of which product went on which surface, so any later discolouration can be traced.

instructionSections.heading: Worked case: a delicate housing
instructionSections.body: A cleaner plans to use a strong product on the housing of a sensor that the manufacturer says must not be exposed to solvents. The label approves the product for hard environmental surfaces only. The correct decision is to stop before any product touches the sensor, check the manufacturer instruction for an approved method, and ask the supervisor or the device owner for the approved product. Record the request, the decision and the time. If the sensor has already been wiped with the wrong product, stop further application, leave it as found, and report it immediately, so that the damage and product can be recorded.

lessons.title: Reusable-device reprocessing boundaries
learningOutcomes: Define reprocessing in the facility context and explain that it is outside this course.
Explain the difference between cleaning the outside of a device and reprocessing a reusable device for return to clinical use.
State who in a healthcare facility holds reprocessing authority, and the regulatory points that limit it.
Describe the escalation steps when a reprocessing request, or an item that appears to need reprocessing, reaches a cleaner.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: the boundary, not the method
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only and teaches where your role stops. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure. This lesson does not describe any reprocessing step, product, concentration, cycle or equipment. If you need that information for your work, ask your facility for the procedure that applies, and treat the reprocessing as the responsibility of the staff named in it.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as reprocessing
instructionSections.body: In a healthcare facility, reprocessing is the set of validated steps that a reusable medical device goes through before it is used again on another patient. It is distinct from cleaning the outside of a device, which removes visible soil from surfaces. The Aged Care Quality Standards Action 3.17 guidance resource (no date shown) describes a facility procedure for reprocessing reusable medical equipment and devices, and it refers to traceability, storage and transport, and workforce training. The Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care advisory (dated August 2024) records that AS 5369:2023 replaced AS/NZS 4187:2014 in December 2023 and sets no transition period.

instructionSections.heading: Why the boundary is strict
instructionSections.body: A device that has been cleaned on the outside may still contain organisms inside a lumen, channel or joint, and a wipe does not reach those areas. A reusable device that is reused without validated reprocessing can transmit infection between patients. For single-use devices the risk is also regulatory. The ACIPC position statement on single-use devices, version 4.0 of February 2024, says that single-use devices must not be reused and that a used single-use device must not be reprocessed or reused. It also states that the TGA considers reprocessing or reuse of a single-use medical device to be a remanufacture, after which the original manufacturer is no longer responsible for its performance and safety (as the ACIPC statement records; the TGA's own text was not read in this session). These points are why a cleaner must never treat reprocessing as an extension of cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Who holds reprocessing authority
instructionSections.body: Reprocessing is carried out only by staff and departments that the facility has authorised for that device class, under the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's procedure. For single-use devices, the ACIPC statement says reprocessing in a health service facility is restricted to a facility that is licensed as a manufacturer. A cleaner has no reprocessing authority under this course, and a verbal instruction from a colleague does not change that. If you are unsure whether a reprocessing task is happening or required, ask the facility infection prevention and control contact before you touch the item.

instructionSections.heading: What a cleaner does when reprocessing comes up
instructionSections.body: If an item appears to be waiting for reprocessing, or someone asks you to reprocess or disinfect a reusable device, do not start the task. Keep the item where it was found or with the designated team, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor. Record the item, the location, the request, the person who made it, and the time. Do not move the item to a clean area or your trolley, and do not wipe it to tidy up. The responsible team decides what happens next under the facility procedure.

lessons.title: Single-use items, damaged items and quarantine
learningOutcomes: Identify single-use labelled items and state that they must not be reused or reprocessed.
Recognise a damaged, defective or unidentified item and state the stop condition that applies.
Describe how an item is placed in quarantine and labelled under the facility procedure, without repairing or testing it.
Record the item, its condition, its location and the escalation recipient on the work record.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It explains how a cleaner recognises items that must not be cleaned for re-use, and how a damaged or doubtful item is kept separate until the responsible team decides what happens next. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure, and this lesson does not teach any of them.

instructionSections.heading: Single-use items
instructionSections.body: A device labelled single use is designed for one patient and one procedure. The ACIPC position statement on single-use devices, version 4.0 of February 2024, says that medical devices labelled as single use must not be reused, and that used single-use devices must not be reprocessed or reused. The statement also notes that a single-patient-use device may be reprocessed under the manufacturer's instructions only where it holds TGA approval and is on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods, and then only for reuse on the same patient. That is a reprocessing decision for authorised staff. A cleaner's role is to recognise the label, keep used single-use items out of stock, and escalate. An opened, expired or part-used single-use item is also not yours to return to stock.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising a damaged or defective item
instructionSections.body: Damage changes what an item is safe to do. A cracked housing may expose internal components, a frayed cable may be an electrical hazard, a split seal may allow liquid into the device, and a bent connector may no longer fit its intended patient-care equipment. Stop work on any item that shows damage, a leak, a smell, heat, a broken label, an open package, or a component that is loose. Do not attempt to fix, tape, test or switch on the item to check it. Your role is to make the item safe, keep it separate, and tell the responsible team. A damaged item that is still in use on a patient is a clinical matter, and the clinical team decides what happens to it.

instructionSections.heading: Quarantine: keep it separate and labelled
instructionSections.body: Quarantine means holding an item apart from clean stock and from routine use until a responsible person decides its status under the facility procedure. Place the item in the designated quarantine location or container, and do not place it on a clean trolley, shelf or in a clean-stock cupboard. Attach the facility's quarantine label, if one is provided, and complete it with the item identity, the date and time, your name and the reason. If the quarantine container is not available, keep the item in a clearly marked place and tell your supervisor the same shift. Quarantine does not mean the item is safe, and it does not mean the item is ready for re-use when it is moved.

instructionSections.heading: Worked case: a cleaning trolley and an opened pack
instructionSections.body: During a round you find an opened sterile-looking pack, a half-used single-use cannula set and a cracked monitor cable on your trolley shelf, left there by someone else. Do not use any of them to clean. Do not return the pack or the set to stock. Move none of the items into clean areas. Make the trolley safe, tell your supervisor, and ask for the items to be collected under the quarantine or waste procedure. Record each item and its condition, and note where it was found.

lessons.title: Clean/dirty workflow, transport and traceability
learningOutcomes: Plan a clean-to-dirty route for a trolley and its contents before work begins.
Keep used equipment, used cloths and contaminated materials separate from clean stock during transport.
Complete a handoff record so that each item can be traced from collection to return.
Identify a route, storage or handoff breach and state the correction and the escalation.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It explains how a cleaner plans and records the movement of equipment and materials around a healthcare site. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure, and the movement of an item for those purposes follows the facility procedure rather than this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Why the direction of travel matters
instructionSections.body: Healthcare facilities usually separate clean areas from used or contaminated areas so that clean stock does not pick up contamination on the way past. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare treat environmental controls, including cleaning and spill management, as part of preventing transmission from the environment to patients. The practical rule is one-way movement: clean stock moves from clean areas to point of use, and used items move from point of use to a designated holding area, without crossing back through clean areas. The shortest route is not always the correct route. If the shortest path crosses a soiled holding corridor, the facility's designated route applies, even when it takes longer.

instructionSections.heading: Planning the trolley and its contents
instructionSections.body: Before you leave the clean store, check the trolley's content list against the work order. Keep clean cloths, containers, product and equipment in their own compartments, and keep used cloths in a bag or bin that is closed and labelled. Never load used equipment onto a trolley that carries clean stock, and do not use one trolley for both unless the facility procedure says so. Confirm the route, the lift or door you will use, and the holding area for used items. Plan the order of the round so that you move from the cleanest area to the most soiled, as the facility procedure directs.

instructionSections.heading: Transport, containment and handoff
instructionSections.body: Transport items so that they are covered, secured and cannot fall or leak. An item that must be moved to a designated area is placed in a labelled container where the procedure requires one, and you do not carry several items in your hands at once. At each handoff, the receiving person confirms the item, the condition and the destination, and you record the handoff. A handoff is not complete until the receiving person accepts it. If the receiving person is not available, keep the item in the designated holding area and do not leave it on a corridor floor or in a clean area.

instructionSections.heading: Traceability
instructionSections.body: Traceability means that you can say, for any item, where it came from, where it went, who handled it and when. A simple record with the item identity, the time, the location and the handoff signature is usually enough, but the exact record format is set by the facility. Traceability lets the team act if an item is later found to be damaged, unlabelled, or in the wrong place. A cleaner who moves an item without recording it breaks the chain and makes it impossible to tell whether the item was cleaned, moved or left in an unsafe place.

lessons.title: Medical electrical systems and powered equipment
learningOutcomes: Identify powered medical equipment and the features that make it a liquid and electrical hazard during cleaning.
Apply the manufacturer's instruction on isolation, power and liquid limits before any external clean.
State the actions that are outside a cleaner's role, including testing, opening, repairing and changing settings.
Recognise a damaged cable, a fault or an unexpected behaviour and state the stop-and-report response.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It is about the outside of powered equipment and the cables and connectors you may be asked to clean. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure. Electrical testing, repair, servicing, opening a housing and changing settings are also outside a cleaner's role, and this lesson does not teach any of them.

instructionSections.heading: Why powered equipment is a different hazard
instructionSections.body: Powered equipment combines liquid, electricity and patient-care function. Liquid entering a housing, a connector or a switch can cause a short circuit, an electric shock, a fire risk or a failure of the device at the moment a clinician needs it. Some powered devices are rated for a level of liquid ingress and wiping, and others are not. The rating is set by the manufacturer and is shown in the instruction, often as an ingress rating on the label. Do not assume that a device which can be wiped is safe to be sprayed, soaked, or wiped at a connector. Treat each device by its own instruction.

instructionSections.heading: Power state and isolation
instructionSections.body: Before you clean the outside of a powered item, follow the manufacturer's instruction on power state. Some instructions require the item to be switched off and unplugged. Others require it to remain connected to a charger or a supply, or they do not permit it to be disconnected while in use. Do not unplug a device that is in use on a patient, and do not switch off a device that a clinician has asked to remain on. If the instruction on power state is unclear or conflicts with the clinical situation, stop and refer. Never remove a patient-connected cable to get better access, and never let a cable or lead lie in liquid while you clean around it.

instructionSections.heading: Cables, connectors and displays
instructionSections.body: Cables, connectors and display panels are the most common points of failure and are often the points where liquid can enter. Keep connectors dry unless the instruction permits a wipe at that point. Do not allow a lead to be pulled, twisted or stretched while you work. Look for splits, exposed wire, discolouration, heat marks and loose strain relief. Damage of this kind is a stop condition: leave the item in place, make the area safe, and report it. A cleaner does not test, tape, or repair a cable.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and report
instructionSections.body: Stop work and report at once if you see smoke, a burning smell, sparking, unexpected heat, a loose or damaged cable, liquid inside a housing, an alarm, a fault code, or a device that powers on or off without being touched. Do not switch the device on or off to find out what is wrong. Make the area safe, keep people away from the item, and tell the clinical team and your supervisor the same moment. Record the device, the observation, the time and the action taken.

lessons.title: Records, incidents and failed processes
learningOutcomes: Complete a work record for an external clean with the asset, product, instruction version, observed condition, exceptions and handoff.
Explain why a record must not state that a condition was achieved when it was not.
Identify a failed or interrupted process, tag it, and escalate it under the facility incident procedure.
Describe how records support traceability, audit and review without changing what happened.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It explains the records you keep for an external clean and how to respond when a step fails. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure, and their records are kept under that procedure rather than under this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: What a complete work record contains
instructionSections.body: A complete record lets another person understand what was done without asking you. For each item it should show the asset identity from the label, the location, the date and time, the product and lot used, the dilution or form, the instruction and its version, the contact condition achieved where one applies, the observed condition before and after, any exception, and the handoff or the person who signed. The exact form is set by the facility, but these fields are the minimum. Write the record at the time of the work, not from memory at the end of the shift, and use the same asset identity as the label.

instructionSections.heading: Honest records: what was achieved and what was not
instructionSections.body: A record is a statement that something happened. If a contact condition was not achieved because the surface dried, the record must say so. Do not sign for a disinfection condition that was not achieved, do not round a time up to meet the minimum, and do not fill a field with a value you did not observe. An honest incomplete record is useful: it shows the team where to focus and it protects the patient, the worker and the facility. A false complete record is the most serious error in this lesson, because the next person will rely on it.

instructionSections.heading: Failed or interrupted processes
instructionSections.body: A process fails when a required step cannot be completed as the instruction requires: the product runs out, the surface dries early, a label is unreadable, an item is damaged, a person is called away mid-task, or the environment changes. Stop the affected step, leave the item in a safe state, and tag it as incomplete or failed using the facility's tag or label. Record the failure, the step that failed, the reason and the time. Escalate to your supervisor the same shift, and follow the facility incident procedure where the failure could affect a patient, a worker or equipment. The failure is recorded, not hidden, and the decision to repeat the work is made by the responsible person.

instructionSections.heading: Worked case: the wipe that dried early
instructionSections.body: A wipe dries before the product's required wet contact time is reached on a bed-side monitor. The worker must not record the surface as treated. The correct record shows the product and lot, the actual contact time, the step that could not be completed, the tag applied, the supervisor told and the time. The item is then assessed by the responsible team and cleaned again only under the procedure that applies.

lessons.title: Competency demonstration and patient safety
learningOutcomes: Explain how screening, classification, instructions, exposure controls, surface work, transport and handoff work together in one task.
Demonstrate stop-work and escalation decisions in a supervised simulation with approved, restricted and unknown equipment.
Describe the difference between written knowledge and observed practical competence, and why only the second supports a work decision.
Explain how patient safety depends on the cleaner stopping at the boundary of their authority.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It brings together the earlier lessons into one supervised demonstration. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure. A demonstration in this course does not authorise any reprocessing, sterilisation or device disinfection, and it does not show competence for those tasks.

instructionSections.heading: What a competent external clean looks like
instructionSections.body: Competence in this course is the ability to complete one task safely from start to finish. Before touching an item, the cleaner confirms the written authority, the asset identity and the classification record, and reads the manufacturer instruction and product label. The cleaner selects protective equipment from the data sheet, performs hand hygiene, and cleans only the surfaces the instruction permits, using the approved method and contact condition. The cleaner keeps clean and used items apart, completes the handoff, and records the outcome honestly. At any point, a cleaner who cannot meet a requirement stops and escalates. Stopping is part of competent work, not a failure of it.

instructionSections.heading: The stop-work decision
instructionSections.body: The most important decision in this course is the stop. Stop when the authority is unclear, when the item is critical, semicritical or unknown, when the instruction is missing or conflicts, when the protection is not available, when the contact condition cannot be met, when the item is damaged or powered in an unexpected way, and when the request goes beyond your list. Stopping does not mean doing nothing. Make the area safe, leave the item as found, tell the responsible person, and record the decision. Patient safety depends on this decision being made consistently, including when someone is pressing you to finish quickly.

instructionSections.heading: Knowledge is not practical competence
instructionSections.body: Passing a written check shows that you can recall rules. It does not show that you can perform a task on a real item, in a real room, with a real trolley and a real colleague asking you for a shortcut. Practical competence is observed by a supervisor against defined criteria, on the facility's equipment, and recorded separately. A completed course, a knowledge check, or a certificate of attendance does not by itself authorise you to carry out any task. The facility decides when a person is competent for a specific task and records that decision.

instructionSections.heading: Worked simulation: the multi-device room
instructionSections.body: In a simulated treatment room you find four items: an approved trolley of external cleaning products, a restricted reusable instrument that is not on your list, a damaged powered unit with a split cable, and an unidentified device with no label. The competent response is to clean the approved trolley's surfaces only as the instructions allow, leave the restricted instrument and the unidentified device exactly where they are, leave the damaged powered unit untouched, make the room safe, and escalate all three. Record each item separately, the decision for each, and the person notified. The task is not complete while any item remains unresolved.

lessons.title: Surface preparation and washing
learningOutcomes: Wash and clean a surface so that paint can key and adhere.
Choose a washing method suited to the surface and the contamination.
Dry and check the surface before the first coat, and stop where damp is present.

instructionSections.heading: Why the surface comes first
instructionSections.body: Paint bonds to the layer beneath it. If that layer is dirty, greasy, chalky, mouldy, wet or already flaking, the bond is weak, and the paint will lift, blister or peel, often within months. Preparation is therefore part of the paint system, not an optional extra. Most early paint failures trace back to the surface rather than to the paint itself. Before any cleaner goes on, you need to know what the surface is made of, what has been on it, and whether it is sound enough to take a new coat. A clean, dry and sound surface gives the next coat something to grip, and the time spent preparing it is what makes the finish last.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect and record the contamination
instructionSections.body: Inspect the surface in good daylight or with a torch held low across it, because flat light hides dull films and fine marks. Look for grease, especially on kitchen and bathroom walls, near cooking areas and around switches. Rub a dry finger across the surface: a fine powder on the finger suggests chalking, which is breakdown of the paint film and needs removing before painting. Look for efflorescence, the white crystalline deposit that can appear on masonry and render, which is usually salt brought to the surface by moisture. Look for mould, which may appear as dark spots, fuzz or a musty patch, and for dust, loose paint and old wax or silicone residue. Tap or lightly scrape the paint to find areas that are loose or flaking. Check for damp by eye and with a moisture meter where the site provides one, and note any stain that suggests water is coming from behind the surface. Record each finding with its location, because each one changes the method.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a washing method
instructionSections.body: Match the method to the contamination. Water and a neutral detergent, applied with a sponge or cloth and rinsed with clean water, suits dust and light soiling on most interior and exterior surfaces. A stronger alkaline cleaner, used only as the product data sheet directs, is used for greasy walls and for removing residue that water does not lift. Chalking and loose powder are usually brushed or wiped off before washing, so that the powder does not smear. Efflorescence is brushed dry first, and then washed, because wetting it first can draw the salt back into the surface. Loose or flaking paint is removed mechanically with scraping or sanding, and this brings in a dust control problem and, on older surfaces, a lead or asbestos question. Where a surface may be old enough to contain lead or asbestos, stop and refer it before any mechanical removal, using “Lead paint and older-surface awareness (refer)”. Do not mix cleaning products. Check each product's safety data sheet and label before use, and keep to the dilution the product states.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure, water and what it can damage
instructionSections.body: Water is the main washing tool, and it can also be the main cause of damage. High-pressure washing can strip sound paint, roughen old timber, damage render and mortar, loosen fixings, and drive water behind cladding, flashings and window frames. Once water is behind a surface, it can show up later as a stain, a blister or rot, and the cause is then hard to trace back to the wash. Use the lowest pressure that does the job, keep the nozzle moving, and keep a sensible distance from the surface. Do not aim the water into vents, gaps, under sills, at switchboards, power outlets or light fittings, or at gaps around window frames. Keep water away from electrical fittings at all times. Any pressure figure used on a job is a site setting checked against the product and surface, and no figure is given in this lesson. Where the pressure needed to remove a contaminant would damage the surface, stop and choose a gentler method, or refer.

instructionSections.heading: Mould and damp: stop and refer
instructionSections.body: Mould is not a surface finish problem to paint over. Where mould or damp is found, stop painting that area and record it. Mould can show the presence of water, condensation or a building fault, and painting over it hides the evidence and tends to fail. Cleaning mould is a separate task with its own controls, and it is covered by the mould guidance in “Moisture ingress and mould warning signs”. Do not paint until the moisture source is known and dealt with, or until the client has agreed in writing to a stated scope. Check the surface for damp after it has been washed and dried, because a surface that looks dry at the surface may still be wet behind.

instructionSections.heading: Drying, checking and protecting the job
instructionSections.body: Rinse the surface with clean water to remove detergent, because any residue left on the surface can stop paint from bonding. Allow the surface to dry fully before the next step. The drying time depends on the surface, the temperature, the humidity and the wind, and the product data sheet for the first coat states the conditions it needs. A surface that feels dry may still hold moisture in its core, so check with a moisture meter where the site provides one, or by a method the product data sheet accepts. Before washing, protect the floor, fittings and adjacent surfaces with drop sheets and masking. Cover power outlets and switches where water could reach them, and keep the wash water away from open windows and doors. Wash runoff can carry detergent into stormwater or gardens.

instructionSections.heading: The limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant a painting licence, a plastering licence, a lead or asbestos removal licence or any authority to undertake regulated work. Licence positions depend on the state, the value of the work and the scope, and they are set out in the safety and regulatory section below and in “Paint systems, primers and coverage” and “Painting quotes, variations and colour approval”.

lessons.title: Paint systems, primers and coverage
learningOutcomes: Select a primer and topcoat that are compatible with each other and with the substrate.
Estimate coverage from the product data sheet and the surface area, and allow for the surface type.
Apply the product in the conditions stated on the data sheet.

instructionSections.heading: What a paint system is
instructionSections.body: A paint system is the set of products that go on a surface in a set order: a primer or sealer, sometimes an undercoat, and a topcoat. Each layer has a job. A primer or sealer is chosen to bond to the substrate, to seal a porous or absorbent surface, to block stains, or to stop a substrate from reacting with the paint above it. An undercoat builds body and evens out colour. A topcoat gives the finish, the colour and most of the durability. Each layer must be compatible with the layer beneath it and with the substrate, meaning the surface the paint goes onto. Products from different manufacturers, or from different chemical families such as water-based and solvent-based, are not always interchangeable over one another. Some primers are made for bare timber, others for plaster, metal, masonry or previously painted surfaces. A system that works on one substrate can fail on another, so the choice is made from the data sheets for the products, not from habit or from the shelf.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the data sheet before you buy
instructionSections.body: The product data sheet is the manufacturer's statement of how the product is meant to be used. Before you choose a system, read the data sheet for each layer and check the substrates it is suited to, its compatibility statements, and any warning about what it must not be applied over. Note the recoat window, which is the time that must pass before the next coat can go on, and the drying time to touch and to handle. Check the stated application conditions, including air and surface temperature, humidity and any limits on direct sun or wind. Note the coverage figure, the film thickness it is quoted at, and the number of coats the system needs. Check the solvent or thinner the product uses, the tools it needs, and the personal protection the safety data sheet requires. Record the product name, the batch number and the data sheet reference on the job record, because a fault that is traced to a batch cannot be investigated without them.

instructionSections.heading: Water-based, solvent-based and over old finishes
instructionSections.body: Mixing water-based and solvent-based products is a common cause of poor adhesion, lifting and wrinkling. Some water-based topcoats do not bond well to an old gloss or oil-based finish, which is glossy and non-porous, so the surface may need to be scuffed, cleaned and fitted with a bonding primer or another compatible system before the topcoat. The data sheet names what it is compatible with, and where it does not name the substrate or the previous finish, do not assume compatibility. A small test patch, left for the time the data sheet gives, is a practical check on a job where the old finish is unknown. Record the test and its result. Do not thin a topcoat or change its system to make it go on more easily unless the data sheet allows it.

instructionSections.heading: Substrate types and what they change
instructionSections.body: Timber needs sealing of knots and resins, and a primer that suits bare timber. Plaster and new plasterboard often need a sealer to stop the surface from absorbing paint unevenly and to control the sheen. Bare metal may need a rust-inhibiting primer that suits the metal and the environment. Masonry and render can be alkaline and damp, so the primer must suit that. Previously painted surfaces need checking for gloss, chalking, flaking and whether the old paint is sound, because the new system can only be as good as the surface under it. Each substrate has its own primer in the data sheet, and the choice of primer is recorded on the system record.

instructionSections.heading: Coverage: how much paint to buy
instructionSections.body: Coverage is the area that one litre of paint covers at the film thickness the manufacturer states. The figure on the data sheet is usually quoted for a smooth, sound surface under stated conditions. Rough, porous and textured surfaces take more paint, so the quantity needs an allowance for the surface type. Begin by measuring the area to be painted: multiply the length and height of each wall, add the other surfaces, and subtract openings that will not be painted. Multiply the area by the number of coats the system needs. Divide by the coverage figure from the data sheet to find the litres needed, then add an allowance for surface and waste. Round up to the nearest container size the product comes in. As a worked example only, with invented numbers: a wall of 40 square metres, two coats, a data sheet figure of 12 square metres per litre, and a 15 per cent allowance gives 80 square metres of coverage needed, which is 6.67 litres, plus 15 per cent, about 7.7 litres, so the job would order 8 litres of that product. Use the data sheet and the site's own figures for the real job.

instructionSections.heading: Application conditions and recoat times
instructionSections.body: Each coat should go on in the conditions the data sheet states. Paint applied in cold, damp, very hot or windy conditions can dry too fast, too slowly, or with a poor film. Painting in direct sun can make the paint dry before it levels, and the dark surfaces heat up faster. Check the surface temperature as well as the air temperature where the data sheet asks for it. Do not recoat before the previous coat has dried for the time the data sheet gives, because a second coat applied too early can lift or soften the first coat. A recoat window that runs out may need the surface to be lightly abraded or cleaned before the next coat, as the data sheet directs. Record the conditions at the time of application.

instructionSections.heading: Check the licence position before the job starts
instructionSections.body: The value of the job can decide whether a painting licence or registration is needed, and the test differs by state. New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). Materials count towards that value. Western Australia: painting work valued at $1,000 or more requires a licence, which is painting contractor registration (WA Government painters' scope of work page, last updated 23 December 2025). Victoria: painting-only jobs need no registration. You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills, such as plastering and painting, to complete a job (Consumer Victoria registration page, last updated 9 July 2025). Queensland: the licence position for painting-only work is not confirmed by an official source. South Australia, Tasmania, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory: the licence position for painting is not confirmed by an official source. Check the position for your state before you buy the materials or accept the job, and check it again if the scope grows.

instructionSections.heading: The limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not give a painting licence, a contractor licence or authority to undertake regulated building work. Completing it does not make you competent to select systems for substrates you have not been trained on, and the product data sheets always take priority over this lesson.

lessons.title: Cutting-in, rolling and edge technique
learningOutcomes: Cut in edges and corners with a clean line and no lap marks.
Roll walls and ceilings with an even film that avoids roller marks and runs.
Plan a wet edge so that the paint is blended before it dries.

instructionSections.heading: Why application decides the finish
instructionSections.body: A room can have a good paint system and good preparation and still look poor because of how the paint was put on. The eye reads the edges, corners and junctions first, and it reads the wall as a whole under the light that falls across it. Cutting in and rolling are the two steps that set the finish. Cutting in is done with a brush before the roller covers the main area, and it defines the lines where walls meet ceilings, skirting, architraves, window frames and other surfaces. Rolling covers the open areas. Both steps are carried out in sections, and the aim is to join each section to the one before it while the paint is still workable. The technique here is general working practice, and the product data sheet for each paint takes priority over it on loading, drying and recoating.

instructionSections.heading: Cutting in and keeping a wet edge
instructionSections.body: Load the brush lightly. Dip only part of the bristles, and tap or wipe off the excess against the side of the tin so that the paint does not drip or build up at the ferrule. Draw the brush along the edge with a steady stroke, using the tip and part of the body of the brush, and keep the line straight by guiding the brush with the other hand or with an edging tool where the surface allows. Work in sections small enough to roll before the cut-in dries. The cut-in should still be wet when the roller reaches it, so that the roller blends the two without leaving a line. A dry edge that the roller meets is the usual cause of a lap mark, which is a dark or lighter band where the paint has dried at different rates. Keep the brush clean between strokes, and never load a dirty or clogged brush with fresh paint. Where a corner or junction is tight, cut in both sides before rolling the centre, so that the centre blends into two wet edges.

instructionSections.heading: Rolling for an even film
instructionSections.body: Load the roller evenly across its sleeve by rolling it in the tray until the nap is saturated but not dripping, and then roll off the excess on the tray's ridge. Start the roll at the edge of the section and roll out in a W or M pattern, so that paint is spread across the area. Once the area is covered, roll out in one direction, with the roller running from the wet edge into the previously finished area, with light pressure. Pressure does the work of spreading, not the roller's weight, so pressing hard forces paint out of the sleeve, leaves thick patches and causes runs and an uneven film. Work from the window or main light source toward the darker side of the room, so that any unevenness is seen while it is still wet. Use a sleeve whose nap suits the surface texture. A smooth sleeve on a textured wall leaves the texture uncovered, and a long-nap sleeve on a smooth wall can leave a heavy orange-peel finish. Keep the roller wet, and avoid rolling the same area repeatedly once the paint has started to tack, because overworking lifts the film and leaves marks.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing, inspection and correction
instructionSections.body: Inspect the finished wall and ceiling under a raking light, which is a light held low across the surface, because flat light hides marks that show clearly at a low angle. Look for lap marks, roller stipple, runs and sags, missed spots (holidays), brush marks at the edges, and any patch where the sheen differs.
