Correct a run or a lap mark while the paint is still wet, using the roller or the brush with light strokes, if the data sheet allows the product to be worked while wet. Do not keep rolling over a mark once it has started to dry, because the attempt to fix it usually makes it worse. Record defects that cannot be corrected, and do not claim that the finish is complete while a known defect is open.

instructionSections.heading: Working safely with brushes, rollers and ladders
instructionSections.body: Use a ladder or a platform that is stable and suited to the task, set up on a firm surface, and do not overreach. Keep the work area clear of trip hazards, with drop sheets secured so that they do not slide. Ventilate the room as the product's data sheet directs, and keep solvent-based products away from ignition sources. Clean brushes and rollers at the end of the day with the cleaner the product's data sheet names, and do not leave solvent-soaked rags in a pile, because they can heat up and ignite.

instructionSections.heading: Value, licence and what this lesson does not give
instructionSections.body: The licence test for painting work is set by the value of the job, not by the technique used to apply paint. A higher standard of finish does not change whether a licence is needed. New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). The position for other states is set out in “Paint systems, primers and coverage” and “Painting quotes, variations and colour approval”. Completing this lesson does not give a painting licence, a certificate or any authority to undertake regulated building work.

lessons.title: Lead paint and older-surface awareness (refer)
learningOutcomes: Recognise the signs that an older surface may contain lead paint.
Stop disturbing older surfaces until their composition is assessed by a competent specialist.
Describe the licence and regulatory position for lead paint work, which the matrix does not record.

instructionSections.heading: Why an older surface is a reason to stop
instructionSections.body: Paint on older buildings may contain lead, and the age of a building is a reason to assess the paint, not proof either way. A painted surface can have lead in the paint film even when it looks clean, and the only reliable way to know is to have it assessed. Lead is harmful when it is breathed in or swallowed, and the most common route on a painting job is dust. The job that causes the most exposure is usually the one that makes the most dust: dry sanding, scraping, grinding, abrasive blasting or heat stripping. Heat stripping can also release fumes. Children and pregnant workers face particular risk, so occupants should be kept away from the work. Because the paint cannot be judged by eye, the safe default is that an older surface is not disturbed until a competent specialist has assessed it and the result is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as a lead process
instructionSections.body: Regulators treat certain paint-removal work as a lead process. The NSW lead notification guidance lists removing paint that contains lead among the processes that involve lead (page metadata published 30 June 2021, last modified 24 September 2021). The South Australian guidance lists dry sanding, buffing and grit blasting as lead processes for removing lead paint. Victoria regulates work that sands, buffs or removes paint with lead levels greater than 1 per cent by dry weight as a lead process (WorkSafe Victoria safety alert, published 20 January 2025). The exact thresholds and duties differ between states, so a painter who is unsure whether a surface contains lead should treat it as potentially lead-bearing until the assessment says otherwise.

instructionSections.heading: What to do when you find an older surface
instructionSections.body: Where an older surface is to be disturbed, stop before any sanding, scraping, heat stripping, grinding or blasting. Keep occupants, children and other trades away from the area, and put up barrier tape. Do not dry sweep the dust, and do not use compressed air or a standard vacuum to clear it, because these spread fine dust. Record the surface, its location, its condition and the reason for the stop. Refer the surface for specialist assessment, and tell the client in writing that the painting work on that surface waits for the outcome. Do not sand a small test patch to check the paint, because the test itself releases dust. Where the assessor advises containment or cleaning methods, follow their written advice and the regulator's requirements, and do not improvise.

instructionSections.heading: Notification timing differs by state
instructionSections.body: Notice rules apply around the start of lead risk work, and the timing differs by state. In New South Wales, the notice must be given seven days before lead risk work starts (SafeWork NSW, lead notifications page). In South Australia, the person conducting the business must notify within seven days of the work being determined to be lead risk work (SafeWork SA, lead risk work page); the commencement trigger is not confirmed by an official source. In the Australian Capital Territory, the notification is due within seven days of determining that the work is lead risk work (WorkSafe ACT). In Victoria, notice to WorkSafe is required before lead-risk work begins, and the guidance gives no fixed timeframe (WorkSafe Victoria, lead-based paint removal). None of these pages names a licence for lead paint removal. Do not assume that a painting licence covers lead paint removal, and confirm the position with the state regulator before accepting any lead paint removal.

instructionSections.heading: Asbestos: the other older-surface question
instructionSections.body: Older buildings may also contain asbestos, and asbestos can look like ordinary sheeting or render. Asbestos limits differ by state. In Victoria, unlicensed removal of non-friable asbestos is limited to an area of 10 square metres in total, and to a total time of one hour of asbestos removal work in any period of seven days, which is cumulative across all employees; the page is for an employer or a self-employed person (Asbestos Victoria, unlicensed asbestos removal, which shows an 'Updated' label and no date). The Victorian page does not list friable asbestos among the unlicensed exceptions, so treat friable material as outside that allowance and confirm with the regulator. In New South Wales, less than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos does not need a licence, and removal above that needs a class B licence, while any amount of friable asbestos needs a class A licence (Service NSW, asbestos removal licence). In Queensland, a licence is not needed for 10 square metres or less of non-friable asbestos, and any amount of friable asbestos needs a class A licence (WorkSafe Queensland). A painter who finds possible asbestos stops, keeps people clear, and refers it. Painting over asbestos-containing material is not a way round the removal rules.

instructionSections.heading: What this matrix does not say
instructionSections.body: The licence matrices used for this course record the painting licence positions but do not record a licence rule for lead paint removal. A painter should not accept lead paint removal work on the basis of a painting licence, and should confirm the state's position with the regulator before quoting, scheduling or starting. The record of that check is part of the job file.

instructionSections.heading: The limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Completing this lesson does not give a lead paint, asbestos or painting licence, certificate or authority to disturb older surfaces. It teaches you to recognise an older surface, to stop, to refer and to record. The assessment of lead and asbestos is done by a competent specialist.

lessons.title: Painting quotes, variations and colour approval
learningOutcomes: Write a painting quote that states the scope, the surfaces, the system, the coats and the exclusions.
Manage variations in writing before they are performed.
Obtain written colour approval and state the effect of a colour change on the price.

instructionSections.heading: A quote states what is included and what is not
instructionSections.body: A painting quote is the document that sets the client's expectations for the job, and most painting disputes start where the quote was vague. It should name the property and the surfaces to be painted, room by room and elevation by elevation, so that the client can see what the price covers. It should state the preparation included, such as washing, filling, sanding and masking, and say whether the preparation is part of the price. It should name the paint system, meaning the primer, undercoat and topcoat, and the number of coats for each surface. It should state how colour is approved, the sheen level and the date the quote is valid until. Exclusions matter as much as inclusions. Repairs to damp, plaster defects, mould treatment, assessment of older surfaces for lead or asbestos, furniture moving and the repair of cladding or timber are commonly excluded, and each exclusion should be written out rather than implied. A quote that says the house will be painted is not enough. Give the client a list that shows exactly what the price covers and what it does not.

instructionSections.heading: Quotes, estimates and what the client can rely on
instructionSections.body: Consumer guidance in Victoria advises clients to compare written quotes for the same work, to confirm what each quote covers, and to watch for cheaper quotes that leave items out or use a base rate that does not cover the finish they want. It also advises asking how changes to the quote or the timeframe will be handled, and recording changes in writing and signed off before they are made (Consumer Victoria, getting quotes; last updated 20 October 2025). The Australian Consumer Law guarantee of due care and skill applies to services. Under it, the work should be of the standard a competent provider with average skill and experience would deliver, and the provider should take reasonable steps to avoid loss or damage (ACCC, consumer rights and guarantees). A quote therefore should describe the work that the business is able and willing to deliver to that standard, and should not promise results the paint cannot give, such as hiding a crack that is not repaired.

instructionSections.heading: Check the licence position before the quote is issued
instructionSections.body: The value of the work and the state where it is done decide whether a licence or registration is needed, and the check belongs before the quote is sent. New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). Since 2015, stand-alone contracts for internal paintwork no longer need a licence, unless the paintwork is part of other home building work. Western Australia: painting work valued at $1,000 or more requires a licence, which is painting contractor registration (WA Government painters' scope of work page, last updated 23 December 2025). Victoria: painting-only jobs need no registration. You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills, such as plastering and painting, to complete a job (Consumer Victoria registration page, last updated 9 July 2025). Queensland: the licence position for painting-only work is not confirmed by an official source. South Australia, Tasmania, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory: the licence position for painting is not confirmed by an official source. Each check should be recorded with the state, the value, the date and the page checked.

instructionSections.heading: Written contracts and variations
instructionSections.body: A variation is any change to the agreed scope. It includes extra coats, extra surfaces, a different system, a change of colour that needs more coats, and repairs that are found during preparation. In New South Wales, the government guidance for residential building contracts says that a variation must be in writing, attached to the contract, and signed by both the client and the contractor or their nominated representative. It also says the builder should give the extra cost and any extra time before the variation work starts, with an exception for urgent work needed to prevent danger or property damage, where the written variation may follow (NSW Government, contracts for residential building work; last updated 29 April 2026). The same page says a written contract is required where the contract price for residential building work is over $5,000 including GST. Whatever the state, a variation should be recorded with its price and its effect on time and coats, and approved in writing before the work is done.

instructionSections.heading: Colour approval and the cost of a change
instructionSections.body: Colour approval should be in writing, and it should identify the product, the colour code or the sample reference, the sheen, and the surfaces the colour applies to. A physical sample painted on a board in the room's light is better than a name on a card, because a colour can look different under other light. State that a colour change after the first coat can require more coats and extra cost, and record the client's acceptance of that before the new colour goes on. Where the client asks for a darker colour part-way through, that is a variation. Stop, record the request, give the client the price and the effect on coats and time, and obtain written approval before the new colour is applied. Keep the approved colour record with the job file so that the finish can be matched if touch-ups are needed later.

instructionSections.heading: Filing and the limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: File the signed quote, each colour approval and each variation with the job record, and keep a note of the licence check. The records protect both the business and the client, and they show what was agreed if the job is later questioned. Completing this lesson does not give a painting licence, a certificate or any authority to quote for regulated building work.

lessons.title: House-sitting scope, keys and security checks
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between house sitting in the owner's home and boarding at the sitter's or another property, using the Victorian definition
Check the house, its security and its hazards before the first night, and record the check
Hold keys and codes under a written register.

instructionSections.heading: Boarding is defined by where the animal stays
instructionSections.body: Whether a pet arrangement is boarding or house sitting turns on where the animal is cared for. The Victorian boarding code describes boarding as holding one dog or cat for payment at a site other than where it normally lives (section 2.1). The Agriculture Victoria boarding establishments page (updated 27 October 2025) says every boarding establishment must be registered with the council for its area as a domestic animal business. The same page says home boarding is limited to up to two animals from one household at any one time, and section 10 of the code applies that two-animal limit. On that definition, an animal that stays in its own home is not boarded at a property other than its normal place of residence. Pet sitting in the sitter's own home may be home boarding. The Agriculture Victoria list of business types does not name house sitting. Stonnington's permit page (no date shown) lists for-profit homecare boarding among the businesses that need a permit, but does not define homecare boarding, which is council-specific.

instructionSections.heading: Boarding rules in other states: what is confirmed and what is not
instructionSections.body: New South Wales Code of Practice No 5 covers dogs and cats in boarding businesses. It requires every animal to be inspected once a day as a minimum, requires vaccination records dated no more than 12 months before admission, sets record-keeping duties, and names no licence. In the ACT, the pet business licensing scheme in Part 3A of the Animal Welfare Act 1992 reaches businesses that board animals, and a licence can run for up to five years. The ACT page treats boarding as covering both daytime and overnight care. In South Australia, the City of Burnside allows a business that runs a kennel for breeding, boarding or training dogs to apply for registration, and development approval is needed first. In Western Australia, the City of South Perth states that a licence is required to run a kennel, or to keep more dogs than the council's no-licence limit, and the council sets that limit. The page does not say whether a licence covers house sitting.

instructionSections.heading: Keys, security and the house check
instructionSections.body: A house sitter holds the client's keys, codes, alarm details and sometimes the car. Record each key and code in a register with the date received, the holder and the date returned, and store the register in a locked place. Never copy a key, and never give a code to another person. Before the first night, walk through the home and check each entry point, the alarm, the gate, the pet door and any hazards such as a pool, a stair gate, a loose fence or a toxic plant. Record the check, and tell the client what you found. If the home is unsafe or the alarm does not work, do not stay in it. Contact the client and the business's escalation contact in {{business:safety.escalation_contact}}, and record the decision. Access and alarm instructions are held in {{business:customers.access_instructions}}. Client information is covered by the privacy approach in “Privacy, security and customer property”.

lessons.title: Pet routines, feeding and medication
learningOutcomes: Follow the owner's written routine for feeding, exercise, toileting and rest, and record each step
Give medication only as the owner and the vet have directed, and record each dose
Recognise the signs of illness or distress that need an immediate call to the owner or vet

instructionSections.heading: The owner's written routine is the standard
instructionSections.body: A pet sitter follows the owner's written routine, not the sitter's own habits. The routine covers meals and portion sizes, the food brand, feeding times, walks and toileting, play, rest, litter or cage care, and any special needs such as a diet or a behaviour plan. Before the first visit, confirm each item with the owner, and record the answers in the client file. Where the owner's routine conflicts with the sitter's view of what is good for the animal, the sitter follows the routine and raises the concern with the owner. A change to the routine needs the owner's written agreement. The business's routine record is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instructionSections.heading: Medication: only as directed, and recorded
instructionSections.body: Medication is a high-risk task. Give medication only where the owner's written instructions and the vet's directions match, and where the dose, the timing and the method are clear. Check the label of the medicine against the instructions before each dose, and record each dose with the time given. Never give a human medicine to an animal, and never double a dose to catch up on a missed one unless the vet's written direction says to. Where a dose is missed or the animal refuses it, call the owner or the vet for guidance and record the call. The business should not give any medication until the owner has provided written direction, and until the business procedure has been followed.

instructionSections.heading: Signs of illness and when to call
instructionSections.body: A sitter must watch each animal at every visit for changes from its normal behaviour. Signs that need an immediate call to the owner or the vet include vomiting or diarrhoea that does not stop, refusal of food or water for a period the vet has set, difficulty breathing, collapse, a seizure, bleeding, a limp that stops the animal walking, a swollen abdomen, and any sudden change in behaviour that is severe. Where the owner cannot be reached, call the vet named in the owner's written authority. The emergency steps for animal first response are set out in “Pet first aid and emergency vet referral”, and the owner's authority to take the animal to care must be on the file before any visit.

lessons.title: Emergency contacts and vet authority
learningOutcomes: Record the owner's emergency contacts, the chosen vet and the written authority for emergency care before the first visit
Describe the limit of the sitter's authority to consent to treatment, and the steps when the owner cannot be reached
Explain the on-call vet arrangement required for Victorian boarding establishments.

instructionSections.heading: Emergency contacts before the first visit
instructionSections.body: Before the first visit, the sitter must hold the owner's mobile number, a second contact who can make decisions, the owner's vet name and phone number, the address of the nearest emergency vet, and the owner's written authority for emergency care, including any spending limit the owner sets. Record each contact on the client file, and check that the numbers work before the owner leaves. A contact who cannot be reached when needed is not a contact. The business's emergency contact procedure is held in {{business:safety.emergency_contact}}, and the escalation contact for the business is {{business:safety.escalation_contact}}. Those are business fields that must be completed for each client's arrangement.

instructionSections.heading: The limit of the sitter's authority
instructionSections.body: A pet sitter is not the owner. The sitter may take an animal to a vet in an emergency where the owner has given written authority to do so, and the authority must state what may be done and what spending is allowed. Without that authority, the sitter should try to contact the owner and the second contact before any treatment is agreed. The sitter must not agree to surgery, sedation, euthanasia or a high-cost procedure on the owner's behalf unless the owner has said so in writing. The sitter must never sign a vet consent form for a treatment the owner has not authorised.

instructionSections.heading: The on-call vet arrangement in Victoria
instructionSections.body: The Victorian Boarding Code requires boarding establishments to hold a signed arrangement with a sufficient number of vets who are available on call to treat animals (section 4.2). It also requires isolation to be available at the premises or at a veterinary clinic (section 5.2). Its records section (section 9) lists the owner's details, the vaccination status, and the veterinarian's name and telephone contact. These are confirmed requirements for boarding establishments in Victoria, and the code is at Revision 1 (October 2004), printed April 2025. The sitter should follow the same standard as good practice, which means a written vet arrangement and the owner's contact record, until the position is confirmed with Agriculture Victoria. Completing this lesson does not create a vet arrangement or give the sitter any authority over veterinary decisions.

lessons.title: Visit logs, photos and handover reports
learningOutcomes: Keep a visit log that records each visit, the routine followed, the observations and any concern
Take and store photos of an animal only under the owner's consent and the business's photo rules
Prepare a handover report that tells the owner what happened, what was not done, and what to do next

instructionSections.heading: The visit log is the evidence of the sit
instructionSections.body: A visit log is a dated record of each visit. It should record the arrival and departure time, the routine steps completed, the food and water given, the toilet breaks and walks, any medication dose, the animal's condition, any change from normal behaviour, and any concern raised with the owner or the vet. A visit log written at the end of the day from memory is weaker than one written at the visit. Write the log at the time, using the same format for every visit, so that a gap is easy to see. The business's log format is held in {{business:quality.evidence_requirements}}. Section 9 of the Victorian boarding code sets the records a boarding establishment must keep, including owner contact details, vaccination status and the vet's details. The log is kept in any case as good practice.

instructionSections.heading: Photos: consent first, storage second
instructionSections.body: Photos help an owner see that the animal is well. They are also personal information about the owner's home and pet. Take a photo only where the owner has agreed to photos in writing, and never photograph the inside of the home beyond what the owner has agreed to show. Do not post photos of an animal or a home on social media without the owner's written consent. Store photos on a secure device or in a secure system, label each photo with the date and the visit, and delete photos at the end of the period the owner agreed. The business's photo rule is held in {{business:jobs.photo_requirements}}. The business should follow the privacy approach in “Privacy, security and customer property”.

instructionSections.heading: The handover report
instructionSections.body: At the end of a sit, the sitter gives the owner a handover report. It should state the dates covered, the routine followed, any change to the routine, the medication given with the times, the observations, any health concern, any call made to the owner or the vet and the advice given, any fault found in the home, and any task not completed with the reason. The report should be factual and should not guess. Where the sitter did not see something, the report should say so. The handover is the point where the owner takes back responsibility, so the report must be clear about what the owner needs to do next, such as booking a vet check or replacing a lock. The handover record is signed or confirmed by the owner, and kept on the client file.

lessons.title: Pricing and extended stays
learningOutcomes: Price a visit or a stay from the time, the travel, the supplies and the risk of the arrangement
Identify the point at which an extended stay or a change of location may become boarding, and stop to confirm the position
Explain the insurance that the Victorian boarding code requires for boarding establishments.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing visits and stays
instructionSections.body: A visit price should cover the travel, the time at the home, the time spent on the log and the report, the supplies used, and the business's share of the costs of any compliance step. A stay price should cover the nights, the number of visits, and the extra supplies and risk. A house sit with an overnight stay in the owner's home carries a different risk from a series of day visits. Build each price from its parts, and record the build. The business's pricing method is held in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}, and the minimum charge in {{business:pricing.minimum_charge}}. Do not make a price depend on any statement about the animal's health, and do not promise outcomes.

instructionSections.heading: When an extended stay may become boarding
instructionSections.body: The line between house sitting and boarding turns on where the animal is cared for. The Victorian boarding code describes boarding as holding one dog or cat for payment at a site other than where it normally lives, and it limits home boarding to two animals from one household. The boarding establishments page confirms the two-animal limit for home boarding. If a sitter takes an animal to the sitter's own home for a stay, the sitter may be running home boarding, and a council registration may be needed. Stonnington's permit page (no date shown) lists for-profit homecare boarding among the businesses that need a permit. The business must stop and confirm the position with Agriculture Victoria and the council before offering a stay in the sitter's own home, or any stay that could be treated as boarding.

instructionSections.heading: Insurance for boarding and what applies to sitters
instructionSections.body: The Victorian boarding code sets public liability of $10,000,000 for boarding establishments. That is confirmed for boarding establishments. The business should not assume that a sitter is exempt, and should confirm the position with its insurer and the regulator before offering a stay that could be boarding. Where a council permit or registration applies, the council may set its own insurance condition, and the sitter must check it before the stay starts. In Victoria, WorkSafe Victoria's WorkCover page (reviewed 19/05/2026) indicates that registration is generally expected once a business takes on employees, and that a sole trader with no other workers does not need to register. Record each insurance check in {{business:compliance.policy_reference}}.

lessons.title: Substrate types and bonding
learningOutcomes: Identify the common plaster substrates and their bonding behaviour.
Select a bonding agent or key coat suited to the substrate and the finish.
Identify moisture and movement that must be resolved before plaster is applied.

instructionSections.heading: Know the substrate
instructionSections.body: Plaster bonds differently to each substrate. Plasterboard has a paper face that takes a plaster finish when the joints are set correctly. Masonry is porous and may need a bonding agent or a scratch coat to key the plaster. Lime-based older plaster can be soft, crumbly or bonded poorly to its backing, and it needs assessment before a cement-based coat is applied over it. Render and concrete may carry salts, dust or release agent that stop bonding. Identify the substrate and its condition before choosing the coat.

instructionSections.heading: Bonding and moisture
instructionSections.body: Bonding fails when the substrate is dusty, greasy, damp or too smooth. Clean and dry the surface, and use a bonding agent or key coat that the product data sheet recommends for the substrate. Check for damp before plastering, because plaster laid on a moisture source will fail and hide the cause. Movement at junctions or cracks can cause the finish to crack later, so note movement and refer it before the coat is applied. A plaster that bonds well to a sound substrate and dries evenly is the result of checking these points first. Before you accept plaster work, check the licence threshold for its value. In New South Wales the figure is more than $5,000 of labour and materials, GST included, for dry and wet plastering (NSW Government pages, last updated 23 June 2026).

lessons.title: Patch, skim and finishing coats
learningOutcomes: Apply a patch and a skim coat in layers suited to the depth and the finish.
Allow each layer to dry before the next is applied, and check the drying.
Finish a skim to a flat, even surface that is ready for paint.

instructionSections.heading: Layers and drying
instructionSections.body: A plaster repair is built in layers. Deep patches are filled in lifts, each thinner than the last, and each lift is allowed to stiffen before the next. A thin skim coat is applied last, over a sound and dry base. Applying a thick layer in one go traps moisture, cracks as it shrinks, and may not bond. Drying takes longer in cold and damp conditions, and the surface must be dry before paint is applied. Check the drying by the colour and the feel of the surface, and by the data sheet time.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing a skim
instructionSections.body: Apply the skim with a flat trowel, working in short passes that overlap. Work from a light source across the wall so that high and low spots show. Let the skim firm enough to be worked, and then finish with a damp trowel or sponge, working from the centre toward the edges. A skim that is worked too early pulls off; a skim that is left too long shows trowel marks. Check the finished surface with a straight edge and under a raking light before it is painted.

lessons.title: Sanding dust and silica exposure controls
learningOutcomes: Identify the dust that sanding plaster produces and the exposure route it creates.
Apply wet methods, extraction and suitable respiratory protection to control dust.
Stop sanding older or unknown material until its composition is assessed.

instructionSections.heading: Where the dust comes from
instructionSections.body: Sanding plaster, joint compound and some sand-based products produces fine dust. Some plaster and sand products contain crystalline silica, and inhaling fine silica dust is a serious health risk. Dust can also come from older coatings and from materials in older buildings that may contain asbestos. The control method depends on what the material is, and an unknown material is treated as hazardous until it is identified or assessed. Check the product safety data sheet for the material before sanding. The workplace exposure standard for respirable crystalline silica is 0.05 mg/m3 as an 8-hour time-weighted average, half the earlier 0.1 mg/m3 figure (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown; Safe Work Australia research page, no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Control the dust at source
instructionSections.body: Use wet methods where the product allows them, because wet material produces much less airborne dust. Where dry sanding is used, use a power sander connected to extraction with a suitable filter, and keep the work area ventilated. Keep occupants and children away, close doors, and cover vents and ducts. Clean up with damp methods and an extraction unit suited to fine dust, and do not dry sweep. Wear respiratory protection suited to the dust and fitted correctly, and change or clean it as the manufacturer directs.

lessons.title: Plastering quotes and scope boundaries
learningOutcomes: Write a plastering quote that states the scope, the coats, the preparation and the exclusions.
Identify the boundary between plastering, painting and other trades, and state it in the quote.
Check the licence threshold for the job value and the type of plaster work before quoting.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and exclusions in the quote
instructionSections.body: A plastering quote should state the surfaces, the number of coats, the preparation included, the finish standard, and the exclusions. Common exclusions are damp repairs, structural cracking, older plaster assessment, lead or asbestos assessment, and making good after other trades. A quote that says plaster the walls leaves the client to guess what is included. Write the finish standard in terms the client can check, such as a flat finish under raking light, and attach the exclusions to the quote.

instructionSections.heading: The boundary with painting and other trades
instructionSections.body: Plastering and painting overlap at the finish. The quote should say whether the plaster is finished ready for paint, and whether painting is included or by another trade. A plasterer who skims a wall to a finish that is not ready for paint, without saying so, creates a dispute. Where a repair involves damp, structural movement or wiring, refer it and exclude it from the quote. Record each variation in writing and obtain approval before it is performed. Consumer Victoria states: “You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills (such as plastering and painting) to complete a job.” A combined quote must address that before it is issued (Consumer Victoria page, last updated 9 July 2025).

lessons.title: Pond ecology, fish and plant balance
learningOutcomes: Describe the producers, consumers and decomposers in a garden pond and explain how they depend on one another
Identify common causes of imbalance, including overfeeding, organic debris, nutrient runoff, low oxygen and pump failure
Choose a first response to stressed fish that checks the pump, aeration and temperature before any other action
Keep pool chemicals and other non-pond products out of a pond with fish or plants, and refer any request the owner's plan does not cover

instructionSections.heading: A pond is a living system
instructionSections.body: A garden pond is a small ecosystem in which water, plants, animals and microorganisms depend on one another. Producers are the plants that make food from light and dissolved nutrients: submerged plants, floating plants, plants with floating leaves, and the microscopic algae (phytoplankton) that float in open water and can colour it green. Consumers feed on other living things. Small grazing animals such as snails, insects and tadpoles eat algae and plant matter, fish and frogs eat those animals, and birds and turtles sit higher in the food web. Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi in the sediment and the filter, break down dead material and return nutrients to the plants. Because each group relies on the others, a problem in one part, such as too much food, shows up in the water quality and in the health of the fish. A pond with clean water, some shade, a range of plants and varied habitats supports the widest range of wildlife, and a balanced pond tends to need less intervention.

instructionSections.heading: Common causes of imbalance
instructionSections.body: Overfeeding is one of the most common causes of poor water. Uneaten food and fish waste add nutrients, feed algae and, as they decompose, use up dissolved oxygen. Leaves, needles and other organic debris add to the same load, and they are hardest to remove once they have started to rot. Nutrients also enter ponds from outside. Fertiliser and other pollutants carried by runoff from lawns and paved areas can reach a pond directly or through the stormwater system, and nutrient-rich water encourages rapid algae growth. When algae die, more organic matter builds up and the cycle speeds up. Warm, still weather lowers the oxygen the water can hold, and warm water also speeds up decay. A stopped pump or a clogged filter removes both mechanical filtration and aeration. Shade is not always a problem. In natural settings, shade and leaf litter combined with clean water support habitats that open, sunlit ponds may not, so cutting back trees is an owner decision with ecological effects, not a routine maintenance step.

instructionSections.heading: First response to stressed fish
instructionSections.body: When fish gasp at the surface, act on the most likely immediate cause first, which is usually low oxygen. Check that the pump is running and that any aeration is working. Measure the water temperature in degrees Celsius and record the time. Check the feeding record and remove uneaten food. If the water is clearly poor, a small partial water change with conditioned water at a similar temperature may help, but it must follow the owner's plan and be gradual. Do not add a chemical to force a result. Record what you found and what you did. If fish are dying in numbers, or an odour or cloudiness stays after these steps, stop the adjustments and refer the matter to the owner and, where appropriate, to a qualified aquatic specialist.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning and water changes
instructionSections.body: Clean the pond gradually. Remove excess debris by hand or with a net, and do not remove all the sediment or all the plants in one session. The bacteria in the filter and the sediment, and the plants, keep the system stable, and a complete clean removes them together, which can cause a sudden fall in water quality. Partial water changes should be modest. Condition tap water to remove chlorine and chloramine before it enters the pond, and match its temperature to the pond as closely as is practical. Sudden changes in temperature or water chemistry are a common cause of fish stress, and a sudden large change should be avoided even when the water looks poor.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping non-pond products out
instructionSections.body: Pool chlorine, pool algaecides, pool pH products and other pool chemicals are formulated for a different system and must not be used in a pond with fish or plants. Pond treatment products are chosen for the specific system and are used only where the owner's instruction and the product label allow them. Read the label and the safety data sheet before any product is used. Storage needs care as well. So keep pond products separate from pool chemicals, out of reach of children and pets, and away from anything that could mix with them. Chemical control of pests, weeds or fish is not taught in this course. Those tasks need product-label checks, state rules and, where a licence applies, the licence, and they sit outside this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: When to refer, and moving fish
instructionSections.body: Refer to the owner when fish die in numbers, when an odour or cloudiness does not respond to the usual steps, when disease is suspected, or when a treatment is requested that is not in the owner's instruction. Moving live fish is regulated. In Western Australia, the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development says that moving live fish within the state needs a translocation approval. Queensland and New South Wales rules on restricted fish, releases and sightings are set out in the water-movement lesson (“Water conservation and environmental release for ponds”).

lessons.title: Pond liner and leak inspection
learningOutcomes: Inspect a pond liner, its edges, penetrations, outlets and pump fittings for signs of leaks and damage
Carry out a bucket test to separate evaporation from a leak, and record the result with its conditions
Identify liner materials and conditions that increase the risk of damage, and report them without recommending a product
Work on liners and edges without damaging the liner or creating a fall, crush or electrical hazard

instructionSections.heading: Scope: maintenance and inspection, not construction
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers inspection, testing and reporting on a pond that already exists. Building a new pond, excavating a pit, laying a new liner or reshaping a pond is a separate course and is outside the scope of this lesson. If a client needs a new liner or structural work, record the findings, refer the work and quote it under the business's approved method. Replacing a liner is not a routine maintenance task for this course.

instructionSections.heading: Where pond leaks occur
instructionSections.body: Pond leaks usually appear at the liner edges, at seams and joins, at places where pipes or outlets pass through the liner, at the waterline where ultraviolet light and wear damage the liner, under rocks, and where tree roots push the liner upward. Liners also fail where they have been stretched, because a stretched liner thins and cracks over time. Pumps, valves, fittings and the connections to a skimmer or bog filter can leak too. Inspect each of these in turn rather than looking only at the water surface, because a leak can be hidden below the water or in the surround. Note any sign of soil or sand washing in along an edge, since that often points to a gap in the edge or the liner beneath it.

instructionSections.heading: The liner itself: materials and condition
instructionSections.body: A liner should be rated for ultraviolet light and for the frost conditions of the site, otherwise it can become brittle or lose its seams. Tarpaulins and similar sheeting should not be used as a pond liner, because some contain heavy metals that can harm fish and plants. Some laminated textured liners can separate their layers in weather, causing leaks, so record the material if it can be identified. Report the material and its condition, and do not recommend a brand or product. Avoid stretching the liner during inspection or cleaning, because stretching shortens its life. Where a liner is covered by gravel or slope protection, record how much of the liner is covered before you start, because covered areas are harder to inspect.

instructionSections.heading: The bucket test
instructionSections.body: A bucket test separates evaporation from a leak. Place a bucket on a step inside the pond so that its water level is close to the pond's level, mark the water level inside and outside the bucket, and leave it for the same period under the same conditions. If the water level in the pond drops more than the level in the bucket, the loss is more likely to be a leak or an outlet fault. Record the start and finish times, the level drop inside and outside the bucket in millimetres, the air temperature in Celsius, the rain and the wind. Repeat the test if the first result is unclear, and report the result rather than guessing. A short test is evidence of loss, but it does not show where the leak is.

instructionSections.heading: Inspecting safely and recording findings
instructionSections.body: Do not walk on a liner in shoes that may puncture it. Use soft-soled footwear with rounded soles, or boards, and keep sharp tools away from the liner. Lift rocks one at a time with a plan, because a rock can fall and cause a crush injury. Keep walkways and edges clear, and be careful on wet edges and steep banks. Work near electrical pumps only after the power is isolated and proven off, and do not use a damaged cord. Connection work and wiring are licensed work in many circumstances; in New South Wales, wiring work is licensed or certified work at any price. Record what you inspected and what you found, including the location of any damage, the method of the test and the result. Do not certify the pond as watertight after a visual check. A bucket test over a short period supports a finding, but a repair is a separate scope that the client must approve.

lessons.title: Wildlife, netting and protected-species boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify common pond wildlife and the situations where wildlife protection rules may apply
Install or check netting so that it protects fish without trapping or harming wildlife
Stop work and refer when nests, eggs, breeding animals or protected species are found
Explain the limits of this lesson: it does not authorise handling, moving or harming native animals, or disturbing their nests and eggs

instructionSections.heading: Ponds attract wildlife
instructionSections.body: Ponds attract birds, frogs, dragonflies, water beetles, turtles, snails and many other animals. Many pond animals use the very shallow water at the edge, where the water is only a few centimetres deep, and well-vegetated ponds can look dry to a person while still supporting these animals. Some of the animals are common, and some are native species that may be protected. A heron may be a threat to fish, but it is a native bird and its protection status depends on the state and the species. Do not assume that a species is common, and do not assume that a rule does not apply because the pond is in a backyard. Native animals are protected under state and territory law (for NSW), and listed threatened species and communities may also be protected under national law.

instructionSections.heading: What the state and national rules say
instructionSections.body: Under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016, NSW's native birds, reptiles, amphibians and mammals count as protected, with the dingo as the stated exception. The state department can grant licences to people or organisations that control, hold or trade protected species, and the page lists bird exceptions in some regions, such as sulphur-crested cockatoos and galahs in several Local Land Services regions. At federal level, threatened species and communities on the official lists are a protected matter, and a proposed action that could significantly affect them goes to the federal environment minister for a decision.

instructionSections.heading: Netting and its risks
instructionSections.body: Netting is used to keep birds away from fish. It must be supported above the water, secured at the edges and tensioned so that it does not drop into the pond, where birds, frogs or turtles can become tangled. Loose, torn or sagging netting is a trap for wildlife. Check netting at each visit, according to the owner's plan, and look for animals caught in it. If an animal is trapped, do not handle or release it unless you are authorised and competent to do so. Otherwise, report the entrapment to the owner and to the appropriate wildlife authority. Keep the netting clear of the water surface so that animals can still reach the edge, and secure the edges so that the net cannot be pulled into the water.

instructionSections.heading: Nests, eggs and breeding animals
instructionSections.body: Frogspawn, bird nests, eggs, young animals and breeding sites are not to be moved, removed or disturbed by a contract worker. If you find one, pause work in that area, keep the disturbance low, and tell the owner. Record the location and the observation. Work in that area may resume only when the owner and the wildlife authority's guidance allow it, and work elsewhere should continue only if it does not disturb the animals.

instructionSections.heading: What this lesson does not authorise
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not authorise you to handle, capture, relocate, kill or harm native animals, to disturb protected habitat, or to remove or relocate frogspawn or nests. Completing this lesson does not give that authority, and it does not give any licence to hold, trade or control protected animals.

lessons.title: Access features: inlet, outlet, overflow, edges and depth
learningOutcomes: Describe the job of the inlet, outlet, overflow and drain point, and check each for blockage, movement or leaks
Measure freeboard and water depth at a fixed reference point, and record them so that later changes can be seen
Inspect pond edges, stones and banks for movement, soil wash-in and exposed liner, and make the area safe
Identify tree-root, erosion and bank problems, and refer repair work without cutting roots near the liner

instructionSections.heading: Access is part of the job
instructionSections.body: A pond service is only as good as the access to the parts that need attention. The pump, the filter, the skimmer, the valves, the outlet, the overflow and any drain point all need to be reachable without stepping on the liner, without lifting heavy stones alone and without working over deep water. Before a visit, check the access route and any path the owner has asked you to keep clear, and note any part that cannot be reached safely. A new pond or a new excavation is a separate course and is not part of this lesson. This lesson covers checking and maintaining the access features of a pond that already exists.

instructionSections.heading: Inlet, outlet and overflow
instructionSections.body: The inlet returns water to the pond, usually from a pump or a filter. The outlet draws water out, for example to a skimmer, a pump intake or a drain point. The overflow lets excess water leave during heavy rain, so that the water level stays below the rim. Inspect each in turn. Check that the outlet has its screen in place, because a suction screen keeps fish, animals and debris out of the pipe. Remove any blockage with the power off and the pump isolated. Look for cracks, loose joints and movement where a pipe passes through the liner, and check that the inlet return still points where it was set. Check where the overflow water goes, and confirm that the discharge point is the one the owner has agreed. One NSW council's stormwater factsheet treats putting stormwater into its sewer as an offence, and it does not mention pond water. The route must be checked before any water is discharged.

instructionSections.heading: Freeboard and water level
instructionSections.body: Freeboard is the vertical gap between the water surface and the lowest point of the pond rim or edge. The water should never run over the top, so the freeboard should stay clear at all times, including during heavy rain. Measure it at a fixed point and record the value in millimetres, with the date. Add a permanent reference mark on a wall or a fixed feature if the owner agrees, so that the next measurement is taken from the same place. A fall in water level is a reason to run a bucket test, as set out in the liner lesson (“Pond liner and leak inspection”). A rise that brings the water close to the rim calls for an overflow check and a note to the owner.

instructionSections.heading: Edges, banks and exit points
instructionSections.body: The edges hold the liner in place and hide it from view. Check that edge stones, slabs and pavers are firm, that none has shifted to expose the liner, and that soil or sand is not washing into the pond along the edge. Where a drainage strip of coarse gravel has been used at the edge, check that it is still free of soil. Stones that are fist-sized or larger, piled to hold steep slopes, are the usual approach to securing an edge in a garden pond, and a loose stone on a steep bank is a fall and crush hazard. Make the area safe before you work on a bank. Check that there is a way out for animals and for people, such as a gently sloped section or an exit aid, because steep, smooth walls can trap animals that fall in. Note wet edges and slippery areas on the record.

instructionSections.heading: Depth, sediment and the bank zone
instructionSections.body: Depth is recorded at the same reference point each time, with a marked pole or a measured line. Record the depth to the sediment as well as the depth of the water, because the difference shows how fast sediment is building up, which links to the sludge work in “Debris, sludge and plant management”. Keep the shallow margins, where many animals live, in good condition and free of debris, and do not make them deeper without the owner's agreement. Depth also matters for winter refuge, which is covered in “Seasonal care and cold-climate notes”.

instructionSections.heading: Trees, roots and embankments
instructionSections.body: Tree roots can push under the liner or lift the edge, and leaf fall adds to the load in the pond. Where a root is under or next to the liner, record its location, photograph it where the business requires, and refer the repair. In an embankment pond, the bank is a dike, and its job is to hold the water. Check for erosion, bare patches, wet spots, cracks and animal burrows, and check that grass or other ground cover is still holding the bank. Large trees on or near a dike are a risk to its structure, so note them in the record and refer any concern to the owner. Do not cut roots close to the liner.

lessons.title: Debris, sludge and plant management
learningOutcomes: Explain why organic debris and sludge build up in a pond and how they change oxygen, nutrients and clarity
Set a routine that removes debris and sludge in small amounts, so that the workload stays low and the bacteria and plants are kept
Hold, label and dispose of sludge and plant matter without moving water, pests or disease to another site
Manage floating and submerged plants and tree litter to keep the pond in balance, and record the volumes removed

instructionSections.heading: Why debris is a workload problem
instructionSections.body: Leaves, needles, dead plant stems and uneaten food all add organic matter to a pond. As this matter decomposes, bacteria use up dissolved oxygen and release nutrients, which feed algae. Decay is faster in warm water, so debris that is left for a week in summer can cause more trouble than the same debris removed in cool weather. Needles and small leaves sink, mix into the sediment and become hard to remove once they have rotted. A pond with a regular, small removal routine needs fewer large, costly clean-ups, which is the main workload saving in this lesson. Reducing the amount that enters the pond also helps. Where the layout allows, a netted cover in leaf season and a plan for trimming overhanging branches, agreed with the owner, reduce the load before it arrives.

instructionSections.heading: A routine that keeps the load low
instructionSections.body: Remove floating debris from the surface with a net on each visit, and in leaf season more often if the owner's plan allows. Clean the skimmer basket and the pre-filter, which are the most common places for debris to collect, as set out in the filtration lessons. Work from the edge inward, and lift debris out rather than stirring it into the water, because stirring releases sediment and reduces clarity. Put debris into a container with a lid, let it drain on site where that is safe and allowed, and keep it apart from the water. Record the volume removed each visit, so that the trend shows whether the routine is keeping pace with the load.

instructionSections.heading: Sludge: where it builds and how to remove it
instructionSections.body: Sludge collects in low corners, under outlets and behind large rocks, where the water moves slowly. Measure the depth of sediment at the reference point described in the access lesson (“Access features: inlet, outlet, overflow, edges and depth”), and remove it in layers rather than all at once, leaving enough to keep the bacteria and plants stable. Use a method that removes sludge with as little water as possible, because every litre removed has to be replaced and then discharged or stored. Hold the sludge on site in a lidded container until the disposal route is confirmed. Sludge can carry pest species and disease, so do not move it, or any water taken with it, to another pond or site.

instructionSections.heading: Plants: keeping the balance
instructionSections.body: Submerged plants add oxygen to the water and compete with algae for nutrients, which is why a pond with a healthy submerged layer tends to be clearer. Floating-leaved plants, such as water lilies, can cover so much of the surface that light no longer reaches the submerged plants. Keep them to an agreed area and reduce leaves moderately if they outgrow it. Remove rotting leaves, dead stems and damaged roots, and trim within the plant basket so that the plant does not spread over the edge. Check that baskets are still firm and that the plant is still growing in its medium. Do not take plants from the wild, because removing native plants from nature is forbidden in many cases. Some plants are regulated as invasive in some states. In Queensland, the state's prohibited-plant page gives examples including anchored water hyacinth, Eurasian water milfoil, floating water chestnut and water soldiers, and says a sighting of a prohibited invasive plant is to be reported to Biosecurity Queensland within 24 hours. In NSW, water hyacinth is a biosecurity zone weed that is to be wiped out where that is practicable, and control order weeds are to be destroyed at once.

instructionSections.heading: Tree litter and the value of shade
instructionSections.body: Tree leaves and shade have a value as well as a cost. Shade and leaf litter, combined with clean water, provide habitat for some species that live only in ponds. The aim is therefore to manage leaf litter, not to remove every leaf from every corner. Net the surface, remove heavy accumulations and keep the litter out of the deep sediment, and if the owner agrees, leave a small, defined area where leaves can settle. Record the agreement, so that a later visit does not undo it by mistake. Removing a tree or cutting it back is an owner decision with ecological and approval effects, and it is not part of routine debris removal.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the workload
instructionSections.body: Record the volume removed, estimated in litres or buckets, the type of material, where it was held, the time taken and the approval for any water movement. This record shows the workload trend and supports the pricing method in the business's approved method ({{business:pricing.pricing_method}}). It also shows the owner why a routine is needed, and it provides the evidence for any change to the plan.

lessons.title: Pumps, UV clarifiers and filters
learningOutcomes: Describe the circulation loop and the reasons the components are placed in the order the system was designed to use
Carry out routine checks and cleaning on pumps, intake screens, aeration and filter media with the power isolated
Carry out safe routine UV clarifier checks, including isolation, lamp care and the rule against looking at a lit lamp
Identify faults, cords and connections that must be reported, and state what the licence covers without implying that this lesson grants it

instructionSections.heading: The circulation loop and the order of components
instructionSections.body: Pond water is drawn in through a skimmer, a pre-filter or a pump intake, moved by a pump through a filter where solids are caught and bacteria break down waste, through a UV clarifier where one is fitted, and returned through a waterfall, stream or return outlet. The order of the filter and the UV unit depends on the purpose the system was built for. A product guide describes two arrangements, one in which the filter sits after the UV unit so that the algae the UV unit clumps are caught, and one in which the filter sits before the UV unit so that particles do not shade the water from the light. Do not change the order of an existing system without the manufacturer's instruction and the owner's agreement, and record the layout you find before you touch anything.

instructionSections.heading: Pumps and aeration: routine checks
instructionSections.body: Check each pump at each visit. Look and listen for changes in noise, flow at the return, and any sign that the pump is running dry or losing its prime. Keep the intake clear. An intake that sits in sludge or weed draws debris into the pump and reduces flow, so check the position of the intake against the sediment depth (“Debris, sludge and plant management”). Clean the intake screen and the pre-filter basket with the power off and the pump isolated. Never reach into a running pump, and never run a pump with no water. Check that the cord is intact along its length, that it is kept out of the water and away from wet ground, and that any extension lead is not in use across the pond. Aeration works on the same principle as the pump: check the air pump, the tubing for splits, and the diffuser stones for blockage, with the power isolated before any connection is handled.

instructionSections.heading: UV clarifiers: isolation and lamp care
instructionSections.body: A UV clarifier contains a lamp that can injure the eyes and skin, so switch it off and isolate its supply before you open the housing. Do not look at a lit lamp. Check that the quartz sleeve around the lamp is clean and free of algae film, and that the seals are intact. A clean sleeve passes more light, and a dirty one can make the unit appear to be working when it is not. Replace a lamp only where the manufacturer's instructions and the owner's plan allow it, and only after isolation. Water passing through the unit should be as clear as the system allows, because particles can shade the water from the light. The unit must also suit the flow the pump gives it, and running it at a lower flow gives longer exposure.

instructionSections.heading: Filters: cleaning with pond water
instructionSections.body: Filter media hold the bacteria that break down ammonia and nitrite, and they should be cleaned without losing those bacteria. Rinse biological media in pond water, not tap water, because chlorine and chloramine harm the bacteria. Clean one section at a time, so that part of the media keeps its bacteria while the rest is cleaned. After a heavy clean, the biological activity recovers slowly, so do not clean all the media on the same visit unless the owner has agreed. Record which sections were cleaned, and check the flow afterwards. Dispose of any media that is damaged or broken down only as the business's waste procedure and the council allow.

instructionSections.heading: Where electrical work stops
instructionSections.body: Routine tasks are visual checks, cleaning of screens and baskets with the power off, checking that a cord is undamaged, and reporting a fault. Connection, wiring, opening fixed electrical enclosures, replacing a cord into a plug or fixed connection, and repairing a pump or UV unit's electrical parts are electrical work. In New South Wales, wiring work is licensed or certified work at any price, and the page treats putting in, fixing, changing, taking out or extending an electrical installation as wiring work. Queensland's electrical safety guidance says submersible pumps need an earthed design or a 12-volt supply, and that equipment should run through a safety switch with cords kept out of the water. Do not use an indoor aquarium heater in a pond.

lessons.title: Water-quality checks: temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, clarity, hardness
learningOutcomes: Carry out simple visual checks of clarity, colour and surface condition, and record them as observations rather than diagnoses
Measure water temperature in degrees Celsius and dissolved oxygen, and explain why both fall or rise with the season, the weather and the load
Read pH and hardness results, and convert hardness between mg/L as calcium carbonate and German degrees using the arithmetic in this lesson
Compare each reading with the owner's plan and the previous visit, and decide the next step without adding any product that is not in the plan

instructionSections.heading: Visual checks come first
instructionSections.body: Begin with what you can see and smell before you test. Clarity is the depth to which light penetrates the water. A simple check is to lower a pale, marked disc on a cord and record the depth at which the mark is no longer visible. Particles reduce clarity, and in a pond they are usually algae or fine sediment. Record colour, surface film, odour and any visible algae, but treat colour as an indicator rather than a diagnosis. The aquaculture source describes green and blue water as dominated by phytoplankton, golden or yellow-brown water as rich in diatoms, and red water as high in iron.

instructionSections.heading: Temperature and dissolved oxygen
instructionSections.body: Measure water temperature in degrees Celsius at a set depth and time, and record it with the air temperature. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cool water, and decay of organic matter uses up oxygen, so both warm weather and heavy organic load can lower the oxygen that fish and other animals need. Dissolved oxygen is most at risk after warm, still nights and after heavy feeding or a large debris load. Check it with the test kit or meter in the way its instructions direct, and read it at a depth where the animals are, not only at the surface. The aquaculture document gives a threshold below which oxygen is said to harm pond life. Use the owner's plan and the trend and the fish's behaviour instead, and refer any sign of distress. Do not use that figure as a target.

instructionSections.heading: pH and why it moves
instructionSections.body: pH measures how acid or alkaline the water is. In a pond, pH moves over a day because plants and algae take up carbon dioxide in daylight and release it at night. Carbonate hardness (KH) buffers pH, so a low KH allows large swings. The pH also controls how much ammonia is in its more harmful form, which is why a reading should be read with the temperature and the ammonia result (“Water chemistry and pH interpretation for ponds”). Use the owner's plan for the target range.

instructionSections.heading: Hardness, its two parts and the units
instructionSections.body: Water hardness has two parts that the test kit may report separately. General hardness (GH) mainly reflects calcium and magnesium. Carbonate hardness (KH) reflects the bicarbonate and carbonate that buffer pH. Test kits report hardness in different units, so the unit must be recorded with every reading. The common units are mg/L as calcium carbonate, which is the same as parts per million for dilute water; German degrees, written as °dGH for general hardness and °dKH for carbonate hardness; and millimoles per litre. The arithmetic conversions are: 1 °d equals 10 mg/L of calcium oxide, which is 17.8 mg/L as calcium carbonate. So to convert mg/L as calcium carbonate into degrees, divide by 17.8. One millimole per litre equals about 100 mg/L as calcium carbonate, or about 5.6 °d. For example, a carbonate reading of 89 mg/L is about 5.0 °dKH, and a general reading of 120 mg/L is about 6.7 °dGH. These are unit conversions, not targets, and they are not a regulatory claim. The owner's plan sets the target.

instructionSections.heading: Recording and out-of-range results
instructionSections.body: Record each reading with its value, unit, time, depth, the instrument or kit used, the reagent batch and expiry date, and any observation. Follow the rules for valid results and corrections in the sampling lesson (“Water sampling and record integrity for ponds”). Compare each result with the last visit and the owner's plan. A single out-of-range result is a reason to recheck the sample and the reagent, not to add a product. If the plan sets an action for the reading, take that action and record it. If the plan does not cover the reading, refer it to the responsible person with the full set of results.

lessons.title: Seasonal care and cold-climate notes
learningOutcomes: Describe how the load on a pond changes across the seasons, and plan the checks each season needs
Explain why depth and cooler water matter for animals in cold weather, and check depth against the owner's plan
Explain why an aquarium heater must not be used in a pond, and what changes if the owner heats the pond
Respond safely to a frozen surface and to frost damage, and refer any decision the owner's plan does not cover

instructionSections.heading: The load changes with the seasons
instructionSections.body: A pond does not run at the same level all year. In spring the water warms, algae begin to grow, and plants restart, so clarity and oxygen need closer watching. In summer the water is warmest, evaporation is highest, and the risk of low oxygen rises on warm, still nights. In autumn, leaf fall adds a large organic load, which is the time to plan netting and debris removal (“Debris, sludge and plant management”). In winter, biological activity slows, animals reduce their activity, and in cold areas the surface may freeze. Record the local climate for each site from the owner and from the observed conditions, rather than assuming it.

instructionSections.heading: Hot weather
instructionSections.body: In hot weather, check the pump and any aeration first, since a stopped pump is the most common cause of a sudden problem (“Pond ecology, fish and plant balance”). Measure the water temperature in degrees Celsius and record the time. Check for shade and cover that the owner has agreed to, because heavy sun can warm a pond quickly, and some shade supports pond habitat. Evaporation makes the level fall, so a steady fall should be checked with a bucket test before any top-up (“Water conservation and environmental release for ponds”). Avoid large water changes in heat, because a large sudden change in temperature stresses fish. Plan visits early in the day when oxygen is likely to be higher and the water is cooler, if the owner's plan allows it.

instructionSections.heading: Depth, hibernation and cold water
instructionSections.body: Many pond animals move into deeper, cooler water in cold weather, where the temperature is more stable. Water is densest at about 4 degrees Celsius and sinks, so under ice the deeper water can stay near that temperature, which many animals use for hibernation. Check the depth at the reference point (“Access features: inlet, outlet, overflow, edges and depth”) against the owner's plan, and record it before winter. A pond that is too shallow may freeze through, which leaves animals without refuge. Feeding usually reduces in cold weather, and the feeding regime is set by the owner's plan. This lesson does not give feeding amounts.

instructionSections.heading: Heaters and the electrical side
instructionSections.body: An aquarium heater must never be used in a pond. Most aquarium heaters are made for indoor use, and their cords and casings are not designed for weather, sunlight or ground contact, so they are a risk to fish and to people. A heated pond keeps fish active through winter, so the feeding and oxygen needs change, and the owner's plan must set them. In Queensland, pumps and any heater should run through a safety switch, and cords must stay out of the water.

instructionSections.heading: Frozen surfaces and frost damage
instructionSections.body: If the surface has frozen, do not force or break the ice, and do not pour hot water on it. Ice can give way under weight, and a sudden change in temperature can stress the animals below. Check the depth, observe the animals without disturbing them, and record the condition. Frost can damage a liner that is not rated for the local frost conditions, and a liner that has become brittle can crack at the edges or at the seams (“Pond liner and leak inspection”). Record any cracking or stiffness, and refer the damage to the owner. Keep pumps and cords out of the ice and out of freezing water, and do not walk on ice.

instructionSections.heading: Seasonal planning and the spring restart
instructionSections.body: Plan the year by season. In autumn, plan the netting, the debris routine and the depth check. In winter, keep the visits to the level the plan sets, and check the depth and the frozen surface. In spring, check the liner and the edges after winter, restart the pump and the aeration, check the temperature and the clarity, and plan the first visits so that the water has time to settle after the restart. Any decision about restocking fish, adding plants or changing the feeding regime belongs to the owner's plan and the specialist advice, and this lesson does not set numbers for any of them.

lessons.title: Pond records and handover
learningOutcomes: Keep a pond log that records each visit in metric units, with the readings, the equipment status and the work done
Correct a record without overwriting it, and explain why a consistent log shows trends that a single reading does not
Prepare a handover note that lists open issues, hazards, referrals and the things that must not be done to the pond
Protect client and site information in records and handovers, and share it only with the people the business's policy names

instructionSections.heading: Why a pond log matters
instructionSections.body: A pond changes slowly, and a single reading can mislead. A consistent log shows the trend in temperature, clarity, oxygen, pH, hardness, water level, pump running and the amount of debris removed. The trend is what tells you that a problem is starting, and that the routine needs to change. A log is also evidence of the care given, of the decisions made under the owner's plan, and of the referrals made. The idea of keeping a simple running log for a pond is common practice among pond keepers, and this lesson takes only that idea. It does not use the text of any example log.

instructionSections.heading: What to record at each visit
instructionSections.body: At each visit, record the date and time, the weather, the air temperature and the water temperature in degrees Celsius. Record the readings from the water-quality lesson with their units, and the clarity and the observations. Record the state of each piece of equipment, including whether the pump and aeration were running, the UV unit if fitted, and the filter sections cleaned. Record debris and sludge removed by volume, the plants trimmed, and any water added or removed with its volume, source, conditioner used and the approval. Record any feeding as the owner's plan describes it, the wildlife observed without any handling, the netting check, any mortality or disease, and any referral. Keep the entries in the order of the visit, so that the record can be read from start to finish.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the record clean
instructionSections.body: Use metric units throughout, with Celsius for temperature, millimetres for level changes and litres for volumes. Record one unit for each parameter, and state the unit on the form. Never back-fill a reading for a time when no test was done, and never estimate a value so that it looks like a pass. Corrections follow the rule in the sampling lesson: one line through the original, the correct value beside it, the initials, the date and the reason. Keep a simple site plan with the positions of the inlet, outlet, overflow, filter and pump, and the depth reference point, so that a new technician can find them. Note the equipment make and model as the owner's records show, and keep a reference to the manufacturer's manual. Do not recommend a product through the log.

instructionSections.heading: Handover to the owner or the next technician
instructionSections.body: A handover note is written at the end of each visit where the pond will be left with someone else, and at the end of a service period. It should state the current condition of the pond in plain terms, the open issues and their owners, the referrals made and their status, the electrical hazards found and whether they are isolated, the wildlife present and any netting that needs checking, and the things that must not be done to the pond. The list of things that must not be done includes adding pool chemicals, releasing or moving fish or sludge, and discharging water without a confirmed route. Add the next visit date and the contact details from the business's approved fields. Record who received the handover and when, and keep a copy in the log.

instructionSections.heading: Privacy and sharing
instructionSections.body: The log describes a client's property, its layout and the people who use it, so it is confidential. Share it only with the client, the responsible person in the business, and the people the business's policy names. Locations of nests, eggs or protected animals should be recorded for the wildlife authority's guidance only, and should not be shared publicly or put on a shared page. The privacy and confidentiality rules in the shared lessons apply to every entry (“Privacy, security and customer property”).

instructionSections.heading: Reviewing the log
instructionSections.body: Review the log at least once a month, or at the interval the owner's plan sets. Look for repeated top-ups, a steady fall in clarity, repeated pump faults, a rising debris load and any run of out-of-range readings. Each pattern is a reason to change the routine, to refer the problem, or to explain the cost to the owner. A pattern caught early usually costs less to fix than a failure that becomes a call-out. The review and any change it leads to are recorded in the log.

lessons.title: Water sampling and record integrity for ponds
learningOutcomes: Choose and use a consistent sampling point for a pond, using the client plan or the previous service record
Handle, label and test a pond sample so that the reading describes the pond rather than the container, the reagent or the sampling spot
Record each pond result with time, location, method, reagent details and tester
