Correct a record without overwriting it, and identify a test that is invalid and must not be recorded as a result

instructionSections.heading: Why a pond result depends on the sample
instructionSections.body: A pond test is only as good as the sample and the record behind it. A reading taken from the wrong place, with an out-of-date reagent, from a container that has held cleaning product, or several hours after a feed, does not describe the pond. It can look plausible and still lead to the wrong action. The record is also evidence. It shows what was tested, where, when, by whom and what was done in response, so that the next visit can see a trend rather than a single number. A pond changes slowly and can be misread, so a consistent method matters more than any one dramatic result. Good sampling and good records also reduce repeat call-outs, which is a workload saving for the business as well as a quality measure.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the sampling point
instructionSections.body: Take the sample from the point that the client plan or the previous service record names. If no point is named, choose one, record it, and use the same point on later visits so that results can be compared. Avoid the filter outlet, the return or waterfall, the skimmer throat and the area directly under a feeding spot, because each can give a reading that is not typical of the pond as a whole. No target depth is set in this draft. Note any change of point, and the reason for it, in the record.

instructionSections.heading: Taking and handling the sample
instructionSections.body: Use a clean container that is kept only for pond sampling. Do not use a container that has held cleaning product, pool chemical or fertiliser. Rinse the container with pond water only where the test-kit instructions allow it, and avoid touching the inside of the container or the cap. Fill it at the planned point, then label it with the date, time, location and tester before you leave that point. Test it promptly. While it waits, keep the sample out of direct sun and away from heat, as the kit instructions direct. Never use the same sampling equipment for two ponds without cleaning it between them, and never move pond water from one site to another. Moving water, sludge, plants or fish can spread pest species and disease, so check the biosecurity rules for your state before any movement.

instructionSections.heading: Test kits and reagents
instructionSections.body: Use the test kit or meter the way its manufacturer directs, and wait for the reaction time the instructions give. Before each round of tests, check the expiry date of every reagent, the calibration of any meter and the condition of the colour chart or cell. Reagents are chemicals in their own right. Store them according to their safety data sheet, keep oxidisers apart from flammable chemicals, which the Safe Work Australia guide describes as incompatible, keep acids apart as each safety data sheet directs because that guide does not address acids, and never keep them in a food or drink container. Dispose of used reagents as the safety data sheet and the site waste procedure direct. Where the kit shows a batch number, record it, so that a faulty batch can be traced later.

instructionSections.heading: Recording, correcting and out-of-range results
instructionSections.body: Write each result with its value, its unit, the time, the location, the method, the reagent details, the tester and any observation about the water, such as clarity, odour, surface film or fish behaviour. A test that was not completed is recorded as not completed, with the reason. Do not back-fill a result for a time when no test was done, and do not estimate a reading so that it looks like a pass. Never overwrite an original entry. To correct an error, draw a single line through it, write the correct value beside it, then initial and date the correction and give the reason. In an electronic system, use the amendment function that keeps the original. If a result is outside the range the client plan sets, follow the plan's action, inform the responsible person and leave the record as it was measured.

lessons.title: Water chemistry and pH interpretation for ponds
learningOutcomes: Explain how pH, ammonia, nitrite, nitrate and carbonate hardness are linked in a pond, and why they are read together
Interpret a set of pond test results and identify which reading drives the next step under the client plan
Refuse to add pool or other non-pond chemicals to a pond, and explain why
Refer a result or a fish-health concern that the client plan does not cover, rather than experimenting with treatment

instructionSections.heading: A pond is a living chemical system
instructionSections.body: A pond holds fish, plants, bacteria and decaying matter in one body of water. The chemistry shifts as these change. Fish waste and uneaten feed release ammonia. Bacteria in the filter and in the pond convert ammonia to nitrite and then nitrite to nitrate. Plants take up some nitrogen and carbon dioxide, and their photosynthesis and respiration change the pH over a day. Because these processes are linked, one reading on its own rarely explains a problem. Read the set of results together, against the last visit, and against the client plan. Do not work from numbers remembered from another system; use the target set for this pond.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the results together
instructionSections.body: Ammonia and nitrite are both harmful to fish, and the level of ammonia that matters depends on pH and temperature, because a higher pH shifts more ammonia into its more harmful form. This is a technique point and no source is checked for it in this draft. Nitrate is the end product of the normal filter cycle, and a rising nitrate with falling ammonia and nitrite usually means the cycle is working. Carbonate hardness, often called KH, buffers pH, so unstable pH readings often point to low buffering. Green water usually reflects algae growth from nutrients and light rather than a fault in one chemical. Dissolved oxygen matters most after warm nights and heavy feeding, and where the client has a test for it, read it alongside the rest (“Water sampling and record integrity for ponds” and “Water-quality checks: temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, clarity, hardness”). Look at the whole set, the trend and the fish behaviour before deciding what the next step is.

instructionSections.heading: No sanitiser, no pool chemicals, and tap water first
instructionSections.body: Pool sanitisers and pool chemicals are not for ponds. A sanitiser that kills microorganisms in a pool can also harm fish, plants and the bacteria that keep the pond working. Chlorine and chloramine in tap water are harmful to fish and must be removed before tap water is added to a pond. Keep pool chemicals, acids and any pond product in separate storage, and do not mix products in one container. Many pool sanitisers are oxidisers. The Safe Work Australia guide treats oxidisers and flammable chemicals as incompatible and suggests keeping incompatible goods at least 3 metres apart when the chance of a reaction is small; that guide does not address acids, so each product's safety data sheet states its own incompatibilities, including with acids. The same separation applies in a pond service vehicle.

instructionSections.heading: Adjusting in the plan's order, and referring when the plan does not cover it
instructionSections.body: The client plan sets which products may be used, in what order and at what dose. Add one product at a time, at the point and in the manner the label directs, and allow the water to mix before retesting. Record each reading and each product added, with amount and time. If readings do not respond as expected, do not add a larger dose to force a result. Recheck the sample and the reagent, compare with the trend, and follow the plan. If the plan does not cover the situation, stop the chemical adjustment and refer to the responsible person. Fish that are gasping, lying still at the surface, or showing sores or unusual colour need a qualified person.

lessons.title: Filtration and circulation diagnostics for ponds
learningOutcomes: Describe the order of a pond circulation loop, from intake through pump, filter and UV unit to the return
Diagnose low flow and poor filtration using observation, the pre-filter and strainer, and any gauge the system has
Isolate a pond pump and filter safely before opening any part of it
Price, record and refer diagnostic work according to the business's approved method and the scope in this lesson

instructionSections.heading: The pond circulation loop
instructionSections.body: Pond water is drawn in through a skimmer, a pre-filter or a pump intake, pushed by a pump through a biological filter and, where fitted, a UV clarifier, and returned through a waterfall, stream or return outlet. The pump moves water through the filter, so that solids are caught and the bacteria in the filter can break down ammonia and nitrite. A fault at any point reduces flow and can change the water quality. Diagnose the loop in the order the water travels: intake, pump, pre-filter, biological filter, UV unit, return. This keeps the inspection logical and avoids opening equipment that does not need attention. Record the layout you find before you change anything, because many pond systems are installed differently. The order of the filter and the UV unit depends on the purpose of the system, so do not change it without instruction (“Pumps, UV clarifiers and filters”).

instructionSections.heading: Reading the signs of a fault
instructionSections.body: Weak flow at the waterfall, a noisy pump, a pump that loses prime, air in the pre-filter, a sump that gurgles, and a filter that stops cleaning well are common signs. A pre-filter full of leaves or sludge is the most frequent cause of low flow, and it is also the cheapest to fix. Air leaks on the suction side, a blocked intake screen, a partly closed valve or a worn impeller can produce similar symptoms. Record the flow you see and the state of the pre-filter and strainer before you clean them, and record them again after the work. A reading means little without a reference, so if the client or the manufacturer gives a normal clean-filter reading or flow figure, record it against the system.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating before you inspect
instructionSections.body: Switch off the pump at its isolator or the circuit breaker before you open a pre-filter, touch the pump or work on any electrical connection. Confirm the pump is off before you put your hands in the water. Relieve pressure before you open a filter lid, as the manufacturer directs, and do not open a pressurised filter. Record the position of each valve before you move it, so that it can be restored. Keep the pump area dry, never use a damaged cord, and keep cords and extension leads out of the water. Queensland's electrical safety office says submersible pumps need an earthed design or a 12-volt supply, and that equipment should run through a safety switch with cords out of the water. UV clarifiers contain lamps that can cause eye and skin harm, so switch the unit off and isolate it before you open it, and do not look at a lit lamp.

instructionSections.heading: What is in scope, and what is referred
instructionSections.body: Clearing a pre-filter, cleaning a skimmer basket, rinsing biological media in pond water (not tap water) and checking flow are generally within the scope of pond maintenance work. Replacing a pump, changing a pump's wiring, altering a fixed electrical connection, and changing outlet pipework or pipe joins are not general maintenance and are referred. In New South Wales, wiring work is licensed or certified work at any price, and the page treats putting in, fixing, changing, taking out or extending an electrical installation as wiring work. In New South Wales, plumbing, draining and gasfitting work must be done by a licensed or certified person whatever the price, and that page does not mention ponds or water features. In Queensland, the QBCC's licensing page sets no dollar cut-off for plumbing or drainage work, so the licence applies at every price, and the page does not list ponds or water features. Refer any such work to the person the rules name.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing and documenting diagnostic work
instructionSections.body: Diagnostic time is real work and should be priced under the business's approved method, not absorbed as free time. Record the symptoms the client described, the flow and readings you took, the checks you made, the action you took, the parts or work you referred, and the time spent. A diagnostic record that says the system is working is only valid if the readings and checks support it. Where the diagnosis finds a fault outside your scope, write a short referral note that describes the symptoms and readings, so that the licensed person can start from the facts.

lessons.title: Electrical, mechanical and confined-space boundaries for ponds
learningOutcomes: Identify the electrical, mechanical and confined-space hazards around a pond pump, light, UV unit or pump pit
Isolate, secure and prove off the power to a pond pump before any inspection that needs it
Recognise when a pit, sump or vault may be a confined space, and refuse entry without authority and a procedure
State where the scope of pond maintenance ends and licensed or specialist work begins, without implying that this lesson grants any licence

instructionSections.heading: Water and electricity around a pond
instructionSections.body: Pond pumps, lights, UV units and cords are often installed close to water, and the water can carry a shock if equipment is damaged or wet. A safety switch, which is a residual current device, reduces the risk of electric shock, but it does not make live work safe and does not give anyone permission to work on the system. Treat any pond electrical equipment as live until it has been isolated and proven dead by a competent person. The Queensland electrical safety office says submersible pumps need an earthed design or a 12-volt supply, and that equipment should run through a safety switch, with cords and appliances kept out of the water. Do not work on a light, pump or cord while the surrounding area is wet.

instructionSections.heading: Where electrical work becomes licensed work
instructionSections.body: In New South Wales, wiring work is licensed or certified work at any price, and the page treats putting in, fixing, changing, taking out or extending an electrical installation as wiring work. A pond maintenance worker may isolate equipment, inspect the outside of it, check that a cord is undamaged and report a fault. A repair, a rewire, a new connection or the opening of a fixed enclosure is for a licensed person. Completing this lesson does not give anyone the authority to do electrical work.

instructionSections.heading: Mechanical hazards and isolation
instructionSections.body: Pumps and their impellers can start when power is restored, and a pump that is off at the switch can still be live at the isolator. Before reaching into a pump, strainer or intake, isolate the power at the isolator, check that the isolator is off, and secure it so that it cannot be switched on while you work, as the site procedure directs. Prove the circuit dead with a proving test where your procedure requires it. Some ponds also have stored pressure in filter housings, hot surfaces on lamps, and pipework that can move. Check the equipment before you touch it, and never reach into a running pump to clear a blockage.

instructionSections.heading: Confined spaces in ponds and water features
instructionSections.body: Pump pits, sumps, vaults, underground chambers and enclosed plant cabinets can be confined spaces. A confined space has limited openings for entry and exit, is not designed for people to work in continuously, and can hold a hazard such as low oxygen, gas, engulfment or a hazard from the water or the equipment. Assess the space before any entry. Entry needs a documented procedure, an assessment of the atmosphere and hazards, a standby person and, where the rules require it, a permit. Do not enter a pit that has standing water or a closed plant cabinet on your own, and never enter a pit to clear it by hand.

instructionSections.heading: The scope boundary
instructionSections.body: Pond maintenance scope usually covers cleaning, inspection, reading equipment from the outside, isolating power as the procedure allows, cleaning intake screens and baskets, and reporting faults. Replacing or rewiring a pump or light, opening electrical enclosures, entering a confined space, altering a controller and changing pipework are outside that scope unless the work order, the client, and the worker's licence and competence all cover them. When a task is outside scope, stop, make the equipment safe as far as the procedure allows, and refer the task in writing with the symptoms and readings.

lessons.title: Water conservation and environmental release for ponds
learningOutcomes: Separate evaporation from a leak in a pond by carrying out a bucket test and recording the result
Limit unnecessary water changes and top-ups, and explain the cost and stress they create
Refuse to release pond water, sludge, plants or fish to stormwater, a waterway or bushland without an approved route and the permit the state requires
Record the volume moved, the route, the approval and the person who approved it

instructionSections.heading: Why pond water loss costs money
instructionSections.body: Every litre lost from a pond has to be replaced, and each top-up changes the water the fish and plants live in. Evaporation on a hot, windy day is normal. A steady loss on a cool, still night can point to a leak, an overflowing or misaligned outlet, or a waterfall that splashes water out of the pond. Unnecessary water changes cost money, add stress for fish, and can upset the bacteria that keep the filter working. Cost reduction starts with finding the cause of loss, rather than adding water every visit without knowing why.

instructionSections.heading: The bucket test and unnecessary changes
instructionSections.body: A simple bucket test separates evaporation from a leak. Place a bucket filled with pond water on a step within the pond, so that its water level is close to the pond's, and mark the level inside and outside the bucket at the start. Leave it for the same period, then compare the two marks. If the pond has dropped more than the water in the bucket, the loss is more likely a leak or an outlet problem, and it should be reported. The method is a practical technique and is not a certified test. Record the weather, the time and the result. Carry out a partial water change only when the test results, the client plan or a qualified specialist calls for one, and record the reason for it.

instructionSections.heading: Topping up with treated water
instructionSections.body: When a top-up is needed, add water that has had its chlorine and chloramine removed, because both harm fish and the bacteria in the filter. Add the top-up slowly and avoid pouring it onto fish or plants. Do not add water from an unknown source, such as a dam, bore or natural waterway, without checking the rules first.

instructionSections.heading: Releasing water, sludge, plants and fish
instructionSections.body: Pond water, sludge and removed plants must not be released into stormwater, a kerb drain, a gutter, bushland or a waterway unless the route has been confirmed in writing by the client, the council and the water authority. Councils regulate discharge routes for stormwater. One NSW council's factsheet treats discharging stormwater into the council sewer as an offence. That is a stormwater rule and does not decide the route for pond water. Fish are a separate matter. In Queensland, prohibited noxious fish cannot be brought in, and sightings of prohibited noxious fish and of sight-only restricted species have a 24-hour reporting limit to Biosecurity Queensland. For restricted fish such as carp and tilapia, the page says caught fish must be humanely killed straight away and disposed of away from water, and that they may not be kept, fed, given away, sold, used as bait or returned to water. In New South Wales, releasing fish into public waters such as rivers, creeks and impoundments needs a fish stocking permit under the Fisheries Management Act. The NSW page also places an abandoned pet fish in the same category as an abandoned cat or dog under section 11 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979. Sludge and plant material may carry pest species and disease, so keep them on site until the approved disposal route is confirmed. Do not assume that any discharge route is allowed.

instructionSections.heading: Recording water movements
instructionSections.body: Record the volume drained, topped up or removed where you know it, the route, the approval or permit relied on, the time, the reason, and the person who approved the move. Where the route is unknown, stop and refer rather than moving the water. A record that shows the route was approved protects the business and the client, and a record that shows the water went somewhere unknown does neither.

lessons.title: Scope, site classification and authority
learningOutcomes: Classify a pool or spa site as residential, spa, public, hydrotherapy or commercial before starting work
Identify the named responsible operator and confirm who holds water-treatment decisions
Compare a work order with the site and state in writing which tasks are inside and outside scope
Stop and refer work when a listed trigger is present

instructionSections.heading: Why classification comes first
instructionSections.body: Pools and spas are not one hazard class. A private backyard pool, a hotel spa, a public aquatic centre and a hydrotherapy pool in a health facility each have different users, different responsible people and different duties. Before you touch a skimmer, a pump or a dosing line, establish which type of water you are working on, who operates it and what your work order allows. The classification decides who may test water, who may adjust chemistry, which records are kept and who must be told about a problem. Do not classify a site from the customer's description alone. Check the signage, the equipment, the operator's details and the venue type.

instructionSections.heading: Who holds responsibility
instructionSections.body: The operator may be the owner, a body corporate, a facility manager or a contracted pool operator. A contractor engaged for surface cleaning or equipment servicing is not automatically the operator. Before work starts, confirm the named responsible person, their contact details and whether they have delegated any treatment, closure or reopening decisions in writing. If nobody is named, treat the site as having no authorised operator and do not start treatment work.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the work order against the site
instructionSections.body: The signed work order is your scope. Check whether it covers cleaning, equipment servicing, chemical dosing, testing or inspection only. Anything beyond the written order needs a new written instruction from the responsible person or a referral to a specialist. A completed cleaning task never, by itself, makes a pool ready for use. Record the task you were engaged for and the tasks you were not engaged for, so that the record cannot later be read as a water-quality approval. If the work order includes a visual look at the safety barrier, record it as a visual check under “Safety barrier visual check and escalation”. A visual check is not a barrier approval.

instructionSections.heading: Operator plans and rules that vary by state and territory
instructionSections.body: Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan. The plan sets which products are used, the target ranges, the testing frequency, the closure triggers and the records to be kept. Where the plan is not available, stop treatment work and ask the responsible person for it. This course gives no target values. Barrier rules, registration and public-pool rules come from each state and territory and from local councils, so they vary across Australia. A rule quoted from one jurisdiction applies to that jurisdiction only. In Western Australia, the Health (Aquatic Facilities) Regulations 2007 cover aquatic facilities open to the public, and the Department of Health page (last reviewed 12 December 2023) says domestic pools are left out. In NSW, a pool's entry on the Swimming Pool Register is not a finding of compliance, as the NSW owner page (last updated 16 March 2026) explains.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer triggers
instructionSections.body: Stop and refer when any of these applies: there is no named responsible operator; you are asked to override a regulatory or operator-plan requirement; the task needs a licence or competence you do not hold, such as electrical, gas or confined-space work; the water shows signs of contamination; a barrier defect leaves the water reachable; or you are asked to certify the pool as safe, compliant or open. A refusal is a correct decision when the trigger is present. Record it with the time, the person asking and the reason.

lessons.title: Pre-start inspection and drowning prevention
learningOutcomes: Complete a pre-start inspection of the pool barrier, gates, signage and access
Identify suction outlet and entrapment hazards and isolate them without altering the outlet
Confirm the pool is closed to users before entering the water area
Record defects and escalate them to the responsible person before work starts

instructionSections.heading: Drowning prevention is the first control
instructionSections.body: Drowning is the most serious hazard around pools, and it is not limited to chemical work. The December 2025 WA guide reports 19 fatal and 174 non-fatal drownings of children under five in swimming and spa pools in WA over the period July 2012 to June 2022. Before any task near the water, check what controls access: the barrier or fence, the gate and its latch, any self-closing function, the depth markings and the signage. Also check whether children, pets or other swimmers could reach the water while you work. Your inspection records what you observed. It does not certify compliance with the law. Certification is done by the authority named for each state: in NSW the certificates come from councils or registered inspectors (NSW owner page, last updated 16 March 2026), and in Victoria the inspector completes the Form 23 barrier compliance certificate (page updated 30 June 2026). Use the visual barrier check in “Safety barrier visual check and escalation”, and the authority table in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check” for the state or territory of the site.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating the water body
instructionSections.body: Do not enter the water area while swimmers are present. Confirm with the responsible person that the pool is closed or that the operator has taken the isolation step. If the pool is still in use, ask the operator to close it, and do not start a task that requires entering the water. Keep covers secured while work is done, and confirm that any emergency information and rescue equipment the operator provides is present and accessible. Do not rely on a sign alone to keep people out.

instructionSections.heading: Suction outlets and entrapment
instructionSections.body: Check suction outlets, main drains and their covers. A missing, cracked or loose outlet cover is a serious entrapment hazard. Do not remove or replace a suction cover unless the work order covers that task and you are competent to do it. Report and isolate a damaged cover according to the operator's instruction, and record its location and condition. Do not leave a damaged cover in service, and do not test suction by placing a body or a limb over an outlet. The Australian Standard AS 1926.3 is named in this course for water recirculation and outlets.

instructionSections.heading: Surfaces, footwear and access
instructionSections.body: Pool decks, steps and tiles are slippery when wet. Wear footwear with grip, keep hoses and chemical containers out of walkways, and mark wet areas. Confirm that the access route to the plant room and the chemical store is clear. Where a route involves stairs or a steep bank, plan the handling of equipment before you carry it (see the shared lesson “Ergonomics and manual handling”, ergonomics and manual handling).

instructionSections.heading: Recording and escalation
instructionSections.body: Record the inspection time, the observed defects, what was isolated, the person told and whether the pool was open to users at the time. Escalate any barrier failure, missing cover, open gate or water-entry risk to the responsible person before you start work. A pre-start record is not a compliance certificate. It records what you checked and what you did about what you found. Record a barrier defect in the same way as the visual check described in “Safety barrier visual check and escalation”, and do not describe the barrier as compliant.

lessons.title: Water sampling and record integrity
learningOutcomes: Collect a water sample from the location and method set by the operator plan
Record test results with time, location, method, reagent details and the tester
Correct a record without overwriting the original and explain the correction
Identify when a test is invalid and must not be recorded as a result

instructionSections.heading: Why sampling and records matter
instructionSections.body: A water test is only as useful as its sample and its record. A result taken from the wrong place, at the wrong depth, with an expired reagent or with a poorly rinsed container is not a valid reading, even if it looks plausible. The record is also evidence. It shows what was tested, when, by whom and what was done in response. Keep the sampling and recording steps consistent with the operator plan, because the plan sets where, when and how often samples are taken.

instructionSections.heading: Taking the sample
instructionSections.body: Use the sampling location, depth and method in the operator plan. Rinse the container with the water being sampled only where the method allows it, and avoid touching the inside of the container or the cap. Take the sample away from the return jets and the dosing point where the plan says so, because fresh chemical can give a misleading reading. Label the sample container with the date, time, location and tester before you leave the point. Test as soon as practical, and do not store samples for a long time unless the plan or the test kit instructions allow it. Where the plan does not say where to sample, stop and ask the responsible person rather than choosing a point yourself.

instructionSections.heading: Testing and reagents
instructionSections.body: Use the test kit or meter in the way its manufacturer directs. Check the reagent expiry date, the calibration status of any meter and the condition of the colour chart or cell. Test reagents are chemicals too. Store them according to their SDS, keep them away from acidic and oxidising products, and never keep them in food or drink containers. Dispose of used reagents as the SDS and the site waste procedure direct.

instructionSections.heading: Recording results
instructionSections.body: Record each result on the form or system the operator uses. Write the value, the unit, the time, the location, the method, the reagent batch where relevant, the tester and any observation about the water. Record a test you did not complete as not completed, with the reason. Do not round or estimate a reading to make it look like a pass. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan, and the plan sets what happens after a result is outside the range it allows.

instructionSections.heading: Correcting records
instructionSections.body: Never overwrite or delete an original entry. If an error is found, draw a single line through the entry, write the correct value beside it, then initial and date the correction and state the reason. In electronic systems, use the amendment function that keeps the original. A record that was written later and dated earlier, or that was completed from memory, is not a valid record. If a test was missed, say so. Do not back-fill a result for a time when no test was done.

lessons.title: Disinfection chemistry and pH interpretation
learningOutcomes: Explain why pH controls the effectiveness of pool chlorine
Interpret a set of test results and identify which reading drives the next action
Apply the operator plan's order of adjustment, not a memorised sequence
Identify incompatible products and keep them separated as the SDS directs

instructionSections.heading: Pool disinfection is a chemical system
instructionSections.body: Chlorine-based sanitisers work by forming chemicals that inactivate microorganisms in the water. Their effectiveness depends on several linked factors: pH, the amount of organic and other contamination, the level of stabiliser in the water, temperature, and the time the water is in contact with the chemical. Changing one factor shifts the others. A pool that looks clear can still be under-treated, and a pool that looks cloudy is not always a problem with chlorine alone. Treat the water as a system, and use the operator plan to decide the target ranges and actions. Do not use numbers from memory.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the results together
instructionSections.body: A single test value means little on its own. Free chlorine tells you how much active sanitiser is available. Combined chlorine indicates that the sanitiser has reacted with contamination; a high combined reading points to a load that needs a different response from simply adding more sanitiser. The pH tells you how much of the free chlorine is in its more active form, so a high pH reduces the effectiveness of a given amount of chlorine. Total alkalinity buffers pH changes, so unstable pH readings often reflect alkalinity. Stabiliser (cyanuric acid), where used, slows chlorine loss from sunlight but can reduce chlorine effectiveness when it accumulates. Calcium hardness affects scaling and corrosion. Read these together before you act.

instructionSections.heading: Adjusting in the plan's order
instructionSections.body: The operator plan sets the order in which adjustments are made. Commonly, pH and alkalinity are corrected before sanitiser is added, because a high pH wastes sanitiser. Follow the order in your plan rather than a memorised sequence. Add one product at a time, at the point and in the manner the product label and SDS specify, and allow the water to mix and the reading to stabilise before retesting. Do not add two different chemical products at the same time or into the same bucket. Do not pour water into concentrated chemical unless the label directs it. This lesson gives no product amounts; take them from the label and the operator.

instructionSections.heading: Hypochlorite, acids and separation
instructionSections.body: Calcium hypochlorite is a dry chlorine product. WorkSafe WA's pool chemicals guidance advises keeping liquid hypochlorite away from acidic products such as pH decreasers and scale removers. The same guidance says dry calcium hypochlorite should be kept away from heat, moisture, acids and two other named chlorine products. Safe Work Australia advises storing incompatible chemicals well apart, because contact can give off gases that are poisonous, catch fire, or attack materials. Keep pool chemicals apart in storage, dosing and spill handling. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan, and the plan sets which products may be used at the site.

instructionSections.heading: What to do when readings disagree
instructionSections.body: When readings disagree with the plan's expectations, do not add a large dose to force a result. Recheck the sample, confirm the reagent, and compare with the previous trend. Then follow the plan's response. If the plan does not cover the situation, stop chemical adjustment and refer to the responsible operator. A cloudy pool, a strong odour, an unusual colour or a sudden change in readings is a reason to refer rather than to experiment.

lessons.title: Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention
learningOutcomes: Describe how automatic and manual dosing systems deliver chemical to pool water
Identify the gas-release risks from mixing or contaminating pool chemicals
Apply segregation rules for hypochlorite, acids and other incompatible products
Respond to a leak, odour or gas release by isolating, moving people away and escalating

instructionSections.heading: What dosing systems do
instructionSections.body: Dosing systems feed chemical into the pool circuit, either manually through a bucket and feed point or automatically through a pump and a controller that responds to a sensor or a timer. Each system has a chemical source, a feed line, a pump or injector, a check valve, an injection point and often a controller. Each part can fail: lines can crack, valves can stick, injectors can block, and controllers can drift. A failed dosing system can deliver too much or too little chemical, or let chemical flow back toward storage. Work on the controller, wiring and mechanical parts is outside the scope of most contract cleaning work and is covered by the electrical and confined-space boundaries in “Electrical, mechanical and confined-space boundaries”.

instructionSections.heading: Gas risk from incompatible products
instructionSections.body: Chlorine-releasing products react with other chemicals in ways that can be dangerous. Incompatible products can give off gases that are poisonous, flammable or damaging to materials when they meet. The most important rule for a pool worker is that acid products and hypochlorite must never mix. WorkSafe WA's pool chemicals guidance keeps liquid hypochlorite away from acidic products such as pH decreasers and scale removers, and keeps dry calcium hypochlorite away from heat, moisture, acids and two other named chlorine products.

instructionSections.heading: Preventing the gas release in daily work
instructionSections.body: Keep separate buckets, funnels, spill kits, spill trays and storage bays for acids and for hypochlorite. Label every container with its product name and hazard. Never use the same scoop, jug or hose for two products. Do not dissolve hypochlorite granules in an acid-contaminated container. Do not clean a dosing line with a different product unless the SDS and the operator plan permit it. Store products away from heat and moisture. Keep the storage area ventilated and clear of other goods. Operator plans set the storage location, bunding and quantities, so check them before you move product. This lesson gives no chemical amounts or storage quantities; take them from the product label, the SDS and the operator.

instructionSections.heading: Leaks, odours and gas release
instructionSections.body: A chlorine odour, a visible vapour, a hissing line or a sudden leak from a dosing pump is an emergency signal. Move people out of the area to fresh air. Do not enter a poorly ventilated room or chemical store to find the source. Do not attempt to fix a leaking line or pump while the leak is active unless you are competent and the SDS and site procedure allow it. Call the emergency number set by the site and the operator, and follow the workplace emergency procedure. Report the event afterward using the site incident process. Respirators are used only where the site risk assessment and the SDS require them, and by people trained to fit and use them.

instructionSections.heading: Dosing system work and licences
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant any authority to repair, wire or reprogram a dosing system. Refer to the operator or a qualified person for that work.

lessons.title: Filtration and circulation diagnostics
learningOutcomes: Describe the main components of a pool circulation loop and their order
Diagnose low flow and high filter pressure using observation and gauge readings
Isolate equipment safely before opening any pressurised or electrical part
Price and document diagnostic work according to the business's approved method

instructionSections.heading: The circulation loop
instructionSections.body: Pool water is drawn from the skimmer and the main drain, passed through a pump and a filter, and returned through return jets. Many systems also include a heater, a chemical feed point, valves and automatic controls. Circulation moves the water through the filter so that particles are removed and the water is mixed with the treatment chemicals. A fault in any part of the loop can reduce circulation. Diagnose the loop in the order the water travels: intake, pump, filter, return. This keeps the inspection logical and avoids opening equipment that does not need attention.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the signs
instructionSections.body: Low flow at the returns, a noisy pump, a pump that loses prime, air in the strainer and a filter pressure that rises after cleaning are common signs. A high filter pressure reading compared with the normal clean-filter reading suggests a dirty or blocked filter. Air leaks on the suction side, a blocked skimmer basket or pump strainer, and a partly closed valve can produce similar symptoms. Record the pressure reading and the state of the basket and strainer before and after you clean them. A reading only has meaning if you know the clean-filter reference for that system, so record it from the manufacturer's data or the site record where it is available.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating before you inspect
instructionSections.body: Turn off power to the pump at the isolator or circuit breaker before you open the strainer lid, touch the pump motor or work on any electrical connection. Relieve pressure before you open a filter lid, as the manufacturer directs. Do not open a pressurised filter. Close valves only as the system layout and the operator plan indicate, and record valve positions before you change them so that they can be restored. Water near electrical equipment is a shock hazard, so keep the pump area dry and never use a damaged cord.

instructionSections.heading: What is in and out of scope
instructionSections.body: Cleaning a skimmer basket, emptying a strainer pot, backwashing or cleaning a filter as the manufacturer directs, and checking gauge readings are generally within a pool cleaning and diagnostic scope. Replacing pump internals, rewiring, changing heater elements, working on the gas side of a heater or altering a controller are outside general contract scope and need competence and authority (see the electrical, mechanical and confined-space boundaries in “Electrical, mechanical and confined-space boundaries”). Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan. Backwashing a filter may produce waste water that the discharge rules control (see “Water conservation and environmental release”).

instructionSections.heading: Pricing and documenting diagnostic work
instructionSections.body: Diagnostic time is real work and should be priced under the business's approved method, not absorbed as free time. Under the Australian Consumer Law, a service must be carried out competently, and it must be supplied within a reasonable period where no time was agreed. Record the symptoms observed, the readings taken, the checks made, the action taken, the parts or work referred, and the time spent. A diagnostic record that says the circulation is fine is only valid if the readings and the checks support it.

lessons.title: Surface cleaning and equipment hygiene
learningOutcomes: Select cleaning methods and products that suit the pool surface and finish
Clean and disinfect pool equipment without cross-contaminating sites
Keep acid cleaners and hypochlorite products separate in use and storage
Record equipment condition and cleaning tasks completed

instructionSections.heading: Surfaces and finishes first
instructionSections.body: Pool surfaces include tiles, grout, coping, steps, plaster, pebble, natural stone, fibreglass and vinyl liners. Each reacts differently to acid cleaners, abrasives, pressure and some chlorine products. Identify the finish before you choose a product. An acid-based tile-line cleaner that works on glazed tile can etch natural stone or damage grout. Test a product on a small hidden area where the surface allows it, follow the product's surface compatibility information, and escalate when you are unsure. This is a surface-compatibility decision, not a matter of habit.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the product and the method
instructionSections.body: Use only products approved for the site and the task. Read the SDS and the label before use. Use the lowest concentration and the least aggressive method that does the job, and keep PPE on for the whole task. Do not mix cleaning products together, and do not use a chlorine-based product and an acid-based product in the same bucket, spray bottle or rinse. Rinse the surface and the equipment between products as the label directs. Do not pour cleaners or concentrates directly into skimmers or returns unless the label and the operator plan allow it.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment hygiene between pools
instructionSections.body: Brushes, nets, skimmer baskets, vacuum heads and pool cleaners can carry algae, biofilm and microorganisms from one pool to the next. Keep equipment dedicated to a site where practicable. If equipment moves between sites, rinse it, dry it fully and clean it according to the site procedure before use. Store wet equipment so that it dries. Record any equipment that cannot be cleaned to standard, and remove it from use. Hygiene is part of the cleaning task, not an extra.

instructionSections.heading: Surface and equipment records
instructionSections.body: Record the surfaces cleaned, the products used, the concentrations where the plan sets them, the PPE used and any surface damage or equipment defect found. A cleaning record is not a water-quality record. It shows only the cleaning work done. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan. Rinse water from cleaning is handled under the site procedure and the discharge rules described in “Water conservation and environmental release”.

lessons.title: Biological contamination and incident escalation
learningOutcomes: Recognise signs of biological contamination in pool water and on surfaces
Take the first protective actions: keep people out of the water, notify the operator, and use PPE
Escalate according to the operator's emergency plan and not make a reopening decision
Record the event, the actions and the people informed

instructionSections.heading: Recognising a biological incident
instructionSections.body: Biological contamination in a pool may be visible or suspected. Examples include faecal matter, vomit, blood, and an unexplained illness reported by swimmers. A serious injury or a drowning event is a different and more urgent emergency. Treat every suspected contamination as a risk to people in the water and to the people cleaning up. Do not assume that the water is safe because it looks clear.

instructionSections.heading: First protective actions
instructionSections.body: The first priority is the people. Stop the task. Make sure swimmers leave the water and that the pool area is controlled, following the operator's plan. Call the emergency number if someone is seriously injured or unwell. Notify the responsible operator or duty manager straight away. Do not enter the water to remove material while swimmers are present. Put on the PPE set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}} before any direct contact, and keep others away from the area while you work.

instructionSections.heading: What you must not decide
instructionSections.body: The operator decides on closure and reopening under the operator plan and the applicable public-health rules. Requirements for responding to a contamination event are set by state and territory authorities. Do not dose the pool to 'fix' the water, and do not tell customers or swimmers that the pool is safe to use. Treating the water is a water-treatment decision that requires the operator's plan and instruction (see the pool chemistry lessons, “Disinfection chemistry and pH interpretation” and “Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention”).

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning up within scope
instructionSections.body: Where the work order and the operator plan allow it, remove visible material from deck surfaces and equipment with disposable tools, bag and seal the waste as the site waste procedure directs, and disinfect contaminated equipment and surfaces using products approved for the site. Keep contaminated equipment separate from clean equipment. Large or complex biological contamination, or any body fluid cleanup beyond pool surrounds, is outside this lesson. Refer it to the operator and to the High-risk cleaning module, where that scope applies.

instructionSections.heading: Exposure and records
instructionSections.body: If you come into contact with pool water or body fluid, wash the area, report it to your supervisor as the site incident procedure directs, and seek medical advice if the operator or your supervisor advises it. Record the event with the time, the number of people in the water, what you observed, the actions you took, and who you told. Do not record a guess about the cause as a fact.

lessons.title: Electrical, mechanical and confined-space boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify the electrical, mechanical and confined-space hazards in a pool plant area
Isolate and lock out equipment before any inspection that requires it
Recognise when a pit, plant room or tank is a confined space and refuse entry without authority
Apply the scope boundary between cleaning or diagnostic work and licensed or specialist work

instructionSections.heading: Water and electricity
instructionSections.body: Pool and spa areas combine water with mains electricity, pumps, heaters, lighting and automation. A fault can deliver a shock through water, through a damaged enclosure or through a wet connection. Protective devices such as residual current devices reduce the risk, but they do not make live work safe and they do not give permission to work on the system. Treat all pool electrical equipment as live until it has been isolated and proven dead by a competent person. Do not work on pool lights, underwater fittings or heater electrics while the area is wet.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical work and licences
instructionSections.body: Licence rules, the classes of work they cover and the authority to test pool equipment differ between states and territories. In Queensland, water equipment became prescribed electrical equipment on 1 April 2025, and a licensed electrician must do wiring or repair work on it. This lesson does not grant any electrical licence, and completing the lesson does not give authority to perform electrical work. A cleaner or diagnostic technician may isolate, inspect the outside of the equipment and report a fault; the repair is for a licensed person.

instructionSections.heading: Mechanical hazards
instructionSections.body: Pumps, motors, belts, couplings and rotating parts can start unexpectedly when power is restored. Before you reach into a pump or strainer, isolate the power, check that the isolator is off, and secure it so it cannot be turned on while you are working, as the site procedure directs. Some plant systems also have stored pressure, hot surfaces or chemical lines. Check the plant before you touch it.

instructionSections.heading: Confined spaces
instructionSections.body: Pump pits, filter chambers, plant rooms, balance tanks and surge tanks can be confined spaces. The Safe Work Australia model code for confined spaces (dated December 2011) treats a space as confined when it is enclosed or partly enclosed, is not built for people to spend time in, and carries a risk from unsafe oxygen, contaminants or engulfment. The code says the hazards and circumstances decide whether a space is confined, not its size alone. Under the code, someone must be designated as a standby person before a worker goes in, and a written permit from a competent person is required before entry to do work in such a space. Initial air testing should happen from outside, with probes or handheld detectors at the access points, and people must not rely on their senses to tell whether air is safe. Check with the regulator for the site's jurisdiction. Do not enter a pit with standing water or a closed plant room alone.

instructionSections.heading: Scope boundary
instructionSections.body: The contract worker's scope is usually limited to cleaning, inspection, checking readings from the outside of equipment, isolating power as authorised, cleaning strainers and baskets, and reporting faults. Replacing or rewiring equipment, opening electrical enclosures, entering confined spaces and altering controllers are outside that scope unless the work order, the operator and the worker's competence and licences cover them.

lessons.title: Water conservation and environmental release
learningOutcomes: Explain why unplanned loss of pool water raises cost and chemical use
Identify the discharge options set by the water authority, council and operator plan for drained, backwash and overflow water
Refuse to release pool water to stormwater or the environment without an approved route
Record water volumes, discharge routes and approvals

instructionSections.heading: Why water loss costs money
instructionSections.body: Pool water is expensive to replace. Every litre lost to splash-out, evaporation, leaks, or unnecessary backwashing must be topped up with mains water and re-treated with chemical. Losses also upset the chemical balance, so a top-up can change pH and sanitiser levels. Cost reduction starts with finding the cause of loss rather than topping up. Check whether the loss matches evaporation on a hot still day or whether it suggests a leak or a backwash that is run too often.

instructionSections.heading: Finding leaks and unnecessary backwashing
instructionSections.body: A simple bucket test helps separate evaporation from a leak. Place a bucket filled to the same level on the top step, and mark the water level inside and outside the bucket over the same period. If the pool drops more than the bucket, the loss is more likely a leak or an outlet problem, and it should be reported. Backwash only when the filter pressure reading and the operator plan indicate that it is needed, and record the reading that triggered it. Backwashing more often than needed wastes water and chemical and adds to the discharge volume.

instructionSections.heading: Discharge routes are set by the authority
instructionSections.body: Where pool water must be removed, the route depends on the local water authority, the council, the state or territory rules, and the operator plan. There is no single national route. Unitywater's domestic pool wastewater policy in South East Queensland is used here as one example. The policy (reviewed 16 July 2025, amended March and April 2026) accepts maintenance water to sewer only as a last option, when garden reuse cannot be done safely or sensibly, and caps that discharge at 0.5 L/s within two windows, 10am to 5pm and 10pm to 5am. It keeps rainwater overflow out of the sewer unless every other option has been ruled out as unsafe or unworkable, and it points to private stormwater drains, garden storage or a seepage option first. A sewer discharge needs written approval from the authority. The Icon Water acceptance guideline for pools in the ACT (version dated August 2016) is a different example: it allows a domestic pool to go to sewer only in limited cases, and says rainwater overflow must stay out of the sewer. Both are examples for one authority each, not state-wide rules.

instructionSections.heading: Chlorine, stormwater and waterways
instructionSections.body: Do not assume that chlorine has evaporated or been used up because a reading is low. The discharge route must be confirmed with the operator, the council and the water authority before any water is moved. The Unitywater policy sets no chlorine limit and describes no dechlorination method. The Icon Water guideline sets a total chlorine ceiling of 5 mg/L as Cl and a pH range of 6.5 to 10.0 for the discharges it covers, rules out sodium thiosulfate as a dechlorinating agent, and says rinse water from acid or strong-detergent cleaning must not go to sewer. Do not invent a dechlorination method; use the one the site's authority states.

instructionSections.heading: Recording water movements
instructionSections.body: Record the volume drained or backwashed where it is known, the route, the authority or approval relied on, the time, the reason, and the operator who approved the discharge. Where the discharge route is unknown, stop and refer. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan, and the plan may restrict when water can be moved and how it is treated before discharge.

lessons.title: Handover, periodic care and records
learningOutcomes: Plan periodic care visits from the operator's schedule rather than from memory
Complete a handover that states what was done, what was not done and what remains
Record evidence that supports each completed task without implying water approval
Communicate defects and referrals in writing to the responsible person

instructionSections.heading: Periodic care follows the operator's schedule
instructionSections.body: Periodic pool care covers cleaning, equipment checks, filter inspection, surface care and scheduled visits. The frequency and content come from the operator plan and the work order, not from a habit. A schedule that is kept in one place, shared with the operator and updated when the work changes saves unplanned visits and prevents tasks from being forgotten. Where the operator plan sets testing and treatment, those visits are recorded separately from cleaning and inspection visits. Where the work order includes a barrier look, a periodic visit may include the visual barrier check in “Safety barrier visual check and escalation”. That check is visual and non-certifying, and a periodic visit does not certify a barrier.

instructionSections.heading: Handover says what is true
instructionSections.body: A handover tells the next person, and the operator, what has been done and what has not. Use three headings: completed, not completed or not in scope, and remaining or referred. A completed cleaning checklist shows that cleaning tasks were done. It does not show that the water is suitable for use, that chemistry is in range, or that the pool is ready to reopen. Never write that a pool is safe, compliant or approved on the basis of cleaning work. Write what you observed and what you did.

instructionSections.heading: Evidence that supports the record
instructionSections.body: Good evidence is specific and dated. Photographs of a cleaned surface, a completed strainer check, a pressure reading or a defect are stronger than a tick box. Record who did the work, the time, the equipment and products used where relevant, and any defect with its location. Keep the record in the form the operator uses, and do not alter a record after it has been sent without marking the change (see “Water sampling and record integrity”).

instructionSections.heading: Defects and referrals
instructionSections.body: A defect is recorded and reported, not fixed silently, when it is outside scope. Write the location, the symptom, the readings if taken, the risk, and the action requested. Give the record to the responsible person in writing. A verbal handover is not enough for a defect that affects safety or water treatment. Keep a copy for the business's own records, as the business's policy requires.

instructionSections.heading: Customer and operator communication
instructionSections.body: Explain to the customer or operator, in plain words, what was done and what was not done. Do not offer opinions about water quality that the work did not measure. Where a customer asks whether the pool is ready for use, the correct answer is the operator's decision under the operator plan. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan.

lessons.title: Safety barrier visual check and escalation
learningOutcomes: Complete a visual barrier check covering gaps, gates, latches, climbable objects, doors, windows, locks and covers, and mark any part not seen as not inspected
Explain why a visual check is not a certificate, and say who certifies a barrier in the job's state or territory
Stop water-side work when a barrier defect leaves the water reachable, and escalate through the set path
Write a barrier check record and defect report that use no compliance wording

instructionSections.heading: Why the barrier check comes first
instructionSections.body: Its job is to keep very young children away from the water when no adult is watching. The December 2025 WA guide reports 19 fatal and 174 non-fatal drownings of children under five in swimming and spa pools between July 2012 and June 2022. A barrier that is propped open, damaged, bypassed or left unlatched offers little or no protection, even if most of it is sound. A look at the barrier before you start work is therefore part of the job, and what you see is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: What you may and may not do
instructionSections.body: This is a visual, non-certifying check. You look for visible defects, record what you can see, and escalate. You do not decide whether a barrier complies with the law. You do not sign, issue or describe any certificate of compliance or non-compliance, and you do not tell an owner or a swimmer that a barrier is safe, compliant or approved. Only the inspector or authority named for the state or territory can inspect and certify a barrier (see “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”). In NSW, the certificates come from councils or registered inspectors. In Victoria, a registered inspector completes a Form 23 barrier compliance certificate. Do not measure a barrier to pass or fail it. Do not adjust a hinge, latch or self-closing device, and do not move, remove or add a barrier part to make the check pass. Those belong to the owner, a licensed or authorised person, or the local permit body, not to you.

instructionSections.heading: What to look at
instructionSections.body: Walk the length of the barrier on both sides, where you can safely reach them, and look for these visible conditions. Gaps: any opening you can see through or under, including a gap at the ground, a gap where a panel has gone, or a gap at the gate. Condition: a broken, bent, rotten, rusted or loose section, or a post that moves. Removable parts: any panel, slat or gate fitting that lifts out or comes off without tools. Gates: whether the gate is hung to open away from the water, whether it returns to the shut position when released from a partly open position, and whether the latch engages. Observe these; do not force the gate. Latch release: whether the release sits high on the water side, can be reached over the barrier by a child, or is shielded; record what you see. Locks: a padlock, deadlock or key lock fitted to a gate, door or window in the barrier. Climbable objects: furniture, barbecues, pots, planters, stacked materials, ladders, water features, trees, shrubs, retaining walls, and pumps or filters close enough that a child could step onto them, on either side. Doors and windows: any door or openable window in the barrier wall. Covers: a pool cover, even a lockable one, does not count as a barrier. Above-ground pools: any ladder or steps that can be removed, and any pump or filter near the wall.

instructionSections.heading: WA reference figures (WA only)
instructionSections.body: The December 2025 WA guide, Rules for Pools and Spas, supersedes the 2016 edition. Its figures apply in Western Australia only. They are listed here only so that you can recognise an obvious defect, not as a test you can use to certify anything. The guide says that water deeper than 30 cm brings a pool under the barrier rule. It sets a barrier height of 1.2 m or more on the non-poolside, with height measured from the finished ground level. The gap under the barrier and under a gate may not be more than 100 mm. Under the guide's first option, a gate latch release must sit 1500 mm or more above the ground on the non-poolside. The horizontal gap between vertical members may not exceed 100 mm. A self-closing hinge that stands out more than 10 mm can help a child climb, so it must be kept clear of non-climbable zones. A gate should open outward, away from the water, rather than toward it. Check the WA guide itself before relying on any figure. No figures for any other state or territory are given in this course. Check the authority for the job's state in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”.

instructionSections.heading: The escalation path
instructionSections.body: Use this path, and stop at the first step that applies. Step 1, immediate danger: if a child or any unsupervised person can reach the water through a gap or an open gate, do not start water-side work. Make the area safe as far as you can without entering the water, tell the owner at once, and call the emergency number if someone is at risk. Step 2, defect found without immediate danger: do not start water-side work while the defect leaves the water reachable. Do not repair the defect yourself unless the work order covers it and you are competent. Step 3, record: write a defect report with the location, what you saw, the time, photographs where your business policy requires them, and the person told. Step 4, business escalation: give the report to the responsible person named in the work order, who decides whether your job continues. Step 5, owner and authority: the owner keeps the barrier working. Tell the owner in writing that a formal inspection or repair is needed, and point them to the authority in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check” for the job's state or territory. Your business escalation contact decides whether any other body is informed. If you refuse to start work, record the refusal, the reason and the person told.

instructionSections.heading: Records and wording
instructionSections.body: Every barrier check record states the date, the time, the site, the parts checked, the parts not inspected, and each defect found. The record uses the words visual check, not compliance check. Write what you saw in plain words. Do not write that a barrier is compliant, safe, certified or approved. If any section of the barrier was not visible or could not be reached safely, record it as not inspected. The record shows what you looked at and what you did about it. It is not a certificate.

lessons.title: Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check
learningOutcomes: Explain why barrier rules differ between states and territories.
Find the barrier authority for the job's state or territory and record the source, the page date and the status
Record a certificate as sighted without interpreting it as proof of current compliance
Refer certification, repair, licence and other questions the sources do not settle instead of answering them.

instructionSections.heading: Australia-wide, with no single rule
instructionSections.body: Pool barrier rules are not one national rule. Each state and territory sets its own requirements through its own laws, and councils or other authorities enforce them. Who inspects differs by place: councils and registered inspectors in NSW, licensed pool safety inspectors in Queensland, councils in South Australia, and pool safety advisers in the Northern Territory. The national framework includes the National Construction Code, which contains the Building Code of Australia, and the barrier standards AS 1926.1 and AS 1926.2, which the ACT page names as AS 1926.1-2012 and AS 1926.2-2007. This lesson names those framework items only.

instructionSections.heading: How to use the table
instructionSections.body: For each job, do four things. First, confirm the state or territory and the local council for the address. Second, find the authority named for that jurisdiction on its official page, and record the page address and the date you read it. Third, ask the owner for any certificate or notice, and record its type, its issuer and its date as sighted. Do not treat it as proof of current compliance. Never apply one state's rule to another. All checks in this pass were made on 3 November 2026.

instructionSections.heading: Western Australia (checked for the December 2025 guide; partly checked for initial inspections)
instructionSections.body: The December 2025 WA guide, Rules for Pools and Spas, supersedes the 2016 edition. The WA publication page (first published 15 November 2024, last updated 26 November 2024) links to it. The guide says that water deeper than 30 cm brings a pool under the barrier rule. It sets a barrier height of 1.2 m or more on the non-poolside, a gap of no more than 100 mm under the barrier and under a gate, and a latch release at least 1500 mm above the ground on the non-poolside under its first option. It caps the horizontal gap between vertical members at 100 mm. It says local governments inspect barriers at intervals of no more than four years and are the permit authorities, and that a building permit is generally needed before a swimming or spa pool is built or installed. The WA Government page on initial barrier inspections (first published 13 November 2024, updated 19 November 2024) covers new private pools and existing pools that have never been inspected. It does not say who may carry out those inspections, gives no deadline and does not name the inspecting authority. The WA Department of Health page (last reviewed 12 December 2023) says the Health (Aquatic Facilities) Regulations 2007 cover aquatic facilities open to the public and leave out domestic pools. Checked for the guide's barrier figures as read in this pass (check the PDF before reliance); partly checked for the initial-inspection page and the Health regulations point.

instructionSections.heading: New South Wales (checked, owner page)
instructionSections.body: The NSW Government owner obligations page (last updated 16 March 2026) says pools that can be filled with water to more than 30 cm are covered. A barrier must reach 1.2 m or more, with height taken from the finished surface, and the gap at the bottom must not exceed 10 cm. Vertical bars may not be more than 10 cm apart, and horizontal climbable bars must be at least 90 cm apart. Gates must stay shut and open outward, not toward the water. They must shut by themselves whatever position they were released from, and they must latch on their own. Registration on the Swimming Pool Register does not show compliance. Councils or registered inspectors can issue a certificate of compliance, which remains in effect for 3 years, or a certificate of non-compliance. Checked for the authority, certificate and measurement points listed on the page. The page is not consistent on the depth wording for portable pools, so confirm the threshold with the council.

instructionSections.heading: Queensland (partly checked)
instructionSections.body: The QBCC pool safety inspector page (last reviewed and published 31 August 2021, with a fee change stated for 1 July 2026) says a licensed inspector under the scheme may inspect a pool and then issue a certificate or a non-conformity notice. Such an inspector may also make minor repairs, such as adjusting a latch or hinge or removing a climbable object, and may erect or repair parts of a barrier, but the page limits that barrier work to a total length of 5 metres and to 6 posts at most. A technician who is not a licensed inspector should not act as one. Partly checked, because the page is dated 2021. The current licence scope must be checked on the QBCC site before reliance.

instructionSections.heading: Victoria (checked for inspectors; partly checked for repairs)
instructionSections.body: The Building and Plumbing Commission page on pool and spa safety barrier inspections (updated 30 June 2026) says that building surveyors, building inspectors and pool inspectors who are registered do these checks. The inspector issues the Form 23 barrier compliance certificate. Where doubt remains about the fence, an inspector does not issue it. After a notice, the owner has 60 days to comply, and the inspector must form an opinion within 60 days of the inspection. The Victorian Building Authority consumer page on pool safety barriers (no date shown) says that pools and spas deeper than 300 mm need a compliant barrier, that owners must keep barriers working, and that a permit may be needed to alter an existing barrier, with advice to check with the council or building surveyor. Checked for the inspector role and the certificate; partly checked for the repair and permit point.

instructionSections.heading: South Australia (checked for council inspections; partly checked for the licensing point)
instructionSections.body: Practice Direction 8 on council swimming pool safety inspections (no version date shown) says councils must inspect all pools and pool safety features completed in a reporting year. The timeframe is two weeks from the point at which a council learns that the works are finished. The inspections are carried out by councils, not by pool service technicians. The SA Consumer and Business Services building licence FAQs (November 2025) list works on a pool or spa as an example of domestic building work, which needs a building work contractor licence. Checked for council inspections; partly checked for the licensing point.

instructionSections.heading: Tasmania (checked; page dated 8 December 2023)
instructionSections.body: The Consumer, Building and Occupational Services page on pool safety barriers (last updated 8 December 2023) says barriers are required for pools and spas with water 300 mm or more deep that were installed from 1994 onward. Covers over a pool or spa do not count as barriers. Licensed builders install barriers under the oversight of a licensed building surveyor, and a licensed building surveyor checks inflatable or relocatable pool barriers before the pool is filled. For pools installed before 1994, the page recommends fitting a barrier but does not require one. Checked, on a page dated 2023.

instructionSections.heading: Australian Capital Territory (checked)
instructionSections.body: The ACT Planning page on home swimming pool safety reforms (no date shown) says the scheme began on 1 May 2024 with a four-year transition. It covers pools and spas deeper than 30 cm at residential buildings. From 1 May 2028, compliant barriers and barrier compliance certificates become mandatory, and certificates issued from then are valid for five years. Authorised persons issue barrier compliance certificates; licensed building surveyors are authorised automatically, and others are authorised under a 2024 appointment instrument. The page cites AS 1926.1-2012 and AS 1926.2-2007. Checked.

instructionSections.heading: Northern Territory (partly checked)
instructionSections.body: The NT Government page on pool fencing and barrier safety standards (no date shown) covers residential properties under 1.8 hectares. It says pools installed after 1 January 2003 need a compliance certificate in the owner's name, issued after a pool safety adviser inspects the barrier. Older pools have obligations that depend on whether the property has been sold or leased since 1 January 2003. The page applies to pools that can be filled to 30 cm or more at the deepest point and names the Swimming Pool Safety Act 2004. Partly checked, because the page is undated and the full text was not read.

instructionSections.heading: What this table does not cover
instructionSections.body: Pool chemical licences, dangerous goods thresholds for pool chemical storage, electrical licences for pool equipment, public-pool registration, and water discharge rules are not covered in this table for any jurisdiction. Use “Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention” for chemical handling, “Electrical, mechanical and confined-space boundaries” for electrical and plant boundaries, and “Water conservation and environmental release” for discharge.

lessons.title: Post-construction final clean sequence (dust-to-finish)
learningOutcomes: Confirm that the area is released by the site and that trades have finished before cleaning.
Sequence the final clean from dust removal to finish cleaning, high to low.
Control dust during the clean, and check the finish before handover.

instructionSections.heading: Release first
instructionSections.body: A final clean starts only when the site has released the area and the trades have finished in it. Confirm the release in writing, and check the access, the hazards and the exclusions. A final clean is not permission to enter a space where trades are still working, and presentation cleanliness is not contamination clearance.

instructionSections.heading: The sequence
instructionSections.body: Remove the dust first, from high surfaces to low, using controlled methods: dust extraction on the tools and wet-wiping where the surface allows it, rather than dry sweeping. Then clean the wet work, the windows, the fixtures and the finishes, and finish with the floors. Keep dust from the wet work away from finished surfaces, and cover what you have finished.

instructionSections.heading: Dust control and the finish
instructionSections.body: Control dust at its source and avoid dry sweeping, because settled dust becomes airborne when disturbed. WorkSafe Victoria advises that cleaning should not rely on pressurised air, sweeping that is dry, or high-pressure water, and it favours wet methods or extraction vacuums (page reviewed 11 March 2025). The exposure standard for crystalline silica dust is 0.05 mg/m³ averaged over 8 hours (same page, reviewed 11 March 2025). The current exposure standards list is being replaced by an exposure limits list starting 1 December 2026, so confirm the figure against the list in force (WorkSafe Victoria hazardous substances page; reviewed 19 May 2026). Check each finished surface under good light, and do not use a method on a new finish that the finish schedule does not allow.

lessons.title: Trade residue, adhesive and paint-overspray removal
learningOutcomes: Identify trade residues, adhesive and paint overspray, and the surfaces they sit on.
Choose a removal method approved for the surface and residue, and test it first.
Refuse scraping or strong solvent where no approved method exists.

instructionSections.heading: Identifying the residue
instructionSections.body: Trade residues on a construction site include cement splash, grout haze, adhesive, sealant, tape residue, plaster splatter and paint overspray. Each sits on a surface differently. Cement and grout bond to the surface by drying into it. Adhesives and sealants can bond chemically to a surface and can leave a film. Paint overspray can be water-based or solvent-based, and the difference matters because the removal method for one can soften or damage the other.
