Identify the residue and the surface before any removal. Ask the site for the product names and the data sheets of the materials that were used in that area, and look at packaging left on site. Where the residue is unknown, treat it as sensitive and stop before using any solvent or scraper.

instructionSections.heading: Surfaces that need care
instructionSections.body: Glass, tile and grout, polished or engineered stone, stainless steel, new paint, timber, vinyl and plastics each react differently to the same method. A steel blade can scratch glass and glazed tile. Strong solvents can soften new paint, cloud plastics and damage some stone finishes. Engineered stone needs particular care, as set out in the safety section below. Where the surface is new or freshly finished, the safest assumption is that it is sensitive until the site or the trade confirms otherwise.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing and testing the method
instructionSections.body: Choose a removal method approved for the surface and the residue, by the site, the trade responsible for the finish, or the product maker. Test it on an inconspicuous area first, such as the back edge of a panel or a corner that will be hidden, and leave it for the time the label or the approved method states. Check the test area for colour change, dulling, softening, lifting of the finish, or any scratch under good light. Work gently and in small areas. Keep the removal within the area released for cleaning, and stop if the surface changes. Do not try a stronger product because the first one did not work. Ask for the approved method instead.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing unapproved methods and recording the request
instructionSections.body: Refuse scraping or strong solvent where there is no approved method. Record the residue, its location, the surface beneath it, the reason you stopped, and who you asked. Request the approved method in writing from the site or the responsible trade. A removal that is not approved can cause damage that becomes a dispute about who caused it, so the written record protects both the business and the client. Chemicals must be managed under the label and the SDS, and a register of hazardous chemicals is required, with the exclusions described in the safety section.

lessons.title: Defect list, punch items and handover sign-off
learningOutcomes: Compile a defect list of marks, damage and incomplete items with their locations.
Separate cleaning items from items that belong to the trades.
Complete a handover sign-off that does not claim clearance or completion beyond the scope.

instructionSections.heading: The defect list
instructionSections.body: Walk each area once in a fixed order, usually from the top of the room downwards and from the entry around the room, so that nothing is missed. List every defect and punch item you can see within the scope you were given: marks and scuffs on walls and doors, scratches, chipped or cracked finishes, missing fittings or covers, residues that did not come off, incomplete trade work such as an unfinished edge, and any damage you think was caused during the build. Give each item a number, a location, a short factual description, and a photograph where the site permits it. Describe what you see, not why it happened. Mark each item as a cleaning item, a trade item, a damage item, or an unknown item that needs a decision. Cleaning items are yours to resolve within scope. Trade items belong to the responsible trade, and you name that trade on the list.

instructionSections.heading: Acceptance criteria before handover
instructionSections.body: Agree the acceptance criteria before the handover, in writing if you can. The criteria say what the cleaning must achieve in each area, which items are in scope, which are excluded, and who may approve exceptions. Check the work against those criteria, not against a general sense that it looks clean. A handover that depends on a verbal agreement is harder to defend, so write down any change that the client or site agrees to during the walk-through, with the time and the name of the person who agreed.

instructionSections.heading: The handover sign-off
instructionSections.body: Sign off only what you checked. The sign-off describes the cleaning that was done, the areas and criteria it covered, the defects and punch items listed, and the items not resolved, with the responsible person for each. It is not a clearance certificate, a building or regulatory sign-off, or a guarantee that the finish meets any standard that was not agreed. Do not write words such as defect-free, complete or approved unless each of those words is true for the scope you checked, and say which scope that is. Date and time the sign-off, and attach the list it refers to.

instructionSections.heading: Recording exceptions and keeping the list current
instructionSections.body: Record each exception and each unresolved item with the person responsible for it, and the date by which it is expected to be resolved if that has been agreed. Keep the list current. When an item is resolved, check it, record the check, and reissue the list rather than editing the old version. A handover that hides an open item is a false record, even if every other line is accurate. If you find a new defect after the sign-off, record it on a new list, and tell the person who signed.

lessons.title: Scope and surface survey
learningOutcomes: Separate low-pressure cleaning from regulated industrial jetting; confirm owner approval, site scope and exclusions.

instructionSections.heading: Low-pressure cleaning is not regulated jetting
instructionSections.body: The first decision on any pressure cleaning job is which kind of work it is. Routine exterior cleaning with a domestic or light commercial cleaner is one kind of work. High-pressure water jetting is another, and it carries a different level of risk. WorkSafe Victoria warns that a water jet can pierce skin and inject contaminated material into the body. Its alert sorts equipment by output in bar litres per minute. Class A covers outputs of 800 to 5,600 bar litres per minute, and Class B covers outputs above 5,600, which the alert describes as presenting a higher risk to the operator. The alert points to AS/NZS 4233.1:2013 for the classes, and says Class B operators must be trained and assessed through a registered training organisation. This lesson does not authorise any jetting at that level. The scope agreed with the owner must say which kind of work is being offered, and any request for industrial jetting, hazardous remediation or Class B equipment is outside this course.

instructionSections.heading: Confirm the owner's approval and the scope
instructionSections.body: Before a job is accepted, establish what is to be cleaned, why it needs cleaning, and what a successful result looks like. Record the address, the surface materials, the area that can be reached, the nearby drains, the people and vehicles on site, any landscaping that may be damaged, and the owner's restrictions. A pressure cleaner is not the default answer. Some surfaces need a rinse at low pressure, some need manual cleaning, and some need a specialist. Put the scope and the exclusions in writing before the work starts. The price is part of the scope. Western Australian consumer guidance says an accepted quote forms a binding contract, and that extra work needs the customer's approval before it is done. The Northern Territory guidance says a quote can become binding once it forms part of a contract, and that no charge applies for extra work unless it was approved. A change to the scope is therefore a new approval, not a line added at the end of the day.

instructionSections.heading: Survey the surface before any water is used
instructionSections.body: Ask the owner about the age of the material, any protective coating, previous leaks, loose pointing, painted sections and past damage. Walk the whole site, not only the area to be cleaned, because runoff, spray and access routes reach beyond it. Look for cracked or loose render, lifting paint, open joints, damaged downpipes and any exposed electrical equipment. Older painted surfaces need a particular check, because paint can contain lead. Photograph each defect with the owner's permission, and mark the excluded zones on a simple site plan. Decide whether the work can be done by the worker, needs a licensed contractor, or needs another specialist, and record that decision before the equipment is unloaded.

instructionSections.heading: Work at height and the licence position
instructionSections.body: Work above ground level is a separate question from pressure cleaning. Safe Work Australia defines high risk construction work as construction work with a fall risk of more than 2 metres, and the control order puts a fall prevention device first, then a work positioning system, then a fall arrest system. In New South Wales a safe work method statement is needed where a fall could be more than 2 metres, and a scaffold licence is needed to erect or alter a scaffold where the fall or falling-object risk is more than 4 metres. South Australia moves the high-risk threshold from 3 metres to 2 metres from 1 July 2026. Elevated platforms are a licence question as well. New South Wales: a boom-type elevating work platform needs a WP high risk work licence where the boom length is 11 metres or more (SafeWork NSW, High risk work licences, last modified 15 June 2026 per page metadata). Western Australia: the WP licence covers boom type elevating work platforms with a boom length of 11 metres or more (WorkSafe WA, published 11 August 2026; last updated 13 August 2026). Tasmania: the WP class covers booms of 11 metres or more (WorkSafe Tasmania, Check the classes, last updated 1 December 2023). Northern Territory: the licence class covers boom-type elevating work platforms with a boom length of 11 metres or more (NT WorkSafe bulletin, no date shown). South Australia: no boom-length licence rule is confirmed by an official source; the SafeWork SA high risk work licence page (last updated 10 January 2024) does not name a boom-type elevating work platform class. Queensland: according to the WorkSafe QLD page, search snippet, date not shown, a WP high risk work licence is needed to operate a boom type elevating platform, and elevated work platforms less than 11 metres in length are not included in that definition. Whether a boom-length threshold applies in Victoria is not confirmed by an official source. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. The national model code measures the boom from the original design, and says that below that length the duty holder still has a duty of care to ensure operators are adequately trained. Scissor lifts do not need the WP licence in Victoria or the Northern Territory.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical and solar limits
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In New South Wales, electrical installation work includes repairing and altering an installation. The same page excludes an electrical article that is connected to, and extends beyond, an electrical outlet. Treat every panel and cable as live. Refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work and referral
instructionSections.body: Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell the supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain. Stop if wind, rain, ice or fading light changes the conditions, if exposed wiring or water near electrical equipment is seen or suspected, if a person or animal enters the exclusion zone, if the task falls outside your training or the written work order, or if you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or written authorisation the work requires. A stop is not a failure. It is the control working as designed.

lessons.title: Pre-start hazard assessment
learningOutcomes: Assess injection injuries, slips, pedestrians, flying debris, wind, traffic, overhead electricity and operating environment.

instructionSections.heading: Injection injury is the first hazard to assess
instructionSections.body: The pre-start assessment is the point where the hazards of the job are named before any equipment is switched on. For pressure work, the first hazard is the water itself. WorkSafe Victoria's alert on high-pressure water jetting says a water jet can pierce the skin, and that contaminated material may be injected into the body. The same alert sets the expectation for controls. Anyone near jetting operations should wear eye protection, and the operator who controls the water flow should wear, at minimum, safety glasses and a face shield. Head protection is to be worn where needed, leg and body armour that can withstand the jet's direct force is needed where there is a risk of injury from the jet, and hearing protection is needed where noise cannot be controlled. Whatever the work, a jet that pierces skin is a medical emergency. Get urgent medical attention, and record the time and the event.

instructionSections.heading: Slips, pedestrians, traffic and debris
instructionSections.body: Wet hard surfaces, drips from the equipment, and water that runs off into a footpath or driveway are slip hazards. Walk the area on a fixed route before setup and note the surfaces that will be wet, the edges that drop away, the steps, and the places where a worker could be pushed off balance by the recoil of the lance. Pedestrians, including children and people with a mobility or sight impairment, may not see a spray zone. Set up an exclusion zone wide enough that the spray and the runoff stay inside it, and keep the zone closed while work continues. If the work is beside a road, the traffic risk is separate from the pedestrian risk. Flying debris from loose paint, grit, leaves and fragments of old sealant can strike people and vehicles. Check for loose material before the first pass and keep people back from the area the debris can reach.

instructionSections.heading: Wind, weather and overhead electricity
instructionSections.body: Wind changes the spray path and can carry overspray over people, vehicles and windows. Stop and reassess when a gust changes the direction or force of the spray, and do not work into a wind that carries spray toward others. Rain makes surfaces more slippery and can change the risk to electrical equipment. Water conducts electricity, so the risk of electric shock rises when equipment is used near water. A Queensland safety alert says equipment used near water should be connected to a safety switch or a residual current device, or fitted with a portable RCD. The same alert says a portable RCD should be tested before each use, or daily, whichever is the longer interval, and inspected every three months by a competent person. Check the position of overhead lines before any hose or lance is raised. In New South Wales, the SafeWork NSW code on work near overhead and underground electric lines (in force from 22 May 2026) sets 3.0 m for ordinary persons near lines up to 132,000 V, and 4.0 m for conductive materials near low-voltage overhead service lines. A wet hose, lance or water jet can conduct, so this course applies the 4.0 m figure near low-voltage lines; that is a course decision, not a figure the code gives for water. Refer to the network operator, and do not work closer to an overhead line than the network operator allows.

instructionSections.heading: The operating environment and the risk assessment
instructionSections.body: Look at the whole environment, not only the surface to be cleaned. Note the drains and where the runoff will go, the location of emergency exits and first-aid access, the lighting, the traction on the ground, the hose route and any place where a hose can be trapped or damaged. Ask about pets, unsecured doors and gates, and any chemicals stored nearby. For each hazard, assess how likely it is and how serious the outcome could be, then decide the control, name the person responsible for it, and set the trigger that stops the work. A risk assessment that names no owner and no stop trigger is not a finished assessment. Recheck the assessment whenever the site changes, when the weather changes, or when a new person arrives. Noise also needs assessment. The exposure standard is 85 decibels as an average over eight hours, and hearing protection is needed where noise cannot be controlled.

instructionSections.heading: Elevated work and the competency boundary
instructionSections.body: If the job requires work above ground level, the fall risk is a separate hazard to assess before the work begins. Safe Work Australia treats construction work with a fall risk of more than 2 metres as high risk, and the control order starts with keeping work on the ground or a solid construction. In New South Wales a safe work method statement is needed where a fall could be more than 2 metres. Any elevated work must be authorised in writing and carried out by a person with the licence the state requires. This lesson does not grant that authority, and it does not grant authority for regulated high-pressure jetting, electrical isolation or confined-space work. Where a task exceeds the trainee's authority, stop and escalate it to the supervisor.

lessons.title: Equipment suitability and inspection
learningOutcomes: Understand pressure, flow, reaction force, pressure ratings, hose compatibility and manufacturer-specified nozzles without prescribing unsafe settings.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure, flow and reaction force
instructionSections.body: Two quantities describe a pressure water system, and they are not the same thing. Pressure is the force the water is delivered at. Flow is the volume delivered in a given time. A cleaner's output depends on both, and the WorkSafe Victoria alert sorts high-pressure equipment by output, expressed in bar litres per minute, which combines the two. The alert places systems with an output of 800 to 5,600 bar litres per minute in Class A, and systems above 5,600 in Class B, which it describes as presenting a higher risk to the operator. A jet also pushes back on the equipment. That reaction force is why a lance is held firmly, why the operator's footing matters, and why a light or unsupported lance can move unexpectedly. This lesson does not set any working pressure or flow for a job. Those values come from the manufacturer's data for the equipment, and a worker who changes them to suit a surface is changing the equipment outside its design.

instructionSections.heading: Ratings, hoses and fittings
instructionSections.body: Every hose, fitting and part in the high-pressure path has a rating, and the rating must be at or above the maximum operating pressure of the equipment. The WorkSafe Victoria alert says hoses, fittings and parts should be the right size and compatible with each other, and rated at or above the equipment's maximum operating pressure. A hose that is rated for less than the machine can deliver is a failure waiting to happen. Check the rating printed on the hose and fitting against the equipment data before use, and do not mix hose brands or fitting types unless the manufacturer says they are compatible. The alert also says equipment and attachments must not be modified without written approval from the manufacturer or another competent person, and that repair and maintenance are for the manufacturer, its agent or a competent person. A modification the owner or worker makes on a site is a modification without approval.

instructionSections.heading: Nozzles and attachments
instructionSections.body: A nozzle sets the shape and the concentration of the jet, and so it changes the force on the surface and the risk to people in the area. Use only the nozzles the manufacturer specifies for the equipment. A nozzle that is worn, damaged, homemade or unidentified is not a suitable substitute, because its output is not known. Do not fit a nozzle found on site, or borrowed from another machine, until its specification has been confirmed against the manufacturer's data. Record the nozzle type and its source on the equipment record. The choice of nozzle must follow the scope and the surface test, not the wish to finish sooner.

instructionSections.heading: Inspection before use
instructionSections.body: Before the equipment is started, inspect it. Look at the hoses for cuts, abrasion, bulges and kinks, and at the fittings for leaks, cracks and worn threads. Check the trigger or control, the lance and its safety features, and the guards. Check the electrical lead and plug for damage, and test the RCD before use at the interval the guidance sets. The Queensland alert says a portable RCD should be tested daily or before each use, whichever is longer, and inspected every three months by a competent person. Do not run equipment with a damaged hose, a leaking fitting or an electrical fault. Tag it out, remove it from use and record the defect. A tag-out is not a repair. Only the manufacturer, its agent or a competent person can repair high-pressure equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Noise and hearing
instructionSections.body: Pressure equipment is often loud, and noise adds to the other hazards of the job. Safe Work Australia's exposure standard is that workers must not be exposed to noise above 85 decibels as an average over an eight-hour day. The page describes the duties to use control measures and provide personal protective equipment as separate duties, and it says that where a worker frequently wears hearing protection to stay below the standard, audiometric testing must be provided. The WorkSafe Victoria alert also calls for hearing protection where noise cannot be controlled. Choose the controls first, and use hearing protection where the controls do not reduce exposure enough.

instructionSections.heading: Training and competency
instructionSections.body: The WorkSafe Victoria alert says operators must be trained by a competent person, and that Class B operators must be trained and assessed through a registered training organisation. It also says trainers must be accredited, and that operators need refresher training at least every two years, and whenever new or more powerful equipment is introduced. This lesson is an introduction to equipment suitability and inspection. It does not give Class B competency, and it does not authorise work on equipment above the Class A range.

lessons.title: Injection injury prevention and site exclusion
learningOutcomes: Explain why a high-pressure water jet is a serious injection hazard even when the entry wound looks small.
Apply the personal protective equipment and exclusion controls that the WorkSafe Victoria jetting alert describes for routine work.
Stop work and seek urgent medical attention when a jet injury or hose failure occurs.

instructionSections.heading: Why injection injury is different
instructionSections.body: A high-pressure water jet can penetrate skin and drive water, dirt or other material into the tissue beneath. The wound at the surface can look minor, while the damage underneath may be much larger, and the material carried into the body may be contaminated. WorkSafe Victoria's high-pressure water jetting safety alert (published 14 September 2022, reviewed 11 May 2023) warns that a jet can puncture the skin and drive contaminated material into the body. The alert gives no first-aid step. Treat any skin contact with a jet as a reason for urgent medical attention.

instructionSections.heading: Immediate response to a jet injury
instructionSections.body: If a jet strikes a person, stop the equipment at once and isolate it as the manufacturer directs. Tell the medical team that the injury was caused by a high-pressure water jet, and tell them what the jet may have carried, such as detergent, dirt or other material from the surface being cleaned. Do not wait to see whether the injury gets worse. Record the time, the equipment, the operator and the witnesses, and report the incident as the employer's procedure requires. Keep the injured person still and call for urgent medical attention.

instructionSections.heading: Keep hands and body away from the jet
instructionSections.body: Never check a nozzle, a spray pattern or a blockage with a hand or any part of the body while the equipment is pressurised. Do not place a hand in front of the wand to test the flow. Before clearing a blockage, changing a nozzle or working on a coupling, isolate the equipment and release the pressure as the manufacturer's instructions direct. Keep the wand pointed at the surface being cleaned at all times, and keep the operator's own feet and legs clear of the line of the jet.

instructionSections.heading: Exclusion zones and site control
instructionSections.body: Set an exclusion zone around the work area before the equipment starts. Keep people, pets and vehicles out of the zone, and use barriers, cones or a supervisor to hold it. Stop the jet immediately when anyone enters the zone, and restart only when the zone is clear. Where the site is shared with other workers or the public, agree the zone with the site controller and record the agreement. The zone must cover the spray, the splash and the path of any loose debris.

instructionSections.heading: Personal protective equipment
instructionSections.body: The WorkSafe Victoria alert (reviewed 11 May 2023) says anyone close to jetting operations needs eye protection, and that the operator who controls the water flow wears at least safety glasses with a face shield. Head protection applies where the risk calls for it. Armour for the legs and body, able to take the jet's full force, is needed where injury is possible, and ear protection is needed where noise cannot be reduced. Check the PPE before every job and replace damaged items. The job pack should name the PPE for the task, and a worker who lacks the required PPE does not start the jet.

instructionSections.heading: Hose failure and equipment condition
instructionSections.body: A flailing hose, an uncontrolled nozzle or a separated hose coupling can strike a person with force. Before use, check that every hose, fitting and coupling is compatible, correctly sized and rated no lower than the equipment's highest operating pressure, as the WorkSafe Victoria alert requires. Do not fit attachments or make changes that the manufacturer or a competent person has not approved in writing. Repair or maintenance should be left to the manufacturer, its agent or a competent person.

instructionSections.heading: Competency boundary
instructionSections.body: The WorkSafe Victoria alert (reviewed 11 May 2023) sorts jetting systems by output in bar litres per minute: Class A covers 800 to 5,600 and Class B covers output above 5,600. Class B operators need training and an assessment of competence delivered by a registered training organisation (RTO), and refresher sessions must be logged no less often than every two years. The alert relies on AS/NZS 4233.1:2013. Compare the stated output of any machine with these bands before deciding whether this applies. This lesson does not provide that competency.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, competency or authority to operate industrial or Class B water jetting equipment. The competency route described in the alert is provided by registered training organisations. Obtain the employer's written authorisation before any work with high-pressure equipment.

lessons.title: Electrical power and exhaust safety
learningOutcomes: Inspect the power supply, leads and connections for an electric pressure cleaner before use.
Explain why a petrol-engine pressure cleaner must not run in an enclosed space.
Identify electrical work that is outside the scope of a cleaning worker and refer it correctly.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical hazards around water
instructionSections.body: An electric pressure cleaner combines electricity with water, which increases the risk of electric shock. Before use, check the power point, the lead and the plug. The power point should be in good condition and suitable for outdoor use. The lead should be undamaged, of a suitable rating, and free of joins. Keep the lead off wet ground and away from the spray. If the power point or lead is damaged, wet or unfamiliar, do not use it, and report it. Where the site has residual current protection, confirm it is working as the manufacturer directs before connecting the equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Testing and maintaining electrical equipment
instructionSections.body: AS/NZS 3760 is the reference standard named for electrical equipment inspection. Follow the employer's test-and-tag or inspection schedule for the equipment, and remove from service any item that fails inspection, shows damage, or has been wet inside its housing.

instructionSections.heading: Petrol engines and exhaust
instructionSections.body: Never run the engine in a garage, shed, enclosed courtyard, under a carport roof or any room with limited airflow. Place the machine outdoors, upwind of people, air intakes and windows, and keep the exhaust directed away from the work area. If a worker feels dizzy, has a headache or feels unwell while the machine is running, stop the machine, move to fresh air and seek medical advice.

instructionSections.heading: Fuel, refuelling and storage
instructionSections.body: Stop the engine and allow it to cool before refuelling. Keep fuel in an approved container, away from the engine, sources of ignition and occupied areas. Do not carry fuel in the cabin of a vehicle used for transport where the employer's rules forbid it.

instructionSections.heading: Fixed wiring and outdoor power points
instructionSections.body: A cleaning worker does not repair, alter or install fixed wiring, outdoor power points or switchboards. If a fault is suspected, stop using that power point, make it safe by not using it, and refer it to a licensed electrician or the site controller. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work includes repairing and altering, so repairs to fixed wiring need a licence or certificate (NSW Government licensing page, last updated 23 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Equipment modification and attachments
instructionSections.body: Do not modify the electrical or engine parts of the equipment, bypass a safety device, or fit an attachment that the manufacturer has not approved. The WorkSafe Victoria alert says attachments and changes need written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person (reviewed 11 May 2023). Report any part that seems faulty and remove the equipment from service until a competent person has checked it.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, a contractor licence or any authority to repair, alter or install electrical equipment or wiring. Repairs to fixed wiring are licensed work in New South Wales (NSW Government licensing page, last updated 23 June 2026).

lessons.title: Chemicals, PPE and exposure prevention
learningOutcomes: Interpret safety data sheets, prevent incompatible chemical use, assess aerosols and ensure suitable eye, hearing and skin protection.

instructionSections.heading: Read the label and the safety data sheet
instructionSections.body: A cleaning product is a hazardous chemical until its label and its safety data sheet say otherwise. The label tells you the product's intended uses, its dilution, the contact time and the first steps for exposure. The safety data sheet gives more detail, including hazards, protection, handling, storage, spill response and disposal. Safe Work Australia's guidance says a copy of the safety data sheet for each chemical in use must be kept in the hazardous chemical register, and must be easy to access for every worker who uses, handles or stores the chemical, and for anyone else who may be exposed to it. The same guidance says the information in a safety data sheet is general, so the worker must work out what applies to the site. Before a product is used, read its label and the current safety data sheet, and confirm the uses and incompatibilities the sheet names.

instructionSections.heading: Incompatible chemicals and mixing
instructionSections.body: Some chemicals must not be mixed or stored together, because a reaction can produce heat, gas or a more hazardous product. Safe Work Australia's storage guidance says that incompatible chemicals should be kept apart and stored well away from each other, and that some hazardous chemicals are not compatible with one another. The working rule is to use one product at a time, as its label directs, and to rinse equipment between products only where the label allows it. Do not combine products to make a stronger solution. Do not use a decanted liquid when its origin, concentration and contents are unknown. Do not combine an acid-based product with a chlorine-based product, and check each safety data sheet.

instructionSections.heading: Aerosols, overspray and exposure
instructionSections.body: Pressure work turns liquid into a fine spray and an aerosol. The spray can carry product onto skin, eyes, clothing and nearby vehicles, and it can be breathed in. Control the spray first. Lower the spray where the product allows it, position the operator so the spray does not drift toward people, and stop when wind carries the spray toward them. Personal protective equipment supports those controls, but it does not make an unsafe spray method acceptable. The WorkSafe Victoria alert says anyone near jetting operations should wear eye protection, and that the operator controlling the water flow should wear at least safety glasses and a face shield.

instructionSections.heading: Selecting PPE for eyes, hearing and skin
instructionSections.body: Select PPE after the task assessment, not before it. For eyes, the alert's minimum for the operator, and eye protection for anyone close to the spray, form the baseline. For hearing, the Safe Work Australia standard is 85 decibels as an average over an eight-hour day, and hearing protection is needed where noise cannot be controlled by other means. Where a worker frequently wears hearing protection to stay below the standard, audiometric testing must be provided. For skin, select gloves that the safety data sheet names as suitable for the product, and wear waterproof clothing where the product or the spray will reach the body. Gloves that are not suitable for a product can fail without warning. Wash facilities and a place to change out of contaminated clothing are part of the control, not an extra.

instructionSections.heading: Spills, runoff and storage
instructionSections.body: Check the spill response in the safety data sheet before use, and keep a spill kit suited to the product. Do not wash a chemical or its wastewater into a stormwater drain. The Victorian EPA guide on stormwater pollution, dated August 2007, says the runoff of wastewater and liquid or solid waste into the stormwater system must be avoided. Store products in their original labelled containers, in a suitable container for each product, and keep them apart from anything they are incompatible with.

instructionSections.heading: Competency boundary
instructionSections.body: This lesson gives the basic approach to chemicals, PPE and exposure. It does not give authority to use a restricted or high-hazard chemical, to remediate contamination, or to carry out work that needs a licence or a training competency. Refer those tasks to the supervisor and to a specialist, and record the referral.

lessons.title: Hazardous or unidentified contaminants
learningOutcomes: Identify surfaces and substances that must not be pressure cleaned until they are identified and assessed.
Explain why pressure cleaning can spread contamination, including mould spores, into air, water and other areas.
Apply stop, containment and referral decisions to a simulated job with unknown or hazardous contamination.

instructionSections.heading: Why contamination changes the job
instructionSections.body: A pressure cleaner moves a large volume of water at force. When the surface is contaminated, the jet can break up the contamination, throw it into the air as fine droplets or aerosol, and carry it into drains, soil and neighbouring areas. A job that looks like a routine clean may therefore spread a hazard, rather than remove it. The first decision on any surface is whether the contamination is known, ordinary and safe to clean with the approved method.

instructionSections.heading: Identify before you clean
instructionSections.body: Look at the surface and its surroundings before the equipment starts. Note any staining, odour, residue, powder, loose material, growth or damage that is not ordinary dirt. Ask the site controller about past spills, chemical storage, animal waste, flooding or repairs. Do not touch, scrape or test an unidentified substance by hand. If the material cannot be identified from the labels, safety data sheets or the site controller's records, treat it as unknown and do not pressure clean it.

instructionSections.heading: Mould and biological growth: full warning
instructionSections.body: Mould is a biological growth that can release spores. Pressure cleaning can spread those spores into the air and carry them, in water, into wall cavities, floor junctions, drains and other rooms, so it is not an appropriate routine method for mould. Do not pressure clean mould, and do not treat this lesson as authority to remove it. A worker who sees mould-like growth, a musty smell, or water damage behind a surface stops, keeps other people away from the area, records what was seen, and refers the job. Mould remediation requires its own assessment, containment, respiratory protection and waste controls, and those are covered in the High-risk cleaning module (family lesson HR04-mould-remediation).

instructionSections.heading: Asbestos and suspect materials
instructionSections.body: Older buildings may contain asbestos-containing materials in sheeting, flooring, fibre cement and other finishes. Pressure cleaning can break these materials and release fibres. The Queensland council page advises against using pressure cleaners on asbestos-contaminated materials (last modified 22 July 2025). If a surface may contain asbestos, do not pressure clean it, do not scrape or cut it, and stop the job. The Safe Work Australia model code on managing and controlling asbestos in workplaces is a model code whose legal effect depends on each jurisdiction (publication date blank). Refer the job to a competent person who can identify the material.

instructionSections.heading: Chemicals, SDS and wash water
instructionSections.body: Before using any cleaning product on an unknown surface, check the product's label and safety data sheet. Do not mix products, and do not use a product on a surface it is not designed for. In Queensland, a council page says pressure-cleaning wastewater is a regulated contaminant under the Environmental Protection Regulation 2014 (Schedule 10) and may not go into gutters or the stormwater system (last modified 22 July 2025). Collect, divert or refer the wash water as the job plan and the site rules require.

instructionSections.heading: Stop, contain and refer
instructionSections.body: Where the contamination is unknown, the response is stop, contain and refer. Stop the equipment, keep people and animals clear, close off the area where practical, and record the location and the appearance of the material. Refer the job to the site controller and to a competent person who can identify the substance or growth. Do not restart until the material is identified and a written method is approved. If a worker feels unwell after contact or exposure, stop work, move to fresh air, and seek medical advice.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, clearance, certificate or authority to remove mould, asbestos, hazardous chemicals or other restricted contamination. A pressure cleaning worker does not give a clearance statement for any surface that was contaminated.

lessons.title: Workflow, zoning and people management
learningOutcomes: Plan safe zones, surface sequence, runoff controls, spot-testing, protected equipment and pedestrian interfaces.

instructionSections.heading: Plan the zones before the first pass
instructionSections.body: A pressure job is easier to control when the site is divided into zones before the first pass. Mark the spray zone, where the jet and the overspray go. Mark the exclusion zone, which is the wider area that people and animals must stay out of. Mark the equipment zone, where the machine, the pump, the fuel and the power connection sit, and keep it outside the spray. Mark the runoff zone, where the wash water will go, and the access route for people and vehicles. Sketch the zones on a site plan and walk them with the team before setup. The plan should be changed when the site changes, and the change should be briefed to everyone who is on site. A zone that exists only in the operator's head is not a control.

instructionSections.heading: Surface sequence
instructionSections.body: Plan the order in which surfaces are cleaned. The sequence should suit the material and the risk to the surface, and it should keep finished areas from being re-soiled by water running off untreated areas. A common working practice is to work from the higher surfaces down, so that runoff from upper areas does not wash over surfaces already cleaned. This is working practice, not a legal requirement, and it must give way to the surface test and the owner's instructions. Where a surface is fragile, it may need manual or low-pressure cleaning, and it may be left until last or handled separately. Record the sequence on the site plan so that the team and the owner can see it.

instructionSections.heading: Spot-testing and trial areas
instructionSections.body: Before a method is used across a surface, test it on a small area that is hidden or otherwise unimportant. Start with the least forceful method and the lowest effective setting the manufacturer's data allows, then increase only if the surface has not reacted. Record the location, the method, the result and the time of the test. If the test causes damage, stop, record it, and change the method or refer the surface to a specialist. Do not widen the method to a larger area until the test result is accepted by the owner. A test on one material does not cover another material on the same building, so each material needs its own test.

instructionSections.heading: Runoff, wastewater and stormwater
instructionSections.body: Plan the runoff before the water is used. The Victorian EPA guide on stormwater pollution, dated August 2007, says the runoff of wastewater and liquid or solid waste into the stormwater system must be avoided. Practical controls include sweeping before wetting, dry-cleaning where the surface allows, directing runoff onto the lawn or a soil area where that is permitted, and capturing the wastewater with a barrier or a sump. For yard and workshop wet cleaning, the same guide says wastewater should go to sewer through a water and oil separator under a trade waste agreement. Do not add detergent to a stormwater path, and do not let runoff reach a drain or a waterway because it seemed too small to matter.

instructionSections.heading: Protected equipment and electrical equipment
instructionSections.body: Protect what the spray can damage. Cover or shield vehicles, plants, windows, light fittings, meters, letterboxes, electrical outlets and any exposed fixture before work starts. Keep electrical equipment away from water. The Queensland safety alert says equipment used near water should be connected to a safety switch or residual current device, or fitted with a portable RCD, and that cords should be kept off the ground so they do not contact water. Route the hose and the cord so that they do not cross the exclusion zone or a walkway, and so that nobody can trip on them.

instructionSections.heading: Pedestrians and the team
instructionSections.body: The pedestrian interface is the edge of the exclusion zone, and it needs a person who controls it. Put a spotter at the edge where the public can reach the zone, with a clear instruction to stop work when someone enters. Use barrier tape, cones and signs to show the route around the zone. Brief the team at the start of each shift on the zones, the stop triggers and each person's role. Operators, spotters and any helpers must know who makes the stop decision. Where work is above ground level, the fall controls in Safe Work Australia's control order apply, and the work must stay on the ground or solid construction where possible. Noise from the equipment affects the team and the public, and the exposure standard for workers is 85 decibels as an average over eight hours. Rotate operators where the noise and the work load require it, and record the rotation.

instructionSections.heading: Handover and records
instructionSections.body: At the end of each stage, record what was cleaned, what was not, what was tested, where the runoff went, and any damage or near miss. Hand over the site to the owner or the supervisor with the exclusions and the open items written down. A handover that is only spoken is hard to check later.

lessons.title: Shutdown and equipment care
learningOutcomes: Follow manufacturer shut-down/depressurisation, inspect hoses and connections and quarantine defective equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure cleaning at height and the access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson sits in the pressure cleaning (all heights) track, which covers ground-level pressure work and work that is elevated or on a roof. High-pressure water, hoses and lances, the machine's power source, electrical supply, exhaust gas and falls from height are all hazards on this track. Safe Work Australia treats construction work with a fall risk of more than 2 metres as high risk construction work, and it lists the control order to follow, starting with doing the work from the ground or a solid surface. NSW requires a safe work method statement where a fall could exceed 2 metres. In South Australia, construction work with a risk of falling more than two metres is high-risk from 1 July 2026, and a SWMS is required, according to SafeWork SA's guidance (March 2026, no day shown); the regulation text itself was not read in this pass. The Victorian, Queensland, Western Australian and Tasmanian pages checked do not state a metre threshold for this work. Where the work is above ground level, the employer's written authorisation is needed in addition to any licence the state or territory requires. The authorisation rule is working practice in this course rather than a checked legal rule. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on a roof or on a solar system.

instructionSections.heading: Why shutdown is still a hazard step
instructionSections.body: A pressure cleaner can hold energy after the engine or motor has stopped, in the pump, the hose and the lance. The end of a job is therefore a hazard step, not a tidy-up step. The Safe Work Australia guide on high pressure water jetting expects a system to be depressurised and locked off when nobody is attending it, when it is idle, and when parts are being swapped or fixed. The same guide asks that planning and pre-start checks cover isolation steps that use locks and tags. The guide does not give a bleed-down method for each machine, and it does not set a specific stored-energy warning. The manufacturer's full shutdown sequence therefore decides the actual steps for the machine in front of you. Treat every machine as still charged until the checks in this lesson show that it is not. The guide defines high pressure by output rather than by one pressure figure, and it notes that systems below its output definition can still be covered where injury is a foreseeable risk. A small domestic-style machine is therefore not outside the thinking in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Shutdown sequence and pressure release
instructionSections.body: Use the sequence in the manufacturer's manual for the specific machine. The order matters. Stop the engine or motor and isolate the power or fuel supply the way the manual says. Shut off the water supply to the machine. Release the stored pressure by the method the manufacturer gives, which is commonly done by operating the trigger gun or lance with the supply shut off. Then confirm the machine is safe by checking that the pressure gauge reads nil, if the machine has one, and that no water flows from the lance or nozzle. Only when those checks pass should any hose, lance or fitting be disconnected. Do not open a coupling while the machine still holds pressure, and do not rely on the machine being switched off to mean it is safe. If the machine will not depressurise, or the release method is unclear, stop and call the supervisor. Do not try to force the coupling or strike it.

instructionSections.heading: Hoses, connections and inspection
instructionSections.body: Inspect each hose assembly, fitting, coupling, trigger gun, lance and nozzle at the end of every job, and before the first use of the day. The Safe Work Australia guide wants a competent person to look over each hose assembly before every use. It classes a hose with broken wires, a deep abrasion, a kink, a blister or a bubble as defective, and it classes a fitting with a crack, corrosion or damaged threads as defective. Check each connection for leaks at the seal and for wear at the thread. Keep hoses flat, in a place that is cool and not damp, because the guide links hose life to pressure cycling, heat, chemicals and abrasion. The guide does not set a replacement interval, so the manufacturer's data and the business's maintenance schedule must set it. The guide is dated December 2013, so check whether a later edition or the manufacturer's data gives different requirements before relying on it for a particular machine.

instructionSections.heading: Quarantine and defect reporting
instructionSections.body: A defective item must be taken out of use at once. Stop using it, tag it as defective, and move it away from the working equipment so that it cannot be picked up by mistake. The guide expects a defective hose to come out of service with a clear marking and tag. It also calls for testing after a hose is new, damaged, re-ended or repaired, keeps test records, and allows only passing hoses back into use. As a trainee, you do not repair the item or test it yourself. Record what you found on the defect log: the item, its identifier if it has one, the date, the defect, and who found it. Report it to the supervisor and request maintenance through the business's own route. Do not fit a spare fitting from another machine, cut out a damaged section and rejoin the hose, or wrap a damaged hose with tape to keep it in service. Each of those actions changes the equipment without authority and removes the record of the defect.

instructionSections.heading: Chemicals, containers and wash water at shutdown
instructionSections.body: Chemicals used in pressure cleaning should stay in their original labelled containers, or in containers labelled with the product name and the hazard information that the safety data sheet gives. Keep containers closed when they are not in use and store them as the safety data sheet directs. Do not mix products unless the label or the safety data sheet allows it. Check the safety data sheet for each product before use, and keep the sheets where the team can find them. Until those rules are confirmed for the work site, follow the site rules and the supervisor's instructions, and record how waste and wash water were handled on the job record.

instructionSections.heading: Competency boundary and the electrical notice
instructionSections.body: Apply the site-specific risk assessment, the verified local requirements and the equipment manufacturer's instructions. This lesson alone does not grant authorisation for regulated high-pressure jetting, hazardous remediation, electrical isolation, fuel system repair or confined-space work. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work covers the physical work of putting in, fixing, changing, removing or extending an installation, and the licensing page leaves out electrical articles connected to an outlet. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

lessons.title: Quality control and handover
learningOutcomes: Capture before/after evidence, waste records, client sign-off, limitations, property defects and incidents.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure cleaning at height and the access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson sits in the pressure cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level pressure work and work that is elevated or on a roof, so falls, high-pressure water, hoses, electrical supply and exhaust gas are all hazards that the inspection and handover can reveal. Safe Work Australia treats construction work with a fall risk of more than 2 metres as high risk construction work. NSW requires a safe work method statement where a fall could exceed 2 metres. In South Australia, construction work with a risk of falling more than two metres is high-risk from 1 July 2026, according to SafeWork SA's guidance (March 2026, no day shown); the regulation text was not read in this pass. The Victorian, Queensland, Western Australian and Tasmanian pages checked do not state a metre threshold for this work. Where the work is above ground level, the employer's written authorisation is needed in addition to any licence the state or territory requires. This is working practice in this course, not a checked legal rule. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on a roof or on a solar system.

instructionSections.heading: Quality is measured against the agreed scope
instructionSections.body: The quality of a pressure clean is judged against the scope the client agreed in writing, and against the test area that was agreed before the main work began. How bright a surface looks from the doorway is not the measure. A surface can look clean while residue is still present, while a sealed or fragile finish has been damaged, or while a sealant has lifted at an edge. Inspection should take place after the surface has dried enough to show its true state, because wet surfaces hide residue, water marks and lifted edges. The inspection checks the agreed scope, the preserved finish, the safe condition of the site, the environmental controls, the return of access to the client and the client's acceptance. Each of these is recorded separately so that a gap in one area does not get lost in a general statement.

instructionSections.heading: Before and after evidence
instructionSections.body: Take the before photographs at the walk-through, before any water is used, and take the after photographs from the same positions, under similar light and once the surface has dried. Number each zone on a simple site plan and label every photograph with its zone number, the date and the time. Include a close-up of any defect, a wide view that shows where the defect sits, and the test patch before and after. Photograph only what the owner or site has agreed may be photographed, and store the images with the job record. Do not use a before photograph taken after the work started, and do not select only the best after photographs. A record that shows the whole zone, including the parts that did not change, is the one that stands up later.

instructionSections.heading: Inspection, limitations and missed areas
instructionSections.body: Inspect every zone in the same order, and check for missed areas, damage, chemical residue, staining, water marks, lifted edges and any change in colour or texture that was not there before. Compare the result with the documented test patch and the photographs. Record limitations honestly. If an area could not be cleaned without risk of damage, record it as a limitation with the reason, such as a fragile sealed finish, a failing render or paint that lifts under pressure. Use plain words for the result. Lightened is not removed, and a reduced stain is not gone. Describe what changed and what did not. Remove barriers only after slip hazards and residual runoff have been dealt with, and check the walkways before the client uses them.

instructionSections.heading: Property defects found before and during the work
instructionSections.body: Record any existing defect at the walk-through, before work starts. Typical examples include cracked render, loose tiles, open joints, lifted paint and a damaged downpipe. Record each defect with its location, a photograph and a short factual description. If a defect is found after the work, record it as found at the point of inspection, not as caused by the cleaning, unless the evidence shows that the cleaning caused it. Keep pre-existing defects in a separate list from any change the work made, so that the handover does not blur the two. Tell the client in writing about any defect that may need a licensed trade or a specialist assessment, and do not offer a repair you are not authorised to carry out.

instructionSections.heading: Waste, wash water and chemical records
instructionSections.body: Keep a waste record for each job. Note the products used, the quantity used where it is known, how the waste and wash water were handled, and where the waste went. Record the handling in the same form for every job so that the owner can compare them. Until the rules for the work site are confirmed, follow the site and council instructions, the product's safety data sheet and the supervisor's direction, and record each step taken.

instructionSections.heading: Client sign-off, quotes and extra work
instructionSections.body: Walk the client through the completed work, the exclusions, the limitations, the concerns and any recommended follow-up. Give the client a concise written account, then ask for written acceptance. Acceptance is the point at which the Western Australian consumer page treats a quote as binding. Work outside the accepted scope needs the client's agreement first, and the Northern Territory consumer page takes the same position on extra work. If the client asks for more work during the visit, record the request and the price, and get the client's written approval before the work is started. Do not treat a verbal comment such as that the surface looks fine as acceptance.

instructionSections.heading: Incidents, near misses and handover
instructionSections.body: Record any incident or near miss on the day it happens, even if nobody was hurt: a slip, a hose failure, a lance strike, a chemical splash, a property contact or a complaint from a neighbour. Report it to the supervisor through the business's incident procedure. Close the handover with the completed checklist, the before and after photographs, the waste record, the defect and limitation list, the signed client acceptance and the incident record, if any. Each item is filed against the job, and the worker signs the handover once every item is present.

lessons.title: Client screening and health-questionnaire boundaries
learningOutcomes: Complete a health questionnaire with a new client and identify the answers that need a medical referral before training
Explain the difference between a screening tool and a diagnosis, and the limits of the trainer's role
Identify the children's-service check categories that were confirmed in Victoria.

instructionSections.heading: Screening is a referral step, not a diagnosis
instructionSections.body: A personal trainer's health questionnaire is a way to find out whether a client needs medical advice before exercise. It is not a diagnosis, and it does not replace the advice of a doctor. The trainer's role is to ask clearly, record the answers, and refer where a medical question is raised. Some industry bodies publish pre-exercise screening tools. AusActive is an industry body, not an official source. The business's screening questions and referral rule are held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}. Follow that document, and use this lesson to understand why each answer matters.

instructionSections.heading: What the trainer must not do
instructionSections.body: The trainer must not tell a client that a symptom is harmless, must not advise on a medication, and must not start a programme for a condition that a medical practitioner has not reviewed. Under the business rule, chest pain, dizziness, breathlessness out of proportion to effort, a recent injury or a recent surgery means the client is referred to a medical practitioner before any further training. Where a client has told the trainer about a condition, the trainer records the condition as the client describes it, and does not state what the condition is. Where the trainer is not sure whether a client is safe to train, the safe decision is to refer and to postpone the start of the programme.

instructionSections.heading: Who the trainer works with: children, permits and checks
instructionSections.body: Some trainers train children. The Victorian government's Working with Children Check page (updated 12 October 2026) lists private tutoring and coaching aimed at children (code 28), commercial gyms and play venues aimed at children (code 32), and sport, recreation and culture clubs that deal with children or are mainly made up of children (code 42). The same page does not say whether self-employed trainers are covered, and it sets no direct-contact rule. A business listing that copies the government text says self-employed workers are covered and refers to direct contact (no date shown; secondary copy). The government explainer (updated 24 July 2026) states that a clearance is valid for five years. No pet-care category appears on the government list. The government page also says an organisation can still require a check for work that is not listed. Where a council permit applies, see “Outdoor and park session safety” and “Booking, packages and client retention”. Completing this lesson does not give any check, certificate or permit.

lessons.title: Programme design and progression
learningOutcomes: Design a programme that starts from the client's referral and questionnaire answers, and states its goals and review points
Progress a programme by a defined rule, and stop or reduce it when the client reports a warning sign
Explain which qualifications the council permits in the research require, and that they are council conditions, not state licences

instructionSections.heading: A programme begins with the screening result
instructionSections.body: A programme is only as safe as the screening that comes before it. The trainer should not design a programme until the questionnaire in “Client screening and health-questionnaire boundaries” is complete and every medical question has been answered or referred. A programme then states the client's goal, the starting level, the sessions per week, the exercises, the intensity rule, the progression rule, the review date, and the points at which the programme must be stopped or changed. The programme is recorded on the client file, and each review is recorded with the date and the decision. The business's programme template is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the approval for each programme is recorded as {{business:pricing.quoting_approval}} where a programme is sold as a service.

instructionSections.heading: Progression with a rule and a stop
instructionSections.body: Progression means increasing the load, the reps, the time or the difficulty. It should follow a rule the trainer can state in one sentence, such as 'add a set when the client completes all sets with good form twice in a row'. A rule with no stop is unsafe. The trainer must stop or reduce the session where the client reports chest pain, dizziness, breathlessness out of proportion to the effort, joint pain that does not settle, or a new injury. Those signs mean the programme goes back to the referral step in “Client screening and health-questionnaire boundaries”, and the trainer should not progress the client until a medical practitioner has advised. Record every stop and the action taken.

instructionSections.heading: Charging more for specialised programmes, within the permit limits
instructionSections.body: A programme that takes more skill, more assessment time or more specialised training can be priced higher than a standard session. The price should cover the assessment, the design and review time, the travel, the equipment and any compliance cost. Council permits set qualification conditions for personal trainers on public land, and they apply only on that council's land. Holdfast Bay's personal training permit terms (titled 2024, with no issue date in the document) call for the primary trainer to hold a Certificate IV-level fitness qualification (or a sport-specific equivalent) from an accredited provider, with current first aid and CPR; the CPR certificate expires yearly. Hornsby Shire Council (no date shown) asks for proof of accredited courses that Fitness Australia or VETAB endorses, matched to the activity taught, plus senior first aid training that is still current. Stonnington's permit listing (no explicit date) asks for a Level 2 first aid certificate, kept current, from a workplace course and registration with a recognised peak body. These are council-specific conditions, not state licences. Completing this lesson does not satisfy any of those permit conditions.

lessons.title: Supervision, emergency and first-aid response
learningOutcomes: Describe the supervision a session needs, including the maximum group size the business sets and the permit limit where one applies
Carry out the first response to a collapse or serious symptom, and state the limit of what the trainer may do
Record the incident and the emergency contact details for each session

instructionSections.heading: Supervision: who is in charge and how many
instructionSections.body: Each session needs a named person in charge, and that person must be able to see every participant. The business sets a maximum group size and a supervision ratio. Where the session is on public land, the council permit may set a limit that the business must not exceed. Hornsby Shire Council in New South Wales caps a group at 18 for the permitted personal training it covers (no date shown). Stonnington in Victoria caps participants at 15 per session under its permit (listing shows no explicit date; confirm with the council). Those are council-specific limits for those councils. The business's group size and ratio are held in the session procedure, {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the supervisor is named in {{business:staff.supervisor_contact}}. The trainer must check the permit for the place and the time before the session starts, and must not let a group grow beyond the limit.

instructionSections.heading: First response to a collapse or serious symptom
instructionSections.body: If a participant collapses, becomes unresponsive, has chest pain, struggles to breathe, or shows signs of a serious injury, the first step is to make the area safe and call emergency services. Stay with the participant, keep them safe, and follow the first-aid training the trainer holds. Stonnington's permit listing asks for a Level 2 first aid certificate, kept current, from a workplace course; Hornsby asks for senior first aid, kept current; Holdfast Bay requires current first aid and CPR. Those are council conditions that apply on that council's land. This course does not treat a first-aid certificate as clinical authority, and it is not a state licence. The trainer must not diagnose, must not give medication, and must not tell the family what the cause is. Record the time of the incident, what was seen, what was done, and who was called. The escalation and emergency contacts are held in {{business:safety.emergency_contact}} and {{business:safety.escalation_contact}}.

instructionSections.heading: Records and the incident after the session
instructionSections.body: After any emergency, the trainer must complete an incident record while the details are fresh. The record should include the participant's name, the time, the location, the session type, the group size, the first aid given, the people called, and any witnesses. The record must be kept under the business's privacy approach, and the client's medical information must be shared only as the business procedure allows. Where the event involves a child, the business must also follow its child-safety procedure. The trainer should not discuss the incident on social media or with other clients. The business should review the incident and record the change it has made.

lessons.title: Outdoor and park session safety
learningOutcomes: Check that a park session is inside the council permit for the place, the time, the group size and the equipment
Carry out a site inspection that identifies the hazards in a public space before a session starts
Apply a dynamic risk assessment during the session, and stop the session when conditions become unsafe

instructionSections.heading: The permit comes before the park
instructionSections.body: A public park or sportsground is council land, and most councils set conditions for commercial activity on it. The sources checked include several permits with specific conditions. Stonnington in Victoria issues seasonal permits, for 1 October to 31 March and 1 April to 30 September. Its listing says training may run only between 6am and 9pm, limits the number of sessions a week, and forbids attaching equipment to trees or pegging it to the ground. It also bans amplifiers (no explicit date shown). Hornsby Shire in New South Wales restricts personal training to designated areas that others can also use, and up to three locations per application (no date shown). Holdfast Bay in South Australia sets sessions between 6am and 8pm, caps sites at three per application (two reserves and one beach), and asks for battery lights whenever work runs outside daylight (no issue date). These are council-specific conditions and apply only on the council that set them. Yoga is named among Hornsby's permitted activities, but Pilates is not named there. Check the permit before every new park, and keep a copy with the session record.

instructionSections.heading: Site inspection and the hazards of a public space
instructionSections.body: Before every outdoor session, inspect the site. Look for uneven ground, holes, tree roots, wet or slippery surfaces, loose equipment, nearby traffic, cyclists and dogs, other park users, and any work underway. Check the shade and the forecast for heat and sun, and plan breaks and water. Where the site has a playground or sports equipment, keep clients clear of it unless the permit allows use. Record the inspection on the session record, with the time and the conditions. Where a hazard cannot be removed, move the session to another area in the permit or cancel it, and record the decision. The business's site inspection checklist is held in {{business:safety.site_hazards}}, and the required personal protective items are in {{business:safety.required_ppe}}.

instructionSections.heading: Dynamic risk assessment during the session
instructionSections.body: Conditions change during a session. A storm can arrive, a dog can run into the group, a participant can become unwell in the heat, or a cyclist can cut across the area. The trainer must assess the risk as it changes and act on it. The method is to stop the activity, make the group safe, decide whether to continue, move, or end the session, and record the decision. Stop the session where any participant has a warning sign of a medical problem, where the weather becomes dangerous, or where the permit conditions can no longer be met. The stop-work authority in “Dynamic risk assessment and stop-work authority” sets out the trainer's right to end the session. Record every stop, with the time and the reason, on the session record.

lessons.title: Booking, packages and client retention
learningOutcomes: Set up a booking and package system that records each session, the terms and the client's health review date
Identify the insurance each council in the research required.
Use client retention methods that do not depend on health claims or unreviewed promises

instructionSections.heading: Bookings and packages that keep the record straight
instructionSections.body: A booking is a promise to a client and a record for the business. Every booking should record the date, the session type, the location, the group size where it applies, the health review date, and the cancellation rule. A package is a set of sessions sold together. The package must state the number of sessions, the period it covers, what happens to unused sessions, and how it can be cancelled. Queensland's Fair Trading page for gym and fitness agreements (last updated 23 July 2024) sets a 48-hour cooling-off period, refunds of prepaid fees within 14 days (less services used and any stated administration fee), and a 12-month cap on prepayment. New South Wales's page (modified 15 April 2026) says an expired membership does not stop direct debits by itself, and that the gym may need a notice period of 30 days, given in writing, to stop them. The business's booking rules are held in {{business:jobs.scheduling_method}}, and the cancellation policy is in {{business:customers.communication_policy}}. Each session in a package still needs its own health review date, because a client's health can change.

instructionSections.heading: Insurance: what the councils required
instructionSections.body: Councils set most of the insurance conditions the sources found for personal training. Stonnington's listing wants cover for public liability and for professional indemnity, with no minimum amounts stated. Hornsby Shire's page wants APRA-approved public liability cover of $20 million or more, with the council recorded on the policy in an interested-party role (no date shown). Holdfast Bay's terms require public liability of at least $20 million and professional indemnity of at least $5 million (no issue date). These are council-specific amounts, and they apply on that council's land. In Victoria, WorkSafe's registration guide (last updated 19 May 2026) says WorkCover registration is generally required where a business employs any workers. A sole trader with no other workers on staff does not need to register, and a small-business exemption applies if there are no apprentices and annual wages stay at or under $7,500 for the financial year. Check each council's permit and the insurer before taking a booking on public land. The business's insurance details are held in {{business:compliance.policy_reference}}.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping clients without making health promises
instructionSections.body: Retention comes from reliable sessions, clear progress records, and a relationship that clients trust. It does not come from promises about health outcomes. A trainer who says that a programme will reverse a condition, cure a complaint or guarantee a result is making a claim the research does not support. New South Wales's consumer summary notes that the Australian Consumer Law rules out misleading statements about what a service does (page modified 15 April 2026). Use reviews of the programme with dates and results the client has recorded, reminders for sessions, and a clear way for the client to report a change in health. Keep the client's information private, as “Privacy, security and customer property” explains. Use retention offers within the approved pricing rules.

lessons.title: Portfolio intake
learningOutcomes: Collect the intake details for a property: owner, address, access, authority and emergency contacts.
Confirm written authority before any key, code or account is used.
Store intake details securely and share only what each person needs.

instructionSections.heading: What an intake must capture
instructionSections.body: A property manager starts with a complete intake record, because later decisions depend on it. Capture the property address and a short description of the property, including the number of levels, the type of building and any shared areas. Record the owner's name, postal and email details, and the best number to reach them. Record the owner's written authority for the manager to act, which is covered in the next section. Note the access arrangements: who lets people in, at what times, and whether a tenant or occupier must be told before entry. Record the emergency contacts for the property, and the process for escalating an urgent issue such as water escaping or a lock failure. Attach any existing asset register, maintenance history and reports that the owner has provided. An intake that leaves any of these fields blank should show the gap and the date it is to be closed.

instructionSections.heading: Written authority and approval limits
instructionSections.body: Do not use a key, code or account until written authority covers that use. The authority should say what the manager may approve, in what categories of work, and up to what amount. It should name the approval route for work above that amount, such as a quote sent to the owner for approval before the work starts. It should also say what happens in an emergency, and which work must always go back to the owner. A verbal instruction is a starting point for a conversation, but it does not authorise access or spending. Confirm the owner's approval for each category of work and record the date of each approval. Where the owner has not set a limit, record that as an open item and do not approve work that needs a quote until the limit is in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Keys, codes and accounts
instructionSections.body: Record every key, code, card and online account that the property uses, and the person who holds each one. Keep the register in a secure location, and limit access to the people who need it for the job. Do not keep codes in an open message thread, a shared note or a sticky note. Where a code or key is handed to a contractor, record who received it, when, and the date it must be returned or changed. When the arrangement ends, return or change every key and code, and update the register with the date. Keep a copy of the owner's authority with the register, so that anyone checking the file can see what was permitted and when.

instructionSections.heading: Sharing information with the right people
instructionSections.body: Share only what each person needs for their task. A plumber needs the address, the access arrangement and the fault. A contractor does not usually need the owner's full contact details or the tenant's personal information. Keep personal information about owners and tenants private, and use it only for the management task. Where privacy obligations apply to the business, they depend on the business's size and activities.

lessons.title: Condition evidence
