learningOutcomes: Record condition evidence that separates pre-existing damage from damage caused during a tenancy or job.
Capture dated, referenced photographs and notes at intake and before handover.
Respect privacy when photographing occupied properties.

instructionSections.heading: Separate existing condition from new damage
instructionSections.body: Condition evidence protects the owner, the manager and the occupant. At intake, record the condition of each room and fixed item with dated, referenced photographs taken from the same positions each time. Note existing marks, chips, stains and wear. When a dispute arises later, the question is what was there before. Without an intake record, a scratch on a floor can be blamed on anyone. Keep the evidence with the asset register so that the condition history of each item is visible.

instructionSections.heading: Photograph with care
instructionSections.body: Photograph the property, not the occupants' private items. Take photographs with the occupant's consent where they are present, and avoid photographing personal papers, mail, medication or children. Keep photographs stored securely and share them only with the owner and people who need them. A photograph taken from a marked position at each inspection makes change easy to see. A condition note that says what was seen, where and when is as useful as a photograph. Taking condition photographs during an inspection means entering the home, so the entry rules below apply. In New South Wales, an inspection needs a minimum of seven days' notice given in writing, and no more than four inspections may take place in any twelve-month period (page last modified 24 May 2024). Entry is generally barred on Sundays and public holidays, and before 8am or after 8pm (page last modified 1 October 2026). In Victoria, a general inspection needs seven days' notice, may not be made in the first three months of the agreement, and can happen no more than once every six months (page last updated 24 April 2025). In Queensland, a routine inspection needs at least seven days' notice on the entry notice form and can happen no more than once every three months (no page date shown).

lessons.title: Vacate and tenancy scope
learningOutcomes: Identify which vacate tasks are within a property manager partner's scope and which belong to the owner or a licensed professional.
Describe the evidence needed at a vacate without making tenancy decisions.
Refer tenancy, bond and leasing questions and record the referral.

instructionSections.heading: Separate work from decisions
instructionSections.body: A vacate involves physical work, such as checking the condition of the property, arranging keys, and organising repairs and cleaning. It also involves decisions: what counts as damage, what is deducted, whether a notice was correctly given, and what the outgoing occupant is responsible for. The second group belongs to the owner, and in many cases to a licensed or regulated process. A property manager partner records the condition and arranges work the owner has approved. Do not make tenancy decisions or promise an outcome to the outgoing occupant.

instructionSections.heading: Refer tenancy and leasing questions
instructionSections.body: Questions about notices, rent, bonds, leasing, and tenancy rights should be referred to the owner and to the relevant state authority or qualified professional. The licence position differs by state. In New South Wales, the NSW licence page for real estate agents says a licence is needed to lease and manage property for clients, and that rent collection falls within it (page last modified 20 October 2026). In Queensland, a current resident letting agent licence is required for that work, and its scope is set out on the licence page (last updated 26 October 2026). Record each question, the person it was referred to, and the date. Do not give legal or tenancy advice that the course does not cover.

lessons.title: Service documentation
learningOutcomes: Use a standard checklist for each service visit so that records are comparable across properties.
Record the service, the findings and the next action in a form the owner can read.
Store service records so they can be retrieved for each asset and each property.

instructionSections.heading: Standard checklists make records comparable
instructionSections.body: Each type of service has its own checklist. The checklist lists what is checked, what is done, what is found, and what is due next. A standard form means that the owner can compare visits across properties, and a new worker can pick up a record without asking the last person what they meant. Keep the checklist short enough to complete on site, with space for brief notes and photographs. Each entry needs a date, the name of the worker, and the asset identifier from the register. Where a checklist item is not applicable to the visit, mark it as not applicable and give the reason, rather than leaving it blank. A blank field looks the same as a missed check, and the reader cannot tell which it is.

instructionSections.heading: Asset identifiers and the register
instructionSections.body: Give every asset in the portfolio an identifier, such as a code on a label, and record that identifier in the asset register. An air conditioning unit, a hot water system, a gate operator and a pool pump are all assets. Use the identifier on every service entry, so the history of one item can be pulled from its own file. Where two items of the same type sit in one property, the identifiers keep them apart. If an asset is replaced, record the date, the old identifier and the new one, and keep the history of the old asset on file. Do not merge the history of a replaced asset into the new one.

instructionSections.heading: Store, retrieve and correct the record
instructionSections.body: File each service record against the property and against each asset, so that both views work. Keep the original record. When an error is found, record the correction as a dated addition that states what was wrong and what the correct entry is. Do not overwrite or delete the original. Set a retention period for records in line with the owner's requirements and the applicable rules. Keep records secure, and limit access to people who need them for the job.

instructionSections.heading: Readable summaries for the owner
instructionSections.body: The owner reads a summary, and the detail stays on file. A useful summary states the property, the asset, the service, the date, what was found, what was done, and what is due next. Use plain words, and avoid technical shorthand that the owner has to decode. Where a photograph supports the summary, include it only with the owner's permission and only if it shows the asset or the finding and nothing personal. Send the summary within an agreed time after the visit. A summary that cannot be checked against the detail on file should not be sent.

instructionSections.heading: A service record is not a regulated certificate
instructionSections.body: A service record shows what a worker checked and did. It does not replace a certificate, report or compliance record that a regulator or a licensed trade issues. Where a regulated service needs a certificate, the licensed trade or authorised person issues it, and the service record refers to that certificate by its number and date. This lesson does not give the worker authority to issue, sign or certify any regulated service, and the worker must not describe a service record as a certificate.

lessons.title: Agent handover
learningOutcomes: Write a factual completion note that states what was done, what was not, and what needs action.
Prepare a rework plan with owners and dates.
Avoid blame language and unverified claims in a handover.

instructionSections.heading: Factual completion notes
instructionSections.body: A handover note records what was done, what was not done, and what is still open. Write it as a list of facts that the next person can check against the file. For each completed item, state the work, the location, the date and the evidence held. For each excluded item, state the work that was left out and the reason. For each open item, state what has been observed, what evidence supports it, and what is not yet known. Keep the note short, factual and dated, and avoid conclusions that the evidence does not support.

instructionSections.heading: Wording: facts, not blame or certainty
instructionSections.body: If an item is not known, write that it is unknown, and do not replace it with a likely cause.

instructionSections.heading: Rework plan and approval
instructionSections.body: Any open item goes into a rework plan with the action, the owner of the action, the due date and the approval status. The owner of the action is a named person, not a team. The approval status states whether the owner or the property owner has approved the action and the spend. Where an open item involves electrical, gas, plumbing or structural work, the plan refers it to the licensed trade or competent person who must assess it. The note does not state that the item is safe or compliant. Send the handover note and the rework plan to the next person and to the owner, and ask for written acknowledgement. Keep the signed copy with the property file. A handover without acknowledgement is an assumption that the next person knows what is open.

lessons.title: Owner reporting and monthly statements (boundaries)
learningOutcomes: Build a monthly owner report from the asset register, service records and approved work.
Separate reported facts from estimates, opinions and unresolved items.
State the boundaries of the report, including any financial handling that is not covered by this course.

instructionSections.heading: A report is built from records
instructionSections.body: A monthly owner report is built from the records already kept: the asset register, the service records, the approved work and the open items. Each figure or statement in the report should trace back to a dated record that the owner can ask to see. Do not write a report from memory, because memory can drop a visit, mix two properties or repeat an old finding as if it were new. Start by pulling the records for the period, then write each line from its record and note the record reference. A report that a reader can trace is worth more than a longer one that cannot be checked. Keep a fixed layout, with the same sections in the same order every month, so that owners can compare one month with the next.

instructionSections.heading: Separating what is known from what is proposed
instructionSections.body: Separate what is known from what is estimated, recommended or still open. A completed item is one that a dated record shows as done. A proposed repair is a recommendation, not a completed item, and it goes in its own section with the quote or estimate that supports it. An unresolved defect is an open item, not a closed one. Where the report includes an opinion, such as a view that a fixture will need replacing soon, label it as an opinion, say who gave it and on what evidence. Show a repair as in progress only if a record shows that work has started. Each section should make clear whether the reader is reading a record, an estimate or a view.

instructionSections.heading: Money in the report and its boundaries
instructionSections.body: Where the report includes money, state the source of each amount and whether it is an invoice, an estimate or a payment. An invoice is a request for payment, an estimate is a projection that may change, and a payment is money received or made. Do not mix them in one line. Handling of rent, deposits, bonds or trust money is not covered in this course. In New South Wales, a licensee keeps client money in a trust account, and that money may be used only for the client it belongs to. The licensee's trust records also go to an audit each year. The NSW licensing page lists collecting bonds and rents tied to a lease among the licensed functions for certain licence classes, and the NSW bond page caps a bond at four weeks' rent. In Queensland, a resident letting agent licence allows the holder to collect rents in the complex and to operate a trust account. Do not carry out or report financial handling until the rules for the state are confirmed, the licence position is confirmed, and the owner has agreed the process in writing.

instructionSections.heading: What the report is not
instructionSections.body: The report is a record of the property and the work, prepared for the owner. It is not an audit of the accounts, not a financial statement, and not a certificate of safety or compliance. A report that says a system is compliant must show the certificate or record that supports it, issued by the person or body authorised to issue it. A report that says nothing about an item should not be read as a statement that the item is fine. State each boundary in the report, so that the owner knows what the report can and cannot support.

lessons.title: Contractor selection, quotes and approvals
learningOutcomes: Select contractors by licence position, scope fit and evidence of competence, without assuming a licence.
Obtain comparable written quotes against the same scope.
Route quotes through the owner's approval before any work is booked.

instructionSections.heading: Check the licence position before selection
instructionSections.body: A contractor is selected for the work, not for their name. For each trade, check the licence position for the state, and ask the contractor to show their licence or registration number and the class it covers. Do not record a licence as held because the contractor says so. In New South Wales, a contractor licence is needed for residential building or trade work, fencing included, where the value of the work exceeds $5,000 with GST included (page last updated 23 June 2026). Record what was checked, when, and by whom.

instructionSections.heading: Compare quotes on the same scope
instructionSections.body: Give each contractor the same written scope, the same access details and the same exclusions, and ask for a written quote against it. Quotes that cover different scopes cannot be compared, and a low quote that leaves out a task is not a saving. Compare the exclusions as carefully as the price. Route each quote to the owner for approval, and book work only after written approval is received. Variations are approved in writing before they are performed.

lessons.title: Compliance calendar: safety certificates (refer to licensed trades)
learningOutcomes: Build a calendar of safety certificate and inspection due dates for each property.
Refer each certificate or inspection to the licensed or authorised person who issues it.
Identify the certificate requirements that are confirmed for the state, and set the rest aside.

instructionSections.heading: A calendar records dates and owners, not compliance
instructionSections.body: A compliance calendar records when each certificate or inspection falls due, who issues it, and who arranges it. It does not show that the property is compliant. The calendar is a tool for making sure a licensed or authorised person does the work at the right time. Build it from the asset register and the owner's documents, and set a reminder period before each due date so that there is time to refer the work.

instructionSections.heading: Requirements and their sources
instructionSections.body: Record each requirement with its source, and do not invent a due date for a requirement you have not sourced.

lessons.title: Leasing and tenancy boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify the leasing and tenancy tasks that are outside the scope of this course.
Describe why the licence position for leasing must be confirmed before any leasing task is accepted.
Refer leasing and tenancy questions and record the referral.

instructionSections.heading: Leasing is not a maintenance task
instructionSections.body: Leasing covers finding and screening tenants, negotiating and signing tenancy agreements, collecting rent and managing bonds and notices. These tasks are not part of property maintenance. In many places they are regulated, and the regulated status differs by state and territory. Official pages checked in this pass confirm the position in New South Wales and set a narrower scope in Queensland. Until the position is confirmed for the property's state, a property manager partner must not accept leasing work, and must not represent that they are licensed to do it.

instructionSections.heading: Refer and record
instructionSections.body: When an owner or a tenant asks for a leasing or tenancy task, record the request, state that the position is being confirmed, and refer it to the owner and to the relevant state authority or licensed agent. Do not give tenancy advice. Keep the maintenance and condition work separate, because it can continue under the owner's instructions while the leasing question is resolved. NSW's guidance separates administrative and receipting tasks from agent functions: a worker who only issues keys to existing tenants and collects rent from them under the manager's direction does not need the licence for those tasks, provided they do not carry out agent functions (page last modified 22 September 2025).

lessons.title: Customer scope and access
learningOutcomes: Confirm the scope, the excluded rooms and the access arrangements before arriving.
Record the agreed access, the occupants and any alarms or pets.
Stop and confirm with the client before entering any room that is not in scope.

instructionSections.heading: Agreeing scope in writing
instructionSections.body: Confirm the agreed scope before the first visit, room by room and task by task. Note which tasks are included, which are excluded, and any tasks that need the client's approval. A scope agreed verbally and not written down is the most common cause of a dispute.

instructionSections.heading: Access, occupants and security
instructionSections.body: Confirm how you will get in, who will be home, and whether an alarm, a key safe, a gate code or a pet needs special handling. Record the access instructions, and do not share codes outside the approved channel. If the client is working from home, agree the working hours and the quiet times.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping at the boundary
instructionSections.body: Do not enter a room that is excluded or unclear. Stop and confirm with the client before you go in. If the client asks for something outside the agreed scope, note the request, explain that it needs approval and pricing, and do not start it.

lessons.title: Occupied-home protection
learningOutcomes: Protect the household's belongings, pets and privacy while cleaning in an occupied home.
Control slip, trip and product hazards around people, especially children and pets.
Leave work areas and documents undisturbed, and stop when the household's needs change the plan.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting belongings and privacy
instructionSections.body: An occupied home has belongings that are personal and important: papers, devices, medicines and keepsakes. Clean around them rather than moving them, unless the client has agreed. Do not read documents, open drawers or look at personal items beyond what the task requires. Keep any photographs to the authorised areas and leave out people and personal papers.

instructionSections.heading: Pets, children and products
instructionSections.body: Keep products away from pets and children, and keep pets and children out of the work area as agreed. Store chemicals out of reach while you are working, and do not leave a wet floor unmarked. Where a household member is working from home, plan quiet times and keep the work out of their workspace unless they agree.

instructionSections.heading: When the plan changes
instructionSections.body: If a household member arrives, a pet escapes or a child enters the work area, pause the affected task, make the area safe, and agree the next step with the client. Do not continue with the original plan when the people or animals in the home have changed.

lessons.title: Handover and rebooking
learningOutcomes: Walk the client through the completed work and the exclusions.
Record the handover, including any issues found and not fixed.
Offer rebooking on the agreed terms, without promising work that is not scoped.

instructionSections.heading: Walking the client through
instructionSections.body: At handover, walk the client through the completed rooms and the exclusions. Say what was done and what was not, and point out any issue that you found and could not fix, such as a damaged fitting or a stain that did not respond to the approved method. Let the client see the areas that you are reporting.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the handover
instructionSections.body: Record the handover with the time, the rooms covered, the exclusions, the issues found and the client's acknowledgement. Keep the record factual. Do not describe the home as sterile or as free of pests, and do not guarantee a result beyond the scope.

instructionSections.heading: Rebooking
instructionSections.body: Offer a rebooking on the agreed terms, and confirm the scope for the next visit against the current record. Do not promise extra tasks that have not been scoped and priced. If the client wants a different scope, note the change for approval.

lessons.title: Mattress cleaning and drying (residential only)
learningOutcomes: Assess a mattress for stains, odour and moisture before offering a treatment.
Choose a method and product that suit the mattress fabric and the soil, and test first.
Refer mould, heavy contamination or moisture damage rather than treating it as routine.

instructionSections.heading: Assess before offering
instructionSections.body: Inspect the mattress before any treatment. Check the fabric and the label, the stains, the odour and whether the mattress is damp. A damp mattress that smells musty may have a moisture or mould problem, which is outside routine mattress cleaning. Record the condition with the client before work starts, and set the expectation that some stains may not come out.

instructionSections.heading: Method, product and drying
instructionSections.body: Use a method and product suited to the fabric, and test on an inconspicuous area first. Do not over-wet the mattress, because excess moisture can soak into the core and be slow to dry. Allow the mattress to dry fully before it is used, and use air movement where the setting allows. Keep the product out of the eyes and off the skin.

instructionSections.heading: Referral
instructionSections.body: Refer visible mould, heavy contamination, bodily fluid stains of unknown origin, and any mattress that will not dry within a reasonable time. These are specialist or out-of-scope tasks. Do not treat them as routine mattress cleaning, and do not promise removal. Conditions vary by state, territory and country, and the local rules and the manufacturer's instructions govern. This lesson does not substitute for them.

lessons.title: Job scope, ownership and safe authorisation
learningOutcomes: Identify who owns and controls the roof, any solar equipment and any shared or strata property affected by the job.
Separate the decisions a worker may observe and record from those reserved to qualified roof, electrical, chemical or environmental specialists.
Apply a hold, restricted-scope or stop-work decision to a paper-based job pack in which authority or evidence is missing.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: SafeWork NSW, Work safely at heights in construction (page date: No date shown); Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: Managing the risk of falls at workplaces (page date: No date shown; partly checked); SafeWork NSW, Work on roofs: commercial and industrial buildings (code of practice) (page date: Cover dated May 2026; commencement 22 May 2026; partly checked); SafeWork SA, High-risk construction work changes for PCBUs and principal contractors (page date: March 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Why ownership and authority come first
instructionSections.body: A roof soft washing job starts with the question of who may let the work happen. The owner of the building, the body corporate or strata manager for common property, the owner of any solar array, and the occupant may each hold a different part of the decision. A request from one occupant does not establish authority over the whole roof, the skylights, the gutters or the equipment mounted on it. Record the name, role and approval date of each person whose consent is needed, and do not schedule roof access until those approvals exist.

instructionSections.heading: Scope the job in writing
instructionSections.body: Write down what is included: which roof planes, gutters, roof edges and related surfaces, the method and the products, and the times. Write down what is excluded: roof repairs, re-sheeting, roof integrity assessment, solar panel cleaning under a separate scope, and high-pressure roof jetting. A soft washing job scope that does not state its exclusions invites a dispute about what was promised. Mark every part of the roof that cannot be seen from the ground as an unknown.

instructionSections.heading: Ground-based alternatives and the height hierarchy
instructionSections.body: Apply the height hierarchy before any roof access is considered. SafeWork NSW's construction guidance (no date shown) puts the options in order: first, ground-level or existing solid-structure working where that is possible; second, fall-prevention devices such as work platforms, roof-edge barriers or scaffolding; third, work-positioning systems; and fall-arrest systems last. For fragile surfaces, the same guidance points to covers over skylights, crawl boards and exclusion zones marked out in the work area. Ask whether any part of the job can be done from the ground with a method that does not need roof access, and record the answer.

instructionSections.heading: Recognise what the worker may and may not decide
instructionSections.body: A worker may observe the roof from a safe position, record visible conditions, photograph them, and report them. A worker may not decide that a roof is structurally sound, that a material is not fragile, that a chemical is compliant, or that a runoff rule is met. Those decisions belong to a competent person, the relevant specialist or the site controller. Keep the observed facts separate from the unverified statements in every record.

instructionSections.heading: Regulatory context for roof cleaning
instructionSections.body: Safe Work Australia's model code on managing the risk of falls (no date shown) says to check with the regulator whether it has legal effect in the jurisdiction; that it has legal effect only where a jurisdiction adopts it is not confirmed by an official source. The NSW code for work on roofs of commercial and industrial buildings took effect on 22 May 2026 (cover dated May 2026) and excludes residential roofs. It lists roof-material cleaning among the work it covers, but its text does not mention gutter cleaning or soft washing, so the NSW position for soft washing is only partly confirmed. Work over 2 metres needs fall-prevention controls; whether the high-risk work rules apply at 2 metres is not confirmed by an official source. SafeWork NSW's construction guidance requires a safe work method statement (SWMS) for work where a person could fall more than 2 metres. In South Australia, from 1 July 2026, construction work that involves a risk of falling more than two metres is high-risk construction work, and SafeWork SA's March 2026 guidance (no day shown) says a SWMS must be prepared before the work starts. Check the rule for the state where the job sits.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work and hold decisions
instructionSections.body: Issue a hold notice when authority, a roof assessment, access planning or a competent person's confirmation is missing. Stop work when the roof is fragile or unknown, the weather changes, a skylight or opening is unprotected, a person or animal enters the exclusion zone, or a solar array or electrical service is found where the scope did not say it would be. A customer's wish to finish the job is not a reason to continue past any of these conditions.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, roof-work authority or height authority. No licence for roof soft washing as such is confirmed. Obtain the employer's written authorisation, and check the state rule, before any roof access.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): SafeWork NSW, Work safely at heights in construction (page date: No date shown); Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: Managing the risk of falls at workplaces (page date: No date shown; partly checked); SafeWork NSW, Work on roofs: commercial and industrial buildings (code of practice) (page date: Cover dated May 2026; commencement 22 May 2026; partly checked); SafeWork SA, High-risk construction work changes for PCBUs and principal contractors (page date: March 2026).

lessons.title: Roof condition, skylights and fragile surfaces
learningOutcomes: Identify conditions, authorisation limits and evidence requirements relevant to roof condition, skylights and fragile surfaces.
Differentiate worker-observable conditions from determinations reserved to qualified roof, electrical, chemical or environmental specialists.
Demonstrate a proportionate stop-work, referral and documented client communication using a paper-based scenario.

instructionSections.heading: Why roof condition decides the job
instructionSections.body: Before anyone thinks about cleaning a roof, the roof itself has to be understood. Its condition decides whether a person can stand on it, where water and chemicals will travel, and which parts of the job must be left alone. Falls through roofs are a serious and well-known cause of injury in construction and trades work. WorkSafe Victoria's 2024 safety alert about a worker who fell from a roof describes a guardrail that came loose from a parapet wall and was found on the ground; the alert does not state the cause, and it says a guardrail may fail where the supporting structure has not been verified. The lesson for a soft-washing worker is that a surface that looks finished can still give way under a person's weight, and that a barrier is only as reliable as the structure behind it. This lesson teaches you to observe the roof, record what you see, separate what you know from what you assume, and stop when the answer is not clear. It does not teach you to walk a roof, judge its structure or sign it off.

instructionSections.heading: Reading a roof from the ground
instructionSections.body: Most of the useful information about a roof can be gathered without setting foot on it. Walk the full perimeter of the property where it is safe and lawful to do so, and photograph each roof plane from more than one angle. Look for sheeting that bends between fixings, cracks or chalky patches in tiles or fibre-cement, rust that has perforated metal, lifted or slipped tiles, displaced ridge capping, cracked mortar, and sealant applied in heavy patches as if to stop leaks. On polycarbonate and acrylic rooflights, look for yellowing, crazing, scratches and any sign that the sheet has been walked on. Note roof-mounted equipment, solar arrays, cables, vents, box gutters and penetrations. Write each observation as you saw it, for example 'ridge capping displaced at the north-east end', and keep a separate column for anything you have only inferred, such as 'the sheeting may be thin'. Zoomed photographs help, but a photograph does not show the strength of a material, so any decision on strength stays with a competent person.

instructionSections.heading: Skylights, rooflights and other openings
instructionSections.body: A skylight is both an opening and a surface that may not carry a person's weight, and it is one of the most common causes of serious falls through roofs. Treat every skylight, rooflight, penetration and other opening as an exclusion zone until a competent person has confirmed how it is protected. The NSW code of practice for work on roofs, which took effect on 22 May 2026, asks that the risk assessment identify brittle or fragile surfaces, skylights, penetrations and other openings before work begins. Where an opening is found, the code expects steps to stop people walking into it, such as barricades or a restraint system. Any cover should be securely fixed, look distinct from the roof sheeting so that it is not lifted off by mistake, and withstand the concentrated load the code sets, which is at least 2 kN. Those checks belong to the competent person and the duty holder. A worker does not decide that a cover is adequate. Mark each opening on the job plan, and confirm that no cleaning path crosses it.

instructionSections.heading: Treating unknown surfaces as fragile
instructionSections.body: The working rule in this course is that every roof material is treated as potentially fragile until a competent person establishes otherwise. That rule is a training position rather than a quoted regulation, and it exists because appearance is a poor guide to strength. Weathered sheeting can look solid and still give way. Older fibre-cement sheets can resemble modern ones and may contain asbestos. Whether the asbestos rules cover roof sheeting is not confirmed by an official source, so the state summary in the asbestos lesson of this course applies. As a working rule in this course, a worker does not disturb suspected fibre-cement and refers it for assessment. A statement that the roof was walked last year, or that the owner has never had a problem, is information to record. It is not an assessment. The question is not whether the roof looks safe. The question is who has assessed it, when, and what they found.

instructionSections.heading: Height and the control hierarchy
instructionSections.body: Work at height is the central issue in roof cleaning. Safe Work Australia's guidance on working at heights lists the control options in order: first, eliminate the risk or minimise it, for example by doing the work on the ground or from a solid structure; second, a fall prevention device such as a barrier, scaffold or elevating work platform; third, a work positioning system; and last, a fall arrest system. WorkSafe Victoria's alert sets out a similar sequence in a slightly different order, with passive devices and work positioning ahead of fall arrest, and ladders or administrative controls at the end. The difference matters because the sequence that applies is the one used by the regulator in the state where the job sits, so this lesson does not choose between them. On the threshold, use the official wording for the state where the job sits. SafeWork NSW requires a safe work method statement (SWMS) for work where a person could fall more than 2 metres, and work over 2 metres needs fall-prevention controls; whether the high-risk work rules apply at 2 metres is not confirmed by an official source. In South Australia, from 1 July 2026, construction work that involves a risk of falling more than two metres is high-risk construction work. Ask first whether any part of the job can be done from the ground, and record the answer.

instructionSections.heading: Overhead lines, solar arrays and other electrical hazards
instructionSections.body: Roofs often carry hazards that are not part of the roof itself. The SafeWork NSW code on work near overhead and underground electric lines (May 2026) says a worker should assume an overhead line is live unless there is an access authority or written documentation from the supply authority. Workers must not measure a line's height directly, and must not use metal tapes to estimate it. For ordinary persons, the code sets a distance of 3.0 metres from lines up to 132,000 V. For conductive materials near low-voltage overhead service lines, it sets 4.0 metres. Queensland's WorkSafe page also sets a 3-metre exclusion zone for powerlines up to 132 kV, and Energy Safe Victoria sets 3.0 metres as the distance within which work near an overhead distribution line needs permission from the network operator; it does not describe a 3 metre no-go zone. Where a line is closer than these distances, or its position cannot be confirmed, stop and refer the work to the supply authority. Solar arrays are a separate hazard. Energy Safe Victoria's guidance (reviewed 15 April 2025) says that PV DC supply cables may still be live when the power is off, and the Western Australian guide (last updated 26 November 2024) says panels keep generating while the mains is disconnected. Electrical testing, isolation and repair of PV systems need a licensed electrician, and plain panel washing is not stated by the official page to need a licence. The working rule is simple. Treat every panel and cable as live, do not touch or isolate them, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instructionSections.heading: Recording what you saw and what you did not
instructionSections.body: A record is useful only if a reader can tell what was seen, when, where, and how much weight to give it. Each entry should carry a date, a location label that matches the job plan, and a photograph reference. Keep three categories apart. Observed means you saw it and can describe it. Inferred means you believe it from indirect evidence, and you say so. Unknown means you cannot see it, or no one has assessed it. A fourth category, determinations, belongs to specialists: whether the roof is structurally sound, whether a sheet is fragile, whether a chemical is compliant, and whether asbestos is present. A worker records these questions and names who must answer them. A line such as 'the roof is in good condition' is a determination presented as an observation. A line such as 'ridge capping lifted at two points, photographs 4 and 5' is an observation that a reader can check.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work and hold decisions
instructionSections.body: A hold means the job does not proceed until a named condition is met, such as written authority from the owner, a competent roof assessment, or confirmation by a licensed person that electrical supply is isolated. A stop-work decision applies when a hazard appears during the job. Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if a surface, access point or platform is unstable or uncertain, if weather or light changes conditions, if a skylight or opening is found unprotected, if a person or animal enters an exclusion zone, if live or damaged wiring is seen or suspected, or if the task falls outside your authorisation. A waiting customer, or a belief that the roof was fine last time, is not a reason to continue past any of these points.

instructionSections.heading: Open points in this draft
instructionSections.body: Check your state or territory regulator before any work above ground level.

lessons.title: Electrical, solar and overhead services
learningOutcomes: Identify overhead services, roof-mounted solar arrays and electrical equipment that change a roof job's risk.
Explain why a solar array's DC cables can remain live when the mains power is switched off.
Apply stop-work and referral rules when a roof has live, damaged or unidentified electrical equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: WorkSafe Queensland, Exclusion zones (powerlines and electrical cables) (page date: No date shown); SafeWork NSW, Work near overhead and underground electric lines code of practice (page date: cover dated May 2026; in force from 22 May 2026); Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); Government of Western Australia (wa.gov.au), Electrical safety at home: solar PV systems (page date: Last updated 26 November 2024); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Building and trades licences and credentials: electrical (page date: Last updated 23 June 2026); Standards Australia, AS/NZS 4836: Safe working on or near low-voltage electrical installations and equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Overhead services near the roof
instructionSections.body: Overhead power lines, service drops and communications cables may run close to a roof, its edges and its gutters. A ladder, a pole, a hose or a tool can reach a line by accident, and contact can be fatal. Before work starts, survey the roof perimeter and the path of any equipment for overhead services. Queensland's WorkSafe page sets a 3-metre exclusion zone for overhead powerlines up to 132 kV, including low-voltage lines usually carried on poles (no date shown). The NSW code of practice on work near overhead and underground electric lines (cover dated May 2026, in force from 22 May 2026) sets 3.0 metres for ordinary persons from lines up to 132,000 V. For conductive materials such as roofing and guttering near low-voltage overhead service lines, it sets 4.0 metres. For non-conductive materials it sets 1.5 metres, for hand-held tools 0.5 metres, and for driving or traversing mobile plant 0.6 metres. Where a line is within reach, or its distance cannot be confirmed against these figures, stop and refer the job to the network operator or a qualified person before the equipment is moved.

instructionSections.heading: Solar arrays on the roof
instructionSections.body: Many roofs carry photovoltaic arrays. Energy Safe Victoria guidance (reviewed 15 April 2025) says that DC supply cables can remain live after the supply is switched off, and that contact with them should be prevented. The WA government guide adds that the panels keep generating during the day even when the main power has been disconnected (page last updated 26 November 2024). A solar array can also generate electricity while light falls on it, so switching off the mains does not make the array safe. Treat every panel, cable and connector as live, and do not touch them.

instructionSections.heading: Isolation and who may do it
instructionSections.body: Energy Safe Victoria's guidance (page reviewed 15 April 2025) says that installing and maintaining PV systems is licensed electrical installation work, and that damaged cables or equipment must be repaired by a licensed electrical installation worker. As a rule for this course, a roof soft washing worker does not test, isolate or repair any solar or electrical system, and refers these to a licensed electrician. The Western Australian guide (last updated 26 November 2024) says DC isolators need to be verified by a licensed electrician. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work, including repairing, needs an electrical licence or certificate (page last updated 23 June 2026). Plain panel washing is not stated by the official pages to need a licence.

instructionSections.heading: Water and electrical components
instructionSections.body: Water on connectors, inverters, junction boxes and wiring can cause a fault or a shock. Soft washing involves water and products, so keep the spray away from electrical components, inverters and any junction box, and keep the spray from the electrical side of any equipment. This is a safe-work rule for this course; no official source reviewed in this draft states it as a legal requirement. Where water reaches electrical equipment, stop, and refer the equipment to a licensed electrician before the job continues.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising a fault and stopping
instructionSections.body: Stop work and refer when you see or suspect exposed wiring, a damaged cable, a burnt or discoloured connector, a panel that is cracked or hot, a smell of burning, a buzzing or spitting sound, or water near an inverter or junction box. Do not touch the fault. Keep people and animals clear of the area. Record what was seen, where, and when, and tell the site controller and the owner in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems, electrical installations, inverters or wiring. Victorian guidance treats PV installation and maintenance as licensed electrical installation work, and says damaged cables or equipment must be repaired by a licensed electrical installation worker. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work, including repairing, needs an electrical licence or certificate. Plain panel washing is not stated by the official pages to need a licence. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): WorkSafe Queensland, Exclusion zones (powerlines and electrical cables) (page date: No date shown); SafeWork NSW, Work near overhead and underground electric lines code of practice (page date: cover dated May 2026; in force from 22 May 2026); Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); Government of Western Australia (wa.gov.au), Electrical safety at home: solar PV systems (page date: Last updated 26 November 2024); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Building and trades licences and credentials: electrical (page date: Last updated 23 June 2026); Standards Australia, AS/NZS 4836: Safe working on or near low-voltage electrical installations and equipment.

lessons.title: Water pressure, roof materials and damage prevention
learningOutcomes: Identify conditions, authorisation limits and evidence requirements relevant to water pressure, roof materials and damage prevention.
Differentiate worker-observable conditions from determinations reserved to qualified roof, electrical, chemical or environmental specialists.
Demonstrate a proportionate stop-work, referral and documented client communication using a paper-based scenario.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure is a damage question as well as a cleaning question
instructionSections.body: Water pressure can do more harm than it removes. The same jet that lifts growth from a roof can crack a tile, strip a coating from metal, drive water under the overlap of a sheet, tear a sealant bead, or erode the mortar that holds a ridge in place. Once the damage is done, water can reach the roof space and the rooms below, often out of sight. Pressure equipment also carries its own hazards. WorkSafe Victoria's safety alert on high-pressure water jetting describes injuries from a jet piercing the skin, from flying debris, from a hose whipping or a coupling separating, and from falls. For a soft-washing worker the first lesson is that the method is chosen to protect the roof and the people around it. A higher pressure is never a shortcut to a better result.

instructionSections.heading: Roof materials and what each one tolerates
instructionSections.body: Each material has its own weak points. Concrete and clay tiles depend on their bedding, their mortar and their interlock, and a jet directed under the lap of a tile can lift it. Metal sheeting depends on its coating, its fixings and its overlaps. A high-pressure stream can remove the coating and expose bare metal, and water forced under sheets can reach the framing and the ceiling below. Fibre-cement sheeting can be brittle, and an older product may contain asbestos, so it must not be abraded or blasted. Refer a suspected sheet for assessment as described in the earlier lessons. Slate and some natural stones are prone to cracking under impact. Polycarbonate and acrylic rooflights can scratch, craze or yellow, and they count as openings under the rules in the previous lesson. Membranes and bituminous surfaces are sensitive to abrasion, and the loss of surface granules or the peeling of sealant are signs of damage. Where the material has not been identified, the method cannot be chosen, and the work is held.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a limit and a method
instructionSections.body: No pressure setting appears in this lesson, and none should be chosen from the worker's own judgement. The limit comes from three places: the roof material manufacturer's guidance, the rating of the equipment and its fittings, and the authorised method for the job. Where any of those is missing, the answer is not to test a higher setting until something works. The answer is to hold the work and find the limit. Low-pressure soft washing works mainly through contact time and gentle application, not through force. A worker who feels the need for more force should stop and ask whether the product, the method or the surface is the real problem. A method that cannot be explained in terms of the material and its limit is not an authorised method.

instructionSections.heading: Damage prevention in practice
instructionSections.body: Damage prevention is mostly about direction and the path of the water. Keep the spray at a low angle so the stream does not run under laps, seams or the edge of a flashing. Do not aim the jet at sealant, at the edges of tiles, or at gaps where water could enter a cavity. Move steadily and do not dwell on one spot. Keep debris moving away from gutters, downpipes and vents, rather than pushing it into a blocked outlet that will overflow onto the wall or the ground. Stop water entering a roof cavity, a vent or a meter box, and check the area below the work for any sign of water. Before the job starts, photograph the roof and record existing damage, such as loose tiles, cracked sheets and failed sealant. A record made before work is what allows a later question about damage to be answered from evidence rather than memory.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment checks and pressure safety
instructionSections.body: Equipment must be checked before each use. Inspect hoses for cuts, bulges and worn covers. Check couplings, fittings and the nozzle. Confirm that every component is rated at or above the equipment's maximum pressure and is compatible with the rest of the set, and record the check. WorkSafe Victoria's alert says operators should wear at least safety glasses and a face shield, that people nearby need eye protection, and that the operator needs body armour where injury is possible. It also says that equipment and its attachments must not be modified without written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person, and that repairs are for the manufacturer, its agent or a competent person. The alert sets training and refresher expectations and names the standard AS/NZS 4233.1 for systems. This lesson does not authorise anyone to operate pressure equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Signs to stop and what to record
instructionSections.body: Stop work in the affected area, and record it, when you see a tile lifting or cracking, a coating coming away from a sheet, sealant peeling or pulling, water being driven under laps or into a joint, mortar crumbling, granules lost from a bituminous surface, a rooflight crazing or cracking, or water appearing inside the building. Do not keep working to see whether the damage gets worse. Mark the area, tell the supervisor, and let the decision owner set the next step. The record should show the photograph, the location, the time, and whether the damage was there before work began or appeared during it. A worker records what is visible. The cause and the repair are for the people competent to decide them.

instructionSections.heading: Run-off and where the water goes
instructionSections.body: Pressure and chemical washing both send water somewhere. Before work starts, identify where the run-off will go: gardens, lawns, stormwater pits, pools, water tanks, neighbouring properties and footpaths. Water that carries product or fine debris is an environmental concern as well as a damage concern. The operational rule for now is to hold the work wherever run-off cannot be controlled, and to record the path on the job plan.

lessons.title: Soft-wash chemicals, SDS and exposure boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify conditions, authorisation limits and evidence requirements relevant to soft-wash chemicals, sds and exposure boundaries.
Differentiate worker-observable conditions from determinations reserved to qualified roof, electrical, chemical or environmental specialists.
Demonstrate a proportionate stop-work, referral and documented client communication using a paper-based scenario.

instructionSections.heading: Why the chemical question is an authority question
instructionSections.body: Chemicals are the reason soft washing is different from a simple rinse. Each product carries its own hazards to the operator, to people nearby, to plants and water features, and to the environment. A product that is approved for one method may be wrong for another, and a mixture that has never been tested may react in a way nobody planned for. The question of which product may be used, in what concentration, by whom and where, is therefore an authority question as well as a technical one. A worker does not settle it by reading a label on the truck or by accepting a supplier's description. This lesson shows how to check the paperwork, set the boundary around the work, and stop when the evidence is missing.

instructionSections.heading: Reading a safety data sheet
instructionSections.body: A safety data sheet, or SDS, is the document that describes a chemical's hazards and how to handle it safely. Manufacturers and importers are responsible for preparing it, and it must describe the hazards, safe handling, storage and disposal, physical and chemical properties, health effects, emergency response and environmental effects. It follows a standard set of headings. When you use an SDS, start with the product identification, the hazard identification and the first-aid measures. Then read the handling and storage sections, the exposure controls and personal protection, the stability and reactivity information, which names the materials to keep apart, and the spill, disposal and environmental sections. Check that the product name and concentration on the SDS match the container label. Check the review date shown on the SDS, because the Safe Work Australia guidance says that SDSs must be reviewed and updated at least every five years. An SDS that is out of date or does not match the product is not an SDS for that product.

instructionSections.heading: The hazardous chemicals register
instructionSections.body: A business or site that uses hazardous chemicals should keep a hazardous chemicals register. Safe Work Australia's guidance says the register lists only hazardous chemicals, includes the current SDS for each listed chemical, is kept up to date, and is kept at the workplace where it can be reached easily. Workers, anyone who could be affected, and emergency services should be able to use it. Non-hazardous chemicals are not listed, and some hazardous consumer products and chemicals in transit are excluded, but the guidance says that chemicals in transit may still need listing if they are present in large amounts or stored often. Safety information for every chemical at the workplace, hazardous or not, must still be available. In practice, the label and the SDS carry that information. The register does not replace the duty to share it.

instructionSections.heading: Products, mixing and incompatibility
instructionSections.body: Use only the products on the authorised product list for the job, and use them only in the way the label and the approved method describe. No dilution rate is given in this lesson. Any dilution comes from the label and the approved method, and the worker does not work it out from memory. Do not mix two products, even two that are sold for cleaning, unless the label, the SDS and the authorised method all allow it. Mixing can produce a reaction that is hazardous in itself, such as a gas release, and the SDS names the materials to keep apart. Keep containers closed when they are not in use, keep them labelled, and never decant one product into an unlabelled bottle. If two products arrive on the same truck and the crew wants to combine them in one tank to save time, the answer is no. Separate them, hold the work, and refer the question to the decision owner.

instructionSections.heading: Setting the exposure boundary
instructionSections.body: An exposure boundary is the area within which people, animals, plants, vehicles, water features and drains could be affected by the product or the run-off. It is set on the plan before any product is handled, not by eye on the day. Mark the wash area, then extend the boundary to cover the places the product or spray could reach, taking account of wind direction, the layout of the building and the paths people use. Check for a swimming pool, a rainwater tank, a garden bed, a pond, parked vehicles, a play area, and any stormwater pit or drain on the property or the footpath. Put up barriers and signs where needed, and keep the public out until the authorised method and the product's label say the area can be reopened. Whether the boundary is set, and whether the work can go ahead, is the decision of the authorised approver. A worker records the boundary and does not decide it alone.

instructionSections.heading: PPE, first aid and spill response
instructionSections.body: Personal protective equipment is chosen from the SDS and the risk assessment, not from habit. Many products call for eye protection and gloves, and some call for protective clothing. Respiratory protection is used only where the SDS and the risk assessment call for it. Keep the first-aid instructions from the SDS on site and make them known to the crew. Keep a spill kit that matches the products on the job, and know how to use it. Other first-aid advice found in older roofing handbooks, such as household neutralising agents, is not adopted in this lesson, because the first-aid measure for each product is the one on its SDS. If someone is exposed, follow the SDS, call emergency services where the SDS or the situation requires it, and report the incident under the business's procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Storage, transport and waste
instructionSections.body: Store chemicals in their original, labelled containers, keep incompatible products apart, and keep them out of reach of the public and away from heat and sunlight. Transport them upright and secured, and check that the vehicle carries the spill kit. Do not pour unused product or rinse water into a drain, a stormwater pit, a garden or a water feature. Dispose of unused product and empty containers as the SDS and the local rules describe. Hold the work and refer any disposal question to the decision owner.

instructionSections.heading: When paperwork is missing
instructionSections.body: A product without a current SDS, without a clear label, or without an approved method is not ready to use, however familiar it looks. A supplier's assurance, a photograph of the front of the container or a verbal description is not an SDS. If the SDS is missing, hold the product, request the current SDS from the supplier or the manufacturer, check the hazardous chemicals register, and tell the decision owner. Record the date of the request and the reply. Do not test the product on a small area to see how it behaves, because that is an application, and it is not authorised by this lesson.

lessons.title: Biological growth, asbestos and unexpected hazards
learningOutcomes: Recognise biological growth on a roof and explain why it can hide the condition of the material beneath.
Identify roof sheeting that may contain asbestos and apply a do-not-disturb and refer decision.
Apply a stop-work and referral decision to an unexpected roof hazard, such as structural damage, nests or a mould-affected roof space.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: WA Department of Health, Guidance note: asbestos cement roofs (page date: Copyright 2016; no publication date shown; partly checked); Queensland Government (asbestos.qld.gov.au), Asbestos guidance (node 79) (page date: No date shown (copyright 2018-2026)); WorkSafe Victoria, Tradies warned to be alert for asbestos (page date: Published 2 February 2018; reviewed 25 March 2022); WorkSafe Victoria, Understand and manage asbestos in workplaces (page date: Reviewed 9 May 2024; no last-updated date shown); SafeWork NSW, Asbestos (page date: No date shown); SafeWork SA, Asbestos removal licence guide for applicants (page date: No date shown); WorkSafe WA, Asbestos licences (page date: Last updated 21 October 2026); WorkSafe Tasmania, Asbestos removal licensing (page date: Last updated 11 November 2025); NT WorkSafe, Asbestos licensing (page date: No date shown); WorkSafe ACT, Asbestos licensing (page date: No date shown); Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: How to manage and control asbestos in the workplace (page date: No date shown; partly checked); NSW Government (environment.nsw.gov.au), Protected species (page date: Updated 7 September 2026; partly checked); SafeWork NSW, Work safely at heights in construction (page date: No date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Biological growth on roofs
instructionSections.body: Moss, lichen, algae and fungal staining are common on roofs in many climates. They can look like ordinary dirt, but they can also hold moisture against the sheeting, hide cracks and loose fixings, and make surfaces slippery. Soft washing is intended for surfaces of this kind, but the growth is also a sign that the roof may have a moisture or ventilation problem. Record the extent of the growth, its position, and any sign of damage beneath it. Do not record that the growth has been removed or that the surface is sound, unless a competent person has confirmed it.

instructionSections.heading: Asbestos in roof sheeting
instructionSections.body: Older roof sheeting, especially fibre cement sheeting, may contain asbestos. A WA Department of Health guidance note dates widespread use of asbestos cement roofing from the 1930s to roughly 1987, and treats 1990 as the boundary for presuming a material may be asbestos. Washing, scraping, cutting or walking on such sheeting can break it and release fibres. Queensland's asbestos guidance says material should be assumed to be asbestos-containing if no sample analysis has been done. Victoria's WorkSafe warns tradies to check pre-1990 buildings for asbestos before starting work, because breaking such materials can free fibres into the air. The Safe Work Australia model code on managing asbestos is listed for its title and model status only, and whether it applies depends on each state. Removal licence rules differ by state. Each state's official source, checked on 3 November 2026, says the following. New South Wales: a friable asbestos removal licence is needed to remove any amount of friable asbestos, and a non-friable licence is needed to remove more than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos. Victoria: removal must be done by a licence holder, and the only unlicensed exception on the page is non-friable asbestos of 10 square metres or less that takes no more than 1 hour in any 7-day period, counted across all employees. Friable asbestos has no such allowance, and work above these limits needs a licence. South Australia: a Class A licence is needed to remove friable asbestos, and a Class A licence also covers removal of non-friable asbestos; a Class B licence is needed for more than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos (source: the SafeWork SA applicant guide, Asbestos removal licence guide for applicants, page date not shown; the main licence page could not be retrieved). Western Australia: a licence is needed to remove asbestos; Class A covers friable asbestos of any amount, and Class B covers more than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos. Tasmania: a licence is needed for any amount of friable asbestos and for more than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos; below that non-friable threshold the code of practice still applies. Northern Territory: a Class A licence covers any amount of friable asbestos, and a Class B licence covers more than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos. Australian Capital Territory: only a Class A licence holder may remove friable asbestos, a Class A licence holder may also remove non-friable asbestos, a Class B licence holder may remove non-friable asbestos, and the page gives no size threshold. Queensland: the page says to assume material is asbestos-containing if no sample analysis has been done, and it does not state a removal licence rule for roof sheeting. None of the removal licence pages checked names roof sheeting as its own category. If the age or material of the roof sheeting is unknown, treat it as possibly containing asbestos, stop, and refer it to a competent person before any washing, scraping or walking on it.

instructionSections.heading: Do not disturb: what to do
instructionSections.body: If suspect sheeting is found, do not pressure wash it, scrape it, drill it, cut it or walk on it. The WA guidance describes high-pressure cleaning of this sheeting as hazardous and unlawful, because it can spread contaminated sludge (guidance note, copyright 2016; no publication date shown). Keep people and animals clear of the area below, and cover or isolate any drainage where it could carry debris. Record the location, the material's appearance, its age if known, and the people told. Tell the owner and the site controller in writing, and do not continue the wash on that section. Removal, encapsulation and clearance of asbestos are specialist tasks that this course does not cover.

instructionSections.heading: Structural damage and unexpected conditions
instructionSections.body: A roof may show rotten timber, loose or lifted sheeting, corroded fixings, sagging, cracked battens or a damaged gutter bracket. These are conditions that change the fall risk and the load on the roof. A worker does not decide whether the structure is safe. Stop, keep the area clear, record the condition, and refer it to a competent person. The worker also does not certify or warrant that the roof is structurally sound after the job.

instructionSections.heading: Nests, animals and biological hazards
instructionSections.body: Birds, bats, wasps and other animals may nest in roof voids, gutters or under sheeting. Some nests carry risks such as stings, droppings and bacteria. Check for nests before access, and do not disturb an active nest. Check the rule for the state before any removal. Keep the work area clear of animals and record the presence of nests so that the owner can decide on removal through the proper channel.

instructionSections.heading: Mould in roof spaces
instructionSections.body: Roof voids can contain mould, particularly where there has been water entry or poor ventilation. Soft washing of a roof surface does not treat mould in the void or the framing, and a surface wash does not provide a clearance. Where mould is visible in a roof void, a loft, a roof space or on framing, stop the work in that area and refer it to a competent person. Mould remediation is covered in the high-risk cleaning module of this curriculum, and that module is not a routine soft washing method.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, asbestos authority, roof-work authority or clearance. State removal licence rules are set out above, but none of the pages checked names roof sheeting as its own category, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point for roof sheeting. The lesson does not describe a removal route and does not authorise any worker to disturb suspect material.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): WA Department of Health, Guidance note: asbestos cement roofs (page date: Copyright 2016; no publication date shown; partly checked); Queensland Government (asbestos.qld.gov.au), Asbestos guidance (node 79) (page date: No date shown (copyright 2018-2026)); WorkSafe Victoria, Tradies warned to be alert for asbestos (page date: Published 2 February 2018; reviewed 25 March 2022); WorkSafe Victoria, Understand and manage asbestos in workplaces (page date: Reviewed 9 May 2024; no last-updated date shown); SafeWork NSW, Asbestos (page date: No date shown); SafeWork SA, Asbestos removal licence guide for applicants (page date: No date shown); WorkSafe WA, Asbestos licences (page date: Last updated 21 October 2026); WorkSafe Tasmania, Asbestos removal licensing (page date: Last updated 11 November 2025); NT WorkSafe, Asbestos licensing (page date: No date shown); WorkSafe ACT, Asbestos licensing (page date: No date shown); Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: How to manage and control asbestos in the workplace (page date: No date shown; partly checked); NSW Government (environment.nsw.gov.au), Protected species (page date: Updated 7 September 2026; partly checked); SafeWork NSW, Work safely at heights in construction (page date: No date shown).

lessons.title: Inspection evidence and restricted client handover
learningOutcomes: Identify conditions, authorisation limits and evidence requirements relevant to inspection evidence and restricted client handover.
Differentiate worker-observable conditions from determinations reserved to qualified roof, electrical, chemical or environmental specialists.
Demonstrate a proportionate stop-work, referral and documented client communication using a paper-based scenario.

instructionSections.heading: What the client is actually receiving
instructionSections.body: At the end of a roof soft-washing job the client receives a document, and that document is often the only thing they keep. It is a record of what was seen, what was done, what was not done, and what remains open. It is not a guarantee that the roof is safe, sound, compliant or clear of asbestos. A restricted handover says so plainly. Commercial roofing businesses tend to rely on a clear inspection report with dated photographs and a short statement of scope, and that practice is a useful model here. The difference is that a soft-washing worker is often not qualified to make the determinations a full roof report would contain, so the handover must stay inside what was observed and authorised, and must name the specialists for everything else.

instructionSections.heading: Evidence that stands up
instructionSections.body: Evidence is useful when a reader can check it. Each photograph needs a date, a location label that matches the plan, and the name of the person who took it. Keep the original file, unedited, in the job folder, and use copies for the handover. Each observation should state where it was made, from what position, and whether it was seen directly or reported by someone else. A note that says 'roof is fine' cannot be checked. A note that says 'ridge capping lifted at the north-east end, photograph 7, observed from the footpath on the stated date' can be. Record the source of every statement that did not come from you, such as the owner's account of earlier repairs, and mark it as reported.

instructionSections.heading: Separating facts, unknowns and determinations
instructionSections.body: Before writing the handover, sort every item into one of three groups. Facts are things you observed and can describe. Unknowns are things you could not see, or things nobody has assessed. Determinations are conclusions that belong to a specialist: whether the roof is structurally sound, whether a material is fragile, whether a chemical is compliant, whether asbestos is present, and whether electrical equipment is safe. A worker does not reach these conclusions in a handover, even when the answer looks obvious. Instead the handover states that the question was not determined, names the person or the type of specialist who must determine it, and records the step required to get the answer. This sorting is the core of the lesson, and a handover that mixes the groups is not acceptable even if every statement in it is accurate.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the restricted handover
instructionSections.body: A restricted handover has a set of plain sections. It states the job, the date, the address and the people involved, and the owner or body corporate that authorised the work. It lists what was done, in the order it was done, and which roof planes, gutters or surfaces were covered. It lists what was not done and why, including any area held for access, asbestos, fragility, electrical hazards or chemical approval. It lists each unresolved item with the person who owns it and the approval still needed. It records what was told to the client and when. It ends with a space for the client's acknowledgement that they received the document and understand the restrictions. Where the business uses an approved sign-off procedure, that procedure governs the form. The handover should be short enough that the client reads all of it, and specific enough that nobody can mistake an open item for a finished one.

instructionSections.heading: Wording that is safe to use and wording that is not
instructionSections.body: Good wording names the observation, the date and the limit. For example: 'Observed from the ground on the stated date. No structural assessment has been carried out, and that is a determination for a competent person.' Or: 'Wash not carried out on the rear plane, pending access approval from the body corporate.' Avoid words that imply a result nobody has verified, such as 'safe', 'compliant', 'certified', 'clear', 'asbestos-free', 'structurally sound' and 'fully decontaminated'. These words can make a client rely on a safety or compliance position that the worker is not able to give. If a client asks for one of these statements, the answer is that the question is outside the job, and the question is referred to the competent person, recorded, and answered in writing.

instructionSections.heading: When evidence is missing
instructionSections.body: A handover does not become complete because the work is finished. If an approval has not been received, a plane is held, an asbestos question is open, or a photograph is missing, the handover must say so. Do not fill a gap with an assumption. If a client asks for a clean certificate while items remain open, decline to issue one, record the request, and state the open items in the handover. If an approval arrives later, issue a dated change note that records the new information and what it changes. Do not re-issue an earlier version of the handover as though it had always said the new thing.

instructionSections.heading: Damage claims, prior damage and what the record can show
instructionSections.body: Clients sometimes report damage after a job and ask whether the job caused it. The record is the first and most useful answer. Before-work photographs that show the same tile or sheet with the same crack are evidence that the damage pre-dated the job. Where the before photographs do not show the area, say so. Do not admit or deny cause in a handover or a message. Record the complaint, the date, the photographs compared, and the person who will answer. Keep the originals, and pass the question to the decision owner. The record should show what was seen, not who was at fault.

instructionSections.heading: Handing over and keeping the record
instructionSections.body: Give the handover to the client, the owner or body corporate that authorised the work, and the decision owner in the business, and record the date, the method of delivery and the acknowledgement received. Keep the signed or acknowledged copy, the photograph index, the observation record, the hold and stop-work logs and any change notes together in the job folder. Customer personal details in the handover are handled under the business's privacy policy, and the policy is not described here.

lessons.title: Short-stay departure-to-arrival turnover planning
learningOutcomes: Confirm the turnover window and permission to enter before going in.
Plan the tasks by their dependencies, including laundry and drying time.
Control the deadline without shortcuts, and escalate where time or access is short.

instructionSections.heading: Confirm the window and the access
instructionSections.body: Before you travel to the property, read the booking handover, the departure confirmation, the next arrival deadline, the property checklist and the access instructions. Compare them. If the departure time, the arrival time or the access code differ between documents, report the conflict to the coordinator before you go in, and do not resolve it by guessing. Never assume that a guest has left because the checkout time has passed. A guest who is still inside is a stop point, not a reason to enter. Confirm in writing, through the channel your business uses, that you have permission to enter, and record the time that permission was confirmed. Permission comes from the booking terms and from the property manager or owner's instructions, so it is the coordinator's job to hold that confirmation and pass it to you.

instructionSections.heading: Plan by dependency
instructionSections.body: Work out which tasks must happen first, because other tasks wait for them. In a typical turnover, access verification and the safety scan come first, then rubbish removal and linen collection. Starting an approved laundry cycle is the task that often sets the finish time, because the cycle, the drying and the return of clean linen all have to happen before the beds are made. Bathroom and kitchen products may need a contact time before they are wiped, and that time must be built in rather than cut short. Keep the clean supplies separate from the used linen so that the two never cross. Allow for the final inspection and any reinspection before you plan the release time. The arithmetic is simple: a laundry cycle that runs for, example, three hours and then needs drying time cannot finish inside a two-hour window, however fast the cleaning is.

instructionSections.heading: The time budget, the buffer and escalation
instructionSections.body: Build a time budget for each zone, with a final inspection buffer. As an example only, a plan might give a two-bedroom unit a set time for each zone and hold back a fixed share of the total as a buffer for the inspection. The figures for your business come from the coordinator's standard, not from this lesson. If the time is not enough, tell the coordinator early, not at the end. Prioritise safety checks and mandatory hygiene tasks, and seek an authorised schedule change rather than cutting steps. Record the start and finish times, the reason for any delay, and the person you told. If a guest is still inside after checkout, contact the coordinator, revise the task order, and record the delay. Do not enter, and do not pressure the guest to leave. Do not omit contact times, do not conceal defects, and do not certify a room you have not inspected.

lessons.title: Linen handling, bed preparation and guest amenities
