learningOutcomes: Separate used and clean linen, and inspect used linen for sharps and contamination before handling.
Sort and launder linen by the care labels and the property policy.
Replenish amenities from the approved inventory, and report shortages and defects.

instructionSections.heading: Used linen: containment before handling
instructionSections.body: Used linen is handled as a containment task first and a laundry task second. Before you touch it, put on the gloves the task requires, and any other PPE the business procedure sets. Stand the bag open next to the bed, not on a clean surface. Inspect the linen before you lift it: look for sharps such as needles or broken glass, and for visible contamination. Do not reach blindly into pockets or folds. If you find a sharp, stop, do not remove it by hand, and tell the coordinator so that the item can be dealt with by the approved route. Gather the linen from the outside inwards, and do not shake it, because shaking spreads particles and any contamination into the air and onto clean surfaces. Place it in a designated bag and close the bag. Heavy contamination, such as bodily fluid in quantity, and any suspected infectious material are not routine linen. Escalate them to the coordinator and follow the business procedure rather than handling them yourself. Wash your hands after the task, and after you remove the gloves.

instructionSections.heading: Sorting, care labels and laundering
instructionSections.body: Sort the linen by the approved fabric and colour groups, and read the care label on each item before you load it. Use the temperature, the cycle and the drying setting the label and the property policy allow. Use only the detergent or product that the approved procedure names, and never improvise an additive such as a bleach or a fabric treatment. Keep chemicals apart, because mixing two products can create a hazard, and follow the label and the SDS for each one. Do not overload the machine beyond its rated load, and report any machine fault, leak, unusual noise or smell to the coordinator instead of working around it. If you cannot read a label, do not guess; set the item aside and ask the coordinator. Record any item that has been damaged or stained during laundering.

instructionSections.heading: Making up beds
instructionSections.body: Clean your hands before you handle fresh linen. Check each mattress and pillow protector for tears, stains and fit, and use the correct size for the bed. Fit the protector flat and smooth, then the sheets, pillowcases and cover in the order the property standard sets. Avoid dragging clean linen across the floor, and keep it off surfaces you have not cleaned. Check the bed from the guest's point of view: the corners are square, the surface is clean, there are no hairs or marks, and the linen is free of creases the standard does not allow. Count the linen for the room against the inventory, and record any shortfall.

instructionSections.heading: Amenities from the approved inventory
instructionSections.body: Replenish towels, toiletries, toilet paper, kitchen consumables and welcome items only from the approved inventory sheet, and use the products and containers the sheet names. Check each item for a sealed pack, an intact label, a readable expiry date where one applies, and cleanliness. Place items as the presentation standard shows. Never refill an unlabelled or unapproved container, and never use personal products from home. Where an item is near its expiry, or its seal is broken, remove it and report it. Count the consumables against the sheet, and report any shortage, damage or missing stock separately from the linen count.

instructionSections.heading: The handover check and reporting
instructionSections.body: Finish with a handover check that covers the beds, the linen count, the amenities and any stain or damage. A stain on a mattress protector or a missing item is not solved by covering it. Isolate the item, mark it so that it cannot be used, and report it with its location, the time and a description. Record the defect and the shortage in the handover, even when the shortage has been made up from another room, so that the coordinator can see the true stock position.

lessons.title: Timed guest-ready turnover and final property release
learningOutcomes: Establish the acceptance criteria and separate what the cleaner approves from what needs coordinator sign-off.
Complete a full timed turnover in a safe order, inspecting from the guest's perspective.
Release the property only after all mandatory checks and approvals are complete.

instructionSections.heading: Acceptance criteria and approvals
instructionSections.body: Before you begin, obtain the property-specific checklist, the presentation standard and any guest safety requirements, such as the position of the smoke alarms or the locking of windows the property uses. Read them through once, and ask the coordinator about anything that is unclear. Then sort the items into two groups. The first group is what you can approve yourself, such as the cleanliness of a surface or the number of towels placed. The second group is what needs the coordinator's sign-off, such as a maintenance fault, a missing safety item, a presentation exception or a guest belonging left in the property. A guest-ready property is one that meets the checklist and has every required approval recorded. It is not simply a property that looks tidy. A tidy room with an open safety item is not ready.

instructionSections.heading: The timed run in a safe order
instructionSections.body: Start with an authorised entry check and a hazard scan before any cleaning. The hazard scan looks for a gas smell, a damaged cord, water on a floor near a power point, a window that will not lock, and any sign that something is wrong with the property. If you find a hazard, stop and report it, as the safety section explains. Then run the turnover in an order that keeps clean work clean: remove rubbish and used linen, dust from high to low so that dust falls onto surfaces you have not yet cleaned, clean the wet areas with their contact times, work through the kitchen, and finish with the floors. Use the correct tools and follow the product directions for each surface. Plan the run against a time budget, with the contact times and the final inspection built in. For example, a two-bedroom turnover might be split into set blocks for each room, with a block held back for the final inspection. Those figures are examples and the coordinator's standard applies. Never operate an unfamiliar electrical or gas appliance just to show that it works.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect from the guest's view
instructionSections.body: Walk in as the guest would. Check the entry, the odour, the lighting, the bedding and its corners, the visible surfaces at eye level and at the edges, the bathroom fixtures, the kitchen, the consumables and the floor edges. Confirm that windows, doors and equipment are in the state the property requires, including any safe state for windows and doors. Record each incomplete or failed item, correct the items that are within your training and scope, and reinspect those items. Report maintenance faults, guest belongings, suspected contamination and stock shortages. Do not hide them to finish early.

instructionSections.heading: Submit the checklist and release
instructionSections.body: When the run is complete and the inspection is done, submit the timestamped completion checklist, the authorised photographs, and the exception records and maintenance tickets. Secure the keys and codes as the procedure directs. Mark the property guest-ready only when every mandatory check and every required approval is complete. If the coordinator has not approved an exception, the property is not released, even if the rest of the work is finished. Record the time of release and the name of the person who approved it.

lessons.title: Damage and lost property
learningOutcomes: Record damage found during a turnover, separating it from cleaning issues.
Handle lost property so that it is recorded, secured and returned through the approved route.
Avoid accusations and avoid repairing damage yourself.

instructionSections.heading: Recording damage as you find it
instructionSections.body: Damage is anything that has been broken, marked, cracked, chipped, torn, burnt, stained into the material or left missing. Record it at the moment you see it, before you clean around it. Write the location in the property, a short factual description, and the time. Take a photograph where the property rules allow it, with the item in view and a reference point so that the place can be found again. Separate damage from cleaning issues in the record. A stain that remains after a proper clean is a cleaning issue if it comes off with the approved method, and a damage issue if it is part of the surface, such as a mark that has soaked into timber or a burn on a benchtop. Do not repair the damage yourself, and do not try to hide it under a mat, a towel or a cushion. A hidden damage item becomes the cleaner's problem later, and it is a false record.

instructionSections.heading: Lost property: recording, securing and returning
instructionSections.body: Lost property is any item that is not rubbish and is not the property's own fixed contents, such as a phone, a bag, keys, clothing or jewellery. When you find it, stop and record it: the item, its description, the exact location where you found it, the time, and your name. Secure the item in the approved place, in a sealed bag or container where the procedure requires one, with a reference number that matches the record. Keep a simple chain of custody, which means the record shows who held the item and when. Pass the item through the approved return route, which is the coordinator or the property manager, not a guest you happen to meet. Do not look through personal items beyond what you need to identify and record them. For example, you may note that a phone is in a case with a particular colour, but you should not unlock it, read messages or photograph its contents. Never keep an item, even for a short time, and never take it home.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the record factual and avoiding accusations
instructionSections.body: Record what you found and when you found it, and leave the attribution of damage to the coordinator and the property manager. Do not state who caused the damage, do not guess at the cause, and do not write opinions about the guest. A record such as 'cracked tile at the base of the shower wall, approximately one finger-width crack, photographed at 10:40' is useful. A record such as 'the guest broke this tile' is not, because the cleaner did not see it happen. If the damage looks like a safety hazard, such as broken glass or exposed wiring, make the area safe first, keep people away, and report it at once. Do not clean up broken glass with bare hands. Send the record through the approved channel, and keep a copy in the turnover log.

lessons.title: Appliance and safety checks
learningOutcomes: Check the visible state of appliances and safety items without operating unfamiliar appliances.
Identify faults, damage and missing safety items, and report them.
Keep the appliance and its power and gas connections undisturbed.

instructionSections.heading: Visible checks only
instructionSections.body: Your check is a visual one. Look at each appliance and its connections as they sit in the room. Check the cord for fraying, cuts, kinks, exposed wire, or a cord that has been taped or joined. Check the plug for scorching, discolouration, a loose fit or a cracked casing, and check the power point it is in for scorch marks, a loose cover or a plate that sits unevenly. Check the appliance housing for heat marks, leaks, or damaged controls. Check smoke alarms and fire blankets where the property has them, for obvious damage, a missing item, or a visible expiry date that has passed. Do not switch on an unfamiliar electrical or gas appliance to show that it works. Do not open its panels, take off its covers, or unplug it, and do not move a heater or a cooktop to see behind it. If the property procedure permits a test of a smoke alarm, follow that procedure and no other.

instructionSections.heading: Reporting faults at once
instructionSections.body: Report any fault, damaged cord, scorch mark, loose plug or missing safety item to the coordinator straight away, before you move on to other tasks. Mark the appliance as not to be used, using the tag or sign the property procedure provides, and leave it unused until a qualified person has checked it. Do not repair a cord by taping it, and do not replace a plug, a socket or a fitting. A gas smell is an emergency, and it is handled differently from other faults. Leave the immediate area, keep others away, and follow the gas steps in the safety section. Do not search for the source of a gas smell yourself, and do not use a flame, a switch or an appliance while you are in the area.

instructionSections.heading: Recording each check
instructionSections.body: Record each check and each fault with the appliance, its location, the time, and what you saw. Use the word checked, not working, unless the check was authorised and included a function test by a person who is allowed to carry one out. Do not record an appliance as safe to use unless the procedure says that a visual check is enough to make that statement. Include a photograph where the property rules allow it, with the fault and a reference point in view. Record who you told and the time you told them. This lesson does not grant any electrical or gas licence, and a visual check is not an inspection or a certificate.

lessons.title: Client permissions and system ownership
learningOutcomes: Identify who must give permission for roof or ground access to a PV array, and record that permission.
Explain why occupancy and system ownership can differ, and why both must be considered before a job is booked.
Apply a hold or referral decision to a booking where permission, warranty or licence questions are unresolved.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Installing solar panels (page date: Last updated 19 October 2026); Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), Consumer rights and guarantees (page date: No date visible on the page (page metadata shows 17 July 2026)).

instructionSections.heading: Who must give permission
instructionSections.body: A solar array is usually fixed to a roof or a ground frame that belongs to someone, and the array may belong to a different person. Before a cleaning job is booked, identify the owner of the property, the person who controls access to the roof or the ground, and the owner of the array. The property owner and any person who controls the roof or the system should confirm the job in writing. A booking taken from a tenant, an agent or a phone call alone does not establish that the owner has agreed to roof access or to any work on the system.

instructionSections.heading: Ownership is not the same as occupancy
instructionSections.body: An occupant may live in a house where the array is owned by a finance company, a body corporate, a previous occupant or an energy services provider. In those cases, the owner's consent and any terms of the arrangement may matter. Do not assume that the person paying the invoice owns the system. Record each party, the basis on which you believe they have authority, and the approval you received. Where ownership cannot be confirmed, hold the booking.

instructionSections.heading: Warranty and manufacturer conditions
instructionSections.body: Manufacturer instructions and warranty conditions may restrict the cleaning methods, products or equipment that are acceptable for a model of panel. Ask the customer for the model reference or the installer's documents, and check the manufacturer's cleaning instructions before a method is approved. Under the ACCC's consumer guidance (page metadata dated 17 July 2026; no date visible), the basic consumer guarantees stay in force whatever a business states, and a manufacturer's warranty adds promises above those guarantees. The worker does not certify that a warranty is valid or void.

instructionSections.heading: Licence questions to resolve before booking
instructionSections.body: Victorian guidance treats PV installation and maintenance as electrical installation work that licensed electrical workers perform (Energy Safe Victoria page reviewed 15 April 2025). Before booking, confirm that the job will not involve electrical work, switching, isolation, inverter or battery work. If the customer asks for any of these, record the request and refer it to a licensed person.

instructionSections.heading: Hold and refer
instructionSections.body: Write the hold notice with the missing approval, the person who must give it, and the date. Do not schedule the job until the approval is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, a solar installation licence or any authority to access a roof, switch or isolate a PV system, or make a warranty statement.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Installing solar panels (page date: Last updated 19 October 2026); Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), Consumer rights and guarantees (page date: No date visible on the page (page metadata shows 17 July 2026)).

lessons.title: Electrical hazards and live-generation assumptions
learningOutcomes: Explain why a PV array must be treated as live whenever light falls on it.
Identify why DC cables can remain live when the mains supply is off, and why switching off an inverter is not assurance of an electrically safe array.
Apply a stop-and-refer decision to any electrical hazard seen during a clean.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); Government of Western Australia (wa.gov.au), Electrical safety at home: solar PV systems (page date: Last updated 26 November 2024); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Building and trades licences and credentials: electrical (page date: Last updated 23 June 2026); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Installing solar panels (page date: Last updated 19 October 2026); WorkSafe Queensland, Electrical Safety and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024: your questions answered (page date: No date shown; partly checked); Government of South Australia (Energy and Mining), Electrical trades (Office of the Technical Regulator) (page date: No date shown; partly checked); Standards Australia, AS/NZS 4836: Safe working on or near low-voltage electrical installations and equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Why a PV array is treated as live
instructionSections.body: A photovoltaic array converts light into direct current electricity. While light falls on the panels, the array can generate electricity, even when the building's mains supply is switched off or the inverter is off. The Western Australian government guide notes that output continues after the mains is disconnected, and that cables between the panels and the inverter are live while the panels generate (page last updated 26 November 2024). Treat every panel, junction, cable and connector as live for the whole job. This is the controlling assumption for every task in this course.

instructionSections.heading: DC cables and the mains switch
instructionSections.body: Energy Safe Victoria's guidance (page reviewed 15 April 2025) says the DC supply cables of a PV system can still carry voltage after the power has been switched off. Turning off the mains at the switchboard therefore does not make the array's DC side dead. The same caution applies to cables that run from the array to the inverter.

instructionSections.heading: Why switching off the inverter is not enough
instructionSections.body: A customer or a worker may believe that switching off the inverter makes the array safe. The WA guide says a licensed electrician has to verify the DC isolators (page last updated 26 November 2024). The safe working rule is to treat the array as live regardless of the inverter's state, and to refer any isolation to a licensed person.

instructionSections.heading: Who may isolate a PV system
instructionSections.body: Energy Safe Victoria describes isolation at the main switchboard, with the supply turned off, locked off and tagged, and points to AS/NZS 4836 for safe working on low-voltage installations (page reviewed 15 April 2025). The same guidance treats PV installation and maintenance as electrical installation work for licensed electrical workers. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work, including repairing, needs a contractor licence or certificate (page last updated 23 June 2026). Queensland's WorkSafe page says an electrical mechanic licence is required to complete electrical work on energy generation and storage systems, and it does not name solar PV (no date shown). Electrical work on panels and inverters is outside the cleaning work taught in this lesson, and whether a licence is needed for panel cleaning alone is not confirmed by an official source. A cleaning worker does not isolate, switch or work on the electrical system.

instructionSections.heading: Water and electrical hazards
instructionSections.body: Water on connectors, inverters, junction boxes and cable entries can cause a fault, a shock or a fire risk. The electrical hazard is greater where a connector is damaged, burnt or loose. Keep the spray away from electrical components and stop when water reaches them.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer
instructionSections.body: Stop work and refer when you see or suspect exposed wiring, a damaged cable, a burnt or discoloured connector, a hot or cracked module, a smell of burning, unusual sounds, or water near electrical equipment. Do not touch the fault. Keep people and animals clear. Record what was seen and tell the owner in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, a solar installation licence, or any authority to work on, isolate or repair a PV system or its wiring. Under the NSW government page on installing solar panels (last updated 19 October 2026), rooftop solar contracts are limited to licence holders in the building and electrical trades, and the wiring falls to an electrical licence holder, a qualified supervisor, or a worker supervised by one. The WA guide directs maintenance to an installer holding accreditation, or to a licensed electrical contractor (page last updated 26 November 2024).

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); Government of Western Australia (wa.gov.au), Electrical safety at home: solar PV systems (page date: Last updated 26 November 2024); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Building and trades licences and credentials: electrical (page date: Last updated 23 June 2026); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Installing solar panels (page date: Last updated 19 October 2026); WorkSafe Queensland, Electrical Safety and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024: your questions answered (page date: No date shown; partly checked); Government of South Australia (Energy and Mining), Electrical trades (Office of the Technical Regulator) (page date: No date shown; partly checked); Standards Australia, AS/NZS 4836: Safe working on or near low-voltage electrical installations and equipment.

lessons.title: Module damage, exposed wiring and faults
learningOutcomes: Inspect an array for visible module damage, exposed wiring and faults, and separate what is seen from what is unknown.
Apply a stop-and-report decision to damaged modules, exposed cables and burnt or discoloured components.
Write a referral record that a licensed person or the owner can act on.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Building and trades licences and credentials: electrical (page date: Last updated 23 June 2026); Standards Australia, AS/NZS 5033: installation of photovoltaic (PV) arrays.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect before cleaning
instructionSections.body: Before any cleaning, walk the array from the ground with binoculars or a camera where access is possible, and record what can be seen. Look for cracked or chipped glass, delamination, discoloration, burn marks, bent frames, loose or lifted modules, exposed cable, damaged junction boxes and connectors, and any sign of water ingress. Do not climb or step onto the array to inspect it. Mark each item as observed, and record the parts of the array that you could not see as unknowns.

instructionSections.heading: Module damage
instructionSections.body: A cracked or chipped module may have an exposed or damaged internal part, and the surface wash can drive water into the damage. A module that is discoloured, bubbling, hot or smelling of burning may have an internal fault. Do not clean a damaged module with a jet or with a product. Hold it, record it, and report it to the owner in writing with a dated photograph.

instructionSections.heading: Exposed wiring and burnt components
instructionSections.body: Exposed wiring, a damaged cable sheath, or a connector with a black or burnt mark is an electrical hazard. Energy Safe Victoria guidance (reviewed 15 April 2025) says DC supply cables can remain live after the supply is switched off, so the damage is treated as live. Do not touch the cable or connector to check it. Keep people and animals clear, keep spray away, and stop the work near the affected part. Refer the damage to a licensed electrician or the installer.

instructionSections.heading: Standards and records
instructionSections.body: AS/NZS 5033 is the Australian standard for installing photovoltaic arrays. Do not cite a clause of AS/NZS 5033 for a cleaning method. Record the array's make and model, the date of inspection, and any damage found, so that the owner and any specialist have a clear record.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer
instructionSections.body: Stop and refer when a module is cracked or its glass is open, when a cable is exposed or damaged, when a connector is burnt or discoloured, when a module is hot or smells of burning, or when water is found in a connector or junction box. Tell the owner in writing, and do not continue cleaning the affected row or string until a competent person has confirmed the next step.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, solar installation licence or authority to repair, replace or isolate any module, cable or connector. Victorian guidance treats PV installation and maintenance as electrical installation work (reviewed 15 April 2025). In New South Wales, the government's licence page (last updated 23 June 2026) treats repairing as part of electrical wiring work, which needs a contractor licence or certificate.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Building and trades licences and credentials: electrical (page date: Last updated 23 June 2026); Standards Australia, AS/NZS 5033: installation of photovoltaic (PV) arrays.

lessons.title: Manufacturer instructions and warranties
learningOutcomes: Find and apply the manufacturer's cleaning instructions for a panel model before approving a method.
Explain why warranty questions are referred and not certified by a cleaning worker.
Record the instruction source and any unknowns that affect the choice of method.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), Consumer rights and guarantees (page date: No date visible on the page (page metadata shows 17 July 2026)).

instructionSections.heading: Why the manufacturer's instructions come first
instructionSections.body: Each panel model may have cleaning instructions from its manufacturer. Those instructions may describe acceptable water temperatures, products, equipment, brushes and the methods to avoid. A method that is safe on one model may damage the surface, the seals or the frame of another. Before approving any method, find the manufacturer's instructions for the model, read them, and choose a method that they allow. Where the instructions cannot be found, record the gap as unknown and use the most conservative approved method that the job plan allows.

instructionSections.heading: Finding the model and the document
instructionSections.body: Ask the customer or the installer for the model reference printed on the panel frame or on the installation documents. Use the model reference to find the manufacturer's current cleaning instructions. Keep a copy of the document, or a reference to it, with the job record. If the customer has only the installer's documents, record which document was used and its date, because the installer's document may not match the model.

instructionSections.heading: Warranty conditions
instructionSections.body: A panel warranty may contain conditions that apply to cleaning, such as approved methods, approved products, or conditions about damage caused by unapproved work. Under the ACCC's consumer guidance (page metadata dated 17 July 2026; no date visible), the basic consumer guarantees stay in force whatever a business states, and a manufacturer's warranty adds promises above those guarantees. A cleaning worker does not state whether a warranty is valid, void or affected by a clean. The worker records the conditions that the customer provides and refers the warranty question to the manufacturer or the installer.

instructionSections.heading: When the method is not covered
instructionSections.body: Sometimes the manufacturer's instructions do not mention a method that the customer or the worker wants to use, such as high-pressure equipment or a stronger product. Do not assume that the method is allowed. Stop, record that the method is not covered, and use only a method that the manufacturer approves. If the question cannot be answered from the instructions, refer it to the manufacturer or installer in writing before using the method.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the decision
instructionSections.body: The job record should show the model, the source of the instructions and its date, the method chosen, the products and equipment used, and any gap or unknown. If a warranty question was raised, record the question, who it was referred to, and the answer when it is received. Do not write a warranty statement in your own words.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, solar installation licence or warranty certification.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), Consumer rights and guarantees (page date: No date visible on the page (page metadata shows 17 July 2026)).

lessons.title: Water application and equipment separation
learningOutcomes: Apply water and spray controls that keep water away from electrical components during a PV clean.
Separate chemical, clean-water and pressure equipment so that products and tools do not cross-contaminate.
Select only approved products and equipment, and record them against the manufacturer's instructions.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: WorkSafe Victoria, High-pressure water jetting safety alert (page date: Published 14 September 2022; reviewed 11/05/2023); Safe Work Australia, Code of Practice: Preparation of safety data sheets for hazardous chemicals (version 2) (page date: Cover dated February 2016); WorkSafe Victoria, Safety data sheets (page date: Reviewed on 30/07/2022).

instructionSections.heading: Keep water away from electrical parts
instructionSections.body: The most important water control in a PV clean is to keep water off electrical parts. That means connectors, junction boxes, cable entries, inverters and the electrical side of any mounting. Direct the spray along the module face, not at the joints between modules, and do not aim a jet at a junction box or an inverter to rinse it. Where water reaches an electrical part, stop, and refer the equipment to a licensed electrician before the job continues.

instructionSections.heading: Low-pressure methods and the manufacturer's limits
instructionSections.body: Where the manufacturer's instructions allow water cleaning, use the lowest effective method that they specify. Pressure equipment is not approved for panels by default. WorkSafe Victoria's high-pressure jetting alert (published 14 September 2022; reviewed 11 May 2023) says jetting equipment and its attachments should not be altered unless the manufacturer or a competent person approves in writing. Do not select a pressure from memory.

instructionSections.heading: Separate the equipment
instructionSections.body: Keep chemical tools, clean-water tools and any pressure equipment separate. Use separate buckets, brushes and cloths for each product, and label them. Do not use a brush that has touched a strong product on a panel, and do not return unused product to a clean-water container. Separation prevents cross-contamination, keeps each product to its approved use, and makes an incident easier to trace.

instructionSections.heading: Water quality and residue
instructionSections.body: Water quality and mineral deposits can affect the surface of a panel. Where the instructions require a particular water quality, record the water source used, and do not assume that the water supply is suitable. Do not use water that the manufacturer does not allow.

instructionSections.heading: Approved products and safety data sheets
instructionSections.body: Use only products that the manufacturer allows, and keep the label and the safety data sheet on site. Safe Work Australia's SDS code (cover dated February 2016) makes the maker or importer responsible for sending an up-to-date SDS to people who may be exposed. The same code places incompatible materials under section 10, which covers stability and reactivity. WorkSafe Victoria's SDS page (reviewed 30 July 2022) says the employer has to make the sheets reachable by the workforce and by emergency responders. Do not mix products. Do not use a strong acid, a solvent or an unidentified mixture on a panel. Record the product name, its concentration as directed on the label, and the time it was applied.

instructionSections.heading: Limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers water and product application for cleaning only. It does not authorise any work on the electrical system, the inverter, the battery or the wiring. It does not authorise roof access, and it does not set a pressure, concentration or dwell time that the manufacturer has not approved.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, a solar installation licence or authority to use pressure equipment on a PV array. WorkSafe Victoria's alert says Class B jetting systems (output above 5,600 bar-litres per minute) need operator training and assessment, delivered by registered training organisations, with refresher training on a two-year cycle (alert reviewed 11 May 2023). This course does not provide that training.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): WorkSafe Victoria, High-pressure water jetting safety alert (page date: Published 14 September 2022; reviewed 11/05/2023); Safe Work Australia, Code of Practice: Preparation of safety data sheets for hazardous chemicals (version 2) (page date: Cover dated February 2016); WorkSafe Victoria, Safety data sheets (page date: Reviewed on 30/07/2022).

lessons.title: Vegetation, nests and biological hazards
learningOutcomes: Identify biological hazards around a PV array, including nests, droppings and vegetation.
Separate routine cleaning of droppings from the removal of nests and the trimming of vegetation, which are outside the cleaning scope.
Apply a check, stop and refer decision to an active nest or a vegetation problem that affects access.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: NSW Government (environment.nsw.gov.au), Protected species (page date: Updated 7 September 2026; partly checked); SafeWork NSW, Work near overhead and underground electric lines (code of practice; page date: cover dated May 2026; in force from 22 May 2026; no separate last-updated date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Biological hazards around arrays
instructionSections.body: Arrays are often mounted where birds, bats, wasps, spiders and other animals shelter or nest. Vegetation can grow over the array and shade it, and leaves or debris collect at the edges and in gutters. These biological hazards can cause stings, bites, slips and contamination. Before access, look at the array and its surroundings for nests, droppings, hives and vegetation that could reach the work area, and record what you see.

instructionSections.heading: Nests and wildlife
instructionSections.body: Do not disturb an active nest. NSW's biodiversity law (the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016) covers native birds, with listed exceptions. Check the rule for the state before any removal. Where a nest is active or its status is unknown, keep the work away from it, record its position, and refer the removal to the owner or the appropriate authority. A cleaning worker does not remove nests under this course.

instructionSections.heading: Droppings and routine hygiene
instructionSections.body: Bird droppings on panels are a routine part of the cleaning job when the method and the PPE allow it. Wear the PPE the job pack names, avoid breathing dust or spray, wash hands after the job, and keep the work area clean. Droppings that are dried and dusty need care, because the dust can carry organisms. Where the droppings are heavy or the area is enclosed, stop and check the job plan before continuing.

instructionSections.heading: Vegetation that affects access or shading
instructionSections.body: Vegetation that shades the array, or grows over the array edge, is not part of the cleaning scope unless the owner separately authorises trimming. Trimming vegetation near an electrical installation can bring electrical and fall risks. Record the vegetation and its effect, and refer the trimming to the owner and to a qualified person. Do not cut vegetation with a tool from the roof or the array edge. The NSW code of practice on work near overhead and underground electric lines (in force from 22 May 2026) says a worker should assume an overhead line is live unless the supply authority has confirmed otherwise in writing. Refer any branch that touches a line to the network operator, and keep people out of the area.

instructionSections.heading: Stop and refer
instructionSections.body: Stop and refer when an active nest is within the work area, when a hive or swarm is present, when a wasp or spider presence causes a risk, when vegetation blocks a safe access route, or when a worker has an allergic reaction. Keep people clear, record the location, and refer to the owner and to the appropriate person. Seek urgent medical care for any sting or bite that causes a reaction.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, pest control licence, tree-trimming authority or any wildlife permit. Vegetation work and nest removal are outside the cleaning course.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): NSW Government (environment.nsw.gov.au), Protected species (page date: Updated 7 September 2026; partly checked); SafeWork NSW, Work near overhead and underground electric lines (code of practice; page date: cover dated May 2026; in force from 22 May 2026; no separate last-updated date shown).

lessons.title: Ground protection and environmental runoff
learningOutcomes: Identify cost-reduction measures for a PV clean that keep the work inside its safety and scope limits.
Explain how ground protection and runoff control reduce both cost and environmental harm.
Apply a decision that trades a time-saving shortcut against the scope, the safety rules and the environmental rules.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: NSW EPA, The drain is just for rain (stormwater fact sheet) (page date: January 2021 (code 20P2719)); Wollondilly Shire Council (NSW), Fact sheet: roof cleaning, roof restoration and stormwater pollution (page date: No date shown; partly checked); Toowoomba Regional Council (QLD), Water pressure cleaning (page date: No date shown; partly checked).

instructionSections.heading: Cost reduction within the scope
instructionSections.body: Cleaning cost is driven by time, travel, materials, equipment, rework and callbacks. A solar clean reduces cost when the job is planned from the ground, when the array is inspected before work starts, when the scope is agreed in writing, and when the method uses only the approved products and equipment. Cost reduction does not mean taking roof access without approval, skipping the inspection, or using a stronger product to finish faster. Those shortcuts increase the risk of damage, incident and warranty dispute, which costs more than the time saved.

instructionSections.heading: Ground-based planning first
instructionSections.body: Where the array can be reached from the ground, or where a ground-based method is possible, plan that method first. Ground-based work avoids roof access and the costs of approval, equipment and supervision that roof access requires. Where the array is on a roof, record why a ground-based method is not possible, and do not treat roof access as the default.

instructionSections.heading: Ground protection
instructionSections.body: Ground protection means protecting the turf, soil, paths, cables, pits and garden beds from the damage that equipment and vehicles can cause. Place boards or mats where a ladder, a trolley or a vehicle will stand. Keep cables and hoses clear of walkways and off the ground where they can be trodden on. Damage to the ground is a cost, and it is also a hazard for trips and for underground services. The site controller decides where equipment may be placed.

instructionSections.heading: Runoff and stormwater
instructionSections.body: Wash water from a solar clean can carry detergent, dirt, bird droppings and any residue from the panel surface. NSW EPA guidance (dated January 2021) says the stormwater drain is for water only, and that chemicals should be kept in bunded, closed and labelled storage rather than tipped in the drain. A NSW council fact sheet (no date shown) states that polluted run-off reaching a drain or waterway is an offence under the NSW Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997, which can carry substantial penalties. For example, NSW EPA guidance (dated January 2021) asks for dedicated washdown areas that do not lead to stormwater drains, so runoff from a site without one should be held or collected as the job plan requires. In Queensland, a council page (no date shown) states that wastewater from pressure cleaning may not be let into kerbside channels or the stormwater network, and cites section 440ZG of the Environmental Protection Act 1994. Use the lowest water volume the method allows, use approved products only, and divert or collect the runoff as the job plan requires. Where runoff reaches a drain, record it, and report it under the site's procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Water and product use
instructionSections.body: Use only the water that the job needs. Leaving a hose running, flooding the array or using unfiltered water where the manufacturer does not allow it wastes water and can damage the array and its warranty. Use approved products at the labelled concentration, and do not increase the concentration to save time. Record the water and product used so that the cost and the environmental impact can be reviewed.

instructionSections.heading: Reducing callbacks
instructionSections.body: Callbacks cost money. A pre-clean inspection, a written scope, a record of the array condition before work, and an approved method all reduce callbacks because they show what was there before the clean and what was done. A record of the condition is the best protection against a later dispute about damage.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, environmental approval or authority to discharge wastewater, to work on the ground in a regulated area, or to access a roof.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): NSW EPA, The drain is just for rain (stormwater fact sheet) (page date: January 2021 (code 20P2719)); Wollondilly Shire Council (NSW), Fact sheet: roof cleaning, roof restoration and stormwater pollution (page date: No date shown; partly checked); Toowoomba Regional Council (QLD), Water pressure cleaning (page date: No date shown; partly checked).

lessons.title: Defects, performance claims and referrals
learningOutcomes: Separate a cleaning observation from a defect finding, a performance claim and a warranty statement.
Record a defect in writing and refer it to the correct person, without certifying the system.
Explain why accreditation references must be current, including the scheme that now applies (Solar Accreditation Australia, per the NSW government page).

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Installing solar panels (page date: Last updated 19 October 2026); Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Building and trades licences and credentials: electrical (page date: Last updated 23 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Observation, defect and claim
instructionSections.body: A cleaning worker may observe that a panel is dirty, cracked, discoloured or loose. Recording that observation is part of the job. Calling it a defect that affects the array's output, or saying that the array will produce more or less power after the clean, is a different statement. Energy-output testing and performance claims are outside this course, and a worker does not make them. Keep the observation, the defect and any claim separate in your record.

instructionSections.heading: Performance claims
instructionSections.body: Customers often ask whether a clean will increase energy output, by how much, or whether the inverter reading is correct. The cleaning course does not include energy-output testing, system servicing or inverter checks. The correct response is to say that output claims and system checks are outside the cleaning scope, and to refer the customer to the installer or a suitably qualified person. Do not quote a percentage, a generation figure or a return on investment.

instructionSections.heading: Recording and referring defects
instructionSections.body: Record each defect in writing with a dated photograph, its position on the array, and what you observed. Give a copy to the owner. Refer electrical defects, such as burnt or exposed components, to a licensed electrician. Refer equipment or installation defects, such as a loose mounting, to the installer or the array owner. Refer warranty questions to the manufacturer or installer. Keep the referral and the outcome on the job record.

instructionSections.heading: Accreditation references
instructionSections.body: Where an installer's accreditation is relevant to a referral, check the current scheme. NSW government guidance (last updated 19 October 2026) says rebate eligibility depends on accreditation with Solar Accreditation Australia, which is the scheme the page names. Do not describe CEC accreditation as current, and correct any older document that does.

instructionSections.heading: What a worker must not do
instructionSections.body: A cleaning worker must not certify that an array is compliant, safe, performing or under warranty. The worker must not isolate the system, change settings or repair a defect. The worker must not promise a result for a defect that a licensed person has not assessed. These statements are reserved to the licensed or accredited person or the manufacturer.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, solar installation licence, accreditation, energy-output certification or warranty authority. Victorian guidance treats PV installation and maintenance as electrical installation work. New South Wales electrical wiring work, including repairing, needs a licence or certificate (page last updated 23 June 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Installing solar panels (page date: Last updated 19 October 2026); Energy Safe Victoria, Safely installing photovoltaic (PV) systems (page date: Reviewed 15 April 2025); NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Building and trades licences and credentials: electrical (page date: Last updated 23 June 2026).

lessons.title: Job records, handover and escalation
learningOutcomes: Complete a standard job record for a PV clean that captures scope, method, observations, exclusions and referrals.
Write a handover that tells the customer what was done, what was excluded and what must be referred.
Use a standard template to reduce repeated admin without removing evidence or checks.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (start of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson: NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Installing solar panels (page date: Last updated 19 October 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Why the job record matters
instructionSections.body: A job record is the evidence of what was agreed, what was checked, what was done and what was referred. It protects the worker and the business in a dispute about damage, a missed exclusion or a warranty question. A record should be complete enough that another person could understand the job without asking the worker.

instructionSections.heading: The fields a solar job record needs
instructionSections.body: A standard record should capture the owner and the array owner, the approvals obtained, the scope and exclusions, the array make and model, the instruction source, the method and products, the equipment used, the before and after photographs, the time taken, any defect or unknown, and any referral made. Keep observations and claims in separate fields. Where a field is not applicable or unknown, write so, rather than leaving it blank.

instructionSections.heading: Using a template to reduce workload
instructionSections.body: A standard template reduces repeated writing and makes records consistent across jobs. Use fixed fields for the items above, and avoid free text where a choice from a fixed list will do. A template does not remove the checks. Each field must still be completed by a person, and the template must not hide an exclusion, a defect or an unknown. Review the template when the method or the regulations change.

instructionSections.heading: Customer handover
instructionSections.body: At handover, give the customer a written summary. It should state what was cleaned, what was excluded and why, any defect observed and who it has been referred to, and any question that is outside the cleaning scope. Do not give a verbal assurance that the panels are compliant, safe, performing or under warranty. Keep a copy of the summary in the job record.

instructionSections.heading: Escalation
instructionSections.body: Escalate any electrical, structural, warranty or environmental concern in writing to the owner and to the qualified person named in the procedure. Record who was told, when and what decision is pending. Do not fix a concern on the spot if it is outside the scope, and do not delete a photograph or change a record after it has been made. Corrections are added as dated entries.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant an electrical licence, solar installation licence, accreditation or authority to certify a system. Completing a record template is not a licence or certification.

instructionSections.heading: Official sources (end of lesson)
instructionSections.body: Official sources for this lesson (end): NSW Government (nsw.gov.au), Installing solar panels (page date: Last updated 19 October 2026).

lessons.title: Confirm the surface before work: natural stone, terrazzo or engineered stone
learningOutcomes: Identify whether a surface is natural stone, terrazzo or possibly engineered stone using documents and non-destructive observation
Explain why a surface that cannot be confirmed is a stop-work case
Record the identification basis, photograph the surface and state a proceed or stop decision
Refuse any test that cuts, grinds or scratches the surface to identify it

instructionSections.heading: Why identification comes first
instructionSections.body: The surface type decides what you are allowed to do. Natural stone such as marble, granite, limestone and slate, and terrazzo, can be honed, polished and sealed under the controls taught in this course. Engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs are different. The national prohibition on their use, supply and manufacture started on 1 July 2024. Installed engineered stone does not have to be removed, but processing it is restricted, and some legacy processing needs notice to the WHS regulator before the work starts (see “The engineered stone prohibition and what it means on a job”). Because the outcome is so different, the first task on every job is to confirm the material, not to assume it. A kitchen benchtop that looks like granite may be engineered stone. A client who says it is granite is giving an opinion, which is useful information but is not an identification.

instructionSections.heading: Checks that do not damage the surface
instructionSections.body: Start with paper. Look for the product label, the installer's documents, the warranty card, the supplier invoice, the builder's specification and any maintenance guide the client has kept. Then look at the surface from a normal viewing distance and in good light. Engineered stone often shows a very even colour and speckle pattern repeated across a large area, and a sheen that looks uniform from every angle. Natural granite shows a crystal structure with variation in grain, and natural marble shows veining that changes across the slab. Terrazzo shows chips set in a matrix. These cues are only reasons to stop and check. They are not a reliable test on their own, and a surface that looks like granite can still be engineered stone. Do not scratch, grind, cut, wet-rub with abrasives or take a sample to test the surface. Cutting, grinding and sanding are named as silica dust-generating processes in the national guidance. Those actions can also change the surface. If the material is still uncertain after the document and visual checks, treat it as engineered stone and stop.

instructionSections.heading: What to record and who decides
instructionSections.body: Record the basis for your decision. A documented identification means a product label, an installer or manufacturer document, or a written confirmation from the responsible person who has the authority to give it. Photograph the surface, any label or document, and any marks or cracks. Write the decision, the date and your name. Terrazzo needs one more point. This is a precaution, not a regulator's statement. Refer any doubt about terrazzo to the responsible person and the state regulator before work.

lessons.title: The engineered stone prohibition and what it means on a job
learningOutcomes: State when the national engineered stone prohibition started and when the import ban started
Explain why installed engineered stone does not have to be removed and why work on it is still restricted
Identify the points on which the sources differ and explain how this course handles them
Decline or refer an engineered stone job in a way that does not suggest the work is lawful

instructionSections.heading: What is banned and from when
instructionSections.body: The national prohibition on engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs commenced on 1 July 2024. The DEWR page dates the import ban to 1 January 2025. Processing and installation are covered: the Asbestos Safety and SA Government pages both say so, and the explanatory material to the import instrument describes the domestic ban in the same terms, with 'processing' defined in WHS Regulation 529A. The DEWR page does not address processing or installation. The explanatory material also notes that some jurisdictions delayed full implementation to 31 December 2024. Porcelain and sintered stone are excluded, and so are finished items that need no processing. The instrument's explanatory material lists further products outside engineered stone, including concrete and cement products, bricks, ceramic tiles, grout, mortar and plasterboard. The WHS Regulation 529A text itself was not read this session, so its exact wording is partly checked.

instructionSections.heading: What installed stone means for you
instructionSections.body: Installed engineered stone does not have to be removed. The SA Government page adds that installed stone can be used safely while it stays undisturbed. The practical point is that the work is the problem, not the stone sitting in the kitchen. Removing, repairing, modifying or disposing of installed engineered stone is restricted. Asbestos Safety says that controlled processing of legacy stone for repair, removal, minor modification or disposal may be allowed, and that the WHS regulator must be notified before the work. Safe Work Australia's guidance of August 2025 says notification is required when work involves processing engineered stone, that the regulator does not need to approve the work before it starts, and that the notice should be kept for five years. WorkSafe Victoria says the uncontrolled dry cutting of legacy engineered stone is not permitted in Victoria, and that a crystalline silica hazard control statement must be prepared before high-risk work starts. None of these points gives permission to take the job. They tell you that a regulated route exists and that it is outside this course.

instructionSections.heading: Natural stone is not banned, and this course does not stretch its rules
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 27/08/2024) says the ban does not reach natural stone, and cites a granite benchtop as not prohibited. This course covers natural stone and terrazzo. The methods taught in “Pre-work surface assessment and test patches” to “Wet work on site: slurry, runoff and slip control” apply to those materials only. If a client, builder or supplier asks you to work on a surface that might be engineered stone, the answer is to stop, record the request and refer it, not to try a method that might work. Do not extend natural-stone methods to a surface that only looks similar.

lessons.title: Respirable crystalline silica: where it comes from and why it matters
learningOutcomes: Describe how respirable crystalline silica is released from stone and terrazzo work
List the dust-generating processes in stone restoration, including honing and polishing
Explain why dry work, dry sweeping and compressed air are stop-work matters
Explain why respiratory protection is the last control, not the first

instructionSections.heading: What silica dust is and how it is released
instructionSections.body: Crystalline silica is a mineral that occurs naturally in many rocks and sands, and it is present in many stones, aggregates and some terrazzo mixes. When these materials are cut, drilled, ground, sanded, sawn or polished, very fine particles can be released into the air. The particles that matter for health are respirable, which means small enough to reach deep in the lungs. Crushing, cutting, drilling, grinding, sanding, sawing and polishing all appear in the national guidance (February 2022) as dust-generating work. For this course, the processes that matter most are honing, grinding, polishing and any dry cutting or dry sweeping that follows them. The national guidance names silicosis, progressive massive fibrosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic bronchitis and lung cancer as health effects of exposure, and also mentions chronic kidney disease and autoimmune disorders.

instructionSections.heading: Why dry work is the stop-work case
instructionSections.body: The NT WorkSafe guide (version 1.1, 29 January 2026) says dry cutting, grinding or polishing without on-tool extraction, water suppression or local exhaust ventilation generates very high levels of respirable crystalline silica. The national guidance rules out compressed air, dry sweeping and general-purpose vacuums for cleaning surfaces and clothing, because they spread the dust into the air. Honing and polishing are wet processes in this course, and they are only safe when the water is running at the point of cut and the slurry is controlled. A task that starts dry, that loses its water feed partway through, or that is cleaned up with dry methods has moved outside the course's safe methods. Stop the task, make the controls work, and record the stop. Do not carry on because the job is nearly finished.

instructionSections.heading: Plan before the first pass
instructionSections.body: Before work starts, list each task that will create dust. Name the control for each task: a wet method, on-tool extraction, local exhaust ventilation or isolation of the area. Check that the control is available and working before the first pass, not after the first dust cloud. In occupied buildings, such as offices or cafes, plan the isolation of the area as well, so that other people are kept away from the work. Victoria's guidance calls for a written silica hazard control statement, which has to exist before high-risk work begins. If any listed control is not available, the work does not start that day.

lessons.title: Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping
learningOutcomes: Apply the control hierarchy to stone dust: engineering controls before personal protective equipment
Set up and check a wet method, on-tool extraction and isolation before a cut or pass
Use only housekeeping methods that the guidance allows for silica dust
Stop work and record the stop when a dust control fails

instructionSections.heading: Engineering controls come first
instructionSections.body: The control hierarchy puts elimination and substitution first, then isolation and engineering controls, then administrative controls, and personal protective equipment last. For stone restoration, the most useful controls are wet methods, on-tool extraction, local exhaust ventilation and isolation of the work area. The national guidance (February 2022) treats wet cutting as an engineering control, says high-dust work can be isolated by shutting it in a closed room with controlled entry, and names local exhaust ventilation as a way to remove dust close to the source. It also ranks personal protective equipment as the least effective method of control. The practical result is that the water, the extraction and the isolation are planned and checked first. Respiratory protection is the backup, and it is covered in “Respirators, fit testing and health monitoring”.

instructionSections.heading: Wet methods and extraction at the point of cut
instructionSections.body: A wet method keeps the surface wet at the point where the machine is cutting or abrading, so that the dust is held in the slurry and does not become airborne. Check the water flow at the start, at each change of grit or pad and at regular intervals during the pass. If the flow stops or drops, stop the machine, restore the flow and check the surface before you continue. On-tool extraction captures dust at the machine. Use an extraction unit that is suited to the task and to the manufacturer's rating. The NT WorkSafe guide of 2026 recommends an M or H class rated vacuum for cleaning dusty areas, and that recommendation should be checked against the state rules before it is taught as a requirement. A fan is not one of the controls named in the guidance, and it moves dust around the room rather than capturing it at source. The national guidance also rules out general-purpose vacuums for cleaning surfaces and clothing.

instructionSections.heading: Isolation and housekeeping
instructionSections.body: Isolation means separating the dusty work from people who are not involved, using barriers, signs and restricted access. In occupied buildings, plan the isolation before the work starts and tell the building manager. Housekeeping means removing the dust and slurry in ways that do not make the air dustier. The national guidance rules out compressed air, dry sweeping and general-purpose vacuums for cleaning. It names low-pressure water, wet sweeping, and a vacuum rated to the class the guidance specifies as the alternatives. Keep the area clean at the end of each shift, and do not leave slurry to dry into a film that can be disturbed later. Clean tools and machines with a wet method before they are stored.

lessons.title: Respirators, fit testing and health monitoring
learningOutcomes: Explain why respiratory protection is the last control for stone dust
Describe when a worker must pass a fit test before wearing a tight-fitting respirator
Explain when health monitoring must be arranged and who pays for it under the guidance

instructionSections.heading: Respiratory protection is the last line
instructionSections.body: Respiratory protective equipment comes after the engineering controls described in “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”. Some risk can remain after those controls are in place, and a respirator is then needed for that residual risk. The national guidance of February 2022 ranks personal protective equipment last in the control order. It places this kind of protection at the weakest end of the ranking and warns against leaning on it by itself. For processing porcelain, sintered stone or engineered stone, the NT WorkSafe guide puts the duty on the business to supply breathing protection to everyone who may be exposed, and says the worker must keep it on for the whole of the processing work. The NT guide is a Northern Territory document, so its duty applies in the Northern Territory. Choose the respirator from a documented risk assessment, not from habit, from a product on a shelf, or from what the worker used on a previous job.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the respirator and the standard
instructionSections.body: The respirator's type, class, filter and standard must match the task and the manufacturer's data. The NT guide names two Australian and New Zealand standards for respiratory protective equipment used in processing porcelain, sintered stone and engineered stone: AS/NZS 1716:2012 and AS/NZS 1715:2009. Those are the standards the NT guide names. A respirator that meets a standard is still only suitable if its class, filter and fit suit the task. Record the choice against the risk assessment, with the model, the class and the filter, and keep the manufacturer's data on file. Do not state them as a requirement for another jurisdiction.

instructionSections.heading: Fit testing comes before first use
instructionSections.body: A respirator protects only if it seals to the face. The national guidance expects a worker to pass a fit test before first wearing a tight-fitting respirator. The guidance also expects a repeat test after a change of make or model, after a change in facial features, and once a year at least. The guidance prefers a quantitative test for full face and powered types. A qualitative test, which depends on the wearer detecting a taste or odour, is for half-face types only, because it can give a misleading pass for the other types.A fit test is specific to a model, a size and a person, so a changed model or size needs a new test. The NT guide also expects a fit check every time the respirator goes on. Facial hair, glasses and damaged seals can defeat the seal, so the fit-test provider's instructions and the manufacturer's directions apply.

instructionSections.heading: Health monitoring is a duty, not a choice
instructionSections.body: The national guidance expects monitoring to begin as soon as someone takes on silica work, whether at hire or when they move onto such tasks, so that early changes in health are picked up. For people already working with these materials without monitoring, the guidance asks for arrangements to be put in place promptly. In the Northern Territory, the NT WorkSafe guide puts on the business the duty to arrange and fund monitoring where silica exposure poses a risk to health. That duty is not limited to the people who create the dust. The NT guide also reaches those who clean up the work area and the tools. The NSW Resources Regulator position paper of April 2025 deals with monitoring for high-risk processing, but its context is mine and petroleum operators, and it is a position paper rather than the regulation itself. The decision to monitor depends on the risk and the work done, not on how long the job lasts. Arrange monitoring through a qualified provider, keep the arrangement on file, and do not attempt to assess a worker's health on the job.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work and the start of a dusty task
instructionSections.body: A dusty task does not start until the controls before it are in place. For a tight-fitting respirator, that means a current fit test for the model and size, a seal check on the day, training in fitting, checking, cleaning and storage, and a monitoring arrangement on file where the risk requires one. If any of these is missing, the worker does not start the dusty task. The worker can take up a non-dusty task, such as setting up the water feed or the barriers, while the supervisor puts the missing record in place. Record the stop, the reason and the date it is lifted.

lessons.title: Chemicals for stone: acid etches, cleaners and sealers
learningOutcomes: Find and read the Safety Data Sheet and product instructions before using any stone chemical
Choose a stone chemical that the manufacturer approves for the material and finish
Store and handle chemicals without mixing products unless the manufacturer allows it
Explain why a test patch comes before any acid etch or strong cleaner

instructionSections.heading: Read before you pour
instructionSections.body: Stone work uses several families of product: acidic etches, alkaline and neutral cleaners, poultices and stain removers, and impregnating and topical sealers. Each product has a Safety Data Sheet, and the SDS is the first source of hazard information. Read the sections on hazards, first aid, personal protective equipment, handling, storage and incompatible materials before the product is opened on site. The label and the product's technical data sheet give the approved use and the dilution. This course does not set dilutions or contact times, because they depend on the product and the stone. Use the product only on the surfaces the manufacturer approves, and only after a test patch as set in “Pre-work surface assessment and test patches”. WorkSafe Queensland's incident alert (page undated; incident March 2022) advises checking labels and SDS for handling, storage and emergency steps, and keeping them within easy reach of workers.

instructionSections.heading: Storage, mixing and waste
instructionSections.body: Store chemicals by hazard class, away from incompatible materials, and keep the lids closed. Do not mix products unless the manufacturer's instructions say that the mixture is approved. Mixing one product with another can produce heat or gases. WorkSafe Queensland's 2022 alert describes sodium hypochlorite added to sulphuric acid, releasing toxic chlorine gas, and warns against mixing incompatible chemicals; acids must therefore never be mixed with bleach or hypochlorite products. Keep the SDS for each product on site and in a location that workers can reach in an emergency. Label any diluted solution with the product, the dilution, the date and the hazard. Follow the SDS and the site's waste procedure, and check the state environment authority before disposing of any residue into a drain or ground.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the product and the test
instructionSections.body: Match the product to the stone and to the finish. An acid etch that suits a honed granite may dull or damage a polished marble or a terrazzo finish, and a cleaner that suits a sealed surface may strip an unsealed one. Use the manufacturer's list of approved uses first, and then test on a concealed patch as set in “Pre-work surface assessment and test patches”. Use the lowest strength and the shortest contact time that the manufacturer states and that the test patch supports. This course's teaching rule is that an acid etch used near people or pets needs a documented control plan before use.

lessons.title: Pre-work surface assessment and test patches
learningOutcomes: Record the material, finish, condition and location of a stone or terrazzo surface before work
Identify cracks, loose edges, joints and previous treatments that change the method
Run a test patch that uses the same dust and water controls as the full job
Decide to proceed, change the method or stop, based on the recorded test result

instructionSections.heading: Assess before you abrade
instructionSections.body: Once the material is confirmed as natural stone or terrazzo, record what the surface is like before any tool touches it. Write down the material, the finish (polished, honed, flamed, tumbled or textured), the condition (etching, staining, scratches, chips, cracks, sealer residue, previous repairs, lifting or loose areas), the location, the traffic and the moisture. Note any fixtures, joints, penetrations and edges. Cracks and loose edges matter because a grinder or a pad can break them, and the break makes dust and a hazard. Use good light and a torch from a low angle to see the surface, and take photographs. These checks are visual and do not damage the surface. Do not use a scratch or cut to find out more about the surface, because that creates dust and changes what you are trying to assess.

instructionSections.heading: Test patches that show the real response
instructionSections.body: A test patch is a small area, usually in a concealed place such as under a fixture or inside a cupboard, that is treated with the proposed method before the whole job is started. The patch shows how the stone responds to the abrasive, the water, the chemical and the contact time. Record the abrasive grit or pad, the machine speed as set by the manufacturer, the water use, any chemical and its contact time, and the result. Look for colour change, scratch pattern, etching, staining, edge rounding and any change in sheen. The test patch must use the same dust controls as the full job, including the wet method and extraction set out in “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”. A test is never a reason to start dry work. If the patch dusts, stop, add the control, and then repeat the test.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding the method from the result
instructionSections.body: After the test, decide one of three things. Proceed when the patch gives the expected result and the controls are in place. Change the method when the patch shows a risk, for example a sequence with a finer grit, a different pad, a different product or a shorter contact time. Stop when the patch shows damage that cannot be managed, when the material is not identified (see “Confirm the surface before work: natural stone, terrazzo or engineered stone”), when a crack or loose edge would be affected, or when a control cannot be set up. Write the chosen method, the grit or product sequence and the controls on the job record. If the result is uncertain, tell the client in writing what is known and what is not, before the work starts. A passing test does not identify the material, and it does not replace the identification record.

lessons.title: Honing and polishing sequence for natural stone and terrazzo
learningOutcomes: Explain why honing comes before polishing and why each grit must remove the scratches of the previous one
Keep the wet method running throughout each honing and polishing step
Inspect a finished surface for scratches, pits, colour change, edge damage and loosening chips
Record the grit sequence, the water and extraction checks and the inspection result

instructionSections.heading: Plan the sequence before the first pass
instructionSections.body: Honing removes marks, levels the surface and opens the stone to the next step. Polishing uses finer abrasives to build the sheen. The two stages run in order, and each stage has to remove the scratch pattern of the one before it. The grit numbers, the pad types, the machine speeds and the number of passes are set by the product or the manufacturer's instructions for the material. This course does not give a national grit sequence or machine speed, because no Australian standard for natural stone restoration method was found and the sequence depends on the stone.
