Use the sequence confirmed by the test patch in “Pre-work surface assessment and test patches”, and write it on the job record before the first pass.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the wet method running through every step
instructionSections.body: The wet method is the main dust control for honing and polishing, and it applies at every grit. Start the water before the machine starts, and keep the flow at the point of cut for the whole pass. Check the flow when you change the grit or pad and at regular intervals. Keep the pads clean and free of debris, because a loaded pad scratches the surface and can heat up. Dry honing and dry polishing are stop-work matters under “Respirable crystalline silica: where it comes from and why it matters” and are not permitted in this course. The NT WorkSafe guide describes dry cutting, grinding or polishing without controls as generating very high silica levels. Where the slurry becomes thick and dry at the edges, stop, restore the flow and clean the edges with the wet method before continuing.

instructionSections.heading: Check the result before you call it finished
instructionSections.body: Inspect the surface under good light and from the angles at which the client will see it. Look for remaining scratches from the coarser grit, pits, colour change, uneven sheen and edge damage. On terrazzo, check each chip for looseness and stop before the grinding exposes or lifts the aggregate. Over-grinding terrazzo changes the look and can loosen the chips, so stop at the point where the matrix and chips are level and the surface is even. If the surface shows damage, stop and refer it, and record the damage in the job record. When the inspection passes, record the final grit used, the water and extraction checks and the result.

lessons.title: Sealing, stain protection and cure times
learningOutcomes: Explain what a sealer or impregnator does and what it does not do
Choose a sealer by stone type, finish and traffic using the manufacturer's data
Apply thin, even coats and respect the stated dwell, buffing and cure times
Give the client written care and re-seal instructions at handover

instructionSections.heading: What sealing does and does not do
instructionSections.body: A sealer or impregnator reduces the absorption of the stone, which makes it slower to stain and easier to clean. It does not make a worn or damaged surface sound, it does not fill cracks, and it does not hide defects. A sealer applied over a surface with dirt, slurry or residue traps the contamination and can affect the finish and the cure. For this reason, sealing comes after the surface is clean, dry to the product's requirement and confirmed as the right stone with a passing test patch (“Pre-work surface assessment and test patches”). Choose the sealer from the manufacturer's data for the stone type, the finish and the traffic it will carry. Some sealers change the sheen, so the test patch should show the finish as well as the protection.

instructionSections.heading: Application and cure
instructionSections.body: Follow the product's instructions for the number of coats, the coverage rate, the dwell time, any buffing and the cure time. Apply thin, even coats. A thick coat does not seal faster, and it can trap solvent, leave a tacky film or leave a line. Remove the excess before it sets, as the product directs. Keep the area ventilated, because many sealers have solvents that the SDS will describe (“Chemicals for stone: acid etches, cleaners and sealers”). Keep the area closed to traffic for the cure time. Temperature, humidity and moisture in the stone change the cure, so read the product data for the conditions on the day and record them. If the surface is not dry when the product requires it, stop and wait.

instructionSections.heading: Handover and client care
instructionSections.body: At handover, tell the client in writing the cure time, the time before the area can be walked on and the time before it can be washed. Give the client the list of cleaning products that the manufacturer approves, and the products to avoid, including acidic cleaners, abrasive pads and solvent cleaners where the product data says they are unsuitable. Explain when the surface should be re-sealed, as the product data sets. Record the product name, batch, application date and coat count. Where a sealer change or a second product is planned, check the compatibility in the product data before application. The care note is part of the job, and it protects the finish that the client paid for.

lessons.title: Wet work on site: slurry, runoff and slip control
learningOutcomes: Explain why slurry is both a waste problem and a dust and slip hazard
Set up containment, collection and drain protection before the first pass
Clean slurry continuously with approved methods and manage wet floors
Respond to slurry that reaches a drain by stopping the water and containing the flow

instructionSections.heading: Slurry is waste, dust and a slip hazard
instructionSections.body: Honing and polishing produce slurry, which is a mixture of water, stone particles and, where a chemical has been used, the chemical. The water keeps the silica dust in the slurry during the work, which is the point of the wet method. Once the slurry dries, however, the particles can become airborne dust again, and a wet floor left unmarked is a slip hazard. Slurry that flows into a drain, a gutter or stormwater can carry stone particles and chemicals into waterways. Council guidance for wet cutting says waste must be kept out of the stormwater network, because slurry can clog pipes and make the water more alkaline. Plan the handling of slurry with the site and the local rules before the first pass.

instructionSections.heading: Containment, collection and drain protection
instructionSections.body: Before the work starts, set up containment. Use barriers, slurry collection mats or a bunded area, and cover or block drains that the slurry could reach, using covers that are suited to the purpose. Where a wet vacuum is used for slurry, confirm that its rating and the manufacturer's instructions allow it for slurry, and do not use a general-purpose vacuum on dust. Collect solids from the containment and store them in a sealed container until disposal. Let settled slurry dry in a contained area only if the site rules allow it, and never sweep it dry. Council guidance says small quantities may be left in lined ditches to dry out, while larger volumes need a licensed recycler or landfill. Dispose of slurry by the site procedure and the state rules. Where settling tanks are used, keep the water and the solids apart as the site plan requires. Keep a clean path for workers and the public, and keep hoses and cords out of the walkway.

instructionSections.heading: Clean as you go and manage wet floors
instructionSections.body: Clean slurry as you go, not at the end of the day. Use low-pressure water, wet sweeping or the rated vacuum. Never use compressed air or dry sweeping. Mark the wet area with signs and cones, and manage access so that people do not walk through the slurry. Wear footwear with good grip, as set by the site induction. If the work cannot be made safe for the floor or the people around it, stop the work and make the area safe before resuming. If slurry reaches a drain, stop the water flow at once, contain the flow, tell the site manager and record the event. Follow the incident reporting procedure for the site.

lessons.title: Quoting restoration work with hazard controls priced in
learningOutcomes: List the items a stone restoration quote must show, including the controls and exclusions
Price the wet method, extraction, isolation, test patches and documentation as scope, not as overheads that can be dropped
Write a variation clause for surprises such as a surface that cannot be identified, no water supply or an occupied space.
Explain why a quote does not grant any authority to do regulated work

instructionSections.heading: What a stone quote has to show
instructionSections.body: A quote for stone restoration is a plan of the work, and it should show the scope in terms a client can check. State the surface, the area, the material and finish as far as they are known, and the identification basis. Show the process: assessment, test patch, the honing and polishing sequence, sealing where it is included, cure time and handover. Show the controls as line items: the wet method and water supply, on-tool extraction or ventilation, isolation of the area, the drain and slurry containment, the respiratory protection and health monitoring arrangements where they apply, and the waste disposal. Exclusions must be written down. Typical exclusions include structural repair, cutting and installation, removal of stains that the test patch shows cannot be removed, and any engineered stone work, which this business does not take (“The engineered stone prohibition and what it means on a job”). A quote that prices labour only, and leaves out the controls, is not a valid quote for this work.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing the controls as scope
instructionSections.body: The controls take time and equipment, and they must be paid for. The water supply, the extraction, the isolation barriers, the slurry containment and the test patch take time before and after the main work. A specialist rate is earned by pricing the identification, the test, the correct sequence, the sealing and the documentation, not by reducing the controls to make the price look smaller. Use the business pricing method and the minimum charge set in the business policy for site setup and isolation. Where the material costs are passed through, use the materials cost policy. If a competitor's price is lower because it leaves out a control, the quote still needs the control, and the difference should be explained to the client rather than hidden. A price that depends on a control being left out is not a price this business offers.

instructionSections.heading: Variation clauses for the surprises
instructionSections.body: Stone jobs produce surprises. The surface may turn out to be engineered stone or may not be confirmed, the water supply may be unavailable, the area may be occupied, or the test patch may show that the finish needs a different and longer sequence. Each of these is a variation. Write the variation rule into the quote: the work stops until the identification is confirmed, the variation is priced in writing and approved before the work resumes, and any extra time or equipment is charged under the variation rate. Do not start unpriced high-hazard work, and do not start work that the variation has not approved. Record each approval.

lessons.title: Customer expectations, pre-existing damage and written limits
learningOutcomes: Explain the normal variation in natural stone and terrazzo and set client expectations before work starts
Photograph and record pre-existing damage before touching the surface
State the limits of the work in writing, including exclusions and what may remain after the work
Handle a client complaint about the finish through the business escalation route

instructionSections.heading: Set the expectation before the work starts
instructionSections.body: Natural stone and terrazzo vary. Colour changes across a slab, veining and fine lines are normal features of the stone, and pits and natural voids are part of the material. Terrazzo has chips of varying colour and size set in a matrix. Restoration changes the sheen and sometimes the colour, and the result depends on the stone, the age of the finish, the wear, the existing sealer and the test patch. Explain this to the client before the work starts, in plain words and in writing. Services under the Australian Consumer Law must be performed with reasonable care and competence, and finished in a timely manner where no time is agreed. Do not promise a mirror finish, a colour match or the removal of a particular mark until the test patch has shown what is achievable. Once the test patch is done, tell the client the result, and record the client's acknowledgement of it.

instructionSections.heading: Record the damage that was already there
instructionSections.body: Walk the site with the client before the work starts, and photograph the existing chips, cracks, stains, etch marks, previous repairs, lifting, loose tiles and grout failure. Record each item with its position and the date. Record anything that is outside scope, such as a crack that needs structural repair or a loose tile that needs re-fixing. Pre-existing damage protects both the client and the business: it shows what was there before the work, and it shows which problems the work did not cause. Tell the client in writing where a stain or mark may not be removed by the work. Record the client's acknowledgement with the photographs in the job record.

instructionSections.heading: Write the limits and handle a complaint
instructionSections.body: State the limits of the work in writing. The limits include what the business will and will not do, that engineered stone is not taken on by this business (“The engineered stone prohibition and what it means on a job”), that structural repair, cutting and installation are out of scope, and that some marks may remain after the test patch and the work. Keep communication respectful and clear, and do not make legal statements about regulated work that the business is not authorised to give. Privacy and access rules apply to the client's home or premises, and the client's property is handled under the business privacy policy. If the client complains about the finish, record the complaint, check it against the test patch record and the photographs, and follow the complaint escalation route in the business policy. A complaint is not resolved by promising a different finish that the work cannot give.

lessons.title: Strata by-laws, common property and access rules
learningOutcomes: Identify the building's by-laws, the common property and the access rules before work.
Distinguish common property from private lots, and clean only what is in scope.
Follow the access and notice rules and escalate any conflict with the owners' corporation or manager.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the rules
instructionSections.body: A strata or common-area building has rules set out in its by-laws and its access arrangements. Before work, obtain the relevant rules: what the common property is, who controls access to it, when work may be done, and what notice is needed. The by-laws differ between buildings, and the building manager or the owners' corporation can confirm them. In NSW, the owners corporation, working through the strata committee, is responsible for repairing and maintaining common property, while owners handle repairs inside their own lot (NSW Government strata repairs page; last updated 22 June 2026). Victoria's Owners Corporations Act 2006 is in force, and its current version shows an effective date of 9 September 2026 (legislation page; duty wording not read). Victoria also lets an owners corporation restrict short stays through a rule backed by three quarters of lot owners (Consumer Affairs Victoria page; last updated 8 January 2025).

instructionSections.heading: Common property and private lots
instructionSections.body: Common property includes the lobby, the stairs, the lifts, the corridors and the shared facilities. Private lots belong to individual owners or tenants. Clean only the common property you are contracted for, and do not enter a private lot unless the owner or the manager has authorised it in writing. Do not move residents' property in common areas.

instructionSections.heading: Access and conflict
instructionSections.body: Follow the access and notice rules, including key and fob control, quiet hours and the route for deliveries. If a resident objects, or if a rule conflicts with the work order, stop that part of the task and refer the conflict to the building manager. Record the conflict and the decision, and do not resolve it yourself.

lessons.title: Common-area and lift/lobby service schedules
learningOutcomes: Build a service schedule for common areas, lifts and lobbies that shows frequency and method.
Keep lift cars and lift controls clean without working on the lift mechanism.
Schedule work around peak use and keep a record of each visit.

instructionSections.heading: Building the schedule
instructionSections.body:
A common-area schedule is the agreement between the cleaner and the building manager about what is cleaned, how often, how, with which products and in what time window. Start by walking the building with the manager and listing each area: the lobby floor and entrance mats, the lift cars, the lift lobbies, the stairwells, the corridors, the letterboxes, the bin areas, the glass doors and the handrails. For each area, record the frequency, the method, the products, the equipment and the time window. Frequencies are a matter for the building manager and the strata committee's arrangements. Any frequency written in a training example is an example only.

High-touch points are the surfaces that many people touch in a day, such as lift buttons, handrails, door plates, intercom panels and letterbox handles. They are usually cleaned more often than corridors or stairwells. Set those surfaces out on their own line in the schedule, so that a visit cannot skip them because the rest of the area looked clean. Record the agreed frequency in writing, and keep the copy on site. Do not work from memory, because a schedule that lives in one person's head cannot be checked or handed over.

Build in a review point. A schedule that is set once and never revisited can drift from what the building needs, especially after a change in use, a new tenant mix or a new fitout. Record the date of the last review and the person who agreed the change.

instructionSections.heading: Lift cars and controls
instructionSections.body: Clean lift car walls, floors, handrails, mirrors and the outside faces of the call buttons and panels with approved methods. Keep liquid away from the buttons, the display and any gap in the panel, because liquid can get into the controls. Apply product to the cloth first, then wipe the surface, rather than spraying the panel directly. Dry the surface afterwards so that no film builds up on the buttons or the floor. Do not open the lift panels, the machine room or the shaft, and do not work on the lift mechanism, the doors or the sensors. Those parts are maintenance and repair work for the lift service company. The New South Wales WorkSafe guidance on lifts states that the people who have management or control of a lift must make sure it is inspected and maintained regularly, and that records of inspection and maintenance must be kept (SafeWork NSW, lifts and escalators page; modified 28 July 2023). In Queensland, the licence categories on the WorkSafe Queensland lifts page name installation of a new unit and repair or modernisation of an existing unit as licensed work, and the page does not mention servicing or cleaning (WorkSafe Queensland, lifts and escalators licence page; no date shown). Report faults at once, such as a sticking button, a sensor that does not respond, a light that is out or a door that does not close fully. The NSW guidance says that when a lift malfunctions, the lift service company should be called to help anyone trapped, and that the service company or building management must take the lift out of service until it is repaired (SafeWork NSW, lifts and escalators page; modified 28 July 2023). Your role is to stop use where the manager agrees, put up a notice, and report it. It is not to try the repair.

instructionSections.heading: Peak use, closures and the visit record
instructionSections.body:
Schedule the heavier work outside peak use, such as the early morning or late evening in a residential block, or the quieter part of the day in a commercial building. Put up signs and barriers where the lobby is in use, and keep walkways clear. Where a lift or a lobby must close for cleaning, agree the closure time with the manager, and give notice to the people who use it in the way the manager has agreed.

Keep a visit record for each area. Record the date, the time, the method, the products, any defect found and the name of the person who did the work. A missed visit is recorded as missed, with the reason, and the manager is told at once. A blank line in a visit record looks the same as a visit that was not done, so the record must show the difference. A complete record is the main evidence that the schedule was met.

lessons.title: Shared-facility hygiene and tenant notice
learningOutcomes: Clean shared facilities with approved methods and dedicated tools.
Give tenants notice of work and closures in the agreed way.
Report damage, contamination and unsafe conditions in shared facilities.

instructionSections.heading: Shared facilities and why hygiene matters
instructionSections.body:
Shared facilities such as laundries, gyms, bin rooms, lounges and pool areas are used by many people, often in close contact, and the same surfaces are touched again and again. Hygiene in those spaces protects residents from contamination and protects the building from complaints, odours and pests. Before cleaning a facility, identify what it is, who uses it and what its own rules say. Some facilities have posted hours, booking systems, equipment rules or cleaning schedules. Follow those rules, and do not use a facility that is closed for maintenance.

Separate the work by area. A bin room is a high-contamination area, a laundry has wet surfaces and lint, and a gym has sweat, handles and equipment that needs its own approved product. Use dedicated tools for each area. A mop or cloth used in a bin room should never be used in a laundry or a gym, because it carries the contamination with it. Store each set of tools separately, and use a colour or label system where the building uses one. The colour system in a training example is an example only, not a standard.

A pool area is a special case. Pool and spa water quality, chemical handling and access rules are set by the owner, the manager and the regulator for the jurisdiction. This lesson does not cover pool water treatment, and it does not authorise any pool work. If your task includes the surrounds of a pool, follow the manager's instructions and the approved method, and stop at the water line unless the work has been defined and approved separately.

instructionSections.heading: Giving notice to tenants
instructionSections.body: Tenants should know in advance when a facility will be cleaned, closed or restricted. Give notice of work and closures in the way the building manager has agreed, which may be a printed notice, an email, a message through the building app or a sign at the entrance. The notice should state the facility, the date, the start and end times, and whether the facility is closed or only restricted. Where the work can change the way people reach their home or use a service, say so clearly, and offer the manager's contact details for questions. Give the notice in time for the people affected to plan. Keep a copy of the notice, the method it was sent by, and the date and time it was posted or sent. A notice that is not given in time, or cannot be shown to have been given, leaves residents surprised and gives the manager no evidence to rely on.

instructionSections.heading: Reporting damage, contamination and unsafe conditions
instructionSections.body:
Report damage, contamination, blocked drains, pest activity, leaking pipes and unsafe conditions to the building manager at once. Give the location, what you saw, when you saw it and whether anyone is at risk. Where a condition is unsafe, close the area off with signs and barriers, and keep people out until the manager confirms it is safe. Do not attempt repairs to equipment, drains, appliances or fittings in the facility, because repairs belong to the person responsible for the equipment.

Record what you found and the time, with a photograph where the building's photo rules allow it. Where the same problem appears again, record each occurrence so that the manager can see the pattern. A written record protects both the cleaner and the building, and it stops a report being lost between the cleaner and the manager.

lessons.title: Tiling basics for handymen: tile check, cut and fix
learningOutcomes: Check tiles and the substrate for size, flatness and condition before fixing.
Cut and fix tiles on a dry, sound substrate with the correct adhesive and spacing.
Identify when a wet area or waterproofing task is referred under “Tile types, substrate assessment and waterproofing boundary”.

instructionSections.heading: Check the tile and the substrate first
instructionSections.body: Before fixing, check the tiles for size, thickness, flatness, colour and any chips or cracks. Lay out a dry run and check the set-out so that cut tiles are not too narrow at the edges. Check the substrate: it must be flat, sound, clean, dry and firm. Tiling over a loose, damp, dusty or deflecting surface gives tiles that lift or crack. Note any substrate fault and fix or refer it before tiling begins.

instructionSections.heading: Cut and fix
instructionSections.body: Cut tiles with a suitable cutter or wet saw, and check each cut against the layout. Spread adhesive with a notched trowel suited to the tile size, and back-butter large tiles where the data sheet requires it. Press each tile into the adhesive and use spacers to keep joints even. Check the tiles are level with a straight edge as you go, and correct lipping while the adhesive is workable. Allow the adhesive to set for the time the data sheet gives before grouting or walking on the surface.

instructionSections.heading: Where tiling stops and referral starts
instructionSections.body: Wet areas and waterproofing are not covered by this basic lesson. Where tiles are to be fixed in a shower, around a bath, or in an area that needs a waterproof membrane, refer under “Tile types, substrate assessment and waterproofing boundary”, because the waterproofing position is recorded as needing a licence check. Before you accept any tiling work, check the licence position for its value in your state. In New South Wales the contractor licence applies above $5,000 of labour and materials, GST included, as the NSW Government page last updated on 23 June 2026 shows. Do not tile over a waterproofing system that you cannot identify.

lessons.title: Tile types, substrate assessment and waterproofing boundary
learningOutcomes: Identify common tile types and their fixing requirements.
Assess a substrate for movement, flatness, moisture and suitability for the tile.
Identify the waterproofing boundary and refer wet-area work where the position is not established.

instructionSections.heading: Tile types need different fixing
instructionSections.body: Ceramic and porcelain tiles differ in water absorption, weight and size, and porcelain is often denser and harder to cut. Natural stone is porous and can stain, and some stones need sealing. Glass and mosaic tiles need a fixing and a grout suited to their size and their backing. Large-format tiles need flatter substrates and a suitable adhesive. Check the manufacturer data for the tile and the adhesive, and record the product.

instructionSections.heading: Assess the substrate and the boundary
instructionSections.body: Refer wet-area waterproofing to a competent or licensed person, and do not tile over a membrane that you cannot identify.

lessons.title: Setting, spacing and grouting
learningOutcomes: Set tiles with even spacing and a level finish across the area.
Achieve full adhesive coverage behind each tile.
Grout joints to the grout's data sheet and clean the surface without damaging it.

instructionSections.heading: Before the first tile goes down
instructionSections.body: Setting is only as good as the bed and the layout beneath it. Confirm that the substrate has been assessed and prepared as set out in “Tile types, substrate assessment and waterproofing boundary”, and that the area is clean, dry and within the moisture limit that the adhesive data sheet gives. Dry-lay the tiles from the chosen centre line or main line so that the cut tiles at the edges are a sensible size. Check the tile batch for shade and size variation before opening the boxes, because a mixed batch can show across a floor. Mix only the adhesive that can be used within its open time, and read that time from the data sheet rather than from habit. Choose the trowel notch for the tile size and the bed thickness that the data sheet gives. A larger tile usually needs a deeper bed, but the actual figures come from the product.

instructionSections.heading: Spacing, level and lippage
instructionSections.body: Use spacers of one consistent width across the area so that the joints run straight and even. The joint width depends on the tile, its edge profile and the grout the data sheet allows, so set it before you start rather than adjusting it tile by tile. Check the face level of each tile against its neighbour with a straight edge laid across the joint, or with a lippage gauge where one is used. Lippage is the step between adjacent tile edges. It can be felt underfoot and it catches the light, so it is checked while the adhesive is still workable. If a tile sits proud, lift it and re-set it while the bed is open. Do not tap a tile down into a bed that is already skinning over, because that pushes the adhesive out and leaves a void behind. Write the finish tolerance in the quote or the task sheet in a form that can be measured, such as a stated gap under a straight edge of a stated length. The numbers must be set for the job and the tile. The format is an example only; no tolerance figure is given in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Adhesive coverage and back-buttering
instructionSections.body: Coverage is the share of the tile back that is in contact with adhesive, and it matters more than speed. Lift a sample tile at intervals, for example after each small section, and look at the back. Contact should show across the area that the data sheet requires, with the adhesive ridges combed in one direction so that air is not trapped. Large tiles, heavy stone and tiles in wet or heavily walked areas usually need back-buttering as well, where the data sheet asks for it. Tap each tile with the handle of a tool after it is set. A solid sound suggests a full bed. A hollow or drummy sound means a void, and that tile is lifted and re-bedded while the adhesive is workable. Hollow areas crack under foot traffic or when the substrate moves. A crack that appears later is far harder to explain than a sample lift taken now, and the record of the lift is the evidence that the bed was checked.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing and mixing the grout
instructionSections.body: Choose the grout type and colour from the tile, the joint width and the use of the area. Check the data sheet for the joint widths the product is designed for. Cement-based grout and epoxy grout behave differently. They need different mixing, working time, cleaning and curing, and some tile faces are sensitive to some products. Mix to the ratio on the data sheet, and measure the water and the powder rather than estimating them. Mix only the amount you can use within the working time. Do not add water to a grout that has begun to stiffen unless the data sheet allows it. If the data sheet calls for a slaking or rest period before the final mix, allow it. Keep grout from different batches apart, or mix them together only if the product allows it, because a shade difference will show across a finished floor.

instructionSections.heading: Grouting, finishing and cleaning
instructionSections.body: Press grout into the joints with a rubber float held at an angle, working diagonally across the joints so that the grout is forced into the gap and the joint fills without voids. Work in small areas that you can finish within the working time. Remove the excess from the tile faces as the data sheet directs, using the float at the stage it names, and do not let grout dry into a haze on the face. Clean the surface with a damp sponge and a clean water change. Rinse the sponge often, because a dirty sponge spreads grout back over the tiles. Polish the surface only with the cloth or product the data sheet names. Natural stone, unglazed tile and some glazed finishes can be marked or etched by acid-based cleaners, so use only the cleaner the data sheet allows. Where the data sheet calls for it, test a hidden area first. Sealing, where it is part of the job, is a separate step with its own data sheet and is not covered here.

instructionSections.heading: Curing, inspection and the finished record
instructionSections.body: Keep foot traffic off the floor, and keep the area dry, for the cure time the data sheet gives. Once the grout has cured, look along the joints in good light for pinholes, shrinkage, low spots and unfilled sections. If the data sheet allows a repair with the same product, fill and finish the defect and record it. Take the finish inspection photographs with the client's permission. If a void or a hollow is found after grouting, record the location, the cause if it is known, and the repair. Do not describe the repair as a guarantee of the floor, because the record shows only what was checked on the day.

lessons.title: Floating floor installation (underlay, expansion gaps)
learningOutcomes: Prepare a substrate and underlay for a floating floor to the manufacturer's requirements.
Leave expansion gaps at walls, fixed objects and transitions.
Identify where licence positions for floating floors are not established in each state.

instructionSections.heading: What a floating floor is, and why the product decides the method
instructionSections.body: A floating floor is laid over a substrate and is held together at its joints rather than bonded or fixed to the substrate. Because it is not fixed down, the whole floor can move as one piece, and most of the installation rules come from that movement. Products differ. Laminate, engineered timber and vinyl plank are installed in different ways, and each manufacturer's instructions set the joint method, the order of laying, the tools and the underlay. Read those instructions before quoting or starting, and keep a copy in the job file. This lesson gives the principles that apply to most floating floors. It does not replace the product's own method.

instructionSections.heading: Substrate flatness and moisture
instructionSections.body: The substrate must be sound, clean and flat within the tolerance the manufacturer gives. Check flatness with a straight edge and a feeler gauge across the area, and mark any high or low spot for grinding, filling or levelling by the method the product allows. Moisture is the most common cause of floating floor failure, so measure it before any underlay goes down. Use the test method the manufacturer names, record the reading, and record the method used. Where the reading is over the limit, stop. A moisture barrier is installed only where the product calls for one, and only as the product directs. Do not lay a floating floor over a substrate that is wet, sweating or showing signs of rising damp. A surface that looks dry is not a measurement, and the reading decides.

instructionSections.heading: Underlay, acclimatisation and the sample row
instructionSections.body: Confirm the underlay type with the product before buying it, because some underlay forms part of the manufacturer's conditions. Acclimatise the planks or boards in the room, flat and unopened where the product allows, for the time the manufacturer gives, so that they reach the room's temperature and humidity before they are laid. Lay the underlay as directed, with seams taped or overlapped as specified and turned up at the walls where the product requires it. Start the first run against a straight reference line, check it for square, and lay a sample row before committing to the layout. Check the end-piece lengths the product allows, so that a short last piece does not appear against a wall. Mix boards from several cartons as you go, so that no shade band or pattern repeat shows across the room.

instructionSections.heading: Expansion gaps at walls, fixed objects and pipes
instructionSections.body: A floating floor moves with changes in temperature and humidity, so it needs an expansion gap at every wall, fixed object, pipe, column, cabinet base and threshold. The gap width comes from the manufacturer's data, and it is not a figure to estimate. Set the gap with spacers during laying, check it at every run, and remove the spacers at the end. Cover the gap with the approved trim, skirting or transition, and fix the trim to the wall or the skirting rather than to the floor, so that the floor can still move beneath it. A floor laid tight to a wall has nowhere to go when it expands, and it then buckles or lifts. Do not hide the gap with sealant unless the manufacturer allows it, because sealant can lock the floor in place and transfer the movement to the joints.

instructionSections.heading: Transitions, doorways and large areas
instructionSections.body: Each doorway, threshold and change of floor covering needs an approved transition strip or trim that allows the floor to move. Where the floor runs a long distance in one direction, the manufacturer may require an intermediate movement joint or a transition. A transition fixed rigidly across the joint can stop the movement and cause the same damage as a tight wall. Choose the transition to suit the height difference between the two floors and the direction of the joint, and fix it as the product directs. Record each transition, its type and its fixing, and photograph the joint before the trim covers it.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing, handover and the client's conditions
instructionSections.body: Remove all spacers before the room is used, and check each joint and each transition for lift, squeaks and a hollow sound. Clean the floor using only the products the instructions allow. Explain the conditions that affect the floor, such as keeping the room within the temperature and humidity range the manufacturer gives, using the mats and furniture protection the manufacturer recommends, and not dragging heavy furniture across it. Give the client the product information and the record of the moisture reading, underlay, gaps and transitions. A warranty is the manufacturer's to give, on the manufacturer's terms. Do not describe any warranty as given by the installer unless the written terms say so.

lessons.title: Cutting tile and silica dust controls
learningOutcomes: Cut tile with wet methods where the product and the tool allow them.
Control silica dust from cutting, using extraction and suitable respiratory protection.
Clean up tile dust with damp methods and avoid dry sweeping.

instructionSections.heading: Wet cutting controls dust at source
instructionSections.body: Many tiles, especially porcelain and natural stone, contain crystalline silica, and cutting them dry releases fine silica dust. Use a wet saw with a constant water supply wherever the tile and the job allow it, because wet cutting keeps most of the dust in the slurry. Keep the water level and flow adequate, and keep the blade wet. Cut outdoors or in a ventilated area where a wet saw is not practical, and keep occupants and children away from the cutting area. The workplace exposure standard for respirable crystalline silica is 0.05 mg/m3 averaged over an 8-hour period, half the former 0.1 mg/m3 figure (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown; Safe Work Australia research page, no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Dry cutting, clean-up and protection
instructionSections.body: Where dry cutting is unavoidable, use a tool with extraction and suitable respiratory protection fitted correctly. Do not use an angle grinder without extraction for tile. Clean up slurry and dust with damp methods. Keep slurry and wash water out of stormwater. Council guidance for Woollahra in New South Wales says runoff that could reach drains must be filtered to below 50 mg/L (total suspended solids) before it is discharged, and small volumes may be left to soak away in a designated area (no document date shown). Larger volumes go to a recycler or landfill. Do not dry sweep tile dust, and do not blow it with compressed air. Keep the cutting area separate from the rest of the work until clean-up is complete.

lessons.title: Tiling quotes, levels and defect boundaries
learningOutcomes: Write a tiling quote that states the scope, the substrate preparation, the tile and the exclusions.
Identify the defect boundary between the tiler's work and the substrate or waterproofing that is excluded.
Check the licence threshold for tiling work before quoting.

instructionSections.heading: What the quote has to state
instructionSections.body: A tiling quote defines the job, so it has to say what is included as well as what is not. State the areas to be tiled, the tile and who supplies it, the substrate preparation that is included, the adhesive, the grout and any sealing, the layout pattern and the cuts, the waste allowance, access and working hours, and the exclusions. Items that are commonly excluded are substrate repairs and levelling, waterproofing, structural work, removal of old floor coverings or tiles, and any testing or removal the job needs for hazardous materials. Where an item is excluded, say so in the quote and offer to price it separately. Do not leave the substrate preparation unstated, because the client will assume it is included.

instructionSections.heading: Setting a finish standard that can be checked
instructionSections.body: A finish standard is only useful if it can be measured on site. A client who expects a flat finish over an uneven substrate will be disappointed unless the levelling is included or quoted separately. Tie the standard to the tile and to the substrate. For example, the quote can state that the finish will be measured with a straight edge over a stated length, and that the result will be recorded at handover. The tolerance figures are set for each job and are not given in this lesson. Wording such as perfectly level or flawless cannot be checked, and a dispute then turns on the wording rather than on the work.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the substrate before tiling
instructionSections.body: Before any tile goes down, record the substrate as it is found: its flatness, cracks, moisture where it is measured, previous adhesives or coverings, movement joints and any visible water staining. Photograph each area with the client's permission, and include a straight edge or scale in the frame where the photograph is meant to show flatness. Record in writing the substrate condition the client has accepted. This record is what separates a setting defect, which belongs to the tiler, from a substrate defect, which may not. Older floor coverings, mastics and adhesives can contain asbestos. If the job may disturb them, stop and refer the testing and removal to a licensed or competent person before any work starts. The asbestos thresholds are not verified in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Defect boundaries and consumer guarantees
instructionSections.body: Defects that come from the tile, the adhesive, the grout or the setting are the tiler's to put right, and the quote and the record define that boundary. Defects that come from substrate movement, an excluded waterproofing system, a previous trade or another unrelated cause sit outside the tiler's work, and they must be recorded with evidence. Whether a quote exclusion limits a consumer guarantee claim is a legal question, and this lesson does not settle it. The ACCC business guidance sets out three service guarantees: care and skill, suitability for a stated purpose, and completion within a reasonable time where no time was agreed. The same page states that a trader's own words or conduct cannot switch these basic rights off. The NSW Government notes that the guarantees operate separately from any warranty a trader gives.

instructionSections.heading: Variations and written approval
instructionSections.body: A variation is any change to the agreed scope, such as extra levelling, a changed tile, an additional cut pattern or a substrate problem found during the work. Price each variation, describe what it adds and what it leaves out, and get the client's written approval before the work is done. Keep each variation with the quote and the substrate record. A verbal approval for an extra area is the most common source of a dispute about who pays, so the record should be complete before the work starts.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the licence position before quoting
instructionSections.body: The licence position depends on the state, the value of the job and the trades involved, so check it before the quote is issued, and check again if the scope grows. In New South Wales, the tiling page sets out a contractor licence or supervisor certificate for work valued above a threshold that includes GST, and it lists waterproofing of wet areas before tiling among the covered work. In Victoria, a job involving only one listed trade, including wall and floor tiling, does not need building practitioner registration, but combining skills on one job does. In Queensland, wall and floor tiling is a QBCC licence class. The page gives a $3,300 limit for incidental work, and the page read did not give a separate tiling dollar threshold. In South Australia, anyone carrying on business as a building work contractor needs the right licence. The guide sets no dollar threshold and does not name tiling.

lessons.title: Tile and grout sealing
learningOutcomes: Select a sealer suited to the tile, the grout and the exposure, using the data sheet.
Clean and dry the tile and grout before sealing, and test the sealer on a small area.
Explain the boundary between sealing and waterproofing, and refer waterproofing work.

instructionSections.heading: Sealing is not waterproofing
instructionSections.body: A sealer protects porous tile and grout from stains and dirt. It does not make a wet area waterproof, and it does not repair a failed membrane or a cracked grout line. Natural stone, unglazed tile and cementitious grout are the usual candidates for sealing, and glazed tile normally needs grout sealing only. Confirm the tile and grout type before choosing a sealer, because some sealers change the look of the surface or are not compatible with some stone. Waterproofing is referred under “Tile types, substrate assessment and waterproofing boundary”.

instructionSections.heading: Clean, test and apply
instructionSections.body: Clean the tile and grout fully before sealing, because any residue is sealed in. Let the surface dry for the time the data sheet requires, and check the moisture before sealing. Test the sealer on a small hidden area and check the appearance after it dries. Apply the sealer in thin, even coats, and do not flood the surface. Wipe off excess before it dries, and keep traffic off the surface until the data sheet's cure time has passed. Record the product, the batch, the coats and the cure time.

lessons.title: Timber floor restoration: scope, boundaries and what this training does not grant
learningOutcomes: Describe the timber floor restoration work that is included in and excluded from the approved scope.
Identify when a job falls outside the scope and must be referred instead of performed.
Explain why completing this lesson does not grant a licence or authority to do regulated work.

instructionSections.heading: What timber floor restoration includes
instructionSections.body: Timber floor restoration brings an existing timber floor back to a clean, serviceable and finished condition. Within an approved scope this can include sanding and screening, filling small surface defects in boards, staining, oiling or sealing, recoating, and cleaning up the dust and residue the work creates. The job is defined by a written scope that names the rooms, the finish to be applied, the surfaces excluded and the outcome the client has agreed. A worker does not widen that scope on their own judgement, even when the extra work looks easy.

instructionSections.heading: What the course excludes
instructionSections.body: Structural timber repair, subfloor and joist work, and any decision that a floor is structurally sound are outside this course and usually outside the job. Installing a new floor belongs to the flooring trade, and floating floors sit in the tiling business. Routine care of sealed timber is covered in the hard floor care course. Work on a floor that may contain lead paint, asbestos adhesive or asbestos-backed vinyl is excluded until a documented assessment has set the controls. In South Australia, SafeWork SA's asbestos licence page (page date not shown) says that removing asbestos-backed vinyl needs a Class A licence.

instructionSections.heading: Training is not a licence
instructionSections.body: Completing this course, or any Skilled lesson, does not give a licence, certificate or authority to do regulated work. Whether a licence, registration or notification is needed depends on the state or territory, the material and the activity. Where a licence is required, the work goes to a person who holds that licence.

instructionSections.heading: Why scope is checked before the first machine starts
instructionSections.body: A sanding job changes the floor quickly. Once a board is cut through, a finish has been stripped, or old material has been disturbed, the damage or the exposure cannot simply be undone. The scope and the site conditions are therefore checked before any machine starts, and any change is agreed in writing before work continues. The scope record protects the worker, the client and the business, and it is the first document an assessor will ask for.

lessons.title: Identify the timber, the board type and the existing finish
learningOutcomes: Distinguish solid timber, engineered boards and other timber floor types by observation and the client's records.
Record the existing finish and the condition of the boards before any work starts.
Decide when a floor needs further assessment before any sanding.

instructionSections.heading: Why identify the floor first
instructionSections.body: A timber floor is not one material. Solid hardwood, softwood and engineered boards with a timber top layer over a different core behave differently under a sander and under a finish. Board type affects how much material can be removed, the sanding sequence, the dust produced and the finish that will adhere. Identify the floor before any machine is used, and record clearly what you can confirm and what you cannot.

instructionSections.heading: Board type and species
instructionSections.body: Look at the edge profile, the end grain, the grain pattern and the board width. Solid boards usually show the same timber through the thickness at the edge. Engineered boards often show a layered core at the edge or a thin top layer that can be sanded through. Hardwood and softwood are not always clear by eye. Do not guess a species to fit a limit.

instructionSections.heading: Existing finish and board condition
instructionSections.body: A film finish such as polyurethane can look glossy and resist a scratch. A penetrating oil or wax often looks dull or patchy. Note any cupping, crowning, gaps, loose or lifted boards, insect damage, staining and water damage. Note any paint, varnish or adhesive that is not part of the original finish. Those marks trigger the pre-start assessment in “Pre-start assessment: lead, asbestos and suspect materials in old floors” before any sanding is planned.

instructionSections.heading: Information from the client
instructionSections.body: Ask for the building age, any previous refinishing, and any product records the client holds. Record what is known and what is not. A product name the client gives you is client-reported information. It is not a confirmed fact, and it must not be used as proof of what the finish is.

instructionSections.heading: Checks that do not create a hazard
instructionSections.body: Use visual inspection and the manufacturer's information. Do not carry out a solvent rub test in an enclosed room, and do not drill or cut a board to see what lies underneath. Both can release dust or disturb material that may need assessment. Where a test is needed, use an approved, written method that the supervisor has signed off.

lessons.title: Pre-start assessment: lead, asbestos and suspect materials in old floors
learningOutcomes: Explain why old paint, varnish, adhesive and vinyl can contain hazardous material that appearance does not rule out.
Apply a stop-and-refer decision when a floor may contain lead or asbestos.
Describe the kind of controls that a documented assessment must set before any disturbance.

instructionSections.heading: Why old finishes are a hazard
instructionSections.body: Timber floors in older buildings can carry layers of paint, varnish and adhesive from earlier work. NSW LeadSmart (page published 18 May 2026) says most Australian homes built before 1970 contained lead paint. Floor coverings and adhesives in older buildings may also contain asbestos. Neither lead nor asbestos can be ruled out by how a surface looks.

instructionSections.heading: Lead in old finishes
instructionSections.body: The main concern is lead dust produced by sanding or scraping. Safe Work Australia's lead page (no date shown) treats grinding and sanding that expose workers to lead dust as lead processes, and links lead risk work to a blood lead level above 5 µg/dL for a female of reproductive capacity or above 20 µg/dL in any other case. Treat the surface as possibly lead-containing until a documented assessment, using a method the assessor specifies, says otherwise.

instructionSections.heading: Asbestos in floor coverings and adhesive
instructionSections.body: Asbestos may be present in older vinyl, floor tiles, sheet flooring and adhesives. In South Australia, SafeWork SA's page (no date shown) says that friable asbestos and asbestos-backed vinyl need a Class A removal licence, and that non-friable material such as floor tiles falls under a Class B licence where more than 10 square metres is removed (the SafeWork SA applicant guide). A worker must not remove, grind or sand suspected asbestos material in order to find out what it is.

instructionSections.heading: The stop-and-refer decision
instructionSections.body: If the assessment cannot rule out lead or asbestos, stop work on that area, keep people out of it, record the finding, and refer it to the supervisor and to the approved assessor or licensed contractor. The error this lesson addresses is carrying on with sanding because the floor looks sound. Do not treat a finish as safe because an earlier contractor worked on it. Clear only the area that the assessment covers, and record that boundary.

instructionSections.heading: Controls once the material is known
instructionSections.body: Where an assessment finds lead or asbestos, the controls come from that assessment and from the regulator's requirements, not from this training. NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) describes wet sanding and wet scraping as the safest way to prepare a surface with lead paint, advises keeping pregnant or breastfeeding women and young children away from renovation work, and advises against open-flame torches. These are NSW government statements, not a national control plan.

lessons.title: Wood dust and formaldehyde: health effects and exposure limits
learningOutcomes: Describe the health effects of wood dust and formaldehyde from engineered boards.
State the exposure values quoted for wood dust and formaldehyde, and say where each value comes from.
Explain why meeting an exposure limit does not replace the control hierarchy.

instructionSections.heading: What wood dust does to the body
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) names occupational asthma and nasal cancer among the lung diseases linked to inhaled wood dust. The same page lists nasal and eye irritation, nosebleeds, skin dermatitis and reduced lung function as effects of exposure. It also reports that the International Agency for Research on Cancer classes wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, with links to cancers of the nose, sinuses and upper throat.

instructionSections.heading: Formaldehyde from engineered boards
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) places formaldehyde in reconstituted wood products such as plywood, particleboard and fibreboard including MDF. The same page describes short-term irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, and treats formaldehyde as carcinogenic under the GHS classification that Safe Work Australia adopts. Treat sanding dust from engineered boards as a formaldehyde source as well as a wood dust source until the product information says otherwise.

instructionSections.heading: Exposure values and what to check
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) quotes, from Safe Work Australia's April 2024 list, softwood dust at 5 mg/m3 averaged over eight hours and 10 mg/m3 short-term, and certain hardwoods such as beech and oak at 1 mg/m3 averaged over eight hours. Formaldehyde is 1 ppm (1.2 mg/m3) averaged over eight hours and 2 ppm (2.5 mg/m3) short-term in that list. The formaldehyde values are confirmed in the April 2024 Safe Work Australia list.

instructionSections.heading: The December 2026 change
instructionSections.body: Safe Work Australia's news page (no date shown) says the new Workplace exposure limits (WEL) take effect on 1 December 2026, replacing the workplace exposure standards list, and that the transition period ends on 30 November 2026. The same page gives no wood dust value, and says formaldehyde is among nine substances where ministers asked for more impact analysis before its limit is updated. Check the current list on the day of the job and record the check.

instructionSections.heading: A limit is not permission
instructionSections.body: An exposure limit is a reference point for checking control. It does not make an uncontrolled sanding process acceptable. The control hierarchy is applied first, and exposure is checked against the limit to confirm the controls are working. A job that is below a limit on one day can exceed it with a different machine, a closed room or a longer shift.

lessons.title: Dust control: extraction, wet cleaning and safe clean-up
learningOutcomes: Set up extraction at each dust source before sanding starts.
Choose a wet or HEPA clean-up method and explain why dry sweeping and compressed air are not used.
Record the extraction check and the waste disposal for each room.

instructionSections.heading: The control order for sanding dust
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) sets out an order of controls: eliminate first, then substitution, isolation and engineering controls, then administrative controls, with PPE last. For sanding an installed floor, the practical controls are to isolate the work area, to substitute a lower-dust method or product where one is approved, and then to use engineering controls, mainly local exhaust ventilation at each dust source. Administrative controls and PPE come only after those, for the risk that remains.

instructionSections.heading: Extraction at the source
instructionSections.body: Local exhaust ventilation should capture dust as close as possible to each dust source, and every dust source on a machine should be controlled. Portable tools should use on-tool extraction connected to a dust collector, with a minimum recommendation of Dust Class M. WorkSafe Victoria notes that dust bags on portable tools alone do not capture fine dust efficiently. Inspect the extraction before each job, and check hoses and ducts for holes and leaks.

instructionSections.heading: Clean-up with wet methods and HEPA
instructionSections.body: Use wet cleaning methods such as mopping and wiping, and damp down surfaces before sweeping, as WorkSafe Victoria recommends; SafeWork NSW's wood dust page (last modified 11 July 2023) gives the same advice. Dry sweeping is listed by WorkSafe Victoria as an activity that generates airborne wood dust, and it is not presented as an acceptable method. Use an industrial vacuum with a HEPA filter, also rated at least Dust Class M, for dust that remains. Use the same approach for dust on clothing and equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Never use compressed air
instructionSections.body: Compressed air must not be used to clear workbenches, and it must not be used to blow dust off skin or clothing. WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) says compressed air re-suspends dust and poses an eye injury risk, and that on skin or clothing it can push air into the circulation, with serious effects including death. A HEPA vacuum is the method to use for clothing.

instructionSections.heading: Keep dust in the room where it is made
instructionSections.body: Seal the work area with plastic and tape, close doors to adjoining rooms, and keep occupants and pets out. Keep the sanding sequence moving so dust is removed at the machine rather than left in the room. Dust from the job must be bagged and labelled according to the approved waste procedure, not left loose in the room or placed in ordinary household bins without approval.

lessons.title: Respiratory protection and fit: the last layer of control
learningOutcomes: Explain why respiratory protection is the last layer of control, after extraction and other measures.
Select a respirator and filter type from the assessment and its markings, and state the standards named by the regulators.
Carry out a fit check before every use of a facial-seal respirator, and record it.

instructionSections.heading: Respirators are the last layer
instructionSections.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) says a respirator is needed where the higher controls cannot hold exposure within the limits. A respirator protects only the person wearing it, and it works only when it fits and is the right type. It is not a substitute for extraction, damp cleaning or isolation of the work area. If the controls are not set up, the job does not start until they are.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the respirator and filter
instructionSections.body: For wood dust, WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) indicates that a non-disposable half-face unit fitted with a P2 filter generally meets the need. The same page points to AS/NZS 1715 for selection guidance, cites AS/NZS 1716:2012 as the marking to look for, and names a powered air purifying respirator (PAPR) as an alternative. For old paint, NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) advises an AS 1716-approved respirator or a P1 or P2 mask with coveralls, and says paper masks often fit poorly and do not block fine dust.

instructionSections.heading: Fit, facial hair and fit testing
instructionSections.body: Facial-seal respirators need clean-shaven users and a fit check every time they are put on. The WorkSafe Victoria page (reviewed 17/04/2026) says a fit test should be carried out, using either the quantitative or the qualitative method. A person with facial hair that breaks the seal cannot be fit checked on a facial-seal respirator, so the assessment must select a different option, such as a PAPR, before the work proceeds.

instructionSections.heading: Care, storage and records
instructionSections.body: Clean and store the respirator after each use, outside the work area. Keep a record of each respirator issued, its fit test, and the training given. A respirator that is damaged, has a poor seal, or breathes poorly is taken out of use.

lessons.title: Solvents, stains, finishes and fire risk in timber restoration
learningOutcomes: Read a product label and safety data sheet before use, and state the controls they require.
Identify the ignition sources that must be removed from a timber sanding or finishing area.
Describe safe storage and disposal of flammable products and contaminated rags.

instructionSections.heading: Read the label and the safety data sheet first
instructionSections.body: Timber restoration uses stains, oils, sealers, strippers, solvents and cleaners, and each has its own hazards. Before opening a product, read its label and its safety data sheet (SDS) for ventilation, personal protective equipment, storage, incompatibilities and disposal. WorkSafe Queensland's incident alert (no date shown on the page; incident dated March 2022) advises checking the label and SDS for how to handle, store and respond in an emergency, and says SDS should be kept within easy reach of workers. Do not mix products or change their strength to get a different result. Use only products the SDS and the manufacturer approve for the floor and the finish.

instructionSections.heading: Vapours in enclosed rooms
instructionSections.body: Solvent and stain vapours build up in closed rooms. The ventilation the job needs is set by the SDS and the job plan. Do not work in a closed room with a product that needs ventilation until the plan has been confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Ignition sources and dust
instructionSections.body: Open flames, sparks and hot surfaces can ignite vapours. SafeWork NSW (last modified 11 July 2023) warns that wood dust can create an explosion risk, and advises keeping flames and sparks away from areas where dust is produced. Remove open flames, spark-producing tools and unnecessary heaters from the work area unless the plan approves them.

instructionSections.heading: No open-flame stripping
instructionSections.body: Do not use an open-flame torch to strip an old finish. NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) says open-flame torches create lead fumes, and advises the lowest setting and no lingering in one spot for a heat gun. If a heat tool is approved in the plan, follow that advice.

instructionSections.heading: Storage and disposal
instructionSections.body: Store flammable products according to the approved storage procedure and the relevant standard. Used rags and cloths that have been in contact with oil or finish must be placed in a labelled container and disposed of as the approved waste procedure says.

lessons.title: Sanders, polishers and electrical safety on wet and dusty floors
learningOutcomes: Inspect a sander, edger or polisher and its leads before each use, and remove faulty equipment from service.
Explain why electrical equipment must be in-service tested and why cords are controlled on a dusty, wet floor.
Control a floor machine safely, including setting it down and handling it, and use hearing protection where the assessment calls for it.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect before every use
instructionSections.body: Before each use, check the sander, edger, polisher and extraction unit. Look at the cord and plug, the housing, the guards, the switch, the abrasive and the connection to the extraction hose. A cracked housing, a damaged cord or a missing guard means the tool is removed from service and tagged. Do not tape a damaged lead and carry on. Record every inspection and every tool removed from service.

instructionSections.heading: In-service testing and tags
instructionSections.body: Confirm that each tool and extension lead has a current test and tag where the requirement applies. Repairs that involve wiring are not part of this course. Electrical wiring work needs a licence. NSW requires an electrical licence for wiring work regardless of cost or type of work. Queensland's classes page says installing wiring needs an open electrical work licence, and that businesses doing electrical work for others need an electrical contractor licence. In Victoria, Energy Safe Victoria issues electrician licences.

instructionSections.heading: Water, cords and residual current protection
instructionSections.body: Floors that are damp from cleaning or finish products increase the risk of electric shock. Keep cords out of the path of the machine and off the sanded area, and do not let them run over wet surfaces. Use residual current protection where the site plan requires it.

instructionSections.heading: Controlling a floor machine
instructionSections.body: A drum or belt sander can pull, kick or jump if the operator loses control. Hold it with both hands, keep it moving over the floor, and do not let it stop in one place with the drum down, because this causes dips and burns. Switch the machine off before setting it down, and lift it clear of the floor. Heavy machines are moved by two people where the assessment requires it. The Safe Work Australia Model Code on hazardous manual tasks places a duty on the PCBU to manage risks from tasks such as lifting, pushing, pulling and carrying, and sets no numeric weight limit.

instructionSections.heading: Noise and vibration
instructionSections.body: Sanders and polishers produce noise that can damage hearing, and vibration that can affect the hands and arms over time. Safe Work Australia's page for the model Code of Practice on managing noise and preventing hearing loss at work (no date shown) confirms the code exists, but the page gives no exposure values. Use the hearing protection and vibration controls the assessment sets, and rotate tasks where the plan calls for it.

lessons.title: Sanding and screening sequence: preparation, grit order and inspection
learningOutcomes: Prepare a room for sanding, including protection, dust control, and checks for fixings and hazards.
Follow the manufacturer's grit sequence from coarse to fine, and explain why grits are not skipped.
Inspect the floor under raking light after each stage and correct marks before finishing.

instructionSections.heading: Preparation before the first pass
instructionSections.body: Confirm that the pre-start assessment is complete and that no suspect area has been disturbed. Remove furniture and fittings where practical, protect skirtings and adjoining surfaces, seal doorways, and set up extraction at the machine before the first pass. Check the floor for nail heads, staples and screws that could damage the abrasive or the machine. Set or remove them with the approved method. Tell occupants and neighbours of the timing and the restricted area.

instructionSections.heading: The grit sequence
instructionSections.body: Use the abrasive sequence stated by the sanding system manufacturer. Work from the coarsest grit needed to the finest. Use the large machine first, then the edger for edges and the hand tools for corners and tight areas. Keep the machine moving so that it does not dwell in one spot. Do not skip grits to save time, because a coarse scratch left under a fine grit shows through the finish. The specific grit numbers are not set in this draft and must come from the product and the manufacturer for the job.

instructionSections.heading: Screening
instructionSections.body: Screening removes the surface finish and light marks with a fine abrasive or screen pad, depending on the system used. It produces less material removal than sanding and still produces wood dust, so the same extraction and wet-clean controls apply. Screening is not a way to remove deep marks or dips. If a mark remains after the approved sequence, stop and assess the cause rather than repeating passes until it disappears.

instructionSections.heading: Inspection under raking light
instructionSections.body: After each grit stage, check the floor under a raking light, which means a light held low across the surface. Raking light shows dips, swirl marks, burn spots, missed areas and uneven edges that are hard to see under overhead light. Mark each defect, correct it with the approved method at the right grit, and check again. Record the inspection at each stage. A burn mark usually means the machine stopped or dwelt on one spot, and the cause must be fixed before the sanding continues.

instructionSections.heading: Clean before finishing
instructionSections.body: Before any finish is applied, remove dust using the damp method and HEPA vacuum described in “Dust control: extraction, wet cleaning and safe clean-up”. Never dry-sweep, and never use compressed air. Allow the floor to dry as the finish manufacturer states before applying the finish. Check the floor again under raking light just before the finish goes on.

lessons.title: Board repair, gaps and stop-and-refer conditions
learningOutcomes: Classify each board defect as cosmetic, structural or suspect before any repair.
Carry out approved cosmetic repairs to gaps and small surface defects within scope.
Stop and refer structural, water-related, rot, insect or hazardous-material defects.

instructionSections.heading: Classify every defect first
instructionSections.body: Every defect is recorded as cosmetic, structural or suspect before any repair. A cosmetic defect is a surface mark, a small gap or a minor chip that the approved scope covers. A structural defect is one that affects the strength or movement of the floor, such as a bouncing or sagging board, a rotten or crushed board, or movement that suggests a joist or subfloor problem. A suspect defect is one where the cause is not clear, such as a dark stain that may be water, insect damage, or a glued joint that may contain hazardous material.

instructionSections.heading: Structural and water-related defects are referred
instructionSections.body: Structural repair, subfloor work and any decision that a floor is structurally sound are outside this course. A bouncing board or sag must be referred to a qualified person. A dark stain that may come from water is referred, because the cause must be found before it is filled or finished. Filling a stain or a soft board to make it look better hides a problem that the next owner will inherit. Record the referral with photos and the location.

instructionSections.heading: Cosmetic repairs within scope
instructionSections.body: Where the scope allows, small gaps and surface chips can be filled with a filler approved for the timber and the finish. Test the filler colour on an offcut or an inconspicuous area first. Fill after the screening stage, not before, so that the filler is not sanded out or pulled from the joint. Allow the filler to cure as the manufacturer states, and sand it flush with the surrounding surface. Sanding filler creates dust, so the same extraction and HEPA controls for wood dust apply.

instructionSections.heading: Loose boards
instructionSections.body: A loose board that moves under foot may point to a fixing or joist problem. Refix a board only by the method stated in the approved scope. Where the cause of the movement is not clear, treat the board as structural and refer it. Do not add screws or adhesive to a board you have not classified.

instructionSections.heading: Suspect adhesive and material
instructionSections.body: A joint or edge that shows adhesive, black mastic or old filler may contain hazardous material. Stop and assess it under “Pre-start assessment: lead, asbestos and suspect materials in old floors” before any cutting, grinding or filling. Do not fill over a suspect adhesive joint, because the filler does not change the hazard and the disturbance may release dust.

lessons.title: Stains, oils, sealers and recoating: finish control and handover
learningOutcomes: Confirm that a finish is compatible with the sanded timber and the scope before applying it.
Apply thin coats and observe the drying, recoat and cure times stated on the product label.
Walk the floor against the acceptance criteria and hand over care instructions with a signed record.

instructionSections.heading: Confirm compatibility and the approved finish
instructionSections.body: The finish must be the one stated in the approved scope and must be compatible with the sanded timber and any finish that remains. Confirm the product name, the batch and the SDS. Test the stain or finish on an offcut or an inconspicuous area first, and record the result, because the same product can look different on different timbers and under different light. Where the client has chosen the colour, record the choice and the test result they accepted.

instructionSections.heading: Applying thin coats
instructionSections.body: Apply thin coats as the product label states. Thick coats do not dry faster, and they can trap solvent, soften, or show brush or roller marks. Sand between coats only where the label allows it, and remove dust with the damp method from “Dust control: extraction, wet cleaning and safe clean-up” before the next coat, as the wood dust guidance recommends. Keep the room ventilated and free of ignition sources during application, as set out in “Solvents, stains, finishes and fire risk in timber restoration”. Do not pool finish in corners or at joints.

instructionSections.heading: Drying, recoat and cure
instructionSections.body: Use the drying and recoat times stated on the label, adjusted for the actual conditions only where the manufacturer allows. Record the time each coat was applied and when the next coat was started. Restrict foot traffic until the cure time stated by the manufacturer has passed. A floor that feels dry can still be soft underneath. Furniture is returned only after the stated cure time.

instructionSections.heading: Slip and traffic risk
instructionSections.body: Freshly coated floors can be slippery, and footprints and furniture can mark them. Post warning signs, control access and keep the area clear until the stated drying time has passed.

instructionSections.heading: Walkthrough and handover
instructionSections.body: At handover, walk the floor with the client under raking light and check it against the acceptance criteria in the scope. Record any remaining defects, and agree in writing how they will be resolved. Hand over the manufacturer's care instructions for the finish, and the record of the products used. Ask the client to sign the handover record. The record is evidence of what was agreed, not a guarantee of how the floor will look in future.

lessons.title: Quoting timber restoration by scope, hazard and evidence
learningOutcomes: List the included, excluded and assessed items that a timber restoration quote must show.
Price the time for assessment, containment, extraction, clean-up and handover, not only the sanding area.
Handle a variation found after inspection with written approval before work continues.

instructionSections.heading: Price what the job actually needs
instructionSections.body: A timber restoration quote that is priced only by the floor area leaves out most of the work. The job includes the pre-start inspection and assessment, the room protection and sealing, the extraction set-up, the grit stages, the screening, the repairs within scope, the finish and its drying time, the damp clean-up, the waste disposal and the walkthrough. Price each stage in the way the business's approved pricing method states. Do not discount the containment and the clean-up, because they are the controls that keep the job safe.

instructionSections.heading: Price the assessment separately
instructionSections.body: A pre-start assessment for lead, asbestos or other suspect material is a separate line in the quote. Its outcome decides whether the sanding can be quoted at all.
