If the assessment finds material that needs licensed removal, that removal is not part of this course and is not quoted as part of a normal timber job. Refer it to the appropriate licensed contractor, and say so in the quote.

instructionSections.heading: State the exclusions in writing
instructionSections.body: Structural and subfloor repair, removal of suspect adhesive or vinyl, repair of water-damaged boards, and any stain repair where the cause is unknown are excluded unless they are scoped and authorised separately. Write these exclusions into the quote so that the client understands what the price does not cover. Any item the business is not authorised to perform must be shown as excluded or referred, not priced as if it were included.

instructionSections.heading: Variations and no promised outcomes
instructionSections.body: If the floor changes after the first inspection, record the change and get written approval for the variation before the work continues. Under the Australian Consumer Law, a service provider must work with reasonable care and competence, and must finish in a timely manner where no time is agreed. Do not promise an exact final colour or an exact appearance on old timber. Explain that the outcome depends on the species, the finish that was there before, the condition of the boards and the products used, and record that explanation in the quote.

instructionSections.heading: Licence position stays with the job
instructionSections.body: A quote does not change the licence position. Before accepting work that may need a licence, notification or accreditation, check the requirement for the state or territory.

lessons.title: Glass and frame survey
learningOutcomes: Record the condition of glass, frames, seals and beading from ground level using a consistent survey sheet.
Separate visible defects from conditions that need a competent person to assess.
Apply stop-work and referral rules to glass or frames that look cracked, loose or unstable.

instructionSections.heading: Purpose of the survey
instructionSections.body: A glass and frame survey is a structured look at the windows or panels before cleaning starts. It records what can be seen from a safe position, so the supervisor can decide the method, the exclusion zone and whether the job should be stopped or referred. The survey is an observation record. It does not certify the glazing or the frame, and it does not replace a building or structural inspection. Keep that boundary clear in every record you write.

instructionSections.heading: What to look for
instructionSections.body: Survey each pane and frame in turn. Note cracks, chips and star breaks in the glass, and the position of each one. Look at the edges of the glass for chipping, and at the beading and gaskets for looseness, gaps or missing sections. Check the frame for corrosion, rot, cracking, movement and fixings that appear loose. Note any protective film, tinting, painted or frosted surfaces, and signs of previous repair or sealant. Record the glazing type where it is visible, such as toughened, laminated or insulated units, but do not state a type you cannot see.

instructionSections.heading: Separate defects from unknowns
instructionSections.body: A visible crack is a defect that you record and report. A panel that might be cracked behind a film, a frame that might be rotten inside its cavity, or a fixing you cannot reach is an unknown. Write unknowns in their own column. Do not turn an unknown into a finding of safe or unsafe. The supervisor or the building owner decides on the next step, and a competent person may be needed to assess the glazing or frame.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work and referral triggers
instructionSections.body: Stop cleaning the affected panel, keep the zone clear, and refer the job when a pane is cracked through, a panel rattles or moves in its frame, a frame is loose from its fixings, glass is held only by sealant, or water or staining suggests a failure behind the glass. Do not push, lean on or test the glass to check it. Mark the area, report it in writing, and wait for a decision.

instructionSections.heading: Recording and communication
instructionSections.body: Use a survey sheet with a sketch or photograph for each elevation, numbered panels, and a column for each defect and unknown. Date the survey, name the surveyor and the supervisor, and record the weather at the time. Give the customer a written copy of the defects you found, and state clearly that the survey does not cover structural or glazing condition beyond what was visible from the ground.

instructionSections.heading: Boundary notes
instructionSections.body: This course does not teach glazing repair, sealant work, frame work or structural inspection of facades, and those tasks are out of scope. If a customer asks you to fix, seal or certify any of them, record the request and refer it. Completing this lesson does not grant any authority to inspect or certify a building, a facade or a glazing system. A ground-level survey avoids the height rules, but a ladder or platform does not: the national working-heights page says to work on the ground where possible (no date shown).

lessons.title: Cleaning sequence
learningOutcomes: Describe a safe top-to-bottom cleaning sequence for a ground-level window or panel.
Explain how a documented sequence supports quality, time estimates and a fair quote.
Identify the points at which the sequence must stop because the access or conditions have changed.

instructionSections.heading: Why sequence matters
instructionSections.body: A consistent cleaning sequence protects the glass, the frame, the public and the worker. It keeps wash water from running back over areas already cleaned, and it keeps the work area predictable. A written sequence is also the basis for a fair time estimate and a quote that reflects the actual work, which is why this lesson links method to revenue.

instructionSections.heading: Set up before the first pane
instructionSections.body: Confirm the scope, the exclusion zone and the wind and weather limits in the job plan. Check the survey sheet from the glass and frame survey for held panels, and do not clean any held panel. Set out the approved product, its safety data sheet and the equipment, and confirm the water supply and any pole is inspected. The set-up is complete when the supervisor has signed the job plan and the zone is marked.

instructionSections.heading: The top-to-bottom sequence
instructionSections.body: Work from the top of the panel down. Wet the surface from the top so the product and water run down through the dirt rather than being left to dry on the glass. Apply the approved product only where the method calls for it and only for the dwell time the product label or safety data sheet states. Agitate the surface with the approved tool, then rinse from the top down. Clean the frame and sill after the glass where the method requires it, so that frame runoff does not dirty the glass. Finish with a squeegee or dry cloth stroke that starts at the top edge and ends at the bottom edge.

instructionSections.heading: Checks during the work
instructionSections.body: Look at each pane after rinsing for streaks, residue and missed areas, and correct them before moving on. Check the exclusion zone and the wind between panels. If a pane shows a new crack, a loose frame or a change in the weather, stop, hold the pane and tell the supervisor. The sequence is only safe while the conditions match the job plan.

instructionSections.heading: Documenting the method and the time
instructionSections.body: Record the sequence used, the product name and the safety data sheet reference, the time taken per panel or elevation, and any panels that were held or excluded. These records support future quotes and show the customer what was done. They must be factual. Do not record a guaranteed finish or a result that was not inspected.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing and revenue
instructionSections.body: A documented sequence lets a business estimate time and materials with more consistency. A higher rate is supportable where the work is more complex, such as a difficult set-up, held panels that need extra coordination, or a large pole job that needs more inspection. Do not promise a rate or a result for work whose scope is not verified. Tie any price to the scope, the exclusions and the method. A quote becomes binding once accepted, and extra work outside it needs the client's approval (Western Australian consumer page, last updated 4 September 2026); the Northern Territory page (no date shown) sets the same rule.

instructionSections.heading: Limits and boundary
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers ground-level and ground-based cleaning only. It does not authorise work on a ladder, a platform or a roof. Where the sequence would need height, the job returns to the access decision in the scope lesson. Completing this lesson does not grant any licence or height authority.

lessons.title: Job authority and high-access scope
learningOutcomes: Identify who holds site authority, who controls access, and which approvals must exist before any height work is considered.
Separate verified site facts from assumptions and unknowns when scoping a high-access window job.
Apply a stop-work or referral decision to a simulated job pack where authority or competence is missing.

instructionSections.heading: Why authority comes first
instructionSections.body: A window job that looks simple from the ground can carry the same fall and falling-object risks as a construction task. Before any height is considered, someone with control of the building or site must confirm in writing what work is wanted, where it will happen, who will be exposed, and who is responsible for the risk. A request from a tenant, a strata committee member or a family member does not by itself establish that the owner or site controller has approved access, equipment or a work area. The first question is therefore not how to reach the windows but who has authority to let the work happen, and on what terms. Under the national working-heights page, high risk construction work is construction carrying a fall risk greater than 2 metres (no date shown).

instructionSections.heading: Scope the work before planning access
instructionSections.body: Write the scope in plain terms: the windows or facade panels included, the levels, the surfaces, any frames or fixtures excluded, the cleaning method, and the hours when work may take place. Mark every part of the scope you cannot see from ground level. Glazing condition, frame condition and the structure that carries any platform or anchor are unknowns until a competent person has checked them. This course does not teach glazing repair, sealant or frame work, or structural inspection of facades. If a customer asks for any of those, record the request and refer it rather than agreeing to it.

instructionSections.heading: Apply the height hierarchy
instructionSections.body: Safe Work Australia's working-heights page sets the control order: work on the ground where possible, then fall prevention devices, then work-positioning systems, with fall arrest last (no date shown). The SafeWork NSW construction page gives the same order and requires a safe work method statement where a fall could exceed 2 metres (no date shown). Ask whether the windows can be reached from the ground by a water-fed pole or another ground-based method, and only then consider access equipment. South Australia sets the high-risk threshold at 2 metres from 1 July 2026 (page dated 5 June 2026). The ACT sets the same 2-metre SWMS trigger (no date shown), and the Northern Territory construction code gives falls of more than 2 metres as an example (code last varied 12 January 2026). The Victorian, Queensland, Western Australian and Tasmanian pages checked give no metre figure, so check the rule for your state before starting.

instructionSections.heading: Recognise stop-work conditions
instructionSections.body: Stop, make the area safe, and report before continuing if any of these apply: there is no written authority from the site controller; the access equipment or anchor has not been inspected; the public or neighbouring property cannot be kept clear of falling objects; the wind or weather is outside the job plan; or the glass or frame looks cracked, loose or unstable. A customer who wants the job finished today is not a reason to work past any of these conditions. The work is also a stop if it falls outside your training or the job pack.

instructionSections.heading: Record facts, assumptions and approvals separately
instructionSections.body: Your job record should keep three kinds of entry apart: what you verified by direct observation, what you were told but could not check, and what remains unknown. For each approval the job needs, record the person who gave it, the date, and the scope they approved. The record must also name who decides on a referral and who must be told of a stop-work decision. Do not write that a job is safe or compliant. Write what was checked, what was not, and what must happen next.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to work at height or to operate any platform. In New South Wales and Queensland, a boom-type platform needs a WP licence at a boom length of 11 metres or more, and a shorter boom may not need it in those states. The Victorian WP class page (reviewed 30 June 2026) gives the class with no boom-length threshold. Check your state or territory rules and obtain written authorisation from your employer before any work above ground level.

lessons.title: Facade and glazing risk screening
learningOutcomes: Identify safety and authorisation decisions associated with facade and glazing risk screening.
Explain the applicable risk hierarchy and specialist responsibilities for facade and glazing risk screening.
Produce a defensible stop-work, competent-person referral or restricted handover using mock evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Where this lesson sits
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level work, water-fed pole work and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Work above ground level, or work from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted. It needs written authorisation from the employer under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson is a desk-based drill. It does not give permission to work at height, on a roof, from a platform, or on a solar system. Safe Work Australia's working-heights page sets the high-risk construction threshold at a fall of more than 2 metres. In NSW, a safe work method statement is needed where a person could fall more than 2 metres. South Australia lowered its high-risk construction threshold from 3 metres to 2 metres, effective 1 July 2026. Check the rule in your own state or territory before any real work.

instructionSections.heading: What facade screening is for
instructionSections.body: Facade and glazing screening is the step where you look at the exterior and separate three things: what you can see, what you cannot see, and who has to decide the rest. It is not an engineering assessment. A worker can record what is visible, such as a crack in a pane, a gap in a sealant line, a loose fixing, a stain that suggests water, or debris on a ledge. Those are observations. A conclusion that a panel is secure, or that an overhead element will stay in place, is an inference, and it needs a building specialist to confirm it. Approval to work is a third thing. It comes in writing from the person who controls the site and the work. Keep the three apart in every record. The point of this lesson is that a visible sign does not tell you the engineered condition, and that missing information becomes an open decision, never a permission.

instructionSections.heading: Applying the risk hierarchy to a facade
instructionSections.body: Safe Work Australia's risk-management code ranks controls from most to least effective. The top levels are to eliminate the hazard, to substitute it or isolate people from it, and to use engineering controls. The lowest level is administrative controls and personal protective equipment, which depend on people behaving correctly. On a facade, eliminating the hazard means taking the elevated work out of scope, so the worker does not go up to look. Isolation means keeping people out of the area beneath a damaged element and marking the boundary. Engineering controls, such as a barrier or a catch zone, are designed by a specialist and are not improvised by a cleaner. Administrative controls include the permit, the signage, the briefing and supervision. Personal protective equipment comes last. A hard hat beneath a cracked overhang does not make the overhang safe, and it does not change the restriction.

instructionSections.heading: Information needed before any work is allocated
instructionSections.body: Before anything is allocated, confirm five things. These are the work order and its exact scope; the name and contact details of the site controller; the current method approval for the work, if one exists; the location-specific risk assessment; and the licence or authorisation status of any equipment that would be used. Also confirm access, the exposure of pedestrians and neighbouring premises, the weather, and whether the building owner or managing agent has been told about any damage. Where any item is missing, record it as an open decision. An open decision means the affected work does not go ahead until a person with authority closes it in writing. It is never treated as silent permission.

instructionSections.heading: The lesson case: cracked glazing under an overhead element
instructionSections.body: The lesson case is a photograph of cracked glazing beneath an overhead facade element, taken after building maintenance. Start from the restriction. The overhead element, and any work near it, is out of scope until a building specialist has assessed it. Do not infer that the panel is structurally sound because it looks intact in the photograph, or because the building is in use. A photograph cannot show the fixing, the load path, or the condition of the element above the glass. The first safe action is to stop and keep people out of the area beneath the element. Tell the site controller and the building contact, record the time and the names of the people told, and request a specialist assessment. Do not remove the cracked glass, do not climb, and do not tell the client that the area is safe. A separate, ground-level scope that sits clear of the overhead element may continue only if the site controller confirms it in writing and the area is isolated from the cracked element.

instructionSections.heading: Role boundaries and the stop-work decision
instructionSections.body: General cleaning training does not sign off rope descent, platform operation, anchor certification, electrical clearance or emergency rescue capability. A trainee who finds that one of these is needed must refer it, not attempt it. Structural assessment of a facade belongs to an appropriate building specialist, and electrical assessment belongs to a licensed electrician. The stop-work rule applies whenever the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; when wind, rain, ice or fading light changes the conditions; when exposed wiring, damaged cable or water near electrical equipment is seen or suspected; when a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; when the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or when you are asked to work above ground level without the required licence or authorisation. When the rule applies, stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming.

instructionSections.heading: Records and communication
instructionSections.body: Use dated records to show the exact observation, the source document, the person notified, the time, the restriction applied, and the response requested. Describe what was seen in plain words, and label each statement as an observation, an inference or an approval. Keep each entry short. Do not write safe, certified or compliant unless the evidence and the authority both support the word. The record is what protects the people who read it later, including the client and the next worker on the site.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and height rules differ by jurisdiction
instructionSections.body: The licence picture is set by each state and territory, so check the rule where you work. For a boom-type elevating work platform, the WP licence applies to a boom of 11 metres or more in New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory. The Queensland definition places platforms shorter than 11 metres outside its scope. The Victorian WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. The national model code uses the same 11-metre threshold, measured from the original design, and expects operators of shorter booms to be trained. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria, and the Northern Territory expects the operator to be competent. Window-cleaning licence status by state: NSW: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; VIC: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; QLD: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; WA: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; SA: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; TAS: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; NT: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; ACT: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04. Pressure-cleaning, roof soft-washing and solar-panel-cleaning licence status: UNCONFIRMED.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. The NSW definition of electrical wiring work includes installing, repairing, altering, removing or adding to an installation, and it also covers supervising that work. Victorian rules on PV installation, on whether PV DC cables stay live when the system is switched off, and on PV panel cleaning could not be read in this pass. As general practice, treat all panels, cables and exposed wiring as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instructionSections.heading: Trainer-led tabletop practice
instructionSections.body: Work through the case using fictitious work orders, drawn plans, photographs of a mock facade and blank record sheets. Annotate a mock facade map with the defects you have observed, the points that are unknown, and the people who must be notified. The trainer checks each entry for accuracy and stops any proposal to carry out unauthorised work on a real building.

lessons.title: Rope access and anchor certification
learningOutcomes: Explain why rope access is a specialist method that this course does not teach or certify.
Identify the anchor and equipment checks that a competent person must complete before rope access is considered.
Decide whether a higher-rate rope-access quote is supportable on the evidence available.

instructionSections.heading: What rope access is, and why it is restricted
instructionSections.body: Rope access uses ropes and harnesses to move a worker down or across a surface, usually with a second rope or line as a backup. It is a specialist method. It depends on correctly rated anchors, rope systems that have been inspected, and a worker who has been trained and assessed to use them. A worker who has completed a window cleaning course has not thereby become competent in rope access. This lesson is about recognising that boundary, not about learning the method.

instructionSections.heading: The standard that applies to fall arrest equipment
instructionSections.body: The ACT working-heights page says its competency-based fall arrest and travel restraint training follows AS/NZS 1891.4:2009 (no date shown). Do not describe the standard as a certification scheme. Equipment used for fall arrest should be selected, used and maintained as the manufacturer directs and in line with the relevant standard (text not read), and a competent person must decide whether it suits the task.

instructionSections.heading: Anchor evaluation
instructionSections.body: An anchor is only as good as its structure and its rating. Before a rope system is trusted, a competent person must confirm the anchor point's location, condition, load capacity and suitability for the surface. Anchors on old, corroded or unknown structures are not verified. Record anchor locations as unknown until verified, and refuse to use an anchor that cannot be verified.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work and referral
instructionSections.body: Stop the job and refer it if the anchor is unverified, the rope or harness is damaged or out of date, the surface is unknown, the wind or weather changes, or the worker is not assessed for the method. Referral goes to the person who holds site authority and to the competent person who would supervise the method. Do not attempt a rope-access job as an improvisation to save time.

instructionSections.heading: Revenue and honest pricing
instructionSections.body: A rope-access job may command a higher hourly rate because of the specialist skill and equipment it needs. That higher rate is only supportable when the evidence shows verified competence, verified equipment, a verified anchor and written authority from the site controller. Under the Western Australian and Northern Territory quote rules, an accepted quote is binding, so its exclusions must be written into it. When the evidence is missing, quote only the ground-based or platform-based work that you are authorised to perform, and state in writing what is excluded.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, rope-access competence or authority to work on ropes or anchors. Completing this lesson is not evidence that a worker or business is certified for rope access. A business must not advertise rope-access certification unless it holds evidence of that certification from a verified source.

lessons.title: Elevated work platforms and competence
learningOutcomes: Identify which platform types require a high risk work licence in the states where the licence matrix confirms the rule.
Check operator competence, platform condition and the rescue plan before an elevated platform is used.
Price elevated platform work only on evidence of licensed operation, equipment and authority.

instructionSections.heading: What an elevated work platform is
instructionSections.body: An elevated work platform lifts a worker and their tools to a working height. Platform types differ. A boom-type elevating work platform extends on an arm and has a platform at the end. A scissor lift raises a platform vertically. Each type has different stability, reach and control characteristics, so each needs its own check. The type of platform decides which licence rules apply, and the rules differ by state and territory.

instructionSections.heading: Licence rules from the official pages
instructionSections.body: In New South Wales and Queensland, a boom-type elevating work platform needs a WP high risk work licence where the boom is 11 metres or more, and a shorter boom may not need it in those states. That threshold is stated on the national model code page (December 2025), the New South Wales page, the Tasmanian page (last updated 1 December 2023), the Western Australian page (updated 13 August 2026) and the Northern Territory bulletin (no date shown). Queensland excludes platforms shorter than 11 metres (no date shown). The Victorian WP page gives the class with no boom-length threshold (reviewed 30 June 2026). Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. Scissor lifts need no licence in Victoria (reviewed 30 June 2026) or the Northern Territory (no date shown), and the national class list names no class for them (no date shown). The other pages checked do not address scissor lifts, so check the rule for your state before use, and do not assume a rule from another state.

instructionSections.heading: Operator competence and the licence question
instructionSections.body: Where a licence is required, only a licensed operator may run the platform. Check the licence class, its validity and that it covers the platform type before the platform moves. A licence held by one worker does not authorise the business to perform the work, and it does not cover the other workers on the job. Record who holds each licence, the class, and the regulator who issued it, and keep a copy of the record on the job. The national model code says a licence must be sighted and should be recorded at induction (December 2025).

instructionSections.heading: Pre-use checks and the rescue plan
instructionSections.body: Before use, check the platform's condition, the manufacturer's inspection record, the outriggers or stabilisers, the ground, the controls, the emergency lowering method and the guardrail or restraint system as applicable. Confirm that the platform will not be overloaded and that the wind and weather are inside the plan. Prepare a rescue plan that says how a trapped or unwell operator is lowered or brought down, who does it, and how quickly. The plan must exist before the platform is raised.

instructionSections.heading: Exclusion zones and public protection
instructionSections.body: The area beneath and around the platform is a drop zone. Tools and cleaning equipment must be tethered or held, and the zone must be kept clear of people and property using barriers or a supervisor. A platform that cannot keep the zone clear is not suitable for the site.

instructionSections.heading: Honest pricing for platform work
instructionSections.body: Platform work can be priced higher than ground-based work because it needs equipment, a licensed operator and planning. That price is supportable only when the licence, the equipment, the operator and the authority are verified, and the platform type is confirmed. Do not quote an elevated platform rate on the basis of a worker's general experience. Put the platform hire or ownership cost, the operator cost and the exclusions in writing, and tie the rate to the verified evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, operator competence or authority to operate any elevated work platform. Boom-type platform licences apply at a boom length of 11 metres or more, as set out above. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start.

lessons.title: Chemical selection and runoff boundaries
learningOutcomes: Identify safety and authorisation decisions associated with chemical selection and runoff boundaries.
Explain the applicable risk hierarchy and specialist responsibilities for chemical selection and runoff boundaries.
Produce a defensible stop-work, competent-person referral or restricted handover using mock evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Where this lesson sits
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level work, water-fed pole work and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Work above ground level, or work from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted. It needs written employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the state or territory requires for the equipment used. Safe Work Australia's working-heights page sets the high-risk construction threshold at a fall of more than 2 metres. South Australia lowered its threshold from 3 metres to 2 metres, effective 1 July 2026. This lesson is a desk-based drill. It does not give permission to apply any product on a real site.

instructionSections.heading: Product approval and the label
instructionSections.body: Every product used on a job must be on the approved list for that job, and it must be used exactly as its label directs. Before a product is used, read the label and find its safety data sheet (SDS). Workers who use or handle a hazardous chemical must be able to reach its SDS easily, and a business with hazardous chemicals at the workplace should hold an SDS for each one. A hazardous chemicals register lists those chemicals with their current SDS and is kept where workers can reach it. If a container has no label, or the SDS is not on site, the product is not used. Record the gap and report it. A product that is approved for one surface is not approved for every surface, and a product that is approved for one purpose is not approved for a different one. Use the label's list of surfaces and its directions as the limit, not the habit of the person holding the bottle.

instructionSections.heading: Surface compatibility
instructionSections.body: A product that is safe on one glazing frame may damage another. Window frames can be aluminium, timber, painted or coated, or made of a plastic that clouds or softens. Seals and sealants can swell, lift or discolour. Glass can be etched by the wrong product, and a coating can be stripped. Surface compatibility is checked against the label, the manufacturer's guidance and the method approval, and then confirmed with a test on a sample area that the site has released for testing. In this desk lesson the test is planned on paper only. Record the surfaces the product is approved for, the surfaces it is not approved for, and the test that is needed before any use. Do not treat a product as compatible because it looks similar to one that worked before.

instructionSections.heading: Runoff: where the water goes
instructionSections.body: Runoff is the water and product that leaves the surface and flows away. The question is always where it goes. In Queensland, a council page on water pressure cleaning says that the wastewater is a prescribed water contaminant that must not enter roadside gutters or stormwater systems, and that letting it do so is unlawful under the state's Environmental Protection Act. The same page describes ways to capture the water, such as sending it to a garden or to a holding tank for collection by a licensed liquid waste contractor, and warns that a drain must be protected from the water. That guidance is for Queensland and for that council.

instructionSections.heading: Landscaped drains and the lesson case
instructionSections.body: The lesson case is an alkaline cleaning product proposed for use above landscaped runoff drains, without product approval. Treat any drain as connected to stormwater until the site confirms otherwise, and keep the product and the wash water off drains, gutters, garden beds, plantings and neighbouring property. Do not test the product over a drain to see how it reacts. The first safe action is to hold the product. Tell the site controller, ask for the approved product for that surface and area, and ask for written runoff controls. If no control is approved, the chemical use does not go ahead. The site controller decides whether a different method, which does not use the product, is used instead. That decision is theirs, not the cleaner's.

instructionSections.heading: Role boundaries and the stop-work decision
instructionSections.body: Hold chemical use until the site confirms surface compatibility, the product's instructions and the runoff controls. General cleaning training does not sign off rope descent, platform operation, anchor certification, electrical clearance or emergency rescue capability. A trainee who finds that one of these is needed must refer it. The stop-work rule applies whenever the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; when wind, rain, ice or fading light changes the conditions; when exposed wiring, damaged cable or water near electrical equipment is seen or suspected; when a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; when the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or when you are asked to work above ground level without the required licence or authorisation. Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming.

instructionSections.heading: Protective equipment is the last control
instructionSections.body: Safe Work Australia's risk-management code places containment, elimination, substitution, isolation and engineering controls above personal protective equipment, and describes PPE as a last resort or a back-up to higher controls. The right order here is to keep the product off the drain, to use the approved product only, and to use the least product that works, and then to wear the gloves and eye protection the SDS sets. PPE does not make a drain safe to receive a product.

instructionSections.heading: Records and communication
instructionSections.body: Record the product name, the label check, the SDS reference, the surfaces the product is and is not approved for, the drain and garden map notes, the decision reached, the person told, and the time. Use the same observation, inference and approval separation as the other lessons in this track. Do not write that a product is safe for an area unless the label, the SDS and the written approval all say so.

instructionSections.heading: Licence and height notes
instructionSections.body: A boom-type elevating work platform needs a WP high risk work licence where its boom is 11 metres or more in New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory. In Queensland, a shorter boom may not need it, because the Queensland definition does not cover platforms shorter than 11 metres. The Victorian WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. The national model code uses the 11-metre threshold, measured from the original design. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria, and the Northern Territory requires the operator to be competent. Completing this lesson is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In NSW, electrical wiring work includes repairing and altering an installation and needs a licence or certificate. Victorian rules on PV work could not be read in this pass. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instructionSections.heading: Trainer-led tabletop practice
instructionSections.body: Create a simulated product-and-drainage review sheet using fictitious container labels, SDS excerpts and a drawn drain and garden map. Use photographs, drawn plans, fictitious work orders and inert desk materials only. Trainer checks each entry for accuracy and intervenes if the learner proposes unauthorised real-world activity, including any test over a real drain.

lessons.title: Inspection evidence and restricted handover
learningOutcomes: Identify safety and authorisation decisions associated with inspection evidence and restricted handover.
Explain the applicable risk hierarchy and specialist responsibilities for inspection evidence and restricted handover.
Produce a defensible stop-work, competent-person referral or restricted handover using mock evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Where this lesson sits
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level work, water-fed pole work and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Work above ground level, or work from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted. It needs written employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the state or territory requires for the equipment used. Safe Work Australia's working-heights page sets the high-risk construction threshold at a fall of more than 2 metres. This lesson is a desk-based drill. It does not give permission to work at height or on a solar system.

instructionSections.heading: What inspection evidence is
instructionSections.body: Inspection evidence is the record of what was actually looked at, from where, with what limits, and by whom. A worker who looks at the frontage from the ground can see the lower glazing and the frames within reach or sight, and can record what is visible. That view does not show the condition of an upper pane, a fixing above the head, a seal on the far side of a frame, or the state of a structural element. A record that says every window was checked is therefore false when only the ground-level windows were seen. Write down the viewpoint for each observation, and state what was not seen. An observation from a photograph is an observation of that photograph, and it is not a finding about the building.

instructionSections.heading: Scope closure and the restricted handover
instructionSections.body: The handover closes the scope in writing. It sets out four parts kept apart from one another. The first is the completed scope: the elevations and areas that were cleaned or inspected under authorisation, and the method used. The second is the excluded elevations: the parts not done, and the reason, such as the restriction on work above ground level or the absence of authorisation. The third is the unresolved conditions: the defects and unknowns observed, with the viewpoint and the time. The fourth is the specialist recommendations and referrals: the person or trade recommended, the person notified, and the time. The handover also states its limits. It does not certify the glazing, the frames or the structure, and it says that nothing above ground level was checked unless that is shown in the completed scope.

instructionSections.heading: Claims and certification
instructionSections.body: A handover must not say that the work is certified, compliant or safe unless the evidence and the authority both support the word. The consumer rules are relevant here. The ACCC states that claims must be accurate and backed by reasonable grounds, that a statement giving a false impression can breach the rules even when each word is literally true, that staying silent can mislead a buyer about something that matters, and that intention does not matter. A statement that all windows are certified safe, made after ground-level observation only, would breach those principles. The correct response is to decline the request in writing, give the reason, and offer the referral instead.

instructionSections.heading: Quotes, scope changes and written agreement
instructionSections.body: The accepted quote sets the scope. In Western Australia, a quote becomes a binding contract once accepted, and the tradesperson must get the customer's permission before doing extra work. Work done without permission does not have to be paid for. In the Northern Territory, an accepted offer on fixed terms binds both parties, and the customer does not have to pay for extra work that was not in the quote unless it was approved beforehand. These are state and territory rules, and the rule where you work applies. In practice, any added elevation, any added element or any change to the method must be agreed in writing before it is done, and the handover must show the scope that was actually agreed.

instructionSections.heading: Hazard and safer-option analysis
instructionSections.body: The lesson case is a client who asks for an all-windows-certified-safe statement after only ground-level observations. Start with the restriction: the upper glazing was not reached under authorisation, so no competence or condition claim about it is supported. Do not give the statement, and do not sign a form that carries it. The safer option is to hand over the ground-level scope with the excluded elevations listed, and to recommend that a building specialist assesses the upper glazing. Any work above ground level would need a separate written scope, an authorised risk assessment and any required licence, and none of that is assumed by this handover.

instructionSections.heading: Role boundaries and the stop-work decision
instructionSections.body: General cleaning training does not sign off rope descent, platform operation, anchor certification, electrical clearance or emergency rescue capability, and a trainee cannot certify a building. The stop-work rule applies whenever the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; when wind, rain, ice or fading light changes the conditions; when exposed wiring, damaged cable or water near electrical equipment is seen or suspected; when a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; when the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or when you are asked to work above ground level without the required licence or authorisation. Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming.

instructionSections.heading: Records and communication
instructionSections.body: Use dated records to show the exact observation, the viewpoint, the source document, the person notified, the time, the restriction applied and the response requested. A verbal summary is not a handover. Send the written handover to the site controller or the client, keep a copy, and record the date it was sent and to whom. If the client disagrees with the excluded elevations, record the disagreement and the response, and do not change the handover to match the request without written agreement and evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Licence notes
instructionSections.body: A boom-type elevating work platform needs a WP high risk work licence where its boom is 11 metres or more in New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory. In Queensland, a shorter boom may not need it, because the Queensland definition does not cover platforms shorter than 11 metres. The Victorian WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. The national model code uses the 11-metre threshold, measured from the original design. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria, and the Northern Territory requires the operator to be competent. Completing this lesson is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In NSW, electrical wiring work includes repairing and altering an installation and needs a licence or certificate. Victorian PV rules could not be read in this pass. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instructionSections.heading: Trainer-led tabletop practice
instructionSections.body: Draft a fictional handover note using fictitious work orders, a drawn elevation and a blank record. Divide the note into completed scope, excluded elevations, unresolved conditions and specialist referrals. Write one refusal letter to a fictitious client who asks for an unsupported certificate. Use photographs, drawn plans, fictitious work orders and inert desk materials only. The trainer checks accuracy and stops any proposal to carry out unauthorised real-world work.

lessons.title: Class setup, mats and space safety
learningOutcomes: Set up a class space that has enough room, a firm surface, clear exits and a clear path for every participant
Check mats, props and equipment before each class, and remove any item that is unsafe
State which parts of the space and permit rules are confirmed in the research and which remain open.

instructionSections.heading: Space, room and exits
instructionSections.body: A class space needs room for each participant to move their arms and legs without touching another person or a wall, a clear path to the exit, and a firm floor. Check the room before each class. Look for loose boards, wet patches, cables, stored items, and furniture that could fall or be knocked. Keep the exits clear and know where they are before the class starts. Record the room, the number of participants and any hazard seen on the class record. The business's room and venue rules are held in {{business:procedures.prestart_checklist}}. Use the venue's own conditions as well as this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Mats, props and equipment
instructionSections.body: A mat must give grip and stay flat. Check each mat for tears, lifting edges and slipperiness before the class starts, and remove any mat that is damaged. Props such as blocks, straps, bolsters and balls should be checked for cracks and for stability. Pilates equipment, such as reformers or springs, needs its own inspection under the manufacturer's instructions, and the manufacturer's manual is held as {{business:equipment.manufacturer_manual_url}}. Do not use equipment that has a loose part, a frayed strap or a spring that is not secure. Record the inspection of each item used in a class, and remove unsafe items from use with a note of the date. The approved product list for cleaning mats is in {{business:materials.approved_products}}.

instructionSections.heading: Heat, outdoor sessions and permits
instructionSections.body: Heated classes, outdoor sessions and classes in hot weather carry a risk of heat illness. Use shade, water, ventilation and breaks, and stop the class if a participant shows signs of heat distress. For outdoor classes on public land, check the council permit. Hornsby Shire Council in New South Wales names yoga and tai chi among the activities its commercial fitness permit covers (no date shown); that is council-specific. Check the permit for each park before the class.

lessons.title: Teaching modifications and injury boundaries
learningOutcomes: Offer a modification for a posture without diagnosing the student's condition
Identify the injury signs that require the class to stop and the student to be referred
Explain why a yoga or Pilates certificate is not a clinical or therapeutic authority, and how that applies to hands-on adjustments

instructionSections.heading: Modifications: offer options, do not diagnose
instructionSections.body: A modification is a change to a posture that makes it suitable for a student, for example a lower position, a support, or a shorter hold. The instructor offers modifications from the start of the class, so that a student who is unsure can choose one without explaining why. The instructor must not diagnose the student's condition, must not name an injury, and must not tell the student that a pain is nothing. Describe what you can see and offer an option. Where a student describes an injury or an ongoing condition, the instructor records it as the student describes it, and refers the student to a medical practitioner or allied health professional for advice before the student attempts any posture that aggravates the condition. The business's modification and referral procedure is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instructionSections.heading: Injury boundaries and when the class must stop
instructionSections.body: The class must stop for an individual where a student reports sharp pain, numbness, dizziness, chest tightness, breathlessness out of proportion to effort, or any sudden injury. The instructor must keep the student safe, avoid moving the student further, and advise medical attention where the symptoms are serious. The screening approach in “Client screening and health-questionnaire boundaries” applies to yoga and Pilates as well. Where a student has an injury that a health professional has told them to avoid a posture for, the instructor must respect that advice and must not coach the posture through pain.

instructionSections.heading: Hands-on adjustments and the limits of a certificate
instructionSections.body: Hands-on adjustments, where an instructor touches a student to guide a posture, carry risk. They need the student's clear consent, a clear reason, and training in the technique. The business should not make hands-on adjustments unless it has the training and the student's consent recorded. A teaching certificate is a qualification, not a clinical or therapeutic authority. It does not allow the instructor to diagnose, treat or advise on a medical condition. Completing this lesson does not give any of those authorities.

lessons.title: Private sessions and premium pricing
learningOutcomes: Run a private session with the same screening and referral steps as a class, and record them
Set a premium price from the time, skill and costs, without making a health outcome claim
Identify the home-visit safety points that are confirmed and those that remain and those that remain open.

instructionSections.heading: A private session is still a screened session
instructionSections.body: A private session often earns a higher rate because the instructor gives more attention and adapts the session to one person. The screening, the consent and the referral steps are the same as in a class, and in a private session they matter more because the instructor is alone with the client. Complete the health questionnaire from “Client screening and health-questionnaire boundaries” before the first session, and repeat it when the client reports a change. Record each modification, referral and stop. The business's private session procedure is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the cancellation rule is in {{business:customers.communication_policy}}.

instructionSections.heading: Private sessions in a client's home
instructionSections.body: Some private sessions take place in a client's home. WorkSafe Victoria's health and safety responsibilities page (reviewed 03/04/2025) states that a self-employed person's work must not put others at risk, within what is reasonably practicable, and that employers must do the same for customers and the public. Treat the home as a workplace for set-up and safety, and check the room before the session, as “In-home safety, lone-work and room setup” explains for mobile massage. Check the access instructions in {{business:customers.access_instructions}} before entering, and use the lone-worker check-in method from “Lone-worker safety and check-ins” at arrival and departure.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing a premium private session
instructionSections.body: A premium private session should be priced from the time it takes, the skill it needs, the preparation, the travel, the equipment and any compliance cost. A premium price must not be used to justify a claim that the session treats a condition or reduces a medical risk. Describe the session by its length, its focus and its included equipment. Advertising and consumer-law rules for health claims were not researched for this course. The pricing method is held in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}, and the minimum charge in {{business:pricing.minimum_charge}}. Check the price against the cost of each step before it is published.

lessons.title: Community class schedules and membership growth
learningOutcomes: Plan a class schedule that keeps each class inside its venue, its permit and its group size
Identify when a children's class engages a Working with Children Check category.
Grow a membership without relying on health claims, and with the consumer-law points checked

instructionSections.heading: Building a schedule inside its limits
instructionSections.body: A community class schedule is a commitment to a venue and to participants. Each class must sit inside the venue's conditions, the council permit where it runs on public land, and the group size the business has set. Before adding a class to the schedule, check the venue's hours, the room size, the number of participants the room allows, and the permit for each public place. The schedule is held in {{business:jobs.scheduling_method}}. Keep the class capacity on the schedule, and do not sell a place beyond it. Where a class is moved to a new venue, the new venue's rules apply from the first session, and the permit must be checked again.

instructionSections.heading: Children's classes and the check categories
instructionSections.body: A community class for children may engage the Working with Children Check. The Victorian government's list (updated 12 October 2026) names private tutoring and coaching aimed at children (code 28), commercial gyms and play venues aimed at children (code 32), and sport, recreation and culture clubs that deal with children (code 42). The government explainer states that a clearance is valid for five years (updated 24 July 2026). A business listing that copies the government text says self-employed workers are covered and refers to direct contact with under-18s (no date shown; secondary copy). Do not offer a children's class until the position is recorded for the venue and the state.

instructionSections.heading: Growing membership without a health promise
instructionSections.body: Membership growth comes from a reliable schedule, a welcoming class, clear communication and good records of attendance. It does not come from claims that a class will cure a condition, improve a diagnosis or reduce a medical risk. Describe the class by its style, its level and its time. Membership terms must state the classes included, the period, the rule for unused classes, cancellation and refund. Queensland's fitness-agreement page (last updated 23 July 2024) sets a 48-hour cooling-off period, refunds of prepaid fees within 14 days, and a 12-month cap on prepayment, for Queensland only. Check the terms before the membership is sold, and record the check. The communication and cancellation policy is in {{business:customers.communication_policy}}, and the pricing method for memberships is in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}.

lessons.title: How a field job moves from request to finished visit
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between a job, a visit and a worker in the app.
Describe the order in which a customer request becomes a completed visit.
Identify which record holds each part of a customer request.

instructionSections.heading: Why the app keeps separate records
instructionSections.body: A field business handles one customer request in several different ways. Someone has to record what the customer wants, when a worker will attend, who that worker is, and what the work costs. If all of this sits in one place, the office loses track of separate trips and the history of a site. The app therefore keeps separate records. The job holds the customer, the site, the scope and the agreed price. A visit is one trip to the site for some or all of that scope. A worker is the person or crew who does the trip.

instructionSections.heading: How the records connect
instructionSections.body: One job can have several visits: a first attendance to diagnose, a return to fit parts and a final check, for example. Each visit has its own window, duration and status. Equipment on site is kept as an asset, so a later repair can be traced to the right unit. Once the job's work is finished, the job feeds the service report and the invoice.

lessons.title: Service areas and their assigned workers
learningOutcomes: Define a service area with a clear boundary and a parent area where one exists.
Place a worker in an area as main base, backup area, or temporary cover.
Explain why an oversized area slows scheduling and dispatch.

instructionSections.heading: What a service area is
instructionSections.body: A service area is a region your team covers. It might follow suburbs, council zones, a postcode group, or a travel radius from your yard. Areas help the app decide which workers are sensible for a job. A worker based on the north side should not be sent across the city without a reason. When you build a hierarchy, create the widest area first and then the smaller areas beneath it. Each area needs an address or map point so the app can work out travel time.

instructionSections.heading: Sizing and membership roles
instructionSections.body: Oversized areas make scheduling slow and dispatch hard to manage. The reference guide suggests keeping an area to about fifty workers, about a thousand visits a day, and no more than twenty qualified workers for a single visit. Treat these as starting points to review, not as Australian standards. Membership records say which area a worker belongs to. A primary area is where the worker mostly works, usually near home. A secondary area is somewhere they can be sent when needed. A relocation area is a temporary home area for a set period. Each worker's home base needs a confirmed map point, or the app cannot calculate their travel.

lessons.title: Opening hours, blocks and shifts
learningOutcomes: Set working hours for a worker or an area, including time slots.
Choose between regular working hours and a shift for a given pattern of cover.
Explain how a shift's status changes what the scheduler uses.

instructionSections.heading: Opening hours and time blocks
instructionSections.body: Working hours tell the scheduler when a worker or an area can take a visit. This same record type can also capture a customer's arrival window or time preference, which makes it useful in several ways. A time slot carves out a block inside those hours, such as a morning block set aside for one type of job. Hours can be set for an area, and a worker's own hours can override them. Keep hours realistic, because the scheduler treats them as fixed until someone changes them.

instructionSections.heading: Shifts for irregular cover
instructionSections.body: A shift suits work that does not follow a fixed weekly pattern, such as on-call duty, overtime or a contractor who works an agreed set of days. A shift runs from a beginning to a finish in the area's time zone, and it may name an area, a worker and a status. A tentative shift is still being planned. A published shift is ready to hand to the worker. A confirmed shift has a named worker, and the scheduler takes confirmed shifts into account. A shift can also be marked as extended time, meaning it falls outside normal working hours.

lessons.title: Job templates for repeat work
learningOutcomes: Build a job template with a duration, required skills, required parts and default visit behaviour.
Explain what happens to existing jobs when a template changes.
Decide when a required skill should be a hard rule rather than a suggestion.

instructionSections.heading: What a template is for
instructionSections.body: A job template standardises a repeat service, such as a single-room clean, a gutter clear or a door adjustment. It carries the expected duration, the skills a worker needs, the parts usually required and a link to any reference article. When a new job uses the template, it copies these values. That saves desk time and keeps quotes consistent across staff.

instructionSections.heading: Changes that do not flow backwards
instructionSections.body: A template change affects jobs created after the change. It does not rewrite jobs already open. The same applies to skills: adding a skill requirement to a template does not change jobs that already exist. Office staff should check open jobs after any template change that affects time or skills. A skill requirement is only enforced where the scheduler is set to check it. Without that check it works as a suggestion.

lessons.title: Jobs and their task lines
learningOutcomes: Create a job with its customer, site and task lines.
Price each task line and explain where discounts are recorded.
Choose the right record change when a visit is cancelled.

instructionSections.heading: The job and its task lines
instructionSections.body: The job is the header for a customer request. Beneath it sit task lines, which are the concrete steps a worker must complete, such as remove old hinge, fit new hinge, test the door. Each task line can be ticked off, so the office sees progress without a phone call. Prices, unit amounts and discounts belong on the task lines too, not only on the header. That way the invoice can be built from the lines themselves.

instructionSections.heading: Cancellations and follow-up jobs
instructionSections.body: When a visit is cancelled, record the cancellation on the job. If the work still needs doing, open a follow-up job linked to the original. Do not reuse the original job, because then you lose the record of how often work is cancelled and why. Deleting a job also removes its linked visits, notes and task lines. Restore a deleted job only if the deletion was a mistake, because restoring brings the linked records back too.

lessons.title: Equipment on site and planned maintenance
learningOutcomes: Record equipment at a site as an asset, including parent and child items.
Set a recurring maintenance plan, giving it a repeat interval and a generation window.
Explain why a plan must be checked after an asset is replaced.

instructionSections.heading: Assets
instructionSections.body: An asset is a piece of equipment or a system at a customer's site that may need repeat service, such as an air conditioner, a pool pump or a commercial dishwasher. Recording assets gives each later job a history. An asset can sit under a parent, such as a plant room with several units beneath it. The reference guide sets limits on how large these groupings can grow.

instructionSections.heading: Maintenance plans
instructionSections.body: A maintenance plan sets how often visits should happen and creates jobs for future visits in batches. It has a start date, an optional end date that matches any contract, a job template, a customer and optionally a site. The frequency and its unit set the gap between visits. The generation window sets how far ahead jobs are created at one time. When a plan covers several assets, you decide between one job covering all of them or one job per asset. Assets lacking rules of their own inherit the plan's rules.

lessons.title: Visits: booking and status
learningOutcomes: Create a visit against a job with a window and an expected duration.
Name the visit status stages and say what moves a visit between them.
Explain why a visit's parent record matters.

instructionSections.heading: What a visit records
instructionSections.body: A visit is one planned trip to a site. It records when the work should start, how long it should take, which job it belongs to and who is assigned. Most visits sit under a job. A visit can also hang off an asset, a customer account, or a lead for a site survey. The parent shows the kind of visit it is. A job-linked visit covers the work itself, while an account-linked visit might be a general check.

instructionSections.heading: Status stages
instructionSections.body: A visit moves through stages: not yet scheduled, scheduled, dispatched, in progress, finished, unable to finish and cancelled. Changing a visit's status can trigger the next step, so make changes deliberately. If a visit is unscheduled, it goes back to not yet scheduled. A visit that cannot be finished should be marked unable to finish, with a reason recorded, so the office can plan a follow-up rather than lose the work. Status names can be renamed to suit your business, but the stage order does not change when you rename them.

lessons.title: Scheduling rules: priority, emergencies and dependencies
learningOutcomes: Set a priority for urgent and routine visits.
Explain how a dependency holds one visit until another finishes.
Describe the steps for booking an emergency visit.

instructionSections.heading: Priority
instructionSections.body: Priority tells the scheduler which visits matter most when the day is full. It can be a fixed value set on a job or a visit, or a calculated value, such as the days left before a due date. The scheduler looks at the visit's own priority first and falls back to the job's. When no free slot exists, a higher-priority visit can displace a lower one. Choose a small scale that the office can remember, and write down what each level means.

instructionSections.heading: Dependencies and emergencies
instructionSections.body: A dependency links two visits so one cannot start before the other is finished. This suits multi-stage work, such as strip-out before a fit-out. An emergency booking uses a view of nearby workers, so the office can send the closest suitable person straight away. Use emergency booking sparingly, because each one moves other visits, and the customers affected must be told.

lessons.title: Changing the schedule: clashes, grouping and gaps
learningOutcomes: Explain what a schedule clash is and what the app shows when one occurs.
Choose a safe default for a clash that cannot be fixed automatically.
Use grouping and gap filling to reduce travel without breaking customer windows.

instructionSections.heading: Clashes
instructionSections.body: A clash happens when a visit overlaps another visit or a worker's absence. The app can fix some clashes by moving visits, but the office must set the rules first. Decide whether a moved visit may go only to its original worker or to any suitable worker. Decide whether unscheduled visits are rebuilt by priority or in their original order. When no valid option exists, the safe default is to leave the visit where it is, flag it at risk and tell the office. Silently removing a visit leaves a customer with no visit. Automatic clash fixing does not apply to capacity-based workers, so check their days by hand.

instructionSections.heading: Grouping and gap filling
instructionSections.body: Grouping nearby visits gathers visits in the same area to cut travel. It can move later visits that day to make room, so check each customer's agreed window before accepting a change. Gap filling looks for work that fits a worker's free time. Both tools change bookings, so the office should run them and review the result, not leave them running unchecked.

lessons.title: Dispatch: sending visits to workers
learningOutcomes: Explain how scheduling a visit and dispatching it differ.
Describe how drip-feed dispatch releases visits one at a time.
Name the steps for telling a worker about a change after dispatch.

instructionSections.heading: Scheduling and dispatch
instructionSections.body: Scheduling decides when a visit happens and who does it. Dispatching sends that visit to the worker's device so they can act on it. Dispatch can be done by hand from the office board, or set to run automatically on a schedule. Automatic dispatch suits stable days. Manual dispatch suits days when plans change often. Each dispatch should name the assigned workers and notify them through the channel the team actually reads.

instructionSections.heading: Drip-feed release
instructionSections.body: Drip-feed dispatch sends visits singly. A later visit is held back until the visit in front of it is finished. This stops a worker being handed a long list that is likely to change, and it reduces confusion when the day shifts. Drip-feed takes more setting up than a full dispatch, but it limits the number of changes a worker must absorb.

lessons.title: Workers: capacity, efficiency and preferences
learningOutcomes: Set a worker's capacity as hours or visits per period.
Explain how an efficiency score affects the planned length of a visit.
Tell apart the three worker settings: favoured, mandatory and barred.

instructionSections.heading: Capacity
instructionSections.body: Some workers, such as contractors, can only work an agreed amount in a period. You can record that as hours per period, for example eighty hours a month, or as a number of visits per period. Capacity records should match contract dates, and the dates should not overlap. The scheduler checks each day against capacity, and does not weigh the week or the month, so the office should review weekly totals by hand.

instructionSections.heading: Efficiency, skills and preferences
instructionSections.body: Workers differ in pace. An efficiency score changes the planned length of each visit assigned to that worker, so the end time is more realistic. Skills describe what a worker can do. Preferences go further: a worker can be favoured, mandatory or barred for a given asset, site or customer. If the asset carries no preference, the app looks at the site and then the customer, and takes the first one it finds. The office should be able to see where a preference came from.

lessons.title: Crews: working as a group
learningOutcomes: Describe when a visit should go to a crew rather than to individual workers.
Explain the membership date rules for crew members.
Set a minimum headcount on a job template.

instructionSections.heading: Why use a crew
instructionSections.body: A crew is a team that attends a visit together, such as a three-person tree removal or a two-person heavy lift. The crew appears as one record in the schedule, but it is made up of individual workers, each with their own availability. A visit given to a team receives the team record and each member who is active at that time. Use a crew only where the job needs several people. Otherwise assign individuals, so the scheduler has more options.

instructionSections.heading: Membership and minimum size
instructionSections.body: Crew membership has its own date range. A worker can join more than one crew only when those date ranges do not overlap. A member must be an active worker of the right type and must already belong to the crew's area for the same time. The crew needs a leader, and the leader's position is the one followed. Job templates may state how many people are needed at minimum and how many are ideal, and the scheduler uses these figures to check the visit is staffed properly. If all members leave a crew, its crew record is switched off.

lessons.title: Time sheets, absences and daily routes
learningOutcomes: Explain how a time sheet moves from entry to submission and approval.
Record an absence so the schedule avoids that time.
Compare a worker's planned route with the actual route for a day.

instructionSections.heading: Time sheets
instructionSections.body: A time sheet records the hours a worker spent on the job. Workers can log time from their phone or tablet, and the office approves it. Sending a time sheet starts the approval process, so approval has to be configured before workers can send entries. Keep the fields simple, because the mobile view shows only a few of them. This should be tested in the field before workers rely on offline time sheets.

instructionSections.heading: Absences and routes
instructionSections.body: An absence logs a block of days when a worker cannot take jobs, such as leave, training or sickness. Recording it stops the scheduler offering visits in that time, and the office can see gaps early. A daily route shows where a worker travelled. The planned route is what the scheduler expected, and the actual route is what the device recorded. Comparing the two helps the office spot unrealistic travel times. Tell workers about any location tracking before it starts.

lessons.title: Parts and stock on the job
learningOutcomes: Attach required parts to a template or job so the right items travel with the worker.
Explain how a request, a transfer and a used-parts record connect.
Record a return with its reason.

instructionSections.heading: Required parts
instructionSections.body: Parts can be listed on a template or on an individual job. A worker sent to a repair without the right part wastes a visit, so the aim is to know what is needed before dispatch. A template's parts list covers the usual need, and a job can add parts it specifically requires. If a part is missing, raise a request linked to the job, so stock and the job stay in step.

instructionSections.heading: Requests, transfers and use
instructionSections.body: A stock request asks for items to be moved to where they are needed, with a date and a location. A transfer shifts stock between two places, for example a depot and a van, and the stock levels update. When a worker uses an item, log it against the job immediately, so the stock count is right and the invoice can include it. Shipments track items in transit, and returns handle items sent back, each with a reason.

lessons.title: Working without signal in the field app
learningOutcomes: Explain what the app downloads before a worker goes offline.
Describe what the pending changes queue shows and how it behaves.
Resolve a conflict between two changes to the same record.

instructionSections.heading: Priming
instructionSections.body: When a worker logs in, the app downloads the visits and related records assigned to them, so they can carry on without signal. This is called priming. The reference guide primes the worker's visits within a window around the current date, by default forty-five days either side, and notes that this window can be configured. Large volumes take longer. A network error stops priming, so the worker should run it again once they have signal. A worker who has not primed before going offline will not have the visits they need.

instructionSections.heading: Pending changes and conflicts
instructionSections.body: Changes made offline join a pending line in the sequence they were created. The queue shows whether each change has reached the server. If two changes conflict, the queue pauses, because later changes may depend on the earlier one. The worker must delete or edit the conflicting change before the remaining items can go up. Whichever edit lands on the server last wins over an earlier one.

lessons.title: Service reports and customer sign-off
learningOutcomes: Explain which report template applies to a job or visit.
Describe what a customer signature records.
Recognise when a final report file needs a connection.

instructionSections.heading: What a service report is
instructionSections.body: A service report summarises a job or visit in a document the customer and the team can sign. It shows the work done and gives the customer a record of the visit. Workers or the office create the report from the job or visit. The default template should always stay active, because reports can fail to generate without it.

instructionSections.heading: Template choice, sign-off and connection
instructionSections.body: Templates are picked in a fixed order: first the one set on the job, next the one on the job's type of work, and last the standard template. Each signature records the signer's role, such as customer or site contact. A report can be previewed offline, but the final file may only be produced after the device reconnects. Check language support for your customers before sending text written right to left.
