lessons.title: Typical job prices and times: mean or median
learningOutcomes: Calculate the mean and the median of a set of job prices or job times taken from your own records.
Explain why one unusually large job can pull the mean away from the typical job.
Choose the summary that fits a pricing or planning question and give a reason for the choice.

instructionSections.heading: Two ways to find the middle
instructionSections.body: When you look back over a month of invoices, you want one figure that tells you roughly what a typical job brings in or takes. Two common answers are the mean and the median. The mean comes from adding every job together and dividing by the number of jobs. Because every job feeds into it, one very big job pushes it upward. The median comes from lining the jobs up from smallest to largest and picking the one in the middle. Half the jobs sit below it and half sit above it, so it does not react to how extreme the biggest and smallest jobs are. With an even number of jobs there is no single middle job, so take the two in the centre and average them. Both figures are simple to produce in a spreadsheet, and both are worth having side by side.

instructionSections.heading: Why one big job changes the picture
instructionSections.body: Suppose the last nine invoices in your records are $180, $190, $200, $210, $220, $230, $240, $250 and $1,450. The last one is a common-area job in a strata building that happened to fall in the same month. These figures are invented for this lesson, but the pattern is familiar. Add the nine invoices and the total is $3,170. Divide by nine and the mean is about $352. That number looks high, and it is pulled up by a single job that most of your work does not resemble. The median is $220, the fifth value once the list is sorted, and it matches the jobs you see most often. Neither figure is wrong. They answer different questions, and the gap between them is information you should look at rather than hide.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the right summary
instructionSections.body: Use the median when your question is about the typical customer or the typical job. If a new customer asks what a standard bond clean usually costs, or you want to know how long a usual kitchen clean takes, the median gives a fair answer. Use the mean when your question is about totals. If you expect 40 jobs next month and each one averages a certain amount, multiplying the mean by 40 gives the total income you can plan around, and that total includes the occasional large job which is part of real income. When the mean and median sit far apart, a few unusual jobs are shaping the average. Find out what those jobs were before you change any price, because they may point to a scope you have not yet priced properly.

lessons.title: Spread and outliers in job times and invoices
learningOutcomes: Calculate the range and the interquartile range (IQR) for a set of job times or invoice totals.
Apply a simple rule to flag an unusually long job and state the reason it was flagged.
Use the spread to decide whether a standard time or quote needs a buffer.

instructionSections.heading: Where the jobs sit, and how far they wander
instructionSections.body: A middle figure tells you where most jobs land but nothing about how far apart they are. Picture two gardeners who each average two hours a job. One finishes almost every visit in about two hours. The other ranges from forty minutes to four hours. Both have the same average, yet only one of them can be scheduled and quoted with confidence. The spread is the measure of that predictability. The simplest spread measure is the range, which is the largest value minus the smallest. It is quick to work out, but a single odd job can set it by itself. A steadier measure looks only at the middle half of the jobs. To get the interquartile range, which people usually call the IQR, find the value a quarter of the way up the sorted list and the value three quarters of the way up, then subtract the first from the second. The IQR ignores the extremes at both ends, so one odd job has much less effect on it.

instructionSections.heading: Finding a job that runs long
instructionSections.body: A job is worth a second look when its time or its invoice sits well above the rest. A common rule of thumb in statistics, which is a general convention and not a legal or market standard, marks any value more than one and a half times the IQR above the upper quartile. Take the upper quartile, add one and a half times the IQR, and any value above that line is flagged. A flag does not mean the job was wrong. It might have run long because the gate was locked, the scope grew, a second person was needed, or the time was entered in the wrong unit. The useful question is what caused the job to run long, and whether that cause will come up again. Only then should it change your standard time or your quote.

instructionSections.heading: Putting the spread to work
instructionSections.body: A narrow spread lets you promise a time with confidence. A wide spread tells you to add a buffer, to split the service into sub-types such as a standard clean and a heavy-soil clean, or to ask better questions at intake. Keep the cause of each flagged job in the job record, so the next quote for a similar site carries the risk forward. Spread also helps when you compare crews. A crew that is occasionally quicker but often much slower may be a worse bet for your schedule than a crew that is a little slower but steady.

lessons.title: Estimating a rate from a sample: repeat customers
learningOutcomes: Write a clear definition of the thing being counted, such as a repeat customer, and apply it to a list of records.
Calculate a share (a rate) from a sample of customers and report it with its sample size and time window.
Explain sampling variation in plain language and show how much a small sample can move.

instructionSections.heading: Why you work from a sample
instructionSections.body: Most owners cannot check every customer who has used the business in the last year, so they work from a sample: the customers they can see in a fixed window of time. A rate, such as the share of customers who book again, is then estimated from that sample. Start with the definition, because the number depends on it. For example, a repeat customer might be someone who has paid for two or more jobs in the past twelve months. Write the definition down and use it every time you count. If the definition changes from one month to the next, the rate will move for reasons that have nothing to do with how the business is doing.

instructionSections.heading: Working out the share
instructionSections.body: Count the customers in your sample, count how many of them meet the definition, and divide the second number by the first. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage. Suppose a mobile massage business has 40 clients in the last twelve months, and 14 of them paid for two or more sessions. Fourteen divided by 40 is 0.35, which is 35 per cent. That is the estimate from this sample. It describes these 40 clients well enough for planning, but it is not a guarantee about the next 40 clients, and it should always be reported together with the sample size and the window it covers.

instructionSections.heading: Sampling variation: the wobble
instructionSections.body: If you took a different group of 40 clients, you would probably get a somewhat different share. That natural movement is called sampling variation, and it is strongest when the sample is small. You can see the effect in your own data by splitting the sample. The following split is only a demonstration. Suppose the first 20 clients in the list, ordered by first booking date, include 9 repeat clients, which is 45 per cent, and the last 20 include 5, which is 25 per cent. Together they give the 35 per cent figure again, but the two halves differ by 20 percentage points. That gap tells you that 40 clients cannot pin the rate down tightly. The sensible response is not to react to each month's figure. Watch the trend over several periods, and treat a small-sample share as an estimate with a wide margin.

lessons.title: Comparing two methods with before-and-after data
learningOutcomes: Write a one-sentence question and a measure before collecting before-and-after data.
Compare the averages and the spread of two groups of similar jobs and judge whether the gap stands out from normal variation.
Make a documented decision to change, keep testing or reject a method, stating what evidence would change that decision.

instructionSections.heading: Why before-and-after comparisons mislead
instructionSections.body: Owners often change something and then look at the numbers that follow. A new quote template, a pre-treatment step for carpets or a new checklist for bathrooms can each be followed by a different figure. The question is whether the difference is real or simply the ordinary movement that appears from one job to the next. Before-and-after comparisons are easy to get wrong because other things change at the same time: the season, the type of customer, the crew, the weather and the mix of jobs. Compare like with like as far as you can, meaning the same job type, a similar size of job and a similar time of year. Write down anything else that changed, because you will need that note when you read the result.

instructionSections.heading: Is the gap bigger than the wobble?
instructionSections.body: Individual jobs vary. A bathroom clean that takes 55 minutes on a Tuesday might take 65 minutes on a Friday for reasons that have nothing to do with the method. A useful habit is to set the size of the difference between your two averages against the spread inside each group. You can use the range or the IQR from the spread lesson for this. If the averages differ by a small amount and the individual jobs overlap heavily, the gap could easily be chance. If the averages differ by a lot compared with how much the jobs swing, and the difference holds across several weeks, the change is more likely to be real. You are looking for a gap that stands out from the normal noise, not just any gap that appears on paper.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding when the answer is unclear
instructionSections.body: When the result is close, collect more data before acting. Keep the recording method the same for both groups, note the job type for each record, and run each method long enough to cover different jobs and different days. For a pricing change, count the quotes sent and the quotes accepted under each format, and check that the two groups of customers were of similar kinds. Set the number of jobs you need before you start, so you are not tempted to stop as soon as one method looks better. Once you have enough data, decide, and write down what result would have changed your mind. A test that is too small is not a failed test. It has not yet answered the question.

lessons.title: Forecasting monthly jobs from a seasonal pattern
learningOutcomes: Calculate a seasonal index for each calendar month from at least two years of the learner's own monthly job counts.
Produce an adjusted three-month level and use it to forecast the next month's jobs.
Compare a past forecast with the actual result and state the size and direction of the gap.

instructionSections.heading: Why a plain average misleads in a seasonal business
instructionSections.body: Many home and commercial services rise and fall with the calendar. Pool and spa work, end-of-lease cleaning, gutter work and garden clean-ups each have busy months and quiet months, and the pattern tends to repeat from year to year. If you forecast next month by averaging the last few months as they stand, you will overshoot the quiet months and undershoot the busy ones. Two steps fix this. First, measure how each calendar month usually compares with an average month. Second, strip the seasonal effect out of recent months so you can see the underlying level of work, and then put the season back in when you forecast. The seasonal pattern in the examples is invented for this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: The seasonal index
instructionSections.body: A seasonal index compares one calendar month with an average month. Take all the job counts for a given calendar month across two or three years and find their average. Then divide that average by the average across all twelve months. An index of 1.00 means an ordinary month. An index of 1.50 means that month usually runs about half as much again as an ordinary month. An index of 0.80 means it usually runs about a fifth below an ordinary month. The twelve indices should balance out to about 1.00 across the year, because each one is measured against the same average. If they do not, the arithmetic needs checking before you go further.

instructionSections.heading: Moving average and forecast
instructionSections.body: A simple moving average is the average of the most recent few periods, recalculated one month at a time as new figures arrive. This lesson uses three months. First, adjust each of the last three months by dividing its actual job count by its seasonal index. The adjusted figure shows roughly how busy that month would have been if it were an ordinary month. Average the three adjusted figures and you have the underlying level of work. To forecast a future month, multiply the underlying level by that month's seasonal index. Refresh the level each month. If the level keeps drifting up or down over several months, the business is growing or shrinking, and a seasonal index alone cannot show that. Once a forecast shows a quiet month, a trade guide suggests spreading recurring visits into off-peak windows and capping plan sales to what the team can deliver.

lessons.title: Reading a profit and loss forecast
learningOutcomes: Build a profit and loss projection in the order sales, direct costs, gross profit, overheads, operating profit, interest, net profit
Calculate gross margin and net profit margin from the lines above them and state the sales base used
Identify which lines in a projection are facts, targets or assumptions, and which need a tax or accountant check

instructionSections.heading: What the statement answers
instructionSections.body: A profit and loss projection shows what the business expects to earn and spend over a period, and what remains after each layer of cost is taken off. Work through it line by line, beginning at sales. Sales come first, then the cost of doing the work, then the running costs of the business, then interest and tax. Every subtotal should be reproducible from the lines directly above it. If a subtotal cannot be recalculated from its inputs, the statement has a fault, however tidy it looks. The statement answers one question for the owner: after the work is paid for and the business is run, how much is left to pay the owner and to repay debt? It does not show cash timing, which is a separate question covered in the cash planning lessons.

instructionSections.heading: Build the layers in order
instructionSections.body: Start with sales for the period. Where the business is registered for GST, sales should be shown net of the GST collected, because that GST belongs to the Australian Taxation Office rather than to the business. The treatment should be confirmed with an accountant. Subtract direct costs, meaning materials and subcontractor labour that go into a specific job, to reach gross profit. Divide gross profit by sales to get gross margin. Next subtract overheads: wages, vehicle running costs, insurance, storage, phone and software, marketing and depreciation on tools and vehicles. Depreciation is a non-cash charge that spreads the cost of a long-life asset over its working life, so it reduces profit without a payment leaving the bank in that month. The result after overheads is operating profit. Subtract interest on borrowing to reach profit before tax, then subtract tax to reach net profit. Net profit margin is net profit divided by sales.

instructionSections.heading: Labour appears in more than one place
instructionSections.body: Employee wages, with the on-costs that attach to them, are an expense line. The owner's own living income is treated differently. In a sole trader structure, the owner's drawings are not a business expense in the same way, so the projection shows the profit available to the owner instead. A company structure pays its owner through salary or dividends, and the lines change again. Check them with a registered tax agent before the projection is used for pricing, borrowing or hiring decisions. Keep owner pay visible as its own line so that the person reading the plan can see what the business would have to earn to support the owner.

instructionSections.heading: Test the statement against itself
instructionSections.body: A projection that looks reasonable can still be inconsistent. Three tests catch most faults. First, check that gross margin changes only when direct cost or price assumptions change. Second, if sales rise while fixed overheads stay the same, net margin should rise, and the amount of the rise should agree with the arithmetic. Third, compare the statement with the break-even point built from the same figures. Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by the contribution margin, which is the share of each sales dollar left after variable costs. If the statement shows a loss at sales above that point, or a profit below it, one of the inputs is wrong. The method for reconciling conflicting break-even figures is taught in “Break-even analysis with a worked calculation”, and it applies directly here.

lessons.title: Reading a projected balance sheet
learningOutcomes: Classify assets, liabilities and equity as current or long-term, and explain the difference in one sentence each
Calculate owner equity from total assets and total liabilities, and check the result against a balanced statement
Explain why unpaid quotes and unpaid invoices must be treated differently on a balance sheet

instructionSections.heading: A snapshot at one date
instructionSections.body: A profit and loss covers a period, but a balance sheet records a single date. It lists what the business owns (assets), what it owes to others (liabilities), and what is left for the owner (equity). The three parts always agree: assets equal liabilities plus equity. This is the test that tells you whether the statement is sound. Profit from “Reading a profit and loss forecast” flows into equity over time, and the cash and equipment that the profit produces show up in assets. A projection that adds profit to equity without a matching change in assets or liabilities has a fault, and the imbalance points to where the fault is.

instructionSections.heading: Current and long-term lines
instructionSections.body: Current assets are cash and items expected to turn into cash within about a year. For a trade business these are usually the bank balance, money owed by clients for completed and invoiced work, and materials held for jobs. Long-term assets include vehicles, tools and equipment, shown at their value after depreciation. Current liabilities are amounts due within about a year: supplier accounts, GST and other tax owing to the Australian Taxation Office, and the repayments due on a short-term loan. Long-term liabilities are borrowings repaid over more than a year, such as a vehicle loan or equipment finance. Equity for a sole trader is the owner's capital plus profit kept in the business, less drawings taken out. A company shows share capital and retained earnings instead.

instructionSections.heading: Money owed is not cash
instructionSections.body: Trade businesses often carry a large balance of unpaid invoices. Those invoices count as current assets only once the work is done and an invoice has been issued. A quote that the client has not yet accepted is not an asset, and it does not belong on the balance sheet at all. Overdue invoices should be reviewed and, where the debt is doubtful, reduced in value rather than left at full face value. A balance sheet that looks strong because of high receivables can hide a cash problem, which is why the cash questions are tested separately in the cash planning lessons.

lessons.title: Writing the assumptions register behind a projection
learningOutcomes: Label each projection input as a fact, a target or an assumption, with the reason for the label
Complete an assumptions register with value, basis, source, date checked, owner and the next check date
Rank assumptions by how much a change would move profit, and choose the first three to verify

instructionSections.heading: Why a projection needs a register
instructionSections.body: Every projection rests on inputs: prices, job counts, costs, wages, interest rates and tax rates. A sample plan can present those inputs as a short table with no basis, date or owner, and a reader then has no way to tell which numbers were measured and which were guessed. An assumptions register fixes that. It is a single list of the inputs behind the statements, each with enough detail that someone else could check it. The register is the first thing a lender, partner or assessor will look for, and it is where a careless projection is exposed first.

instructionSections.heading: Three labels for every input
instructionSections.body: A fact comes from a record you can point to: a signed invoice, a supplier bill, a bank statement or a government rate published with a date. A target is what you intend to achieve, such as six jobs a month before the first quarter closes. An assumption is a belief you have not yet tested, such as the claim that one in five enquiries will become a booked job. The labels matter because they change how much weight a number can carry. Targets and assumptions should never be presented as facts, and they should always have a named check. Interest rates and tax rates in a sample plan are not facts for your business. Replace them with the rate in your loan offer or a current rate from an Australian source, or leave the rate blank until you have one.

instructionSections.heading: Columns and sensitivity
instructionSections.body: The register needs these columns: the input, its value and unit, its label, its basis, its source and the date checked, the person responsible, the next date it will be checked, and what changes in the plan if it is wrong. The last column is the most useful. Once every row has a value, change each important assumption by a fixed amount, for example ten percent lower job count or a higher material cost, and watch the effect on operating profit. The assumptions that move profit most are the first ones to verify. Those that move it very little can stay as they are until the next review.

lessons.title: Base, storage and service hours for a mobile trade business
learningOutcomes: Compare a home base, a rented workspace and a shared yard against the needs of a mobile trade business
Describe a secure storage plan for tools, stock and ladders, including what must be kept apart
Set service hours, a booking window and a confirmation step, and write them into the business plan

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a base for mobile work
instructionSections.body: A mobile trade business spends most of its working time at client sites, so the base is a place to store, load and plan rather than a place to meet clients. Three options are common: a home base, a rented workspace or a shared yard, and a sample plan may describe a rented office with a fitted workshop. Choose on function. The base needs secure storage for tools and stock, room to load a vehicle, and a place to do admin without clutter. A home base can be cheaper, but its use may be restricted by council, strata or landlord rules. Record the base, its cost, its access hours and the reason for the choice.

instructionSections.heading: Storage and separation
instructionSections.body: Tools, ladders, paint, fixings and consumables all need a defined place. Lockable storage protects both the stock and the client's property, and the vehicle should be secured whenever it is parked at the base. Keep chemicals and paints apart from food and from personal items, and store them according to their safety data sheet. The storage lessons “Storage, spills and disposal” and “Buying tools and equipment in stages” give the procedures in more detail. A simple stock list kept at the base shows what has been used, what must be bought and what has gone missing.

instructionSections.heading: Service hours and the booking window
instructionSections.body: Clients need to know when they can reach the business and how far ahead they can book. Write service hours as the times the phone, email or booking page is answered, separate from the hours the crew is on site. Set a booking window, which is the earliest and latest point at which a job can be scheduled, so that the owner can plan travel and capacity. State how a booking is confirmed and how a late enquiry is handled, including any out-of-hours message. The scheduling method should match the job scheduling field used in the business settings. A sample plan that opens an office at a fixed time can be used as a model for the format only; the hours themselves must reflect the owner's real availability.

lessons.title: Business ratios from the plan: margin, liquidity and how fast clients pay
learningOutcomes: Work out gross margin, the margin left after all costs, current ratio, debt to equity and receivable days from one profit and loss and one balance sheet
Explain what each ratio compares, and what a change in it would suggest about prices, costs, cash or client payment
Choose a first action from a ratio result, and explain why a rule-of-thumb threshold is not a legal test

instructionSections.heading: Ratios turn figures into comparisons
instructionSections.body: A single figure, such as a net profit of $22,100, says little about the business on its own. A ratio divides one figure by another so that businesses of different sizes can be compared, and so that the same business can be tracked over time. Every ratio needs two things stated: the numerator, which is the item on top, and the denominator, which is the base it is compared against. A ratio without its base is not a finding. Calculate ratios from the statements built in “Reading a profit and loss forecast” and “Reading a projected balance sheet” for the same date or period, and state the period beside each result. Ratios from different periods or different statement bases should not be compared directly.

instructionSections.heading: Margin, liquidity and debt
instructionSections.body: Gross margin and net profit margin both use sales as the denominator. A falling gross margin usually means the direct cost of each job has risen, or prices have been reduced or discounted; it is the first place to look when profit falls. Net profit margin shows how much of each sales dollar the business keeps after overheads, interest and tax. The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities. A result above one means current assets exceed current liabilities on paper, but it depends on how quickly receivables are paid and how much of the cash is committed. Debt to equity divides total liabilities by equity. The thresholds used in some sources, such as a current ratio of two, are rules of thumb that prompt a question. They are not legal tests.

instructionSections.heading: How fast clients pay
instructionSections.body: Receivable days estimate how long, on average, clients take to pay. Divide receivables by sales for the period and multiply by the number of days in the period, usually 365 for a year. A result close to the payment terms on the invoice is a healthy sign. A result much higher means money is being held by clients, which strains cash even when profit is good. The cause is usually invoicing delay, missing deposits, unclear payment terms or a client dispute. The fix is a process change, such as invoicing on completion and following up at a set day. A lower price is rarely the right first response, because it reduces margin and does nothing about the timing.

lessons.title: Defining a pool service offer and its boundaries
learningOutcomes: List each pool service the business will offer and describe what is included and excluded
Set a frequency, a visit length basis and the supplies for each service without using sample figures
Identify the services that fall outside the business's scope and must be referred
Decide which services need a licensed person or the operator's written instruction

instructionSections.heading: Why the offer comes first
instructionSections.body: A pool service that cannot say exactly what it does will price badly, promise too much and carry risks it did not plan for. The sample business plan lists a range of services: regular maintenance, chemical balancing and filter cleaning, algae removal, opening and closing, emergency cleaning and repairs, tile and grout cleaning, water testing and acid washing. That list is a structure to work through. It is not a set of services the business should offer, and the sample descriptions, prices and response times are hypothetical placeholders. Do not copy them. Write the offer from your own capacity, your training and the scope rules in “Scope, site classification and authority”.

instructionSections.heading: Describing each service
instructionSections.body: For each service, write four things: what is included, what is excluded, how often it is needed, and what it depends on. Regular maintenance covers skimming, vacuuming and brushing, basket emptying, the filter check and the routine chemistry readings the plan allows. It excludes repairs, water-treatment decisions outside the plan and electrical work. Chemical balancing depends on the operator plan and the test method. Filter cleaning depends on the manufacturer's trigger and the equipment condition. Algae removal depends on a diagnosis and on the product in the plan. Opening and closing depends on the operator's written instruction and the season. Write each service in this way, so that a client, a worker and an assessor read the same thing.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and the referral list
instructionSections.body: Some work is outside the business's scope even when the client asks for it. Electrical work, gas work, heater installation, liner replacement, draining, structural repair and any act that requires a licence are referred. Write a referral list that names each excluded task and the person or type of business it is referred to. A referral list protects the business and the client, and it prevents a worker from taking on a task they are not authorised to do.

instructionSections.heading: Emergency and after-hours work
instructionSections.body: An emergency service may be attractive, but it commits the business to availability and to a response. Do not state a response time or an availability that the business cannot sustain. If emergency work is offered, write what the emergency is, who decides it is an emergency, what is done on arrival and what is referred. Any emergency that involves electrical, gas, chemical or drowning risk goes through the referral and stop-work rules first.

lessons.title: Market, customers and competitors for pool services
learningOutcomes: Define target customer segments by who decides, what they buy and how frequently they need the service
Size a market only from a stated source and date, and label any estimate as an assumption
Describe competitors by what can be observed, with the date of observation
Mark any market figure from a US or older source as historical and not an Australian fact

instructionSections.heading: Segments and who decides
instructionSections.body: Pool services serve different customers with different decision-makers. Home owners decide for a single private pool. Body corporate committees and strata managers decide for shared pools. Commercial operators, such as hotels, resorts and holiday parks, decide through managers and contracts. Property managers and estate agents often decide for rental and sale properties. Green-pool restoration is a separate segment, because the work is a one-off restoration before any routine service. The sample plan lists residential, commercial, green-pool and mobile services, and it names real estate agents and property managers as an audience. Use this as a structure, and write your own segments.

instructionSections.heading: Sizing the market
instructionSections.body: A market size claim needs a source, a date and a definition. The sample plan shows available, served and target market boxes with placeholder figures, and those figures are hypothetical. In Australia, a figure for pools, pool owners or pool service spend must come from a named source with its date checked. Any US or foreign figure must be labelled historical and not used as an Australian fact. Where no source is found, write the estimate as an assumption and state how it was made.

instructionSections.heading: Competitors
instructionSections.body: Identify direct competitors, meaning other pool services for the same customers, and indirect competitors, meaning other ways customers solve the problem, such as doing it themselves or a general handyman. For each competitor, record only what can be observed: the services listed, the public scope, the online booking, the reviews, the stated emergency offer and the date seen. Do not guess their prices, their customer counts or their staff numbers. Write strengths and weaknesses from the observations, and say where a point is your view rather than a fact.

instructionSections.heading: Trends and regulation
instructionSections.body: Trends such as demand for eco-friendly service, automated cleaners or online booking should be written with a source and a date. Pool barrier, registration, operator and environmental rules depend on the state, territory and council, and they are covered in the pool-standards and water-conservation lessons rather than in this market analysis.

lessons.title: Pricing pool visits and service packages
learningOutcomes: Build a price for a visit from its costs: labour time, travel, supplies, equipment, insurance and overheads
Set a minimum charge and a policy for chemicals and materials
Price extras separately and agree them in writing before the work
Test a package price against the costs and the business's target, without using sample prices

instructionSections.heading: Costs before price
instructionSections.body: A price for a pool visit starts from the costs of the visit. Labour time includes the set-up, the work, the record and the travel between sites. Supplies include the chemicals the plan allows, the spare parts and the consumables. Equipment has a cost, which is spread over the jobs it serves. Insurance and the business overheads, such as vehicle, phone, software and accounts, have to be recovered too. The sample plan lists several pricing structures, including fixed, hourly and per-session prices, but its numbers are hypothetical and are not used here. Set your own figures from your own costs and record how each figure was made.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing method and minimum charge
instructionSections.body: Choose a method and write it down. A common approach is a visit price made of time, travel and supplies, with a minimum charge so that a short visit still covers its costs. Set the minimum charge from your own costs and state it in the pricing policy. A minimum is a protection, not a discount. Also decide whether a visit price changes for access difficulty, distance, dirty pools or repeat neglect, and write the rule in advance, so the client knows how the price is worked out.

instructionSections.heading: Chemicals and materials
instructionSections.body: Decide whether chemicals are included in the visit price, charged as a separate line, or passed through at cost. Each option has a cost to the business and a risk of dispute. Whichever policy is chosen, record it, show the amount on the invoice, and keep the supplier's receipt. Materials such as replacement baskets or seals are priced as extras, with the price agreed in writing first. Do not sell a product that the operator plan does not allow.

instructionSections.heading: Packages and discounts
instructionSections.body: A package bundles visits or services at one price, often with a commitment period. A package must still cover its costs at the frequency it promises. Test each package against the visit cost. A discount that takes the price below cost cannot be sustained, and it harms the business and the service. Write any discount as a stated rule with its conditions, and check that it leaves a margin.

instructionSections.heading: Testing the price
instructionSections.body: Test the price against the business's target in three ways: whether the visits in a month cover the fixed costs, whether a single visit covers its direct costs and its share of overheads, and whether the margin matches what the owner needs. The assumptions behind these tests belong in the assumptions register described in “Writing the assumptions register behind a projection”. Where a price is marked as an assumption, record it as one.

lessons.title: Marketing, referrals and retention for pool service work
learningOutcomes: Choose marketing channels for each customer segment and state the reason for each
Set up a referral route with property managers, real estate agents, builders and other trades
Plan retention activities such as service follow-up and annual service agreements
Check every marketing claim against the evidence and the advertising rules before it is published

instructionSections.heading: Channels that match the customer
instructionSections.body: A pool service reaches home owners, body corporates, commercial operators and property managers through different channels. The sample plan lists social media, content marketing, an email newsletter, paid search, brochures, referral programmes, direct sales calls and partnerships. Those are a useful list of channels. Choose the channels that reach the segments in your own analysis, and state the reason for each one. Record how many enquiries each channel brings, so that the channels that do not work can be dropped.

instructionSections.heading: Referral and partner routes
instructionSections.body: The most reliable source of pool work is often a referral from someone who already trusts the service. Property managers, real estate agents, builders, pool installers and other trades can refer clients. Set up each partner route in writing. State what the partner gets, what the business gets, and how referrals are logged.

instructionSections.heading: Claims and advertising
instructionSections.body: Every marketing claim needs evidence. Words such as safe, chemical-free, eco-friendly, guaranteed, certified or the best must be avoided unless the business can show the evidence and the claim is accurate. Testimonials must be genuine, given with permission, and not invented. Check each claim, and each advertising channel, before publication.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping customers
instructionSections.body: Retention is cheaper than acquisition. Build routines that keep customers informed: a short note after each visit with the readings and the tasks done, a reminder before a seasonal task, and an offer of an annual service agreement with its terms written out. Follow up on any complaint and record the outcome. A loyalty discount is a pricing decision and follows the rules in “Pricing pool visits and service packages”.

instructionSections.heading: Tracking what works
instructionSections.body: Track the enquiries, the conversions, the cost of each channel and the retention rate by segment. Review the tracking at a set date. Stop or change any channel that costs more than it returns.

lessons.title: Operations, staffing, equipment and compliance for pool service work
learningOutcomes: Describe the operating process from enquiry to completed visit and record
Set out who may do which tasks, and the supervision and training each task requires
Plan the equipment list, its maintenance and the storage of chemicals
List each compliance requirement with its status, marked as checked or still to be checked

instructionSections.heading: The operating process
instructionSections.body: Write the process from the first enquiry to the completed visit: the enquiry, the site visit, the quote, the agreement, the scheduling, the visit, the record, the invoice and the follow-up. The sample plan lists quotations, scheduling, site visits and staff training as the core of its process. Keep those steps, and add a step for the operator's written instruction on any treatment task. Each step names the person who does it and the record it creates.

instructionSections.heading: Staff, tasks and training
instructionSections.body: Write a list of the tasks each person may do. Some tasks, such as surface cleaning and basket emptying, can be done by a trained worker under supervision. Others, such as water treatment decisions, chemical dosing beyond the plan, electrical work and gas work, need the operator or a licensed person. The sample plan lists staff roles such as a manager, a sales specialist and an operations manager. Those roles are a structure only. Record the training each task needs, and the supervision in place until a worker is signed off.

instructionSections.heading: Staff engagement
instructionSections.body: The US guide suggests hiring through local advertisements and through people the owner knows. Contractors and employees differ in status, so the distinction must be checked against Australian rules.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment, maintenance and storage
instructionSections.body: List each item of equipment, its maintenance schedule and its storage. Include the vacuum and hoses, brushes, test equipment, the pump or filter tools, the vehicle and the chemical store. Test kits and gauges should be checked against the maker's instructions. Chemicals are stored separated by type, locked and away from fuel and people, and the vehicle carries them securely.

instructionSections.heading: Compliance register
instructionSections.body: Set up a compliance register. For each requirement, record the source, the date checked, the authority and its status. Where a requirement has not been checked, name the individual responsible for checking it. Requirements to record include business registration, any licence or competence for each service, electrical and gas work restrictions, dangerous goods, workplace health and safety, insurance and records. No entry may be marked as checked without a source and a date.

lessons.title: Financial plan structure, assumptions and break-even for pool service work
learningOutcomes: Describe the parts of a financial plan for pool service work: forecast, profit and loss, cash flow, balance sheet and break-even
Write an assumptions register that links volume, price and cost for each forecast line
Work out a break-even point in words and with the business's own inputs
Identify the financing needs and state each one with its basis

instructionSections.heading: The parts of the finance section
instructionSections.body: A financial plan for pool service work usually contains a sales forecast, a income and expense statement, a cash flow statement, a balance sheet, a break-even analysis and a statement of financing needs. The sample plan has all of these as blank tables with zero entries, so it shows the structure only. The business's numbers must come from its own volumes, prices and costs, with the assumptions written down.

instructionSections.heading: The assumptions register
instructionSections.body: Every forecast line rests on an assumption. For a pool business the main ones are the number of visits per week, the number of clients on each service, the average price per visit, the chemical and supply cost per visit, the travel time and cost, the labour cost, the insurance cost, the vehicle and equipment cost, the overheads and the owner's pay. Write each assumption, its value, its basis and its date. The method is taught in “Writing the assumptions register behind a projection”.

instructionSections.heading: Profit, cash and the balance sheet
instructionSections.body: The income and expense statement shows the income and costs over a period. The cash flow statement shows when money comes in and goes out, which can differ widely, because clients pay later than the visit and some costs fall before any income. The balance sheet shows what the business owns and owes at a date. Read these together with “Reading a profit and loss forecast” and “Reading a projected balance sheet”, and check that a profit does not hide a cash shortfall.

instructionSections.heading: Break-even
instructionSections.body: The break-even point is the level of activity at which income equals costs. In words: divide the fixed costs for the period by the margin each visit contributes after its direct costs, and that gives the number of visits needed to break even. Use only the business's own fixed costs, margin and assumptions. “Break-even and sales forecast by stage” describes the method for a stage-by-stage break-even. Avoid using a sample plan's break-even table, because its figures are placeholders.

instructionSections.heading: Financing needs
instructionSections.body: State the financing needs in two parts: the start-up costs, such as equipment, vehicle, initial supplies and registration fees, and the working capital needed to cover the time before cash comes in. For each need, state the amount it is built from, the source of the funds and the date needed.

lessons.title: Pool service business plan (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Complete each field of the pool service business plan from the business's own information
Link services, customers, pricing, marketing, operations and finance to the same definitions
Mark each compliance item as checked with a source, or leave it out
Submit the assembled plan for assessor sign-off against the rubric

instructionSections.heading: How the template works
instructionSections.body: You build the plan field by field. Each field asks for one part of the plan and says what a good answer contains. When every required field is complete, the system assembles one document that you keep. There are no model answers, and the output document contains only what you write. Do not copy the sample plan's text, names, prices or figures. Where you do not yet know an answer, name the individual responsible for confirming it.

instructionSections.heading: Consistency across the plan
instructionSections.body: Use the same names for the same things throughout. A segment named in the customers field must be the segment used in the pricing and marketing fields. A service named in the services field must be the service priced in the pricing field. An assessor checks this first, and inconsistency is the most frequent reason a plan is returned.

instructionSections.heading: Sources and dates
instructionSections.body: Every market, cost and compliance statement shows its source and the date checked, or is marked as the author's observation. Foreign and historical figures are labelled as such and are not used as Australian facts.

lessons.title: Defining needs, outcomes and specifications
learningOutcomes: Distinguish an output or performance specification from a conformance specification, and choose the style that fits a given purchase.
Write a requirement that states what is needed in testable terms, without unnecessary design detail.
Identify when a specification adds excess cost or shuts out suitable alternatives, including brand-name requirements.
Name sources of information for a specification and state what each one is used for.

instructionSections.heading: A need is not yet a specification
instructionSections.body: Buying starts with a need: something the business must achieve, such as clean floors across three sites each night, or a vehicle that can carry a particular load safely. A requirement turns that need into a statement of what the item or service must do, who it serves and when it is needed. A specification goes one step further and describes the characteristics a supplier must meet, so the buyer can tell whether an offer is acceptable. Many poor purchases come from skipping the first two steps. The buyer jumps to a product name, asks for a price on that name, and then finds the product does not do what the business needed. Before writing anything, ask what the business must achieve, how success would be measured, what the item must never do, and what would make a supplier unacceptable. Those four answers form the base of any specification, whichever style is chosen.

instructionSections.heading: Three styles of specification
instructionSections.body: An output specification describes the result the buyer needs and leaves the method to the supplier. It usually names key performance indicators, such as the share of work passing inspection or the time taken to finish a task, and it states the standard each result must meet. A performance specification describes how the item must behave under stated conditions, for example the load it must carry, the noise it may make or the energy it may use, and the test that will prove it. A conformance specification describes the item in detail: the design, dimensions, materials, method or referenced standard that must be matched. Checking then means comparing what arrives with the description. Guides use these three terms differently, so write down the definitions your purchasing policy uses and state them in each request. A practical test is to ask who carries the design risk. If the buyer fixes the design and the design fails, the buyer carries that risk. If the buyer fixes the result, the supplier carries more of the risk and has more room to propose an efficient design.

instructionSections.heading: Avoiding excess cost, gaps and lock-out
instructionSections.body: Over-specification is a common source of excess cost. A specification that asks for features the business will never use raises the price, narrows the field of suppliers who can bid, and can make the item harder to maintain. Under-specification has the opposite problem: the offer looks cheap, but gaps in the description lead to disputes, variations and rework once the work starts. Brand names are a frequent cause of lock-out. Naming one brand tells suppliers that nothing else will be accepted, even when an alternative could meet the same performance measures. If a brand is named for compatibility or another real reason, say so, and add the words or equivalent together with the performance criteria an equivalent must meet. Whatever style is chosen, a good specification is clear, complete enough to be checked, and free of terms that two readers would understand differently. A useful test is to give the draft to two people who did not write it and see whether they would assess an offer in the same way.

instructionSections.heading: Where the information comes from
instructionSections.body: The best specifications are built with the people who will use the item and with the market that will supply it. Users show what the work really involves. A short walk-through with the staff who will run a machine often reveals requirements that a manager would not think to write down. Suppliers can explain what the market offers, which standards are common and which costs drive the price. Early market engagement, usually through a request for information, lets a buyer test assumptions before committing to a document. Published sources also help: government reports, trade directories, industry standards and benchmarking data can show what good practice looks like. Competitors' public material can be useful, but a buyer must never use confidential information from one organisation to shape a request sent to another. Record where each requirement came from, because that record explains the reason for each requirement when someone later asks why an offer was accepted or rejected.

lessons.title: Cost types and budgeting for purchasing
learningOutcomes: Classify a cost as direct or indirect, and explain the basis used to share out an indirect cost.
Classify a cost as fixed, variable or mixed, and state the period and activity range the classification relies on.
Choose a budgeting method for a cost line and give a one-sentence reason.
Calculate a budget variance, label it favourable or unfavourable, and split it into volume and price effects.

instructionSections.heading: Direct and indirect costs
instructionSections.body: A direct cost can be traced to one cost object, such as a job, a product batch or a client contract, in a way that is practical to record. The chemicals used on one job and the hours a technician records against that job are direct costs. An indirect cost supports several jobs or the whole business and cannot be traced to a single cost object without an allocation. Supervision, insurance, rent and the cost of the office system are typical examples. Indirect costs are shared out using a basis, such as hours worked, floor area or number of jobs. The basis matters, because it changes the cost recorded against each job and therefore the price a client should be quoted. Anyone who reads an all-in price should be able to see which costs were shared out and why. This distinction is about how a cost is traced to what it supports. It is separate from whether the cost moves with volume, which is covered next.

instructionSections.heading: Fixed and variable costs over a period
instructionSections.body: A fixed cost stays the same in total across a range of activity over a stated period. A variable cost changes in total as activity changes. Rent for a month is fixed for that month, even when the number of jobs goes up or down. Materials used per job are variable: more jobs mean more materials. Many costs are mixed, with a fixed part and a variable part, and need splitting before they can be budgeted. The label depends on two things: the period being looked at and the range of activity expected. Over a longer period more costs become variable, because a lease can be renegotiated or a supervisor can be hired or let go. A cost can therefore be fixed for a quarter and variable over a year. When you label a cost, state both the period and the range, so the label is not mistaken for a permanent fact.

instructionSections.heading: Budgeting methods and when each fits
instructionSections.body: An incremental budget starts from last period's spend and adds an allowance for change. It is quick to prepare, but it carries forward spending that nobody has tested. A zero-based budget requires every line to be justified again from nil at each cycle. It takes more effort, but it exposes spending that exists only because it always existed. An activity-based budget links costs to the activities that drive them, which helps show what a service really consumes. A fixed budget sets one amount for one planned level of activity. A flexible budget restates the allowed amount at the level of activity that actually occurred, which makes the comparison fairer when volumes move. A rolling budget is extended forward by a set period as each period closes, so it always covers the next interval. A common practical approach for a small business is a fixed annual budget, reviewed each quarter, with a flexible view for volume-driven lines such as consumables.

instructionSections.heading: Building a purchasing budget and reading a variance
instructionSections.body: A purchasing budget starts with the expected volume of work, because volume drives most consumable and service purchasing. Past purchase prices give a baseline, but they should be adjusted for known supplier price changes and for market information. Supplier quotes and published price indices help check those adjustments. A variance is the actual result minus the budget. For a cost line, an actual below budget is a favourable variance and an actual above budget is an unfavourable one. Do not judge a variance by its sign alone. Split it into a volume effect, which is the change in activity multiplied by the budgeted cost per unit, and a price or usage effect, which is the change in cost per unit multiplied by the actual activity. The two parts show whether spending rose because more work was done or because each unit cost more. Budgets also carry a behavioural risk: managers may spend what is left in a line at the end of a period to protect next year's allowance, so review the reason for every large variance.

lessons.title: Market analysis and buying contexts
learningOutcomes: Separate the macro environment from the micro market when reading a supply market, and name a source for each.
Explain the five forces that shape a market, and name the force that matters most for a given purchase.
Compare a price with a like-for-like comparator, and state the difference between price analysis and benchmarking.
Classify a purchase as a straight re-buy, a modified re-buy or a new task, and set the effort to match.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the market before buying
instructionSections.body: Before a buyer commits to a supplier, it helps to understand the market that supplier operates in. Some pressures sit outside both the buyer and the supplier: political decisions, economic conditions, social trends, technology, legal requirements and environmental pressures. These are the macro environment, and they are usually read from external sources such as government statistics, trade publications and reputable news reports. The micro environment is closer to the purchase: the suppliers able to meet the need, the customers and other buyers competing for the same capacity, and the firms that might enter the market. A supplier's financial reports help show whether it is stable enough to hold a long contract. A code of ethics sets how buyer and supplier should behave. The purpose of this reading is practical. It tells the buyer how many suppliers can meet the need, how much each one can shape price and terms, and how much risk the buyer carries if one of them fails.

instructionSections.heading: Porter's five forces
instructionSections.body: Michael Porter's five forces model describes the pressures that limit the profit available in a market. Rivalry among existing competitors is stronger when there are many firms of similar size, growth is slow, fixed costs are high and products are hard to tell apart. The threat of new entrants depends on barriers to entry: set-up and capital costs, economies of scale, customer switching costs, access to distribution and the expectation that incumbents will respond hard to a newcomer. Where barriers are low, new firms are more likely to enter and push prices down. The threat of substitutes is high when customers can meet the same need another way at a comparable cost, because that limits what a supplier can charge. The bargaining power of suppliers rises when a few suppliers dominate, when substitute inputs are scarce, when the buyer is a small customer for the supplier and when switching away is costly. The bargaining power of buyers rises when there are many alternatives, large volumes, standard products and low switching costs. In most purchases, the supplier-power force decides how much room the buyer has to negotiate.

instructionSections.heading: Market structures and what they mean for the buyer
instructionSections.body: A monopoly exists where one seller supplies a market and entry is blocked by high barriers. In that case the seller usually holds the stronger position, because the buyer has no real alternative to switch to. A buyer facing a monopoly can reduce its need for the item, look for substitutes, change the specification so that other suppliers can offer a compliant alternative, shape contract terms that allow for future competition, or decide whether to make the item in-house. Where many sellers compete, the buyer has more leverage, although that leverage depends on how similar the offers are. Some manufacturing industries need large investment and skilled labour, which raises barriers to entry and fixed costs. When demand falls, those fixed costs can make rivalry intense. No structure is good or bad in itself. The point is that the buyer should identify which structure applies before setting its negotiating approach and contract terms.

instructionSections.heading: Price analysis, benchmarking and buying contexts
instructionSections.body: Price analysis compares the price paid with a comparator that is like for like. Useful comparators include the previous price for the same item and specification, a published index or catalogue price, a competing quote for the same scope, and a should-cost estimate built from the materials, labour and overheads the supplier must cover. Comparing a service with a different scope, volume or delivery term produces a misleading result. Benchmarking reaches wider. It compares performance, unit cost, service levels or process steps with a reference group, so the buyer can see what good practice looks like and whether a supplier is out of line. Its purpose is learning and improvement. A buyer must not use benchmarking to pressure a supplier with another supplier's confidential terms, and must not pass one supplier's confidential price to another. The buying context sets the effort. A straight re-buy is a routine repeat from the same supplier, to the same specification, with little search and little negotiation. A modified re-buy is a familiar purchase where something has changed, such as the specification, supplier, price, volume or terms, so it needs a review and usually more people. A new task is a purchase the business has never made before. It is the highest-risk context, because there is no experience to rely on, so it calls for wide information search and a larger decision group. Extending an existing contract with new services is a common trap. The label on the old contract does not settle the context. Each new service is judged by how new it is to the buyer.

lessons.title: Cost-down, value for money and cost-benefit
learningOutcomes: Explain value for money as a combination of whole-of-life cost and fit for the stated need, and identify the non-price factors that also count.
List the one-off, running and exit costs that belong in a whole-of-life comparison.
Apply value analysis to a cost-down review without removing a function the outcome still needs.
Prepare a simple cost-benefit analysis for a purchase decision, and record the non-financial benefits separately.

instructionSections.heading: Value for money is not the lowest price
instructionSections.body: The Commonwealth Procurement Rules make value for money the core rule of procurement. Paragraph 3.4 calls achieving value for money the core rule of the rules, and it requires consideration of financial and non-financial costs and benefits. Under paragraph 4.4, officials responsible for a procurement must be satisfied, after reasonable enquiries, that the procurement achieves a value for money outcome. Paragraph 4.5 says price is not the sole factor: an official must consider the financial and non-financial costs and benefits of each submission, including quality, fitness for purpose, the supplier's experience, performance and ethical conduct, flexibility and innovation, environmental sustainability and whole-of-life costs. The value-for-money page does not define the term. This lesson uses a working definition: value for money is the best combination of whole-of-life cost and quality for the stated need, judged against the specification. A low price that fails the need is poor value. A higher price that meets the need at a lower total cost can be the better buy. Record the judgement and its reasons, so that another person can see why the choice was made.

instructionSections.heading: Whole-of-life cost
instructionSections.body: Whole-of-life cost is the total cost of owning and using an item or service over its life, and the purchase price is only one part of it. Paragraph 4.6 of the rules gives examples, including maintenance and operating costs, transition-out costs, licensing costs, and decommissioning, remediation and disposal costs. For a small business the same idea applies. Running costs include consumables, energy, servicing and insurance. Training people to use the item is a cost. The cost of getting out of the arrangement, such as moving to another supplier or removing equipment at the end, is also a cost. Total acquisition cost is a narrower idea that adds delivery, installation and set-up costs to the price. The gap between the cheapest quote and the lowest whole-of-life cost often sits in running and exit costs, which are easy to overlook when comparing quotes on the first page.

instructionSections.heading: Cost-down and value analysis
instructionSections.body: Cost-down is the deliberate reduction of the cost of a product or service without losing the function the business needs. It can be done by changing the specification, for example by accepting a material that performs the same function at a lower cost, or by changing the way the work is delivered. Value analysis asks three questions about each element: what function it performs, what it costs, and whether another element could perform the same function for less. Removing an item from the specification can be a valid cost-down step, but only after the function it performs has been identified and confirmed as unnecessary, or moved to another item. Removing a function the outcome still needs produces failure, rework or disputes, and those costs can exceed the saving. Repeating the current contract and waiting for the market to deliver a lower price is not cost-down. It leaves the cost choices untouched. A cost-down review is strongest when it starts from the specification and the whole-of-life picture, because that is where the real cost choices sit.

instructionSections.heading: Cost-benefit analysis for a purchase decision
instructionSections.body: A cost-benefit analysis compares the quantified costs and benefits of a decision over a stated period. List every cost: the price, set-up and transition costs, training, trial periods, running costs, maintenance and the cost of exit. Then list every benefit that can be measured in money, such as savings in consumables, fewer call-backs or less downtime. Benefits that cannot be measured in money, such as lower environmental impact or reduced risk to staff, should be recorded separately, with the reason, rather than forced into a dollar figure. Where one supplier could stop supply, a contingency source or extra stock has a cost too. Put that cost in the analysis as a risk line, state how often a failure might happen as an assumption, and record where the assumption came from. Test the result against the assumptions that matter most, and note what result would change the decision. Scale the analysis to the purchase. A detailed study of a small item can cost more than it saves. Paragraph 4.4(e) asks that the effort put into a procurement fit its size and breadth.

lessons.title: Chart of accounts for a service business
learningOutcomes: Set up a numbered chart of accounts for a service business, grouped by asset, liability, equity, income, cost of sales and expense.
Post a client deposit, a completed job and a staff payroll amount to the correct accounts.
Identify which tax points in the chart must be confirmed by a registered tax agent before use.

instructionSections.heading: What a chart of accounts does
instructionSections.body: A chart of accounts is the numbered list of every account your business uses to record money. Each transaction, such as a card payment from a client, a receipt for cleaning products or a payment to a staff member, is posted to one account, so that the totals at month end mean something. For a small service business the list can be short, but it has to answer a few questions: how much cash you hold, what clients owe you, what you owe, what you earned, what each job cost in materials, and what the business spent on running costs. The numbers used in this lesson are an illustrative layout, grouped into assets, liabilities, equity, income, cost of sales and expenses. They are not an official standard, and your bookkeeper or accounting software may use a different scheme. What matters is that every account has a number, a plain description and one clear use, so that two people posting the same transaction choose the same account.

instructionSections.heading: The accounts a service business needs
instructionSections.body: Start with assets. Cash at bank holds the balance of the business transaction account, and a small cash float is kept separately only for minor purchases. Trade debtors hold invoices that have been issued but not yet paid, for example a commercial client who pays on account. Consumables stock holds cleaning products, materials and supplies bought for future jobs, and the cost moves into cost of sales when the product is used on a job. Equipment such as a tool, a machine or a pressure washer, and any vehicle you own, sit in non-current assets, with accumulated depreciation recorded in a contra account. Liabilities include trade creditors, client deposits received in advance, GST collected, PAYG withholding payable for amounts held back from staff pay, and superannuation payable for staff. A client deposit for a booking is owed as work, so it is a liability and not income until the job is done. Equity holds the owner's capital and drawings. Income separates service sales from product sales and any call-out fees, so you can see which service earns money. Expenses group advertising, insurance, vehicle running costs, phone and internet, storage, wages, workers compensation premiums, licences and registrations, bank fees and depreciation.

instructionSections.heading: Australian terms and what still needs checking
instructionSections.body: Use your ABN on invoices and in the accounts set-up. Keep GST and PAYG as separate ledger accounts. The ATO's record-keeping guidance says to set GST aside in a separate ledger account where GST credits are claimed, and it points to PAYG payment summaries for amounts withheld from payments. The ATO's GST guidance sets the rate at 10 per cent and applies it to most sales of goods and services in Australia. The ATO's registration page puts the GST turnover threshold at $75,000, so whether your business must register depends on its own turnover. The ATO's PAYG withholding guidance explains that a business may need to hold back an amount from some payments, pass it to the ATO on due dates set by its withholding status, and issue the right payment summary. The ATO superannuation page gives the general super guarantee rate as 12.00 per cent from 1 July 2025, so set up a superannuation payable account to hold the amount owed until it is paid to the fund. That page was last updated on 17 April 2026, so recheck the rate for the period you are recording. Ask a registered tax agent to confirm each of these before you rely on the chart.

lessons.title: Keeping records for a service business
learningOutcomes: Keep a job record for each booking that links the quote, the condition record, the invoice and the payment.
Reconcile the bank account and the GST ledger each month, and resolve any difference before the next month begins.
Write a retention schedule that states how long each kind of record is kept and when it is disposed of.

instructionSections.heading: What must be kept, and for how long
instructionSections.body: The ATO's employment and payroll records guidance says employee payment and PAYG withholding records are kept for 5 years, but the Fair Work Ombudsman says time and wages records are kept for 7 years, so the schedule must not apply the 5-year period to time and wages records. The period runs from the later of when the record was made or obtained, and when the transaction or related act was completed. Where a review period runs longer, the records must be kept until that period ends. For a service business, the records to keep include records of all cash and electronic transactions, including reconciled card and EFTPOS sales; records that support business expenses claimed as deductions; records of the business portion of an expense that also has private use, such as a vehicle or a phone; a separate GST ledger account where GST credits are claimed; and PAYG payment summaries for amounts withheld from payments. This is a teaching summary, not the full list, so check the ATO page for the complete list before you set the schedule. Superannuation paid for staff is recorded against the payroll, and the general super guarantee rate for the period is 12.00 per cent from 1 July 2025.

instructionSections.heading: The job record as the evidence for each job
instructionSections.body: A job record is the single file that proves what was booked, what was agreed, what was done and what was paid. Open it when the booking is confirmed, not after the job. Attach the quote, the booking confirmation with the included and excluded items, the pre-work condition record and the photographs, and the consent for photographs where it was given. Add the time on site, the products and consumables used, the handover note and any complaint. Then link the invoice and the payment, so that the income, the deposit and the balance can each be traced to the job. Store photographs under the job number, not in a general camera roll, so that they can be found when a client raises a question months later. Keep the record secure, and limit who can open it. When a client asks for a copy, check what the record contains before sending it, and remove any information that does not belong to that client. The job record is also the source for the complaint register, so a complaint should always point back to the job it concerns.

instructionSections.heading: The monthly routine: reconcile, check GST, prepare the BAS
instructionSections.body: A monthly routine keeps small problems small. Each week, file receipts and supplier invoices against the job or the expense type they belong to. Each month, reconcile the bank account: match every bank line to a receipt, an invoice, a payment or a transfer, and note any line that cannot be matched. Check that the GST ledger balances against the sales and purchases recorded for the period, and that client deposits are still held as liabilities for jobs not yet completed. Record PAYG withholding and superannuation for staff as they are incurred, not when the bill arrives. Good practice is to base each business activity statement on complete and accurate records rather than estimates. Ask your registered tax agent for the lodgement and payment schedule that applies to your business. Keep the reconciliation sheet with the month's records, so that anyone checking the books can see how each difference was resolved.

lessons.title: Equipment, vehicles and depreciation for a service business
learningOutcomes: Separate a purchase that is used up in one period from an asset that is kept for several periods.
Set up an asset account and a matching accumulated depreciation contra account for one item of equipment.
Explain why the instant asset write-off or another depreciation treatment must be confirmed for the year by a registered tax agent.

instructionSections.heading: Why some purchases are kept as assets
instructionSections.body: Not every payment is an expense in the month it leaves the bank. A tool, machine or vehicle that the business keeps and uses for several years is first recorded as a non-current asset at its cost. Its cost is then spread across the years in which it helps earn income, through depreciation. The asset account keeps the original cost, so the amount paid stays visible. Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset account that sits beside it and builds up each period. The carrying amount, sometimes called book value, is the cost less the accumulated depreciation. Depreciation expense is the amount charged to the income statement for the period. Posting it does not move any money, because no cash leaves the bank when the entry is made. Land is listed among non-current assets in many charts, but it is not normally depreciated as an accounting convention, so a land account should not have a depreciation partner account.

instructionSections.heading: Working out an annual charge, and recording a sale
instructionSections.body: A simple way to spread cost is the straight-line method. Take the cost of the asset, deduct any amount you expect to get at the end of its life (often nothing for small equipment), and divide the result by the number of years you expect to use it. The answer is the yearly charge, which can be split into months if the asset is bought part-way through a year. Keep a register that lists each asset with its date first used, its cost, the method, the expected life, the charge to date and the carrying amount. When an asset is sold, compare the sale price with its carrying amount. A sale above that amount produces a gain on sale of assets, which the chart records as income. A sale below it produces a loss. Remove both the cost and the accumulated depreciation from the books when the asset leaves the business, so that nothing is left behind on the balance sheet.

instructionSections.heading: Australian tax treatment and what still needs checking
instructionSections.body: The tax treatment of a business asset is a separate question from the book entry, and the two can differ. The ATO's instant asset write-off page sets the per-asset threshold at $20,000 for assets first used or installed ready for use on or after 1 July 2023, for businesses with aggregated turnover under $10 million. That page was last updated on 28 August 2026, and its worked examples apply the rule to 2025–26, so check whether it applies to the income year you are recording. Whether a particular asset qualifies, whether the write-off continues in the current year, how the book depreciation should match the tax claim, and the depreciation rates for each class of asset are for a tax agent to confirm. Vehicles used partly for private purposes need a separate treatment, which a tax agent should confirm. Ask a registered tax agent to confirm each point before the figures go into a tax return.

lessons.title: From source document to journal and ledger
learningOutcomes: Name the steps of the accounting cycle from source document to closing, in order.
Write a balanced journal entry for a transaction, with the correct account on the debit side and the credit side.
Post journal entries to ledger accounts, and find the balance of each account.

instructionSections.heading: The accounting cycle in order
instructionSections.body: The accounting cycle is the repeating set of steps that turns everyday transactions into financial statements. It begins with a source document, such as an invoice, a receipt, a bank statement or a payroll summary, which shows what happened and when. The transaction is then analysed to decide which accounts change and by how much. It is recorded in the journal, posted to the ledger, checked through a trial balance, adjusted for items that belong to the period but are not yet in the books, closed at the end of the period, and reported in the income statement and balance sheet.
