The steps are the same for a small service business as for a large one. Keeping them in this order lets someone else trace each figure back to its source.

instructionSections.heading: Journal entries and the debit and credit rule
instructionSections.body: A journal entry is the first written record of a transaction. Each entry has a date, a description, at least one account to debit and at least one to credit, and amounts whose debit total equals its credit total. Which side an amount goes on depends on the type of account. Asset and expense accounts increase on the debit side and decrease on the credit side. Liability, equity and income accounts increase on the credit side and decrease on the debit side. A debit is not good and a credit is not bad; they are simply the two sides of every account. An entry that does not balance must be found and corrected before it is posted, because an unbalanced entry makes every later total unreliable.

instructionSections.heading: Posting to the ledger and checking the balances
instructionSections.body: The ledger holds one account for each item in the chart. Posting copies each journal line to the matching ledger account, on the side named in the entry. An account that normally carries a debit balance, such as cash or an expense, has its balance worked out as the debits less the credits; an account that normally carries a credit balance, such as a liability or income, has its balance worked out as the credits less the debits. Keep the ledger in account-number order, and record the source document reference beside each posting, so the trail can be followed. Where GST credits are claimed, the ATO's record-keeping guidance says to keep the GST in a separate ledger account, so the GST element is posted there rather than to the expense or asset account. The ledger balances are the input to the trial balance, which is covered in “Trial balance, adjusting entries and closing the books”.

lessons.title: Trial balance, adjusting entries and closing the books
learningOutcomes: Prepare an unadjusted trial balance from ledger balances, and explain what it does and does not prove.
Prepare adjusting entries for accrued expenses, prepaid expenses, depreciation and doubtful debts.
Place the closing entries in order, and explain what remains open in the post-closing trial balance.

instructionSections.heading: What the trial balance proves and what it does not
instructionSections.body: An unadjusted trial balance lists every ledger account with its balance, placed in a debit or a credit column. If the two columns total the same, the debits and credits have been entered equally, which is a useful arithmetic check. It does not prove that each amount sits in the right account, that an entry was not missed, or that the period's items are complete. An error such as a payment posted to the wrong expense account still balances. The trial balance is therefore a checkpoint between the ledger and the financial statements, not a finished report, and it is the starting point for adjustments.

instructionSections.heading: Adjusting entries for items that belong to the period
instructionSections.body: Adjusting entries are made at the end of a period so that income and expenses fall into the period they relate to. Accrued expenses are costs the business has incurred but not yet paid or billed, such as wages earned by staff up to the period end, and they are recorded against a liability. Prepaid expenses are payments made in advance, such as insurance for a year. Only the part used in the period is expensed, and the rest stays as an asset until it is used. Depreciation is the period's share of a non-current asset's cost, as set out in “Equipment, vehicles and depreciation for a service business”. An allowance for doubtful debts is an estimate of client invoices that may not be paid, shown as a contra-asset against trade debtors. Unearned income, such as a client deposit for work not yet done, is moved to income only as the work is performed, which links to the deposit treatment in “Chart of accounts for a service business”. Each adjustment needs a description and a note of the reason it is needed.

instructionSections.heading: Closing the books and preparing the statements
instructionSections.body: Once the adjusted trial balance is agreed, the statements are prepared. The income statement shows the period's income less its expenses. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at the period end. Closing entries then reset the temporary accounts to nil for the next period. Income and expense accounts are transferred to an income summary account, the income summary is transferred to owner's equity, and owner's drawings are transferred to equity, because drawings are not an expense. Balance sheet accounts are not closed. A post-closing trial balance is then prepared to show that only the permanent accounts still carry balances and that the debits and credits still agree. Some businesses also post reversing entries at the start of the next period for certain accruals, so that the first payment is recorded simply. Whether and how to do this is a bookkeeping choice, and it should be applied consistently.

lessons.title: Explaining the organisation's infection control policy to the team
learningOutcomes: Confirm the current infection control rules before a briefing
Explain infection risks and their controls to a team in plain words
Record the briefing and the questions raised, and check understanding

instructionSections.heading: Start from the current policy
instructionSections.body: A briefing is only as reliable as the policy it describes. Before briefing the team, confirm which version of the organisation's infection control policy applies and where its procedures are kept. Industry codes may also apply. If you cannot find a current version, say so in the briefing and escalate it; do not work from memory or from an older copy.

instructionSections.heading: Explain the risks, not only the rules
instructionSections.body: Staff follow controls more reliably when they know the hazard a control addresses. Describe the infection risks in the team's own tasks, such as close personal contact, handling laundry or cleaning a shared surface, and link each control to its risk. Share the results of any infection risk assessment with the group regularly, not only once at induction.

instructionSections.heading: Use words everyone can follow
instructionSections.body: Define technical terms before using them. Useful terms include standard precautions, transmission-based precautions, carrier, colonisation and contamination. A short glossary in the team pack lets staff look up words later. Leave time for questions, and answer them or record them to pass to the policy owner later.

lessons.title: Standard precautions and hand cleaning during personal care
learningOutcomes: Explain standard precautions and why they apply to every person
Choose between soap and water and an alcohol-based rub using the visible-soil test
Apply the five moments for cleaning hands during a personal-care visit

instructionSections.heading: Standard precautions apply to every person
instructionSections.body: Standard precautions are the baseline controls used for every person, whatever their diagnosis. The reasoning is that many body substances and surfaces can carry microbes, so the same baseline applies to everyone. Hand hygiene is a core control. Equipment and surfaces that may have been in contact with fluids from the body must also be handled so that spread is stopped.

instructionSections.heading: Two kinds of microbes, and the visible-soil test
instructionSections.body: Hands carry two groups of skin microbes. Transient microbes sit on the surface, pass easily to others and to surfaces, and are removed by washing or by an alcohol-based rub. Resident microbes live deeper in the skin and are not removed easily by routine washing; they matter mainly during invasive procedures. When hands look dirty, wash them using soap and water, because a rub is not a substitute in that case.

instructionSections.heading: The five moments
instructionSections.body: The five moments set out the points at which hands need cleaning: before touching a person; before a clean or aseptic task; after a risk of body fluid exposure and after removing gloves; after touching a person; and after touching the person's surroundings when you leave. The source credits this model to WHO.

lessons.title: Personal protective equipment and personal hygiene at work
learningOutcomes: Select gloves, gown, eye protection or mask for a task using the expected exposure
Put on and remove gloves so that you do not contaminate yourself
Apply personal hygiene and food-handling controls that limit spread

instructionSections.heading: Choose protective equipment for the expected exposure
instructionSections.body: Personal protective equipment is a set of barriers used singly or in combination, that protects skin, clothing and mucous membranes. Gloves, masks, eye protection, gowns and face shields are chosen for the exposure you expect. Gloves are needed when you handle fluids from the body, or equipment that carries them, touch broken skin or mucous membranes, or carry out an invasive task. Change gloves between clients and never reuse them.

instructionSections.heading: Keep your own skin and personal items separate
instructionSections.body: Unbroken skin blocks most microbes. Seal any cut or scrape under a waterproof dressing before work. Keep your towels and clothing, your razors and toothbrushes, and similar belongings to yourself, never with clients. Clean your hands regularly, especially after using the toilet, before handling food, and after contact with clients or equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Food and drink in a care setting
instructionSections.body: When food is prepared in a care setting, clean your hands at the start and finish of food preparation, keep your fingers off your hair and face, and keep hot items hot and chilled items cold. Store cooked and uncooked food apart, use separate utensils and boards, and wash utensils and surfaces after use.

lessons.title: Handling body fluid spills and contaminated sharps
learningOutcomes: Isolate and protect an area before cleaning a body fluid spill
Clean and disinfect a spill using the approved product's label and the organisation's procedure
Handle, contain and report a used sharp and any contact with fluids from the body

instructionSections.heading: Isolate and protect first
instructionSections.body: When a body fluid spill occurs, the first task is to isolate the area and protect yourself. Keep others away, and dress in gloves, a waterproof apron and goggles. If the spill is large, a person is hurt, or the situation is beyond the procedure you have been trained for, stop and call for help through the escalation route. This lesson does not authorise work beyond your training.

instructionSections.heading: Clean and disinfect using the product label
instructionSections.body: Blot the fluid using disposable paper towel or the product the procedure names. Where the procedure calls for a chlorine-releasing granular product, cover the spill and leave it for the contact time on the label. Collect the waste, bag it, clean the surface using hot, soapy water, dry it, and then dispose of towels and gloves. The source gives a bleach dilution and contact time, and this lesson does not reproduce them. The dilution and contact time must come from the approved product's label and the organisation's procedure. Never mix cleaning products.

instructionSections.heading: Sharps: contain, do not recap
instructionSections.body: Never recap, bend or break a used needle. Handle the sharp by its barrel and place it straight into a puncture-resistant sharps container. Do not overfill the container. The source refers to container standards and a yellow labelling scheme.

instructionSections.heading: After an exposure: flush, report, record, seek advice
instructionSections.body: If blood or body fluid reaches your skin, rinse the skin under running water, wash it with lukewarm water and a mild soap, and tell the responsible person about it. Record it in the organisation's incident system and seek medical advice. The source names a specific incident form.

lessons.title: Checking how well infection control works, and improving practice
learningOutcomes: Investigate an infection control event promptly and identify its cause
Set up a simple audit schedule and feed back results within a set time
Use aggregate reports to find hazards, improve controls and identify training needs

instructionSections.heading: Investigate events promptly
instructionSections.body: An infection control event, such as a missed hand hygiene moment, a sharps injury or a spill handled outside procedure, needs a prompt investigation. Find the cause in the system as well as in the person. Was the procedure clear, was the equipment available, was training current? Record the event, the cause and the action taken, and check later that the action worked.

instructionSections.heading: Audit on a schedule with simple tools
instructionSections.body: Audits need not be complicated. Observation audits can be run weekly by a supervisor, covering items such as hand cleaning at each of the five moments and personal items that interfere with hand cleaning. Larger audits, such as a review of sharps handling, can be annual or more frequent. Build the audit tool from your organisation's own policy. The source gives examples from a UK hospital setting. Those examples and the figures in them are not used here.

instructionSections.heading: Feed back quickly and train where gaps appear
instructionSections.body: Audit results help only when staff see them soon enough to act. Share results with the team within a short time, recognise what went well, and agree one fix for each gap. Where the same gap shows across the team, arrange a refresher on that topic. Core training topics are hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, sharps, waste, spills, equipment decontamination, and linen handling.

lessons.title: Chemical compatibility and SDS decision exercises
learningOutcomes: Explain hazards and scope boundaries for chemical compatibility
Demonstrate an authorised procedure with appropriate controls
Document outcomes and escalate exceptions

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Identify the actual task
instructionSections.body: Start with the soil, surface, people present and intended outcome. A disinfectant is not automatically needed for every cleaning task. Check the work order, product label, manufacturer surface guidance and site procedures before choosing a product.

instructionSections.heading: Read the SDS alongside the label
instructionSections.body: Find hazard identification, safe handling, exposure controls, first aid, accidental release, storage and incompatibility information. The SDS informs risk assessment; the current product label gives specific use instructions. If documents conflict or are unavailable, stop and ask the supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Test the compatibility decision
instructionSections.body: Compare the proposed product against the surface and existing residues. Acidic descalers may damage acid-sensitive stone; oxidisers may affect some finishes. Never mix products, including bleach with acids or ammonia-containing products. Do not infer compatibility from colour, fragrance or marketing terms.

instructionSections.heading: Choose a safer response
instructionSections.body: For an unknown residue or unlabelled container, isolate it from use and escalate. Never sniff, taste or experimentally combine chemicals. For a sensitive finish, use the authorised alternative or request specialist guidance.

instructionSections.heading: Document the decision
instructionSections.body: Record the task, product name, relevant label directions, surface, PPE/ventilation requirements, identified hazards, selected controls and any stop-work escalation. A supervisor reviews decisions before independent use.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: Electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In Victoria, PV installation and maintenance is licensed electrical installation work, and PV DC cables may stay live when the power is off. NSW electrical wiring work includes repairing. On the Victorian, Western Australian and New South Wales pages checked, plain panel washing is not stated to need a licence, and any electrical work on a PV array is referred to a licensed electrician. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

lessons.title: Safe measuring, dilution and dispensing demonstration
learningOutcomes: Explain hazards and scope boundaries for controlled dilution and dispensing
Demonstrate an authorised procedure with appropriate controls
Document outcomes and escalate exceptions

instructionSections.heading: Confirm whether dilution is permitted
instructionSections.body: Many products are ready to use. Only dilute a concentrate when the manufacturer explicitly specifies it and the workplace authorises the task. Confirm the required ratio, units, temperature, application method and contact time.

instructionSections.heading: Prepare the dispensing station
instructionSections.body: Use a designated ventilated area, suitable PPE, stable measuring equipment, a compatible labelled container and spill controls. Keep food and personal items away. Check that the container is clean and not holding unknown residues.

instructionSections.heading: Calculate using an example
instructionSections.body: For an explicitly authorised 1:20 concentrate-to-water ratio and a final 2.1 L batch, one part concentrate plus twenty parts water equals 21 parts: 100 mL concentrate and 2,000 mL water. Ratios are not universal; verify whether the label specifies concentrate-to-water or concentrate-to-total before calculating.

instructionSections.heading: Dispense without exposure
instructionSections.body: Follow the manufacturer’s order of addition, use accurate measures, avoid splashes and never improvise with drinking cups. Close the original container promptly. Do not decant into beverage bottles.

instructionSections.heading: Label, verify and store
instructionSections.body: Apply required product identity, concentration, preparation/expiry details and hazard information. Check the mixture against the instruction before release. Clean the station and record who prepared it. If a calculation or label is uncertain, do not use the mixture.

lessons.title: Evaluate ingredients without relying on natural claims
learningOutcomes: Distinguish the documented requirements for ingredient evaluation from unsupported product claims.
Demonstrate correct verify–authorise–record–escalate decisions for a customer worksite.
Describe when local legislation, product labelling or specialist review governs the task.
Explain the applicable limits and safeguards for evaluate ingredients without relying on natural claims.

instructionSections.heading: Why natural claims are not evidence
instructionSections.body: Words such as natural, plant-based, eco-friendly, non-toxic and biodegradable appear on many cleaning products, and customers often assume they mean the product is safe for every surface, every person and every place. A natural origin does not decide whether a product is safe, effective or suitable for a task. Plant-derived materials, essential oils and fragrance blends can irritate skin or airways, and acids and alkalis from natural sources can still damage stone, metal or finishes. This lesson teaches you to evaluate an ingredient from its documented evidence, and to record your decision so that it can be checked.

instructionSections.heading: Gather the documents before you judge
instructionSections.body: Start from the product, not from its marketing. Obtain the product label, the current safety data sheet (SDS) and the full ingredient or composition information the supplier provides. Check that all three refer to the same product, formulation and version, and note their dates. Read the hazard statements, the signal word, the first-aid and handling sections, the PPE advice and the disposal guidance. Where the composition is not disclosed, or the SDS and label disagree, the product is not yet evaluated and is treated as unverified until the supplier supplies the missing information. Keep the documents on file with their revision dates.

instructionSections.heading: Separate claims from verified criteria
instructionSections.body: A claim is what the packaging or sales material says. A verified criterion is a result that a recognised third party has tested against a stated standard, or a fact stated in the SDS and composition. When a product says it is certified or eco-friendly, ask what the claim refers to, which standard or test it rests on, who verified it, and whether that verification covers this formulation and this version. A manufacturer's self-declaration is useful information but is not the same as independent verification. A claim with no stated basis does not count as evidence and should not be repeated to a client.

instructionSections.heading: Judge exposure, surfaces and the people present
instructionSections.body: Judge the product by the way it will be used. Look at the concentration and dilution the approved method calls for, the route of exposure (skin, eyes, inhalation or ingestion), how long people and surfaces will be in contact with it, and the ventilation of the space. Check whether any occupant is vulnerable, such as a child, an older person or a person with asthma, and whether the client has reported a fragrance or other sensitivity. Check the surface as well: a product suited to sealed tiles may etch natural stone or damage a timber finish. Use the surface compatibility information from the manufacturer or the approved method. Where any of these points cannot be confirmed, the product is not used on that task.

instructionSections.heading: Decide and record
instructionSections.body: With the documents and the exposure picture in hand, choose one of four decisions: use the product as the approved method states, use it only with named controls such as dilution, ventilation or a test patch, refer it to a supervisor or specialist, or do not use it. Record the product, the documents checked, the reason for the decision, the controls and the person who approved it. Do not mix products to improve performance, do not raise the concentration to get a stronger result, and do not make a disinfectant claim the product does not support. A product that cannot be evaluated is recorded as not evaluated.

instructionSections.heading: Worked check on a fragrance-sensitive client
instructionSections.body: A scented botanical product is proposed for a poorly ventilated childcare area after a customer reports fragrance sensitivity. The botanical name and the natural claim do not answer the question. The evidence needed is the composition, the SDS hazard statements for the fragrance and any carrier, the ventilation and occupancy of the space, and a comparison with unscented authorised options. The right action is to pause the product, compare the unscented authorised options against the site's risk controls, and record why the chosen option was selected. The customer hears what was checked and what was not, without any claim that the product is safe for the room.

instructionSections.heading: Legal limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not authorise the use of any product for a regulated task. Check the label, the SDS and the employer's approved products list before any use.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop, leave the area safe and tell your supervisor before using a product if its label, SDS or composition is missing, if the documents do not match the product in hand, if a client or occupant reports a reaction or sensitivity, if the surface may be damaged, if the product would be mixed with another or used stronger than the approved method, or if a supervisor asks you to skip a verification step to meet a deadline. Do not proceed on an unverified product, claim or exposure-control method.

lessons.title: Control procurement, decanting and storage
learningOutcomes: Distinguish the documented requirements for procurement and storage from unsupported product claims.
Demonstrate correct verify–authorise–record–escalate decisions for a customer worksite.
Describe when local legislation, product labelling or specialist review governs the task.
Explain the applicable limits and safeguards for control procurement, decanting and storage.

instructionSections.heading: Why control starts before the product arrives
instructionSections.body: Many chemical problems in cleaning businesses trace back to a product nobody can identify: a drum with no label, a bottle decanted into a drink container, a supplier substitute sold under the old nickname, or incompatible products stored side by side. This lesson covers how to control what you buy, how to transfer product safely from bulk containers to working containers, and how to store stock so that a worker can always tell what it is, what it is for and what to do if it spills. Procurement and storage are not paperwork. They are the controls that make a product safe to use.

instructionSections.heading: Procure only approved products
instructionSections.body: Keep an approved products register that records, for each product, the supplier, the product name and version, the formulation or composition reference, the SDS date, the approved uses and the storage requirements. A product is bought only if it is on the register or has been added after review. When a delivery arrives, check its label and SDS against the register and the order. A new formulation sold under an old name is a different product until it has been reviewed, because the nickname on an order is not evidence of identity. Hold any stock that does not match, and do not release it to a worker until the SDS, the label and the compatibility review have been completed and recorded. Ask the supplier to notify you of formulation changes in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Decant only into suitable, labelled containers
instructionSections.body: Decanting is a transfer, and every transfer is a chance for a mistake. Use only containers that are clean, undamaged, compatible with the product and designated for chemicals. Never decant into a food or drink container, a bottle that has held food, or an unlabelled container. Label each working container with the product identifier, the main hazards from the SDS, the date of transfer and the initials of the person who made it. Measure the product with a graduated container or the approved dispensing system, follow the PPE and handling advice in the SDS, and never top up one product with another. Record each transfer, including any spill and how it was cleaned up. Where the label or SDS does not cover decanting, the transfer waits until a supervisor has checked it.

instructionSections.heading: Store stock so it can be identified and separated
instructionSections.body: Store products closed, labelled and upright where the label requires it, in a dedicated and ventilated area that is secure from unauthorised access. Separate products that the SDS says are incompatible, and keep acids, alkalis and oxidisers apart from each other and from other products where the SDS directs. Keep chemicals away from food, and keep working containers where the person using them can see the label. Check the storage area regularly for leaks, damaged or bulging containers, corroded lids and missing labels. Where expiry or supplier guidance applies, rotate stock so the oldest product is used first. A damaged or unidentified container is isolated, recorded, and its disposal is referred to a competent person under local rules.

instructionSections.heading: Count and record the stock
instructionSections.body: Run a stock check at a set interval, recording the stock on hand, the expiry dates, any damaged containers and any product found without a label. Compare the count with the register and recent purchases, and investigate any difference you cannot explain. A product with no SDS on file is a control failure, and it is withdrawn from use until the file is complete. The check is also the moment to confirm that working containers are labelled and that the approved products list is current.

instructionSections.heading: Worked check on a supplier substitute
instructionSections.body: Suppose a supplier substitutes a differently formulated concentrate under the same informal product nickname. The new drum looks like the old one and the order uses the same name. The correct decision is to hold the new stock and not release it. Request the fresh SDS, the new label and the composition, and check them against the register and the compatibility guidance for the surfaces the product will be used on. Record the substitution in the register, withdraw any working container of the new product until it has been reviewed, and tell the supervisor. Release the stock only after the review is recorded and the approved uses are updated.

instructionSections.heading: Legal limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not authorise the purchase, transport, storage or use of any regulated product. Check the label, the SDS and the employer's approved products list, and follow the local rules for disposing of residues.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop and tell your supervisor before using or moving a product if its identity cannot be confirmed, if its label or SDS is missing or damaged, if you find an unlabelled or leaking container, if a product has been put into a food or drink container, if incompatible products are stored together, or if you are asked to use stock that has not been released. Isolate the container, keep people away from any spill, and do not pour it into another container.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Learning goal and job context: This lesson teaches read labels and sds for routine cleaning work. Start with the actual job scope, site instructions, manufacturer directions and worker training. Never treat a general lesson as authority to perform restricted or specialist work.

Core procedure: Locate product identity, hazard pictograms, directions, first-aid, storage and disposal on the container. Match the exact product and formulation to its current SDS; use SDS sections on hazards, handling, exposure controls, first aid and spills rather than relying on a generic product family.

Decision-making in the field: Before acting, ask: What is the surface or equipment? What is the soil or hazard? Which product or method is approved? What could harm a person, property or food? If the answer is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.

lessons.title: Remove soil before disinfecting
learningOutcomes: Explain and apply: remove soil before disinfecting

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Overview
instructionSections.body: In this lesson, practise remove soil before disinfecting using an authorised work order and a realistic Australian cleaning-site scenario. Work only within training, employer procedures and site-specific instructions.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body: Remove visible debris and soil using the appropriate detergent and method before applying any disinfectant. Follow product-specific surface contact time where disinfection is required.

instructionSections.heading: Understand the difference
instructionSections.body: Cleaning physically removes soil; disinfection is an additional process intended to reduce specified microorganisms when the situation requires it. Disinfectant is not a substitute for removing visible dirt.

instructionSections.heading: Follow product instructions
instructionSections.body: Check approved label instructions for target surface, preparation, dilution, application and contact time. Do not invent contact times or use a product on an incompatible finish.

instructionSections.heading: Verify the process
instructionSections.body: Confirm soil removal, coverage and that the surface stayed treated for the labelled time. Report situations requiring specialist infection-control guidance.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: Electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In Victoria, PV installation and maintenance is licensed electrical installation work, and PV DC cables may stay live when the power is off. NSW electrical wiring work includes repairing. On the Victorian, Western Australian and New South Wales pages checked, plain panel washing is not stated to need a licence, and any electrical work on a PV array is referred to a licensed electrician. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

lessons.title: Cleaning versus disinfection
learningOutcomes: Explain and demonstrate cleaning versus disinfection

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level, water-fed pole and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Any work above ground level, or from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted: it needs employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body: Cleaning physically removes soil and reduces contamination; disinfection uses an approved product or process to inactivate targeted microorganisms on suitable surfaces. Determine whether disinfection is required from the work scope, risk assessment and site protocol. When required, remove visible soil first unless the product specifically supports a validated one-step method. Read the label for approved surfaces, dilution, application method, wet contact time and rinsing requirements, especially on food-contact surfaces. Do not substitute a household product for a healthcare-grade requirement. Never promise that a surface is sterile after routine cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Learning focus
instructionSections.body: Choose cleaning and disinfection appropriately. Cleaning physically removes soil and reduces contamination; disinfection uses an approved product or process to inactivate targeted microorganisms on suitable surfaces. Determine whether disinfection is required from the work scope, risk assessment and site protocol. When required, remove visible soil first unless the product specifically supports a validated one-step method. Read the label for approved surfaces, dilution, application method, wet contact time and rinsing requirements, especially on food-contact surfaces. Do not substitute a household product for a healthcare-grade requirement. Never promise that a surface is sterile after routine cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Worked workplace scenario
instructionSections.body: A team wipes a high-touch surface with disinfectant and dries it immediately. The assessor asks them to check the actual label contact time and repeat the approved process if necessary.

instructionSections.heading: Guided practice
instructionSections.body: Given three scenarios, justify cleaning alone or cleaning plus disinfection, and demonstrate label-based preparation and contact-time compliance.

instructionSections.heading: Quality and safety checks
instructionSections.body: Before signing off, confirm that the method matches the authorised site scope and current product labels, that no uncontrolled hazard remains, and that evidence is factual and privacy-safe.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

lessons.title: Product selection and evidence
learningOutcomes: Compare products on the evidence the label, SDS and supplier provide, rather than on marketing claims.
Identify the information that supports a sustainability claim and what it does not prove.
Record the product choice and the evidence used to make it.

instructionSections.heading: Environmental claims need evidence
instructionSections.body: Many products carry claims such as biodegradable, low toxicity, plant-based, recyclable or certified. A claim is useful only when it can be checked. Ask what the claim refers to, what standard or test supports it, who verified it and whether it applies to the product as sold. A biodegradable claim may refer to a single ingredient, under specific conditions, and not to the whole product. Treat a claim without a source as unverified.

instructionSections.heading: What the label and SDS tell you
instructionSections.body: The label and SDS give the hazards, the handling information, the disposal advice and the ecological information where it is provided. The ecological section of an SDS may give information about aquatic toxicity and persistence. Compare the hazard statements, the signal words and the disposal guidance between products. A product with fewer hazards and simpler disposal may be a better choice, provided it still does the job. Check the supplier's data and the date of the information.

instructionSections.heading: Record the choice
instructionSections.body: Record the product, the reason for choosing it, the evidence used and the date. This creates a record the business can review, and it helps when a product is changed or a customer asks why a product was used. Keep a short list of approved products with their evidence, and review the list when a new product or a new claim is presented.

lessons.title: Correct dosing and dilution
learningOutcomes: Dose products to the label concentration, so that cost and waste are controlled.
Explain how over-dosing and under-dosing both create cost, waste and quality problems.
Choose a dosing method that reduces waste and avoids unmeasured pouring.

instructionSections.heading: Why dosing controls cost
instructionSections.body: Product cost on a job is driven by how much is used, not only by the price per litre. Over-dosing uses more product than the job needs, adds to waste and leaves residue that attracts soil and needs more rinsing. Under-dosing may not clean, so the job is repeated and the labour cost rises. Correct dosing is therefore a cost-reduction control and a quality control at the same time. The dilution on the label is the starting point, and the approved procedure may set a different concentration for a specific surface.

instructionSections.heading: Dosing methods
instructionSections.body: Measure product with a graduated container or a dosing system where the business has one. Pour-by-eye is the most common source of error. Use the same measuring method each time, label the bucket or bottle with the dilution, and check the mix at the start of each job. Where a dispensing system is used, check it regularly for accuracy and leaks, and record the calibration or check where the procedure requires it. Do not top up a dilution with more concentrate to save time.

instructionSections.heading: Waste and rework
instructionSections.body: Track the waste from over-mixing: a bucket made up for a job that is then thrown away. Mix only what is needed for the work area, and keep the rest in its labelled container. Repeated jobs caused by under-dosing or poor technique cost more than the product saved, and they can also reduce the customer's trust. Record any job that needs rework because of product or dosing issues, so the cause can be fixed.

lessons.title: Waste segregation and wastewater
learningOutcomes: Separate waste into general, recycling, sharps and hazardous streams as the site and the rules require.
Describe the points to check before wash water or product residue is discharged.
Identify when waste must be referred to a specialist or to the customer's own disposal route.

instructionSections.heading: Waste streams
instructionSections.body: Waste from service work usually falls into several streams: general waste, recycling, green or garden waste, sharps, hazardous product residue and empty chemical containers, and wash water. Each stream has its own container, colour and disposal route set by the site, the council and the state or territory. Keep the streams separate so that hazardous material does not end up in general waste or recycling. Do not put sharps, chemical containers or liquids in general waste bins, and do not overfill bags.

instructionSections.heading: Wash water and discharge
instructionSections.body: Wash water from cleaning can carry product residue, oils, soil and detergent. Whether that water may go to a drain, a sewer, a stormwater drain or a garden depends on the rules of the council, the water authority and the state or territory. In many places, discharge to a stormwater drain is not allowed, and discharge to a sewer may need approval. Where there is no approved route, collect the water and refer it to the supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Specialist and customer waste
instructionSections.body: Some waste, such as contaminated material from a spill, unidentified residue, sharps found on a site or large quantities of a product, must go to a specialist or to a disposal route approved by the customer and the business. Do not take such waste home or put it in a customer's bin unless the procedure allows it. Record what the waste is, how much there is, where it was put and who received it.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish detergents, degreasers, descalers, disinfectants and specialist products by function and approved use.
Identify the soil and substrate before choosing a product category.
Explain why a disinfectant does not replace removal of heavy visible soil.

instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches product categories for routine cleaning work. Start with the actual job scope, site instructions, manufacturer directions and worker training. Never treat a general lesson as authority to perform restricted or specialist work.

instructionSections.body: Before acting, ask: What is the surface or equipment? What is the soil or hazard? Which product or method is approved? What could harm a person, property or food? If the answer is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.

lessons.title: Reading a written cleaning procedure and closing out the task
learningOutcomes: Locate the purpose, the finished standard, the hazard controls, the timing guide and the steps in a written cleaning procedure.
Explain why a timing guide is a planning aid and not a target to be used without checking it against the site.
Complete the close-out routine in the right order: equipment, storage, PPE, hand hygiene and the job record.

instructionSections.heading: How a usable cleaning procedure is laid out
instructionSections.body: A clear cleaning procedure does five things in a fixed order. It states the purpose of the task. It sets a required standard, which is the finished result you must reach. It lists the equipment and the hazards, with a control for each hazard. It gives an indicative time. Then it sets out numbered steps. A worker who knows where each of these sits can check any step in seconds, and can tell at a glance whether a procedure is complete.

instructionSections.heading: Read the standard before the steps
instructionSections.body: The steps are only a route to the standard. Before you pick up a cloth or a mop, read what finished looks like for that surface, such as dust-free, streak-free or an even sheen. If a finish is damaged, the standard may not be reachable with the method in the procedure. That is a fault to report, not a reason to work harder with the same method.

instructionSections.heading: Treat the hazard controls as a checklist
instructionSections.body: The hazard table tells you what to control before you start: slips and falls, manual handling, electrical equipment, chemical use and the rest. The controls it lists are minimum controls. Where the site's approved procedure or the state or territory rule is stricter, follow the stricter one. Tick off each control you have applied before you begin the numbered steps.

instructionSections.heading: Timing guides are planning aids
instructionSections.body: A procedure may give an indicative time for an area. Use it as a rough guide for planning only. It assumes conditions that may not be present, such as clear floors, light soil or easy access. Your business should measure its own rates on its own surfaces before it quotes or schedules work, and should record the actual time taken. The timing figures in the source document are unverified and are not Australian benchmarks, so this lesson does not use them.

instructionSections.heading: Close-out is part of the job
instructionSections.body: The last steps are not optional tidying. Put equipment away, clean the tools, store cords, pads and brushes in the designated place, remove PPE, perform hand hygiene and record the job. An incomplete close-out is how the next job starts with dirty or damaged tools, and how a fault goes unreported.

lessons.title: Interior glass and mirror cleaning: squeegee sequence and streak-free finish
learningOutcomes: Clean interior glass and mirrors to a streak-free, mark-free finish, using a dampen-then-squeegee method for glass and a wash-then-buff method for mirrors.
Choose the correct method and access arrangement for panes within easy reach and for panes above the height set in the business risk assessment.
Identify the products and tools that must be kept away from glass and mirror surfaces.

instructionSections.heading: What falls under glass in this lesson
instructionSections.body: The items covered are interior windows, glazed doors, flyscreens, mirrors (including bathroom and bedside mirrors) and window ledges. A pane passes only when it shows no streaks, spots, smears or prints when viewed from both sides. Frames, tracks and sills must also be dust-free and grit-free. External faces of windows may sit under a separate cleaning arrangement, which this routine standard does not set.

instructionSections.heading: Panes within easy reach: dampen, then squeegee
instructionSections.body: Begin with the upper edge of each pane and treat one pane at a time. Dampen the surface with a cloth loaded with solution, using long horizontal sweeps followed by vertical sweeps, so the pane never dries before the blade arrives. Set the squeegee at the top corner and draw it across in a single pass, then start each new pass so it slightly overlaps the one before. Clear the rubber edge of the squeegee between passes so that no grit scratches the pane. Once a pane is done, wipe the sash and sill and soak up any runoff.

instructionSections.heading: Panes above the height set in the business risk assessment: two people and approved access
instructionSections.body: Work on any pane above the height set in the business risk assessment only with approved access equipment and a second person positioned before the first move. The second person lifts the bucket and cloth up to the worker, holds the base steady and keeps people away from it. One worker climbs at any given moment. The washing and blade technique is the same as on the lower panes, but the climber stays inside the ladder's footprint and repositions the ladder rather than stretching.

instructionSections.heading: Mirrors: wash, then buff
instructionSections.body: Wash a mirror with a moistened cloth in passes that keep its reflective face wet, then buff it with a second, dry cloth. Streaks become visible when you tilt your head and view the mirror at an angle in good light, so check it that way and clear any you find. Wipe the frame too, so that dust does not transfer back onto the glass.

instructionSections.heading: Products to keep away from glass
instructionSections.body: Use a neutral glass cleaner (a neutral detergent) mixed to the strength printed on its label. Powder, paste and grit-based cleaners are not for glass or mirrors, since they scratch the surface and leave a haze behind. Solution containers stay off furniture and window sills, and any splash is mopped up before it dries into a mark.

lessons.title: Step ladders and ladders for interior high cleaning
learningOutcomes: Inspect a step ladder or ladder before use, and remove it from service if it is damaged.
Set up a ladder on a flat, firm surface, fully open where it is a step ladder, and keep it in the correct working position.
Apply the two-person rule and the single-climber rule to every task above floor-level reach.

instructionSections.heading: Why interior ladder work goes wrong
instructionSections.body: Most falls on interior tasks happen because the worker reaches too far, climbs above the safe top step, stands on something that was never meant to be climbed, or carries items while climbing. The ladder is one control and the working position is the other. Both are set before the first step is taken.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing and inspecting the equipment
instructionSections.body: Use only ladders that meet the Australian Standard the site specifies. Before each use, check the rungs or treads for looseness, and check screws, rivets, bolts, feet and locks for damage or looseness. Store ladders covered and supported so they do not sag. Remove a damaged ladder from service, tag it, and report it.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up
instructionSections.body: Place the ladder on a hard, flat, clear surface. Do not set a ladder on carpet edges, loose surfaces, boxes or furniture. A step ladder must be fully open and locked before anyone climbs it. Keep the work between shoulder height and arm's reach. If a point is out of reach, move the ladder rather than leaning or stretching sideways.

instructionSections.heading: Two people, one climber
instructionSections.body: When the work sits above floor-level reach, a second person steadies the base of the ladder and keeps passers-by away from it. Only one worker climbs at a given moment. The partner passes items up and receives them back down, and stays at the base for as long as the ladder is in use.

instructionSections.heading: Climbing, carrying and rotating work
instructionSections.body: Never carry kit up or down a ladder. Have the partner pass items up, or use a tool belt if the site approves one. Never climb onto window sills or ledges. Where the job is long, share the high work between people so that nobody spends extended time at height.

lessons.title: Carpet shampoo and hot-water extraction: step sequence and drying
learningOutcomes: Sequence a carpet shampoo and extraction job from debris removal through to drying and handover.
Control solution volume, the area treated per pass and the recovery-tank level so the carpet dries without damage to furniture or the carpet.
Recognise machine and electrical faults that require the machine to be stopped and reported.

instructionSections.heading: Preparation before any solution goes down
instructionSections.body: Vacuum first, so loose grit is lifted before shampoo goes down and cannot turn into muddy residue. Shift the furniture to a suitable spot, and inspect the carpet for marks needing pre-treatment. Lift chewing gum with a scraper before wet work begins. Put up signage and a barrier before the unit is wheeled in.

instructionSections.heading: Making up the solution and adding defoamer
instructionSections.body: Mix the shampoo in the tank following the product label, and put the defoamer into the recovery tank before extraction begins, so foam does not reach the motor. Never let the unit run without solution, and never drive it over its own cord. Use no more water than the method specifies; surplus water prolongs drying and complicates finishing.

instructionSections.heading: Working in small sections
instructionSections.body: On a walk-behind extractor, work roughly three square metres per section. Keep any pre-sprayed patch to around twenty square metres or less, so the solution is still moist when you extract it. Begin at the spot most distant from the exit and move back toward it, so you do not tread on finished carpet.

instructionSections.heading: Extraction passes
instructionSections.body: With a hand-wand machine, pull the wand back slowly with the suction engaged, and repeat the pass over the same ground to take out the solution. On a heavy stain, make a second extraction pass over the same spot to lift more soil. Empty the recovery tank before it reaches its fill line. A full recovery tank loses suction and leaves the carpet wet.

instructionSections.heading: Drying and close-down
instructionSections.body: Let the carpet dry fully before furniture is returned. When the job ends, drain and flush the water tank, clean the water jet after every use, and wipe the unit down. For a battery unit, plug it into the charger as the maker specifies. Store the unit in its assigned place.

lessons.title: Ride-on sweeper for car parks, courtyards and entrances
learningOutcomes: Complete a pre-operation check and review the manufacturer's manual before using a ride-on sweeper.
Operate the sweeper's controls in the correct order, and shut it down safely at the end of a run.
Name the noise, heat, debris and exhaust hazards this machine presents, and apply a control to each.

instructionSections.heading: Who may operate, and what the operator must know
instructionSections.body: Only a trained and authorised person may operate a ride-on sweeper. Before the first use, the operator reads the manufacturer's manual, knows where every control and attachment is and what it does, and works under supervision until the supervisor is satisfied. Passengers are never carried on the machine. This lesson does not give anyone authority to operate plant.

instructionSections.heading: Hazards on the machine
instructionSections.body: The rotating brush can throw debris into the air and into the eyes of the operator or a bystander. The hydraulic drive, the motor and the exhaust can become hot during operation, so they must not be touched while running or soon after. Exhaust fumes can make an operator dizzy or queasy, so the sweeper is not run where fumes can collect. Noise over a shift can harm hearing, and vibration adds to body strain. Smoking and open flames are not allowed near the machine, and the operator avoids repeated stooping and twisting when clearing it.

instructionSections.heading: Starting, moving and stopping
instructionSections.body: Open the suction flap, start the sweeping and side brushes, free the parking brake, and press the accelerator gently to the speed the job needs. To slow down, lift off to neutral and then apply the service brake. Engage the parking brake when you stop. Never lift the hopper while the centre broom is still turning; halt the broom first, then operate the hopper.

instructionSections.heading: Clearing the route before you sweep
instructionSections.body: Lift out big items by hand and place them in the waste container before the sweeper passes over the area. Large objects can jam the brush or damage the machine. Check the route for pedestrians and vehicles, and set signs and cones so people know the sweeper is working.

instructionSections.heading: Shutdown, filter and storage
instructionSections.body: When the run ends, switch off the roller and the side brush, engage the parking brake, and check and clean the filter as the manufacturer directs. Empty the debris bin when it is full or at the end of the shift. Wash down the machine and park it in its assigned storage area. Never walk away from the unit while the engine is still running.

lessons.title: Air blower on paved entrances, landings and balconies
learningOutcomes: Prepare an external area for blowing by clearing objects and surveying the area, neighbours and wind.
Blow debris in a controlled direction, away from cleaned areas, and collect it with a dustpan and banister brush.
Apply eye, hearing, respiratory and smoking controls for blower work.

instructionSections.heading: What blowing does and does not do
instructionSections.body: An air blower moves loose leaves and light debris quickly across open hard surfaces. It does not remove grease, stains or compacted soil, and those need the approved wet method. Blowing also lifts dust and fine debris into the air, so the work must control who is nearby and where the air is aimed.

instructionSections.heading: Set the direction before you start
instructionSections.body: Look over the site first, and set the nozzle or chute so air pushes the debris where you intend it to go. Open a lane along the centre line of the area first. Then work outward on alternating sides, so the debris is pushed away from cleaned sections and not back across them.

instructionSections.heading: Protect the operator and bystanders
instructionSections.body: Wear eye protection, hearing protection and any respiratory protection the task requires. Keep both hands on the blower while it runs. Debris can bounce back and strike the eyes, so keep people, pets and vehicles clear of the air stream. Do not smoke while you operate the blower or refuel it, and keep fuel and flames apart.

instructionSections.heading: Finish with a collection step
instructionSections.body: Blowing by itself leaves debris heaped against walls, door sills and fire doors. Sweep each heap into a dustpan with a banister brush; then place what you have collected in the general waste container. Do not blow debris into drains, gutters or neighbouring spaces.

lessons.title: Toilet and shower detailed procedures
learningOutcomes: Explain the hazards and quality standards for toilet and shower hygiene.
Apply a toilet and shower procedure that keeps toilet tools apart from other surfaces.
Stop and correct a cross-use of tools, and record the event.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the bathroom before you start
instructionSections.body: A residential bathroom with a toilet, a shower screen, chrome fittings and a porous grout line presents several surfaces that respond differently. Visible soap film and an odour point to a combination of soap residue and organic soil. Before work, identify the fixture materials, confirm the agreed scope, check ventilation, and read the product labels. The grout is porous, so it takes up soil and product, which is one reason to keep the cleaning sequence and the product choice deliberate.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up and working in order
instructionSections.body: Prepare a designated toilet-only tool set and keep it apart from every other tool. Remove loose debris first. Apply approved products to compatible surfaces, following the label directions, and work from less contaminated areas to more contaminated ones. Use separate cloths for the toilet exterior and the bowl. Avoid aerosol-generating methods, which spread fine droplets, and rinse where the label instructs. Finish by drying and inspecting the surfaces.

instructionSections.heading: When a tool crosses zones
instructionSections.body: A worker may want to use the toilet cloth on a shower tap to save time. Stop, replace the cloth with a clean one from the correct zone, and explain the contamination pathway: soil from the toilet can move onto a surface people touch with their hands. Record the correction. The time saved is never worth the transfer.

instructionSections.heading: Quality standard and records
instructionSections.body: The finished bathroom has no cross-use of toilet tools, no unapproved chemical mixing, no damaged finish, visible soil removed, and fixtures inspected. Record the product used where required, any exceptions, the corrective actions and the supervisor's sign-off.

lessons.title: Complete bathroom practical and inspection
learningOutcomes: Explain the hazards, boundaries and quality standards for an end-to-end bathroom service.
Complete the bathroom practical and inspection using authorised methods.
Record results and escalate unsafe or out-of-scope conditions.

instructionSections.heading: Context and safety boundaries
instructionSections.body: A two-bathroom property must be cleaned to an agreed checklist while occupants are present. Translate the work order into a timed sequence, the contamination zones, and the quality acceptance criteria before you start. Follow the site-specific procedures, the current product labels and supervision. Stop if the task becomes unsafe or falls outside your authorisation.

instructionSections.heading: Preparation and method
instructionSections.body: Carry out a pre-start risk check. Stage clean and sanitary tools separately, and keep the toilet tools apart from the basin tools. Clean the high and low contact points in an orderly sequence, manage the waste, and change cloths at the right points. Inspect mirrors, taps, shower tracks, toilets and floors against the checklist, correct defects, record exceptions, and hand over without exposing private details.

instructionSections.heading: Reasoned workplace decision
instructionSections.body: During the practical, the assessor places a toilet brush in the basin. Stop the task, isolate the affected tools and surfaces, and demonstrate recovery: remove the item from use, re-clean the surface with clean tools and the approved product, and record the event.

instructionSections.heading: Quality standards and records
instructionSections.body: The assessor checks hazard control, hygiene segregation, finish protection, inspection accuracy, correction and handover. Record the product used where required, the exceptions, the corrective actions and the final supervisor sign-off. Completion means observable safe work and verified quality, not a ticked checklist.

instructionSections.heading: Transfer to the workplace
instructionSections.body: Before using this method at a real site, compare the practice setting with the actual surfaces, occupants, chemical instructions, equipment condition and scope. Where any assumption differs, reassess the risk and obtain approval before continuing.

lessons.title: Food-contact cleaning and sanitising workflow
learningOutcomes: Explain the hazards and quality standards for food-contact surface hygiene.
Apply the cleaning and sanitising workflow in the correct order, using the label concentration and contact time.
Stop when a sanitiser is applied over soil, and redo the sequence.

instructionSections.heading: Confirming what kind of task this is
instructionSections.body: A shared kitchen with preparation benches, a sink, a chopping area and food awaiting storage needs a clear decision first: is this routine cleaning, or an authorised food-safety sanitising task that the site has specified? Confirm with the supervisor. Protect the food and utensils before you start, and remove or cover food awaiting storage so that it cannot be contaminated by the work.

instructionSections.heading: The sequence
instructionSections.body: Remove or protect the food, and segregate tools by zone. Remove debris, then wash with a suitable detergent. Rinse if the procedure requires it. Apply an approved food-contact sanitiser at the concentration and for the contact time stated on its label. Rinse after sanitising only if the label directs it, and let the surface air-dry, or dry it by an approved method. Document the completion.

instructionSections.heading: Why soil comes first
instructionSections.body: A worker who sprays sanitiser over visible crumbs has skipped the most important step. Sanitisers act on clean surfaces, and soil protects micro-organisms and reduces the effect of the product. Stop the sequence, remove the soil, and redo the steps from the beginning. Do not treat the sanitising step as a way to cover soil.

instructionSections.heading: Release and records
instructionSections.body: The result is correct sequence, approved product at the right concentration, full contact time, no food contamination, and safe release for use. Release is given by the person the site authorises, and the record shows the product, the concentration, the contact time and the release decision.

lessons.title: Complete kitchen practical and verification
learningOutcomes: Explain the hazards, boundaries and quality standards for kitchen competency and handover.
Complete the kitchen practical and verification using authorised methods.
Record results and escalate unsafe or out-of-scope conditions.

instructionSections.heading: Context and safety boundaries
instructionSections.body: An occupied home kitchen has dishes, food preparation areas, an appliance exterior and mixed surface finishes. Plan a safe sequence that protects the food, respects the client's property, and separates food-contact cleaning from general cleaning. Follow the site-specific procedures, the current product labels and supervision, and stop if the task becomes unsafe or outside authorisation.

instructionSections.heading: Preparation and method
instructionSections.body: Confirm the scope, allergies or site restrictions before you start, and protect the food and personal items. Identify the materials and soils, and clean the general and food-contact areas with dedicated tools. Sanitise only where it is specified and authorised. Check the sinks, taps, benches, handles and floors, and inspect for residue, odour and damage. Hand over any exceptions.

instructionSections.heading: Reasoned workplace decision
instructionSections.body: The assessor reveals a contaminated cloth used on a preparation bench. Stop, re-clean with the correct tool and sanitise as the procedure requires, and explain the corrective reporting.

instructionSections.heading: Quality standards and records
instructionSections.body: The kitchen should meet the food protection, cross-contamination control, surface compatibility, scope and final inspection requirements. Record the product used where required, the exceptions, the corrective actions and the final supervisor sign-off. Do not describe the kitchen as food-safe beyond the service scope and the inspection performed.

lessons.title: Appliance identification
learningOutcomes: Identify the common appliance types and the parts that are within cleaning scope.
Recognise the manufacturer's labels and documents that set the cleaning method.
Stop and escalate for any appliance that is unidentified or has no cleaning guidance.

instructionSections.heading: Knowing what you are cleaning
instructionSections.body: Appliances in a home or workplace include ovens, cooktops, rangehoods, dishwashers, microwaves, refrigerators, washing machines and dryers. Each has a different mix of accessible parts, electrical controls, heating elements, seals and moving parts. Before you clean one, identify the make and model from its data plate or label, and find the manufacturer's cleaning guidance if the site holds it. Identification sets which parts are cleaned, which are left alone, and which products are allowed.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and the parts you may clean
instructionSections.body: Within routine cleaning, the accessible exterior, the interior surfaces that the manufacturer says can be cleaned, the removable racks and trays, and the door seals and handles are usually in scope, subject to the work order. Electrical panels, switches, sockets, fixed wiring, gas connections, motors and control boards are not cleaned with liquid, and are not opened or dismantled by a cleaner. The work order and the manufacturer's guidance mark the boundary.

instructionSections.heading: When identification fails
instructionSections.body: If the appliance cannot be identified, or the manufacturer's guidance is not available, do not guess the method. Clean only the exterior with a mild, approved product that is suitable for the surface, leave the rest, and record the appliance as unidentified. Ask the supervisor for the manufacturer's guidance before cleaning further.

lessons.title: Isolation and temperature
learningOutcomes: Confirm that a hot or energised appliance is cool and isolated before cleaning.
Recognise isolation steps that a cleaner may use and those that only a licensed person may do.
Stop and escalate where isolation is unclear or disconnection would be needed.

instructionSections.heading: Temperature first
instructionSections.body: Oven interiors, cooktop surfaces, grills and the glass of some appliances stay hot for a long time after they are switched off. Confirm the appliance is cool before you touch the interior, or clean a surface that is still warm. Heat also changes how a product behaves, so the cleaning method is chosen for a cool surface. A burn is a common and avoidable injury in appliance cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Isolation: what a cleaner can and cannot do
instructionSections.body: A cleaner may switch an appliance off at its own control, and may use the site's approved lock-out or tag-out step where the procedure gives one. A cleaner must not disconnect a fixed appliance from the electrical supply or the gas supply, must not open the panel behind the appliance, and must not remove a hard-wired connection. Those steps are for a licensed person, and the cleaner reports the need rather than carrying it out.

instructionSections.heading: When isolation is unclear
instructionSections.body: If you cannot tell whether an appliance is switched off, or whether a control is live, stop, leave the controls alone and escalate to the supervisor. Do not assume that a dark display means that the appliance is isolated. Record the appliance, the time and the decision taken.

lessons.title: Product and ventilation selection
learningOutcomes: Select a product approved for the appliance surface and for the soil.
Set ventilation appropriately before using a product with fumes.
Refuse an unapproved product, and escalate for an approved alternative.

instructionSections.heading: Matching product to surface and soil
instructionSections.body: Appliance surfaces include stainless steel, painted metal, glass, enamel, plastic and seals, and each reacts differently to products. Oven cleaners, degreasers and general cleaners are different products, and an oven-specific product is used only on an oven interior that it is approved for. Read the label and the appliance manufacturer's guidance to confirm the product suits the surface and the soil.

instructionSections.heading: Ventilation and fumes
instructionSections.body: Some cleaning products give off fumes, particularly oven and heavy-degreasing products. Open windows or switch on extraction where the site allows, and keep the cleaning area ventilated during and after use. Do not use a product in a closed space without ventilation, and keep people who are not involved out of the area. The SDS sets the ventilation requirements for each product.

instructionSections.heading: Refusing an unapproved product
instructionSections.body: If a client or colleague asks for a product that is not approved for the appliance, refuse it, explain the surface risk, and ask the supervisor for an approved alternative. Do not test a product on an appliance surface unless the procedure allows it, because a damaged finish is hard to reverse.

lessons.title: Removable components
learningOutcomes: Identify which removable parts the manufacturer allows a cleaner to remove.
Remove and clean removable parts without damaging seals, fittings or wiring.
Stop before any step that needs tools, dismantling or a technician.

instructionSections.heading: Which parts come out
instructionSections.body: Racks, shelves, trays, crumb trays, grease filters and some door panels are commonly removable by the user. Whether a specific part can be removed is set by the manufacturer's guidance and the work order. A part that is held by screws, clips that need force, or a fixed connection is not removed by a cleaner unless the procedure says so. When you are unsure, leave the part where it is and check.

instructionSections.heading: Removing and cleaning without damage
instructionSections.body: Remove parts carefully, supporting heavy items and keeping track of small fittings. Clean removable parts at a sink or in a suitable area away from electrical controls, and dry them before they are refitted. Do not force a part out of its housing. Check seals and gaskets for tears or deformation and report them.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping before dismantling
instructionSections.body: Stop before any step that requires tools, dismantling the appliance, removing a panel, or disconnecting a wire or hose. These steps are beyond routine cleaning. Record the part that you could not safely remove, and escalate to the supervisor for the appropriate person.

lessons.title: Residue removal and reassembly
learningOutcomes: Remove residue from appliance parts with an approved method that does not damage the finish.
Reassemble only the parts the manufacturer and the work order allow.
Stop and escalate when reassembly needs a technician or a part is damaged.

instructionSections.heading: Residue and the right method
instructionSections.body: Baked-on residue and grease build up in corners, around seals and on removable parts. Remove loose residue first, then apply the approved product for the surface and the soil, and allow the product its contact time. Scrapers and abrasives can scratch the finish and leave a surface that holds more residue. Use the method the manufacturer and the approved procedure give.

instructionSections.heading: Reassembly is limited
instructionSections.body: Reassemble only the parts that you removed in line with the manufacturer's guidance and the work order. Refit each part in its original position, check that it seats properly, and do not force it. Confirm that no tool, cloth or product has been left inside the appliance, and that no wire, hose or seal has been displaced.

instructionSections.heading: When to stop
instructionSections.body: Stop if a part is damaged, if reassembly needs a tool to fix the part in place, or if a wire, hose or gas connection has been disturbed. Those are technician tasks. Record the state of the appliance, what was reassembled, and what remains for the technician.

lessons.title: Functional handover
learningOutcomes: Check the appliance is clean, dry, correctly reassembled and free of left-behind items.
Describe the appliance's state at handover without claiming function that has not been tested.
Hand over with a record, and escalate any appliance that is not safe to return to use.

instructionSections.heading: What handover covers
instructionSections.body: At handover, check that the appliance is clean, dry, correctly reassembled, and free of cloths, products and tools. Check that the work order's items are complete and that the surrounding area is left safe. The handover describes what was cleaned and what was not. It does not describe the appliance as working or safe unless someone with the authority to test and confirm function has done so.

instructionSections.heading: Function is not the cleaner's claim
instructionSections.body: A cleaner does not normally test the electrical or gas function of an appliance. Switching an appliance on to see whether it works is a test that the cleaner may not be authorised or trained to carry out. Where function is part of the work order, the appropriate person tests it under the procedure. Otherwise, the record says that function was not tested.

instructionSections.heading: When an appliance is not ready
instructionSections.body: If an appliance has a fault, a torn seal, a displaced connection or a hazard, do not hand it over as ready. Record the defect and the hold, tell the supervisor, and tell the client what is not yet done. A handover that hides a defect is a false record.

lessons.title: Scope, project phases and authority
learningOutcomes: Distinguish rough, intermediate and final builders' cleaning.
Locate the signed handover, the site controller and the access permit before entering.
Stop entry to any area with active trades, and obtain a revised safe access window.

instructionSections.heading: Three stages of builders' cleaning
instructionSections.body: Builders' cleaning happens in stages that follow the trades. Rough cleaning removes the larger, authorised debris while work is still going on.
