Intermediate cleaning follows the progress of the trades and keeps the work area workable. Final cleaning prepares completed areas for handover. Knowing the stage tells you what the area is, what hazards are still active, and what the client expects. A final clean does not give you permission to enter an active building site.

instructionSections.heading: Confirming authority before entry
instructionSections.body: Before you enter, identify the construction stage, the site controller, the access permit, the rooms agreed for your work, the excluded hazards, the approved hours, and the person who can sign off completed work. If any of these is missing, do not enter until it is confirmed in writing or through the site's documented process.

instructionSections.heading: Presentation is not contamination clearance
instructionSections.body: A room can look finished and still have active trade work, unfinished services or unidentified materials. Never confuse a presentable room with a room that is safe or clear of contamination. Where the supervisor asks for a photograph of a finished room while electricians are testing live circuits, document the unfinished stage, stop entry into that area, and obtain a revised safe access window before continuing.

instructionSections.heading: Working from the sample work order
instructionSections.body: Read the work order with the authorising contact, the allowed zones, the active-trade exclusions and the handover criteria. Write down the questions that must be resolved before mobilising, and do not start until the answers are recorded.

lessons.title: Construction induction and simultaneous operations
learningOutcomes: Confirm the site induction, pedestrian and vehicle segregation, permits and emergency routes.
Stay out of plant routes and never remove a barrier to shorten travel.
Withdraw and escalate when a plant route crosses the cleaning area.

instructionSections.heading: What the induction covers
instructionSections.body: A site induction tells you the local hazards, the emergency assembly point, the incident procedure, the restricted zones, the vehicle routes and who the site controller is. It does not, on its own, certify that you are competent for every task on the site. Treat the induction as the start of the controls, not the end of them.

instructionSections.heading: Simultaneous operations change the picture
instructionSections.body: Trades, deliveries and temporary barriers move during the day, so the controls are checked at each shift start. Stay out of plant routes. Do not remove or step around a barrier to save time. If a forklift route crosses the corridor that you were assigned, do not work around moving plant. Withdraw to the designated safe location and request an approved revised pedestrian route from the site controller.

instructionSections.heading: Reporting a changed hazard
instructionSections.body: Keep a written channel for reporting a newly opened hazardous zone, and use it. A changed condition is reported as soon as it is seen, with the location and the time. The report is what allows the site to close the gap.

instructionSections.heading: Walking the plan
instructionSections.body: Use the supplied site plan to trace the permitted access route and the evacuation route, and locate the exclusion boundaries. Practise the escalation when a simultaneous operation changes the route, so that the response is automatic under pressure.

lessons.title: Hazard recognition and unknown materials
learningOutcomes: Recognise warning signs of silica, lead, asbestos, sharp metal or glass, wet cement, electrical and biological hazards without touching the material.
Isolate suspected uncontrolled hazardous material from a safe position.
Report the material to the site controller and leave removal to qualified specialists.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising the signs
instructionSections.body: Some hazards on a construction site can be recognised by what you see. Dusty cut masonry can carry crystalline silica. Damaged insulation, peeling suspect coatings and older building materials may contain asbestos or lead. Sharp offcuts and broken glass are physical hazards. Unsecured wiring is an electrical hazard, unlabelled drums are a chemical hazard, and wet uncured materials such as cement can cause burns and skin damage. Biological hazards may be present in some situations. Recognise these signs, but do not sample or handle the material to identify it.

instructionSections.heading: Appearance cannot identify the material
instructionSections.body: You cannot tell asbestos, lead or the concentration of silica by looking at them. A powder that resembles harmless dust may be hazardous, and a bag labelled offcuts may contain something else. Treat any suspicious or unidentified material as outside routine cleaning. Do not empty a bag to see what is inside, and do not sweep the powder up because it looks like dust.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating and reporting
instructionSections.body: Isolate the area from a safe position, keep other workers out, and report the material to the site controller. Record its location and what you observed without disturbing it. Ask for the documented material and dust plan. Only qualified and authorised specialists may identify and remove regulated material.

instructionSections.heading: Sorting the situation
instructionSections.body: In practice, a hazard card may be routine authorised work, something that needs supervisor clarification, or an immediate stop-work condition. Routine work is the cleaning that the plan already covers. Clarification is needed where the material is known but its handling is not set out. Stop-work applies to any unidentified or uncontrolled hazardous material. The person who resolves each issue is named in the site plan.

lessons.title: Silica dust exposure fundamentals
learningOutcomes: Explain how silica dust is created and why it is a respiratory hazard.
Identify the dust-control approach set by the site's risk assessment.
Stop and escalate when dust control is absent or not verified.

instructionSections.heading: Where silica comes from
instructionSections.body: Crystalline silica is found in many common building materials, including concrete, masonry, stone, tile and some grouts and renders. Cutting, grinding, drilling and sweeping dry material can release fine respirable silica dust into the air. Fine dust is the concern because it can reach the deep parts of the lungs and it may not be visible. Dusty cut masonry is a warning sign.

instructionSections.heading: Controls before cleaning
instructionSections.body: Dust is controlled at its source first. The site's documented risk assessment sets the control, such as wet methods, dust extraction on the cutting tool, or enclosure. Cleaning must not create dust. Dry sweeping and the use of compressed air disturb settled dust and put it back into the air. A cleaner works to the controls that the site has verified, not to a general belief that a method is safe.

instructionSections.heading: When controls are not verified
instructionSections.body: Stop when dust control is absent, when the site cannot show the controls in place, or when the dust source is unknown. Keep others away, and report to the site controller. Do not clean up silica dust with a household vacuum, because its filtration is not designed for fine respirable dust.

instructionSections.heading: Exposure limits and monitoring
instructionSections.body: Exposure is managed against the workplace exposure limits that apply. The exposure list that applies is changing in Victoria on 1 December 2026, so current limits must be checked before they are cited. Air monitoring and health surveillance may be needed, and the site determines whether they are required.

lessons.title: Dust suppression and extraction
learningOutcomes: Compare wet methods, site-approved on-tool extraction and hazard-appropriate industrial vacuums.
Identify the runoff, electrical and slip hazards that wet methods introduce.
Reject equipment that is not approved for the hazard, and obtain a documented alternative.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing from the site risk assessment
instructionSections.body: The dust control is selected from the documented site risk assessment and the equipment instructions. A general rule that a HEPA filter is safe is not a basis for choosing equipment. The hazard, the material and the jurisdiction determine what is suitable. Filtration, seal integrity, maintenance and waste handling all vary, so the equipment must be the kind that the risk assessment names.

instructionSections.heading: Wet methods and their side effects
instructionSections.body: Compatible controlled wet methods can reduce dust, but they introduce other hazards. Water on the floor creates slip risk. Water near electrical equipment creates an electrical hazard. Runoff can carry contamination into drains and onto neighbouring property, and water can damage some materials. Plan the route of the runoff and the protections that stop it leaving the work area, before the water is used.

instructionSections.heading: Extraction equipment
instructionSections.body: Industrial vacuums and on-tool extraction need the right filtration for the material, intact seals, and maintenance records. A household canister vacuum with a new HEPA filter but no approval for silica is rejected for the task. Never empty a suspected hazardous-dust collector unless you have the approved training and the approved method for it. Obtain a documented suitable alternative from the responsible supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing and recording
instructionSections.body: Compare the equipment against the risk assessment, check the evidence that the equipment is approved for the material, quarantine any item that is not approved, and record the water protections in place. Keep the choice and the reason on the job record.

lessons.title: Respiratory protection and fit
learningOutcomes: Explain why respiratory protection is the last control in the hierarchy.
Carry out a user seal check before wearing a respirator.
Stop work when a respirator does not fit, is damaged or is not the type the site specified.

instructionSections.heading: Last, not first
instructionSections.body: Respiratory protection is the last layer of control in the hierarchy. It does not replace controlling the dust at source, and it does not work if it does not fit. The site's risk assessment decides whether a respirator is needed, and which type. A cleaner who chooses a respirator for themselves on a hazard they have not assessed is making a decision that belongs to the site.

instructionSections.heading: Fit and the user seal check
instructionSections.body: A respirator only protects when it seals to the face. Facial hair, damaged seals, incorrect sizing and an unchecked strap can all stop a seal. Before wearing the respirator, carry out a user seal check as the training and the manufacturer's instructions describe. The check is done each time the respirator is put on.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping when protection fails
instructionSections.body: Stop work if the respirator does not pass the seal check, if the seal breaks, if the filter is clogged or damaged, or if the wrong type has been supplied for the material. Leave the area, report the problem to the supervisor, and do not continue without a suitable respirator.

instructionSections.heading: Looking after the respirator
instructionSections.body: Store the respirator clean and dry, inspect it before use, and replace filters on the schedule the manufacturer and the site set. A respirator that is worn with a damaged filter gives false protection.

lessons.title: Debris segregation and waste containment
learningOutcomes: Separate authorised ordinary waste, recyclables, sharps, chemical residues and suspected hazardous waste.
Use labelled containers and approved routes that prevent dust release.
Secure unidentified contaminated debris and seek a corrected waste plan.

instructionSections.heading: Streams of waste
instructionSections.body: Construction debris falls into several streams: authorised ordinary waste, offcuts, recyclable materials, sharp objects, chemical residues and suspected hazardous waste. Keep the streams apart in labelled containers. The site waste classification and disposal plan decides which stream a material goes into. If the classification is missing, quarantine the area and ask the site controller before moving anything.

instructionSections.heading: Handling sharps and containers
instructionSections.body: Do not compress bags by hand, and do not retrieve sharp debris without an approved method. Use containers and routes that prevent dust from escaping and stop unauthorised members of the public from getting into the waste. Keep lids closed and loads secured on the way to the container.

instructionSections.heading: When a skip is wrong
instructionSections.body: A skip marked general waste may contain suspect insulation and broken glass. Do not re-sort it by hand. Record the issue, the location and the contents as far as you can see them without disturbing them, and seek a corrected waste-management plan. The skip is a waste problem for the site to resolve with the right people.

instructionSections.heading: Waste classification and transport
instructionSections.body: Classification, transport and disposal rules vary by state and territory and by waste type. Follow the site plan and the approved route.

lessons.title: Materials and surface protection
learningOutcomes: Distinguish cured from uncured coatings, delicate flooring, adhesives and new installations.
Obtain the finish schedule and manufacturer method before selecting an agent or tool.
Record defects and stop when no approved method or product specification is available.

instructionSections.heading: New surfaces need more care
instructionSections.body: A newly installed surface may be uncured, porous or covered by a temporary protective film. An uncured coating can be damaged by a product that would be safe on the cured version. Porous stone takes up product and can stain. Protective films can be damaged by some solvents. Before you select an agent, pad or method, check whether the surface is cured, what it is, and whether it has a protective layer.

instructionSections.heading: Use the finish schedule
instructionSections.body: Obtain the finish schedule and the manufacturer's cleaning instructions before you clean. The approved method is the one the schedule and the manufacturer give. A test on an inconspicuous approved area can confirm compatibility, but it does not override a missing SDS or an unsafe chemical combination, and it does not replace the approved method.

instructionSections.heading: When there is no specification
instructionSections.body: A contractor may ask for adhesive removal on new stone without a product specification. Do not scrape the residue or apply a strong solvent to remove it. Record the residue and its location, and request the stone supplier's approved method through the site. Stone can be etched or stained by a method that seems reasonable, so the specification is the control.

instructionSections.heading: Photographs and protection of information
instructionSections.body: Photograph pre-existing defects only with permission. Protect occupants and customer information in any photograph, and do not photograph people or private documents.

lessons.title: Equipment inspection and decontamination
learningOutcomes: Inspect cords, guards, wheels, extraction hoses, seals, filters and labels before use.
Tag out damaged equipment and stop its use.
Clean and decontaminate equipment only by the approved procedure for the material collected.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect before every use
instructionSections.body: Before use, inspect the electrical cord, the guards, the wheels, the extraction hoses, the seals, the filters and the labels against the manufacturer's guidance. Check the maintenance status as well. A machine that looks fine may have a torn seal or a blocked filter that you cannot see from the outside, so the inspection covers each part in turn.

instructionSections.heading: Tagging out damaged equipment
instructionSections.body: Damaged equipment is tagged out, removed from use and reported. Do not improvise electrical or filtration repairs. A torn extraction seal on a unit with an unknown dust history is tagged out, prevented from further use, and reported for competent inspection. Return to service only after the competent person approves it.

instructionSections.heading: Decontamination by approved method
instructionSections.body: Reusable equipment is cleaned and decontaminated only by the approved procedure for the material it actually collected. The method depends on the material, so the cleaner does not choose a method on appearance. Emptying a collector is done only by trained personnel using the manufacturer's method. Preserve the service logs, and report any unsafe disposal or filter change.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the log
instructionSections.body: The equipment log records the inspection result, the equipment identifier, any defect, the quarantine action, the responsible person and the return-to-service approval. A log that is filled in without the inspection is a false record.

lessons.title: Client handover and quality evidence
learningOutcomes: Agree measurable acceptance criteria before the work starts.
Record exceptions, defects and unresolved exclusions explicitly.
Decline certification claims that a cleaning walkthrough cannot support.

instructionSections.heading: Agree the criteria first
instructionSections.body: Before work starts, agree measurable acceptance criteria with the client. These cover the rooms in scope, the accessible surfaces, the documented defects, the waste clearance, and any hygiene or contamination verification that qualified parties will carry out. A criterion that is not measurable cannot be checked, so write each one so that someone else can verify it.

instructionSections.heading: Evidence and privacy
instructionSections.body: Photograph only where authorised. Do not photograph personal records, security plans or people without permission. Keep a defects register that records each defect, its location and its status. Record exceptions explicitly, so that the handover shows what was not done.

instructionSections.heading: What a cleaning completion is not
instructionSections.body: Final cleaning completion is not a laboratory clearance certificate, an asbestos clearance or a regulatory sign-off. A visual walkthrough does not show that a space is free of silica dust or other contamination. Clearance comes from the qualified and authorised professional who performs the test. If the client asks you to sign a silica-free certificate after a visual walkthrough, decline that certification. Provide the contracted cleaning checklist, and refer any exposure clearance to the authorised competent professional.

instructionSections.heading: The mock final walkthrough
instructionSections.body: In a final walkthrough, check each room against the agreed list, log the defects, and record the unresolved exclusions. Mark the work complete only against the approved scope, and state clearly what is outside that scope.

lessons.title: Site rules: approved products, plug-in equipment and reporting
learningOutcomes: Identify which products and equipment are approved for a job before opening or using them.
Move a plug-in machine to another socket using the switch-off sequence.
Report a defective machine, a hazard or an accident to the supervisor without delay, without attempting an electrical repair.
Explain why a machine is never lifted or dragged by its cord.

instructionSections.heading: Use only what the business has approved
instructionSections.body: Every product and machine used on a job should come from the list your business has approved. A product brought from home, an unlabelled bottle or a borrowed machine may not match the safety data, the dilution rules or the equipment checks that the business relies on. If you find a product you did not expect, do not use it and do not pour it into another container. Tell the supervisor, who will confirm whether it is approved. Your business records its approved list in the job or site record, so check there before you open any container.

instructionSections.heading: Plug-in equipment and the safe way to move a plug
instructionSections.body: Electrical hazards are a main risk with cleaning machines in occupied buildings. Vacuums, scrubbers and extractors have cords that can be damaged, that can trip people, and that can be drawn into water. When a machine must move to another socket, switch the machine off at the machine, switch the wall socket off, and only then remove the plug. Take hold of the plug body, not the cord. Move the machine by its body or handle, never by its lead. The site rule is also that you do not unplug any plug on site unless you have been directed to handle it. Ask first when the plug belongs to the client, the building or another contractor.

instructionSections.heading: Defective equipment and electrical repair
instructionSections.body: If a cord is cut, a plug is cracked or warm, a switch sticks or a machine smells of burning, stop using it at once. Set the machine aside and label it as defective in the way your business directs. Tell your manager straight away. Electrical equipment is never repaired by the worker, even for a small fault such as a loose plug or a cut cord that could be taped. Repairs are arranged by the business through a suitably qualified person. Confirm them with the business before relying on any testing record.

instructionSections.heading: Misuse, hazards and reporting
instructionSections.body: Tampering with the equipment or materials you were given is misuse, whether it happens on purpose or through carelessness. Removing a guard, bypassing a safety switch, using a machine for a task it was not built for, or mixing products to get a stronger result all count as misuse. Your duty to report extends to every hazard you notice while working, not only to equipment faults. Report it to your manager immediately. The business then assesses the hazard and decides how to remove or reduce the risk. Do not decide alone that a hazard is too small to mention. Report every accident, however minor, and report near misses too, because a slip you recovered from shows where a control needs to change.

instructionSections.heading: Personal protective equipment before the first task
instructionSections.body: Wear the personal protective equipment that the job sheet lists for every task, not only when you expect to be close to a chemical. Check the PPE before you start. Gloves with tears or holes, or eye protection that is scratched or fogged, do not protect you and should be replaced before you begin.

lessons.title: Colour-coded cloths: a business-set system that keeps areas apart
learningOutcomes: Explain why separate cloths for separate areas prevent cross-contamination.
Read the business's colour key and apply it without assuming a colour's meaning from another business.
Remove from use and replace a cloth that has crossed into an area it was not assigned to.

instructionSections.heading: What the colour system is for
instructionSections.body: A colour system keeps cloths, mops and tools tied to one area of a site, so that soil, micro-organisms or product residue collected in one area does not travel to another. The colour itself does not protect anyone. The protection comes from the rule that each colour is used only in its assigned area and is not swapped between areas during a job. A cloth used in a washroom is safe to keep in use only while it stays in the washroom.

instructionSections.heading: Each business sets its own colours
instructionSections.body: Colour meanings differ between businesses, between sites and sometimes between clients. One example scheme assigns one colour to toilets and urinals, another to general areas, and a third to food-preparation areas. A different business may use a different set of colours for the same areas, or may use shapes, labels or bag colours instead. Do not assume a colour's meaning from anything you have seen elsewhere. The colour key is set by management, recorded in the business's procedures and shown at the site or on the job sheet. If the key is missing for a site, ask before you start.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up cloths and tools by area
instructionSections.body: Before you start, list the areas you will clean and check that each has its own set of cloths and tools. Keep the sets apart in the kit or on the trolley so that you cannot reach into the wrong set without noticing. Label holders or bags where the business uses them. Do not carry a loose cloth in a pocket or on your shoulder between areas. A cloth that drops on the floor is no longer clean for any area, so set it aside and take a replacement from the correct set.

instructionSections.heading: Working between areas
instructionSections.body: Work through the area order the business sets, which is usually from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest. When you move from one area to the next, do not carry a used tool across the threshold. Change gloves or wash your hands as your procedure requires before you handle cloths for a different area. Before each move, ask one question: is this cloth, mop or tool assigned to the area I am about to enter? If the answer is not clear, do not use it there.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising a crossed cloth and recovering
instructionSections.body: A cloth has crossed when it has been used in an area it is not assigned to, has touched a surface from another area, or has dropped onto a floor that you have not yet cleaned. Take it out of use and keep it apart from your clean cloths until it is handled the way the business directs. Clean the affected surface again with a correctly assigned cloth, then record the event and tell your supervisor, following the business's correction procedure. Do not decide on your own that the transfer was harmless.

lessons.title: Dusting and damp wiping: top-down order and controlled moisture
learningOutcomes: Dust vertical surfaces from the top down so that dust does not land on finished work.
Apply a damp wipe by loading the cloth rather than the surface.
Prevent product spray from reaching floors, edges and fittings during damp wiping.
Check and clean the equipment after the task and before storing it.

instructionSections.heading: Why order matters in dusting
instructionSections.body: Dust falls. If you clean a low surface first and then a higher one, the dust you knock loose from the higher surface lands on work you have just finished. Working from the top down means each pass deals with what the surfaces above have released, and the lowest surfaces are dealt with last. Use overlapping strokes so that you leave no gaps. Turn or refold the duster when its face is loaded, so that each stroke picks up dust rather than moving it around.

instructionSections.heading: Dry dusting first
instructionSections.body: Use a dry duster for the dusting stage, because its purpose is to lift loose dust before any moisture is involved. Dust vertical surfaces such as frames, panels and wall faces from the top down. Draw dust out of corners and along edges with the tip of the duster rather than leaving it in the angle. A dry duster will smear a sticky or greasy film rather than lift it. When you find a film, note it for damp wiping or for a different method, and do not keep working the dry duster over it.

instructionSections.heading: Damp wiping and where the solution goes
instructionSections.body: Damp wiping removes soil that dry dusting cannot lift. Make up the cleaning solution exactly as the product label or the business's approved method directs, and do not make it stronger to save time. Apply the solution to the cloth, not directly onto the surface, so that you control where the product goes. Wipe with smooth, even strokes. The working rule is that the cloth takes the product and the surface receives only the cloth. Over-spray can run onto floors, skirting, edges and electrical fittings. It creates a slip hazard on floors and can damage finishes and fittings.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the rinse clean
instructionSections.body: Where a surface needs a rinse, use clean water and a clean cloth, then wipe the surface dry. A loaded rinse cloth spreads soil back onto the surface, so change the water and the cloth when they are visibly dirty. Keep damp-wipe cloths and rinse cloths in their assigned sets, as set out in “Colour-coded cloths: a business-set system that keeps areas apart”, and do not use a cloth from one area on another area's surfaces.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting the finish and signing the area
instructionSections.body: Where the business's procedure requires a test on a hidden or less visible part of a surface before a product is used, complete the test first and record the result. Put on the protective gloves and other PPE the job sheet lists before you open a product. Place a warning sign where a wet surface or a fall risk has been created, and keep it in place until the area is dry.

instructionSections.heading: Checking and storing the equipment
instructionSections.body: After the task, check the duster, cloths, buckets and trigger sprays for condition and cleanliness before you store them. Rinse and dry reusable items as the procedure requires, and replace any worn cloth. Equipment left dirty or wet becomes the next job's cross-contamination source, so finish this step before you leave the area.

lessons.title: Dry sweeping and mopping: route order, bucket position and drying
learningOutcomes: Plan the working order so that you finish at the exit and do not walk over cleaned floor.
Dry sweep with a dustpan and brush and place the waste in the bag the business specifies.
Park the bucket on the already-mopped side and avoid carrying dirty water across cleaned floor.
Keep warning signs in place until the floor is completely dry.

instructionSections.heading: Clear the floor first
instructionSections.body: Before you dry sweep or mop, remove moveable objects from the floor area, such as bins, chairs, mats and loose cables. Set them where they will not block the route. Anything left on the floor will either stop the mop or be missed, and it leaves a line of soil under the mop head. If an object cannot be moved safely, report it rather than working around it blind.

instructionSections.heading: Plan the route from the far end
instructionSections.body: Work from the point furthest from the exit back toward the exit. This keeps you from walking over floor you have already finished, and it leaves you a clean, dry route out. In a large room, divide the floor into sections and finish each section before starting the next. Do not leave a section half-wet across a route that people must use.

instructionSections.heading: Dry sweeping
instructionSections.body: Dry sweeping lifts loose dust and debris before any moisture is applied, which stops the soil being smeared into a film. Sweep in the direction the procedure sets, gather the waste into a pile, and lift it with a dustpan and brush. Place the waste into the refuse bag the business specifies. Do not sweep debris into a corner to deal with later. Sharp or hazardous items are not swept in with ordinary debris. Handle them as the procedure directs.

instructionSections.heading: Mopping and the position of the bucket
instructionSections.body: Park the bucket on the already-mopped side, moving it forward as you progress, and never set it over floor you have not yet mopped. Dip the mop, wring it to the level the procedure sets, and mop in overlapping passes. Change the water when it is visibly dirty, rather than spreading soil across a larger area. Do not let the mop head dry out between passes, and do not leave solution pooled on the floor.

instructionSections.heading: Warning signs and drying
instructionSections.body: Place a warning sign wherever a wet floor creates a fall risk, and keep it in place until the floor is completely dry, not just until you have left the area. A floor often looks dry while the surface under a shoe is still slippery, especially in corners, at edges and under mats. Where drying takes a long time, rope off the route or use a barrier. Check the surface before you remove the sign.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing the floor
instructionSections.body: When the floor is finished, return the bucket and equipment to the allocated place, not to the walkway. Record the floor area completed and whether the drying check was met before the sign came down.

lessons.title: Vacuuming: inspect, clear, control the cord and shut down safely
learningOutcomes: Pick up large and sharp objects by hand before vacuuming, using gloves for sharp items.
Vacuum systematically, with extra passes over heavy-traffic areas, edges and corners.
Control the cord so that it stays behind the operator and is never overstretched.
Shut down the machine, wind the cord and store the machine in its allocated place.

instructionSections.heading: Check the machine before the first pass
instructionSections.body: A vacuum is only as safe as its condition. Before you start, check the cord, plug, hose, wheels, filter and bag or container against the business's inspection checklist. If the machine fails any check, do not use it. Set it aside and report it, as “Site rules: approved products, plug-in equipment and reporting” describes. Also confirm the machine suits the job. A vacuum rated for dry dust may not be suitable for wet debris or unknown material, and “Vacuum systems” sets out how to match the machine to the job.

instructionSections.heading: Clear large and sharp objects first
instructionSections.body: Before you switch the machine on, pick up large objects by hand. These include bottle caps, coins, nails, pieces of packaging and any debris that could block the hose, jam the brush roll or strike you. Pick up sharp objects such as glass fragments with protective gloves, and place them in the sharps container or the waste container the business specifies. Vacuuming over glass or metal can damage the machine and injure the operator or other people in the room.

instructionSections.heading: Sequence and passes
instructionSections.body: Vacuum the area in a systematic pattern rather than wandering across it. Give extra attention to heavy-traffic routes, along skirting boards and in corners, where soil collects. Overlap each pass slightly so that no strip is missed. Plan the route so that you do not step on the cord or drag the machine across it.

instructionSections.heading: Controlling the cord
instructionSections.body: Keep the cord behind you as you move, so that it is never under the machine's wheels or in front of your feet. Do not overstretch the cord, because a tight cord can pull the plug or damage the cord where it meets the machine. Do not pull the machine by its cord, and do not run it over the cord. Keep cords out of doorways and off stairs, and follow “Stairs, balustrades and handrails: stable stance and safe layout” when you vacuum stairs or landings.

instructionSections.heading: Shutting down, winding and storing
instructionSections.body: When you finish, switch off the power at the machine before you unplug it. Then switch off the socket and remove the plug at the plug body, as “Site rules: approved products, plug-in equipment and reporting” describes. Wind the cord back onto the machine in a controlled way, keeping it off the floor and away from the wheels. Empty or service the bag or container as the procedure directs, then store the machine in its allocated place. A machine left in a walkway is a trip hazard, and others may use it or damage it.

lessons.title: Stairs, balustrades and handrails: stable stance and safe layout
learningOutcomes: Place warning signs on landings and keep the route clear for other people.
Clean a handrail or balustrade with both feet on the floor, without leaning over or reaching.
Keep equipment and cables off the stairs and to one side of the landing.
Wipe spills at once and dry the treads before leaving them.

instructionSections.heading: Why stairs need their own rules
instructionSections.body: Stairs combine three hazards: a fall from height, a slip on a wet tread, and an object that blocks someone's path. Most of the controls therefore concern where you stand, where your equipment sits, and how quickly you dry what you have wet. People who use the stairs may not see the section you are cleaning, so signs and a clear route matter as much as the cleaning itself.

instructionSections.heading: Signs and the route
instructionSections.body: Place a warning sign on every landing you are working on, and at any point where a person could reach the stair you are cleaning. Keep the route clear. If someone needs to pass, stop, step aside to a safe position, and let them through before you continue. Do not cross a stair that is still wet while you are carrying equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Your stance and reach on the rail
instructionSections.body: When you clean a handrail or balustrade, both feet stay planted on the floor for the whole task. Leaning over the rail and reaching past your comfortable range are both ruled out. Move your position along the stair instead, so that each section comes within reach from a stable place. If a section cannot be reached safely from the floor, stop and tell the supervisor, who will decide on a safe method or access arrangement. Do not stand on a tread, the rail or any object to gain height.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment, buckets and cables
instructionSections.body: Keep all equipment to one side of the landing so that it does not obstruct anyone. Never place a vacuum or a bucket on a stair tread, where it can be knocked over or tripped over. Keep electrical cables clear of the treads and the handrail, where they can snag. If a cable must run near the stair, route it along the wall and secure it so that it cannot slide onto a step.

instructionSections.heading: Drying as you go
instructionSections.body: Leave every surface as dry as practicable. Wipe any water spill straight away, because a wet tread is one of the most likely causes of a fall on stairs. Use a drying cloth on each section after it is cleaned, and check the treads you have just finished before you move on. If a stair is still wet at the end of the task, the warning sign stays in place.

lessons.title: Bathroom risk assessment
learningOutcomes: Identify at least six common bathroom hazards before touching any surface.
Apply the order of controls to a routine bathroom hazard.
Stop work and escalate when a condition falls outside routine cleaning scope.
Record pre-existing damage and hazards before work begins.

instructionSections.heading: Why the walk-through comes first
instructionSections.body: A bathroom looks ordinary, but it concentrates hazards that are easy to miss once cleaning starts: wet floors, glass and sharps hidden in bins or behind fittings, loose tiles, damaged electrical fittings close to water, and residues from products that should never be mixed. Before you open a product or pick up a cloth, walk the room from the doorway. Confirm the authorised scope for this job, who is on site, whether ventilation is working, where the power points are, and a clear route out if something goes wrong. The walk-through is short, but skipping it is how most avoidable injuries in routine cleaning begin.

instructionSections.heading: Scanning without touching
instructionSections.body: Look before you reach. Check the floor for broken glass and standing water, the basin and shower area for loose tiles or unstable fittings, the wall near power points for damaged plates or cords, and the bin for sharps or bodily fluids. Notice any sour or chemical smell, which may indicate residues or a leak. Do not pick up an unknown sharp with your hands, and do not clean up an uncontrolled biological spill as if it were routine dirt. If you cannot see clearly into a bin or cabinet, treat its contents as unknown until the supervisor has assessed them.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding whether the task is routine
instructionSections.body: Routine bathroom cleaning covers soil that is known, surfaces that are compatible with an approved product, and hazards you can control with the PPE and method in your procedure. A hazard is outside routine scope when its nature or quantity is unknown, when it involves bodily fluids beyond what the procedure covers, when it involves exposed live electrical parts or gas, or when it would require a product you have not been trained or authorised to use. In those cases you stop, protect people from the area, and call the supervisor. Specialist response is a separate job with its own scope, and this lesson does not authorise it.

instructionSections.heading: Applying controls in order
instructionSections.body: Where a hazard is within scope, use the order of controls. First remove the hazard if you are authorised to do so, for example by picking up a dry, visible piece of debris with a suitable tool. Second isolate it, for example by closing the bathroom door, placing a wet-floor sign, or unplugging an appliance that is safe to unplug. Third rely on safe work procedures, such as a defined cleaning sequence and dry-floor finishing. PPE is the last layer, not a substitute for the first three, and it must match the product SDS and the site risk assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Recording what you found
instructionSections.body: Record the hazards you found, the controls you applied, and any damage that existed before you arrived. Photographs are valuable where the site permits them, provided they do not capture occupants or private property. A short, factual note is better than a long opinion. If you stopped work, record the time, the condition, who you told, and what you left untouched. This record protects you, the client and the business, and it gives the supervisor what they need to decide the next step.

lessons.title: Zone and cloth segregation
learningOutcomes: Assign dedicated cloths and tools to bathroom zones before work starts.
Explain why toilet tools must not be used on clean-touch surfaces.
Recover safely from a cross-zone mistake by segregating and re-cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Why zones matter
instructionSections.body: A bathroom has zones with different levels of contamination. The toilet bowl and floor around it are the most contaminated. Basins, taps, mirrors and shower screens are touched frequently, so they matter for hygiene and for appearance. If a toilet cloth is used on a basin tap, the soil from the toilet moves onto a surface people touch with their hands. Zone segregation keeps that transfer from happening, and it is the simplest control in a bathroom clean.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up the cloth system
instructionSections.body: Before you start, assign dedicated cloths and tools to each zone according to the site colour code or written procedure. Colour coding is useful only when everyone on the site uses the same meaning, so never assume that a colour means the same thing at every business. Keep toilet brushes and toilet cloths in their own zone, separate from vanity tools, and keep floor tools separate from both. Store clean tools away from used tools and away from the bin.

instructionSections.heading: Working in order
instructionSections.body: Work from cleaner zones toward dirtier zones where the site procedure allows. Clean mirrors and clean-touch surfaces first, then the basin and taps, then the shower, and finish with the toilet and the floor. Replace a cloth when it becomes visibly soiled, and always replace it when you move from a dirty zone to a clean one. Remove gloves when you change tasks, perform hand hygiene, and put on fresh gloves. Gloves are a barrier, not a replacement for hand hygiene.

instructionSections.heading: Recovering from a mistake
instructionSections.body: If a toilet cloth touches a vanity handle, stop the sequence. Withdraw the cloth from use and place it in the designated dirty container. Tell the supervisor if the procedure requires it. Re-clean the affected surface with a clean tool, using the approved product, and then recheck it. Record what happened and what you did. The record matters because it shows the site that the control worked, and it lets the supervisor adjust the set-up if the mistake repeats.

lessons.title: Fixtures, soils and material compatibility
learningOutcomes: Identify the main fixture materials in a bathroom before selecting a product.
Distinguish soap film, mineral scale, body oils and dirt, and match each to an approved method.
Justify an exclusion where a product or method is unsuitable for the surface.

instructionSections.heading: Identify the material first
instructionSections.body: Fixtures do not respond the same way to the same product. Glazed ceramic, enamel, acrylic, chrome, stainless steel, sealed stone and unsealed natural stone each have their own sensitivity to acids, alkalis, abrasives and solvents. Before choosing a product, look at the surface, check the site record if one exists, and ask the client or supervisor if the material is uncertain. If you cannot identify it, treat it as sensitive and use the gentlest approved method.

instructionSections.heading: Match the soil to the method
instructionSections.body: Soap film, mineral scale from hard water, body oils and ordinary dirt need different approaches. Soap film is usually removed with a mild, compatible detergent. Mineral scale may need an acid-based product on suitable surfaces, but acid can etch natural stone and damage some finishes, so it must not be used on sensitive surfaces without approval. Body oils and grease respond to a degreaser that is compatible with the finish. Dirt in a joint or fixing may need a mechanical method that does not scratch the surface. One product is rarely right for every soil in the room.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the label and testing
instructionSections.body: Read the product label and SDS for intended surfaces, dilution, ventilation, PPE and contact time before use. Test on an inconspicuous area only where the manufacturer and the site procedure allow it, and wait for the test area to dry before judging the result. Never mix products, and never transfer product into an unlabelled container. Record the product name and the test result if a test is carried out.

instructionSections.heading: When to exclude a method
instructionSections.body: Some requests are outside what the cleaner should do. A client who asks for an acidic descaler on marble is asking for a method that can etch the surface. The correct response is to explain the risk, use only a stone-compatible approach that the site allows, and escalate any persistent marks to the supervisor for a specialist assessment. Excluding a method is a professional decision. Record the limitation in the job notes so the client understands what was and was not done.

lessons.title: Sanitary cleaning sequence
learningOutcomes: Apply a fixed fixture-by-fixture sequence for a full bathroom clean.
Follow product contact time and rinsing instructions rather than guessing them.
Control splashing and wet-floor hazards during and after the clean.

instructionSections.heading: Set up before you start
instructionSections.body: Prepare the room before the first product is opened. Ventilate as the site allows, set out a warning sign if occupants could enter, and lay out clean tools in the order you will use them. Remove rubbish and loose debris, but do not disturb sharps you cannot identify. Once the room is ready, the sequence begins. Skipping set-up leads to cross-contamination and slips later in the clean.

instructionSections.heading: Work from top and clean toward dirty
instructionSections.body: Clean higher and cleaner surfaces first so that drips and splashes fall onto areas you have not yet cleaned. Start with mirrors and accessible touchpoints, then move to the basin and taps, the shower screen and fittings, and finally the toilet exterior and interior. Use the separate sanitary tools for each stage. Finish with the floor, moving toward the exit so you do not walk over finished surfaces. Leave slip-prone floors dry or controlled until they are safe to walk on.

instructionSections.heading: Products, contact time and rinsing
instructionSections.body: Use the product label for dilution, contact time, rinsing and disposal. A common error is assuming that a disinfectant works immediately or that one contact time applies to every product. Contact time is set by the product, so the cleaner must wait for the stated time before wiping, rinsing or moving on. Where a product is not labelled as a disinfectant, do not describe the surface as disinfected. Keep product use within the label and within the site procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing and checking
instructionSections.body: After the floor is finished, walk the room and check for residue, streaks and wet spots. Confirm that toilet tools are back in their zone and that the bin is emptied as the procedure requires. A clean that looks finished is not automatically verified. Record the checks you completed and any limitations, and leave the room in the state the site procedure requires for handover.

lessons.title: Final inspection and handover
learningOutcomes: Inspect a bathroom along a fixed route from the doorway to the floor.
Separate removable soil from damage or staining that routine cleaning cannot resolve.
Hand over with a factual, privacy-safe record of what was done and what was not authorised.

instructionSections.heading: A fixed inspection route
instructionSections.body: Inspect the bathroom in the same order every time, starting at the doorway. Check the mirror edges, taps, basin and drain surrounds, shower screen, grout, the toilet contact points, skirting, corners and the floor. Look for visible soil, streaks, residue, misplaced items and equipment left behind, and check the floor for slip hazards. A fixed route stops you from missing a surface that you have already stopped looking at.

instructionSections.heading: Soil, damage and limitations
instructionSections.body: Distinguish removable soil from damage, staining or deterioration that routine cleaning cannot resolve. Discoloured grout that remains after safe cleaning is usually a limitation, not a cleaning failure. Do not apply an unapproved stronger chemical to remove it. Record the location and the limitation, and let the supervisor decide whether a specialist is needed.

instructionSections.heading: Photographs and privacy
instructionSections.body: Photograph only where the site's privacy and consent policy allows. Exclude people, personal documents and unnecessary belongings from the frame. A photograph is evidence of a condition, so frame the surface and keep the context neutral.

instructionSections.heading: Handover without overpromising
instructionSections.body: Record unresolved issues factually, including what was attempted and what was not authorised. Explain the outcome to the client or supervisor without promising sterilisation or infection-free conditions. Close out the job by confirming the record is complete and the handover has been accepted by the person authorised to accept it.

lessons.title: Food-contact safety and scope
learningOutcomes: Identify the type of kitchen and the authorisation that applies before handling food-contact items.
Recognise tasks and conditions that are outside a routine cleaner's scope.
Prepare a controlled work area and record what is in and out of scope.

instructionSections.heading: Confirming the kitchen type and the authority
instructionSections.body: A domestic kitchen, a short-stay kitchen, an office kitchenette and a regulated food premises carry different expectations. Before handling benches, utensils, food-contact equipment or stored food, read the work order and the site's food safety plan, and identify which of these you are in. A routine cleaner must not assume authority to dismantle appliances, to handle exposed food, or to carry out food-business verification. When in doubt, the authorised site contact decides.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing the work area
instructionSections.body: Ask the authorised site contact to secure or remove exposed food, and to clean or move utensils and personal items before products are applied. Identify the handwashing facilities, water access, ventilation, waste routes and chemical storage. Keep clean and dirty equipment separate, and never place chemical containers on food preparation surfaces.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising exclusions and escalating
instructionSections.body: Report pests, suspected contamination, damaged food-contact materials, inaccessible equipment and uncontrolled electrical hazards. Do not use unapproved pesticides, do not dispose of food without authorisation, and do not certify that a food business meets regulatory standards. Record what is in scope and what is out of scope, so that the client and supervisor know where the boundary sits.

instructionSections.heading: The start-work check
instructionSections.body: Before starting, confirm that the area has been released for cleaning, that suitable products are available, and that the site instructions state any sanitising and final rinse that are required. Photograph only when authorised, and without capturing private information.

lessons.title: Degreasing without damage
learningOutcomes: Distinguish loose food residue, light oil films, hardened grease and mineral deposits.
Select an approved degreasing method that suits the surface.
Degrease a surface in a controlled sequence without damaging its finish.

instructionSections.heading: Identify the soil and the surface
instructionSections.body: Grease is not one thing. A light oil film on stainless steel behaves differently from hardened grease on an oven shelf or a baked-on residue on a painted panel. Loose crumbs and food residue come off with dry methods first. Before applying a degreaser, identify the surface: stainless steel, laminate, painted surfaces, glass, coated metal, sealed stone and timber all respond differently. Damaged coatings and porous surfaces may need specialist advice rather than a stronger product.

instructionSections.heading: Choose an approved method
instructionSections.body: Read the product label and SDS for the intended surface, dilution, PPE, ventilation, dwell time and rinsing. Check the appliance or benchtop manufacturer's guidance where it is available. Avoid aggressive abrasives on polished stainless steel and coated surfaces, because they leave scratches that hold more grease later. Avoid acidic or strongly alkaline products on sensitive stone, timber or finishes unless the product is approved for that surface.

instructionSections.heading: Degrease in a controlled sequence
instructionSections.body: Remove loose debris first so that it does not smear. Apply the authorised product using the label method and wait for the specified time without letting the product dry where the label prohibits that. Agitate with a compatible non-scratching tool, lift the residue, rinse if the label directs, and dry the surface where appropriate. Keep drips away from food, power sockets and appliance controls. Degreasing near electrical controls needs extra care, and the product must not be allowed to enter switches or vents.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the result and escalating
instructionSections.body: Inspect the surface from more than one angle, because streaks and residue often show only in side light. Repeat the method only within the approved method. Record baked-on or inaccessible grease as a limitation rather than increasing the chemical strength without approval. Where a surface is damaged by the process, stop, record the damage, and report it. Do not hide the damage by applying another product.

lessons.title: Appliance and handover checks
learningOutcomes: Identify the authorised appliance boundaries from the work order before cleaning.
Clean accessible appliance parts safely, away from energised electrical parts.
Complete a closeout inspection and handover that does not overstate the service delivered.

instructionSections.heading: Setting the boundary
instructionSections.body: Check the work order for the authorised appliance exteriors, shelves, accessible removable parts, and the listed exclusions. Do not open electrical panels, disconnect fixed services or dismantle gas equipment. Do not spray liquid into switches, sockets, motors or control boards. Isolate an appliance only by an authorised, safe procedure. If an appliance is not within the work order, leave it as it is and record that it was excluded.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning accessible parts safely
instructionSections.body: Allow hot equipment to cool as required, and check for sharp edges, unstable shelving and glass. Use the manufacturer-approved methods for doors, seals, handles, benches and exterior controls. Keep cloths and liquids away from energised electrical parts. Never mix chemicals, and do not use an oven-specific product outside its approved application.

instructionSections.heading: Inspecting the whole room
instructionSections.body: Check the touchpoints, splashbacks, sink edges, appliance handles, floor corners, waste area and every item on the work order. Confirm that no food, utensils or personal items were contaminated or moved. Identify pre-existing damage, faults, inaccessible deposits and incomplete work, and report them rather than hiding them.

instructionSections.heading: Handover with evidence
instructionSections.body: Return only the authorised items to their agreed positions, remove supplies and waste, and leave the floor safe. Complete the checklist, record any sanitising step required by the site procedure, and escalate unresolved risks. Do not claim the room is food-safe beyond the service scope and the inspection actually performed.

lessons.title: Public and occupied-area safety
learningOutcomes: Assess foot traffic, trip routes, cables, wet floors and emergency exits before each work zone.
Use barriers and signs without relying on them alone to stop entry.
Pause affected work and reroute when occupancy changes.

instructionSections.heading: Assessing the zone before you start
instructionSections.body: Before each work zone, assess the foot traffic, the trip routes, cables, wet floors, cleaning odours, ventilation, accessibility and emergency exits. An occupied area can change in minutes, so the assessment is repeated when people arrive or the traffic pattern changes. Identify the person responsible for escalation before you begin.

instructionSections.heading: Barriers, signs and sections
instructionSections.body: Use the site-approved signage and barriers. Signs and barriers are a warning, not a physical block, so never rely on signs alone to prevent a person from entering. Work in manageable sections and check that the surface is safe before reopening it. Keep accessible exits and paths open, and do not spray near people, food or electronics.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting people, documents and privacy
instructionSections.body: Protect confidential desks and documents. Clean around sensitive items rather than moving them without permission. If the task exceeds your training, consent, safe access or the agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others, report promptly, and document the reason. Do not substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Worked example: a busy corridor
instructionSections.body: During lunch, a corridor becomes busy while the floor is wet. The cleaner isolates the area, offers an accessible alternative route, and waits for the floor to dry safely before removing the controls. The corridor is reopened only when the surface is safe to walk on.

lessons.title: Vacuum systems
learningOutcomes: Match the vacuum's rating, filtration and attachments to the job.
Inspect the cord, hose, bag, filter and seals before use.
Stop and escalate when the dust or material is unknown or the vacuum is not rated for it.

instructionSections.heading: Matching the machine to the job
instructionSections.body: Vacuum systems are not interchangeable. Identify whether a machine is a dry vacuum, a wet-capable vacuum or a specialist machine, and read its manufacturer rating. Never assume that a dry vacuum can collect liquid or hazardous dust. Match the filtration, the floor head and the power supply to the job, and check the capacity for the amount of material you expect to pick up.

instructionSections.heading: Inspecting before use
instructionSections.body: Inspect the cord, the hose, the bag or container, the filter, the seals and the attachments before you plug the machine in. A damaged power cord is not used. Replace the component, or remove the machine from service and report it, rather than taping it up and continuing. Check the bag or container is seated and that the filter is clean enough for the job.

instructionSections.heading: Unknown dust and hazardous material
instructionSections.body: When you encounter unknown fine dust, such as renovation dust, stop. A household vacuum is not suitable for dust that may be hazardous, because its filtration may let fine particles back into the air. Follow the site's procedure for dust containment and filter changes, and escalate the material for identification before continuing. Do not guess what the dust is.

instructionSections.heading: Handling bags and filters
instructionSections.body: Handle a full bag or container so that dust is not released. Follow the site procedure for emptying, and for disposing of the bag or filter. Record any filter change and any escalation of suspect material.

lessons.title: Wet cleaning systems
learningOutcomes: Select a flat mop, bucket system or scrubber based on floor type, soil, traffic and drying time.
Control slip and moisture hazards with barriers, signs and drying.
Stop and switch method when a surface shows moisture damage or pooling.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the system
instructionSections.body: Wet cleaning systems differ in how much water they put on a floor. A flat mop with a microfibre head uses little solution and dries quickly, which suits sealed hard floors. A bucket system with a wringer lets the cleaner control how wet the mop is. A scrubber applies more agitation for heavy soil. Choose the system according to the floor type, traffic, the amount and type of soil, and how long the floor must take to dry before people can walk on it.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping clean solution separate
instructionSections.body: Where the system allows, keep clean solution separate from dirty recovery water. Change the solution when it is visibly dirty, and do not keep reusing dirty water to make the floor look clean. Dirty water spreads soil and can leave residue. Keep containers labelled and do not pour product into unlabelled bottles.

instructionSections.heading: Controlling moisture and slip risk
instructionSections.body: Wet floors are slippery, so place signs and barriers before you start, and keep pedestrian routes open where the site allows. Avoid flooding seams, joins and electrical outlets. Water that sits in joints or under edges can damage timber and some substrates. Dry the floor where the procedure requires it, and check that the floor is safe to walk on before you leave the area.

instructionSections.heading: When to change method
instructionSections.body: Stop and change method if you see pooling, swelling, staining or a change in the colour of timber, or if water is reaching a joint that the floor finish cannot tolerate. Use the approved low-moisture method instead. Record the change and the reason. A general wet-cleaning lesson is not authority to carry out a restricted or specialist task on a sensitive floor.

lessons.title: The hotel room standard and why guests judge cleanliness
learningOutcomes: Describe the parts of a guest-ready room standard: what is seen, touched, smelt and found.
Explain why one visible fault can shape a guest's view of the whole room.
Identify which parts of the standard come from the business's written quality standard and which need a coordinator's decision.

instructionSections.heading: What a room standard covers
instructionSections.body: A room standard is the set of conditions a room must meet before the next guest arrives. It is more specific than a general sense that a room is tidy. It covers what a guest sees (surfaces, the bed, the bathroom, the floor), what a guest touches (the points many hands use), what a guest smells, how the air and temperature feel, and whether the supplies a guest expects are in place. Higher-tier accommodation sets the bar higher, because guests arrive with firm expectations and compare rooms closely. A standard only helps when it is written down and applied the same way each time, so that two cleaners given the same room produce the same result.

instructionSections.heading: Why one small fault changes the whole judgement
instructionSections.body: Guests rarely inspect a room methodically, but they notice what is out of place. A dusty lamp, a smear on the bathroom mirror or a hair in the basin can lead a guest to wonder what else was missed. The judgement forms quickly, from the points a guest looks at and touches first, and it then colours the rest of the stay and any review that follows. For that reason the cleaner does not treat the parts that are easy to see as the whole job. Every listed point counts, including the ones that are not on a guest's first glance.

instructionSections.heading: Clean has three parts
instructionSections.body: In this group a room counts as clean only when three things are true. It looks clean, with no dust, marks or residue on the surfaces a guest sees. It has been treated where it matters, which means high-touch surfaces have been disinfected with a product used as its label directs. And it is neutral in smell and comfortable in temperature. A room can look clean and still fail on touch or smell, so each part is checked separately. The lessons that follow in this group break these three parts into practical steps.

instructionSections.heading: Where the standard comes from
instructionSections.body: The standard comes from the business's written quality standard and from any requirements the property sets for itself. The cleanliness of accommodation may also be governed by state or territory law or by local rules. The source article behind this lesson describes state-level rules in a different market, and those rules are not used here. Do not present this lesson as a statement of legal obligation. Where the business or property has a specific standard, that standard governs the job.

lessons.title: Room sequence: top to bottom and dirty to clean
learningOutcomes: State the order of work for a room turnover and the reason for each stage.
Explain why dry work comes before wet work and why the floor is finished last.
Plan the room sequence inside a time window without skipping a stage.

instructionSections.heading: Why order matters
instructionSections.body: Order decides how much work has to be repeated. Dust settles onto surfaces that are already clean. Cleaning product and dirt move from one area to the next on cloths and hands. Clean linen cannot be placed on a surface that is still being worked. A fixed sequence stops these problems before they start. The sequence in this lesson rests on three rules: remove soiled items before cleaning begins, do dry work before wet work so that dust is not pushed into damp surfaces, and finish with the floor so that it is not walked over until the other work is done.

instructionSections.heading: The sequence in practice
instructionSections.body: Start by removing all linen and then clearing rubbish and used items from the room, so that the room is empty of soiled material. Dust from the highest point down across the whole room, which is dry work. Then wipe and disinfect the high-touch surfaces in the room. Clean the bathroom next, as the most contaminated area, using its own cloths and products. Make the bed with clean linen once the bathroom work is finished. Restock to the approved list, and then vacuum, sweep or mop the floor. Check the odour and temperature, and finish with the final walk-through. Plan the order within the time window set in “Short-stay departure-to-arrival turnover planning”, and allow time for the final walk-through in every plan.

instructionSections.heading: Working the room in one direction
instructionSections.body: Work round the room in one direction without going back to areas already finished. Start near the entry and move around the room, so that you finish each area before moving on. Do not leave a stage half done while you go to another area. Keep the cloths and products for each zone separate, as your business method sets out, so that bathroom cloths do not go onto room surfaces. Change a cloth when it is no longer picking up dust or when it has been used on a dirty area.

instructionSections.heading: Why the bathroom comes before bed-making
instructionSections.body: Some hotel procedures make the bed earlier in the order. This lesson places the bathroom before the bed so that clean linen is not handled after the bathroom work, and so that bathroom splashes do not land on a bed that has just been made. Hands are washed and gloves changed between the two stages in any case. Your business method may set a different order for a particular property. If it does, keep the same reasons and record the agreed order on the checklist.

lessons.title: Dusting and wiping high-touch surfaces
learningOutcomes: Dust a room from the highest point to the lowest, in a fixed order.
List the high-touch surfaces in a guest room and explain why they need disinfecting, not only wiping.
Apply an approved product so that the label's contact time is respected.

instructionSections.heading: Why dusting carries weight
instructionSections.body: A small amount of dust shows clearly on a dark or polished surface, and a guest who notices it may assume the rest of the room was not properly cleaned. Dusting is therefore a visible part of the standard, not a formality. It is done in one direction, from the highest points to the lowest, so that anything knocked down by one pass is caught by the next. Dry dusting is done before any wet work, so that wet cloths are not left with dust to push about.

instructionSections.heading: Top-to-bottom dusting in practice
instructionSections.body: Start with the high points: light shades, the tops of wardrobes and cupboards, artwork and picture frames, and fittings on the walls. Then work down through the window sills and blinds, the tops of furniture, the bedside tables and the desk, and finally the low items such as the base of lamps. Lampshades and light fittings are dusted only with the power off and the item cool and stable. Anything you cannot reach safely is reported under “Reporting damage and maintenance faults” rather than reached by improvised means. Use the dry or lightly damp cloth that your method sets, and avoid any tool that moves dust into the air.

instructionSections.heading: High-touch surfaces need disinfecting
instructionSections.body: High-touch surfaces are the points a guest's hands use most often: the remote control, the telephone, door handles inside and outside, light switches, drawer and cupboard handles, the mini-fridge door and handle, and the bedside controls. These need wiping with an approved disinfectant, used exactly as its label directs. The label states the contact time the product needs to work, and the surface must stay wet for that time. Wiping a surface and drying it at once does not satisfy the step unless the label allows it. A surface that looks clean may still need disinfecting.

instructionSections.heading: Cloth and product discipline
instructionSections.body: Apply the product to the cloth rather than spraying it onto electrical items, switches and the telephone. Keep the cloth just damp, so the surface is wet only where the label requires it. Fold the cloth to a clean face as you go. Replace the cloth when it is no longer picking up residue or when it has been used on a dirty area. Keep the zone coding from your business method, so that a cloth used in the bathroom does not reach the room's surfaces.

lessons.title: Bathroom checks for evidence of a previous guest
learningOutcomes: Describe the signs that a previous guest's presence can leave in a bathroom.
Carry out the bathroom check in a fixed order, under good light, as a separate final step.
Decide what to do with a mark that cannot be removed, and with an item that appears to belong to a guest.

instructionSections.heading: What the check is for
instructionSections.body: Once a bathroom has been cleaned, the last check is whether anything from the previous guest is still there. The signs can be small: a hair in the basin or on the tiles, water marks on glass, fingerprints on the mirror or taps, traces of product on the shelf, a greasy film on the glass, and drip marks on the outside of the bin. Any of these tells the next guest that the room was not fully reset, and it lowers trust in the rest of the room. The check is a separate step, done after the cleaning is complete and with fresh eyes.

instructionSections.heading: How to run the check
instructionSections.body: Stand at the doorway first and look across the whole bathroom with the light on. Then work round in a set order: basin and taps, mirror, shower or bath walls and screen, toilet inside and outside, floor edges and corners, the bin and the outside of it, and the back of the door and its hook. Marks often show only at an angle, so check the glass and tiles against the light. Run a clean cloth along edges and joints to feel for residue that the eye misses. Where a fitting is within reach and safe to check, include the extractor grille and the light fitting.

instructionSections.heading: What to do with what you find
instructionSections.body: If the approved method can clear a sign, clear it and recheck that exact spot. If it cannot be cleared, or if it looks like damage (chipping, a loose fitting, a leak, or growth that looks like mould), stop and report it under the business's procedure. Do not hide a mark by covering it. Do not sort through a guest's belongings. If an item appears to belong to a guest, follow the property's lost property procedure, described in “Damage and lost property”, and do not keep, sell or discuss the item.

instructionSections.heading: Hair, personal care items and electrical items
instructionSections.body: Remove hair with a cloth or the approved tool, not by hand. Keep product residue off cloths used elsewhere in the room. Hair dryers and other small electrical items are checked for a damaged cord or case and reported if faulty. Do not open the case or attempt a repair. Lint traps are cleaned as the business's procedure sets. Appliance identification for in-room appliances is covered in “Appliance identification”.

lessons.title: Bed making to the hotel standard
learningOutcomes: Build a bed in a fixed sequence of layers so that it looks the same each time.
Check each layer for stains, tears, lint and hair before the bed is accepted.
Handle clean linen so that it stays clean from the store to the bed.

instructionSections.heading: Scope, and the link to the linen handling lesson
instructionSections.body: Used linen handling, sorting, laundering and amenities are covered in “Linen handling, bed preparation and guest amenities”. Read that lesson before this one. This lesson covers the bed itself: how it is built, how it looks, and the checks made before it is accepted. The first stage of the room sequence removes the linen, which is when the mattress, protector and base are seen for stains and damage. Those checks are made at that point and are part of this lesson's standard.

instructionSections.heading: Building the bed in layers
instructionSections.body: Build the bed in a fixed order so that it looks the same every time. Fit the mattress protector flat and smooth, with no creases across the top. Place the bottom sheet and square the corners, tucking the sheet so it is smooth on the mattress. Add the top sheet with its decorative edge in the set position, and fold it at the head of the bed as the property's standard requires. Place the blanket or duvet, then the bedspread or throw. Set the pillows last, with the open side facing away from the door. Smooth each layer before the next one goes on, because creases trapped under a later layer are hard to remove.

instructionSections.heading: Clean hands and clean linen
instructionSections.body: Handle clean linen only with clean hands, and keep it off the floor. Do not drag linen across the room. Carry it against the body, away from bins and from any bathroom area. Do not place clean linen on the bathroom floor, on a bin, or on any surface that has not yet been finished. Wash or sanitise hands, or change gloves, after handling rubbish or cleaning products and before touching clean linen.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the bed before you leave it
instructionSections.body: Stand at the foot of the bed and look at it from the door side, as a guest would first see it. Check that each layer is square and that nothing hangs unevenly. Look for hairs, crumbs and lint. Press the top of the bed to check it is firm and free of lumps. Check each pillow before placing it, and reject any cover that is stained, torn or thin. If a cover is stained, torn or thin and there is no spare in the room, do not use it. Report it under the spare linen procedure.

lessons.title: Restocking to a list
learningOutcomes: Restock a room by working through the approved list in the room's layout order.
Check each item for presence, count, condition and expiry before it is placed.
Report a shortfall without substituting an item that is not on the approved list.

instructionSections.heading: Why restock against a list
instructionSections.body: Guests look for items and expect them in the places they know. A missing pen, an empty tea caddy or a set of glasses that is not set out is noticed on arrival, and it costs more trust than a guest would expect from so small an omission. A written list makes sure every item is checked in the same way for every room. Without a list, cleaners tend to restock what they remember and miss what they do not. The list is the record of what the room should contain.

instructionSections.heading: Working the list
instructionSections.body: Read the list in the order the room is laid out, not in the order items were used. For each item, check that it is present, counted, in good condition and within any expiry date. Replace anything damaged, expired or stained with approved stock. Keep clean items clean: handle glassware and mugs by the base or the rim, and keep tea and coffee materials sealed. Empty, clean and dry any container such as an ice bucket before refilling it from the approved supply. Tick each line only after the item is in place.

instructionSections.heading: Presenting the items
