instructionSections.body: Position matters, because guests look at a room in a fairly set way. Place stationery, the information folder and menus where a guest first looks for them. Set glassware and mugs where the list places them. Do not overfill a shelf, and do not hide items inside drawers unless the list says so. Items for use, such as toiletries and laundry bags, go where a guest can reach them without moving other things.

instructionSections.heading: Shortfalls and substitutions
instructionSections.body: If an item on the list is short, do not replace it with a similar item from another room or from a personal supply. Record the shortfall with the item name and the room, and tell the coordinator so that stock can be refilled. A substitution is only made where the list names an approved alternative. Food and drink items follow the property's food-handling rules for storage and presentation.

lessons.title: Odour and temperature checks
learningOutcomes: Describe what a neutral room smells like on entry and why a fragrance is not a fix.
Find and remove a likely odour source in a fixed order of checks.
Check the room temperature against the business's target and record the reading, or report the fault.

instructionSections.heading: Why air matters
instructionSections.body: Guests judge a room within moments of entering, and many notice the air before anything else. A room should smell neutral: not sharp from cleaning product, not heavy from air freshener, and free of the lingering smell of earlier occupants, cooking, smoke or pets. Air freshener does not solve an odour. It covers it for a short time, and the source remains. If a smell is still present after the room has been cleaned, it has a cause, and the cause needs to be found and dealt with.

instructionSections.heading: Finding the source
instructionSections.body: Work from the most likely source outwards. Check the bin and the floor beneath it, the bathroom drain and floor edges, the mini-fridge (empty, clean inside, door seal included), the wardrobe, the bedding and soft furnishings, and the carpet edges. Check any vent or fan grille you can reach. Open windows where the property and the weather allow, and let the air clear before the final check. Also check the surfaces you have just treated, because a product that has not been rinsed or allowed to dry can leave its own smell.

instructionSections.heading: Temperature
instructionSections.body: The room should feel comfortable for a guest on arrival. Check it against the single target the business sets for its rooms, using a thermometer or the property's own control, and do not rely on feel alone. The target comes from the business's written quality standard, and this lesson does not set a figure. If the room is outside the target, adjust the setting only if you are allowed to, or report it. Record the reading where the checklist asks for it.

instructionSections.heading: Why a fragrance is not a fix
instructionSections.body: Do not use a strong air freshener, spray or candle to cover an odour unless the business's approved product list allows it. Strong fragrance can cause complaints from guests with sensitivities, and a candle is a fire risk in an occupied room. A room that smells of nothing in particular is the aim. If you cannot find or remove a source, report it rather than hiding it.

lessons.title: Final room walk-through with a checklist
learningOutcomes: Walk a finished room in a fixed order, and tick each checklist item as it is checked.
Check the room from the guest's point of view, from the doorway and across the whole room.
Record or fix every item that does not pass, and raise it before the room is released.

instructionSections.heading: The purpose of the walk-through
instructionSections.body: The final walk-through checks the finished room the way a guest will first see it. It catches what the earlier stages missed: a dusting point that was skipped, a stray item, a light left on, a bed slightly out of square. It is not a repeat of every task. It is a structured look with a checklist, done once the work is finished and before the room is released. How the release itself is signed off is covered in “Timed guest-ready turnover and final property release”.

instructionSections.heading: Walking the room in a fixed order
instructionSections.body: Stand at the entrance and look at the room as a whole first. Then walk round in one direction: the entry and door, the window and curtains, the bed, the bedside table and lamp, the desk or table, the wardrobe and storage, the mini-fridge and kitchen area if present, the bathroom, and the floor last. Hold the checklist and tick each item as you reach it. Do not tick from memory, because memory is what the walk-through is meant to replace.

instructionSections.heading: What the checklist must cover
instructionSections.body: A walk-through checklist should cover, at minimum, what this group teaches: no items left by the previous guest; the bed made to standard; surfaces dusted and high-touch points disinfected; the bathroom checked for signs of the previous guest; the restock list complete; the floor finished; the odour and temperature recorded; windows, doors and lights secured or set as the property directs; and no damage left unreported. A business uses its own approved checklist, and this lesson does not replace it.

instructionSections.heading: Acting on a fault found
instructionSections.body: If a check fails, fix it if the fault is within your task and tools, and recheck the same item. If it cannot be fixed within your role or the time available, record it and tell the coordinator before the room is released. The walk-through does not end when the first fault is found. It ends when every item is either passed or recorded.

lessons.title: Reporting damage and maintenance faults
learningOutcomes: Separate faults that cleaning can fix from faults that must be reported.
Write a report that states what was found, where, how big, whether it is safe, and whether the room can be used.
Stop work and raise an urgent report when a fault creates a hazard.

instructionSections.heading: Why report rather than repair
instructionSections.body: A cleaner finds things that are not cleaning problems: a stain that will not lift from carpet, a torn mattress protector, a cracked tile, a loose fitting, a tap that drips, a window that will not lock. Unless the job and the cleaner's authority allow it, the task is to report these, not to repair them. Reporting early keeps the room available, protects the guest, and stops a small fault from being blamed on the cleaner later. A report made at the time, with a time stamp, is the record that protects everyone.

instructionSections.heading: What to report, and how
instructionSections.body: Report anything the room standard cannot fix with approved cleaning. The report should describe what you found, where it is, how big it is, whether it is safe, and whether the room can be used. Take a photo if the business requires one, and make sure it shows the fault clearly. Include the room number and the time. Use the business's reporting channel, whether that is a system, a form or a message to the coordinator, and keep the wording factual. Do not guess a cause, and do not describe what someone else must have done.

instructionSections.heading: Damage and lost property
instructionSections.body: Damage found after a guest has left is recorded in the same way as damage found before. Do not discuss blame or costs with guests or with on-site staff, and send questions about them to the coordinator. Items that appear to belong to a guest are handled under the property's lost property procedure, described in “Damage and lost property”. Cleaners do not keep, sell or dispose of them.

instructionSections.heading: Hazards and stopping work
instructionSections.body: If a fault creates a hazard, such as exposed wiring, a leak, broken glass or a loose ceiling fitting, keep others away from it, make the area safe only if this can be done without risk, and report at once. Do not stand on furniture or unstable items to reach a fault. Stop work on the affected item or area, and continue elsewhere only if the hazard does not reach the other work. Follow the business's emergency procedure for anything that is urgent.

lessons.title: Food contamination pathways and zoning
learningOutcomes: Distinguish biological, chemical, physical and allergen cross-contact risks in a kitchen.
Map raw-food, ready-to-eat, waste and wash-up zones before moving equipment.
Decide to stop or isolate when a contamination pathway appears.

instructionSections.heading: Why contamination is not only visible dirt
instructionSections.body: A kitchen can look clean and still carry contamination. Microorganisms, chemical residues, physical fragments, and allergens such as nuts or dairy can move from one surface to another on a cloth, a mop, a glove or a tool. A cleaner who is careless with a tool can carry raw-food residues across to a ready-to-eat bench in seconds. Contamination is therefore a question of pathways, not just of visible soil. The cleaner's job is to prevent transfer.

instructionSections.heading: Zoning the kitchen before you move equipment
instructionSections.body: Before you move any equipment or open any product, identify the zones: raw food handling, ready-to-eat preparation, waste, and wash-up. Confirm whether food preparation is under way, which surfaces are food-contact surfaces, and who approves release of an area back to use. Allocate tools to zones, carry contaminated tools in closed containers, and work in a sequence that moves from cleaner areas toward dirtier ones. Colour coding helps identify tools, but a colour is not a sanitising process, and a contaminated tool must be cleaned appropriately before reuse.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding when to stop
instructionSections.body: Stop and isolate the area when a tool or cloth has crossed from a raw-food zone to a ready-to-eat zone, when food is in an area being cleaned, or when you do not know what a residue is. Notify the food safety supervisor or the site contact and follow the site corrective-action procedure. Do not return the area to use on your own judgement, and do not claim food safety verification without authorised evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Handover and the limits of appearance
instructionSections.body: At handover, separate dirty equipment and failed work from the areas ready for use, and record the method, the observations, any exceptions, and who accepted or rejected the handover. A successful appearance is not enough to prove that a surface is sanitary. Sanitising, where required, and verification are separate steps set by the site's food safety plan. Your record shows what you did, and it lets the supervisor verify the outcome.

lessons.title: Chemicals, SDS, labels and food-contact compatibility
learningOutcomes: Verify product approval, dilution, contact time, rinsing and incompatible agents from the label and SDS.
Identify an unlabelled or unknown product and stop its use.
Keep chemicals separate from food and food-contact items during storage and use.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the product before using it
instructionSections.body: Every chemical in a kitchen must be traceable to its label and its safety data sheet. Before you use a product, read the original container label for the intended use, the dilution, the contact time, the rinsing requirement, and any food-contact statement. Then check the SDS and the site's chemical register, where the site keeps one. If you cannot confirm the product, you do not use it. An unidentified bottle is not a cleaning product until someone can name it and show its label.

instructionSections.heading: Storage, dispensing and labelling
instructionSections.body: Store chemicals below and apart from food, ingredients and food-contact items. Keep incompatible products apart, and never store a cleaning product near an open food container. Dispense only from the original container or from a labelled secondary container that carries the product name and hazard information as the site procedure requires. Never transfer a cleaning chemical into a food container, a drink bottle or any unlabelled vessel.

instructionSections.heading: Compatibility and mixing
instructionSections.body: Do not mix products to improve performance. Mixing can produce hazardous gases or reduce the effectiveness of the product. If a product is not suited to the surface or the food-contact condition, do not use it, and escalate for an approved alternative. Where a product is food-contact approved, use it only as its label and the site procedure direct.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping when something is unknown
instructionSections.body: When you find an unlabelled spray bottle beside uncovered food, quarantine the product, keep it away from the food, and prevent anyone from using it. Identify the source by asking the supervisor and checking the site's records, consult the SDS and the label where you can, and report the event under the site procedure. The supervisor decides whether the surrounding food or surfaces need to be discarded or re-cleaned. Your role is to isolate, identify and report.

lessons.title: Utensils, smallwares and dishwashing
learningOutcomes: Pre-remove soil and load utensils so that they wash effectively.
Inspect washed utensils for residual grease, food and damage.
Hold items from service and reprocess them when residue or a failed indicator is found.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing items for washing
instructionSections.body: Dishwashing works only when the items are prepared properly. Remove gross soil before loading, so that the wash water is not overloaded and the cycle is not used to do the scraping's work. Load items so that they are not nested, so that water and product can reach every surface. Keep smallwares apart from items that might damage them, and keep knives and sharp items in a safe position in the basket.

instructionSections.heading: Running the approved process
instructionSections.body: Use the site-approved wash and sanitise process. The manufacturer's instructions and the site procedure set the temperatures, the product dosing and the cycle selection. Do not change the cycle or the dosing to speed up the work. Check the operational indicators that the site procedure requires before you unload, and record the result.

instructionSections.heading: Inspecting the output
instructionSections.body: After unloading, inspect each item for residual grease, food, cloudiness or damage. A completed cycle does not prove that utensils are clean. A short cycle that leaves visible residue, or an indicator that shows a failure, means the items are held from service and reprocessed through the approved process. Investigate the loading and the process controls, because the cause may be overloading or a fault in the machine.

instructionSections.heading: Handover and records
instructionSections.body: Record which items were held, why they were held, and what was done to reprocess them. Do not return held items to service until the inspection is passed and the record is complete. A record that says a cycle was completed, when the items were not inspected, is a false record.

lessons.title: Benches, preparation surfaces and allergen cross-contact
learningOutcomes: Identify which allergens have been used on a surface and whether equipment is shared.
Clean a bench using the validated plan and dedicated tools.
Refuse to promise an allergen-free status and escalate any uncertain cross-contact.

instructionSections.heading: Why allergens need their own step
instructionSections.body: Allergens such as peanut, tree nut, dairy, egg, gluten and sesame are present in many foods, and very small amounts can cause a reaction in a sensitive person. A bench that has been used for peanut preparation can carry peanut residue even when it looks clean. Allergen control therefore depends on a validated cleaning plan, dedicated tools where the plan requires them, and a verification step that the site owns. A visually clean bench does not show whether an allergen has been removed.

instructionSections.heading: Before cleaning
instructionSections.body: Confirm which allergens were used on the surface, whether the equipment is shared with other preparation, and who owns the allergen verification. Find the site's validated allergen cleaning procedure and the tools assigned to it. Do not use a general-purpose cloth on an allergen-controlled bench unless the procedure allows it.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning and handover
instructionSections.body: Remove visible debris first. Clean the surface following the validated plan, using dedicated tools where the plan requires them. Then request the verification and the release decision from the person who owns the allergen control. Record the handover as a clean zone only once the approved release has been given. Do not describe the bench as allergen-free in your own words.

instructionSections.heading: Escalation
instructionSections.body: If you are uncertain whether a cross-contact has occurred, or whether the validated plan was followed, stop and escalate to the food safety supervisor before the bench is used for an allergen-controlled order. An uncertain allergen condition is not a judgement to make alone.

lessons.title: Grease, extraction and hot kitchen hazards
learningOutcomes: Identify hot surfaces, sharp sheet metal, slippery grease and fire-risk build-up near cooking equipment.
Decide which extraction and hood components are within an accessible external-clean scope.
Stop and escalate for internal ductwork, fire suppression or interlocked equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising the hazards
instructionSections.body: Kitchen extraction and cooking equipment combines heat, grease and moving parts. Surfaces near ovens, fryers and cooktops can stay hot for a long time after the equipment is switched off. Sheet metal in hoods and filters has sharp edges. Grease that has built up on hoods, filters and ductwork is slippery underfoot and can be a fire risk when it reaches heat. Before you touch equipment, check that it is cool, switched off and secured, and that the work is within your authorised scope.

instructionSections.heading: The accessible external clean
instructionSections.body: Where the site authorises it, a cleaner may clean accessible external surfaces of a range hood and the removable grease filters, using an approved degreaser. Confirm the equipment is cool and that controls are locked out or switched off as the procedure requires. Assess the chemical compatibility of the product with the metal finish and any coating. Keep water and product away from electrical controls and lights. Work with the filter removed on a safe surface, not balanced on a hot hob.

instructionSections.heading: The limits of the job
instructionSections.body: Internal duct cleaning and complex extraction systems are not routine work for a general cleaner. Do not enter or scrape powered ductwork, do not defeat fire suppression or interlocks, and do not remove access panels that the procedure does not allow you to remove. Where the system is complex, the work is referred to a competent specialist. This lesson does not grant any such licence or authority.

instructionSections.heading: Escalating grease that could start a fire
instructionSections.body: Escalate immediately where grease build-up appears to be an imminent fire concern, such as thick grease in a duct or near an open flame, or where you notice damaged fire suppression components. Do not attempt to clear it yourself. Notify the supervisor and the site contact, keep people away from the equipment, and record what you saw with the time and location.

lessons.title: Cold rooms, refrigerators and drainage
learningOutcomes: Plan a cold-room or refrigerator clean that does not disrupt food temperature control.
Clean reachable surfaces without blocking drains or contaminating stored goods.
Stop and escalate before disconnecting equipment that holds high-risk food.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting the food first
instructionSections.body: A cold room or refrigerator holds food under temperature control, and the cleaner's task must not interrupt that control. Before you move food or switch off any cold storage, coordinate with the site management, who confirm the temporary storage arrangements and who is responsible for monitoring temperatures. A cleaner does not have the authority to shut down refrigeration or to move high-risk food on their own decision.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning reachable surfaces
instructionSections.body: Clean the reachable interior surfaces, shelves, door seals and handles according to the approved procedure. Keep water and product away from stored goods, and do not let water run into drains in a way that contaminates food or blocks the drain. Report damaged seals, leaks, odours and blocked drains to the supervisor. Never perform restricted refrigeration servicing, such as work on the refrigerant circuit or the electrical controls.

instructionSections.heading: When the unit must be switched off
instructionSections.body: Do not disconnect a refrigerator holding high-risk food without a validated temperature-control plan. Where the plan exists, the site manager confirms the temperature monitoring, the temporary storage and the time limits before the power is interrupted. Record the temperature before and after the work, and record who approved the interruption.

lessons.title: Floors, spills, waste and pest signs
learningOutcomes: Plan waste removal routes that avoid crossing ready-to-eat preparation spaces.
Control slip hazards on wet kitchen floors during and after cleaning.
Report pest evidence and broken glass for authorised response without disturbing them.

instructionSections.heading: Waste routes and containers
instructionSections.body: Waste is a contamination pathway. Remove it on agreed routes, using sealed or suitable containers, and avoid crossing ready-to-eat preparation spaces with it. When bins overflow near a preparation line, the first step is to separate the clean and dirty traffic and restrict access to the area, rather than carrying the waste through the work zone. Ask the supervisor which route and which container the site requires.

instructionSections.heading: Wet floors and slip control
instructionSections.body: Kitchen floors become slippery with grease and water. Keep wet floors barricaded until they are safe to walk on, and do not reopen a wet traffic zone while the slip hazard persists. Use the site's floor-cleaning method, and dry the surface where the procedure requires it. Do not sweep contamination into food areas, and do not allow mop water to reach food or equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Pests and sharp debris
instructionSections.body: Report pest activity, droppings and any evidence of pests to the supervisor for an authorised response. Do not apply pesticide yourself, because pest control products are used under their own rules and by authorised people. Broken glass and contaminated materials are reported for an authorised response before you clean them up, unless the site procedure says you can do so safely with the right tools.

instructionSections.heading: Clean after assessment
instructionSections.body: Clean the affected surface only after the hazard has been assessed and the site has authorised the cleaning. Record what was found, who was told, and the time, so that the site can track recurring pest evidence and trace the cause.

lessons.title: Cleaning schedules and verification records
learningOutcomes: Record each planned cleaning control with item, area, method, responsible worker, time and result.
Identify a false or prefilled sanitising record as a control failure.
Record unsuccessful results and corrective action instead of signing them off.

instructionSections.heading: What a verification record is for
instructionSections.body: A cleaning schedule lists the controls that the site relies on. A verification record shows that each control was carried out and checked. For each planned control, the record should show the item, the area, the method, the worker responsible, the date and time, the observations, any exceptions, and the verification result. The record is useful only if it is true. A record that shows work that was not done gives the site false confidence, and it removes the chance to correct the problem.

instructionSections.heading: Who signs
instructionSections.body: The person who signs a record must have observed the work or reliably verified it. A supervisor who asks a cleaner to sign off a sanitising check they have not performed is asking for a false record. Refuse the sign-off, document the real result, and state who must verify the control. Where a control has failed, the failure is recorded as a failure, with the corrective action and the person informed.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping records
instructionSections.body: Maintain records under the location's retention policy, and keep them accessible for the people who need them. Do not pre-fill entries. Do not alter a record after the fact without a clear note of the change, who made it, and why. Honest records, including records of failures, are what let a site improve.

lessons.title: Chemical competency: reading labels and safety data sheets
learningOutcomes: Read a product label and state the hazard, dilution, protective equipment and first aid directions before first use.
Find and interpret the safety data sheet for a named product in the site record.
Dilute and apply a product to its label directions, water first, without combining it with any other product.
Store and dispose of used and unused product so that customers, colleagues and property are not exposed.
Stop work and escalate when a product has no label, no safety data sheet or unknown contents.

instructionSections.heading: Why chemical competency comes first
instructionSections.body: Chemical competency means knowing what a product does, how strong it is, what it can damage, and what happens when it meets another product. Most avoidable chemical incidents in cleaning come from three habits: mixing products to get a stronger result, using a product from a container nobody can identify, and skipping gloves for what seems a small job. Every later method in this set, including mopping, buffing, washing and washroom cleaning, depends on handling products correctly. Before you open any product, you should be able to say what it is, how it is applied, and what to do if it reaches skin or eyes.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the label and the safety data sheet
instructionSections.body: The manufacturer label is the first document to read. Check the product name, hazard warnings, directions for use and dilution, protective equipment, first aid and storage directions. The detailed document is the safety data sheet, or SDS. The source material for this lesson uses the term COSHH data sheet, which belongs to a UK framework; on Australian jobs use the term SDS. Under the national model work health and safety approach, a business keeps a hazardous chemicals register, and the register must be kept up to date and readily accessible with a current SDS for each listed chemical. State and territory regulators confirm how that position is adopted, so check your own jurisdiction. The SDS sections you will use most are hazard identification, first aid, handling and storage, and personal protection. If a label is missing, faded or torn, do not use the product.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the site before the first use
instructionSections.body: Before using any product, check the site binder or digital record for a risk assessment and an SDS for that exact product. If either is missing, stop and ask your supervisor before you use it. This rule applies even to products that look familiar, because similar bottles can hold different concentrations. Customer-supplied products are used only if the business has approved them and their SDS is on file. Confirm the approval rule in your business procedure before you accept a customer's product.

instructionSections.heading: Diluting and applying correctly
instructionSections.body: Fill the bucket with water first, then add the measured product. Adding the product first causes foaming, and a splash from a bucket that is already diluted is less concentrated than one that is not. Measure to the label and do not estimate. Never combine two products, including two products from the same range, and never add anything other than water to a dilution unless the label directs it. Replace the lid straight after use, and keep trigger sprays switched to off when they are not in use. The label check does not end when the bottle is open: read the dilution again each time you prepare a new bucket.

instructionSections.heading: Protective equipment, ventilation and disposal
instructionSections.body: Wear gloves whenever you handle a cleaning product. The source states that gloves are issued to every employee and worn at all times with chemicals. Add eye protection when the label or SDS warns of splashing, and when you are diluting a concentrate. Open windows or doors where possible so fumes disperse, and treat ventilation as part of the duty of care for your own team and the customer. Spent solution goes to a sluice or other designated disposal point. Never pour product into a kitchen sink or a toilet bowl. Dispose of unused product so that a customer, child or pet cannot reach it.

lessons.title: Safe use and care of electrical machines
learningOutcomes: Complete a pre-use safety check on an electrical machine, covering its test label, plug, flex and casing.
Connect and disconnect a machine using the socket-switch sequence.
Route the flex so it cannot be run over, caught or damaged while the machine is operating.
Tag a faulty machine, remove it from service and report it.
Explain why repairs to fixed wiring or to a machine's internal parts are outside a cleaner's role.

instructionSections.heading: Why electrical equipment needs a routine check
instructionSections.body: Electrical cleaning machines combine water, moving parts and long cables, and each of these creates a route to injury. Faults usually start small: a nicked flex, a cracked plug, or a filter packed with fine dust that makes a motor run hot. The source sets a pre-use routine and a rule that only trained people operate electrical equipment. Your part is to look, feel and listen before the machine is switched on, and to stop the moment something is wrong. The checks are short, but a fault that was missed in a two-minute check can become a shock in the middle of a job.

instructionSections.heading: Test labels and the pre-use check
instructionSections.body: Each machine should carry a label showing when it was last tested and when the next test is due. The source calls this a PAT test. Read the date on the label first. Then run your hand along the flex from the plug to the machine, looking for cuts, flattened sections, bare wires, or electrical tape standing in for a repair. Check the plug and pins for scorch marks, bent pins or cracks. Look at the casing for cracks, and check the bag or filter, because a blocked filter can make the machine overheat. The source requires a register listing all machines, so record the check.

instructionSections.heading: Connecting, running and disconnecting
instructionSections.body: Before you plug in, make sure the socket switch is off. Plug in, then switch on. When you have finished, switch the socket off before you unplug the machine from the wall. Keep the flex behind you while you work, so you are never walking over it or dragging it through a wet area. Where a flex must cross a walkway, make the crossing safe with a cable cover or a clear route, and let the supervisor know. Check that the building has a protective device, such as a circuit breaker or safety switch, that cuts supply if a fault occurs. The source states that circuit breakers are expected to be fitted.

instructionSections.heading: Faults, storage and who fixes what
instructionSections.body: A machine with a fault is not used. Tag it as faulty, remove it from service, and report it to your line manager. Do not tape over damaged flex, and do not open a casing to look inside. Repairs go to an approved contractor, as the source requires for checking and repair. Store machines upright, with the cable loosely coiled and not trailing. Wet or dusty machines are dried and wiped down before they are put away. Work on fixed wiring, power points or building circuits is licensed electrical work and is outside this lesson; the licence notice in this lesson explains the boundary.

instructionSections.heading: Protective equipment and ventilation
instructionSections.body: Wear gloves and full enclosed shoes when you use electrical equipment, because the source identifies hand and foot injury as the risk. Gloves are also worn when you handle bags and filters. Add eye protection when dust or product spray is present. Open windows or doors where possible, so that any fumes from products used with the machine do not build up around you or the customer.

lessons.title: Storing equipment, chemicals and consumables
learningOutcomes: Wash, dry and position mops, buckets, cloths and dust pans so they are ready for the next job and do not hold stagnant water.
Apply the colour system so that equipment from one zone never moves into another.
Store heavy chemical containers at a safe height and position, labelled and closed.
Rotate stock so older product is used first.
Keep fire exits and walkways clear of stored items.

instructionSections.heading: What the storage area is for
instructionSections.body: The store is where equipment, chemicals and consumables spend most of their time, and it is where many incidents begin: a leaking container on a shelf, a mop left in a bucket for days, or a fire exit blocked by a stack of cartons. A clean, tidy and odour-free store reduces accidents, extends the life of equipment, and keeps clean areas separate from dirty ones. The source states that the store must be free of smells and clutter, and that rubbish is removed from it.

instructionSections.heading: Washing and drying equipment
instructionSections.body: Wash mops, buckets and cloths after each use. Hang mop heads head up so they dry without holding stagnant water. Store buckets upside down with cloths hung over the top to air-dry. Wash and dry dust pans, and store them in their colour group. Buffing pads are washed and hung to dry, and buffers are not stored with a pad or base plate still fitted. Gloves used for washroom work are washed and kept in their own colour group.

instructionSections.heading: Colour coding as a control
instructionSections.body: Colour coding separates equipment by zone so that a cloth used on a toilet never travels to a kitchen or office surface. The source gives the example of all red cloths stored together and all blue buckets together. The colour-to-zone map is set by your business, so use the map it gives you rather than a guess. Keep each colour in its own place and check the groupings at every restock.

instructionSections.heading: Chemical storage rules
instructionSections.body: Store heavy containers on the floor or below chest height, slightly away from walls, following the label and safety data sheet. Keep the products you use most within easy reach, and rotate stock so older containers are used first. Every container is labelled and has its lid securely fitted or its trigger switched off. Fire exits are kept clear at all times. Store a product only where its SDS is on file, as set out in “Chemical competency: reading labels and safety data sheets”.

instructionSections.heading: Protective clothing and the end-of-shift check
instructionSections.body: Wear the protective clothing your business requires when you handle chemicals, machines or consumables in the store. At the end of the shift, confirm the store is clear of rubbish, the colour groups are correct, the chemicals are in their positions and fire exits are open. Record any defect you cannot fix, so the next person knows about it.

lessons.title: Mop sweeping hard floors
learningOutcomes: Check a vacuum, dust pan and sweep mop head before use, including the vacuum's test label.
Sweep a floor edge first, then in figure-of-eight passes, without raising a dust cloud.
Remove chewing gum and sticky matter before sweeping, so the mop head is not contaminated.
Clean and store the mop head, dust pan and vacuum according to the colour system.
Stop and escalate when the floor is wet, slippery or contains an unidentified substance.

instructionSections.heading: What dry mop sweeping does and does not do
instructionSections.body: Dry mop sweeping lifts loose dust, grit and small debris from a floor without water. It is quick, and it suits large open areas and the first pass of a floor job. It works only while the mop head is clean and in full contact with the floor. Once a mop head is wet, greasy or full of debris, it spreads dirt instead of collecting it. Dry sweeping does not remove grease, marks or residue, which need a wet method under the approved procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing before the first stroke
instructionSections.body: Check the vacuum you will use afterwards. Confirm its test label is valid, the plug is intact, the flex has no bare wires or tape, the bag is not full and the filter is clear. Use a clean mop head and a colour-coded dust pan and brush. Put on gloves before you touch the mop head, pick up large rubbish or check the vacuum bag and filter, because the source notes that chewing gum and rubbish can carry bacteria. Look at the floor for chewing gum and sticky patches first. Scrape gum up with a suitable tool into a refuse bag. A sticky mop head does not sweep effectively.

instructionSections.heading: The sweeping pattern
instructionSections.body: Start at the outside edges of the area and work along the walls so that dirt collects toward the middle. Then move to the point furthest from the door and sweep in figure-of-eight passes, working back toward the exit. Keep the mop head in contact with the floor, so dust is held rather than lifted into the air. Pause halfway through to check the mop head, and vacuum it if it is loaded. When the sweep is finished, vacuum the mop head and the floor around the area where it rested.

instructionSections.heading: Floor condition and safety while sweeping
instructionSections.body: A dry sweep should end with a floor that is free of debris, clean and dry, and not slippery. Do not sweep over a wet patch as though it were dry, because the mop will fail and the patch becomes a slip hazard. Sign-post any wet area, and make any trailing cable or open socket safe before you sweep near it. Take extra care when staff are still on the premises: keep the work area separated from people and do not sweep through them.

instructionSections.heading: After the sweep
instructionSections.body: Store mop heads head up in a holder, because heads stored face down collect dirt. Wash and dry dust pans, and store them by colour. Safety check and damp wipe the vacuum after use. Dispose of collected refuse in the designated waste area, and log any floor defect or hazard you found.

lessons.title: Single-solution wet mopping
learningOutcomes: Prepare one diluted solution to the product label directions, water first, and mark the bucket.
Mop in manageable sections, edges first, working from the far point toward the door.
Remove overspill from skirting boards with a clean damp cloth before the floor is mopped.
Wring the mop without tipping the bucket, and keep the bucket behind you at all times.
Confirm the floor surface type before choosing a method, and leave the floor dry and free of slip risk before removing signs.

instructionSections.heading: Why one solution and one method
instructionSections.body: Single-solution mopping uses one diluted product in one bucket. That keeps the method simple and reduces the chance of mixing products. It is a wet method, so the risks are slips, over-wetting and damage to floors that cannot take water. Good mopping is planned before the bucket is filled: the surface type, the level of soil, the area to be done in one go, and how long the floor needs to dry.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing the solution
instructionSections.body: Fill the bucket with water first, then add the product at the dilution the label or the approved procedure gives. Do not add a second product, and do not pour product into a bucket of mop water without measuring it. Mark the bucket with the product and the time it was made, so the team knows what is in it. Check that the mop and cloths are washed and clean before you start. Confirm the floor surface type from the approved procedure before you choose the method, because not every floor takes a wet mop.

instructionSections.heading: Mopping technique
instructionSections.body: Work in a section you can reach comfortably, because over-stretching is a manual handling risk and produces uneven results. Keep the bucket behind you so you never step through the mop water. Start at the outside edges of the room and wipe overspill off the skirting boards with a clean damp cloth. Use a scouring pad only for stubborn marks, and only on a surface that is not polished, as the approved procedure directs. Then mop the middle of the room, working from the point furthest from the door toward the door, and rinse the mop often so that you are not spreading dirty water.

instructionSections.heading: Wringing, drying and finishing
instructionSections.body: Wring the mop out over the bucket, with the bucket held between your feet so that it cannot tip and pour water across the floor. Change the mop water when it looks dirty. Leave the area signposted until the floor is fully dry. Remove warning signs and close ventilation only once the floor is dry, because a damp floor is still a slip hazard. A floor that dries quickly means customers are less likely to slip.

instructionSections.heading: Storage after the job
instructionSections.body: Mop heads go head up to air-dry. Buckets are washed and stored upside down with cloths hung over the top. Keep the whole set in its colour group, so that the mop used on floors is never used on a washroom or kitchen surface.

lessons.title: Floor buffing with a rotary machine
learningOutcomes: Complete the electrical pre-use check and the pad check before buffing starts.
Select a buffing pad by colour, using the manufacturer's colour guide and the task.
Buff the edges first, then the middle, with the cable kept behind the operator.
Stop, unplug and check the pad halfway through the task.
Store the buffer and pads correctly after use.

instructionSections.heading: What buffing does and the risks it carries
instructionSections.body: Buffing uses a rotating machine and a pad to work the surface of a floor. It restores sheen and removes light build-up. The machine is heavy, spins quickly and draws a cable across the work area. Hands and feet are exposed to pads, base plates and any product used on the floor. The source states that only trained employees use electrical equipment, and the operator must be able to stop the machine at once. A trained operator treats the machine as a live hazard from the moment it is connected.

instructionSections.heading: Pad selection and condition
instructionSections.body: Pads are colour coded. The source notes that the darker the pad, the more abrasive it is. Choose the pad that the manufacturer's colour guide and the job specification call for, and do not choose by feel. Check the pad before you start, and turn or replace it when it is dirty or worn. Do not store the buffer with the pad and base plate still fitted.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical pre-use checks and the cable
instructionSections.body: The pre-use checks match “Safe use and care of electrical machines”: a valid test label, an intact plug, no bare wires or tape on the flex, and a safe socket. Keep the cable behind the machine at all times, so the pad never runs over it. Before you plug in, make sure the socket is switched off, and switch it off again before you unplug.

instructionSections.heading: Buffing sequence and pauses
instructionSections.body: Buff the outside edges of the room first, then the middle, starting from the point furthest from the exit and working back toward it. Halfway through, stop, unplug the machine and check the pad. Turn or replace the pad if it is dirty. After buffing, mop sweep the debris that has been pushed out from under the skirting boards. Before you leave, confirm the floor is clean, dry and not slippery, and that any wet area is signposted.

instructionSections.heading: Care after use
instructionSections.body: Safety check and damp wipe the buffer after each use. Wash the buffing pads and hang them to dry. Store the buffer upright in the position the manufacturer gives, with the pad off. Clean, well-maintained machines last longer and give a more consistent result, which the source ties to better service for the customer.

lessons.title: Suction (vacuum) cleaning of floors and carpets
learningOutcomes: Complete the pre-use check on a vacuum, covering the bag, filter, hose and beater bar height.
Remove large debris by hand, wearing gloves, before vacuuming.
Vacuum the edges first, then the middle in overlapping passes, working back toward the exit.
Work busy traffic areas with the pile and then against it, to lift the pile.
Keep barrier mats clean at the surface, at the edges and in the mat well.
Empty, clean and store the vacuum and tools after use.

instructionSections.heading: Why vacuuming needs its own checks
instructionSections.body: A vacuum combines electricity, moving air and a hose that can block. A blocked filter makes the motor overheat, and a beater bar set at the wrong height leaves carpet pile uneven or fails to lift dirt. A vacuum is also a dust generator, so the way it is used, and the condition of its bag and filter, matter for the people who breathe the air afterwards. The source treats vacuum checks as part of the electrical equipment routine, and requires that only trained employees use electrical equipment.

instructionSections.heading: The pre-use check
instructionSections.body: Check the test label, the plug, and the flex for damage, bare wires and tape. Check the bag and filter: a full bag or a blocked filter reduces suction and causes overheating. Look through the hose for any blockage, and clear it with the correct tool rather than with your hand. Set the beater bar height for the carpet pile or floor you are working on. Record what you found.

instructionSections.heading: Clearing debris and managing the cable
instructionSections.body: Put on gloves before you pick anything up. Remove large items by hand and place them in a bin bag. Run the cable behind you, so you cannot trip over it or catch the vacuum on it. Connect only after the socket is switched off, and switch the socket off before you unplug. Wear gloves and eye protection when you handle the bag and filter, because dust and bacteria are present.

instructionSections.heading: Vacuum pattern and busy areas
instructionSections.body: Vacuum the outside edges of the room first, then work the middle in overlapping passes, moving back toward the exit. In doorways and other busy traffic areas, vacuum with the pile and then against it, which lifts the pile and draws out dirt that a single pass leaves behind. Once the floor is complete, check the edges for any build-up of dirt.

instructionSections.heading: Barrier mats and care after use
instructionSections.body: Where barrier mats are fitted, fixed or leased, they are kept clean: no dirt on the surface, around the edges, or underneath in the mat well. This applies only where barrier mats are fitted. After use, switch off the socket, unplug, safety check and damp wipe the vacuum, and dispose of the rubbish. Clean the dust pan and brush, and store them by colour.

lessons.title: Wall washing
learningOutcomes: Cover every electrical socket and switch with masking tape before the wall is wet.
Dust the wall from the bottom up, including the skirting board, before washing.
Apply product to the cloth rather than the wall, and wash bottom to top in figure-of-eight passes.
Rinse and remove product from top to bottom, so that no run marks are left.
Recognise when a wall is out of safe reach and stop for suitable access equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Why walls need a fixed method
instructionSections.body: Walls collect dust, fingerprints and splashes, and the build-up is usually heaviest in a band near the floor. Done carelessly, wall washing leaves run marks, lets liquid reach electrical fittings, and sprays product onto furniture and the customer. A fixed sequence (protect, dust, apply, wash, rinse, check) keeps the wall, the fittings and the people nearby safe. The source emphasises that the customer's property should not be damaged, and that neither the property nor the customer should be sprayed with chemicals.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting the wall, the floor and the fittings
instructionSections.body: Before any product touches the wall, cover every electrical socket and switch with masking tape, working from the bottom up. Place plastic sheeting under the bucket to protect carpet or flooring. Move furniture where you can, and get the client's agreement for anything that cannot be moved. When the work is finished, remove the tape with dry hands only, because wet hands near a socket are an electrical hazard.

instructionSections.heading: Dusting, applying and washing
instructionSections.body: Dust the wall from the bottom up, including the skirting board, to remove loose material before any liquid is used. Apply the diluted product to your cloth rather than spraying the wall, because spray causes overspray onto people and nearby items. Wash in figure-of-eight passes from the bottom of the wall to the top. The lower band is usually dirtier and needs longer contact time, so reapply product to the cloth where the lower band needs it.

instructionSections.heading: Rinsing and checking the result
instructionSections.body: Remove the product with clean water and a clean cloth, working from top to bottom in figure-of-eight passes, so that drips run into areas you have already rinsed. Rinse the cloth often. A finished wall has no run marks, and the skirting board is clean and free of dust. Check each section of wall in good light before you move on.

instructionSections.heading: Walls out of safe reach
instructionSections.body: If a wall is higher than you can reach safely from the floor, stop. Do not stretch, lean or stand on furniture. Use suitable access equipment in line with the site's work-at-height rules, or arrange another method with the supervisor. This lesson does not cover height work. The window and exterior lessons carry their own rules for that work.

lessons.title: Dusting, damp wiping, washing and polishing furniture and surfaces
learningOutcomes: Fold and turn a duster so every part of the cloth is used and dirt is not spread.
Dust a surface from the edges inward, and dust the legs and sides from top to bottom.
Damp wipe or wash furniture with a cloth loaded with product, not with product sprayed onto the surface.
Apply polish to a dry surface using a cloth, and buff the treated areas to a high sheen.
Respect clear-desk limits by cleaning only clear areas and never moving or removing a client's papers.

instructionSections.heading: What these tasks have in common
instructionSections.body: Dusting, damp wiping, washing and polishing are the everyday surface tasks in most cleaning jobs. They look simple, which is why shortcuts creep in. The method is the same across all four: work from the edges inward, keep cloths clean, keep product off the air as far as possible, and finish with a surface that is clean, dry and free of smears. The source covers desks, furniture, glazed items, telephones and display furniture, and sets out the same care for each.

instructionSections.heading: Dusting
instructionSections.body: Fold the duster into thirds, then into thirds again, so that all of the face is used. Turn the cloth whenever it starts to clog. Dust the surface from the outside edges first, then the middle, using overlapping figure-of-eight passes. Dust the legs and sides from top to bottom, so that loosened dirt falls onto surfaces you have not yet cleaned. The aim is to remove dust, not to move it to the next surface.

instructionSections.heading: Desks, papers and glazed items
instructionSections.body: Clean only the clear areas of a desk. Do not move, remove, or read papers, and do not lift personal items to clean underneath them. Where a client runs a clear-desk routine, do not assume the desk is ready; ask the supervisor. Telephones are cleaned and sanitised as required, using a product approved for the surface. Glazed items, including framed pictures, mirrors, glazed noticeboards, display cases and bookcases, are cleaned using the glass method your business uses, and the cleaner must not allow product to run into the frame or onto the wall behind.

instructionSections.heading: Damp wiping, washing and polishing
instructionSections.body: Damp wiping and washing use a cloth loaded with diluted product. Do not spray the surface, because overspray reaches people and nearby items. Wipe the edges of the furniture first, then the middle, and do the legs and sides from bottom to top with product. Remove the product with a clean cloth and clean water, from the edges to the middle, and wipe the legs and sides from top to bottom. For polishing, the surface must be completely dry. Spray polish onto a clean duster rather than onto the surface, apply it to the outside edges first, then the middle, then the sides and legs, and buff all treated areas to a high sheen. Never sniff a duster to check whether it has polish on it.

instructionSections.heading: Blinds, curtains and care after use
instructionSections.body: Blinds and curtains are cleaned by the method that suits the material: washed where the material is washable, and aired or dry cleaned where appropriate. Where curtains are removed for cleaning at an approved premises, they must be replaced until they are returned. Curtain cleaning and blind-cleaning frequency are agreed with the client and recorded in the job system. After use, wash buckets, cloths and dusters thoroughly, hang the cloths to dry, store the bucket upside down, and keep the colour system.

lessons.title: Cleaning toilets, wash basins, urinals and washrooms
learningOutcomes: Set up a washroom safely with a cleaning-in-progress sign, ventilation and colour-coded equipment.
Protect yourself from infection by covering cuts, wearing gloves throughout and washing hands at the end.
Clean in the order dirty areas first, then clean areas, with washroom cloths and brushes kept for washroom use only.
Remove chewing gum and waste from urinals and toilets before cleaning them.
Restock consumables, report faulty fixtures and judge the finished washroom against the stated standard.

instructionSections.heading: Why washrooms need the strictest routine
instructionSections.body: Washrooms carry some of the highest concentrations of germs in most buildings, and cleaners work close to them. The rule in the source is that equipment and materials used here are never used outside the washroom. That rule stops germs moving into kitchens and office surfaces. The task also happens in a space that customers may be using, so the cleaner must be courteous, careful and visible. The source names a hygiene areas standard from the British Institute of Cleaning Sciences framework.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up and protecting yourself
instructionSections.body: Put a cleaning-in-progress sign on the door so that customers know the washroom is being serviced. Where the washroom is shared, follow your workplace rules on who may enter and when. Check your hands for open cuts before you put gloves on, and cover any cut with a waterproof plaster. Gloves are worn for the whole task. Eye protection is used when splash or spray is possible. Open windows or doors where possible, and make sure no chemical fumes are present in the area while you work.

instructionSections.heading: The cleaning order
instructionSections.body: Turn off the urinal water supply if you can. Empty all bins, and use a litter picker to remove chewing gum and waste from the urinals. Flush the toilet with the lid down to reduce splash, and push the water past the U-bend with the brush. Apply toilet cleaner to the urinal and the toilet. Disinfect the dirty areas first: the door locks, the toilet roll holder, the base and flush of the toilet, the tiles around it, the cistern, the seat and lid, and the brush holder. Then do the outside of the urinal, its tiles and the floor around it. Clean the clean areas next, from the sink, taps and tiles to the soap dispenser, the dryer or towel dispenser, and the exit handle. Use the cloth colour your business has assigned to washroom clean-up areas, and rinse the cloth often. Use a separate colour for the toilet and urinal rinse work, and never use either set outside the washroom. Scrub the inside of the toilet with the toilet brush, flush with the lid down, and scrub the urinal with the brush or a scouring pad before rinsing it.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing the washroom
instructionSections.body: Turn the urinal water back on. Restock toilet roll, soap and paper towels. Clean the mirrors. Mop the floor using the single-solution method in “Single-solution wet mopping”. Take off your gloves, wash your hands, and replace any plaster you are wearing. Report any broken seat, fixture or fitting. Remove waste according to the customer's disposal guidelines. Do not leave any product within reach of a customer.

instructionSections.heading: The washroom standard
instructionSections.body: A finished washroom meets the following standard. Walls, doors and cubicle partitions are washed with a disinfectant on a regular schedule. Towel holders and dispensers are clean, dry and free of dust and marks, with clean towels fitted. The outside of hand dryers is clean, dry and free of smears. Sanitary ware, including sinks, basins, baths, WC bowls, seats, covers, taps, outlets, plugs, urinals, brushes, toilet roll holders and tiled surfaces, is free of scum, grease, hair, scale, dust, soil, spillage and removable stains. Soap dispensers are filled, working, with clean nozzles and clean external surfaces, and bar soap is replaced when needed. Supplies are stocked at all times. Mirrors are free of smears.

lessons.title: Spray buffing with a rotary machine
learningOutcomes: Complete the electrical and pad pre-use checks for a spray buffer and record the results.
Select a pad by colour, using the manufacturer's guide and the task.
Use gloves, eye protection and ventilation when a spray buffing product is in use.
Connect and disconnect a spray buffer using the socket-switch sequence.
Stop, tag and report a faulty spray buffer.

instructionSections.heading: What spray buffing is, and what this version covers
instructionSections.body: Spray buffing combines a rotary machine, a pad and a light application of product to bring up the shine on a floor surface. It uses the same electrical equipment and chemical rules as floor buffing, and the source treats it as a separate procedure because of the product and the finish. This lesson covers the full procedure from the source: the equipment checks, pad selection, personal protection, ventilation, the connection sequence and the service sequence. Follow the steps in order, and check any product against its label and the manufacturer directions.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical and pad checks
instructionSections.body: Only trained employees use electrical equipment. Check the test label before use, and confirm that the plug, the flex and the casing are intact, with no bare wires or tape. Keep a register of machines. Select the pad by colour for the task, using the manufacturer's guide, because the darker the pad, the more abrasive it is. At the end of the task, repeat the safety checks, so that any damage caused during use is found.

instructionSections.heading: Products, protective equipment and ventilation
instructionSections.body: Wash and check all equipment before use, so that products are not mixed by accident. Wear gloves at all times when you use chemicals or handle pads and base plates. Wear goggles, because your hands and eyes can be exposed to product and dust. Open windows or doors where possible, so that people nearby are not breathing fumes. Keep customers away from the work area, and sign-post it.

instructionSections.heading: Connection sequence and service method
instructionSections.body: Before you plug the machine in, switch the socket off. When you unplug, switch the socket off before you remove the plug from the wall. The service sequence for spray buffing, including how product is applied, the order of passes, and any drying or rinsing step, is not yet written from the source. Until the sequence is approved, follow the written spray-buffing procedure your business supplies.

lessons.title: Window cleaning from the ground and with extension equipment
learningOutcomes: Set up a window-cleaning area with barriers and warning signs before any glass is wet.
Wear the gloves and eye protection required for window work, and explain why each is needed.
Apply a diluted cleaning solution with a ferret or dolly, allow contact time, and remove it with overlapping figure-of-eight passes.
Use extension equipment for glazing that cannot be reached from the ground, and apply the stop-work rule when it cannot be reached safely.
Inspect finished glass, frames and ledges for smears, runs and standing water, and correct them.
Wash, dry, colour-code and store window equipment so that clean and dirty equipment never mix.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson and what it does not grant
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches the ground-level method for internal and external glazing, and the method for glazing you can reach safely with extension equipment. The scope of work for each site decides which glazing is included. Where the work includes internal and external glass, the cleaner cleans both in line with the site's scope. Work that needs a ladder, a platform, a rope or any other form of height access is not covered by this method, and the lesson does not give you the authority or the training to do it. Completing this lesson does not make you licensed or authorised for height work of any kind.

instructionSections.heading: Protective clothing and equipment
instructionSections.body: Gloves and goggles are worn for window cleaning every time. Glass cleaning solutions, dust and bacteria on frames and sills can reach the skin and the eyes during wiping and during the rinse, so both must be covered. Before you start, check and wash every piece of equipment: buckets, cloths, ferrets, blades and extension poles. Wash them so that two products are never mixed by accident, because mixed chemicals can give off fumes that could be breathed in. Well-kept equipment lasts longer, and it gives the customer a better result. Confirm each chemical has its manufacturer's label displayed and that you know its dilution before you open it.

instructionSections.heading: Access, barriers and ventilation
instructionSections.body: Before you wet any glass, set out a barrier around the area where you are working, and display warning signs where people will see them. The barrier stops pedestrians and customers from walking under or through the work. Open windows or doors where possible, so that you and your colleagues are not standing in fumes. For glazing you cannot reach from the ground, use the extension pole instead of stepping onto furniture, boxes or a ladder. If the extension pole cannot reach the glass safely, the stop-work rule in this lesson applies.

instructionSections.heading: Applying, removing and checking the solution
instructionSections.body: Apply the diluted solution to the glass with a ferret or a dolly, so that the whole pane is wet. Leave the solution for its contact time, so that it can loosen the dirt; do not scrub the glass dry while it is working. Remove the solution with overlapping figure-of-eight passes, starting at the top corner of the pane. Wipe the blade on a clean part of the cloth after each pass, because a dirty blade is the most common cause of smears. Wipe the window frames and ledges to remove any water that has run off the glass. Then check the pane for runs and smears in good light, and correct any faults before you move to the next pane.

instructionSections.heading: Height and ladder work: the stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: You must stop work and report to your supervisor, and must not climb or place a ladder, when any of the following applies: the glass cannot be reached from the ground or with the supplied extension equipment; you would need to stand on furniture, a box, a step or a ladder; the surface you would stand on is not stable or is wet; you cannot see the work area clearly; there are overhead power lines or other hazards near the work area that you have not been trained to manage; or you are unsure whether the work is covered by your training. Stopping is the correct action, and it is not a failure. The supervisor decides how the glazing is cleaned, and by whom.

instructionSections.heading: Licence notice: working at height
instructionSections.body: Working at height, including on ladders, platforms and rope-access systems, may require a specific training qualification or a licence in the state or territory where the work is done. This lesson does not grant a licence, a certificate or any authority to do height work. A worker who has completed this lesson must not carry out height work unless the required training or licence is held and the work is authorised.

instructionSections.heading: Storage and colour coding
instructionSections.body: Buckets, cloths, ferrets and blades must be washed thoroughly after use. Stand buckets upside down so they air dry, and hang the cloths and ferrets over the top. Store window equipment in colours that are kept for window work, for example all red cloths together and all blue buckets together. Keep clean equipment and dirty equipment apart, so that a dirty cloth never touches a clean area. Colour coding also keeps unpleasant odours and germs away from the customer.

lessons.title: Stain removal: identify, test, treat and record
learningOutcomes: Identify the stain and the surface or material before choosing any method.
Remove as much of a stain as possible by absorption, scraping or gentle abrasion before any chemical is applied.
Test an inconspicuous area with the approved product, and judge the result before treating the stain.
Apply an approved stain remover, allow contact time, and work from the outside of the stain toward its centre.
Rinse, blot and check the area, and repeat or refer when the stain remains.
Record the stain, product, test result and outcome for each stain treated or referred.

instructionSections.heading: Stain removal is a method, not a guess
instructionSections.body: The aim is a stain-free surface that the customer can use straight away, and a surface that is not damaged in the process. Stain removal follows four principles. First, identify the stain and the material it sits on. Second, test an inconspicuous area before any product touches the stain. Third, use only an approved product and the manufacturer's method. Fourth, record what was done and what happened. The source for this lesson sets these as the working standard, and the source's wording is not reproduced here. Where a source statement reads as a negation of its own steps, this lesson uses the positive principle and the reviewer is asked to confirm the intent.

instructionSections.heading: Identify the stain and the surface first
instructionSections.body: Before you choose a method, find out what the stain is, how old it is, and what it is on. The material matters as much as the stain. Some synthetic materials can be damaged by organic solvents, so check the material and the manufacturer's directions before you use a solvent-based product. Some stains need a product chosen for that stain type. If you cannot identify the stain or the material with confidence, do not treat it until the supervisor or the manufacturer's guide has confirmed the method. Stop and identify first, because a wrong product can set a stain or damage a surface.

instructionSections.heading: Protect yourself and the area
instructionSections.body: Wear gloves whenever you use a stain remover, a spot treatment or a chewing gum remover, because the product can irritate the skin and the dust on a surface can reach your hands. Open windows or doors where possible so that no one nearby breathes fumes. Set out a barrier around the area, so that dirt is not walked into the damp area and people do not slip. Check that each chemical has its manufacturer's label displayed before you open it, and keep sprays switched off when a container is not in use.

instructionSections.heading: Remove first, then treat
instructionSections.body: Take off as much of the stain as you can before any chemical goes on. Use absorption, where you blot up liquid with a clean cloth. Use scraping for solids, carefully and without damaging the surface. Use gentle abrasion only where the surface allows it. Then try water on the stain before any product is applied, because water sometimes lifts a stain without a chemical. Stop if water spreads the stain or changes the surface, and report it.

instructionSections.heading: Test, treat, work and check
instructionSections.body: Spot test an unnoticeable area with the approved product before you use it on the stain, and wait for its contact time. Look for any change in colour, texture or the surface itself. If the test area changes, do not use the product on the stain. Once the test is clear, spray the approved product onto the stain and allow the contact time, checking the progress regularly. Work with a small scrubbing brush from the outside of the stain toward the centre, so the stain does not spread outward. Rinse the surface with water, and blot it dry with a white cloth or white paper towel. Check whether the stain has gone. If it is still present, repeat the treatment once, as set out in the procedure, and then refer it if it remains.

instructionSections.heading: When to stop and refer
instructionSections.body: A stain must be referred to the supervisor, and not treated further, when the test area changes; when the stain does not respond after the repeat; when you cannot identify the stain or the material; when the stain is on building fabric, such as graffiti or staining on a structure, which may be a separate quoted service; or when a treatment would need a product or method that is not on your approved list. Referral is a sound decision. The record must say why the stain was referred, and what was seen during the test.

instructionSections.heading: Record the result
instructionSections.body: Each stain treated or referred needs a record. Write down the location and surface, the stain type, the product name and dilution, the result of the test area, and the outcome. If the stain was not removed, write down what remained and who was told. The recording step is a team documentation rule, and it lets the business show what was done to a customer's surface. Keep the record with the job file.

lessons.title: Stripping, drying and reapplying emulsion polish on hard floors
learningOutcomes: Describe the order of work for stripping old polish: outside edges first, small sections, slurry removed before it dries.
Inspect a buffer and wet pick-up for electrical and mechanical faults before and after use.
Choose a buffing pad by its colour and abrasiveness for the stage of the job.
Apply and cross-weave polish coats, letting each coat dry before the next, and explain how drying time affects slip risk.
Store the buffer and wet pick-up so the pad, base plate, blade and tank are not left in a state that damages the machine.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of the task
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers the full cycle for a hard floor finished with emulsion polish. The old polish film is loosened with a stripper and worked off with a rotary buffer. A wet pick-up machine then lifts the resulting slurry. The bare floor is dried and checked, and new polish is laid down in thin, even coats. The work happens in a single area, but its risks run through the whole job: chemical contact and fumes, an electrical lead near a spinning pad, a slip hazard on wet or freshly polished floor, and damage to the floor finish if the steps are done out of order. The operator must be trained on the machines before running them. This lesson does not authorise any plant use and does not replace the product's safety data sheet.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment checks before work starts
instructionSections.body: Check each electrical machine before switching it on. Confirm that the electrical safety test date is current and recorded on the site register. Look over the plug and the lead for cuts, cracks or bare conductors, and reject any lead that has been repaired with electrical tape. On the wet pick-up, check that the squeegee blade is intact and that the float is sound. Choose the buffing pad by colour. A darker pad is more abrasive than a lighter one, so pick the pad for the stage of the job as set in the approved method. Wash all equipment before any chemical is mixed or used, so that residue from an earlier product cannot react with the new one. Every chemical container must carry a legible manufacturer's label.

instructionSections.heading: Preparing the room
instructionSections.body: Cover any fittings, walls, skirting and surfaces that the stripper or polish could reach. Use plastic sheeting and secure it with masking tape. Open doors and windows where possible, because stripper vapour can be harmful and moving air helps the floor dry sooner. Put on gloves and eye protection before opening any container. Set up barriers so that no one walks across the floor while it is wet or unprotected.

instructionSections.heading: Stripping in sections
instructionSections.body: Work from the outside edges toward the centre. Apply stripper to the edges with an edging tool and let it sit for the contact time the manufacturer specifies. Wipe any stripper that has landed on the skirting boards so that chemical does not build up there. Next, mop stripper onto the central area, allow contact time, and scrub the film off with the buffer. Use overlapping figure-eight passes and move from the edges inward. Keep each section small enough that you can finish and clear it before the chemical dries. Pick up the slurry with the wet pick-up, working from dry floor toward wet floor, so you never step on liquid you have not yet cleared. Slurry must not be left to dry on the floor, because dried residue is much harder to remove and can leave marks.

instructionSections.heading: After stripping and before polishing
instructionSections.body: If a standard alkaline stripper was used, neutralise the floor as the procedure directs. The source method names vinegar for this; confirm the neutralising step against the product label before use. Once the polish film is gone, the floor is unprotected and will mark easily. Keep shoe soles clean and avoid walking back over treated areas. Let the floor dry completely and check that it is clean before any polish goes on. Rinse the wet pick-up's tank and wipe the blade before storing it.

instructionSections.heading: Applying the polish
instructionSections.body: Polish the outside edges of the room first, then let that band dry before working across the open floor. Apply polish with a mop using figure-eight overlapping sweeps across the middle. Keep polish off the outer edges during the main application. Wipe any polish that reaches the skirting boards straight away. Buff the floor between coats using the buffing method in the same procedure set. Wait until each coat is dry before applying the next. Lay the second coat at right angles to the first (cross-weave). Apply a third coat only if the surface still needs it. Remove the plastic sheeting only after the final coat is dry.

instructionSections.heading: Operating electrical machines safely
instructionSections.body: Keep the cord behind you so the spinning pad cannot run over it. Never drape the cord over your shoulder. A faulty machine could give an electric shock, and a snagged cord can pull you off balance. Keep the buffer under control at all times. Only trained operators run the machine. Electrical equipment must stay clean, maintained, tested and in good repair. Any machine that is damaged or whose test has lapsed comes out of service and is reported.

instructionSections.heading: Storage and end of use
instructionSections.body: Never store a buffer with the pad and base plate still fitted. Safety check the machine and damp wipe it after use. Store it upright with the base plate balanced on top. Wash the buffing pads and hang them to dry. Wash out the wet pick-up, wipe the blade, rinse the float and let everything dry. Wash buckets and cloths, store buckets upside down so they air-dry, and store all equipment in its colour group so clean and dirty items never mix.

lessons.title: Machine scrubbing and drying with a wet suction machine
learningOutcomes: Complete the before-use checks on a wet suction scrubber, including electrical status, pad condition and fluid levels.
Select the pad and fluid flow setting for the surface being cleaned and explain why each matters.
Move the machine at a steady speed and monitor the floor during the pass so the scrub and dry result is achieved.
Carry out end-of-use checks, empty and clean the waste tank, and store the machine safely on charge or upright.

instructionSections.heading: What this machine does and where the risks sit
instructionSections.body: A wet suction scrubber applies cleaning solution to the floor through a brush or pad, scrubs the surface, and then pulls the dirty liquid back into a waste tank. It is a battery-powered electrical machine with rotating parts, a fluid circuit, a charging point and a heavy body. The main risks are electrical faults, a fall or slip on wet floor, chemical contact and fumes, and damage to the floor finish or to the machine if the pad, fluid flow or speed is wrong. The procedure set out here is written for trained operators. Completing this lesson does not qualify you to operate the machine on a site.

instructionSections.heading: Before-use checks
instructionSections.body: Before the machine is used, confirm that it is unplugged from its charging source. Check the electrical safety test date against the site register, and look over the plug and lead for damage, bare wires or tape repairs. Inspect every part of the machine for obvious damage, including the body, the anti-splash skirt, the wheels and the brush or pad holder. Condition the machine and check that every fluid level is correct for the job. Select the brush or pad that suits the surface. Secure the anti-splash skirt.
