Check that the battery holds enough charge to finish the area. Switch the machine on, then set the fluid flow to the level the job requires.

instructionSections.heading: Selecting pads and fluid flow
instructionSections.body: Pads are colour coded by abrasiveness. A darker pad is more abrasive, so choose the lightest pad that will do the job for the surface and the soil. Too much fluid leaves the floor slippery and wastes solution, while too little leaves the surface under-cleaned. Match the flow to the surface and adjust it during the job if the floor is drying too fast or leaving a film. Chemicals must be labelled and must be washed out of the equipment before a different product is used, so that two products are never mixed by accident.

instructionSections.heading: Running the machine
instructionSections.body: Move the machine across the floor at a steady pace that gives the scrub and suction time to work. Going too fast leaves the surface dirty, and going too slowly can over-wet the floor or damage the finish. Watch the floor as you work and check the result on each pass, not just at the end. Keep ventilation open where possible, because fumes from cleaning products are harmful and air movement helps the floor dry faster. Keep the machine under control at all times and never leave it running unattended. Keep electrical checks in mind throughout: stop immediately if the machine behaves unusually, the lead is pinched, or the floor is too wet to work on safely.

instructionSections.heading: End-of-use checks
instructionSections.body: After use, complete the listed checks to confirm that the machine has not been damaged during the job. Empty the waste fluid tank and remove any residue from inside it, following the site's waste disposal procedure. Remove the brush or pad, safety check and damp wipe the machine, and wash the pad and let it dry. Put the machine on charge if it needs it, using the charging point, and store it upright. Never store the machine with a pad or brush still fitted.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the job
instructionSections.body: Record the before-use check, the fluid settings used, the area covered, the end-of-use check and the disposal of the waste. A faulty machine, a missed test, or a damaged part must be reported and tagged out before the next use. Recording the checks is what shows the machine was safe and the work was done to standard, not the time spent on the floor.

lessons.title: Litter picking on external grounds and entrances
learningOutcomes: Barrier and sign an outdoor work area so that vehicles, colleagues and the public can see where work is happening.
Pick up litter, cigarette ends, gum and waste from the listed external surfaces and planting areas without disturbing the planting more than necessary.
Separate general litter from sharps and contaminated waste, and handle each category in the way the procedure requires.
Describe the post-job checks for equipment, personal hygiene and the external areas.

instructionSections.heading: Why litter picking carries more risk than it looks
instructionSections.body: Litter picking appears to be low-skill work, but the outdoor setting adds hazards that indoor cleaning does not have. Vehicles and pedestrians share the space. Hedges, verges and planting beds can hide sharps, broken glass and contaminated waste. Dust, pollen and bacteria can reach the skin and eyes. The aim of this lesson is to keep the worker visible and protected, to keep sharps and contaminated waste separate from general litter, and to leave the grounds clean and tidy without creating new hazards for other people.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment and personal protection
instructionSections.body: Check each litter picker and each sack before use, and wash the equipment as the procedure requires so that residues do not carry from one site to another. Wear the gloves issued to you at all times while picking. High-visibility clothing must be worn whenever you are picking litter, because you will be working outdoors where vehicles are moving. Always use the sharps containers and collection points the site has approved. Wash your hands thoroughly after each litter pick, even when the gloves seemed intact.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up the work area
instructionSections.body: Barrier off the area so that vehicles, employees and customers can clearly see where you are working. The boundary of the external area to be cleaned must be confirmed with the site before work starts. Do not start in an area that is not on the agreed boundary plan.

instructionSections.heading: Picking up litter and waste
instructionSections.body: Work through the external areas on the scope list: entrances, car parks, paving, paths, steps, ramps, walkways, terraces, ledges, signage, fixed seating, lighting columns, bollards and the outside of the premises. Pick up litter, cigarette ends, chewing gum and general dirt. Place general litter into the designated sacks. Keep your body out of hedgerows, and reach in with the litter picker where possible. Only a foot should go into a hedge bed, and only when the procedure allows it. Take sacks to the skip or the customer's designated collection area. Empty and replace all waste bins in their original positions.

instructionSections.heading: Sharps and contaminated waste
instructionSections.body: If you find a needle, syringe or other sharp, stop and mark the location clearly so no one else touches it. Call a trained colleague to bring the sharps container and dispose of the item under the sharps procedure for bodily fluids and sharps. Never pick up a sharp with your hands. Place all sharps in a rigid sharps container, never in a sack. Store the sharps containers in a locked storage area and dispose of them through the site's approved route. Litter pickers and bins must be washed regularly, and the needle-stick containers must be kept sealed.

instructionSections.heading: Protected areas and finishing the job
instructionSections.body: Some areas are protected by security screening, netting or protective cages. You may remove the protection temporarily to clear debris, dirt, dust and litter, but it must be replaced to its original condition before you leave. The finished area should look clean and tidy, be free of litter, gum, cigarette ends, staining and bodily fluid, and show no sign of food pests or vermin. Disinfectant may be used where it is appropriate. Remove barriers only after the area is clear and safe.

lessons.title: Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)
learningOutcomes: Describe the protective steps before contact with a body fluid spill, including covering open cuts and selecting the spill kit and PPE.
Contain, absorb, disinfect and remove a body fluid spill in the order the procedure sets, allowing the disinfectant its full contact time.
Remove a sharp using a litter picker or grips and place it in a sharps container, never in general waste.
Dispose of soiled materials, PPE and equipment through the clinical waste route the site uses, and explain the decontamination of reusable tools.

instructionSections.heading: High-risk warning
instructionSections.body: Body fluids and sharps can carry blood-borne and other infectious agents. A needle stick or a splash to the eye or to broken skin is a serious incident. This lesson is written as a high-risk task. It is written to be complete, not reduced. Work on any body fluid spill or sharp only after the training your employer requires, with the spill kit and PPE provided, and with a supervisor or first-aid trained colleague aware of what you are doing. If the spill is large, the material is unknown, or you cannot carry out the steps safely, stop, protect the area and call for help. Completing this lesson does not qualify you to clean biohazard or crime-scene material, which is covered by separate high-risk lessons.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting yourself before you start
instructionSections.body: Check your hands for open cuts, grazes and broken skin. Cover any open wound with a waterproof dressing before you put on gloves. Put on the gloves and eye protection provided. Use the spill kit's protective clothing as the kit instructions require. Keep bystanders away, and rope off or barrier the area. Keep ventilation open where possible, because cleaning products give off fumes that should not be breathed. The equipment in the spill kit is single-use for the spill and should not be reused for other jobs.

instructionSections.heading: Clearing the sharps first
instructionSections.body: If there are sharps or needles in the spill, remove them before anything else. Use a litter picker or grips from the sharps container, not your hands. Place each sharp directly into an appropriate sharps container, and place the container on the floor while you put contaminated items into it, as the procedure directs. Never put a sharp into general waste, and never try to recap or bend a needle.

instructionSections.heading: Containing and absorbing the spill
instructionSections.body: Cover the liquid with the absorbent granules from the spill kit, or another approved absorbent. Work from the outside of the spill toward the centre so the spill does not spread. Scoop up as much of the contamination as possible with a scoop or scraper. Use absorbent paper towel to pick up the rest. Put every item used in the clean-up into the clinical waste bag as you go.

instructionSections.heading: Disinfecting and finishing the area
instructionSections.body: Spray the approved disinfectant over the area and leave the full contact time on the label, because the disinfectant needs that time to reduce the numbers of bacteria to a safe level. Mop or wipe the area and rinse it clean. Repeat the disinfect and wipe steps for any stubborn residue. Give the area a final rinse and let it dry. Check that no residue remains before the area is released for use.

instructionSections.heading: Disposal and decontamination
instructionSections.body: Put all soiled materials and used PPE into the clinical waste bag and seal the bag. The source procedure states that contaminated items are sent for incineration. Litter pickers, scoops and other reusable tools must be disinfected before they are used again. Wash your hands thoroughly after removing gloves, and put a fresh waterproof dressing on any plaster or wound that has been exposed. Keep colour coding for cloths and buckets so clean and contaminated items never mix.

instructionSections.heading: What the finished job looks like
instructionSections.body: The area should look clean and dry, be free of visible residue, and smell neutral once the disinfectant has been allowed to work. The customer should not be exposed to harmful bacteria or to needles. All waste is sealed and removed through the designated route. The sharps container is closed and stored in its locked area. The incident is recorded and reported, even when no one was hurt.

lessons.title: Cleaning stairs, landings, balustrades and handrails
learningOutcomes: Clean hard and carpeted stairs in the top-to-bottom order the procedure requires, working from the edges and corners inward.
Clean balustrades, handrails and skirting boards with a damp cloth and a bucket that is changed when dirty.
Check the vacuum cleaner before and after use and position the vacuum so the cable stays clear.
Leave stairs dry, free of runs and chemical build-up, and safe to walk on.

instructionSections.heading: Why stairs are a slip and manual handling hazard
instructionSections.body: Stairs combine a slip risk, a fall risk and a manual handling risk. A wet or sticky step is dangerous, and so is a step that has been over-chemicalled and not rinsed. Working on stairs also means reaching, bending and carrying, so the worker should limit the area cleaned at one time to a size they can manage safely. A stairwell is usually a shared route, so the job must leave it passable and safe before the worker moves on.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment and electrical checks
instructionSections.body: Before using a vacuum cleaner, check that it has a current electrical safety test date recorded on the site register. Look over the plug and lead for damage, bare wires or tape repairs. Check the bag and filter, because a blocked filter can make the vacuum overheat. Check the hose for blockages and check the height of the beater bar against the floor covering. Confirm that all chemicals carry a legible label. Only trained employees may use electrical equipment. After the task, repeat the safety checks to confirm the machine has not been damaged during use.

instructionSections.heading: Protection and ventilation
instructionSections.body: Wear gloves at all times when using chemicals. Gloves and eye protection should be worn when using chemicals and the vacuum, because dust and bacteria can reach the eyes and skin. Open a window or door where possible, so that fumes do not build up in a stairwell that has little airflow.

instructionSections.heading: Removing gum and litter first
instructionSections.body: Before cleaning, check the stairs, landings, balustrades and handrails for chewing gum. Remove gum with a scraper or a gum remover, following the stain removal method for the surface. Pick up any large litter. Clearing large items first stops them from being pushed into the corners during cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Dry and hard stairs
instructionSections.body: On a hard surface, sweep from the top step to the bottom. Start with the edges and corners, then sweep toward the middle of each tread. When mopping, mop from the top down. Give extra attention to the corners, edges and nosings, which collect dust and debris. Wipe any run marks straight away so none are left on any surface. Check that the floor is not over-wet. The floor should not feel sticky when dry, which is a sign of too much chemical.

instructionSections.heading: Carpeted stairs
instructionSections.body: On carpeted stairs, use the vacuum to remove surface dirt and dust. Position the vacuum either below or above you, depending on where the power point is, so that the cable stays clear of the path you are working along and does not come under your feet on the stairs.

instructionSections.heading: Balustrades, handrails and skirting
instructionSections.body: Damp wipe the balustrades and the skirting boards. Keep the bucket on a landing behind the line of work so you do not carry water up or down the stairs. Change the water as soon as it becomes dirty, rather than spreading dirt across the next section. Wipe all skirting so that dust, debris and chemical build-up are removed. Check the handrails for smears and wipe them dry.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing and storing the equipment
instructionSections.body: Wash the bucket and cloths thoroughly after use. Store the bucket upside down so it air-dries, and hang the cloths over the top. Keep equipment colour coded so clean and dirty items do not mix. Safety check the vacuum and damp wipe it after use. Empty and dispose of the rubbish according to the site's waste procedure. Clean the dust pan and brush, and store them by colour.

lessons.title: Cleaning passenger and goods lift interiors
learningOutcomes: Obtain permission and isolate a lift for cleaning with the doors open, so the worker is not in a confined space.
Select the cleaning material for each lift surface: car walls, handrails, doors, floor, tracks and control panel.
Clean the doors and door tracks inside and out, and vacuum the floor tracks, without pressing any call button.
Return the lift to service and record the job, scheduling the work to cause minimal inconvenience to the building.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and the boundary of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers cleaning the interior surfaces of a lift car, the landing door faces and tracks that can be reached safely, and the control panel surfaces. It does not cover opening the lift shaft, working in the lift pit or machine room, or adjusting or repairing any lift component. Those tasks are mechanical or electrical work that belongs to the lift service provider. Completing this lesson does not grant a licence or authority for that work.

instructionSections.heading: Permission and timing
instructionSections.body: Always ask the building's responsible person for permission before isolating a lift. Where a passenger lift is used by staff and visitors, schedule the internal clean at a time that causes the least disruption to the people working in the building. The isolation step should be done only after the permission is confirmed and recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating the lift safely
instructionSections.body: Isolate the lift with the doors open, so that you are not working in a confined space and so that the lift is safe to enter. Use the lift's isolating switch to take the car out of service, following the building's procedure. Keep the control buttons in mind during isolation: the call button must not be pressed while you are working, because it would bring the lift back into use or send it to a floor while you are inside. Confirm the lift is isolated before you enter the car.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment and electrical checks
instructionSections.body: Before using the vacuum cleaner, check that it has a current electrical safety test date recorded on the site register. Inspect the plug and lead for damage, bare wires or tape repairs. Check the bag and filter, since a blocked filter can make the vacuum overheat. Check the hose for blockages and set the beater bar height for the floor covering. Confirm that every chemical has a legible label. Only trained employees may use electrical equipment. Repeat the safety checks at the end of the task. Wash and dry cloths and tools, and keep them colour coded.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing materials for each surface
instructionSections.body: Identify the dirt on each surface first. Dirt on the car walls, handrails, doors and control panel may need a different product from the dirt on the floor. Choose the material that suits each surface from the approved product list, and use the same wall-washing method used for other walls in the building. Use the same floor methods used for other hard and carpeted floors, selected by the floor covering in the car. The source names mop sweeping, single-solution mopping and suction cleaning as the methods for these floors; the full methods are not written in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning the car and doors
instructionSections.body: Clean the car walls, then clean the handrails and control panel with care, wiping the buttons with a lightly dampened cloth so that no liquid enters the panel. Clean the car floor using the method for its covering. Clean the doors inside and outside to remove marks and fingerprints. Clean around the door tracks and frames, and vacuum the floor tracks to remove dirt and dust. Be careful not to press any call button on the control panel while you work.

instructionSections.heading: Returning the lift to service
instructionSections.body: When the clean is finished, check that all cloths, tools and vacuum cleaners have been removed from the car and the landing area. Return the lift to service by changing the isolating switch back, following the building's procedure. The source wording on this step is unclear about the switch position, so the building's written procedure must be checked before this lesson is used. Confirm that the lift responds normally, and record the job.

instructionSections.heading: Storing equipment and finishing
instructionSections.body: Safety check and damp wipe the vacuum cleaner after use. Empty the rubbish according to the building's waste disposal procedure. Clean the dust pan and brush and store them by colour. Clean materials and well-maintained machines last longer and keep the service consistent.

lessons.title: Cleaning personal computers, keyboards and screens
learningOutcomes: State which IT equipment is in scope for a cleaning job and confirm the scope before work starts.
Explain why water and silicone-based polish must be kept away from computer equipment, and why power must be switched off before the surface is cleaned.
Clean a keyboard, screen and computer base with a damp, not wet, cloth and a cotton bud in the gaps between keys.
Replace every item moved during the job so the customer's workstation is left as it was found.

instructionSections.heading: Scope first
instructionSections.body: IT equipment is often excluded from a general cleaning contract unless the customer names it as part of the work. That covers computers, monitors, printers, photocopiers, fax machines, televisions and similar equipment. Before starting, confirm with the customer or the contract whether the computer equipment is in scope. If it is not in scope, do not clean it, and record the decision. If it is in scope, follow this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Why electronics need careful handling
instructionSections.body: Computer equipment is sensitive to dust, water and silicone-based polish. Liquid and polish can short-circuit components, leave a film that damages screens and key surfaces, and cause a fault that the customer will blame on the cleaner. Your job is to prevent water and polish from reaching the equipment, to keep electricity and liquid apart at every step, and to clean the surface only with the method set out here.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment and personal protection
instructionSections.body: Check that every item of equipment you use is clean and washed before use. Confirm that each chemical carries a legible manufacturer's label. Gloves must be worn at all times when using chemicals, and gloves and eye protection are needed when handling the cleaning solution. Keep windows or doors open where possible so that fumes from cleaning products do not build up in the room.

instructionSections.heading: Powering down safely
instructionSections.body: Always ask the customer for permission before switching off or unplugging a computer or monitor. Ask the user to remove any CDs or DVDs from the work area. Switch off the computer and the screen at the mains, then unplug them from the socket. Water and electricity must never come into contact, so do not wet the equipment or its power points at any stage.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning the keyboard, screen and base
instructionSections.body: Remove surface dirt and debris from the keyboard with a mini vacuum or a soft, dry paint brush. Dust the screen with a dry, non-linting cloth to remove surface dirt. Apply the cleaning solution to the cloth, not directly to the equipment, and wipe the keys with the damp cloth. Clean between the keys with a cotton bud that has been dampened with the solution. Wipe the computer base with a damp cloth only if the base has been unplugged and is easy to reach. Never let the cloth drip, and never spray solution onto the screen or keyboard.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing the workstation
instructionSections.body: Replace any CDs or DVDs that were moved. Put back everything that was moved off the desk, in the same place, so the customer is not concerned about their property. If you switched off and unplugged the computer, plug it back in and switch it on again as the customer expects. Buckets and cloths must be washed, and stored colour coded. Buckets are stored upside down to air-dry, with cloths hung over them.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the job
instructionSections.body: Record whether the computer equipment was in scope, whether the customer gave permission to switch it off, which items were cleaned, and what was replaced. Note any fault, damage or dispute on the job sheet before you leave.

lessons.title: Induction before cleaning work starts
learningOutcomes: Name the topics an induction must cover before a worker starts cleaning on a site.
Find the chemical register, the safety data sheets, the risk assessment records and the emergency details for a site during an induction walk-through.
Explain when an induction, or the part of it that has changed, must be repeated.
Complete an induction record that states the tasks the worker is cleared for and the tasks they are not yet cleared for.

instructionSections.heading: Status of this lesson
instructionSections.body: The uploaded source gives the title of an induction annex but not its text, so this lesson is a general outline written by the team and is not the business's own induction policy. It must be replaced with the annex text once that text is supplied and reviewed. Nothing in this lesson sets how long an induction takes, and nothing in it grants a licence, a certificate or any authority to do regulated work.

instructionSections.heading: Why the induction comes first
instructionSections.body: A new worker does not yet know the hazards on a site, where the safety information is kept, or who to call when something goes wrong. The induction passes that knowledge from the supervisor to the worker before the first task, rather than during it. It also creates a record that the information was given, which protects both the worker and the business if a question arises later.

instructionSections.heading: The topics an induction covers
instructionSections.body: A cleaning induction usually covers the standard operating procedures that apply to the worker's tasks, the chemicals in use and where their labels and safety data sheets are kept, the protective gear each task needs, the colour-coded equipment system and where it is stored, and the hazards that belong to the site itself, such as wet floors, fixed plant and restricted areas. It also covers the fire exits, the assembly point, the first-aid point, how to report an injury, a near miss or damage, and who the supervisor is and how to reach them.

instructionSections.heading: Walking the site
instructionSections.body: The supervisor takes the worker around the site rather than only describing it. At each stop the worker sees the chemical store, the sharps and waste points, the equipment store, the amenities, the exits, and the areas where entry is restricted. The worker should be invited to ask questions at every stop. The supervisor then asks the worker to point out one hazard and its control, in the worker's own words, before moving on.

instructionSections.heading: The induction record and sign-off
instructionSections.body: The induction record names the worker, the date, the supervisor and the site. It lists the topics covered and the tasks the worker is cleared to do at that point. Where a worker is cleared for some tasks but not others, the record says so in plain terms. Both the worker and the supervisor sign it, and the record is kept with the business's training records. The policy the induction follows is recorded by reference, using the business's own policy reference.

instructionSections.heading: When an induction must be repeated
instructionSections.body: Repeat the induction, or the part of it that has changed, after a change of task, a change of site, a new chemical or machine, a new hazard on the site, or any incident that shows the worker may not have understood something. A worker who was inducted for one task is not cleared for a different task until the part of the induction about that task has been covered and recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Legal position
instructionSections.body: Work health and safety law in each state and territory sets the duties of a business to inform, instruct and train its workers. Check them against the law of each jurisdiction before the induction is finalised.

lessons.title: Sharps and body fluids: policy, reporting and records
learningOutcomes: State the policy rules for sharps and body fluids that apply before any clean-up starts.
Describe the stop-and-report steps to take when a sharp or an unexpected fluid is found.
Describe the reporting and record steps after an injury, a near miss or a spill, including what the supervisor must record.
Explain why only trained workers may carry out the “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)” clean-up, and what an untrained worker does instead.

instructionSections.heading: Status of this lesson
instructionSections.body: The uploaded source gives the heading of the sharps and body fluids annex but not its text. This lesson is a team-written overview that sits alongside the clean-up procedure in “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)”. When the annex text is supplied, this lesson must be checked against it and corrected wherever the two differ. Nothing in this lesson grants a licence, a certificate or any authority to handle clinical waste or to carry out post-exposure care.

instructionSections.heading: Stop before you touch
instructionSections.body: The most common risk with a sharp is that it cannot be seen. Do not reach into rubbish, bedding, gaps behind furniture, or the gaps in a bin to find it. Stop, keep your hands away from the item, and call your supervisor. If you have a cut or broken skin on your hand, seal it under a waterproof dressing, and only then put on gloves. Do not handle the item until you are cleared to do so.

instructionSections.heading: Who may clean up
instructionSections.body: Only workers who have been trained for body fluid and sharps clean-up may carry out the procedure in “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)”. Any other worker stops, keeps people away from the area, and reports the event. Making an area safe is different from clearing it. The supervisor decides who clears the area, and records the decision.

instructionSections.heading: Containers and waste
instructionSections.body: Sharps go into a rigid, labelled sharps container, and never into general waste or a loose sack. The container is set down where it cannot tip, and it is kept locked away between jobs. Body fluid waste and contaminated materials go into the clinical waste route the business uses.

instructionSections.heading: Injuries and near misses
instructionSections.body: If a sharp cuts or punctures your skin, wash the wound straight away, tell your supervisor, and get the first-aid and medical care that the business's process sets out. Record the time, the item, the place and the names of any witnesses. A near miss is reported in the same way, even when no injury happens. Reporting does not mean you caused the problem. It lets the business remove the hazard.

instructionSections.heading: What the supervisor records
instructionSections.body: For each sharps or bodily fluid event, the supervisor records what happened, the clean-up that was done, who did it and what training they held, the disposal route, and any follow-up care that was arranged.

instructionSections.heading: Legal and regulatory position
instructionSections.body: The duties for storing, transporting and disposing of sharps and clinical waste, and the response required after an exposure, vary by state and territory and by the type of premises. None of these is confirmed in this lesson. The rules that apply must be checked before this policy is used on any site.

lessons.title: Manual handling for cleaning work
learningOutcomes: Identify the manual handling tasks in a cleaning job, including carrying, pushing, pulling, lifting and reaching.
Assess a load or a movement before it is attempted, and decide whether to reduce it, split it, use an aid, or get help.
Apply the controls for manual handling: planned routes, mechanical aids, team lifts and working within reach.
Report a manual handling hazard, strain or near miss, and name the control that was used.

instructionSections.heading: Status of this lesson
instructionSections.body: The uploaded source gives the title of a manual handling annex but not its text. The only manual handling statement in the source is a short line about keeping to manageable areas, and it is used here. The rest of this lesson is a general outline written by the team. This lesson grants no licence or certificate.

instructionSections.heading: Where manual handling happens
instructionSections.body: Manual handling is any task that involves lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling, carrying, holding or reaching. In cleaning work it appears when you move a full bucket, a vacuum, a floor machine, a bin of waste, a box of stock, a ladder or a piece of furniture, and when you stretch to reach a high or low surface. Repetition matters as much as weight. Many small movements repeated through a shift can cause as much harm as one heavy lift.

instructionSections.heading: Plan the movement before you start
instructionSections.body: Before you lift or move anything, look at the load, the route you will take, and the place where it will be set down. Check any weight that is marked on the container. Clear the route of trip hazards and wet patches. If the load is unstable, awkward, too heavy for one person, or blocks your view, do not attempt it alone.

instructionSections.heading: Use aids and a second person
instructionSections.body: Use a trolley or a cart, a hoist where the site provides one, or a second person for a load that is large or heavy. Where a load can be divided, divide it rather than making one difficult trip. When you lift with someone else, agree a signal beforehand so that you both lift and set down at the same moment.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the body in a safe position
instructionSections.body: Keep the load close to your body, keep your back in its natural position, and move with your legs rather than twisting your trunk. Avoid bending and twisting at the same time, and avoid reaching far above the shoulders or far out in front of the body. Where the work allows it, change position and take short breaks between tasks.

instructionSections.heading: Work in manageable areas
instructionSections.body: Clean in areas that you can reach and control comfortably. Move the equipment rather than leaning, stretching or overbalancing to reach a surface. The stairs procedure in “Cleaning stairs, landings, balustrades and handrails” uses the same principle, which is to work in a manageable area rather than attempting a whole stairwell in one movement.

instructionSections.heading: Reporting and records
instructionSections.body: Report any sore back, strain, near miss or unsafe load to your supervisor on the same day. Record the task, the load or the movement, the control that was used, and whether help was needed. Repeated reports about the same task are a signal that the task or the equipment needs to change.

instructionSections.heading: Legal position
instructionSections.body: They must be checked before this policy is finalised.

lessons.title: Cleaning audit: inspecting, recording and signing off a clean
learningOutcomes: Describe the order of an audit, from reading the standard to signing off the area.
Check a cleaned area against the quality standard in the relevant SOP and the agreed job brief for that customer.
Record each defect with its location, its type and the action it needs, and take photographs where the business requires them.
Decide whether a defect needs a re-clean, a follow-up or an escalation, and record the outcome.

instructionSections.heading: Status of this lesson
instructionSections.body: The uploaded source gives the title of a cleaning audit annex but not its text. This lesson is a general outline written by the team. A completed audit is not a licence, a certificate or an authority for any regulated work.

instructionSections.heading: What an audit is for
instructionSections.body: An audit checks finished work against a standard before it is handed over. It catches defects while the cleaner who did the work can still correct them, and it gives the business evidence that the work met the scope. An audit looks at the area against the same standard each time. It is not a personal judgement of the cleaner who did the work.

instructionSections.heading: The standard you audit against
instructionSections.body: Each area is audited against three things: the quality standard in the relevant SOP, the agreed job brief for that customer, and any requirement that applies to that particular site. Read all three before you start. If the standard is unclear for an area, stop and ask your supervisor rather than inventing a standard of your own.

instructionSections.heading: Walking the audit
instructionSections.body: Start at the entrance or another fixed point and move in one direction, so that nothing is missed. Check surfaces at the height people use them and in the light they use them. Check the detail as well as the main floor or surface: edges, skirting boards, corners, fixtures, the back of doors and the washroom fittings. Check the equipment and the storage area used for the job, as well as the work area itself.

instructionSections.heading: Recording defects and scores
instructionSections.body: Record each defect separately, with its location, its type and a short description. Typical types include a smear, a missed area, a residue, damage, a safety issue and an equipment fault. Where the business uses a score, apply it the same way to every area. A safety issue is never offset by a good score elsewhere. It is stopped and reported before anything else happens.

instructionSections.heading: Photographs
instructionSections.body: Photograph a defect where the business's evidence rules require it, for example before and after a re-clean, or to record damage. Take each photograph from the same position every time, and include a clear reference such as the room name or the fixture. Do not photograph people, or customer property beyond what the record needs.

instructionSections.heading: Acting on what the audit finds
instructionSections.body: Decide the action for each defect: re-clean it now, schedule a follow-up, change the method or the equipment, or escalate it to the supervisor. Record the action and the person who will take it. Do not sign an area off while it has an open safety issue or an open re-clean.

instructionSections.heading: Sign-off and handover
instructionSections.body: Sign an area off only when every defect has been resolved, or has been recorded with an agreed follow-up. The sign-off record names the area, the date, the auditor, the standard that was used, any open items and, where it applies, the customer representative.

instructionSections.heading: Legal position
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not set any statutory basis for an audit. Where an audit is used to show that a legal duty has been met, or where a customer contract requires it, the rules that apply in each state and territory have not yet been confirmed here, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.

lessons.title: Walking a new site before the first shift
learningOutcomes: Locate the storage room, waste points and emergency contacts on a site walk-through.
Find the safety data sheets kept on site and explain what they are for.
Confirm the agreed task list and closing routine with the site contact before work starts.

instructionSections.heading: Why walk the site first
instructionSections.body: A walk-through turns an unfamiliar building into a map you can work from. Workers who skip it lose time searching for supplies, miss areas that sit out of normal sight lines, and learn the client's expectations only after something goes wrong. Walking the site with the person who manages it is the cheapest way to ask questions while there is still time to act on the answers.

instructionSections.heading: What to note on the way round
instructionSections.body: Record where supplies are stored and who holds the keys. Mark every waste point, including the ones tucked behind partitions or in rarely visited corridors. Note any switches, power points or hinges that carry a colour marker, because the markers often show where a surface is meant to be handled differently. Check where emergency numbers are posted and where the safety data sheets are kept, then read one sheet to see which sections cover handling and first aid. Finally, read the agreed task list and the closing routine, such as lights, doors and alarm.

instructionSections.heading: Turning notes into a working plan
instructionSections.body: Put your observations on a short site card and keep it with the job file. Any task that falls outside the agreed list should be marked as a question rather than a decision. Do not invent scope on the day. A short written message to the site contact keeps the record clear and protects both sides.

lessons.title: Teaching a cleaning task in four stages
learningOutcomes: Explain a cleaning task in four stages: purpose, demonstration, supervised practice and review.
Run a supervised practice run and give specific, observable feedback.
Record what a worker demonstrated, not only that they attended a session.

instructionSections.heading: Why a fixed sequence helps
instructionSections.body: A cleaning task is easiest to teach when the trainer follows the same stages each time: say what the task is for, show the steps, let the worker perform them under observation, then review the result together. Skipping a stage usually shows up later as a missed step or a shortcut that nobody noticed at the time.

instructionSections.heading: Explaining and showing
instructionSections.body: Begin by naming the outcome the task must achieve, then describe the steps in plain words and in order. Demonstrate at normal speed, then again slowly, pointing out the step where people most often go wrong. Keep the explanation short. Long talks about cleaning are hard to remember once the worker is on the floor.

instructionSections.heading: Practising and reviewing
instructionSections.body: Let the worker carry out the whole task while you observe without taking over. Interrupt only for a safety issue or a repeated error. Afterwards, compare the result with the intended outcome, name one thing done well, and agree on one thing to improve. Repeat the practice until the worker completes a full run without prompts. Record what was demonstrated; attendance alone is not evidence of skill.

lessons.title: Packing the waste-collection kit before a route
learningOutcomes: List the core items for a waste-collection kit and state what each item is for.
Pack the kit so that supplies stay within reach during the route.
Check the kit against the site card and act on any shortage before leaving the storage room.

instructionSections.heading: Why a waste route needs its own kit
instructionSections.body: A waste route moves from desk to desk, and for much of it you are carrying a full collection bin. A planned kit keeps supplies within reach, so you are not walking back to the storage room for each item. Build the kit before you leave the storage room, and keep it the same for each site so the routine stays predictable.

instructionSections.heading: The core items
instructionSections.body: Bring a wheeled collection bin with a tie-off bag and a carry tote for small items. Carry liners in three sizes matched to the bins on the route. Add a dusting cloth, a small brush, a set of cloths for touch points, and a spray bottle of approved sanitiser. Take a plastic drop sheet to lay down where full bags will wait, and a scoop for ash and small debris. Wear the personal protective equipment set for the site, usually eye protection and gloves.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the kit within reach
instructionSections.body: Place the most-used items on top of the tote and the heaviest items low on the bin. Keep small items where your hand reaches without looking. Use a caddy or tote that fits the bin, so your hands stay free for doors and for moving between cubicles.

lessons.title: Running the waste route in a fixed order
learningOutcomes: Describe the order of a waste route from the storage room to the drop point.
Empty, reline and check each desk bin and sanitise each touch point in turn.
Identify when a bin, area or item has been missed and correct it before leaving the floor.

instructionSections.heading: Starting and moving through the space
instructionSections.body: Begin with a check of your protective equipment and the kit, then move through the area in a steady loop. Keep to one direction on every pass so that no desk is skipped. Hold the bin close to your body and do not let it drift out to the side. Where corridors and cubicles branch off, work in short zig-zags, finishing each row before you move on, so you do not double back.

instructionSections.heading: At each desk
instructionSections.body: Empty the desk bin into the collection bin, check that spare liners are in its base, and fit a fresh liner if one is needed. Replace a liner that is torn, wet or holding food. Wipe the desk top with a sanitised cloth, lifting only what you need to lift. Pick up loose rubbish around the bin and beneath the desk. If a chair or the bin itself has to move to reach under the desk, put it back before you leave.

instructionSections.heading: Touch points and small items
instructionSections.body: Items people touch often, like switches, handles and push plates, are sanitised with a cloth kept only for that job. Empty pencil sharpeners and punches as you pass them. Leave boxes and stacked items where they are, unless they are clearly marked for disposal. Ask the site contact before you move anything of value.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing the route
instructionSections.body: Once the collection bin reaches capacity, knot the bag shut and set it on the drop sheet at the designated point. Return the kit to the storage room, place used cloths in the laundry basket, and set the kit up for the next visit.

lessons.title: Fitting, tying and replacing bin liners
learningOutcomes: Choose a liner size that fits a given bin and check the fit before tying.
Seat, tie and stock a liner so the next replacement is quick.
Decide when a liner must be replaced rather than reused.

instructionSections.heading: Matching the liner to the bin
instructionSections.body: Each bin needs a liner that sits fully over the rim and is big enough to tie off. A liner that is too small sinks inside the bin and gathers at the bottom. A liner that is too large folds over the rim and stops the lid from closing. Use the liner size the site card lists for each bin, and check the fit as soon as the first liner is in.

instructionSections.heading: Seating and tying
instructionSections.body: Open the liner so its mouth lies flat over the rim, then smooth it down into the bin before tying. Keep two or three spare liners in the base of the bin, folded or tied, so the next change is quick and the route does not stop. Tie the working liner snugly and check that no waste is caught in the knot.

instructionSections.heading: When to replace
instructionSections.body: Replace a liner that is torn, wet, leaking or holding food. Also replace it when it is nearly full and the next collection point is far away. Never press waste down by hand or with a foot, because sharp items may be hidden in it. If the bin is too full to take another item, replace the liner.

lessons.title: Separating recycling from general waste on the route
learningOutcomes: Set up a two-stream collection and keep each stream pure from desk to drop point.
Decide where an unclear item belongs by checking the site guide rather than guessing.
Handle recycling bags so they are tied, separated and delivered to the right point.

instructionSections.heading: Two streams, two containers
instructionSections.body: Where a site separates recycling, the route uses two collection bins that travel together: one for general waste and one for recyclables. Match the colour and label of each bin to the site's signs. Keep each stream pure, because a single wrong item can make a whole recycling load unacceptable to the recycler.

instructionSections.heading: Sorting at the desk
instructionSections.body: Empty each desk bin into the stream that matches each item. If you are unsure where an item belongs, check the site guide or ask the site contact. If it is still unclear, place the item in general waste rather than guessing. Do not tip recyclables and general waste into one bag to save a trip.

instructionSections.heading: Items that cause contamination
instructionSections.body: Some items spoil recycling even when they are recyclable in principle. Food residue on paper and card is the most common example. Follow the site guide for what counts as acceptable. Keep recycling bags apart on the drop sheet, label them if the site asks, and do not mix the contents when moving them to the outside bin.

lessons.title: Cleaning and sanitising waste bins
learningOutcomes: Choose between a light clean and a heavy clean for a waste bin based on the soil present.
Remove crusted matter before applying a cleaning solution, and apply the product at the label strength.
Dry and reline a bin before returning it to service.

instructionSections.heading: When a bin needs more than a wipe
instructionSections.body: Most bins need only an outside wipe at each visit. A bin needs a deeper clean when residue has built up inside, when it smells, or when a spill has dried onto the surface. Decide first whether the soil is light or heavy, because that choice sets the method.

instructionSections.heading: Light soil
instructionSections.body: Take the bin to the cleaning area and mist both the interior and the exterior with a sanitising solution made up to the label. Dry it off with a cotton rag or kitchen paper. Check the seams and the base, where residue tends to collect.

instructionSections.heading: Heavy soil
instructionSections.body: Scrape hard, crusted matter from the inside with a putty knife first, so the solution can reach the surface. Fill the bin with cleaning solution at the strength on the label and leave it to soak for the time the label gives. Scrub using a nylon brush or a green scrub pad. A melamine sponge can lift marks, but use it lightly on painted or glossy surfaces. Rinse, then dry the inside completely before reuse.

instructionSections.heading: Returning the bin
instructionSections.body: Fit a fresh liner and seat it, then return the bin to its place on the route. A bin that goes back damp develops odour and leaves wet rings on the floor and the liner.

lessons.title: Emptying ashtrays and smoking urns without a fire risk
learningOutcomes: Explain why an ashtray must be treated as hot until it has been checked.
Empty a sand-filled or non-sand ashtray using the correct method and protective equipment.
Replace ashtray filler when scooping no longer clears it.

instructionSections.heading: Heat is the first hazard
instructionSections.body: Smoking urns and ashtrays often hold embers that look out but are still burning inside. Treat every ashtray as hot until you have checked it. Embers never go into a plastic liner or any general waste bin, because the bag can melt or start a fire. If you are unsure how to handle a particular urn, ask the site contact for their method before you touch it.

instructionSections.heading: Sand-filled urns
instructionSections.body: Wear eye protection and gloves. Lift cigarette ends and debris out of the sand with a scoop, making several passes so the sand is clear. Put the debris into a sealed plastic bag once it has cooled, and close the bag so the smell stays inside. Some sites use cat litter as the filler. The same method applies. Replace the filler when scooping no longer clears it: empty the old material into a sealed bag, wipe the base and rim with a damp cloth, then refill to just below the rim and level the surface.

instructionSections.heading: Non-sand ashtrays
instructionSections.body: Remove the ashtray where possible and empty it into a sealed bag once the contents are cool. If it cannot be removed, scoop the debris out. Wipe clean with a damp cloth, use soapy water for stubborn stains, and dry the ashtray before it goes back into use.

lessons.title: Emptying desk sharpeners and punches
learningOutcomes: Empty a pencil sharpener's receptacle and clear its cutters without damaging the unit.
Empty and wipe a hole punch and return it to service.
Report equipment that will not clear rather than forcing it.

instructionSections.heading: Why small office equipment needs its own step
instructionSections.body: Desk sharpeners and punches gather shavings and punched dots, which jam the mechanism and spill onto desks. Empty them as you pass during the route rather than waiting for a complaint. Where a unit has a plug, unplug it before you touch the cutters or the receptacle.

instructionSections.heading: Pencil sharpeners
instructionSections.body: Unplug the sharpener first. Lift it over the bin, take out the receptacle and tip the shavings into the bin. If the cutters are clogged, wipe the blades using a dry cloth. Material lodged in the grooves can be picked out with a blunt tool, for example a bent paper clip. Keep oils, greases and abrasive products away from the mechanism, and never soak the unit in water. Refit the receptacle, return the sharpener to its place, plug it in and test it.

instructionSections.heading: Hole punches
instructionSections.body: Take the receptacle off the base and tip the dots into the bin. Wipe dust from the body using a dry, lint-free cloth; fit the receptacle back and set the punch in its usual place. Test it with a sheet of scrap paper if the site allows.

lessons.title: Carrying and disposing of full waste bags
learningOutcomes: Keep a waste bag to a weight that can be lifted and carried safely by one person.
Remove a full bag from a bin using a method that protects the back and the hands.
Dispose of a bag at an outside bin by placing it by hand, never by throwing it.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the load manageable
instructionSections.body: A full bag is often the heaviest thing a cleaner lifts on a route. Keep each bag to a weight you can carry comfortably, with a clear view ahead. If a bag is very heavy, split it into two smaller bags or use the bin's wheels rather than heaving it. Do not overfill a bin, because a heavy bag is harder to pull out and more likely to split.

instructionSections.heading: Removing a bag from a bin
instructionSections.body: Tie the bag closed before you move it. Tip the bin onto its side and draw the bag out, keeping your back straight and bending at the knees. If the bag sticks because a vacuum has formed inside the bin, stop and ask the site contact whether small air holes can be added to that bin. Do not alter a bin yourself, because it may belong to the building.

instructionSections.heading: Getting bags into the outside bin
instructionSections.body: Never throw a bag from a distance. Walk up to the outside bin, lift the lid, and place the bag inside by hand. Do not lean into the bin or stand on its edge. Never press waste down with a hand or a foot. If the bin needs compacting, use a tool made for the job rather than a body part, because sharp items can be hidden in the waste.

lessons.title: Filling spray bottles with three dilution methods
learningOutcomes: Fill a spray bottle using a dilution control system, a pre-measured pack, or a measuring cup.
Set the strength of a bottle from the product label and the manufacturer's directions.
Label and check each bottle before it goes into use.

instructionSections.heading: Why the fill method matters
instructionSections.body: Solution strength decides how well a product works and how safe it is to use. A bottle made up too weak may leave residue or fail to disinfect. A bottle made up too strong can damage surfaces and leave a film. The label and the manufacturer's directions set the strength. The fill method is a reliable way to deliver that strength.

instructionSections.heading: Using a dilution control system
instructionSections.body: Switch on the water supply and remove the trigger sprayer from the bottle. Place the bottle under the fill tub, select the product, and press the solution button. Release it when the bottle is full. The system mixes the product and water. Fit the trigger sprayer back and label the bottle.

instructionSections.heading: Using pre-measured packs
instructionSections.body: Remove the trigger, fill the bottle with water and leave room for the pack. Open the pack and add its contents to the water. Replace the trigger and check that the pack matches the product written on the bottle's label.

instructionSections.heading: Measuring with a cup
instructionSections.body: Take off the trigger, add water to the bottle, leaving space for the chemical. Measure the amount the label gives into a cup, pour it into the bottle, and replace the trigger. Mix by gently turning the bottle. Do not shake a full bottle.

lessons.title: Closing a waste route and resetting the kit
learningOutcomes: Confirm that every full bag has reached its collection point before closing a route.
Return and reset the kit so it is ready for the next visit.
Record shortages and missed areas on the job sheet.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing is part of the job
instructionSections.body: A route is not complete until the kit is back in the storage room and set up for next time. Leftover waste, dirty cloths and empty bottles left in corridors create hazards and slow the next shift. Close the route in the same order each time, so nothing is missed.

instructionSections.heading: Bringing the kit back
instructionSections.body: Empty the collection bin at the designated point, check that no waste is left inside, and wipe its outside. Return the tote and the tools to storage. Put used cloths into the laundry basket or hang them to dry, as the site rules say.

instructionSections.heading: Resetting for next time
instructionSections.body: Refill spray bottles, fit spare liners in each bin on the list, and check that the drop sheet and scoop are present. Note any shortages on the job sheet. A kit that is ready at the start of the route is what makes the next route quick.

lessons.title: Planning the dusting sequence from high points down
learningOutcomes: Explain why high points are dusted before lower surfaces.
Plan a dusting route that uses each tool once per pass.
Walk a room in one direction so that no surface is dusted twice.

instructionSections.heading: Why order matters
instructionSections.body: Dust that falls from a high surface lands on work you have already finished. Working from a room's highest point downward, and from the far side back toward the entry, keeps completed areas clean and stops you from covering the same ground twice. The order is a method, not a preference.

instructionSections.heading: Sequencing the tools
instructionSections.body: Begin at the storage room with protective equipment on. Take the extension duster first for the high work, then return to collect the cloths, the brush and the polish for desk-level work. Going back and forth costs time, so plan the sequence to use each tool once per pass.

instructionSections.heading: Moving through the space
instructionSections.body: Walk the room in one direction, moving between rows and cubicles in short passes. Watch ceiling corners, light fittings, ledges and sills as you go. Finish with the lower surfaces and the floor-level furniture, then return the tools to storage.

lessons.title: Dusting desks, shelves and office seating
learningOutcomes: Dust fabric and leather seating from the top down using the right cloth or mitt.
Dust a desk lamp safely and return it to its exact position.
Apply furniture polish only when the client has asked for it, and only with the grain.

instructionSections.heading: Fabric and leather seating
instructionSections.body: Dust chairs and sofas with a cloth, a mitt, or a wand. Begin at the upper edge of the back and the arms, and work down to the seat face. Keep strokes in one direction so that the fabric nap wears evenly. Do not press so hard that the surface is marked.

instructionSections.heading: Desk lamps
instructionSections.body: A lamp may still be warm from use, so check it before you touch it. Dust from the top down with a cloth or mitt, lift the base to clean underneath, and set the lamp back exactly where it was.

instructionSections.heading: Desk tops and shelves
instructionSections.body: Desk tops and shelves are usually solid timber or laminate. Dust the open areas of a desk without moving papers. On shelves, work from the top shelf to the bottom and from the back forward. Remove items only where you must, wipe the shelf, and put each item back in its original place.

instructionSections.heading: Polish and client requests
instructionSections.body: Apply furniture polish only when the client has asked for it. Apply it to a cloth rather than directly onto the surface, and wipe along the grain of the wood. Polish left on a surface attracts dust, so use it sparingly.

lessons.title: Dusting horizontal blinds without leaving streaks
learningOutcomes: Set a horizontal blind into the correct position for dusting both faces of each slat.
Dust the room-facing and window-facing sides of the slats in a planned sequence.
Check a blind at an angle and correct any dust line that remains.

instructionSections.heading: Why blinds need a set method
instructionSections.body: Horizontal slats collect dust on both faces. A single pass leaves a line on the face you missed, which shows as a streak once light hits the blind. Dust both faces of every slat in a planned sequence so each face is covered once.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up the blind
instructionSections.body: Lower the blind fully. Angle the slats so they face slightly downward, into the room. Use a short-handled duster, static or microfiber, since a long handle makes the slats harder to control.

instructionSections.heading: The two passes
instructionSections.body: First, dust the room-facing side in one sweep, beginning at the top rail and moving downward, working across the width as you go. Second, ease the bottom rail away from the window, turn the slats the other way using the tilting control, and dust the window-facing side from the bottom rail upward. Angle the slats before each pass so the duster meets every face square-on.

instructionSections.heading: Why streaks form and how to catch them
instructionSections.body: A streak appears when a face is skipped, or when a slat is dusted in the wrong direction and dust rolls onto the next slat. After finishing, look at the blind from a slight angle. If a line is visible, go back over that slat with the duster.

lessons.title: Dusting high points, walls and vents
learningOutcomes: Choose the right tool to reach ceilings, walls and vents.
Dust a painted wall, working downward, using a flat mop head and its pad, changing the pad when it is loaded.
Dust vents in line with their slats, and report any vent that cannot be reached safely.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a tool for height
instructionSections.body: An extension duster lets you reach high surfaces from the floor. For painted walls, a flat mop fitted with a microfiber pad covers more area per pass than a duster does. Where dust is heavy or high up, a backpack vacuum fitted with a brush head, held on a long wand, lifts the dust away rather than moving it along.

instructionSections.heading: Walls
instructionSections.body: Adjust the mop so its head reaches the upper edge of the wall while the handle sits at a comfortable angle. Start beside the ceiling and draw the mop down in one vertical stroke to the skirting, then shift sideways and draw it up again. When you meet an obstacle, step around it with the mop and carry on to the upper edge. Keep working across the wall until the whole surface is covered, and swap the pad once it is visibly loaded.

instructionSections.heading: Vents
instructionSections.body: Fit a microfiber duster to a telescopic pole, or use a static duster that extends. Adjust the length so it reaches each vent. Sweep along the line of the vent's slats, so dust is carried along rather than pushed back into the grille. A heavily soiled vent may need a backpack vacuum with a brush head instead.

instructionSections.heading: Height and footing
instructionSections.body: Never stand on furniture, chairs or desks to reach a high point. Check what rests on the upper face of each shelf before you dust, so that nothing is knocked down onto you or the floor. If a high point is beyond the reach of your tools, do not improvise a platform. Report it to the site contact so that a safe method of access can be arranged.

lessons.title: Laundering dusters and cloths between routes
learningOutcomes: Wash microfiber dusters and cloths at the dose the label gives, working them by hand.
Clean a static duster by submerging its head and spinning off the water.
Keep cloths from different zones apart so that none crosses between zones.

instructionSections.heading: Why cloth care matters
instructionSections.body: A dirty duster does not remove dust. It moves dust from one surface to the next. Clean dusters and cloths after each route so that the next surfaces are not contaminated. Keep cloths for different zones apart, so a cloth used in a washroom never reaches a desk.

instructionSections.heading: Washing by hand
instructionSections.body: Half-fill a bucket with warm water, then add a neutral cleaner or laundry detergent at the dose the label gives. Push the sleeves and cloths through the solution with your hands. Remove each one, rinse it in clean warm water, and squeeze out the water. For a static duster, submerge the head, lift it and move it up and down gently, then squeeze and spin off the water before hanging it by the handle.

instructionSections.heading: Drying and storing
instructionSections.body: Dry cloths and duster sleeves fully before you store them, since damp fibres can develop an odour. Fold microfiber cloths in quarters while in use, and store clean ones in a clean container away from chemicals.

lessons.title: Dusting safety: footing, eyes and dust exposure
learningOutcomes: Choose eye protection and, where dust is heavy, a fitted dust mask before dusting.
Reach high points from a stable floor position without standing on furniture.
Identify loose or unstable items and report them rather than moving them.

instructionSections.heading: Eyes and breathing
instructionSections.body: Wear eye protection while dusting, because dust and debris can fall from above. When dust is heavy, such as in a storeroom that has not been cleaned for some time, add a dust mask. A mask protects only if it fits the face, so check the seal before you start.

instructionSections.heading: Footing and reaching
instructionSections.body: Do not stand on chairs, desks or furniture to reach. Use an extension tool and keep both feet on a stable floor. Watch for cables and items on the floor as you move between desks.

instructionSections.heading: Items on shelves
instructionSections.body: Look at what rests on the upper face of shelves and cabinets before you dust. Heavy or fragile items can fall when a shelf is touched. If an item looks unsafe to move, leave it, then ask for help or report it to the site contact.

instructionSections.heading: Recording near misses
instructionSections.body: If something nearly falls or you nearly lose your footing, record it with its location so the site can address it. A near miss recorded early is far cheaper to fix than an injury.

lessons.title: Washroom finishing order and standard
learningOutcomes: Set out the washroom in the correct working order so that finished surfaces are not re-soiled.
Describe what a finished washroom should look and smell like before you sign it off.
Explain why the floor is left until last and why drains are run with water at the end.

instructionSections.heading: Why the order matters in a washroom
instructionSections.body: A washroom is judged quickly. Users notice odour first, then residue on the taps, streaks on the mirror and dust on the high points. Most of these faults come from doing the work in the wrong order. If you wipe a basin and then dust a ceiling vent above it, the falling dust lands on the clean basin. If you mop before you have finished the fixtures, splashes and drips land on a floor you have just cleaned. A fixed sequence lets each surface be finished once, with the dirty work done before the clean work.

instructionSections.heading: Set up and restock before you touch a surface
instructionSections.body: Begin by stocking the consumables: toilet paper, paper towel, soap and sanitiser. Replace the bag in the bin and remove any waste. Doing this first means you are not reaching back into the washroom with soiled gloves after you have cleaned the fixtures. Carry the supplies in on a caddy so the chemicals you need are within reach. Put out a 'cleaning in progress' sign or a wet floor sign by the door before you begin, so people know the room is being serviced.

instructionSections.heading: Dust high, clean wet, end with the floor
instructionSections.body: Work from the high points down. Reach vents and fittings with an extension duster on vents, light fittings, the tops of partitions and the corners where cobwebs collect. Then move to the basin and counter, cleaning the bowl and the surrounding surfaces with a cloth that has been wetted with an approved cleaner. Polish the mirror and the taps last, because the wet work will mark them. Clean the toilet exterior, seat, hinges, flush control and the base, then the interior of the bowl. Clean the touchpoints, meaning door handles, dispenser buttons and light switches, before the floor. The floor is the final stage, so that anything that falls during the earlier work is caught and removed.

instructionSections.heading: Drains and the finished standard
instructionSections.body: Floor drains that are not used regularly can lose the water seal in their trap, which lets odour rise into the room. Run clean water through each floor drain once the job is complete to keep the seal in place. After that, check the finished washroom against the standard: no dust or cobwebs on vents, corners, partitions or lights; no residue on the hinges, flush control or the base of the toilet; mirrors clear of streaks; dispensers full; and no odour. If any of these checks fails, correct it before you leave.

lessons.title: Break area reset: sequence, touchpoints and floor
learningOutcomes: Sequence the break-area clean so that surfaces are finished once and not re-soiled by later work.
Identify the touchpoints and the food-contact areas that need attention in every break-area visit.
Carry out the floor stage correctly, including moving furniture and protecting the finished floor.

instructionSections.heading: Think about how food and people use the room
instructionSections.body: A break room collects food residue, crumbs, spills and handprints. Cabinets, appliance doors and the sink take the most soil from food handling, while light switches, door handles and the fridge handle take the most contact. Plan the clean around those two patterns. The work is not only about looking clean. Food residue left on cabinet faces or in the sink basket attracts pests and odour, so those areas need the same care as the floor.

instructionSections.heading: Start with the waste and the consumables
instructionSections.body: Before you wipe anything, empty the bin. Take out the full bag, then seat a new liner snugly over the rim so it stays put when waste is dropped in. Refill paper towel, hand soap and any other consumables. Doing this first stops food waste from dropping onto surfaces you have already cleaned.

instructionSections.heading: Work the room in a steady loop
instructionSections.body: Move through the room in one direction so that you never walk back over finished work. Start on the far side from the exit and work toward the door. Dust the high surfaces first with an extension duster, then change to a dry cloth for the lower dusting. At the sink, sanitiser goes on a sanitiser to one cloth and wipe the cabinet fronts, handles, the counter and the splashback, then rinse the cloth and wipe any overspray off nearby walls and objects. Move on to the touchpoints. Clean the fridge, dishwasher and microwave exteriors, and the exterior of the stove, using the cloth colour set for those zones.

instructionSections.heading: Polish the sink and the floor
instructionSections.body: Polish the sink last, because the splashes from the earlier work will mark it. A stainless steel sink can be polished with a steel-appropriate product, and a glass cleaner can be used on the taps and the chrome around the sink. Once the upper zones are finished, move the furniture out of the way of the mop and the vacuum. Move the floor mats out of the area and set up a wet floor sign by each entrance. Clear chairs away from the tables so that the floor under and around them can be reached. Begin on the far side and mop back toward the exit, so you never step onto the section you have just washed. Once the floor has dried, remove the sign and return the mats and chairs to their positions.

lessons.title: Microwave interior and exterior care
learningOutcomes: Describe the common microwave types and finishes you will meet on site.
Clean the interior from the top down, removing the turntable or cook tray for separate washing.
Clean the exterior and controls without letting liquid reach the vents or the control panel.

instructionSections.heading: Know what you are cleaning
instructionSections.body: Microwaves in workplaces come as over-the-range units, built-in units and countertop units. Their finishes are usually painted enamel or polished steel. The finish sets which cloth and cleaner you use: enamel tolerates a general cleaner well, while stainless steel should be wiped along the grain and never scoured. Before you start, look for vents, a control panel and any removable tray. Those features tell you where liquid must not go and what needs to be taken out.

instructionSections.heading: Interior: top down, then remove and wash the tray
instructionSections.body: Lift out the turntable or cook tray first and clean it on its own, resting it on paper towel while you work. Then apply cleaner to a cloth or spray the interior surfaces directly, and wipe from the ceiling down the sides and back. Finish with the cavity floor, collecting loose crumbs and tipping them into the bin so they do not drop onto the tray you have just cleaned. Clean the interior of the door and the door seal. For baked-on spots, apply product, let it sit briefly to soften, then loosen and wipe. Do not force a scraper against the interior lining.

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, controls and returning it to use
instructionSections.body: Use a cloth dampened with cleaner, not a soaked one, on the control buttons, the door handle and the door frame. Spray the cloth, never the controls or the vents. Wipe the exterior of the body and the top, then dry the surfaces that have been wet. Replace the tray in its correct position before the unit is switched on. Check the interior has no smell of cleaner, because a residue can taint food that is heated afterwards.

lessons.title: Stainless steel: grain-aware cleaning and polishing
learningOutcomes: Tell a brushed stainless steel surface from a polished one and choose the method that suits it.
Clean stainless steel with the grain, starting with the gentlest method and stepping up only as needed.
Apply a polish evenly, then buff it off without leaving marks.

instructionSections.heading: Why stainless steel needs its own method
instructionSections.body: Stainless steel withstands corrosion and rust, which makes it a common choice for appliances, lift doors, sinks and water fountains. Its protective layer depends on the surface being kept clean. Fingerprints, food films, and hard-water deposits left on the surface can dull it or start discolouration if they are not removed. The main risk is not the soil itself but the damage done while removing it, which is why the method should start gently and only step up when needed.

instructionSections.heading: Find the finish and the grain
instructionSections.body: Stainless steel has several finishes. The one most often met in buildings is a brushed finish, which shows fine lines running in one direction. Those lines are the grain. A polished finish looks more like a mirror and shows marks more clearly. Before you start, run your eye along the surface in a low light and find the line of the grain. Every wipe, including the final buff, should follow that direction. Wiping across the grain leaves fine scratches that stay visible.

instructionSections.heading: Start gently: glass cleaner first
instructionSections.body: For light soil, use glass cleaner on a blue cloth and move along the grain until the metal is dry. Work across the whole surface before you move on. A lint-free cloth gives the best finish and does not leave fibres behind. Stop here if the surface is clean.

instructionSections.heading: Step up: mild detergent, then polish
instructionSections.body: For tougher soil, dilute a gentle detergent of near-neutral pH, roughly 7 to 8, in a spray bottle according to the maker's instructions. Dampen a cloth with it rather than soaking the metal, and wipe along the grain. Dry straight away with a second dry microfiber cloth, still moving with the grain. Only once the metal is dry should polish go on. Put a small amount on a clean cloth, work it along the grain with light overlapping strokes, and check that the film is even. Follow the polish label for the amount and how long to leave it before buffing.

lessons.title: Dust mopping hard floors and removing dry soil
learningOutcomes: Describe the parts of a dust mop and fit or change a head without contaminating the clean side.
Dust mop a room in controlled passes, gathering dust without lifting it back into the air.
Clean the dust mop's head after use and return it to storage ready for the next job.

instructionSections.heading: Why dust mopping comes before wet cleaning
instructionSections.body: Dry soil such as grit, hair and crumbs is abrasive when it is pushed around on a wet floor. Removing it first means the wet clean lifts only the film and marks, not grit that scratches the surface. Dust mopping is the standard first pass for hard floors, and it should be done before any mop water is used.

instructionSections.heading: Heads, fastenings and the clean side
instructionSections.body: Dust mop heads fasten to the frame in several ways: a zip, ties, a slot pocket, snaps, or a breakaway fitting. The head should be changed when it is full of soil or has lost its ability to hold dust. For a zip-fastened head, open the zip, draw the frame out of the soiled head, and bag that head for laundering. Thread the frame into a fresh head and close the zip. For a flat-style dust pad, the pad is peeled from the holder and a new one is pressed on, so the hook-and-loop backing grips. Keep the clean head in a clean bag until it is needed.

instructionSections.heading: The dust mopping pass
instructionSections.body: Remove floor mats before you start. Start in a corner and keep the head on the floor the whole time. Walk backwards with an even, steady push, moving across the room in overlapping passes. Each pass should be a few centimetres over the previous one so no strip is missed. Push the dust into a pile near the centre of the room. Lift the head only at the end to shake it lightly into the pile, then sweep the pile into a dust pan with a broom and empty it into the bin.
