Work carefully: lifting the head and swinging it up throws dust back into the air.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning the head after the job
instructionSections.body: Take the dust mop back to the cleaning cupboard before cleaning it. Work a stiff bristle brush through the head above a bin so the dust drops in. A backpack vacuum can draw the dust out instead. Do not shake a dirty head in an occupied area. Once clean, hang or store the head so that it cannot touch the floor, and let it dry if it has been damp.

lessons.title: Wet mopping with a bucket and wringer
learningOutcomes: Prepare the floor and the solution so the wet mopping starts with a clean, dry-soil-free surface.
Wring and load the mop so that the floor is damp, not flooded.
Tackle corners and edges before the open floor, working toward the exit so that no finished floor is walked on.

instructionSections.heading: Clear the floor before the water goes down
instructionSections.body: Wet mopping only works on a floor that has already been dust mopped or vacuumed. Before the bucket comes in, lift any mats and scrape off adhesive labels and chewing gum with a putty knife, held at a shallow angle so the floor is not gouged. Set out wet floor signs by each room entrance so people know the floor is wet and do not walk onto it while it dries.

instructionSections.heading: Make up the solution and wring the mop
instructionSections.body: Fill the bucket with cold water to the marked level, then add pH-neutral floor detergent at the dose on the product label. Do not add more than the label allows, because excess product leaves a film. Dunk the head, then run it through the wringer and press the handle down to squeeze out the surplus. The head should be damp, not dripping. A head that is too wet floods the floor, and one that is too dry lifts less soil.

instructionSections.heading: The mopping stroke and order
instructionSections.body: Stand upright and keep your back neutral. Avoid twisting at the waist. Mop the corners and edges before the open floor, using the head to reach into the angles. Fill the open floor by moving the mop in a looping pattern that carries you backward toward the exit. Keep the bucket on the unwashed side and behind your body, so that you never step onto a section you have just mopped. Overlap each stroke by a short distance so that no strip is missed. Re-wring the mop whenever the head is no longer damp, and replace the bucket water once it looks soiled, because dirty water puts soil back on the floor.

instructionSections.heading: Finish, dry and tidy up
instructionSections.body: When the last area is done, take the bucket and wringer back to the cleaning cupboard rather than leaving them in the room. Remove the wet floor signs only when the floor has dried. A floor that still shows a sheen or a streak has not been cleaned properly, so check the finish before you move on. If the floor shows a film, a scrub or a recoat may be needed, and that should be reported to the supervisor rather than attempted with the wet mop alone.

lessons.title: Flat-mop microfiber system with a charging bucket
learningOutcomes: Load a charging bucket with the right amount of solution and the right number of pads.
Attach a pad to a flat mop, then use it so that the pad stays evenly damp.
Use the flat mop in the same order as a bucket mop, with the pad replaced when it is spent.

instructionSections.heading: What the flat system does differently
instructionSections.body: A flat mop carries a microfiber pad on a holder, and the pads are wetted in a charging bucket rather than a wringer. Microfiber pads trap soil in their fibres, so a clean pad lifts more soil with less solution. The system also means fewer hands-on steps: the cleaner does not twist the mop head by hand. The method is only as good as the pad, so the pad must be clean and the charging bucket must be set up correctly every time.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up the charging bucket
instructionSections.body: Add cold water to the charging bucket in the amount suited to the number of pads being used, following the marks on the bucket. Add pH-neutral floor detergent at the label dose. Load the pads with the white backing uppermost, so the microfiber side sits in the solution. Close the lid and fasten each flap so nothing spills in transit. Grip the bucket by its handle and move it firmly from side to side so the pads take up the solution evenly. Set the bucket down and open the lid when you are ready to mop.

instructionSections.heading: Mopping with the flat head
instructionSections.body: Set a telescopic handle to a height that suits you. Lower the holder into the bucket to take up a damp pad. The pad should be damp, not dripping. Stand upright, tackle the corners and edges before the open floor, then fill the open floor with a steady fanning motion, moving backward toward the exit. Keep the bucket on the unfinished side, behind you, so that you never walk on a section you have washed. Overlap each pass by a short distance. When the pad is saturated or grey, replace it, rather than rinsing it on the floor.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing the flat mop job
instructionSections.body: When the last area is complete, take the flat mop and the charging bucket back to the cleaning cupboard. Take out any unused pads, rinse them, squeeze them, and hang them up to air dry. Dirty pads go into a laundry bag. Dry the holder with a cloth. Rinse the bucket inside and out, dry it, and store it in its marked place. Remove the wet floor signs once the floor has dried.

lessons.title: Changing mop heads and pads, and treating heel marks
learningOutcomes: Remove a dirty bucket mop head and fit a clean one, using the clamp type on the handle.
Remove a microfiber pad from a flat mop holder and attach a clean one without contamination.
Choose a method for heel marks that does not scratch the floor, and test it before full use.

instructionSections.heading: Why heads and pads are changed, not just rinsed
instructionSections.body: A mop head that is full of soil or has dried with residue will put that soil back onto the floor during the next room. Changing it between rooms, or when it is visibly soiled, keeps the clean floor clean. The change must be done in a way that does not contaminate the clean head or the handle. Gloves are required for every change, because the head is in direct contact with the soil and the cleaner's hands.

instructionSections.heading: Bucket mop heads: the clamp types
instructionSections.body: Bucket mop heads are held on the handle by one of several clamp types. Some use a jaw collar that tightens around the head. Others use a spring-loaded bar that is pressed against the handle, a wing-nut bracket, or a locking wheel that holds a plastic bar against the head. Before changing a head, identify the clamp type. Loosen the clamp, slide the soiled head off, and bag it for laundering. Seat the new head where the clamp grips it and tighten until it is held firm. Give the head a tug to check it does not slip.

instructionSections.heading: Flat mop pads: the hook-and-loop attachment
instructionSections.body: Flat mop pads attach to the holder with a hook-and-loop backing. To take off a soiled pad, pin the pad down with one foot and steady the holder with the other, then lift the holder so the backing lets go. Once it has come loose, turn the holder a quarter turn and use its tip to lift the pad clear, then bag it. To fit a fresh pad, lay it flat and press the holder squarely onto it so the hook surface grips. Check that the pad is square before use.

instructionSections.heading: Dealing with heel marks
instructionSections.body: Heel marks are black scuffs left by shoes on vinyl and similar floors. They are usually lifted with a gentle method first, and the mop head should be the first tool used. Clip a white, non-abrasive pad onto the head to lift scuffs during the wet pass. As an alternative, work a soft pad over the scuffs before the wet pass begins. Test any method in a small area first, and check that it does not dull or mark the floor. Do not use a harsh scouring pad on a floor that has a sealed finish, because it can remove the finish. If the marks do not lift, report the floor to the supervisor.

lessons.title: Emptying, rinsing and storing a mop bucket
learningOutcomes: Drain and flush a bucket and wringer at a sluice without spilling dirty water on the floor.
Lift a heavy bucket safely using the handle and the rim, with the knees bent.
Store the bucket and wringer clean and dry in the cleaning cupboard.

instructionSections.heading: Why the bucket needs a proper finish
instructionSections.body: A bucket that is left with dirty water, grit or product residue in it becomes the source of the soil you thought you had removed. The next time it is filled, the residue dissolves into fresh solution and goes back onto the floor. The finish of the job is therefore part of the cleaning, not an extra. Empty the water, rinse the bucket and wringer, and dry them before storage.

instructionSections.heading: Empty at a sluice, not a corridor
instructionSections.body: Take the bucket to a sluice or a utility sink, which is designed to take dirty water. Remove the wringer first and rinse it under cold water, wiping off soil and product residue. Leave the wringer to one side, clear of the working zone, so that it cannot collect dirt in transit. Pour the water out at the sink, never onto the floor.

instructionSections.heading: Lifting safely
instructionSections.body: Use your legs, not your back. Keep one hand on the handle and the other on the rear lip of the base, bring the load close to your body, and tip it into the sink from the back edge. If the bucket has a drain tap in its lower back, open the tap into the sink instead of lifting the bucket at all. For a heavy bucket, ask for help rather than straining.

instructionSections.heading: Rinse, dry and store
instructionSections.body: Run a hose from the sink tap into the bucket, working from the rear to the front so the water carries grime away from you. Rinse the sides as well. Dry the bucket inside and out with a cloth, drop the wringer back in, and store the bucket in the designated area of the cleaning cupboard. Leave the bucket upright and clear of the floor to dry.

lessons.title: Stairwell dry removal and damp cleaning
learningOutcomes: Choose between a backpack vacuum and a dust mop for dry soil on steps and landings.
Damp clean steps and landings using a flat mop pad, moving from the top down and keeping a clear exit.
Manage the work area so that no one is at risk of a slip or fall on a wet tread.

instructionSections.heading: Stairs carry soil in a different way
instructionSections.body: Stairwells collect grit, leaves and dust on the treads and the landing edges, and the nosing of each step is where most of it sits. Dry soil on steps is best taken up before any wet work, so that the damp pad does not turn it into a film. The main safety issue is that stairs are used on the move, so the cleaning must be arranged so people can still pass safely while the work is done.

instructionSections.heading: Dry removal: vacuum first, dust mop as the fallback
instructionSections.body: A backpack vacuum is the quickest tool for dry soil on stairs, because the wand reaches the nosing of each tread. Where a backpack is not available, a dust mop can do the job, but it is slower. With either tool, work from the top landing down. For a vacuum, set the nozzle at the outer edge of each tread and sweep across to the far side before stepping up. For a dust mop, walk the head across each tread in a steady motion, keeping the head on the surface, and gather the soil into a pile on the landing.

instructionSections.heading: Damp cleaning using a flat mop
instructionSections.body: After the dry work, set out a wet floor sign by each entrance to the stairwell and lay one clean, damp pad on every landing, drawn out of the charging bucket. Carry a small liner in a back pocket for used pads. Start on the top landing, mopping the corners and edges and then the open area. Then work down the flight standing on a finished tread, reach the next tread with the damp pad, drawing it across the width and then toward the nosing. Swap the dirty pad for the clean one waiting on the landing, and drop the dirty pad into the liner. Pass the liner down to the following landing, and repeat until the base is reached.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing the stairwell
instructionSections.body: Once the stairwell is complete and the treads and landings are dry, remove the signs from the entrances. Carry the flat mop and bucket back to storage, put the soiled pads in the laundry basket, then rinse and dry the bucket before storing it. Check the nosings and the handrails for any remaining film, and report a persistent film to the supervisor.

lessons.title: Vacuuming rooms with a backpack or upright machine
learningOutcomes: Set up a backpack or upright vacuum safely, including harness fit and cord handling.
Vacuum a room in a fixed direction so that corners, edges and under-desk areas are reached.
Apply the site's door-status marking and outlet-selection rules correctly, and leave each room as the client expects.

instructionSections.heading: Check the machine before you plug it in
instructionSections.body: Start in the cleaning cupboard with the machine. Inspect the collection bag or bin, the filter set and the cord. Look along the cord for cuts, scrapes, or bare conductors, and check the plug for damage. If a plug has lost its earth pin, do not use the machine; tag it and report it. A backpack machine should be fitted to the body before you start. Adjust the harness so the weight sits on the hips rather than the shoulders, and clip the tools onto the waist belt so they do not drag.

instructionSections.heading: Route and direction
instructionSections.body: Work in a consistent direction through each room so that you do not walk back over finished areas. A counter-clockwise route from the door works well for most rooms. Enter the room, turn right as you go in, and work around the perimeter back to the door. Vacuum the corners, edges and the areas under desks as you pass them, and push chairs in to the desk so that the floor beneath them is reached. Then clear the centre of the room with overlapping passes.

instructionSections.heading: Power, cords and outlets
instructionSections.body: Use the outlets that the site has identified for vacuuming. Many sites mark these with a coloured dot so that they are not confused with outlets that power equipment. Never disconnect a computer or similar equipment to free an outlet. Let the cord hang loosely so the plug is never under strain, and disconnect by gripping the plug body, not the cord. Plan the cord route so that you do not cross a path where people walk.

instructionSections.heading: Bins, furniture and mats
instructionSections.body: Look for a bin that has not been emptied. If one is found, lift it, vacuum underneath, and return it to the exact spot it came from. For furniture that is upholstered, use the upholstery tool with the hose, and spot clean only where the soil is visible. Vacuum the walk-off mats after the room, rolling them up and vacuuming underneath before you put them back.

instructionSections.heading: Hallways and door status
instructionSections.body: In a corridor, keep your back upright and hold the wand close to your body, sweeping it left and right as you walk ahead. Continue until the full width is covered, then disconnect and move on. Switch lights off once a room is complete. Door status is recorded with a colour dot placed on the middle hinge. A red dot means that the door stays locked before, during or after vacuuming. A green dot means that the door is shut without a lock afterwards. A yellow dot indicates the door is left as it was found. Follow the dot shown on each door, and do not change a door's state without the dot telling you to.

instructionSections.heading: Returning the machine
instructionSections.body: Replace the bag when it is about two-thirds full, so that suction is not lost. When the job is finished, return the machine and attachments to the cleaning cupboard. Check the bag and filters, then wipe the exterior of the machine, wind the cord neatly, and store the machine in its assigned place.

lessons.title: Back-pack vacuum filters, muffler and bag care
learningOutcomes: Identify the bag, micro-filter, dome filter, sound muffler and cap in a backpack vacuum.
Service each filter and the muffler at the interval the site sets, and reassemble them in the right order.
Recognise when a filter or bag has reached the end of its life and tag it for replacement.

instructionSections.heading: What filtration does for the machine
instructionSections.body: A backpack vacuum only performs as well as its airflow allows. A clogged bag, a full cloth filter or a dirty dome filter restricts that airflow, so the machine loses suction and the dust it fails to trap goes back into the room. Regular service of the filters and the muffler keeps the suction at the level the machine was built for. The schedule below is a general guide; the machine maker's manual and the site's rules set the actual intervals.

instructionSections.heading: The parts and how they sit together
instructionSections.body: Remove the twist cap on the upper part of the machine first. Under it, a paper micro-filter bag sits inside a micro-cloth filter. The cloth filter can be shaken out and washed, and the paper bag is discarded when full. Lower in the machine is a dome filter that contains a foam medium, and a sound muffler sits at the bottom. The muffler reduces noise and is also a filter in its own right, so it should be rinsed as part of the service.

instructionSections.heading: Routine service
instructionSections.body: Empty the micro-cloth filter by shaking it into a bin each time the bag is changed. Hand wash it once a month and let it air dry completely before refitting. Once a week, clean the foam in the dome filter and rinse the sound muffler, then let both dry before refitting. Replace any part that is torn, hardened or no longer holds dust. Before refitting, clear loose dust from the housing with a microfiber cloth, so none of it reaches the new bag.

instructionSections.heading: Reassembly order
instructionSections.body: Start with the dome filter and muffler, then slot a fresh paper bag into the cloth filter and seat that pair in place, finishing with the cap. Wipe the exterior of the housing with a dampened microfiber cloth, leave it to dry, and test the machine on a short run before it goes into use. Any machine that loses suction after service should be tagged and checked by the supervisor.

lessons.title: Walk-off mats and elevator door tracks
learningOutcomes: Vacuum a walk-off mat using a set pass pattern so that the soil is drawn out from the full mat.
Describe the lock-out steps that must be in place before any work near lift doors and tracks.
Clean lift door tracks with the right tool and product, and stop if the lift cannot be made safe to work near.

instructionSections.heading: Walk-off mats collect most of the entrance soil
instructionSections.body: A walk-off mat at an entrance traps grit and moisture before it reaches the remainder of the building. If the mat is not vacuumed, the soil works its way into the floor covering beyond it. The mat should be vacuumed on a regular schedule, and its pattern of passes matters: a single pass leaves soil in the matting. A set number of passes in each direction, starting from the edge where people step on, draws the soil up from the full depth of the mat.

instructionSections.heading: The pass pattern for a walk-off mat
instructionSections.body: Use an upright or backpack vacuum. Begin at the edge people step onto and run ten strokes over the first three metres. Follow with five strokes lengthwise and five crosswise. Lift the mat and vacuum the floor beneath it too, since soil collects there.

instructionSections.heading: Lift doors and tracks: confirm lock-out before work
instructionSections.body: Lift door tracks are a place where fingers and tools can be caught when the doors move. Before any work near the doors, the lift must be taken out of service at the site's lock-out point, and the lift should not be called to that floor while work is in progress. Use the site's lock-out procedure and confirm it with the building contact. If the lock-out cannot be confirmed, do not start the work. Do not reach into the door gap, and do not work on the lift's motors, controls or door mechanism. Those are for the lift contractor.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning the tracks
instructionSections.body: With the lift locked out, vacuum the track with a backpack hose and a crevice tool to remove dry grit. Apply an approved track cleaner suited to the metal or coating, work the grooves using the grout brush; wipe away residue with paper towel. Check that no residue is left in the groove. Do not spray cleaner into the door mechanism or the lift's electrical parts. When the track is dry, reinstate the lift according to the site's procedure and confirm it is working before you leave.

lessons.title: Slip, trip and housekeeping priorities
learningOutcomes: Identify slip, trip and housekeeping hazards in a warehouse before cleaning.
Prioritise hazards by their likelihood and the harm they could cause.
Keep walkways clear and escalate hazards that are outside cleaning scope.

instructionSections.heading: Where the slips and trips come from
instructionSections.body: In a warehouse, the common slip and trip hazards are wet or oily floors, loose packaging, cables across walkways, damaged floor edges, pallets left in the path, and uneven surfaces at dock plates and thresholds. Cleaning can add to the problem when water, product or waste is left on the floor. Walk the area before cleaning, and note the hazards you find.

instructionSections.heading: Setting priorities
instructionSections.body: Prioritise hazards by how often people pass them and how serious a fall would be. A wet floor on a main pedestrian route at a loading dock is a higher priority than a small piece of packaging in a quiet corner. Deal with the highest-priority hazards first, and escalate those that you cannot control within your scope, such as damaged racking or a broken dock plate.

instructionSections.heading: Housekeeping limits
instructionSections.body: Housekeeping means keeping the walkways and the work area clear, dry and free of waste. It does not include moving stored goods, clearing racking, or working in traffic aisles without a traffic control plan. Keep clear of any vehicle route, and do not step into the path of moving equipment. Leave the area safe and record what you could not clear.

lessons.title: Approved cleaning equipment and floor compatibility
learningOutcomes: Identify the decision gate for powered cleaning equipment on a warehouse floor.
Recognise when the observed floor or the equipment does not match the authorised plan.
Write a restricted-scope referral that separates observed conditions from unverified ones.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the site and the job records
instructionSections.body: Before any warehouse cleaning starts, review the documented work order, the named supervisor, the risk controls and the site movement plan. Pay particular attention to equipment authorisation and the condition of the surface.

instructionSections.heading: The equipment decision gate
instructionSections.body: Confirm the equipment assignment, the operator's competency, the floor's load rating and its compatibility with the site plan. Compare what you observe with the site's current authorised plan. If the plan and the observed conditions differ, suspend the affected task and document the discrepancy. A large powered scrubber on a surface with an unknown load rating and pedestrian crossover is a case for stopping, not for proceeding.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and referral
instructionSections.body: A cleaner may identify and report hazards, but may not stand in for a traffic controller, a plant isolation officer, an engineer or a hazardous-material specialist. Do not operate unapproved powered equipment on unsuitable flooring. Where the floor or the equipment is outside authority, the work is restricted and referred.

instructionSections.heading: Documentation
instructionSections.body: Record the time, the location, the work-order identifier, what was observed as distinct from what was inferred, the supporting record, the person notified, and any response. Leave the affected area restricted until written authority has been given.

lessons.title: Privacy, security and customer property
learningOutcomes: Explain and apply: privacy, security and customer property

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Overview
instructionSections.body: This lesson develops practical competence in privacy, security and customer property for routine professional cleaning work. Apply the employer’s site procedures and stop if a task falls outside your training or authority.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body: Keep keys and access codes confidential. Secure the premises when leaving, report breakage immediately and avoid handling cash, medication or valuables unless explicitly authorised.

instructionSections.heading: Prepare and verify
instructionSections.body: Treat access codes, keys, addresses, alarm instructions and client information as confidential. Use only approved communication and storage systems. Do not share site details, photographs or client stories on personal messaging or social media.

instructionSections.heading: Perform the work safely and professionally
instructionSections.body: Before moving objects, check whether movement is necessary and permitted. Photograph only where the work order and privacy requirements allow, and frame images to avoid personal documents and identifying details.

instructionSections.heading: Check, record and escalate
instructionSections.body: If property is damaged, missing or unexpectedly unsafe, stop the affected task, protect the area, notify the designated contact promptly and record objective facts. Never conceal damage or attempt unauthorised repair.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

instructionSections.body: Electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In Victoria, PV installation and maintenance is licensed electrical installation work, and PV DC cables may stay live when the power is off. NSW electrical wiring work includes repairing. lessons.title: Customer discovery and site assessment
learningOutcomes: Ask discovery questions that reveal the customer's needs, priorities, constraints and budget range.
Carry out a site assessment that identifies the scope, access, hazards and the surfaces involved.
Record the discovery and assessment so that the quote and the work order match the site.

instructionSections.heading: Discovery before the quote
instructionSections.body: Discovery is a short, structured conversation that finds out what the customer needs and why. Ask what they want done, what they have tried, what matters most to them, when they need it, who will be present, whether there are pets or children, and what they have already decided. Listen for needs the customer has not stated, such as a deadline or a guest arriving. Do not promise a result before you have seen the site. Record the answers in the customer record so that the next person can see them.

instructionSections.heading: Site assessment
instructionSections.body: A site assessment confirms the discovery by looking at the place. Note the size, the number of rooms or surfaces, the access and parking, the condition and finish of surfaces, the soil level, the presence of hazards such as wet floors, height, electrical items, unknown products or unsafe structures, and any restrictions on water, noise, waste or hours. Take photographs only with consent and under the privacy procedure. Record anything that changes the scope, the time or the method.

instructionSections.heading: Match scope to the site
instructionSections.body: Once the assessment is complete, check whether the customer's needs can be met safely and within the business's approved services. If the site needs a different method, a longer time or a referral, say so before the quote is issued. Record the assessment, the scope agreed and any item excluded. A quote built on a site visit is more accurate, and it protects the customer and the business from disputes later.

lessons.title: Customer communication and records
learningOutcomes: Communicate with the customer in writing and by phone so that each message is clear, timely and recorded.
Keep customer records that are accurate, current and held in the approved system.
Handle a change, complaint or query through the approved channel with a record of each step.

instructionSections.heading: Communicate clearly and on time
instructionSections.body: Confirm each booking in writing, with the date, time window, address, scope and any access arrangement. Send a reminder before the job, and tell the customer as soon as there is a change, such as a delay or a clash. Use plain language and avoid promises you cannot keep. When a customer asks a question you cannot answer, say you will check and confirm the answer in writing by a stated time. Keep the tone courteous even when the customer is frustrated.

instructionSections.heading: Keep accurate records
instructionSections.body: A customer record holds the contact details, the service history, the agreed scope, the access arrangements, the preferences and any special requirements. Update the record after each change, and date each update. Do not keep personal notes in unapproved places. Record only the information the business needs to deliver the service, and keep it secure. Where the customer asks to see or change their record, handle the request through the approved channel.

instructionSections.heading: Complaints and changes
instructionSections.body: A complaint or change request is recorded when it is received, with the facts, the customer's words and the date. Pass it to the designated contact, and tell the customer who will respond and when. Do not argue, blame another worker or agree to a refund or remedy without authority. Record the outcome and tell the customer the result in writing. Close the record only when the customer has been told the outcome.

lessons.title: Privacy and customer confidentiality
learningOutcomes: Identify the personal information that a service business collects and holds.
Describe the confidentiality practices that protect that information in daily work.
Explain what to do if personal information is lost, sent to the wrong person or accessed without authority.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as personal information
instructionSections.body: Personal information is information about an identifiable person. In a service business it includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, schedules, access codes, photographs of people or homes, household details, payment details and staff records. Think of anything that would let someone identify or locate a person, or learn about their home, as personal information. Keep it only for the purpose of delivering the service, and only for as long as the business needs it.

instructionSections.heading: Confidentiality in daily work
instructionSections.body: Keep customer and staff information out of conversations, messages and social media that are not part of the job. Do not leave documents or screens visible in a customer's home, and do not discuss one customer's information with another. Use only the approved systems. Lock devices when you leave them. Send information only to the person who needs it, and check the address before you send it. Do not keep copies of personal information on a personal device or account.

instructionSections.heading: Breaches and the privacy position
instructionSections.body: A privacy breach occurs when personal information is lost, sent to the wrong person, or accessed without authority. If it happens, stop the activity that caused it where possible, recover the information if you can, and report it to the designated contact immediately. The business decides on any notification to the customer or the regulator. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner states that the Privacy Act applies to organisations above the $3 million AUD annual turnover threshold, and that small businesses at or below that threshold are generally outside it.

lessons.title: Consent, dignity and boundaries
learningOutcomes: Explain the purpose and limits of consent, dignity and boundaries
Apply the principle to a service-business situation

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level, water-fed pole and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Any work above ground level, or from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted: it needs employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires for the equipment used. instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Learning outcome
By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to obtain consent and preserve dignity while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

Workplace procedure
Introduce yourself and explain the cleaning task in plain language. Confirm the person is comfortable with your presence and the work area; respect refusals and requests for privacy. Follow the authorised service plan and your role boundaries. Do not provide personal care, handle medication, make financial decisions or move mobility aids without permission and training. If consent is unclear or the person appears distressed, pause the task and contact the designated coordinator.

Decision boundaries
Before acting, confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation. If the task exceeds training, consent, safe access or agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others as appropriate, report promptly and document the reason. Never substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

Worked workplace example
A client asks the cleaner to help with medication. The cleaner politely explains that this is outside the cleaning role and contacts the care coordinator through the agreed process.

Guided practical exercise
Role-play a first visit where the client declines bedroom access and requests an out-of-scope personal task. Demonstrate respectful language and documentation.

Assessment and feedback
An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Seeks meaningful consent, respects refusal and maintains the professional scope without coercion. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to communicate respectfully across different needs while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

Workplace procedure
Ask how the person prefers to be addressed and communicate directly with them where appropriate. Use clear short explanations, allow processing time and check understanding without patronising language. Respect language, cultural practices, hearing or vision differences and personal routines. Use approved interpreters or communication supports when required; do not assume family members may receive confidential information. Record agreed preferences only in authorised systems.

A resident cannot hear a spoken warning about a wet floor. The cleaner moves to a visible position, uses the person’s preferred communication method and confirms they understand the temporary route change.

Practise explaining a delayed task to three clients with different communication preferences; obtain consent and document a preference without unnecessary personal details.

Assessment and feedback
An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Adapts communication respectfully, checks understanding and safeguards confidential information. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

Use approved identification and introductions when entering a customer's premises.
Refuse to disclose another client's identity, share keys or access codes, and escalate an identity challenge to the supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction

instructionSections.heading: Prepare and verify
instructionSections.body: Use approved identification and introductions so customers know who is entering their premises. Confirm the correct address, booking and authorised contact before requesting entry.

instructionSections.heading: Perform the work safely and professionally

lessons.title: Client service and complaints for a service business
learningOutcomes: Confirm a booking, its scope, its exclusions and what the client must provide, before the work starts.
Set expectations about the result, the time window and pre-existing defects, and record what was agreed.
Handle a complaint in a fixed order: listen, acknowledge, check the record, offer options within your authority, record the outcome and follow up.

instructionSections.heading: Service starts at the first contact
instructionSections.body: For a service business, the client's experience begins with the first enquiry, not with the first visit. Answer enquiries promptly, and say clearly what you can do, when you can do it and what it will cost. Confirm every booking in writing, with the date, the time window, the address or site, the scope, the package and the list of included and excluded items. Ask open questions about what the client wants to achieve and what problem they are trying to solve. Then ask what the job needs from the client: access to water and power, parking, a gate code, the location of any pets, and any building or strata rules that apply on the day. Most client dissatisfaction comes from expectations that were never stated. A client who knows what is excluded is less likely to be surprised at handover. Keep the language plain, and avoid promising a result you have not yet inspected.

instructionSections.heading: Setting expectations and recording them
instructionSections.body: Expectations need to be agreed before work begins. Explain what a good result looks like for this job and what it cannot achieve. For example, an odour that comes from damp under a floor may not be removed fully by surface cleaning, and an old mark on a wall may stay visible after treatment. Tell the client if the time on site will be longer than expected, and tell them early rather than at the end of the visit. Link this conversation to the condition record taken before work, so that you and the client can point to the same pre-existing defects. Where the client asks for something outside the agreed scope, give a clear price and a clear time before doing it, and confirm the change in writing. At handover, walk the client through the finished areas, point out any limits, and ask them to confirm they are satisfied with the result they can see. Keep a short handover note with the date, the time the job finished and any open point.

instructionSections.heading: Handling a complaint in a fixed order
instructionSections.body: A complaint is a useful signal, and it is also a chance to keep the client. Start by listening without interrupting or correcting the client, even if you think they are mistaken. Acknowledge the inconvenience and the effort the client has taken to raise it, and say you want to sort it out. An apology for the experience is appropriate even before the cause is known, but do not admit fault you have not checked. Next, check the facts against the job record, the condition photos where they were taken, and the booking confirmation. Do not blame the client, the product or another worker. If you do not know the answer, say so and give a time when you will come back with it. Offer options that you have the authority to deliver, such as returning to correct the work, removing a residue at no extra charge, or a partial credit where the work cannot be corrected. Record the complaint with the date, the client's contact details, the detail given, the action agreed and the outcome. Then follow up after the fix, confirm that the client is satisfied, and close the record. If the matter involves injury, damage to property or a claim against the insurance policy, stop negotiating and pass it to the person you have named for escalation.

lessons.title: Customer complaint log and response (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Log every complaint with its date, channel, reference and the customer's words
Check the facts against the job record before writing a response
Record the outcome, follow-up actions, escalation and closing review

instructionSections.heading: Why every complaint is logged
instructionSections.body: A complaint is any expression of dissatisfaction that the business has to respond to, including one made in passing to an employee. A log turns scattered complaints into a record that shows patterns, such as the same service, the same crew or the same kind of job. Log every complaint, including those resolved on the spot. The log protects the customer and the business, because it shows what was said, what was checked and what was agreed.

instructionSections.heading: Facts before response
instructionSections.body: Write the complaint in the customer's words first, before adding your own view. Then check the facts against the job record, the checklist, photos, the quote and any variation. Record what you checked, where you checked it and what it showed. The response should follow those facts. If the facts show the business did not meet the agreed scope, say so plainly and state what will be done. If they show the work met the scope, explain what was done and why, without blame. Do not argue the customer out of their experience. Respond within the time the business sets, using the channel the customer used unless they asked for another.

instructionSections.heading: Outcome, follow-up and escalation
instructionSections.body: Record the outcome agreed with the customer, whether the customer is satisfied, and any follow-up action with an owner and a due date. Escalate complaints that involve injury, property damage, a threat of legal action, or a repeated issue, using the business escalation contact. Record when the complaint was closed and who reviewed it. Review the log each month to look for patterns, and decide which checklist, procedure or training needs to change. Keep the customer's personal information to what the complaint needs, and store it under the business privacy procedure.

lessons.title: Equipment inspection, isolation and fault-response simulation
learningOutcomes: Explain hazards and scope boundaries for equipment fault management
Demonstrate an authorised procedure with appropriate controls

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. instructionSections.heading: Pre-use condition check
instructionSections.body: Inspect the plug, cord, casing, wheels, guards, filters, tanks and attachments according to the equipment manual. Check the site power arrangements and whether inspection tags or other local controls apply. Do not operate damaged equipment.

instructionSections.heading: Set up safely
instructionSections.body: Select the correct machine for the task and floor, maintain clear walkways, manage cords and wet-area hazards, and use manufacturer-approved accessories. Confirm the operator is trained and authorised.

instructionSections.heading: Recognise warning signs
instructionSections.body: Unusual vibration, burning smell, sparking, damaged insulation, leaking liquid, overheating or unexpected shutdown requires immediate cessation. Do not open electrical housings or attempt unauthorised repairs.

instructionSections.heading: Isolate and report
instructionSections.body: Stop operation, disconnect power only when safe, prevent others using the equipment, apply the workplace out-of-service tag/process and notify the responsible person. Follow emergency procedures for smoke, fire or injury.

instructionSections.heading: Return-to-service control
instructionSections.body: Only an authorised competent person may assess or repair equipment. A supervisor confirms the fault is resolved and records clearance before the machine returns to service.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Learning goal and job context: This lesson teaches select equipment for surface and task for routine cleaning work. Start with the actual job scope, site instructions, manufacturer directions and worker training. Never treat a general lesson as authority to perform restricted or specialist work.

Core procedure: Choose a tool based on surface finish, soil type, access, contamination zone and manufacturer instructions. Match vacuum filtration and floor equipment to the material and debris. Use separate tools for sanitary areas and food-contact surfaces; test a new method on an inconspicuous area only when authorised.

Decision-making in the field: Before acting, ask: What is the surface or equipment? What is the soil or hazard? Which product or method is approved? What could harm a person, property or food? If the answer is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.

Worked workplace scenario: A stiff brush would scratch a polished stone vanity. The cleaner selects a soft compatible cloth and reports the remaining deposit.

Guided supervised practice: Compare six surface/soil cards with available brushes, cloths, mops and vacuums; justify each selection and identify two exclusions.

Evidence and feedback: The assessor observes the task and checks whether the learner: matches tools to surfaces and prevents cross-contamination and abrasion. A learner must explain any unsafe choice, correct it and repeat the demonstration. Record observations, required coaching and reassessment rather than awarding competence from attendance alone.

Core procedure: Before use, check power supply, plugs, cords, guards, hoses, wheels, filters, tanks, batteries and accessories as applicable. Confirm inspection tags or site requirements. instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Learning outcome
By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to move, store and maintain equipment safely while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

Workplace procedure
Plan loading routes, lifts, trolley capacity and safe handling before bringing equipment on site. Check wheels, cords, batteries, containers and restraints. Keep clean and contaminated tools separated; segregate bathroom and food-area supplies. Store products upright in labelled containers within approved locked or restricted locations, with SDS accessible. Never block fire equipment, exits or electrical panels. Charge batteries only in authorised areas following manufacturer instructions. Log and isolate faults.

Decision boundaries
Before acting, confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation. If the task exceeds training, consent, safe access or agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others as appropriate, report promptly and document the reason. Never substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

Worked workplace example
A storage cupboard is full and a worker proposes leaving chemicals in a public stairwell. The supervisor rejects the option, secures supplies in an approved location and reports the capacity issue.

Guided practical exercise
Inspect a staged trolley and storeroom with eight faults. Correct safe issues, isolate damaged equipment and write a concise fault report.

Assessment and feedback
An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Demonstrates safe movement, contamination segregation, compliant site storage and fault isolation. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

lessons.title: Water-fed poles and ground-based operations
learningOutcomes: Explain why ground-based methods are the first option in the height hierarchy and where they still carry hazards.
Inspect a water-fed pole system and identify conditions that stop its use.
Apply overhead-line, wind, public-exclusion and runoff controls to a simulated ground-based job.

instructionSections.heading: Why ground-based methods come first
instructionSections.body: A water-fed pole lets a worker clean windows or panels from the ground, so the worker's feet stay on a stable surface. This is why ground-based methods come first in the height hierarchy. A ground-based method is not risk-free, however. The pole is long, often conductive, and can strike overhead services, people or property. It can also fail at its joints or under wind load. The method reduces the need for height; it does not remove the need for planning, an exclusion zone and a stop-work rule.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect the equipment before use
instructionSections.body: Before each job, inspect every pole section, joint, seal, hose, filter and nozzle. Look for cracks, dents, bent sections, worn or missing seals, damaged threads and fittings that do not match. Do not fit attachments that the manufacturer has not approved. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for maximum length, water supply and any detergent. A pole with any defect is removed from service, tagged, and reported.

instructionSections.heading: Overhead electrical lines
instructionSections.body: Conductive poles can contact overhead power lines and transfer current to the operator. Before extending a pole, survey the area above and beside the work for overhead lines, service drops and any structure that could carry electricity. In New South Wales, the SafeWork NSW code (May 2026) sets 4.0 m for handling conductive materials such as scaffolding, roofing, guttering and pipes near low-voltage overhead service lines, and 3.0 m for ordinary persons near lines up to 132,000 V; the code does not address water-fed poles, so this course treats a water-fed pole as conductive as a precaution. The rule is firm: if a line is within reach, or you cannot confirm the clearance, stop, keep the pole down, and refer the job to the network operator or a qualified person before continuing.

instructionSections.heading: Wind, public protection and falling objects
instructionSections.body: A long pole acts like a sail in wind and can become unstable. Set a wind threshold in the job plan and stop when it is exceeded. Keep the public and property out of the drop zone beneath the work area using barriers or a supervisor, and do not allow anyone to walk under a working pole. Plant the base on firm, level ground. If the footing shifts or the pole sways beyond control, lower it and reassess.

instructionSections.heading: Runoff and chemicals
instructionSections.body: Wash water, detergent and any approved cleaning product must not run into stormwater. Use only products with a safety data sheet available on site. Choose the lowest-impact method the job allows and collect or divert runoff where the job plan requires it.

instructionSections.heading: Limits of the method
instructionSections.body:
A pole does not make an unsafe surface safe. If the surface can only be reached by climbing, leaning out or working from an unstable platform, the ground-based method does not apply and the job returns to the access decision in the scope lesson. Never extend a pole to the point where you are using it to climb, to pull yourself up, or to reach beyond a safe footing. Record each limit you reached and what you did instead.

Licence notice: This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to work at height, near overhead lines or with pressurised equipment.

lessons.title: Stormwater, vegetation and runoff protection
learningOutcomes: Identify conditions, authorisation limits and evidence requirements relevant to stormwater, vegetation and runoff protection.

Demonstrate a proportionate stop-work, referral and documented client communication using a paper-based scenario.

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the pressure cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level pressure work and elevated or roof-level applications. High-pressure water, hoses and lances, electrical supply, exhaust gases and falls are all hazards on this track. Work above ground level is restricted to workers who are authorised by the employer and who hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Learning purpose and outcome
instructionSections.body: Explain why stormwater, vegetation and runoff protection changes the risk and permission profile of a roof-cleaning job. Learners must distinguish direct observation, tentative inference and specialist approval. No real roof work takes place in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Authorisation and boundary review
instructionSections.body: Using a simulated job pack, identify the site controller, stated job scope, contractor competencies, authorised exclusions, and missing permits relevant to stormwater, vegetation and runoff protection. A customer request alone never validates access or controls.

instructionSections.heading: Hazard recognition and hierarchy
instructionSections.body: Analyse this scenario: A downpipe drains toward a creek and planting beds; wash-water capture has not been planned. Begin with alternatives that avoid working at height. Mark fragile areas, skylights, public exposure, electrical installations and environmental unknowns wherever relevant; do not invent specialist approvals.

instructionSections.heading: Safe decision and escalation
instructionSections.body: The controlling principle is: Do not allow uncontrolled chemical wash water to enter stormwater, soil or waterways. Prepare a restricted-scope or stop-work decision. Identify which roof, electrical, work-at-height, chemical or environmental professional must resolve outstanding safety matters.

instructionSections.heading: Documentation and communication
instructionSections.body: Record what is known, the provenance of photographic or paper evidence, the person notified, the decision owner, and the unresolved approval. Never issue an unconditional safety or compliance certificate.

instructionSections.heading: Facilitated simulated practice
instructionSections.body: Conduct the paper-based exercise: Trace a fictional site drainage plan and document containment questions for an environmental specialist. The trainer examines reasoning, absence of unsupported assurances, escalation accuracy and readable records; no hazardous activity is simulated physically.

In Victoria, PV installation and maintenance is licensed electrical installation work, and PV DC cables may stay live when the power is off. In NSW, electrical wiring work, including repairing, needs an electrical licence or certificate. Electrical testing, isolation and repair of PV systems need a licensed electrician, and plain panel washing is not stated by the official pages to need a licence. lessons.title: Working models for a trainer: employed, facility-contracted or independent
learningOutcomes: Compare employed, facility-contracted and independent working models using the same six criteria
Identify the costs and records each model places on the trainer, and list each Australian legal or tax point to be checked.
Choose a model for a stated situation and write the reasons and the trade-offs being accepted

instructionSections.heading: Three working models
instructionSections.body: A personal trainer can work in at least three broad ways. In the first, the trainer is employed by a gym, studio or other employer, who pays for time on the floor and a different rate for each training session. In the second, the trainer contracts their services to a facility and pays a fee per client or a monthly fee for the use of the space, carrying their own costs. In the third, the trainer runs an independent business, for example travelling to clients' homes or working from a studio they lease. Each model moves costs, risk and records between the trainer and someone else. The source describes the first two in detail. The third is an addition in this lesson and uses the same comparison method.

instructionSections.heading: What employment gives you, and what it takes
instructionSections.body: As an employee, marketing, equipment and facility costs usually sit with the employer. Some employers provide training, uniforms or group class opportunities, and some invite trainers to comment on equipment and layout. The trade-offs are real. Employers may set dress and grooming standards, minimum hours and sales goals, and the pay for each session can be lower than an independent trainer could earn. The source gives a pay share as a percentage of the client fee. That figure is not used, because it is not an Australian benchmark. The source's account of US employer tax reporting is NOT APPLICABLE in Australia and is not used.

instructionSections.heading: What a facility contract asks of you
instructionSections.body: Under a facility contract, the trainer pays a fee to use the space, per client or per month, and carries their own operating costs. The trainer also has no say over how the facility runs, so changes to the room, hours or policies are outside their control. The source suggests a newcomer may price a little under local competitors. That suggestion is not used here as a rule, because it has no Australian basis. Fees must cover the space, insurance, marketing, equipment, records and the trainer's own tax, so a rate that merely sounds cheap is not a plan. Training clients on a facility's premises without paying the facility is a serious breach. The source says this can lead to prosecution. The source also names a professional conduct code, which was not read for this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: What running your own business asks of you
instructionSections.body: An independent trainer sets fees from their experience and from what the local market will pay. They carry all marketing costs, all travel time between clients' homes, any health questionnaires and client release forms, and all record-keeping. They must also meet their tax obligations on earned income. Before you rely on any of them, check current official guidance, then speak with a registered accountant or an insurance broker (see “Professional advisers: when to ask, and what to bring”).

instructionSections.heading: Choose a model with the same criteria for each
instructionSections.body: Compare the three models on six criteria: the monthly income you need, how stable that income is, how much control you have over hours and location, the travel and admin load, the marketing cost you carry, and the records you must keep. Then check the working arrangement itself. Whether a worker is an employee or a contractor depends on how the work is actually done, not on what the agreement calls it.

lessons.title: Discovering needs and qualifying a prospect without pressure
learningOutcomes: Ask needs-discovery questions that uncover a prospect's goal, why it matters and what has stood in the way before, and record the answers
Qualify a prospect honestly on need, budget, schedule and readiness, including a clear decision not to proceed
Present one option and invite a decision, and accept a not-now answer with a recorded follow-up date

instructionSections.heading: Selling is an honest offer you can ask for
instructionSections.body: Service providers need to be at ease requesting payment from a prospect for the service. Asking is part of the work, and it is not the same thing as pressure. The honest version is a clear offer, a fair price and a plain question about whether the prospect wants it. Good service also makes the provider a guide, who helps the prospect choose what suits them. That may mean recommending a smaller start, or a different provider.

instructionSections.heading: Find the need before you describe the service
instructionSections.body: People often decide on feelings and then explain the decision with facts, so the most useful early question concerns what the person wants and why it matters to them. Ask open questions. What goal has been on your mind? For how long has that goal been with you? Why does it matter now? What has got in the way before? Listen, then reflect back, in your own words, what you heard. The aim is to describe a service that fits what this person wants, not to steer them towards a yes.

instructionSections.heading: Qualify honestly, including a clear no
instructionSections.body: Qualification means checking the fit before you sell. Four checks help. Does the service meet the need you have heard? Can the person afford the option you would recommend? Can they keep to the times you offer? Are they ready to put in the effort? If the answer to any of these is no, say so plainly, and refer the person to a suitable option, a later start or a different provider. Before you send any offer, also confirm the work involved, your own capacity, the deadline and the payment terms. Business Queensland's guidance on preparing quotes suggests not quoting for work you cannot deliver to the customer's satisfaction. After a first full session, four plain questions help: did the session suit you, do you want to carry on, is the cost workable for you, and which day suits the next booking? These are honest checks, not a closing script.

instructionSections.heading: Present the option, and accept the answer
instructionSections.body: Describe the option by its outcome, what is included, the price, how many sessions are involved, the timing and the cancellation terms. Explaining the benefits before the price, and why the price is what it is, reduces the chance of losing the prospect on price alone. A programme differs from a set of separate sessions. It moves each session towards a stated goal, and its start and finish use the same measures, so that progress can be shown. Then ask for the decision. If the answer is not now, agree a follow-up date and channel, record both, and keep to them. A timed follow-up, with a request for feedback if the prospect does not go ahead, shows which part of the offer did not justify the price. Do not repeat the same request on every contact.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the emotional side honest
instructionSections.body: Empathy is a skill. Name the feeling you heard, such as frustration or worry about starting again, and show that you understand it. Do not use fear, false deadlines or invented scarcity, and do not promise results you cannot show. Check every statement about price, savings, results or availability against evidence before you make it. Where a single price is advertised, the ACCC's advertising and selling guide (dated July 2021; confirm it is the current version) indicates that it should include the total, with any tax, fee or levy. Consumer law may apply to how a service is sold, so check the rules that apply in your state or territory and with the ACCC.

lessons.title: A trainer's weekly time budget and honest availability
learningOutcomes: Build a weekly time budget that covers all seven categories of work, using hours drawn from a logged week
Publish availability that matches across every channel, and includes travel time for home visits
Refuse an unavailable time honestly, offer a real alternative or a referral, and record the action taken

instructionSections.heading: Your hours limit your income
instructionSections.body: A personal trainer's time is finite. Income from sessions depends on how many hours are available for training, and every other task competes with those hours. Planning starts by writing down the hours you work in a normal week, and deciding how many of them go to clients. Keeping that figure honest matters more than making the plan look full.

instructionSections.heading: The seven parts of a working week
instructionSections.body: A realistic week includes time for working with clients, managing client records and programmes, looking for new customers, preparing marketing and advertising materials, other business duties such as invoicing and accounts, your own exercise, and personal time and home life. Leave out any one of these and the plan will fail in practice. A plan that gives the whole week to clients leaves no time to find the next client, and no time to rest.

instructionSections.heading: Publish availability you can keep
instructionSections.body: Set the hours you are available, and publish them in the same form on your website, booking page and messages. Include travel time for home visits, so that a 45-minute session does not hide an hour of driving either side. Keep to the times you offer, because reliable hours build trust. Availability is not a device for creating scarcity. Describe the hours you really offer, and do not invent a shortage.

instructionSections.heading: When the schedule is full
instructionSections.body: If a prospect asks for a time you cannot offer, be direct. Offer a different time you truly have, suggest a later start if it suits them, or refer them to another trainer. Keep a record of any referral. A short, honest answer keeps a relationship that may lead to work later, and it protects the quality of the sessions you already run.

instructionSections.heading: Build the budget from a logged week
instructionSections.body: Plan from the hours you actually use, not the hours you hope to use. Log your time for one normal week, sorted into the same seven categories. Compare the log with the plan, and move hours until the plan balances. Repeat the log after about a month. Admin time is easy to underestimate, so the log is the check. The method for estimating admin hours in “Owner time and admin workload before the first job” can be used here.

lessons.title: Professional advisers: when to ask, and what to bring
learningOutcomes: Name the adviser needed for each business decision, and the decision it supports
Prepare a one-page brief with the facts an adviser needs before a meeting
Confirm ownership of business assets, and record each piece of advice, the decision and who made it

instructionSections.heading: Advice is a cost you choose to spend
instructionSections.body: Some decisions in a service business need a specialist. The skill is to match the adviser to the decision, bring a short brief, and record what you were told. Advice is worth paying for when a decision is hard to reverse, when a large amount of money is at stake, or when a mistake would be costly to fix. Where you can, ask for a fixed-fee quote, and say which question you need answered.

instructionSections.heading: Business structure
instructionSections.body: The main structures are a sole trader, a partnership, a company and a franchise. Each one shapes who is liable for the business's debts and how much paperwork it takes. A lawyer should advise on the structure you choose, and an accountant should advise on the tax and cash consequences. The source describes the same set of structures, and treats a lawyer as essential for the founding documents of a company or partnership.

instructionSections.heading: Money, records and tax
instructionSections.body: An accountant can help set up the records that show money coming in and going out. Ask for a simple system that records each invoice, expense and payment in one place, with a reference number on each. Keep the advice in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Brand, website and design
instructionSections.body: A web developer or graphic designer can help shape the visual identity and a website that explains the service clearly. Before you pay, check who will own the domain name, the logins, the design files and the content. The business should hold these in its own name, so that it keeps control if the designer changes. Confirm the arrangement in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Insurance, premises and contracts
instructionSections.body: An insurance broker can compare policies and build cover around the risks of the work. Compare quotes on the same scope, limits, exclusions and conditions. A real estate agent can help find premises, and a lawyer should review a lease before you sign it. Contractors can carry out repair and maintenance of the premises you use.

instructionSections.heading: Prepare a brief and record the advice
instructionSections.body: Before a meeting, write a one-page brief. Include the business and the decision, the facts an adviser needs, the numbers you already hold, the deadline, and the question you want answered. After the meeting, record the advice, the decision you made, who made it and when. This record protects the business if the decision is questioned later.

lessons.title: Authenticity: choosing what your yoga or fitness brand is true to
learningOutcomes: Describe the two kinds of authenticity a teaching brand can rest on: fidelity to a tradition, and honesty about personal practice
Choose the kind that fits your training and your intended clients, and state it in one plain sentence
Check each brand claim against what happens in your class, and record the evidence for it

instructionSections.heading: Authenticity is a promise about what is real
instructionSections.body: Clients use the word authentic to mean that a teacher is what they appear to be. In a yoga or fitness business, that realness can come from two places. The first is a tradition: a named style, its history, its vocabulary, and a discipline the teacher has been trained in and can describe in their own words. The second is the teacher's personal practice: why they teach, what their body has taught them, and what they actually do with a room of people. Neither source is automatically better. They attract different people, and a brand that claims both without choosing can look muddled. Before you write any public description, decide which source your teaching draws on most, and be ready to explain how it does so.

instructionSections.heading: Matching the kind of authenticity to the client
instructionSections.body: A teacher who trains in a set method and teaches it closely will usually attract clients who value rigour, a consistent sequence and a clear line back to the source. Those clients ask about training and notice shortcuts. A teacher who builds classes from several disciplines, and who speaks openly about their own path, tends to attract clients who want approachable, adaptable sessions and a relationship with the teacher. Those clients respond to honesty and to being invited in. Problems start when the two are mixed without intent. A class that presents itself as strictly traditional, but changes the sequence each week and plays loud music, will lose the traditional clients and look like a gimmick to everyone else. Choose a primary source, let any secondary influences sit beside it openly, and say so.

instructionSections.heading: Turning a claim into something you can show
instructionSections.body: Words such as traditional, authentic, certified, lineage and original carry weight with clients, so each one needs evidence behind it. Keep the training certificate, the course record, the dates the work was completed, and a written account of any lineage you describe, including who taught you and what they taught you. If you cannot name the source of a term, do not use the term. Treat each one as a claim that must be true and provable, because consumer law may treat a misleading description of a service as a problem. Check the current Australian consumer law position before you rely on this point.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the promise consistent across every channel
instructionSections.body: A brand is what the client experiences from the first search result to the last class. Your website, your timetable, your social posts, your bio and the words you use at the start of a class should describe the same teacher and the same method. Use the business name held as {{business:business.display_name}} on every channel so that clients can find one consistent offer. Read each channel side by side. If the website calls the class gentle and the class itself is intense, the gap will show. Ask a client who has attended for about three months to describe your class in their own words, and compare that answer with your written description. Where the two differ, change the description or change the class, and record which one you chose and why.

lessons.title: Differentiation and protecting what is yours
learningOutcomes: Name three points of difference for a teaching offer, each tied to a practice the teacher actually delivers
Distinguish a general idea or style that others can use from a specific name or created material that may be protectable, and check the Australian position before relying on it.
Run a name check and a differentiation check before a new class or program name is published

instructionSections.heading: Differentiation is a choice a client can point to
instructionSections.body: A class timetable often looks much the same from one suburb to the next. Differentiation means a client can point to one thing another teacher does not offer, and that thing matters to them. Good points of difference are concrete: the size of the group, a plan for people who are new to exercise, the time of day, a setting such as a beach or a park, a clear progression across weeks, a community of regulars, or a method of feedback. Weak points are labels with nothing behind them. Write three points of difference, and for each one name the part of the class where a client will see or feel it. If you cannot name that moment, the point is not yet a difference you can deliver.

instructionSections.heading: Separating ideas from things you can own
instructionSections.body: Ideas, general styles and common poses are not owned by any one person. Anyone can teach a sequence of standing poses, combine two approaches, or teach at dawn. A specific brand name, a logo, a written program with its own wording, or recorded material you created may be capable of protection, depending on its form and how it is used. Check the current guidance from the national intellectual property office and take advice from a qualified IP adviser before you file, rely on protection, or raise a complaint against another teacher. Overseas cases in which teachers have tried to protect a fixed class format have drawn public opposition. Those cases are historical and non-Australian, and they do not establish any Australian position.

instructionSections.heading: Checking a name before you commit to it
instructionSections.body: Before a new class name appears on a website, a timetable or a flyer, run a name check. Search the public trademark register, search business names and domain names, and search the websites and social profiles of teachers in your area and online. Look for names that sound like yours, share its key word, or describe the same offer in a way that could confuse a client. A name that simply describes what the class is, rather than distinguishing it, is usually harder to own. Record each search, its date and its result. If a conflict is possible, take advice before launch, because changing a name after signs are printed is expensive.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping a record of what you created
instructionSections.body: If you write a course outline, a written program, a set of cueing notes or a recorded class, keep dated drafts and a note of who wrote each part. This record shows what you made and when. It is still good practice. It lets you explain how a class was built, it helps when a colleague you worked with later disputes a shared program, and it reduces the risk of reusing another teacher's written material by accident. Where you use shared material from someone else, get their written permission and keep it on file with {{business:compliance.policy_reference}}.

lessons.title: Value that justifies a price, and respect for where a practice comes from
learningOutcomes: Explain why a higher price needs a benefit the client can see and experience, not a label alone
Write a value statement for a class or program that names the audience, a checkable change, the method and the deliverable, without health or treatment claims
Make and record a decision on how a practice's origins are named, credited and described, and state where the matter is contested

instructionSections.heading: A higher price needs a benefit the client can feel
instructionSections.body: Clients pay more when they can see what they are getting. A brand name on its own rarely does that work. A teacher who wants to charge above the local average needs a value that shows up in the room: a small group that allows individual feedback, a clear progression across weeks, a written home plan, a booking system that works, or a cool-down that follows a demanding session. Ask what a client will notice after the third session that they would not notice at a cheaper class. If the answer is only the name, the price rests on the name alone, and that is fragile. Build the premium on something the class delivers and the client can describe in their own words.

instructionSections.heading: Writing a value statement with a checkable outcome
