instructionSections.body: A value statement connects four things: who the class is for, what changes for them, how the method produces that change, and what they receive. Keep it specific enough to check. A statement such as 'a six-week beginner block for adults returning to exercise, with a written home plan and a progress check at week three' can be verified against the program. A statement that promises to transform a body or cure back pain cannot be verified, and it makes a health claim. Avoid outcome promises about health, injury or weight. Describe what the class does and what the client does in it.

instructionSections.heading: Respecting where a practice comes from
instructionSections.body: Some practices, including many forms of yoga, come from traditions that are religious or cultural for some people. Teachers and communities disagree about how such practices should be sold. Some argue that a spiritual practice should not be commercialised. Others argue that teaching it widely and well is a valid way to share it. This lesson does not settle that debate, and it claims no legal rule. As a business owner, you can still take practical steps. Name the source of a practice accurately. Do not imply a lineage, a credential or a religious endorsement that you do not hold. Do not use sacred terms as decoration, and do not describe a practice in a way that mocks its origins. Write down your own position on attribution, so that you can explain it to a client who asks and so that your staff give the same answer.

instructionSections.heading: Making the same value visible in every channel
instructionSections.body: The value you describe must match what happens in the room. Put the value statement on the website, the timetable and the bio, and check it against the class plan each term. When a claim changes, change it everywhere on the same day. Use the business name held as {{business:business.display_name}} on every channel so that clients can find one consistent offer. Then ask a small group of current clients to tell you, in their own words, what they pay for. If their answer differs from your value statement, that gap is the next job to fix. Where a class plan relies on a particular safety or evidence standard, keep the reference recorded under {{business:compliance.policy_reference}}.

lessons.title: Choosing an ideal client and a training specialty
learningOutcomes: Write a one-sentence ideal-client statement from a set of real client records
Explain why a specialty narrows the market and still leaves room for referrals to other providers
Check a specialty and its refusal criteria against the scope and the anti-discrimination rules.

instructionSections.heading: A specialty states who you serve and the result you deliver
instructionSections.body: A specialty is a short, plain answer to two questions: who you work with, and what change they can expect. It need not be a clever slogan. Its job is to let a prospect see quickly that the service is meant for them. Many providers avoid narrowing because they fear losing work. In practice a clear focus makes marketing easier to write, makes referrals easier for other people to pass on, and lets you build repeatable skills for one kind of client.

instructionSections.heading: Build the profile from records, not guesses
instructionSections.body: Start with the clients who have stayed longest and reached what they came for. Look for patterns in goals, weekly availability, distance from the business, how they found you, and what they say they value. Record the patterns in a short table. A profile built from memory tends to describe the clients you wish you had. A profile built from records shows the clients you already serve well.

instructionSections.heading: Say who you refer on, and why
instructionSections.body: Every specialty leaves some enquiries outside its scope. Explain the fit and refer the person to a suitable provider, rather than deflecting without a reason. Declining someone because of age, disability, sex, race or another protected attribute can breach anti-discrimination law. Health suitability is screened through its own process, not through the specialty.

lessons.title: Writing a value-led message and checking your claims
learningOutcomes: Rewrite a list of features as client-facing benefits
State a unique selling point in one sentence and apply it to a headline and one closing prompt
Identify claims that need evidence, written permission or a legal check before publication

instructionSections.heading: Lead with the outcome, then the method
instructionSections.body: Clients buy a result they can picture, along with how the process feels. A feature names what you do, such as a 45-minute circuit. A benefit names what changes for the person, such as climbing stairs without planning rest stops. Turn each feature into a benefit by asking what the client would notice in their week. Put the benefit first in every headline, post and flyer, and keep the method as supporting detail.

instructionSections.heading: One unique selling point, stated once
instructionSections.body: The unique selling point is the single reason a prospect would choose you over another option. It must be true, specific and provable in your own practice. Write it as one sentence and use the same sentence across channels. If you cannot state it in one sentence, the offer is not clear enough yet.

instructionSections.heading: Claims need evidence, consent and a legal check
instructionSections.body: Advertising must not mislead. Claims about results, such as weight loss, pain relief or body shape, need evidence you can show and must not promise outcomes that depend on the person. Testimonials and before-and-after images need the person's written permission and must reflect a real experience. The Australian Consumer Law turns on whether conduct is misleading or deceptive.

instructionSections.heading: Headline and closing prompt
instructionSections.body: A headline says who you help and the outcome, in one line. The sub-heading names the service area and the format. The closing prompt is one clear next step, such as booking a first session. Avoid competing actions on one page, and keep any testimonial block to genuine, permitted quotes.

lessons.title: Choosing lead sources and the four-stage offer chain
learningOutcomes: Rank lead sources by enquiries produced per hour of effort, using the learner's own figures
Describe the four stages of the offer chain and the job each stage does
Find the largest drop-off in a funnel and choose one change to test

instructionSections.heading: Rank channels by return on effort
instructionSections.body: Lead sources differ in how quickly they start a conversation and how much effort they take. Personal contact, calls to people who already know you, and referrals often produce enquiries faster than broad public advertising, but each business should confirm this from its own numbers. Compare channels on one measure: enquiries produced per hour of effort over a set period, such as 30 days. Record the counts rather than relying on how a channel feels.

instructionSections.heading: Four stages of the offer chain
instructionSections.body: The lead source brings a prospect in. The entry offer is a low-commitment first step, such as a trial session, a free assessment or a short introductory block. The core offer is the main ongoing service most clients buy. The back-end offer is a further programme or product for clients who are already satisfied. Each stage needs deliberate design, because a weak stage drags down the ones after it.

instructionSections.heading: Find the bottleneck, then change one thing
instructionSections.body: Count prospects at each stage over the same period. The stage with the largest percentage drop-off is the bottleneck. Improving a stage that already converts well rarely changes income much. Fix one thing at the bottleneck, test it for 30 days, and count again. Adding leads does not repair a broken step; it only sends more people through the same leak.

lessons.title: Referral and reactivation as a repeatable follow-up system
learningOutcomes: Map each step of the enquiry-to-client process and set a time target for each
Write a referral request that is specific and timed to a client milestone
Plan a reactivation message for former clients that respects consent and opt-outs

instructionSections.heading: Fix the process before adding leads
instructionSections.body: Many businesses think they lack enquiries when the real problem is slow or uneven handling after an enquiry arrives. Write each step from the first reply through to the initial visit: reply, call or consultation, offer, booking and follow-up. Set a time target for each step. A prospect who waits two days for a reply may already have chosen someone else. Follow-up wins many enquiries, so keep a dated record of each follow-up.

instructionSections.heading: Ask for referrals at the right moment
instructionSections.body: The strongest moment for a request is after a client reaches a milestone they value, or when they say they are satisfied. Make the request specific: say what kind of person you help, and offer an easy route for passing on your details, such as a card or a booking link. Thank each person who refers and tell them what happened. Track the source of every referral so you know which requests work.

instructionSections.heading: Reactivate former clients with an honest check-in
instructionSections.body: Former clients often respond to a short message that asks about their goals and offers a no-pressure next step. Keep the tone plain. Where a message is sent electronically, the Spam Act applies, so confirm consent before sending. Remove anyone who opts out at once. A reactivation list is a list of people who may welcome contact, not a list to be emailed in bulk.

lessons.title: Partnerships and location agreements
learningOutcomes: Score potential partner businesses against stated fit criteria
Describe what a written partnership note and a venue agreement should cover
Identify the referral payment, insurance and workplace points that have not yet been confirmed and need advice

instructionSections.heading: Partner with businesses that already serve your clients
instructionSections.body: The best partner already serves people like your ideal client, has a sound reputation, and is close to your service area. Depending on the area, candidates include allied health and wellness businesses, retailers of sports or nutrition products, and early-childhood providers. Score each candidate on client overlap, reputation, distance and whether you already have a relationship. Avoid businesses that compete for the same clients with the same service.

instructionSections.heading: Make the partnership mutual and in writing
instructionSections.body: A partnership works when both sides gain something useful, such as a joint talk, a free assessment for the partner's staff, or a shared article. Put the arrangement in a one-page note: what each side provides, how referrals are passed on, how client information is shared, and how either side may end it. Any referral payment is a separate decision. It must be disclosed, recorded in writing, and checked for legal and professional-conduct issues before use. Cash payments for referrals are not assumed in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Location agreements set the terms
instructionSections.body: Training at a private gym, studio or a client's home is a commercial arrangement. The written agreement should state the revenue split, who pays for insurance and cleaning, access and cancellation terms, who holds client records, and what happens if the venue closes. The percentage a venue accepts is a negotiation, not a standard.

lessons.title: Keeping in touch: newsletters and a consent-based contact plan
learningOutcomes: Explain the consent, sender identification and unsubscribe requirements for commercial electronic messages in Australia
Build a contact cadence that mixes a regular newsletter with personal touches
Keep a consent record and action each opt-out within five business days

instructionSections.heading: Why steady contact matters
instructionSections.body: People cannot refer you if they have forgotten you. A regular newsletter keeps the business visible without constant selling. The content is what earns attention: training tips checked for accuracy, schedule changes, a member story used with permission, and a clear next step. Keep the tone plain and the frequency predictable, so readers know what to expect.

instructionSections.heading: Consent comes first
instructionSections.body: Under the Spam Act 2003, a commercial electronic message needs the recipient's consent. Consent may be express, given knowingly, or in limited cases inferred from an ongoing relationship. Each message must identify the sender accurately, with correct contact details, and must carry an unsubscribe option that is clear, free and easy to use. The ACMA guidance checked on 2026-11-02 says opt-out requests must be acted on within five business days. A purchased list does not transfer responsibility for consent.

instructionSections.heading: Plan the cadence with personal touches
instructionSections.body: A monthly newsletter works well alongside a handful of personal touches, for example a note of thanks after a milestone, a birthday card, or a check-in after a long absence. Record each touch with its date, so you can see whether the plan is too heavy or too light. Stop any touch when the person asks you to stop.

lessons.title: A focused weekly marketing hour and a network map
learningOutcomes: Choose one marketing task for a fixed weekly hour and prepare for it in advance
Map personal and professional contacts into closeness tiers, with consent and contact notes
Review a task after four weeks and stop it if it produces no result

instructionSections.heading: Protect a fixed hour
instructionSections.body: Marketing often loses out to client work. A fixed weekly hour, with one task and no distractions, produces more than scattered effort. Prepare the materials the day before: the list, the message, the contact details, the venue address. Choose the task most likely to create an enquiry that week. Examples include sending the newsletter, sending personal messages to clients who have said yes to receiving your updates, or visiting nearby businesses to introduce yourself.

instructionSections.heading: Map your network
instructionSections.body: Your network includes people who know your work well, people who know you a little, and people who know of you. List them and mark the closeness of each relationship. Note how each person could open a door: by referring a client, hosting a talk, or passing on your details. Record the consent status and the last contact date. Do not send promotional messages to the whole list.

instructionSections.heading: Measure the output
instructionSections.body: After each hour, record what it produced: messages sent, conversations started, meetings held. Review after four weeks. A task with no measurable output should be changed or stopped, not repeated from habit.

lessons.title: Group-training format: definition, group size and layout
learningOutcomes: Define the format in terms of group size, individual coaching and programme
Identify design mistakes that turn a small group into a large class with fewer people
Plan a layout with zones sized to the group, and check the limits that apply

instructionSections.heading: What the format is
instructionSections.body: A small-group session is run by one trainer for a group of about four to six people, in which each person's programme is adjusted to their level, limits and goals. The group shares the session, but the coaching is individual. A good trainer can coach a beginner and an advanced member side by side, so neither feels left behind. Name the service clearly and describe it in the same terms everywhere.

instructionSections.heading: Avoid the common design mistakes
instructionSections.body: Several mistakes are common. Running the session as a large class with fewer people, with loud music, a timer and everyone on the same machine, makes members ask why they pay more. Adding small-group sessions as one line on a price list, with no plan to market them, rarely fills a group. Charging a large-group price for a smaller group, and not organising the room for it, both erode value. Each has a design fix: a plan for each member, a clear offer, and a room laid out for the number of people.

instructionSections.heading: Use zones, not open floor
instructionSections.body: Plan the room in zones, each sized for one group, with equipment within reach of that zone and clear walkways between zones. Crowding two groups into a small room, so that everyone works in one tight spot, makes coaching harder and raises the risk of collisions. Check the venue's and any council occupancy limits and fire egress rules.

lessons.title: Pricing a small-group session against the one-to-one rate
learningOutcomes: Set a group rate as a percentage of the one-to-one rate and test it against hourly earnings
Calculate expected hourly earnings at a planned fill rate
Explain why unlimited group access and unclear inclusions reduce value and create compliance risk

instructionSections.heading: Anchor to the one-to-one rate
instructionSections.body: Set the group rate as a percentage of your one-to-one rate, then test whether a full group earns more per hour than one-to-one would. A group rate set too low can earn less than a single one-to-one session, even with a full group. The one-to-one rate is the anchor and the hourly test is the check. The percentage is a starting point for testing, not a fixed rule.

instructionSections.heading: Plan for a fill rate below full
instructionSections.body: Not every session will be full. Estimate the average fill rate from your bookings and use that figure, not the maximum group size. Earnings per hour equal the group rate multiplied by the average number of paying members. Recalculate after each month of data.

instructionSections.heading: Avoid unlimited group access
instructionSections.body: Unlimited access makes each session seem less valuable and reduces the average income per session. Use session packs or memberships with clear terms, and state the expiry, cancellation and inclusion terms before sale. Those terms must be fair and not misleading.

lessons.title: Keeping small-group members: why they leave and what to do
learningOutcomes: Classify reasons clients leave as controllable or outside the business's control
Set check-ins that catch dissatisfaction early
Use the member's original goal to guide retention actions

instructionSections.heading: Clients leave for predictable reasons
instructionSections.body: Small-group members leave for a range of reasons. Some are outside your control, such as moving house or a change in work hours. Others come from the service itself: the member does not feel they fit the group, the coaching feels thin, or the sessions do not match the goal. Some reasons are unclear, and a short exit conversation can help. Sorting reasons this way shows where effort will change outcomes.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the reason for joining visible
instructionSections.body: Members who joined for a goal tend to stay longer when it stays visible. Revisit the goal at set points, compare it with progress data, and agree the next step with the member. A general check-in adds little. A specific conversation about the goal shows whether the programme still fits.

instructionSections.heading: Catch dissatisfaction early
instructionSections.body: Use short check-ins at about weeks two, six and twelve, and a brief exit form for anyone who stops. Treat each sign of dissatisfaction first as a coaching question: is the programme too easy or too hard, is the member getting enough attention, does the group time suit them? Act on the largest controllable reason first. Booking and package terms are covered in the booking and retention lesson and are not repeated here.

lessons.title: Coaching inside a group session
learningOutcomes: Pre-plan a group session with a modification for each member
Apply a coaching rhythm that gives each member frequent, brief attention
Stop or modify an exercise when a member reports warning symptoms, and follow the referral route

instructionSections.heading: Plan each member before the session
instructionSections.body: Before the session, read each member's notes and write their modification for the main exercises. A written plan keeps your attention on people instead of the next exercise. Include the member's current goal and any limitation flagged at screening. The plan is a set of starting points, to be adjusted when a member's day goes differently.

instructionSections.heading: Use a short, regular coaching rhythm
instructionSections.body: A simple rule helps. When you pass a member, watch for about three repetitions, then give one correction or one encouraging comment and move on. Over a session, every member should get frequent contact. Members who feel ignored often leave without saying why. Apply the rule the same way across the group.

instructionSections.heading: Keep effort within safe limits
instructionSections.body: The aim is effort the member can sustain with good form, not effort that matches the fittest person in the room. Watch for changes in form, breathing or colour, and for any report of pain, dizziness or chest discomfort. Stop the exercise, follow your emergency procedure and the referral route, and record the event. Screening and emergency response are covered in the screening and supervision lessons and are not repeated here.

lessons.title: Tracking progress and writing a group programme that scales
learningOutcomes: Choose two or three objective measures that match a member's goal and record them the same way each time
Write a group template with progressions and regressions for each movement
Explain where a group programme sits between a fully individual plan and a fixed template

instructionSections.heading: Track a few measures that match the goal
instructionSections.body: Choose two or three measures linked to the goal, such as body weight, circumference measurements, or a repeatable performance test. Use the same method each time, at a consistent time of day and on a fixed schedule. Explain to the member what each measure shows and what it cannot show. Body-composition estimates vary between methods, so compare results only within one method. Record only what the member has agreed to have recorded, and store it securely.

instructionSections.heading: Write one template with levels
instructionSections.body: A group programme can be written as one template in which each movement has a regression, a base version and a progression. Each member chooses a level at the start of a block. This sits between two extremes: a fully individual plan for each member, which takes considerable time, and a fixed daily workout that cannot change. A middle design gives much of the individual benefit at a workload a trainer can sustain.

instructionSections.heading: Keep a simple workout record
instructionSections.body: Record what each member did, the level used, any change made, and the progress measure. Review the record every four weeks and adjust the group template where several members show the same pattern.

lessons.title: Setting up the business: name, structure, break-even and cash flow
learningOutcomes: Pick a trading name and check it for conflicts and implied credentials
Calculate break-even sessions from fixed costs and contribution per session
Build a three-month cash-flow view and list the registration, tax and insurance points that have not yet been confirmed

instructionSections.heading: Name and brand
instructionSections.body: A business name ought to describe the service and be memorable. Check that no other business already uses it, and whether it can be protected as a trade mark. Avoid names that suggest a qualification, accreditation or affiliation you do not hold. A simple logo and a consistent set of colours build credibility more than an elaborate design.

instructionSections.heading: Structure and registrations
instructionSections.body: Choose a legal structure, such as sole trader, partnership or company, with advice on liability and tax. An Australian Business Number, GST registration, business insurance and any industry registration are separate questions. On industry registration: an AUSactive page checked on 2026-11-02 describes a route into its Register of Exercise Professionals that requires a relevant qualification, current first aid and agreement to its code.

instructionSections.heading: Break-even and cash flow
instructionSections.body: Break-even sessions equal fixed costs divided by the contribution each session makes, where contribution is the session price minus the variable cost of that session. Fixed costs include rent, insurance and software. Variable costs include venue hire per session and consumables. A profitable business can still run short of cash when income arrives late, so build a monthly cash-flow view for at least three months. Sample figures in business plan templates are not used; every figure here is the learner's own.

lessons.title: A focused niche and the fit test for choosing one
learningOutcomes: Explain how a focused niche narrows the market and makes an offer easier to describe and refer
Score candidate offers against seven fit factors, with an evidence note for each factor marked yes
Reject a candidate that fails the values check, and state the reason in writing

instructionSections.heading: What a niche does for the business
instructionSections.body: A niche is a chosen group of clients who share a situation and a result they want, and your offer is designed for that group. Instead of describing a service to everyone, you describe it to people for whom it is the obvious answer. The benefit is clarity. A prospect can tell in one sentence whether you are for them, and a friend can pass your name to the right person. The cost is that you decline some work you could technically do. Make that trade on purpose. A niche is not a promise about income, because income depends on prices, delivery and demand, which the rest of this course covers.

instructionSections.heading: Weigh the advantages of focus against staying broad
instructionSections.body: Focus has real advantages. You can draw on experience you already have, clients recognise your real strengths, and the work can sit closer to what you care about. Staying broad has real costs. The message becomes vague, prospects are unsure what you are strongest at, and referrals are harder because people cannot describe you to someone else. Write both lists for your own business before you choose. A focus that gives you no advantage over your current offer is a new label, not a niche.

instructionSections.heading: Use seven fit factors to compare candidates
instructionSections.body: List three to five candidate offers. For each one, check how many of seven factors it meets: you are drawn to the work; you feel the offer is genuine when you describe it; it matches your values; it uses your talents; it draws on something particular to you; it builds on experience you have; and it fits a story you can tell honestly. Mark each factor yes, partly or no, and keep a short evidence note beside each yes, such as a past job, a qualification or a client comment. Read the answers as well as the totals. A candidate that scores well on everything except values should be rejected, because a niche you do not believe in tends to wear down.

instructionSections.heading: Choose a niche you can keep delivering
instructionSections.body: A niche should be work you can deliver well for years, not only during the first months of enthusiasm. Ask whether you would still choose it after a busy season, a difficult client and a slow month. If the honest answer is no, the candidate has failed, however well it scores on paper. Record the decision, the scores and the date, so that you can later check whether the reasons still hold.

lessons.title: Plus factors: combining your background into one offer
learningOutcomes: List plus factors across five areas of work, study, interests, life experience and community ties, and mark the evidence for each
Combine two or three plus factors into one offer statement that names a client group and a result
Test each combination for a named buyer and for the business's ability to deliver it

instructionSections.heading: Distinct offers often combine several things
instructionSections.body: Most people can name one skill. A stronger offer often combines several things at once: work from an earlier career, a training path, an interest that shows up in the service, a language, or a local connection. When two or three of these meet in one service, the result is harder to copy, because nobody else has the same mix. The aim is a combination that a particular group of clients would recognise as useful. A list of achievements is not the aim.

instructionSections.heading: Build an honest inventory
instructionSections.body: Write down your plus factors across five areas: work history, study and training, interests and hobbies, life experience, and community or language ties. For each item, note the evidence you hold: a certificate, a client reference, a portfolio, dated work records or a clear personal account. An item with no evidence can still be part of your story, but it must not be presented as a credential or a result.

instructionSections.heading: Combine two or three factors into one offer
instructionSections.body: Pick the combinations that point at a client group and a result. For example, a former teacher who also does handyman work could offer after-hours repairs to families with young children, with a short walk-through of the home beforehand. Test each combination with two questions. Would a specific group pay for it? Can you deliver it well? A bundle that nobody would buy is a hobby, however interesting it is.

instructionSections.heading: Keep each combination inside what you are qualified to do
instructionSections.body: Combining factors can make an offer sound more expert than it is. Describe only the training and experience you hold, and do not let a plus factor imply a trade qualification, licence or clinical role you do not have. Where a combined service involves licensed work, the licence rules have not yet been confirmed in this lesson and must be checked with the relevant state or territory authority before you advertise the service.

lessons.title: Buying triggers: the reasons clients act, and how to speak to them honestly
learningOutcomes: Name the five common buying triggers and give one service example of each
Rank the triggers for a target group using real enquiries, reviews or messages
Write a client message for each chosen trigger that makes no unverified claim and is checked for health-claim and consumer-law risk

instructionSections.heading: A trigger is the reason a client acts
instructionSections.body: A client moves from interest to booking when something they care about becomes urgent or valuable enough to act on. That is the buying trigger. A message works best when it speaks to a trigger the client already feels and shows how the service answers it. A trigger is not the feature list. A carpet clean is a feature. The trigger might be a landlord who needs a bond returned in full, or a family who wants a tidy home before visitors arrive.

instructionSections.heading: Five triggers to test
instructionSections.body: Test five common triggers: money, time, relationships, health and peace of mind. Money covers saving money and earning it. Time covers reclaiming hours and creating open space in a diary. Relationships covers the people in a client's life, and whether a service brings people closer, helps them communicate, or helps them through a change. Health covers wellbeing, and it carries the most risk, because any health claim must be true and supported by reasonable grounds. The ACCC's advertising guide (July 2021) says health and therapeutic claims need reasonable grounds, usually scientific evidence. Do not promise treatment. Peace of mind covers reducing worry, knowing a job is done properly, and having someone to call when something goes wrong.

instructionSections.heading: Find the triggers your group responds to
instructionSections.body: Do not guess. Collect about ten real enquiries, reviews or messages from the group you serve, or from people very like them, and mark which trigger each message shows. Pay attention to the words clients use, because those words usually name the trigger. Count the marks, rank the triggers, and choose one or two to lead with. A trigger can matter without being the lead reason, so keep the others in your file for later messages.

instructionSections.heading: Write the message around the trigger, with honest proof
instructionSections.body: For each chosen trigger, write one message that names the client's situation, describes the service in plain words, gives one piece of proof you hold, and offers a clear next step. Keep urgency honest. Give a date only if it is real, and a price only if it is the price you charge. Avoid false deadlines and invented scarcity, because they damage trust and may breach consumer law. The ACCC guide says limited-time offers and short supply must be stated clearly and must be genuinely available.

instructionSections.heading: Money and health claims need the most care
instructionSections.body: A money claim, such as a saving, needs the numbers behind it. Price comparisons such as was/now or two-price claims need records behind them, according to the ACCC guide. A health claim needs more care still. A service can describe what a session includes and how it is run. As a working rule, do not claim to treat, cure or prevent any condition. Australian health-claim rules have not been checked against an official source in this lesson, so check with the relevant regulator before using any health wording. The service should point people with a health concern towards their own health provider. Follow-up email or text that promotes the service can fall under the Spam Act, which requires consent and an unsubscribe option (ACMA).

lessons.title: Testing a working niche and sharpening it with client response
learningOutcomes: Write a working niche statement that is marked as provisional and has a review date
Answer the ten decision questions for the two strongest candidates and record the answers
Use prospect response and an affordability check to decide whether to keep, refine or replace the niche

instructionSections.heading: Settling on a focus takes time
instructionSections.body: Many people find it hard to settle on one focus, and the decision can take months. Treat your first niche statement as a working niche: a provisional choice you intend to test, review and possibly change. Writing it down, with a review date you can keep, makes the decision concrete without locking you in. Being unsure is normal. What matters is that the decision is tested against evidence on a schedule, rather than left open indefinitely.

instructionSections.heading: Test the working niche by offering it
instructionSections.body: The quickest way to sharpen a niche is to describe it to real people and see what happens. Speak with about ten prospects in the group, offer the service in its working form, and record what you hear: questions asked, objections raised, quotes accepted, and enquiries that went no further. Silence is information too. Make each approach relevant and honest, and do not pressure anyone: the ACCC's 2026 media release on unsolicited selling reports that many approaches were pressured or misleading. The response is the feedback that tells you whether to keep the niche, refine its wording or replace it.

instructionSections.heading: Ten questions to narrow the choice
instructionSections.body: When two or three candidates remain, answer ten questions for each. Which clients have you enjoyed working with most? Which clients come to you without much effort? What work gives you the most energy? When in the working day do you feel most at ease? How do you want your days to look in this business? Which option has the strongest buying triggers for its group? Which option is most commercially sensible? Which is easiest to deliver well? Is anyone else serving this group successfully? Their success is evidence that demand exists, though it is not a reason to copy them. Would you rather commit now and aim for profit sooner, or keep your options open for longer? Write each answer in full. A candidate with strong triggers but weak personal fit will show up clearly.

instructionSections.heading: Check whether the group can afford you
instructionSections.body: A niche only works if the group can pay the price the business needs. Not every decision is about money, but choosing a group that cannot afford the work is not a sound plan. Compare the price you need with what the group can reasonably spend, using the test in “Defining target segments from customer data” of need, ability to pay and reachability. Before quoting anyone, confirm their budget, timing and deadline, and check your own capacity; Business Queensland advises this. If the gap is large, you have three options: change the group, change the offer or price, or keep looking. A change to price must rest on evidence and on your costs, not on hope.

instructionSections.heading: Decide at the review date
instructionSections.body: On the review date, look at the response log, the answers to the ten questions and the affordability check. Then choose one of three outcomes: keep the working niche and write its final statement; refine the wording, the group or the offer, and test again; or replace it with the next candidate. Record the outcome and the reason. Stopping to reconsider is a legitimate business decision, not a failure.

lessons.title: Processing-plant wet cleaning: dry removal, drains and protein-safe rinsing
learningOutcomes: Remove dry debris by hand tools before any water is applied to a food-processing surface.
Explain why a hot rinse or steam can set protein soil onto equipment.
Clear floor drains and channels during the wet clean, then record the result.
Keep water away from electrical equipment, motors and dry stored goods during a wet clean.

instructionSections.heading: Dry removal comes before any water
instructionSections.body: In a processing area the first job is to take away solid material by hand. A shovel, scraper or squeegee moves trim, shell, vegetable matter and similar debris into a container or onto a conveyor that carries it out of the building. A hose is the wrong first tool here, because it pushes solids into drains, under equipment and toward product. In a food-service kitchen the same logic applies on a smaller scale: a dustpan with a long handle collects solids and paper, and a damp cloth or mop contains spilled liquid. Dry sweeping is avoided wherever food is exposed, because it lifts particles into the air where they can settle on food or work surfaces.

instructionSections.heading: Rinse with cool or lukewarm water
instructionSections.body: Once the solids are gone, a rinse lifts the fine residue left by seafood, red meat, poultry, produce, dairy or egg material. Cool or lukewarm water works best. Hot water and steam can bake protein onto a surface, the way an egg fixes itself to a dry pan. Proteins set when they are heated, so a rinse that is too hot makes the next step harder and leaves the surface less clean. Keep water and spray away from motors, control panels and electrical units. Where belts are lifted on metal bars for cleaning, remove the bars before the equipment runs again, or the belt and equipment can be damaged. Disassemble parts such as band saws, pipes and stuffers so the rinse reaches the surfaces underneath.

instructionSections.heading: Drains, coolers and moisture in storage
instructionSections.body: Floor drains and channels belong to the clean, not to a separate task. A drain that holds old food debris becomes a source of odour and a place where microorganisms and pests can build up, so it is cleared and flushed during every wet clean. Coolers that hold wet product, such as seafood, red meat, poultry, dairy or produce, need regular cleaning too. Keep water out of dry goods stores: moisture that carries into a dry store can damage packaging and product. The supervisor of the wet clean should check the drains, the cooler floors and any area that is often overlooked, and record that the check was made.

lessons.title: Choosing a sanitiser for food-contact and processing surfaces
learningOutcomes: Explain why a sanitiser cannot work on a surface that still carries food soil.
Name the main classes of sanitiser and state where each one is unsuitable.
Apply the selection factors of contact time, temperature, organic load, pH, surface compatibility and cost.
Choose a product only from the label and the site's approved list, not from habit.

instructionSections.heading: What a sanitiser does and does not do
instructionSections.body: Sanitising lowers the count of microorganisms on a surface that has already been cleaned. It is a second step, not a replacement for cleaning. Soil acts as a shield: when a sanitiser meets fat, protein or mineral deposits, it is used up on that material and reaches fewer microorganisms. Sanitising is also not a substitute for pest control. A surface that is sanitised while pests remain active can be re-contaminated soon afterwards, so the pest question is settled first (see “Pest control principles for food plants, stores and food-service zones”).

instructionSections.heading: Classes of sanitiser and where they fit
instructionSections.body: The main classes are the halogens, a group that includes chlorine, bromine and iodine, plus phenol-based products and quaternary ammonium compounds. Chlorine-based products are among the most widely used in food settings. Iodine-based products can stain belts and other absorbent materials. Phenol-based products should not be used in food processing areas, because their odour can pass into food and the strong smell can hide whether a room has actually been cleaned. Quaternary ammonium compounds have a place in food processing, but their cost usually limits how much they are used.

instructionSections.heading: Five selection factors and surface compatibility
instructionSections.body: Choose a sanitiser by weighing five factors. The first is contact time: if an item will be soaked, the speed of action matters less than the total time in contact. The second is temperature: chlorine becomes less effective as the temperature rises. The third is organic load: a surface with much food residue uses up the sanitiser on the residue. The fourth is acidity: chlorine works better when the solution is more acidic. The fifth is price, which limits how much of a sanitiser a site can use. Compatibility with the surface sits beside these factors. Chlorine in high concentration forms an acid in solution and can pit stainless steel over time, so the surface material decides how strong the solution can be. Mineral deposits and milkstone also block a sanitiser from reaching the microorganisms beneath, so they are removed first.

lessons.title: Detergent choice, application and residue removal in processing areas
learningOutcomes: Choose a detergent by soil type, surface, water quality and application method.
Explain why dwell time and mechanical action matter before rinsing.
Rinse detergent away completely, since leftover traces can make people ill.
Keep incompatible detergent types apart and follow the label and SDS for each product.

instructionSections.heading: Match the detergent to the soil and the surface
instructionSections.body: A detergent is picked for the job it must do. Five things decide the choice: the type of soil (fat, protein, raw residue, baked-on food or chemical scale), the surface (solid, mesh, stainless or galvanised), the hardness of the water (hard or soft), the method available (spray, foam or manual) and the price of the product and its use. Alkaline products are generally used for fats and proteins, while acid products are used for mineral scale. Low-foaming products suit high-pressure equipment, and high-foaming products suit foam application or manual work. These are general chemistry points; the product's label and SDS, and the supplier's technical information, confirm what a particular product is for.

instructionSections.heading: Apply, allow dwell time and agitate
instructionSections.body: A detergent works through its chemistry and through time. High-pressure systems meter detergent into the water stream, and the force of the spray lifts residue from the surface. Foam is applied and left for several minutes before rinsing, so the foam can loosen the soil. Stubborn soil on parts that cannot be sprayed is brushed or scrubbed with pads. Disassembled parts such as mixers, whisks and beaters are first soaked in warm water to loosen debris; the source uses warm water for this soak, and no Australian soak temperature is confirmed here. A commercial kitchen commonly runs a sink with four bays: the first compartment removes large soil, the second holds the detergent wash at the temperature set by the product label, the third rinses and the fourth sanitises.

instructionSections.heading: Rinse until no detergent remains
instructionSections.body: Detergent residue is a food-safety problem in its own right. The source warns that even trace detergent left in food may upset the stomach and intestines, with symptoms that look like food poisoning, so every trace has to go. Rinse using water that is clean and fit to drink. Foam left on a surface after the rinse means the rinse has not finished. Where the site procedure requires a rinse check, perform it and record the result. A surface that is only partly rinsed must be rinsed again before the sanitising step begins.

lessons.title: Sanitising equipment and parts: immersion, spray, air-drying and handling
learningOutcomes: Choose immersion, spray or wipe sanitising to suit the size and fixed or loose nature of the item.
Explain why sanitised items are air-dried rather than towel-dried.
Verify hot-water sanitising with a thermometer and a timer.
Store sanitised items so they cannot be contaminated again before use.

instructionSections.heading: Choose the sanitising method for the item
instructionSections.body: Loose utensils and small parts are dipped into a sanitising solution or hot water for the period the procedure sets. Fixed plant, including belts, saws and tables, is sprayed with a hand-pumped unit in a small operation, or with a pressurised unit in a large facility. A hand-held spray bottle does table sanitising in a restaurant. For hot-water sanitising, Queensland Health's cleaning and sanitising guidance gives a hot-water temperature of 77 degrees Celsius held for a minimum of 30 seconds.

instructionSections.heading: Let the surface air-dry
instructionSections.body: After the sanitising contact time, the surface is left to air-dry. Drying with a towel can carry microorganisms from the cloth or from the hands onto a surface that was just sanitised. Parts that cannot be immersed must be sprayed to cover the full surface, and enough solution must be applied to stay wet for the contact time. A surface that dries too fast before the contact time has ended has not been sanitised.

instructionSections.heading: Handle and store sanitised items
instructionSections.body: Sanitised items are stored on a clean rack or shelf, not on a bench that has not been sanitised. Keep sanitised parts apart from raw materials, and keep tools colour-coded by zone so that a tool used in one area is not carried into another. The colour-coding principle is covered in “Colour-coded cloths: a business-set system that keeps areas apart”. The person handling sanitised items should wash their hands before touching them, as the site procedure requires.

lessons.title: Pest control principles for food plants, stores and food-service zones
learningOutcomes: Explain why pests need controlling before a surface is sanitised.
Describe a pest control programme as an ongoing plan with a named responsible person.
Respond to a pest sign by stopping, recording and reporting, without applying a pesticide unless authorised.
State that pest-control licensing in Australia has not yet been confirmed and that this lesson grants no licence.

instructionSections.heading: Pests are a sanitation and food-safety problem
instructionSections.body: Flies, cockroaches, rodents and insects that infest stored food are more than a nuisance. They carry microorganisms on their bodies and can physically contaminate food with fragments, hair, feathers and droppings. Regulators inspect food premises for signs of pests and for conditions that let pests thrive, and contaminated stock can be seized or destroyed. A surface that has been sanitised while pests remain active can be re-contaminated soon afterwards, so sanitising does not hold if the pest question is still open. This is why the order of work matters.

instructionSections.heading: The order of work and a programme, not a one-off fix
instructionSections.body: Where nothing is active, the usual order of clean and then sanitise holds. Where pests are active, they are dealt with ahead of the sanitising step. Pest control is a planned programme with named responsibility, scheduled inspections and records. Finding one rodent or one colony of insects is a signal to review the whole area: how incoming stock is inspected, how it is stored, whether the building lets pests in, how housekeeping is done and how often checks are made. Treating only the visible sighting leaves the cause in place and tends to bring the problem back.

instructionSections.heading: Pesticides, responsibility and the limits of this lesson
instructionSections.body: Senior management carries the final accountability: it names a capable individual to run the pest programme and backs that person with resources. Anyone who applies a pesticide must use a product that is needed, apply it exactly as the label directs, and confirm that people, food and the environment are not put at risk. Pesticide use is not a task for an untrained cleaner. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to apply a pesticide.

lessons.title: Harbourage and exclusion: building layout, clearances and gaps
learningOutcomes: Identify harbourage: cracks, gaps, hollow spaces and clutter where pests shelter.
Explain why equipment and stock should be sealed, raised or spaced so cleaning reaches them.
Report gaps and openings that let pests in, without making building repairs outside the worker's scope.
Describe the outdoor measures that reduce shelter and entry points.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as harbourage
instructionSections.body: Harbourage is any space that gives pests shelter, a route in or a place to breed. In a food building this includes cracks and pores in the surfaces of walls and floors, hollow spaces behind equipment, gaps around pipes that pass through a wall or floor, and clutter stored against walls. Equipment lifted only a few centimetres above the ground, or set very close to a wall, is awkward to clean and often shelters cockroaches. The rule is simple: if a cleaner's cloth cannot reach it, or a pest could hide in it, it is harbourage.

instructionSections.heading: Clearance, stacking and sealing
instructionSections.body: Make every area used to handle or store food easy to reach for routine cleaning. Fix cabinets and equipment flush against a wall or floor where design permits, or leave a clear space of at least about 15 centimetres (six inches) so the floor and wall can be cleaned and inspected. Stock sits on pallets rather than the ground, with a gap of roughly 45 centimetres (18 inches) beneath it and space between it and the walls. That US source treats the spacing as a rule of thumb. Openings around pipes, drains and vents are sealed, and doors and openable windows get close-fitting screens.

instructionSections.heading: Outside the building and the report
instructionSections.body: The outside of a food building should stay clean and tidy. Grass and shrubs are kept short and trimmed, paved approach paths are kept tidy, and drainage is sloped so water does not pool and create breeding places. Lights are placed away from the building and aimed so that flying insects are drawn away from entrances and glazing. Waste containers are kept raised off the ground. Where the gap is in the building fabric itself, like a door bottom or a pipe penetration, the cleaner records and reports it to the responsible person. Repairs that require a licensed trade are outside this lesson, and the licensing rules for those trades are not covered here.

lessons.title: Dry waste areas and waste containers as pest and contamination sources
learningOutcomes: Explain how caked food residue in a waste container becomes a breeding source for flies and similar pests.
Clean a waste container by loosening, washing and draining it, and state what is not done.
Manage waste so bags are tied, lids are closed and containers are emptied at a set frequency.
Keep wash-down wastewater within the trade-waste rules that govern the premises.

instructionSections.heading: Why the base of a bin matters
instructionSections.body: A bin that looks empty can still hold a layer of food residue caked onto its base and sides. This material feeds flies and similar pests and gives them somewhere to breed, and it also carries microorganisms. Regular emptying does not remove the caked layer, so a waste container needs its own cleaning step. The source notes that a trace of residue left in a container can support very large numbers of flies, which is why the cleaning step is not skipped when a bin is emptied. The specific figures the source gives for bacteria carried by flies come from a historical US study and are not used in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Clean the container by loosening, washing and draining
instructionSections.body: Before washing, break up the crusted layer at the base of the container with a scraping tool and a hoe. Then wash the container with water and an approved product, and spray it to remove the loosened residue. Let the container drain, and keep the wash-down water out of food and dry goods. Waste containers are set up raised on racks or a concrete base, so that cleaning underneath is possible and pests have less shelter. Enclosed containers are kept closed.

instructionSections.heading: Manage waste at a set frequency
instructionSections.body: Waste food is removed from food areas at least once a day, or more often where the site's risk assessment asks for it. Bags are tied shut before they go into an outdoor container. Waste areas are cleaned on a schedule set by the responsible person, with some areas needing cleaning daily and others weekly, and with spills cleaned as they happen. Keep sharps out of general waste and follow the site's separate sharps procedure. Where wash-down water goes to a drain depends on the trade-waste rules that govern the premises, which have not yet been confirmed for this lesson, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.

lessons.title: Sanitation programme and zoned inspection checks
learningOutcomes: Write a sanitation programme that states each task, its frequency and the person responsible.
Inspect a food area by zone, marking each check yes or no and recording each deficiency.
Close a deficiency by correcting it, checking the correction and recording the result.
Explain why a written programme lets a new worker work out the tasks without help.

instructionSections.heading: Write the programme in specific terms
instructionSections.body: A sanitation programme is written so that a new worker can follow it without asking. Each task states what is done, where, how often and by whom. The source gives the example of one employee who scrapes and sprays a waste container weekly, another who cleans restrooms each day, and another who inspects monitoring devices and baiting points each day. Assigning named tasks to named people shows where responsibility sits and lets management see whether the programme is being done. A checklist is a useful way to assign the duties.

instructionSections.heading: Inspect by zone with a yes or no record
instructionSections.body: A preventive programme depends on regular inspection. The inspection form is matched to the business, but in general it covers zones such as the exterior grounds, the building exterior, the building interior, dry and refrigerated storage, preparation areas, dishwashing, the indoor waste area, toilets and locker rooms, the lunch room, utility and office areas, and public areas. Each item is marked yes or no. A no marks a deficiency that must be corrected, and the entry on the far side of the form notes what is wrong. The inspection record is then reviewed and signed by the responsible person. This lesson does not reproduce any published inspection form; the zone structure is described in new words.

instructionSections.heading: Close deficiencies and keep the record honest
instructionSections.body: A deficiency found on inspection is recorded, corrected and checked. Where pest evidence or poor housekeeping is found, the inspector logs it, assigns the corrective action to a named person and sets a date for re-inspection. A zone that looks clean is not passed until each item on the form has been checked. Records are completed during the inspection itself and are not filled in later from memory. A checklist with every item ticked and no deficiencies recorded, when problems were seen, is a false record.

lessons.title: Control points: writing the check that shows a task is finished
learningOutcomes: Write a control point as an observable check that a second person could confirm.
Link each control point to the step in the procedure that produces it.
Set a check frequency for shared and public areas, and name who records it.
Explain why a written site standard is a starting point that each site adapts.

instructionSections.heading: A standard is a first draft for your sites
instructionSections.body: A written cleaning manual describes what a job should look like, but it cannot see the building in front of you. The most useful way to use an inherited manual is to treat it as a first draft. The business keeps the parts that fit its sites, changes the parts that do not, and adds the checks its own customers expect. A standard only works when the people doing the work can see what it asks for. Before you adopt any set of task instructions, read it against the sites you actually clean and note where a step does not fit. Record the change, the reason for it and who approved it, so the next worker does not have to discover the same gap.

instructionSections.heading: What a control point is
instructionSections.body: A control point is a short statement, placed at the end of a task sheet or beside its steps, that says what must be true when the work is complete. It sits apart from the method. The method tells the worker what to do. The control point tells the worker and the checker what the result must look like. A good control point names a surface or area, a condition and a way to see that condition. A phrase such as looks clean fails this test, because two inspectors can disagree about what it means. A phrase that names the surface, the condition and the viewing position can be checked in a few seconds by anyone standing in the room.

instructionSections.heading: Writing checks that someone else can confirm
instructionSections.body: Start each control point from the finished surface and work backwards. Ask what a person entering the room would notice first, what a hand run along the surface would find, and what would show up under normal light. Prefer counts, positions and states. A bin is empty and its liner is fitted. A handrail has no marks along its full length. A floor has no standing water, and its warning sign comes down only once it is dry. Keep each control point to one condition, because two conditions in one line let a check pass when one of them has failed. If a check needs a tool, name the tool, such as a torch for checking streaks on glass, so the checker does not have to improvise.

instructionSections.heading: Linking each control point to the method
instructionSections.body: Every control point should trace back to a step. If the control point says the glass door panels are free of finger marks, a step must say when the glass is cleaned and with what. A control point with no step behind it is a gap in the standard. A step that produces nothing a control point checks may be unnecessary, or the check is missing. Walk the task from the first step to the last and mark which control point each step serves. Doing this on paper before a new task goes live catches most gaps. It also tells the worker which step to return to when a check fails, so the whole job does not have to be repeated.

instructionSections.heading: Check frequency in shared and public areas
instructionSections.body: Some areas need checks during the working day as well as at the end. Lobby glass, entrance doors, lifts and standing bins are seen by visitors throughout the day, so one end-of-shift check lets a marked state stand for hours. Set the frequency on the task sheet as a number of checks or a fixed interval, and name the person who records each check. Heavily used areas need more frequent checks. Where a customer or building manager has set a higher expectation, the business standard should reflect it. Frequency is a business decision that must be written down, not left to a worker's judgement on the day.

instructionSections.heading: Recording and acting on a failed check
instructionSections.body: A failed control point is information. Record which check failed, where it failed and what was found, then return to the step that produces that result. Do not sign off an area with a known failure, and do not quietly correct a result without recording it, because the record is how the business learns that a step is weak. If the same control point fails across different workers and sites, the problem is more likely to be the method or the equipment than the people, and it should go to the supervisor for review.

lessons.title: Microfibre cloths: what they do, their limits and when to retire them
learningOutcomes: Explain how a microfibre cloth picks up soil, and why it works best when damp rather than wet.
Identify the product types and surfaces that limit where a microfibre cloth can be used.
Decide when a microfibre cloth is worn out and must be retired.
Keep microfibre cloths within the task and area system that the business has set for them.

instructionSections.heading: How the fibre does its work
instructionSections.body: A microfibre cloth is made from very fine synthetic fibres. Each fibre is thin, and the cloth as a whole presents a large surface, so it can take up fine particles that a looser cotton cloth would push around. The fibres also carry a light static charge, which helps them hold dust. Damp fibres draw liquid into the weave by capillary action. Those features make microfibre effective, and they work best when the cloth is damp. A dripping cloth carries water onto surfaces and floors. A dry cloth on a greasy surface may only move the film about. Treat the cloth as a tool that does its job at the right moisture level.

instructionSections.heading: Water first, and check the chlorine limit
instructionSections.body: The source material describes these cloths as suited to damp use with water alone, and it advises keeping them away from chlorine-based disinfecting products. This lesson records that advice as a source statement. Follow the supplier's written limits. The practical rule is the same either way. Read the label of any product before it goes near a microfibre cloth, and do not assume that a product safe on a hard floor is safe on a cloth. Use only the products the business has approved for the cloths, and keep the cloths stored away from chemical containers.

instructionSections.heading: Where microfibre works and where it does not
instructionSections.body: Microfibre suits routine upkeep on lightly soiled surfaces. On old or damaged surfaces the fibres catch on rough patches, and a snagging cloth can leave lint or drag. Heavy grease, dried-on residue and set-in soil need a different method or a stronger approach, and the job should not be forced with a microfibre cloth. The source also notes that relying on microfibre for a single job, for example high dusting, may not give the best result. A cleaning system that uses the cloths across several tasks, with cloths assigned by area and by task, gives better and more consistent results than ad hoc use. Set the tasks in the business standard rather than leaving them to habit.

instructionSections.heading: Folding, refolding and cloth-use rules
instructionSections.body: Use one face of the cloth at a time. Fold it so that a clean face is ready while the previous face loads with dust or soil, and refold as each face fills. The source gives a rule of thumb that a standard cloth provides about eight usable faces and that one cloth is normally enough for one area or one room. That is historical hospital practice, not a rule for every job. Treat it as a first guide, then set the business's own cloth-use rule from how quickly each cloth loads, the surfaces it covers and the soil level of the area. Where two areas share a cloth, cross-contamination control under “Colour-coded cloths: a business-set system that keeps areas apart” applies.

instructionSections.heading: Retiring a worn cloth
instructionSections.body: Retire a microfibre cloth when it no longer lifts dust or residue as it did, when its fibres have torn or pilled, or when it has snagged a surface. A cloth that has been used on a dirty area does not return to a clean area, however it looks after washing. Move retired cloths out of the clean set and into the used-cloth route the business sets. Where the business tracks cloth life, record early failures, because a run of them points to a laundering fault, a wrong product or a surface that is too rough for the fibre.

instructionSections.heading: The environmental claim, stated carefully
instructionSections.body: It is tempting to assume that a water-dampened cloth uses less product than a sprayed or soaked method. The source describes the water-dampened design but does not measure product use, so this lesson does not claim a saving. Whether microfibre reduces product use on a given job depends on the surface, the soil, the dilution and the method, and it has not been measured in this draft. If the business wants to make an environmental claim, it should first measure product use and waste on its own jobs. Until then, treat the water-dampened method as a cleaning technique and not as evidence of a lower environmental impact.

lessons.title: Plastic chopping boards: wash, sanitise, rinse and dry on edge
learningOutcomes: Put a plastic chopping board through the scrape, wash, rinse, sanitise, rinse and dry sequence in the order given.
Use a sanitising product only at the label's dilution and contact time, with the PPE that the label sets.
Store a board so that it drains and dries and does not hold water.
Recognise a board that cannot be cleaned to standard, and take it out of use.

instructionSections.heading: Why boards get their own steps
instructionSections.body: A chopping board holds food residue in its knife grooves and its surface, so a quick wipe is not enough. Because the board is used for food, the business's food-safety plan and the rules that apply to food-contact items matter as well as the cleaning method. This lesson covers the cleaning and drying steps for plastic boards as the source sets them out. It does not set food-premises requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Scrape, wash and rinse first
instructionSections.body: Scrape heavy debris and soiling into the bin before any water touches the board. Wash the board in a detergent solution made up to the label, using a brush or scrubber to work into the grooves. Rinse it in fresh water to remove the detergent, because detergent left on the board can interfere with a sanitiser. Change the wash water when it is visibly soiled. If residue will not lift with the brush, soak the board briefly in the detergent solution, then scrub again. Do not move on to the sanitising step until the board is visibly free of residue.

instructionSections.heading: Sanitise at the label's dilution and time
instructionSections.body: The source soaks plastic boards in a sanitising solution for a time set by the source, and it gives a dilution for its product. Both are historical values for a product named in a 2012 hospital manual. This lesson does not endorse that product and does not use those figures as current instructions. Use only a sanitiser on the business's approved products list, make it up to that product's label, and hold the board in contact for the time the label gives. Contact time is the time the sanitiser needs to work, not the time it takes to wipe. If the label gives no time, stop and check the safety data sheet and the approved method before using it. Never mix this sanitiser with another product in the same container or sink.

instructionSections.heading: Rinse, dry and store on edge
instructionSections.body: Rinse the sanitised board in fresh water to remove the sanitiser, then stand it on its edge so that both faces shed water and air out. Laying the board flat traps water in the grooves and underneath, which lets residue and odour build up. Store the dry board on its edge in its allocated place, away from chemical containers. A board that is still damp should not be put away.

instructionSections.heading: Working safely with the sanitiser
instructionSections.body: Sanitising is a chemical-hazard step. Wear the gloves and any eye protection the approved product's label lists, and make up the solution where there is adequate ventilation. The source warns against inhaling sprayed product and asks for ventilation, and those points carry over to any sprayed product. Rinse and dry your hands after use, and protect the skin if contact is prolonged. Keep the sanitiser container closed when it is not in use, and keep it labelled with the product name and dilution. If a product gets into your eyes or onto your skin, follow the first aid steps on the label and the safety data sheet, and report it to your supervisor at once.

instructionSections.heading: Boards that must come out of use
instructionSections.body: Take a board out of use when it has deep grooves or cracks that the brush cannot clean, when it has warped, or when a smell does not clear after the full sequence. Report it to the supervisor and have it replaced under the business's equipment process. Do not try to repair a cracked board with tape or filler, and do not keep using a board whose surface has been lost. A board that is out of use is stored apart from the boards in service, so that nobody picks it up by mistake.

lessons.title: Choosing your service list and checking local demand
learningOutcomes: Sort each planned service into own-trade work, referral work or out of scope, with a stated reason.
Check local demand and competitor offers using at least five dated sources, and record what the checks showed.
Write a one-page service list in plain customer language that contains no unverified claims.

instructionSections.heading: Why a narrow service list helps
instructionSections.body: A service list that says the business will fix anything tends to attract vague enquiries, and it makes it harder for a customer to picture what will happen when they call. A shorter list of specific jobs, named in the words customers actually type into a search box, lets people judge quickly whether the business is the right one for them. Start by writing down every task you have done well in the last few years, paid or unpaid. Then sort the list. Some tasks sit in a clear category, such as hanging doors or patching plasterboard. Others touch licensed trades, such as new power points, gas appliances or plumbing connections. Put those in a separate column marked referral, because a licensed tradesperson does that work, not the handyman. Keep the own-trade column to tasks you can repeat to a good standard.

instructionSections.heading: Testing whether people want the work
instructionSections.body: Demand means that people in your area are looking for the work and are willing to pay someone to do it. Check it with at least five local sources: search results for each service in your suburb or town, local community groups, public job-posting sites, noticeboards that property managers and body corporates publish, and conversations with other local tradespeople. Count how often each service appears, and note whether the requests come from homeowners, landlords, agents or strata managers. A service that appears repeatedly and comes from several types of client is worth testing. A service that nobody asks for is not worth advertising yet, however well you can perform it. Write down the date of each check, so the record stays honest when conditions change.

instructionSections.heading: Studying competitors without copying them
instructionSections.body: Look at eight to ten local operators who offer work similar to yours. For each one, record the services listed, the way each service is described, whether they quote by the hour, by the job or with a call-out fee, the reviews they show, and any licence or insurance claims they make. Treat each claim as something to verify, not as a fact to repeat. Do not reuse their wording, their prices or their photos. The aim is to find gaps: a service that nobody describes clearly, a suburb nobody covers, or a concern customers have that the competitors do not answer, such as clear written quotes or a site visit within a set number of days. Gaps are where a new business can be useful, provided it can deliver what it promises.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding on the result
instructionSections.body: Bring the evidence together on one page. Show the services you will offer, the services you will refer, the places you will work, the demand you found and the gaps you plan to address. If the evidence shows that every service you offer is crowded, narrow the list to one or two specialities, widen the area you serve, or change the mix. Revisit the page after three months of real enquiries. A decision made from a single search is weak evidence, and a list that changes every week means the evidence is not yet clear enough to act on.

lessons.title: Owner time and admin workload before the first job
learningOutcomes: Estimate the weekly hours of admin a small trade business creates, task by task, using measured examples.
Compare available working hours with the admin and job hours, and identify any shortfall.
Set up one simple record system for bookings, quotes, invoices and receipts that share a reference number.

instructionSections.heading: Admin is part of the work
instructionSections.body: Clients see the site visit and the finished job. They do not see the quote drafted at the kitchen table, the message answered late at night, the receipt photographed in a hardware car park, or the invoice sent a week after the work finished. Those tasks take real time, and new owners usually underestimate them. List every admin task the business will carry: enquiries and bookings, site visit notes, quotes, scope confirmations, invoices, payment follow-up, receipts, supplier orders, tool and vehicle records, insurance and licence renewals, website updates, marketing and tax records. Put a rough time against each task for each job or each week. Do not rely on memory alone. Time three or four real tasks, and use those results instead of guesses.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the hours against the week
instructionSections.body: Add the admin hours to the hours of on-site work and travel. Compare the total with the hours you can realistically give the business each week. If admin takes most of the week, replies will be slow, and slow replies lose jobs. Avoid planning admin for the evening after a full day on site unless you have decided that pattern is sustainable. Schedule admin in blocks during the working week, such as one morning for quotes and one block for invoices and receipts. Blocks reduce the constant switching between tasks that makes admin feel endless.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up simple systems first
instructionSections.body: Choose one place for each type of record: a booking list, a quote register, an invoice register and a receipt folder. Use the same reference number on the quote, the job sheet, the invoice and the receipt, so that any job can be traced across all four. Use one business phone number and one email inbox, so enquiries do not get lost between devices. Keep templates for quotes, scope confirmations and invoices. If you use software, check that the invoices it produces contain what an Australian tax invoice must show, and check whether your registration requires you to issue them. Confirm the required content with the ATO before relying on any template. A system that is not kept up to date is worse than paper, so choose the simplest tool you will actually maintain.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding what to change when the numbers do not fit
instructionSections.body: If the total hours exceed what you can give, there are three choices: delay the start date, bring in help for admin, or narrow the services so each job needs less paperwork. Choose the option that protects your response time and your record keeping. After the first month, replace the estimates with the measured figures and repeat the comparison.

lessons.title: Start-up costs, cash runway and business banking
learningOutcomes: List the one-off and recurring costs of starting a trade business, and separate the essential costs from the later ones.
Estimate how many months of living and business costs the owner can cover before income is steady.
Set up separate business banking and a receipt routine that supports the tax records.

instructionSections.heading: Sorting the costs into types
instructionSections.body: Start with five groups: registration and licensing fees set by the state or territory, insurance premiums, website and online listing costs, marketing materials, and equipment. Add a sixth group for transport, phone and data, and software for accounts or bookings. Inside each group, separate one-off costs, such as a first set of tools or a logo, from recurring costs, such as insurance premiums, subscriptions or a phone plan. Enter each amount only after you have checked it with the supplier or the authority, and record the date of the check. Leave out any amount you cannot yet check. Do not copy a figure from a guide. The guide this lesson draws on gives US-based amounts, and those are not used here.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding what is needed now
instructionSections.body: Mark each cost as needed before the first job, needed within the first three months, or needed later. Few trade businesses need every item on the first day.
