A vehicle the owner already has, a basic phone plan and a simple booking method may cover the first jobs, provided the required registration and insurance are in place. Items that protect against serious loss, such as insurance and any required registration, come first. Items that add convenience, such as a larger tool set or a paid advertising campaign, can wait until work is coming in.

instructionSections.heading: Working out the cash runway
instructionSections.body: Cash runway is the number of months the owner can keep paying living costs and business costs before the business earns enough to cover them. Add the monthly living costs, the monthly business costs and an allowance for the months with little work. Divide the cash set aside by that monthly total. Set the allowance honestly. The first months of a trade business are often slower than the owner expects, and a plan that assumes full work from the first week is fragile. If the runway is short, delay the start, reduce the start-up list, or keep some paid work while the business builds.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping business money and records separate
instructionSections.body: Open a separate business bank account before the first invoice, and pay business costs and receive business income through it. Keep every receipt, and write down the business purpose of each purchase. Mixing personal and business money makes records hard to check and creates problems at tax time. Avoid funding the start with expensive debt where a cheaper option exists. Speak with a registered tax agent about which costs are deductible and how vehicle expenses are recorded.

lessons.title: Milestone planning: six months, one year and five years
learningOutcomes: Write milestones for six months, one year and five years, each with a measure that can be checked from records.
Answer the planning questions on clients, time, admin, travel and hiring in writing.
Review the milestones on a fixed schedule, and record any change together with its reason.

instructionSections.heading: Why plan in milestones
instructionSections.body: Many owners start because they want more control over their work, better returns for their hours or the freedom to choose their clients. Those reasons can carry an owner through the early period, but the daily demands of running a business can wear them down. A written set of milestones gives a fixed reference point. It shows whether the business is moving toward what the owner wants, and it signals when a change of course is needed. A milestone plan is a private planning tool. It is different from a formal business plan for a lender, which needs more financial detail. “How a cleaning business plan is structured” sets out the structure of a formal plan.

instructionSections.heading: Setting three milestones with checkable measures
instructionSections.body: Describe what the business looks like at six months, at one year and at five years. Each description should contain something you could check: the number of repeat clients served, the share of enquiries answered within a set time, the share of work that comes from referrals, the hours worked on site each week, whether a team member is employed, and what the records show. Avoid phrases such as doing well or growing strongly. A measure you cannot check tells you nothing about whether you are on track.

instructionSections.heading: Answering the planning questions
instructionSections.body: Use these questions to test the milestones. How many fresh clients must come in each month, and how many existing clients can you keep? What will you spend each month on tools and their upkeep? How many hours each week will admin take? What is the longest travel time you will accept for a job? Which sources will bring in the bulk of the work? At what point will the first team member join, and when will a second follow? Keep the answers realistic. A plan that assumes a large number of new clients in six months needs strong evidence for that claim. Also write down what you want the business to be after five years: a small operation, a larger team, or a business you eventually hand to someone else.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the plan honest and reviewing it
instructionSections.body: Review the milestones on a fixed date each quarter, and record what has changed and why. Small adjustments are normal. Frequent large changes suggest the original numbers were not based on evidence, and then the plan needs a fresh look at the demand evidence from “Choosing your service list and checking local demand” and the cash position from “Start-up costs, cash runway and business banking”. Keep the plan to one or two pages, so it stays readable and gets used.

lessons.title: Insurance for property trade work in Australia
learningOutcomes: Identify the insurance types a small property trade business should consider, and describe what each one covers in general terms.
Compare quotes using the same scope of work, the same limits, the same exclusions and the same conditions.
Keep a register of policies, certificates and renewal dates that a client or a regulator can check.

instructionSections.heading: What insurance is for
instructionSections.body: Insurance shifts the expense of a serious mistake or accident away from the owner and the client. A tradesperson can damage a client's property while working, and a member of the public can be hurt on a site. Those events can cost far more than a year of premiums. Insurance also builds trust, because many clients, property managers and councils ask for proof of cover before they engage a trade. The guide this lesson draws on describes general liability insurance and workers compensation. The Australian term for cover against claims from third parties for injury or property damage caused by the work is public liability insurance.

instructionSections.heading: The main types to consider
instructionSections.body: Public liability insurance covers third-party claims for injury or property damage caused by the work. Workers compensation insurance covers employees for injuries at work. Tools and equipment cover and motor vehicle cover protect the business's assets. Choose the types that match the actual work, the people who will do it and the clients it serves. Then confirm each choice with the insurer or with an adviser who is authorised to give the advice.

instructionSections.heading: Comparing quotes like for like
instructionSections.body: Obtain at least two quotes for the same scope of work. Compare the limit of cover, the excess, the exclusions, the work the policy says it covers, any restriction on height, roof or electrical work, the claims process and the renewal terms. A lower premium is not a better policy if it excludes the work you do. Check that the person giving advice is authorised. The ASIC register is the place to check it, and the check should be made on the ASIC site before any advice is accepted.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the evidence
instructionSections.body: Keep a register of each policy with the insurer, the cover type, the limit, the start date, the renewal date and where the document is kept. Send a copy of the current certificate to a client when a job requires it. Renew before the expiry date, because a lapse can end cover for work already in progress. Tell the insurer when an employee, a new service or a new vehicle is added, because undisclosed changes can affect a claim. This lesson does not recommend any insurer or broker.

lessons.title: Business registration and licence checks by state and territory
learningOutcomes: Identify which registrations and licences the state or territory may require for each task on the planned service list.
Check each task against the state or territory rule, and record the source, the date and the result of the check.
Set out the business identity steps (name, structure, Australian Business Number and GST timing), with each step marked as checked or still to be checked.

instructionSections.heading: Start with the work, not the paperwork
instructionSections.body: Licence rules usually depend on the type and value of the work, so begin by writing down the work the business plans to do. Break each service into the tasks it involves. Then check each task against the rules in your own state or territory. The guide this lesson draws on describes a contractor licence process in one US state: check the state rules, choose a business name, complete training, sit an exam and apply. Those steps do not apply in Australia. Each state and territory has its own licensing and registration rules, with different thresholds, categories and fees. The existing lesson “Scope, consent and trade boundaries” sets out the trade boundary and the licence notice, so read it first, then check the current rules with the state authority.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up the business identity
instructionSections.body: Choose a business name you are entitled to use. A trading name that differs from the owner's legal name is a question to check with the state or territory. Decide the business structure. A sole trader, a company, a partnership and a trust each carry different tax and liability features, so the choice should be made with a registered tax agent or an accountant. Confirm the current steps and any fees before applying for an Australian Business Number. Register for GST when GST turnover reaches the threshold. The ATO states that a GST turnover of $75,000 or more requires registration, as checked on 2026-11-02.

instructionSections.heading: Checking licences and renewals
instructionSections.body: If a state or territory requires a licence or registration for a task, record the licence category, the holder's obligations, the renewal date and any conditions. Some categories allow only certain work, so a licence may not cover everything on the service list. Keep the licence or a verified register entry in the business file, with the expiry date. Check for each licence category whether it can transfer to a business or an employee. Completing a course, passing an exam or finishing an apprenticeship is not the same as holding a licence. The licence is the authority issued by the state or territory, and this lesson does not issue, grant or confirm any licence.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping a compliance record
instructionSections.body: Record every check: the state or territory rule, the source and the date checked, the decision, and who made it. Repeat the checks each year and whenever a new service is added. A record shows a client or an auditor that the rules were looked at before the work was accepted, and it helps the owner notice when a change affects the business.

lessons.title: Buying tools and equipment in stages
learningOutcomes: Build a list of tool categories needed for the first three to five planned services.
Decide for each tool whether to own, borrow, hire or refer it, and record the reason.
Keep a tool register with purchase, inspection and storage details.

instructionSections.heading: Starting from the services, not the shop
instructionSections.body: The most common way to overspend is to buy tools for jobs that have not been booked. Start from the first few services on the list. For each service, write down the tasks it requires and the tool categories each task uses: measuring and marking, fixing and fastening, cutting, power tools, access equipment, cleaning and protection, and personal protective equipment. Tools the owner already has come first. A tool needed once a year may be better hired or borrowed, provided the hire is safe and the operator is competent. Record the reason for each decision so it can be reviewed later.

instructionSections.heading: Buying in the order of use
instructionSections.body: Buy the tools used most often for the first services, and add the rest as work arrives. A practical test is to buy a tool when a booked job needs it and when the cost of hiring it for the year would be higher than the cost of owning it. Keep the receipt for every purchase, linked to the job or service it supports. Choose tools that suit the materials and tasks actually taken on, and check each tool's rated use before buying. Quality matters most for tools that carry load, cut or fasten, because a failed tool causes injuries and rework.

instructionSections.heading: Looking after what is bought
instructionSections.body: Inspect each tool before use, clean it after use, and store it where it cannot damage or injure anyone. Check the cords, guards and switches of power tools. Inspect ladders and access equipment before each use, as set out in “Ladders, elevated access and fall prevention”. A tool register lists each tool with its purchase date and cost, a serial number or other identifying mark, the date of the last inspection and any repair. Keep the register in the vehicle folder or in cloud storage, and update it after every repair.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting against theft and damage
instructionSections.body: Tools are a business asset and are often stolen from vehicles. Keep the most valuable tools locked away, mark them with an identifier, and photograph them for the register. Check with the insurer whether tools and equipment are covered, and whether any storage condition applies to tools kept in a vehicle.

lessons.title: Finding local customers without relying on bidding sites
learningOutcomes: Choose two or three local customer-finding methods that fit the service list and the owner's available time.
Plan a letterbox or property-agent approach that respects consent, council rules and privacy.
Track each enquiry to its source, and review which methods produced jobs after a set period.

instructionSections.heading: Why local methods still matter
instructionSections.body: Many enquiries come from people who live near the business or need the work done close to home. Online bidding sites put a business in competition with many others at once. Local methods allow a business to build a reputation in a small area, with fewer rivals for each job. These methods work best when the service list is clear (“Choosing your service list and checking local demand”) and the owner can respond quickly. Because local methods take time, choose two or three rather than trying everything at once.

instructionSections.heading: Letterbox drops and printed offers
instructionSections.body: A letterbox drop puts a printed offer into homes on a chosen street or in a chosen suburb. Use a clear photo of the owner's own completed work, a short list of services and one way to respond. Check whether the local council allows distribution, and respect any no junk mail sign on a letterbox. Track the number of letters delivered, the enquiries received and the jobs won, so the cost of each lead can be judged. Printed mail is not governed by the Spam Act 2003, but the content must still be accurate and must not imply a licence or an insurance cover the owner does not hold.

instructionSections.heading: Property managers, agents and strata contacts
instructionSections.body: Property managers, agents and strata managers often need small repairs done quickly, between tenancies or on common property. Introduce the business in person or by letter, bring a short service list, and offer a trial quote. Once the business holds insurance, provide a certificate when the agency asks for one. Agents usually have preferred trades and set their own contractor requirements, so follow those conditions. A lasting arrangement grows from reliable work and clear quotes, not from underpricing other trades.

instructionSections.heading: Vehicle signage, cards and a simple web page
instructionSections.body: Business cards work well when handed over at the end of a job, with the client's permission to give them out. A simple web page with a short service list, photos of the owner's own work used with consent, and a contact method is enough to begin. Keep the business details accurate, because enquiries will check them.

instructionSections.heading: Recording where each enquiry came from
instructionSections.body: Ask every caller how they found the business, and record the answer against the enquiry. After six to eight weeks, compare the enquiries, quotes and jobs for each method. Drop any method that produced no jobs, and put more time into the methods that did. This record helps the owner spend marketing money on what works.

lessons.title: Online job platforms: choosing and setting up a profile
learningOutcomes: Compare online job platforms on fees, lead quality, contract terms and the time each one needs.
Write a profile with accurate business details, evidence of work and a clear service description.
Measure the cost of each platform lead and decide whether to keep, change or stop using each platform.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding whether the time is worth it
instructionSections.body: Online platforms connect people who need work with tradespeople who respond to their requests. They can provide steady leads, but they also bring competition, lead fees, subscriptions and the time spent on bids that never turn into jobs. The guide this lesson draws on names several US sites. Those sites are not Australian services, and their fees and terms are not used here. Before joining any platform, find out whether it operates in the owner's area, what it charges, whether the charge is per lead, per job or by subscription, how it ranks profiles, and what its terms say about contact details. Check each point on the platform's own terms page.

instructionSections.heading: Building the profile around evidence
instructionSections.body: A profile is often the first contact a client has with the business. Include the trading name and the owner's name as the owner presents them to the public, the suburbs or regions served, the locations travelled to for work, the specialities, and the website if there is one. Add photos of the owner's own completed work, with client consent. Show a rate or a range if the platform allows it. Write a short description covering what the business does well, how quickly it responds and how it adapts to a client's needs. Ask a friend or family member to read it back. Every licence or insurance claim must match what the owner holds and can show.

instructionSections.heading: Testing with a small number of platforms
instructionSections.body: Start with one or two platforms and a fixed trial period. Record every lead, bid, reply, job and invoice against the platform it came from. At the end of the trial, calculate the cost of each lead and the cost per job won, including the time spent bidding. Keep the platforms that produce jobs at an acceptable cost, and stop the rest. Ask each completed client for a review where the platform allows it and the client is willing to give one.

instructionSections.heading: Protecting client information
instructionSections.body: Client contact details and addresses are personal information. Do not share them outside the platform, do not post them publicly, and do not contact a client through a channel the platform prohibits. Read the platform's privacy statement before uploading any client photo or detail. Keep the profile details consistent across platforms, so clients do not see conflicting information.

lessons.title: Winning bids without underpricing
learningOutcomes: Reply to a bid request with a personalised message that names the client's job and proposes a clear next step.
Prepare an accurate estimate for a site visit or a remote quote, with inclusions, exclusions and assumptions stated.
Avoid underpricing by checking every bid against the estimate and the hourly rate or minimum charge.

instructionSections.heading: The first reply shapes the next step
instructionSections.body: A bid request is often one of several a client receives. The first reply should show that the request was read. Use the client's name, refer to the job by its details, and say what happens next, such as a call, a site visit or a written quote by a set date. Speed matters, because a prompt reply signals that the business will be responsive on the job. Where a platform shows the client's phone number with the request, a call to discuss the job is a normal reply to it. Avoid a generic template sent to every request, because clients notice when a message does not match their question.

instructionSections.heading: Offering a site visit when the scope is unclear
instructionSections.body: A bid made from a photo or a short description can be wrong. Offer a site visit when the job involves access problems, hidden conditions or more than one service type. Bring a portfolio of the owner's own work, the service list and the estimate form. A visit also shows the client how the business works. Record what was seen, what the client asked for and what the client did not ask for, so the scope can be confirmed in writing.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing from the estimate, not from competitors
instructionSections.body: Cutting a price to win one job can leave the business with a loss it cannot recover. Build the price from the estimate (“Estimating a job from labour, materials and extras”) and from the hourly rate or minimum charge (“Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge”). If the scope is not yet clear, state the assumptions and what would change the price, rather than guessing low. Competitor prices are a guide, not a target, and a comparison is only useful with businesses whose insurance, licences and costs are similar. Some estimating guides add a 10 to 20 percent allowance to estimates for unexpected work; if the owner uses one, state it as an assumption. Keep the quote valid for a stated period. Tell the client what is included, what is excluded and what would need a variation. If a warranty or guarantee is offered, state its terms clearly. Under the Australian Consumer Law, services must be carried out with due care and skill, be fit for the purpose stated, and be supplied within a reasonable time where no timeframe is agreed, as the business.gov.au guide sets out. Check the current rules before writing any warranty wording.

instructionSections.heading: Asking for references and reviews
instructionSections.body: Clients who trust the business are more likely to hire it. Offer references where the client has agreed to share them. Ask each client for a review after the job, and include the review link in the next message where the platform allows it. Keep the reviews on file with their date and the client's permission to use them.

lessons.title: Turning one-off jobs into repeat clients
learningOutcomes: Plan a follow-up sequence for past clients that is accurate, consented and respectful of unsubscribe requests.
Design a check-in or maintenance package with a defined scope, price, exclusions and cancellation terms.
Record repeat work and referrals against each client, so their value can be measured.

instructionSections.heading: Why repeat work changes the business
instructionSections.body: Most property trade enquiries are one-off jobs, so a business can end up in a constant search for new clients. Repeat work reduces that pressure. A client who trusts the business will call again for the next small job, and that client is more likely to recommend it to friends and neighbours. The aim is a base of clients who call regularly, while the business still takes new work. Repeat work also makes the week easier to plan, which reduces the admin load described in “Owner time and admin workload before the first job”.

instructionSections.heading: Staying in touch after the job
instructionSections.body: Contact the client a few days after the job to check that the work is performing as expected, and ask for a review if the client is pleased. Then plan a light touch two or three times a year, such as a seasonal reminder or an offer to inspect the property. Keep messages short and useful. A message that gives a real reason to reply, such as a seasonal check or a warning about a known issue, works better than one that only says hello. Electronic messages must follow the Spam Act 2003, which requires consent, accurate sender identification and an unsubscribe option that works. The ACMA guidance, checked on 2026-11-02, says unsubscribe requests must be acted on within five working days. The wider outreach rules are set out in “Finding your first customers through direct, consent-based outreach” and “Referrals and repeat work from existing clients”.

instructionSections.heading: Designing a check-in or maintenance package
instructionSections.body: A package bundles a defined set of services into a regular arrangement at a set price. For example, a yearly property check with a fixed list of items, a set number of minor repairs and one price. The package must be clearly defined: what is included, what is excluded, what happens when extra work is needed, how often it runs and how the client can cancel. Check the margin of the package against the hourly rate and minimum charge (“Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge”), because a package that suits the client but does not cover the time loses money.

instructionSections.heading: Offering repeat-client terms carefully
instructionSections.body: Discounts for repeat clients can help, but only when the business can afford them. Calculate any discount as a percentage of the normal price, and check the margin after it is applied. Benefits that cost less than a discount may be better, such as priority booking or a free annual inspection with a defined scope. Record the benefit in writing so the client knows what to expect.

lessons.title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short jobs, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instructionSections.heading: Factors that move the rate
instructionSections.body: A rate depends on skill, experience, how scarce the skill is locally, the range of work offered and the cost of running the business. An owner who offers several services that a client can book in one visit may justify a higher rate, because the client saves time. A narrow range of basic tasks in a crowded market may need a rate closer to local norms. Experience matters too. A new business should price honestly and review the rate regularly, rather than cutting it to win work. Use the local evidence from “Choosing your service list and checking local demand”, “Finding local customers without relying on bidding sites” and “Online job platforms: choosing and setting up a profile”, not a published national average. The guide this lesson draws on gives a US national average, and that figure is not used here.

instructionSections.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instructionSections.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. If only part of the paid time can be billed, the rate must be higher than it would be if every hour could be billed. For example, if sixty of every hundred paid hours are billable, the costs of all one hundred hours must be recovered from the sixty, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week. A Jobber guide puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours. That is a general range rather than an Australian figure, so check your own log against it.

instructionSections.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instructionSections.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income needed to live on. A business.gov.au pricing guide says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each will be allowed for. Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation are treated for the owner's situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by the billable hours to reach the base rate. A personal-training pricing guide from AIPT works backwards from a target income, dividing by working weeks and then by weekly hours, with tax and business costs added on top. Its example figures are not used here. Review the base rate each quarter, and compare it with what clients accept and with the local evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instructionSections.body: Short jobs can cost more in time than they earn, because travel and setup do not shrink with the size of the task. A minimum charge or a call-out fee covers the time needed to attend the site and start work. Set the minimum so that a short job still covers travel, setup and admin. State it before the visit, and explain it to the client in plain terms. A contractor pricing guide suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, setup and cleanup. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here.

lessons.title: Estimating a job from labour, materials and extras
learningOutcomes: Build an estimate that shows labour, materials, subcontract costs, permits, cleanup and travel as separate lines.
Estimate job time from a checked scope and the owner's own record of similar jobs.
Identify the assumptions and risks that could change the estimate, and state them in the quote.

instructionSections.heading: Check the site before pricing
instructionSections.body: An estimate built from a photo or a phone description often misses access problems, the condition of surfaces and hidden work. Visit the site when the job is not simple. Note the access route, the working height where relevant, the condition of surfaces or items, any existing conditions that affect the work and any hazards that need controls. Write down what was seen in the same terms that will appear in the scope. Where a site is unsafe, or the work lies outside the owner's permitted scope, record that and refer the work before pricing it.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the scope and estimating the time
instructionSections.body: Write the scope as an ordered list of tasks, with the finish expected for each. Estimate the time for each task from the owner's records of similar past jobs. Where no record exists, time a sample task, note the result and update the estimate after the job. A trade article from Carters Trade Leader suggests comparing the original quote with the actual labour time, then feeding the gap into the next quote. Add time for setup, travel, cleanup and handover. A scope that says clean the rooms is weak. A scope that names the rooms, the tasks in each, the materials or products and the finish expected is useful.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing labour, materials and extras
instructionSections.body: Labour is the time for each task multiplied by the hourly rate from “Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge”, or the minimum charge if that is higher. Materials are the cost of each item, including delivery and an allowance for waste where the task needs one. A subcontract line is the quoted price of a licensed or specialist provider brought in, and the owner must check that the subcontractor holds the required licence and insurance before the line is added. Cleanup and waste disposal are costs too, and so are fuel and travel if they are not already in labour. Show each cost on its own line, so the client can see where the money goes.

instructionSections.heading: Stating what could change the price
instructionSections.body: List the assumptions behind the estimate, such as the access, the condition of the surfaces or items, the existing conditions and the client's choice of finish. Add a clear line that names what would trigger a variation, and state that the variation will be agreed in writing before the extra work starts. An estimate that names its risks protects both the owner and the client when the job reveals more than was expected. Some estimating guides add 10 to 20 percent to estimates for unexpected work; if the owner does so, state the allowance as an assumption.

lessons.title: Markup, margin and presenting the final quote
learningOutcomes: Distinguish markup from margin, and calculate the price for each method from the same cost base.
Check the arithmetic of a quote formula, and identify whether the label matches the calculation.
Present a quote with inclusions, exclusions, validity, GST treatment and variation terms.

instructionSections.heading: Markup and margin are different
instructionSections.body: A markup is the percentage added to a cost to reach a price. A margin is the share of the price that remains as profit after the cost is paid. The same cost gives different prices depending on which method is used. If a cost is one hundred units and a markup of fifty per cent is added, the price is one hundred and fifty units. If the same cost must produce a margin of fifty per cent, the price is two hundred units, because the cost must be half of the price. The two methods are not interchangeable, so a quote should state which one has been used.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the source's formula before using it
instructionSections.body: The guide this lesson draws on divides a total cost by 0.50 and calls the result a markup of fifty per cent. Dividing by 0.50 doubles the cost. That result is a margin of fifty per cent, which is the same as a markup of one hundred per cent on cost. The guide's arithmetic is correct, but its label is not. This lesson does not use that formula as a markup. The correct calculations are: price equals cost multiplied by one plus the markup, or price equals cost divided by one minus the margin. A contractor pricing guide (Contractor+, 23 September 2026) makes the same point: dividing the whole visit cost by one minus the target margin gives the price for that margin, while adding the same percentage to cost gives a lower margin. Its figures are illustrative. This is recorded as a source correction for reviewer confirmation.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the method and presenting the quote
instructionSections.body: Choose markup or margin as the method, apply it consistently to labour and materials, and state how the markup covers overheads and profit. Check that the price covers total overheads, including card fees, insurance and software, and not only the direct costs of the job (Business Victoria guide, undated). Present the quote as separate lines for labour, materials, subcontracts, permits and cleanup, then the total. State whether the price includes GST, and confirm with the ATO how GST must be shown on a quote. The ATO states that a business must register for GST once its GST turnover reaches $75,000 (ATO page last updated 14 September 2026). State the validity period, the inclusions and exclusions, any warranty or guarantee terms, the variation process and the payment terms.

instructionSections.heading: Walking the client through the quote
instructionSections.body: Go through the quote with the client in person or by phone, line by line. Explain each assumption and the trigger for any variation. A client who understands the quote is less likely to dispute the final invoice. Keep a copy of what was agreed, and keep any written confirmation of it.

lessons.title: Deciding on your first team member
learningOutcomes: Decide whether the business is ready to hire, using repeat demand, cash and workload evidence.
Decide between an employee and an independent contractor using the working arrangement, not the label.
Screen and interview a candidate using skills checks, references and a check of any licence claim.

instructionSections.heading: Confirming the business is ready
instructionSections.body: Hiring is often the step that makes a small business feel fragile. Before hiring, check the evidence: repeat work and steady enquiries, a cash buffer that covers wages and on-costs for several months, and admin and job records showing that the extra capacity is needed. The milestone plan in “Milestone planning: six months, one year and five years” is the place to write the hiring trigger. A hire made because the owner is busy for one month often becomes a loss when the work drops away.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the working relationship
instructionSections.body: Decide whether the person will be an employee or an independent contractor. The label in a contract does not decide the relationship. The way the work is done, who controls it, who supplies the tools, and whether the person works for others all matter. Employment obligations, including minimum pay under the applicable award or agreement, leave, superannuation, workers compensation and payroll tax, must be checked before any offer is made. Confirm them with the Fair Work Ombudsman or a registered employment adviser.

instructionSections.heading: Screening for skills and reliability
instructionSections.body: Set the skills the role needs, and test them. A practical task or a short site test shows more than a résumé. Check references from people who have seen the candidate work, and check any licence or certificate the candidate claims to hold on the state or territory register. Ask how the candidate handles a job that goes wrong, how they communicate with clients, and how they plan their day. Trust matters, because the person will enter client homes and represent the business.

instructionSections.heading: Taking care with friends and family
instructionSections.body: Hiring someone you know can work, but the relationship can make it hard to give direction, correct errors or end the arrangement. If you hire someone close to you, agree the role, the hours, the pay and the expectations in writing, and treat the arrangement as a work relationship. Where the budget allows, hire for a skill the owner does not have, because that adds capacity rather than copying the owner's skills. Look for someone who finishes tasks without constant direction.

lessons.title: Setting up your first employee: cover, pay, schedule and feedback
learningOutcomes: List the cover, registration and pay steps to complete before an employee's first working day.
Plan a weekly schedule that groups jobs by area to reduce travel time.
Set up a feedback routine that keeps the employee and the business improving.

instructionSections.heading: Cover before the first day
instructionSections.body: Before the first working day, confirm the workers compensation cover for the employee in the state or territory where the work is done. Confirm that the business's public liability cover applies when an employee works on client sites, and check the policy conditions on supervision and licensed work. Keep the policy number and the certificate in the business file.

instructionSections.heading: Pay and records
instructionSections.body: Register as an employer with the tax office and set up the payroll reporting the ATO requires. Pay the employee at least the minimum under the applicable award or agreement, and pay superannuation at the super guarantee rate. The ATO page checked on 2026-11-02 gives that rate as 12.00 per cent for 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027. Payroll software or a payroll service can help, but the owner remains responsible for the payments. Late pay is the quickest route to losing a worker and to starting a dispute.

instructionSections.heading: Scheduling for travel and skill
instructionSections.body: Plan the week so the employee and the owner are not spending the day in traffic. Group jobs by suburb or region, and keep a quieter day for the jobs further away. Work alongside the employee on the first few jobs, so that the owner can check the standard of work, how it is recorded and how the client is handled. Give each day a plan listing the job, the address, the scope, the materials, the access arrangements and the expected finish time. Record the start and finish time of each job, and its outcome. The schedule should also show when the owner will be on site, so that clients know who to expect.

instructionSections.heading: Feedback and handover
instructionSections.body: Hold a short feedback conversation each week for the first month, and a monthly one after that. Ask the employee what would make the work easier, what the business could do better and what they need. Write down the changes agreed, and check them at the next meeting. Plan for the possibility that a good employee will leave. Keep job records, standards and client details in the business systems rather than only in one person's head, so the work can pass to someone else without loss.

lessons.title: Working zones in a dental surgery: where contamination can and cannot go
learningOutcomes: Describe where contamination travels in a dental operatory and why the room is divided into zones.
Apply the rule for movement between the two zones.
Choose the correct glove and the correct storage point at changeover.

instructionSections.heading: Why the operatory is zoned
instructionSections.body: A dental treatment room has two kinds of working space. The first is the contaminated side, where patient fluids such as blood and saliva can land through splashing, spattering or transfer. It takes in the operating field and the area where instruments are cleaned. The second is the clean side, which holds reception, offices, staff rooms, sterile items and stock. The division keeps contamination inside the first side and stops it reaching the second. Everyone who works in the room has to understand where that line sits, not only the clinician.

instructionSections.heading: How far contamination travels
instructionSections.body: Splashes and large droplets usually land within roughly a metre of the patient's mouth. Finer aerosols produced during treatment can carry further than that. The source therefore treats the whole operatory as at risk while treatment is under way. Any surface or item within reach of the treatment is taken to be contaminated by that treatment. Surfaces left uncovered by a barrier are wiped down once each patient has left. An item placed on the contaminated side and not used is still treated as contaminated.

instructionSections.heading: Moving between the two sides
instructionSections.body: Staff may step from the clean side onto the contaminated side once they have gloved, but gloved hands carrying contaminated material do not travel back. Stock moves from clean storage into the room. Contaminated items never return to clean storage. Bulk stock such as glove boxes, cotton rolls and gauze stays on the clean side, covered against splashes and aerosols. Personal bags, spare clothing and personal belongings stay out of both sides.

instructionSections.heading: Your part at changeover
instructionSections.body: A cleaner who enters the room at changeover puts on fresh gloves before touching any working surface. Gloves that were on during assistance with the last procedure are not reused for the cleaning task. Working surfaces are wiped with neutral detergent by the method the practice's written protocol sets. Barrier coverings on hard-to-clean equipment are removed and replaced as the protocol requires. Never move a contaminated item into clean storage, and never open a clean drawer while wearing contaminated gloves.

lessons.title: Dental unit waterlines: biofilm, flushing and water quality
learningOutcomes: Explain why biofilm forms inside dental unit water tubing.
Describe the controls that keep waterlines in a safe state.
Report a waterline fault without handling or dosing the water system.

instructionSections.heading: Why waterlines need attention
instructionSections.body: The narrow tubes that feed the handpieces, the three-way syringe and the ultrasonic scalers carry water slowly, and their inner surface is large compared with the volume they hold. Under those conditions, organisms from the environment can settle and build a film called biofilm. The film can release organisms into the water sprayed on patients and staff. Among the organisms the source flags from waterlines are Pseudomonas aeruginosa, one group of atypical mycobacteria, and Legionella. Biofilm is therefore regarded as a store of contamination, not as a nuisance.

instructionSections.heading: Water quality targets
instructionSections.body: The source asks that water used to cool or irrigate during tooth preparation and scaling meet at least the national drinking-water standard. It sets a bacterial count limit for coolant water in non-surgical work, and a tighter limit when care is given to people whose immune defences are weakened. Surgical procedures use sterile water or saline. Test results are checked against those limits.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the lines in a safe state
instructionSections.body: The main controls are flushing the lines after each patient and again at the opening of each day, flushing after a long break, fitting anti-retraction valves so that fluid from the mouth cannot travel back into the lines, and treating the water by a method the manufacturer approves. Any treatment product is handled under the manufacturer's directions by a person trained to do it. A cleaner does not mix, dose or connect a water treatment product unless the role and training specifically allow it. Valves cannot stand in for flushing, and flushing cannot stand in for valves.

instructionSections.heading: Your part
instructionSections.body: A cleaner reports leaking lines, missing or damaged valves, a test kit past its use date, or water that looks or tastes unusual at the chair. A cleaner does not disconnect a line or interfere with a valve.

lessons.title: Burs, handpieces and sharps at the chairside
learningOutcomes: Explain why careless handling of sharps is the leading cause of puncture injuries in a dental surgery.
Remove a loose sharp safely without touching it with bare fingers.
Seal and hand over a sharps box for licensed collection under the site plan.

instructionSections.heading: Where sharps injuries come from
instructionSections.body: The source names careless handling of sharps, during treatment and afterwards, as the chief reason for puncture injuries at dental chairs. Tight working space and a limited view of the field make things worse. Burs, scalers, scalpels, orthodontic wires and needles all belong to that group, and the risk runs through the whole changeover, not only through the procedure itself.

instructionSections.heading: Burs and handpieces
instructionSections.body: A bur is removed from its handpiece before the handpiece leaves the unit, so that a bur does not travel with it. Reusable burs go into a stand, not into a general container. Before changeover begins, the assistant checks that the operator has taken off any burs or orthodontic wires. A cleaner does not remove a bur from a handpiece unless the role and training allow it.

instructionSections.heading: Hand passing and trays
instructionSections.body: Blades like scalpels and scalers are never handed directly from one worker to another. They are dropped into a puncture-resistant receptacle straight after use, and they travel to the instrument area inside a lidded box that resists punctures. Disposable sharps go straight into a sanctioned sharps box at the chairside, near the spot where they were used.

instructionSections.heading: Containers and collection
instructionSections.body: Sharps containers stand upright, out of children's reach, and are never overfilled. The source asks for sealing at the fill line, or at roughly three-quarters capacity, followed by collection by a licensed waste contractor under local rules. The cleaner hands sealed containers to the person responsible for collection and does not collect or transport them to a disposal site.

instructionSections.heading: Needles
instructionSections.body: A needle is not recapped unless the practice uses a recapping device or a single-handed technique designed for that purpose. Bending or snapping a used needle by hand is never acceptable. Disposable needle and syringe combinations go directly into the sharps container.

lessons.title: Extracted teeth, amalgam and dental clinical waste
learningOutcomes: Separate medical waste from general waste at the point it is collected.
Handle a bag of clinical waste without compacting or overfilling it.
Choose the correct route for an extracted tooth, including one with a dental amalgam restoration.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as clinical waste
instructionSections.body: Clinical or medical waste from a dental practice includes recognisable human tissue, with teeth treated separately, and any material or solution that carries free-flowing blood. The rules that govern disposal are the state and territory regulations and the local environment authority's guidance, not one national rule. Separate waste at its origin into medical and non-medical streams, colour code and label medical waste, and use bags that meet the applicable clinical waste bag standard.

instructionSections.heading: Handling bags and containers
instructionSections.body: The usual barrier kit of gloves, a face mask and goggles applies whenever clinical waste is handled. Bags and boxes are not overfilled, and nothing is pressed down inside them. Clinical waste and sharps boxes wait in secure storage for a licensed contractor, who collects them for approved treatment. Chemical waste, including some dental chemicals and mercury, never goes to a landfill tip that compacts waste.

instructionSections.heading: Extracted teeth
instructionSections.body: Once an extracted tooth has been rinsed free of visible blood, grit, soft tissue and spit, it may be given back to the patient on request. Otherwise it could be enclosed in paper, or set in plaster inside a disposable cup, then put in ordinary rubbish under the local rule. Certain states and territories restrict burning teeth that carry dental amalgam, because mercury vapour is released, so those teeth must not go into medical waste or sharps containers. Check the local rule before disposing of any tooth.

instructionSections.heading: Chemical waste from imaging
instructionSections.body: Imaging chemicals and some disinfectants have their own disposal route. The source refers to a companion practice guide for the detail, which this lesson does not reproduce. Use the practice's documented chemical waste route, and never pour a chemical into a general drain unless the written plan allows it.

lessons.title: Mobile dental visits to care homes and private homes
learningOutcomes: Describe how instruments and materials are carried to and from a mobile visit.
Separate waste and sharps during a visit and carry them back to the practice.
Prepare an impression for transport so it is safe to handle.

instructionSections.heading: Why home and care visits differ
instructionSections.body: Dental care given in a residential care facility, a home or a hospital bed takes place away from the fixed surgery. Facilities there are often limited, and water, power and waste collection can be hard to arrange. The source applies the same standard precautions as in the surgery and expects staff to carry the protective equipment they need.

instructionSections.heading: Carrying instruments and materials
instructionSections.body: Clean instruments and materials travel in a lidded box of metal or stiff plastic so they are not damaged or spilled. Used instruments return to the practice inside a sealed, hard-walled box. Where possible they are cleaned during the visit using detergent solution, or misted with a product that keeps debris from hardening, before they travel. Impressions and try-ins travel in sealed plastic boxes, and impressions are rinsed to clear visible blood and spit before they reach the laboratory.

instructionSections.heading: Waste on the road
instructionSections.body: Waste is separated where it is generated. General waste goes into the facility's general waste. Sharp items and clinical waste follow the state rules, and a sharps container labelled to the Australian standard travels with the team back to the practice. Clinical waste is never left in the facility's general bin.

instructionSections.heading: Your part on the visit
instructionSections.body: The assistant carries the containers and waste bags, checks every seal and lid before leaving the room, and notes any missing supplies or facility problems for the practice. The assistant does not leave used items in the facility's rooms or bins.

lessons.title: Front-of-house areas: housekeeping, toys and shared devices
learningOutcomes: Apply a housekeeping method that avoids raising dust or aerosols.
Clean toys and shared devices on a set schedule.
Keep clinical and general cleaning tools separate.

instructionSections.heading: Housekeeping surfaces are still surfaces
instructionSections.body: Floors, walls, curtains and reception furniture carry lower risk than the clinical contact surfaces, but the source requires them to remain clean and sanitary under the public health rules that apply in each state and territory. Dust, soil and transient organisms still collect on them, so they stay on a written schedule.

instructionSections.heading: Toys and shared objects
instructionSections.body: Toys in waiting areas act as objects that carry germs between people. Wiping their firm surfaces with detergent wipes suited to firm clinical surfaces, on the practice's schedule and after a busy period, reduces the organisms that move around. Follow the product's own directions, and do not use general household spray in its place.

instructionSections.heading: Keyboards and handsets
instructionSections.body: Keyboards in the operatory can harbour microbes, so they are shielded in the treatment areas and wiped down between appointments with a product the manufacturer permits. Outside the treatment areas, keyboards are wiped down regularly. Standard keyboards cannot be submerged, and repeated saturation damages them, so flat or sealed keyboards are preferred where the practice can use them. Telephone handsets, door handles and window sills belong on the weekly schedule.

instructionSections.heading: Dusting and mopping without spreading dust
instructionSections.body: Cleaning must not stir up dust or spray. Damp dusting, mops that trap dust, and vacuums fitted with filtered exhaust are preferred, and brooms are kept out of clinical spaces. Mops and cloths are rinsed once used and left to air dry before the next use, or single-use heads are chosen. Keep separate mops for clinical and general areas, which the Malaysian guideline also advises. Lunchroom crockery is never washed in hand basins or instrument basins, and food is never stored with dental materials, specimens or medicines.

lessons.title: Waste rules that differ between countries: reading a foreign guideline against Australian rules
learningOutcomes: Explain why a guideline from another country is used for comparison, not as the local rule.
Identify two points where the Malaysian waste section differs from the Australian sources.
State the principles that hold across waste systems and the action to take when a difference appears.

instructionSections.heading: Why compare two guidelines
instructionSections.body: A guideline written in another country describes how a dental practice there handles clinical waste. Reading it next to the Australian rules shows where the systems differ, so that a worker knows which rule to check. Local rules still apply in full. This lesson uses the waste section of the Malaysian guideline as the example. It marks each point that differs from the Australian sources, the ADA guideline and “Clinical waste: segregation, containers and handling”.

instructionSections.heading: Where the two systems differ
instructionSections.body: The Malaysian section allows fluid from suction and blood to go to the sewer, and it caps how long a sharps bin may stay in use before it is closed and passed on for high-temperature destruction. The Australian sources place clinical waste, fluid included, with licensed collection, and close sharps containers at the fill line or at about three-quarters capacity. The Australian sources prevail for this set. The Malaysian section uses its own bag colours, which are not used here. The Malaysian statute references are not used.

instructionSections.heading: Principles that carry across
instructionSections.body: Whichever system applies, the same principles hold. Separate waste where it is made. Use the right container and label. Do not overfill or compact. Keep sharps in their own container. Store securely until collection, and keep a record. Ask the practice manager for the written waste plan, and ask for the local rule on liquids and on each container type before you handle them.

instructionSections.heading: What this means for your work
instructionSections.body: Do not pour clinical fluid down a drain because a document from another country allows it. Ask first.

lessons.title: Dental laboratory items and equipment sent for repair
learningOutcomes: Prepare an impression or appliance for laboratory transport so it is safe to handle.
Explain the decontamination record needed before equipment leaves for repair.
Refuse to send an item that has no decontamination record and report it.

instructionSections.heading: Items that leave and come back
instructionSections.body: Impressions, bite records, prostheses and orthodontic appliances can carry blood and saliva, so they are a route by which infection can pass between the surgery and the laboratory. Before they leave the surgery, they are rinsed to clear visible blood and grit, then disinfected. They travel in sealed containers or bags. Gloves are worn when handling them and when pouring models, and personal protection stays on until disinfection is complete.

instructionSections.heading: Coming back from the laboratory
instructionSections.body: Laboratory items return to the surgery cleaned and disinfected. Items that will be used in surgery are heat sterilised where practical, and chemically sterilised where heat cannot be used. Laboratory tools that become contaminated, such as burs, polishing points and rag wheels, are cleaned, then disinfected or sterilised per the maker's directions. Where the maker's directions are not available, heat-tolerant items are cleaned and heat sterilised, and other items are cleaned and disinfected to the level the source sets. The practice protocol confirms that level.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment sent for repair
instructionSections.body: Instruments from both the clinic and the laboratory are decontaminated before they leave for repair, to the level each item needs. The decontamination is recorded, so the repairer and the practice both know the item is safe to handle. An item that arrives back from repair is checked for any sharps that are still in it, and those are handled through the sharps route in “Burs, handpieces and sharps at the chairside”.

instructionSections.heading: Your part
instructionSections.body: A cleaner packs and labels items for transport, checks that the decontamination step has been recorded, and never sends an item that has not been cleaned or whose status is unknown. Any item without a record is held back and reported to the practice manager.

lessons.title: Dental radiography: barrier envelopes, holders and imaging touch points
learningOutcomes: Describe the handling sequence for a digital receptor and a film holder for one patient.
Explain why the clinician, not the assistant, positions the holder inside the mouth.
Clean the imaging unit's touch points and replace damaged barrier covers.

instructionSections.heading: Why imaging is a cross-infection point
instructionSections.body: Intraoral imaging puts receptors, film packets and holders into the mouth. Those items touch saliva and sometimes blood, and the hands that handle them can carry organisms onward to the next person. The controls described cover the glove, the holder, the envelope, and the disposal route.

instructionSections.heading: Routine imaging
instructionSections.body: Gloves without powder are worn for every imaging task and changed between patients. Each patient receives a clean holder that is sterilised or heat-treated, and digital receptors go inside a barrier envelope. The clinician seats the holder inside the mouth, and fingers never go in to position it. Once the procedure ends, the envelope comes off the receptor and goes into clinical waste. The holder is then cleaned. If it cannot go through the autoclave, it is disinfected before its next use. Film packets used without a barrier are cleaned along with the holder, then disinfected before they go for processing.

instructionSections.heading: Patients at higher risk
instructionSections.body: The source gives an extra set of steps for patients identified as high risk. Those steps are not reproduced in this lesson. Follow the practice protocol for those patients.

instructionSections.heading: The imaging unit and the cleaner
instructionSections.body: The handles and controls of the imaging unit are touch points that “Shared clinical equipment and surface barriers” says should be wiped between patients. A barrier cover that is torn or soiled is replaced. Developer and fixer solutions and other imaging chemicals follow the practice's chemical waste route. The Malaysian sewer route for X-ray solutions is not adopted here (see “Waste rules that differ between countries: reading a foreign guideline against Australian rules”).

lessons.title: Why the healthcare environment carries infection risk
learningOutcomes: Name two pathways that carry microbes from a surface to someone being looked after.
Justify why cleaning intensity varies with the item and how likely that item is to hold microbes.
Name the decisions a cleaner must refer to clinical staff rather than make alone.

instructionSections.heading: Why surfaces matter
instructionSections.body: A microbe may remain alive on a bed frame, a light switch or a trolley handle long after the last person who touched it has left. Reports of single cases and investigations into outbreaks have tied neglected surroundings to infections picked up in care settings. Reliable cleaning cuts that link, so it counts as infection control rather than housekeeping alone.

instructionSections.heading: Two routes from the environment
instructionSections.body: Infection can reach a patient straight from a contaminated device that touches them. It can also arrive by a longer path: a worker's hands collect organisms from a dirty item and then contact a patient. The second path is easy to miss, because the surface looked fine and the worker's hands felt fine.

instructionSections.heading: Matching effort to risk
instructionSections.body: Items do not all need the same method. Something shared between patients needs attention before each new use. A wall that people rarely handle may need less frequent work. The effort depends on what the item is, how often hands reach it and how likely it is to hold contamination. Intensive care areas and isolation rooms may need extra cleaning where antibiotic-resistant organisms are a concern.

instructionSections.heading: Standard precautions as the baseline
instructionSections.body: Baseline controls apply to all people in a care setting, regardless of diagnosis. They include cleaning your hands, wearing protective gear where the risk demands it, orderly cleaning routines, and careful handling of needles, rubbish and bedding. Additional measures, which the guideline labels transmission-based precautions, come into play when a given infection calls for them.

instructionSections.heading: Where your role stops
instructionSections.body: Deciding which precautions apply, whether a patient is isolated and who may visit are clinical and infection prevention decisions. Your part is to clean to the written schedule, use the stated product, report anything that looks wrong and pass questions upward. Patients and visitors can also help by telling staff when something looks unclean.

lessons.title: Sorting surfaces into cleaning tiers
learningOutcomes: Sort the surfaces in an area into minimal-touch and high-contact groups.
Describe the routine detergent method for each group.
State when a cleaning method changes because of a multi-resistant organism.

instructionSections.heading: Two groups of surfaces
instructionSections.body: The guideline divides room surfaces into two families. Floors and ceilings sit in the low-contact family because hands seldom land on them. The busier family includes handles, rails, bedside tables, switches, benchtops and the wall beside a toilet, since these pass microbes between people. Every facility drafts its own list from a risk review and records it in a policy document.

instructionSections.heading: Method for minimal-touch surfaces
instructionSections.body: Mixed to the manufacturer's dilution, detergent serves floors, walls and back-office rooms well. Damp mopping outranks dry mopping for everyday floors. Patient-room walls and blinds merit a detergent wipe-down whenever they look grimy.

instructionSections.heading: Method for high-contact surfaces
instructionSections.body: These items are attended to more often than minimal-touch ones, with a general-purpose detergent matched to the material and the expected dirt. Pre-soaked wipes suit one item or a small patch. On a general ward they are seldom the main tool and never replace a cloth and a mix.

instructionSections.heading: When the method steps up
instructionSections.body: Intensive care and isolation rooms receive more work when a multi-resistant organism is a worry. In that case the routine clean grows heavier: a detergent pass comes first and a disinfectant pass follows, so each surface is wiped twice. The facility decides when to step up, and you follow the written instruction for that area.

lessons.title: Documented cleaning schedules and outsourced cleaning
learningOutcomes: Describe the content a written cleaning schedule has to include.
List the four elements an outsourced cleaning service must document.
Explain how a schedule is altered when one particular microbe is present.

instructionSections.heading: What the schedule must contain
instructionSections.body: Every healthcare organisation should hold a written cleaning schedule. It names who is responsible for each task, sets out the roster, states how often each area or item is cleaned, and lists the product to use for each area. Staff also need education and training that matches their tasks, covering both routine and special cleaning.

instructionSections.heading: Outsourced cleaning
instructionSections.body: A contract cleaner must set down how the work will be performed. That document covers four headings: how often and how each task is done; who works the roster, from permanent and part-time staff to relief workers and supervisors; what supplies and equipment are provided, including fluids and paper goods; and how the contractor manages the service on the ground. The B5.1 table offers a benchmark other settings may tailor.

instructionSections.heading: Changing the schedule for a known organism
instructionSections.body: Every infection risk gets weighed, and the timetable changes whenever a known microbe is in the building. The guideline's illustration involves Clostridium difficile: surfaces get a detergent wash followed by hypochlorite. The illustration makes the point; the strength, mixing and wait time are set by the product label and the facility's approved instruction.

instructionSections.heading: Local adjustment
instructionSections.body: The frequency table is a yardstick, not a law for every site. Each facility drafts its own timetable that fits its setting, then checks how that timetable performs. If the timetable seems wrong for your room, tell your supervisor in writing. Never alter a frequency or a product by yourself.

lessons.title: Detergent first: physical cleaning before any disinfectant
learningOutcomes: Explain why hands-on or machine cleaning must come before any disinfectant.
Choose between a two-step and a two-in-one clean for a given surface.
Identify the situations in which a disinfectant is needed.

instructionSections.heading: Physical cleaning comes first
instructionSections.body: The guideline regards physical cleaning as the single most important step. Surfaces are wiped or scrubbed with a detergent mix before any disinfectant goes on. A disinfectant used alone, without the physical clean, is not recommended, because it does not lift the soil that can shelter organisms, and a treated-looking surface can still be carrying them.

instructionSections.heading: When a disinfectant is needed
instructionSections.body: In acute wards, a disinfectant goes on when it is uncertain whether a stain is blood or plain dust, or when a multi-resistant organism, Clostridium difficile or an infection needing extra precautions is present or suspected. In offices and quieter settings such as long-term care, the facility judges the need for disinfectant from the odds of contamination, the way the bug travels and the danger to other people.

instructionSections.heading: Two accepted methods
instructionSections.body: A two-step clean runs a detergent pass, then a disinfectant pass. A two-in-one clean uses one blended detergent and disinfectant product, such as a combined wipe or liquid, but only when real wiping action is applied rather than spraying alone. Any disinfectant must be on the Therapeutic Goods Administration register and carry label claims for the microbe in question.

instructionSections.heading: Chemical hazards during this work
instructionSections.body: Disinfectants are chemicals. Read the label and the safety data sheet before use, wear the protective equipment they call for, ventilate as the label directs, and do not combine products unless the label allows it. This lesson gives no mixing ratios or contact times. Use the label and the facility's approved instruction for each product.

lessons.title: Cleaning tools, solutions and preventing cross-contamination
learningOutcomes: Describe the routine care needed for mops, cloths and cleaning solutions.
Explain how colour coding reduces cross-infection.
Explain why a tool gets dried or replaced before its next use.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the solution clean
instructionSections.body: Any cleaning plan has to stop solutions and tools turning into sources of contamination. Solutions are made up each day, or as often as required, and refreshed on the facility's timetable. A bucket that serves several rooms can move organisms from one room to the next.

instructionSections.heading: Mops and cloths
instructionSections.body: Mops and cloths get washed and air-dried before they are reused. Disposable heads and cloths are the other route. A cloth that returns to the bucket unrinsed and undried can deposit organisms on the next surface, so it is processed as the facility method describes.

instructionSections.heading: Colour coding
instructionSections.body: Facilities rely on checklists, colour-coded equipment, cleaning manuals and model contracts to keep standards consistent. Colour coding lowers the chance of carrying organisms between areas, because each colour is reserved for a defined area or task. Learn the colour scheme for your site before you start, and never take a coloured cloth into a different zone.

instructionSections.heading: New tools under review
instructionSections.body: Some newer methods, like microfibre cloths made to very fine standards and mists of hydrogen peroxide, may eventually cut down chemical reliance. Their effectiveness against different microbes, and their dependability across daily routines, still lacks solid proof. Only adopt such methods with a facility's sign-off in writing.

lessons.title: High-touch items: minimum intervals for patient rooms
learningOutcomes: Name the four risk levels used in the guideline's routine cleaning frequency table.
Give the minimum frequency for three high-touch items at the significant-risk level.
Explain why the table is a benchmark and not a ceiling.

instructionSections.heading: The four risk levels
instructionSections.body: Within the guideline, the B5.1 table places each area into one of four hazard bands. The most severe band is an outbreak in a high-hazard zone; the next includes intensive care, high dependency, burns, renal and theatre suites; the third is the usual general ward; the fourth covers rehab wards, long-term care and offices. Although built around acute hospitals, the table may inform other settings.

instructionSections.heading: High-touch items
instructionSections.body: Door handles in patient rooms are cleaned twice daily at the very-high level and once daily at each of the other three levels. Light switches are cleaned daily at the two highest levels and weekly at the two lower levels. Telephones are cleaned twice daily at the two highest levels, daily at the significant level and weekly at the low level. Bed rails and bedside tables are cleaned most often at the highest level, with extra cleaning after a patient is discharged.

instructionSections.heading: What the frequency means
instructionSections.body: A frequency is a floor, not a ceiling. A facility can clean more often, and a surface that is visibly soiled, or that a known organism has reached, is cleaned straight away. The table does not replace an alert, a spill procedure or a direction from the infection prevention team.

instructionSections.heading: Products for these items
instructionSections.body: For these high-contact items the table names a medical-grade surface cleaner or detergent wipe, with a disinfectant added wherever a multi-resistant organism is in play. The product should carry a Therapeutic Goods Administration listing as a medical device in a stated class.

lessons.title: Beds, equipment, curtains and mattresses: minimum frequencies
learningOutcomes: Give the minimum frequency for beds, mattresses and bed curtains at two risk levels.
State when equipment must be cleaned after each use.
Identify the items that need a disinfectant step when a multi-resistant organism is present.

instructionSections.heading: Beds and frames
instructionSections.body: At the three highest risk levels the bed frame is cleaned daily, and its underside is cleaned weekly. The whole bed is cleaned on discharge. At the low level, beds are marked not applicable in the routine frequency line, so the facility's own instruction governs.

instructionSections.heading: Mattresses and curtains
instructionSections.body: Mattresses are cleaned weekly and on discharge at the two highest levels, and monthly and on discharge at the two lower levels. The guideline would rather see a mattress with a completely waterproof cover. Bed curtains follow their own cycle: weekly on discharge at the highest level, monthly at the high level, every six months at the significant level and yearly at the low level. Curtains come down sooner if the patient carried a multi-resistant organism or another infection.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment in use
instructionSections.body: Equipment that is not attached to a patient, such as infusion pumps and pulse oximeters, is wiped between patients at the three highest levels and weekly at the low level. Drip stands get a clean at their contact points after every use at all levels, while IV stands are cleaned after use only at the two highest levels. Oxygen kit, nebulisers and patient slides or boards are cleaned after use, and the table gives a monthly or discharge cycle for lower-risk areas.

instructionSections.heading: Surfaces that change the method
instructionSections.body: Where a multi-resistant organism is present, several items in the table move to a detergent plus disinfectant method. Those items include beds, chairs, mattresses and commodes. Work from the facility's organism instruction rather than the default line.

lessons.title: Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals
learningOutcomes: List the six factors the guideline sets for choosing a cleaning or disinfection product.
Name three products or uses the guideline rules out for general cleaning.
Explain why alcohol is not used on large surfaces or on spills.

instructionSections.heading: Six factors for choosing a product
instructionSections.body: Six considerations apply. The Therapeutic Goods Administration must have approved the product for that exact use. Its stated purpose has to fit the task. The maker's directions must be achievable on site. The product has to suit the material or room. Trained staff and available resources must be able to use it properly. And it has to act on the target organisms within the time it needs to do so.

instructionSections.heading: Products ruled out for general cleaning
instructionSections.body: Strong high-level disinfectants and liquid sterilants are kept out of routine cleaning, because the manufacturer's directions for those hazardous agents rule that use out. Products meant for instruments are never wiped across room surfaces. Large surface areas are not treated with alcohol, which can ignite, and alcohol does not suit spill clean-up either.

instructionSections.heading: Hypochlorite is a specific-use product
instructionSections.body: Routine spill work does not require sodium hypochlorite. It can be brought in for special cases once a risk assessment has weighed the setting, the spill, the transmission risk and the surface involved. It stays away from upholstery.

instructionSections.heading: The label governs
instructionSections.body: Concentrations, dilutions and contact times come from the label and the facility's approved product list. A product you know well is not automatically approved for the area you are working in, and a product approved for one use may not be approved for another.

lessons.title: Carpets, soft furnishings, walls and blinds
learningOutcomes: Describe the routine vacuuming and periodic cleaning method for carpets in patient areas.
State the method for cleaning a spill on soft furnishings.
Explain when walls and blinds are cleaned.

instructionSections.heading: Carpets
instructionSections.body: Carpets in lobbies and general patient zones get a daily vacuum run by a machine whose filter traps very fine particles, so dust does not drift back out. Deep cleaning happens on the schedule the facility sets, using a technique that throws up little mist and leaves little film.

instructionSections.heading: Soft furnishings
instructionSections.body: Upholstery that has been spilled on gets a detergent mix, never hypochlorite. Wet extraction is another option. Once treated, open up the room as much as you can so the piece is fully dry before anyone sits on it.

instructionSections.heading: Walls and blinds
instructionSections.body: Patient-room walls and blinds get a detergent wipe-down once dust or grime appears. Window curtains are replaced on a fixed cycle, and they go to the laundry early if they pick up soil or have been near a multi-resistant organism.

instructionSections.heading: Why the method matters
