instructionSections.body: The guideline asks for carpet cleaning that produces little spray and leaves little residue, and it warns against the wrong chemical on upholstery. For soft furnishings the drying time is part of the method, not an optional extra.

lessons.title: Managing spills of body fluid at work
learningOutcomes: Describe the response to a spot, a small spill and a large spill.
Name the contents of a spill kit and explain why each item is disposable.
Say when a disinfectant belongs in the spill response and when it does not.

instructionSections.heading: Prompt action
instructionSections.body: Acting fast on a spot or a spill involving blood or bodily fluid is good infection control and matches workplace safety duties. Once the mess is up, clean the patch and apply any disinfectant the risk review requires. Leaving it lets microbes spread and exposes the next person.

instructionSections.heading: The method depends on setting and volume
instructionSections.body: In a patient area, a little spill can be dealt with using a detergent mix alone. A heavy release, such as a large quantity of vomit or urine, must first be boxed in. Visible solids are taken up with disposable absorbent paper, broken glass or sharps are lifted with forceps rather than fingers, and free liquid is soaked up using a granular clumping absorbent.

instructionSections.heading: Three levels of response
instructionSections.body: A spot gets dabbed up straight away with a damp rag or a paper towel, and the debris is binned. A small patch, roughly 10 cm across or less, is soaked up with absorbent material that goes into a sealed bag; the surface is then cleaned with warm detergent on a disposable cloth. A larger patch is covered in granular absorbent, scooped with a single-use scraper and pan into a watertight container, and mopped with detergent. The guideline's table also shows a hypochlorite wipe-down with drying for the small and large levels, but that step follows the risk assessment in “Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals” and is not automatic.

instructionSections.heading: Disinfectant and alcohol
instructionSections.body: A disinfectant is not needed for every spill. Where one is required, particularly under transmission-based precautions, use a TGA-listed product with the right label claim. Alcohol is not used to clean spills. Soft furnishings are cleaned with detergent rather than hypochlorite.

instructionSections.heading: The spill kit
instructionSections.body: Each clinical room keeps a spill kit containing a scoop, a scraper, one-use gloves, a protective apron, a face mask, goggles, granular absorbent, clinical waste bags with ties, and detergent. Discarding every item after one use prevents carry-over between incidents.

lessons.title: Shared clinical equipment and surface barriers
learningOutcomes: Pinpoint the handled areas on shared clinical equipment.
State the cleaning rule for shared equipment between patients.
Describe when a surface barrier is used and how it is replaced.

instructionSections.heading: Why shared equipment matters
instructionSections.body: Shared clinical equipment only meets intact skin, so it is unlikely to infect anyone directly. It can still act as a carrier, moving organisms from one patient to the next through the parts that hands and skin touch during care. The guideline's examples are the knobs and handles on dialysis units, x-ray units, instrument carts and dental chairs.

instructionSections.heading: The cleaning rule
instructionSections.body: Between patients, wipe the handled parts of shared equipment with a detergent mix. Any departure needs a documented risk assessment to back it. Frequencies for particular shared items sit in the B5.1 table, the same reference relied on in “High-touch items: minimum intervals for patient rooms” and “Beds, equipment, curtains and mattresses: minimum frequencies”.

instructionSections.heading: Surface barriers
instructionSections.body: A moisture-impermeable covering, such as cling film, a plastic bag, a sheet, or tubing, forms a barrier between contamination and equipment. Fit it so that all parts requiring protection are enclosed, then strip it off and disinfect what lies underneath between patients. Where no covering can be applied, cleaning the surface still applies.

instructionSections.heading: When a barrier is required
instructionSections.body: Put a barrier on equipment that gloved hands handle repeatedly during treatment, on items prone to splatter from bodily fluids, and on surfaces that are awkward to clean. Leaving any of these uncovered needs a documented risk analysis. The guideline lists air-water syringes, bed boards and keyboards as illustrations.

lessons.title: Checking cleaning quality without over-relying on sampling
learningOutcomes: Describe the systems a healthcare facility uses to check cleaning standards.
Explain why a visual check does not confirm that a surface is free of organisms.
Give reasons why routine swabbing of the environment is not the usual method of verification.

instructionSections.heading: The systems that support checking
instructionSections.body: A facility checks cleanliness through several channels: lists to tick off, colour-matched equipment to prevent crossover, cleaning handbooks, template outsourcing agreements, infection-control advice and ongoing oversight. Jurisdictional authorities may impose cleaning expectations on health sites, whether the work is outsourced or internal. This document does not explain those expectations; verify them locally.

instructionSections.heading: Visual checks and their limits
instructionSections.body: Most cleaning audits rely on eyesight. The guideline notes that microbes are too small to see, so a surface that looks spotless can still carry them. Objective alternatives, including black-spot audits and tests that detect adenosine triphosphate, are under study and are not standard in most facilities.

instructionSections.heading: Why routine sampling is not used
instructionSections.body: Sampling the environment for microorganisms has known limits. It detects only some organism types, the amount shed by patients varies, residual detergent or disinfectant can skew results, and sampling technique differs between people. These limits make results hard to read, so routine sampling is not recommended. It still has a place in specific situations, such as an outbreak or an unexplained infection, as one part of a wider risk approach.

instructionSections.heading: What a cleaner can check
instructionSections.body: You can confirm that a surface looks clean and dry, leaves no film, that the right product and method were used, and that the record is complete. These checks matter, but they do not replace the schedule, the method or the supervisor's review.

lessons.title: Reusable equipment: risk categories
learningOutcomes: Name the three risk categories used for patient-care items.
Match a category to the contact site it describes.
Explain why a cleaner must not classify an item by appearance.

instructionSections.heading: The three categories
instructionSections.body: Equipment that touches patients falls into three categories by infection hazard. The top category is critical, the middle one is semi-critical, and the lowest is non-critical. Critical devices penetrate sterile areas of the body and need sterility at the moment they are used. Semi-critical devices meet mucosa or damaged skin; they are disposable or undergo sterilisation after every use. Non-critical devices touch only unbroken skin, where careful cleaning is usually adequate.

instructionSections.heading: Examples from the guideline
instructionSections.body: Scalpels and other surgical tools, urinary and cardiac catheters, implants and probes placed inside sterile cavities fall under critical. Breathing-support and anaesthetic kit, certain endoscopes and laryngoscope blades are semi-critical. Stethoscopes, blood pressure cuffs, non-invasive ultrasound heads and commodes are non-critical.

instructionSections.heading: Single-use and reusable devices
instructionSections.body: Devices meant for repeat use have to appear on the Therapeutic Goods Administration register. Anything labelled disposable is never reprocessed. A site that chooses to reprocess such items needs a TGA licence, takes on a manufacturer's responsibilities and must submit to audit. This lesson does not confer any right to reprocess.

instructionSections.heading: Why appearance is not enough
instructionSections.body: Two items can look alike yet fall into different categories. A blood pressure cuff and a flexible device that goes into the body may both be grey plastic objects beside a bed, but one touches intact skin and the other does not. The category depends on the contact site and the maker's labelling, so a cleaner checks the facility list rather than guessing.

lessons.title: Reprocessing steps and storage: awareness and limits
learningOutcomes: State why cleaning comes before disinfection or sterilisation.
Describe the two methods of cleaning instruments and their protective equipment.
Explain the storage rule that keeps a reprocessed item at its level.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of this lesson
instructionSections.body: This lesson explains the principles so you can spot poor practice and protect yourself and others. It does not authorise any cleaner to reprocess critical or semi-critical instruments. Reprocessing is carried out only by people the facility has trained and authorised, under its written procedure and the manufacturer's instructions. Medical equipment courses treat reprocessing as outside the external cleaning role.

instructionSections.heading: Clean first, always
instructionSections.body: Detergent-based cleaning lifts dirt and organic matter. It has to happen before high-level disinfection or sterilisation, since retained protein undermines both. Whatever remains after cleaning cannot be neutralised later. Start on instruments promptly after use, before residue sets, and disassemble detachable parts.

instructionSections.heading: Automated and manual cleaning
instructionSections.body: Ultrasonic baths and washer-disinfectors lower the amount of manual handling and suit robust basic instruments. Load hinged instruments open, stop items overlapping, and separate components when possible. Hand scrubbing is reserved for fragile instruments or sites without automation: brushing removes soil while fluid is forced through lumens. Required protection: a plastic apron, heavy gloves and a face shield, and no leaning into splashes or sharp tips.

instructionSections.heading: Disinfection and sterilisation
instructionSections.body: Disinfection inactivates most vegetative microbes via heat or chemicals, but falls short of sterility. Heat-resistant goods are generally steam-sterilised, whereas heat-sensitive goods need a low-temperature process. Validated sterilisation aims for a sterility assurance benchmark near one in a million (10 to the power minus six), and records prove each cycle ran.

instructionSections.heading: Storage keeps the level
instructionSections.body: Storage has to preserve each item's reprocessed status. Sealed sterile packs stay dry, clean and clear of sharp edges, and the wrap keeps out contamination while stored. Inspect surfaces regularly for cracks or breaks, and repair or discard any item that no longer works or cannot be reprocessed properly.

lessons.title: Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits
learningOutcomes: Name the five WHO hand hygiene moments as adopted in Australia.
Choose between an alcohol hand rub and soap with water for a given situation.
State the hand-care rules that keep hand hygiene effective.

instructionSections.heading: Why hands matter
instructionSections.body: Any organism that spreads by contact or by droplets can ride on the hands. Organisms may live on the hands at all times or be picked up during work, and they can pass from a patient to a surface and then to another patient. The guideline cites published studies in which better hand hygiene went with fewer infections caused by some antibiotic-resistant organisms. It is one control within a wider approach, not a stand-alone fix.

instructionSections.heading: The five moments
instructionSections.body: The five moments endorsed by the WHO and adopted in Australia identify when cleaning shields the patient from the worker's hands, the patient from their own organisms during invasive care, and the worker and setting from the patient's organisms. Clean on both sides of each patient encounter: on approach, before an aseptic task, after body-fluid exposure, after the encounter, and after touching the environment. A further cleaning follows glove removal.

instructionSections.heading: Non-clinical moments
instructionSections.body: Beyond direct care, hands need cleaning at shift start and finish, around meals, after toilet use, whenever visibly dirty, after handling laundry, equipment or waste, after nose or mouth contact, and after keyboard use in clinics. Outbreak periods add entries and exits from patient zones.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the product
instructionSections.body: Alcohol-based rubs typically outperform ordinary or antiseptic soaps against common germs. They work well on many bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi, and reasonably on enveloped viruses. Certain viruses lacking an envelope, norovirus among them, respond less reliably, and Clostridium difficile spores survive exposure. Soap mechanically removes organisms, which is why it suits visibly grimy hands. If C. difficile or viruses lacking an envelope are of concern and no gloves were worn, scrub with soap and rinse, then dry carefully.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the skin healthy
instructionSections.body: Cuts receive waterproof coverings. Keep nails trim and clean, avoid false nails, and steer clear of chipped varnish. Discourage watches and rings; a plain band may stay but should be turned while cleaning. Routine emollient keeps skin healthy and encourages steady practice. Individual facilities write their own jewellery and nail rules.

lessons.title: PPE for cleaning tasks: choosing, putting on and taking off
learningOutcomes: List the three factors used to decide which protective equipment is needed.
Put on protective equipment in the correct order.
Remove protective equipment in the order that avoids self-contamination.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing protective equipment
instructionSections.body: Select protective equipment through a task-specific assessment: estimate the chance of touching blood or other fluids, identify the fluid, and consider how the organism is likely to travel. Typical items are aprons, gowns, gloves, masks, goggles and visors, each needing a Therapeutic Goods Administration listing or recognised equivalent.

instructionSections.heading: When gloves are needed
instructionSections.body: Gloves are worn when direct contact is expected with blood, body fluid, mucous membranes or broken skin, or when touching kit or surfaces that look or might be contaminated. They do not reveal a needle puncture, so they never substitute for the sharps measures in “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”. When donning a full set, gloves come last.

instructionSections.heading: Putting on
instructionSections.body: Start by washing your hands. Drape the gown from neck to knee and out to the wrists, wrap it round the back, and tie it at the neck and waist. Position the mask's straps at the crown and nape. Set goggles or a visor over the eyes and face and tighten it for fit. Gloves are the last layer and extend over the gown's cuffs.

instructionSections.heading: Taking off
instructionSections.body: Strip off at the threshold or in an anteroom. Begin with gloves, since their exterior is contaminated: grasp one glove's exterior with the other gloved hand and peel it away, hold it, slide a bare finger beneath the second glove's wrist and draw it inside out over the first. Wash your hands. Lift goggles by the strap or arms, as the lens is contaminated. Loosen the gown, draw it off the shoulders using only the inner side, turn it inside out, and roll it for disposal. Remove the mask by the ties, never touching its front. Wash your hands the moment everything is off.

instructionSections.heading: Respirators
instructionSections.body: A standard surgical mask may be lifted off where care is delivered. Removing a P2 respirator means washing hands, leaving the room, or entering an anteroom, placing the sealed respirator into a container and washing again. The guideline presents this as a footnote to the removal order.

lessons.title: Sharps: handling, containers and injury response
learningOutcomes: Describe the safe handling rules for sharps during cleaning and disposal.
Explain the container and placement rules for used single-use sharps.
Sequence the first-aid and reporting steps after a sharps injury.

instructionSections.heading: Where sharps injuries happen
instructionSections.body: Sharps injuries can happen during procedures, while scrubbing used instruments, when binning needles and when moving sharp tools after a procedure. The guideline wants care at every one of those points, since the risk spans the whole job rather than the procedure alone.

instructionSections.heading: Handling rules
instructionSections.body: Use an instrument, never bare fingers, for needles, tissue retraction and blade loading or unloading. Announce a sharp as it changes hands. Avoid hand-to-hand transfer: set the sharp down in a tray or a designated safe area. Round-tipped blades are preferred where the procedure allows. Minimise handling. Do not recap, bend or break a needle after use.

instructionSections.heading: Binning single-use sharps
instructionSections.body: Whoever used a single-use sharp is responsible for binning it at once in an approved container positioned where the sharp was used. Containers need clear labels, must resist punctures and leaks, and meet the Australian standards the guideline names. Never let one go above the three-quarter line. Keep them beyond children's reach and fixed or wall-mounted so they cannot topple. Reusable sharps being sent for reprocessing travel in a lidded, puncture-resistant container.

instructionSections.heading: Safety-engineered devices
instructionSections.body: Devices with built-in protection, such as guarded syringes and blades with covers, lower the injury risk. The current NHMRC guideline is dated 2019. Where a facility chooses them, it must back them with training.

instructionSections.heading: After an injury
instructionSections.body: Seek care without delay after a sharps injury. Where skin is broken, wash the site promptly with soap plus water or, lacking water, use alcohol rub. Avoid squeezing. Alert your supervisor at once and ask what aftercare, such as post-exposure prophylaxis, applies; it is most effective when started early. File an incident report with date, time, mechanism and, if known, the source person. The guideline notes that few exposures become infections, and fast action lowers the chance further.

lessons.title: Clinical waste: segregation, containers and handling
learningOutcomes: Describe the standard precautions for handling waste.
State where waste is separated and how containers are identified.
Explain why waste classification depends on local law.

instructionSections.heading: No single national definition
instructionSections.body: Because Australia has no one nationwide meaning for clinical waste, facilities must follow the state or territory rules for clinical and associated waste, with reference to the Australian standard for that waste. This lesson therefore covers general principles only.

instructionSections.heading: Principles that apply everywhere
instructionSections.body: Protect yourself with baseline precautions whenever you handle waste, and wash afterwards. Waste is sorted at its source. Each stream goes into its designated receptacle, marked by hue and a written tag, and is managed under the site's waste plan. Staff receive instruction in the correct method.

instructionSections.heading: The same principles in every area
instructionSections.body: The guideline applies one rule to decide whether waste is clinical or general, no matter where it originates, including isolation rooms and routine patient areas. Do not reclassify waste because a room is quiet or a bag seems small.

instructionSections.heading: Waste that looks ordinary
instructionSections.body: Dressings and cloths can carry blood or bodily fluid even though they look innocuous. Handle such possibly contaminated items as the facility directs, and do not place them in general waste before their category is verified.

lessons.title: Soiled and clean linen: handling and storage
learningOutcomes: Describe how used linen is bagged and carried.
State where used linen may and may not be rinsed, sorted or washed.
Explain the storage conditions for clean linen.

instructionSections.heading: Policy first
instructionSections.body: Every healthcare facility keeps written rules on collecting, moving and storing linen. A site that washes its own linen also needs operating procedures in line with the Australian laundry standard the guideline cites. Your local procedure sets the detail for your workplace.

instructionSections.heading: Used linen
instructionSections.body: Lift soiled linen carefully so organisms are not dispersed into air or onto uniforms. Protective gear should keep exposed skin and mucosal surfaces covered. Bag linen at its point of use in the correct laundry container. Do not rinse or sort in patient zones, and never launder it in a household machine. Linen contaminated with body fluid goes into a sealed leak-proof bag for transport. Clean hands after handling used linen.

instructionSections.heading: Patient personal items
instructionSections.body: A household-type washer may take only a patient's personal clothing, never facility linen. Use a suitable detergent with hot water. Without hot water, wash one patient's load at a time. Dry those items in a dryer.

instructionSections.heading: Clean linen
instructionSections.body: Clean linen belongs in a tidy, dry space shielded from airborne particles, dust, damp and pests, and it is never mixed with soiled stock. A trolley or shelf that has carried used linen cannot be used for clean linen.

lessons.title: Enhanced cleaning under added controls for infection spread
learningOutcomes: List the additional controls layered over baseline practice when an infection spreads by touch, droplet or air.
Set out the cleaning expected in an acute area when an infection is suspected or confirmed.
State how long transmission-based precautions stay in effect.

instructionSections.heading: What the added controls involve
instructionSections.body: These controls apply to patients who may carry, or do carry, an infection passed by touch, droplets or airborne particles. They are always layered over baseline controls. When one illness travels by several routes, several sets are combined.

instructionSections.heading: The measures in acute settings
instructionSections.body: On an acute ward, the bundle of transmission-based measures comprises: baseline controls maintained; protective items chosen to fit the route (gloves, gown or apron, surgical or P2 masks, eye protection); equipment reserved for one patient; a private room or grouping with others infected by the same agent; air-handling as specified; intensified scrubbing and disinfecting the patient's immediate area; and limits on transfers within and between sites. Route-specific protection is detailed within B2.2 through B2.4, which should be read before use.

instructionSections.heading: Environmental cleaning under precautions
instructionSections.body: On an acute ward where a possible or verified agent needs transmission-based precautions, scrub surfaces with detergent mix, then apply a TGA-listed product suited to hospital use, using the two-step or two-in-one technique. In clinics and calmer settings, facility policy weighs contamination odds, transmission route and danger to people nearby before choosing disinfection.

instructionSections.heading: Duration
instructionSections.body: Transmission-based precautions last for a set span: until the symptoms have eased, or as infection control specialists advise for that organism. Never end a precaution on your own view; that call belongs to the infection prevention or clinical team.

instructionSections.heading: Crockery and utensils
instructionSections.body: Dishes and cutlery from a patient managed under these added controls need no special holding. They are handled like anyone else's and go through the dishwasher. Disposable tableware is unnecessary.

lessons.title: Coughing habits and breath hygiene in shared areas
learningOutcomes: Describe how respiratory droplets reach surfaces and other people in a shared area.
Apply the coughing habit and the hand cleaning step that follows it.
Report a respiratory symptom or an empty supply to a supervisor without confronting the person.

instructionSections.heading: Why breath and cough matter in a service area
instructionSections.body: Some germs leave the body in the small drops produced when someone coughs, sneezes or speaks, and a few remain in the air for longer. A worker who walks through a waiting room, a corridor or a lift can collect these on the hands, then carry them to the lips, the nostrils or the eyes. Respiratory hygiene is the group of habits that stops those drops reaching the next person or the next object. The guideline starts these habits at the moment of first contact, which for a cleaner usually means meeting a visitor or patient in a shared space.

instructionSections.heading: What you do about your own cough
instructionSections.body: When you cough or sneeze yourself, hold a tissue over your nose and mouth. Without a tissue, turn your face into the crook of the arm rather than using a palm, since hands spread germs onto everything they reach. Drop the used tissue into the closest lidded bin, then clean your hands. Hand cleaning applies again after any touch of an object that has been near someone's breath or secretions, such as a tissue resting on a chair.

instructionSections.heading: Supporting the system around you
instructionSections.body: The facility should stock tissues, lidded bins and hand cleaning products at the points where people need them. Your task is to spot an empty dispenser or an overflowing bin and report it. Never confront someone who is coughing. Pass the concern to your supervisor, who can apply the site policy. That policy may ask a symptomatic person to wear a mask and to keep a gap from other people in shared spaces. The source sets a specific gap distance.

lessons.title: Terminal cleaning after a patient leaves
learningOutcomes: Distinguish routine, scheduled and terminal cleaning.
Sequence a terminal clean from linen and waste removal through to the final check.
Explain why detergent comes before disinfectant on high-touch items after discharge.

instructionSections.heading: What terminal cleaning is for
instructionSections.body: After a patient departs a room, the space is not simply tidied for the next arrival. The source separates three kinds of cleaning. Routine cleaning keeps the patient zone free of organic matter while someone is staying there. Scheduled cleaning deals with dust and soil on surfaces that people do not usually touch. Terminal cleaning follows discharge or transfer, reaches the immediate patient space and the surrounding care area, and aims to strip out organic material and cut microbial contamination so that none passes on to the next occupant. Treat it as its own task with its own checklist, not as a longer routine clean.

instructionSections.heading: Sequencing the work
instructionSections.body: Begin only when the discharge is confirmed and the people who own the equipment have removed it or cleared it. Remove and bag linen and waste first, following “Clinical waste: segregation, containers and handling” and “Soiled and clean linen: handling and storage”. Work from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest, and from the ceiling downward, so that debris does not fall onto surfaces already cleaned. Clean high-touch items such as bed rails, call bells, switches, door handles, taps and over-bed tables with detergent first, because organic material can block a disinfectant from reaching the surface, as “Detergent first: physical cleaning before any disinfectant” explains.

instructionSections.heading: Disinfection and drying
instructionSections.body: Apply disinfectant only where the risk review or the item's frequency table requires it, using a product on the approved list under “Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals”. Keep the surface wet for the product's contact time before you wipe, and allow it to air dry instead of wiping it early. The source describes heavier methods for outbreaks and specialised areas. Those are covered in “Enhanced cleaning under added controls for infection spread” and are not repeated here, and no product concentration or dosing from the source is used in this lesson.

lessons.title: Dust and infection control during building work near patients
learningOutcomes: Explain why building dust is an infection hazard in patient areas.
Identify the boundary between the construction clean and the hospital clean.
Check barriers and dust controls before starting cleaning near active works.

instructionSections.heading: Why building work is an infection issue
instructionSections.body: Demolition, drilling, sanding, and the stripping of ceilings and floor coverings release dust into the air and onto surfaces. People with weakened defences, and areas such as operating rooms, dialysis units and bone marrow units, are harmed by that dust. The source therefore treats building work as an infection control task with its own risk assessment, not as ordinary maintenance.

instructionSections.heading: Two kinds of clean
instructionSections.body: The construction team cleans the works zone after the day's labour stops, or more often when needed, to remove heavy soil, dust, debris and building material. The hospital clean begins outside the hoarding, where the works zone stops, and is done by facility staff. Know where that boundary sits before you start, because each team has different tasks and each has to deal with dust left on its side.

instructionSections.heading: Matching the work to the risk
instructionSections.body: Before work starts, the infection prevention team looks at three things. The first is the kind of building activity, graded from A, a visual check with little dust, to D, major demolition or new construction across several shifts. The second is the patient area affected, graded from low risk, for example offices, to highest risk, including intensive care, operating rooms, isolation rooms and units caring for people with weakened immunity. The third is the precautions class, which the source reads from a matrix that combines the first two. The matrix is not reproduced here. Learners use the matrix their own infection prevention team has approved.

instructionSections.heading: Precautions you may see on site
instructionSections.body: Higher precaution classes call for dust containment, sealed barriers between the works zone and the remainder of the building, changes to air handling, sealed waste containers, dust mats at entrances, HEPA-filtered vacuums in clinical areas, wet cleaning in place of sweeping, and no taking down of barriers until the infection prevention team has inspected the job. Check that barriers are intact before each shift begins, and report any gap immediately.

lessons.title: Staff health checks, immunity records and staying away when unwell
learningOutcomes: Explain why staff health checks protect patients and colleagues.
State when to report an illness and stay away from care areas.
Name the records a care-area worker should keep and show.

instructionSections.heading: Why staff health is part of infection control
instructionSections.body: Workers can catch infections at work and can pass them to patients, colleagues and residents. A staff health programme therefore covers the start of employment, ongoing training, immunity records and the decision to stay away when unwell. Health checks happen when someone is hired and again when their duties change significantly. A new worker should not start in a care area until the checks are complete and they are cleared to work.

instructionSections.heading: Training and your part in it
instructionSections.body: Infection control training is expected at induction and then kept current through evidence of further education. The training covers occupational hazards such as bloodborne infections and tuberculosis. Your part is to attend, keep your own training records, and tell your employer when a training record is due.

instructionSections.heading: Immunity and vaccination
instructionSections.body: Staff who may handle blood, other body fluids or sharps are expected to be protected against hepatitis B, and the source sets out a testing approach for people whose immune response to the vaccine is weak. The source also encourages staff without immunity to some other diseases to consider vaccination. The schedules are not copied into this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Staying away when unwell
instructionSections.body: Staff with symptoms that may come from an infection should report them, and should not attend work while they are likely to pass the infection on. The source names categories such as chest and airway infections, stomach bugs, eye infections, weeping skin sores when the worker would touch patients or food, chickenpox, and shingles where the rash could reach patients. You do not diagnose yourself. You tell your supervisor before the shift where you can, and the site's staff illness policy decides when you return.

lessons.title: Splash or skin exposure to body fluid: first response and reporting
learningOutcomes: Identify the splash and skin routes of exposure to body fluid.
Carry out the first response for a splash to the eye, mouth or skin.
Complete the exposure report with the details needed for follow-up.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as an exposure
instructionSections.body: An exposure happens when blood or another body fluid reaches the body in a manner able to carry infection. The source lists four main routes: a puncture from a sharp, a splash into the mouth, nostrils or eyes, contact with broken skin, for example a cut, a sore or dermatitis, and a bite. The fluids of concern include blood and several others, namely spinal fluid, joint fluid, the fluid around the lungs, abdominal fluid, the fluid around the heart, and amniotic fluid. This lesson covers the splash and skin routes and the reporting steps that apply to every route. Puncture management is in “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”.

instructionSections.heading: First response at the spot
instructionSections.body: Lather the exposed skin and any wound with soap, then rinse it under a running tap. Let a wound bleed freely, and do not squeeze or scrub it. Do not use antiseptic as a first step, because the source advises against it. For a splash to the eyes, flush with clean water or saline. If you wear contact lenses, rinse the eyes at both stages, before and after lens removal, as the site allows. For a mouth splash, spit and rinse repeatedly with clean water. Remove contaminated clothing as soon as it is safe to do so.

instructionSections.heading: Reporting promptly
instructionSections.body: Inform your supervisor and the IPC team straight away. Every exposure is logged and then followed through. The record needs the date and time, what you were doing, the type of fluid or tissue, how it reached you, how much and for how long, and the state of the skin. If a sharp was involved, record the device. Any testing of the person the fluid came from and of you follows clinical decisions, is confidential, and is set by occupational health and the treating clinicians.

lessons.title: Microbes and the stages from carriage to illness
learningOutcomes: Sort a listed organism into bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites using its description.
Explain how carrying a microbe differs from being infected or unwell, with one example of each.
Explain why a product that works on bacteria may not work on a spore-forming organism.

instructionSections.heading: Microbes are not all alike
instructionSections.body: Microorganisms are too small to see with the eye alone. The ones that matter in a care setting fall into four broad families: bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Protozoa are single-celled organisms that behave like parasites, so they are usually grouped with them. The families differ in how they multiply, how they survive on a surface and how they respond to cleaning products. You do not need a laboratory background to use this. What counts is knowing that a method suited to one family may fail against another, and that the facility product list, not a guess, decides what you use.

instructionSections.heading: Bacteria, spores and the limits of disinfectants
instructionSections.body: A bacterium is a single-celled organism without a nucleus. Many bacteria are killed by a properly applied disinfectant spray or wipe. Some bacteria can form spores, a dormant and tough form that tolerates heat, drying and many chemicals. Spores are the main reason a surface can look clean and still carry a risk. Destroying spores in general requires sterilisation, which happens in controlled equipment such as an autoclave and is not a cleaning task. Chemical disinfectants that kill bacteria will not reliably kill their spores. Where the facility names a spore-forming organism, use the product it lists for that organism and no other.

instructionSections.heading: Viruses need a living host
instructionSections.body: A virus cannot multiply by itself. It enters living cells and uses them to make new copies. Inside, it carries genetic material wrapped in a protein shell, and some viruses also carry an outer envelope that helps them attach to cells. Enveloped viruses tend to respond more readily to cleaning products than viruses without an envelope, which is why product choice matters (the product rules are in “Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals”, and the envelope point is in “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits”). For you, the practical point is that a virus left on a surface can be picked up by the hands, so surface cleaning and hand hygiene belong together.

instructionSections.heading: Carriage, infection and illness are separate stages
instructionSections.body: Microbes can live on or in a person without causing harm. When they multiply but no signs appear, the person is colonised, and a colonised person can still pass organisms to others. That is why standard cleaning applies to every person and not only to those who look unwell. Infection begins when microbes start to damage cells, usually with local signs such as pain, swelling or redness. Disease follows when the damage disturbs normal body function and the person feels unwell. The three stages differ, and a person can move between them. Your role is to treat every person and every body fluid as a possible source, and to refer any sign of infection to the nurse in charge.

instructionSections.heading: What decides whether infection takes hold
instructionSections.body: The learner guide names three factors: how many harmful organisms get into the body, how quickly the organism can reproduce, and how strong the body defences are. Your work affects the first factor directly. Cleaning reduces the number of organisms in the environment, hand hygiene limits how many reach a person, and correct cleaning stops organisms building up in soiled places. Damp buildings can grow fungi that cleaning alone does not resolve. Visible mould is outside this lesson and falls under the high-risk cleaning module, which has its own controls and warnings.

lessons.title: Where spread can be interrupted: the six links
learningOutcomes: Name the linked conditions that must all be present for infection to spread.
Match a worker action to the link in the chain that it breaks.
Explain why the chain can be broken at more than one point and why early action matters.

instructionSections.heading: Six linked conditions
instructionSections.body: Infection spreads only when several conditions coincide. An infectious agent must be present. It needs a reservoir where it lives, a way out of that reservoir, a mode of travel, a way into a new person, and a susceptible person who can be infected. Remove any one link and the spread stops. A separate factor, the level of exposure, decides how likely infection becomes once a microbe reaches a person. It depends on the environment, temperature, how many organisms there are, the person immune strength and how many people share the space.

instructionSections.heading: Reservoirs go well beyond people
instructionSections.body: Many workers assume the reservoir is always a sick person. In practice a reservoir can be a piece of equipment, blood or other body fluid, food, water, soil and waste, a surface, or a frequently touched place such as a door handle, a light switch or a call bell. Animals and birds can also act as reservoirs. Surfaces and equipment are where cleaning acts on the reservoir, and that is why the cleaning schedule matters even when nobody in the room is unwell.

instructionSections.heading: Exits and entries are body openings and broken skin
instructionSections.body: Organisms leave a body through the nose, mouth, the bowel and genital openings, and through broken skin. They enter through the eyes, nose, mouth, bowel and genital openings, and through broken skin. A cut or abrasion is therefore both a possible exit and a possible entry, which is why “Cuts, abrasions and skin conditions at work” deals with covering cuts before any task. The fastest way to break these links is to keep your own breaks in skin covered and to avoid touching your eyes, nose or mouth with contaminated gloves or hands.

instructionSections.heading: Modes of transmission and the controls that break them
instructionSections.body: Microbes travel by contact, whether direct with a person or indirect through a surface or object; by droplets from coughs and sneezes; by airborne particles; by vectors such as ticks, mosquitoes, fleas and flies; and by penetrating injury such as a needle stick. Each mode has a matching break. Hand hygiene and gloves break contact spread. Covering coughs and sneezes breaks droplet and airborne spread. Keeping waste sealed and out of reach breaks spread through waste. Tidy, controlled work areas break spread through vectors. Sharps handling breaks the penetrating route, and “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response” covers it. The controls work best together, because no single one is reliable on its own.

lessons.title: Who is most at risk and where infection can come from
learningOutcomes: Name four factors that leave a person less able to resist infection.
Name four sources of infection that come from outside the human body.
State who decides on extra precautions for a susceptible person.

instructionSections.heading: Susceptible people
instructionSections.body: Some people have weaker defences against infection. Very young children and newborn babies have immune systems that are still developing and have had less exposure to common organisms. Older people are often frailer, have less reserve, and rely on others for everyday tasks, which adds to the chance of injury and then infection. People living with long-term conditions such as diabetes, people undergoing cancer treatment, people with burns and people with cognitive impairment are also more susceptible. Current infection, an ongoing disease, some medicines that dampen the immune response, and several conditions at once can all lower defences.

instructionSections.heading: Lifestyle and environment
instructionSections.body: The guide lists smoking, heavy alcohol use, poor diet, lack of exercise and drug use as factors that weaken general defences. In a care setting, close contact with other people raises the risk, because more people in a shared space means more chances for organisms to pass between them. Hospitals hold more people who carry infections, so the chance of touching a contaminated surface or breathing airborne organisms is greater there. Your work is to keep the environment as clean as the schedule requires, because you cannot control the people who move through it.

instructionSections.heading: Sources that are not people
instructionSections.body: Infection can come from food that is badly cooked or past its best, and from poor hygiene around food. Water can carry organisms that are swallowed or inhaled as droplets. Soil can carry worm eggs. Waste that is poorly managed can cause infection by contact or by breathing in its fumes. Animals can transmit infection through body fluids, scratches and bites, and birds through airborne particles from plumage or droppings. Vectors such as ticks, mosquitoes, fleas and flies spread disease through bites and stings. Poor sanitation, including damp buildings and unclean surfaces, can allow fungal infection to grow. Treat any bite, scratch or sting that breaks the skin as an injury to wash and report.

instructionSections.heading: What this means for your work
instructionSections.body: Knowing who is more susceptible tells you where a lapse matters more, for example in a neonatal area or a burns unit. It does not give you authority to decide on extra precautions. That decision belongs to the nurse in charge or the infection prevention team. When extra measures are needed, carry them out discreetly. A person condition is confidential, so you must not describe it to other people in the building, and you must not move a person in a way that signals a diagnosis. Privacy and dignity apply alongside infection control.

lessons.title: Personal hygiene, clean work clothing and staying away when unwell
learningOutcomes: Describe the personal hygiene routine expected before and during a shift.
Explain how work clothing is kept clean and how a soiled uniform is handled.
State when a worker must not attend work and whom to tell.

instructionSections.heading: Personal hygiene is part of the barrier
instructionSections.body: You are a route that organisms can take, so your own hygiene counts as an infection control measure. The guide sets out a daily routine: shower with soap or body wash, wear clean clothing each day, use deodorant, brush the teeth and floss daily, keep nails clean and short, cover the nose and mouth during coughs and sneezes, and discard used tissues straight away. Mouthwash and cleaning the hands after a smoking break are also listed. Hand hygiene is the most important step and is covered in full in “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits”, so it is not repeated here.

instructionSections.heading: Clean clothing and uniforms
instructionSections.body: Work clothing should be clean when each shift begins. Keep two or more days of clean clothing on hand so a change is always possible. If a uniform becomes soiled, change it straight away and avoid wearing it for the rest of the shift. An apron worn over the uniform reduces how often that happens. Where the facility supplies scrubs or other hospital clothing, the guide says it should be laundered on site, so that it does not pick up organisms at home, in the car or on public transport. Where you work in the community, you usually wash your own clothing, and some facilities ask for personal clothing to be bagged and taken home for laundering. Follow the procedure your employer gives you, and treat stains with the stain removal method it sets.

instructionSections.heading: Staying away when unwell
instructionSections.body: A worker who has a transmissible infection should not come to work or go out in public while infectious. The guide applies this to workers with a cough or fever, and it applies to any transmissible illness. Tell your supervisor before the shift starts, because a late call leaves the team short and may expose residents or patients. Do not diagnose yourself and do not give advice to colleagues. Follow your employer illness procedure and any return-to-work requirement. Agency staff should ask on arrival at each placement, because policies differ between sites.

instructionSections.heading: Where this sits with the rest of your work
instructionSections.body: Personal hygiene supports the cleaning methods described in other lessons, but it does not replace them. A clean uniform does not protect a surface you have not cleaned, and a clean surface does not protect a person when the hands touching it are dirty. Keep all parts of the routine in place every shift.

lessons.title: Respiratory hygiene, cough etiquette and waiting areas
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate the cough etiquette steps for a person with respiratory symptoms.
Name four items a facility should supply for respiratory hygiene.
Describe how spacing and signage in a waiting area reduce spread.

instructionSections.heading: Why coughs and sneezes matter
instructionSections.body: Respiratory infections such as influenza and COVID-19 spread through the droplets released when people cough or sneeze. Cough etiquette aims to stop those droplets reaching other people and surfaces. The guide expects everyone with symptoms of a respiratory infection to follow it, and that includes staff, visitors and clients.

instructionSections.heading: Cover, bin, clean
instructionSections.body: When you cough or sneeze, shield your nose and mouth with a paper tissue or the crook of your elbow when no tissue is to hand. Put a used tissue straight into the nearest bin, never into a pocket. Then clean your hands using soap and water, or hand rub, following the method in “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits”. The guide specifies ordinary, non-antimicrobial soap for this step, so check which soap your facility supplies.

instructionSections.heading: Supplies and layout a facility should provide
instructionSections.body: The guide expects waiting and public areas to hold tissues and a no-touch bin for used tissues. Hand-rub dispensers, which contain alcohol, should be placed where people actually need them, such as the doorway of a ward or next to a bed. Every sink should have soap and single-use paper towels. Posters and visual signs in the languages visitors use should be placed by area doorways as reminders. The guide also suggests asking visitors to report any airway infection on arrival, so that staff can help them practise cough etiquette. Anyone who is coughing should sit away from other people in the waiting room.

instructionSections.heading: Your role as the cleaner
instructionSections.body: You top up tissues and bins and report empty dispensers and missing soap or towels straight away, because staff and visitors depend on them. You clean the high-contact points in a waiting area on the schedule (see “Cleaning sequence, routine cleaning and checklists”). You do not remove or cover signs. If a person is coughing, you do not confront them. You point them to the tissues and the hand rub and tell the reception or the nurse, who will manage the situation.

lessons.title: Cuts, abrasions and skin conditions at work
learningOutcomes: Describe the sequence for covering a cut or abrasion before any further task.
Explain why an open wound changes which precautions apply.
State when a skin condition must be reported to the supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Broken skin is an open route
instructionSections.body: A cut or abrasion gives microbes a route past the skin barrier. The guide names broken skin as both a portal of entry and a portal of exit (see “Where spread can be interrupted: the six links”). Cuts are difficult to prevent in cleaning work, even with careful work, so the question is how well a cut is covered and managed. Any open skin means more care with gloves, dressings and hand hygiene, and the protection should be checked before every task.

instructionSections.heading: Cover, glove and report
instructionSections.body: Follow your workplace policy for cuts. Wash the area using soap and water first and dry it. Cover it with a waterproof dressing, or with gauze or a sterile bandage if a waterproof one is not available. Gloves go on over the dressing before any further task. Tell your supervisor about the cut before the next task starts. Replace the dressing daily, and sooner if it becomes wet or soiled. Creams should be used only as your doctor directs for a skin condition. The guide points to hand creams with a water base that are listed on the ARTG, the TGA listing database; check that listing for the product you use.

instructionSections.heading: Skin conditions go to the supervisor
instructionSections.body: Any rash or other skin condition should be reported to your supervisor, who decides whether the condition limits the tasks you can do. Do not hide a rash because it seems minor, and do not decide for yourself that it is harmless. Do not diagnose it from pictures or from advice on the internet. Follow your employer policy on return to clinical contact, and keep the information private to those who need it.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the skin working as a barrier
instructionSections.body: Warm water is kinder to the skin than hot water, and drying the hands fully with paper towel helps prevent cracking. Use hand rub where the procedure allows. Where you handle irritant chemicals, wear heavy-duty gloves, because a chemical burn or dry crack gives organisms an easier route in. The routine skin care in “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits” applies to every shift.

lessons.title: Gowns, aprons, masks, eye protection and gloves: choosing and changing
learningOutcomes: Select a gown, apron, mask, eye protection or glove type that matches the fluid or splash risk listed by the facility.
Identify which masks give little protection and which are regulated for higher-risk areas.
State when each protective item must be changed, replaced or discarded.

instructionSections.heading: Gowns and aprons
instructionSections.body: Gowns and aprons protect clothing from body fluids and splashes, and they reduce the spread of organisms by direct contact. A gown has to resist fluid, and it is put on over ordinary clothing for clinical tasks. The learner guide cites a four-level scale for gown protection, taken from a US document, ANSI/AAMI PB70. A standard disposable apron has one grade; thicker aprons are used in kitchens. An apron should fit closely around the body. Fasten it at the rear, with the tie behind the neck, and never at the front, because a soiled knot can spread contamination. Change an apron after each client and as soon as it is soiled, and put it into the nearest appropriate bin.

instructionSections.heading: Masks and what they protect against
instructionSections.body: The guide sorts masks into three groups. Cloth-type masks offer little protection and the TGA does not regulate them, so do not use them where a fluid or droplet risk is listed. Surgical masks are regulated, and levels 1 to 3 reflect increasing fluid resistance, with the higher levels used in higher-risk areas. A surgical P2 or N95 respirator is the same but also resists fluid. Fit the mask as the manufacturer directs so that it covers the mouth and nose, and tighten it on the face. Keep your hands off the outer face of the mask while it is on. Discard a mask after use, and discard it straight away if it becomes wet. A mask should never sit around the throat or in a pocket between uses, and it is changed between clients.

instructionSections.heading: Eye protection and face shields
instructionSections.body: Wear eye protection when there is a chance of blood or other body fluid splashing, and during any cleaning task where splashing is possible. Eye protection should give clear vision without fogging or distortion, sit snugly, and shield the sides and the front. Single-use eyewear goes in the bin after use, and reusable eyewear is cleaned after each use. A face shield gives wider protection across the whole face. It suits an exposure site, any chance of body fluid contact, a splash injury risk, or work with a person carrying a contagious organism. Remove eye protection by the headband or strap, never by touching the outside, which may be contaminated.

instructionSections.heading: Gloves: type and fit
instructionSections.body: Gloves stop organisms passing between skin, and they are needed whenever you handle body fluid. Single-use gloves are discarded after each use and never washed for reuse. Non-sterile gloves cover possible contact with body fluid or mucus. Sterile gloves are for procedures that require sterility, and general-purpose gloves, usually thicker rubber, are for cleaning instruments and general cleaning. Glove materials include latex, vinyl and nitrile, and nitrile resists chemicals and punctures better. Where the latex allergy risk is present, offer non-latex gloves. Keep nails short and clean so they do not tear the gloves. Use heavy-duty gloves for any task with a puncture or cutting risk. The guide also shows a numbered grade chart taken from a supplier. That chart is not adopted here, because the grades differ between facilities and the facility list governs.

lessons.title: Clean zones, contaminated zones and signage
learningOutcomes: Name the items that go in a clean zone, and the items that must stay apart in a contaminated one.
Explain how records, medicines and clean stock are kept out of contaminated areas.
Choose the correct sign category for a given instruction or hazard.

instructionSections.heading: Two zones in every workplace
instructionSections.body: A clean zone holds sterile storage, equipment storage, medicines and administration records. A contaminated zone receives items that have been used or soiled, such as reusable instruments waiting for reprocessing, and it includes the receiving area of the reprocessing centre. The two zones must stay apart. Once a clean item has touched something from the contaminated zone it can no longer be trusted, and the organisation has to re-clean or discard it, which costs time and resources.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the direction of travel one way
instructionSections.body: Material should move from clean to contaminated, and not back. Reusable instruments that have been used remain in the soiled space until reprocessing is complete, and they are never stored alongside sterile equipment. Single-use items that cannot be reprocessed are dropped into the waste container the facility designates. Where the facility uses separate bins for items soiled with body fluid, use them. Records and medicines are never carried into a contaminated area, and records are never stored with soiled stock.

instructionSections.heading: Aseptic principles that apply to support staff
instructionSections.body: Aseptic technique is a clinical procedure, and you do not perform it. The guide does, however, list principles that a support worker needs to understand. The first is the environment: before entering a clean area, check for anything that could let organisms reach a patient, such as an open window, an unclean surface or another activity in progress. The second is no-touch technique. Keep the clean area clean by using gloves, cleaning surfaces, and never letting body fluid enter it. The third is hand hygiene, which must be done before entering a clean area.

instructionSections.heading: Signs that tell people what to do
instructionSections.body: Signage identifies clean spaces, soiled spaces and places with a hazard. They can also tell people to act before going into a space, such as putting on protective items, taking off contaminated clothing or cleaning their hands. The guide sets out six sign groups: those that require an action, those that forbid one, those that warn, those that give emergency information, those that signal danger, and those that simply inform. Some signs use only pictures. Before relying on a picture-only sign, make sure the people it is for will understand it. Do not cover, move or remove a sign. Report a missing or damaged one at once.

lessons.title: Cleaning sequence, routine cleaning and checklists
learningOutcomes: Order the tasks in a room from the least contaminated area to the most contaminated area.
Explain why a checklist is used for routine cleaning.
Describe the routine floor and bench cleaning steps for a clinic room.

instructionSections.heading: Work from clean to dirty and from high to low
instructionSections.body: The order of work protects surfaces you have already cleaned. Clean from high to low, so that dust and splashes fall onto areas you have not cleaned yet. Clean from the least contaminated surface to the most contaminated one, and finish in the most contaminated area. Wipe benches and tables before vacuuming or mopping, so that anything falling from them is picked up by the floor clean. Starting in the cleanest room and finishing in the dirtiest is the same principle applied to the whole area.

instructionSections.heading: Routine cleaning and cleaning before and after tasks
instructionSections.body: Routine cleaning runs at the opening and closing of each day, around specified tasks, and at intervals the schedule fixes. The guide wants benches and tables cleaned around each session and whenever they appear dirty. Wipe the surface with a mild detergent dissolved in warm water, then dry it with a single-use towel. Swap in a clean cloth for every new area so a single soiled cloth cannot spread contamination through the room. Any soiled surface, or any surface a patient touched, is wiped between patients with the same approach.

instructionSections.heading: Floors and walls
instructionSections.body: Carpeted areas get daily vacuuming, and hard floors get daily vacuuming followed by mopping. Dampen the floor with detergent solution, then pick up the surplus with a clean, dry cloth or mop. In a poorly ventilated or chilly room, wipe the floor by hand so moisture does not linger. Any wet area must be signed to stop slips and falls. Walls can be cleaned less often than floors, except where they sit in a soiled area or may be splashed. A mild solution in warm water is gentler on wall finishes and on the hands of the worker than hot water; if hot water cannot be avoided, switch to heavier gloves.

instructionSections.heading: Checklists, posters and hot spots
instructionSections.body: A checklist shows what has been done and stops a task being missed, so tick each item when it is finished and report any item you could not complete. Cleaning posters placed on the walls help to show the order. Surfaces that many hands touch, for instance handles on doors, wall switches, flush levers, keyboards, bed controls, call bells and wheelchair grips, need cleaning more often than the rest, and the schedule sets how often. The minimum frequencies for these items are set out in “High-touch items: minimum intervals for patient rooms”.

lessons.title: Terminal cleaning after transmission-based precautions
learningOutcomes: List the steps of a terminal clean in order.
Explain the difference between a two-step clean and a two-in-one clean.
Describe the protective items and hand hygiene steps during and after the clean.

instructionSections.heading: What a terminal clean is
instructionSections.body: A terminal clean decontaminates a room once the person has left it by discharge or transfer, from a space under transmission-based controls. It goes further than routine cleaning: it includes a full clean and a disinfection step for the whole room. The clinical team decides when the precautions end and when the room can be released (see “Enhanced cleaning under added controls for infection spread” for the duration rule). Do not start a terminal clean until the nurse in charge has confirmed the room is free to clean.

instructionSections.heading: Protect yourself first
instructionSections.body: Before going in, put on a surgical mask, eye protection, a gown and gloves, as the guide describes. Clinical equipment that the patient used must be cleaned or removed according to its method, and only after the clinical team has released it. Keep the protective items on for the whole clean, and change the gloves at the points set out in the procedure.

instructionSections.heading: The working order
instructionSections.body: The guide sets out a sequence. Replace soiled privacy screens and drapes around the bed, disposable ones included. Wipe down every surface, piece of furniture and fitting with a damp cloth to pick up dust. Wash the glass, ledges and window frames. Clean every surface of the bed, including the mattress, and then go over the floor with a mop. Mop the floor. Take off the protective items, clean your hands, then put on new gloves. Clean the equipment itself and put it back into its store. Discard the waste correctly. Finish with hand hygiene. Keep to this order so that you do not re-contaminate areas already cleaned.

instructionSections.heading: Two-step and two-in-one approaches
instructionSections.body: A two-step clean uses a detergent first, then a disinfectant. The guide names two disinfectant choices for the disinfection step after the detergent clean: a TGA-listed product for hospital use that works against viruses, or a chlorine product, for example sodium hypochlorite. A two-in-one clean relies on one product that merges both jobs: either a TGA-listed product effective against viruses, or a detergent blended with hypochlorite. Your facility policy chooses the approach. Follow the label for dilution and contact time. The guide gives no dilution figure, and some organisations do not allow bleach at all, so check the facility list rather than relying on memory.

instructionSections.heading: Hazards during a terminal clean
instructionSections.body: In this work watch for slick floors, liquid on powered equipment, heavy loads, chemical vapours from spills or products, and skin reactions to chemicals. Ventilate the room where the product allows it, sign wet floors, and keep the chemicals away from electrical items. Report any fumes or skin reaction at once.

lessons.title: Cleaning equipment care, vacuums and cleaning-tool hazards
learningOutcomes: Select a vacuum that controls dust and state the bag-changing rule.
Describe how a shared, non-disposable item is cleaned between clients.
Name five hazards in cleaning equipment work and a control for each.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a vacuum that controls dust
instructionSections.body: Dust is a route for organisms, so a vacuum must have suitable suction and must not release dust and bacteria back into the air. The guide gives two options: a correctly vented or ducted vacuum, or a dust-holding mop used with detergent solution. Never use a vacuum to pick up clinical waste. Carpets need daily vacuuming, so the machine must be working properly before the day begins.

instructionSections.heading: Vacuum upkeep and bag changing
instructionSections.body: Dispose of a full vacuum bag without spilling its contents, and replace it with a clean one. Do not overfill a bag and do not reuse it. Clean the filters and the cleaning heads regularly, and check that the cleaning head is free of hair and debris before use. A neglected machine throws dust into the air, so keeping it in good order is part of infection control, not an extra job.

instructionSections.heading: Cloths and reusable shared items
instructionSections.body: Launder cloths after each use, and discard any that cannot be washed. Take a fresh cloth into every new area. Reusable mop heads are washed hot after each use. Non-disposable items, for example stethoscopes, medical equipment, hoists, slings, walking frames, trolleys and trays, are cleaned between each client. Use the manufacturer instructions for the product and method, and check the product before you apply it, because the manufacturer may list unsuitable methods and products. Protective wraps and covers can shield awkward items like keyboards, and each one is replaced between clients.

instructionSections.heading: Hazards in cleaning equipment work
instructionSections.body: The guide lists five hazards: slippery wet ground, liquid reaching powered equipment, heavy lifting, vapours from chemicals or spilt products, and irritation of the skin caused by chemicals. Control them by signing wet areas and drying floors, keeping water and liquids away from electrical equipment, asking for help or using lifting aids for heavy items, ventilating and reading the product label for fumes, and wearing gloves suited to the chemical. Check the manufacturer instructions before cleaning any electrical item.

lessons.title: Body fluid exposure: first response and reporting
learningOutcomes: Put the first-response steps in order after blood or other body fluids reaches the eyes, mouth or skin.
List the details an incident report for a body fluid exposure must include.
Explain why the supervisor must hear about an exposure straight away.

instructionSections.heading: What counts as an exposure
instructionSections.body: The guide names blood, urine, sputum, mucus, faeces, semen, vaginal fluid and vomit as body fluids that carry risk. Exposure can happen during toileting, showering, bed bathing, changing catheter bags, cleaning up a body fluid spill, sharp injuries, wound management, brushing teeth or feeding. Treat any contact with these fluids as an exposure until your supervisor tells you otherwise. Sharp injuries are covered in “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”, and this lesson covers splashes and contact with the eyes, mouth and skin.

instructionSections.heading: First response on the skin, eyes and mouth
instructionSections.body: Where fluid has reached the skin, wash the exposed area thoroughly using soap and water. If the eyes are affected, rinse them with tap water or saline while holding the eyelids open, and do not rub them. If fluid gets into the mouth, spit it out and keep rinsing until none is left. Take off any soiled clothing and have a shower if it is needed. Move away from the source of the splash first if that is needed to make the area safe.

instructionSections.heading: Instruments, reporting and documentation
instructionSections.body: Rinse or wipe any used instrument promptly so that it is ready for reprocessing. Report the exposure verbally to the right person straight away, so that the workplace can decide whether further steps are required. Documentation may then be required of you. A serious exposure calls for an incident report. It should record the events, who was involved, who saw it, where it happened and how far any injury extends, the object responsible for the injury, the kind of fluid, and how much of it reached the worker.

instructionSections.heading: Why speed matters
instructionSections.body: Blood-borne viruses such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV can be transmitted through contact with blood. Prompt reporting lets the employer arrange counselling, testing and treatment where these are needed. Decisions about testing timing, follow-up and treatment belong to clinicians and the workplace occupational health process. Keep the identity of the source person private, and share it only with those who need it for the response.

lessons.title: Recording risks, hazard reports and breaches
learningOutcomes: Complete a risk record with the activity, hazard, rating, control measures and timeframe.
Write a hazard report that includes type, location, risk, who is at risk and action taken.
Name the first person to tell about a breach and the other people a report may need to reach.

instructionSections.heading: Writing a risk record
instructionSections.body: Begin by naming the activity and the hazards in it. Decide who is at risk and how likely and how serious the harm could be. List the control measures already in place and any new control you recommend, and set a timeframe for each. The guide lays out five columns: what the worker is doing, the danger involved, how serious the danger rates, the measures in place, and when each measure is due. For example, showering a client who has dementia brings risks of a wet floor, aggression or resistance, and falls. Controls include a shower chair and grab rails, and each has a timeframe. Keep the record in the form your employer uses.

instructionSections.heading: Hazard reports
instructionSections.body: Spotting a hazard at work means you are obliged to report it. The guide treats this as a legal duty. Write up a hazard report, then hand it to the supervisor or the WHS representative. A hazard report should give the type of hazard, its location, the risk it poses, who is at risk and the action taken. For urgent hazards, speak to the supervisor first and then complete the written report.

instructionSections.heading: Breaches of infection control
instructionSections.body: Infection control policies are written to keep everyone safe. The employer must create, explain and train workers in those policies, and workers must learn and follow them. Examples of breaches named in the guide include skipping hand cleaning at the required moments, putting protective items on or taking them off incorrectly, attending while unwell, reusing a needle meant for one use, reusing equipment that has not been reprocessed, weak respiratory etiquette, and disregarding signs. A breach is reported to the supervisor, not corrected publicly. Agency staff may not know the local policy, so a reminder and the correct protocol are often the right first step, before any formal document is written.

instructionSections.heading: Who receives which report
instructionSections.body: Go to the supervisor first, speaking directly and without delay, and bring one or two possible fixes so the supervisor can accept one or suggest a different option. Other people may need a report depending on the situation: a registered nurse, a general practitioner, other health professionals, a carer, a family member or guardian, and the regulating bodies. The regulator, which the guide calls the responsible authority, creates and enforces the rules, and investigates when there are repeated breaches. Share information only with people who need it, and keep records in the designated clean administration area (see “Clean zones, contaminated zones and signage”).

lessons.title: Assessing infection risk: grading risks and ranking controls
learningOutcomes: Place a risk into a likelihood and a consequence category and read the rating from a matrix.
Rank three control options from the most reliable to the least reliable.
Explain why protective equipment is a last layer and not the first choice.

instructionSections.heading: Likelihood and consequence
instructionSections.body: Assessing a risk means looking at how likely it is to happen and what its consequence would be. The questions to ask include what influences the risk, its probability, its consequence, its rating, which controls can be used, which stakeholders must be told, the timeframe, who is responsible, what limits the analysis, and whether the plan creates a new risk. The guide uses five likelihood categories, from almost certain to rare, and five consequence categories, from insignificant to severe. A numerical scale, such as 1 to 5, can be used instead. Either system works, but the matrix has to be designed for the workplace and checked as the work goes on.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the matrix
instructionSections.body: A risk matrix places likelihood on one axis and consequence on the other. The square where the two meet gives the rating, which the guide shows as low, medium, high or extreme. The guide presents its matrix as a template, so use the matrix your employer has adopted rather than copying the example. The organisation sets what each rating requires. A high or extreme rating normally needs a supervisor decision and a control before the work continues, but the exact response is set by the employer procedure and is not stated by the guide.

instructionSections.heading: Ranking controls by reliability
instructionSections.body: The hierarchy ranks controls from the most reliable to the least reliable. At the top sits elimination, which takes away what creates the danger. Next is substitution, which replaces the hazard with a safer alternative, such as a single-use item in place of a reusable one where the procedure allows it. Isolation keeps the hazard away from people, for example by holding waste in a locked space. Engineering controls change the equipment or the environment, such as a ducted vacuum. Administrative controls are the policies, procedures, schedules and signs. Protective equipment is at the bottom. It matters, but it does not remove the hazard, so it is used on top of the higher controls and not in place of them.

instructionSections.heading: Reasonably practicable and organisational procedures
instructionSections.body: The guide lists factors for deciding what is reasonably practicable: how probable the hazard is, how much damage it could do, how well the hazard and its controls are understood, whether suitable controls exist and can be used, and what the controls cost, including whether that cost is grossly out of line with the risk. Cost does not decide the matter on its own, and a control has to suit the hazard. The guide also lists specific controls that follow organisational procedures: removing a dangerous process altogether, wearing protective items properly, redesigning the way work is done, keeping the hazard apart, putting up signs, fitting protective devices, handling items safely, and following the infection control policy. These should be applied in the order the hierarchy sets.

lessons.title: Theatre infection control: standard and additional precautions
learningOutcomes: Distinguish standard precautions, which apply to every patient, from additional precautions that depend on how an infection travels.
Explain why the theatre applies the same baseline to every patient, including patients with a blood-borne virus.
Identify who in the theatre is responsible for checking standards and how the check is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Two layers of precaution
instructionSections.body: Infection control in a theatre rests on two layers. The first is the baseline that applies to every patient at all times, whatever the diagnosis. Its contents are hand cleaning, protective items for any contact with blood or other body fluids, careful handling of patient equipment and linen, avoiding sharps injuries, cleaning of the environment and dealing with spills, and careful waste handling. The second layer is added where a particular route of spread needs it: airborne, droplet or contact precautions. The second layer always sits on top of the first and never replaces it.

instructionSections.heading: Why the baseline treats all fluid as a risk
instructionSections.body: The operating-theatre paper regards every sample of blood, every blood product and all other body fluids as a possible carrier of infection, whatever the diagnosis, and however risky a case looks.
