It identifies two main workplace routes for HIV and hepatitis B: needles and blades carrying blood or other body fluids that pierce the skin, and splashes that land on the eyes, on damaged skin or in a wound. Blocking those routes means avoiding sharps injuries and placing a physical barrier between workers and every source of blood or other body fluids. The learner guide reaches the same conclusion through its standard precautions and its sharps rules (see “Body fluid exposure: first response and reporting” and “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”).

instructionSections.heading: Additional precautions and the size figures
instructionSections.body: Beyond the baseline, the same document also lists extra measures for three routes, and gives size figures for two of them. The learner guide gives no size figures for those routes. The additional measures for a particular case come from the theatre infection-control plan that the clinical team sets. The learner guide lists possible measures such as isolation, special ventilation, enhanced cleaning and extra protective items (see “Enhanced cleaning under added controls for infection spread” and “Terminal cleaning after transmission-based precautions”).

instructionSections.heading: Terminology and blood-borne virus patients
instructionSections.body: The theatre document uses the term universal precautions for the baseline. The learner guide uses standard precautions, and it governs where the two differ, so this lesson uses standard precautions for the same principle. According to the same paper, a person living with hepatitis B, hepatitis C or HIV receives the same care as anybody else, under the baseline. The learner guide adds a confidentiality rule: a person condition is not disclosed to others, and any extra measure is carried out discreetly. Taken together, the rules mean the same care for everyone, with no disclosure.

instructionSections.heading: Who checks the standard
instructionSections.body: Responsibility for following the standards rests with every person working in theatre or in a clinical role. Co-ordinators must confirm that cleanliness expectations are satisfied, and take corrective steps when they are not. It makes theatre operational managers responsible for regular audits, with a written record. The learner guide places the duty to write policies and train workers on the employer, and places the duty to follow them and report breaches on each worker. The facility written role descriptions decide who does what in practice.

instructionSections.heading: Jurisdiction and references
instructionSections.body: The theatre document is undated and unattributed, and it contains UK-style references such as a trust waste policy. Its jurisdiction is unknown, so it is treated here as practice content only. UK-only policy references do not apply in Australia. State and territory law and the facility policy govern waste, reporting and the theatre plan.

lessons.title: Sharps and instruments in theatre
learningOutcomes: Describe how a sharp instrument moves between a surgeon and an assistant without being handed directly.
State the disposal rules for used needles and disposable blades in the theatre.
State the steps a cleaner takes when they find a sharp in the theatre.

instructionSections.heading: Scope of the surgical points
instructionSections.body: This lesson covers how sharps are handled in the theatre. The surgical technique described in the theatre document is for trained theatre clinicians working in the operating setting. It is not a cleaning method and must not be applied to the work of cleaning contractors. Cleaners follow only the final section of this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Moving sharps between clinicians
instructionSections.body: A sharp is never handed across by hand between a surgeon and an assistant. The surgeon places sharps safely. Each sharp travels in a dish reserved for sharps, and the dish holds one sharp at any moment. Where two surgeons work at once, each keeps a personal dish. The learner guide sets the baseline: a sharp is not handed to another person by hand, and is placed in a puncture-resistant tray for handover. Any dish the theatre uses must meet that puncture-resistant standard.

instructionSections.heading: Blades and needles
instructionSections.body: Where practicable, use one-piece disposable scalpels so that no blade has to be pulled from a reusable handle. Where a removable blade is used, detach it with an appropriate device rather than with the fingers. Lift a needle with grooved forceps or a needle holder, never with the fingers. Do not resheath or recap a used needle. Spent needles and single-use sharps go into a facility-approved bin without delay.

instructionSections.heading: Glove tears and needlestick events
instructionSections.body: When a glove splits or a needle pricks someone, take the glove off, scrub the hands with the surgical solution, fit a fresh glove, and take the implicated needle or tool out of the sterile zone. Address a needle prick or a mucous membrane splash once it is safe to do so. The learner guide adds the wound steps: clean the wound using soap and water, press on any bleeding, cover the wound with a waterproof dressing, tell the supervisor straight away, and complete the incident report. For wounds, the learner guide governs.

instructionSections.heading: Containers and filling
instructionSections.body: Sharps containers must be approved, puncture-resistant and water-proof, clearly labelled, and usable with one hand. The theatre document says to close a container when it is three-quarters full. That figure is not an Australian rule and is not adopted. Use the facility fill line. Do not reopen a sealed container, and do not place a sharps container where it blocks cleaning. Sharps waste leaves the site with a licensed operator, who destroys it by incineration.

instructionSections.heading: Surgical technique not used here
instructionSections.body: Several surgical points in the theatre document, including how to close the skin, how to manage drainage and how to use laser cutting, are not reproduced in these lessons. They belong to surgical training and are not support-worker content.

instructionSections.heading: What cleaners do
instructionSections.body: A cleaner never picks up a sharp by hand, and never recaps or bends a needle. If a sharp is found on the floor, in linen or in a dish, stop, keep others away, alert the nearest theatre team member, and let them retrieve it with an approved tool. Record the find as a hazard. A glove torn during cleaning is replaced at once, after hand washing.

lessons.title: Theatre attire, gloves, footwear and jewellery
learningOutcomes: Choose and use gloves, including double gloving for high-risk procedures, under the theatre plan.
State the rules for headwear, footwear, jewellery and nails in the theatre.
Describe which items come off before someone exits the theatre.

instructionSections.heading: Gloves have two jobs
instructionSections.body: Gloves guard the person wearing them against the patient blood and wound exudate, and they also stop organisms on the wearer hands from reaching the surgical site. The theatre document says double gloving reduces hand contamination and protects the wearer against viral transmission, and it recommends double gloving for high-risk procedures. The learner guide adds that gloves are single-use, never washed for reuse, replaced when damaged, and that hands are cleaned before and after putting them on. Where the two sources cover the same point, the learner guide governs.

instructionSections.heading: Gowns, masks and eye shields
instructionSections.body: Scrubbed staff face the greatest splash risk. The theatre document recommends fluid-resistant face masks, which give both an airborne barrier and splash protection. For heavy contamination it advises gowns that are impermeable, with waterproof sleeves that reach well down the arm and a front panel covering the full length of the body; for scrubbed staff losing a lot of fluid it suggests plastic aprons; and for the eyes it names goggles or a face shield that covers the whole face. Everyone who wears protective items is trained in their fit and use, and the equipment is checked, maintained and restocked so that it is always available.

instructionSections.heading: Headwear
instructionSections.body: Disposable headwear is required for scrubbed staff, since they stand near the surgical field, which matters most in laminar flow rooms. Hats are also needed in laminar flow rooms when a prosthesis is being implanted. Headwear is discarded after use and is never worn outside the theatre.

instructionSections.heading: Footwear
instructionSections.body: Footwear should fit well and have impervious soles. Open footwear is not worn. Protective boots, such as galoshes or rubber boots reaching the calf, are the better choice over standard shoes. Shoes are wiped down each time they are worn, and a set routine at the close of each session makes sure that happens. The learner guide asks for footwear that protects against dropped sharps, which fits with this.

instructionSections.heading: Jewellery and nails
instructionSections.body: Chains, earrings and gem-set rings are removed. Plain bands can remain on for both scrubbed and unscrubbed staff, but surgeons may be asked to take them off, mainly when metal implants are in use. The learner guide allows only a plain flat band, and only where the organisation permits it, so the theatre policy decides. False fingernails are not worn in the theatre.

instructionSections.heading: Visitors and leaving the theatre
instructionSections.body: A visitor entering a main theatre changes into theatre clothing first. Scrubbed staff wear disposable caps, masks and footwear close to the field. Before exiting, take the surgical mask off (never let it hang on the neck), remove the cap, and put a fresh white jacket over the theatre clothes whenever you leave the unit, particularly when walking through public corridors.

lessons.title: Movement, case order and cleaning between cases in the theatre
learningOutcomes: Explain how closed doors and controlled movement reduce airborne contamination during a case.
Describe how the order of cases on a list can make cleaning more effective.
Carry out the between-case clean for a theatre table and touch surfaces, including clearing away blood and any other fluid.

instructionSections.heading: Where microbes in a theatre come from
instructionSections.body: According to the operating-theatre paper, germs that enter an open, clean wound come from the skin of the patient, from the hand of the surgeon, or from airborne microbes that land in the wound or on tools. The bulk of airborne microbes in a theatre originate with the team members, while the patient contributes only a small share. The number of microbes dispersed rises with movement. Managing traffic through the room is therefore part of infection control. Doors should stay shut so the air handling works as designed, and foot traffic should be kept to the lowest level while a procedure runs.

instructionSections.heading: The order of cases on the list
instructionSections.body: The same paper requires that the operating table and any items touching the patient are cleaned between one person and the next. It observes that scheduling a case that sheds many microbes at the close of the list can simplify cleaning, although that order is unnecessary when the between-patient clean already does its job. The learner guide principle that work moves from clean to contaminated supports the same approach. Follow the list order that the facility sets.

instructionSections.heading: What the between-case clean involves
instructionSections.body: The theatre document calls routine cleaning adequate between cases. The learner guide sets the method for a between-patient wipe. It uses a mild detergent solution, a single-use towel, a sequence from the least soiled surface to the most soiled, disinfection where the facility requires it, and a final drying pass. Routine cleaning counts as adequate only when it includes this wipe. The learner guide governs the method.

instructionSections.heading: Blood, body fluid and instruments
instructionSections.body: Wipe blood and any other organic matter from kit, walls and floors promptly. Before instruments travel to central processing in a sealed container, knock off heavy soil in the theatre. Use mechanical washing where practicable. If machine washing is not possible, wash by hand in a basin of warm detergent solution, never beneath a running tap. The learner guide sets a ceiling of thirty-five degrees for preliminary cleaning. Immerse instruments before scrubbing, and never scrub them while any part of them sits above the water.

instructionSections.heading: Containing fluids and handling specimens
instructionSections.body: Fluids from the patient are kept inside a liquid-proof drape or a sealed suction set, ideally disposable. This is a clinical measure. Samples and tissue pieces are placed in leak-proof tubs or biohazard bags before they are carried away. Swabs and sponges soaked in blood sit in a basin until the theatre team counts them and seals them in a plastic sack. Cleaners do not count swabs. Specimens are carried only by staff the facility has authorised.

instructionSections.heading: Surgical steps not used here
instructionSections.body: Closing and drainage steps and wound dressings in the theatre document are surgical technique and are not used in this lesson.

lessons.title: Theatre skin preparation, hand decontamination and who checks the standard
learningOutcomes: Describe the hand decontamination requirement before a procedure, and the basis for choosing an alcohol or water-based skin preparation.
Explain how theatre co-ordinators and operational managers check the cleanliness standard.
Separate the parts of this lesson that apply to cleaning work from those that apply only to clinicians.

instructionSections.heading: Hand decontamination
instructionSections.body: The operating-theatre paper treats hand cleaning as a major way to cut infection, and asks that hands be cleaned using a suitable technique. The theatre protocol names the method, and the learner guide hand hygiene rules apply throughout (see “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits”). Alcohol-based rub does not work on visibly dirty hands, so wash using soap and water first in that case. The surgical hand scrub is a clinical task and is not described further here.

instructionSections.heading: Skin preparation
instructionSections.body: According to that paper, alcohol mixtures outperform water mixtures for preparing skin, so alcohol is the favoured choice. The alcohol needs to air dry completely before work goes on. Skin preparation is a clinical task for theatre staff. Cleaning contractors do not prepare patient skin and must not touch a prepared site.

instructionSections.heading: Standards and audits
instructionSections.body: Co-ordinators carry the duty to verify cleanliness expectations and to act when they slip. It makes theatre operational managers responsible for regular audits of the standards, with a written record. The learner guide makes the employer responsible for policies and training, and each worker responsible for following them and reporting breaches to a supervisor. Where the two sources overlap, the facility written role descriptions decide.

instructionSections.heading: What cleaning contractors take from this lesson
instructionSections.body: Work only to the written instruction for each area that the co-ordinator provides. Report any standard that is not being met to the co-ordinator. Keep the audit records and checklists as the co-ordinator asks, and do not alter them.

instructionSections.heading: Parts of the theatre document not used
instructionSections.body: The theatre document includes a passage on post-mortem workers. That setting is outside this course and is not used. Its references to a trust waste policy and to a clinical waste section are UK-style, do not apply in Australia, and the clinical waste section is empty in the source. Waste rules come from “Clinical waste: segregation, containers and handling” and from state or territory law.

lessons.title: First-shift walkthrough
learningOutcomes: Perform the named task within an approved scope and site safety rules
Explain and demonstrate safe decisions in realistic work situations
Provide observable evidence of work quality and appropriate escalation

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Learning context and safe boundaries
instructionSections.body: A new cleaner arrives at an occupied home for a two-hour routine clean. The client is working from home and one room is excluded. The learner must follow the actual site induction, product instructions, employer procedures and supervisor direction. Do not undertake work beyond training or authorisation.

instructionSections.heading: Step-by-step field procedure
instructionSections.body:
1. Confirm the assignment, address, contact and arrival window from the authorised work order; never assume access or entry permission.
2. On arrival identify yourself, confirm the client or site contact and clarify permitted rooms, pets, alarms and any immediate hazards.
3. Walk the route from entry to storage and exit; locate water, power and waste facilities only where permission is given.
4. Prioritise tasks against the agreed scope and available time; communicate conflicts before changing the service.
5. At closeout check equipment, secure access as instructed and send a factual completion report.

instructionSections.heading: Worked decision and reasoning

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Learning outcome
By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to verify identity and authorised entry while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

Workplace procedure
Check the scheduled site, address, shift window, nominated supervisor and current access instructions in the approved system. Complete required induction before working, including evacuation assembly point, restricted areas, emergency contacts and incident reporting route. Use only credentials issued to you. Never tailgate through secured doors or share access codes. If access fails, notify the nominated contact and record the delay.

Decision boundaries
Before acting, confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation. If the task exceeds training, consent, safe access or agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others as appropriate, report promptly and document the reason. Never substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

Worked workplace example
At a corporate office, an unfamiliar contractor offers to hold a secure door. The cleaner declines, uses their own authorised access and reports an unexpected visitor if required by site policy.

Guided practical exercise
Role-play entry at a mock building with a failed badge, a restricted laboratory and a missing induction record. Complete an access checklist and choose the safe next action.

Assessment and feedback
An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Uses authorised access, locates emergency arrangements, recognises restricted zones and records access exceptions. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

instructionSections.heading: Step-by-step field procedure
instructionSections.body:
1. Complete a dynamic hazard check, including slips, electrical equipment, ventilation and public access.
2. Set out tools, segregation controls and wet-floor precautions before beginning.
3. Demonstrate a consistent high-to-low sequence, correct product use and prevention of dirty-to-clean transfer.
4. Manage interruption: pause, secure chemicals and equipment, and restore safe access before resuming.

instructionSections.heading: Worked decision and reasoning

instructionSections.heading: Practice and feedback

instructionSections.heading: Quality and completion criteria
instructionSections.body: Evidence must show accurate scope interpretation, safe sequencing, correct tool/product selection, respectful communication, and reliable handover. Critical safety failures require stopping the practical and retraining.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction

instructionSections.heading: Perform the work safely and professionally

instructionSections.body: In this lesson, practise plan the cleaning sequence using an authorised work order and a realistic Australian cleaning-site scenario. Work only within training, employer procedures and site-specific instructions.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body: Confirm scope, identify high-risk surfaces, gather supplies and work systematically from cleaner to dirtier areas and generally high to low to reduce recontamination.

instructionSections.heading: Plan zones and priorities
instructionSections.body: Read the scope and identify rooms, exclusions, high-touch areas, access limits and required outcomes. Prepare clean supplies before entering a contaminated area.

instructionSections.heading: Sequence to avoid rework
instructionSections.body: Generally work from cleaner to dirtier areas and higher to lower surfaces, subject to the site procedure. Allow required product dwell times and keep wet areas protected until dry.

instructionSections.heading: Close each zone

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body: Use designated cloths and equipment for sanitary areas, change tools when soiled, perform hand hygiene at task transitions and avoid returning dirty tools to clean surfaces.

instructionSections.heading: Separate cleaning pathways
instructionSections.body: Use designated cloths, mops and equipment for toilets, bathrooms, food areas and general areas under site rules. A colour system works only if everyone follows the local chart.

instructionSections.heading: Prevent transfer
instructionSections.body: Change gloves and perform hand hygiene at appropriate transitions; never carry a used toilet cloth into a kitchen. Keep clean supplies separate from used items during transport.

instructionSections.heading: Respond to a breach
instructionSections.body: If contaminated equipment touches a clean or food-contact surface, stop, isolate the affected items, reprocess the surface using approved procedures and report if necessary.

lessons.title: Job planning and scheduling
learningOutcomes: Estimate the time for a job using the scope, the site size and the method.
Plan a day's route so that travel, access windows and breaks are built in.
Re-plan when a job runs over, a customer changes the time or access fails.

instructionSections.heading: Estimate time from the scope
instructionSections.body: Estimate time from the scope, not from the price. Count the rooms, the surfaces, the methods and the drying time. Add time for set-up, the site induction, the pre-start checks, the clean-up and the handover. Record the estimate and the basis for it, so that the next estimate can be improved from actual times. An estimate that is too short leads to rushed work, while an estimate that is too long wastes capacity.

instructionSections.heading: Plan the route and the day
instructionSections.body: Plan the day in the order that reduces travel, respects access windows and fits the team's breaks. Keep a buffer for delay between jobs, particularly where traffic or parking is unpredictable. Group jobs in the same area where possible. Check the access times and the customer's preferred windows before confirming the order. Record the planned times so that the team and the customer have the same information.

instructionSections.heading: Re-plan when conditions change
instructionSections.body: When a job runs over or a customer changes the time, tell the next customer as early as possible with a revised time. Do not promise a time that the team cannot meet. If access fails, record it and move the job to another slot where possible. Use the record of actual times to adjust the next estimate.

lessons.title: Read the job scope
learningOutcomes: Identify scope, inclusions, exclusions and access windows in a work order before arrival.
Clarify contradictory or missing instructions with the coordinator before allocating time.
Produce a clarification request and workable task sequence without assuming authorisation for extra work.

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level, water-fed pole and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Any work above ground level, or from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted: it needs employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body: Review customer instructions, inclusions, exclusions, access windows, staff eligibility and evidence requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Purpose and learning outcome
instructionSections.body: After this lesson, the learner can demonstrate read the job scope in a routine cleaning workplace, identify limits of their authority and document the result. The following procedures are examples; always apply the approved site process and task instructions.

instructionSections.heading: Detailed workplace method
instructionSections.body: Read the site address and access instructions in the authorised job system, verify the correct customer and booking window, and review scope, exclusions, priority rooms, site contacts and completion evidence. Identify dependencies such as water, power, keys, parking and other contractors. Clarify ambiguous or contradictory instructions before arrival. Do not infer consent to perform extra tasks or handle client possessions.

instructionSections.heading: Safety, boundaries and escalation
instructionSections.body: Before proceeding, confirm the actual work scope, hazards, material or equipment suitability and who can authorise changes. Stop and seek direction when work is unsafe, outside training, or the requested result conflicts with a site instruction. Record facts, not assumptions.

instructionSections.heading: Worked example
instructionSections.body: A turnover order says “full clean” but the inventory lists only bathrooms and kitchen. The cleaner contacts the coordinator to confirm whether bedrooms and linen are included before allocating time.

instructionSections.heading: Supervised practical
instructionSections.body: Review a sample work order containing missing access instructions, an unclear appliance task and a conflicting completion time; produce a clarification request and task sequence.

instructionSections.heading: Assessment and corrective feedback
instructionSections.body: An assessor observes the learner and verifies: Identifies scope and exclusions, asks timely questions and creates a workable task order without assuming authorisation. If any critical safety action is missed, provide coaching and require a new demonstration. Attendance alone is not proof of competence.

lessons.title: Job checklist and sign-off (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Complete the pre-start, during-job and completion checks with an observation behind each tick
Record a scope change and agree it before extra work starts
Record the customer's inspection and sign-off, or the reason it was not given

instructionSections.heading: What a job checklist protects
instructionSections.body: A job checklist is a record that the job was checked at the points where things usually go wrong: before work starts, during the work, and at completion. It also records the customer's confirmation that the work matches what was agreed. Without a checklist, a job can be finished and still not match the quote, and a problem can be found by the customer rather than by the crew. The checklist should be short enough to complete on site and specific enough to show what was done. It does not replace the SOP for the task. It confirms that the SOP was followed and that the site was ready.

instructionSections.heading: Pre-start, during and completion
instructionSections.body: Before work starts, confirm the job reference and scope, the access instructions, the hazards visible on arrival, and the equipment needed. If a hazard cannot be controlled, record it and do not start the affected task until it is controlled or a decision has been recorded by the person the business names. During the job, record the checks that matter for quality and safety, such as surface protection, chemical contact time or the position of a ladder, and record any change in scope when it happens. At completion, record the work done against the scope, take the agreed photos, leave the area clean, remove equipment and waste, and tell the customer what was done and what was not.

instructionSections.heading: Customer sign-off
instructionSections.body: Customer sign-off confirms that the customer has inspected the work and agrees that it matches the agreed scope. Use the sign-off method the business has set. Make sure the customer knows what they are confirming, and do not ask for a signature before the work has been inspected. If the customer disagrees, record the concern in their words and the action agreed. Do not mark the job complete until the concern is resolved or escalated under the complaints procedure.

lessons.title: Customer needs and building trust in a service business
learningOutcomes: Describe three customer needs in observable terms
Explain why trust is the main barrier for in-home and on-site services
Test a market claim against local evidence before using it

instructionSections.heading: Start with what the customer is buying
instructionSections.body: A customer does not buy hours of work. They buy a result, a reliable arrival, and the feeling that someone they can trust is working in their home or building. The sample plan names three needs: professional conduct, convenience and trustworthiness. Turn each need into something a customer can observe. Professional conduct shows up as a punctual greeting, a tidy appearance and clear communication. Convenience shows up as booking times that suit the customer, a simple access routine and an easy way to change a visit. Trust shows up as the screening, training and damage process covered in the trust sections that follow.

instructionSections.heading: Trust is the main barrier
instructionSections.body: Many customers worry about a stranger on their property, about theft and about breakage. The sample plan reports that screening and training ease these concerns, and it treats insurance as the answer to damage a client blames on the business. Those are sensible ideas, but each claim needs evidence. Before you say that workers are screened, confirm that a screening step exists and is recorded. Before you say a loss is covered, check the policy and its limits with your insurer. A trust claim you cannot evidence damages credibility faster than making no claim at all.

instructionSections.heading: Trust is slow to build
instructionSections.body: A new business has no reviews, no referrals and no track record. The sample plan admits that goodwill takes time and that brand recognition is hard to establish at the start. Plan for that gap. Expect fewer repeat customers in the first months, budget time for follow-up with each early client, and ask every satisfied client for a referral or a review. Early clients are your evidence, so treat each job as the first step in a relationship rather than a one-off sale.

instructionSections.heading: Testing the market story
instructionSections.body: For example, a cleaning sample plan describes a market that has moved from individual housekeepers towards companies, with customers changing providers often. It also claims that some households now avoid hiring house help because of security concerns. These statements come from a plan written for another country at an unstated date, so they are hypotheses and not Australian facts. Test them locally by speaking with enough prospects and recent clients to see a pattern, choosing that number before you start. The Victorian Government's 'Who is my customer?' guidance also advises checking assumptions about buyers with research rather than guesswork, including speaking with prospects and with staff at rival businesses. Ask what they used before, what made them change, and what they would need to hear from a new provider. Record the answers with dates.

instructionSections.heading: Mapping competitors by type
instructionSections.body: The sample groups competitors into two types: individual operators who work for one or a few clients, and independent companies whose quality varies. Map your own market the same way, then add the competitors your customers name. For each type, note the price band, the trust signals it shows and the gaps you could fill. Where service quality varies widely, a consistent and documented way of working can be a real point of difference, but only if you can show it.

instructionSections.heading: From needs to a marketing message
instructionSections.body: A marketing message should answer one need, in one sentence, with proof behind it. A statement such as 'every visit follows a documented screening and damage process' has evidence behind it. A statement such as 'the best providers in town' does not. Build your message from evidence you already hold. Review the channels you use, because the sample names social platforms that may have changed since it was written. Choose channels by asking where your local customers look for a service.

lessons.title: Positioning on training and professionalism
learningOutcomes: Define a market position in one sentence tied to a customer need
Convert a training program into a visible, evidenced promise
Write a damage response the team can use on site

instructionSections.heading: What positioning means
instructionSections.body: Positioning is the reason a particular customer picks your business over a similar service. It is not a slogan. Both sample documents position the business on trained staff and professional conduct. The business plan puts training first. The proposal extends the standard from the first greeting through to the way damage is handled. Positioning built on training works only when customers can see the training, and only when the team behaves the same way on every job.

instructionSections.heading: Make training visible
instructionSections.body: The sample plan describes three kinds of training: a method for doing the work, working effectively in a team, and a continuing learning system. Each can become a promise. 'Every new team member completes a documented induction before working unsupervised' is a promise you can keep and show. 'Our staff are highly trained professionals' is not. Keep the induction record, the method sheets and the refresher dates, and be ready to show them when a client asks what training their team has had.

instructionSections.heading: Professionalism happens at specific moments
instructionSections.body: The sample proposal treats professional conduct as something that runs through the whole visit: the greeting, the handling of access, the way the work is done, and what happens when something is damaged. Write down those moments for your own team. For each one, state the expected behaviour in a sentence or two. The damage moment matters most, because it is when customer doubt is highest. Write a short response process before the first job: stop, make safe, tell the client the same day, record the damaged item with photos, and follow the agreed resolution steps. Brief every team member on it and rehearse it.

instructionSections.heading: Appearance and the look of professionalism
instructionSections.body: The sample plans use uniforms and magnetic signs on vehicles to create an impression of professionalism. Any uniform or vehicle signage only works if it matches the team that arrives. A branded vehicle with an untidy crew sends a mixed message. Check that the signage shows the business name the client will recognise, that uniforms are clean and fitted, and that vehicles are roadworthy and parked with care. Rules on vehicle signage and advertising are set by each state or territory, so check the local rule in each one where you work.

instructionSections.heading: Environmental products as a supporting message
instructionSections.body: For example, a cleaning sample plan written for another country, at an undated time, says its chemicals are environmentally sound. That is not an Australian fact. The plan also notes that other companies use similar products, so the claim is not a major point of difference. Use it as a supporting message only, and only after checking it. Any environmental or green claim must match the product's documentation. The ACCC's guidance on false or misleading claims covers 'green' and 'non-toxic' claims and expects them to be based on reasonable grounds. Check the safety data sheet and the supplier's technical information, and write down which products the claim covers. Do not describe a product as green or safe in general terms if the documents only cover some of its uses.

instructionSections.heading: Protect the message
instructionSections.body: Every promise in marketing is a commitment the team must keep on every job. Review the promises each quarter against the records: training records, complaints, damage reports and client feedback. If a promise is not being kept, either change the promise or fix the practice before you advertise it again.

lessons.title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instructionSections.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instructionSections.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the job types you do well, the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A fortnightly service on a route you already run is worth far more to a small business than a single large job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. If you cannot state them, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one.

instructionSections.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instructionSections.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach a person who makes the buying decision, and whether the job falls within the licence and insurance you hold. Property managers, strata managers, real estate offices, body corporate committees, holiday rental managers, aged care and childcare facilities and small offices are examples of prospects that some service businesses serve, but add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Write one short profile for each segment on the list, as business.gov.au suggests when identifying a target market. Before you contact anyone, confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline, as Business Queensland advises before sending a quote. Keep only business contact details that are published for business use, and keep the list secure. Whether the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business depends on its turnover and other factors, so check the OAIC's small business guidance. Do not use bought or harvested contact lists. ACMA's guidance says that buying a list does not remove the need to show consent.

instructionSections.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instructionSections.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely in the near future. Examples include a public notice of planned building works, a new business opening on a street where you already work, a change of occupier at a site you already service, a new commercial fit-out, or a competitor that has closed in your area. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. Do not monitor private people, use personal information that is not public, enter private property, or turn up at a home to make an offer. If a signal concerns a private person rather than a business or a public body, leave it alone. Public registers are useful signals about businesses and public bodies. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts, and each agency publishes an annual plan of what it intends to buy. Some councils publish a planning permit register with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register in Victoria's open data portal, so check the register for your own council.

instructionSections.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instructionSections.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the business or the notice. It makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or from the business's own published material, such as a notice about works or a business listing with an obvious gap in its service range. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. Where the message goes by email, text or another electronic channel, check the consent and unsubscribe rules in the safety section before anything is sent. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves, so a specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage as well as a compliance step.

instructionSections.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instructionSections.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. Stopping is part of the approach. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

lessons.title: Networking: warm contacts, trade partners and local businesses
learningOutcomes: List the warm contacts and local businesses that could send or receive work, and write one specific request for each group.
Draft a written referral arrangement with a complementary trade that covers referrals, complaints and any reward.
Introduce your business in under a minute at a local event or group, within that group's rules, and state the referral you want.

instructionSections.heading: Start with the people who already buy from you
instructionSections.body: Every business owner you pay for a service is a possible route to new work. Your accountant, mechanic, vet, physiotherapist, bookkeeper, dentist, real estate agent and the owners of the local shops you use all meet people who need what you offer. Write a list of these contacts, then tell each one what you do, what kind of client you want next, and what a suitable introduction would look like. Ask one direct question rather than handing over a long pitch: do you know anyone who needs this at the moment? Follow up once a quarter with a short update, because people remember the ones who keep them informed.

instructionSections.heading: Form written partnerships with complementary trades
instructionSections.body: Complementary trades serve the same customers without competing for the same job. Examples include a gardener and a pool technician, a cleaner and a carpet cleaner, a handyman and a locksmith, a dog walker and a pet sitter, or a personal trainer and a massage therapist. Before either party refers anyone, agree in writing what each does with a referral, how the handover works, who speaks to the customer first, how a complaint is handled if the partner's work goes wrong, and whether any reward is paid. Also agree what happens when a lead falls outside one partner's scope or licence. Put the agreement in a short document that both sides sign, and keep any reward at a level both sides can explain to a customer.

instructionSections.heading: Example: approaching a property or building business with a specific offer
instructionSections.body: A property or building business is one example of a business that can have recurring needs suited to home-service work. Property managers, real estate offices, strata managers and builders' site offices are typical examples. Examples of such needs include turnaround cleans between tenancies, gardening for common areas, minor repairs in vacant units, and clean-ups before inspections. The same approach applies to any business with a recurring need you can meet: arrive with one written offer for that need, a clear description of how you price it, and two or three questions about what the current supplier misses. Book the meeting in advance, follow the reception and site rules, and do not attend a site where you have not been invited. Leave a short document with your insurance details, licence details and contact details, and note the agreed next step before you leave.

instructionSections.heading: Use business groups and events with a prepared introduction
instructionSections.body: Local business groups, trade associations, council-run business sessions and networking events can introduce you to other owners. Some councils keep a directory of local business networks, from informal dinner groups to formal referral organisations that trade referrals between members. Wyndham City Council in Victoria is one example, so check the directory for your own council. Before you attend, read the group's rules on visitors and on pitching. Prepare an introduction of about thirty seconds that says who you help, what problem you solve and what kind of introduction you would welcome. Listen more than you speak, ask two or three questions about the other person's business, and offer one practical tip that costs them nothing. If a group forbids pitching, follow that rule even if you think your service would help the room. Record who you met and what each person offered, and follow up within two working days.

instructionSections.heading: Be present at community events where the rules allow it
instructionSections.body: School fairs, sports club days, community markets and neighbourhood events let people in your area see your name and your work. Before you book a stall or a sponsorship, check the organiser's rules on trading and promotion, and any fees or insurance the organiser requires. Keep your table focused on the service and one practical tip, such as a seasonal checklist, with a simple quote-request sheet beside it. Collect contact details only with the person's agreement, and tell them what you will do with those details. Count the enquiries that became paid work so you can decide whether returning next season is worth the cost.

lessons.title: Online presence: community groups, profiles and consent-based content
learningOutcomes: Read a community group's rules and write a helpful answer or post that complies with them.
Prepare a before-and-after or completed-work post from a finished job, with written consent and identifying details removed.
Set up an opt-in email list and state the sender identity and unsubscribe approach before the first send.

instructionSections.heading: Join the groups where your customers already ask questions
instructionSections.body: Local neighbourhood groups, parents' groups, strata and body corporate owner groups, and pet owner or garden communities are where future customers ask for help. Join the groups that match your service area, not only groups for other tradespeople. Before you post anything, read the group rules, including whether business posts, offers and direct messages are allowed. Answer questions with specific, practical help, such as how to tell whether a piece of equipment needs servicing or when a routine task is due, and mention your business only where the rules and the question allow it. Do not message members first to offer your service unless the group rules and the member have clearly allowed it. ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, so check whether a direct message counts as a commercial message before you send one.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the profile customers find accurate
instructionSections.body: When someone searches for your service in your area, your online business listing is often the first thing they see. Keep the business name, service area, service list, hours and contact method accurate and current. Add photos of completed work only when the customer has agreed to that use, and never use photos from other businesses without their permission. Reply to every enquiry within a time you state on the listing, and say so if you cannot respond out of hours. An accurate, responsive listing also makes it easier to ask for reviews later, because customers who want to thank you will find it.

instructionSections.heading: Share completed work with consent and no identifying details
instructionSections.body: Before-and-after photos, or photos of any finished job, show results clearly, but they can expose a customer's home or site, routine and identity. Ask for written consent before you post, and say where the photo will appear. Before posting, crop or blur the street number, street sign, number plates, faces, children, pets and personal items, and remove location data from the file. Do not name the customer or describe the property or site in a way that identifies them. Cropping is part of the preparation, not a replacement for consent. If the customer withdraws consent, remove the post and any copies you control, and record the date.

instructionSections.heading: Post useful seasonal tips on a schedule you can keep
instructionSections.body: A small number of practical tips, posted regularly, builds more trust than frequent promotion. Choose one platform first, and plan a simple calendar tied to local conditions, such as an opening or closing checklist, a maintenance check before the wet season, care advice during hot weather, or a spring clean-up. Write each post as a short, practical instruction a customer could use that day, and end with one optional next step. Keep the posts that get answers, and drop the formats that do not. Post no more often than you can answer the replies.

instructionSections.heading: Build an opt-in email list for people who asked to hear from you
instructionSections.body: An email list lets you contact people who chose to hear from you again. Offer a useful resource, such as a seasonal checklist, in exchange for an email address, and make the sign-up a clear, separate choice that is not pre-ticked. The sign-up should say what you will send and how often. Every commercial message must identify you as the sender and include a working way to unsubscribe, and you should act on each unsubscribe within five working days at the latest, and sooner where you can. The rules come from the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's avoid-spam guidance (read 2026-11-03) summarises them: the sender must be identified accurately, and the unsubscribe option must be free, work for at least 30 days and be honoured within five working days. “Finding your first customers through direct, consent-based outreach” covers consent and spam rules in more detail.

lessons.title: Referrals and repeat work from existing clients
learningOutcomes: Plan a review or referral request that is made after the client confirms the result and that the client can decline easily.
Write a next-service offer with a date, a scope and a price approach, and schedule the check-in that follows it.
Write referral reward terms, including the condition for payment, before any referral is made.

instructionSections.heading: Ask at the moment the client is most satisfied
instructionSections.body: The best time to ask for a review or referral is after the client has confirmed that the result is right, usually at sign-off or when the invoice is paid. Ask in one sentence, name the next step you would like, such as a review or the name of one person who might need the service, and make it easy to decline. Record what you asked and what the client said. Timing matters: in one Baylor Keller Center experiment, a late reminder brought in more reviews than an immediate one. Sending a review link or QR code is allowed, and Google provides one for this purpose. Do not write reviews for clients or invent them. Do not screen out unhappy clients in a way that hides complaints. Asking only happy clients is called review gating, and Podium, a review software vendor, says Google treats it as a violation. The ACCC's guidance on online reviews says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on what the review says. Google also bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews, including for changing or removing negative reviews, so check each platform's terms before offering any incentive.

instructionSections.heading: Offer the next service before the client leaves
instructionSections.body: Repeat work is one of the most dependable sources of growth for a small service business. At the end of each job, propose the next step with a date: a fortnightly pool service, a quarterly carpet clean, an annual gutter and roof check, a spring garden plan, or a handyman visit to finish a list of items. Put the proposed scope, the interval and the price approach in writing, and confirm that the client agrees before you change their schedule. A written next step turns a passing comment into a booked job. If the written offer goes by email or text, check the electronic message rules first: ACMA's guidance indicates that inferred consent is narrow and does not cover a message sent just after a purchase.

instructionSections.heading: Check in at the interval that suits the service
instructionSections.body: Schedule a check-in after a period that suits the work. For a clean or a repair, a suggested starting point is about ninety days, which is a choice to test, not a benchmark. For a pool or a garden it may be after the next seasonal visit. The check asks whether the result still holds, whether anything has changed and whether there is other work to quote. Keep it short and useful, record what the client said, and close the loop with a reply. If the check is sent by email or text, check it against the electronic message rules in “Online presence: community groups, profiles and consent-based content”. A check-in that only asks about the result may not be commercial, but a message that promotes any service can be, even when it is framed as a reminder. ACMA's summary (read 2026-11-04) does not say whether one-to-one messages are covered, so check that point before you send.

instructionSections.heading: Re-contact previous clients before their busy periods
instructionSections.body: Many home-service needs follow the calendar: spring clean-ups, pool opening before the warm months, gutter checks before the wet season, garden work before holidays, and carpet cleaning before a lease handover. Plan a short message to previous clients a few weeks before each period. Offer the slots you can actually deliver, on written terms, with a clear way to opt out. Do not use the message to pressure anyone, and do not contact a client who has asked not to hear from you. ACMA's guidance says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days, so record each opt-out as soon as you receive it and stop sending to that client. At the end of the period, review the response and note which timing worked.

instructionSections.heading: Set referral rewards in writing before anyone refers
instructionSections.body: A referral reward works best when the client knows the terms before they refer someone. Decide what you will offer, such as a credit on the next service or a small thank-you, and write down the condition for payment, which is normally that the referred person has completed a paid job. Tell the referrer the terms, keep a record of each referral and whether the reward was paid, and never promise a reward you cannot deliver. Keep the arrangement simple and fair. Research on referral programmes found that stating the referrer's reward in the invitation increased referrals in a set of studies, so say what the reward is in the invitation. Get the referred person's consent before any referral message is sent, because the referrer's word alone may not be enough. Check any cash-based reward, and its tax or contract effect, with an adviser before you start. No business.gov.au or ACCC guidance on referral rewards was found, so those points remain unconfirmed.

lessons.title: Service improvement and growth
learningOutcomes: Identify the service improvements that increase repeat work without reducing safety or quality.
Describe how to offer additional services that the team can deliver safely and profitably.
Measure the effect of a change before deciding whether to keep it.

instructionSections.heading: Grow by doing the current job better
instructionSections.body: The most reliable growth in a service business comes from repeat customers who are satisfied with the scope, the timing, the communication and the result. Use the job records and the customer feedback to find the points where the service fails or delights. A missed item that causes a complaint, a late arrival that is not communicated, or a product that leaves a residue are all improvements. Choose one improvement at a time, make it, and check whether it reduced the complaint or increased repeat work.

instructionSections.heading: Add services the team can deliver safely
instructionSections.body: Additional services can increase revenue, but only when they match the team's skills, equipment and licences. Before offering a new service, check the scope, the hazards, the licence requirement and the price, using the service offer and pricing lessons. A recommended add-on, such as an oven clean for a regular kitchen client, should be defined with its scope, time and price, and offered only where it can be done safely. List it on the written quote as a separate option, so the customer can choose it. Do not offer a restricted or licensed service that the business does not hold the licence for. Licence and training rules differ by state or territory and by type of work, so check the rule where you operate.

instructionSections.heading: Measure before you keep a change
instructionSections.body: Decide in advance what result a change should produce, such as fewer complaints, more repeat bookings, or less time per job. Record the measure before and after the change, and review it after a fixed period. A change that does not produce the result is reviewed or reversed. Do not claim growth from a single job or from a feeling. Keep the record so that the decision can be explained to the team and the customer.

lessons.title: Defining target segments from customer data
learningOutcomes: Sort existing customer records into candidate segments using at least three fields
Test each candidate segment for need, ability to pay and reachability
Calculate a compound growth rate from a start value, an end value and a number of years

instructionSections.heading: What a segment is and why it comes first
instructionSections.body: A segment is a group of customers who share a recurring need, can pay for the service at the price you charge, and can be reached through a channel you are allowed to use. Choose segments before you choose channels. The channel depends on where the group already looks for help, so a business that picks a brochure or an advert first and works out its audience afterwards usually pays to reach people who will never book. Your segments should be written down, tested and dated, not held as an impression of who your customers are.

instructionSections.heading: Start with the customers you already have
instructionSections.body: Your own records are the cheapest source of segment data. Export invoices or bookings for the last twelve months into a spreadsheet with one row per customer. Add columns only for things you already hold or can ask about with consent: property type, household or business type, how often they book, how long they have stayed, what they bought first, and how they found you. Do not add a field the service does not need. Limit personal detail to what the job requires. Each extra personal field may add privacy obligations, so check them before collecting it.

instructionSections.heading: Look for patterns that predict value
instructionSections.body: Sort the rows by booking frequency and then by total value. Look for traits that the most valuable and most loyal customers share, and count how many of each trait appear in that top group compared with the rest. The point is to show the pattern in numbers rather than in memory. A pattern found in a handful of customers is a hypothesis to test in the next step, not a segment yet.

instructionSections.heading: Test each candidate segment
instructionSections.body: Give every candidate three tests. Need: does the group have a recurring problem that your service solves? Ability to pay: does the group pay the price you plan to charge, and do its members buy this type of service now? Reachability: can you contact the group through a channel you can lawfully use? Before you commit, also compare the candidate with the number of rival providers, how often the need recurs, and where buyers prefer to purchase. A candidate that fails one test is either redefined so it passes, or set aside. Write down the reason for each rejection so the decision can be reviewed later and not repeated by accident.

instructionSections.heading: Size the segment and state the date
instructionSections.body: A segment is only useful if you know roughly how many people or businesses fit it. Count from a source you can name and date, such as a local council figure, an official statistical release or your own records, and write the year beside the number. Then apply a growth assumption and show the arithmetic. Compound growth over a number of years is calculated as the end value divided by the start value, raised to the power of one over the number of years, minus one. The sample plan this lesson draws on gave a potential-customer count and a growth rate for an earlier United States market. Those figures are removed here: they are not Australian and are not current. Use the method only: a start count, an end count, the number of years and a growth rate calculated from a source you can name and date.

instructionSections.heading: Write one profile per segment
instructionSections.body: Finish with a short profile for each kept segment. Keep it brief, as government small-business guidance on target markets suggests, and make each profile specific to one group: who the customers are, the recurring problem they have, what they value most, and the one reason they would choose your business. The sample plan described its target groups by household income and house value. Those thresholds were set in United States dollars in 2002, so they cannot be carried into an Australian plan. Replace them with measures from your own records, in Australian dollars and dated, or leave them out if you cannot source them.

lessons.title: Choosing marketing channels and measuring them
learningOutcomes: Compare at least three marketing channels using cost, reach to the chosen segment and expected response
Calculate cost per new customer for each channel from a supplied log
Set up a way to tag each new customer with the channel that brought them

instructionSections.heading: Match channels to the segment
instructionSections.body: A channel is a route to a segment: a printed brochure, a partner group, a referral, a directory listing, a local newspaper section or a website. Start from the segment profile written in “Defining target segments from customer data” and ask where that group already pays attention. A channel that reaches many people outside the segment costs money without adding customers. The sample plan this lesson draws on used three routes: a colour brochure placed through clubs whose members fit its target profile, a referral incentive, and an advertising campaign in the weekly home section of two local newspapers. Those choices suited a United States residential cleaner in the early 2000s. Local business networks and referral groups are another route to test. Some councils publish directories of them, so search your own council's listings. A Victorian council directory is one example. Before you copy any route, test whether it reaches your segment in your own area today.

instructionSections.heading: Compare channels on the same basis
instructionSections.body: Put every channel in one table with the same columns: the cost to run it for a set period, the number of people in the segment it reaches, the expected response rate, the expected number of new customers, and the time until the first job. Expected figures are estimates, so write down how each one was made, so you can check it later. Then shortlist the one or two channels with the lowest expected cost per new customer that still reach the segment, and test them with a fixed budget before committing the full amount.

instructionSections.heading: Measure cost per new customer
instructionSections.body: The main test of a channel is its cost per new customer. Divide the total cost of the channel in a period by the number of new customers who arrived through it in that period. Compare that figure with what a new customer is worth to you, using the average first-year value of a customer from your own records. A channel that costs more per customer than a customer is worth loses money, even when it produces many enquiries.

instructionSections.heading: Tag every enquiry
instructionSections.body: A channel can only be measured if each enquiry is tagged. Ask every new customer at booking how they heard about you, and record the answer against a fixed list such as brochure, club, referral, newspaper, website or other. Keep the other category small and review it each month. Unexplained budget lines hide the same problem. The sample plan put most of its budget into a single line labelled only other, so that line could not be judged until it was broken into named activities. The plan's amounts are removed here because they are United States figures.

instructionSections.heading: Set a target and review on a fixed date
instructionSections.body: Set a target for each measure, such as a maximum cost per new customer, and review the channel table on a fixed day each month. The sample plan set a marketing objective for reducing its customer acquisition cost each year. That was an early 2000s United States target, and its size is removed here. Use the wording only: a direction, a size and a period. Each review should end with a decision for each channel: keep, change or stop, recorded with its reason.

lessons.title: Referral incentives that respect consumer and spam rules
learningOutcomes: Write a referral reward with clear conditions, a cap and a payment trigger
Identify the consumer and messaging checks that apply before a referral message is sent
Calculate the cost of a referral reward per referred paying customer

instructionSections.heading: Why referrals work and where they fail
instructionSections.body: A referral incentive asks an existing customer to bring in someone they know, in return for a reward. The sample plan this lesson draws on argued that a financial reward would motivate that behaviour, and that people like to pass on a good deal to friends. That is a reasonable starting point. Referral schemes fail when the terms are vague, when the reward is paid before any real work is done, or when the business sends messages to people who never agreed to hear from it.

instructionSections.heading: Design the reward on paper first
instructionSections.body: Write three things before the scheme is announced: the reward, the trigger and the cap. The reward is what the referrer and the new customer receive. The trigger is the event that releases the reward, and for most home services it should be a completed first paid job. The cap is the maximum reward per referrer in a set period. The sample plan proposed a free visit as the reward. That is a United States example from the early 2000s. Before offering any reward in your own business, compare its value with your cost to deliver it.

instructionSections.heading: Cost the reward per paying customer
instructionSections.body: Divide the total reward cost in a period by the number of referred customers who completed a first paid job. The result is the cost per referred paying customer, and you can compare it with the cost per new customer from other channels in “Choosing marketing channels and measuring them”. When the reward is paid only after a paid job, and that job is profitable, the reward is a known cost rather than an open promise. The sample plan budgeted its referral incentives as a named line that rose over the period. Its amounts are removed here because they are United States figures. The principle is that a referral line should be budgeted and not left open.

instructionSections.heading: Consumer and messaging checks
instructionSections.body: Before a referral scheme goes live, check three things. First, an electronic message that promotes a service can be a commercial electronic message under the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). Whether a message a customer forwards on the business's behalf is covered needs a legal reading before you rely on it. Second, reward terms and promotional claims should not mislead customers. Misleading-conduct rules in the Australian Consumer Law may apply, but the ACCC guide cited here does not cover reward terms, so check the current ACL text. Third, some reward or prize schemes may fall under state or territory promotion rules, which differ between states and territories. Check them against current official sources before any scheme goes live, and record the check and its date.

instructionSections.heading: Do not buy or harvest contacts
instructionSections.body: Referral messages should only go to people who have agreed to be contacted, or to people a customer has introduced to you with that introduced person's consent. Whether that consent is enough under the Spam Act and privacy rules needs a legal check. Never import a list of contacts to send a reward offer. Buying a list does not free the sender from proving that each person agreed, so do not buy or scrape contact lists. Never create a referral that did not happen in order to claim a reward. A scheme built on harvested contacts is a compliance problem and also damages the trust that referrals depend on.

lessons.title: Growth options and market share for a service business
learningOutcomes: Place a growth option for a service business in one of the four Ansoff quadrants, by asking whether the service and the customer group are existing or new.
Calculate market share from a supplied sales figure and a supplied total market figure, and state whether the total is confirmed.
Choose one growth option, state its main risk, and name the measure that will show whether it works.

instructionSections.heading: The Ansoff matrix asks two questions
instructionSections.body: The Ansoff matrix is a planning grid for growth. It asks two questions: is the service you sell new or existing, and is the customer group you sell to new or existing? The answers place each growth option in one of four quadrants. The options carry different levels of risk, because a business knows more about some services and customers than others. Use the matrix to compare options before you spend money on one of them. It shows where the risk sits, but it does not decide the choice for you.

instructionSections.heading: Market penetration: existing service, existing customers
instructionSections.body: Market penetration means selling more of the service you already offer to the customer group you already serve. It is usually the lowest-risk option, because the business already knows the service and the customers. Ways to do it include more repeat bookings, a reminder system, a loyalty offer, or a stronger local presence. The limit is that a local market may already be well served, so growth can come only from taking clients from rivals or from clients using the service more often. Measure it with the number of repeat clients and the share of the market you hold, which is explained below.

instructionSections.heading: Market development and product development
instructionSections.body: Market development means selling an existing service to a new group of customers, such as households in a different suburb, a different type of property, or commercial clients instead of households. The business keeps the same service but must learn the new customers' needs, prices and buying habits. Product development means offering a new service to the customers you already serve, such as adding a related task to the same visit. This option uses the trust you have already built, but it needs new skills, equipment and pricing. Both options carry more risk than penetration, and each needs a test before the business commits to it. Before you test a new group, check your assumptions about it with research rather than guesswork. The Victorian Government's 'Who is my customer?' guidance suggests comparing how many competitors exist, how often buyers need the service and where they prefer to buy.

instructionSections.heading: Diversification: new service, new customers
instructionSections.body: Diversification has the highest risk, because both the service and the customer group are new. It can spread income across more than one kind of work, but the business is then learning two things at once. Consider it only when a simpler option has been tested and has reached its limit, or when a clear need exists and the business already has the skills to meet it. Treat a diversification as a separate project with its own costing, insurance check and review date, rather than as an add-on to the current work.

instructionSections.heading: Market share: the proportion you hold
instructionSections.body: Market share is the proportion of a market that one business controls. It is usually measured by sales revenue: your sales divided by the total sales of the market, written as a percentage. The calculation is simple, but the total market figure is often the hard part. A total may come from a survey, an industry report or an estimate, and each source has limits. Write the source and date of the total next to the share, and leave out the figure if you have not checked it. Read the share with the size of the market beside it. A share can rise even while your sales fall, if the whole market falls faster than you do.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing and measuring one option
instructionSections.body: Pick one growth option for the next period, not all four at once. Name its main risk, and the measure that will show whether it works, such as repeat bookings per month, or your share of the market in a named area. Set a review date, and decide in advance what result would mean stop and what would mean continue. Recording the decision in the business plan keeps the choice visible when the market changes.

lessons.title: Preparing a marketing plan: mission, present position and goals before channels
learningOutcomes: Write a short mission statement that says why the business exists, and test it against one real decision the business faces.
Describe the present position of a service business using facts, and separate each fact from an opinion.
State the basic assumptions the marketing plan depends on, and set a measurable goal before choosing any channel.

instructionSections.heading: Why preparation comes before the plan
instructionSections.body: A good marketing plan depends more on the work done before writing than on the writing itself. A plan written without that work tends to list activities that do not connect to the business's purpose or its limits, so it is hard to act on and hard to measure. The preparation has four parts: a mission, an honest view of the present position, a set of basic assumptions, and goals. Only when these are clear should you choose channels, budgets and activities. Those are covered in the marketing plan template lesson, which is the next step after this one.

instructionSections.heading: A mission that can settle a decision
instructionSections.body: A mission statement says, briefly, why the business exists and whom it serves. Keep it short enough to say aloud. A useful test is whether the mission would help you choose between two real options. For example, a business whose mission is to keep local homes safe and clean would decline a job it cannot do safely, even if the job pays well. A mission that cannot separate two options is too vague to guide a plan. Write it in plain words, and avoid slogans that could describe any business at all.

instructionSections.heading: Present position: facts before opinions
instructionSections.body: Before you plan, describe where the business stands, using questions that have answers you can check. What is the financial position? What do competitors charge and offer? How do existing clients describe the business? Which markets will you target, and which can you reach? Mark each answer as a fact, from your records or a checked source, or as an opinion, such as a belief about the market. When a fact and an opinion conflict, the fact wins. Where the answer is not known, write it down as a gap, and give a date by which it will be filled.

instructionSections.heading: Basic assumptions that limit the plan
instructionSections.body: Make the assumptions behind the plan explicit.
