Decide whether the business is an innovator, which creates a new service to meet a new need, or an imitator, which improves a service that already works for others. Set the geographic limits you can serve well, and count the cost of travel and time within those limits, because a distant job can cost more than it earns. Write down any other assumption the plan depends on, such as the number of jobs per week, the price per job, or the availability of staff. Give each assumption a date and an owner, so it can be checked later. Check the assumptions about buyers against research before you rely on them. The Victorian Government's 'Who is my customer?' guidance suggests comparing how many competitors exist, how often buyers need the service and where they prefer to buy.

instructionSections.heading: Goals and measures before channels
instructionSections.body: A goal states a result to reach by a date, such as a number of new bookings from referrals within six months. A goal is useful only if you can measure it, which means a baseline, a target, a date and a data source. Set few goals, with one or two measures for each. Only then choose the channels and activities that support each goal. A channel chosen before its goal is hard to judge, because nothing says what success looks like. When the plan is running, review the goals on a fixed date, keep what works, and change what does not.

lessons.title: Finding your first customers through direct, consent-based outreach
learningOutcomes: Write an initial message that offers help without an immediate sale
Book a discovery call and ask about the customer's problem
Follow up consistently without spamming

instructionSections.heading: Outreach is a numbers game with a human face
instructionSections.body: Most first customers come from many conversations. Plan a daily routine of outreach, follow-up and engagement. Expect to send far more messages than you receive replies.

instructionSections.heading: Open with value, not a pitch
instructionSections.body: A short message that names something specific about the person and offers a no-cost check or tip is a more relevant opening than a sales pitch. The ACCC's 2026 media release on unsolicited selling reports that many approaches were pressured or misleading, so a relevant message that clearly names who is writing stands apart. Ask what is hardest for them right now.

instructionSections.heading: Discovery call first
instructionSections.body: On the call, ask about the problem, what they have tried, what it cost and what they would change. Listen more than you talk. Offer a proposal only when they ask, or when you have confirmed the problem and your fit.

instructionSections.heading: Consent and spam rules
instructionSections.body: Unsolicited commercial electronic messages in Australia are regulated by the federal Spam Act 2003 (Cth). The basis for sending is consent, which can be express or, in narrow cases, inferred. An existing relationship is not, on its own, permission to send marketing: inferred consent needs an ongoing relationship with marketing tied to it, and it does not cover a message sent just after a purchase. Each message must identify the sender and include a free unsubscribe that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. A business email address published online does not by itself allow marketing messages. Check current ACMA guidance and the Act's text before any bulk messaging. Do not buy or scrape contact lists.

instructionSections.heading: Follow-up and referrals
instructionSections.body: Follow up on a planned schedule over a few weeks, spaced out, and stop once the messages agreed in advance have been sent. Ask every customer for a referral and a review, with their consent.

lessons.title: Scaling up and running a time-limited campaign
learningOutcomes: Increase outreach volume in a planned way
Run a two-week limited-places campaign with clear terms
Check capacity before promising more work

instructionSections.heading: Scale on purpose
instructionSections.body: Once a few customers pay, increase outreach and take on more work. Most of the early gain comes from effort, so plan the hours you can give it without damaging quality.

instructionSections.heading: Capacity first
instructionSections.body: Before you promise more jobs, check how many you can deliver well each week, including travel, admin and rest. Business Queensland advises checking your own capacity and deadlines before quoting, and quoting only work you can deliver to the customer's satisfaction. Overbooking can hurt reviews and referrals.

instructionSections.heading: A limited-places campaign
instructionSections.body: Run a promotion for a fixed period, with a stated number of places. Be honest: if the places are genuinely limited by your capacity, say so, and open the next round when you have capacity. The ACCC's advertising guide (July 2021; check the current version) expects limited-time offers and short supply to be stated clearly and to be genuinely available. Do not invent scarcity.

instructionSections.heading: Measure and stop
instructionSections.body: Track enquiries, bookings, price accepted and quality. Stop or change the campaign when the quality or the margin falls.

lessons.title: Building your reputation as the expert in your service
learningOutcomes: Set a regular habit of sharing useful, practical content
Turn your experience into content that customers find useful
Direct interested people to a way to contact you or join a list

instructionSections.heading: People buy from people
instructionSections.body: Customers hire people they trust. Show your experience and your results. A licensed professional or a specialist operator can build trust by sharing what they actually do.

instructionSections.heading: Give value most of the time
instructionSections.body: Most of your content should teach or help, with no ask. Make an offer only occasionally. Useful content includes how-to tips, before-and-after photos with the reasons behind the work, and common mistakes to avoid.

instructionSections.heading: Choose where your customers look
instructionSections.body: Use the platforms your customers use: Google Business Profile, Facebook or Instagram for households, LinkedIn for property managers, or local community groups. Post consistently on one or two platforms rather than many.

instructionSections.heading: Reviews and proof
instructionSections.body: Ask every customer for a review, not only the satisfied ones. Filtering by mood before inviting reviews can breach platform rules. Do not offer discounts or other rewards in exchange for Google reviews. A link or QR code to the review page makes asking simple. Get the customer's consent before publishing a review, photo or name, and keep a record of it. Privacy law may apply to customer details; whether the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies depends on the business's turnover and activities, so check the OAIC small business guidance. Respond to every review, including negative ones, calmly and factually.

instructionSections.heading: Capture interest
instructionSections.body: Give people a next step: a booking link, a short guide or a newsletter. Ask only for the information you need. A newsletter that promotes your business sent by email or text needs the subscriber's consent and a working unsubscribe option under the Spam Act.

lessons.title: Marketing plan (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Choose three marketing channels and state the reason, cost basis and owner for each
Plan at least three months of activities with a channel, an owner and a done date for each
Define three measures with a formula, a data source and a baseline before the plan starts

instructionSections.heading: What a marketing plan is for
instructionSections.body: A marketing plan decides where the next customers will come from, how much will be spent to reach them, and how the business will know whether it worked. It is not a list of everything that could be posted. Most home-service businesses grow from a small number of sources: repeat work, referrals, a listing that people search for, and direct contact with people who have agreed to hear from them. The plan should choose three channels and explain why. Choosing more spreads the budget too thin to judge any one of them.

instructionSections.heading: Defining customers and choosing channels
instructionSections.body: Start from the target customer table in the business plan. For each segment, write what the customer needs, where they look for a provider and why they would pick this business over another. Then choose three channels that reach those people. For each channel, state the reason, the cost basis (a fee, staff time or materials) and the person responsible. Direct contact should only go to people who have agreed to receive it. An existing relationship does not, on its own, allow marketing messages; inferred consent can apply only in narrow cases, such as an ongoing relationship with marketing tied to it. A business email address published online does not by itself allow marketing. Record the basis for each contact. Electronic messaging and privacy rules apply to outreach.

instructionSections.heading: Budget, monthly activities and measures
instructionSections.body: Set a monthly budget and split it across the three channels, keeping a small part for follow-up. Plan activities by month, with one channel, one owner and one done date for each. Define three measures before you start. Repeat customers are counted as a share of jobs in a period. Acquisition cost for a channel is the money spent on it divided by the number of new customers it brought, measured over the same period. Referrals are counted as the number of new customers who name a source. Record a baseline before the plan begins so that any later change is visible rather than remembered.

lessons.title: A clean look is not the same as a controlled risk
learningOutcomes: Explain in your own words why a surface that looks clean can still carry microorganisms.
Describe the two separate jobs a cleaning routine does: removing soil, and reducing the chance that organisms spread.
Identify the Australian national guideline that applies to infection control in care settings, and say when to ask the infection-prevention lead for direction.

instructionSections.heading: A clean look is not the same as a controlled risk
instructionSections.body: People often treat a tidy, visibly clean room as a safe one. In care settings that link is only partly true. Removing visible soil improves how the room looks, supports the confidence of residents, families and inspectors, and supports the wider infection-control effort. A room can still look spotless while microorganisms remain on touch points that nobody has checked. Your work therefore has two aims: remove soil, and reduce the chance that organisms move from a surface to a person.

instructionSections.heading: Why soil comes off before any disinfectant
instructionSections.body: Organic soil such as blood, food residue, grease and body fluids can shield microorganisms, and it can reduce how well a disinfectant works. The approved sequence is therefore to remove visible soil with the approved detergent first, then apply a disinfectant only where the approved procedure requires one, and leave it for the contact time on the product label. This is the same soil-first principle taught in the chemicals lesson on removing soil before disinfecting (“Remove soil before disinfecting”).

instructionSections.heading: The Australian reference point
instructionSections.body: For infection control in Australian healthcare and residential care, the reference point is the national infection-prevention guideline for healthcare issued by the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), which is listed in the source references below. The UK cleaning procedure that supplied some background for this lesson uses its own national standards, inspection programmes, colour code and cleaning frequencies. Those are UK-only. They are not Australian requirements, and this lesson does not use their figures. Where a UK document and the Australian guideline differ, follow the Australian guideline and your provider's approved procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Changing the routine when a precaution applies
instructionSections.body: Some rooms carry a notice about a transmission-based precaution. When that notice applies, the order of work, the product or the cloth colour set may change. Read the notice, check the approved procedure, and confirm any change with your team leader or the infection-prevention lead before you start. Do not decide alone to skip a touch point or to swap a product, even if the swap looks equivalent to you.

instructionSections.heading: Use the high-touch list, not your eyes alone
instructionSections.body: Each room type has a written list of high-touch points, such as door handles, light switches, bed rails, call bells, taps, bedside tables, handrails, chair arms and shared keyboards. Work through the list and tick each item. Your eyes tell you what looks dirty. The list tells you what must be handled, whether or not it looks dirty. Where the list and the room disagree, follow the list and report the difference.

lessons.title: Planning a deep clean alongside routine work
learningOutcomes: Describe how a deep clean differs from routine cleaning, and why routine cleaning continues while it is planned and carried out.
List the conditions that justify a deep clean: built-up soil, hard-to-reach areas, and surfaces that the routine cannot restore.
Plan a deep clean with a written method, agreed access and a signed record of the result.

instructionSections.heading: What a deep clean is
instructionSections.body: A deep clean is an enhanced programme of work on the same surfaces, not a separate kind of cleaning. It usually brings extra equipment, a stronger approved method or a specialist skill, and it targets soil that has gathered gradually or areas that the routine cannot reach each cycle. It does not replace routine cleaning. The usual schedule continues, and the enhanced work is fitted around it.

instructionSections.heading: When a deep clean is justified
instructionSections.body: Look for grime that collects on edges, fixtures and skirting and does not lift with routine wiping; for marks that remain after the approved routine method has been used correctly; for areas with restricted access behind or beneath fixed items; and for high-use zones where daily work has fallen behind. Also check whether the finish itself is the cause. A worn or damaged surface can keep collecting soil, and the remedy may be repair or replacement, not more scrubbing. A space that is easier to reach and clean needs less deep work over time.

instructionSections.heading: Planning around people who are using the space
instructionSections.body: Enhanced work is often noisy, wet or uses stronger products, so it can disrupt the people using the site. Sequence the work so occupants are affected as little as possible. Agree access times with the site lead, use barriers and signs, and keep the routine service running in the areas not being worked. Where the site has clinical, care or customer roles, consult those people before the start, not after.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the result
instructionSections.body: Keep a record that shows the scope, the reason, the method, the products used, the equipment, the areas completed, any item that was replaced or sent for repair, and a sign-off by both the cleaning lead and the site lead. The record is the audit trail. It lets a later inspection show what was done, when, and by whom, and it shows what was not done and why.

lessons.title: Letting a contractor onto a live site: plan, sign-in and sign-off
learningOutcomes: Explain what a method statement and a risk assessment must show before a contractor starts.
Apply a sign-in and site-briefing step for a contractor working on a shared site.
Describe how supervision and the signed completion record keep specialist work accountable.

instructionSections.heading: Why a contractor needs a written plan first
instructionSections.body: Specialist work carries risks that routine cleaning does not, and the people using the site are entitled to know how the work will be done. Before a contractor starts, the site needs a written method statement that sets out the steps, the equipment and the products, and a risk assessment that names each hazard and the control for it. The site manager checks both documents before entry is allowed. A verbal explanation does not replace either document.

instructionSections.heading: Sign-in and a site briefing
instructionSections.body: Contractors report to the agreed point, usually the facilities or estates contact, before they enter. The site records each person's name, company, arrival time and the staff member who signed them in. The contractor is then briefed on the occupied areas, the access times, the barriers, the emergency and incident route, and the rules for noise, closure and escort. The same reasons that apply to inducting the site's own staff apply to outside workers.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping disruption and risk low while work is underway
instructionSections.body: The contractor's plan should show the sequence, the barriers and signs, and the times when noise or strong products are allowed. The routine cleaning or housekeeping team should watch the work at the agreed checkpoints. They must not assume the plan is being followed. If the contractor wants to change the method, the change goes to the site lead for review before the work continues, and the decision is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: The completion record as an audit trail
instructionSections.body: When the work is complete, the outside worker and the area manager (for example the ward, department or housekeeping manager) each sign the completion record. The record shows the work that was planned, the work that was done, any approved variation and any defect left in place. That signed record is the audit trail that lets the site show later that the work was done as agreed.

lessons.title: Training a cleaner to observed competence, task by task
learningOutcomes: Describe the stages a cleaner moves through, from induction to observed competence in each task.
Keep a training record by person, task and date, and identify which tasks a person is not yet authorised to do.
Explain the difference between attending training and being assessed as competent in a task.

instructionSections.heading: Training is a sequence, not a single course
instructionSections.body: A cleaner moves through several stages. Induction covers the site rules, hazards, equipment and the route for reporting problems. Mandatory training covers workplace safety and infection-prevention content the site requires. Supervised practice on live work puts the new cleaner beside a trained person who watches, corrects and signs off each task. Where the role calls for it, supervisory and leadership development follows. Each stage builds on the one before, and a later stage does not make up for a gap in an earlier one.

instructionSections.heading: Attendance is not the same as competence
instructionSections.body: Attending a session shows the person received information. Competence is the demonstrated ability to carry out a task to the standard, and a supervisor records it by observation. The UK source refers to certificated competence through a UK qualification. This lesson therefore uses observation-based competence records, which work in any setting.

instructionSections.heading: Matching each person to the tasks they are authorised for
instructionSections.body: Each person's record should list the tasks they are authorised to do. A cleaner who is competent in dusting and damp mopping is not automatically authorised for machine scrubbing, chemical mixing or a specialist job. The supervisor keeps the list current, shows it on the roster or the job sheet, and removes a task from the list when training lapses or the method changes.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the record current
instructionSections.body: Record the date, the trainer, the task, the method used, the outcome and the next review. Refresh the training when a method, product or piece of equipment changes, and after an incident or a repeated defect that suggests a gap. A record that has not been reviewed is a record that cannot show current competence.

lessons.title: Service request intake and classification
learningOutcomes: Explain the boundary for service request intake and classification and identify when work must stop.
Prepare a task-specific, documented decision for service request intake and classification under company and local requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Why intake comes first
instructionSections.body: Every request starts as a claim about work, and the first decision is whether your business should accept that work at all. Intake is the point where a request is written down, understood and sorted before any quote is given or any equipment is loaded. A request that looks routine can hide unidentified materials, access limits or a need for a licence, so classify it on evidence and not on how familiar it sounds. This lesson covers how to collect the facts, how to sort the request into one of four outcomes, and how to record the decision so that the next person can see why it was made.

instructionSections.heading: Collect the facts before you classify
instructionSections.body: Obtain the request in writing where you can. Record the site address, the named site contact, the person who can approve the work, the expected result in the client's own words, and any materials, products or equipment the client expects you to use. Ask about access and occupancy: who is on the premises, whether children, animals or people with health conditions are present, which areas are restricted, and when the site can be entered. Keep what you have observed separate from what someone has told you and from what is still unknown. Photographs taken within safe access help the record, but a photograph does not identify an unknown substance or confirm that a surface or structure is safe. A client's statement that something is harmless or routine is not proof.

instructionSections.heading: Classify the request into one outcome
instructionSections.body: Once the facts are gathered, place the request in one of four outcomes. Accept means the work sits within the worker's documented training, the business's approved methods and products, and the authority the site has given. Accept with controls means the work is in scope once named controls, such as ventilation, an exclusion zone or a second worker, are in place. Hold means facts or authority are missing, so no work starts until they arrive. Refer means the work involves a licensed trade, a regulated material, a specialist method or a risk the business is not competent to manage, so it goes to an appropriately authorised provider. A quote given during intake is not work permission, and a hold or refer outcome must be stated in both the quote and the job record.

instructionSections.heading: Worked decision on an unidentified residue
instructionSections.body: Suppose an office manager asks for removal of a dark residue on office carpet, and nobody knows what it is or how it got there. The request cannot be classified as routine cleaning. The correct classification is uncharacterised: the material is not identified, its hazard is not known, and the client's wish to have it removed does not change that. The response is to request photographs, the product history, any cleaning records, the building's access rules and a qualified inspection. The cleaner does not label the residue, does not test it with cleaning products, and does not promise that it will come out. The client is told why the job is on hold, and the named approver is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Record the decision and the restart conditions
instructionSections.body: Record the classification, the scope and any exclusions, the controls required, the decision (accept, accept with controls, hold or refer), the person who approved it and the date. Keep a copy of what the client was told. Before work restarts, confirm who can restart it, which control check must be completed, and which documents must travel with the job. If a risk stays unresolved, escalate it to a competent specialist rather than closing the intake record.

instructionSections.heading: Licence notice
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, permit or authority to do any work. Some tasks that appear in a service request need a licence, a permit or a specific authorisation in some states and territories. Completing this lesson does not make a worker competent or authorised for any regulated task.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before resuming if the scope is unclear, if a hazard is identified or suspected and not yet understood, if the request calls for work outside your training or the work order, if the client asks you to start before authority is confirmed, or if people or animals enter the area while work is in progress.

lessons.title: Shift planning and service-level scope
learningOutcomes: Explain and demonstrate shift planning and service-level scope

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Learning outcome
By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to translate a service schedule into a workable shift while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

Workplace procedure
Read the signed scope and site-specific schedule: areas, frequency, timing, service standard, exclusions, chemicals permitted and required records. Separate daily high-touch work from periodic tasks and special requests. Sequence work around occupancy, access restrictions and drying time. Allocate staff according to competency and available hours, allowing time for inspections and waste transfer. Escalate any conflict between the schedule and safe completion; do not silently omit work.

Decision boundaries
Before acting, confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation. If the task exceeds training, consent, safe access or agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others as appropriate, report promptly and document the reason. Never substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

Worked workplace example
A client asks for a deep carpet extraction during a routine evening clean. The shift lead records the request as outside scope and seeks approval and suitable trained operators rather than adding it without authority.

Guided practical exercise
Given a three-hour office schedule and a list of 15 tasks, create a timed route, identify two infeasible tasks and draft a clear scope-clarification message.

Assessment and feedback
An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Creates a realistic prioritised plan, preserves contracted scope and flags capacity or access conflicts early. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

instructionSections.heading: Learning outcome
instructionSections.body: By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to translate a service schedule into a workable shift while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

instructionSections.heading: Workplace procedure
instructionSections.body: Read the signed scope and site-specific schedule: areas, frequency, timing, service standard, exclusions, chemicals permitted and required records. Separate daily high-touch work from periodic tasks and special requests. Sequence work around occupancy, access restrictions and drying time. Allocate staff according to competency and available hours, allowing time for inspections and waste transfer. Escalate any conflict between the schedule and safe completion; do not silently omit work.

instructionSections.body: Before acting, confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation. If the task exceeds training, consent, safe access or agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others as appropriate, report promptly and document the reason. Never substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Worked workplace example
instructionSections.body: A client asks for a deep carpet extraction during a routine evening clean. The shift lead records the request as outside scope and seeks approval and suitable trained operators rather than adding it without authority.

instructionSections.heading: Guided practical exercise
instructionSections.body: Given a three-hour office schedule and a list of 15 tasks, create a timed route, identify two infeasible tasks and draft a clear scope-clarification message.

instructionSections.heading: Assessment and feedback
instructionSections.body: An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Creates a realistic prioritised plan, preserves contracted scope and flags capacity or access conflicts early. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: Electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In Victoria, PV installation and maintenance is licensed electrical installation work, and PV DC cables may stay live when the power is off. NSW electrical wiring work includes repairing. On the Victorian, Western Australian and New South Wales pages checked, plain panel washing is not stated to need a licence, and any electrical work on a PV array is referred to a licensed electrician. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

lessons.title: Environmental impact across the job
learningOutcomes: Identify where a service job affects the environment: products, water, energy, waste, travel and materials.
Choose practices that reduce the impact without reducing safety or the quality standard.
Explain the trade-offs between environmental and safety or quality decisions.

instructionSections.heading: Where the impact comes from
instructionSections.body: Service work affects the environment through the products used and how much is used, the water and energy consumed, the waste produced and where it goes, the fuel used for travel, the packaging and materials brought onto site, and the wash water that leaves the site. Walk through a typical job and list each point. Most impact comes from over-use of products, poor dosing, unnecessary travel, and waste that is not sorted. Identify the largest items first, because those are where a change makes the most difference.

instructionSections.heading: Practical reductions
instructionSections.body: Reduce product use by dosing correctly and mixing only what is needed. Use microfibre and reusable cloths where they suit the surface and the procedure. Reduce water use by using a bucket method rather than running taps, and by using a trigger spray rather than a hose where it is enough. Reduce energy by turning off equipment when not in use. Reduce travel by grouping jobs by area. Sort waste at the point it is made so that recyclables are not contaminated. Each reduction must be checked against the safety and quality standards before it is adopted.

instructionSections.heading: Trade-offs and safety first
instructionSections.body: A lower-impact product is not always the right choice. A product with fewer environmental claims may still be the safer or more effective product for the surface, and a less effective product may need more use and more waste. Never reduce a safety control, a protective equipment requirement or a disinfection step to save resources. Where an environmental choice and a safety choice conflict, the safety choice takes priority, and the trade-off should be recorded.

lessons.title: Water and energy efficiency
learningOutcomes: Use water and energy efficiently during a job without reducing the quality or safety of the work.
Describe the common sources of water and energy waste on service jobs.
Check the water-use restrictions and discharge rules that apply before using water on site.

instructionSections.heading: Water use on a job
instructionSections.body: Water is used to mix products, rinse surfaces, fill buckets and run equipment. Waste usually comes from running taps, rinsing longer than needed, filling buckets to the top, and using a hose where a bucket and cloth would do. Use a bucket method for most cleaning, and change the water when it becomes soiled. Use a trigger spray with the minimum volume that wets the surface. Check whether the site has water-use restrictions, and do not use water where a restriction applies or where the discharge route is not approved.

instructionSections.heading: Energy use on a job
instructionSections.body: Energy is used by vacuums, pressure washers, floor machines, heaters, dryers and lighting. Switch off equipment when it is not in use, and do not leave a machine running while you move between rooms. Use the lowest effective setting for each machine, and keep filters and brushes clean so that the machine works efficiently. Turn off lights in areas you have finished where the customer agrees and the work is not affected. Check equipment for faults that increase energy use, such as a motor that runs hot, and record the fault.

instructionSections.heading: Efficiency and safety
instructionSections.body: Efficiency must not reduce safety or quality. Do not reduce water or the rinse step where the product label or the procedure requires it. Do not turn off ventilation or lighting where it is needed for safe work. Where a machine has a setting that reduces energy but reduces its effectiveness, test it on a hidden area and record the result before using it on the visible area.

lessons.title: Measure and improve outcomes
learningOutcomes: Choose a small set of measures for product use, water, waste and rework that the business can record consistently.
Record the measures and review them against a baseline.
Decide on one improvement at a time and check its effect.

instructionSections.heading: Choose measures the business can keep
instructionSections.body: A measure is only useful if it is recorded consistently. Choose a few measures that the team can record without extra work, such as the volume of product used per job or per dilution, the number of bags of general waste per job, the number of jobs needing rework, and the fuel or travel time per job. Record the baseline for each measure over a set period before making a change. Do not choose a measure that cannot be collected reliably, because the result will not be trusted.

instructionSections.heading: Review and decide
instructionSections.body: Review the measures at a fixed interval, such as monthly. Compare the results with the baseline, look for the causes of the largest changes, and decide on one improvement. Record the decision and the reason. Check the effect after a fixed period, and keep the change only if it improves the measure without reducing safety or quality. A change that does not work is reviewed or reversed, and the record shows the decision.

instructionSections.heading: Report the results
instructionSections.body: Share the results with the team so that people can see the effect of their work. Report the measures and the decision, not only the good results. Where the results are shared with customers, use only measures that are accurate and that the business can support. Do not make environmental claims that the measures do not show.

lessons.title: Kit classes
learningOutcomes: Describe the classes of kit used in service work: tools, equipment, products, protective equipment, consumables and documents.
Explain why each class needs different storage, checks and handling.
Assign each item in the business's kit to a class.

instructionSections.heading: The kit classes
instructionSections.body: A job kit is the set of items a team takes to a job. Group the items into classes so that each is handled correctly. Tools and equipment are the machines and hand tools that are used and maintained. Products are the cleaning and maintenance chemicals, which carry labels and SDS. Protective equipment is the gloves, eye protection, respirators and other items that protect people. Consumables are the cloths, bags, dressings and sponges used up on each job. Documents are the work orders, SDS copies, checklists and records. Each class has different rules for storage, transport and checks.

instructionSections.heading: Why the classes matter
instructionSections.body: Products must be kept with their labels and SDS, separated by incompatibility, and secured in transport. Protective equipment must be kept clean, dry and in date. Tools and equipment must be inspected before use. Consumables are used up and must be counted. Documents must be current and confidential. A kit that mixes these classes without a rule leads to lost SDS, mixed products, damaged equipment and missing protection. Keep a list of the classes and the items in each class for the kit.

instructionSections.heading: Assign and review the kit
instructionSections.body: For each item in the kit, decide its class, its storage place and its check. Record the list and update it when items are added or removed. Review the kit each time the job type changes, so that the team takes what the job needs and nothing that it does not, and so that an item that is no longer used is removed from the kit and its products are returned to the store.

lessons.title: Task-to-item mapping
learningOutcomes: Map each task in a job to the items needed to carry it out safely.
Build a kit for a specific job from the task map, rather than from habit.
Identify missing or extra items before the team leaves the store.

instructionSections.heading: Build the map from the tasks
instructionSections.body: Start from the tasks in the work order and the procedure. For each task, list the tools, equipment, products, protective equipment, consumables and documents it needs. A bathroom clean needs a toilet brush, a bucket, a cloth for the basin, a cloth for the toilet, a separate cloth for the glass, the approved products, the gloves named on the labels and the work order. Mapping from the tasks prevents the team taking items they do not need, and forgetting items they do need.

instructionSections.heading: Use the map to check the kit
instructionSections.body: Compare the kit to the map before leaving the store. Check that each task has its items and that each item is in its class. Check that any product in the kit has its SDS and label, that the protective equipment named for each product is included, and that the cloths and equipment are separated by zone. Record any item that is missing or extra, and resolve it before the team leaves.

instructionSections.heading: Update the map when the job changes
instructionSections.body: When a new task is added, a surface changes or a product is replaced, update the map and the kit list. A map that is not updated becomes wrong, and the team will either take items they do not need or miss items they do. Keep one approved map for each job type, and record the version and the date.

lessons.title: Consumable quantities
learningOutcomes: Estimate the consumable quantities needed for a job from the task map and the size of the work.
Track the use of consumables against the estimate to find waste and shortages.
Set a reorder level that avoids both running out and over-stocking.

instructionSections.heading: Estimate from the task map
instructionSections.body: Estimate consumables from the task map and the size of the job. Count the cloths by zone, the bags by the volume of waste, the gloves by the number of zone changes and product changes, and the dressings and sponges by the number of expected uses. Record the estimate and the basis. An estimate that is based on the job's actual tasks is more useful than a fixed number for every job, because it reflects the work and the risk.

instructionSections.heading: Track use and find waste
instructionSections.body: Record the consumables used on each job, or at least the total used per week. Compare the use with the estimate. Where use is much higher than the estimate, look for the cause: a cloth used for too many zones, gloves changed too often without reason, or a product that is wasted through over-mixing. Where use is much lower than the estimate, check that the items were not left out of the kit. Use the comparison to adjust the estimate.

instructionSections.heading: Reorder and avoid waste
instructionSections.body: Set a reorder level for each consumable so that the team does not run out during a job. Do not over-stock items that expire, such as dressings and some products, or that take up space and are damaged in storage. Use older stock first, and check expiry dates at each stock check. Do not reduce the number of gloves or cloths to save cost where it would mean breaking the zone or protection rules.

lessons.title: Transport and containment
learningOutcomes: Contain each class of kit during transport so that nothing spills, mixes or moves.
Describe the containment measures for products, waste and wet items.
Identify the transport rules that must be checked before carrying dangerous goods.

instructionSections.heading: Contain by class
instructionSections.body: Each class of kit needs its own containment in transport. Products should be in sealed, labelled containers, upright, in a tray or bunded area where the vehicle has one, and separated by incompatibility. Waste should be in sealed bags or lidded bins. Wet cloths and mop heads should be in a separate bag so that water does not reach the products or the documents. Equipment should be secured so that it cannot move or fall. Documents should be kept dry and out of the way of spills, and copies of SDS should be available in the vehicle.

instructionSections.heading: Vehicle and driver practices
instructionSections.body: Secure the load with straps, racks or lockable boxes before driving. Keep chemicals out of the passenger cabin and keep the vehicle ventilated. Do not carry chemicals next to food or drink. Check the containers for leaks at the start of each day and after each stop. If a container leaks, stop, contain the leak as the SDS directs, ventilate the vehicle if safe, and report it.

instructionSections.heading: Dangerous goods
instructionSections.body: Some products and quantities are dangerous goods under transport rules. In Victoria, the vehicle licence limits for dangerous goods are set by quantity, as stated in the licence notice in this lesson. Check the product's classification and those limits before transporting any larger quantity, and do not transport a product that you have not confirmed as permitted.

lessons.title: Kit handover and reconciliation
learningOutcomes: Reconcile the kit against the job map and the stock register at the end of a job or shift.
Hand over the kit with the state of each item, any damage and any product used.
Record any loss, damage or shortage and resolve it.

instructionSections.heading: Reconcile at the end
instructionSections.body: At the end of a job, check the kit against the job map and the stock register. Account for every tool, piece of equipment, product, protective item and document. Note the products used, the quantity remaining and any product that is damaged, leaking or expired. Check that the SDS for each product is still in the kit and that no product has been moved to a place where it is not stored safely. A kit that is not reconciled at the end of the job becomes a loss that nobody can trace.

instructionSections.heading: Hand over clearly
instructionSections.body: Hand the kit to the next person or to the store with a written list of its contents and its state. Tell the receiver about any item that is damaged, low, expired or needs cleaning, and any product that is leaking or opened. The receiver should confirm the count and the state, and sign or record the handover. Do not leave the kit in the van or at the customer's premises without a handover.

instructionSections.heading: Record loss, damage and shortage
instructionSections.body: Record any loss, damage or shortage with the item, the quantity, the time, the job and the likely cause. A missing product must be reported, because it may be a safety issue if it has been taken or spilled. A damaged item must be removed from use and checked. Investigate repeated shortages to find the cause, such as a missing item from the map, a theft risk or a packing practice that causes damage.

lessons.title: Inventory movements
learningOutcomes: Record each movement of equipment and products into and out of the store.
Keep a running balance that shows what is on hand, what is in use and what is missing.
Use the movement record to find losses, waste and reorder needs.

instructionSections.heading: Record each movement
instructionSections.body: Every movement of equipment and products should be recorded: what was taken out, to which job or vehicle, by whom and when, and what came back. The same applies to returns, transfers between vehicles, disposal and damage write-off. A simple movement record with these fields is enough for most businesses. Record movements at the time they happen, not at the end of the week, because a late record cannot show when a loss occurred.

instructionSections.heading: Keep a running balance
instructionSections.body: From the movement record, keep a running balance for each product and key item. The balance shows what should be on hand, and a stock count checks it. A difference between the balance and the count is a loss, a recording error or waste, and each must be investigated. Use the balance to plan reorders, and to see which products are used fastest and which sit unused.

instructionSections.heading: Use the record to act
instructionSections.body: Use the movement record to find patterns: a product that disappears at one site, a product that is wasted through over-mixing, or an item that is out for long periods and may be lost. Act on the pattern and record what was done. Products that are approaching expiry or that have been damaged should be moved to a separate location and recorded as such, so that they are not used by mistake.

lessons.title: Replacement and lifecycle
learningOutcomes: Describe the lifecycle of equipment, tools and protective items from purchase to retirement.
Compare the cost of repair, replacement and continued use using the maintenance record.
Decide when an item must be retired for safety, quality or cost reasons.

instructionSections.heading: The lifecycle
instructionSections.body: Each item moves through a lifecycle: purchase, first use, regular maintenance, repair, and eventually retirement. The lifecycle differs by item. A machine with a motor may last for years if it is serviced, while a cloth or a glove has a short life by design. Protective items have expiry or replacement points set by the manufacturer. Record the purchase date, the expected life and the maintenance schedule for each item, so that replacement can be planned rather than forced by failure.

instructionSections.heading: Repair or replace
instructionSections.body: Use the maintenance record to compare the cost of repair with the cost of replacement, including the downtime of the item. An item that needs repeated repairs, that cannot be repaired to its original safety standard, or that costs more to keep than to replace should be considered for replacement. Some items must be retired regardless of cost, such as a damaged protective item, a machine with a failed safety device, or a cracked ladder. A safety-related fault is not a cost question.

instructionSections.heading: Retire safely
instructionSections.body: Retire an item by removing it from the kit and the store, marking it as retired, and disposing of it through the approved route. Do not sell or give away a retired item that is unsafe, and do not leave it in the store where it could be used by mistake. Record the retirement, the date, the reason and the disposal route. Replacement should be checked against the task map so that the new item is suitable for the work.

lessons.title: Building a sales forecast from stages
learningOutcomes: Build a sales forecast from named stages, each with a trigger, a capacity and a revenue estimate
Cross-check a forecast total against its segment totals and against its stated objectives
Explain the gap between a forecast and a growth target, and record the decision taken

instructionSections.heading: Why stages beat a single guess
instructionSections.body: A forecast built from stages ties revenue to the steps the business must take first. The sample plan this lesson draws on did this. Its first month was set aside for legal and accounting set-up, office equipment and training design, with little or no trading expected. From the second month, enquiries began to turn into contracts, and staff were added only as contract volume justified each step. Every stage in a forecast should have a trigger, such as a number of confirmed contracts, and a capacity, such as the number of jobs a team can complete in a week.

instructionSections.heading: Set up the stage table
instructionSections.body: Make one row for each stage. The columns are the stage name, the trigger that starts it, the number of jobs per month, the average revenue per job, the monthly revenue and the team capacity. Include a set-up row with zero revenue if no trading happens in that period. Where a stage asks for more jobs than the team can deliver, the excess is a capacity problem rather than a sales result. Cap the jobs at capacity and record any surplus demand separately, so the forecast shows what can be delivered.

instructionSections.heading: Source each input
instructionSections.body: Each input should come from something you can check: the enquiries you have received, the share of enquiries that became paid jobs, the average job price from your records, and the segment size from “Defining target segments from customer data”. The sample plan assumed that a large part of its new clients after the second month would come from word of mouth. That assumption drives the whole forecast, so it must be stated and tested, not assumed. The plan also described its forecast as conservative. Write down what would have to be true for it to be too low, and what would have to be true for it to be too high.

instructionSections.heading: Cross-check the totals
instructionSections.body: Add the segment totals and confirm that they equal the grand total. The sample plan's forecast figures are removed here because they are United States figures from the early 2000s. Use the check only: add the segment totals, confirm they equal the grand total, then compare growth from year to year using your own dated figures.

instructionSections.heading: Compare the forecast with the stated objectives
instructionSections.body: The same plan's executive summary described very high projected growth, and its financial objectives set a high growth rate for three years. Its own forecast showed much slower growth in the first two years. Those rates are removed here as United States figures. That gap is the finding. A forecast does not have to match an objective, but the difference must be named, explained and then either closed by a stated action or resolved by changing the objective. Write the decision down with its date, so the next review can test it.

lessons.title: Setting an expense budget as a percentage of sales
learningOutcomes: Set a total expense budget as a percentage of planned sales
Split a budget group into named lines, each with a definition
Calculate budget as a percentage of sales and compare actual spend with budget each month

instructionSections.heading: Start from planned sales, not from spending wishes
instructionSections.body: An expense budget expressed as a percentage of sales ties what you can spend to what you expect to earn. Take the sales forecast from “Building a sales forecast from stages”, choose a percentage for each cost group, and multiply. The percentage is a planning target rather than a fixed rule, so write down the reason for each one. If the reason is that last year's spend was like this, say so and check whether it still holds.

instructionSections.heading: Name every line
instructionSections.body: A line labelled other hides what the money is for. Split each group into named lines and give each a short definition. The sample plan this lesson draws on budgeted its marketing expenses in three lines: printed material, economic incentives for referrals, and other. Its figures for one year are removed here. The other line made up most of the total and was not explained. Check the addition, then ask what the line contains before you approve it. The amounts are removed because they are United States figures; the problem they show is the point.

instructionSections.heading: Work out the percentage
instructionSections.body: Divide the total for a cost group by the sales for the same year. The same plan's marketing budget rose as a share of sales over the period. Its percentages are removed here because they are United States figures. The share rises when the budget grows faster than sales, and that pattern is worth questioning in any plan.

instructionSections.heading: Phase the spending
instructionSections.body: Spending does not have to be even across the year. The sample plan front-loaded spending in the first quarter to build visibility, held it at a steady level, and then lifted it before a seasonal peak. Phase your budget against the same months as your forecast stages, so spending rises when the revenue it supports is expected. A budget that front-loads spending needs a cash plan so the business can pay for it before the revenue arrives.

instructionSections.heading: Monitor actual against budget each month
instructionSections.body: Each month, record actual spend against each named line, work out the variance in dollars and as a percentage, and decide what to do. A variance is a question, not a verdict. Ask whether it came from a higher price, a change in the number of jobs, or a one-off cost, and record the answer. Set a threshold in advance, such as a variance above a stated percentage, that triggers a review.

lessons.title: Controls and KPIs: repeat business, satisfaction, revenue and expenses
learningOutcomes: Define at least four KPIs, each with a formula, source, owner, target and action threshold
Calculate repeat rate, satisfaction score with response rate, revenue variance and expense ratio from supplied data
Show how a percentage increase compounds over several periods

instructionSections.heading: What controls are for
instructionSections.body: A control is a regular check that shows whether the plan is on track. The sample plan this lesson draws on named four things it would monitor: revenue, monthly and annual; expenses, monthly and annual; repeat business; and customer satisfaction. Those four cover money coming in, money going out, customers coming back and customers' experience of the service. Start with them, then add one measure for each part of the plan that could fail without being noticed.

instructionSections.heading: Define each KPI in full
instructionSections.body: A key performance indicator without a definition cannot be checked. For each measure, write its name, its formula, the data source it is taken from, how often it is reviewed, the person responsible for it, its target, and the threshold that triggers action. Use the same definition every time, so that one month can be compared with the next. Changing the definition halfway through a year makes the trend meaningless.

instructionSections.heading: Repeat rate and satisfaction
instructionSections.body: Repeat rate is the number of customers in a period who had a previous job, divided by the number of customers served in that period. Satisfaction is the number of survey responses scoring 4 or 5 out of 5, divided by the number of responses. Always record the response rate beside the satisfaction score, which is the number of responses divided by the number of surveys sent. A score from a small number of replies says little about the customers who did not reply.

instructionSections.heading: Revenue variance and expense ratio
instructionSections.body: Revenue variance is actual revenue minus forecast revenue, divided by forecast revenue, shown as a percentage. Expense ratio is total expenses divided by revenue for the same period. Compare the expense ratio with the budget percentages from “Setting an expense budget as a percentage of sales”, and treat a drift in either direction as something to explain.

instructionSections.heading: Targets compound
instructionSections.body: The sample plan set a quarterly objective for repeat customers. That rate is removed here as a United States figure. Compounding is the point: a rate applied each period multiplies, it does not simply add. Targets are easy to misread, so check whether each is per period, compounded or measured against the same base.

instructionSections.heading: Act on thresholds
instructionSections.body: A threshold names the point at which someone must act. For example, if repeat rate falls below a set level for two periods in a row, the owner reviews the service and records the cause and the action. A KPI that never triggers any action is not doing its job, and a threshold set after the results are known is not a real threshold.

lessons.title: Milestone planning with owners and dates
learningOutcomes: Build a milestone table with one named owner, start and end dates, a budget line and dependencies for each milestone
Sequence dependent milestones so that each starts only after its input is due
Define the evidence that shows each milestone is complete

instructionSections.heading: Milestones are dated, checkable outcomes
instructionSections.body: A milestone is an outcome that someone can check, such as printed brochure approved and delivered, or referral terms signed off. It is not a task list. The sample plan this lesson draws on listed key marketing programmes: completing the marketing strategy, producing printed material, generating customers from referrals and running two advertising campaigns. It said each one should be finished on time and on budget. Write each programme as an outcome with a finish that can be seen.

instructionSections.heading: One owner per milestone
instructionSections.body: Each milestone has one named person accountable for finishing it. Others can contribute, but the table records one name. Shared ownership usually means no owner. For a solo business the owner is you. For a team, the owner is the person with authority to approve the spend and sign off the result. Record the role as well as the name, so the milestone survives a change of staff.

instructionSections.heading: Dates, dependencies and sequence
instructionSections.body: Give each milestone a start date and an end date, written in day-month-year format. Then record the milestones it depends on. A printed brochure cannot be delivered before its design is approved, and a campaign cannot start before its budget is approved. Sort the table by dependency first and by date second, and check that no milestone starts before the milestones it depends on have ended.

instructionSections.heading: Link each milestone to a budget line
instructionSections.body: Each milestone's cost should come from a named line in the expense budget from “Setting an expense budget as a percentage of sales”. A milestone with no budget line is an unfunded commitment. A milestone whose budget is used up before it is finished is at risk, and the owner must say so at the next review, not after the money is spent.

instructionSections.heading: Define the evidence of completion
instructionSections.body: A milestone is complete only when its evidence exists: a signed-off design, a delivery receipt, a count of referred customers who completed a first paid job, or a dated invoice. A note that says done is not evidence. Write the evidence next to the milestone, and record where it is stored before the milestone starts.

instructionSections.heading: A caution about the sample table
instructionSections.body: The milestone table in the sample plan is partly garbled in the text available for this course. Its dates and budgets cannot be reliably matched to its rows, so this lesson uses the structure only and does not reuse the sample's dates or amounts. The part worth copying is the structure: one owner, dates, a budget, and a status for each milestone.

lessons.title: Reporting documents for a cleaning site
learningOutcomes: Sort site documents by purpose: supply, staffing, quality and client reporting
Design a form that records what is needed and nothing more
Set an owner, frequency and retention period for each form in a form register

instructionSections.heading: Why site documents matter
instructionSections.body: Site documents create a record that work was requested, done, checked and paid for. The sample proposal lists about a dozen reporting documents, from a material requisition to a daily housekeeping schedule. Each one answers a question a client, an insurer or a supervisor may ask later. Before you add a form, write down the question it answers. If you cannot write the question, the form should not exist.

instructionSections.heading: Sort the documents by purpose
instructionSections.body: Group forms by what they prove. Supply forms track what was requested, bought and used: the material requisition, the supply requisition, the stock inventory and the dispenser monitoring sheet. Staffing forms record attendance and overtime: the absence report and the overtime request, plus an endorsement form where a sign-off is needed. Quality forms show the work was checked: the site inspection checklist, the daily restroom checklist and the weekly report. Incident and performance forms form a system of their own and are covered in the next lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Design a form people will complete
instructionSections.body: A usable form has a reference number, a date, the site, the name of the person completing it, the item or task, the quantity or result, and a signature or initials. Limit each form to what its question needs. Put the most important field first. Use tick boxes for routine answers and free text only for exceptions. Avoid personal identifiers you do not need. The sample incident and appraisal forms include a personal number field. Do not copy a national identity number field into any form unless a clear legal need has been confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Requisitions follow a flow
instructionSections.body: A material requisition moves through a set flow: the site requests the item, a supervisor approves it, purchasing orders it, the site receives it, and the stock record is updated. Each step needs a named owner and a date. A requisition with no receipt step cannot show what was actually used. The sample requisition has numbered lines, codes, units and quantities, which is a sound basis for this flow.

instructionSections.heading: Daily and weekly records
instructionSections.body: A daily checklist should take about a minute to complete, and be complete enough to show that the job was checked. The weekly report summarises the week: hours worked, issues, supplies used, inspection results and open actions. Build the weekly report from the daily records rather than from memory, so that the summary matches what happened on site.

instructionSections.heading: Control references and versions
instructionSections.body: The sample uses reference codes made from an operations prefix, a form type and a number. A numbering pattern works only if one person controls it. Keep a form register with the reference, the current version, the owner, the frequency, the place where completed forms are filed and the retention period. Withdraw old versions from the site and date every new version.

instructionSections.heading: Paper or digital
instructionSections.body: Paper or digital records both work, as long as each entry can be traced to a person, a date and a site. Where the scope requires photographs, define when they are taken, what they must show and where they are stored, using the photo requirements for your business.

lessons.title: Documenting and automating the repetitive parts of your business
learningOutcomes: List the systems your business needs, from enquiry to payment
Prioritise the automation with the most time saved
Test each automated process before relying on it

instructionSections.heading: Document everything you repeat
instructionSections.body: Each time you do a task more than twice, write it down. A one-page document and a short recorded walk-through are often enough. The aim is that someone else could pick the process up.

instructionSections.heading: Master systems list
instructionSections.body: List every process: enquiry, quote, booking, reminders, job checklist, invoicing, payment and review requests. Visibility comes first.

instructionSections.heading: Prioritise
instructionSections.body: Automate the processes that save the most time or prevent the most errors. Leave rare or complex processes until later.

instructionSections.heading: Build simply
instructionSections.body: Use the tools you already have, such as a calendar, a booking form, invoicing software and a shared document. A virtual assistant can run parts of the process. Keep the system simple enough to explain in a few minutes.

instructionSections.heading: Test before you rely on it
instructionSections.body: Run a test booking or test invoice through the whole process. Check the reminders, the payment and the record. Keep manual checks until the automation has worked several times.

lessons.title: Quality policy, scope and measurable objectives
learningOutcomes: Explain what a quality policy commits a business to and what it does not do.
Write a scope statement that names the services covered and any clause excluded, with a reason.
Turn a general quality aim into two objectives that can be measured.

instructionSections.heading: What a quality policy is for
instructionSections.body: A quality policy is a short statement of what the business promises its clients and staff. The sample manual commits the firm to meeting its own and its clients' expectations, to forming lasting ties with customers, to improving its systems, to using its resources well and to complying with the laws that apply to it. A policy is a commitment, not a procedure. The procedures sit beneath it and must support what the policy says. A policy that nobody can act on is a notice on a wall.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and exclusions
instructionSections.body: The scope marks out which services the system governs. In the sample, the services listed are janitorial work, laundry, pest control and general housekeeping. It also records one excluded clause, the one covering design and development, because the firm offers no new services. An exclusion is only valid if the reason holds. If the business starts a new service, the excluded clause must be brought back in. Write the scope so a new supervisor can tell at a glance whether a service is covered.

instructionSections.heading: Objectives that can be measured
instructionSections.body: The sample sets objectives such as reducing client complaints, improving margin and stabilising the customer base. These are useful aims, but an objective needs a measure, a date and an owner before it can be checked. Turning 'reduce complaints' into 'log every complaint for three months and compare the count with the prior three months' gives a result that can be shown to the management review. The sample also notes that the customer decides what quality means, so feedback from clients should shape the objectives.

instructionSections.heading: Standards named in the sample
instructionSections.body: The sample states that it applies a version of an international quality standard. Its figures and retention periods come from a 2012 sample for a non-Australian operation, so they are not Australian facts. Confirm the current edition of any standard before naming it in a business document.

lessons.title: Weekly toolbox talks and safety alerts
learningOutcomes: Plan and run a short weekly toolbox talk that a crew can take part in.
Choose and post a safety alert that suits the sites the crew works on.
Record attendance, topics and actions from each talk.

instructionSections.heading: Why a short regular talk helps
instructionSections.body: In the sample, a weekly safety meeting is run on each work site by the supervisor, with a senior operations deputy plus a safety officer, while the training lead also attends. The purpose is to keep everyone informed of changes that affect their safety and wellbeing. A talk of ten to fifteen minutes, held on a fixed day each week, works well for a crew because it is regular and focused. It also gives workers a place to raise hazards they have noticed.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing topics and alerts
instructionSections.body: Choose a topic from the week's real work: a chemical that was used more, a near miss, a change to a method, or a hazard seen on a site. The sample also posts weekly safety and health alerts on work sites, drawn from internal and external material where management judges them relevant. Use alerts that match what the crew actually does. A generic alert that is never connected to the work is quickly ignored.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the talk and following up
instructionSections.body: Record the date, the site, the people present, the topic and any action agreed. An action might be a change to a procedure, a request for equipment, or a report to the manager. Check at the next talk whether the action was completed. The sample does not set legal requirements for these talks. Check whether a weekly talk meets the consultation duties that apply under Australian WHS law. See “WHS duties and consultation” for the consultation duties and check the local arrangements.

lessons.title: Teaching a new cleaner: the training sequence
learningOutcomes: Sequence a new worker's training from classroom content to supervised practice to final evaluation.
Use a demonstrate, watch, do and repeat cycle for each task.
Write a final evaluation that states what was achieved and what needs repeating.

instructionSections.heading: The order of training
instructionSections.body: The sample firm teaches theory before any on-the-job work, so trainees learn the basic knowledge and skills before they begin. New recruits are introduced to their section by the supervisor, taken through key company policies, and then gathered for a larger, organised training once they know the section's operations. The first organised training covers the specific standards and procedures for each type of site, the equipment used and the detergents needed.

instructionSections.heading: Demonstrate, watch, do and repeat
instructionSections.body: On the job the trainer first does the task while the trainee watches, then the trainee does a specific part of the task alone under observation. The sample stresses that a trainee who has not picked up the task should be taken through it again until it is fully understood. Move between sites when a task differs, for example from a rooms-based housekeeping task to an office-based janitorial one, so the trainee sees how the methods change.

instructionSections.heading: Supervised work and evaluation
instructionSections.body: After training, the new worker is given a permanent set of tasks and works under close supervision for the opening days. The sectional supervisor keeps the trainee in the assigned area and checks the work. A trainer then walks the work as a field supervisor and completes a final evaluation. The evaluation is passed to the manager responsible for training, who decides whether the training was effective. Keep the evaluation separate from the induction record, which is covered by “Staff onboarding and induction record”.

lessons.title: Approving suppliers and checking goods on receipt
learningOutcomes: Describe the checks used to approve a supplier and the record kept for it.
Check a delivery against its order at the point of receipt and record any problem.
Trace a product back to its source using the receiving record.

instructionSections.heading: Approving a supplier
instructionSections.body: The sample firm approves suppliers by reference to qualifications, any licences held, insurance, track record, experience and references. Every supplier and each approval decision is entered on a register of cleared suppliers. Approval is not a one-time event: the sample reviews every supplier each year, and records any problem on a log. Checking that a supplier holds a licence is a check only. It does not grant or confirm that the supplier may carry out any particular work.

instructionSections.heading: Checking goods on receipt
instructionSections.body: Each delivery is inspected on arrival and matched to the purchase order for quantity and specification. Faults go on the receiving record, and the buyer who placed the order judges how much harm each fault caused the business. Where problems recur with one supplier, the operations manager raises them with the supplier first. If the problems continue, the sample says an alternative supplier should be found.

instructionSections.heading: Traceability
instructionSections.body: The sample requires every product to be traceable to its source. The receiving record shows what was received, from whom and when, which supports product recall and stock rotation. Keep the record in a form that can be found quickly, and keep the product's own instructions and safety information with the stock.

lessons.title: Reviewing a contract before accepting the work
learningOutcomes: Set out the client requirements in writing before costing a contract.
Use a contract check sheet covering time frames, staffing, pricing, payment terms and escalation.
Explain why an unpriced staffing or time requirement puts the margin at risk.

instructionSections.heading: Understanding the requirement
instructionSections.body: The sample firm requires the operations manager to read every enquiry, to confirm the contact person and to resolve any unclear requirement with the client in writing before costing. Client documents and confidential information remain the business's responsibility until handed back to the client. A requirement that is not written down is a requirement that cannot be priced or defended.

instructionSections.heading: Costing and the decision to tender
instructionSections.body: The operations manager prices the chemicals, consumables, labour hours and kit, and prepares a cost-benefit comparison for the head of the business. The directors then decide whether the company has the skills and funds to meet the client's needs and finish the work well. Only then is the tender drafted, verified for correctness and sent.

instructionSections.heading: The contract check sheet
instructionSections.body: When a contract is awarded, the operations manager compares the tender with the signed contract. The sample's review covers the schedule windows, the number of workers needed, the price, when and how payment is made, the rules for raising prices mid-contract, and any capital outlay. A filled-in sheet is the proof that the review happened. A price that does not cover the staffing the contract requires will erode the hourly rate of every job under it, so check the labour hours against the price before signing.

lessons.title: Checking measuring and mixing equipment
learningOutcomes: Describe how hand-held measures and mixing flasks are checked and recorded.
Identify a mixing or storage practice that introduces a hazard.
Describe the corrective action when a check is missed.

instructionSections.heading: Why measures must be checked
instructionSections.body: Dilution and mixing depend on measuring equipment that reads true. The sample firm checks and calibrates handheld gauges and mixing flasks at a fixed interval, and records each check in the records diary. The interval the sample uses is the firm's own rule. Check whether a six-monthly interval suits any particular product or site. Set the interval from the manufacturer's instructions and the product's directions.

instructionSections.heading: Following the maker's method
instructionSections.body: Follow the manufacturer's instructions strictly when calibrating an instrument. Keep heavy-duty cleaning concentrates away from glass tools kept in the mixing room, because the combination can introduce a hazard. Check that the equipment is suitable for the product before use, and keep the product's own safety information with the mixing station.

instructionSections.heading: Corrective action when a check is missed
instructionSections.body: The sample describes what to do once a check has been skipped. The operations manager decides whether any chemical use could have been compromised and logs it. The staff member is retrained and re-signs the training record. The cause is investigated, the calibration procedure reviewed if needed, and the event recorded on the improvement report.

lessons.title: Site risk controls: staff cover, property security and labelling
learningOutcomes: Name the common site risks in the sample: absence, property security, mislabelled items and power loss.
Choose a control for each risk and explain how it is checked.
Keep a risk table that is reviewed when the work changes.

instructionSections.heading: Staff absence
instructionSections.body: The sample treats unplanned absence as a serious risk, because a shortage of people leads to unfinished work and complaints.
