Its control is to plan more people than a job strictly needs, so a relief worker is available. The sample offers a case in which a two-person job is covered by three people. That is one firm's policy, not a standard. Whatever ratio is chosen, the roster must show who the relief worker is and how they are called in.

instructionSections.heading: Property security and labelling
instructionSections.body: Where a worker might leave a room door open, the client's property is at risk. The sample's control is a supervisor check after the work is finished, so workers take responsibility for locking rooms before they leave. Items sent for cleaning are also at risk of mix-up and loss. The sample uses a laundry docket checked against the bag contents, and asks owners to mark their items. Use the same logic for any shared item: a record, a check and an identifier.

instructionSections.heading: Power loss and keeping clients informed
instructionSections.body: Some risks are outside the business's control, such as a power failure that leaves work incomplete. The sample states that the business must keep the customer informed when this happens, and it names backup power as a control at sites where it is needed. Record each risk in a table with its control, the person who checks it, plus the date it is next reviewed.

lessons.title: Standard operating procedure (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Write a purpose and scope that a new person can read and apply without help
Reference every chemical and equipment item to its label, safety data sheet or manual
Give each step a visible check and a defined response when the check fails, with records and change approval named

instructionSections.heading: What a standard operating procedure is for
instructionSections.body: A standard operating procedure (SOP) is a written method for doing a task the same way each time, so that a new person can do it safely and a supervisor can check it. It is more than a checklist. An SOP states its purpose and scope, the equipment and materials used, the steps, the checks made during and after the task, the records kept, and who may approve a change. Write it for the person doing the job, in the order they will do it. Where a step depends on a product label or a manufacturer manual, refer to that document rather than copying a figure into the SOP.

instructionSections.heading: Equipment, chemicals and checks
instructionSections.body: List each item of equipment the procedure uses, with its purpose, the check made before use, and the person responsible for maintenance. For each chemical or material, record the product name, its use, the dilution or concentration taken from the label or safety data sheet, where that document is kept, how the product is stored and how its waste is handled. Do not write dilution figures from memory or from another product. Each step should have a visible check, such as a surface test, a gauge reading or a visual inspection, and the SOP should say what to do if the check fails. A check that cannot be completed means the step is not finished.

instructionSections.heading: Records, change control and review
instructionSections.body: State what is recorded, when, where, and for how long the record is kept. State who may change the SOP, what evidence supports a change, and how the new version reaches the people who use it. Record a version number and a review date. An SOP changed informally in the field drifts away from what is written, so changes should go through the named approver before they are used. Where the procedure covers a licensed or authorised task, state who is authorised and where that authorisation is recorded. The SOP does not grant the authorisation.

lessons.title: Electrical, battery and fuel safety
learningOutcomes: Identify electrical, battery and fuel hazards on a garden or outdoor site before starting work.
Inspect corded tools, extension leads, battery packs and fuel containers and remove defective items from service.
Refuel and store petrol engines and batteries using the controls in this lesson.
Stop work and refer any mains wiring, fixed electrical or gas task to a licensed tradesperson.

instructionSections.heading: What this lesson covers and what it does not
instructionSections.body: Outdoor work brings electricity, batteries and fuel into wet, uneven and crowded places. A mower lead can be cut by a spade, a battery pack can overheat in a hot ute, and a petrol can left beside a running trimmer is a fire waiting to happen. This lesson teaches you to recognise those hazards, apply the controls that a worker is allowed to apply, and stop and refer everything else. It does not authorise you to install, repair, rewire or connect any fixed electrical installation, irrigation controller mains supply, outdoor lighting circuit or gas appliance. Those tasks need a licensed electrician or other licence holder under the rules that apply in your state or territory. Finishing this lesson does not give you a licence, a certificate or authority to do regulated electrical or gas work. Check {{business:compliance.licence_requirements}} before any task that goes beyond inspecting and reporting.

instructionSections.heading: Recognise electrical hazards on site
instructionSections.body: Start every job by looking at the power supply before you plug anything in. Look for outlets without protective covers, boards placed on wet grass or bare soil, and leads that cross paths, gates or driveways where vehicles run over them. Check each extension lead for cut or nicked insulation, exposed copper, cracked plugs, heat marks, and connectors that have been taped together. A lead that works is not automatically a safe lead. Where your tools or outlets are supplied with residual current device (RCD) protection, confirm that it is present and working using the test button before use. Where a site has no RCD protection and you are not sure whether the outlet is protected, do not assume it is. Stop, use a tool that is known to be protected, and ask your supervisor. Treat any buried or overhead cable you cannot identify as live until a competent person confirms otherwise. Work near overhead power lines, and tree work above a set height or near lines, is outside this business and needs the licensing that applies to it.

instructionSections.heading: Batteries, chargers and fuel
instructionSections.body: Lithium-ion battery packs used in blowers, trimmers and mowers store a lot of energy. Damage can cause overheating, swelling, smoke or fire. Inspect each pack before use. A pack that is cracked, leaking, swollen, hot to touch or smells unusual must come out of service. Do not charge a damaged pack, do not drop it into a bin, and move it to a clear, non-combustible area away from fuel and dry vegetation. Charge only with the charger supplied for that battery and at a location that is cool, dry and ventilated. Do not charge a hot battery straight after heavy use. Petrol and two-stroke fuel need separate handling. Store fuel only in approved containers that are clearly labelled, away from ignition sources and out of direct sun. Refuel engines only when they are switched off and cool. Wipe up spills before starting the engine. Never refuel a running engine, and never smoke near fuel. Petrol engines in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces produce carbon monoxide, so do not run them in sheds, garages or under covered areas without fresh air.

instructionSections.heading: Controls, isolation and when to stop
instructionSections.body: Use the hierarchy of control. The first choice is to avoid the hazard, for example by using a battery tool where it is suitable instead of a long extension lead. Next, substitute a safer tool or fuel system. Then separate people from the hazard, for example by keeping leads out of the walking path and out of the cutting zone. Only after those steps should you rely on PPE, such as eye protection, hearing protection and gloves that suit the task. Before adjusting, clearing a jam or changing a blade, switch the tool off, remove the battery or unplug it, and wait for moving parts to stop. Keep cords clear of blades and wheels, and never run a cord through standing water or under a wet tarp. Stop work immediately if a tool trips its RCD repeatedly, if a lead becomes warm, if you smell burning or if fuel leaks. Tell your supervisor, make the area safe and record the event. Do not attempt to fix a fault in fixed wiring, a switchboard or a garden lighting circuit yourself.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check what you do, not only what you can describe. During a site check, you should be able to point to the defective item, explain why it is unsafe, show the correct removal from service and name the person you would inform. The pass evidence is an inspection record for each tool, lead and battery, with photographs taken with consent showing any defect and its isolation. Escalate immediately to the supervisor for any exposed wiring, any shock, any fuel leak near an ignition source, any swollen or smoking battery, and any electrical fault in fixed wiring or a controller. Where the fault involves mains supply, the decision to repair belongs to a licensed electrician, not to the crew.

lessons.title: Weather, heat, ultraviolet and wildlife
learningOutcomes: Plan work around heat, ultraviolet exposure, lightning and wind before a job starts.
Recognise the early signs of heat illness in yourself and co-workers and apply the work-rest and hydration controls.
Decide when to stop work, seek shelter and report, using the business's escalation steps.
Recognise common wildlife hazards on outdoor sites and respond without handling animals or nests.

instructionSections.heading: Why weather is a work hazard
instructionSections.body: Outdoor work is exposed to conditions that change during a shift. A cool morning can become a hot afternoon, a light breeze can turn into a gusty front, and a thunderstorm can arrive faster than the forecast suggests. Heat, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, lightning, strong wind and wet ground all change how tools behave and how people think. Heat stress reduces concentration, which increases the risk of cuts, falls and vehicle incidents. Lightning and strong wind can bring down branches, lift tarpaulins and make ladders unstable. Before any job, check the forecast and any official weather warnings for the site, and read the business's weather procedure. Write down the conditions under which you will continue, modify the work, or stop. This is the weather trigger matrix for the job, and it should be agreed with your supervisor before work begins. It is a planning tool, not a guarantee, so it must be reviewed again as the day changes.

instructionSections.heading: Heat, UV and work-rest planning
instructionSections.body: Heat illness develops gradually. Early signs include headache, dizziness, unusual tiredness, heavy sweating that stops, cramps, nausea and irritability. Any worker who shows these signs must stop, move into shade or a cool area, drink water if they are alert, and be checked by a supervisor. A person who is confused, vomiting, not sweating, or who collapses needs urgent medical help, and the emergency procedure applies. Plan the heaviest tasks for the cooler parts of the day where possible, and schedule regular rest in shade. Keep drinking water available and encourage small regular drinks rather than large amounts all at once. For UV, use the business's sun-protection controls. Shade, long sleeves, a broad-brimmed hat, sunscreen and sunglasses reduce exposure, and shade-seeking should be built into the work plan rather than left to individuals. Do not rely on a cloudy sky as protection. The approach to heat and UV is to change the work, not to push through it.

instructionSections.heading: Lightning, wind and wet conditions
instructionSections.body: When lightning is in the area, stop working outdoors and move to a fully enclosed vehicle or building. Wait for a set period after the last thunder before going back outside, following the business's rule. Do not shelter under isolated trees or in open structures such as gazebos, and keep clear of metal fences and equipment during a storm. Strong wind can throw debris, bring down dead branches and make ladders and elevated platforms unsafe. Stop height work and any task that uses a tall tool when gusts make footing or control uncertain. Wet ground and slippery surfaces increase slip risk around mowers, hoses and irrigation fittings. Adjust your method, not only your footwear. Stop and reassess when conditions change, and record the change and the decision in the job record.

instructionSections.heading: Wildlife and insects
instructionSections.body: Garden sites contain animals, insects and nests that can injure people. Snakes, spiders, bees, wasps, ants and some caterpillars and marine animals can cause bites, stings or allergic reactions. Treat every nest, hive, burrow and unexplained animal as a hazard. Do not handle, disturb or attempt to remove an animal, and do not use a pesticide on a wildlife hazard unless the business's licensing and training allow it for that product and task. Many native animals are protected and their disturbance may be regulated, so refer the situation to the supervisor and, where needed, to a competent specialist. Before cutting into dense growth, leaf litter or log piles, look and listen first and move slowly. Keep a clear route to the vehicle and carry the first-aid kit and any allergy medication that the worker is authorised to use. Anyone with a known severe allergy must tell the supervisor before the job starts.

instructionSections.heading: Escalation and verification
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check decisions rather than paperwork. In a practical check, a worker should explain which weather conditions would change the plan, show the shade and water arrangements, identify the nearest shelter, and name the person to inform. Stop work immediately for lightning in the area, for a worker who shows heat illness signs, for a wildlife hazard that cannot be isolated, or for wind that makes the task unsafe. Escalate to the supervisor and record the event. Do not restart until the supervisor confirms the conditions have changed.

lessons.title: Biosecurity and invasive species
learningOutcomes: Recognise plants that may be invasive, declared or restricted without relying on touch or guesswork.
Stop, avoid spreading suspect plant material and clean tools and footwear where required.
Decide whether material can be moved, composted, chipped or disposed of, and where the decision needs an authority.
Record species uncertainty, the referral and the client's notification.

instructionSections.heading: Why biosecurity matters on a garden job
instructionSections.body: Garden and landscape work moves plants, soil, seed and fragments from one property to another. Weeds and pests spread when a seed head is shaken off, a cutting is dropped in a green-waste bin, or a boot carries soil into the next yard. Some plants are declared or restricted because they damage native bushland, waterways, crops or infrastructure. A declared plant may need to be reported, controlled or destroyed under specific rules, and moving it may be an offence. The rules are set by each state and territory and by local government, and their lists differ. Your job on site is to recognise the risk, stop the spread, and refer the decision to someone with the authority to make it. Identifying a plant is not the same as having authority to remove or treat it.

instructionSections.heading: Recognising suspect plant material
instructionSections.body: Many weeds look like ordinary garden plants when they are young. Look at the growth habit, leaf arrangement, flower and seed structure, and any unusual sap, thorns or fruit. Compare what you see with a reliable identification source, such as a state or territory weed guide or a qualified botanist, and note any uncertainty. Do not identify a plant by smell or taste, and do not handle sap or fruit with bare hands. If a neighbour, client or sign tells you a plant is a declared weed, take it seriously and stop cutting that plant until you have checked. Photograph the plant and its location with the client's consent, and do not collect seed or cut material for identification unless the process allows it. Keep the plant separate from other green waste so it does not contaminate the rest of the job.

instructionSections.heading: Stopping spread during work
instructionSections.body: Stop cutting or moving any suspect plant as soon as you are unsure of its identity. Clean tools, gloves, boots and equipment before they leave the infected area, using the method approved by the business and suitable for the plant. Wash mower decks and trimmer heads, and brush soil and seed from boots and wheel rims. Do not blow leaves or clippings onto a footpath, into a drain or across a boundary into a neighbouring bushland or waterway. Use bagging, covered trailers and tarps where the material is at risk of falling or blowing away. Work from the cleanest area to the most infested area so that you do not carry seed across clean ground. Where the material cannot be controlled, stop and refer to the supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding what happens to the material
instructionSections.body: Once a plant is identified with confidence, you can decide what happens to the material, but only within the rules that apply. Ask four questions. Is the plant declared, restricted or otherwise regulated in this location? Can the material be moved off the property, and if so, what documents or containment are required? Is composting or chipping allowed, or will the material have to go to a specified disposal facility? Does the client or the land owner have a duty to report the plant? If you cannot answer every question from a reliable source, keep the material on site, contain it, and refer the decision. Do not state to the client that a plant is safe to compost or dispose of until the answer is confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and referral
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the reasoning, not just the final bag. A competent worker can explain what triggered the stop, how the plant was confirmed or left unconfirmed, what cleaning and containment were used, and who was informed. Good practice is a referral record with the species name if known, the location, the photographs taken, the containment used and the owner's notification. Do not certify that a site is free of an invasive plant. You can record that a plant was identified, controlled or referred, and what evidence supports that statement.

lessons.title: Waste stream separation and lawful disposal
learningOutcomes: Separate clean green waste, diseased or invasive plant matter, treated timber, chemicals and sharps at the point of collection.
Confirm that a disposal destination accepts each waste stream before the load leaves the site.
Load and secure waste so that it does not blow, leak or enter drains.
Complete a waste record that supports the client's handover and any audit.

instructionSections.heading: Why waste separation saves money and protects sites
instructionSections.body: A garden clean-up produces several kinds of waste, and each kind has its own handling and disposal route. Clean green waste such as lawn clippings, small prunings and leaves usually goes to a green-waste facility. Diseased or invasive plant matter may need to be contained, treated or sent to a specified destination. Treated timber, chemical containers, paint tins, batteries and sharps are not general green waste. When these streams are mixed, the whole load can be rejected at the gate, the crew may pay for a second trip, and a contaminated load can spread disease or chemicals. Separation at the source is faster and cheaper than sorting at the disposal site. It is also one of the simplest ways to show the client that the job was done properly. Waste separation depends on knowing what is in the load, so the first step is always a site walk to identify the waste types before collection begins.

instructionSections.heading: Sorting at the point of collection
instructionSections.body: Set up separate, labelled containers before collection starts. Use one container or pile for clean green waste, one for diseased or suspect plant matter, one for treated timber, and one for any chemical or sharps item that the business is authorised to handle. Keep the chemicals and sharps out of general containers altogether, and do not compact them into a bin with clippings. If a chemical container is leaking or unlabelled, do not open it. Move the container to a safe, ventilated, contained area, and stop until the supervisor confirms the product and the handling route. Treated timber is often not accepted in green-waste streams. Keep it apart, and confirm its acceptance at the destination before it is loaded. Sharp items, such as broken glass, needles and metal, need puncture-resistant containers and a clear label. Do not hand-sort mixed heaps. Use tools and a defined work area to reduce contact with hazards.

instructionSections.heading: Confirming destinations and rules
instructionSections.body: Before loading a vehicle, confirm where each waste stream is going. Ask the disposal facility what it accepts, whether it requires a manifest or booking, whether it will accept diseased or invasive material, and whether it has a separate stream for treated timber, liquids and sharps. Write the answers down with the date and the name of the person who gave them. Acceptance rules and the rules for transporting regulated waste differ between states, territories and local councils, and this draft does not confirm them for any particular location. Where a waste type is regulated, such as certain liquids, asbestos-containing material or hazardous chemicals, the crew must not handle it under this lesson. Stop, contain the area, and refer it to the supervisor and to a licence holder or specialist service. Do not guess a destination, and do not send mixed loads to a facility that has not confirmed it will accept them.

instructionSections.heading: Loading, transport and records
instructionSections.body: Load each stream into the correct vehicle or container, and secure it so that it cannot shift, blow or leak in transit. Use a cover or net for loose material, and check the load before the vehicle leaves the property. Keep loads off the kerb or footpath, and do not let material enter the stormwater system. Make a waste record for every load. Record the date, the site, the waste types and estimated volumes, the container or vehicle used, the destination, the time of arrival, and the receipt or ticket number. If anything goes wrong, such as a spill, a leaking container or a rejected load, record it and inform the supervisor. The waste record is part of the job's evidence, and it should be handed over with the final inspection described in the handover lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Verification and escalation
instructionSections.body: A supervisor should check the sorting decisions as well as the paperwork. A competent worker can point to each stream on a site, explain why a stream is kept apart, name the destination that accepts it and show the receipt. Escalate immediately when a container is leaking, a chemical is unlabelled, sharps are mixed into a green-waste load, or a destination will not confirm acceptance. Do not hide a rejected load or send it somewhere else without authority. Record the rejection and the decision that followed.

lessons.title: Pool cleaning start-up essentials and licence status checklist
learningOutcomes: List the equipment, vehicle, paperwork and office items a pool service needs before its first visit
Identify each start-up step in the US guide and state whether it applies in Australia, with its status
Explain that a course certificate or a registration number is not a licence and must not be implied by the business documents
Complete a start-up readiness list in which every regulatory item is marked as checked or still to be checked

instructionSections.heading: What a pool service needs before its first job
instructionSections.body: The US start-up guide lists the basic items a pool service carries: pool cleaning tools, the chemical products for pool treatment, a vehicle large enough to carry supplies, business cards, invoices, contract forms, a diary, a laptop and a printer. Those practical items apply in Australia too. Add a test kit for sanitiser and pH, a net and skimmer, a vacuum and hoses, brushes, spare seals, and the storage needed to keep chemicals apart from each other and from the vehicle's fuel and from people. The vehicle must carry the chemicals securely.

instructionSections.heading: The licence step: not applicable as written
instructionSections.body: The US guide tells the reader to find out which business licence is needed at the local council office. It also says that a licence protects the business legally, lets it buy supplies at trade prices, and makes clients more inclined to hire. Those points describe US local government and US practice, and they do not apply in Australia. In Australia the registration, licence or competence needed for pool work depends on the state or territory, the council, the kind of pool and the task. This lesson grants no licence and no registration, and it should never be read as implying either.

instructionSections.heading: Pool operator courses are not a licence
instructionSections.body: The US guide describes several training courses for pool operators and technicians, and it lists their fees and certificate terms. Those courses, their certificates, their fees and their validity periods are US-specific. None of them is used or endorsed here. Their names are not repeated as recommendations. Completing any course in Australia is not, by itself, a licence or an authority to operate a pool. See “Licences, permissions and restricted work” for the general licence rules.

instructionSections.heading: Finding staff and telling people about the service
instructionSections.body: The US guide suggests hiring through local advertisements, through friends and family with pool experience, and by using additional help once the business grows. The guide also suggests delivering business cards to acquaintances, approaching apartment communities, condominium managers, real estate agents and banks that hold properties with pools, and advertising in local newspapers. “Marketing, referrals and retention for pool service work” covers the marketing plan.

instructionSections.heading: Readiness list
instructionSections.body: Before the first job, list each item in four groups: practical equipment, vehicle and storage, paperwork and office items, and regulatory status. Every regulatory item is marked either as checked with the source and date, or still to be checked. A start-up is ready only when every equipment item is in place and every regulatory item is either checked or marked clearly as still to be checked, with a named person responsible for confirming it.

lessons.title: Australian service agreement checklist for pool service work
learningOutcomes: Record the client's requirements and special conditions before a price is confirmed
Write a service agreement that states the services, the frequency, the price, the payment terms and the exclusions
State the responsibilities that stay with the owner or operator, including supervision, barriers and water-treatment decisions
Identify the clauses that must be checked against Australian law before use

instructionSections.heading: Meeting the client and recording the details
instructionSections.body: The US guide recommends meeting the client face to face or speaking by phone, noting the services and any special conditions, and asking how often the client wants the work. Offer any extra services you will include, and agree their price before signing. Those steps are sound practice, and they are kept here in Australian terms. Record who makes the decisions, who holds the water-treatment responsibility and whether the site is a home pool, a body corporate pool or a commercial pool. The operator's role and the owner's role are different and must be stated.

instructionSections.heading: Drafting the agreement
instructionSections.body: Draft the agreement in a word processor so you can copy and keep it. The guide advises that it should be easy to read, free of errors, and printed for signing. Include the date, the business name and address, the contact details, and the registration or business number held. Where no number is confirmed, leave the field blank rather than inventing one.

instructionSections.heading: Services, frequency and exclusions
instructionSections.body: Describe each service visit in detail: the pool surfaces, the equipment checked, the baskets emptied, the vacuum, the test readings taken, and the records left. State the visit frequency, whether weekly or monthly. Name the person who supplies chemicals, tools and utensils. State what is excluded: water-treatment decisions outside the operator plan, electrical and gas work, heater repair, liner repair, draining and winterising unless separately agreed. Exclusions protect both parties, and the guide notes that clear written terms prevent misunderstanding.

instructionSections.heading: Price, payment and extras
instructionSections.body: State the price for the service, a breakdown if one is needed, and the payment terms: whether payment is monthly, weekly or fortnightly, the method, and how long the client must pay. Price each extra task separately and agree it in writing before it is done. Do not state any price in a template; set your own prices from your costs, as “Pricing pool visits and service packages” describes.

instructionSections.heading: Access, start date and responsibilities
instructionSections.body: Record the start date, the days and times of service, and any access arrangements, such as gates, codes, keys and animals. State the owner's responsibilities: keeping the water level, supervision of swimmers, barrier and gate condition, and the operator plan. State the operator's responsibilities where a separate operator is named. Copies of the signed agreement must be given to the client ahead of work starts.

instructionSections.heading: Insurance and advice
instructionSections.body: The agreement should not promise a safety outcome, such as safe water or a compliant barrier, that the service cannot deliver. Template contracts and online contract tools named in the guide are US services and are not endorsed. Any template used in Australia must be checked against Australian law by a suitable adviser before use.

lessons.title: Pool service records, invoices and customer paperwork
learningOutcomes: Prepare an invoice with the details needed for pool service work, and leave the tax and business number status blank where not checked.
Keep copies of quotes, agreements, visit records and enquiries in an organised, retrievable way
Connect each invoice to the visit record and agreement it relates to
Explain the privacy and retention points that apply to customer records, and check each one for Australia.

instructionSections.heading: What an invoice must show
instructionSections.body: The US guide advises that invoices are used to bill clients and that each form should carry the business's contact information and a licence number. An invoice in Australia should show the business name, contact details, the date, a unique invoice number, the client, a description of the service and the price, and the total. Do not add a number to an invoice that you have not confirmed.

instructionSections.heading: Linking invoices to visits
instructionSections.body: Every invoice should link to the agreement and to the visit record that supports it. A visit record shows the date, the time, the services done, the readings taken, the tasks not done and the referrals made. The record is the evidence for the charge. Without it, a dispute about the service is hard to resolve. Keep the record and the invoice together, using the same job number.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping copies and organising files
instructionSections.body: The US guide advises keeping copies of every business dealing, including enquiries about the services, in a file that can be accessed when needed. Use one file per client, with the agreement, the visit records, the invoices, the payments and any correspondence. Keep a calendar of visits so that each visit can be matched to its record.

instructionSections.heading: Privacy and customer details
instructionSections.body: Customer records contain names, addresses, phone numbers and access details, such as gate codes. Limit access to people who need it, store records securely, and share customer details only for the service.

instructionSections.heading: Corrections and disputes
instructionSections.body: Never change a past record silently. If an entry is wrong, make a dated correction that states what was changed and why. Keep the original. Send any dispute to the owner or the business owner for decision, and keep the record of the dispute with the job.

lessons.title: Pump and sand filter: parts, flow path and valve settings
learningOutcomes: Trace the water path through a centrifugal pump plus a sand filter and its multi-position valve
State what each valve setting does and which settings must never be used while the unit is on
Explain why a filter takes out particles but does not disinfect the water
Identify the warning labels and keep them in place, readable and undamaged

instructionSections.heading: How the parts connect
instructionSections.body: Picture the reference unit as four linked stages. A centrifugal pump, with an electric motor driving it, starts the flow. Water enters through a lidded lint and hair catcher whose basket catches the larger objects, then leaves the pump through its discharge port. A hose runs that flow to the control valve sitting on top of a fast-flow sand filter. Inside, the sand catches debris on its upper face, the water seeps through the bed, climbs a central tube, and goes out through the valve on its way to the pool again. As debris piles up the gauge reading rises and the return flow falls. That is the signal that a backwash is due, and “Backwash triggers, rinse and chemical cleaning for the sand bed” explains how to carry one out.

instructionSections.heading: The valve settings and what they do
instructionSections.body: The six-way valve gives six working settings and one winterising setting. Filter is the normal running setting: flow passes down through the sand and to the pool again. Backwash reverses the flow through the bed and sends it to waste. Rinse follows a backwash and settles the bed before the water goes to waste. Waste bypasses the filter and empties to the waste connection, which suits vacuuming to waste or drawing the level down. Recirculate sends water round the filter without passing it through the sand. The closed setting stops all flow. The manual is emphatic that the pump must never run against a closed valve, because the air-relief path stops working and pressure can build dangerously. A pump run with no flow is also heavily damaged, and the NO FLOW position must never be chosen while the motor is energised.

instructionSections.heading: What a filter cannot do
instructionSections.body: A sand filter takes suspended matter above the waterline. It does not disinfect the pool. Disinfection is a separate step, and the chemistry must be kept in balance for the water to stay clear. Chemistry decisions rest with a qualified pool service or the operator. The manufacturer also states a minimum circulation volume per day.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure and warning labels
instructionSections.body: The manufacturer warns that the system runs under pressure. If it is put together wrongly, or if air is trapped in the circulation side, parts can separate and cause serious harm. A warning label is attached to the filter body and must stay there. Any safety label that has become unreadable or is missing needs replacing. The manual forbids testing a filter with air or any gas under pressure, since compressed gas stores energy and can cause severe injury if a component fails.

instructionSections.heading: Why loss of flow matters
instructionSections.body: A filter that stops running, or that filters poorly, leaves the water cloudy. Cloudy water hides the floor, so a swimmer may dive into or onto something they cannot see, with a risk of serious injury or drowning. Treat any loss of flow or clarity as a same-day report, as “Supervision, behaviour rules and drowning prevention at home pools” explains.

lessons.title: Pump and filter installation checks
learningOutcomes: Check the base, placement and access for a pump and filter before the unit is connected
Confirm that the filter sand, the valve and the clamp match the manufacturer's specification
Use thread sealant and fittings that suit plastic pipe and avoid petroleum-based products
Refuse to connect the unit to any pump that exceeds the filter or the valve pressure limit

instructionSections.heading: Siting and access
instructionSections.body: The manual asks for a level, firm base, near the pool, with room and light for routine maintenance. A sand filter holding water and media is heavy, so plan the lift and use help and suitable equipment. Keep electrical controls off the filter. Whoever starts the pump must be able to move away from the filter before it runs.

instructionSections.heading: Media and internal parts
instructionSections.body: Use only the sand type the manufacturer names, in the quantity on the nameplate. Substituting other media changes how the filter performs and is not allowed. Before pouring sand, check the underdrain at the base for cracked or loose laterals, which can be damaged in transit. Half fill the tank with water first, pour the sand slowly so that its weight does not break the laterals, and take out the sand guide once the level is right. Wipe any sand off the upper section of the tank, plus the valve seat.

instructionSections.heading: Valve seating and clamp
instructionSections.body: Place the valve on the tank flange with its o-ring in position, orienting it so the ports face where you need them. Push the valve fully down so the two flanges meet. Fit the plastic clamp across both flanges, seating the screws and nuts in the retainer slots. Tighten the clamp screws and check the joint by eye. The manual warns that a badly assembled tank valve can come off and cause serious injury or damage, so check the clamp before every start.

instructionSections.heading: Ports, pressure ceiling and fittings
instructionSections.body: Each valve port is marked for its connection: pump discharge to the pump port, waste line to the waste port, pool return to the return port. The nameplate gives the top working pressure, and the manual forbids connecting the filter or its valve to any pump that could exceed it. Use sealant on tapered pipe threads, but only a type suited to plastic. Avoid petroleum-based products. Tighten threaded fittings by hand and then a small further turn, without forcing them, because tapered plastic threads crack under excess force. Fit the pressure gauge in the port opposite the pump port. The suction line should be no narrower than the pump inlet.

instructionSections.heading: Chemical storage distance
instructionSections.body: The manual asks that pool chemicals never be stored within a stated distance of the pump, filter or valve, and that they be kept cool, dry and well ventilated. Fumes and spills from chemicals corrode filter and pump parts, and weakened parts can come loose. The distance in the manual is product-specific and is not used here.

lessons.title: Start-up, air bleeding and priming a pump and filter
learningOutcomes: Carry out the start-up sequence in the order the manual sets, with the valve and pump changes in the right order
Open and shut the air bleeder safely, and recognise when a constant flow of water shows that air is cleared
Prime a pump correctly and explain why a dry pump and a low pool level cause damage
Record the operating pressure at the time the filter was cleaned as the reference for later backwash decisions

instructionSections.heading: Before the first start
instructionSections.body: Clean out a new pool prior to it is filled, because heavy dirt and big particles can harm the pump plus the sand filter. Check that the backwash hose is open so water can run to waste. Turn the valve to backwash. Fill the pump pot with water before the pump is started. Keep the vents on the underside of the motor free of debris so the motor can cool. Check the valve clamp. A clamp that is not fully closed, or air in the filter, can let the valve top come off with serious injury or damage.

instructionSections.heading: Running dry and the test cord
instructionSections.body: Never operate the pump without water in it. Dry running damages the seals and the housing, and it can let water escape and flood the area. The manufacturer also supplies a test cord, which is for a brief operating check and is not a permanent supply. The time limit for the test cord is set for that product and is not used here. Use the cord only as directed and only for the period the manual allows.

instructionSections.heading: Bleeding air and starting
instructionSections.body: Open the bleeder mounted on the filter, move away from the filter, and switch the pump on so that it can prime. Close the bleeder once water comes out in a steady stream with no air in it. Stop the pump, then turn the valve to filter. Check that every suction and return line is clear. Open the bleeder again, move clear, start the pump, and close the bleeder once the flow is steady. The unit is now filtering. Make sure the outflow reaches the pool, then record the gauge reading taken while the filter is unused and clean. That reading is the reference for every later backwash decision.

instructionSections.heading: New sand and the first backwash
instructionSections.body: Sand is washed before dispatch, but transport can still wear it, so the manufacturer asks for a longer first backwash, continued until the water runs clear. The handbook adds that once a new pool is running, its filter needs a backwash and a clean after the initial runs to clear construction debris. Small bubbles that appear in the pool just after a start or a backwash are normal for a short time. If they keep coming, check the water depth and the strainer lid, as “Pump strainer, suction valves and the vacuum route” describes.

instructionSections.heading: Priming a pump that will not pump
instructionSections.body: The UK handbook says a pump that will not prime usually has an air leak ahead of it. Typical causes are a strainer lid that is not sealed, a union that is not fully tight, or a missing gasket. Confirm that the pool has water in it before you try, because priming a dry pump in a pool with low water can cause expensive damage. Shut the valves ahead of the pump; then set the multiport valve to waste, fill the strainer to the brim, refit the lid firmly, and switch the pump on. Open one suction valve. If the pump does not begin moving water soon after, stop it, close the valve, then try again. Open the other valve only once the first is working, and do it gradually. Log every attempt.

lessons.title: Backwash triggers, rinse and chemical cleaning for the sand bed
learningOutcomes: Choose the backwash trigger the manual names and explain why a timer alone is not a trigger
Carry out a backwash and rinse in the order the manual gives, with the pump off at each valve change
Describe the chemical cleaning steps for a sand bed in addition to the precautions they need
Decide when a sand bed needs chemical cleaning and when it must be referred

instructionSections.heading: Deciding when to backwash
instructionSections.body: The manufacturer offers three ways to decide. The most precise, on a unit that has a flow meter gives a drop in flow of a stated share from the clean-filter flow. A rougher method is to watch the flow from the pool's return fittings and backwash when it weakens. The most common, and least precise, is to backwash once the gauge climbs a stated amount above the clean-filter reading. The manufacturer warns against using a timer alone, and notes that backwashing too often also reduces filtration. Weather, rain, dust, pollen and water temperature all change how fast a filter loads. The proportions and amounts are specific to the product and are not used here, so work from the manual for the unit in front of you.

instructionSections.heading: Backwash and rinse
instructionSections.body: Stop the pump. Confirm that the intake and backwash hoses are unobstructed, turn the valve to backwash, move clear, and switch the pump on. Keep backwashing until the waste water runs clear, which is the manufacturer's end point. Stop the pump, turn the valve to rinse, move clear, and run the pump briefly to settle the bed before stopping it again. Turn the valve to filter, confirm the return line is clear, open the bleeder, switch the pump on, then close the bleeder once the flow is steady. Note the filter pressure. It must not rise above the figure recorded when the filter was first started. If it is still higher after a proper backwash, the bed needs a chemical clean.

instructionSections.heading: Chemically cleaning the bed
instructionSections.body: The manufacturer names cleaners that strip grease, scale and rust from the sand in a single operation. Those product names are American and are not used here. Choose a sand-bed cleaner that is listed for the filter and approved for use in Australia, and read its label and safety data sheet before opening it. Mix it exactly as the label directs. Backwash first. If the filter sits below pool level, stop the pump, then close the valves so the pool cannot drain. Open the filter drain and let the tank empty. Turn the valve to backwash, take off the pump strainer lid, and confirm the backwash hoses are clear. With the pump operating, pour the solution slowly into the strainer until the sand is saturated. Stop the pump, then leave the filter on backwash for the soak period the manual gives. Refit the lid and finish with a normal backwash. The cleaning solution must stay beyond the pool edge.

instructionSections.heading: Looking after yourself during the clean
instructionSections.body: The cleaning solution is a chemical. Wear the protective equipment named in its safety data sheet, including eye protection and gloves. Pouring a corrosive or irritating liquid into a running strainer risks splashes, so pour slowly, keep the lid area clear, and keep the solution beyond the pool edge. The manufacturer warns that chemical fumes and spills corrode the filter and the pump parts, and that corroded parts can fail. Store unused cleaner separately, as “Pool chemical handling and storage at home” describes.

instructionSections.heading: When to refer
instructionSections.body: If the pressure is still too high after a proper backwash and a correct chemical clean, or the flow stays weak, refer the filter to the owner or operator. A worn or cracked valve, a damaged bed or a suspected internal fault is not a routine task. Record the readings before and after each step, and the reason for the referral.

lessons.title: Electrical connection, bonding and motor safety for a pool pump
learningOutcomes: Identify the electrical hazards of a pool pump and explain why isolation comes before any work
Describe the protective devices and bonding requirements in the manual and state which parts are product-specific and not applicable in Australia
Recognise a damaged or unsuitable cord, a wrong voltage and an extension lead, and refer each one
State the electrical tasks that must be carried out by a licensed electrical worker and that this lesson grants no licence

instructionSections.heading: Why a pump counts as live
instructionSections.body: According to the manufacturer, the pump draws electrical power and can produce both suction and pressure within the water system. Wired and plumbed correctly, it works safely. The electrical hazard exists whenever the pump is connected to supply, whether or not it is turning. A switched-off pump can still be live. Treat every pump as live until its supply has been isolated, tested and confirmed off.

instructionSections.heading: Protective devices and bonding
instructionSections.body: The manufacturer asks for a residual current device at the supply point. It also describes bonding that ties the motor, the metal parts of the pool, metal conduit and any metal pipework to a single common conductor. That document refers to a United States electrical code, which does not apply in Australia. Its conductor sizes, breaker ratings and voltage-drop tables are specific to the product and to the US, and they are not used here.

instructionSections.heading: Matching the supply
instructionSections.body: Wire the motor to the voltage on its wiring diagram. Connecting the wrong voltage damages the motor and voids the warranty. Keep the cable run as short as practical and sized so the voltage at the pump does not sag enough to cause harm. Confirm the supply voltage before connection and record it. Never alter the motor wiring to suit a supply you have not verified.

instructionSections.heading: Cords, plugs and extension leads
instructionSections.body: A cord-connected unit must plug only into an earthed socket protected by a residual current device. If that protection cannot be confirmed, call a qualified electrician. Keep the cord out of the earth, clear of mowers and trimmers, and do not run it through an extension lead. Replace a damaged cord without delay. The supplied test cord is for checking operation before installation and must not be used as a permanent connection.

instructionSections.heading: Work on the pump, with the motor
instructionSections.body: Keep hands off the pump whenever it is energised or still connected to power, because dangerous voltage can cause serious or fatal injury. Earth the motor before it is connected to supply, and never earth it to a gas pipe. Motor servicing is for a motor service centre. Electrical isolation, wiring and motor replacement are licensed work in most places, and this lesson grants no licence for them.

instructionSections.heading: Symptoms that need a licensed person
instructionSections.body: The UK handbook says that if an electric motor refuses to start, the fuse should be checked. A motor that hums may have a jammed impeller, in which case the supply is cut and the maintenance company is called. Those are the points where a service worker stops and refers. Do not open the motor, its terminal box or any control enclosure.

lessons.title: Component care, inspection and seasonal shutdown of a pump and filter
learningOutcomes: Carry out a visual structural inspection of the filter, valve and pump components and decide what must be replaced
Replace the valve top with its diverter assembly in the order the manual gives, using the correct lubricant
Explain why a pressure vessel is never serviced under pressure
Prepare equipment for a seasonal shutdown, with the freezing and antifreeze rules for the climate and the manual

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning and inspection
instructionSections.body: Wash the outer surface of the pump plus filter assembly using a gentle cleanser in water, then rinse. Solvents are not to be used. At each service, check the parts for soundness. Corroded, bent or visibly defective items can let the filter cover or its fittings come off, with serious injury or damage as the result. Replace any such part and record the replacement. Clean the pump strainer basket at the interval set out in “Pump strainer, suction valves and the vacuum route”, and inspect its O-ring, swapping it out if it is worn. The pump seal needs no lubricant. Motor work is reserved for a motor service centre.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure and restarting
instructionSections.body: A filter is a pressurised vessel and must never be opened or serviced while it holds pressure. Release the tank pressure, then open the air bleeder before any work begins. When the unit is restarted after work, open the bleeder and move away from the filter, as “Start-up, air bleeding and priming a pump and filter” sets out.

instructionSections.heading: Replacing the valve top plus diverter
instructionSections.body: If the valve stops working properly, the usual remedy is to replace the valve top plus diverter as one assembly. Stop the pump, then open the bleeder to release internal pressure. Turn the handle to winterise, remove the six cover screws with their washers and nuts, and lift the valve top away with the diverter. The diverter carries the sealing gasket, so handle it with care to protect the sealing face. Wipe the valve body sealing face with a soft lint-free cloth and check it for scratches or nicks. A damaged face means the valve body needs replacing. Grease the replacement valve top O-ring with silicone grease or soapy solution, never a petroleum product. Set the new handle to winterise, align the recess with the small bump on the body, fit all six screws with washers, and tighten them in a crossing sequence until they are snug. Do not overtighten.

instructionSections.heading: Seasonal shutdown
instructionSections.body: The manufacturer's shutdown steps are written for freezing climates. They cover backwashing, setting the valve to winterise, removing the drain plug, draining the pump body and pipework, and protecting the equipment from the weather. Where a shutdown is required, follow the operator's written instruction. Keep the valve on winterise during shutdown so the diverter does not press against its seal.

instructionSections.heading: Antifreeze and covers
instructionSections.body: If emptying the pump is not possible, the manufacturer permits only propylene glycol as an antifreeze, because other antifreezes are very poisonous and will harm the pump. Use no other kind. Shelter the equipment from the weather with a canvas cover or sheeting, but do not wrap the motor in plastic, since condensation can build up inside it. A dry, sheltered location is best for a removable pump.

lessons.title: Weekly home pool routine and water level
learningOutcomes: Set out a fixed weekly visit sequence for a home pool and mark each task as done, skipped or referred
Confirm the water level against the minimum height at the skimmer opening and explain why a low level harms the pump
Empty and inspect skimmer and strainer baskets and decide when a basket needs attention before the next visit
Name the tasks a routine visit does not cover and the written instruction needed before they start

instructionSections.heading: Why a fixed weekly sequence matters
instructionSections.body: A home pool needs a short visit that repeats the same way each week more than it needs a large occasional effort. The UK handbook behind this lesson describes a weekly routine that takes only a short time when the pool and plant are well designed. The routine works because the same tasks happen in the same order, so a skipped step becomes visible quickly. Choose a set day and record every visit on the same form. Readings and observations then line up across weeks, and a change in water level, debris or filter pressure can be seen rather than remembered. The handbook is a 2011 UK document. Its times, products and temperatures are not Australian facts. What transfers is the sequence and the reason for each step.

instructionSections.heading: Confirm the water level before anything runs
instructionSections.body: Read the water level before the pump is started. The pump draws water through the skimmer opening, and when the level falls below the point the skimmer weir needs, the pump begins to draw air. Air in the suction line stops circulation and can harm the pump. Water leaves a pool through splashing, evaporation and backwashing, so in hot weather the level can drop noticeably in a week. Top up only to the level the equipment is designed for and the operator plan allows. If you cannot see the skimmer weir or the level is unclear, avoid running the pump until the level is confirmed. Write the level and any top-up on the record. A large top-up every week can indicate a leak, and that is a referral item rather than a routine task.

instructionSections.heading: Baskets, strainers and skimming
instructionSections.body: Empty the skimmer basket plus inspect the pump strainer basket at the frequency the site plan sets. Where trees overhang the pool, leaves and blossom can fill a skimmer basket quickly, so the visit frequency may need to rise in some seasons. The skimmer catches floating debris and the filter traps the fine particles that pass it. A full basket reduces flow. The UK handbook sets a weekly check for the pump strainer, while the manufacturer manual for one pump sets a more frequent interval. Where the two differ, use the more frequent interval unless the operator plan sets another. Before closing a strainer lid, check the lid seal and the O-ring. Torn mesh, cracked lids or a damaged seal go to the owner or operator for replacement.

instructionSections.heading: The chemistry check and what the visit may change
instructionSections.body: Test sanitiser and pH using the kit method the owner or operator has agreed. Read the colour in daylight against a white background, compare it with the card in the kit, and record the reading as a value with the time, method and tester. Compare the result with the target in the written plan. The handbook says to check pH and sanitiser before use, even on a pool that is serviced regularly. Make only the adjustments the plan allows for the visit. Cloudy water changes which readings can be trusted, so record the cloudiness and refer it. The disinfection and pH decisions themselves are covered in “Disinfection chemistry and pH interpretation”, and the dosing rules are covered in “Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention”.

instructionSections.heading: Tasks a routine visit does not include
instructionSections.body: Do not empty a pool to clean it or to lower its level without professional advice. Water pressure from the ground can push a concrete shell upward and can lift or displace a liner. An empty pool is also more dangerous for anyone who falls in, because injuries are more likely than in a full pool. Winterising, equipment repair, electrical work and gas work all sit outside a routine visit. Each of them needs a separate written instruction and, where it applies, the licence described in the licence notices of “Pool chemical handling and storage at home”, “Home pool heating systems: operation and safe limits” and “Home pool troubleshooting and liner repair”. A routine visit records what was checked. It does not show that the water is safe to use.

lessons.title: Supervision, behaviour rules and drowning prevention at home pools
learningOutcomes: Describe the supervision rules for children and non-swimmers at a home pool and state which ones a service worker can enforce
Identify the handbook rules on diving, horseplay, depth marking and glass near the pool
Explain why no cover, gate or device is treated as a complete drowning control
Record drowning-prevention advice given to an owner and the points that need the owner's action

instructionSections.heading: Drowning is the main hazard at a home pool
instructionSections.body: A home pool is a drowning hazard before it is a cleaning job. Water can be dangerous even in shallow depth, and a small child can drown in a small amount of water. The UK handbook behind this lesson makes the point that the most effective defence is constant supervision, teaching and common sense, not one device. Your visit is a chance to look at the safety arrangements and to tell the owner what they must keep doing. You do not take over supervision during a visit, and you do not assume that a barrier is adequate because it exists. Note what you see, tell the owner, and refer barrier questions to the owner or to the relevant authority.

instructionSections.heading: Supervision and the people who use the pool
instructionSections.body: Every member of a household should be taught to swim as early as is practical. Small children should be kept away from the water unless an adult is present, and they should enter only when an adult says they may. Adults watch swimmers continuously while the pool is open for use, and that includes older swimmers. Watching people in the water is not the same as keeping the whole pool in view, so the rule is that a named, responsible adult watches the water continuously. Never allow small children to swim unsupervised. Visitors' children should come onto the grounds only by invitation and when an adult has agreed to supervise them.

instructionSections.heading: Behaviour rules at the pool
instructionSections.body: The handbook sets rules you can check and reinforce on a visit. Ban horseplay and bombing, do not run around the edge of the pool, plus do not push or hold other people under the water. Dive only from the designated place, which is the place designed for diving. Mark the deep and shallow ends clearly, and display diving prohibitions where the pool has no designed diving area. Keep glass containers and glass products beyond the pool edge surround, because broken glass causes cuts and can enter the water. These rules only protect people when they are enforced, so record which rules the owner's household is not following on the day.

instructionSections.heading: What a barrier cannot do on its own
instructionSections.body: Gates, covers, alarms, moving floors and fences all depend on people. A gate has to be closed and locked, a safety cover has to be placed over the pool once nobody is using it, and a moving floor has to be locked in position. The handbook states that no single product is a foolproof safety device. Treat every barrier as one layer and never describe a pool as safe because it has a cover, fence or device. Barrier design, height, gate and alarm requirements are set by state, territory and council rules. The pool-standards lessons that cover them are not part of this set.

instructionSections.heading: Clear water is a safety condition
instructionSections.body: The water needs to be clear enough to see the whole bottom at all times. If you cannot see the bottom, the pool must not be used until the cause is found and corrected. Poor clarity can come from low filtration, unbalanced chemistry or a filter that needs cleaning, and the handbook links clarity directly to safety. Report the cause to the owner or operator. Do not decide that a pool is usable because the surface looks acceptable from the edge.

instructionSections.heading: Insurance and written advice
instructionSections.body: The handbook suggests that the owner ask an insurer about public liability cover for the pool plus its equipment. Give the owner drowning-prevention advice in writing, date it, and record the owner's response. Do not give legal or liability advice.

lessons.title: Sand filter backwash, rinse and return to filter
learningOutcomes: Explain what a sand filter removes and why the pressure gauge decides when to backwash
Carry out a backwash, rinse and return-to-filter sequence in the order set by the manufacturer manual
State the rule that the multiport valve is never moved while the pump runs, and explain why
Record the reference pressure on a clean filter and the post-backwash pressure, and refer a filter that will not clean

instructionSections.heading: What the filter is for
instructionSections.body: A sand filter holds back the fine material that the skimmer plus the baskets let through. Water moves down through a bed of sand, then climbs a central pipe on its way back. Debris builds up in the bed over time, the gauge reading goes up, and the return flow shrinks. The UK handbook behind this lesson asks for a daily turnover in the bathing season and gives run times for it. The product manual sets a minimum turnover of its own and defers to local health rules. The operator plan and the equipment maker's manual are the references for run time.

instructionSections.heading: Deciding that a backwash is due
instructionSections.body: Backwash when the gauge has climbed past the reference reading you took after the previous backwash, or when a flow meter shows the drop that the manual names as the trigger. The handbook and the manual use different pressure increases, and the manual also gives a flow-based trigger, so use the manual for the unit in front of you. The manual cautions against backwashing on a timer, since frequent backwashing reduces filtration. Rain, pollen, wind and bather load all change how fast the bed fills. Write the reference reading, the trigger you used and the date on the record.

instructionSections.heading: Running the valve through its settings
instructionSections.body: Stop the pump, the heater and any cleaner before the valve is touched. Attach the waste hose if one is fitted. Put the handle on backwash, start the pump and let it run until the sight glass shows clear water. Stop the pump, turn the handle to rinse, run the pump briefly to settle the bed, then halt it. Put the handle on filter, open the return line, open the air bleeder, switch the pump on, then close the bleeder once the outflow is steady. Read the gauge and note it. Both sources use the same order: backwash, rinse, then filter, with the pump stopped at each change.

instructionSections.heading: Why the handle is never moved under flow
instructionSections.body: The multiport handle must not be moved while the unit is running. The handbook says so plainly, and the manual asks for the pump to be stopped before any valve change. Moving the handle under flow can wear the spider gasket and damage the valve seal. The manual also warns that a clamp which is not fully closed can let the valve top come off under pressure. Turn the handle in one direction only, since reversing it wears the gasket. Stop the pump at its switch, check that it has stopped, and only then move the handle.

instructionSections.heading: Early runs in a new pool
instructionSections.body: Once a new pool is filled, backwash the filter, then clean it again after the first few runs, because construction debris can clog the bed. The manual asks for a longer first backwash, because transport can wear the sand. After any backwash, hold the filter in filter position until the water is clear, and then go back to the routine. If the water remains cloudy after backwashing, look at the chemistry before extending the run time.

instructionSections.heading: When the bed will not clean
instructionSections.body: If the pressure remains well above the reference after a proper backwash, or the flow stays weak, the bed may need a chemical clean. “Backwash triggers, rinse and chemical cleaning for the sand bed” covers that work, which needs the product named in the manual, its safety data sheet and a safe method. Do not add cleaner while the filter is connected to the circuit. Do not open or service the tank before the pressure has been released, as “Component care, inspection and seasonal shutdown of a pump and filter” describes. If the fault persists after a correct backwash, refer it to the owner or operator.

lessons.title: Pump strainer, suction valves and the vacuum route
learningOutcomes: Open and close a pump strainer in the correct order without drawing air into the system
Set the the valves on the intake side for normal circulation and for vacuuming
Explain the risk from a blocked suction fitting and the supervision rule that follows
Stop the pump, then isolate power before any work on the pump or its motor

instructionSections.heading: The job of the pump strainer
instructionSections.body: The strainer basket sits ahead of the pump together with stops debris before it reaches the impeller, where it could cause damage. The UK handbook makes that point. To open the strainer, release the lid's screw thread or clamp and lift the lid off. First close the suction valves ahead of the pump together with set the multiport valve, so that water in the pipework does not drain back out. Reopen the valves after the lid goes back on. Check the lid seal and the O-ring. A worn seal lets air into the pump, which lowers the flow and makes priming harder.

instructionSections.heading: Valve positions at the intake
instructionSections.body: Most installations fit a small group of valves on the intake side. One serves the skimmer line and another the main drain. With normal circulation both ought to be fully open. When vacuuming via the skimmer, open the skimmer valve fully and close the main drain valve. A separate vacuum point has its own valve, and that valve is set to suit the route in use. Balance the flow by opening the valves gradually until the straining sound from the pump stops. Never start the pump with the valves in a position you have not checked.

instructionSections.heading: Blocked suction outlets
instructionSections.body: A blocked suction fitting can cause serious or fatal drowning. A suction outlet can hold a person firmly, so a blocked outlet is an entrapment risk. The product manual says young children who use pool equipment need a responsible adult watching them at all times, and must not use the product only when they are under constant adult supervision. Before a swim, confirm that the outlets and the strainer are clear, and refer any cracked or missing outlet cover to the owner or operator. Do not fit or remove an outlet cover unless the owner has given written instruction and supplied the correct part.

instructionSections.heading: Isolating power before pump work
instructionSections.body: Keep hands off the pump whenever it is energised or still connected to power. Dangerous voltage can cause serious or fatal injury. Switch the pump off at its isolator, confirm the supply is dead, and only then open the strainer or the motor housing. Motor servicing belongs to a motor service centre. The handbook notes that if a motor refuses to start, the fuse should be checked, and that a humming motor may have a jammed impeller. In that case, cut the power supply and contact the maintenance company. Electrical work itself is covered in “Electrical connection, bonding and motor safety for a pool pump”.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the valve settings
instructionSections.body: Note the position of every valve before you change anything, so that the system can be restored to its normal state. A valve left in the wrong setting is a common reason for weak flow, and the fault often goes unnoticed until the next visit. Record the strainer condition, the state of the lid seal, the valve settings and the gauge reading when you finish.

lessons.title: Vacuuming, vacuum to waste and automated cleaners
learningOutcomes: Set up a pool vacuum through the skimmer or a vacuum point and remove trapped air from the hose
Vacuum at the speed and direction that keeps debris from being stirred back into suspension
Choose between normal vacuuming and vacuum to waste, and explain the effect on the water depth
Remove automated cleaners, hoses and cables from the pool prior to any swimming, and record it

instructionSections.heading: Setting up the vacuum
instructionSections.body: Fit the vacuum head to the pole and the hose, then lower the head into the water beside the skimmer. Lower the hose gradually gradually so the water fills it and the trapped air rises out of the open end, which sits above the waterline. Connect the line to the skimmer via an adaptor plate fitted to the skimmer or, if no plate is fitted, take out the skimmer basket plus push the hose into the suction opening at the foot of the skimmer. A vacuum point takes the hose directly. The UK handbook lists leaves in the skimmer, a kinked hose, a choked strainer or an unprimed pump as the usual reasons for poor suction, and it names a dirty filter as the most frequent one.

instructionSections.heading: Technique and flow balance
instructionSections.body: Once the hose is connected, open the vacuum valve fully and partly close the other suction valves until the flow is balanced. A straining sound from the pump means the balance is off. Open the valves gradually until the sound stops. Never lift the head above the waterline while the unit is running, since the pump can lose its prime. Work the head slowly over the floor and up any slope. Moving it quickly stirs the dirt back into the water. Suction weakens as the filter loads, and a backwash, as “Sand filter backwash, rinse and return to filter” describes, usually restores it.

instructionSections.heading: Vacuuming to waste
instructionSections.body: Where the floor is heavily soiled, vacuum to waste so the debris skips the filter. Start in the usual way, then halt the pump; then set the multiport valve to waste, open any waste valve, and restart. Water is drawn out and discharged through the waste outlet, bypassing the filter. The pool level falls during this, so overfill before starting and top up when you finish. Record the estimated volume removed, because it affects the water balance and the chemistry.

instructionSections.heading: Automated cleaners and entanglement
instructionSections.body: Automated cleaners come as vacuum, pressure or self-contained electric types. Electric units contain strainers and filters which need regular attention, so the owner should know which type is installed. The handbook is clear that hoses, cables and cleaners must be taken beyond the pool edge before anyone enters it, because they can tangle or trap a swimmer underwater. Record the removal at the close of the visit, and tell the owner if a cleaner has been left in.

instructionSections.heading: Liner pools and footing
instructionSections.body: On a liner pool, discourage standing on steep slopes, particularly in warm water, because feet can crease a pliable liner. Use only the waterline cleaner the liner maker recommends. Avoid household cleaners, concentrated acid, steel wool and metal brushes, all of which damage the finish. Keep the water temperature within the limit the liner maker sets.

lessons.title: Pool chemical handling and storage at home
learningOutcomes: Read the label and safety data sheet for a pool chemical before it is handled
Explain why chemicals are never mixed before they are added to the water, plus the risk involved
Pre-dissolve and add a chemical in the order and manner the label and the handbook describe
Store and separate chemicals so that children, incompatible products and the filter equipment are protected

instructionSections.heading: Why these products are hazardous
instructionSections.body: The UK handbook states that every pool chemical is potentially dangerous and needs careful handling. Each container carries the instructions for use and storage, and those instructions take precedence over habit or memory. Combining products before they reach the water can release a toxic gas or cause an explosion, and the handbook says this must never happen. The safety data sheet for each product lists its hazards, first aid, protective equipment and storage rules. Read it before handling the product and keep it where it is reachable reached on site.

instructionSections.heading: Adding a product safely
instructionSections.body: Dissolve each product on its own in a dedicated, labelled bucket filled with water drawn from the pool. Stir with a wooden or plastic paddle and pour the solution slowly near an inlet or around the edge of the pool, so it spreads without splashing. Undissolved product can mark the pool finish, so it must never be tipped in as a lump. Rinse the container in the pool once it has each use and avoid using it for a different product. Wash your hands afterwards, and keep children away from the chemicals throughout.

instructionSections.heading: Containers and storage
instructionSections.body: Never move a one chemical into the container meant for another product, and never reuse a used container from a different product. Keep the chemicals in a dry, cool, lockable place and separate each type from the others. The product manual for the filter asks for pool chemicals to be kept a stated distance from the filter, the pump together with the valve. Keep the store ventilated and away from fuel and heat.

instructionSections.heading: Empty containers and surplus product
instructionSections.body: The handbook directs that empty containers be rinsed in pool water and then discarded. Its household disposal route is UK practice and must not be used in Australia until the Australian disposal rules have been confirmed. Dispose of containers and surplus product by the route the label and the local authority require, and record which route you used. Never pour surplus product down a drain or onto the ground.

instructionSections.heading: What this lesson does not authorise
instructionSections.body: This lesson does not grant a licence, permit or authority to handle, store or transport dangerous goods, and it does not replace the operator's instruction or the product's safety data sheet. Treatment decisions are covered in “Disinfection chemistry and pH interpretation” and “Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention”.

lessons.title: Home pool heating systems: operation and safe limits
learningOutcomes: Describe how a heat pump, an electric heater, a gas heater, an oil-fired heat exchanger and a solar collector heat pool water
Explain why every heater needs water flow and why thermostat, time clock and flow switch settings are checked
Identify the safety devices on a gas heater and what each one does
Name the installation and connection work that needs a licensed person and state that this lesson grants no licence

instructionSections.heading: Heating needs water moving through it
instructionSections.body: A pool heater transfers heat to the water passing through it, so the filter pump has to be running before any heater can work. The UK handbook makes this point directly: the heater does nothing unless the circulation pump is moving water. Confirm that the pump is operating and the flow is steady before you read the heater settings. Low flow trips the safety devices and leaves the heater off. That is a flow problem first, not a heater fault to be reset again and again.

instructionSections.heading: Heat pumps and electric heaters
instructionSections.body: A heat pump operates like a refrigerator running in reverse. A fan draws air across a coil holding a fluid that boils at a low temperature, a compressor raises the vapour's temperature, and a heat exchanger hands that heat to the pool's water. Keep the face of the unit free of covering, and keep the air path across the plant room and out of it unobstructed. Condensate from the drain tube is a normal sign that the unit is working. An electric heater works something like a large kettle and shows indicator lights for its elements and its supply. Some sites run the heater on an off-peak supply through a time clock, and a power interruption can reset that clock, so check it after any outage.

instructionSections.heading: Gas heaters and their safety devices
