instructionSections.body: A gas heater has an isolator on the control panel, its own on and off switch, a thermostat, and a gas tap on the supply. Three safety devices protect it. An over-temperature thermostat shuts the heater down when it overheats and resets when it cools. A gas safety shut-off valve closes the supply if the pilot or flame goes out, and the heater then has to be relit. A pressure switch stops the heater when water flow stops and resets once flow returns. Never bypass, tape over or alter these devices. In South Australia, gas fitting work on a gas heater, including a pool heater, must be done by a person holding a gas fitter's registration under the Plumbers, Gas Fitters and Electricians Act 1995, with flue, gas supply and ventilation part of that work.

instructionSections.heading: Oil, solar and thermostat settings
instructionSections.body: Oil heaters either pass the pool water straight through or heat it through an exchanger. The handbook warns that flues must not end close to windows or property boundaries, and that the oil level must be checked because many call-outs come from an empty tank. Solar collectors are regulated by a differential device that compares water and air temperature, and the collectors work best with enough flow through them. Set a thermostat above the water temperature to call for heat, and the heater stops once the pool reaches that setting. Do not change a thermostat to force a result without the owner's written instruction.

instructionSections.heading: Who may install and connect
instructionSections.body: Gas installation, gas connection and flue work are limited to licensed or registered persons. Electrical connection of any heater needs a licensed electrician, who should confirm the supply before installation. Oil and boiler work needs the appropriate qualified trade. This lesson grants no licence, registration or authority to install, connect, service, repair or adjust a heater.

lessons.title: Pool covers: handling, storage and the limits of a cover
learningOutcomes: Identify heat-retaining, winter debris and power-operated covers and what each is for
Explain why no cover is a complete safety control and what other measures the owner must consider
Handle, roll, clean and store a cover so that it is not damaged and does not become a hazard
Record the state of the cover and any referral needed for a lockable or power-operated cover

instructionSections.heading: Cover types
instructionSections.body: Heat-retaining covers rest on the surface, cut evaporation and the heat lost to cold wind, and need no fixings. Bubble covers are a common heat-retaining type. Winter debris covers are stretched across the pool, keep leaves and blossom out, and are fixed to the surround. Power-operated covers can be locked and come in fabric or slatted plastic. The UK handbook notes that floating covers keep much debris out, but debris can drop back in when the cover is lifted. Identify the cover type before you handle it.

instructionSections.heading: A cover is not a complete safety control
instructionSections.body: The UK handbook is direct that no swimming pool cover is a complete safety control. A safety cover only protects when it is laid over the pool while nobody is using it, and only when it is checked and kept in working order. A winter debris cover, even one in sound condition and firmly anchored, must not be relied on for any level of safety. In some cases fencing or other measures are needed, and that is judged case by case. Supervision still applies whenever the pool is open, as “Supervision, behaviour rules and drowning prevention at home pools” explains. Record what you see, and never describe a cover as a barrier or certify it.

instructionSections.heading: Handling and rolling
instructionSections.body: Use a suitable roller to make a cover easier to manage. A cover should not be left rolled or folded, and never left in strong sunlight in that state, because the material can be damaged. Lift a floating cover slowly so debris sitting on it does not drop back into the water gradually a cover left on the pool during icy weather deteriorates, so take it off or inspect it during cold spells.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning and storage
instructionSections.body: Before storage, clear away all debris and wash the cover. Avoid solvents, because they make the material shrink. Store it somewhere sheltered, away from heat and concentrated chemicals. Keep a winter debris cover above the waterline where possible. A heavy snow load can press the cover down onto the water, which then carries the weight. If a cover has frozen in place, leave it alone, because forcing it will damage the material.

instructionSections.heading: Power-operated and lockable covers
instructionSections.body: A lockable cover only protects when it is locked. At each visit, check the lock, the drive, the controls and the cover edges, and record any fault. The drive is electrical equipment, so any wiring or drive repair goes to a licensed electrician. Do not run a power cover that shows a visible fault, or that has anyone in its path.

lessons.title: Home pool troubleshooting and liner repair
learningOutcomes: Diagnose low and high filter pressure, air bubbles, cloudy water and slippery surfaces using the checks in the handbook
Separate the faults a service worker may check from faults that need a licensed electrical, gas or heater person
Carry out a basic patch repair to a vinyl liner using the method and the precautions described
Record each fault, the checks made, the result and any referral

instructionSections.heading: A set order for diagnosis
instructionSections.body: Most faults on a home pool have a simple cause. Work through the checks in a fixed order: water level, flow to the pump, baskets and strainer, valves, the filter gauge, then the chemistry. Most faults show up in the first three. The UK handbook lists likely causes for each symptom, and that list is a useful reference, but it is a guide to thinking rather than a sequence of fixes to apply without judgment. Record each check, its result and any change you make. Electrical, gas and heater faults fall under the licence rules in “Home pool heating systems: operation and safe limits”, and electrical checks on the pump are covered in “Electrical connection, bonding and motor safety for a pool pump”.

instructionSections.heading: Pressure, flow and air
instructionSections.body: A low gauge reading usually points to a shut valve, a full basket or a falling water level. A high reading usually points to a dirty filter or a closed return valve. If the gauge has risen, backwash as “Sand filter backwash, rinse and return to filter” describes. If the reading does not come down after a correct backwash, refer it. Air bubbles entering through an inlet just after the pump starts, or after a backwash, are normal for a short time and should clear once the flow settles. If they continue, check the water depth and the seal on the strainer lid. A persistent air leak on the intake side needs referral, because it may point to a defective joint or valve.

instructionSections.heading: Cloudy water and slippery surfaces
instructionSections.body: Cloudy water means the usual sanitiser reading cannot be relied on until the water clears. Check pH and sanitiser first. The handbook suggests a heavy shock dose may be needed, which is an operator decision under the plan. Keep the filter running until the water clears, and use a flocculant only where the plan allows. A slippery floor or wall usually means algae is starting. Check pH and sanitiser, then follow the algae treatment on the product label. Do not use a product the plan does not include.

instructionSections.heading: Patching a vinyl liner
instructionSections.body: The handbook describes a patch that can be fitted while the pool has water in it. Cut a patch a little wider than the opening, then ease off its corners, and spread the adhesive named by the liner maker onto it. Place the patch across the hole and smooth it outwards from the centre to push the water out, so that water pressure helps hold it in place. Keep the patch dry while the adhesive cures, for the time the instructions give. Sharp objects are a common cause of liner damage, so ask the owner to keep sharp toys above the waterline. Large tears, seams and any liner replacement go to the liner maker or a qualified installer.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical, gas and heater faults
instructionSections.body: The UK handbook says that if an electric motor refuses to start, the fuse should be checked, and that a humming motor may have a jammed impeller. In that case, cut the power and refer the fault. The handbook also notes that a heater can trip after a power interruption, after low flow, or because the thermostat is at below the pool temperature. Reset the time clock and check the flow before anything else. Gas, electrical and oil faults need a licensed person, and this lesson grants no licence for them. Do not open an electrical enclosure or gas control to look for a fault.

lessons.title: Pool circulation system: components and how they connect
learningOutcomes: Name the main components of a pool circulation system and explain what each one does
Describe how water flows from the pool through the skimmers as well as drains, the pump together with the filter, and passes to the pool
Explain why the water level has to be held at the right height for the loop to work
State the warning on attaching a vacuum line to a skimmer and follow it

instructionSections.heading: How the loop is built
instructionSections.body: The textbook treats a pool system as a set of components with shared operating needs, although no two systems are identical. A typical layout has water inlets that return filtered water to the pool, skimmers that draw in surface water, skimmer baskets that catch floating debris, a main drain at the deepest point that draws from the floor, a drain manifold that collects every suction line, and a pump that moves the water. Water goes through the pump plus the filter and returns through the inlets. The loop only works while it stays full. The textbook notes that a water level that is low draws air into the closed loop and stops circulation.

instructionSections.heading: Suction-side components
instructionSections.body: Skimmers are water-level baskets with piping that carries pool water into the system, and the fill water needs controlling to hold the level at the right height. Skimmer baskets sit inside the skimmers and catch debris, and they are lifted out and cleared at intervals. The main drain sits at the lowest point, gathers debris from the basin floor, and can also empty the pool when needed. The drain manifold gathers water from each line, and each line has its own regulating valve. Valves are normally set so that each skimmer draws evenly, with a smaller share from the main drain. The main trap, or pump strainer, sits ahead of the pump plus can be opened to remove anything the skimmer baskets missed.

instructionSections.heading: Pump, filter and return components
instructionSections.body: The pump builds pressure that forces the flow into the filter media, then to the pool again, while creating suction on the intake side that pulls water from the skimmers and the drain. A lever-operated backwash valve is fitted. In normal running it directs flow down through the filter, then when it is reversed the flow climbs back through the bed to clean it. A sight glass shows how clear the water leaving the filter is during backwashing. The pressure gauge on the filter shows operating pressure. The reading taken on a clean system is the usual operating pressure, and a rise above it means the filter is loading. A chlorinator feeds a chemical into the circulation before the water returns. Dosing is covered in “Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention” and heaters in “Home pool heating systems: operation and safe limits”.

instructionSections.heading: The pool vacuum and the skimmer warning
instructionSections.body: A pool vacuum has a foot with a pair of connections: a pole that reaches the floor in deep water, plus a hose that reaches the surface and fits a skimmer. Adjusting the manifold valves sends all the suction to the one skimmer where the hose is fitted. The textbook gives a clear warning here. When a vacuum line is fixed to a skimmer inlet, switch the pump off first. While the pump runs, the suction at the skimmer is powerful enough to trap and break fingers. Apply this every time a line is connected, and do not let anyone place a hand over a skimmer opening while the motor is on.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the textbook with care
instructionSections.body: The textbook's component list skips a number and some of its sentences are unclear. Use it for the names and functions of the components only. Check each function against the manufacturer's manual for the real system, and confirm the layout with the owner or operator. Do not rely on a diagram or a figure from the textbook until it has been confirmed for the site.

lessons.title: Sanitiser choice and water balance: principles without target values
learningOutcomes: Explain why pool water has to be sanitised and what the sanitiser is for
Compare chlorine and bromine as sanitisers in terms of odour, cost and use
Explain why correcting one water value can disturb another, and why the operator plan sets the order
Recognise that the textbook's target values are generic or US-based and are not used as Australian targets

instructionSections.heading: Why the water is sanitised
instructionSections.body: The textbook explains that keeping pool water chemically safe depends on controlling harmful bacteria that could be present. Sanitising is the treatment that destroys those organisms. Clear water is a separate aim, and filtration removes particles but does not kill organisms. Sanitising is therefore part of every treatment plan, and the operator decides which product is used and how it is applied.

instructionSections.heading: Chlorine and bromine
instructionSections.body: The textbook names two sanitisers. Chlorine and bromine do broadly the same job. Chlorine is more likely to produce an odour that bothers bathers. Bromine is milder in odour but much dearer to run. Their proportions and reading ranges differ, so a plan written for one cannot simply switch to the other. The textbook discusses chlorine throughout. Whichever sanitiser is used, the plan must name the product, the test method and the target range for that product.

instructionSections.heading: Target values are not given here
instructionSections.body: The sources in this set disagree about target ranges for free chlorine and for pH. The textbook gives generic figures, the UK handbook gives figures for UK pools, and the manufacturer manual gives figures for its own product. None of them is an Australian standard, and this lesson does not set a target. Refer any doubt to the operator.

instructionSections.heading: Why one correction disturbs another
instructionSections.body: The textbook notes that sanitiser and pH have to be kept in step, and that correcting one can upset the other. That is why the order of adjustments matters, and the operator plan sets it. “Disinfection chemistry and pH interpretation” explains how to read results together and which reading drives the next action. A service worker follows the plan's order and records each change.

instructionSections.heading: Testing and recording
instructionSections.body: A reading is useful only when the sample is taken correctly, the test follows the kit's method, and the result is logged with the time and the tester. Free chlorine is the value that controls sanitising, and total chlorine is a different measure. Confirm which one the plan uses before testing, and record each reading and each adjustment against the plan.

lessons.title: Pool cleaning equipment: tools for the water, the walls and the floor
learningOutcomes: Name the pool-specific cleaning tools and state the job each one does
Choose a brush for a pool surface by the finish, following the manufacturer's guidance
Run a weekly cleaning sequence that moves debris towards the drain and removes it from the water
Recognise that housekeeping and hotel cleaning equipment in the textbook is out of scope for pool work

instructionSections.heading: The tools a pool service uses
instructionSections.body: The US start-up guide and the textbook both name the core pool tools: a pool vacuum with its head, pole and hose; a debris net or collector for leaves and insects; brushes for the walls; a test kit for pH and sanitiser; and the chemicals the plan allows. The skimmer and its basket are part of the circulation system and are covered in “Pool circulation system: components and how they connect”, and the vacuum method is in “Vacuuming, vacuum to waste and automated cleaners”. This lesson deals with the walls, the surfaces and the debris.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a brush
instructionSections.body: The US guide suggests a firm brush for concrete, a softer one for fibreglass, tile and vinyl, and a metal-bristled brush only for heavy algae and never on vinyl. Those are US guide statements. The real rule is that the brush must suit the finish, and the manufacturer's finish guidance for the pool is the reference. Use a soft brush on any surface that scratches easily, and keep metal bristles away from liners and from any finish the manufacturer prohibits. Work a long-handled brush from the shallow end towards the deep end, overlapping each stroke, so the loosened dirt is carried to the main drain.

instructionSections.heading: Debris and daily checks
instructionSections.body: The guide advises lifting leaves and insects off the surface with a collector, every day where trees overhang, and using a cover where leaves fall heavily. The textbook adds that skimmer baskets and the filter must be checked, and that the pump ought to be looked at every day. A blocked filter clouds the water, so confirm that water moves freely through it, and clean or replace the filter once it does not. That point matches “Backwash triggers, rinse and chemical cleaning for the sand bed”.

instructionSections.heading: A workable weekly order
instructionSections.body: A practical weekly order is to brush the walls and the waterline, lift off floating debris, empty the baskets, vacuum the floor in overlapping passes, check the pump and filtration unit, and test the water as the plan requires. Use the same order every week so that nothing is missed. Record what was done and anything that needs attention.

instructionSections.heading: Hygiene and out-of-scope items
instructionSections.body: Clean each tool after use, dry it, and keep it away from chemicals. Where several pools are served, keep a separate brush and net for each, so organisms are not carried between them. Equipment hygiene is covered in “Surface cleaning and equipment hygiene”. The textbook's housekeeping section lists mops, dustpans, carpet machines, vapour cleaners, laundry equipment and hotel trolleys. Those items are outside pool work and are not used here, and neither is a lawn scarifier.

lessons.title: Pool chemicals: types, hazards and safe handling
learningOutcomes: Name the main pool chemical types listed in the textbook and state what each is used for
Explain the hazards of each type and why incompatible products must be kept apart
Read the safety data sheet for a pool chemical before it is handled, and follow its protective requirements
Apply the extra care the textbook requires for small pools and baby pools

instructionSections.heading: The chemical types in the textbook
instructionSections.body: The textbook lists several products used to clean and treat pool water: granular or tablet forms of a chlorine donor, namely trichloroisocyanuric acid and sodium dichloroisocyanurate, which dissolves quickly; hydrochloric acid, liquid chlorine, and an alum-based clarifier. Chlorine donors kill bacteria and algae. Acids lower pH and clean surfaces. Alum is a clarifier that makes fine particles clump so the filter can catch them. The textbook gives a chlorine content for one of the products. Each product has its own hazards, and its safety data sheet is the reference.

instructionSections.heading: Hazards and separation
instructionSections.body: The products listed in the textbook are hazardous and must not be mixed. Chlorine donors and acids are incompatible, and combining them can release a toxic gas. The handbook and the textbook both stress keeping products apart and never moving one product into another's container. The separation rules are described in “Pool chemical handling and storage at home”, and the chemistry rules in “Disinfection chemistry and pH interpretation”. Storage must be cool, dry, ventilated, lockable, and kept away from the filter together with the pump.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the safety data sheet
instructionSections.body: Read the safety data sheet for each product before handling it. It gives the hazards, the protective equipment, first aid, storage and disposal. Keep the sheet where it is reachable found on site. The textbook does not replace the sheet, and where any protective advice in this lesson differs from the sheet, the sheet governs.

instructionSections.heading: Small pools and baby pools
instructionSections.body: The textbook warns that extra care is needed when cleaning baby pools with these products. A small amount of water changes concentration quickly, so a little product can produce a high level in the water. Use a reduced dose only where the plan allows one, keep children well away, and record the product, the amount and the time. If the plan does not cover the small pool, refer the question to the operator.

instructionSections.heading: What this lesson does not authorise
instructionSections.body: This lesson grants no licence or permit to handle, store or carry dangerous goods, and it does not replace the operator's instruction or the safety data sheet.

lessons.title: SA public pool standard: scope, definitions and responsibility
learningOutcomes: Identify the pool and spa types the South Australian standard covers.
Define owner, operator and knowledgeable person in the standard's terms.
Explain who answers for water quality while bathers are using a public pool.
State where the South Australian figures stop applying and what must be confirmed first.

instructionSections.heading: What the standard is and what it covers
instructionSections.body: This South Australian standard, last revised in 2013, sits under the state's 2011 public health legislation. Its scope takes in swimming, spa, waterslide and hydrotherapy facilities, using the wording of the 2013 general regulations. Councils rely on it when enforcing the law, and owners and operators treat it as a practical guide. Some disinfection provisions are adopted by the regulations themselves, so falling short of them carries penalties under those regulations. Because the document is dated, check the current regulation text before you act on any number taken from it.

instructionSections.heading: Why water quality rules exist
instructionSections.body: Bathers carry more into a pool than most people expect. Micro-organisms, saliva, sweat, urine, skin cells, hair, sunscreen and dirt all reach the water. Water that is untreated or poorly treated may lead to infections of the eyes, ears, skin and gut. The standard links fatal amoebic meningoencephalitis cases in SA to pools that were neglected, and it notes that unbalanced chemistry can cause rashes and red eyes. Spas and hydrotherapy pools carry more risk, since warm, bubbling water lets microbes multiply fast, and a small spa can host a crowd that is heavy for its volume.

instructionSections.heading: Definitions you will use on site
instructionSections.body: A knowledgeable person has the know-how to take charge of public pool operations so its water meets the regulations. An operator runs the pool day to day, understands how it works, and is capable enough to keep it compliant. An owner or occupier is anyone with a right to occupy or direct the premises, including whoever is responsible for them day to day. Free chlorine is the uncombined portion that can still act on organisms. Total chlorine is the free portion plus the combined portion. Turnover rate is the time needed to cycle a volume equal to the entire basin through the filter media. Bather load is the number of people in the water at one time.

instructionSections.heading: Responsibility for water quality
instructionSections.body: An owner needs to ensure a capable, knowledgeable person runs a public pool any time users can enter it. Whenever the public can use the pool, owner and operator both answer for keeping the water within the required limits. If an operator lets the water fall out of line, the authority may rule that person unfit for the role and tell the owner to appoint a qualified replacement. Hydrotherapy pools follow the same principle and also expect trained supervision of users who have an impairment.

instructionSections.heading: Where this standard stops
instructionSections.body: This is an official South Australian source, and it takes priority over informal, foreign or generic pool advice that conflicts with it. Its figures are aimed at public facilities in SA. Other states and territories have their own rules, and none of them have been checked here. A site operator plan must not conflict with the regulations. Completing this lesson does not give anyone authority to operate a pool.

lessons.title: Pool water clarity and seeing submerged bathers
learningOutcomes: Describe the clarity requirement in the South Australian standard, including the test disc and the depth at which it must be visible.
Explain why water clarity is a drowning-prevention control as well as a hygiene control.
Carry out a disc test and decide whether the pool may open.

instructionSections.heading: What clarity means under the standard
instructionSections.body: Clarity is how clear or free of cloudiness the water is, and it is judged by how far through the water you can see. The regulations require a 150 mm dark disc, or one that stands out against the floor colour, to be readily seen at the pool's deepest point. Filters strip out suspended and colloidal particles, which is what keeps the water clear. Clarity is a requirement in its own right, not an optional tidy-up step.

instructionSections.heading: Why clarity is a drowning-prevention control
instructionSections.body: Clear water lets people estimate depth, see hazards on the floor, and notice someone who has slipped under. The standard also asks for light-reflective internal surfaces, because they help staff notice murky water, sloppy cleaning and swimmers lying under the surface. When the water is cloudy at the deep end, a submerged person can be invisible to lifeguards and fellow bathers. Treat any clarity failure as a safety failure, not only a cosmetic one.

instructionSections.heading: Doing the disc test
instructionSections.body: Use a disc that meets the size and colour rule, and lower it to the pool's deepest point. Check that it is clearly visible from the pool edge in the lighting that the public will have. If it cannot be seen, the pool fails the clarity requirement and stays shut to bathers until the water passes. Record the result, the depth tested, the time and the lighting. Then identify the likely cause, such as filter performance, turnover, chemistry, debris or a cleaning gap, and pass it to the operator.

instructionSections.heading: When clarity fails
instructionSections.body: A failed disc test is a reason to keep the pool closed, not a reason to test again until it passes by luck. Fix the cause first, which may need a filter check, more circulation, chemistry correction or debris removal. Retest after the fix and before reopening. Do not dilute the test by moving the disc to a shallower spot or by changing its colour.

lessons.title: pH plus total alkalinity limits in SA public pools
learningOutcomes: Read a pH plus total alkalinity result and say whether it sits inside the South Australian band for the sanitiser in use.
Explain how pH plus total alkalinity influence how well disinfectant works, how comfortable bathers are, and how long equipment lasts.
Describe a sequenced, measured adjustment followed by a retest.

instructionSections.heading: Why pH and alkalinity come first
instructionSections.body: Disinfectant only works well when the water's pH sits in the right band. pH shapes how well the sanitiser kills organisms, how comfortable the water feels to bathers, and how well the water treats surfaces, metal fittings, pipework and pumps. The effect is strongest with chlorine. Total alkalinity acts as a buffer that resists pH swings. The standard measures it as calcium carbonate, so use that figure when you judge whether pH will hold steady.

instructionSections.heading: The pH band for each sanitiser
instructionSections.body: For chlorine-treated pools, and for pools treated with UV with hydrogen peroxide, keep pH between 7.2 and 7.6. Bromine-treated pools use a slightly wider band, from 7.2 and 7.8. These bands come from the standard's tables for each sanitiser. Water below the band causes eye discomfort, speeds up chloramine formation, and makes chlorine disappear faster. It can also etch exposed cement finishes and corrode metals. Water above the band lowers chlorine's effectiveness, raises the chlorine dose needed, dries skin, clouds the water and encourages scale.

instructionSections.heading: Total alkalinity limits
instructionSections.body: Where a pool is treated with a chlorine product, a bromine product or the UV-peroxide system, total alkalinity has to stay between 60 and 200 mg/L. Where gaseous chlorine is in service, or BCDMH supplies the bromine, the recommended minimum rises to 150 mg/L and the working range becomes 150 and 200 mg/L. Above 200 mg/L, fittings and surfaces scale, the water clouds, and pH tends to climb. Very hard source water may need treatment before it enters the pool. Below 60 mg/L, pH becomes unstable and metals are more likely to corrode.

instructionSections.heading: Corrosion and why acidic water matters
instructionSections.body: Water running below pH 7 eats into concrete shells, render and tile bedding, so tiles can rise. Metal parts, from pumps and ladders to underwater lights and heat exchangers, also corrode. Corrosion narrows flow paths and affects water quality. A balanced pool protects its equipment as well as the bathers.

instructionSections.heading: Adjusting safely in sequence
instructionSections.body: Change one parameter at a time, in the order given in the operator plan. Add a measured dose, circulate the water, and retest before making the next change. Keep acid-based and alkaline adjusters apart from disinfectant products, and check each product's safety data sheet for storage and dosing. Never combine products in one container or add them together at the skimmer. If a result stays outside the band after a reasonable dose, stop and escalate rather than keep adding product.

lessons.title: Chlorine disinfection and the 10 mg/L closure rule
learningOutcomes: Explain how chlorine disinfects pool water through hypochlorous acid.
Distinguish free chlorine from total chlorine, and state the South Australian minimum free chlorine levels.
Apply the immediate-closure rule when total chlorine exceeds the regulated threshold.

instructionSections.heading: How chlorine disinfects
instructionSections.body: Chlorine gas and chlorine compounds both yield hypochlorous acid on contact with water, and that acid is what kills organisms. The acid is small and carries no charge, so it can cross bacterial cell walls and disable the enzymes inside. The hypochlorite ion that forms as pH rises is far less effective, because its negative charge keeps it out of the cell. Your pH reading therefore indicates how much active disinfectant is on hand. Other compounds that behave the same way in water, like sodium and calcium hypochlorite, work the same way.

instructionSections.heading: Free and total chlorine
instructionSections.body: Free chlorine is the uncombined portion that remains available to kill organisms and break down organic contaminants. Combined chlorine forms when chlorine reacts with ammonia or nitrogen compounds from bathers, and it is far less useful as a disinfectant. Total chlorine is the free portion plus the combined portion. A pool can show a healthy-looking free reading while its combined chlorine is climbing, so measure both.

instructionSections.heading: Minimum free chlorine levels
instructionSections.body: Unstabilised public pools need 1.0 mg/L of free chlorine at 26 degrees Celsius or cooler, and 2.0 mg/L above that temperature. Spa pools need at least 4.0 mg/L of free chlorine. Hydrotherapy pools need at least 2.0 mg/L, and a suggested 4.0 mg/L applies when such a pool runs near its upper temperature under heavy loads. The total chlorine reading may exceed the free reading by no more than 1.0 mg/L. Stabilised pools have their own rules, covered in “Stabilised chlorine and cyanuric acid limits”.

instructionSections.heading: The immediate-closure threshold
instructionSections.body: Under regulation 8(4) of the South Australian Public Health (General) Regulations 2013, a public swimming pool must immediately be closed to the public when the total chlorine concentration exceeds 10 mg/L, and regulation 9(6) applies the same rule to spa pools. That is an emergency control, not an advisory limit. Close the pool, keep people out of the water, tell the operator, and do not reopen until the operator has brought the chlorine within limits and a retest confirms it. Reopening on an estimate is not something this lesson allows.

instructionSections.heading: Handling chlorine products
instructionSections.body: Chlorine gas is toxic, and concentrated chlorine compounds are oxidisers and corrosives. Store them away from acids and from other incompatible products, follow the safety data sheet, and never work in an enclosure where you suspect a gas leak. If you smell chlorine strongly in an enclosed plant room, leave, raise the alarm, and follow the site emergency procedure.

lessons.title: Stabilised chlorine and cyanuric acid limits
learningOutcomes: Explain why sunlight destroys free chlorine and why a stabiliser is used outdoors.
State the stabiliser range for outdoor public pools, and the ban that applies indoors.
Decide what to do when stabiliser concentration is too high or too low.

instructionSections.heading: Why sunlight drives chlorine loss
instructionSections.body: Sunlight breaks up free chlorine in pools used outdoors. Stabilisers such as cyanuric acid and its chlorinated relatives are added because they latch onto hypochlorite and form a larger molecule. That reduces losses to sunlight and extends the period during which the chlorine keeps disinfecting.

instructionSections.heading: The trade-off with stabilised chlorine
instructionSections.body: Much of the chlorine in a stabilised pool is locked up with the stabiliser and cannot disinfect, so the chlorine concentration has to be higher than in an unstabilised pool. If stabiliser climbs too far, disinfection slows because the chlorine is locked away, and the time needed to destroy pathogens becomes unacceptably long. Keep the stabiliser inside the band, not as high as possible.

instructionSections.heading: The standard's range and the indoor prohibition
instructionSections.body: For outdoor public pools that use stabilised chlorine, the prescribed cyanuric acid range is 30 to 50 mg/L. The regulation sets the chlorine range at 30 to 50 mg/L. Regulation 8 says cyanuric acid must not be used to stabilise chlorine in a public swimming pool in an enclosed structure, and regulation 9 says it must not be used to stabilise chlorine in a public spa pool, indoor or outdoor. The regulation's definition of swimming pool includes a hydrotherapy pool, so the enclosed-structure rule for public swimming pools applies to a public indoor hydrotherapy pool. The cyanuric acid provisions do not name hydrotherapy pools.

instructionSections.heading: Why stabiliser has to be replaced
instructionSections.body: Losses through evaporation, spray, filter washing and vacuuming away all take water, and the stabiliser with it. Stabiliser therefore runs down over time and must be topped up by partial water replacement. It cannot be removed by chlorine dosing. Only dilution through water replacement brings it down, and the operator must plan this. Do not add more stabiliser to a pool already above the range.

lessons.title: UV with hydrogen peroxide systems for indoor pools
learningOutcomes: State where the UV-peroxide approach is cleared in SA, including its capacity limit.
Explain why hydrogen peroxide is needed to give a residual, and why the UV unit must run continuously.
Check the three operating criteria and decide whether the system is compliant.

instructionSections.heading: Where the system is approved
instructionSections.body: The UV-and-peroxide approach is cleared for indoor swimming, spa, hydrotherapy and waterslide facilities up to 500,000 litres. It is not approved for outdoor use under the standard. The UV unit disinfects water as it passes through, but UV leaves no residual in the rest of the system, so it cannot protect water that has already left the unit. Hydrogen peroxide supplies the residual disinfecting capacity.

instructionSections.heading: Why the unit has to run around the clock
instructionSections.body: To work well, the system has to run around the clock. Turning the UV unit off overnight leaves the pool without the disinfection it needs, and the residual may then fall behind the bather load. Monitor the unit's run status and treat any shutdown as an event to escalate.

instructionSections.heading: The three operating criteria
instructionSections.body: The unit must give a UV dose of at least 30,000 uWs per cm squared. Flow past the UV unit may not exceed 150 L/min, and that rate must still satisfy the pool's turnover requirement. Peroxide must not fall below 40 mg/L. Table 7 also sets pH at 7.2 and 7.6 and total alkalinity at 60 and 200 mg/L.

instructionSections.heading: Water clarity, pH and the UV dose
instructionSections.body: UV leaves pH untouched, but hydrogen peroxide makes the water slightly acidic, so the pH must be raised into the band. Tint, murkiness and dissolved chemistry can block UV from reaching organisms, and bacteria can shelter in turbid water or slimes. Filter and treat the water before it reaches the UV unit. Dirty water reduces the effective dose even when the unit is working.

instructionSections.heading: Handling concentrated hydrogen peroxide
instructionSections.body: Concentrated peroxide acts as a strong oxidiser and has a sharp odour. Store it apart from incompatible materials, keep containers closed, and follow the safety data sheet for dosing and spills. Work with splash protection.

lessons.title: Bromine, BCDMH and bromamines in public pools
learningOutcomes: Describe how bromine disinfects and why its pH band differs from chlorine.
State the bromine minimums that apply to ordinary, hydrotherapy and spa pools.
Explain bromamine build-up and the shock-dose rule.

instructionSections.heading: How bromine disinfects
instructionSections.body: Every bromine disinfectant forms hypobromous acid in water, and that acid is the working disinfectant. Bromine is less pungent than chlorine, tolerates a broader pH band, and kills at a comparable rate. No stabiliser can shield it from ultraviolet light, so outdoor bromine pools shed disinfectant faster in sun. Compare this with the stabiliser rules in “Stabilised chlorine and cyanuric acid limits”.

instructionSections.heading: Ways bromine gets into the water
instructionSections.body: One approach combines a bromide salt with a strong oxidant, like a hypochlorite solution or a persulphate product. Another uses BCDMH, which comes as tablets or granules. BCDMH is acidic, around pH 4.5, so it drags total alkalinity down quickly, and wherever it is dosed, total alkalinity needs to sit between 150 and 200 mg/L. Some of the chlorine released with BCDMH can remain active alongside the bromine, especially after a fill with fresh water.

instructionSections.heading: Bromine minimums
instructionSections.body: For ordinary swimming, wading and waterslide water, bromine should read 2.0 mg/L or more below 26 degrees Celsius, and 4.0 mg/L or more from 26 degrees up. Hydrotherapy pools need at least 4.0 mg/L, and under heavy loads near the top temperature the suggested level is 8.0 mg/L. Spa pools need at least 8.0 mg/L. Bromine pH must sit between 7.2 and 7.8.

instructionSections.heading: Bromamines and when to replace water
instructionSections.body: Bromamines arise when bromine encounters ammonia or organic nitrogen-bearing compounds. Ammonia-based bromamines still kill organisms, produce no harsh smell or eye sting, and so breakpoint treatment is usually not needed for bromine. Organic bromamines from bathers are more stable and can build up, hindering disinfection. Replace part of the water to reduce them. Spa water exchange has to follow the regulations, as “Public spa pools: temperature, replacement and cleaning” explains.

instructionSections.heading: Shock dosing only when the pool is empty of bathers
instructionSections.body: Shock dosing breaks down organic build-up that water replacement cannot shift. For bromine, the standard's superbromination level is at least 20 mg/L, and it is only permitted while the water holds no swimmers. Bromine-chlorine systems may also need superchlorination to break down chloramines, which converts bromide into active bromine.

lessons.title: Breakpoint chlorination, chloramines and cleaning-product cautions
learningOutcomes: Describe the four zones of breakpoint chlorination and the point at which free chlorine appears.
Explain why chloramines cause the chlorine smell and eye irritation, and what reduces trichloramine.
Identify cleaning products that should be kept away from pools and explain why.

instructionSections.heading: The breakpoint process
instructionSections.body: Breakpoint chlorination means dosing enough free chlorine to turn chloramines and ammonia-based nitrogen compounds into harmless nitrogen gas. Chlorine is first consumed by reducing agents that are already dissolved. Adding more, the total chlorine climbs while bather-derived nitrogen compounds become monochloramines. Past a peak, further chlorine oxidises the chloramines, and total chlorine falls almost to zero. This is the breakpoint. Beyond it, extra chlorine appears as free chlorine, which is the disinfectant you want.

instructionSections.heading: Where chloramines come from
instructionSections.body: Sweat and urine bring amino acids and nitrogen-rich breakdown products into the pool. These combine with chlorine to produce monochloramines and then dichloramines. Trichloramine can form when chlorine is added before the breakpoint has been reached. Trichloramine is volatile, so it escapes into the air above the pool and causes the strong chlorine smell, and it causes severe eye irritation.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping pH in the band to limit trichloramine
instructionSections.body: Trichloramine formation increases at low pH, slows as pH rises, and is minimal between pH 7.5 and 8.0. That is one reason why the chlorine pH range is set at 7.2 and 7.6. Keep breakpoint chlorination going so trichloramine effects stay small. A strong chlorine smell is a sign of a combined chlorine problem, not of an excess of free chlorine, so check combined chlorine and pH before adding more chlorine.

instructionSections.heading: Cleaning products that must stay clear of the pool
instructionSections.body: Chlorine can react with phenolic substances to make chlorinated phenols, which irritate the eyes badly and taste unpleasant. Phenols turn up in many cleaning products, and the standard advises against using them in or near pools and spas. Keep phenolic products off the pool deck, out of pool-cleaning buckets, and away from pool equipment. Check labels on every cleaning product before you use it near a pool. Reading the label is part of the work, not an extra step.

lessons.title: Algae control and superchlorination with no bathers
learningOutcomes: Explain how algae reduce disinfectant efficiency and create hazards on the pool surface.
State the South Australian superchlorination level and the condition under which it is applied.
Describe the post-treatment steps that must be complete before a pool reopens.

instructionSections.heading: Why algae are a problem
instructionSections.body: Algae are one of the main contributors to pool pollution. They can shelter bacteria, and they reduce how well disinfectants work, chlorine included. Algae tie up chlorine and generate smells, murkiness, staining and slime. Slime on surfaces is also a trip-and-fall risk on the surrounds. If algae turn up in chlorinated water, the standard reads that as a sign that free chlorine has fallen short.

instructionSections.heading: Superchlorination for heavy growth
instructionSections.body: Heavy algal growth can be treated by superchlorinating the pool. That means holding the free chlorine level above 10 mg/L while nobody is using the pool. After treatment, dead algae ought to come away with brushing. If it does not, repeat the dose until the algae is gone. Take dead algae out by hand or with equipment before users return. Algaecide is another option, but it is a chemical in its own right and must be handled and dosed according to its safety data sheet and the operator plan.

instructionSections.heading: Why no bathers may be present
instructionSections.body: Superchlorination takes free chlorine well above normal operating levels. Only run it while nobody is using the pool, with the access route secured. Shock dosing in general, and the bromine version in particular, is also restricted to times with no swimmers present. Treat any request to dose a pool still in use as a stop.

instructionSections.heading: Before the pool reopens
instructionSections.body: Reopening needs three checks: the algae has been removed or killed and dead material is gone, the free chlorine (or bromine) has returned to the band for the pool type, and the clarity check in “Pool water clarity and seeing submerged bathers” passes. The reopening decision belongs to the operator, but the evidence has to show all three points.

lessons.title: Pool pollution: sweat, urine and nitrogen load
learningOutcomes: Identify the main sources of pool pollution and the role of bathers.
Explain why nitrogen compounds from sweat and urine use up disinfectant.
Describe how timing and pool surrounds affect the pollution load.

instructionSections.heading: Bathers are the main pollutant source
instructionSections.body: Bathers are the biggest contributors of nitrogen-based matter to the water, delivered through sweat and urine. In public pools, children produce the greatest volume of urine. Heat speeds up sweating. The pollution load also comes from dust, leaves and grass cuttings blown or carried into the water, and from algae growth, which is covered in “Algae control and superchlorination with no bathers”.

instructionSections.heading: What sweat and urine contain
instructionSections.body: A swimmer working hard in water around 24 degrees Celsius, on a day when the air is around 38 degrees, can lose up to a litre of sweat an hour. Sweat carries salts, calcium and magnesium, and nitrogen compounds including urea, creatinine, ammonia nitrogen and amino acids. Its pH sits roughly between 4 and 6.8. Urine is more complex, containing a mix of breakdown products, and it is harder to treat because nitrogen is so concentrated in it.

instructionSections.heading: Why nitrogen reduces disinfection
instructionSections.body: Ammonia from sweat and urine binds to chlorine in a matter of minutes, forming chloramines. Urea first has to be broken down by hydrolysis, a step that can take about three or four hours in ordinary conditions, and enzymes can speed that up. Because of these reactions, the standard requires breakpoint chlorination to be held continuously to keep organic nitrogen under control.

instructionSections.heading: Managing the load on a busy day
instructionSections.body: On hot days, school carnivals and busy weekends, the load rises quickly. Increase the frequency of testing and check the breakpoint and pH more often. Keep leaves, grass and dust out of the water with skimmers and surface cleaning, and make sure filters are running as the plan requires. A clear pool does not mean the nitrogen load is low, because the compounds that cause problems are dissolved and invisible.

lessons.title: Infection hazards: bacteria, viruses and amoebae
learningOutcomes: Name the main bacteria, viruses and amoebae that pool disinfection is designed to control.
Explain how the nose-entry route links amoebae to diving and jumping.
Connect each infection route to the disinfection and hygiene control that addresses it.

instructionSections.heading: Organic matter feeds bacteria
instructionSections.body: Organic material in the water feeds bacteria, and it comes from people, animals and surroundings. Disinfectants destroy or inactivate the harmful bacteria. Escherichia coli signals faecal contamination. Staphylococci and streptococci point to contamination from the upper airways and skin. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that takes advantage of weak disinfection, can infect eyes, ears and skin. Mycobacterium marinum produces lumps under the skin and may spread into damp surrounds.

instructionSections.heading: Viruses resist chlorine better than bacteria
instructionSections.body: Many viruses spread from person to person through pool water, and enteroviruses withstand chlorine better than bacteria do. Adenoviruses have been tied to sore throats, pink eye and raised body temperature. Enteroviruses cover polio and coxsackie viruses, as well as hepatitis A, and they can bring on bowel infections, jaundice, nerve involvement and rashes. Effective disinfection and clean, well-managed water are the main controls.

instructionSections.heading: Amoebae and the nose-entry route
instructionSections.body: Two protozoa, Acanthamoeba and Naegleria fowleri, occur naturally in the environment. In neglected water they can trigger a deadly form of meningoencephalitis, a brain infection. Infection follows contaminated water being drawn up through the nose, a risk during dives, leaps or laps. The organisms are destroyed by keeping the disinfectant at the required level in the water. The standard notes fatal cases in SA that were linked to neglected pools. Treat any disinfection failure as a serious hazard, and never assume an amoeba risk is only a spa problem.

instructionSections.heading: Predisposing factors and the health effects table
instructionSections.body: The standard's table of health effects lists how each group of organisms causes illness and what makes infection more likely. Factors that raise risk include heavy microbial loads, long exposure, high temperatures, injury, skin lesions, weakened immunity, low disinfectant levels, aerosol spray from contaminated water, immersing the head, and swallowing water. Your job is to keep every factor you control within the standard, and to report any cluster of illness to the operator.

lessons.title: Filtration, turnover and automatic dosing requirements
learningOutcomes: State the turnover limits for each pool type in the South Australian standard.
Calculate the flow needed to meet a turnover limit for a given pool volume.
Explain what auto-dosing and sensing must do, and what a worker must still check manually.

instructionSections.heading: Continuous circulation through the filter
instructionSections.body: Each public pool and spa needs a filter system that keeps water moving through it non-stop. Enough water has to run through the filter to keep it clean and clear. That is measured as turnover: the time needed to cycle a volume equal to the entire basin through the filter media. Turnover is a condition for every pool type the standard covers, not an optional extra.

instructionSections.heading: Turnover limits by pool type
instructionSections.body: A swimming pool needs its whole volume filtered no less often than every six hours. A wading pool needs it no less often than every two hours. A waterslide pool needs it no less often than hourly. A spa needs its volume cycled at least every half hour. Hydrotherapy water needs its volume cycled no less often than every two hours, with under an hour suggested for busy pools, for example ones running fitness classes. Where requirements vary, a separate filter is recommended.

instructionSections.heading: Filter types and hydrotherapy pools
instructionSections.body: The standard calls a sand filter one that uses sand and gravel media. For hydrotherapy pools it says a dedicated filtration system is ideal, and it does not recommend cartridge units or diatomaceous earth types for them. Backwashing reverses water flow to clean the filter, and it removes water and disinfectant, so follow the operator plan for timing and for managing the discharge.

instructionSections.heading: Auto-dosing and sensing
instructionSections.body: Each pool must have auto-dosing and sensing equipment that watches and corrects the pH and sanitiser level around the clock, keeping them in the ranges set by the standard's tables. The equipment does not remove the need to test. Check its readings against a manual test, know what its alarms mean, and escalate any fault. Repair, wiring and controller work is licensed where a licence applies.

instructionSections.heading: Working out the flow needed
instructionSections.body: To check turnover, divide the pool volume in litres by the minutes allowed for turnover to get the minimum flow in L/min. For example, a 300,000 litre swimming pool with a six-hour limit needs about 830 L/min through the filter. Verify that the pump, filter and pipework can deliver that flow, and that the flow is not reduced by a dirty filter.

lessons.title: Public spa pools: temperature, replacement and cleaning
learningOutcomes: State the temperature limits, alarm point and control accuracy for a public spa.
Explain the spa filtration, skimming, replacement and cleaning requirements.
Give the spa disinfectant minimums for chlorine and bromine.

instructionSections.heading: Why spas need stricter control
instructionSections.body: Public spas carry much more suspended material per litre than swimming pools. The reasons are the small volume, a high bather load for that volume, the raised temperature, aeration, and heavy organic loading. Infection is usually linked to high microbial levels in poorly maintained spas, because the warm, aerated environment supports many kinds of harmful organism. Those are the reasons the spa rules are tighter than the swimming pool rules.

instructionSections.heading: Temperature and alarm
instructionSections.body: Water should stay at or below 40 degrees Celsius, with 35 to 37 degrees as the aim. The thermostatic control has to hold the set temperature within 0.5 degrees either way. An over-temperature alarm must be fitted so the operator is warned if water passes 40 degrees. Heat stress is a real risk at high temperatures and long exposure, so a heater fault that pushes the water above the limit is a closure event.

instructionSections.heading: Filtration, skimming and turnover
instructionSections.body: The spa needs a filter that circulates water continuously, and its full volume has to be cycled every half hour or sooner. A weir or skimmer must draw off surface water nonstop while the spa is running. Auto-dosing and sensing must keep pH and disinfectant within the spa ranges.

instructionSections.heading: Replacement and weekly cleaning
instructionSections.body: On every day it operates, swap out a minimum of 20 percent of the spa water, or empty the spa fully each week. The spa also needs cleaning no less often than weekly during weeks it operates. Water replacement has to follow the regulations for spas, not the swimming pool practice.

instructionSections.heading: Disinfectant minimums for spas
instructionSections.body: A chlorinated spa needs free chlorine of 4.0 mg/L or more, and total chlorine can sit no higher than 1.0 mg/L above the free value. The pH band is 7.2 and 7.6, and total alkalinity is 60 and 200 mg/L, or 150 and 200 mg/L where BCDMH or gaseous chlorine is involved. Bromine in a spa needs at least 8.0 mg/L, with pH held between 7.2 and 7.8. Stabilisers are not permitted in spa pools.

lessons.title: Spa bather warnings, health exclusions and supervision
learningOutcomes: Describe the bather warning notice that has to sit right beside a public spa, and why each point is there.
Explain the heat, infection and drowning risks that the warnings control.
Check the notice and the supervision arrangements before a spa is opened.

instructionSections.heading: Where the warning notice goes
instructionSections.body: A bather warning notice has to be posted somewhere eye-catching right beside the spa, where anyone about to get in can read it. A notice placed out of sight, behind furniture or away from the entry does not meet that purpose. Check the notice every time you open or inspect the spa, and replace it if it is faded, damaged or missing.

instructionSections.heading: The points the notice must convey
instructionSections.body: Bathers should keep their heads out of the water. Anyone affected by drugs or alcohol must stay out, and no single session may run longer than 20 minutes. Children may only use the spa under supervision. Swallowing spa water is not permitted. Anyone with an open wound, anyone feeling unwell, and anyone pregnant should keep out of the spa. Each point controls a specific risk, so the notice is a safety control and must stay legible and complete.

instructionSections.heading: Why these points matter
instructionSections.body: Head immersion and swallowing water carry infection risk, because warm aerated water can hold high microbial loads. Heat stress builds with high temperatures and long exposure, especially for people with heart conditions or a predisposition to stress. Children can slip under the surface or get into difficulty unobserved. Open wounds give organisms a route in. The 20-minute limit reduces the cumulative heat and exposure load.

instructionSections.heading: Supervision and refusing entry
instructionSections.body: The operator must make sure children are supervised whenever they use a public spa. Attendants have authority to deny entry where a person appears unwell, under the influence, or otherwise likely to be at risk, and the standard supports that approach for waterslides and spas alike. Escalate repeated breaches to the operator, and record the incident.

lessons.title: Hydrotherapy pools: temperature, disinfection and vulnerable users
learningOutcomes: State the temperature, humidity and disinfectant requirements for a hydrotherapy pool.
Explain why hydrotherapy pools need a higher disinfectant level than ordinary pools.
Describe the supervision and exclusion points that protect vulnerable users.

instructionSections.heading: Why hydrotherapy pools run differently
instructionSections.body: Hydrotherapy pools run at a higher temperature and need a higher disinfectant level, because warm water accelerates the loss of disinfectant. They serve people rehabilitating after injury or sickness, people whose immune systems are weakened, and people with intellectual impairment, plus people who exercise there. Because of these users, the standard treats running a hydrotherapy pool as work needing extra care.

instructionSections.heading: Temperature and air conditions
instructionSections.body: Hydrotherapy water should stay at or below 38 degrees Celsius, with 28 to 35 degrees as the aim. The thermostat must hold the set temperature within 0.5 degrees either way, and an over-temperature alarm must be fitted to warn above 38 degrees. Air in the pool zone should sit within 10 degrees below the water, and humidity should stay between 50 and 75 percent, with draughts kept down.

instructionSections.heading: Turnover, replacement and disinfectant
instructionSections.body: The full pool volume has to be filtered no less often than every two hours, and under an hour is suggested for busy pools. For heavy bather loads, the standard recommends replacing about a quarter of the water each week. Free chlorine must be at least 2.0 mg/L, and under heavy loads at high temperature the standard suggests at least 4.0 mg/L. For bromine, the minimum is 4.0 mg/L, with 8.0 mg/L suggested when the water is hot and heavily loaded.

instructionSections.heading: Stabilisers and microbial growth
instructionSections.body: Stabilisers are barred from indoor hydrotherapy water, and the standard discourages them in outdoor water as well. Warm water and a heavy organic load make these pools a favourable home for microbes, so a fast-acting disinfectant is the right choice.

instructionSections.heading: Supervision and exclusions
instructionSections.body: The standard suggests trained staff supervise users constantly, and that people with impairments get special arrangements. Some medical conditions rule out hydrotherapy, including unstable heart conditions, active infections and open wounds. Users should be supervised, and the operator must have a way to refuse entry where a user is not suitable. Hydrotherapy pool use by people living with HIV carries no risk that can be measured for other users when the pool is properly disinfected and supervised.

lessons.title: Waterslides, flumes and receiving pools
learningOutcomes: Describe the minimum staffing and sight-line requirements for a waterslide.
State the daily flume inspection and the closure rule for a faulty flume.
Describe the receiving pool and turnover requirements, and the bather warnings that must be displayed.

instructionSections.heading: Staffing and sight lines
instructionSections.body: The standard sets minimum attendant positions for a waterslide. One observer must stand at the head of each flume to supervise riders entering it. A second observer must stand at the receiving pool to supervise riders leaving the flume and emerging from the water. Each observer needs a clear line of sight along the whole run, or a signal device telling the top attendant that the next rider can go. A communication system has to connect the attendants at each end.

instructionSections.heading: Daily inspection and closure
instructionSections.body: Each day, before use, the entire flume needs inspecting for faults or damage that could injure users. If the inspection finds a faulty or damaged flume, the slide shuts until repairs are complete. The fee arrangement should not reward riders for running or horseplay in order to fit in extra rides.

instructionSections.heading: Design checks an operator should look for
instructionSections.body: Starting points need sturdy handrails, a grip-friendly floor and either a canopy of about two metres or another device that regulates entry. The flume must keep riders within the slide at any speed, and designers should steer clear of sharp turns and rapid runs of drops and curves. The flume's end must discharge into a receiving pool with water depth of between 900 mm and 1 m, and that depth has to reach at least three metres out ahead of the flume. Pool surrounds should measure no less than 1.2 m across, light-coloured, impervious and non-slip, and the pool colour must let staff see every rider.

instructionSections.heading: Turnover, flow and make-up water
instructionSections.body: A waterslide pool needs its entire volume filtered no less often than hourly, given the heavy bather load. Roughly four-fifths of the flow should come off through the overflow channels and skimmers, and about one-fifth from below the surface. A self-filling make-up system has to hold the working level. Where turnover requirements vary, a separate filter is recommended.

instructionSections.heading: Warnings that must be displayed
instructionSections.body: A sign must sit prominently at the entry and at the flume. It tells riders to leave the pool immediately on discharge, limits tandem riding to adults with small children, forbids horseplay and carrying glass or pointed items, and asks riders to remove jewellery and glasses that could cause injury. It advises that people who are pregnant, who have weak limbs or a weak back, who have heart ailments, or who have any condition that could be worsened by use, should not use the slide. It also lets management turn people away.

lessons.title: Scope and definitions: Victorian barriers for spas and pools
learningOutcomes: List the pool and spa types that the Victorian note brings within scope.
Identify the water depths and features that fall outside the barrier rule.
Define the terms used in the note: swimming pool area (this lesson's pool zone), barrier height, non-climbable zone, boundary barrier and young child.

instructionSections.heading: Who the note is written for
instructionSections.body: Victorian rule (VBA Building Practice Note SP 02, Version 3, 26 September 2023). The note is written for designers, builders, building surveyors, owners, plumbers and electricians, and it covers barriers for indoor and outdoor pools.

instructionSections.heading: Features outside the barrier rule
instructionSections.body: A pool, under the note, is an excavation or structure able to hold water deeper than 300 mm and used mainly for swimming, wading, paddling, bathing or similar activities. A shallower feature therefore falls outside the barrier rule. The VBA consumer page on pool safety barriers also exempts bird baths, fountains, water tanks, fish ponds, dams, and personal-hygiene baths or indoor spas emptied after each use. Judge each feature by its depth and how it is used, not by what it is called.

instructionSections.heading: Terms used in the note
instructionSections.body: Barrier height is measured at right angles to the finished ground level (FGL). A boundary barrier separates two neighbouring properties. A non-climbable zone is the strip on and beside a barrier, running its full length including any gate, meant to stop young children from climbing it. The note calls the enclosed area the swimming pool area: the area containing the pool or spa, enclosed by a barrier. The note does not define pool zone, so this lesson uses that term for the same area. A young child is a child under five. A spa counts as part of the pool.

instructionSections.heading: The whole lot is not the pool zone
instructionSections.body: The pool area must be a separate area enclosed by a barrier. Enclosing the whole property does not satisfy the barrier requirement, and access must not be directly available through a building door.

instructionSections.heading: Standards that sit behind the rule
instructionSections.body: The note names AS 1926.1-2012 as the barrier standard and refers to NCC 2022. The 2012 edition of AS 1926.1 was not read for this lesson, so the standard is cited by name only, and its current edition has not yet been confirmed. Check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.

lessons.title: When a Victorian pool barrier is needed and construction precautions
learningOutcomes: State the barrier depth rule from the VBA consumer page, and check the construction requirements with the building surveyor.
Describe the site fencing and excavation precautions that the VBA Building Practice Note SP 01 sets out.
State the builder requirement and the 12-month and six-month time limits for pool and barrier building work.

instructionSections.heading: What the barrier must do
instructionSections.body: The Victorian Building Authority consumer page on pool safety barriers states that a barrier must be capable of containing water to a depth greater than 300 mm, and that a pool which cannot hold more than 300 mm of water is exempt. The same page says safety barriers must comply with AS1926.1-2012. Check the building requirements with the building surveyor before starting, and record the barrier position with the building surveyor.

instructionSections.heading: Site fencing and excavation guarding
instructionSections.body: The VBA Building Practice Note SP 01 says excavation of a pool shell can be a hazard. The site fencing considered under regulation 116 must include provisions to restrict access during excavation, during construction, and once the pool can contain water. Where the relevant building surveyor decides protection work is required, it must be provided before and during construction. Check the building requirements, including site fencing, with the building surveyor before starting, and record the check.

instructionSections.heading: Builder type and time limits
instructionSections.body: The VBA consumer page says pools, spas and safety barriers must be constructed by a registered builder, or by an owner-builder who has an owner-builder certificate of consent. The VBA Building Practice Note SP 01 says building work for a swimming pool and barrier must commence within 12 months of the building permit's issue date and be completed within six months of the work commencing, citing regulations 53 and 54. Note the permit's issue date and the planned start date against these limits.

lessons.title: Victorian barrier geometry: height, non-climbable zones and gaps
learningOutcomes: Measure barrier height from the finished ground level and compare it with the Victorian figure for internal and boundary barriers.
Explain non-climbable zones and check their reach against the note.
Check mesh, gaps, steps, ledges and intersecting barriers against the note.

instructionSections.heading: Measuring height and the non-climbable zones
instructionSections.body: Victorian rule (VBA Building Practice Note SP 02, Version 3, 26 September 2023). Height is measured at right angles to the finished ground level (FGL). SP 02 numbers five non-climbable zones (NCZ 1 to NCZ 5), and this lesson calls them Zone 1 to Zone 5. Zone 1 is a 900 mm vertical plane on the outside of an internal barrier. Zone 2 is a quadrant with a 900 mm radius from the top of Zone 1. Zone 3 is a quadrant with a 900 mm radius from the top of the barrier, on the outside. Zone 4 covers vertical openings of 10 to 100 mm, 900 mm high and 300 mm deep, on the inside. Zone 5 applies to boundary barriers. An internal barrier of 1800 mm or more needs no non-climbable zone. The barrier standard is AS 1926.1-2012, cited by name only.

instructionSections.heading: Boundary fences used as barriers
instructionSections.body: A boundary fence serving as the pool barrier must be at least 1800 mm high on the inside. Zone 5 is a quadrant with a 900 mm radius down from the top of the inside face. Owners and occupiers must maintain the barrier and adjacent vegetation, and plants that could help a child climb are not permitted within the non-climbable zones.

instructionSections.heading: Steps, ledges and crossing barriers
instructionSections.body: Steps or level changes that abut a barrier must be set back at least 500 mm from it. This set-back does not apply to boundary barriers. Projections and indentations more than 10 mm deep should not be climbable. Where a lower internal barrier meets a boundary fence, the top rail decides the outcome. If the top rail is 50 mm wide or less and meets the boundary barrier at 45 to 135 degrees, the junction meets the rule. Otherwise, the lower barrier must reach 1800 mm and extend at least 900 mm from the intersection.

instructionSections.heading: Mesh panels, openings and bottom gaps
instructionSections.body: A non-boundary mesh barrier must be at least 1200 mm high where its openings are 13 mm or less, and at least 1800 mm where openings are over 13 mm and up to 100 mm. Openings wider than 100 mm are not allowed. Under a 25 kg weight applied at any point on the top, the barrier must stay at 1200 mm or more. Openings are measured horizontally across the widest part. For mesh or perforated barriers, the gap at the base must stay within 100 mm when a 100 N vertical lift force is applied.

instructionSections.heading: Glass barriers
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says glass must comply with AS 1288. High-risk glass must be Grade A safety glazing of the minimum thickness that AS 1288 prescribes. AS 1288 is cited by name only, and its wording was not read for this lesson.

lessons.title: Victorian pool gates, doors and self-closing latches
learningOutcomes: State what the note requires of a pool gate's closing and latching, and explain what a failure shows.
Identify the door arrangements the note allows, and those it rules out, for outdoor and indoor pools.
Explain why child-resistant doorsets are limited to indoor pools.

instructionSections.heading: Gates must shut and latch unaided
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says gates must be self-closing and self-latching under AS 1926.1-2012. A gate that does not close and latch itself leaves the barrier open, so release each gate from the open position and check that it closes and latches itself.

instructionSections.heading: Gate posts and footings
instructionSections.body: Moving posts can stop a gate from latching. SP 02 says footings for posts and gates should be poured monolithically or as one footing across the opening, which keeps the posts from spreading and the gate from failing to latch. Record any gate that swings loose between its posts as a defect.

instructionSections.heading: Garages, sheds and building doors
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says tool sheds, garages and barbecues should sit outside the pool area, citing AS 1926.2-2007, Appendix B. Access to an outdoor pool must not be directly available through a building door, so a door from the house or a garage opening into the pool area does not meet the rule.

instructionSections.heading: Doors leading out of a building
instructionSections.body: Child-resistant doorsets may only be used for indoor pools and the indoor part of a combined indoor and outdoor pool, so they must stay out of barriers that protect outdoor water. A new outdoor pool or spa area must not be directly accessible from a building.

instructionSections.heading: Indoor pools and side-hung doors
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says an indoor pool is fully enclosed by walls on all sides, roofed, and accessed from within the building. A side-hung door used as part of an indoor pool barrier must swing away from the pool, be self-closing and self-latching, and have a non-climbable zone on its outside. Permit drawings for indoor pools must show the barrier, child-resistant doorsets and the door swing direction.

lessons.title: Victorian pool zone layout and climbable objects
learningOutcomes: Identify the layout rules for the pool zone, including doors that open onto it.
Explain why climbable plants must be kept out of the non-climbable zones, and why barbecues and sheds sit outside the pool area.
Check above-ground pool walls against the 1.2 m barrier height.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the pool zone separate
instructionSections.body: Victorian rule (VBA Building Practice Note SP 02, Version 3, 26 September 2023). SP 02 calls this area the swimming pool area, meaning the area containing the pool or spa and enclosed by a barrier; this lesson uses pool zone for the same area. The pool area must be a separate area enclosed by a barrier, and access must not be directly available through a building door. Enclosing the whole property does not satisfy the requirement.

instructionSections.heading: Sheds, garages and barbecues
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says tool sheds, garages and barbecues should sit outside the pool area, citing AS 1926.2-2007, Appendix B. Keep them outside the pool zone when you check a layout.

instructionSections.heading: Climbable objects near the barrier
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says plants that could help a child climb are not permitted within the non-climbable zones. Trees and other objects a child could use to climb over the barrier should also be kept clear of it, and checked at every visit.

instructionSections.heading: Above-ground pools
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says an above-ground pool wall must be at least 1.2 m above finished ground level and non-climbable. Where the wall meets that rule, the pool wall can act as the barrier.

lessons.title: Victorian mesh barrier load and base-gap checks
learningOutcomes: State the SP 02 load checks for mesh barrier panels and the lift check for the gap at their base.
Explain how the 25 kg top-load check is applied and what result it must give.
Decide whether a mesh panel passes the SP 02 height and base-gap checks.

instructionSections.heading: What SP 02 checks on mesh panels
instructionSections.body: Victorian rule (VBA Building Practice Note SP 02, Version 3, 26 September 2023). A non-boundary mesh barrier must keep its height at 1200 mm or more when a 25 kg weight is applied at any point on its top. The gap at the base of a mesh or perforated barrier must stay within 100 mm when a 100 N vertical lift force is applied.

instructionSections.heading: Footings for posts and gates (recommended)
instructionSections.body: SP 02 recommends pouring footings for posts and gates monolithically or as one footing across the opening. It notes that spreading posts can stop a gate from latching properly. This is a recommendation, so it is not a pass or fail check in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Gates: what SP 02 does and does not require
instructionSections.body: SP 02 does not set out a general self-closing and self-latching requirement for gates under AS 1926.1-2012. For a door that forms part of an indoor pool barrier, it does require self-closing and self-latching under AS 1926.1-2012. Gate operation is not one of the checks in this lesson.

lessons.title: Victorian suction outlets, main drains and entrapment
learningOutcomes: Explain how suction outlets and main drains can trap a bather.
Describe the Victorian checks on main drain covers and suction spacing.
Identify which pool drainage connections need a VBA drainage inspection and compliance certificate under SP 02.

instructionSections.heading: How entrapment happens
instructionSections.body: Building Practice Note SP 02 (Version 3, 26 September 2023) refers to AS 1926.3-2010 for water reticulation; that standard is named here but was not read for this lesson. A suction outlet or main drain can hold a bather, along with hair or a limb, when its cover is missing, cracked or fitted wrongly. Treat a missing, cracked or loose outlet cover as an immediate hazard.

instructionSections.heading: Main drain covers and their paperwork
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says designers must supply the manufacturer's design and test data for the main drain cover. Check that this data is on file before the cover is accepted.

instructionSections.heading: Suction spacing
instructionSections.body: SP 02 says suction points must be at least 600 mm apart. Compare the spacing drawn on the plans with this figure, and record any difference.

instructionSections.heading: Recirculation and drainage connections
