instructionSections.body: SP 02 says recirculation and filtration designs must be given to the relevant building surveyor with the building permit application. It also says a below-ground backwash connection to sewer needs a VBA drainage inspection and compliance certificate, and an above-ground backwash connection valued at $750 or more needs a compliance certificate. Electrical work on the pool equipment is a separate matter and is licensed where a licence applies.

lessons.title: Victorian pool permit drawings, build time limits and stop-and-report steps
learningOutcomes: State what SP 02 requires a permit drawing to show for an indoor pool and its barrier.
Describe what SP 02 says about recirculation and filtration designs at the permit stage.
Describe how a worker escalates an unpermitted or non-compliant barrier situation.
State the SP 01 start and finish time limits for swimming pool and barrier building work.

instructionSections.heading: Permit drawings
instructionSections.body: Victorian rule (VBA Building Practice Note SP 02, Version 3, 26 September 2023). For an indoor pool, building permit drawings must show the barrier, the child-resistant doorsets and the direction the door swings. Recirculation and filtration designs must be given to the relevant building surveyor with the building permit application.

instructionSections.heading: Barrier standard
instructionSections.body: SP 02 names AS 1926.1-2012 as the barrier standard. Check the barrier against that standard, and report any shortfall rather than adjusting it on site.

instructionSections.heading: Stop, record and report
instructionSections.body: Workers do not move a barrier or precaution to get round a permit problem. They stop, record and report, and they do not put the fence back themselves.

instructionSections.heading: Time limits for pool and barrier work
instructionSections.body: Victorian rule (VBA Building Practice Note SP 01, Version 2.0, 27 April 2023). The building work has 12 months from the permit's issue date to begin, and six months from the start to finish. The note links these limits to regulations 53 and 54, which were not read for this lesson.

lessons.title: Handover, competency and specialist referrals
learningOutcomes: Explain the boundary for handover, competency and specialist referrals and identify when work must stop.
Prepare a task-specific, documented decision for handover, competency and specialist referrals under company and local requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Why close-out and referral matter
instructionSections.body: A job is not finished when the last cloth is put away. It is finished when the authorised work has been completed and recorded, the work that was not authorised has been excluded and reported, and the next person knows what they can and cannot do. This lesson covers three linked decisions: the handover of completed work to the client or site, the check that the worker is competent for the task being signed off, and the referral of tasks, hazards or claims that belong to a specialist. Each one needs a clear record. Without it, a client may later believe that work was done that was not, or that a site is safe when nobody checked.

instructionSections.heading: Write an accurate handover
instructionSections.body: A handover states what was done, where, with which products and methods, and when. It also states what was not done and why, such as an area excluded because the material was uncharacterised, a stain left untreated because its cause was unknown, or a repair outside the cleaning scope. Record any residual condition you observed, such as damage that was present before the work or a surface that was unsuitable for the method. Use plain, factual language, and avoid words that imply certainty you do not have. Before-and-after photographs, where the site allows them, support the record. The client should receive a copy or summary and the chance to ask questions before the job is closed.

instructionSections.heading: Decline unsupported certification
instructionSections.body: Clients sometimes ask a cleaner to certify that a site is clean, safe, decontaminated or free of a hazard. A cleaning business should not give that certification unless it holds a qualified person's evidence for it and the certification is within its authority. Where a client asks for it on a site you could not assess, decline the certificate, report only the observed and authorised work, and refer the certification question to an appropriately qualified specialist. Write the reason in the record.

instructionSections.heading: Check competency before sign-off
instructionSections.body: A worker signs off a task only when they are competent for that task and the method used. Competency is shown by a combination of records: the training completed, the supervised tasks signed off by a competent person, and a practical verification of the specific method. A training certificate is evidence of training, not proof of current competence for a specific task. Check that the worker has performed the method under supervision, that the record is current, and that any licence the work requires is held by the person who did it. Where a worker is not verified, the sign-off belongs to a verified person, and the record must show who signed off what. Review competency records when equipment, products or methods change.

instructionSections.heading: Refer what is outside the approved scope
instructionSections.body: Refer a task or hazard to a specialist when it is outside the worker's training or the business's authority, when the material or hazard is unidentified, when the work needs a licence the business does not hold, or when the client wants a result the approved method cannot give. A referral is a written handover to a specialist with the facts: the site, the request, what was observed, what was reported, what was done, what remains unknown, and any photographs or product information you hold. Record the referral with the person it went to and the date. The cleaning job is either held or closed with the excluded work stated, and the client is told who will take over that work. Do not give an opinion you are not qualified to give, and do not pass on a claim you could not verify.

instructionSections.heading: Worked example on an unknown site
instructionSections.body: Consider a client who asks, at handover, for a certificate that a site is fully decontaminated. The site had an unknown contamination history. The cleaner's record shows what was cleaned, with which approved products, and what was not assessed. The cleaner declines the certificate, explains that the business cannot verify the decontamination status of the site, and refers the certification question in writing to a qualified specialist. The handover says that the observed cleaning was completed and that decontamination was not assessed.

instructionSections.heading: Licence notice
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work, and it does not qualify a worker to sign off licensed work. Check the licence rules where the work takes place, and make the referral to a provider who holds the relevant authority.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop, refer and tell your supervisor if you are asked to sign off a task you did not perform or are not verified to perform, if the client asks you to certify a condition you cannot verify, if the record would be incomplete without the excluded work being stated, or if a hazard is found after the handover has been drafted. Do not close the job until the record matches the work done.

lessons.title: Complete site inspection case study
learningOutcomes: Apply the approved procedure to complete site inspection case study
Identify limits of authority and escalate hazards
Demonstrate and document the procedure in a supervised simulation

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Set inspection boundaries
instructionSections.body: Obtain the signed scope, site map, inspection checklist and acceptance standards. Separate contractual inclusions from optional requests. Confirm access permission and any hazards before entering. Never assume that a visually tidy room meets hygiene or safety requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Build an evidence-based sampling route
instructionSections.body: List rooms, surfaces and high-touch points. Use a consistent clockwise or zone-based route, prioritising agreed critical items. Mark inaccessible areas as not inspected rather than passing them. Identify what requires direct observation versus documentary evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Assess objectively
instructionSections.body: Record each finding against a stated acceptance criterion: location, condition, expected standard and observed deviation. Distinguish cosmetic preferences from agreed defects and immediate hazards. Do not infer microbial safety from appearance alone.

instructionSections.heading: Escalate significant findings
instructionSections.body: Stop and isolate unsafe conditions within authority. Report sharps, suspected biological contamination, chemical exposure, damaged electrical equipment or unsafe access to the designated responsible person; do not improvise specialist remediation.

instructionSections.heading: Conclude and communicate
instructionSections.body: Summarise pass, fail and not-inspected outcomes, corrective priorities and any limitations. Arrange follow-up verification with a responsible person and protect client confidentiality in reports.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: Electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In Victoria, PV installation and maintenance is licensed electrical installation work, and PV DC cables may stay live when the power is off. NSW electrical wiring work includes repairing. On the Victorian, Western Australian and New South Wales pages checked, plain panel washing is not stated to need a licence, and any electrical work on a PV array is referred to a licensed electrician. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

lessons.title: Defect rectification and reinspection exercise
learningOutcomes: Apply the approved procedure to defect rectification and reinspection exercise
Identify limits of authority and escalate hazards
Demonstrate and document the procedure in a supervised simulation

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Classify defects

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Purpose and learning outcome
After this lesson, the learner can demonstrate define acceptance criteria in a routine cleaning workplace, identify limits of their authority and document the result. The following procedures are examples; always apply the approved site process and task instructions.

Detailed workplace method
Read the approved work order line by line. Separate included tasks, exclusions, client preferences, frequency and evidence obligations. Write criteria that an independent inspector can observe: for example, a specified mirror is free of visible streaks under normal room lighting, rather than “looks perfect”. Identify material limitations and pre-existing damage. Do not promise stain removal or restoration outside the agreed scope.

Safety, boundaries and escalation
Before proceeding, confirm the actual work scope, hazards, material or equipment suitability and who can authorise changes. Stop and seek direction when work is unsafe, outside training, or the requested result conflicts with a site instruction. Record facts, not assumptions.

Worked example
A property manager requests a “spotless” kitchen but the work order excludes the inside of the oven. The supervisor records oven interior as excluded, defines checks for benches, sink and appliance exteriors, and asks for written approval before any extra work.

Supervised practical
Give learners a sample scope with ten tasks, two exclusions and three ambiguous phrases. Have them create a checklist with an observable criterion and evidence type for each included task.

Assessment and corrective feedback
An assessor observes the learner and verifies: The checklist matches authorised scope, distinguishes exclusions, contains measurable observations and flags ambiguity before work begins. If any critical safety action is missed, provide coaching and require a new demonstration. Attendance alone is not proof of competence.

Before proceeding, confirm the actual work scope, hazards, material or equipment suitability and who can authorise changes. Stop and seek direction when work is unsafe, outside training, or the requested result conflicts with a site instruction. Record facts, not assumptions.

Supervised practical
Inspect a staged bathroom and kitchenette containing six cleaning defects, two pre-existing damage marks and one unsafe-access item. Record each correctly.

Assessment and corrective feedback
An assessor observes the learner and verifies: Identifies defects systematically, avoids unsafe access, differentiates cleaning issues from damage and reports inaccessible areas. Avoid people, addresses, documents, valuables, security codes and personal possessions unless explicitly necessary and authorised. Safety, boundaries and escalation
Before proceeding, confirm the actual work scope, hazards, material or equipment suitability and who can authorise changes. Stop and seek direction when work is unsafe, outside training, or the requested result conflicts with a site instruction. Record facts, not assumptions.

A cleaner photographs a stained countertop but a customer invoice with personal details is visible. They reposition the shot to exclude the invoice, record the condition and upload only through the approved system.

Supervised practical
Review eight sample photographs. Decide which may be used, which need retaking and which must be withheld; then create a short evidence register with location, purpose and permission.

Assessment and corrective feedback
An assessor observes the learner and verifies: Collects relevant evidence without exposing private information, accurately labels records and preserves originals. If any critical safety action is missed, provide coaching and require a new demonstration. Attendance alone is not proof of competence.

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Learning outcome
By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to produce an accurate end-of-shift record while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

Workplace procedure
Reinspect completed zones against the actual contract checklist. Record completed work, exclusions, access restrictions, defects, incidents, consumables and follow-up requests. Distinguish an observed defect from a suspected cause. Photograph only where authorised, avoiding personal information. Secure keys, alarms and equipment using the site process, and confirm the site is left safe. Hand unresolved hazards directly to the appropriate supervisor; never mark unverified tasks complete.

Decision boundaries
Before acting, confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation. If the task exceeds training, consent, safe access or agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others as appropriate, report promptly and document the reason. Never substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

Worked workplace example
A restroom is closed for a plumbing fault. The cleaner records that it was not cleaned, adds the access restriction and notifies the supervisor rather than ticking the entire floor as complete.

Guided practical exercise
Perform a simulated shift closeout with a missed task, a broken vacuum and an access issue; produce a complete handover and explain the escalation priority.

Assessment and feedback
An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Reports truthfully, verifies work, secures the site and assigns unresolved items for follow-up. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.

learningOutcomes: Confirm site, authorised scope, safe access, serviceable kit and assigned tasks before beginning work.
Communicate a clear go/no-go decision with identified hazards, exclusions and support needed.

instructionSections.body: Capture approved prestart evidence, report exceptions and obtain supervisor approval for scope or safety changes.

instructionSections.body: After this lesson, the learner can demonstrate record and communicate readiness in a routine cleaning workplace, identify limits of their authority and document the result. lessons.title: Incident and performance forms as one system
learningOutcomes: Record an incident with facts, immediate action and a follow-up date
Rate performance against defined, observable standards, with evidence
Link incident, performance and training records so that corrective action is proportionate and documented

instructionSections.heading: One system, several forms
instructionSections.body: The sample proposal includes an incident report, a performance appraisal form, an absence report and an overtime request. These work as a system because they share a person's record and a supervisor's review. An incident can lead to training. A pattern in site inspections can feed a performance review. Absence patterns can point to a rostering problem. Design the forms so that each one points to the next step, and so that a person's file can be read in order.

instructionSections.heading: Record incidents as facts first
instructionSections.body: An incident record states the date, the time, the place, the people involved, what happened, what was done straight away, whether anyone was hurt, any witnesses, and the follow-up date. Write facts before opinions, and keep the description specific. 'The mop bucket was left on the stairs at 4 pm' is usable. 'The worker was careless' is not. The sample incident form has an explanation area and a section for the level of corrective action. Complete the explanation first, and decide on any action only after the facts are recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Corrective action must be proportionate
instructionSections.body: The sample offers three levels of action: a verbal warning, a written warning, and suspension with referral to human resources. The levels exist for a reason, but each step needs a procedure and a record. For most first incidents the right response is feedback, a retraining step and a dated note. Record the response and the reason for it.

instructionSections.heading: Keep safety incidents separate from discipline
instructionSections.body: An injury, a near miss, a chemical exposure or damage to a client's property is first a safety event. It must be reported, treated and recorded under the workplace safety procedure before any discipline is considered. A disciplinary form does not replace an injury record.

instructionSections.heading: Rate performance against standards
instructionSections.body: The sample appraisal uses nine competency areas, including job knowledge, quality of work, productivity, dependability, attendance, teamwork, personal hygiene, safety awareness and supervisor ability. Each area is rated as exceeding, achieving or below standard, and where a person achieves the standard the rater adds a marginal or proficient level. Define each area in observable terms before the review. For example, quality of work should mean the checklist items completed to standard on inspected jobs, not the supervisor's general impression.

instructionSections.heading: Link the forms into a plan
instructionSections.body: A below-standard result should lead to a sequence: documented feedback, then support or retraining, then a performance improvement plan if the result does not change. The sample says that a below-standard result calls for help from the operations team. Write the improvement plan with specific actions, a named support contact and a review date. A plan without support is a warning, not an improvement plan.

instructionSections.heading: Handle personal and health matters carefully
instructionSections.body: The personal hygiene area in the sample appraisal needs particular care. Record what was observed and what was asked, in factual terms, and discuss it privately. Do not record medical diagnoses or health details unless the person has given consent and there is a confirmed reason. Store performance and health-related information securely, and limit who can read it.

lessons.title: Objective defect classification
learningOutcomes: Classify missed tasks, incomplete cleaning, damage concerns and pre-existing conditions using evidence
Record factual observations and limitations without compromising privacy or safety
Demonstrate a documented decision, corrective action and verification workflow

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level, water-fed pole and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Any work above ground level, or from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted: it needs employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Purpose and scope
instructionSections.body: Objective defect classification is used to verify agreed cleaning outcomes, not to guarantee sterility, restoration or an outcome beyond the signed scope. Read the work order, site instructions, product constraints and client acceptance criteria. Identify what can be observed safely, what requires specialist authorisation, and which uncertainties must be escalated. Classify missed tasks, incomplete cleaning, damage concerns and pre-existing conditions using evidence.

instructionSections.heading: Prepare the inspection
instructionSections.body: Before inspecting, confirm the correct location, work-order version, completion status and any access restrictions. Use a consistent inspection sequence from entrance to exit, top to bottom where appropriate, and clean to dirty. Separate immediate safety hazards from ordinary presentation defects. Choose evidence that is proportionate, lawful and approved by the site. Never disturb hazardous material, open restricted storage or test electrical equipment without authorisation.

instructionSections.heading: Perform and document
instructionSections.body: For each finding record the zone and exact location, the agreed criterion, what was observed, when it was observed, and whether it is a defect, a limitation or a question. Distinguish objective observations from interpretation: “visible residue at basin tap base” is preferable to “poor cleaning”. Photograph only when permitted; avoid faces, personal documents and identifying belongings. Never modify an original record to conceal an error.

instructionSections.heading: Respond and verify
instructionSections.body: Where the finding is within scope, assign a safe corrective action to an authorised worker, agree priority and record completion. Reinspect the same criterion rather than assuming the problem is resolved. Escalate damage, exposure risks, disputes and work outside the contract. If a product or procedure requires specialist testing, record that testing was not performed; do not invent a result.

instructionSections.heading: Worked workplace example
instructionSections.body: A stained grout line cannot be restored by routine cleaning; distinguish a persistent stain from missed soil. A sound response identifies the agreed standard, makes a factual observation, records the limitation, requests approval when required, and communicates the outcome without assigning blame.

instructionSections.heading: Guided practical
instructionSections.body: Sort ten anonymised findings into service defect, pre-existing condition, safety issue or scope query. The learner must explain each choice, identify at least one privacy or safety constraint, record a finding with a timestamp and location, and show how a supervisor would verify any correction.

instructionSections.heading: Common mistakes and corrections
instructionSections.body: Avoid treating a photograph as proof of disinfection, confusing a pre-existing defect with a missed task, recording personal information unnecessarily, or closing a finding without reinspection. Correct these by using a scope-linked checklist, objective descriptions, minimum-necessary evidence and a documented closeout step.

instructionSections.heading: Knowledge and transfer
instructionSections.body: Explain why the agreed acceptance criterion must be identified before judging a surface. Describe how to record an observation that a different inspector can independently verify. State when inspection must stop and be escalated. Apply the same process to a new site with different privacy and access requirements.

lessons.title: Incident and damage report (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Make the area safe and get help before recording anything when someone may be hurt
Record facts, witnesses and immediate action in sequence, with opinion marked as opinion
Set follow-up actions with an owner, a due date and a check that the action worked

instructionSections.heading: Why reports are written at once
instructionSections.body: An incident is any event that could have caused harm or loss, or did: a near miss, an injury, damage to property, or a complaint about damage. A good report is written while the facts are fresh, and it separates what happened from what anyone thinks caused it. Start with safety. If someone may be hurt, make the area safe and get first aid or emergency help before writing anything. Then record the facts with times, places and names, the immediate action taken, and the people who saw it. Causes come later, and they are marked as initial until they are checked.

instructionSections.heading: Facts, witnesses and immediate action
instructionSections.body: Describe what happened in the order it happened. Write what was seen, heard or measured, and mark any opinion as opinion. Record the immediate action in the order it was taken, with times. For each witness, record their name, how to contact them, and a short summary in their own words. Ask whether they agree to be contacted, and record the answer. Photographs should show the scene, the damage, and any product or equipment involved, and the report should say who took them and when. Keep personal and health information to what the business needs, and store it under the business's privacy procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Follow-up, notification and learning
instructionSections.body: Follow-up actions turn the report into change. Each action needs an owner, a due date and a closed date, and it should address the cause rather than only the symptom. Check the business incident procedure for who must be told and when. Whether a particular incident must be notified to a regulator depends on the state or territory and on the type of incident. The report exists to decide what will change, not to assign blame.

lessons.title: Pricing by hours per project
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate project hours, including set-up, travel and checking time
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instructionSections.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instructionSections.body: The sample business plan says its prices will be based on the expected number of hours per project. Hours are a sound starting point for cleaning work, because the crew, the travel, the set-up and the quality checks all become time. Once you know the hours, you can see the cost, the margin and the effect of a change in scope. A flat price with no hours behind it hides both risk and waste, and it cannot be defended when a client asks why a job costs what it does.

instructionSections.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instructionSections.body: Take the total cost of running the business over a period and divide it by the productive hours in that period. Total cost includes wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation, where your staff arrangements require them, vehicle running costs, equipment, consumables, insurance, administration and premises. Productive hours are the hours a crew is doing chargeable work, not the paid hours on a roster. Use billable hours as the divisor, not the full working week. For example, if you pay for 40 hours and 30 of them are chargeable, the cost per productive hour is higher than the hourly wage.

instructionSections.heading: Estimate the hours
instructionSections.body: Break each job into tasks, such as a room, a bathroom, a window or an area. Estimate the time for each task at a standard speed, then add set-up, pack-down, travel between sites and a checking allowance. Use ranges where the job is uncertain. Add a set allowance for delays outside your control, such as delivery delays, staff absence and weather, and size it from your own records. After each job, record the actual hours and the reason for any difference, and use the gap to correct the next estimate. Over time, your standard times become reliable for your own team and your own methods.

instructionSections.heading: Turn hours into a price
instructionSections.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour to get the cost of the job. Add a margin that reflects your target and the risk in the job, such as difficult access, poor condition or a tight deadline. Apply your materials policy and your minimum charge. The result is a price with a visible basis. If a client wants a lower price, you can show which hours or which part of the scope they are asking you to remove, which keeps the discussion on the work rather than on the person.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the quote honest
instructionSections.body: A quote should state the scope, the hours or price basis, the exclusions, what the client must provide, and how long the quote is valid. Do not show the internal cost per hour to the client unless your policy says to. Record every change to the scope and re-quote when the scope changes. Quotes issued without a scope or without exclusions can lead to disputes.

instructionSections.heading: Review your estimates
instructionSections.body: Compare estimated and actual hours for at least the first ten jobs of each type. If the variance is consistently above an agreed threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules. A pricing method is not finished when it is written. It is finished when actual hours match quoted hours closely enough for the work to make money.

lessons.title: Price for sustainable delivery
learningOutcomes: Build a price from the true cost of delivering the job, including labour, materials, travel, equipment and overheads.
Explain why a price below the cost of safe delivery is not sustainable.
Record the pricing basis so that every quote can be checked and approved.

instructionSections.heading: Count the full cost of the job
instructionSections.body: A job's price must cover everything needed to deliver it safely and to the standard. Count the labour time, including set-up, travel, the site induction, the handover and the administration. Count the materials and products used, the wear on equipment, the cost of protective equipment, the cost of waste disposal, the insurance and licences the work requires under the rules where you operate, and a share of overheads such as the vehicle, phone, software and training. Test the price against all overheads, not only the job's materials and labour, because card fees, insurance and software are easy to miss. Unpaid time, such as re-quoting or chasing payment, is also a cost of the business. A price that counts only the product and the hour on site will not sustain the business.

instructionSections.heading: Price for the job, not the hour alone
instructionSections.body: Pricing by the hour is simple, but it rewards slow work and hides the cost of travel and set-up. Pricing by the job, by the area or by the unit is often clearer for the customer, provided the scope is described and the cost basis is known. For routine work with a known scope, a flat price is usually easier to set. Where the scope or time may shift, an hourly basis is the safer choice. Choose the method that matches the service and record it. Where a job needs extra time for safety controls, such as a walk-through, an access permit or a safe method, that time must be in the price. A safe method is not optional and must not be discounted away.

instructionSections.heading: Minimum charges and the basis for discounts
instructionSections.body: Set a minimum charge that covers the cost of travel and set-up for a short job. A minimum is easier to defend when its contents are written down, such as travel inside the service area and a fixed block of on-site time. Record the basis for any discount, such as a repeat contract or a block booking, and check that the discounted price still covers the full cost of delivery. Do not discount the safety controls, the qualified labour or the licensed work. Any price that is below the calculated cost must be approved and recorded with the reason.

lessons.title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a home-service business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instructionSections.heading: What break-even means
instructionSections.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level the business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. The figure is useful for setting prices, deciding when to hire and checking whether a new channel can pay for itself. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages that go into it.

instructionSections.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instructionSections.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of jobs in a month. They include rent or an office share, insurance, phone and software subscriptions, vehicle registration and loan repayments. Variable costs move with each job. They include consumables, cleaning products used on a job, subcontractor fees and the payment fees charged on each sale. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales: divide the variable cost in a period by the sales in the same period. Bank guidance (ANZ) defines the two cost types and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss. Check that percentage across at least three periods before relying on it, because a single unusual month can mislead.

instructionSections.heading: The formula
instructionSections.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. The quantity one minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales that is left to cover fixed costs. Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 18% becomes 0.18. Then the contribution margin of an 18% variable cost is 0.82.

instructionSections.heading: Work the calculation in order
instructionSections.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source and date. Then compute the contribution margin. Then divide the fixed costs by it. Finally convert the result into a number of jobs at your average job price, and round up to whole jobs, because a part job does not cover costs on its own. The sample plan's fixed cost and variable cost figures are removed here because they are United States figures from 2002. Its break-even figures did not reconcile with its own inputs, so none of them is used. The method is the check: divide fixed costs by the contribution margin, then test the result against inputs you can source.

instructionSections.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instructionSections.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit. Then write down the reconciled figure with its inputs and drop the others. A plan that states a break-even figure without its inputs cannot be checked, and a figure that cannot be checked should not be used to set prices.

lessons.title: Scope of works for a service site
learningOutcomes: Write a scope of works that lists areas, tasks, frequencies, standards, responsibilities and exclusions
Use frequency language that a client and a team can both check
Select products by surface compatibility, and state the source of that check

instructionSections.heading: What a scope of works does
instructionSections.body: A scope of works sets out what work will be done, where, how often, to what standard, by whom, and what is excluded. The price and the rostered hours rest on it. The sample proposal uses a scope with clearly separated areas, tasks and frequencies, and it attaches reporting forms to the same contract. Write yours so that a new team member and the client's site manager would reach the same understanding of the job.

instructionSections.heading: Divide the site into areas
instructionSections.body: The sample proposal groups the site into general floors, restrooms, locker rooms and windows. Each area then has its own task list. Walk the site before you write the scope, and draw a simple zone map. Label each area, note its surfaces and fittings, and record who uses it and how often. A scope written from an office floor plan, without a walk, is a common reason for underpriced work.

instructionSections.heading: Use frequency language that can be checked
instructionSections.body: The sample uses daily, once per shift, weekly, monthly, quarterly and semi-annual frequencies. These are useful because each can be checked against a record. The frequencies are sample values from a janitorial contract, written for an undated, non-Australian site, so they are not an industry standard. Define each term once in the scope. Write 'once per shift' only after the shift is defined. Avoid 'as required' or 'when needed', because no one can check completion against them. Where a task depends on a trigger such as a spill or a complaint, write the trigger and the response time.

instructionSections.heading: Standard work instructions at the point of work
instructionSections.body: The sample plan posts a step-by-step work instruction on the back of the restroom door, with a schedule for initials. This is good practice, because the instruction sits where the work happens. A standard work instruction is a short numbered sheet for one task or one area. It lists the materials, the PPE, the steps, the standard and a sign-off grid. Keep each sheet short, date it and give it a version number. Remove superseded versions from the site.

instructionSections.heading: Surfaces, chemicals and compatibility
instructionSections.body: The sample proposal warns against using an acid-based cleaner on stainless steel. The principle applies generally. Each surface tolerates only some products, and some products damage or discolour surfaces or create hazards when mixed. Before a product goes into a scope, check the product label, its safety data sheet and the surface manufacturer's care guidance. Record the product, its approved surfaces and its use. Do not mix products unless the label and the safety data sheet allow it. Do not let staff choose products from memory.

instructionSections.heading: Say who supplies what
instructionSections.body: The sample notes that matting is charged under a separate janitorial contract. Make that kind of split explicit in your own scope. State which party supplies consumables, equipment, replacement parts and any site stock. Also state what the team does about damage, vandalism and security matters. The sample requires graffiti to be reported to security rather than cleaned by the team. Each reporting rule belongs in the scope, with a contact and a timeframe.

instructionSections.heading: Exclusions and price
instructionSections.body: Exclusions protect both parties. Name each item that is not included, such as specialist treatments, exterior work, height work or biohazard response, and say whether it can be quoted separately. Then link the scope to hours using the method in the pricing lesson. Every area, frequency and standard in the scope should have a time figure behind it.

lessons.title: Building an offer that justifies a higher rate
learningOutcomes: Write an offer with a clear promised outcome, time frame and conditions
Identify the friction and risk the customer carries and reduce them
Price the offer on value and cost, not only time

instructionSections.heading: A bad offer versus a good offer
instructionSections.body: "I will clean your house" is a service. "I will leave your kitchen and bathrooms ready for guests within 3 hours, or I will redo the rooms that fail the checklist at no charge" is an offer. The customer buys the result and the certainty of getting it.

instructionSections.heading: The five parts of an offer
instructionSections.body: A clear outcome; a defined time frame; the work the customer must do; the certainty you provide (checklists, photos, guarantee); and the risk you carry. Keep each part specific and checkable. Put the scope and exclusions in writing, because a written quote can become binding once it is accepted (business.gov.au, 1 August 2025).

instructionSections.heading: Reducing friction
instructionSections.body: Make the booking, access and handover simple. Fewer steps and fewer decisions for the customer usually allow a higher price, because the customer is paying for convenience and reliability.

instructionSections.heading: Guarantees and claims
instructionSections.body: A guarantee must be something you can deliver and are able to pay for. In Australia, consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law apply to services, and they cannot be removed by contract. Claims about results, including any measured percentage improvement, must be substantiated. Check current ACCC guidance before publishing any measurable claim. A written workmanship warranty is an optional extra that sits on top of the consumer guarantees rather than replacing them, and a 'no refunds' line does not override a customer's rights for services (business.gov.au, 27 May 2025).

instructionSections.heading: Pricing on value
instructionSections.body: Price from the outcome and the risk, then check against your cost and time. A premium rate is justified when the customer can see the result, the certainty and the saved time. Government guidance says a quote should recover every cost and add a margin, so check the price against cost before deciding on any premium (business.gov.au, 1 August 2025). Stepped packages, with each higher level adding something the customer can see, are one way to present the offer (Jobber Academy, published May 2021, updated 8 October 2024). Show one clear total and say whether GST is included; Western Australia's consumer agency guidance asks for this (WA Consumer Protection, updated 4 September 2026).

lessons.title: Quote and proposal (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Write a scope that states the work, the area and the finish in observable terms
List inclusions and exclusions so that each one can be checked on site
Record the site assumptions, price basis, time window, terms and acceptance method in one document

instructionSections.heading: What a quote does and what a proposal adds
instructionSections.body: A quote is an offer to carry out a defined piece of work for a stated price, on stated conditions, for a stated period. A proposal is a fuller document that explains the approach, but it still needs the same defined scope, price and conditions. Both fail when the wording promises more than the price pays for. The aim of this template is to make the scope observable. A person reading the quote should be able to say what is included, what is not, which conditions were assumed, and what happens if those conditions change.

instructionSections.heading: Scope, inclusions, exclusions and site assumptions
instructionSections.body: Write the scope in terms of the work, the area and the finish, not the feeling the customer wants. Inclusions list each item of work the price covers, one row per item. Exclusions list what a reasonable customer might expect but which is not in the price, such as a particular material, access that is not provided, or heights the business does not work at. Where an exclusion depends on a condition, state the condition. Describe the site conditions you assumed when pricing, including access, power, water, the state of the surfaces and any constraint. If those conditions change, the change should trigger a variation that is priced and agreed. Price and agree extra work in writing before it starts (WA Consumer Protection, updated 4 September 2026).

instructionSections.heading: Price, time window, terms and acceptance
instructionSections.body: State the price basis clearly, because a fixed price, a rate per hour and an estimate make three different promises. Say whether the price includes GST or other tax, or record that the tax treatment is still to be confirmed. Western Australia's consumer agency guidance on quotes asks for the total including GST and a statement of whether GST is included; check the rule that applies in your state or territory. Give a time window and name the factors that could move it. Terms should cover payment, cancellation, variations and the remedy if work does not meet the agreed scope. Whether a given term can be enforced depends on the law that applies, so check standard terms with an adviser. A remedy should describe what the business will do, and should not promise a result that depends on things outside its control. Consumer guarantees cannot be excluded by contract, so a remedy clause should not try to remove them (ACCC guide, July 2021). Set a validity date, which lets you re-price if material costs move, and record how acceptance is given. Follow the business's quoting approval process before the quote is issued.

lessons.title: Pricing and margin worksheet (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Calculate total job cost from labour, materials, travel and an overhead allocation, each with a stated basis
Calculate a price from a chosen margin, using the formula that matches the margin type stated
Check the final price against the minimum charge and the rounding rule, and record any decision that departs from them

instructionSections.heading: What the worksheet is for
instructionSections.body: The pricing worksheet builds a price from what the job costs to do, then adds a margin that the business has chosen on purpose. It answers three questions: what the job costs to deliver, what margin this kind of job needs, and what price results. It is not a way to find the highest price the market will tolerate, which is a separate question covered in the offer lesson. Use it before every quote that is not a repeat of a job already costed, and keep it with the quote so that the reason for a price can be seen later.

instructionSections.heading: Labour, materials, travel and overheads
instructionSections.body: Labour is the hours for each task multiplied by the labour rate set by the business, including paid time that is not billed separately, such as setup, packing and necessary travel. Record the basis for each hours figure: timed on a previous job, estimated, or taken from a standard the business uses. Some estimating guides suggest a buffer of 10 to 20 percent on job estimates for unexpected work; if the business adds one, state it as its own line with its basis. Materials are the quantity used, multiplied by the unit cost, with a waste allowance written as a percentage you choose and can explain. Travel is the time or distance cost of the job. Overheads are the monthly fixed costs of running the business, divided by the billable hours expected in a month, giving an overhead amount per hour that is applied to the job. Record the method so that it can be checked. Where the business has a materials cost policy or a minimum charge, apply it and record that it was applied.

instructionSections.heading: Margin, price and the minimum charge
instructionSections.body: Gross margin is the share of the price that remains after the job cost, calculated as (price minus cost) divided by price. Markup is a different measure: the amount added to cost, calculated as (price minus cost) divided by cost. The same job gives different numbers under the two methods, so the worksheet must state which one is used. To calculate a price from a gross margin target, divide total cost by one minus the target. To calculate a price from a markup, multiply total cost by one plus the markup. Round the price under the business rule, then check it against the minimum charge. If the price falls below the minimum charge, the business must either apply the minimum or decline the job, and the worksheet must record which. Some estimating guides suggest setting a floor margin for each job, and changing the price or scope when a job falls below it.

lessons.title: Lone-worker safety and check-in scenario
learningOutcomes: Apply the approved procedure to lone-worker safety and check-in scenario
Identify limits of authority and escalate hazards

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. Panels can produce voltage in daylight even when the rest of the system is off. Cleaning on this track does not include electrical work, isolation of the system, opening enclosures, or cable or connector repair. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Identify lone-work conditions
instructionSections.body: Review whether the task occurs without nearby support, including after-hours premises, isolated properties and travel between sites. Check organisational lone-work policies and any site-specific risk assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Establish contact and escalation
instructionSections.body: Confirm supervisor, expected start and finish, check-in intervals, communication device, location-sharing permissions and missed-check-in escalation procedure before starting. Do not rely on a single unreliable channel.

instructionSections.heading: Control access and personal safety
instructionSections.body: Verify authorised entry, lighting, exits and safe parking. Avoid entering where occupants, animals, threats or hazardous conditions create unmanaged risk. Do not confront an aggressive person or attempt to investigate a suspected crime.

instructionSections.heading: Respond to missed contact
instructionSections.body: Use the approved escalation tree: attempt agreed contact, notify supervisor and arrange a welfare response where warranted. In immediate danger, contact emergency services using the applicable local number.

instructionSections.heading: Document and review
instructionSections.body: Record check-in outcomes and safety concerns without collecting unnecessary personal location history. Debrief near misses and update the risk assessment before repeating the work.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: Electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In Victoria, PV installation and maintenance is licensed electrical installation work, and PV DC cables may stay live when the power is off. NSW electrical wiring work includes repairing. On the Victorian, Western Australian and New South Wales pages checked, plain panel washing is not stated to need a licence, and any electrical work on a PV array is referred to a licensed electrician. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instructionSections.heading: Overview

instructionSections.heading: Observe without exposure
instructionSections.body: Do not touch unknown substances or enter restricted areas to investigate. Check site induction information, warning signs, task instructions and changes since the last visit. Keep bystanders away from a suspected hazard.

instructionSections.heading: Record and act

instructionSections.heading: Choose effective controls

instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body: Infection hazards can be transferred through hands, contaminated tools, touch surfaces, droplets or other pathways depending on the organism and setting. Routine cleaners should not diagnose disease or assume that every stain is infectious. Identify plausible transfer routes by tracing where hands, cloths and equipment move during a job. Prioritise high-touch points and prevent transfer from toilets or waste to clean preparation areas. Follow the site infection-prevention plan and escalate unknown biological hazards or outbreak-specific requirements. Cleaning removes soil; disinfection is a separate process when required by the task and product instructions.

instructionSections.body: Before beginning, identify when hand hygiene is required: on entry where directed, before handling clean supplies, after glove removal, after handling waste, after contamination and at task transitions. instructionSections.heading: Instruction
instructionSections.body:
Learning outcome
By the end of this lesson, demonstrate the ability to recognise and report safeguarding concerns while respecting the approved service plan, site procedures and limits of the cleaning role.

Workplace procedure
Be alert to immediate danger, unexplained environmental hazards, coercion, neglect indicators or threatening behaviour without attempting to diagnose or investigate. Record only directly observed facts and the person’s own words when relevant. Follow the organisation’s safeguarding and mandatory-reporting procedures applicable to the service and jurisdiction. If someone is in immediate danger, use emergency services and the site emergency plan. Do not promise secrecy or confront a suspected perpetrator.

Decision boundaries
Before acting, confirm authorisation, hazards and the person responsible for escalation. If the task exceeds training, consent, safe access or agreed scope, pause the affected work, protect others as appropriate, report promptly and document the reason. Never substitute an improvised method for a required specialist procedure.

Worked workplace example
A cleaner notices a blocked exit and hears a client say they feel unsafe. They ensure immediate safety within their competence, record the exact statement and notify the safeguarding contact promptly.

Guided practical exercise
Review four scenarios involving possible neglect, a privacy concern, an immediate threat and an ordinary housekeeping issue; classify urgency and draft factual reports.

Assessment and feedback
An assessor should observe a complete demonstration and confirm: Distinguishes emergency from routine escalation, records facts without speculation and protects the person’s privacy. If a critical safety, privacy or consent step is missed, provide targeted feedback and require reassessment before signoff.
