lessons.title: Scoring a hazard: likelihood, severity and the risk band
learningOutcomes: Score a hazard for likelihood and for severity using the five-point scales of the agreed scheme.
Calculate a risk value from the two scores and assign it to the correct band.
State the action each band requires before work starts.
Find a scoring or banding error in a completed register.

instructionSections.heading: Why score a hazard at all
instructionSections.body: A risk assessment turns a list of hazards into a decision about what to do first. A hazard that scores high needs a different response from one that scores low, and the score is what lets a supervisor see where effort and authority should go. The register this lesson is built on scores every hazard twice: once for the risk as it stands with the routine controls in place, and once for the residual risk after any further controls are added. Scoring is a trained judgement, written down, so everyone on the team uses the same method and a second person can follow the reasoning. The scheme is a business choice.

instructionSections.heading: The two scales
instructionSections.body: Likelihood asks how often the harm could happen in the circumstances of the job, on a scale from 1 for something that almost never happens up to 5 for exposure that happens often and routinely. Severity asks how bad the outcome would be if the harm happened, on a scale from 1 for a minor injury with no lost days up to 5 for a death. Score likelihood by thinking about the task as it is actually done on that site, not about every conceivable accident. Score severity by thinking about the most likely serious outcome of the hazard, not the best case. Two errors appear often. The first is lowering likelihood because a control is listed, before that control has been checked. The second is scoring severity for a minor event that could easily have been far worse. Write one short line of reasons next to each score so a reviewer can see how it was reached.

instructionSections.heading: Multiplying and banding
instructionSections.body: The risk value is likelihood multiplied by severity. Because both scales run from 1 to 5, the only products that can occur are the whole numbers 1 to 6, 8 to 10, 12, 15, 16, 20 and 25. The scheme places 1 to 6 in the Low band, 8 to 12 in the Medium band and 15 to 25 in the High band. Every value a pair of scores can produce falls into one band, so no row is left without a band. A likelihood of 4 with a severity of 4 gives 16, which is High. A likelihood of 3 with a severity of 3 gives 9, which is Medium. Check the arithmetic on every row. A register whose numbers cannot be reproduced from the two scales cannot be relied on, however sensible the wording looks.

instructionSections.heading: What each band requires
instructionSections.body: A Low result may be tolerable, but it is still worth re-examining the job to see whether the exposure can be lowered, and where one job brings several hazardous activities together, a method statement is prepared for that job. A Medium result means the job is reworked, or the exposure reduced, before it begins, and the scheme may need senior sign-off once specialist advice has been sought. A High result is not acceptable as it stands. The job must be redesigned or extra controls added, and those controls must be assessed for suitability before work starts. A high score is never a reason to begin early with a warning sign in place. Work does not start until the band's requirement has been met and recorded.

lessons.title: Walking a site and writing a hazard entry
learningOutcomes: Define the scope of a site clean, including areas, tasks and exclusions.
Walk a site in a planned order and note hazards by location and task.
Write each hazard as one entry that names the task, the place, the people affected and the harm path.
Record the walk so another person can repeat it.

instructionSections.heading: Define the scope before the walk
instructionSections.body: The scope is the list of areas and tasks the crew is responsible for, and it must be written before the walk so the walk checks the right things. A commercial scope typically separates reception and public-facing spaces, corridors and communal spaces, service spaces behind the public areas, washrooms, kitchens and tea points, meeting rooms, stairs and lift lobbies, stores and waste areas, and office waste handling. Each area should be named in the plain words the client and the crew use. The scope also states exclusions. If specialist work, outdoor work, roof access or high-hazard clean-up is not part of the job, the scope says so, because a hazard outside the scope is handled by someone else and must be referred. Record the client contact and the building facilities team, since the walk and the register will need their input.

instructionSections.heading: Walk the site in a fixed order
instructionSections.body: Walk the site in one fixed order, for example from the entry point to the top of the building and back down, so nothing is missed and the route can be repeated. Look up, down and to the sides. Check floor surfaces, lighting in corridors and stairwells, cable runs, traffic routes, equipment storage, waste points, first aid and welfare facilities, emergency exits and assembly points. Ask the site contact about past incidents, unusual visitors, areas that flood, and any tasks that have caused problems before. Separate two kinds of hazard during the walk. Fixed hazards belong to the building, such as a step or a lift lobby layout. Task hazards belong to the cleaning work, such as the chemicals used or a machine that is run near people. Both are entered, but they are controlled by different people, so the entry says which.

instructionSections.heading: Writing one entry per hazard
instructionSections.body: Each entry names one hazard, the people who could be affected, and the harm path. A useful entry describes the mechanism rather than the category. Writing chemicals alone is too vague. Writing transfer of a diluted product from an unlabelled bottle during bathroom cleaning tells the reader what the hazard is, where it arises and how harm could follow. Name the people who could be affected, such as the crew, occupants, visitors, contractors or the public, because a control that protects the crew may not protect a passer-by. Describe the existing controls as they actually exist on the day of the walk, not as the policy says they should be. Entries that combine two hazards make the controls muddy, so split them.

lessons.title: Ranking controls and checking residual risk
learningOutcomes: Rank candidate controls from the most effective type to the least effective.
Choose controls for a named hazard and explain why higher-ranked options were used first.
Re-score a hazard for residual risk and justify the result.
Explain why a control on paper alone is not a control.

instructionSections.heading: The ranking of control types
instructionSections.body: Controls are ranked from the most effective to the least effective. Elimination removes the hazard, for example by not using a product or not doing a task in that way. Substitution replaces the hazard with a less harmful option, for example a product that does not need mixing, a single concentrate diluted with water, or battery equipment instead of a noisy mains machine. Engineering controls change the workplace itself, for example a HEPA-filter vacuum, a guard, a physical barrier, good lighting or a cable management system. Administrative controls change how people work, for example a written procedure, a roster, supervision, signage, a briefing or an exclusion zone. Personal protective equipment is the last line. It protects the wearer but does not remove the hazard, so it never replaces a higher control. The source register relies heavily on administrative controls and PPE, so the reader should ask at every row whether a higher control is possible before accepting the lower one.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing controls for a named hazard
instructionSections.body: Start with the highest-ranked option that can be applied to the task, then add lower-ranked controls only where the higher ones do not remove the risk enough. For a wet floor in a busy stairwell, the options include a barrier that closes one side, a sequence that cleans the stairs in a set direction while the public is kept off, timing the work outside peak movement, and footwear with good grip. The barrier and timing are higher than the footwear, so they are relied on first, and the footwear remains as a further layer. Write each control as an action the crew can check. Avoid phrases such as be careful or take care, because nobody can verify them. A control that depends on a person remembering something every time needs a check, such as a supervisor walk-through or a sign-off at the end of the task.

instructionSections.heading: Residual risk and what makes a control real
instructionSections.body: After the controls are chosen, the hazard is re-scored with the controls in place. This is the residual risk. A residual score that is lower than the starting score is only credible when each control is in place and working. A control that is listed but never shown to the crew, never supplied, or never checked is not in place, and the residual score must not count it. If the residual score is the same as or higher than the starting score, the controls have not worked, and the task must not start until the controls are redefined and re-assessed. Completing this lesson does not make a learner the person who decides on controls for a business.

lessons.title: Cleaning chemicals: mixing, spills and containers
learningOutcomes: Identify the chemical hazards in a cleaning register, including mixing, splashing, inhalation and spills.
Select the least harmful product for a task and explain why mixing is avoided.
Follow the safety data sheet for a product's spill response instead of a general rule.
Store, label and dispose of containers so that a wrong product is not used by mistake.

instructionSections.heading: The chemical hazards on a register
instructionSections.body: A cleaning register usually carries two chemical entries. The first is contact with hazardous substances during use, dilution and mixing, which can cause inhalation harm, eye and skin irritation and absorption through the skin. The second is a spill of a cleaning chemical, which can affect the person who clears it, the people nearby and anyone who walks through the wet area. The controls start with product selection. Choose the product with the least harmful profile for the task, and select a product that needs only one concentrate diluted with water, so that two products are never combined. Keep a current safety data sheet for each product and a risk assessment for the chemical use, as the register notes. The safety data sheet for each product is the authority on its hazards, first aid and spill response.

instructionSections.heading: Dilution, ventilation and never mixing
instructionSections.body: Dilute only the concentrate named for the task, in the amount the label states, and do it in a ventilated area. Make up only the solution needed for the task, seal stock containers when they are not in use, and reseal the concentrate straight away after dilution. WARNING: Never mix two cleaning products together, and never add a product to another to make it stronger. Mixing products can release gases that harm the people in the space, and the harm can come on quickly. Labels must be legible and match the contents, and a container with an unknown or faded label is not used. Keep product away from food areas and out of reach of anyone without training. Access to the store must be controlled so that only trained people can take product out.

instructionSections.heading: Spills and the safety data sheet
instructionSections.body: When a spill happens, stop the task and keep people away from the area. Use the spill kit and the personal protective equipment named in the register for that product, and only if the operative is trained for the task. Do not rely on a general rule about what to pour onto a spill. Some products must not be diluted with water, and the right response depends on the chemical. Read the spill section of the safety data sheet for that product and follow it. Once the spill is contained, clear it into a closable container, label the container and record the event. A spill that cannot be contained with the controls in the register is escalated, and the area is left closed until someone trained has dealt with it.

lessons.title: Slips, trips and falls on floors and walkways
learningOutcomes: Identify the slip hazard from liquid on a floor and the trip hazard from clutter or cables in a walkway.
Set up a barrier and signage that keeps occupants off a wet floor.
Keep walkways clear of equipment, waste and stock while work is in progress.
Report a floor or lighting defect so it is fixed or the area is closed.

instructionSections.heading: Two different floor hazards
instructionSections.body: Slips from liquid happen when a floor is made wet by cleaning, spills or rain, and a person's footing has less grip than the task needs. Trips from the floor happen when something at foot level is not seen, such as a cable, a bag of waste, a trolley, a mat that has rucked up or an uneven joint. The two hazards are controlled differently. Liquid is controlled by keeping the water in the work area, by drying it and by keeping people off it. Trips are controlled by keeping routes clear and visible. A register entry should name which hazard it describes, because a control that suits one can make the other worse. A wet floor with a cable across it, for example, presents both at once.

instructionSections.heading: Barriers, signage and sequence
instructionSections.body: A wet floor is kept out of traffic routes wherever possible. Work is sequenced so that the crew cleans away from the route, moves in one direction and leaves a dry route behind. A barrier closes the wet section, and signage is placed at both ends so people can see it from either side. WARNING: A sign on its own is not a barrier. A sign with no barrier does not stop someone walking in, so the barrier comes first. Non-essential people are kept out of the section while it is wet. The drying time is written into the sequence so that the floor is not reopened too early. Where a route cannot be closed, the work is moved to a quieter time, and the route is kept clear before the crew arrives.

instructionSections.heading: Clutter, cables, lighting and reporting
instructionSections.body: Walkways are kept free of trolleys, cable runs, equipment, stock and waste while work is in progress. Trolleys and buckets are parked off the route, not left beside a door or a corner. Cables are routed along walls or secured where they cross a walkway. Mats are checked for curling edges and corrected or removed. Each planned route is checked before the work starts, because the building may have changed since the last visit. Lighting along routes is checked, and a dark route is not used until it has been reported and lit or closed. Defects, such as an uneven joint, a loose mat or a damaged floor surface, are reported on the same day to the supervisor, and the facilities team is told too. The area stays closed until it is dealt with. Footwear with good grip is a further layer of protection and is not a substitute for barriers or a clear route.

lessons.title: Stairs, hop-ups and step ladders
learningOutcomes: Identify the falls hazards on stairs, landings and steps, and the falls hazards from hop-ups and step ladders.
Choose the lowest-risk way to reach a high point before using any step equipment.
Inspect a hop-up or step ladder before use and withdraw it when it is defective.
Explain why only people holding training and authorisation may work from height.

instructionSections.heading: Stairs, landings and steps
instructionSections.body: A falls hazard on stairs comes from a missed step, a slippery nosing, a loose stair rod, debris on a landing, or a load carried in a way that blocks sight of the next step. The register treats stair cleaning as a job with its own written plan, so the stair work must follow that plan and not memory. Stair and landing spaces are used with the handrail in hand, and the lift is used where it is the approved access route for the task and the load. Stair and landing lighting is checked before work starts. Bulk items, bins and equipment are not stored on stairs or landings, because they force people to step around them. A damaged stair, handrail or tread is reported to the supervisor and the facilities team, and the affected section stays closed until it is checked. The building owner or duty holder is responsible for maintaining the stairs; the crew's duty is to report and to keep the stairs clear.

instructionSections.heading: Hop-ups and step ladders
instructionSections.body: A hop-up or step ladder is used only if the high point cannot be reached safely from the ground, using long-handled or extension equipment. Before any use, inspect the equipment for cracks, bent or missing steps, loose hinges or locks, worn feet and damage to the platform. Equipment that is defective is withdrawn from use, tagged as not fit for use and reported. Set the equipment on a firm, level surface, open and locked where it has a locking mechanism, and do not place it on a box, a chair, a trolley or any other unstable base to gain height. Do not stand on the top step or the platform the equipment is not designed for. Keep three points of contact where possible, and do not overreach. A second person is nearby when the task is at a height the register requires supervision for. WARNING: Never use a chair, a bin or a stacked item to reach higher.

instructionSections.heading: Authorisation and the standard named in the register
instructionSections.body: Elevated work is done only by people who hold training and authorisation from the business for that equipment and that height. This lesson does not authorise anyone to do elevated work and is not a licence or a certificate for that work. The register cites a South African standard for elevated-work equipment, which does not apply in Australia and is not carried into this lesson.

lessons.title: Dust, airborne particles and eye irritation
learningOutcomes: Identify how cleaning can put dust into the air and into the eyes of the crew and occupants.
Choose a damp or dry-wipe method that does not raise dust for each surface.
Select and use filtered vacuum equipment where the register requires it.
Stop work in windy or blustery conditions where dust or debris would be moved.

instructionSections.heading: How cleaning raises dust
instructionSections.body: Dust in an office or a common area is a mix of settled particles, fibres, skin cells, paper and the debris from the building. Cleaning can lift it into the air and into the breathing zone of the crew and occupants, and it can get into the eyes. The register identifies two effects. One is respiratory irritation from airborne dust. The other is foreign matter in the eye, such as grit or fibre. Both can be reduced by the method chosen, so the first control is to choose a method that does not raise the dust in the first place. Working near people, and cleaning in a sequence that moves dust back on to cleaned surfaces, increases the exposure for everyone in the space.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the method for the surface
instructionSections.body: Dry sweeping is not used where a damp or wet method can do the job, because it lifts dust into the air. Dusting uses a damp or dry-wipe method chosen for the surface, and the dust is captured on the cloth rather than dispersed. Work top to bottom, so dust falls onto surfaces that are cleaned later. Where a vacuum is needed, use a vacuum with a HEPA filter if the register requires one for the area, and keep its filters and bags in good condition so that fine dust is not blown back into the room. WARNING: Do not blow dust into the air to clear it, and do not shake a cloth or duster in an occupied room. Eye protection is worn where the register requires it, and it must meet the standard the register names for that task.

instructionSections.heading: Weather, eyes and the cleaning programme
instructionSections.body: Outdoor cleaning stops during strong gusts that would carry dust or debris, which applies to entrances, car parks and open walkways. If an eye is affected by dust or grit, the first step is to follow the first aid instruction on the relevant safety data sheet and the site procedure, and to report the event. An eyewash station or kit is provided where the register requires one, and its location is known to the crew. The cleaning programme itself reduces dust. A regular schedule that stops dust and waste from building up in corners, grilles and ledges means less dust is disturbed during each clean. WARNING: If a person has a persistent eye problem after exposure, they seek medical advice and do not continue the task that caused it.

lessons.title: Electrical hazards: fixed wiring and portable equipment
learningOutcomes: Separate fixed electrical systems, which crew never touch, from portable equipment, which crew inspect and use.
Carry out a pre-use inspection of a portable machine and withdraw it when it is defective.
Keep liquids and cords clear of electrical outlets and equipment during work.
Explain why fixed wiring work is not part of the cleaning task.

instructionSections.heading: Fixed wiring is not a cleaning task
instructionSections.body: Fixed wiring, permanent systems and fixtures are installed, tested and maintained by the building's duty holder and by the people who are licensed or authorised to do that work. The cleaning register tells crew not to touch, alter or interfere with wiring, cables or electrical systems, and to report damage, defects and failures to the supervisor and building facilities team straight away. The reason is that a cleaner who opens a fitting, moves a cable or wets a switch can cause a shock or a fire, and a visual check cannot show whether a system is safe to touch. WARNING: Do not open a switchboard, a power point, a light fitting or a data cabinet, and do not move a cable that appears to be live or damaged. Stop, keep others away and report it. Licence notice: fixed electrical work is licensed or authorised work in many places, and this lesson does not grant any electrical licence or authority to do it.

instructionSections.heading: Portable equipment: test, inspect and use
instructionSections.body: Portable equipment brought to site is tested before it arrives, using the formal testing process the business uses for portable equipment, which the register refers to as PAT testing and which is commonly called test and tagging in Australia. Before each use, the operative inspects the machine: the cord, the plug, the casing, the guards and the tag. A defective machine is not used. It is tagged as not fit for use, withdrawn and reported to the supervisor. Crew are trained in the safe use of each machine and follow the manufacturer's instructions. Equipment is never used in a way that the manufacturer does not allow, and sockets and leads are never overloaded.

instructionSections.heading: Liquids, leads and the working area
instructionSections.body: Liquids are kept well away from electrical outlets and equipment. The mop bucket, the spray bottle and the wet cloth are placed where a spill cannot reach a power point or a cord. Leads are routed so that people cannot trip over them or drag them through water. Where a lead must cross a walkway, it is secured and marked, as “Slips, trips and falls on floors and walkways” describes. WARNING: Stop and isolate a machine if the cord is damaged, if it gets hot, if it trips the circuit, or if you feel any tingle from it. Do not handle a machine or a plug with wet hands, and do not reach into water to free a cord.

lessons.title: Sharps, body fluids and waste areas
learningOutcomes: Identify sharps and body fluids as hazards in public and waste areas, and separate routine clean-up from specialist work.
Respond to a discovered needle or sharp without touching it, and get the right people involved.
Clean a small body fluid spill with the controls in the register, and clean before disinfecting.
Dispose of contaminated materials under the procedure and local rules.

instructionSections.heading: Sharps in public and waste areas
instructionSections.body: Sharps and drug paraphernalia are found in public toilets, stairwells, car parks, bins and general waste areas. The register treats a needle or sharp as a hazard for anyone nearby, including the crew, occupants and the public. The risk comes from a puncture, and the outcome can be a serious infection. The first rule is that no one picks up a needle by hand. If one is seen, the operative stops, keeps others away, and notifies reception and the building facilities team straight away, then informs the operations supervisor. Only trained and competent people who are wearing the protective equipment in the register may remove a sharp, using a sharps kit. The sharp is then disposed of in a sharps container under the company's procedure and the local authority's requirements. WARNING: Never reach into a bin, bag or gap by hand to look for a sharp.

instructionSections.heading: Body fluids and human waste
instructionSections.body: Contact with human waste or bodily fluids is a biological hazard. It can spread infection through the mouth, nose, eyes or a cut. The register allows routine crew to clean up small amounts after training, using personal protective equipment and a segregated area. The steps are to keep occupants away from the area, to scrape residues into a closable container, to clean the surface with detergent first, and only then to disinfect. Wash the hands and forearms with warm water and soap, and dry them with disposable towels or a hot-air dryer, after removing the protective equipment. Do not eat, drink or smoke in the area. A cut or graze is covered with a waterproof dressing and washed at once with soap and running water.

instructionSections.heading: Scope limits and specialist response
instructionSections.body: Routine clean-up of a small, known spill is the limit of the crew's scope under this lesson. Large spills, unknown material, decomposed remains, trauma scenes, and any clean-up involving a hazard the crew cannot name are specialist work. The high-risk course in this platform covers specialist biohazard work and is not authorised by this lesson. When the scope is exceeded, the operative stops, secures the area as far as possible, keeps people away, and escalates to the supervisor and the client. The register does not allow the crew to improvise a response that is outside their training.

lessons.title: Infection risk and rodent-borne hazards in the register
learningOutcomes: Explain how an infectious agent reaches a person from a surface, a body fluid or contaminated cloth.
Apply the hand hygiene and contaminated-item steps that remain sound in the register.
Identify the rodent and water hazards in a waste area, and the controls for cuts and grazes.
Identify which infection controls in a dated register must be checked against current guidance before use.

instructionSections.heading: How an infection reaches a person
instructionSections.body: An infection reaches a person through a route. Usually the route is a contaminated surface, cloth or body fluid, then the hands, then the mouth, nose or eyes. The register's infectious disease entry is based on that route. Its controls work on each step: keeping surfaces clean and disinfecting them in the right order, washing the hands before eating and after touching a contaminated surface, using protective equipment as the register names it, bagging contaminated cloths and equipment, and making sure the work area has good ventilation. The entry was written as a dated document, and its guidance reflects public health advice from the time it was written. The register's historical self-isolation period and any other time-limited advice are not carried into this lesson. WARNING: Current public health advice must be checked with the relevant state or territory health authority before any infection entry is written or changed.

instructionSections.heading: Hand hygiene and contaminated items
instructionSections.body: Wash the hands using soap and running water, then dry them with a clean towel, a hot-air dryer or disposable towels. Sanitiser is a fallback only where water cannot be reached. When coughing or sneezing, use a tissue or the inside of the elbow to cover the face, and bin the tissue at once. Do not touch the face with hands that have not been cleaned. Contaminated cloths, mop heads and protective equipment are sealed in bags and sent for disposal under the procedure, and a contaminated item is never reused. Anyone feeling unwell stays away from work, and the supervisor is told. The register's remaining controls, such as ventilation and separation of cleaning cloths by area, support these habits and do not replace them.

instructionSections.heading: Rodents, water and leptospirosis
instructionSections.body: Rats and mice are common in service-area waste rooms and near waterways. Their urine can carry the bacteria that cause leptospirosis, which is spread when contaminated water or damp soil reaches a cut, a graze, the eyes or the mouth. The register treats the risk as higher where water collects or where the waste area is near a river. The controls are that the crew has been taught about the water-related hazard, that protective equipment and washing facilities are on site, that cuts and grazes are covered with a waterproof dressing or gloves before work starts, and that any cut is washed at once with soap and running water and covered. Hands, face and forearms are washed before food, drink, cigarettes or phone use. WARNING: Avoid standing water in a waste area unless the controls in the register are in place. Report any rodent sighting or droppings to the building facilities team and do not pick up a dead animal with bare hands.

lessons.title: Hand tools, blades and powered floor machines
learningOutcomes: Identify the injury paths from hand tools, blades, scrapers and brooms, and the controls for each.
Identify the injury paths from powered floor machines, pressurised water and vacuum cleaners.
Inspect a machine before use and withdraw it when it is defective.
Keep people out of the working area of a running machine.

instructionSections.heading: Hand tools, blades and scrapers
instructionSections.body: Hand tools cause cuts, puncture wounds, bruises and impact injuries. The risk rises when a blade is used in a way that puts the hand in the path of cut, when a scraper is pushed toward the body, when a tool is left on a floor or ledge, or when a broom handle or brush head is swung without looking. The register requires that only competent people use tools, that only the equipment the business supplies is used, and that the crew wears eye protection, gloves, footwear with good grip and work clothing. Blades are retracted or covered when not in use and are changed with the tool switched off or the blade fully withdrawn. A scraper is worked away from the body and the hand is kept behind the cutting edge. A damaged or blunt tool is replaced rather than forced.

instructionSections.heading: Powered floor machines and pressurised water
instructionSections.body: Powered floor machines, such as rotary and scrubbing machines, can cause impact, entanglement and crush injuries, and their cords and hoses can cause trips. Pressurised water and steam equipment can cause burns, eye injury and skin puncture from a high-pressure jet. A jet can penetrate skin even when it looks harmless, and a hose can whip if the connection fails. Vacuum cleaners can cause entanglement with cords and hoses, and their motors and cables can overheat. The register's controls include battery equipment where possible, a test record for each electrical machine, inspection before every use, guards and protective features kept in place as the manufacturer requires, a service schedule, and a defect procedure that withdraws a machine and labels it unfit.

instructionSections.heading: Access, the running machine and the defect
instructionSections.body: Non-essential people are kept out of the work area of any running machine, and the area is closed off by barriers and signage. A machine is never reached into while it is running, and a blockage is cleared only after the machine has been switched off and isolated. The cord is kept clear of the machine's path and out of the operative's feet. Before each use, the crew checks the machine's guard, the cord, the handle, the brushes or pads, the hose and its connections, and the emergency stop. A defect is reported, and the machine is withdrawn from use and tagged as not fit for use until it is repaired and checked. WARNING: Never operate a pressure lance, nozzle or hose that is not fully connected, and never point a jet at a person, at an electrical outlet or at yourself to test it.

lessons.title: Manual handling, noise and hand-arm vibration
learningOutcomes: Identify the manual handling hazards in a cleaning task and reduce each load to a manageable size.
Use mechanical aids and team lifts where the register requires them, with one person controlling the lift.
Identify the noise and vibration exposures from equipment and the controls for each.
Report early symptoms of hearing loss or hand-arm vibration injury.

instructionSections.heading: Manual handling of loads
instructionSections.body: Manual handling hazards cover lifting, lowering, carrying, pushing and pulling, and they produce strains, sprains, cuts, abrasions and impact injuries. A cleaning task rarely involves one heavy item. It more often involves many small loads, repeated bending and reaching, and long days of carrying bins and bags. The register controls the risk by breaking the load into manageable sizes, using team lifts with one person controlling the lift, using mechanical aids such as trolleys and lifting aids where practical, and using passenger lifts for equipment where the building allows it. Labels on delivered boxes are checked for the indicated weight. Each operative works within their own ability, takes scheduled pauses and rotates tasks. Where a manual handling hazard cannot be brought under control by these means, a written manual handling review is carried out for that task before it continues. WARNING: Do not lift a load you cannot control, and stop if a route is blocked or a load becomes unstable.

instructionSections.heading: Noise from equipment
instructionSections.body: Repeated exposure to noise from machines can cause hearing loss that builds slowly and is often not noticed until it is well established. The register requires a noise assessment wherever the noise level passes an exposure action value, which is a term taken from another jurisdiction. Where a noise assessment is required, low-noise equipment is chosen when buying, machines are serviced and maintained in working order, and defective machines are withdrawn. Health monitoring is carried out, and operatives report symptoms such as ringing or muffled hearing themselves. Hearing protection is used where the assessment requires it.

instructionSections.heading: Hand-arm vibration
instructionSections.body: Hand-arm vibration comes from holding and guiding handheld or floor machines for long periods. Over time it can damage the nerves and blood supply in the hands and arms. Low-vibration equipment is selected, machines are serviced and inspected both before and after each session, and defective equipment is withdrawn. Gloves to the standard named in the register are provided. Operatives are told about the effects of vibration, and they report tingling, numbness, pale or white fingers, or reduced grip early, so the task can be changed before harm becomes permanent.

lessons.title: Vehicles, pedestrians and site lighting
learningOutcomes: Identify the vehicle and pedestrian hazards on car park and loading routes, and keep to the approved routes.
Set up exclusion zones and barriers that stop members of the public entering work areas.
Check lighting before work starts and refuse to work where light is unsafe.
Choose the right timing for work in relation to daylight and building use.

instructionSections.heading: Vehicles and car park routes
instructionSections.body: Car parks, loading areas and vehicle routes are where crew are most likely to be struck by a moving vehicle that they cannot see or hear. The register tells operatives to keep off roadways and out of the path of vehicle traffic, to stay on the approved walking paths at the site boundary and in the car park, and to follow the directional signs. Where the work is near a vehicle route, the crew wears high-visibility clothing that conforms to the standard the register names; that standard belongs to the AS/NZS 4602.1 series; the Standards Australia store shows AS 4602.1:2024, but its text has not been reviewed for this draft, so its requirements have not yet been confirmed until checked against that edition. Where people and vehicles share a space, barriers separate them, and the work is supervised and monitored. WARNING: Do not cross a vehicle lane to reach a bin or a door, and stay out of a loading area while a vehicle is reversing or manoeuvring.

instructionSections.heading: Public and third-party exclusion
instructionSections.body: Members of the public, visitors, residents and contractors can walk into a work area without knowing it is unsafe. The register protects them with barriers and posted warnings where needed, and by planning and coordinating the work so that the public and site staff do not come into contact with the crew's activity. Equipment and materials are kept inside the exclusion zone and are never left unattended. Equipment is removed from the site or stored in the store cupboard overnight, and the site access and entrance are controlled while work is in progress, with the work supervised or monitored throughout. An unattended trolley is a hazard to the public, so the crew does not leave one in a corridor, even for a short time.

instructionSections.heading: Lighting and timing
instructionSections.body: Poor light causes misjudged footing, missed hazards and slips. The register asks for daytime work where it is practical, and for sufficient light levels in any area where work is done. Existing building lighting is supplied and kept in repair by the client, and task lighting is brought in where the crew identifies a need. Operatives do not work where the lighting level presents a danger. A route that is dark is reported and is not used until it has been lit or closed. Where work must be done in low light, the crew checks the route beforehand, uses task lights, and works with a second person nearby.

lessons.title: Lone working, harassment and personal safety on site
learningOutcomes: Decide when lone working is avoided, and set up the buddy or supervision arrangement where it is not.
Describe the check-in and monitoring arrangements that apply to a lone worker.
Respond to harassment, a threat or a trespasser without escalating the situation.
Report an incident of harassment or violence to the named contacts.

instructionSections.heading: When lone working is avoided
instructionSections.body: The register's first control for lone working is to avoid it where that is possible. Where a task cannot be done without a second person, a buddy system is applied, so that two people share the work and can summon help. Where possible a site supervisor is present, and the client's security or reception staff monitor the cleaning employee on site. A regional supervisor looks in on crews at their sites. Senior staff decide whether a particular lone worker faces a risk, and that decision is recorded. The register does not allow a lone worker to be sent to a location without a check-in. A lone worker who cannot make contact at the agreed time is treated as a potential incident until the check-in is made.

instructionSections.heading: Harassment, threats and violence
instructionSections.body: Harassment and violence can come from the public, residents, site staff or others. The register's approach is to stop the work, secure the area, inform the client, the building facilities team and the business head office, and be polite. The operative does not retaliate or try to make the situation worse, because a calm response is the one most likely to end it. The business investigates a reported incident, and notifies the client and any regulator where appropriate. WARNING: Leave the area as soon as it is safe to do so. Do not confront anyone, do not block a door, and do not stay in a place where you feel unsafe.

instructionSections.heading: Trespassers and unfamiliar people
instructionSections.body: If someone is found on the premises without permission, the crew does not challenge them, does not follow them and does not try to remove them. The crew politely requests that they go, if it is safe to do so, and then reports the event to the building facilities team. A locked or unfamiliar area is not entered alone to investigate. The site contact is told, and the report records the time, the location and a description of the person without any attempt to identify them beyond what is seen. Personal safety is always placed above the cleaning task.

lessons.title: Site rules, welfare, phones and emergencies
learningOutcomes: Follow the fire and evacuation arrangements for a site, including the assembly point and the stop-work rule.
Apply the mobile phone, music and smoking rules that apply on site.
Confirm that welfare facilities are adequate before workers are placed at a site.
Explain the site induction and the emergency information the crew must know before access.

instructionSections.heading: Fire, evacuation and the stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Before any crew member is given access to a site, they receive the site's induction, including fire and evacuation training, and the site's fire and evacuation information is posted where it can be read. The building facilities team tests the fire alarm, and the crew knows where the assembly point is before they start work. If a fire or smoke is reported, the operative stops work, reports it to the building facilities team and moves to the assembly point. The crew does not return to the building until the building facilities team has confirmed that it is safe. WARNING: Do not re-enter the building, do not investigate a smell or smoke, and do not use a lift during an evacuation. Smoking is allowed only in the marked area, and anyone found smoking elsewhere on site is asked to leave.

instructionSections.heading: Phones, music and attention
instructionSections.body: Mobile phones, radios and music players are a source of distraction, and a distracted operative is less able to see a hazard or hear a warning. The register forbids using a mobile phone or music player on site in operational areas, and it forbids using a phone while running any machine. A phone may be used in the mess or rest room, and in an emergency, for example to call the building facilities team or the supervisor. The crew does not use a phone while walking, while carrying a load or while at a machine. A personal device with the sound off is kept in a pocket or locker rather than in the hand during work.

instructionSections.heading: Welfare facilities
instructionSections.body: Welfare facilities are the toilets, hand washing, drinking water, rest areas and first aid cover that crew need during the working day. The register requires the client's premises to be inspected before workers are placed there, so that adequate welfare arrangements and provisions are confirmed. Crew wash the face and arms before food, drink, cigarettes, phone use or medication, and cover any cut or graze with a waterproof dressing before starting work. Soap, towels and a first aid kit are stocked on site.

lessons.title: Reviewing, briefing and signing off a risk assessment
learningOutcomes: Complete the document control details of a risk assessment, including the revision history and review history.
Brief the crew on the register and record who was briefed and what was covered.
Identify the events that trigger a review, and revise the register by issuing a new revision.
Explain what a briefing record does not prove.

instructionSections.heading: Document control
instructionSections.body: A risk assessment is a controlled document. It carries a document number and revision, the revision date, the client or site address, the name of the person who prepared it and the name of the person who approved it. A revision history records each change, the author, the date and the items revised, and a review history records each review and its comments. The first issue is revision 00. Where the register is changed, the change is made as a new revision, and the old revision is kept on file. A document with a blank revision date, a blank site address or no review history cannot show which controls applied on a given day. The approval is given by a person with the authority to approve the work, and that authority is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Briefing the crew
instructionSections.body: Once a register is approved, every person who will work under it is briefed on it. A briefing covers the hazards and controls that apply to the tasks, the protective equipment, the chemical use, the infection controls and the reporting arrangements. Short team briefings on safety, chemicals, infection control and protective equipment are the usual format, and each one is recorded with the date, the topics, the people present and the questions raised. The briefing record asks each operative to acknowledge receipt and comprehension of the document, and to commit to its controls and to the directions of the supervisor and the facilities team. WARNING: A briefing record shows that a briefing took place. It does not show that a control works, and it does not transfer responsibility from the business. Verify each control on site.

instructionSections.heading: When to review and revise
instructionSections.body: A review is triggered by events, not only by the calendar. The events that trigger a review are a change of site or area, a new chemical or product, new equipment, an incident or near miss, a complaint, a change in building use or working pattern, a control found not to work, and new guidance that has been checked. A review also happens at the review date the business sets. When the review changes a control or a score, a new revision is issued with the reason, the crew is re-briefed on the change and the old revision is withdrawn from the site. A revision that is not briefed is not in force for the crew who did not receive it.

lessons.title: Site risk assessment worksheet
learningOutcomes: Complete the document control, scope and scoring sections of a site risk assessment.
Enter one hazard per row in the hazard register, with scores, bands, controls and residual risk.
Record the actions that must be done before work starts, and the holds that apply where a band requires them.
Complete the briefing and review sections so the document can be signed off against the rubric.

instructionSections.heading: What this worksheet produces
instructionSections.body: This worksheet is a fill-in document. As you work through it, you complete each field in turn, and the system then assembles your entries into one finished site risk assessment for the site file. You are not given model answers, and the finished document contains only what you have written. The worksheet follows the method taught in “Scoring a hazard: likelihood, severity and the risk band”, “Walking a site and writing a hazard entry”, “Ranking controls and checking residual risk” and “Reviewing, briefing and signing off a risk assessment”: scope first, then a hazard register scored for likelihood and severity, controls chosen by rank, residual risk checked, actions and holds recorded, and the crew briefed. An assessor reviews the assembled document against the rubric and signs it off.

instructionSections.heading: Scope and document control first
instructionSections.body: Begin with the document control fields: the document number and revision, the date prepared, the site address and service area, and the names and roles of the person who prepared the assessment and the person who approves it. Then write the scope in plain terms. List every area and task that is included, and then list the exclusions. A scope that says only general cleaning cannot be checked against a site, so name the areas. Confirm the scoring scale in use by ticking each item in the scale checklist. Do not begin the register until every item is ticked, because a score is only meaningful against a known scale.

instructionSections.heading: The hazard register
instructionSections.body: Enter one hazard per row. For each row, name the hazard in mechanism terms, identify the people who could be affected, and describe how harm could occur. Score likelihood from 1 to 5 and severity from 1 to 5, then multiply them to give the risk value. Find the band for the value using the agreed scale. Write the existing controls, ranked from the highest type to the lowest, and then score the residual likelihood and severity with those controls in place. Find the residual band. Where a row is in the Medium or High band, an action or hold must be written for it. Use the hazard category checklist to confirm that each category was considered, even where it does not apply, and record in the not-applicable field the reason for each category that does not apply.

instructionSections.heading: Actions, holds and briefing
instructionSections.body: Record each action that must be done before work starts, with the person responsible and the due date. Where a band requires that work does not start until controls have been redefined or verified, write the hold clearly, so that a supervisor on the day can see it. Enter the briefing record: each person briefed, their role, the date they were briefed and their signature, with the signature only from the person who was briefed. Record the topics covered and the questions raised in the briefing. A signature shows that the briefing took place; it does not show that a control works, so the controls must be verified on site separately. The next review date and the review triggers are then recorded, so the assessment is revisited when the site, the equipment, the chemicals or the work changes.

instructionSections.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instructionSections.body: This lesson is part of the solar panel cleaning track. Panels are usually mounted on roofs or elevated structures and are connected to DC and AC electrical circuits. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instructionSections.heading: Purpose and competence
instructionSections.body: This lesson teaches the worker to recognise changing conditions and stop unsafe work. Apply employer procedures, the site induction and the actual work order. This is general training, not authorisation to perform specialist rescue, hazardous-material response or medical treatment. The learner must identify limits of authority and explain when to stop and escalate.

instructionSections.heading: Prepare and confirm authority
instructionSections.body: Before work, identify the designated supervisor, site contact, emergency number, nearest safe exit, incident reporting channel and any worker-specific restrictions. Check the current site instructions rather than relying on a previous visit. Confirm that any required equipment and communications are available. If essential controls are missing, do not commence the affected activity.

instructionSections.heading: Safe operating procedure
instructionSections.body: Pause when new people, equipment, weather, contamination, aggression or access restrictions change the job. Withdraw to a safe location, secure only what can be secured without exposure, notify the supervisor and wait for a revised plan. Do not improvise hazardous work.

instructionSections.heading: Worked workplace example
instructionSections.body: During cleaning a worker notices an unidentified powder and a strong odour. They stop, isolate themselves from the area and request specialist assessment rather than sweeping or vacuuming.

instructionSections.heading: Communicate, record and resume
instructionSections.body: Communicate the location, hazard, people potentially affected, actions taken and assistance required. Record time and facts promptly without naming uninvolved clients or speculating about causes. Only resume after the responsible person confirms the hazard is controlled and the work plan is safe. For dynamic risk assessment and stop-work authority, practise repeating the decision sequence under changed conditions.

instructionSections.heading: Common errors and corrective coaching
instructionSections.body: Common errors include continuing because the job is nearly finished, treating PPE as the only control, concealing near misses, improvising outside training, and sharing client information in unsecured messages. The assessor should ask the learner to identify the unsafe decision, select a stronger control, and document who can authorise resumption.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical notice
instructionSections.body: Electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In Victoria, PV installation and maintenance is licensed electrical installation work, and PV DC cables may stay live when the power is off. NSW electrical wiring work includes repairing. On the Victorian, Western Australian and New South Wales pages checked, plain panel washing is not stated to need a licence, and any electrical work on a PV array is referred to a licensed electrician. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

lessons.title: What counts as height work and how falls happen
learningOutcomes: Describe which tasks count as height work on a service job, including the access route as well as the working position.
Name the main routes a worker can fall by on exterior and trade jobs.
Explain why a trigger height taken from another jurisdiction must be checked before use in Australia.
Identify the falling-object risks that apply below any elevated task and the control for each.

instructionSections.heading: Why the height is not the whole story
instructionSections.body: Many serious falls on trade and exterior jobs happen at heights the worker did not think of as work at height. Someone reaching a gutter from a bench, leaning over a balcony rail to wash a window, or standing on the highest step of a stepladder to change a light fitting is doing height work, even though nothing about the job feels dangerous. The useful question is not how high the job is in general, but what would happen if the worker lost their footing from their working position, or from the route they took to get there. One source ranks falls near the top of the causes of construction deaths; that comparison relates to an overseas industry and is not used in this lesson.

instructionSections.heading: Where the trigger sits
instructionSections.body: The sources in this pack do not agree on a trigger height. One training deck uses one fixed height figure as its trigger for height work. A contractor procedure applies fall protection from a fixed height, stated in imperial units. A third source takes a wider view and counts any position from which someone could be hurt by falling, including positions below ground level, and it treats the route up and down as part of the task. None of these figures is an Australian legal trigger. In New South Wales, a separate rule requires a construction safe work method statement where someone could fall more than two metres; that rule is confirmed in the project licence matrix, but it is not a general trigger for every service job. A business should therefore set its working rule from its own risk assessment and a checked state rule, and leave out any figure it has not checked.

instructionSections.heading: The routes a fall takes
instructionSections.body: The sources describe five main routes. The first is falling from an edge, such as a roof, balcony, deck, platform or the open side of a structure. The second is falling through an opening, or through a surface that cannot bear weight, such as a skylight, a rotten board, a translucent roof sheet or an uncovered floor hole. The third is falling from ladders and step equipment, through overreaching, slipping, a moving base or a tipping ladder. The fourth is falling from a platform that tips, runs away or lacks guard components. The fifth is falling into an excavation or pit, or from a lower level where a worker is leaning or working off balance. Each route needs a different control, so the risk assessment in “Writing a risk assessment for height work” names the route for every position.

instructionSections.heading: Falling objects belong to the same plan
instructionSections.body: A tool, a bucket, a length of flashing or a piece of glass that drops from height can seriously injure a person below. The controls are practical. Keep tools in pouches or on lanyards, keep materials well clear of the edge, cone or barricade the area beneath the work, and tell anyone below before anything is raised or lowered. Hand lines and purpose-built containers are safer than throwing items up or down.

instructionSections.heading: The route is part of the task
instructionSections.body: Getting up and getting down form part of the exposure. Two of the sources mention climbing with tools. A worker should keep both hands free while climbing, and should carry tools only in a belt built for that purpose. Heavier items should be hauled up or lowered inside a proper container. The route should be walked before the first climb, checked again after any change, and kept clear of trip hazards such as cables, hoses and debris.

instructionSections.heading: Weather and surface change the picture
instructionSections.body: Rain, ice, wind, heat and glare each change how well a person keeps their footing and how well they can see the surface. A wet roof tile or an icy deck board can turn a safe position into an unsafe one within minutes. Stop and reassess when conditions change, not only at the start of the day, and treat any weather limit the business has set as a stop condition.

lessons.title: The hierarchy of controls for height work
learningOutcomes: Order the height-work controls by how dependable they are.
Explain why personal arrest equipment is a later choice than a physical control or avoidance.
Apply the hierarchy to a worked service job and record the reason for each level chosen or rejected.
Recognise when a lower-level control is being used because a higher level was not checked.

instructionSections.heading: Why the controls are ranked
instructionSections.body: Controls differ in how much they depend on people doing the right thing every time. A control that removes the fall exposure works whether a worker is tired, rushed or inexperienced. A control that only tells people what to do depends on their attention at each moment. The Victorian regulator sets out a ranking that begins with eliminating the hazard and ends with personal protective equipment. The training and contractor sources in this pack use the same idea with different words: first stop the need to go to height, then stop the fall, then limit what a fall can do, and only then rely on personal equipment and procedure.

instructionSections.heading: The levels, from the top
instructionSections.body: The top level is avoidance: do the work from the ground, use an extension tool, build components at ground level and lift them into place, or change the design so no access is needed. The next level is physical prevention: guardrails, edge protection, covers over openings, a fully boarded platform with rails, or a scaffold. Below that sits restraint, which stops a worker reaching the edge at all. Arrest comes next. It accepts that a fall can start and stops it through a harness and an energy-absorbing device. Every level depends on a rescue plan that is ready before the work starts. One source calls fall arrest the final layer of protection, and another ranks restraint as the safest personal option. The Victorian page places personal protective equipment lowest, as the least dependable control, to be used only when nothing else fits, as an interim measure, or alongside a higher control.

instructionSections.heading: Mapping the order to the Australian framework
instructionSections.body: The order above is a working ranking for this course. Where a business writes the control into a formal risk register, it should map each control to the level of the hierarchy used in the state or territory where the work happens. The practical rule holds regardless: a personal harness is the lowest of the physical choices and is never a substitute for a guardrail or a ground-based method that can be used.

instructionSections.heading: Applying the order to a job
instructionSections.body: Start at the top of the list for every job, and move down only with a written reason. A written reason can be checked later, and an unwritten one cannot. In practice, gutter cleaning should move to ground-based equipment where a suitable tool exists. If it does not, a guardrail or a stable platform goes in place. If neither is feasible, a restraint keeps the worker clear of the edge. Only when all of those are excluded should an arrest system be used, with its clearance checked and a rescue plan ready. A harness should not be the first control just because it is easy to carry.

instructionSections.heading: Engineered controls are not automatic
instructionSections.body: A guardrail counts as a control only if it is complete, fixed and at the right height. A platform counts only if its decking is full and secure. A higher control can be written into a plan and not be on site, so check each control on arrival and record what was seen. A plan that names a guardrail that is not fitted is not a plan with a guardrail.

instructionSections.heading: Administrative controls support the physical ones
instructionSections.body: Training, permits, supervision, signs and barriers manage people. They do not change the fall itself. Training and supervision matter, and the sources insist on both, but they cannot replace a physical control where falling is possible. A warning sign at the foot of a ladder is a reminder, not an edge guard, and it must not be the only control for a fall exposure.

lessons.title: Fall protection and arrest systems
learningOutcomes: Name the four categories of personal protection against falls and what each one allows.
Identify the four parts of an arrest system and what each part does.
Explain how the clearance below a worker is estimated, and why the lanyard length alone is not enough.
Explain why an arrest system must not be used until a rescue plan has been prepared.

instructionSections.heading: Personal fall protection comes after the physical controls
instructionSections.body: Personal fall protection is equipment the worker wears. The sources in this pack treat it as a secondary control, to be used after physical controls are excluded, or alongside them. Two of the sources add that the worker needs instruction in its use and in inspecting it, and that it must not be the only control where a physical measure can be fitted. A system can look correct on paper and still fail, because it is fitted badly, anchored to the wrong point, or used without a rescue plan.

instructionSections.heading: Four categories with different purposes
instructionSections.body: Work positioning keeps a worker supported by a harness on a tensioned line, leaving both hands free; it must not be depended on alone to stop a fall. Rope access uses specialist ropes to reach areas that are hard to get to, and it demands a high level of training. Restraint prevents a worker from reaching a fall hazard at all; one source calls it the safest category. Arrest is the one category that lets a fall begin and then halts it with control. The choice should follow the order in “The hierarchy of controls for height work”: use restraint where it works, and arrest only where restraint cannot be used.

instructionSections.heading: The four parts of an arrest system
instructionSections.body: The anchorage is the fixed point the whole system depends on. The body support is a harness, and the sources do not accept a body belt for arrest on site except for specialist work. The connecting device is the link between harness and anchor, such as a deceleration lanyard, an inertia reel, a rope grab or a fall-arrest block. The descent or rescue arrangement is the means of getting the worker down after the arrest. Each part must match the others. A strong anchor paired with a harness that does not fit is not a working system.

instructionSections.heading: Working out the clearance
instructionSections.body: An arrest system stops a fall over a distance. That distance adds the free fall before the lanyard becomes taut, the stretch of the energy absorber, the length of the lanyard itself, the height of the worker from the attachment point to their feet, and a safety margin. Sources describe these terms, and one asks how far a worker could fall with a lanyard attached. Use the calculation method in the business's approved procedure, and check the result against the manufacturer's stated figures before choosing the connector.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the swing under control
instructionSections.body: A worker who is off to one side of the anchor can swing into a structure when they fall. One source describes placing the device vertically above the work area and limiting the swing to a sector above the anchor. Position the anchor so the worker stays within the swing limit, or use another anchor or method.

instructionSections.heading: Anchorage must be fit for the purpose
instructionSections.body: The anchor must take the force of a fall and must not be damaged by the lanyard. Sources give a rated load per worker and a safety factor in units that are not Australian, and those figures are not used here. Keep the principles that hold. The anchor must stand apart from any platform, placed above the worker where possible, without sharp edges, and checked by a competent individual. Several sources list items that must not be used as anchors, including light pipe, electrical conduit and timber handrails.

instructionSections.heading: Rescue planning belongs to the system
instructionSections.body: A worker held in a harness can be injured by the arrest itself and can become unconscious while still suspended. Before an arrest system is used, the plan must name the rescuer, the rescue method and the rescue equipment at the work location. Do not work alone at height where an arrest system is used. “Suspension trauma and rescue planning” covers suspension trauma and the rescue plan in detail.

lessons.title: Inspecting and fitting harnesses and lanyards
learningOutcomes: Carry out a before-use check covering a harness and a lanyard, covering webbing, stitching, buckles, connectors and energy absorbers.
Decide whether an item must be withdrawn from service, and say why.
Fit a harness correctly and have the fit checked by a second person.
Record the item identity, the in-service date and each inspection in a log.

instructionSections.heading: Inspection is the everyday check that matters most
instructionSections.body: A harness or lanyard that looks sound on the outside can still fail under load. The sources agree that an item should be inspected before each use and again afterwards, and that a competent individual should examine it at set intervals. An item that has taken a fall or an impact load comes out of service at once, even if it looks undamaged. This lesson teaches the worker's own check. It does not replace a periodic examination by a competent individual, and completing the lesson does not make the worker that person.

instructionSections.heading: Work through the item in the same order every time
instructionSections.body: Use a fixed order so nothing is skipped. For webbing, look for cuts, tears, fraying, abrasion, discolouration, heat marks and stiffness that suggests chemical contact, and run the strap through your hands to feel for hard spots and stretching. Stitching that carries the load is often in a different colour; any stitch that is missing, cut, frayed or incomplete is a reason to withdraw the item. For buckles and adjusters, look for distortion, sharp edges, cracks and corrosion, and operate each one to confirm it locks and releases. For connectors, check the body and the gate for distortion, cracks and corrosion, and confirm the gate closes and locks fully. For the energy absorber, check that the two ends of its cover are sealed and undamaged, with no cuts, tears or heat damage, and that it has not opened.

instructionSections.heading: The lanyard needs its own check
instructionSections.body: Inspect the full length of the lanyard, including each end, each splice or stitched join, and any shock-absorbing pack. Confirm the length matches the length used in the clearance calculation. A lanyard that has been shortened, knotted or joined with a connector that is not approved for it must be withdrawn. A lanyard used for fall arrest must never be relied on for positioning or for hauling materials.

instructionSections.heading: Protect the equipment in use
instructionSections.body: Keep lanyards away from sharp edges and abrasive surfaces, and use edge protectors where a lanyard runs over a corner. A lanyard that is cut or abraded is unsafe. Store equipment away from heat, sunlight and chemicals, and keep records so that every item can be traced.

instructionSections.heading: Fitting the harness
instructionSections.body: Fit the harness before you go up, then check the fit after you have connected. Put the harness on properly rather than stepping into it on the ground, which wets and dirties it and can expose it to chemicals. Fit the leg straps first, then the chest strap, and keep the back attachment point high on the rear of the harness. A slack harness can injure the skin and body during a fall, so tighten it until it fits closely. Have a second person check the fit, including the straps and buckle positions, before the worker goes up.

instructionSections.heading: When an item must come out of service
instructionSections.body: Remove an item from service at once if it shows any of the following: a cut or tear in the webbing; a missing or broken stitch; a distorted or cracked connector; a buckle that does not lock; an energy absorber that has opened, or has been exposed to heat or chemicals; or any impact load from a fall. Tag the item, store it apart from usable equipment, and tell the supervisor. Only a competent individual may decide whether an item that has taken a load can return to service, and the item stays out of use until that decision is recorded.

instructionSections.heading: Life, storage and records
instructionSections.body: Clean equipment with the method the maker recommends and let it dry in the shade rather than in direct sunlight. A non-Australian source gives a service life and a shelf life; those figures are not used here. Record the in-service date, the serial or item number, each inspection, and the date of any withdrawal.

lessons.title: Choosing and using ladders for trade and exterior work
learningOutcomes: Choose a ladder type and rating for a given task, load and surface.
Check a ladder before use and withdraw one that has a defect.
Set up and climb a ladder with the correct angle, landing extension and three-point contact.
Decide when a ladder is not the right tool, and when a ladder needs a fall-protection measure.

instructionSections.heading: A ladder is a way of getting to a place
instructionSections.body: A ladder gets a person to a place. It is not a good place to work from for long, and two of the sources treat ladders as a significant route into falls from elevation. This lesson sets out a decision path. First, can the task be done without climbing? Second, is a ladder suitable? Third, if a ladder is used, can it be set up and used safely? A ladder suits short, light work.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the type and rating
instructionSections.body: Choose the type first. Step ladders and platform steps are self-supporting. Extension and straight ladders lean on a wall and need a landing point at the top. Each ladder has a rated load that must cover the worker, clothing, tools and materials together, and exceeding it can make the ladder collapse. The material matters as well. Metal conducts electricity, so metal ladders stay away from live services, and timber or fibreglass ladders are chosen for specific tasks. Read the rating label and confirm it is legible before the ladder is used.

instructionSections.heading: Setting up on a firm base
instructionSections.body: Set up on a firm, level base. Where the ground is soft or sloped, use levelling feet or do not use that ladder. Keep doors and walkways clear, or block them off. Where a ladder can be fixed at the upper end, secure it, and where it cannot be secured, have a second person foot it while the worker climbs. For a leaning ladder, use the angle the maker states. A non-Australian source also asks that the top of a straight ladder extend above the landing.

instructionSections.heading: Climbing and working on the ladder
instructionSections.body: Face the ladder, hold the stiles rather than the rungs, and keep three-point contact on the ladder at all times. Carry nothing in the hands: use a tool belt, or hoist tools with a rope once the worker is in position. Avoid overreaching; the belt buckle stays between the stiles, and move the ladder rather than leaning to one side. The highest rung of a step ladder is not a standing place. Do not climb while tired, unwell, or affected by any substance that impairs balance.

instructionSections.heading: When a ladder needs a fall-protection measure
instructionSections.body: Where the worker must lean or reach from a ladder at a working height above the trigger that the sources set, counted from the foot of the ladder to the worker's feet, one source requires fall protection where it is appropriate. The figure is non-Australian, so do not use it. One source also require a lanyard to be attached at the working height before the task begins, and released last when the worker descends. The clearer rule is this: the higher the position and the further the worker reaches, the stronger the case for a platform, a scaffold or a different method.

instructionSections.heading: Check before and after the work
instructionSections.body: Inspect the ladder before each use and again afterwards. Check the rails for bends, splits, twists or breaks. Check the rungs or steps for bends, cracks or missing parts. Check the joints, bolts, rivets and hinges for tightness, the locks, spreaders and safety bars for function, and the feet and levellers for wear. A ladder that fails any check is removed, tagged and reported. Keep inspection records for ladders in regular use.

instructionSections.heading: Authority to use access equipment
instructionSections.body: The duty to manage work at height applies in each state and territory. Some states set licence or authorisation rules for certain elevating equipment. This lesson does not state those rules. Check the rule for the state where the work happens before any ladder task is planned. This lesson does not grant any authority.

lessons.title: Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use
learningOutcomes: Identify who may erect, alter and dismantle a scaffold or a mobile tower, and when specialist authority is needed.
Check a mobile tower before climbing: ground, verticality, outriggers, castors, brakes, platform boarding and tag.
Identify scaffold defects that stop use, including gaps, missing guardrails and the toe boards, an unstable base and unsafe access.
Explain why tagging, handover certificates and inspection records are part of the safety control.

instructionSections.heading: What a scaffold is for
instructionSections.body: A scaffold is a temporary framework that people stand on or work from, or that gives access to a work position. The sources in this pack describe several types, including independent tied, mobile, free-standing, system and tube-and-fitting scaffolds. The common hazards are collapse, gaps in the platform, contact with overhead electrical lines, unauthorised access, untrained erection, falling objects and an incomplete structure. A mobile tower is a single unit on castors. It is quick to set up, but it can tip if its base, load or height is wrong.

instructionSections.heading: Who builds and changes a scaffold
instructionSections.body: Erecting, altering and dismantling a scaffold are specialist tasks. One source says these should be done only by a qualified scaffold erector. In New South Wales, only licensed scaffolders may erect, alter or dismantle a scaffold where the fall risk exceeds four metres; that rule is confirmed in the project licence matrix. Do not remove ties, braces, guardrails or boards to make a task easier. One source warns that tampering with scaffold components can lead to prosecution and fines, and the same principle applies in any state.

instructionSections.heading: Tags and handover
instructionSections.body: A scaffold should carry a tag showing whether it can be used safely, who checked it and when. A competent individual should check a new or changed scaffold before it is used, and the handover should come with a completion certificate. A tag that is out of date, missing or red means the scaffold is not used until a competent individual has checked it again.

instructionSections.heading: Walk the scaffold before use
instructionSections.body: Walk the whole structure before the first use each day, and again after any change, impact or storm. Check the base is level and stable and that the uprights are vertical. Check that every horizontal member is rigid at each joint, and that diagonal bracing is in place. The platform must be fully boarded, the boards secured, and there must be no gap through which a person or tool could fall. Check the handrails, the mid-rails and the toe boards at every open edge, and check that access is by a suitable ladder that extends above the landing, not by climbing the frame.
