Look for overhead lines, unsafe fixings and anything hanging from the structure.

instructionSections.heading: Mobile towers
instructionSections.body: A mobile tower is often safer than a ladder, and the sources recommend one where safer access is not available. Before erection, check that the castors roll freely, that the components are sound, and that the brakes and locks work. On a suspended floor, check that the floor can carry the load. Before use, the tower must be vertical and square, the platform must be fully boarded, the outriggers placed properly and locked in position, the wheels locked, and the tower tagged. The sources give a height above which stabilisers are required and another above which the tower is tied off, and they require the aluminium quantity schedule from the maker to be followed. The control is what matters: stabilise and tie the tower where the maker and the risk assessment require it.

instructionSections.heading: Moving a tower
instructionSections.body: Do not move a tower with anyone on it unless the maker allows it and the surface is clear. Lock the wheels before anyone climbs. Keep the surface flat and finished, because a rough or sloped surface changes the risk of tipping. Come down before any movement, and check the tower again when it is set back up.

instructionSections.heading: Records
instructionSections.body: Keep the erection certificate, the tags, the inspection records and the component list for each scaffold or tower. One source expects an inspection at regular intervals, recorded on a form.

lessons.title: Elevated work platform pre-use checks
learningOutcomes: Carry out a pre-use walk-round of an elevated work platform covering the machine, the basket, the controls, the ground and the overhead hazards.
Name the operator's three main duties before a platform is used.
Identify the conditions that stop a platform from being used.
Explain the fall-protection rule for a platform occupant and why the lanyard is attached to the basket.

instructionSections.heading: What a MEWP is
instructionSections.body: A MEWP, also called an elevated work platform, is a machine that lifts people and their tools. Common types include scissor lifts and boom-type platforms, which can be self-propelled, truck-mounted, tow-behind, push-around, or static booms. The sources list the hazards as falls from the basket, falling objects or people, crush injuries, electrocution, tipping, ground collapse, wind, collisions, equipment failure, and suspension trauma after a fall. Each one has a control in the pre-use check.

instructionSections.heading: The operator's three duties
instructionSections.body: One source describes three jobs for the operator. The first is to make sure the machine can be used safely. The second is to check overhead, ground and surrounding hazards. The third is to operate the machine safely. The jobs run in that order, and the operation stage does not start until the first two are complete.

instructionSections.heading: The machine walk-round
instructionSections.body: Before the first use each day, walk round the machine. Look at the wheels and tyres, the toe boards plus the guardrails, any hydraulic leak, the structure, the hoses and the wiring. Check that the controls work from the base and from the basket, as the maker's instructions describe, and that the emergency controls at the base work. Check the safe working load and the number of occupants the platform allows, and check that the labels and decals are present and readable. A machine with a defect that affects safety is tagged and kept from use. Use the maker's schedule and the business's records.

instructionSections.heading: Overhead and ground hazards
instructionSections.body: Look up before a boom is unfolded. Overhead lines, other equipment, branches and structures can contact the platform. Treat every overhead line as live until its owner or the network confirms otherwise. Check the ground: the machine must stand on a firm and flat base, and the worker should look for buried services, soft or loose ground and holes. Walk the route before driving, and watch where the machine is heading. Wind is a hazard that can tip a platform, and the wind limit is set by the maker.

instructionSections.heading: Inside the basket
instructionSections.body: Remain inside the basket. Do not climb on guardrails, and do not stand on the rails or mid-rail. A worker in the basket wears a harness connected to the basket anchorage by a restraint lanyard, as one source requires, and the maker's guidance sets the lanyard style. Keep the work within the basket's reach limits. Set up barriers, a spotter and an exclusion zone for people below. Discuss the rescue plan before the platform is raised, and read the operator's manual for each model before first use.

instructionSections.heading: Driving and operating
instructionSections.body: Drive a self-propelled platform in the lowered position where the maker allows, because that is the safest position for travel. Only a trained and competent operator may operate the machine. Keep watching where the machine is heading. Keep to the maker's load and slope limits. Tipping is the risk that the limits exist to prevent.

instructionSections.heading: When the platform stops being safe
instructionSections.body: Stop, and lower the platform, if a control becomes unreliable, a warning light or alarm activates, the ground moves, the wind rises, a person is hurt, or a line is contacted. If the platform contacts a power line, the business's emergency procedure applies. The power must be isolated before anyone moves or touches the machine.

lessons.title: Roof and fragile-surface work
learningOutcomes: Identify the fall and falling-object risks of roof work, including the roof edge, openings and fragile material.
Recognise fragile and brittle roofing, and the controls that apply before a person walks on it.
Describe the access, edge and anchor requirements a roof job needs.
State the stop-work decision for a roof that is unsafe or unknown.

instructionSections.heading: Why roofs need their own rules
instructionSections.body: A roof combines several hazards. A person can fall off the edge, fall through a surface that cannot bear weight, slip down a pitched surface, be struck by falling objects, and be affected by the weather. One source describes falls off the edge, falls through fragile roof sheets and skylights, and slips from the eaves on pitched roofs. Another adds that age, sun, pollution, chemicals, storms and overloading all make a roof less reliable over time. Treat each roof as unknown until its condition has been checked.

instructionSections.heading: Fragile and brittle surfaces
instructionSections.body: A brittle roof is one that will not carry a person at every point on its surface, because of its material, age or weathering. The sources name plastic, glass, mineral fibre and thin corrugated sheeting as typical examples. Skylights, old fibre-cement and worn tiles can also fail. Before anyone walks on a roof, find out what it is made of, look for signs of failure such as crazing, discolouration, rust through, soft spots and cracked sheets, and then decide the controls. Do not test a sheet by stepping on it. The worker's judgement is not a control. The fragile areas must be marked, covered or avoided, and crawling boards or a platform used wherever the roof has to be crossed.

instructionSections.heading: Edges and openings
instructionSections.body: The edge is usually the main fall risk. Where an edge is unprotected, use a guardrail, a parapet at a safe height, a scaffold or work platform, a warning line with a restraint or arrest measure behind it, or a safety net. Where a warning line is used, anyone working between the line and the edge needs a harness and fall arrest. Cover or guard every skylight, roof light and opening before work near it starts.

instructionSections.heading: Access to the roof
instructionSections.body: The sources recommend a stable, independent scaffold or tower for access to a roof, even for short work. It must be tied in or supported so it cannot rock or tip. Plan the rescue route before access is set up. A ladder is for access to the start of the roof only and must extend above the edge. The ladder rules are in “Choosing and using ladders for trade and exterior work”, and the scaffold and tower checks are in “Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use”.

instructionSections.heading: Falling material and tools
instructionSections.body: Keep materials and tools clear of the edge, secure them against wind, and never throw them up or down. Catch netting or boards stop small items from falling. Keep people from walking under roof work. One source asks that stacking and storage on roofs be kept to a minimum and secured against wind, and that waste be taken off by a chute or container rather than thrown.

instructionSections.heading: Weather on the roof
instructionSections.body: Wet, icy, windy or hot weather changes the risk. One source says that wet, windy or icy conditions can make footing and control much harder, so controls must be applied. Stop roof work in gusty wind, rain or ice, and reassess after any change.

instructionSections.heading: Overhead services and solar
instructionSections.body: Overhead lines, inverters and the cabling of solar arrays add risk on a roof. Check for them before the work starts. The solar and electrical rules are in the solar course and in “Electrical, solar and overhead services”, and this lesson does not authorise any work near electrical systems.

lessons.title: Edge protection, floor openings and covers
learningOutcomes: Identify when edge protection is needed, and what it must do.
Check a guardrail system for height, rails, toe board, fixing and strength before use.
Cover or guard an opening so that it cannot be stepped into or fallen through.
Decide when a warning line or a restraint is used, and what neither of them can do.

instructionSections.heading: Why the edge and the opening come first
instructionSections.body: A physical edge or opening control removes the need for each worker to make a correct decision every minute. The sources in this pack list open sides and edges, holes, wall openings, skylights, concrete forms with exposed reinforcement, excavations and walkways as places where protection is needed. Treat any unprotected side near the work as an active fall exposure until it has been controlled.

instructionSections.heading: What a guardrail system must do
instructionSections.body: A guardrail system is a top rail, a mid-rail and a toe board. Guardrail heights and loads are set out in the sources, and the figures they give are not Australian. The mid-rail sits halfway up between the top rail and the working surface, and the toe board stops materials sliding off. The top rail is expected to resist a push at any spot on its upper edge, and the mid-rail a push along its length, without failing. The control holds whatever the figure: the rail must be complete, fixed, at the right height, able to stop a body pushing against it, and inspected before first use and after any impact.

instructionSections.heading: Covering an opening
instructionSections.body: An opening is a gap in a floor, roof, deck or wall. Cover it with a cover that is secured against wind and against being moved, and mark it clearly. Before any cover is removed, barricade the area so that no one steps into the opening. Skylights and roof lights are openings too, and they need a rail or a strong cover. Wall openings at height need a guardrail, a barrier or another fall control.

instructionSections.heading: Warning lines and restraint
instructionSections.body: A warning line is a marked rope, chain or line, fixed a set distance back from an edge. It warns people. It does not stop a fall. One source says that anyone working between the line and the edge needs a harness and an arrest system. A thin rope on its own does not guard an edge: one source judges a single nylon rope to be an improper guard for an open floor, and the same logic applies to tape or light cord that a person can step over or pull down. Restraint lines, where used, stop a worker reaching the edge, and their anchor and length must be checked under “Fall protection and arrest systems”.

instructionSections.heading: Nets, mesh and fixed barriers
instructionSections.body: A safety net catches a person who falls. It must be placed as close as practical below the work, and installed and checked by a competent individual. Use a net where a guardrail cannot be installed, and check it before each installation and again after it. Mesh or toe boards fitted to a rail also stop small materials falling.

instructionSections.heading: Protruding steel and excavation edges
instructionSections.body: Protruding reinforcing steel and the unprotected ends of scaffold tubes create a fall and impalement hazard. Cap or cover each end before work near it. Excavations with straight sides and an unprotected drop also need protection. For trenches, the national excavation code from Safe Work Australia (2015) says a trench 1.5 metres or deeper needs its walls held up by supports, benching or battering, wherever a cave-in could bury a person, whatever the depth (national model code; state adoption to be checked). Where workers must stand close to an unprotected excavation edge, they need a restraint or lifeline arrangement.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the controls in place
instructionSections.body: Do not remove an edge control to pass a tool or a material through. If a control must come down for a task, plan a temporary replacement control, record the reason, and get the supervisor's sign-off before the work starts. Put the control back as soon as the task allows, and inspect it again.

lessons.title: Suspension trauma and rescue planning
learningOutcomes: Recognise the early signs of suspension trauma and the response each one needs.
Name the components a rescue plan must cover before any arrest system is used.
Describe the categories of rescue named in the sources and the conditions under which each applies.
State the stop-work condition where no safe rescue arrangement exists.

instructionSections.heading: A harness can save a life and still injure
instructionSections.body: A worker held in a harness after a fall can be injured by the arrest itself, and can become unconscious while still suspended. The sources describe a condition often called suspension trauma. It can follow when a person hangs motionless, with circulation affected in the legs, and the person may faint. One source gives time markers for fainting and for death. The response does not depend on the exact timing. The rescue must be fast, and the plan must exist before the work starts.

instructionSections.heading: Early signs and first response
instructionSections.body: Watch for the early warning signs: a rush of light-headedness or nausea, a flushed or tingling feeling, numbness, faintness or anxiety; treat any of them as a warning. A suspended worker who is unconscious needs rescue as soon as it can be done safely. If a rescue cannot be started straight away, the sources suggest moving the legs or supporting the feet, and raising the lower legs where that can be done, to ease the strain. That response buys time. It is not the rescue, and it must not replace the rescue plan. Medical help is still needed after the rescue, whatever the apparent severity.

instructionSections.heading: What a rescue plan must cover
instructionSections.body: Before any arrest system is used, the plan must name who will rescue, which rescue method will be used, where the rescue equipment is kept, how the rescuer will reach the worker, and how emergency services will be called. One source says that a rescue plan which has not been practised cannot be depended on. Where the existing rescue method is not judged safe enough, the work does not start until a safe method is found. Work in teams: a lone worker cannot be rescued in time, and the sources prohibit lone working at height where fall arrest is used.

instructionSections.heading: Four categories of rescue
instructionSections.body: The sources sort rescues into four kinds: getting a casualty down from a distance, hauling a casualty up from a distance, the worker descending under their own power, and helping a second person who is on the way down. A rescuer should avoid descending or being suspended to reach someone else where that can be avoided, because it can create a second casualty. The sources name methods that include a rescue ladder, pulling a person in through a window or balcony, pulling a person up through an opening, lowering, climbing or descending the structure, an elevated platform, and a crane basket. The method is chosen to fit the location and the risk assessment.

instructionSections.heading: Rescue using an elevating platform
instructionSections.body: Where a platform can reach the suspended worker, an operator trained for that platform positions it beneath the worker. The platform's capacity must cover both the worker and the rescuer. An unconscious worker may need two rescuers to move them into the platform. The lanyard is disconnected only once the worker is secure in the platform, and reconnected to a platform anchor where possible. The worker is then lowered and given first aid.

instructionSections.heading: Raising and lowering a worker
instructionSections.body: Raising a worker needs two or more capable people hauling on a second line, with the slack taken up so that the rope does not slip. Lowering needs a rescuer anchored to a strong point, and someone at the bottom to guide the descent. In both cases, first aid and treatment for suspension trauma as well as for other injuries follow once the worker is safe.

instructionSections.heading: After the rescue
instructionSections.body: Do not let the worker stand straight away after a rescue. The sources advise against it and call for medical assessment, even where the worker seems well. Take the worker for examination at a medical facility. Report the fall to the supervisor and to the business's escalation contact. The equipment that was in use is withdrawn and recorded under “Inspecting and fitting harnesses and lanyards”.

lessons.title: Writing a risk assessment for height work
learningOutcomes: Identify each height-related hazard in a task, using the positions, routes, equipment and conditions.
Choose and record the control for each hazard using the hierarchy in “The hierarchy of controls for height work”.
Write a work-at-height plan that names the rescue arrangement, the people, and the stop-work conditions.
Recognise an incomplete or unreasoned plan, and return it for correction.

instructionSections.heading: Planning comes before the climb
instructionSections.body: A plan for height work is set down before anybody leaves the ground. The sources agree on several points: hazards are identified before work begins, the most suitable equipment is chosen, the weather is taken into account, the people doing the work are competent, the hazards from fragile surfaces and falling objects are managed, and equipment is inspected before and during use. A risk assessment serves as the written record of that planning, and one source requires it to be written before height work starts.

instructionSections.heading: What the assessment must cover
instructionSections.body: A height assessment covers the task and its duration, the positions and heights, the access route, the surfaces and their condition, the equipment and its inspection, the people and their training, the weather and its limits, the rescue arrangement, the public and people below, and the stop-work conditions. Record each hazard as one line, with the likelihood and severity scores used in the business's scheme (see “Scoring a hazard: likelihood, severity and the risk band”), the control, and the residual risk (see “Ranking controls and checking residual risk”).

instructionSections.heading: Scoring a fall
instructionSections.body: Score a fall by the height, the surface below, and the likely injury. A short fall onto a hard surface can be serious, and a fall onto a clear surface can still injure with a bad landing. Do not lower the score because a control is planned. Score the risk as it stands, and then score the residual risk after the control is in place and has been checked. Write the reason beside each score, so that a reviewer can follow it.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing the controls in the plan
instructionSections.body: For each hazard, write the highest feasible control from the hierarchy in “The hierarchy of controls for height work”, and the reason any higher option was rejected. Name each physical control to be inspected, such as the guardrail, platform, scaffold, tower or ladder, and each personal control with its type and its rescue method. Do not list a control that will not be on site on the day.

instructionSections.heading: Cross-checking the plan against the specific lessons
instructionSections.body: Check the plan against the lessons that match its equipment: ladders (“Choosing and using ladders for trade and exterior work”), scaffolds and towers (“Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use”), mobile elevated platforms (“Elevated work platform pre-use checks”), roofs and fragile surfaces (“Roof and fragile-surface work”), edges and openings (“Edge protection, floor openings and covers”), and rescue (“Suspension trauma and rescue planning”). Check that every state or territory rule in those lessons has been confirmed before the plan relies on it.

instructionSections.heading: Briefing and sign-off
instructionSections.body: The plan is briefed before work starts. Everyone involved should know the plan, their role, the rescue arrangement and the stop-work conditions. The supervisor signs off where the business requires it, and the record goes with the job. The height-work authorisation record (“Height-work authorisation record”) records the day's checks and any negative responses.

instructionSections.heading: When the plan is not enough
instructionSections.body: A plan that cannot be carried out safely must be changed or stopped. Examples include equipment that cannot be set up on the surface, a rescue arrangement that is not ready, weather that turns, or a control that is missing. Stop, make the area safe, and tell the supervisor before continuing.

instructionSections.heading: The licence and authority boundary
instructionSections.body: Some elevating equipment and scaffolding work need licences or authorisation in some states, and the rules differ by state. A plan that assumes a licence the worker does not hold is not a valid plan. The state rules are set out in “Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use” and “Elevated work platform pre-use checks”, and they are confirmed only where marked. Completing this lesson grants no authority.

lessons.title: Height-work authorisation record (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Complete every field of the height-work authorisation record for a supplied job, with evidence where a check requires it.
Justify each negative response with a reason and a control, and decide whether the work may proceed.
Name a rescue arrangement that is ready on site before the work starts.
Return the record for correction when any required field is blank or unsupported.

instructionSections.heading: What this record is for
instructionSections.body: The height-work authorisation record brings together the checks a supervisor and a worker make before height work starts. It is not a licence and it does not authorise anyone to work at height. It works only when it is filed with a risk assessment or a safe work method for the same task, and the task it describes is the one that is done. You build the record field by field through this lesson. The system assembles the finished fields into one document that you keep and that is signed off by an assessor.

instructionSections.heading: How to work through it
instructionSections.body: Complete the four templates in order. The first covers the job and the management checks, the second the equipment and access checks, the third the negative responses, and the fourth the confirmation and rescue plan. Answer every field. Where a check does not apply, write not applicable and the reason. Where a check is answered No, the response goes into the negative-response template with its control. Do not sign the record until the checks have been made on site, rather than from memory or from a plan.

instructionSections.heading: Evidence on site
instructionSections.body: Each check should be backed by something you have seen: an identifier, a tag, a measurement, a photograph where the business allows it, or a named person who confirmed the item. A check written from a plan alone does not count. The clearance in the calculated-clearance field must show its factors, and the figures must come from the approved method and the manufacturer, not from an unchecked source figure.

instructionSections.heading: Negative responses and the stop rule
instructionSections.body: A negative response is not a failure of the form, but it is a signal that a control is missing. Each one needs a reason and a control. Where the control cannot be put in place, or the reason does not hold, the work does not proceed. Stop the work, make the area safe, and tell the supervisor. The same applies to any open item that affects safety at the time of signing.

instructionSections.heading: Confirmation and rescue
instructionSections.body: The worker and the supervisor both sign the record. Both must have seen the checks made. The rescue arrangement is part of the confirmation: it names the rescuer, the method and the equipment on site, and it is practised before first use. The business's emergency and escalation contacts are kept with the record.

lessons.title: Writing a cleaning element specification as an outcome
learningOutcomes: Write an outcome statement for a named element
Explain the difference between a task instruction and an outcome statement
Judge an element as acceptable or unacceptable against its written outcome

instructionSections.heading: Describe the outcome, not only the task
instructionSections.body: A cleaning element specification describes the state an item must be in when cleaning is finished, not only the steps taken to get there. The Irish manual builds its approach on element specifications, roughly fifty-five elements for a typical ward, each with a short statement of the result required. For a radiator, for example, the statement describes the whole unit, including its parts, as clean and in good repair with no visible residue. A statement written that way can be checked by two different people and give the same answer.

instructionSections.heading: What a good statement contains
instructionSections.body: A good statement is patient-focused, clear to the staff who clean the element, measurable, in line with infection control requirements, and comparable with similar facilities. It sets out a pass condition and a fail condition in plain words. Keep one element to one statement, so that a score is not argued over two items at once. Test each statement by asking whether a trained person could look at the element and say yes or no.

instructionSections.heading: Scoring against the statement
instructionSections.body: The auditor scores each element as acceptable (1) or unacceptable (0), and leaves out any element that is not present in a room. A failed element is recorded with its reason and a time set for fixing it. Faults that belong to maintenance rather than cleaning are noted as findings for the maintenance route.

lessons.title: Full clean versus check clean: choosing the right work for an element
learningOutcomes: Define a full clean and a check clean
Choose which kind of clean applies to an element on a given day
Explain why over-cleaning wastes resources without adding infection control value

instructionSections.heading: Two kinds of work
instructionSections.body: A full clean means the whole element is cleaned every time it is scheduled, to its written specification. A check clean means the operator inspects each aspect of the item and cleans only the aspects that fall short of the standard. The element is then in the same state as after a full clean. The two terms describe the work itself. The schedule tells you when each one applies.

instructionSections.heading: Use the cue of use and soil
instructionSections.body: The Irish manual's principle is that an element which is clearly clean and has had no use since the last clean does not need cleaning again. An element that looks dirty does need it, even if nobody has used it. This is the heart of a daily routine. Over-cleaning uses staff time and product without adding infection control value, so frequency should follow how often an element gets dirty and how many people use it.

instructionSections.heading: Where the Australian standard overrides
instructionSections.body: The Irish frequencies are minimums that local practice applies, and they are not Australian requirements. In SA public healthcare facilities the SA standard governs. Its standard clean is required routinely even when a surface looks clean, so a check clean does not replace a scheduled standard clean in a SA facility. Where a SA schedule lists a standard clean, clean at the scheduled frequency regardless of appearance. The check-clean approach can apply only where the local schedule allows it.

lessons.title: Scoring a cleaning audit: room, element and area percentages
learningOutcomes: Calculate a room percentage from element scores
Calculate a functional area average from room percentages
Check a published total before relying on it

instructionSections.heading: The room score
instructionSections.body: Each element scores 1 if it is acceptable and 0 when it fails. Elements that are not present in a room are left out of the count. The room percentage is acceptable points divided by achievable points, multiplied by 100. A room with 45 acceptable points against 50 achievable scores 90 per cent.

instructionSections.heading: The area score
instructionSections.body: An area's score is the average of its room scores. Average the room percentages, not the raw points, so that rooms with different numbers of applicable elements count equally.

instructionSections.heading: Check the arithmetic before you publish
instructionSections.body: Totals can be wrong. The Irish manual's worked example lists six room scores, listed in order as seventy, sixty, sixty-five, seventy, ninety and sixty-five and prints a total of 430. Those values actually add to 420, and their average is 70 per cent. The printed total, and the 71 per cent that followed from it, are therefore wrong. Always re-add the values yourself, and correct any sheet that does not add up before it is saved or reported.

instructionSections.heading: Recording the result
instructionSections.body: Record each failed element with its reason and a time for action. Report the area score together with the number of rooms it was calculated from, so that a later reader can check the figure.

lessons.title: Corrective action time frames and the maintenance boundary
learningOutcomes: Match an audit finding to a corrective action time frame
Separate a cleaning fault from a maintenance fault
Write a maintenance request that states the infection risk

instructionSections.heading: Time frames follow risk
instructionSections.body: The Irish manual ties corrective action to the risk category of the area. Findings in the highest risk areas are to be acted on immediately and the cleaning kept constant, while lower risk findings move to a routine, lower-intensity response. The manual also separates maintenance issues that create a risk to infection control or to safety from those that do not. The time frame table in the uploaded text is garbled, so no hour counts are quoted here. Use the facility's own time frames, and do not apply any Irish figures in Australia without checking them.

instructionSections.heading: The maintenance boundary
instructionSections.body: A fault that cannot be cleaned away and that holds soil, such as a cracked tile in a shower room, is a maintenance matter with an infection control risk, so it is reported for urgent action. A fault that does not create that risk goes on the planned maintenance list. The boundary between cleaning and maintenance for each item, such as light fittings and ventilation units, should be written into the service agreement with a named responsible person or department, and reviewed when a dispute arises.

instructionSections.heading: Writing the request
instructionSections.body: A useful maintenance request states what the item is, where it is, why it cannot be cleaned, what risk it creates, and when the fault was first reported. Keep a copy, and check at the following audit that the fault was closed.

lessons.title: Microfibre systems: laundering, drying and damp-mop limits
learningOutcomes: Apply the one-cloth-per-area rule in a microfibre system
State the laundering and drying rules for microfibre products
Set and observe a time limit for damp microfibre mops

instructionSections.heading: The system and its approval
instructionSections.body: A microfibre system holds soil through static attraction, which helps with awkward places. The Irish method statement uses it only where the local infection team has approved it, and it requires a trained operator. Use a single fresh cloth for each room or area, and a new mop head for every area. Keep dust control items and damp mop heads in labelled net bags so that areas do not mix.

instructionSections.heading: Laundering
instructionSections.body: Launder microfibre products separately from other cloths and mops. Use a pre-wash, a main wash, then two rinses. Do not use fabric softener or bleach. Use only a neutral detergent and avoid recycled water systems. The method statement gives heat and time targets for the product, and an upper limit for drying heat. Check the supplier's current instructions and the Australian laundering requirements for the facility before using any figure.

instructionSections.heading: Drying and damp mops
instructionSections.body: Dry microfibre mops after use. Because it is hard to monitor a damp mop, the safer rule is to dry it after use. Microfibre can also take a long time to dry when net bags constrict the mops during washing.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the area
instructionSections.body: Record any area that cannot be reached, so that it is not left untreated for over a day. Measure the system's performance by looking for dust after cleaning.

lessons.title: Dust control and damp dusting in clinical areas
learningOutcomes: Describe the dust control method using a dust head kept on the floor
Explain why dry dusting is not permitted
Choose the correct damp dusting product for a surface

instructionSections.heading: Dust control on floors
instructionSections.body: Dust control uses a head that stays touching the floor during the pass. Make figure-eight passes that overlap, starting at the far end of the area and moving toward the door. Lift and remove large litter by hand first, and scrape gum off the floor before the pass. Keep the head in contact throughout, so that dust is held rather than thrown up. Once it is full, swap the head out and send it for laundering or disposal under local policy.

instructionSections.heading: Why dry dusting is not permitted
instructionSections.body: Dry dusting lifts particles back into the air instead of removing them. The Irish manual says plainly that dry dusting is not allowed. In its place, the cleaner damp dusts. Routine damp dusting uses detergent and water, not chemical disinfectant. The cloth is turned often and rinsed, the solution is changed when it turns dirty, and a dry cloth is used at the end where a surface needs it.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a product for the surface
instructionSections.body: For most general surfaces, warm water with a detergent is the default. Alcohol wipes can decontaminate some equipment, but they can damage other items and are unsuitable where soil is visible. Detergent wipes may suit some items, following the maker's instructions. The SA standard adds that a damp cloth is the expected tool for dusting, and that brooms and feather dusters should be kept out of healthcare areas.

lessons.title: Ward-level authority over cleaning resources and standards
learningOutcomes: Describe what a ward manager can influence in cleaning
Explain why a stable team builds quality
State the limits of ward-level authority over cleaning

instructionSections.heading: Stable teams on each ward
instructionSections.body: The Irish manual argues that cleaning works best when cleaning staff are attached to one ward or department and the ward manager has a real say in standards, frequency and performance. Constant movement of staff between areas makes it hard to build working relationships with patients and the ward team. The manual also warns that staff working side by side on different pay or conditions can damage team spirit, particularly where employed and outsourced staff do similar work.

instructionSections.heading: What the ward manager can do
instructionSections.body: The manual lists what a ward manager requires the ability to do. They can influence what is cleaned and how often, build a working relationship with the cleaning team, get technical support from the cleaning service department, get urgent cleaning done quickly, and recommend that payment be held back for weak performance. A ward management system supports this by giving each ward a plan of the tasks, when they happen, who does them, and the standard time each job should take.

instructionSections.heading: The limits of ward authority
instructionSections.body: Ward authority does not override the infection control schedule, the facility's risk classes or the conditions of the service contract. In SA, a change to frequency, method or risk class goes through clinical management and infection prevention, as described in “Functional area risk classes and what they change” and “Special circumstances: sensitivities, co-located aged care and kitchenette products”. Withholding approval of work or recommending a payment reduction is a contract matter and must follow the contract's process, not an informal instruction to the cleaners.

lessons.title: Scoring tenders on quality and price, and choosing activity or quality specifications
learningOutcomes: Explain how quality and price can be scored together in a tender
Apply a relative price scoring rule to a set of bids
Distinguish an activity-based specification from a quality-based one

instructionSections.heading: Why not the lowest price alone
instructionSections.body: The Irish manual argues that choosing the cheapest tender can lower quality, press down wages and conditions, and reduce the service over time. It recommends awarding on best value, which weighs quality as well as price. The contracting team sets the weights before the tenders are opened, so that the scoring is fair and can be defended later.

instructionSections.heading: How a score is built
instructionSections.body: A common approach gives each bid a technical score and a price score and adds them. The price score can be relative. The lowest acceptable price gets the full points, and each higher price loses points in proportion to how far above the lowest it sits. With 40 price points available, a bid 10 per cent above the lowest loses 10 per cent of 40 and scores 36. Technical criteria can use a rating scale with a weight for each rating, for example 0 per cent for bad, 50 per cent for medium, 80 per cent for good and 100 per cent for excellent, weighted against the points given to each criterion.

instructionSections.heading: Activity-based and quality-based specifications
instructionSections.body: An activity-based specification lists the operations, the surfaces and the frequencies. A quality-based specification states the quality outcome required and leaves the method to the supplier, perhaps with minimum frequencies. Programmed cleaning is an activity-based approach that gives each room a code for its full-clean and spot-check frequencies, and the terms of that code must be defined. An abnormally low bid should be questioned in writing before it is accepted. If the reply does not show that the standard can be met, the bid is eliminated.

instructionSections.heading: References that do not apply here
instructionSections.body: The manual cites European procurement law, Irish tax and social insurance certificates and Irish professional registers. These do not apply in Australia. Use Australian procurement rules and state requirements.

lessons.title: Steam cleaning: training, eye and hand protection, and detector precautions
learningOutcomes: State the training and competency condition that must be met before steam cleaning
Select eye and hand protection for steam work
Identify the electrical, detector and set-up precautions for a steam job

instructionSections.heading: Training comes first
instructionSections.body: Steam cleaning must wait until training is complete and competency has been tested, and only where local policy has recommended steam for that area. This is a high-hazard task. The steam is hot, the pressure nozzle can injure skin, and the machine has an electrical connection that must be kept dry and undamaged.

instructionSections.heading: Protection and set-up
instructionSections.body: Wear eye protection and protective gloves for the whole job, and keep any open skin away from the nozzle. Check the cord and plug before every use. Plug in with the switch off, keep your hands dry, and do not change fittings while the machine is plugged in. Fill the unit with water as the maker directs, attach the accessory for the surface, and wait for the unit to warm up before you start.

instructionSections.heading: Electrical items and detectors
instructionSections.body: Do not steam electrical equipment. Excess steam can set off fire or smoke detectors, so warn the site before you start and plan for it. For wall cleaning, cover the power sockets first. Use the warning sign so people keep clear of the work area.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing the job
instructionSections.body: After use, drain the used-water tank, wipe the machine and wash the accessories, return them to the trolley, and wind the flex back onto its clip. Let the area dry before the furniture goes back. Record the machine's condition, and report any fault before the next use.

lessons.title: Replenishing dispensers and consumables without contaminating new stock
learningOutcomes: Replenish soap, towel and tissue dispensers in the right sequence
Avoid contaminating new stock during refilling
Check dispensers for faults and report them

instructionSections.heading: Replenishing is part of the washroom clean
instructionSections.body: Replenishing is not a separate chore that can be done in any order. Check whether the dispenser needs refilling, then open it as the maker directs, damp-dust its outside, the nozzle or pump and its bracket, and discard the cloth under local policy. Refill or replace the contents without overfilling, close the dispenser, and then check that the kit is clean and back in its place.

instructionSections.heading: Handling stock
instructionSections.body: Open new packs only when they are needed for refilling. Do not leave stock on the ground or on a ledge where dirt can settle on it. Overfilling a dispenser can stop product coming out correctly, which wastes stock. Look for foreign material inside the unit before refilling.

instructionSections.heading: Refill or replace, and faults
instructionSections.body: Where a dispenser takes a refill pack or cartridge, replace it rather than topping up an old container. The SA standard does not accept topping up of liquid soap and disinfectant containers, and it expects those containers to be disposable. Report cracked, broken or faulty dispensers, and any scale deposits, to the supervisor. Do not clean dispensers with hand hygiene products; use the washroom cleaning product approved for the area.

lessons.title: Functional area risk classes and what they change
learningOutcomes: Identify the risk class of an area from its clinical use
Explain how a risk class changes the cleaning frequency
Describe who must be consulted before a risk class is raised or lowered

instructionSections.heading: Why areas carry different risk
instructionSections.body: A functional area is any part of a facility where cleaning takes place, such as an operating room, an intensive care unit, a ward or an office. The standard places each area in one of three bands based on how likely its surfaces are to become contaminated, how vulnerable the patients there are, and how likely people are to be exposed. Areas in the high band are cleaned more often than moderate areas, and moderate areas are cleaned more often than low band areas. The band tells you how often an area needs its scheduled work. It does not tell you which product to use, because the method depends on the element and the kind of clean.

instructionSections.heading: Reading the bands
instructionSections.body: Intensive care, high dependency, operating, recovery and procedure rooms, emergency departments, renal and haemodialysis units, and transplant, haematology and oncology units sit in the high band. General wards, labour and birthing areas, autopsy rooms, reprocessing areas and treatment rooms sit in the moderate band. Plant rooms, records storage, administration and other low-use public spaces sit in the low band. The published list is long and may change, so read the band for each area from the facility's own schedule rather than from memory of a similar room in another hospital.

instructionSections.heading: Changing a band
instructionSections.body: A band may be raised where patients in an area are more at risk, for example moving a moderate ward to high. A band must not be lowered unless the nature of patients or the service level has shifted materially. Any change, up or down, is agreed with clinical management and with the infection prevention team or the state infection control service. A new area that is not on the list is risk-assessed on the same three factors and checked with the same people before a schedule is set. During an outbreak in any area, that area is treated as very high risk until the infection prevention coordinators downgrade the outbreak.

lessons.title: Standard, transmission-based, discharge and spot-and-spill cleans
learningOutcomes: Name the four types of clean used in the SA standard
Select the correct clean for a given trigger
Explain how a single case differs from an outbreak in method and frequency

instructionSections.heading: Four kinds of clean
instructionSections.body: The standard asks for four kinds of clean. A standard clean means the routine, timetabled work carried out regardless of whether an element looks dirty. A transmission-based clean applies when a patient is a suspected or confirmed case of a disease that spreads by contact, droplet or air. A discharge clean happens after one patient leaves a space and ahead of the next admission. A spill or spot clean responds to anything visibly soiled or to a body fluid spill. These are layered: a discharge clean is added on top of the standard clean, and a spill clean is added on top of whatever clean is running.

instructionSections.heading: Single case or outbreak
instructionSections.body: A transmission-based clean has two forms. For a single case, or several unrelated cases, the frequency stays at the standard level but the method rises to detergent plus disinfectant on most elements inside the room the case occupies. For an outbreak, meaning a higher-than-expected number of cases of one infection or two or more connected cases, both the frequency and the method increase across the entire functional area. An outbreak clean takes precedence over the usual scheduled clean until the infection prevention coordinators downgrade it.

instructionSections.heading: Methods that never change
instructionSections.body: Lavatories, bidets and commodes always get detergent and disinfectant. So does every element in a wet area, including showers. Other elements such as bed rails, overbed tables and lockers are normally cleaned with detergent alone, unless a transmission-based precaution or an outbreak applies. Know which elements in your area belong to which group before you start.

lessons.title: Discharge clean: sequence from assessment to remaking the bed
learningOutcomes: Perform the steps of a discharge clean in the right sequence
Remove and bag used linen without spreading contamination
Check the sharps container and waste before leaving the room

instructionSections.heading: Before you touch anything
instructionSections.body: A discharge clean takes place after the patient has left and before the following patient enters. First check whether a transmission-based precaution applied to the patient who left. Then walk the room and note what must be replaced: toilet tissue, hand towels, soap, hand rub, gloves and the sharps container. Make this list before you start on the bed, so nothing is missed at the end.

instructionSections.heading: Working order inside the room
instructionSections.body: Work from least soiled to most soiled and starting from the highest surfaces down. Begin by stripping the bed and bagging the linen where it lies, rolling sheets carefully to limit the spread of aerosols. Put on fresh gloves once the linen is out of the way. Then clean the door, its handle and touched areas, walls only where they look dirty, switches, thermostats and wall-mounted items. Move on to furnishings and flat surfaces, then equipment such as drip stands, the locker, the bed frame and mattress. Clean the bathroom and the floors near the end. Use a fresh cloth for each bed space, and never dip a used cloth back into the clean solution.

instructionSections.heading: Finishing and leaving
instructionSections.body: Before you leave, check the sharps container and replace it once it reaches the fill point in the standard. Put in a new linen bag, then close waste bags without pressing down on them with your hands. Take off your gloves, clean your hands with hand rub unless they look dirty, and leave the room without gloves on. Remake the bed, restock the room, and return the equipment you moved to its storage area. The standard sets the fill point for sharps containers at three-quarters full. The Irish manual uses a different fraction; in SA the standard governs.

lessons.title: Concentration, contact time and when to change a cleaning solution
learningOutcomes: Explain why both concentration and contact time affect cleaning outcomes
Decide when a cleaning solution must be replaced
Distinguish a detergent clean from a disinfectant clean

instructionSections.heading: Detergent or disinfectant
instructionSections.body: A detergent lifts soil and organic matter, and most hard surfaces are cleaned well with warm water with a pH-neutral detergent, used as the maker instructs. A disinfectant destroys or neutralises most infective germs, but it should not serve as a general cleaner unless the product is a combined detergent and disinfectant. Two approaches exist. A two-step clean uses a detergent clean followed by a disinfectant. A two-in-one clean uses a single product that combines both and relies on mechanical action. Some chlorine products must be rinsed off after the contact time, which adds a step.

instructionSections.heading: Concentration and contact time
instructionSections.body: Under-strength mixes may fail to kill microorganisms reliably. A solution stronger than the label allows wastes product, can harm fittings and fixtures, and creates a workplace risk, so stronger is not safer. Make the solution to the label dilution and water temperature. Contact time is how long the product must stay wet on the surface to work; wiping early cuts its effect. Read every claim carefully. A label may say a product kills a named organism in its ordinary form while the spore form needs a different approach. The facility's infection control coordinators approve products and their claims.

instructionSections.heading: When to replace a solution
instructionSections.body: Solutions pick up contamination during use, and carrying it onto clean surfaces spreads microorganisms. Replace the solution on the manufacturer's schedule. Replace it sooner if the area is heavily soiled, or if the solution looks dirty, and straight after a bodily fluid spill has been cleaned. Do not add fresh product to old solution to stretch it.

lessons.title: Dust, aerosols and HEPA-filtered vacuums near clinical areas
learningOutcomes: Choose dust control methods that do not spread particles
Explain why spray bottles are avoided in healthcare rooms
State the filter requirement for vacuums used near clinical areas

instructionSections.heading: Dust control
instructionSections.body: Dust settles on surfaces and moves on air currents. Tools that stir dust into the air, such as brooms and feather dusters, should be avoided in healthcare areas. Dust using a damp cloth so the dust is captured, not sent back into the room. Work from the highest surfaces down, so that dust falling from higher areas is picked up when you reach the lower ones.

instructionSections.heading: Aerosols and sprays
instructionSections.body: Spray bottles and equipment that makes a fine mist can create aerosols. Aerosols carry chemical irritation to the eyes and to the mucous membranes, and they can carry droplets further than a surface spill does. Squeeze bottles that place product onto a cloth or directly onto a surface generate far less mist. Apply product to the cloth, not into the air.

instructionSections.heading: Vacuums near clinical areas
instructionSections.body: A vacuum for carpet work near clinical areas should have a HEPA filter, which traps very fine particles. Its filters should be changed on a planned maintenance schedule. A general-purpose vacuum with a worn bag or an unknown filter can push fine dust back into the room, so check the bag and filter before every use.

lessons.title: Colour coding is a local choice: what applies in SA
learningOutcomes: State whether the SA standard requires colour coding
Explain what colour coding is meant to prevent
Apply a facility's colour scheme consistently

instructionSections.heading: Not required in SA
instructionSections.body: The SA standard does not require colour coding for cleaning items and tools in SA healthcare facilities. A facility can opt to adopt it voluntarily. Its purpose is to make sure that cloths, mop heads, buckets, aprons, gloves used in one area must never go into another, which lowers the chance of infection spreading between areas.

instructionSections.heading: The examples in the standard
instructionSections.body: The standard gives an example taken from schemes used in other jurisdictions. It assigns separate colours to bathrooms and toilets, to general areas, to food areas, and to isolation areas. These are examples only and do not form a required SA scheme. If a facility adopts a scheme, the colour must be easy to read and lasting on each item, and staff need training in how the system works.

instructionSections.heading: Other references that differ
instructionSections.body: Other reference documents use different colour assignments, including the Irish manual that is reviewed elsewhere in this set. Where another document conflicts with the SA standard, the SA standard governs in SA facilities. Do not adopt a colour chart from another document without the infection prevention team approving it for the facility.

lessons.title: Staying away from work when unwell, and vaccination for healthcare cleaners
learningOutcomes: Explain the illness policy that applies before a shift in clinical areas
Identify when a worker must not enter a healthcare area
Describe the immunisation support that a healthcare cleaner should be offered

instructionSections.heading: Illness and entry to patient areas
instructionSections.body: Everyday illnesses like colds, flu and stomach bugs can reach patients through touch, droplets or airborne particles. Healthcare settings should make it clear that workers should stay home with an acute illness that is probably infectious, such as fever, coughing or influenza-type symptoms, diarrhoea or vomiting. The SA standard ties this expectation to the stand-down periods in the NHMRC national guidance on infection control (2019 edition). Confirm the current exclusion periods for your role with the infection prevention team, because this lesson does not state them and the 2019 edition exclusion periods were not reviewed for this draft.

instructionSections.heading: Vaccination
instructionSections.body: Healthcare workers, including cleaners, can face a raised risk of several diseases that vaccination can prevent, and they can carry community infections to patients and colleagues. Access to vaccination programs should be offered. The recommendation that applies to a given worker depends on how likely they are to touch patients or handle bodily fluids. The SA policy directive on immunisation for healthcare workers gives the detail; cite the current version rather than one remembered from earlier.

instructionSections.heading: After an exposure
instructionSections.body: A worker who may have been exposed to bodily fluids or other infectious hazards needs a documented route. The facility should run a scheme against sharps injuries, with prompt follow-up and preventive treatment where indicated, a breathing-protection scheme for anyone entering an airborne isolation room, and a review and reporting process involving WHS staff and infection control coordinators. Your part is to report at once and follow that route.

lessons.title: Checking that cleaning worked: visual, white glove, UV markers and ATP
learningOutcomes: Name the verification methods listed in the SA standard
Explain the limit of a visual check
Describe where verification records are kept

instructionSections.heading: A look is not enough
instructionSections.body: Microorganisms cannot be seen, so a surface can look clean and still carry them. Verification gathers evidence that the method worked and that the schedule was followed. A visual inspection is the first tool. Supervisors also observe cleaning technique against written procedures, to verify that the method is followed as written and not only that the result looks acceptable.

instructionSections.heading: Methods with their limits
instructionSections.body: A white glove test can show dust: a gloved hand wiped across a surface picks up residue that the eye may miss. Fluorescent markers are placed on high-touch surfaces before cleaning, then checked under a UV light afterwards; if the marker has gone, the marked soil was removed. ATP tests measure residual organic matter and are common in food processing. Each method has a limit. White glove and marker checks show that dust or marked soil is gone, and ATP shows organic residue. None of them proves that microorganisms are gone.

instructionSections.heading: Sampling and records
instructionSections.body: Routine environmental microbiological sampling has considerable limits and is not routinely advised for routine use. It has a place in outbreak investigation and in validating a cleaning system; see “Checking cleaning quality without over-relying on sampling” for the wider sampling discussion. Whichever method is used, keep the checklists and reports together in one central place, so that results can be compared over time.

lessons.title: Internal audits: how often each area is audited and the pass mark
learningOutcomes: State the audit frequency and rotation for each risk class
Calculate whether an area has met its pass level
Explain why audits rotate between rooms

instructionSections.heading: Coverage by risk class
instructionSections.body: Internal audits must cover every functional area across all risk classes. For a high-risk area, half of its rooms are audited once in a one-month period. For a moderate-risk area, half of its rooms are audited once in a three-month period. For a low-risk area, every room is audited once in a twelve-month period. Each class also has an pass level: 90 per cent for high-risk areas and 85 per cent for moderate and low-risk areas. An area's audit score must be meet or exceed its level. These figures come from the South Australian Health standard (2014, updated in 2017). They apply to South Australian facilities only, may be out of date, and are not a national rule.

instructionSections.heading: Rotation between periods
instructionSections.body: In the high and moderate bands, rooms not audited this period are picked up next period, so every room is covered over time. Before an audit, the auditor reviews the earlier record to see which sections were covered and which actions are still open. Without that, the same rooms get audited each time and problems elsewhere go unseen.

instructionSections.heading: Who audits and what follows
instructionSections.body: The auditor needs a firm grip on the standard and on the processes it sets. An auditor may come from the cleaning service, from another part of the facility or from the contractor, but should be joined by someone from the audited area's staff, such as the unit manager, so that issues are confirmed on the spot. Cleaning staff join the review of results. Each area receives its score sheet with clear actions. Results and improvement plans go to the governance committee plus the infection prevention committee.

lessons.title: External audits: at least every two years, and yearly when internal audits cannot be shown to work
learningOutcomes: State the minimum interval for an external cleaning audit
Name the conditions that move the external cycle to yearly
Describe what an external audit reviews

instructionSections.heading: The minimum cycle and who may audit
instructionSections.body: The standard recommends an external audit no less often than every two years. The auditor must be qualified and must work for neither the facility nor the cleaning provider. The auditor may come from the wider health service, from another facility in the same local network, or from an outside agency. The external audit reviews the facility hygiene program as a whole: the skills and knowledge of staff, all cleaning policies, the in-house audit schedule, every result and variance, and the action plans. Its scope covers the work of nurses, cleaners, contractors and facility managers.

instructionSections.heading: What a qualified auditor brings
instructionSections.body: A qualified auditor should have technical knowledge of infection control hazards and risks, familiarity with cleaning standards, and an understanding of how audits are run. Communication, cultural sensitivity, skill at settling disputes and solving problems also matter, along with planning and organising ability.

instructionSections.heading: When the cycle tightens
instructionSections.body: If the facility cannot show that its internal audit process assesses cleaning against the pass levels, or that follow-up action is taken when a level is missed, a further external review should be booked inside 12 months. If the next external audit finds the in-house process sound and follow-up actions in place, the cycle returns to the two-year interval. Otherwise the cycle stays at yearly until an effective in-house process is shown.

lessons.title: Special circumstances: sensitivities, co-located aged care and kitchenette products
learningOutcomes: Identify when the standard schedule might have to be adjusted
Name who must agree a change to the schedule or product
Select products that meet the kitchenette requirement in a clinical setting

instructionSections.heading: Adjusting for a patient's condition
instructionSections.body: The standard allows the schedule to deviate where a patient's medical condition calls for it. One example is a patient with multiple chemical sensitivities, who may react to routine cleaning products. The facility can then plan a different product or method for that area. Any such change is agreed with clinical management and the infection prevention service. The SA policy guideline on idiopathic environmental intolerance and multiple chemical sensitivity (2016) covers the wider context; its text is not reproduced here.

instructionSections.heading: Aged care beside acute beds
instructionSections.body: Some facilities, particularly in rural areas, have aged care residents in the same building as acute patients. In those settings the cadence of cleaning and spot cleaning in shared areas might need to rise to match the risk of body fluid contamination. Raise the gap with clinical management and the infection prevention team, and record the agreed change.

instructionSections.heading: Kitchenettes in clinical areas
instructionSections.body: Where food is handled in a clinical or ward setting, such as a kitchenette, every detergent and sanitiser used there needs food-grade status and no perfume. This rule is separate from the disinfectants used on patient surfaces. A fragranced general spray is not acceptable in a kitchenette, whatever it is used for elsewhere in the building.

lessons.title: Licences, permissions and restricted work
learningOutcomes: Explain the boundary for licences, permissions and restricted work and identify when work must stop.
Prepare a task-specific, documented decision for licences, permissions and restricted work under company and local requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Why restricted work needs its own check
instructionSections.body: Some work that looks like cleaning is in fact regulated work. A worker who starts it without the right licence, permit or authorisation exposes themselves, the client and the business to legal and safety risk. This lesson teaches you to ask a set of questions before any task starts: does the work fall under a licensed trade, does it involve a regulated material or hazardous remediation, does the site require a permit or an approval from the owner or manager, and does your employer or insurer restrict the work? A yes to any of these means the task is restricted until it is cleared.

instructionSections.heading: Four sources of restriction
instructionSections.body: Restrictions come from four places. The first is licensing law: some trades and some equipment require a licence or certificate issued under state or territory rules, and each licence covers a defined class of work. The second is regulated materials: suspected asbestos-containing material, and other materials with specific removal rules, must not be disturbed by an unqualified worker. The third is site and owner permission: building managers, body corporates, tenants or clients may set their own rules for access, products, noise or specialised methods. The fourth is employer and insurer policy: your business may place certain tasks outside its approved scope even where the law would allow them. A single task can be restricted by more than one of these at once.

instructionSections.heading: Test the task before accepting it
instructionSections.body: Before accepting, describe the task in plain words, with the location, the materials and the method. Ask whether any part of it involves electrical wiring or fittings, gas, plumbing, structural change, roof or height access, the removal or disturbance of building materials, or a product or process that needs a special permit. Where the answer is yes or you are unsure, the task is restricted until you have checked the licence rules for the state or territory, the site owner's permission and your employer's written authority. Repairing electrical wiring is licensed work in New South Wales, where the licensing rules name repairing as part of electrical wiring work.

instructionSections.heading: Handle suspected asbestos correctly
instructionSections.body: A customer may ask a cleaner to remove a section of suspected asbestos-containing wall lining, or to dust, sand or scrape a surface that may contain it. Treat the material as hazardous until a competent person identifies it. Do not cut, scrape, sand, drill, sweep dry or otherwise disturb it, and do not carry out tests that would expose anyone to fibres. Keep other people out of the area, record what you saw and what the client reported, and refer the work to an appropriately authorised provider.

instructionSections.heading: Confirm permission with the person who holds it
instructionSections.body: A permission is valid only when the person who has authority gives it in writing and it covers the exact task, location and method. A client's verbal agreement does not authorise restricted work, and neither does a colleague's assurance. Find out who controls the site, such as an owner, body corporate or facilities manager, and ask them to confirm access, working hours, any restricted products or methods, and any approval they need to give. Record the name, the date and the scope of the permission before work starts.

instructionSections.heading: What a training certificate does and does not do
instructionSections.body: A training certificate shows that a person completed a course on a topic. On its own it does not grant a licence, permit or authority, and it does not show that the holder is currently competent for a specific task. Before a restricted task starts, check that the required licence is current and covers the work, that the employer or site has authorised the task in writing, and that a competent person has verified the worker's skills for the method being used. This lesson gives you the decision steps. It does not grant any authority.

instructionSections.heading: Licence notice
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant the right to perform any licensed, permitted or restricted work, and it does not make the learner a licence holder. A high risk work licence for boom-type elevating work platforms applies where the boom is 11 metres or more in New South Wales and Queensland, so a shorter boom may not need it in those states. Victoria's WP class has no boom-length threshold. Work above ground level from ladders, scaffolds or platforms is restricted and needs your employer's written authorisation, and the licence rules where you work must be checked before it starts.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before resuming if the task needs a licence, permit or authority you do not hold, if a client or colleague asks you to start before permission is in writing, if you find or suspect a regulated material such as asbestos-containing material, if a licensed system such as electrical wiring is involved, or if the task changes after you have been briefed. Keep people away from the area and do not resume until the decision-maker has given written approval.

lessons.title: How a cleaning business plan is structured
learningOutcomes: Name the sections a cleaning business plan needs, in order
Explain which decision each section supports
Label every number in a plan as a fact, a target or an assumption

instructionSections.heading: What the plan is for
instructionSections.body: A business plan is a working tool. It sets out what you will sell, who will buy it, how you will deliver it, what it will cost, and how you will know whether it is working. A bank, a landlord, a supplier or a large client may ask to see one, but the first reader should be you. If a section does not change a decision you will make, it does not need to be long.

instructionSections.heading: The sections and their jobs
instructionSections.body: A cleaning plan usually has ten parts. The executive summary is one page: what the business does, who it serves, where it works, who runs it and the headline goal. The mission states the standard you promise. The market section covers customer needs, competitors and trends. The marketing approach says how customers will find you. Objectives set marketing and financial targets with dates. The marketing mix covers pricing, service area, advertising and complaint handling. Positioning explains why a customer should choose you. Strategy sets the order of actions. Forecasts show break-even and sales by stage. Controls name what you measure, how often, and who checks it. Write the executive summary last, but place it first.

instructionSections.heading: How the sections depend on each other
instructionSections.body: The sections form a chain. The services you list decide the work, the work decides the hours, the hours decide the price, and the price together with your costs decides break-even. The staffing plan must match the forecast. If you change one link, check the others. A plan that promises a premium service but prices at the lowest rate in the market does not hang together, and a reader will notice before you do.

instructionSections.heading: Reading numbers honestly
instructionSections.body: Every number in a plan is one of three things. A fact is verified, such as an invoice or a signed contract. A target is what you want to reach, and it needs a date and a reason. An assumption is a belief you use for planning, and it needs a note on how you will test it. The sample plan this lesson draws on includes targets for growth, customer acquisition cost and overhead reduction with no workings shown. Treat those as targets and not as benchmarks. The sample is undated and written for a non-Australian market, so its figures are historical and are not current Australian data.

instructionSections.heading: Services: list only what you can deliver
instructionSections.body: Plans often list every service the owner has heard of. The sample plan includes laundering, ironing, and fumigation with pest control. Check the state and territory rules that apply to pest control and fumigation before any pesticide use. Before any regulated service appears in your plan, confirm the licence or authority needed in your state or territory, and whether you hold it. This lesson does not grant or describe any authority to carry out those services. Services you have not been trained or authorised to deliver should be marked as out of scope for now.

instructionSections.heading: Starting from a home
instructionSections.body: The sample plan proposes a home-based start for the first six months. Before you run any business from a residence, check what your local council allows, what your home and vehicle insurance covers, and what your lease or strata rules say.

lessons.title: SWOT analysis for a small cleaning business
learningOutcomes: Separate internal factors (strengths and weaknesses) from external factors (opportunities and threats)
Support each SWOT item with evidence, or label it as an assumption
Pair SWOT items to choose one action with an owner and a date

instructionSections.heading: What a SWOT is for
instructionSections.body: A SWOT analysis sorts the business's situation into four boxes. Strengths and weaknesses sit inside the business, so you can change them. Opportunities and threats come from outside, so you respond to them. The value lies in the actions the analysis leads to. A grid of adjectives that nobody acts on is a poster, not an analysis. Keep each box to about five to seven items, and rank the top three in each.

instructionSections.heading: Strengths need evidence
instructionSections.body: The sample plan lists an enthusiastic leader, a training program that records how the business works, and experienced, dedicated staff. Each is a plausible strength, but it only becomes useful when a result shows it. A leader's energy matters less than a completion rate, a complaint rate or a count of repeat bookings. Ask for the measure behind each strength. If none exists, record the strength as an assumption and plan to measure it.

instructionSections.heading: Weaknesses need a response
instructionSections.body: The sample names three weaknesses: the industry is labour-intensive, trust takes time to build, and a start-up has little brand recognition. None of these is a reason to stop. Each one needs a response written beside it. Labour intensity points to a pricing approach based on hours and to scheduling that keeps crews productive. Slow trust points to a referral process and early client follow-up. Limited brand recognition points to a consistent and visible standard on every job.

instructionSections.heading: Opportunities that can be tested
instructionSections.body: The sample lists a large part of the market that is unaware of the business, a shift away from individual housekeepers, changing consumer habits that favour outsourcing cleaning, and a model that can be scaled. For each one, write which customers it applies to, how many local prospects it describes, and what action it allows. An opportunity you cannot act on this quarter belongs on a later list. The scalability claim, for example, stays a hypothesis until you have a repeatable process and a trained second team.

instructionSections.heading: Threats and their causes
instructionSections.body: The sample lists staff turnover and strong competitors. Turnover has causes you can influence: pay, rostering, the quality of induction, supervision and whether people feel their work is valued. Competitors are a threat only when you can name them and compare them. Write down the three nearest competitors by name, what they charge, and where they are weaker than you.

instructionSections.heading: From grid to action
instructionSections.body: Pair items to decide what to do. A strength matched with an opportunity suggests a move to pursue, such as a referral offer to a group that already trusts your work. A weakness matched with a threat suggests a protective action, such as a fixed rostering rule that keeps staff. Choose one action from each pairing, give it an owner and a review date, and set the rest aside until the first action is complete.

lessons.title: Break-even and sales forecast by stage
learningOutcomes: Calculate break-even jobs per month from fixed costs and contribution per job
Build a stage-based sales forecast with a conservative case for cash planning
Separate profit forecasts from cash timing

instructionSections.heading: What the sample plan gives you, and what it leaves out
instructionSections.body: The sample plan includes a break-even heading and a sales forecast, but the break-even section has no working in it. The sales forecast is written in stages: a set-up month with little or no trading, a second month in which enquiries begin to turn into contracts, a first team working together, and a second team trained once demand allows. The stage structure is useful. The arithmetic is missing, and you must add it yourself.

instructionSections.heading: Break-even in jobs
instructionSections.body: Break-even is the point where income covers all costs. Start with fixed costs per month, meaning costs that continue whether or not you clean, such as insurance, software, a share of home office costs, phone, vehicle finance, and any owner drawings you treat as a cost. Next, find contribution per job: the price minus the variable costs of that job, such as consumables, fuel and the direct labour on the job.
