Divide fixed costs by contribution per job to get the number of jobs needed each month, and round up. This is a planning figure. Recheck it whenever prices or costs change.

instructionSections.heading: Forecast by stage
instructionSections.body: Build the forecast around the stages your business will pass through. Stage one is set-up, with costs and no trading. Stage two is the first paying jobs, usually done by the owner and one helper. Stage three is the first full team, and stage four is a second team, once demand supports it. For each stage, write the number of jobs per week, the average price, the hours per job and the staff cost. Make three cases: base, conservative and upside. Use the conservative case for cash planning and the base case for targets. The sample plan says it prefers a cautious forecast, and that principle is sound.

instructionSections.heading: Cash timing is a separate problem
instructionSections.body: A business can be profitable on paper and still run short of cash. Clients may pay thirty days after an invoice, while wages, fuel and insurance fall due sooner. Build a monthly cash-flow table that shows when money comes in and when it goes out, and check the lowest balance across the year. Break-even tells you the volume you need. Cash flow tells you whether you can survive the time it takes to reach that volume.

instructionSections.heading: Growth targets are not forecasts
instructionSections.body: The sample plan sets aims such as growth above 100 per cent a year, double-digit growth for three years, and profit in the first year. These are targets. A forecast is built from job counts, hours, prices and costs, and each assumption can be tested. Put the targets next to the forecast and check whether the forecast supports them. If it does not, change the target or the plan, and record which one you changed. The sample's figures are historical and non-Australian, so they are not benchmarks for an Australian business.

instructionSections.heading: Compare and revise
instructionSections.body: Each month, compare actual jobs, revenue, hours and costs with the base case. Record each difference and its cause. Update the forecast when two or three months show the same pattern. A forecast that is never compared with actual results is an opinion.

lessons.title: Define the service offer
learningOutcomes: Describe each service the business offers in terms of its scope, its exclusions and the skills and equipment it needs.
Decide which services the business will not offer, and state why.
Record the service offer so that quotes, work orders and marketing all describe the same thing.

instructionSections.heading: Describe the service, not the hope
instructionSections.body: A service offer is a precise description of what the business will do for a customer. It states the tasks included, the surfaces or areas covered, the standard of work, the frequency if the service is recurring, and what is excluded. A vague offer such as 'we clean houses' invites every request and every dispute. A clear offer, such as 'a routine clean of kitchens and bathrooms in homes of up to three bedrooms, excluding ovens, windows and carpets', lets the customer and the team know what to expect.

instructionSections.heading: Match the offer to skills, equipment and rules
instructionSections.body: For each service, list the skills the team has, the equipment it needs, the products it will use and any licence, registration or permit required by the state or territory. Some services are regulated, such as work on electrical installations, gas, asbestos, work at height with some equipment, and some animal-related or personal-care services. Where the business does not hold the required licence, the service must be excluded or referred. Your business's licence requirements are recorded in {{business:compliance.licence_requirements}}.

instructionSections.heading: Decide what you will not offer
instructionSections.body: Excluding a service is a business decision and should be recorded. Services may be excluded because they are outside the team's competence, need equipment the business does not own, carry hazards the business cannot control, or need a licence the business does not hold. State the excluded services clearly in the offer and in the customer communication, so that the customer can go elsewhere where needed. The services the business offers are described in {{business:services.service_description}}.

lessons.title: Defining business needs and the services to offer
learningOutcomes: Write a one-sentence need statement that describes the client problem a service solves.
Write a measurable result for a service, with the test, the conditions and the person who checks it.
Assess a proposed service for competition, client switching, substitutes, cost and risk before adding it to the menu.

instructionSections.heading: Start with the need, not the equipment
instructionSections.body: A business needs analysis asks what the client must achieve, and only then what the business will provide. For a service business, this means describing the client's situation before choosing a service. A client may want a property to look good for a sale in six weeks, a surface protected from weather over winter, or an odour left by a pet removed. Each of those needs leads to different work, different products and a different price. Write the need as one sentence that names the client, the situation and the gap between what they have now and what they want. Separate the need from the wish: a client may ask for a particular treatment, but the need may be to remove visible wear before a sale. Then test whether the business can deliver the need at a profit, with the equipment, skills and time it has. A service that is easy to sell but cannot be done well with the available skills is not a good service to add. Keep the need statement on the service menu so the team can see why each service exists.

instructionSections.heading: Stating what the service must achieve
instructionSections.body: Each service needs a stated result that the team and the client can check. Write the result in terms of what the client will see or be able to use at the end, not in terms of effort. For example, no visible marks on a floor when viewed in normal daylight from one metre is checkable, while the floor looks great is not. For each result, write the test: the light or instrument used, the distance, the checklist, and who makes the final call. Keep the result separate from the method. The result says what must be true at the end, and the method describes how the team gets there. If you write the method in detail, say why, for example because an insurer, a manufacturer or a licensing rule requires it. Link the result to the condition record taken before work, so that the client and the team agree on what counts as finished. Where a result depends on something the team cannot control, such as the age of a surface or a pre-existing fault, write that limit into the result as well.

instructionSections.heading: Testing the offer against the market and your own capacity
instructionSections.body: Before adding a service, test it against four pressures. The first is competition: list the other providers, what they charge and what they include, and how easily a client can compare you with them. The second is the client's switching cost: a client who has used one provider for years may not move unless the new offer is clearly better. The third is substitutes: a do-it-yourself product or a cheaper, lower-skill provider may meet part of the need, and your offer must show what the client gains from paying for yours. The fourth is your own capacity, cost and risk. A new service may need equipment, training, extra time per job, extra insurance cover and a stock of consumables, and the work itself may carry a risk of injury to a person or damage to a client's property. Estimate how many jobs per month the service must win to pay for those costs, and check that figure against the time you actually have. Decide to launch, to trial or to drop the service, and set a date to review the decision.

lessons.title: Planning how a service business earns and delivers
learningOutcomes: Describe, in one sentence, the customer a service serves, including the need and a group the business can reach.
Explain what a client receives from a service as a result they can check, and identify how the work is delivered and who does it.
Separate costs that rise with each job from costs that stay the same, and calculate the monthly job count needed to cover fixed costs from supplied figures.
Identify at least one dependency in a service model, and set a fallback and a test for it before money is committed.

instructionSections.heading: Why plan the earning and the delivery together
instructionSections.body: A service business earns money only when a client pays for work that was delivered properly and on time. Keeping the customer, the work, the money and the risks in separate documents can leave the parts unchecked against each other. This lesson gives you one framework, the five-question service check, to test the whole model before you commit time, equipment or staff. The five questions are: who pays and what do they need; what exactly does the client receive; how is the work delivered and by whom; how does money come in and what does each job cost; and what does the model depend on. Answer them in order, then go back and confirm that each answer agrees with the others. A business plan should set direction, show how goals will be reached, and identify and manage risks, so this model sits inside that larger plan. The check is a thinking tool that exposes gaps. It is not a forecast, and the figures belong in a profit and loss forecast and a cash flow forecast once the logic holds (not confirmed by an official source).

instructionSections.heading: Question one: who pays, and what do they need
instructionSections.body: Start by listing the people who could need the service, then narrow the list to a group you can reach and can afford to serve. Describe who might need the service and has the budget for it, then test those assumptions with real enquiries or market research (testing method not confirmed by an official source). Divide the market into smaller groups that buy for different reasons, and look at the age, location and income of each group, what it cares about, and who makes the buying decision. A useful customer description says who the person or household is, what problem they face, who decides, and where they look for a provider. Busy households in one suburb with a pool they do not want to maintain themselves is specific enough to plan around. Everyone who owns property is not. Write the need as one sentence, because every later question depends on it. If you cannot write that sentence, you do not yet know who the customer is.

instructionSections.heading: Question two: what the client actually receives
instructionSections.body: The client does not buy your tasks. They buy a result they can see, use or rely on. Describe the result as a change the client will notice at the end of the job, such as a lawn that is cut, edged and cleared of clippings by the time they get home, or a door that opens and locks without force. Then state what is included and what is not, because an unclear scope leaves room for disagreement about what the client was promised. Add any promise that goes with the result, such as an arrival window or a return visit if the result is not met, and promise only what your time and skills can deliver. The result also has to beat the client's alternatives, which may be doing nothing, doing the work themselves or using a cheaper provider. Name the alternative your client is most likely to choose, and state what your service gives them that the alternative does not.

instructionSections.heading: Question three: how the work is delivered, and by whom
instructionSections.body: Describe the steps that turn a booking into a finished result. These usually run from the first contact, through booking and scheduling, arrival and the work itself, to a check of the result and the client's sign-off. For each step, write who does it: a named person, a vehicle, a tool, or an outside contractor. Be specific about what a job needs at minimum, because that minimum sets how much work you can sell in a day. Time each step on a trial job, including travel, set-up and pack-down, since desk estimates can leave these out. If one person carries out every step, say so, because that person is also the single point of failure. Where a step needs a licence, a qualification or a supervised trainee, record that requirement beside the step and check it separately, as the safety section explains.

instructionSections.heading: Question four: how money comes in, and what each job costs
instructionSections.body: Revenue is the money the business earns before any costs are taken out. Decide the pricing basis for each income source: a fixed price per job, an hourly rate, a regular plan paid in instalments, an add-on sold with the main service, or a call-out fee. A business can have more than one source, but each source needs a basis you can explain. Next, sort every cost into one of two groups. Variable costs rise or fall with the number of jobs, such as consumables, fuel, booking fees and the pay of a helper who is paid per job. Fixed costs stay roughly the same whether you work or not, such as vehicle finance, insurance, software subscriptions, phone plans and premises rent. Business.gov.au defines a fixed cost as a cost that is "not part of producing a good or service" (Key financial terms), so the wording here is a working description and not the official definition. The price of a job less its variable cost is the contribution that job makes towards fixed costs, which this course calls "contribution per job". Divide the monthly fixed costs by the contribution per job, and you have the number of jobs a month the model needs to break even. This break-even formula and the "contribution per job" term are the course's own method, not an official definition: business.gov.au's key financial terms page defines break-even as the point when a business's income equals its expenses, and does not state this formula. Keep that sum on paper, because it shows how the model behaves when work is slow.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing a pricing basis
instructionSections.body: There are three broad ways to set a price, which business.gov.au calls cost-plus pricing, going rate pricing and value pricing. Cost-based pricing starts from the total cost of making and supplying the job and adds a mark-up. Competition-based pricing, which the page calls going rate pricing, places your price at or near the market price leader. Value-based pricing bases the price on the value the service gives the client, such as time saved or a risk avoided, and not just on cost. Each approach can fail. A cost-based price that ignores what the client will pay can lose work, and a value-based price that ignores your costs can lose money on every job. Check each price against its variable cost and its share of fixed costs before you publish it, and review prices at least once a year, or whenever costs change. Discounts reduce the contribution, so test whether a discounted job still covers its variable costs and makes a contribution to fixed costs.

instructionSections.heading: What the model depends on
instructionSections.body: Every service model rests on a few things the business cannot run without and may not control. Look for four kinds of dependency. People: one trained worker, a key subcontractor, or the owner's own availability. Supplies and tools: one product line, one vehicle, one booking platform or one software provider. Conditions outside your control: weather, seasonal demand, access to client sites, or a change in a rule or a price. Clients: a large share of income from one client or one referral source. For each dependency, write what happens if it fails, how long recovery would take, and what fallback you have. A fallback might be a second subcontractor, a waiting list, a minimum notice period, a materials clause in the quote, or a cash reserve. Where a dependency involves a licence, an insurance cover or a regulated product, record it as open until the authority or insurer that governs it has confirmed the requirement.

instructionSections.heading: Checking the whole model before money is committed
instructionSections.body: Read the five answers together. Choose one client group and follow it through the model. Does the result that group wants match the work you deliver? Does the way they find you reach the people who can book? Does the price cover the job and make a contribution to fixed costs? Is there a fallback for each dependency the work relies on? Where a link is missing, name the gap in one sentence. Pick the gap that would hurt most if you were wrong, and set a small, low-cost test for it, such as offering a fixed number of booking slots to a set number of prospective clients and recording how many accept. Set a date to review the result and write the outcome beside the model. Only then decide whether to buy equipment, hire, sign a lease or take on a contract. A test is not proof of demand. It is a way to avoid spending money before you know whether the model holds.

lessons.title: Designing your life and your freedom number
learningOutcomes: Describe your core values and the working life you want
Calculate the income your business must replace to cover your lifestyle
Write a dated goal for time you want back

instructionSections.heading: Why start with your life, not the business
instructionSections.body: A business is a tool for the life you want. Before you quote a job, decide what you want less of (for example, financial worry), what you want more of (for example, time with family), and what a normal week should look like. These answers set the limits for how much work you take and what you charge.

instructionSections.heading: Your freedom number
instructionSections.body: Work out your lifestyle cost: rent or mortgage, bills, insurance, vehicle, tax, savings and personal spending. That total is the income your business must reach before you can say it has replaced your job. A separate dream number can be set later, once the first one is reached.

instructionSections.heading: Time you want back
instructionSections.body: Write down how many hours per week you want to claim back and what they are for. Use this when you decide how many jobs per week you can safely take, and how much travel time each job adds.

instructionSections.heading: Writing it down
instructionSections.body: Keep the answers in one document. Revisit them every three months. The goalposts can move; the point is to have a clear reason for the work.

lessons.title: Finding your service pillars and your market
learningOutcomes: List the skills you can sell, the topics you care about and the people who need them
Choose a core service and one or two adjacent services
Name the customer group you will serve first

instructionSections.heading: Start with a list, not a decision
instructionSections.body: Write every skill, interest and piece of experience you have. Be specific: "gutter clearing on two-storey homes" is more useful than "cleaning". Then narrow it to the skills you are paid for today or can learn quickly.

instructionSections.heading: Choose your pillars
instructionSections.body: Choose one main service and one or two supporting services that share the same customers or equipment. A pool technician who also cleans pool fences can sell both to the same households.

instructionSections.heading: Who needs it
instructionSections.body: Name the customer group, what they struggle with and what they would pay to avoid. A stronger offer comes from a narrow customer: "owners of short-stay apartments in one suburb" beats "anyone who needs cleaning".

instructionSections.heading: Check the market
instructionSections.body: Speak to five people in the customer group before you commit. Ask what they paid last time, what went wrong and what they would change.

lessons.title: Testing your offer before you charge full price
learningOutcomes: Run a small paid or free pilot with written terms
Collect feedback and evidence that the offer works
Update the offer and move to full pricing

instructionSections.heading: Iterate, do not guess
instructionSections.body: Your first offer will change. The only reliable way to improve it is to deliver it to real customers and listen. Start now, with a small number of jobs.

instructionSections.heading: Pilot with written terms
instructionSections.body: Offer a limited pilot, for example five jobs at a reduced rate or free in return for feedback and a written testimonial. Put the scope, the time, what you need from the customer, and what happens if the result is not met into a short written agreement.

instructionSections.heading: Collect evidence
instructionSections.body: Record photos before and after, the time taken, what went wrong, and the customer comments. Ask for a short review you can publish with consent.

instructionSections.heading: Move to full pricing
instructionSections.body: Update the offer from the feedback, then offer the same service at full price to the pilot customers first, and then to new customers. Note which price and scope they accept.

lessons.title: Business plan (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Complete every section of the business plan template, or mark a section not applicable with a written reason
Link the customer, service, pricing and marketing sections so they use the same definitions
Record the assumption behind each financial target so an assessor can test it

instructionSections.heading: What this template is for
instructionSections.body: A business plan is a working record of the decisions behind your business: who you serve, what you sell, what you charge, how people hear about you, and what the money has to do. This template is not a bank form and it is not a sales pitch. Its job is to show whether the parts fit together. If your prices do not cover your costs at the volume you need, the plan should show that before you spend money. Enter your own facts and figures in each field. This lesson does not supply prices, market sizes or licence numbers, and it does not confirm which registration or insurance requirements apply in your state or territory.

instructionSections.heading: Working through the sections in a useful order
instructionSections.body: Start with the customer and service sections, because every later number depends on what you sell and to whom. Write the market and competitor sections from your own observation, with dates and sources, and keep any overseas figure marked as historical. Then complete the pricing approach, which should point to the pricing and margin worksheet, and the marketing approach, which should point to the marketing plan. Only after those are settled should you set financial targets, the break-even point and cash flow. Write the executive summary last, as a short statement drawn from the sections above. Finish with risks, where each risk has a named response and an owner.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the plan usable
instructionSections.body: A plan that is never reviewed stops being trusted. Put a review date and a version number on it. When a figure changes, record the old value, the new value, the reason and the date rather than overwriting the history. A good plan is short enough to read in one sitting and specific enough that another person could check each claim. Where you are not sure of a fact, write that you are not sure and say what would settle it.

lessons.title: Freedom and cash plan (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Separate personal costs, business costs and the tax set-aside into three totals
Calculate break-even jobs per month from contribution per job, not gross job value
Check whether the required jobs fit within the weekly hours available, including non-billable time

instructionSections.heading: Why this plan starts from your life
instructionSections.body: The freedom number from the earlier lesson states what you want your life to cost. This template turns that into money: what you spend each month, what the business has to take in after its costs, and how many billable hours that needs. Many operators underestimate the hours that do not earn money, such as travel, quoting, bookkeeping and rework. Include them as their own line. A plan that leaves them out can look achievable on paper and then fail in the first month of trading.

instructionSections.heading: Separating personal costs, business costs and the set-aside
instructionSections.body: Keep three lists apart. Personal costs are what you spend to live. Business costs are what the business spends to operate, which can include vehicle running costs, tools, consumables not charged to customers, insurance, phone and software, and bank fees. The set-aside is money held back for tax and any other obligation you carry. This template does not tell you what rate to use. Add a cash buffer expressed as a number of months, so that a slow month does not force a price cut.

instructionSections.heading: Working out break-even jobs and the hours check
instructionSections.body: Add the cash buffer to the monthly target, then divide the total by the contribution each job makes after its materials and travel. The result is the number of jobs needed per month, rounded up to a whole job. Then test the hours. Jobs multiplied by the hours per job, plus the non-billable hours, must fit inside the hours you can work each week. If they do not fit, the plan needs a higher contribution per job, lower fixed costs, a different target or more hours. Seeing that before you start is far cheaper than discovering it after you have taken on customers.

lessons.title: Work planning, teams and interfaces
learningOutcomes: Explain the boundary for work planning, teams and interfaces and identify when work must stop.
Prepare a task-specific, documented decision for work planning, teams and interfaces under company and local requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Why planning is a safety control
instructionSections.body: Many incidents on a job site happen where two groups of workers meet without agreeing who controls what. Work planning turns a job into a sequence of tasks, names who does each task, and sets the points where work must pause. This lesson covers how to plan a job for a small team, how to share a site with other people and other contractors, and how to set clear authority for stopping and restarting work. The aim is not a long document. The aim is that everyone on the site knows what is happening, when, who is in charge and what would make them stop.

instructionSections.heading: Build the plan from the approved scope
instructionSections.body: Start from the accepted scope, not from the client's wish list. List the tasks in the order they must happen, the materials and equipment each task needs, the workers authorised for each task, and the time each task takes. Mark any task that needs a permit, a licence or a specialist, and keep it out of the crew's plan until it is cleared. Include the breaks, drying or contact times that the label or the approved method sets, and the points where the area must be checked before the next task begins. A plan that depends on a task nobody is authorised to do is not a plan.

instructionSections.heading: Allocate roles and supervision
instructionSections.body: Name one lead for the job, who holds the authority to start, pause and stop work. Name each worker's task and check that it is within the worker's documented training. A worker who is new, or not yet verified for a method, works under supervision and does not perform a task alone that they have not been signed off for. Brief the whole team before the job starts, and again whenever the plan changes. Record who attended, what was agreed and who holds stop authority.

instructionSections.heading: Manage interfaces with the site and other contractors
instructionSections.body: An interface is any point where your work meets another person's work, a building system, an occupant or a shared area. Before work starts, identify the site controller or facilities manager, and find out who else will be working in the same zone, on the same day or nearby. Two tasks that are each safe can be unsafe together: a cleaner working beside a contractor who is spraying, grinding or working at height needs the work sequenced or separated, and the site controller must agree the sequence. Do not assume that simultaneous work is safe. Agree who isolates which area, how it is marked and who restarts work once the other party has finished. Keep a written interface schedule and a list of who can stop and restart each activity, and give a copy to the site controller.

instructionSections.heading: Worked scenario on shared access
instructionSections.body: Suppose a maintenance contractor is spraying nearby while cleaners are booked for the same zone. The cleaner does not decide alone to carry on. The response is to hold the start of the cleaning task in that zone, tell the crew lead, and contact the site controller to agree the isolation, the sequence and the exclusion area. The agreement is recorded with the times, the names of the people who agreed it and the restart condition. If the site controller cannot confirm the sequence, the cleaning stays on hold.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the team within its authority
instructionSections.body: Planning fails when a team quietly expands the scope. If a client or occupant asks for an extra task on the day, do not add it to the plan on the crew's own judgement. Return to the lead and the approver, and update the plan only once the new task has been checked against the worker's training, the approved methods and any licence or permit it needs. Record every change with the reason and the person who approved it.

instructionSections.heading: Licence notice
instructionSections.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant any licence, permit or authority to perform regulated work, and coordinating work on a site does not authorise any task within it.

instructionSections.heading: Stop-work rule
instructionSections.body: Stop and tell the lead immediately if another party starts work that is not in the agreed sequence, if an isolation or exclusion area has been removed, if a person enters the zone without the required briefing, if the task moves outside the written plan or the worker's authority, or if the lead or site controller cannot be reached when a decision is needed. Make the area safe, keep people out, and do not restart until the person named in the plan gives the restart condition.

lessons.title: Staffing in stages: the first team, then new teams
learningOutcomes: Set a demand trigger for each hiring stage, linked to the break-even figure
Describe an induction gate that must be passed before unsupervised work
Explain what a team lead must be able to do before a second team starts

instructionSections.heading: Why staffing follows demand
instructionSections.body: The sample plan describes staffing in stages. The first week of jobs is done by a team, new employees are hired as contracts increase, and a new team is trained only once enough demand exists. The logic is sound. Hiring ahead of demand adds wages before revenue arrives, and hiring behind demand loses jobs and strains the people already working. Move one stage at a time, and let a measure you can see trigger each move.

instructionSections.heading: Setting triggers
instructionSections.body: A trigger is a level of demand that justifies the next hire. Derive it from the break-even work in the previous lesson. For example, a trigger might be a set number of booked hours per week, held for a set number of weeks, with a cash reserve in place. Write the trigger as a number and a rule, such as 'booked hours above a set level for three consecutive weeks'. The exact figure depends on your own costs and local market, so set it for your business and review it. Do not copy a figure from another business or from a sample document.

instructionSections.heading: The induction gate
instructionSections.body: The sample plan trains new employees on cleaning methods first, then on teamwork and professionalism. Turn that sequence into a gate. A new team member does not work unsupervised until they have completed induction on methods, workplace safety, chemicals, customer conduct and reporting, and a supervisor has signed off each task they are allowed to perform. The gate protects the client and the worker, and it creates a record.

instructionSections.heading: Teams work better when roles are clear
instructionSections.body: The sample plan prefers teams because they are more efficient, and it notes that some clients want a single cleaner instead. A team needs defined roles: a lead who checks the scope and the standard, workers who carry out the tasks, and a handover at the end of each visit. Team training is training in those roles, in the order the work is done, and in how to raise a problem quickly.

instructionSections.heading: Building a second team
instructionSections.body: A second team is built around a proven lead, not around a headcount. Before the second team starts, the lead should have run full jobs without supervision, be able to complete the scope checks, and be able to take a new person through the induction gate. Copy the induction, the scope and the standards, not the people. Keep the first team as the reference point, and check the second team's first five jobs against the same standards.

instructionSections.heading: Turnover and retention
instructionSections.body: The sample plan names employee turnover as a threat. Turnover has causes you can change: pay, rostering, the quality of induction, supervision, feedback and whether the work is valued. Pay and conditions must follow the award or agreement that applies to each worker.

instructionSections.heading: Employee or contractor
instructionSections.body: Whether a worker is an employee or a contractor affects pay, superannuation, insurance, tax and how much control you have over the work. The sample plan does not address this. Decide the classification by examining the actual working arrangement, not the label alone, and record your reasons.

lessons.title: Employment relationship awareness
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between an employee, a contractor and a subcontractor for a job.
Identify the factors that decide the relationship and why the label chosen by the parties does not decide it alone.
Recognise when a worker is a worker for workers compensation and work health and safety purposes.

instructionSections.heading: Why the relationship matters
instructionSections.body: How a person is engaged affects their pay, their tax, their insurance, their leave, and the duties the business owes them. The label on the contract does not decide the relationship alone. What matters is how the work is actually done: who controls the hours, the methods and the equipment, who bears the financial risk, whether the person runs their own business, and whether they can send a substitute. Getting this wrong can leave the business with unpaid obligations and an uninsured worker.

instructionSections.heading: Workers compensation and worker status
instructionSections.body: Workers compensation rules and work health and safety duties apply to workers, and the definition of worker can extend to some contractors. WorkSafe Victoria states that WorkCover registration is generally required if the business employs any workers, and that a contractor may count as a deemed worker of the business it depends on. Other states use their own tests, and some state insurers state that a contractor working under a contract of service is a worker even with an ABN. The rules must be checked for each state and territory where the work is done.

instructionSections.heading: Before engaging anyone
instructionSections.body: Before engaging a person to do work, decide the relationship, check the insurance position, and record the decision. Ask the person how they run their business, whether they have their own insurance and licences, and whether they will provide their own equipment. Where the relationship is unclear, seek advice from the relevant regulator, the tax authority or a qualified adviser before the work starts. Do not decide the question only from the contract's wording.

lessons.title: Pay and recordkeeping fundamentals
learningOutcomes: Describe the records a business keeps about the hours, pay and entitlements of people it engages.
Explain why accurate time records support pay, safety and dispute resolution.
Identify where the pay rules must be checked, rather than relying on this lesson for them.

instructionSections.heading: Why records matter
instructionSections.body: Records of hours, pay, leave and engagement are both a legal requirement for employers and a practical tool. They show that people were paid correctly, they support the business if a payment is questioned, and they help the business plan rosters and job times. The records should be accurate, complete and made at the time the work is done, not reconstructed later from memory.

instructionSections.heading: What to record
instructionSections.body: For each person engaged, record the start and end time of each shift, the breaks, the jobs and sites worked, any allowance or expense claimed, and the pay rate that applies. For a contractor, record the invoice, the agreed rate and the date paid. Keep signed or approved timesheets, and keep payslips or payment records where they are required. Do not record a time that was not worked, and do not alter a record without a dated note.

instructionSections.heading: Where pay rules come from
instructionSections.body: Pay rates, penalty rates, allowances, superannuation, leave and the record-keeping rules are set by national and state law and by any applicable award or agreement. These rules change and vary by industry and by the person's classification. This lesson does not state any pay rate, penalty or entitlement, because none is confirmed here. Check the current rules with the Fair Work Ombudsman, the relevant state authority or a qualified adviser before setting any pay.

lessons.title: WHS duties and consultation
learningOutcomes: Explain the primary duty of care that a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) owes to workers and others.
Describe a worker's duty to take reasonable care and to cooperate with the business's safety controls.
Explain the purpose of consultation with workers and the steps for consulting, which must be confirmed for each state or territory.

instructionSections.heading: Who has duties
instructionSections.body: Under the model work health and safety laws, a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) has a primary duty to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers while they are at work, and of others who may be affected by the work. Safe Work Australia states that a self-employed person operating their own business is a PCBU, and that a self-employed person may be simultaneously a PCBU and a worker. Workers also have duties: to take reasonable care for their own health and safety, not to adversely affect the safety of others, and to follow the reasonable instructions and procedures the business sets.

instructionSections.heading: What reasonably practicable means
instructionSections.body: Reasonably practicable is the standard that the PCBU must meet. It requires the business to consider the risk, what the business knows or should know about it, the ways to control it, and the cost of the control in relation to the risk. A PCBU must choose the control that is reasonably practicable and keep it under review. This is why a cheap control that does not reduce the risk is not enough, and why a safety control that is practical must be used even if it costs more than the business would prefer.

instructionSections.heading: Consultation with workers
instructionSections.body: Under the model laws, a PCBU must consult workers on matters that affect their health and safety. Consultation means sharing information, listening to the views of workers, taking those views into account, and telling workers what has been decided. Safe Work Australia's guidance on the PCBU duty points to further guidance on consultation with multiple duty holders.

lessons.title: Equal opportunity and respectful work
learningOutcomes: Describe respectful behaviour and the forms of discrimination and harassment that the business must prevent.
Identify what to do when a worker or customer experiences discrimination or harassment.
Explain why the business's equal opportunity obligations must be checked for each state and territory.

instructionSections.heading: Respectful work
instructionSections.body: Respectful work means that each person is treated fairly, without being excluded, mocked or disadvantaged because of who they are or what they believe. In a service business the team works in other people's homes and sites, so the way the team treats each other is seen by customers. Respect covers how a worker talks to a colleague, how a supervisor gives feedback, and how a worker responds to a customer's request. It also covers the sharing of tasks, shifts and access to training.

instructionSections.heading: Discrimination and harassment
instructionSections.body: Discrimination is treating a person less favourably because of an attribute the law protects, such as sex, race, disability, age, religion or family status, depending on the law that applies. Harassment is unwelcome conduct that a reasonable person would expect to offend, humiliate or intimidate. Both can occur between workers, between a worker and a customer, or between a worker and a third party. The protected attributes and the rules differ between Commonwealth and state and territory laws, and must be confirmed for the location and the business.

instructionSections.heading: What to do when it happens
instructionSections.body: A worker who experiences or sees discrimination or harassment should be able to raise it through a clear route. The business should take the concern seriously, record the facts, protect the person from further harm and deal with the matter through its procedure. Do not retaliate against a person who raises a concern in good faith. Where the conduct is serious or may be unlawful, the person may also contact the relevant state or territory or Commonwealth body; the bodies and their processes must be confirmed for the location and have not yet been confirmed in this lesson.

lessons.title: Compliance change and verification
learningOutcomes: Describe a process for finding and recording changes to the rules that apply to the business.
Verify that the business's licences, registrations, insurance and policies are current.
Update the procedures and tell the team when a rule changes.

instructionSections.heading: Find the change
instructionSections.body: Rules that apply to a service business change. Licences are renewed or reclassified, councils change local laws, state regulators issue new guidance, and national model laws are adopted in some states and not others. Set a regular check, such as monthly for licences and insurance and quarterly for rules and guidance, and record each check. Use the official source for each rule, and record the source, the URL and the date checked. A change reported in a newsletter or a forum must be confirmed against the official source before the business acts on it.

instructionSections.heading: Verify and record
instructionSections.body: Verify that each licence, registration, permit and insurance policy is current, that the holder is the person doing the work, and that the scope of the licence covers the work. Record the expiry date and set a reminder before renewal. Where a rule changes, record what changed, when it takes effect, which procedures are affected and who must be told. A change that takes effect in the future, such as a changed exposure limit list, must be planned before the date.

instructionSections.heading: Update and tell the team
instructionSections.body: Update the affected procedures, checklists and training, and tell the team and any subcontractor what has changed and when it takes effect. Record that the update was made and that the team was told. Keep the old version of the procedure for the period of the change, so that work done before the change can be checked against the rule that applied at the time.

lessons.title: Where the team leader role starts and stops
learningOutcomes: Name the main duties a crew leader carries on a cleaning team.
Explain how a team leader's role differs from a manager's role in general terms.
Separate core, secondary and other-person tasks in a written role description.

instructionSections.heading: What the role is for
instructionSections.body: A team leader keeps a small group moving toward one shared result, such as finishing a set of rooms to standard before a handover time. The leader handles the practical problems that slow the work and the interpersonal problems that come between people. On a cleaning crew this means knowing who is doing which part of the job, building the day's plan, checking progress as the shift runs, and telling the supervisor where the job stands. The leader also gives people feedback so they can improve.

instructionSections.heading: How it differs from a manager's role
instructionSections.body: Both roles settle problems, allocate tasks and track progress. The distinction lies in scale and authority. A team leader usually works with a smaller group, while a manager may oversee several groups and the leaders within them. Decisions about discipline, formal performance outcomes and pay are commonly held above the team leader, but the exact split depends on how the business is set up and how each worker is engaged.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping core work separate from everything else
instructionSections.body: Every role collects extra requests. Some are reasonable and some belong to someone else. Write down the tasks that the role must deliver, the tasks that support them, and the tasks that sit with another person or team. Extra work is sometimes needed for a short time, but the lead is judged mainly on the core tasks. Practise declining a request in a calm, specific way, explain the reason, and offer to take the question to the supervisor when the answer is not yours to give.

lessons.title: Delegating work in a repeatable cycle
learningOutcomes: Describe the four stages of a delegation cycle.
Decide what to retain and what to pass to a named worker.
Give a delegated task a clear standard, purpose and check point.

instructionSections.heading: Why passing work on matters
instructionSections.body: A lead who holds every task personally becomes the bottleneck for the crew. Delegation moves routine work to people who can do it, frees the lead for the decisions only the lead can make, and gives workers a stake in the result. Passing a task on does not mean abandoning it. The lead still sets the standard, checks the result and owns the outcome, while the worker carries out the steps.

instructionSections.heading: The four stages
instructionSections.body: Start with your own preferences: which tasks you keep, and how much check-in you want while a task is under way. Next, know your people: match each task to a worker's skills, and use the task to develop someone who is ready to grow. Then state the purpose, meaning why the task matters and how it fits the crew's goal. Finally, assess and reward. Compare the result with the agreed standard, give specific feedback, and recognise good work so the next delegation is welcomed rather than dreaded.

instructionSections.heading: Retaining the work that needs your authority
instructionSections.body: Sort your workload into tasks that need your authority, tasks that need your judgement, and routine tasks that have a clear standard. Keep the first two. Hand over the third group, and keep the sign-off for any step the business reserves for the lead. Delegating a safety-critical sign-off without a written authority is an error, not a time saving.

lessons.title: Setting SMART goals for the crew
learningOutcomes: Rewrite a vague crew goal into a SMART goal with a measure and a deadline.
Break a crew goal into milestones with a named owner for each.
Check whether a goal fits the business's values before it is set.

instructionSections.heading: Why goals need structure
instructionSections.body: Distractions are constant on a cleaning crew. Urgent phone calls, a damaged item at a client's door, and a missing consumable can push the planned work aside. A goal written with enough detail gives the lead a map to return to. Without one, the crew works hard and still drifts away from what the business needs.

instructionSections.heading: The SMART test
instructionSections.body: A goal should be specific, meaning it describes what success looks like on the job. It should be measurable, with a number or a checklist score that shows progress. It should be attainable, which means a stretch is fine but not an impossible one. It should be realistic about the time, materials and people available. It should be timed, with a deadline for the final result and for the milestones along the way. Test each goal against all five words before you publish it.

instructionSections.heading: Milestones, owners and values
instructionSections.body: Split each goal into milestones that can be checked within a shift or a week. Give every milestone one owner, so there is no doubt about who reports on it. Finally, compare the goal with the business's stated values. A goal that rewards speed by sacrificing the client's trust does not fit the business, even if it looks good on a chart.

lessons.title: Communicating, listening and giving feedback
learningOutcomes: Brief a crew on plans and reasons so that people can repeat them accurately.
Ask questions that draw out what a worker thinks before giving a view.
Give specific, timely feedback that describes the work, not the person.

instructionSections.heading: Communicating more than feels necessary
instructionSections.body: A new or changed plan is easily misunderstood when people are working in different rooms. Tell the crew what the goal is, what is changing, why it is changing and who to ask. Repeat the key points at the start of each shift. When a lead thinks a message has been said enough, it is often just starting to land with the people who were not in the room.

instructionSections.heading: Listening and asking questions
instructionSections.body: Hear out many kinds of people, rather than only the ones who side with your view. When someone raises a concern, ask why they see it that way before deciding what to do. If the same concern comes up from several people, treat it as a signal worth checking, even if it sounds minor. Asking questions also shows that the lead values the crew's view, which makes people more willing to speak up about a problem early.

instructionSections.heading: Feedback that helps
instructionSections.body: Feedback works best when it is close in time to the event, specific about the action, and about the work rather than the person. Describe what was seen, say what standard applies, and ask the worker what got in the way. Finish with the next step and a time to check. Praise should be just as specific, so the worker knows exactly what to repeat.

lessons.title: Leading by example and recognising the crew
learningOutcomes: Identify three behaviours a lead must model to get the crew's standard.
Apply rules consistently to every crew member, including the lead.
Plan a recognition practice that fits the business's budget and values.

instructionSections.heading: Leading by example
instructionSections.body: A crew copies what the lead does, not what the lead says. If the lead cuts corners, the crew learns that corners can be cut. Show the attitude and behaviour you want: arrive on time, follow the checklist, clean up after yourself and speak respectfully to the client and the crew. A lead who takes part in the work, rather than standing back, earns more trust when the crew needs help on a hard job.

instructionSections.heading: Consistent rules and fair treatment
instructionSections.body: Crew members need confidence that rules bind everyone equally. Apply the same standards to the lead, to new workers and to long-standing staff. When an exception is needed, explain it openly so nobody assumes favouritism. Balance matters too: a crew that works on weekends or late shifts should also get breaks and time to rest, and the lead should watch for signs of overload.

instructionSections.heading: Recognition that costs little
instructionSections.body: Acknowledgement is among the most useful instruments a lead can use. It does not need to be expensive. A short message after a good week, a shout-out at the shift briefing, or a shared lunch after a hard job all work. Name what was done well and why it mattered to the client or the crew. Tie recognition to the values the business has stated, so that the crew sees a clear link between behaviour and the standard.

lessons.title: Building team alignment through structure, systems and interaction
learningOutcomes: Diagnose a crew problem at the structural, systematic or interactional level.
Explain why trust is needed for a crew to make hard calls under pressure.
Choose one practical fix for a misalignment and record how it will be checked.

instructionSections.heading: Alignment and trust
instructionSections.body: A crew is aligned when its members understand their roles, agree on how the work gets done and communicate openly. Trust sits underneath all three. When people do not trust each other or the lead, they hide problems, protect themselves and avoid decisions. Under pressure, a crew with trust makes difficult calls faster and more calmly.

instructionSections.heading: Three levels to check
instructionSections.body: Look at the structure first: who is responsible for what, and do the roles on paper match what happens on site? Next look at the systems: are the checklists, schedules, handover notes and escalation paths in place and used? Finally look at interaction: how do crew members communicate with one another during the shift, and do they raise problems early? A misalignment usually shows up at one level and is caused at another, so check all three before changing anything.

instructionSections.heading: Taking over a crew
instructionSections.body: A new lead often meets resistance, sometimes because the crew valued the previous leader or has not yet built confidence in the newcomer. Expect this and do not take it personally. Be steady in applying the agreed standard, communicate the plan clearly, and show through small wins that the crew's effort is noticed. Trust is built through consistent behaviour over time, not through a single speech.

lessons.title: Shared working habits, a written charter and what conflict teaches
learningOutcomes: Write team norms that are specific enough to spot a deviation.
Draft a short team charter that includes how conflict will be handled.
Describe how a crew should learn from a conflict after it has been resolved.

instructionSections.heading: Why norms are written down
instructionSections.body: Every crew develops habits. Some are helpful, such as a radio check at the start of each job. Others are harmful, such as leaving a problem for the next shift. Written norms make the expected habits visible. They also become a yardstick. When someone does something that does not match a norm, it is easier to raise it calmly because the expectation was agreed in advance.

instructionSections.heading: A charter that plans for trouble
instructionSections.body: A charter records why the crew exists, its norms, its roles, how decisions get made and how conflict is handled. Conflict will happen even in a good crew, so agree early how it will be raised and by when it will be addressed. Teams that discuss their working habits openly at the start tend to deal with problems sooner. Agreeing these habits is not always comfortable, but the discomfort is smaller than the cost of unspoken friction.

instructionSections.heading: Learning from conflict and the human side
instructionSections.body: Even small conflicts create discomfort. After a disagreement is settled, ask the crew what the norms need to say to prevent it next time. Protect a few minutes for the individual alongside the job itself: a brief check-in at the start of a shift often shows that a worker is struggling with something outside work. Address that first, then plan the job. A crew that feels heard is more willing to follow the norms when a hard day comes.

lessons.title: Handling a difficult person on the crew
learningOutcomes: Recognise four common patterns of difficult behaviour and the effect each has on a crew.
Apply a private, specific conversation approach that describes impact without attacking the person.
Decide when to follow up and when to escalate to the supervisor.

instructionSections.heading: Check yourself first
instructionSections.body: Before raising anything, test whether the behaviour is the true issue or whether your own reaction is amplifying it. Notice whether you have had the same kind of difficulty with other people. Talk it through with a trusted colleague so you can see the situation clearly. Strong feelings such as anger, embarrassment or fear are normal, but they should not set the course of the conversation.

instructionSections.heading: Four patterns and what they do
instructionSections.body: Some workers are constantly critical and rarely satisfied. Some present themselves as the expert and talk down to others. Some go quiet, agree in the meeting and then do little. Some are forceful and insist on their own way. Each pattern affects the crew differently. The critic drains morale, the self-promoter undermines colleagues, the quiet worker shifts the load, and the forceful worker can intimidate others into silence. Identify the pattern, because it shapes the conversation.

instructionSections.heading: Speak privately and follow up
instructionSections.body: Trying to change someone's character in a group rarely works and often makes the person defend the behaviour more. Instead, understand what the person values, because that often explains their choices. Speak to them in private, describe the specific behaviour and its effect on the job, and agree a small number of specific steps. Follow up after a set time. If the behaviour continues or escalates, write down the facts and take them to the supervisor. Where the behaviour is hurtful or intimidating, limit contact and keep the working relationship to what the job needs.

lessons.title: Facing conflict early and staying objective
learningOutcomes: Name a conflict early and set out the facts before proposing a solution.
Mediate between two crew members without taking sides.
Choose which fights to take on and which to leave, using the resources available.

instructionSections.heading: Name the conflict early
instructionSections.body: Many leads hope a conflict will fade. It usually grows. Naming a disagreement calmly, while it is still small, gives the people involved a chance to resolve it. The aim is not to win but to acknowledge that a problem exists and to work on it. Differences of opinion about method can be useful when they are aired openly, because they often reveal a better way of doing the job.

instructionSections.heading: Mediating without taking sides
instructionSections.body: When you mediate, hear each person separately, then together. Keep your own view out of it unless you are asked for it. Look for the shared interest, such as getting the job done to standard before the client returns. If the other party is not a crew member but a client or another contractor, define the limits of what you can agree on and what needs the supervisor's decision. A mediator who appears to favour one side loses the crew's trust quickly.

instructionSections.heading: Choosing battles and working with others
instructionSections.body: Not every disagreement is worth a formal process. Consider how much the issue matters, how much support you have, and whether you can win without damaging the crew. Look for collaboration within the crew and with other teams that share the same aim. Where a proposed arrangement conflicts with the business's standards, do not agree to it just to end the dispute.

lessons.title: Ethical decisions and raising a concern
learningOutcomes: Apply six basic ethical guidelines to a workplace decision.
Work through an ethical dilemma using a set sequence of steps.
Describe the internal routes available for raising a concern and the order to use them.

instructionSections.heading: Basic guidelines for a team leader
instructionSections.body: Several guidelines help a leader decide well. Follow the law that applies to the work. Tell the truth in records and to clients, including about mistakes. Show respect to everyone the work touches. Deal with people in the manner you would hope to receive yourself. Avoid harm, including harm from chemicals or methods that are permitted yet still damaging. Bring affected people into decisions rather than deciding alone what helps them. These guidelines do not replace the business's code of conduct, but they help a leader apply it when a rule is unclear.

instructionSections.heading: Working through a dilemma
instructionSections.body: A dilemma arises when two sound principles conflict, or when it is unclear what the right action is. Start by setting out the principles you hold. Gather the relevant facts, including what was done, by whom and when. Analyse which principles apply and which conflict. Rank them by the priority each should hold in this case. Talk the situation through with a trusted person, then decide on a plan and note its moral implications. Keep the record so the reasoning can be checked later.

instructionSections.heading: Raising a concern
instructionSections.body: When a worker or client is affected by a wrong practice, the concern should be raised clearly and early. Start with the immediate supervisor, or with the person named in the business's procedure. Where the matter involves the supervisor, go to the next level. Many businesses provide an anonymous hotline or reporting channel for serious concerns. Record the facts, the date and the route used. Whether a person who raises a concern has legal protection turns on the kind of concern and the employer.

lessons.title: Keeping yourself effective in a leading role
learningOutcomes: Distinguish burnout from burn-down and name a warning sign for each.
Write a personal development plan that lists weaknesses, goals and support.
Plan personal time and an outside source of support as part of the role.

instructionSections.heading: Burnout and burn-down
instructionSections.body: Burnout comes from long periods of overload, frustration and time pressure. It is usually easy to notice because the leader feels exhausted and wants to stop. Burn-down is quieter. The leader still cares about the work but has lost the energy and drive that once came with it. Because burn-down shows less, it can go unnoticed for longer. Both affect the crew, because a lead who has lost energy stops giving clear direction and stops noticing problems.

instructionSections.heading: Personal development
instructionSections.body: Begin with an honest inventory of shortcomings, including recent ones that caused trouble. Group related weaknesses so they feel manageable, for example communication under pressure. Note the strengths you can build on. Turn each weakness into specific goals with dates. Find a mentor who will be candid with you and keep you to your deadlines. Use training the business provides, and ask for support for training that fits the plan.

instructionSections.heading: Time away and shared load
instructionSections.body: A lead who never switches off eventually makes poor decisions. Schedule time away from work that you can rely on, and protect it. Share the load by building up one or two capable crew members who can cover routine decisions. Looking for a peer group of other leads to talk with about the realities of the role can help you avoid isolation. Asking for help is part of doing the job well, not a sign of failure.

lessons.title: Staff onboarding and induction record (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Record training completed separately from competency observed by a named person
Write the authorised tasks and restrictions that define what the new person may do alone
Record licences or outside authorisations as held and checked, without treating the record as a grant

instructionSections.heading: What an induction record shows
instructionSections.body: An induction record shows that a new person was introduced to the business, its standards and its hazards, and that they can carry out each task they are permitted to do. It is different from a training certificate. A course can show that someone attended a session. The induction record shows what they are authorised to do, what was observed, and who made that decision. Keep the two apart, so that a person is not authorised for a task simply because they completed a course that did not test that task.

instructionSections.heading: Training completed and competency observed
instructionSections.body: List the training completed, with its date, the trainer or provider, and where the evidence is kept. Then list each task the person will perform, and record whether competency has been observed and found adequate, observed but not yet adequate, or not yet observed. A task becomes authorised only after a named observer has seen the person perform it to the standard. Record the method used, such as a demonstration on site, a supervised job, or a practical check set by the business. Competence is shown by doing the task to the standard, not by describing it.

instructionSections.heading: Authorisation, restrictions and sign-off
instructionSections.body: The authorised task list is the boundary of what the person may do alone. Write restrictions in the same table, such as tasks that need supervision and tasks that are not yet authorised. Where a task needs a licence or an authorisation from an outside body, record the licence held, the issuer and the expiry date from the document shown, and check them. This record does not grant or confirm any licence. Sign-off needs both the person's acknowledgement and the supervisor's signature. Set a date for the first review.

lessons.title: Staff performance review (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Rate each chosen standard against dated, sourced evidence
Record the staff member's own evidence and comments before the rating is final
Write an improvement plan with actions, support, a measure and a due date

instructionSections.heading: Start from written standards
instructionSections.body: A performance review compares what a person did with the standards the business has written for their role. If standards are not written down, the review becomes a judgement about personality, which is unfair and hard to defend. Before the review, collect the role description, the standards in the induction record, and any procedures the person must follow. Choose the standards that matter for this period, usually a handful, rather than every item in the role. Each standard should be something that can be observed, such as following the job checklist, completing records on time, or handling a customer concern under the complaints procedure.

instructionSections.heading: Evidence, rating and fairness
instructionSections.body: For each standard, record the evidence you have, its type, its date and its source. Evidence might be a completed checklist, an entry in the complaint log, an observation made on site, or a customer comment. Rate each standard on the scale the business has defined, and write a comment that links the rating to the evidence. Give the person a chance to add their own evidence and comments before the review is finished. Do not rate on evidence you have not seen. If a single incident is used, say so and give its date, rather than letting it stand for the whole period.

instructionSections.heading: Improvement plans and the next review
instructionSections.body: Where a standard is not met, write a plan with one or two actions the person can take, the support the business will provide, a measure that shows improvement, and a due date. Agree the plan with the person rather than handing it to them. Set the next review date. If a performance concern is serious or repeated, the business disciplinary procedure and the employment obligations that apply must be followed.

lessons.title: Proposal for a new client (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Complete every field of the proposal so that a client can read it without asking what an item means
Write a commitment statement and a references section that the business can support with evidence or written consent
Build a price table in Australian dollars that states the GST position and shows how each line was calculated
Use product and environmental claims only where the business holds evidence it can show on request

instructionSections.heading: What a proposal does
instructionSections.body: A proposal is the document a prospective client reads after a first contact, a call on the phone or a site visit. It has to answer three questions in a fixed order: who is making the offer and whether the client has reason to trust them, what exactly the business will do in the client's space, and what that work will cost. This template keeps those answers in separate sections so the price never appears without the scope beside it. A proposal is not the agreement. The binding terms sit in the client service agreement (“Client service agreement”) and the quote terms in “Quote and proposal”, and this lesson refers to them without repeating them. The scope method is taught in “Scope of works for a service site”, and the hours-based pricing method is taught in “Pricing by hours per project”. The pricing worksheet (“Pricing and margin worksheet”) produces the numbers that go into the price table.

instructionSections.heading: Describe the business with facts you can check
instructionSections.body: Claims about the business are where a proposal most often goes wrong. Years in operation, team size, training and any awards must each match what the business can show. Write the years as a whole number and record the month and year the business started trading, so the figure can be checked against records. The team table lists the people who will attend the site, their role on this job and how long each person has worked for the firm. Do not list someone who is not rostered to the job, because a proposal that names a person who never arrives damages the trust it was written to build. A commitment statement such as a promise of punctuality is only useful if the business records its punctuality and can produce that record. Write each promise as something that can be measured.

instructionSections.heading: References with written consent
instructionSections.body: A reference is a person who has agreed that a prospective client may contact them. Ask each person before their name goes into the proposal, and record the date and what they are willing to talk about. A testimonial written for a different service, a different business or a different year should be labelled as such, or left out. Edited, merged or invented testimonials should not be used. Check the misleading-conduct rules in the Australian Consumer Law against current guidance before relying on any testimonial.

instructionSections.heading: Products, methods and environmental claims
instructionSections.body: List the products and methods the team uses, and the surface or task each one suits. A product list with no purpose attached adds length without giving the client anything to check. Environmental and health claims are the highest-risk part of this section. Words such as natural, non-toxic, non-hazardous or eco-friendly need evidence the business holds, such as a product label, a safety data sheet or a certification, and the claim must match what that evidence says. Where the evidence is thin, describe what the business does instead, for example which products are used on which surfaces and which are avoided.

instructionSections.heading: Pricing with GST and a visible basis
instructionSections.body: Show each price in Australian dollars and state whether the amounts include GST. Each line in the price table needs a unit, such as per visit, per hour, per room or per square metre, and a quantity that matches the scope. The line totals are the rate multiplied by the quantity, and the total is the sum of the lines less any offer. Show a discount as a reduction from the full price the business has charged for the same service on other occasions. Write the offer with its condition and its end date, and check the price display rules in the Australian Consumer Law before using it. The ATO GST registration page gives a turnover threshold of $75,000 or more, or $150,000 or more for a non-profit organisation. Check the GST rate and how GST must appear on a quote with the Australian Taxation Office or a qualified adviser. If prices change before a client accepts, honour a proposal already issued at the old rate, and give repeat customers two to four weeks' notice of a new rate.

instructionSections.heading: Inclusions, exclusions, complaints and acceptance
instructionSections.body: State what is included and what is not, taken from the scope of works rather than from a generic list. Where the proposal and the agreement could conflict, the agreement wording should be checked first and the proposal corrected. A satisfaction statement is useful only when it names the complaint route and a response time the business can meet. Check before use whether a line in a proposal can affect a consumer guarantee under the Australian Consumer Law. Check any satisfaction or liability wording against the Australian Consumer Law before use. Keep the acceptance block simple: the method of acceptance, such as a signature or a written reply that quotes the proposal reference, and the date it is recorded.

lessons.title: Client service agreement (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Complete each clause so that the client, the business and the team can each state what happens without guessing
Convert any fixed-hours, cancellation or payment term into an Australian term with a workable notice period, and check any term whose legal effect is uncertain before use.
Link each operational term (access, quality, damage, exclusions) to the lesson or schedule that holds its detail

instructionSections.heading: What an agreement is for
instructionSections.body: A service agreement records what the business will do, when it will do it, for how long, for what fee, and what happens when something goes wrong. Both parties come back to it when a dispute starts, so each term has to be precise enough to act on. This template is built around a fixed-hours model: the client pays for a reserved block of team hours, not for a promised result. That model can work, but it has to be explained plainly. A client who expects a finished result and receives a time block will feel misled, however accurate the contract is. The scope clause in this template states the difference. The fill-in proposal is “Cleaning proposal for a new client”, the quote terms are in “Quote and proposal”, the access detail is in “Site brief and access sheet for each client”, and the payment detail is in “Payment and overdue account schedule”.

instructionSections.heading: Converting terms for an Australian business
instructionSections.body: Several terms in the source model come from a different legal system and must not be carried over. The source sets payment, late-fee, interest, lien, judgment and collection-cost terms that depend on another country's state law, along with a dishonoured-cheque fee and a recovery of legal and collection costs. None of these appear in this agreement. Payment detail sits in “Payment and overdue account schedule”, where each term is checked against the rules in the business's own state or territory before use. Sales tax language is replaced by GST-inclusive pricing. The source presents the business as holding a licence, insurance and a bond, all three. In Australia the business states the insurance it holds and the licences or registrations that apply, with the state or territory where each applies. This template does not confirm that any licence, bond or insurance is required. Clauses that stop a client from hiring the business's own staff can raise competition-law questions, so this template leaves them out. If the business wants one, it takes advice first, and the status of such a clause has not yet been confirmed, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.

instructionSections.heading: Fixed hours and what the client is paying for
instructionSections.body: A fixed-hours clause says the client pays for a reserved number of team hours for each visit. Write three things: the reserved hours, the team size, and the rule for finishing early or running over. A team of two working for two hours is not the same as one person working for four hours, and the agreement should say which unit is used. The scope is an activity list that the client can check, and the clause states that the reserved block is the basis of the fee and does not guarantee a result. If the team cannot finish in the reserved time, the clause says what the client is told, how any extra time is approved and how it is charged. Extra time and extra work are agreed in writing before they begin.

instructionSections.heading: Notice, cancellation and rescheduling
instructionSections.body: The source sets its own notice periods for cancellation by either party and for schedule details. Those choices belong to one business and are not a standard. Set the notice periods your business can meet from its own roster, and write them as whole numbers of days. Test each one with a single question: could the roster absorb a change at this notice? A period the business cannot meet will not protect it when a job is lost. Where a client's notice is short and the business cannot refill the visit, the clause states the fee and the situation exactly, so that the client knows what applies.

instructionSections.heading: Access, exclusions, quality and damage
instructionSections.body: Operational clauses carry the most risk when they are vague. Access details such as keys, lock boxes, alarms and pets belong in the site brief (“Site brief and access sheet for each client”). The agreement refers to that brief and does not hold the detail. Quality is a complaint route with a response time, not a promise that no fault will occur. Damage is handled as a notice, an inspection and a remedy, with the remedy stated as repair, replacement, or a value agreed in writing. The exclusions list states what the business will not do, such as work above a set height, moving heavy items, or handling items the business has not agreed to handle.
