Each limit is set from the business's own risk assessment. The height and weight figures in the source are not carried over. Check every liability cap or exclusion of responsibility before use, because consumer guarantees may apply.

instructionSections.heading: Team, insurance, licences and governing law
instructionSections.body: State who the team are, whether they are employees or subcontractors, and how new team members are trained and supervised. Write the position for this business, and leave it blank until checked. The insurance field lists each policy held, the type of cover, the insurer, the policy number and the expiry date. The licence field lists each licence or registration held that applies to the work, and the state or territory where it applies. Do not list a licence the business does not hold. The governing-law field names the state or territory whose law applies, which is the one where the business operates.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the agreement current
instructionSections.body: Both parties accept the agreement in a way that can be recorded. Record the date, the version number and the name of the person who accepted. An agreement that changes must be reissued with a new version number. The client is told what changed and the date it takes effect, and the business keeps the earlier version on file. A change made verbally is not a change until it is written down and sent.

lessons.title: Site brief and access sheet for each client (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Record access, keys, alarms and pets so the team can enter and leave a site without relying on memory
Identify site hazards and name the control the business will use for each one before the first visit
Store access details in a way that protects the client's privacy and security

instructionSections.heading: What the brief is for
instructionSections.body: The site brief is one record that the office and the team read before anyone arrives. It replaces the conversation at the door and the note left on the bench. Its job is to answer the questions that otherwise cause wasted visits: how the team gets in, what is in and out of scope, which items are off limits, what near the work could cause harm, and who to call. A brief is only as good as the walk-through or call that produced it, so every entry records who gave the information and when. The client service agreement (“Client service agreement”) refers to this brief and does not repeat its detail.

instructionSections.heading: Access and keys without recording secrets
instructionSections.body: Record how the team gets in: a key held by the office, a lock box, a code, or the client present. Record where the access detail is kept, not the detail itself. A full alarm code or key number written into an open file creates a security exposure for the household and for the firm. The brief can say that the alarm arrangement is held in the business's secure record, and the code is kept in the approved store. Record who may give instructions on the day, and what the team does if access fails: which number to call, and that the team does not wait outside for an unknown period.

instructionSections.heading: Preparation, requests and items the team will not handle
instructionSections.body: Clients are often asked to clear items that delay the work: papers on desks, items on floors, valuables, and rooms they do not want cleaned. Write each request as a checkable action, such as 'benches clear of papers before arrival', and record what happens when a request is not met. If the team would have to move items, the brief says whether that is included, and any extra time is agreed in writing before the visit. Items the team will not move, such as heavy furniture above the business's own weight limit, appliances that must be pulled out from a wall, or electronics the business does not handle, are written down, as are items that must be left alone. Products the client asks the team to use or avoid are recorded, and any product the client supplies is recorded with the client's responsibility for it.

instructionSections.heading: Pets, occupants and the team's rule
instructionSections.body: Each animal in the home is listed with its usual location and whether it is secured during the visit. Ask about every animal at each visit, including animals the client says are no trouble. Animals can act differently when the household is out, so the brief records what the client expects. If an animal appears to threaten the team, the team does not enter, and the office contacts the client. The business does not provide childcare or pet care, and this is listed as an exclusion. The arrangement for children and visitors is recorded, together with the business's policy on who may be in the home during the work.

instructionSections.heading: Site hazards and the controls that go with them
instructionSections.body: A site hazard is anything that could injure a team member or damage the property. Examples include stairs without rails, slippery tiles, unstable shelving, a pool or spa, a roof space, a balcony, animals, sharps, chemicals already on site, electrical equipment and any height the team is not permitted to work at. For each hazard, the brief names the control: the task is not done, the team is told before arrival, a second person is present, or the work is referred to another service. Heights and manual handling limits come from the business's own risk assessment. Work at height and some chemicals may need a licence or authorisation, which this lesson does not grant.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the brief current
instructionSections.body: A brief expires when the site changes. Set a review date and check it before each scheduled visit. Update the brief when the access method, the alarm arrangement, the pets or a hazard changes. Each change records the date, the person who gave the information and the person who approved it, and creates a new version number. The client confirms the brief before the first visit, and the confirmation is kept with the record.

lessons.title: Payment and overdue account schedule (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Write a payment schedule with an invoice method, a due period, a GST statement and accepted payment methods that a client can follow
Set overdue steps that are written, dated and within what the business is permitted to do in its own state or territory
Leave every payment, interest, fee and debt term out until its state or territory rule has been checked and the check recorded

instructionSections.heading: Why payment terms sit in a separate schedule
instructionSections.body: Payment terms are where a service agreement most often goes wrong. The source for this lesson sets payment terms written for another country and its state laws: a due date on receipt, a returned-cheque fee, a late fee after a period set by the source, an annual interest rate, collection costs, attorney fees and property liens. None of these is carried into this schedule. Each Australian term must be set and checked against the rules for the business's own state or territory. A separate schedule lets the payment detail be checked and changed without reissuing the whole agreement, and it keeps every item still to be checked in one place where it can be resolved. The client service agreement (“Client service agreement”) refers to this schedule.

instructionSections.heading: Invoices and the due period
instructionSections.body: State when an invoice is issued, for example at the end of each visit or at the start of each month, how it is sent, and the number of days allowed for payment. The due period is a commercial choice. It should be one the business can justify, and it should be checked against the rules in the business's own state or territory. Write the basis for the number in one plain sentence, and leave the number out until the check is recorded. Check the current tax invoice requirements with the Australian Taxation Office before issuing invoices, because the ATO page used here does not cover them. The invoice should then show the business name, the ABN, the date, a description of the work, the quantity, any GST component the ATO requires, and the amount due.

instructionSections.heading: GST and the amount the client sees
instructionSections.body: State whether the amounts include GST. The schedule says when the GST component is shown on the invoice. Confirm the GST display rule with the Australian Taxation Office before issue, because the ATO page used here does not address display. The GST statement must match the statement on the proposal (“Cleaning proposal for a new client”) and in the agreement (“Client service agreement”).

instructionSections.heading: Accepted payment methods and surcharges
instructionSections.body: List only the methods the client has agreed to, such as bank transfer, card or a payment link, and say how each one is used. Do not request payment in a way the client has not agreed to. If a surcharge applies to a method, check the surcharge and disclosure rules for the business's state or territory before setting it, and show it clearly before the client pays. For recurring work, some trade sources suggest offering monthly autopay, which can help cash flow. These are trade and vendor views, not measured results, and autopay is used only if the client agrees to it. Cash and cheque payments, where the business still accepts them, are recorded in the same way as other payments and given a receipt.

instructionSections.heading: Overdue accounts, step by step
instructionSections.body: An overdue account needs a sequence, not a threat. Write each step with the day it happens, starting with a reminder. A common sequence is a reminder, a second reminder that states the amount and the due date, a call or a written notice, and then a decision on whether visits are paused. A pause is considered only after checking the rules for pausing a service in the business's state or territory and giving any written notice those rules require. Each step records what the business will do and how the client can resolve the matter. Before any formal recovery step, the business takes advice on the debt recovery rules that apply in its state or territory. This schedule does not include property liens, judgments, collection costs or attorney fees, because these come from another country's form. A qualified adviser must check any such step for the business's state or territory before it is added.

instructionSections.heading: Late fees, interest and gratuities
instructionSections.body: A late fee or interest charge is not included by default. If the business wants one, check that the rules for its state or territory allow it, disclose it in advance, and leave it out until that check is recorded. The source's fixed late fee and annual interest rate are not carried over. A gratuity is optional. If the business accepts one, the schedule says how it is handled and that it is never a condition of service. Tax treatment of gratuities is not confirmed in this schedule, so check with the Australian Taxation Office or a tax adviser before relying on it.

instructionSections.heading: Failed and returned payments
instructionSections.body: Record what the business does when a payment fails, such as a declined card, a reversed transfer or a returned cheque. The first step is a reminder with a request for a new payment.

lessons.title: Business plan outline for a cleaning business (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Complete each section of the plan in the order that lets later sections depend on earlier decisions
Write the executive summary last, using only statements that appear in the sections
Record the review date, version and reviewer, so that the plan is maintained rather than filed and forgotten

instructionSections.heading: What this plan is and what it is not
instructionSections.body: A business plan records the decisions behind a business and tests whether they fit together. It is not a sales document, and it does not replace the financial projections that an accountant or adviser prepares. This template follows the general shape of a plan: a summary, the business, its services and customers, the market and competitors, the marketing and pricing approach, the operations and team, the finances, the milestones and risks, and the attachments. It poses questions under every heading and does not supply answers. The earlier lessons explain how to answer them: “How a cleaning business plan is structured” covers the structure, “Customer needs and building trust in a cleaning business” customer needs, “SWOT analysis for a small cleaning business” the SWOT analysis, “Break-even and sales forecast by stage” break-even and forecasting, and “Staffing in stages: the first team, then new teams” staffing. This lesson refers to those lessons and does not repeat them. The market and competitor sections are completed in more depth in “Market, customer and competitor analysis”, the pricing in “Pricing and margin worksheet”, the break-even worksheet in “Freedom and cash plan”, and the marketing channels in “Marketing plan”.

instructionSections.heading: The order in which to write it
instructionSections.body: Write the sections in the order that the decisions depend on each other. Start with the services and the customers, because every later number depends on what is sold and to whom. Then complete the market and competitor summary from “Market, customer and competitor analysis”, followed by the pricing and marketing approach. The operations and team come next, because the number of jobs a team can deliver sets the revenue that is possible. The financial targets and break-even come after that, and the funding need comes last among the financial sections. The executive summary and the mission are written last, because they can only summarise decisions that already exist. A plan written in the opposite order tends to fit its numbers to its story.

instructionSections.heading: Facts, targets and assumptions
instructionSections.body: Label each number. A fact is observed or recorded. A target is a goal the owner sets. An assumption is a belief that a target depends on, and it needs a date and a way to test it. An overseas or historical figure is labelled as historical and is not used as a current Australian figure. Where a figure cannot yet be sourced, write that it is not yet sourced and say what would confirm it. A reader should be able to tell, for every number in the plan, which of the three it is.

instructionSections.heading: Keeping the plan alive
instructionSections.body: Set a review date and a version number. When a figure, a service or a price changes, record the old value, the new value, the reason and the date, rather than overwriting the history. A plan that is reviewed once and then left stops matching the business. Name the person responsible for the next review, so the date is not left to chance.

instructionSections.heading: What the plan cannot settle
instructionSections.body: Registration, licences, insurance, tax obligations and employment status depend on the work done and on the state or territory where it is done. The plan states each of them as a question to be checked, until a source has been checked and recorded. A plan that presents an unchecked legal or tax position as settled will mislead its owner and anyone who reads it.

lessons.title: Market, customer and competitor analysis (editable template)
learningOutcomes: Record each market observation with its source, date and method, and keep observation separate from estimate
Define customer segments by who decides, what they buy and how often, with evidence for each segment
Compare competitors on observable points and name a gap that the business can actually serve

instructionSections.heading: Why this analysis comes before the numbers
instructionSections.body: A market analysis is a set of checked observations, not a story about a large market. The business needs to know who is likely to buy its service, where those people look for a provider, how many of them are within reach, and which alternatives they already use. Those answers decide the price band, the marketing channel and the number of jobs in the financial targets. The business plan (“Business plan outline for a cleaning business”) takes its market summary from this analysis. The method for customer needs is taught in “Customer needs and building trust in a cleaning business”, and the SWOT method in “SWOT analysis for a small cleaning business”. This lesson builds on them and does not repeat them.

instructionSections.heading: Local observation first
instructionSections.body: Start with what can be observed locally: the number of providers you can find, the kinds of customers you meet, the services people ask for, and the prices quoted in public. Record each observation with its date, its place and the method used to see it. An observation is evidence for a claim, and a claim needs at least one observation behind it. Where a published statistic is used, record the publisher, the year of the data and the place it covers. Public open-data sets can show local activity at area level: Victoria's building permit activity dataset, for example, can be filtered by suburb or postcode, and a council planning permit register can show which projects are at application stage. Each council publishes its own register, so check yours. Use such data to count activity in an area, not to contact individuals. A figure from another country, or a figure from an earlier period, is historical and must be labelled as such. It is never used as a current Australian fact, and it is never the basis of a target.

instructionSections.heading: Estimating the reachable market
instructionSections.body: The reachable market is the number of customers who could realistically buy from this business. Build it from the bottom up. Count the households or sites in the service area, then work out the share that fit the service type, the share that would pay the price the business can offer, and how often each one buys. Write the steps as a short calculation with the source of each input. Round the result sensibly and state how confident you are in each input. A large total market with a small reachable share is still a small market for this business, and the number of jobs in the targets must fit the reachable share.

instructionSections.heading: Segments defined by the decision
instructionSections.body: A segment names the person who decides, the service they buy, how often they buy, and how they find a provider. Two groups who look alike on paper can make different decisions. A household booking a one-off service and a household on a fixed schedule are different segments. Do not define a segment by an income band alone, because an income band does not show how a person chooses a provider. Each segment needs at least one observed need and one channel through which it can be reached.

instructionSections.heading: Competitors on observable points
instructionSections.body: List direct competitors, which sell the same service to the same customers, and indirect competitors, which meet the same need in another way, such as a self-service option, an employed cleaner or a different service. For each, record only what can be observed: the services offered, the public prices with their dates, the service area, how reviews are handled, and what the competitor does well. Do not record a competitor's weaknesses from hearsay. Where reviews are used, record the platform, the date read and the number of reviews read, and count the themes that recur rather than selecting the ones that suit the argument.

instructionSections.heading: The gap and whether it lasts
instructionSections.body: A gap is a need in a segment that no current competitor meets well, and that this business can meet with what it has. The gap must link to one service in the business plan and one segment in this analysis. Then test how durable the advantage is. A process, a training approach or a product choice can be copied within a short time. A long-standing referral relationship is harder to copy. Record the answer, and mark any advantage that could be copied quickly as temporary.

lessons.title: What cleaning validation proves, and what routine checks do not
learningOutcomes: Distinguish a routine check that a clean was done from validation that a method reliably reaches a set standard.
State the questions a cleaning process must answer before any testing is designed.
Explain why one passing result is not enough to validate a method.
Recognise that the formal validation rules in the source are pharmaceutical and are not Australian food-service requirements.

instructionSections.heading: Routine checks are not validation
instructionSections.body: A routine check asks whether a clean took place on a given day. Validation asks a harder question: does the method, carried out as written, bring a surface or an item of equipment to a set level of cleanliness each time, for the soils and surfaces it is meant to handle? The guide treats validation as the proof that contamination between batches and products is held in check. It also argues that a process cannot be confirmed as working until it has been validated, and that the process itself has to be built properly before validation becomes straightforward. Heavy sampling after a clean does not, on its own, show that the clean works.

instructionSections.heading: The questions a process must answer first
instructionSections.body: Before a test is designed, the process should be questioned. When does an item reach a state that can be called clean? Is a visual inspection a dependable standard, and what does looks clean actually mean? Does the item need physical scrubbing, or does a solvent rinse do the job, and what is the scrubbing achieving? How much does the outcome of a manual clean wander between runs and between products? Which detergent or solvent suits the soil best? Must each product that touches the equipment have its own method? How many passes of the method does each item need before it is truly clean? The answers reveal whether the method works at all, and they can also point to redundant steps that could be dropped to save time and materials.

instructionSections.heading: One result is not validation
instructionSections.body: A single good result shows that the method worked once. Validation needs evidence that the method works consistently, which is why a documented study across several runs is expected rather than one clean that happened to pass. A negative result also needs a check: if a test finds nothing, the question is whether the test could have detected the residue at all. The formal pharmaceutical rules are not food-service requirements in Australia. This lesson takes the reasoning and the questions, and does not set any pharmaceutical standard for a commercial cleaning business.

lessons.title: Protocol content and approval for a cleaning study
learningOutcomes: Set out the elements that a validation protocol for cleaning must contain.
Explain why the test methods are shown to work before the study is run.
Explain why several successive runs are used to show a method works.
State who must approve the protocol before it is executed.

instructionSections.heading: What a protocol holds
instructionSections.body: A validation protocol records, in advance, how the study will be run, so that the results can be judged against a written plan. The guide sets out the content in detail. It covers the objective and scope; the people who perform and approve the study; the equipment details; the procedure for cleaning each product and system; the named cleaning agent; how many consecutive cycles; the number of runs needed to complete the study; the sampling method, with the reason for choosing it; the sample locations; acceptance criteria with the reason they were set; and the test methods and the data that support them. Each element is written so that a second person can follow the study without asking the author.

instructionSections.heading: Test methods come first
instructionSections.body: The guide is clear that the test methods used on the samples must be shown to work before the study begins. A protocol that relies on an unproven test cannot demonstrate anything, because the result itself is uncertain. The protocol names each test method and states its the lowest amount it can detect and the lowest it can quantify reliably.

instructionSections.heading: Repeat the cycle and gain approval
instructionSections.body: Cleaning is usually shown to work by running the procedure several times in succession. The guide typically expects three successful applications in a row. The runs should mirror the most demanding conditions the equipment will meet, such as the largest number of consecutive runs of one product. Management must approve the protocol before any run takes place. A protocol approved after the study is over does not govern that study.

lessons.title: Difficult spots and the hardest-case selection
learningOutcomes: Select a worst-case scenario that reflects the most difficult realistic situation.
Name the awkward areas and give the reason each one is sampled.
Distinguish dedicated equipment from multi-use equipment in the study scope.
Record which equipment and product configurations were covered and why.

instructionSections.heading: Pick the hardest realistic case
instructionSections.body: A validation study should cover the situation in which the cleaning is most demanding. The guide asks for the study to reflect the harshest production conditions, for example the point reached after the greatest number of successive runs of one product, or the moment a long campaign ends. With multi-use equipment, the protocol names the product that is most resistant to removal because of its toxicity, potency or poor solubility. Where equipment forms a connected train of parts, each arrangement of that train is assessed, and not merely the principal unit.

instructionSections.heading: Map the awkward areas
instructionSections.body: Some places resist cleaning more than others: gaskets, sample ports, panes of glass, joints, threads and inner faces that cannot be opened for inspection. The guide asks that the hardest of these be swabbed and included in the sampling plan and that each choice be justified. A sketch or a written description of each area makes the plan clear to a second person. Repeat samples should not come from the same spot each time, and sampling points rotate across the separate components.

instructionSections.heading: Dedicated and multi-use equipment
instructionSections.body: Dedicated equipment serves one product only, so fewer products must be considered for carry-over and the study is smaller. Multi-use equipment needs the most demanding product chosen from all the products it handles. For primary packaging and similar shared equipment, the guide expects microbial evaluations for risk assessment, identification of the most demanding products, assessment of every configuration of the equipment train, and cleaning records made as each event happens.

lessons.title: Sampling: swabs, rinse samples and sample locations
learningOutcomes: Explain the two accepted sampling methods, direct surface swabbing and rinse sampling, and when each is used.
Explain why a result needs its sampled area, and why residue can be patchy.
Explain why a rinse result has to measure the residue, rather than only the purity of the liquid.
Describe the link between sampling and recovery testing.

instructionSections.heading: Two accepted methods and when to use them
instructionSections.body: The guide recognises two acceptable routes. Direct surface sampling, usually by swab, tests the surface itself. Indirect sampling collects residue into a rinse liquid, which is then tested. Combining both is frequently the strongest option, especially when some parts are out of swab reach. Which route fits depends on the apparatus and on how soluble the residue is: swabbing suits stubborn spots and residues that do not dissolve well, while rinse sampling suits residues that dissolve and internal areas that cannot be opened up.

instructionSections.heading: Residue is not spread evenly
instructionSections.body: Residue is patchy. A swab taken from one small spot may miss the highest level present, so a low result does not prove that the whole surface is clean. A swab result means nothing unless the swabbed area is known, which is why the protocol defines the swab area. Each sampling site needs a stated justification. The swabbing technique in the study must match the technique used in the recovery test, so that the two can be compared.

instructionSections.heading: A rinse has to measure the residue
instructionSections.body: A rinse sample is useful only if the residue itself is measured in the rinse. A rinse that proves only that the liquid meets its own purity specification says nothing about the residue left on the equipment. The guide is firm on this point: where a rinse is the sampling route, the residue must be measured directly in its extraction solvent. Rinse samples can also cover large areas that cannot be swabbed completely, but the rationale behind the chosen rinse volume, and the surface it stands for, must be written down.

lessons.title: Setting residue acceptance limits and their rationale
learningOutcomes: Explain why a residue limit needs a logical, written rationale.
Explain why a limit must sit within what the analytical method can measure.
Describe the three bases the source gives for product carry-over limits and when the strictest applies.
Explain why detergent residue needs its own acceptance limit.

instructionSections.heading: A limit needs a written basis
instructionSections.body: The guide insists that a residue limit rest on a logical argument that is written down. A limit is not a figure picked because a test happens to return it. It answers the question of how clean counts as clean, and part of that answer depends on how capable the analytical system is. Current instruments can read residues far under parts per million, into parts per billion. A limit set beneath what an instrument can read cannot be checked, and a limit set above what the product could cause is not protective.

instructionSections.heading: Bases for carry-over limits
instructionSections.body: For carry-over from one product into the next, the guide names three bases and asks that the most demanding of them rule. The first caps how much of a previous product could reach the largest largest daily intake of the subsequent product, expressed as a small fraction of a therapeutic dose. The second caps how many parts per million of one product may appear in another. The third requires that no residue be seen left on equipment once cleaning ends, with spiking trials used to find the level where residue first shows. For potent, allergenic or highly active substances, the guide suggests a limit below what the best method can detect, which in practice can mean dedicated equipment. It also warns that unidentified by-products can persist, so the rationale behind any limit must stand up to scientific scrutiny.

instructionSections.heading: Detergent limits and checkable limits
instructionSections.body: Detergent residue needs its own acceptance figure. The guide expects detergent clearance to be assessed and acceptable amounts to be set, ideally zero detectable residue, and it asks that any possible breakdown of the detergent be considered. A limit that no method can actually measure is of little use. Each limit should be stated alongside the test that will check it and the analytical floor below which a result cannot be reported.

lessons.title: Analytical methods: validate before you test, and show recovery
learningOutcomes: Explain why a test method has to be proven at the concentrations it will read.
Explain how a recovery study shows whether residue can be taken off a surface and measured.
Describe the independent checks that keep analytical data reliable.
State that laboratory handling of solvents and samples needs the controls in each SDS.

instructionSections.heading: Validate the method across its working range
instructionSections.body: The guide requires each analytical test to be proven at the concentrations it will meet in real samples. A method that is accurate at high levels may fail at the trace levels a cleaning study looks for. Validation also fixes the detection floor and the reporting floor, which show the smallest amount the method can register and the smallest amount it can quantify with acceptable reliability. The protocol cites these floors so that a reader can tell what a negative or low result actually means.

instructionSections.heading: Show recovery with the sampling route
instructionSections.body: The sampling route and the analytical method have to be tested together. A known quantity of residue is placed on a surface, sampled with the same technique the study will use, extracted and analysed, and the recovered share and its spread are recorded. Until that is done, a sample result cannot be trusted, because the residue may never have left the surface. The guide adds that a negative outcome may simply reflect poor sampling rather than a clean surface.

instructionSections.heading: Keep the data open to checking
instructionSections.body: A second person checks the analytical data, and dates are recorded accurately. Raw data are retained so that every result can be traced to its sample. The guide cites an inspection outcome in which a cleaning study failed partly because the swab route had never been validated by recovery, rinse filtering went unchecked, some rinse samples went unanalysed, dates were wrong and no second person reviewed the data. This is offered as a warning, not as an Australian rule. Laboratory solvents, reagents and samples need the controls in their SDS and the site's laboratory procedure.

lessons.title: Removing cleaning agents: detergent and sanitiser residue checks
learningOutcomes: Explain why residues of detergent and sanitiser are treated as contamination.
Describe a rinse design that removes cleaning agents to the required level.
Describe the simple checks a commercial site can use, and their limits.
Keep residue checks within the site's approved method.

instructionSections.heading: Leftover cleaning agent is contamination
instructionSections.body: A cleaning agent left behind can contaminate the next product and can distort a test result. The guide expects detergent clearance to be evaluated, acceptable levels to be defined, and zero detectable residue to be the aim. Sanitiser residue is treated the same way. The guide also asks that active ingredients and detergent be measured separately rather than as one combined impurity figure, because a combined figure can conceal the specific residue of concern.

instructionSections.heading: Build the rinse into the method
instructionSections.body: The rinse is designed into the method rather than tacked on afterwards. Rinse water is chosen for its quality, and rinsing continues until the agent has gone. Foam left on a surface after rinsing shows that the rinse is unfinished. Where the site procedure asks for a final rinse check, it is carried out using the approved method and recorded. A rinse that merely confirms the water is pure says nothing about the surface.

instructionSections.heading: Simple checks on a commercial site
instructionSections.body: A commercial site seldom runs a full validation, but it can use a straightforward residue check where its procedure calls for one. The check should target the agent last used on the item, by a method the site has approved. A visual look for foam or film is a routine check and is not a residue measurement. Results are recorded, and any failed rinse is repeated before the item goes back into use. These checks sit alongside the label, the SDS and the approved product list; they do not replace them.

lessons.title: Validation reports, records and revalidation after change
learningOutcomes: State what a validation report must conclude, including its limitations.
Explain why cleaning and use records are written as the work happens.
Identify the changes that trigger a review or repeat of a validation.
Explain why a non-sterile process may need a data review rather than a full repeat.

instructionSections.heading: The report reaches a verdict
instructionSections.body: A validation study closes with a final report, approved by management, that states whether the method passed validation. The evidence must show that residues were brought down to a tolerable amount. The report also records the limits governing the method, such as the analytical floor below which cleanliness cannot be judged. A report that lists figures without reaching a verdict is incomplete, and a report that claims more validity than the data show is wrong.

instructionSections.heading: Records made as the work happens
instructionSections.body: The cleaning record is completed while the cleaning takes place, showing what was done, when, by whom and with which agent. The guide expects these logs to be kept for each event as it occurs. An entry written later from memory, or filled in ahead of time, does not show what was done. Each record links the cleaning to the job, batch or run it followed, so a result can be traced back.

instructionSections.heading: Review or repeat after a change
instructionSections.body: A validation does not last forever. The guide expects a review, and sometimes a repeat, whenever equipment, product, cleaning agent, procedure or analytical method changes. For a non-sterile process run on standard plant, a review of existing data may give enough assurance that control is maintained, provided the sanitation regime remains suitable. A change of cleaning agent or procedure usually calls for a fresh look at residues and their limits. Every change is logged, and the decision to review or repeat is signed.
